About this text

The Supreme Text of Monastic Discipline, known in Sanskrit as the Vinaya Uttaragrantha and in Tibetan as Dulwa Zhung Dampa, is a canonical Vinaya text belonging to the Mūlasarvāstivāda monastic code. It forms part of the extensive Vinaya collection within the Kangyur and is catalogued as Toh 7. The text takes the form of a detailed legal and disciplinary analysis, structured around questions posed by the Elder Upāli to the Buddha, and concerns itself with fine points of monastic law — particularly the rules governing the root offense of unchaste conduct, exploring edge cases and hypothetical scenarios with considerable technical precision. As a supplementary or "upper" treatise to the core Vinaya, it extends and refines the foundational rules of the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition, occupying an important place in the broader body of texts regulating the conduct and communal life of Buddhist monastics.

Translation

In the Indian language: Vinaya Uttaragrantha. In the Tibetan language: The Supreme Text of Monastic Discipline. Homage to the All-Knowing, the Auspicious One.

The First Section.

In brief:
Three of animal kind, and three pathways,
What is entered and what is re-entered, two modes,
What is taken hold of, and what is thrust in again,
The teeth, what is not touched, and like a sow.

Then the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, if a monk, by means of a drug or a mantra, transforms a human woman so that she is born in an animal existence, and then engages in unchaste conduct with her, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat. "Venerable One, if a monk, by means of a mantra or a drug, transforms himself so that he is born in an animal existence, and then engages in unchaste conduct together with a human woman, what becomes of that?" "If he retains the perception of himself as a monk, since it constitutes engagement in sexual intercourse, it becomes a defeat. If he does not retain the perception of himself as a monk, it becomes a grave offense." "Venerable One, if a monk, by means of a mantra or a drug, transforms both himself and a human woman so that both are born in an animal existence, and they engage in unchaste conduct with each other, what becomes of that?" "If he retains the perception of himself as a monk, since it constitutes engagement in sexual intercourse, it becomes a defeat. If he does not retain the perception of himself as a monk, it becomes a grave offense."

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, when you said 'it becomes a defeat immediately upon insertion,' how much constitutes insertion into the mouth?" "Upāli, when the tip passes beyond the teeth." "How much constitutes insertion into the pathway of defecation?" "When the tip passes beyond the opening of the rectum." "How much constitutes insertion into the pathway of urination?" "When the tip passes beyond the labia."

"Venerable One, if a woman has been split in two and all three openings have also been damaged, and a monk joins half to half and engages in unchaste conduct, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. "Venerable One, if a monk engages in unchaste conduct with a woman who has been cut at the waist, using any one of the three openings that remains undamaged, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat. "Venerable One, if a monk engages in unchaste conduct with a woman whose head has been severed, what becomes of that?" If it is done through the pathway of defecation or the pathway of urination, it becomes a defeat. But if it is done through the mouth, through a wound, or through a hollow in a bone, it becomes a grave offense.

The Blessed One has declared that engaging in sexual intercourse — unchaste conduct — with a non-human woman becomes a defeat. What sort of being is a non-human? One possessed of all limbs. The same should be understood to apply to those who have taken on animal form.

"Venerable One, if something is thrust in with repetition, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. "Venerable One, if a monk engages in unchaste conduct by inserting beyond the outer teeth into the inside of the mouth, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. "Venerable One, if a monk inserts into the pathway of defecation, the pathway of urination, or the mouth without touching, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. "Venerable One, if a monk engages in unchaste conduct with the hairless, burned corpse of a sow, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. And the same should be stated for all animal existences.

In brief:
Another's limb, and one who is born with two sex organs — likewise so.
Two who are damaged, one who is bound,
The fourth with two, and the seventh.

"Venerable One, if a monk inserts a male organ into another's female organ, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. "Venerable One, if a single monk enters into union for the purpose of unchaste conduct alone, is there a defeat?"

"Upāli, what does it mean for something to be elongated?" It is like a bolster or cushion.

"Venerable One, if a monk enters into the crouch of a bee-keeper's hive and the woman is sitting outside, and while she remains there in that position he wraps around and engages in unchaste conduct, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat.

"Venerable One, the Blessed One has spoken of 'violation while alive.' How much violation counts as 'while alive'?" "As much as a wound has appeared, or it has decayed, or decomposed, or been eaten by creatures — to that extent it is said to be 'while alive.'" "How much violation counts as 'not while alive'?" "As when both ends of it have become equal — that is 'not while alive.' For a corpse the same should be stated likewise." The same should be stated in the same way also for non-humans, those born in animal existences, males, hermaphrodites, and male hermaphrodites.

"If wrapped around and inserted, it does not become a defeat." The Blessed One having declared this, the monks asked: "If monks wrap around with thick felt or coarse cloth and insert, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. "If wrapped around with cotton, silk, or thin cloth and inserted, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat.

"Venerable One, if a monk inserts perceiving a passage as a passage, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat. "If he inserts perceiving a passage as not a passage, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat. "If he inserts perceiving what is not a passage as not a passage, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. "If he inserts perceiving what is not a passage as a passage, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense.

"If a monk inserts perceiving a wrapped one as wrapped, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. "If he inserts perceiving a wrapped one as unwrapped, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. "If he inserts perceiving an unwrapped one as wrapped, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. "If he inserts perceiving an unwrapped one as unwrapped, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat.

"Venerable One, if one who has not yet received full ordination prepares for unchaste conduct and is inserted into by one who has not yet received full ordination, what becomes of that?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "If one who has not yet received full ordination prepares and is inserted into by one in the act of receiving full ordination, what becomes of that?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "If one who has not yet received full ordination prepares and is inserted into by one who has fully received ordination, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat. "If one in the act of receiving full ordination prepares and is inserted into by one in the act of receiving full ordination, what becomes of that?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "If one who has fully received ordination prepares and is inserted into by one who has fully received ordination, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat. "If one who has fully received ordination prepares and, having received full ordination, inserts, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat. "If one who has fully received ordination prepares and is inserted into by one who has not fully received ordination, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense.

Just as a monk who, through the conditions of unchaste conduct, incurs a defeat, and likewise one who has given up the training — so also for a fully ordained nun it becomes a defeat. For a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā), a novice nun, and a male novice it becomes a wrongdoing.

In brief:
The group of eighty, the mark,
the unequal value yet the mark;
the seventh who has received full ordination performs the act —
the eleven dice pieces are likewise so.

"Venerable One, if a monk counts himself as belonging to both assemblies of the group of eighty, what becomes of that?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "What is the fortunate portion belonging to the Dharma in that case?" It is the first. "If having taken it he conceals it, it becomes a transgression through knowingly speaking a falsehood." When it has been completed, the value is to be assessed.

"Venerable One, among the marks set and established by people, if a monk moves a more valuable mark to a less valuable location, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. "If he moves a less valuable mark to a more valuable location, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat.

"Venerable One, if a monk steals an object of no value, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat.

"What is meant by an object of no value?" It is something that, though it has become precious, cannot have a price assessed upon it. "If a monk steals an object that has no assessable value, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. "What is meant by an object of no value?" It is something so small that a price cannot be set upon it. "Venerable One, if a monk steals an object that cannot be assessed, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat. "If he steals an object that can be assessed, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense.

"Venerable One, if a monk who has set out to steal changes his ordination status and, having become a nun, then steals, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat. "If a nun who has set out to steal changes her ordination status and becomes a monk, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat.

"Venerable One, if one who has not yet received full ordination sets out to steal and steals before receiving full ordination, what becomes of that?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "If one who has not yet received full ordination sets out to steal and steals in the very act of receiving full ordination, what becomes of that?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "If one who has not yet received full ordination sets out to steal and then steals after having received full ordination, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat. "If one in the very act of receiving full ordination sets out to steal and steals in that same act of receiving full ordination, what becomes of that?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "If one sets out to steal during the very act of receiving full ordination and steals after full ordination has been completed, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat. "Venerable One, if a monk who has received full ordination sets out to steal after receiving full ordination and then steals after receiving full ordination, what becomes of that?" It becomes a defeat. "If one who has received full ordination sets out to steal and steals before full ordination has been completed, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense.

"Venerable One, if a monk throws dice in the open sky, what becomes of that?" It is the same as the matter in itself. However, if he does so by supernatural power, there is no offense. "Venerable One, if a monk throws dice by a route that is not the proper one, what becomes of that?" If by doing so he exceeds the boundary of that place, it becomes a grave offense.

"Venerable One, if a monk says to merchants, 'They are going,' what becomes of that?" It becomes a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, in a case where merchants say to a monk, 'Noble One, please carry goods that are subject to a toll-station past the toll-station without having reached the toll-station point' — if a monk then carries them, what becomes of that?" It becomes a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, in a case where merchants say to a monk, 'Noble One, please carry goods that are subject to a toll-station past the toll-station without having reached the toll-station point, and take for yourself half of whatever toll is assessed there' — if the monk then carries them, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense.

"Venerable One, in a case where merchants say to a monk, 'Noble One, please carry goods that are subject to a toll-station past the toll-station without having reached the toll-station point, and take for yourself all of whatever toll is assessed there' — if the monk then carries them, what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense.

"Venerable One, if goods that merchants have made subject to a toll-station have not reached the toll-station point and a monk shows them a different route, what becomes of that?" It becomes a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, in a case where merchants say to a monk, 'Noble One, please carry goods that are subject to a toll-station past the toll-station without having reached the toll-station point' — if the monk then carries them, what becomes of that?" It becomes a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, in a case where merchants have made goods subject to a toll-station, and those goods have reached the toll-station point, and the merchants say to the monk, 'Noble One, please release us from this toll-station place and carry the goods past, and take for yourself half of whatever toll is assessed here' — if the monk then carries them out of that statement, what becomes of that?" The value of the toll is to be assessed.

"Venerable One, in a case where merchants have made goods subject to a toll-station, and those goods have reached the toll-station point, and the merchants say to the monk, 'Noble One, please release us from this toll-station place and carry the goods past, and take for yourself all of whatever toll is assessed here' — if the monk then carries them out of that statement, what becomes of that?" The value of the toll is to be assessed.

In summary:

The robe-rack, the fourth of the fabric goods,
And theft, the third of the root downfalls,
Three kinds of engagement, and doubt,
And other continents — these do not apply to non-humans.

"Venerable One, if a monk, first with a mind to steal, cuts the initial plank of a robe-rack and then, at a later time, appropriates the rest with a sense of ownership — what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense.

"Venerable One, if a monk, when first cutting a plank of a robe-rack, does so with a sense of ownership but later comes to regard it as theft — what becomes of that?" The value is to be assessed.

"Venerable One, if a monk steals a plank of a robe-rack with a mind to steal, and at the time of stealing, robes happen to be draped over that robe-rack, and he takes the rack together with the robes — what becomes of that?" The value of the robe-rack plank is to be assessed.

"Venerable One, if a robe-rack with robes draped upon it and set in place is stolen by four monks or more — what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. However, if what is divided among them individually amounts to five māṣas each, it comes to a defeat.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, into how many types does theft fall?" "Upāli, there are six: theft by deception, theft by force, theft by snatching from one who is asleep, theft by snatching from one who is carrying something, theft while feigning to protect, and Dharma-theft."

"Venerable One, the Blessed One has taught that theft falls into six types — which of them incurs a defeat?" All of them except Dharma-theft incur a defeat.

"Venerable One, the Blessed One has taught that stealing five māṣas incurs a defeat — can a monk incur a defeat by stealing three māṣas?" Upāli, yes, there is such a case: when three māṣas constitute one quarter of something.

"Venerable One, can a monk steal five māṣas and yet not incur a defeat?" Yes, there is such a case: when what exceeds five māṣas constitutes one quarter of something.

"Venerable One, the Blessed One has taught that stealing five māṣas does not incur a defeat — what kind of five māṣas, when stolen, would incur a defeat?" A nāṇaka of twenty māṣas. "What is a māṣaka?" Four kākinīs. "What is a kārṣāpaṇa?" One made with all ornamental markings.

"Venerable One, the Blessed One has taught that stealing five māṣas does not incur a defeat — can a monk steal a thousand kārṣāpaṇas and still not incur a defeat?" Yes, there is such a case: when he takes it perceiving it as something abandoned.

"Venerable One, the Blessed One has taught that stealing five māṣas incurs a defeat — can a monk steal five māṣas and yet not incur a defeat?" Yes, there is such a case: namely, if he steals one at a time, or two at a time, or three at a time, or four at a time, and the total never reaches five.

"Venerable One, if a monk takes a large implement perceiving it as his own, and then hides it with a mind to steal — what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense.

"Venerable One, if, in that case, a monk takes something with a mind to steal and then hides it with a sense of ownership — what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense.

"Venerable One, if a monk steals something with doubt and a divided mind — thinking 'Is this that one, or is this it, or is this not it?' — what becomes of that?" It is in accordance with the actual thing.

"Venerable One, if a monk steals without permission from the western continent of Aparagodānīya — what becomes of that?" If, reckoned by the measure of that continent, five māṣas are stolen, it results in a defeat.

"Venerable One, if one steals without permission from the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha — what becomes of that?" If, reckoned by the measure of that continent, five māṣas are stolen, it results in a defeat.

"Venerable One, if one steals without permission from the northern continent of Uttarakuru — what becomes of that?" Upāli, in that continent there is no taking what is not given, for everything there is held in common. However, if a mind to steal arises, it becomes a grave offense.

"Venerable One, if a monk steals without permission on behalf of another — what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. But if he thinks, "This belongs to that person," there is no offense.

"Venerable One, if a monk perceives a non-human being as a non-human being and steals from it without permission — what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. If one perceives a non-human being as a human, it becomes a grave offense. If one perceives a human as a non-human, it becomes a grave offense. If one perceives a human as a human, it results in a defeat.

In brief:

A stūpa, relics, and a scripture volume,
what is dedicated to the Saṅgha, one from one,
two perceptions, and dwelling accordingly —
the last is a household not yet found.

"Venerable One, if a monk steals the ornaments of a stūpa or the ornaments surrounding a stūpa — what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. "If a monk steals relics — what becomes of that?" It results in a defeat. "Venerable One, if a monk steals a scripture volume — what becomes of that?" The value of the scripture volume is to be assessed.

"Venerable One, if a monk steals without permission from the Saṅgha of the four quarters — what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. "Venerable One, if a monk steals without permission from many persons — what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense; but if from that the individual share of each amounts to five māṣas, and he steals that, it results in a defeat.

"Venerable One, if a monk steals without permission from what has been dedicated — what becomes of that?" It results in a defeat.

"Venerable One, if many monks steal without permission by passing something from one to another — what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. However, each one's individual appropriation is to be assessed according to the value of however much each made his own.

"Venerable One, if a monk perceives something as belonging to another and steals it without permission — what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense.

"Venerable One, if a monk perceives what is fully appropriated as fully appropriated and steals it without permission — what becomes of that?" It results in a defeat. "If one perceives what is not fully appropriated as fully appropriated and steals it without permission — what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. "If one perceives what is fully appropriated as not fully appropriated and takes it without permission — what becomes of that?" It becomes a grave offense. "If one perceives what is not fully appropriated as not fully appropriated" — there is no offense.

"Venerable One, the Blessed One has said that stealing a large implement without permission results in a defeat. Is there then a case where a monk steals a large implement without permission and yet it does not result in a defeat?" Yes, there is: namely, if it is stolen from the very place where it was deposited and stored.

"Venerable One, if a monk, regarding a find that does not fall under his authority, declares 'I have authority over this' — what becomes of that?" Since he knowingly speaks a falsehood, it constitutes a transgression. But if the intention was merely approximate, it becomes a grave offense. If the claim is fully established, the value is to be assessed.

"Venerable One, is there a case where a single monk, having entered a house and taken something without permission, incurs a defeat?"

"Upāli, there is such a case. How does it come about? If a monk, with the intention of taking without permission — that is, with the intention of theft — prepares himself and then enters, or enters and then prepares himself, and death results, it entails a defeat. Likewise, if the training has been surrendered, the same applies to a nun: it results in a defeat. In the case of a female trainee, a novice nun, or male novices, it constitutes a grave offense.

In brief:
Three animal rebirths, and existence through karma,
The existence of the mother, and the fourth,
Two wombs, and sustaining life,
Perception, and the fourth.

Venerable One, if a monk, by means of mantra or medicine, transforms a human being into an animal rebirth and thereby separates that being from life — what becomes of that? It results in a defeat.

Venerable One, if a monk, by means of mantra or medicine, transforms himself into an animal rebirth and thereby separates himself from human life — what becomes of that? If he retains the perception of being a monk and thereby acts in a manner that a monk ought not to act, it results in a defeat. If he does not retain the perception of being a monk, it constitutes a grave offense.

Venerable One, is there a case in which a monk separates his father and mother from life, and yet incurs neither a defeat nor an uninterrupted offense (ānantarika)? There is: when one's parents have taken rebirth in the animal realm.

Venerable One, is there a case in which a monk kills his father and yet incurs neither a defeat nor an uninterrupted offense? Upāli, because what is called 'father' is that which generates the karmic existence of beings — if it is the defiled karmic existence that has been killed, then it is in that sense a defeat, but an uninterrupted offense, no.

Is there a case in which a monk does not kill his mother and yet incurs neither a defeat nor an uninterrupted offense? Upāli, because what is called 'mother' is that which generates craving — if it is craving that has been killed, it is in that sense a defeat, but an uninterrupted offense, no.

Venerable One, if a monk intends to kill his mother but instead kills another woman — what becomes of that? It constitutes a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk intends to kill another woman but does not kill her — what becomes of that? It constitutes a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk, having prepared to kill his mother but without having killed her, causes another woman to be separated from life — what becomes of that? It constitutes a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk, having prepared to kill another woman, causes his mother to be separated from life — what becomes of that? It constitutes a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk kills an animal rebirth that is within the womb of a human woman — what becomes of that? It constitutes a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk does not kill a human being that is within the womb of a female animal — what becomes of that? If the one in the womb is perceived as a human, it results in a defeat. If not perceived as such, it is a transgression.

Venerable One, the mother is the one who generates, while the other is the one who nurtures. If one is separated from life, which of the two results in a defeat and which in an uninterrupted offense? It is the one who generated.

Venerable One, if a monk perceives a human as a human and kills that person — what becomes of that? It results in a defeat. If the monk perceives a human as other than a human and kills that person — what becomes of that? It constitutes a grave offense. If the monk perceives what is not a human as a human and kills it — what becomes of that? It constitutes a grave offense. If the monk perceives what is not a human as not a human and kills it — what becomes of that? It constitutes a grave offense.

In brief:
Doubt of the second kind,
Self and arhat equally,
Two thieves and mistaken perception of another,
The seventh, and the last as well.

Venerable One, if a monk, while wavering in doubt and uncertainty — thinking 'Is this that person, or is this not that person?' — thereby causes that one to be separated from life, what becomes of that? It results in a defeat.

Venerable One, if a monk causes himself to be separated from life — what becomes of that? It constitutes a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk, having prepared to kill his father and mother, kills himself instead — what becomes of that? If the father and mother had died previously, it results in a defeat and also in an uninterrupted offense."

But if he himself had done so at an earlier time, it results in a grave offense and does not constitute an uninterrupted offense.

Venerable One, if a monk intends to kill an arhat but instead kills an ordinary person — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk intends to kill an ordinary person but instead kills an arhat — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk has prepared to kill an arhat and instead kills an ordinary person — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk, having prepared to kill an ordinary person, instead separates an arhat from life — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, a thief being led away for execution makes his escape, and whether it be a village constable or a royal constable who then pursues him from behind, a monk comes along just ahead of them and is asked by them, "Did you see a thief who fled past?" and that monk, while harboring an intent to kill that thief, points him out to them — what becomes of that? It results in a defeat.

Venerable One, a thief being led away for execution makes his escape, and whether it be a village constable or a royal constable who then pursues him from behind, a monk also comes along just ahead of them and is asked, "Did you see a thief who fled past?" and that monk likewise harbors an intent to kill that thief, yet does not point him out to them, and they then separate him from life — what becomes of that? It constitutes an offense.

Venerable One, if two are traveling together, one intending to kill the other and the other is indeed killed — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

If one who has not yet received full ordination prepared to kill someone and kills that person before receiving full ordination — what becomes of that? It constitutes an offense.

If one who has not yet received full ordination prepared to kill someone and then kills that person in the very moment of receiving full ordination — what becomes of that? It constitutes an offense.

If one who has not yet received full ordination prepared to kill someone, and then, having received full ordination, kills that person — what becomes of that? It results in a defeat.

If one, during the very moment of receiving full ordination, having prepared to kill someone kills that person during that same moment — what becomes of that? It constitutes an offense.

If one, during the very moment of receiving full ordination, having prepared to kill someone, kills that person after having received full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in a defeat.

If one who has already received full ordination, having prepared to kill someone, kills that person after full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in a defeat.

If one who has already received full ordination, having prepared to kill someone, kills that person before receiving full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, is there such a thing as a single monk incurring defeat by entering a household for the purpose of being separated from life himself? Upāli, there is — it is as when a monk has prepared to kill and then enters within. Just as a monk incurs defeat through the condition of being separated from life, so too is it for one who returns his training, and for a nun it equally results in a defeat. For a probationer nun, a male novice, and a female novice, it constitutes an offense.

In brief:

Pure, and the Teacher is seen clearly —
the one who has more to learn, the teacher, affliction,
and lapse, release, fear,
birth, gain — these are such cases.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "I am pure" — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "I am the Teacher" — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "I am a hearer of Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa" — what becomes of that? If he announces a prophetic declaration regarding the former abodes, it results in a defeat.

But if he says, "From the time I took refuge in Śākyamuni onward, I have taken refuge in all perfectly and fully awakened buddhas," that results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "I am one who has nothing more to learn" — what becomes of that? If he announces a prophetic declaration regarding the abandonment of afflictions, it results in the final offense. But if he says, "I am learning no craft whatsoever," that results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "I am one who has something to learn" — what becomes of that? If he announces a prophetic declaration regarding conduct appropriate to one who still has to learn, it results in the final offense. But if he says, "I am training in the holy life," that results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "I have no afflictions" — what becomes of that? If he announces a prophetic declaration regarding the abandonment of afflictions, it results in the final offense. But if he says, "I have no alms-bowl, or robe, or any of the requisites for a monk's livelihood," that results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "I have lapsed" — what becomes of that? If he says, "I have lapsed from the fruits of the ascetic life," it results in the final offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "I am released" — what becomes of that? If he says, "I am released from entanglement, bondage, underlying tendencies, secondary afflictions, and what has passed while being thoroughly enmeshed," it results in the final offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "I have no fear" — what becomes of that? If he announces a prophetic declaration regarding the abandonment of fear, it results in the final offense. But if he says, "By fear, I am not frightened in the least," what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "This is my last birth" — what becomes of that? If he announces a prophetic declaration regarding the exhaustion of birth, it results in the final offense. But if he says, "Birth is exhausted, stopped, separated, thoroughly separated — in this way, this is the last birth," that results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "I have fully attained" — what becomes of that? If he says, "I have attained the fruits of monkhood," it results in the final offense. But if he announces a prophetic declaration regarding a worldly thing, that results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "How wonderful! How remarkable that you have become like what I am!" — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

In brief:

Unripened, patience, self-comparison,
abandonment, the second fruit,
the four perceptions, what is to be attained,
and lastly the worldly — these are such cases.

Venerable One, suppose a venerable monk is asked, "Venerable one, have you the fruit of exhausted defilements?" and that monk, while carrying carefully an unripened fruit from a tree, replies, "It is unripened" — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "I have attained the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the supreme fruit" — what becomes of that? It results in the final offense.

Venerable One, if a monk has himself written and says, "Who wrote this? — I am an arhat" — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, suppose a householder asks a monk, "Have you attained the fruit?" and that monk, carrying flowers and ripened fruits, replies, "It is unripened" — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "I have declined" — what becomes of that? If he declares that he has declined from an attainment he actually possesses, it results in the final offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "I am not one who has entered the stream, not one who returns once, not one who never returns, not an arhat" — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "At the mountain called Gro-ba I attained the fruit of stream-entry; on the slope of the mountain called Ri-dgu-pa, the fruit of once-returning; at Vulture Peak, the fruit of non-returning; and in the grove called Öma, the supreme fruit" — what becomes of that? It results in the final offense.

Venerable One, if a monk perceives a human being as something other than human and then declares a teaching surpassing the human — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. If he perceives a non-human as human, it results in a grave offense. If he perceives a non-human as a non-human, it results in a grave offense. If he perceives a human as human, it results in the final offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "Whatever is to be attained by a śrāvaka — that I have attained" — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "Today I did not enter meditative absorption into a worldly dhyāna — not in the evening, not at any time since then" — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk says, "Come here by prophetic declaration" — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

In brief:
Through messenger, written letter, sign language,
through another's words, or passed from one to another,
through one who is mad, or whose mind is disturbed,
through one who is ill, mute, or foolish — these are the last category.

Venerable One, if a monk declares a teaching surpassing the human through a messenger — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Likewise, through a written letter, through a sign, through instructing another, or passing it from person to person — in every such case it results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk declares a teaching surpassing the human to one who is mad — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Likewise, to one whose mind is disturbed, to one tormented by illness, to one who is mute, and to one who is foolish — in every such case it results in a grave offense.

In brief:
To one who is asleep, to one who is delirious, to one who is intoxicated,
to one who has gone into meditative absorption, and likewise
by voice, by bodily gesture, in a secluded place, or by mantra —
from one person to another, these are the last category.

Venerable One, if a monk who is a noble one speaks a teaching surpassing the human to another monk in the noble language, and that monk does not understand the noble language — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. If a noble one speaks in a border dialect and that monk does not understand the border dialect — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. If one who speaks a border dialect speaks in a border dialect and that monk does not understand the border dialect — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. If one who speaks a border dialect declares a teaching surpassing the human to a monk in the noble language, and that monk does not understand the noble language — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk teaches a teaching surpassing the human through a bodily gesture — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk perceives a secluded place as non-secluded and declares a teaching surpassing the human — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk makes himself invisible through a mantra or medicine and then declares a teaching surpassing the human — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if a monk declares a teaching surpassing the human while learning it from another — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if a monk declares a teaching surpassing the human on behalf of another — what becomes of that? It results in an offense.

Just as the consequences arising from a monk's speech apply in the ways described, the same applies to one who has given back the training, and the same outcomes apply to nuns. For female probationers, novice nuns, and male novices it results in an offense.

This concludes the section on defeat offenses from the questions of the Venerable Upāli.

In summary:
Not asleep, as when asleep, likewise stirring;
those without striving, and their counterparts;
the seventh likewise, and others —
these are gathered together with their classes.

The Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable One, if one strives while not asleep and then lies down and emits semen — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if one strives while asleep and, upon waking, semen is emitted — what becomes of that? If one strove, it results in a grave offense. If one did not strive, there is no offense.

Venerable One, you have said that emitting semen that has already gathered into a blister results in a grave offense — how much swelling constitutes a blister? It is blocked from the place as soon as it has blistered. Venerable One, you have said that the Blessed One has prohibited stirring — how much stirring is prohibited? It is prohibited from the place as soon as there is stirring.

Venerable One, if semen is emitted without any striving — what becomes of that? If there is no experience of pleasure, there is no offense.

Venerable One, if a monk, through the emission of semen, undergoes a change of sex and becomes a nun — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense arising from a Saṅgha remainder offense. Venerable One, if a nun, through the emission of semen, undergoes a change of sex and becomes a monk — what becomes of that? It results in an offense arising from a downfall.

Venerable One, if a monk extracts semen from another's male organ — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if one who has not received full ordination strives and emits semen while not fully ordained — what becomes of that? It results in an offense. If one who has not received full ordination strives and emits semen in the very act of receiving full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in an offense. If one who has not received full ordination strives and emits semen after having received full ordination — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder offense. If one strives in the very act of receiving full ordination and emits semen in the very act of receiving full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in an offense. If one strives in the very act of receiving full ordination and emits semen after full ordination is complete — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder offense. If one strives after full ordination is complete and emits semen after full ordination is complete — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder offense. If one begins to strive after receiving full ordination and emits semen while not yet fully ordained — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Just as when a monk incurs a Saṅgha remainder offense through the emission of semen, so too with one who has given back the training it is likewise a Saṅgha remainder offense. For a nun it is according to the actual act. For female probationers, novice nuns, and male novices it results in an offense.

In summary:
The body, doubt, the tooth, and likewise
wound, hair, and nail —
the fourth, the second, and the seventh —
are also gathered into their classes.

Venerable One, if a monk makes full bodily contact with a woman whose faculties are impaired — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if a monk whose own bodily faculty is impaired makes full bodily contact with a woman — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if both parties have impaired bodily faculties and the two make full bodily contact with one another — what becomes of that? It results in an offense.

Venerable One, if a monk, while doubt, uncertainty, and suspicion arise in him that this woman may not be a woman, makes full bodily contact with her — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if contact is made through a wound — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if contact is made with a tooth — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if contact is made with a wound — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if contact is made through hair — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if contact is made with hair — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if contact is made with a nail — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if contact is made by means of a nail — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk makes contact with a human woman while perceiving her as human — what becomes of that? It is a remainder for the Saṅgha. If he makes contact with a human being while perceiving that being as non-human — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. If he makes contact with a non-human while perceiving her as human — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. If he makes contact with a non-human while perceiving her as non-human — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk makes contact with a clothed woman while perceiving her as clothed — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. If he makes contact with a clothed woman while perceiving her as unclothed — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. If he makes contact with an unclothed woman while perceiving her as clothed — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. If he makes contact with an unclothed woman while perceiving her as unclothed — what becomes of that? It is a remainder for the Saṅgha.

Venerable One, if one who has not received full ordination prepares to make full bodily contact and then makes contact while not yet fully ordained — what becomes of that? It results in an offense. If one who has not received full ordination prepares to make contact and then makes contact at the moment of full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in an offense. If one who has not received full ordination prepares to make contact and then makes contact after full ordination has been received — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. If one who is at the moment of receiving full ordination prepares to make contact and then makes contact at the moment of full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in an offense. If one who is at the moment of receiving full ordination prepares to make contact and then makes contact once fully ordained — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. If one who has already received full ordination prepares to make contact and then makes contact while fully ordained — what becomes of that? It is a remainder for the Saṅgha. If one who has already received full ordination prepares to make contact and then makes contact before full ordination has been received — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

In summary:
Perceiving otherwise, a corpse, bones,
sexual characteristics, a male, a soft one,
a hermaphrodite, a father, a mother's brother's wife,
in meditative absorption, lying down, and going about.

Venerable One, if a monk, out of desire for one woman, makes full bodily contact together with another — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if contact is made together with a woman's corpse — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if a monk makes contact with a woman's fleshless skeleton — what becomes of that? It results in an offense.

Venerable One, if a monk makes full bodily contact with a woman and, in the course of that act, his sexual characteristics transform and he becomes a nun — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if a nun makes full bodily contact with a man and, in the course of that act, her sexual characteristics transform and she becomes a monk — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk makes full bodily contact with a man — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if a monk makes contact thinking it to be something soft or pleasant — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Thinking it to be soft or warm — that too results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if a monk makes full bodily contact with a paṇḍaka together with a man — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. If he makes full bodily contact with a paṇḍaka together with a woman — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if a monk makes full bodily contact with a woman who is in meditative absorption — what becomes of that? It results in a Saṅgha remainder offense. Venerable One, if a monk makes full bodily contact with a woman who is asleep — what becomes of that? It results in a Saṅgha remainder offense. Venerable One, if a monk makes full bodily contact with a woman who is dwelling in another state of existence — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Just as a monk incurs a Saṅgha remainder offense through full bodily contact, so too does one who has given back the training incur a Saṅgha remainder offense. For fully ordained nuns it results in a root downfall. For female probationers, novice nuns, and male novices it results in a misdeed.

In summary, by means of voice, body, a secluded spell, conjuring one thing from another, sending a message, a written letter, a hand-sign, saying it through another — these are the seven. The divisions concern paṇḍakas: male paṇḍakas, and paṇḍakas who are good and those who are wicked.

Venerable One, if a noble monk speaks licentious words to a woman in the noble language, and that woman does not understand the noble language — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. If a noble one speaks in a border dialect, and that woman does not understand the border dialect either — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. If a border person speaks in a border dialect, and that woman does not understand the border dialect — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. If a border person speaks licentious words to a woman in the noble language, and that woman does not understand the noble language either — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if a monk directs his body as a visual gesture and speaks licentious words to a woman — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if a monk perceives a secluded place as secluded and speaks licentious words to a woman — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if a monk renders himself invisible by means of a spell or a drug and speaks licentious words to a woman — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if a monk causes another to speak licentious words to a woman — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if a monk speaks licentious words to a woman on behalf of another — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if a monk speaks licentious words to an emanated woman — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Venerable One, if a monk causes a message to be conveyed to a woman — what becomes of that? It results in a grave offense. Likewise, a written letter, a hand-sign, saying it through another, and passing it from one to another — all of these result in a grave offense.

Venerable One, if one who has not received full ordination frames licentious words and speaks them as one who has not received full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in a misdeed. If one who has not received full ordination frames them and speaks them as one who is on the verge of full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in a misdeed. If one who has not received full ordination frames them and speaks them having fully ordained — what becomes of that? It results in a Saṅgha remainder offense. If one who is on the verge of full ordination frames them and speaks them as one on the verge of full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in a misdeed. If one on the verge of full ordination frames them and speaks them as one fully ordained — what becomes of that? It results in a Saṅgha remainder offense. If one who is fully ordained frames them and speaks them as one fully ordained — what becomes of that? It results in a Saṅgha remainder offense.

If one who is fully ordained frames them and speaks them as one not fully ordained — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

Venerable ones, if a monk says to a woman, "Share equally with me in a great matter" — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a monk says this to a hermaphrodite — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If he says it to a man — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If he says it to a female hermaphrodite — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

Venerable ones, if a monk says to a woman, "How splendid" — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. Venerable ones, if a monk says to a woman, "You are a sinful one" — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

In brief:
A madwoman, one mentally disturbed,
one afflicted by illness, one delirious, one simple-minded,
one asleep, one intoxicated with alcohol, one drunk —
and a nun, and one in meditative absorption.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable one, if a monk speaks words of base conduct to a mad woman — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. The same applies likewise to one who is mentally disturbed, one tormented by illness, one delirious, one simple-minded, one asleep, one intoxicated with alcohol, and one who is drunk.

If, when a monk has spoken words of base conduct to a woman, the gender changes and she becomes a nun — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a nun has spoken words of base conduct to a man, and the gender changes and he becomes a monk — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that when a monk speaks words of base conduct to a woman it is a Saṅgha remainder offense. Is there any case in which a monk speaking words of base conduct to a woman does not become a Saṅgha remainder offense? There is: namely, when it is for the sake of another. Venerable one, if a monk says it to a man — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If he says it to female probationers and female novices — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder offense. If a monk says it to a male novice — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a nun says it to a man — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a female probationer says it to a man, a monk, or a male novice — what becomes of that? It results in a misdeed. If a female novice says it to a man, a monk, or a male novice — what becomes of that? It results in a misdeed. If a male novice says it to a woman, a nun, a female probationer, a female novice, a monk, or a male novice — what becomes of that? It results in a misdeed.

Venerable one, if a monk speaks words of base conduct to a woman who is in meditative absorption — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

In brief:
The fourth, combined with two, and different perceptions —
these are spoken of as base conduct.
The same applies to conduct throughout —
this is to be proclaimed in full.

Venerable one, if a monk perceives a non-human woman as non-human and speaks — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If he perceives a non-human as human — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If he perceives a human as non-human — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If he perceives a human as human — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder offense.

Venerable one, if a monk perceives a human woman as a woman and speaks — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder offense. If he perceives a woman as a man — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If he perceives a man as a woman — what becomes of that? It likewise results in a serious offense. If he perceives a man as a man and speaks — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

Venerable one, if a monk, while perceiving someone as another, speaks words of corrupt conduct to a certain woman — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

The third and fourth Saṅgha remainder rules are complete. Just as the conduct in question applies to corrupt speech, so too it applies to all related conduct.

The Noble Vinaya. The second fascicle.

In summary:
Two dharmas with a fourth making six aspects,
Two faculties to be procured,
The seventh, and those below it,
Two of the fourth, and one from one.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, what is the dharma that is neither past, nor future, nor present, yet is the culmination of the completion of all karma?" The Blessed One replied: "Upāli, it is nirvāṇa." "Venerable one, what is that which comes and goes, and is yet the culmination of the completion of all karma?" "Upāli, it is the act of conveying a message." "What becomes of conveying such a message?" "It is a Saṅgha remainder offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk takes a message from a madman, delivers it to the madman, and then gives back a reply to the madman — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a monk takes a message from a madman, delivers it to the madman, and gives back the reply to someone in their natural state of mind — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a monk takes a message from a madman, delivers it to someone in their natural state of mind, and gives back the reply to the madman — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a monk takes a message from a madman, delivers it to someone in their natural state of mind, and gives back the reply to that person in their natural state of mind — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

Venerable one, if a monk takes a message from someone in their natural state of mind, delivers it to someone in their natural state of mind, and gives back the reply to that person in their natural state of mind — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder offense. If a monk takes a message from someone in their natural state of mind, delivers it to someone in their natural state of mind, and gives back the reply to a madman — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a monk takes a message from someone in their natural state of mind, delivers it to a madman, and gives back the reply to someone in their natural state of mind — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a monk takes a message from someone in their natural state of mind, delivers it to a madman, and gives back the reply to the madman — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense."

Just as for a madman the four permutations yield two outcomes, so likewise for one whose mind is disturbed the four permutations yield two outcomes; and the same four permutations yielding two outcomes apply equally to those who are of sound mind and those who are not of sound mind.

"Venerable one, if a monk takes a message from one of sound mind, delivers it to one of sound mind, and gives back the reply to one of sound mind — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder offense. If a monk takes a message from one of sound mind, delivers it to one of sound mind, and gives back the reply to one not of sound mind — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a monk takes a message from one of sound mind, delivers it to one not of sound mind, and gives back the reply to one of sound mind — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a monk takes a message from one of sound mind, delivers it to one not of sound mind, and gives back the reply to one not of sound mind — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

Venerable one, if a monk takes a message from one not of sound mind, delivers it to one not of sound mind, and gives back the reply to one not of sound mind — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a monk takes a message from one not of sound mind, delivers it to one not of sound mind, and gives back the reply to one of sound mind — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a monk takes a message from one not of sound mind, delivers it to one of sound mind, and that reply is then delivered back to one of sound mind — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a monk takes a message from one not of sound mind, delivers it to one of sound mind, and gives back the reply to one not of sound mind — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

Venerable one, if a monk says to a householder, 'Go and obtain a woman,' — what becomes of that? It is a wrongdoing. Venerable one, if a monk says to a householder, 'Obtain this particular woman,' — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense."

If a message is taken from one not fully ordained, delivered to one not fully ordained, and the reply is then delivered back to one fully ordained — what becomes of that? It is a wrongdoing. If a message is taken from one not fully ordained, delivered to one not fully ordained, and the reply is delivered back to one not fully ordained — what becomes of that? It is a wrongdoing. If a message is taken from one not fully ordained, delivered to one not fully ordained, and the reply is delivered back to one who is fully ordained — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder. If a message is taken from one not fully ordained, delivered to one fully ordained, and the reply is delivered back to one who is fully ordained — what becomes of that? It is a wrongdoing. If a message is taken from one not fully ordained, delivered to one fully ordained, and the reply is delivered back to one who is fully ordained — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder. If a message is taken by one not fully ordained, delivered to one fully ordained, and the reply is delivered back to one who is fully ordained — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder. If a message is taken by one fully ordained, delivered by one fully ordained, and the reply is delivered back to one not fully ordained — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

Venerable one, if the very same person who has been given a penalty has himself also completed that penalty, and is himself also engaged in the act of satisfaction — can it come about that he himself has also performed the act of satisfaction? It can. This is how it comes about: a person who has already performed the act of satisfaction incurs a Saṅgha remainder offense, and without having been put under restraint he goes before the Saṅgha and requests the act of satisfaction. The Saṅgha grants him the act of satisfaction and he performs it. Then two Saṅgha remainder offenses arise: one offense is put under restraint for one day, and the other offense is put under restraint for two days. He then requests the penalty from the Saṅgha, and the Saṅgha likewise imposes the penalty. Having carried out one day of penalty, he is released from the penalty for one offense. The second penalty he is carrying out. The third is the act of satisfaction in progress. The fourth is the act of satisfaction already completed.

Venerable one, if a monk acts as go-between for a human woman and a human man — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder. If a monk acts as go-between for a human woman and a non-human male — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a monk acts as go-between for a non-human female and a human man — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a monk acts as go-between for a non-human female and a non-human male — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

Venerable one, if a monk perceives a human as a human and acts as go-between — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder. If a monk perceives a human as a non-human and acts as go-between — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a monk perceives a non-human as a human and acts as go-between — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

Venerable one, if a monk acts as go-between by relaying from one to another — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder.

In brief:
A young woman, a wife, a pregnant woman,
A eunuch, a hermaphrodite, a female eunuch —
The entire Saṅgha by its vows
Is comparable to two of these marks.

Venerable one, if a monk acts as go-between for a young unmarried woman — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. Venerable one, if a monk acts as go-between in the absence of the householder's son — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. Venerable one, if a monk acts as go-between for one dwelling in the womb — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. Venerable one, if a monk acts as go-between for a woman in her prime — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a monk acts as go-between for a eunuch or female eunuch — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

Venerable one, when the entire Saṅgha is assembled, and —

— a householder arrives and says: "With my words, please tell this householder such-and-such to give a sister, a daughter-in-law, or a granddaughter" — and if the entire Saṅgha accepts that message and conveys the reply, what becomes of the entire Saṅgha? It results in a remainder offense for the Saṅgha. If the entire Saṅgha deliberates and a single monk conveys the message and delivers the reply, what becomes of the entire Saṅgha? It results in a remainder offense for the Saṅgha. But if a single monk, acting on his own judgment, conveys the message and delivers the reply, it still results in a remainder offense for the Saṅgha.

If a monk acts as go-between for a nun or for one dwelling in chastity observing the religious life of another, what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. Venerable one, if a monk accepts such a message, and immediately upon accepting it his gender changes and he becomes a nun, and then he conveys and delivers the reply — what becomes of that? It results in a remainder offense for the Saṅgha. Venerable one, if a nun accepts the message, conveys it and delivers the reply, and then her gender changes so that she becomes a monk — what becomes of that? It results in a remainder offense for the Saṅgha. Venerable one, if a monk accepts the message, conveys it, and while the gender-change is actually occurring he delivers the reply — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. Venerable one, if a monk accepts the message, and then the man's gender changes, and while the gender-change is occurring he conveys the message and delivers the reply — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. Venerable one, if a monk accepts the message, and in the case of a woman who has acquired male characteristics delivers the message while she is in the process of acquiring male characteristics, and then delivers the reply — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable one, a man has made an appointment together with a woman, and arising from that appointment the man says to a monk, "Noble one, have you seen such-and-such a woman?" and the monk, while searching, reports back saying, "She is sitting by that wall over there" — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If the man then says, "Noble one, please go and tell that woman to come here," and the monk goes and says that to her — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

Just as acting as go-between results in a remainder offense for the Saṅgha, so too does surrendering one's training — it likewise results in a remainder offense for the Saṅgha. For those in training, for male novices and female novices, it results in a misdeed.

In brief:

Without permission and the proper measure,
oneself, another, and uncovered above —
fallen back after having begun, likewise so,
and finally, the matter of the changed characteristic.

Venerable one, if a monk builds a dwelling without having obtained permission for the materials — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If he obtains permission for the materials but does not build the dwelling — what becomes of that? It results in a misdeed. If permission is granted to build the dwelling but he makes it exceed the proper measure — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If he himself begins it and then abandons it without completing it — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. Venerable one, if another person makes something improper into something proper — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If he makes it without covering the top — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If, having begun, he falls back — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. Likewise, abandoning one's own livelihood, and all instances of claiming novice status — these result in a serious offense. Likewise, the detailed account concerning eunuchs and the rest is as given in the presentation of surrendering one's training. If one who has not received full ordination begins, and it remains without full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in a misdeed.

If one begins without full ordination and it remains without full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in a misdeed. If one begins without full ordination and then full ordination is completed — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If one begins when full ordination is being completed and it remains in the process of being completed — what becomes of that? It results in a misdeed. If one begins upon full ordination and it remains upon full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in a Saṅgha remainder. If one begins upon full ordination and it is not upon full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense.

If a venerable monk begins to build a dwelling and, his status having changed so that he has become a nun, it is completed — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a venerable nun begins to build a dwelling and, her status having changed so that she has become a monk, it is completed — what becomes of that? It results in a misdeed. If one who has been given the training does it — what becomes of that? It results in a Saṅgha remainder. If a nun does it — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. For a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā), a male novice, and a female novice, it results in a misdeed. The same applies likewise to a great monastery.

In brief:
Through messenger, letter, gesture,
through another's words, or passed from one to another,
one who is mad, mentally disturbed, or ill,
one who is mute, foolish, or asleep,
one who is in agony or intoxicated,
one in meditative absorption, or an outsider —
these are the exemptions.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable Blessed One, you have declared that if a monk, out of resentment and without releasing that resentment, falsely accuses a pure and blameless monk who has committed no offense with a defeat, it results in a Saṅgha remainder. Is there a case where a monk who falsely accuses another with a defeat, even though that monk has committed no offense, does not incur a Saṅgha remainder?" "Yes, there is. If a monk accuses through a messenger, it results in a serious offense. Likewise, if the accusation is conveyed through a letter, a gesture, another's words, or passed on from one to another — all of these result in a serious offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk falsely accuses a mad monk — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. Likewise, if the accusation is directed at one who is mentally disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is foolish, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one who is in agony, one who is intoxicated, one in meditative absorption, or one dwelling elsewhere — in all such cases it results in a serious offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk falsely accuses those outside this tradition — non-Buddhist wanderers (tīrthikas), brahmins, those who practice universally, and wandering mendicants — what becomes of that? It results in a misdeed."

In brief:
By speech, by body, by solitude,
by mantra, and by another toward another — seven ways.
Toward laypeople and so forth,
and the status too is transmitted in four modes.

"Venerable one, if a noble monk accuses a monk in the noble language and that monk does not know the noble language — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If a noble monk makes the accusation in a border dialect, and that monk likewise does not know the border dialect — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If one from the borderlands accuses in the border dialect, and that monk does not know the border dialect — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If one from the borderlands accuses in the noble language, and that monk does not know the noble language — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk accuses a monk when no body is in view — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a secluded place as secluded and makes the accusation there — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk renders himself invisible through mantra or medicine and then accuses a monk — what becomes of that?"

It results in a serious offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk has another person make the accusation against a monk — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk accuses a monk on behalf of another — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense."

"Venerable one, if one has prepared to make an accusation against someone not yet fully ordained, and it is concluded before full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in a wrongdoing. If one has prepared to make the accusation before full ordination and it concludes at the moment of full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in a wrongdoing. If one has prepared to make the accusation before full ordination and it concludes after full ordination — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder. If one has prepared to make the accusation at the moment of full ordination and it concludes at the moment of full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in a wrongdoing. If one has prepared to make the accusation at the moment of full ordination and it concludes after full ordination — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder. If one has prepared the accusation once full ordination is complete and it concludes once full ordination is complete — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder. If one begins after full ordination and carries it out before full ordination — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk accuses a layman — what becomes of that? It results in a wrongdoing."

"Likewise, if one accuses a paṇḍaka, or accuses and expels a nun, or accuses one's father, or one's mother, or one who has slain an arhat, or one who has shed the blood of a Tathāgata with malicious intent, or a tīrthika, or one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, or a thief in residence, or one who was previously involved in a dispute, or one against whom an offense was previously established — in all such cases it results in a serious offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk accuses a monk — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder. Likewise, if one accuses those monks who have divided the Saṅgha, or those who are residing in a different location, or those who side with them, or those who have handed back their training — in all cases it becomes a Saṅgha remainder."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a fully ordained person as fully ordained, makes the accusation — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder."

"Venerable one, if a monk makes the accusation against a monk, and then the ordination status shifts and that person has become a nun — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder."

"Venerable one, if a nun makes the accusation against a nun, and the ordination status shifts and that person has become a monk — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a fully ordained person as fully ordained, makes the accusation — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder. If a monk, perceiving a fully ordained person as not fully ordained, makes the accusation — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If one perceives someone not fully ordained as fully ordained and makes the accusation — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If one perceives someone not fully ordained as not fully ordained and makes the accusation — what becomes of that? It results in a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a human being as a human being, makes the accusation — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder. If one perceives a human being as a non-human and makes the accusation — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If one perceives a non-human as a human being and makes the accusation — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense. If one perceives a non-human as a non-human and makes the accusation — what becomes of that? It results in a serious offense."

In brief:
The extreme, and likewise the without-interval,
One must not kill — the one against the other.
Accusation by letter and by proper grounds — likewise so,
The one who elaborates, and the same applies.

"Venerable one, if a monk accuses a monk who himself has come forward and declared, 'I have engaged in unchaste conduct, the act of sexual intercourse' — accusing him groundlessly with theft, with killing, or with lying — what becomes of that? It becomes a Saṅgha remainder."

"Venerable one, if a monk accuses a monk who himself has come forward and declared, 'I have stolen a great valuable item' — accusing him groundlessly with killing, with lying, or with unchaste conduct — what becomes of that? It is a Saṅgha remainder."

"Venerable one, if a monk himself has come forward and declared, 'I have taken a person's life' — and a monk accuses that monk groundlessly with lying, with unchaste conduct, or with theft — what becomes of that? It becomes a Saṅgha remainder."

"Venerable one, if a monk himself has come forward and declared, 'I have proclaimed to a person a Dharma that is supreme over the human' — and a monk accuses that monk groundlessly with unchaste conduct, with theft, or with killing — what becomes of that? It becomes a Saṅgha remainder."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk accuses a monk groundlessly with a matter entailing defeat, it becomes a Saṅgha remainder. If that is so, what becomes of a monk who accuses a monk groundlessly with an action without interval? If the accusation concerns killing one's father, killing one's mother, or killing an arhat, it becomes a Saṅgha remainder. If the accusation concerns causing a schism in the Saṅgha or, with malicious intent, drawing blood from the Tathāgata, it becomes a grave offense."

"Why is that? Upāli, accusing someone of killing father, mother, or an arhat — that accusation is one made with reference to a matter entailing defeat. Accusing someone of causing a schism in the Saṅgha or, with malicious intent, drawing blood from the Tathāgata — that accusation is one made with reference to a grave offense. A grave offense does not render one no longer a monk; it is something to be confessed. If a monk accuses a monk groundlessly with a matter entailing defeat, it becomes a Saṅgha remainder. If the accusation made groundlessly is a Saṅgha remainder, it becomes a downfall. If the accusation made groundlessly is a downfall, a matter of individual confession, or a grave offense, it becomes a wrongdoing. Likewise, if the accusation made groundlessly is a grave offense, it also becomes a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk accuses a nun, what becomes of that? It becomes a Saṅgha remainder."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk accuses a monk, it becomes a Saṅgha remainder. If that is so, what becomes of a monk who accuses a female probationer, a male novice, or a female novice? It becomes a grave offense."

"If a nun accuses a nun, what becomes of that? It becomes a Saṅgha remainder."
