"If a nun accuses a monk, what becomes of that? It becomes a Saṅgha remainder."

"If a male novice accuses a female probationer or a female novice, it becomes a wrongdoing."

"If a female probationer accuses a nun, a female probationer, a male novice, or a female novice, it becomes a wrongdoing."

"If a male novice accuses a monk, a nun, a female probationer, or a female novice, it becomes a wrongdoing."

"If a female novice accuses a monk, a nun, a female probationer, or a male novice, it becomes a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk himself has written something and says, 'This letter states: you have incurred a defeat through unchaste conduct' — what becomes of that? It becomes a grave offense. Just as with a groundless accusation, the same applies when the charge is leveled by such a written letter — it is to be stated in full."

In brief:
The motion to unite, equanimity,
The recollection of the dispute,
The fourth with the ongoing and the permanent,
Faith and the solitary, space and
Carrying it further — treat all the same.

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, if a monk is instructed with a motion and the act by quorum of four without first being instructed to gather — is this to be called 'instructed' or 'not instructed'? Does the instruction take effect or not?"

"Upāli, it does not take effect, and moreover the Saṅgha incurs a transgression along with the past."

"Venerable one, if a monk is instructed to unite by a motion and an act by quorum of four — is this to be called 'instructed' or 'not instructed'? Does the instruction take effect or not?"

"Upāli, it takes effect, and the Saṅgha does not incur a transgression along with the past."

"Venerable one, if a monk is instructed to unite without the act of expulsion having first been performed — is this to be called 'instructed' or 'not instructed'? Does the instruction take effect or not?"

"Upāli, it does not take effect, and the Saṅgha incurs a transgression along with the past."

"Venerable one, if the act of expulsion has been performed and he is then instructed to unite — is this to be called 'instructed' or 'not instructed'? Does the instruction take effect or not?"

"Upāli, it takes effect, and the Saṅgha does not incur a transgression along with the past."

"Venerable one, if the act of expulsion has not been performed and he is instructed by a motion and an act by quorum of four — is this to be called 'instructed' or 'not instructed'? Does the instruction take effect or not?"

"Upāli, it does not take effect, and the Saṅgha incurs a transgression along with the past."

"Venerable one, if the act of expulsion has been performed and he is then instructed by a motion and an act by quorum of four — is this to be called 'instructed' or 'not instructed'? Does the instruction take effect or not?"

"Upāli, it takes effect, and the Saṅgha does not incur a transgression along with the past."

"Venerable one, if a monk has not raised the matter and has not taken note of it, yet remains in a state of personal verbal discomfort — should he be instructed or not?"

"Upāli, he should not."

"Does the instruction take effect or not?"

"Upāli, it does not take effect."

"Venerable one, if a monk has raised the matter and has taken note of it, yet remains in a state of personal verbal discomfort — what is the outcome? He has committed an offense. Should he be instructed or not?"

"Upāli, he should be instructed."

"Does the instruction take effect?"

"Upāli, it takes effect."

"Venerable one, if a monk has raised the matter and has taken note of it, yet remains in a state of personal verbal discomfort — what is the outcome? He has committed an offense. Should he be instructed or not?"

"Upāli, he should be instructed."

"Does the instruction take effect?"

"Upāli, it takes effect."

"Venerable one, if one who is within the boundary instructs those who are beyond the boundary — is this to be called 'instructed'?"

"Upāli, it is not."

"If one who is beyond the boundary instructs those who are within the boundary — is this to be called 'instructed'?"

"Upāli, it is not."

"Venerable one, if the presiding monk who performs the act is within the boundary and instructs those who are beyond the boundary — is this to be called 'instructed'?"

"Upāli, it is not."

"Venerable one, if the presiding monk who performs the act is beyond the boundary and instructs those who are within the boundary — is this to be called 'instructed'?"

"Upāli, it is not."

"Venerable one, if one who has performed the act presses against the boundary, grasps the boundary, or stands or sits at the boundary and gives instruction — is this to be called 'instructed'? Does the instruction take effect?"

"Upāli, it is to be called 'instructed,' and the instruction takes effect."

"Venerable one, if the presiding monk who performs the act has not given instruction, and four persons are dismissed from within the boundary — is this to be called 'dismissed'?"

"Upāli, it is not."

"Venerable one, if the presiding monk appointed to perform the act dismisses four persons from within the boundary — is this to be called 'dismissed'? Or is it so only if they are dismissed one by one, two by two, or three by three?"

"It is to be called 'dismissed' only when dismissed one by one, two by two, or three by three."

"Venerable one, if monks residing in the four quarters of a single boundary give instruction to four monks — is this to be called 'instructed,' and furthermore, can it be the case that no offense at all is incurred and the Saṅgha is not thereby divided?"

"Upāli, there is such a case: when each gives consent to the other and instruction is given one to one, two to two, or three to three — provided the number falls short of four. And why? Because a large group may not perform an act upon a large group."

"Venerable one, may a presiding monk who is present in one direction perform all acts pertaining to the four stations of abiding?"

"Upāli, he may. In such a case, the presiding monk who performs the act should be at the edge of the boundary of all four stations of abiding — whether at a throne, a low seat, a bamboo —"

— leaning against a door-bolt and sitting — then acts of that kind may arise in those stations: whether an act requiring four, an act requiring five, an act requiring ten, or an act requiring twenty — such acts may duly come to be performed there. And why? Because the presiding monk performs the act on their behalf, and it is he who completes the count for them.

"If one who is present on the ground gives instruction to those who are present in the sky, is that considered a valid instruction?"

"Upāli, it is not."

"Venerable one, if the one performing the act is present in the sky and gives instruction to those who are present on the ground, is that considered a valid instruction?"

"Upāli, it is not."

The same is to be said regarding the remaining four categories of the Saṅgha. Just as the precepts are administered to monks, so too for nuns it becomes a matter of the remaining members of the Saṅgha. For probationer nuns, novice monks, and novice nuns, it is an offence.

Here ends the section on the remaining members of the Saṅgha from among the questions of Upāli.

In brief: the last offence, the royal caste, and the remaining aggregates — likewise the mouth, vegetables, sugar, fermented drink, molasses, butter, and what is not manifest.

"Venerable one, if a female lay devotee (upāsikā) who lacks faith comes to a monk and says, 'Venerable one, I saw a certain monk commit the first and last offence' — should one proceed in accordance with the words of that faithless lay devotee or not? One should not. Nor should one have her search for that person. Instead, one should ask her: 'Is there a witness?' If she says there is, then both should be questioned, and if they agree, proceed in accordance with the words of the faithless lay devotee, and let her search for that person as well. But if she then says, 'The first and last offence has not occurred — what I saw was the second, third, or fourth offence' — then let the monk be confronted. Just as for the first, so too for the second, third, and fourth last offences, the same procedure applies."

"Venerable one, if a faithless female lay devotee comes before monks and says, 'Venerable ones, I saw a certain monk behave improperly at the mouth aperture' — should one proceed in accordance with the words of that faithless lay devotee or not? One should not, nor should one have her search for him. Ask her: 'Is there a witness?' If she says there is, question both of them. If they agree, proceed in accordance with the words of the faithless lay devotee and let her search for the person as well. But if she then says, 'It was not the mouth aperture that was used improperly — it was the anal aperture' — then let that monk be confronted. As for the mouth aperture, so too for the urinary aperture and the anal aperture."

"Venerable one, if a faithless female lay devotee comes before monks and says, 'Venerable ones, I saw a certain monk behave improperly with a woman of the royal caste (kṣatriyā)' — should one proceed in accordance with the words of that faithless lay devotee or not? One should not, nor should one have her search for him. Ask her: 'Is there a witness?' If she says there is, question both of them. If they agree, proceed in accordance with the words of the faithless lay devotee and let her search for the person as well. But if she then says, 'It was not with a woman of the royal caste that he behaved improperly — it was with a brahmin woman' — then let that monk be confronted. As for a woman of the royal caste, so too for a brahmin woman, a merchant-caste woman, a white-complexioned woman, a dark-complexioned woman, a tawny-complexioned woman, a tall woman, a short woman, a very beautiful woman, an ugly woman, a colored woman,

a woman of medium build, a woman who walks, a woman who is seated, a woman who stands upright, a woman who is lying down — for all of these as well, the procedure is to be set forth in full.

Reverend ones, if a faithless laywoman comes before the monks and says, "Reverend ones, I have seen a monk commit an accumulation of transgressions and an offense" — should one act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman, or not? One should not. Should one let her search for that person, or not? One should not. Ask her, "Is there a witness in this matter?" If she says there is, question both of them, and if they agree, then act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman and let her search for that person as well. But if she then says, "The first accumulation of transgressions did not occur, but the second, third, fourth, and fifth accumulations did occur" — then proceed in the same way up through the fifth.

Reverend ones, if a faithless laywoman comes before the monks and says, "Reverend ones, I have seen a monk commit the first Saṅgha-remainder offense" — should one act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman, or not? One should not. Should one let her search for that person, or not? One should not. Ask her, "Is there a witness in this matter?" If she says there is, question both of them, and if they agree, then act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman and let her search for that person as well. But if she then says, "The first Saṅgha-remainder offense did not occur, but from the second, third, and fourth up through the thirteenth Saṅgha-remainder offense did occur" — then let the monk be confronted. Just as with the first, so too with the second, and from the third up through the thirteenth Saṅgha-remainder offense — it is the same.

If a faithless laywoman comes before the monks and says, "Reverend ones, I have seen a monk expel semen into a mouth" — should one act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman, or not? One should not. Should one let her search for that person, or not? One should not. Ask her, "Is there a witness in this matter?" If she says there is, question both of them, and if they agree, then act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman and let her search for that person as well. But if she then says, "It was not into the mouth that an offense was committed, but rather semen was expelled outside the teeth, at the lips" — then let the monk be confronted.

Reverend ones, if a faithless laywoman comes before the monks and says, "I have seen a monk expel semen into the urinary passage" — should one act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman, or not? One should not. Should one let her search for that person, or not? One should not. Ask her, "Is there a witness in this matter?" If she says there is, question both of them, and if they agree, then act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman and let her search for that person as well. But if she says, "It was not that an offense was committed by way of the urinary passage — rather, semen was poured into the thigh" — then let the monk be confronted.

Reverend ones, if a faithless laywoman comes before the monks and says, "I have seen a monk expel semen into the fecal passage" — should one act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman, or not? One should not. Should one let her search for that person, or not? One should not. Ask her, "Is there a witness in this matter?" If she says there is, question both of them, and if they agree, then act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman and let her search for that person as well. But if she then says, "It was not that an offense was committed by way of the fecal passage — rather, this one expelled semen into the nose" — then let the monk be confronted.

Venerable ones, if a faithless laywoman comes before the monks and says, "Venerable ones, I saw a monk drinking fermented grain-mash at an improper time," should one act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman, or not? One should not. Should one let her search for that person, or not? One should not. Ask her, "Is there a witness in this matter?" If she says there is, question both of them, and if they agree, then act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman and let her search for that person as well. But if she then says, "He did not drink fermented grain-mash at an improper time — rather, this one drank some medicinal water made from meat-broth" — then let the monk be confronted.

Venerable ones, if a faithless laywoman comes before the monks and says, "Venerable ones, I saw a monk drink sugarcane wine," should one act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman, or not? One should not. Should one let her search for that person, or not? One should not. Ask her, "Is there a witness in this matter?" If she says there is, question both of them, and if they agree, then act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman and let her search for that person as well. But if she then says, "He did not drink sugarcane wine — rather, this one drank some medicinal water from boiled herbs" — then let the monk be confronted.

Venerable ones, if a faithless laywoman comes before the monks and says, "Venerable ones, I saw someone eating meat at an improper time," should one act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman, or not? One should not. Should one let her search for that person, or not? One should not. Ask her, "Is there a witness in this matter?" If she says there is, question both of them, and if they agree, then act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman and let her search for that person as well. But if she then says, "He did not eat meat at an improper time — rather, this one ate some molasses" — then let the monk be confronted.

Venerable ones, if a faithless laywoman comes before the monks and says, "Venerable ones, I saw a monk eating food at an improper time," should one act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman, or not? One should not. Should one let her search for that person, or not? One should not. Ask her, "Is there a witness in this matter?" If she says there is, question both of them, and if they agree, then act in accordance with the words of the faithless laywoman and let her search for that person as well. But if she then says, "He did not eat food at an improper time — rather, this one ate some butter" — then let the monk be confronted.

Whatever a faithless laywoman says, having seen some truth yet speaking of something unverified — let the monk be confronted. The section on unverified matters is complete.

The noble Vinaya text, the third fascicle.

In summary:

Loss of the very thing itself, burning,
mental agitation, not consecrated,
improper, and past the time —
these are the marks, the fourth, and the transmission of three.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, is it the case that a robe that has passed beyond ten years is the very same robe, yet loses one year?" The Blessed One said: "Upāli, yes. If, however, the monk, without interruption in his robe-holding, finds a robe on the very last day of the ten days and consecrates it, but then dawn breaks beyond the boundary without that robe being present — then that robe has passed ten days and lost one night."

"Venerable one, if a monk loses a robe that he had set aside as relinquished, should he confess a transgression?" "Upāli, he should confess." "Having confessed the transgression, should he relinquish what has been received?" "Upāli, he should not."

"Venerable one, if a robe that a monk had set aside as relinquished is burned or eaten, should that remnant also be relinquished?" "Upāli, it should not. One should confess the transgression alone. However, if a piece of one cubit square or more remains, it should be relinquished."

"Venerable one, if a monk's mind becomes disturbed immediately upon finding a robe, from what point should the ten days be counted?" "From the day his own mind returns to its normal state, the counting begins."

"Venerable one, could there be a case where a monk holds eight or nine robes without consecrating or dedicating them for his entire lifetime without incurring a transgression?" "Upāli, there could be. This is when, day by day, the monk takes the robe out of his keeping and consecrates it for another."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that when ten nights have passed a robe must be relinquished — could there be a case where a monk holds a robe beyond ten nights without incurring a transgression?" "Upāli, there could be. This is when the material is fit for a robe but the stitching is not fit, or when the stitching is fit but the material is not fit, or when neither is fit. What is unfit material? Wool of a female yak, wool of an ox, wool of a goat, wool of a wild animal, mixed wool, and wool not yet woven into cloth — a robe of such material, even if kept beyond ten days, constitutes a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that a monk may keep an extra robe for up to ten days — could there be a case where a monk keeps an extra robe for his entire lifetime without incurring a transgression?" "Upāli, there could be. This is when the period has elapsed within ten days."

"Venerable one, can it be that the very same robe is one that may be kept without transgression and yet is also one that incurs transgression by being kept?" "Upāli, it can be. For example, a monk keeps a precious robe, then the sun sets and he becomes a nun — if she then keeps it, a transgression arises."

"Venerable one, if a monk finds a robe and ten nights pass, and then the sun sets and he becomes a nun, and then ten more nights pass — what becomes of that?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment."

"Venerable one, if a nun finds a robe and ten nights pass, and then the sun sets and she becomes a monk, and then ten more nights pass — what becomes of that?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives ten nights as ten nights and dawn breaks — what becomes of that?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment."

"Venerable one, if he perceives it as not ten nights — what becomes of that?" "There is no transgression."

"If it is not ten nights and he perceives it as ten nights — what becomes of that?" "That is a wrongdoing."

"If ten days have not been completed and he perceives them as not completed — there is no transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk finds a robe in a place that has been put under suspension by the Saṅgha, can that robe become one that must be relinquished?" "Upāli, it can. It is when that monk's robe has become one to be relinquished, yet that monk has neither relinquished the robe nor been separated from it nor confessed the transgression — and in the meantime the Saṅgha has lifted the suspension. If that monk then finds a robe, it must be relinquished."

"Venerable one, if those who have been given a training keep an extra robe beyond ten nights — what becomes of that?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment."

"Venerable one, if a nun keeps an extra robe beyond ten nights — what becomes of that?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment."

"If female probationers, male novices, and female novices keep an extra robe beyond ten days, it becomes a wrongdoing."

In brief:

The Saṅgha's first day and boundary,
being pressed and encircled without that being done,
the boundary not cut and not covered —
likewise the robe that passes through four nights.

Then the venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, is it permitted to consecrate a Dharma-robe belonging to the Saṅgha?" "Upāli, it is not permitted." "Venerable one, if such a circumstance arises, is it permitted?" "Upāli, it is permitted."

"Venerable one, if a monk has consecrated a Dharma-robe belonging to the Saṅgha and then, without a Dharma-robe of his own, passes beyond the boundary — is he said to be separated from his Dharma-robe or not?" "He is said to be separated." "Should that Dharma-robe be relinquished?" "Upāli, it should not." "Should the wrongdoing be confessed?" "It should be confessed."

"Venerable one, if a monk places his Dharma-robe on the ground and dawn breaks in the sky, or places it in the sky and dawn breaks on the ground — is he said to be separated from his Dharma-robe or not?" "He is said to be separated."

"Venerable one, if a monk places his Dharma-robe inside the boundary and dawn breaks beyond the boundary, or places his Dharma-robe beyond the boundary and dawn breaks inside the boundary — is he said to be separated from his Dharma-robe or not?" "He is said to be separated."

"Venerable one, if a monk, while pressing upon a boundary, standing at a boundary, or sitting at a boundary — taking it as the boundary — places his Dharma-robe between the boundaries and dawn breaks — is he said to be separated from his Dharma-robe or not?" "He is said to be separated."

"Venerable one, can it occur that a monk is inside the boundary and his Dharma-robe is also placed inside the boundary, yet he becomes separated from that Dharma-robe?" "Upāli, it can. It is when the vow of the Dharma-robe has not been properly declared."

"Venerable one, in a place where no boundary has been demarcated, from what distance is a monk said to be separated from his Dharma-robe?" "Upāli, one should understand it as extending as far as the surrounding area of the monastery, or a building, or a covered walkway, or a surrounding structure, or a park used in common by the monks, or an outer enclosure, or a grove, or a pond."

"Venerable one, if a monk dwells in a single dwelling under a single roof and also places his Dharma-robe there, can it occur that he becomes separated from his Dharma-robe?" "Upāli, it can — when various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), wandering ascetics, brahmins, practitioners, and those who wander about dwell there, and where lodging has been divided among them separately."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives what is beyond the boundary as beyond the boundary, what results?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment." "If he perceives what is inside the boundary as beyond the boundary, what results?" "It becomes a wrongdoing." "If he perceives what is beyond the boundary as inside the boundary, what results?" "There is no offense." "If he perceives what is inside the boundary as inside the boundary, what results?" "There is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk places his Dharma-robe inside the boundary and dawn breaks beyond the boundary, and then the night shifts and he becomes a nun — what results?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment." "Venerable one, if a nun places her Dharma-robe inside the boundary and dawn breaks beyond the boundary, and then the night shifts and she becomes a monk — what results?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment."

"Venerable one, before whom should a monk consecrate a Dharma-robe?" "Upāli, a monk may consecrate a Dharma-robe before a monk or before a male novice. A male novice may consecrate a Dharma-robe before a monk or before a male novice. A nun may consecrate a Dharma-robe before a female probationer or before a female novice. A female probationer may consecrate a Dharma-robe before a nun, a female probationer, or a female novice. A female novice may consecrate a Dharma-robe before a nun, a female probationer, or a female novice. The withdrawal and the reassignment are to be done in the same way."

"Venerable one, when the training has been given and dawn breaks beyond the boundary without a Dharma-robe, what results?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment." Likewise, for a nun it is also fully described as a transgression entailing relinquishment. For female probationers, male novices, and female novices, it is a wrongdoing.

In brief:

A disturbed mind and the time having passed,
and likewise the permissible cases —
likewise the impermissible and the established,
likewise the complete four and the night.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, when the Blessed One has declared that a monk may store a robe for one month even at a distance, and the monk's mind becomes disturbed as soon as he obtains the robe, from what point shall that month be counted?" "From the time when he recovers his own mind."

"Venerable one, when the Blessed One has declared that a monk may hold a robe in expectation for one month even at a distance, is there a case in which a monk may store it for his entire lifetime without incurring a transgression?" "Upāli, there is — provided he keeps to the time-limit of one month."

"Venerable one, when the Blessed One has declared that a monk may store a robe for one month even at a distance, what kind of robe is meant?" "Any one of the seven permissible kinds — those which the Blessed One has not prohibited and has allowed."

"Venerable one, when the Blessed One has declared that a monk may store a robe for one month even at a distance, is there a case in which a monk stores a robe for more than one month without incurring a transgression?" "Upāli, there is — when the cloth of that robe has become fit for use as fabric but the thread is not fit, or when the thread is fit but the cloth is not, or when both are unfit. The impermissible cases are: wool from a female sheep, wool from cattle, wool from goats, wool from deer, mixed wool, and cloth that has not been woven. A robe of such kinds, even if stored for more than one month, results only in a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, when the Blessed One has declared that a monk may store a robe for one month even at a distance, is there a case in which a monk stores a robe for six months without incurring a transgression?" "Upāli, there is — when thirty days have passed since the robe was obtained and the Saṅgha has rendered a formal decision establishing it as stored."

"Venerable one, when the Blessed One has declared that one who has not received the three Dharma-robes may store a robe for one month, suppose a monk has himself received the three Dharma-robes and he obtains a robe for someone who has not yet received the three Dharma-robes — may he also store it for one month at a distance?" "No. And why? When one has the complete three Dharma-robes, whatever other robes he obtains — whether he has taken them up or not — all of these, even at a distance, are to be stored for ten days only. For one who has not yet received the three Dharma-robes, if he obtains a robe that counts as a Dharma-robe, that too is to be stored at a distance for ten days only. But if he obtains one that does not count as a Dharma-robe, even at a distance it may be stored for one month. If it is stored beyond that, it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment."

"Venerable one, if a monk who is storing a robe for one month perceives a full month as having elapsed and dawn breaks, what results?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment." "If he perceives that a full month has not elapsed, what results?" "There is no fault." "If it is not a full month yet he perceives it as a full month, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." "If a full month has not elapsed and he perceives it as not having elapsed, what results?" "There is no fault."

"Venerable one, if a monk has obtained a robe and is storing it for one month, and during that time there is a change of status and he becomes a nun, and the month passes, what results?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment." "Venerable one, if a nun has obtained a Dharma-robe and is storing it for one month, and there is a change of status and she becomes a monk, and the month passes, what results?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment."

"Venerable one, if a training has been given and the permitted period of one month of storing the robe at a distance is exceeded, what results?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment." "Venerable one, if a nun exceeds the permitted period of one month of storing a robe at a distance, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." For female probationers, male novices, and female novices, if they hold a robe beyond the permitted month at a distance, it is a wrongdoing.

In brief:

Messenger, written letter, hand signal,
through an intermediary, one to another,
having become mad, and mentally disturbed,
sick, mute, and foolish —
for laypeople and so forth:
this is the last of the trainings given.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, if a monk were to give an old robe to an unrelated nun, the Blessed One has declared this becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment. Venerable one, if a monk gives an old robe to an unrelated nun through a messenger, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." "Likewise, if it is conveyed through a written letter, a hand signal, through an intermediary, or passed along from one to another, all of these become wrongdoings." "Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a mad nun, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." "Likewise, if it is given to one who is mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, foolish, mute, or deaf-mute, all of these likewise become wrongdoings." "Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a pandaka, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." "Likewise, if it is given to an expelled nun, one's own father or mother, one who has slain an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a non-Buddhist adherent, one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, one in a place of thieves, one dwelling separately, one not residing in the community, one who has previously caused a schism, and one who has previously committed an offence — if a robe is conveyed to any of these, all become wrongdoings." "Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who sides with that faction, or one who has been given a training rule — what results?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment."

In brief:

Shared, washed, and of the Saṅgha,
two marks, and unsuitable,
relinquished, another's, and worn —
the seventh and the fourth likewise —
and last, a nun.

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a shared robe, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." "If he gives one that has been washed, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." "Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe belonging to the Saṅgha, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." "And if it is something that would be fully used by a person, and it has been fully used and is soiled, that too becomes a wrongdoing. However, if bedding articles are given, there is no offence." "Venerable one, if a monk has given an old robe to an unrelated nun and then undergoes a change of gender and becomes a nun — what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." "Venerable one, if an unrelated monk has given a robe to a nun and then undergoes a change of gender and becomes a monk — what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." "Venerable one, if a monk gives an old robe to an unrelated nun, and the nun then undergoes a change of gender and becomes a monk, and then washes it — what results?" "It is a wrongdoing. Likewise it should be applied to a monk as well."

"Venerable one, are there cases in which a monk giving an old robe to an unrelated nun does not become a transgression entailing relinquishment?" "Upāli, there are. For example, if the robe is of acceptable material but the exchange is not permissible, or if the exchange is permissible but the material is not acceptable, or if both are not acceptable — and what is not acceptable is this: wool of a she-goat, wool of a sheep, wool of cattle, wool of deer, mixed wool, or wool not woven into cloth. Giving a robe of such material becomes a wrongdoing." "Venerable one, if a monk gives away a robe that has been relinquished, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." "But if what is given is something that has not been relinquished, it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment. However, if what is given is one that has already been relinquished, it is a wrongdoing." "Venerable one, if a monk gives another's robe, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." "Venerable one, are there cases in which a monk, while in possession of a suitable robe that has entered into a village, can relinquish that robe while it has not yet left his body?" "Upāli, there are."

How so? If that monk has entered inside a house, and the robe has been soiled with excrement, urine, or some other impurity, and he then has it washed by a nun who is not a relative, it becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment. "If one has it washed by someone who has not received full ordination, and she remains one who has not received full ordination, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." "If one has it washed by someone who has not received full ordination, and she is in the process of receiving full ordination, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." "If one has it washed by someone who has not received full ordination, and she has since received full ordination, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." "If one has it washed by someone who has not received full ordination, and she is in the process of receiving full ordination, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." "If one has it washed by someone who has received full ordination, and she is in the process of receiving full ordination, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." "If one has it washed by someone who has received full ordination, and she has since received full ordination, what results?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment." "If one has it washed by someone who has received full ordination, and she has not received full ordination, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a fully ordained nun as fully ordained and has an old robe washed by her, what results?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment." "If he perceives a fully ordained nun as one who has not received full ordination, it is a wrongdoing." "If he perceives one who has not received full ordination as fully ordained, it is a wrongdoing." "If he perceives one who has not received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, it is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a nun who is not a relative as one who is not a relative, and has an old robe washed by her, what results?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment." "If he perceives one who is not a relative as a relative, there is no offense." "If he perceives a relative as one who is not a relative, it is a wrongdoing." "If he perceives a relative as a relative, there is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk has an old robe washed by a nun who is not a relative, what results?" "It becomes a transgression entailing relinquishment." And if it is washed by a female novice in training, a novice nun, a laywoman, a tīrthika female wanderer, a brahmin woman, a female wanderer, or a female mendicant, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." Likewise, if one has it washed by someone abiding in another destiny, it is also a wrongdoing.

If a nun has a robe washed by a monk, a novice monk, a tīrthika male wanderer, a brahmin, a male wanderer, a male mendicant, or by someone abiding in some other destiny, what results? It is a wrongdoing. If she has it washed by a layman or a laywoman, what results? It is a wrongdoing. If by a female novice in training or a novice nun, it is a wrongdoing. The same applies in detail to washing and beating.

In brief:

One who has become mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
One who is ill, one who has recovered, and one who is dull,
Hermaphrodites and the like,
And one who has surrendered the training — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that whichever monk has a robe washed by a nun who is not a relative incurs a transgression entailing relinquishment. Venerable one, if a monk has a robe washed by a nun who is mad, what results?" "It is a wrongdoing." Likewise, if the robe is washed by one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is mute, one who is dull-witted, one who has recovered from illness, a hermaphrodite nun, a nun who has been expelled from the Saṅgha, one who has killed her father, one who has killed her mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, one who has taken to theft, one who has previously committed an offense, or one who was previously in a state of disturbance — if a robe is washed by any of these, what results? In every case it is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk has a robe washed by a nun who is causing a schism in the Saṅgha, or one who is living separately,

one who is siding with the schism, or one who has been given a training — if a robe is obtained from any of these, what results? It is a transgression entailing relinquishment.

In brief:

By messenger, letter, gesture and sign,
through a third party, or from one to another,
one who has gone mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is ill, one who is mute, one who is dull-witted,
one who is asleep, one who is drunk, one who is intoxicated,
one in meditative absorption, a traveler, a paṇḍaka.

Venerable one, if a monk obtains a robe from a nun who is not a relative, by way of a messenger, what results? It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, by letter, by gesture, or through an intermediary — in every case it is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one, if a monk has a robe washed by a mad nun and thereby obtains the robe, what results? It is a wrongdoing. If a monk has a robe washed by a mad nun and others of that kind and thereby obtains the robe, what results? In every case it is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one, if a monk obtains a robe from a nun who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who is living separately, one who is siding with the schism, or one who has been given a training — what results? It is a transgression entailing relinquishment.

In brief:

The unsuitable, and the fourth and second of the kinds,
the seventh, and likewise those of the same designation —
monk and nun in each such case —
this is the summary of what falls into the category.

Venerable one, is it possible that a monk who obtains a robe from a nun who is not a relative does not incur a transgression entailing relinquishment? Upāli, yes, there is such a case. It is as follows: when the robe is acceptable as a cause but the relationship as kin is not acceptable; or when the relationship as kin is acceptable but the robe is not acceptable as a cause; or when neither is acceptable. As for unacceptability: wool of a bull, wool of a female camel, wool of a goat, wool of a deer, or wool mixed from these, or cloth of a kind that has not been woven — if a robe of such a kind is obtained, it is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one, if a monk takes a robe from a nun who is not a relative while perceiving her as not a relative, what results? It is a transgression entailing relinquishment. If one perceives a non-relative as a non-relative and is wrong in that perception, there is no offense. If one perceives a relative as a non-relative, it is a wrongdoing. If one perceives a relative as a relative, there is no offense.

Venerable one, if a monk perceives a fully ordained nun as not fully ordained and then obtains a robe from her, what results? It is a transgression entailing relinquishment. If one perceives a fully ordained one as not fully ordained, it is a wrongdoing. If one perceives one who is not fully ordained as fully ordained, it is a wrongdoing. If one perceives one who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained, it is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one, if one who is not fully ordained obtains a robe from a nun who is not a relative, and hands it to one who is not fully ordained, what results? It is a wrongdoing. If one who is not fully ordained obtains a robe and hands it to one who is fully ordained, what results? It is a wrongdoing. If one hands it over while not fully ordained and then becomes fully ordained and hands it on, what results? It is a wrongdoing. If one who is fully ordained in training hands it to one who is fully ordained in training, what results? It is a wrongdoing. If one who is fully ordained in training hands it to one who is fully ordained, what results? It is a wrongdoing. If one who is fully ordained hands it to one who is fully ordained, what results? It is a transgression entailing relinquishment. If one who is fully ordained hands it to one who is not fully ordained, what results? It is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one, if a monk is in the process of receiving a robe from a nun who is not a relative and in the meantime changes status and becomes a nun, what results? It is a wrongdoing. Venerable one, if a nun is in the process of receiving a robe from a monk who is not a relative and in the meantime he changes status and becomes a monk and hands it over, what results? It is a wrongdoing. Venerable one, if a nun is in the process of receiving a robe from a monk who is not a relative and that nun herself changes status and becomes a monk, and then receives it from the monk who is not a relative, what results? It is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one, if a nun is in the process of receiving a robe from a monk who is not a relative, and that monk also changes status and becomes a nun, and she then receives it from that nun, what results? It is a wrongdoing. If she receives it from a probationer or a novice nun, what results? It is a wrongdoing. If a nun receives a robe from a monk or a novice monk, what results? It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if she receives it from a probationer or a novice nun, it is also a wrongdoing. If a novice monk receives a robe from a nun, a novice nun, or a probationer, it is also a wrongdoing.

In brief:

By messenger, by letter, by gesture,
through another's word, passed one to another,
one who has become mad, one mentally disturbed,
one ill, one mute, one dull-witted,
one asleep, one delirious,
one intoxicated, one gone elsewhere, one who is a non-Buddhist —

Venerable one, the Blessed One declared that whatever monk receives a robe from a householder who is not a relative, or from a householder's retinue, it shall be relinquished. Is there then any case in which a monk receives a robe from a householder or a householder's retinue and yet it does not become a relinquishment downfall? Upāli: Yes, there is. If in any case it was received through a messenger, it becomes a wrongdoing; even if one obtains the robe, it is only a wrongdoing. Likewise, through a letter, through a gesture, through another's word, or through anything passed from one to another — all of these become wrongdoings. Venerable one, if a monk receives a robe from a mad householder and thereby obtains the robe, what results? It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if one obtains a robe having received it from one who is mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, mute, dull-witted, dumb, asleep, delirious, intoxicated, or residing elsewhere, what results? It is a wrongdoing. If one obtains a robe having received it from non-Buddhist outsiders — other ascetics (śramaṇas), brahmins, wanderers, or mendicants — what results? It is a wrongdoing.

In brief:

The fourth of the improper ones, and the second,
the seventh — the marks are just the same;
likewise the eunuch and the hermaphrodite,
and the monk who is such — the same applies.

Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk receives a robe from a householder's retinue, the householder not being a relative, and yet it does not become a relinquishment? Upāli: Yes, there is. In any case in which the material of the robe is proper but the kin-relationship is improper, or the kin-relationship is proper but the material is improper, or both are improper — the improper material being: wool from a female sheep, goat's wool, cattle wool, deer wool, or any such mixed or unwoven material — if one receives such a robe and obtains it, it is a wrongdoing. Venerable one, if a monk perceives one who is not a relative as not a relative and receives a robe from them and thereby obtains it, what results? It becomes a relinquishment downfall. If one perceives a non-relative as a relative, there is no offense. If one perceives a relative as a non-relative, it becomes a wrongdoing. If one perceives a relative as a relative, there is no offense. Venerable one, if a monk perceives a human as a human and receives a robe from them and thereby obtains it, what results? It becomes a relinquishment. If one perceives a human as a non-human, it becomes a wrongdoing. If one perceives a non-human as a human, it is also a wrongdoing. If one perceives a non-human as a non-human, it is also a wrongdoing. If one who has not received full ordination requests a robe and an unordained person obtains it, what results? It is a wrongdoing. If one who has not received full ordination requests a robe and a fully ordained person obtains it, what results? It is a wrongdoing. If one without full ordination makes the request, and having since received full ordination then obtains it, what results? It is a wrongdoing. If one who is fully ordained makes the request and a fully ordained person obtains it at that point, what results? It is a wrongdoing. If one who is fully ordained makes the request and then, having received full ordination in the meantime, obtains it, what results?

It is a wrongdoing. If one who is fully ordained makes the request and a fully ordained person obtains it, what results? It is to be relinquished. If one who is fully ordained makes the request and one who has not received full ordination obtains it, what results? It is a wrongdoing.

Venerable ones, if a monk requests a robe from a layman or a layman's attendant who is not a relative, and then, his sex having changed so that he has become a nun, she obtains it, what results? It is to be relinquished. Venerable ones, if a nun requests a robe from a layman or a layman's attendant who is not a relative, and then, her sex having changed so that he has become a monk, he obtains it, what results? It is to be relinquished. Venerable ones, if a monk requests a robe from a layman and that layman's sex likewise changes so that he obtains it from a woman, what results? It is to be relinquished. Venerable ones, if a monk requests from a layman's attendant and that attendant's sex likewise changes so that he obtains it from a man, what results? It is to be relinquished. The same should be stated likewise in the case of a nun.

Venerable ones, if a monk requests a robe from a hermaphrodite and obtains the robe, what results? It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, in all cases involving hermaphrodites of either kind, it is a wrongdoing.

Venerable ones, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk requests a robe from a layman or a layman's attendant who is not a relative, it becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment. Given that, if a monk makes the request to a nun and obtains the robe, what results? It is to be relinquished. If he makes the request to a female probationer, a novice nun, a fully ordained monk, or novice monks and obtains the robe, what results? It is a wrongdoing.

Venerable ones, if a nun makes the request to a layman or a layman's attendant and obtains the robe, what results? It is to be relinquished. If a nun makes the request to a nun, a female probationer, a novice nun, or novice monks and obtains the robe, what results? It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, for female probationers and novice monks as well, it is a wrongdoing, and this should be explained in full.

Now, with regard to making requests, just as has been set out above, what distinctions exist in relation to the upper robe and the lower robe? There are two kinds each of upper and lower robes: the upper robe of a monk and the lower robe of a monk, and the upper robe of a layman and the lower robe of a layman. If a monk has received a layman's upper robe and lower robe, and then makes a request from a layman's upper robe and lower robe — if what is obtained proves to be superior, he should not keep it; and if there is a surplus, he should not give it away. If a monk obtains a layman's upper robe and lower robe that is either insufficient or with a surplus, that is a wrongdoing; and if obtained, it is a transgression requiring relinquishment.

If a monk has received a monk's upper robe and lower robe, and then makes a request from an upper robe and lower robe — if what is obtained proves insufficient, he may request it; but if there is a surplus, he must return it. If a monk does not return the surplus upper robe and lower robe, or requests more than is needed, that act of requesting is a wrongdoing; and if obtained, it is a transgression requiring relinquishment. In all such cases — whether a layman's upper robe and lower robe were obtained as superior or with surplus, or whether a monk's upper robe and lower robe were surplus and not returned, or obtained in excess — it is to be relinquished. As for the remaining matters, just as was done in the order of preceding rules of training, so too shall this rule of training be applied.

In summary:

Sending a message, a letter, a physical gesture,
having another speak on one's behalf, one by one —
the insane, the mentally disturbed, the sick,
the sleeping, delirious, intoxicated,
those in meditative absorption, travelers, and non-Buddhists —

this was asked of the buddha, the Blessed One, by the venerable Upāli.

The venerable one then asked: the Blessed One declared that if a householder or a householder's attendant who is not a kinsman has set aside a sum of money for robes for a monk, and that monk, without having been invited beforehand, arouses even a slight degree of conceptual thought for the purpose of procuring robes and thereby successfully obtains them, it becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment. Venerable one, if a monk arouses conceptual thought and obtains robes by means of a message, what is the result? It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, through a letter, through a physical gesture, through having another speak on one's behalf, or through passing the request from one to another — all of these are wrongdoings.

Venerable one, if a monk arouses conceptual thought toward an insane person and obtains robes, what is the result? It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if he does so toward one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, one who is asleep, one who is delirious, one who is intoxicated, or one who has entered meditative absorption — and likewise toward those outside this teaching, namely tīrthika non-Buddhists, whether wandering ascetics, brahmins, practitioners, or wanderers — if conceptual thought arises and robes are obtained from them, it is a wrongdoing.

In summary:

The non-kinsman rule, and the fourth rule, and the second;
the seventh rule, and those characteristic cases just the same;
those concerning the hermaphrodite (pandaka), and the case of the same;
and what applies to the hermaphrodite monk applies just so.

Venerable one, is there any case in which conceptual thought arises toward a householder or a householder's attendant and yet relinquishment does not follow? Upāli replied: Yes, there is. Namely, when the material basis for the robe is suitable but the kinship relation is not; when the material basis is not suitable but the kinship relation is; and when neither is suitable. As for what is not suitable as material: wool from a female sheep, wool from a goat, wool from a cow, wool from a wild animal, or a mixture of these, or materials that have not been woven — if conceptual thought arises for the sake of a robe of such material and one obtains it, it is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one, if a monk perceives one who is not a kinsman as not a kinsman, arouses conceptual thought, and obtains robes, what is the result? It becomes an offense requiring relinquishment. If he perceives one who is not a kinsman as a kinsman, what is the result? There is no offense. If he perceives a kinsman as not a kinsman, it is a wrongdoing. If he perceives a kinsman as a kinsman, there is no offense.

Venerable one, if a monk perceives a human being as a human being, arouses conceptual thought, and obtains robes, what is the result? It becomes an offense requiring relinquishment. If he perceives a human being as not a human being, what is the result? It is a wrongdoing. If he perceives a non-human being as a human being, what is the result? It is a wrongdoing. If he perceives a non-human being as a non-human being, what is the result? It is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one, if one who has not received full ordination arouses conceptual thought and obtains robes before receiving full ordination, what is the result? It is a wrongdoing. If one who has not received full ordination arouses conceptual thought and obtains robes at the moment of receiving full ordination, what is the result? It is a wrongdoing. If one who has not received full ordination arouses conceptual thought and obtains robes after having received full ordination, what is the result? It is a wrongdoing. If one arouses conceptual thought at the very moment of receiving full ordination and obtains robes at that same moment, what is the result? It is a wrongdoing. If one arouses conceptual thought after having received full ordination and obtains robes after having received full ordination, what is the result? It becomes an offense requiring relinquishment. If one arouses conceptual thought after having received full ordination and obtains robes before full ordination, what is the result? It is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one, if a monk has aroused conceptual thought toward a householder or a householder's attendant who is not a kinsman, and in the interval his status changes and he becomes a nun, and she then obtains robes, what is the result? It becomes an offense requiring relinquishment. Venerable one, if a nun has aroused conceptual thought toward a householder or a householder's attendant, and in the interval her status changes and she becomes a monk, and he then obtains robes, what is the result? It becomes an offense requiring relinquishment. Venerable one, if a monk has aroused conceptual thought toward a householder who is not a kinsman, and in the interval that householder's status changes and he becomes a woman, and the monk accepts robes from her, what is the result? It becomes an offense requiring relinquishment.

Venerable one, if a monk has aroused conceptual thought toward a householder's attendant who is not a kinsman, and in the interval that attendant's status changes and he becomes a man, and the monk accepts robes from him, what is the result? It becomes an offense requiring relinquishment. The same is to be applied in the case of a nun as well.

Venerable one, if a monk has aroused conceptual thought toward a hermaphrodite and then obtains robes, what is the result? It is an offense of wrong conduct. Similarly, with regard to a neuter person and a female neuter, it is likewise an offense of wrong conduct. Venerable one, if a monk arouses conceptual thought for the sake of some requisite other than robes and then obtains it, what is the result? It is an offense of wrong conduct. Venerable one, if a monk arouses conceptual thought for the sake of a monk, a nun, a female probationer, a female novice, or male novices, what is the result? It is an offense of wrong conduct.

Just as a monk who arouses conceptual thought incurs an offense requiring relinquishment, so too does one who has returned the training, and a nun likewise incurs an offense requiring relinquishment. For male novices, female probationers, and female novices it is to be elaborated as an offense of wrong conduct. Just as this text on the rule of training applies, so too is the second rule of training to be elaborated in full.

In brief:
By messenger, letter, gesture,
Through another, or passed from one to the next,
The mad, the mentally disturbed, the sick,
The mute, the dull-witted, the asleep,
Those intoxicated, the stupefied,
Those in meditative absorption, and outsiders.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that after being solicited four, five, or six times one should remain silent and not speak. If that monk then actually obtains the robes, that is well and good. But if they are not actually obtained, then one may offer more beyond that in order to bring the robes to actual completion — and if, having offered more beyond that, the robes are actually obtained, it becomes an offense requiring relinquishment. Venerable one, is it then possible that a monk who, beyond four, five, or six solicitations, gives more in order to obtain robes, and yet those robes are actually obtained, does not incur an offense requiring relinquishment?

Upāli, that is indeed possible. In any case, when by a messenger one has gone beyond four, five, or six solicitations and accepted more in order to obtain robes, and the robes are actually obtained, it becomes an offense of wrong conduct. Likewise, whether done by letter, by gesture, through another's words, or passed from one to the next — all of these become offenses of wrong conduct.

Venerable one, if a monk has gone beyond four, five, or six solicitations of a madman and accepted more in order to obtain robes, and the robes are actually obtained, what is the result? It is an offense of wrong conduct. Similarly, with regard to one who is mentally disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, and one who is deaf — in all such cases it is an offense of wrong conduct. Venerable one, if a monk has gone beyond four, five, or six solicitations of a sleeping person and accepted more in order to obtain robes, and the robes are actually obtained, what is the result? It is an offense of wrong conduct. Similarly, with regard to one who is intoxicated from drink, one who is stupefied, one who has entered meditative absorption, one dwelling elsewhere, and those outside this tradition — other non-Buddhist renunciants (tīrthikas), brahmins, ascetics, and wanderers — if a monk has gone beyond four, five, or six solicitations and accepted more in order to obtain robes, and the robes are actually obtained, what is the result? It is an offense of wrong conduct.

In brief:
The unsuitable, the fourth, and the seventh —
The same applies to gender as well;
The hermaphrodite and the female neuter,
With the neuter last of all.

Venerable one, is it possible that a monk who has gone beyond four, five, or six solicitations in order to obtain Dharma robes does not incur an offense requiring relinquishment? Upāli, that is indeed possible. In any case, if the material for the robes is suitable but the thread is unsuitable, or the thread is suitable but the material is unsuitable, or both are unsuitable — the unsuitable being: wool from a female sheep, wool from cattle, wool from goats, wool from wild animals, or a mixture of these —

If, however, the cloth has not yet been woven, and a monk solicits beyond four, five, or six times on account of such robes, every instance constitutes an offense requiring confession.

Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a human being as a human being, solicits from that person beyond the limit — what is the result? It incurs relinquishment. If he perceives a human being as a non-human, it is an offense requiring confession. If he perceives a non-human as a human being, it is an offense requiring confession. If he perceives a non-human as a non-human, it is an offense requiring confession.

Venerable one, if a monk solicits from one who has not yet received full ordination and obtains from one who has not yet received full ordination — what is the result? It is an offense requiring confession. If he solicits from one who has not yet received full ordination and obtains at the very moment that person receives full ordination — what is the result? It is an offense requiring confession. If he solicits from one who has not yet received full ordination and obtains after that person has received full ordination — what is the result? It is an offense requiring confession. If he solicits at the very moment of full ordination and obtains at the very moment of full ordination — what is the result? It is an offense requiring confession. If he solicits at the very moment of full ordination and obtains after full ordination has been completed — what is the result? It is an offense requiring confession. If he solicits when full ordination has been received and obtains when full ordination has been received — what is the result? It is a transgression requiring relinquishment. If he solicits when full ordination has been received and obtains before full ordination has been received — what is the result? It is an offense requiring confession.

Venerable one, if a monk solicits beyond four, five, or six times, and in the course of that solicitation the person's status changes so that the person becomes a nun and then the monk obtains the robe — what is the result? It incurs relinquishment. Venerable one, if a nun solicits and then the person's status changes so that the person becomes a monk, and the nun then obtains the robe — what is the result? It incurs relinquishment. Venerable one, if a monk solicits from a male householder and that householder then changes gender and becomes a woman, and the monk obtains from her — what is the result? It incurs relinquishment. Venerable one, if a monk solicits from a male householder's attendant and that attendant then changes gender and becomes a man, and the monk obtains from him — what is the result? It incurs relinquishment. The same is to be applied in the corresponding manner for nuns as well.

Venerable one, if a monk who has already solicited from a close relative four, five, or six times for the sake of obtaining robes goes beyond that limit and solicits again for the sake of robes, and robes are thereby directly obtained — what is the result? It is an offense requiring confession. In the same way, the same applies to hermaphrodites and to all female neuters: it is an offense requiring confession.

Venerable one, if a monk solicits on behalf of other monks, probationary nuns, male novices, or female novices — what is the result? It is an offense requiring confession. Venerable one, if a monk solicits on behalf of other requisites — what is the result? It is an offense requiring confession. Venerable one, if one who bestows the training solicits beyond six times — what is the result? It incurs relinquishment. If a nun solicits in the same way — what is the result? It incurs relinquishment. For probationary nuns, female novices, and male novices, it is an offense requiring confession.

In brief:

By messenger, by written letter, by hand signal,
Through an intermediary, from one to the next,
While in a state of madness, with a disturbed mind,
While sick, while mute, while simpleminded.

Venerable one, if a monk arranges by message for wool to be spun — what is the result? It is an offense requiring confession. In the same way, by written letter, by hand signal, through an intermediary, passed from one to the next, while insane, with a disturbed mind, afflicted by illness, while mute, while dumb, while blind, and while simpleminded — all of these equally constitute an offense requiring confession. Just as a monk who causes another to spin wool from raw wool incurs a transgression requiring relinquishment, in the same way one who bestows the training incurs a transgression requiring relinquishment. For nuns, probationary nuns, female novices, and male novices it is an offense requiring confession.

Just as in this chapter on the training rule it is explained in full with respect to wool that is naturally black, so too it is to be applied in the same way to naturally black wool. As for any distinctions to be made in that context, there are four: those who perceive what is naturally black as naturally black are to be treated as four.

In the same way, everything is to be stated for the second of the two training rules as well. As for the distinctions to be made in that context: when a monk perceives white wool as inferior and mixes them, this is to be treated as four cases.

In summary:
Another's not-yet-received, and received,
and those gone to non-Buddhists, and other destinies,
the improper mark, and the fourth,
and the seventh of the Sugata.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk has wool carded within the limit of six years it is to be relinquished. Venerable one, if a monk has another do the carding, what results?" "It is an offense." "If he has it done for the sake of another, what results?" "It is an offense." "Venerable one, if a monk causes what belongs to another to be made as though it were his own, what results?" "It is an offense." "If he has a layman do it, what results?" "It is an offense."

Likewise, if he has it done by a male novice, or one who has given back the training, or one who previously quarreled, or one who previously committed an offense, or one who is in hiding, or one who dwells separately, or one who does not dwell in the community — in all these cases it becomes an offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk has it done by non-Buddhist ascetics outside this community, by brahmins, by wanderers, or by mendicants, what results?" "It is an offense." "Venerable one, if a monk has those dwelling in other destinies do it, what results?" "It is an offense."

"Venerable one, is there a case where a monk has wool carded within the limit of six years and yet it does not incur relinquishment?" "Upāli, there is. It is when the material is suitable for the purpose but the mixing partner is not suitable, or when the mixing partner is suitable but the material is not, or when neither is suitable. The unsuitable cases are: when it has been mixed with the wool of a female animal, the wool of a cow, the wool of a goat, or the wool of a deer, and has not been woven — these incur an offense of confession."

"Venerable one, if a monk is engaged in having wool carded within the limit of six years, and in the meantime his sex changes so that he becomes a nun, what results?" "It is an offense." "Venerable one, if a nun is engaged in having wool carded within the limit of six years, and in the meantime her sex changes so that she becomes a monk, what results?" "It incurs relinquishment."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving that six years have passed when in fact they have passed, authorizes the carding, what results?" "There is no offense." "If he perceives that they have not passed when in fact they have passed, what results?" "It is an offense." "If he perceives that they have passed when in fact they have not, there is no offense." "If he perceives that they have not passed when in fact they have not, and causes it to be done, it incurs relinquishment."

"Venerable one, if a monk has wool carded within the limit of six years to the measure of the Sugata's Dharma robe, what results?" "It is an offense." "Venerable one, if one not fully ordained begins within the limit of six years and has not yet received full ordination, what results?" "It is an offense." This is also to be elaborated through seven transmission chains.

In summary:
By messenger, written letter, hand-signal,
having another say it, and from one to the next,
one who has become mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one afflicted by illness, one who is mute, one who is dull.

"Venerable one, if a monk authorizes the carding by means of a messenger within the limit of six years, what results?" "It is an offense." Likewise, through a written letter, through a hand-signal, through having another convey it, through passing it from one to another — in all these cases, and also for one who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is dull, one who is mute, and one who is deaf — in all these cases it also becomes an offense.

Just as it incurs a transgression requiring relinquishment when a monk causes wool to be carded within the limit of six years, so too one who bestows the training incurs a transgression requiring relinquishment. For nuns it is an offense requiring confession. For probationary nuns, female novices, and male novices it also becomes an offense requiring confession.

In summary:
Another's not-yet-received, and received,

Laypeople, tīrthikas, beings of other destinies, and those who are unsuitable — likewise the marks. The fourth and seventh are to be understood accordingly.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable Blessed One, you have declared that if a monk makes a sitting mat from an old blanket — without mixing in a full cubit of the Sugata's measure from an old blanket, so as to discolor it — it becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment. Venerable One, if a monk cuts off one finger or half a finger less than the Sugata's measure and makes a sitting mat from it, what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment." "Venerable One, if a monk has another do it, what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If he has it done for the sake of another, what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If another makes what was not proper become proper, what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If he has a layperson do it, what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." If one who has received the training does it, one who was previously in dispute does it, one who had previously committed an offense does it, or if those in hidden positions are made to do it — in all these cases it becomes an offense.

"Venerable One, if a monk has other tīrthikas — other ascetics, brahmins, wanderers, or itinerants — do it, what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If he has one who dwells in another of the destinies do it, what does it become?" "It becomes an offense."

"Venerable One, are there cases in which a monk cuts one finger or half a finger less than the Sugata's measure and makes a sitting mat from it, yet it does not become a transgression requiring relinquishment?" "Upāli, there are. In any case where the material of that sitting mat is suitable but the edge-trimming is unsuitable, or where the edge-trimming is suitable but the material is not, or where both are unsuitable — as for what is unsuitable: if a sitting mat is made from she-camel's wool, cattle wool, goat wool, deer wool, mixed wool, or unwoven material of such kinds, it becomes an offense."

"Venerable One, if a monk cuts one finger or half a finger less than the Sugata's measure and is in the act of making a sitting mat when a change of marks occurs and one becomes a nun — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "Venerable One, if a nun cuts one finger or half a finger less than the Sugata's measure and is in the act of making a sitting mat when a change of marks occurs and one becomes a monk — what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment."

"Venerable One, if a monk perceives as smaller what is smaller than the Sugata's measure, mixes it in, and has a sitting mat made from it — what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment." "If one perceives as larger what is smaller, and has it done — what does it become?" "There is no offense." "If one perceives as smaller what is larger, mixes it in, and has it done — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If one perceives as larger what is larger, mixes it in, and has it done — what does it become?" "There is no offense."

"Venerable One, if one who has not received full ordination cuts one finger or half a finger less than the Sugata's measure and begins making a different sitting mat, and while still without full ordination — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If one begins without full ordination and it is still during the ceremony of full ordination — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If one begins without full ordination and one has received full ordination afterward — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If one begins during the ceremony of full ordination and it is still during that ceremony — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If one begins during the ceremony of full ordination and afterward has received full ordination — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If one begins after having received full ordination and afterward one has received full ordination — what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment." "If one begins at the time of having received full ordination and afterward one has not received full ordination — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense."

In summary:
Message, letter, gesture,
Having another say it, and one to one,
One who has gone mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
One who is ill, one who is mute, one who is dull.

"Venerable One, if a monk cuts one finger or half a finger less than the Sugata's measure —"

— if one has had it done through a messenger with half a finger less, what does it become? It becomes an offense. Likewise, if one has had it done through a letter, a gesture, having another say it, passing it from one to another, through one who has gone mad, one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is dull, one who is mute, or one who is deaf — all of these become offenses. Just as a monk who has had a covering mat made incurs a transgression requiring relinquishment, so too if one who has relinquished the training has had it made, it also becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment. For a nun, a female trainee, a male novice, and a female novice, it is an offense.

In summary:
Sky, miraculous power, and conjured form,
Mantra and the other three — so likewise.
The improper, the second characteristic,
The fourth, the seventh relay — so too.

Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk shears sheep's wool beyond three leagues it becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment. Venerable One, if a monk shears sheep's wool from the sky beyond three leagues — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If he shears it by miraculous power — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If a conjured form acting as an enabler shears it — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "Venerable One, if a monk renders himself invisible by means of mantra or medicine and shears it — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If he shears it for the benefit of another — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If he sends it to another — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense."

"Venerable One, are there cases in which a monk may shear sheep's wool beyond three leagues without it becoming a transgression requiring relinquishment?" "Upāli, there are. If a monk who has set out on a road finds a piece of sheep's wool and carries it himself up to the limit of three leagues, and then finds another piece of sheep's wool and discards the first and takes the second and goes on — in that case there is no offense."

"Venerable One, if a monk shears wool that is improper — wool other than sheep's wool, such as the wool of a female yak, the wool of an ox, the wool of a goat, or the wool of a deer, mixed with what is improper — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense."

"Venerable One, if a monk shears sheep's wool beyond three leagues, and then his characteristic changes and he becomes a nun, and he transgresses the boundary — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "Venerable One, if a nun shears sheep's wool beyond three leagues, and then her characteristic changes and she becomes a monk, and he transgresses the boundary — what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment."

"Venerable One, if a monk shears sheep's wool beyond three leagues, perceiving a league as a league — what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment." "If he perceives a league as not a league — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If he perceives what is not a league as a league — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If he perceives what is not a league as not a league — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense."

"Venerable One, if one who has not received full ordination shears a piece of sheep's wool, and while not yet having received full ordination transgresses the boundary — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If one shears it without having received full ordination and transgresses the boundary at the very moment of receiving full ordination — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If one shears it without having received full ordination and then, having received full ordination, transgresses the boundary — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If one shears it at the very moment of receiving full ordination and transgresses the boundary at the very moment of receiving full ordination — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If one shears it at the very moment of receiving full ordination and then, having received full ordination, transgresses the boundary — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If one has received full ordination, then shears it, and afterward, having received full ordination, transgresses the boundary — what does it become?"
