"It becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment." "If one has received full ordination and shears it, and then transgresses the boundary without having received full ordination — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense."

In summary:

In summary:

A messenger, a written letter, a hand-signal,
Having another convey it, passing it from one to another,
Having become mad, being disturbed in mind,
Being ill, being mute, being simple-minded.

The venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "If a monk, venerable sir, sends more than three leagues' worth of sheep's wool as a messenger-gift — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "Likewise, if it is sent by written letter, by hand-signal, by having another convey it, by passing it from one to another, by a madman, by one disturbed in mind, by one tormented by illness, by a simpleton, by a mute, by a deaf-mute, by a blind person — in all such cases it becomes an offense." "Just as a monk who exceeds three leagues' worth of sheep's wool incurs a transgression requiring relinquishment, so too does giving the training to one who is not a relative incur a transgression requiring relinquishment. For a nun, a female probationer, a male novice, and a female novice, it becomes an offense."

The Noble Vinaya, the fourth section. In summary:

A messenger, a written letter, a hand-signal,
Having another convey it, passing it from one to another,
Having become mad, being disturbed in mind,
Being ill, and beings of various kinds,
Householders and the like —
The giving of the training is the last.

The venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk shears the wool of a nun who is not a relative, it becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment. If a monk causes the wool to be sheared by sending a messenger — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "Likewise, if it is done by written letter, by hand-signal, by having another convey it, by passing it from one to another and having it sheared — in all such cases it becomes an offense." "If a monk causes the wool of a mad nun to be sheared — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "Likewise, if it is caused to be sheared in the case of one disturbed in mind, one tormented by illness, a mute, and a deaf-mute — in all such cases it becomes an offense." "If a monk causes a laywoman to have it sheared — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "Likewise, if it is caused to be sheared by an eunuch, by an expelled nun, by one's father, by one's mother, by one who has killed an arhat, by one who with malicious intent has shed the blood of a Tathāgata, by those who have gone over to non-Buddhists, by those in a place of thieves, and by those who were previously in schism — in all such cases it becomes an offense." "If a monk causes a nun who is creating a schism in the Saṅgha, or who has taken sides, or who has been given the training, to have it sheared — what does it become?" "It becomes a relinquishment." "If one who has been given the training causes a nun who is not a relative likewise to have her wool sheared — what does it become?" "It becomes a relinquishment."

In summary:

What is shared, what has been washed,
Likewise the Saṅgha's two marks,
What is improper, what entails relinquishment,
And what is unknown — likewise so.
The seventh and the fourth,
And the nun is the last.

"If a monk causes a shared piece of sheep's wool to be sheared — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If he causes a washed piece to be sheared — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If a monk causes a piece of the Saṅgha's sheep's wool to be sheared — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If it is something that has been fully used by a person and upon being fully used has become soiled — it becomes an offense. But if it is a bedding article that is caused to be sheared, there is no offense." "If a monk causes a monk who is not a relative to have a piece of sheep's wool sheared, and that monk then changes status and becomes a nun — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "If a nun causes a nun who is not a relative to have a piece of sheep's wool sheared, and that nun then changes status and becomes a nun — what does it become?" "It becomes an offense." "Venerable sir, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk causes a nun who is not a relative to have her wool sheared, it also becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment —"

"Venerable sir, are there cases where a monk causes a nun who is not a relative to have a piece of sheep's wool sheared, and yet it does not become a transgression requiring relinquishment?" "Upāli, there are. If wool that is mixed with unsuitable kinds is caused to be sheared — unsuitable wool being the wool of a female donkey, the wool of a cow, the wool of a goat, or the wool of a deer — if what is caused to be sheared is mixed with any of these, it becomes a minor offense."

"Venerable sir, if a monk causes relinquished sheep's wool to be sheared, what does it become?" "If it has not yet been relinquished, it becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment. If it has been relinquished, it becomes a minor offense."

"Venerable sir, if a monk causes another's sheep's wool to be sheared, what does it become?" "A minor offense."

"Venerable sir, if someone not yet fully ordained causes a piece of sheep's wool to be sheared, and that person remains not fully ordained — what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If the wool was caused to be sheared while not yet fully ordained, and that person is in the process of receiving full ordination — what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If it was caused to be sheared while not yet fully ordained, and full ordination has since been completed — what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If it was caused to be sheared while in the process of receiving full ordination, and that person remains in that process — what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If it was caused to be sheared while in the process of receiving full ordination, and full ordination has since been completed — what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If it was caused to be sheared after full ordination has been completed, and that person is fully ordained — what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment." "If it was caused to be sheared after full ordination, and that person is not fully ordained — what does it become?" "A minor offense."

"Venerable sir, if a monk perceives one who is not a relative as not a relative and causes her to shear sheep's wool, what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment." "If he perceives one who is not a relative as a relative, there is no offense." "If he perceives a relative as not a relative, it is a minor offense." "If he perceives a relative as a relative, there is no offense."

"Venerable sir, if a monk perceives a fully ordained nun as fully ordained and causes her to shear sheep's wool, what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment." "If he perceives a fully ordained nun as not fully ordained, it becomes a minor offense." "If he perceives one not fully ordained as fully ordained, it becomes a minor offense."

"If a monk causes a nun who is not a relative to shear sheep's wool, what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment." "If he causes a female probationer, a female novice, a laywoman, a non-Buddhist female ascetic of another order, a female wanderer, or any other being dwelling elsewhere to do so — all of these become minor offenses."

"If a nun causes a monk, a male novice, a non-Buddhist male ascetic of another order — whether a brahmin, a follower of a practice, a wanderer, or any other being dwelling elsewhere — to shear wool, what does it become?" "A minor offense. Also toward a male householder or a female householder, a minor offense. Toward a female probationer, a male novice, and a female novice, likewise a minor offense. And washing and combing should be understood in the same way."

In brief:
By messenger, letter, gesture,
and through another's word, and from one to another —
through one who has become mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is ill, a deaf-mute, and one who is dumb —

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed Buddha: "Venerable sir, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk takes gold or silver with his own hand, or causes it to be accepted, it becomes a transgression requiring relinquishment. Venerable sir, if a monk causes a messenger to accept gold and silver, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "Likewise, through a letter, a gesture, through another's word, and through a chain of intermediaries — if acceptance is caused in all these ways, do all become minor offenses?" "All become minor offenses."

"Venerable sir, if a monk causes a madman to accept gold or silver, what does it become?" "A minor offense. Likewise, if acceptance is caused through one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, a deaf person, a mute, or a dumb person — all become minor offenses."

"Venerable sir, if a monk takes gold or silver from a madman, what does it become?" "A minor offense. Likewise, if one takes gold or silver, or causes acceptance of it, from one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, a mute, a deaf person, one with a speech impediment, one who is intoxicated, or one who has gone to dwell elsewhere — all become minor offenses."

In brief:
A close relative, a maternal kinsman,
the fourth and the seventh,
the eighth, and householders and so forth,
other householders, and a nun —

"Venerable sir, is there any case in which a monk taking gold and silver, or causing acceptance thereof, from these does not become a transgression entailing forfeiture?" "Upāli, there is: when it has been taken from a non-intimate and one perceives it as a different kind of requisite."

"Venerable sir, if while a monk is taking gold and silver his ordination status changes and he becomes a nun, what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture." "Venerable sir, if while a nun is taking gold and silver her ordination status changes and she becomes a monk, what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture."

"Venerable sir, if a monk takes a fraction of gold or a fraction of silver, what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture." "But if he takes a fraction of iron or a fraction of copper, or causes acceptance of such, it becomes a minor offense."

"Venerable sir, if a monk, perceiving gold as gold, takes it, what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture." "If he perceives gold as not being gold, there is no offense." "If he perceives what is not gold as gold, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If he perceives what is not gold as not gold, there is no offense."

"Venerable sir, if someone who has not yet received full ordination takes gold or silver and receives it before receiving full ordination, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If one who has not yet received full ordination takes it and receives it at the moment of receiving full ordination, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If one who has not yet received full ordination takes it and receives it after having received full ordination, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If one who is at the moment of receiving full ordination takes it and receives it at the moment of receiving full ordination, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If one who is at the moment of receiving full ordination takes it and receives it after having received full ordination, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If one who has received full ordination takes it and receives it after having received full ordination, what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture." "If one who has received full ordination takes it and receives it before full ordination, what does it become?" "A minor offense."

"Venerable sir, if a monk directly causes a layperson to accept gold and silver, what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture. Likewise, the following, if they directly take or cause acceptance: a hermaphrodite, a eunuch, an expelled nun, a father, a mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who with malicious intent has caused the Tathāgata to bleed, one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, a thief, one who dwells separately, one who does not dwell in the community, one who has approached the wrong side, one who was formerly involved in a dispute, one from whom an offense has previously arisen, and one who has surrendered the training — if any of these directly take or cause acceptance, all become transgressions entailing forfeiture."

"Venerable sir, are there cases in which a monk takes gold and silver with his own hand, or causes acceptance, without committing an offense?" "Upāli, there are. In such cases, the monk, though taking gold and silver, has not aroused the thought of making it his own — and therefore, thinking that since what is improper cannot serve as a proper article, he takes something else instead."

"Venerable sir, if a monk takes gold and silver on behalf of another, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "Venerable sir, if one who has been given the training takes or causes acceptance of gold and silver, what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture." "Venerable sir, if a nun takes gold and silver with her own hand, or causes acceptance, what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture." "Venerable sir, if a female probationer, a male novice, or a female novice takes gold and silver with their own hand or causes acceptance, what does it become?" "A minor offense."

In brief:
Through messenger, written letter, gesture,

saying on another's behalf, relaying from one to another, being insane, being mentally disturbed, being ill, being mute, and traveling to another place.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable sir, when the Blessed One declared that whatever monk engages in barter with various kinds of goods, it becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture — venerable sir, if a monk engages in barter with various kinds of goods through a messenger, what does it become?" "A minor offense. Likewise through a written letter, through gesture, on another's behalf, saying on another's behalf, or relaying from one to another." "Venerable sir, if a monk engages in barter with various kinds of goods together with a madman, what does it become?" "A minor offense. Likewise if done together with one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, a simpleton, a mute, a deaf person — and likewise if done with various kinds of goods together with one who has taken up residence in another destiny — in all these cases it becomes a minor offense."

In brief:
The marks, the fourth, the seventh — thus it is.
Likewise one who has received the training,
one who is similar, one who is a relative,
and a nun — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable sir, if a monk engages in barter with various kinds of goods and in the midst of doing so changes his status and becomes a nun, and then the acquisition is completed — what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture." "Venerable sir, if a nun engages in barter with various kinds of goods and in the midst of doing so changes her status and becomes a monk, and then the acquisition is completed — what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture." "Venerable sir, if a monk, perceiving a human being as a human being, engages in barter with various kinds of goods — what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture." "If he perceives a human being as not being a human being, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If he perceives one who is not a human being as a human being, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If he perceives one who is not a human being as not a human being, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "Venerable sir, if one who has not received full ordination engages in barter with various kinds of goods while not yet fully ordained, and the acquisition is completed while still not fully ordained — what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If set out while not fully ordained but the acquisition is completed when nearly fully ordained, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If set out while not fully ordained but completed after full ordination, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If set out when nearly fully ordained and completed when nearly fully ordained, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If set out when nearly fully ordained and completed after full ordination, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "If set out after full ordination and completed after full ordination, what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture." "If set out after full ordination but completed while not fully ordained, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "Venerable sir, if one who has been given the training engages in barter with various kinds of goods, what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture." "Venerable sir, if barter is done with various kinds of goods together with a relative, what does it become?" "A minor offense." "Venerable sir, is there any case in which a monk engages in barter with various kinds of goods and yet it does not become a transgression entailing forfeiture?" "Upāli, there is: when like exchanges with like — coming afterward there is no offense." "Venerable sir, if a nun engages in barter with various kinds of goods, what does it become?" "It becomes a transgression entailing forfeiture." For a female probationer, a male novice, and a female novice — it becomes a minor offense. In this training rule, buying and selling are likewise to be elaborated at length accordingly.

In brief:
The same item, loss,
another region, non-Buddhists (tīrthikas),
what has not been burned, what is white,
the insane, the marks, a messenger,
existence, livelihood, and the nun.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable sir, are there cases where keeping hold of the same almsbowl results in an offense, and cases where keeping hold of the same almsbowl does not result in an offense?"

Upāli replied: "There are such cases. For instance, if a monk keeps hold of a large almsbowl and then undergoes a change of marks and becomes a nun, and in that state continues to keep it, it becomes a minor offense."

"Venerable sir, if a monk loses the almsbowl he has set aside, should he confess the transgression?" The Blessed One replied: "Upāli, he should confess it." "After confessing the offense, if he finds the bowl again, must he set it aside?" "Upāli, no, he need not."

"Venerable sir, the Blessed One has declared that a monk should not keep an extra almsbowl beyond ten days. Are there cases where a monk may keep an extra almsbowl beyond ten days without incurring an offense?" "Upāli, there are. For instance, if a monk sends an almsbowl to another monk in a different region, that monk may keep it for a very long time without any offense."

"Venerable sir, what becomes of a monk who keeps an almsbowl belonging to a non-Buddhist? It becomes a minor offense." "Venerable sir, what becomes of a monk who keeps an unburned almsbowl, a small almsbowl, or a large almsbowl? It becomes a minor offense." "Venerable sir, what becomes of a monk who keeps a white almsbowl? It becomes a minor offense."

"If a monk obtains an almsbowl and then immediately goes insane, from what point does the count of ten days begin?" "It begins from the moment he recovers his own mind." "Venerable sir, are there cases where a monk may keep an extra almsbowl beyond ten days without incurring a forfeiture?" "Upāli, there are. For instance, if a monk acquires an almsbowl and then, after ten days have passed, undergoes a change of marks and becomes a nun, there is no offense. Also, if a monk acquires an almsbowl and immediately upon acquiring it undergoes a change of marks and becomes a monk again, there is no offense."

"Venerable sir, are there cases where a nun may keep an extra almsbowl beyond ten days without incurring an offense?" "Upāli, there are. For instance, if that nun, immediately upon acquiring the almsbowl, undergoes a change of marks and becomes a monk, there is no offense."

"Venerable sir, are there cases where a monk may keep an extra almsbowl for a very long time without incurring an offense?" "Upāli, there are. For instance, if a monk sends a messenger to another monk on account of an almsbowl, and that monk takes possession of the almsbowl and keeps it for a very long time, there is no offense."

"Venerable sir, are there cases where, although a monk has one almsbowl and that one almsbowl is still present, it becomes subject to forfeiture?" "Upāli, there are — if it is kept without having been consecrated." "Venerable sir, are there cases where a monk may keep an extra almsbowl for as long as he lives without incurring a forfeiture?" "Upāli, there are — if that monk passes away before ten days have elapsed."

"Venerable sir, if one keeps an extra almsbowl beyond ten days after having received the training, what results?" "It becomes subject to forfeiture. If a nun keeps an extra almsbowl beyond ten days, it becomes a forfeiture offense. For a female probationer, a female novice, and male novices, it becomes a minor offense."

In brief:
A messenger, a letter, a hand signal,
saying through another, one to one,
having gone insane, mental disturbance,
illness, being deaf and mute, a migrating being.

Then the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable sir, the Blessed One has further declared that if a monk who has fewer than five almsbowls available for use nevertheless seeks another almsbowl, it becomes subject to forfeiture. Venerable sir, if a monk seeks a second almsbowl through a messenger and obtains one, what results?" "It becomes a minor offense." "Just as with the messenger, so too with a letter, a hand signal, saying through another, and all cases of passing the request along from one to another — all become minor offenses."

"Venerable sir, if a monk seeks a second almsbowl from an insane person, what results? If he obtains the almsbowl, it becomes a minor offense." "Likewise, in the cases of one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is deaf, one who is mute, one who is dumb,

and those dwelling in other places — if a monk seeks a second almsbowl from them and obtains one, in all such cases it becomes a minor offense.

In summary:

From tīrthikas and hermaphrodites,
The seven kinds are likewise so;
Those in common, and the fourth,
Implements, and nuns.

Venerable sir, if a monk solicits a second almsbowl from an external non-Buddhist — another ascetic, a brahmin, a wanderer, or a mendicant — and obtains an almsbowl, what results? It becomes a minor offense. Venerable sir, if a monk seeks a single vessel belonging to a tīrthika and obtains it, what results? It becomes a minor offense. Venerable sir, if a monk seeks a second almsbowl from a hermaphrodite and obtains one, what results? It becomes a minor offense. Likewise, if he seeks one from a neuter male or from a neuter female, or from a person of double characteristics, and obtains an almsbowl, it becomes a minor offense.

Venerable sir, if a monk takes another almsbowl while already possessing an almsbowl, and the status of that bowl then changes so that it comes to belong to a nun, and he then obtains it, what results? It must be relinquished. Venerable sir, if a nun, while already possessing an almsbowl, seeks a second one, and her status then changes so that she becomes a monk, and he then obtains it, what results? It must be relinquished.

Venerable sir, if a monk, while already possessing an almsbowl, seeks a second one from a householder or from a householder's attendant, and both parties then undergo a change of status, and after that change the bowl is obtained, what results? It must be relinquished. Venerable sir, if a nun seeks a second almsbowl from a householder or a householder's attendant, and both parties then undergo a change of status, and after that change the bowl is obtained, what results? It must be relinquished.

If one solicits while not yet fully ordained and obtains it while not yet fully ordained, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one solicits while not yet fully ordained and obtains it at the very moment of receiving full ordination, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one solicits while not yet fully ordained and obtains it after full ordination, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one solicits at the very moment of full ordination and obtains it at the very moment of full ordination, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one solicits at the very moment of full ordination and obtains it after full ordination is complete, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one solicits after full ordination is already complete and obtains it from someone fully ordained, what results? It must be relinquished. If one solicits after full ordination is already complete and obtains it from someone not yet fully ordained, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

If two monks jointly solicit a single almsbowl, what results? It becomes a minor offense. Venerable sir, if a monk, perceiving a human being as a human being, solicits an almsbowl and obtains one, what results? It must be relinquished. If he solicits while perceiving a human being as a non-human, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If he solicits while perceiving a non-human as a human being, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If he solicits while perceiving a non-human as a non-human, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

Venerable sir, if a monk seeks a second almsbowl by means of his own goods or by payment, what results? It becomes a minor offense. Venerable sir, if one who has abandoned the training seeks a second almsbowl while already possessing one and obtains it, what results? It must be relinquished. Venerable sir, if a nun seeks a second almsbowl while already possessing one and obtains it, what results? It must be relinquished. If probationary nuns, female novices, or male novices seek a second almsbowl while already possessing one and obtain it, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

In summary:

Through messenger, letter, hand signal,
Speaking through another, and one-to-one relay,
One gone mad, one mentally disturbed,
One ill, one deaf, and those who journey elsewhere.

Thus did the venerable Upāli put these questions to the Blessed One, the Buddha.

Venerable sir, the Blessed One declared that if a monk has a non-relative weaver weave a robe for him, it must be relinquished. If a monk has it woven through a messenger, what results? It becomes a minor offense. Likewise, through a letter, a hand signal, speaking through another, one-to-one relay, or having it woven on behalf of another — in all such cases it becomes a minor offense.

Venerable sir, if a monk has a mad weaver weave a robe for him, what results? It becomes a minor offense. Likewise, if the weaver is mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, simpleminded, mute, deaf, or a being who is a non-human dwelling in such a state — in all such cases it becomes a minor offense.

In summary:

The neuter, the hermaphrodite, and one of common sex marks —
Likewise that category of the impermissible seven,
The fourth order, trainees, and fully ordained nuns.

Venerable sir, if a monk has a neuter weaver weave a robe for him, what results? It becomes a minor offense. Likewise, a hermaphrodite, a female neuter, and one with both sex characteristics — in all such cases it becomes a minor offense. Venerable sir, if a monk has a robe of common ownership woven, what results? It becomes a minor offense. Venerable sir, if a monk has a non-relative weaver weave a robe, and that weaver's status changes and she becomes a fully ordained nun, and the monk then receives it, what results? It must be relinquished. Venerable sir, if a monk or a fully ordained nun has a non-relative weaver weave a robe, and the weaver's status changes — and after that change the robe is received — what results? It must be relinquished.

Venerable sir, is there a case in which a monk has a non-relative weaver weave a robe yet it need not be relinquished? Upāli, yes there is. If the material for the robe is allowable but the relationship is not allowable, or the relationship is allowable but the material is not allowable, or neither is allowable — in such cases the material is not allowable. Having a robe woven from the wool of a she-camel, the wool of a cow, the wool of a goat, the wool of a deer, or mixtures of these — all such cases become minor offenses.

Venerable sir, if one who has not received full ordination has it woven and one who has not received full ordination receives it, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one who has not received full ordination has it woven and one who is in the process of receiving full ordination receives it, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one who has not received full ordination has it woven and one who has fully received full ordination receives it, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one who is in the process of receiving full ordination has it woven and one in the process of receiving full ordination receives it, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one who is in the process of receiving full ordination has it woven and one who has fully received full ordination receives it, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one who has fully received full ordination has it woven and one who has fully received full ordination receives it, what results? It must be relinquished. If one who has fully received full ordination has it woven and one who has not fully received full ordination receives it, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

Venerable sir, if a monk perceives a non-human as a non-human and has a robe woven for that being, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one perceives a human as a non-human, it becomes a minor offense. If one perceives a non-human as a human, it becomes a minor offense. If one perceives a human as a human and has a robe woven, what results? It must be relinquished.

Venerable sir, if a monk perceives a non-relative as a non-relative and has a robe woven for that person, what results? It must be relinquished. If one perceives a relative as not a relative, there is no offense. If one perceives a non-relative as a relative and has a robe woven, it becomes a minor offense. If one perceives a relative as a relative and has a robe woven, there is no offense.

Venerable sir, if a trainee who has relinquished a precept has a robe woven by a non-relative weaver and obtains the robe, what results? It must be relinquished. The same applies to a fully ordained nun as it does to a monk, exactly as before. And just as the preceding cases apply from the training downward — if the robe is obtained while in the process of receiving full ordination, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

If one who has not yet received full ordination gives rise to the intention and obtains the robe before receiving full ordination, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one who has not yet received full ordination gives rise to the intention and obtains the robe in the very process of receiving full ordination, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one who has not yet received full ordination gives rise to the intention and obtains the robe after having received full ordination, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one who is in the very process of receiving full ordination gives rise to the intention and obtains the robe in the very process of receiving full ordination, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one who is in the very process of receiving full ordination gives rise to the intention and obtains the robe after full ordination has been completed, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one who has completed full ordination gives rise to the intention and, as a fully ordained monk, obtains the robe, what results? It must be relinquished. If one who has completed full ordination gives rise to the intention and obtains the robe before full ordination has been completed, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

Venerable sir, if a monk perceives a human weaver as human, gives rise to the intention, and has the robe completed before him, what results? It must be relinquished. If one perceives a human as non-human, it becomes a minor offense. If one perceives a non-human as human, it becomes a minor offense. If one perceives a non-human as non-human, it becomes a minor offense.

Venerable sir, if a monk perceives a non-relative weaver as a non-relative, gives rise to the intention, and has the robe completed before him, what results? It must be relinquished. If one perceives a non-relative as a relative, what results? There is no offense. If one perceives a relative as a non-relative, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one perceives a relative as a relative, there is no offense.

If one who has been given a precept gives rise to the intention and has the robe completed before him, what results? It must be relinquished. Venerable sir, if a fully ordained nun gives rise to the intention and has the robe completed before her, what results? It must be relinquished. If male novices and female novices give rise to the intention and have the robe completed before them, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

In brief:
By messenger, by letter, by hand-signal,
by having another say it, by passing it from one to another,
for one who has gone mad, for one whose mind is disturbed,
for one who is sick, for one who is deaf-mute — these are the cases.

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable sir, the Blessed One has said that if a monk, having given a robe to a monk, seizes it back or causes it to be seized back, it must be relinquished. If a monk seizes it back by messenger, what results? It becomes a minor offense. Likewise, if one does so by letter, by hand-signal, by having another say it, by relaying it from one to another, or by seizing it on behalf of another — all of these become minor offenses.

Venerable sir, if a monk gives a robe to a mad monk and then seizes it back, what results? It becomes a minor offense. Likewise, if one seizes back a robe given to one whose mind is disturbed, to one tormented by illness, to one who is dull-witted, to one who is mute, or to one who is deaf-mute — all of these become minor offenses.

Venerable sir, if a monk gives a robe to ascetics of other traditions who are tīrthikas (non-Buddhists) — whether wandering renunciants, brahmin ascetics, wandering practitioners, or peripatetics — and then seizes it back, what results? All become minor offenses. Venerable sir, if one seizes back a robe given to someone dwelling in another destination, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

In brief:
The same applies to laypeople and the rest,
and likewise to the common mark;
what is not supreme and not permissible is the same,
and the fourth and the seventh are likewise so.

Venerable sir, if a monk gives a robe to a layperson and then seizes it back, what results? It becomes a minor offense. Likewise, if one seizes back robes given to a eunuch, to an expelled nun, to one's father, to one's mother, to one who has killed an arhat, to one who has shed the blood of a Tathāgata with malicious intent,

to one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), to one who is a habitual thief, to one who previously caused a schism, or to one against whom a prior offense has arisen — if one seizes back a robe given to any of these, it becomes a minor offense in every case.

Venerable sir, if a monk gives a robe to a probationer, to one who is not resident, to one who dwells separately, or to a monk who previously caused a schism, and then seizes it back, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

If one causes a layperson to seize back a robe given to one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, to one who has sided with that person, or to one who has surrendered their training, it becomes an offense requiring forfeiture in every case.

Venerable sir, if a monk gives a robe to a nun, to a female trainee, to a female novice, or to a male novice, and then seizes it back, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

Venerable sir, if a monk gives a robe to another monk and then causes a layperson to seize it back, what results? It becomes an offense requiring forfeiture.

Likewise, if one causes a layperson to seize back a robe given to a probationer, to a eunuch, to an expelled nun, to one's father, to one's mother, to one who has killed an arhat, to one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, to one who has shed the blood of a Tathāgata with malicious intent, to a non-Buddhist, to one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, to a habitual thief, to one who dwells separately, to one who is not resident, to one who previously caused a schism, to one against whom a prior offense has arisen, to one who has sided with a schismatic, to one who has surrendered their training, to a monk, to a nun, to a female trainee, to a male novice, or to a female novice — in every case it becomes an offense requiring forfeiture.

Venerable sir, if two monks share a robe in common and afterwards one of them seizes it back, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

Venerable sir, if a monk gives a robe to another monk and seizes it back, and in the interim that monk has changed status and become a nun and received full ordination, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

Venerable sir, if a nun gives a robe to another nun and seizes it back, and in the interim that nun has changed status and become a monk and received full ordination, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

Venerable sir, if a monk gives a robe of less than one cubit to another monk and then seizes it back, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

Venerable sir, is there any case in which a monk gives a robe to another monk, seizes it back, and yet it does not become an offense requiring forfeiture? Upāli, yes, there is. How so? When the material of the robe is permissible but the weaving is not permissible; when the weaving is permissible but the material is not permissible; or when both are not permissible. That which is not permissible is as follows: wool from a female sheep, wool from cattle, wool from a goat, wool from a wild deer, or a mixture of these, or a fabric woven in a manner like these — if such a robe is given and then seized back, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

Venerable sir, if a monk perceives a fully ordained person as fully ordained, gives him a robe, and then seizes it back, what results? It becomes an offense requiring forfeiture. If he perceives a fully ordained person as not fully ordained, gives him a robe, and then seizes it back, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If he perceives a person who is not fully ordained as fully ordained, gives him a robe, and then seizes it back, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If he perceives a person who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained, gives him a robe, and then seizes it back, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

Venerable sir, if one intends to seize from a person who is not fully ordained and does seize from a person who is not fully ordained, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one intends to seize from a person who is not fully ordained and the seizure is accomplished with respect to a fully ordained person, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one intends to seize from a person who is not fully ordained and the seizure is accomplished with respect to a fully ordained person who has been so fully ordained, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one intends to seize from a fully ordained person and the seizure is accomplished with respect to a fully ordained person, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If one intends to seize from a fully ordained person and the seizure is accomplished with respect to a person who is fully ordained, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

If one intends to seize from a fully ordained person and the seizure is accomplished with respect to a fully ordained person who has been so fully ordained, what results? It becomes a defeat. If one who is fully ordained intends to seize and the seizure is accomplished with respect to one who is not fully ordained, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

Venerable One, if one who has undertaken the training gives a robe to a monk and then takes it back, what results? It becomes a defeat. Venerable One, if a monk takes a robe that a nun has given, what results? It becomes a minor offense. Venerable One, if a nun takes a robe that a monk has given, what results? It becomes a minor offense. Venerable One, if a nun takes back a robe that she herself gave to another nun, what results? It becomes a defeat. If a nun takes back a robe she gave to a monk, a female probationer, a male novice, or a female novice, what results? It becomes a minor offense. For female probationers, female novices, and male novices, the detailed treatment of minor offenses applies.

In brief:
A troubled mind, and when the time has passed,
shared in common — likewise these apply;
as the fourth type of unfit case has it,
the seventh concerns the time and the nun.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable One, the Blessed One has declared that a monk should keep an examined robe until the time of the robe-offering ceremony, and that if he keeps it beyond that time it becomes a defeat. Venerable One, is there a case where, even though the time has passed, it does not become a defeat? Upāli, yes there is — when the monk's mind became agitated at the very moment he obtained the robe.

Venerable One, is there a case where a monk may keep an examined robe for his entire lifetime without it becoming a defeat? Upāli, yes there is — when the period up to the time of robe-offering has been made a fixed term.

Venerable One, if a monk keeps an examined robe past the time of the robe-offering and, the ordination status having changed, he becomes a nun, what results? It becomes a defeat. Venerable One, if a nun keeps an examined robe past the time of the robe-offering and, the ordination status having changed, she becomes a monk, what results? It becomes a defeat.

Venerable One, if a monk keeps an examined robe that is held in common past the time of the robe-offering, what results? It becomes a minor offense. Venerable One, is there a case where a monk keeps an examined robe past the time of robe-offering and it does not become a defeat? Upāli, yes there is — when the material of that robe has become suitable but the thread is not suitable, or the thread has become suitable but the material is not suitable, or both are not suitable. What is not suitable? Wool of a female deer, wool of cattle, wool of goats, wool of wild animals, or a mixture of these. A robe of such materials, when it has not yet been woven into cloth, if kept past the time of robe-offering, becomes a minor offense.

Venerable One, if a monk perceives the time of robe-offering as having passed when it has in fact passed, and keeps a robe, what results? It becomes a defeat. If he perceives the time as not having passed when it has in fact passed, and keeps a robe, what results? There is no offense. If he perceives the time as having passed when it has not in fact passed, and keeps a robe, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If he perceives the time as not having passed when it has not in fact passed, and keeps a robe, what results? There is no offense.

Venerable One, if a robe is kept for one who is not yet fully ordained, and the time passes while he is still not yet fully ordained, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If a robe is kept for one who is not yet fully ordained, and the time passes when he is in the act of receiving full ordination, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If a robe is kept for one who is not yet fully ordained, and the time passes after he has received full ordination, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If a robe is kept for one who is in the act of receiving full ordination, and the time passes while he is in that act, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If a robe is kept for one who is in the act of receiving full ordination, and the time passes after he has received full ordination, what results? It becomes a minor offense. If a robe is kept for one who has already received full ordination, and the time passes after full ordination has been received, what results? It becomes a defeat. If a robe is kept by one who has received full ordination and the time passes when he is no longer fully ordained, what results? It becomes a minor offense.

Venerable one, if the proper time has not yet come and the king has dismissed the assembly, how should a monk proceed with a robe that has been kept? Exactly as if one had entered into the proper procedure. Should a robe that has been kept be called "past ten days" or "not past ten days"? It should be called "past ten days."

Venerable one, may a robe that has been kept be made into an out-of-season robe? Upāli: It may not.

Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said "Keep the robe until the time of the robe-offering ceremony," venerable one, when is the time of the robe-offering ceremony? Upāli: It is when the proper time has come. Until the proper time has come, it is at all times out of season.

Venerable one, if a robe is kept past the time for making the robe offering, as set forth in the training, what results? It becomes a defeat.

Venerable one, if a nun keeps a robe past the time for making the robe offering, what results? It becomes a defeat. For probationers, novice monks, and novice nuns, it is a minor offense; that is to be stated in full.

In brief:
The improper, the fourth, and likewise
the seventh, which is the obstruction;
the vow, the Saṅgha,
the sky-mark, and the nun.

The venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that even at great distance, if a monk is separated from his robe for six days, then if he is separated for longer than that it becomes a defeat. Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk, even though separated from his robe for more than six days, does not incur a defeat? Upāli: There is. In whatever way the material for that robe has become permissible but the thread is not permissible, or the thread has become permissible but the material is not permissible, or both are not permissible — what is not permissible is: the wool of a female yak, the wool of cattle, the wool of goats, the wool of deer, and mixtures of these. Similarly, if one is separated from a robe that has not been woven for more than six days, it becomes a minor offense.

Venerable one, if a monk perceives as elapsed what has elapsed and is separated from his robe, what results? It becomes a defeat. If he perceives as not elapsed what has elapsed and is separated from it, there is no offense. If he perceives as elapsed what has not elapsed and is separated from it, it becomes a minor offense. If he perceives as not elapsed what has not elapsed and is separated from it, there is no offense.

Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk, even though separated from his robe for more than six days, does not incur a defeat? Upāli: There is. In whatever case, when that monk was coming, one of any of the eight obstructions arose for him.

Venerable one, if a robe is kept for one who has not received full ordination and is separated from him while he has not received full ordination, what results? It is a minor offense. If it is kept for one who has not received full ordination and is separated from him in the act of receiving full ordination, what results? It is a minor offense. If it is kept for one who has not received full ordination and is separated from him after full ordination has been received, what results? It is a minor offense. If it is kept for one in the act of receiving full ordination and is separated from him in the act of receiving full ordination, what results? It is a minor offense. If it is kept for one in the act of receiving full ordination and is separated from him after full ordination has been received, what results? It is a minor offense. If it is kept by one who has received full ordination and is separated from him after full ordination has been received, what results? It becomes a defeat. If it is kept after full ordination has been received and is separated from him when he is no longer fully ordained, what results? It is a minor offense.

Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk, even though separated from his robe for more than six days, does not incur a defeat? Upāli: There is. In whatever case, that monk has obtained the vow of non-separation from his robe.

Venerable one, if a monk has consecrated a robe belonging to the Saṅgha, kept it, and is then separated from it after more than six days — should that be called "separated" or "not separated"? Upāli: It should be called "separated." Does it become a defeat? Upāli: It does not.

It is a transgression alone that must be confessed.

Venerable one, if a monk has left a robe inside a household and then departed into the sky, and more than six days have passed — what results? It becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

Venerable one, if a monk has left a robe inside a household and is separated from that robe for more than six days, and in the meantime his status changes and he becomes a nun — what results? It is a minor offense.

Venerable one, if a nun has left a robe inside a household and is separated from that robe for more than six days, and in the meantime her status changes and she becomes a monk — what results? It becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

Venerable one, if one who has been granted a training rule is separated from a robe for more than six days — what results? It becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. If a nun is separated from it, it is a minor offense. For a trainee nun and a novice nun as well, it is a minor offense.

Venerable one, if a male novice is separated from a robe for more than six days — what results? It is a minor offense.

The Vinaya, the excellent teaching. Fifth fascicle.

In brief:
By messenger, letter, hand-sign,
through another's word, and one by one —
one who has become mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is sick, one who is mute, one who is deaf,
one who is asleep, one who stutters, one who is intoxicated,
one in meditative absorption, and one gone to non-Buddhists.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk seeks his rains-retreat cloth very hastily or keeps it for an exceedingly long time, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. Venerable one, if a monk has sought the rains-retreat cloth through a messenger very hastily and finds the cloth — what results? It is a minor offense. If he has kept it for an exceedingly long time — what results? It is a minor offense.

Just as with a messenger, so too with a letter, a hand-sign, another's word, and through transmission one by one from person to person.

Venerable one, if a monk has sought the rains-retreat cloth from a madman very hastily and finds the cloth — what results? It is a minor offense. If he has kept it for an exceedingly long time — what results? It is a minor offense.

Just as with a madman, so too with one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one who stutters, one who is intoxicated, one in meditative absorption, and likewise with non-Buddhist ascetics outside this teaching — other wanderers, brahmins, practitioners, and wandering mendicants — if he has sought from them very hastily and finds it, it is a minor offense. If he has kept it for an exceedingly long time, it is also a minor offense.

In brief:
What is improper and likewise its characteristics,
the seventh that is common and the same —
the superior, the cotton cloth,
the fourth, and also the nun.

Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk has sought the rains-retreat cloth very hastily and kept it for an exceedingly long time yet does not incur an offense entailing forfeiture? Upāli: There is. When the material of that cloth is improper, or when the thread is improper though the material is proper, or when both are improper. What is improper is: mare's wool, cow's wool, goat's wool, deer's wool, and the like when blended — if from such material a rains-retreat cloth has not been woven on a loom, and one seeks it very hastily or keeps it for an exceedingly long time, it is a minor offense.

Venerable one, if a monk seeks the rains-retreat cloth very hastily or keeps it for an exceedingly long time and in the meantime his status changes and he becomes a nun — what results? It is a minor offense.

Venerable one, if a nun seeks the rains-retreat cloth very hastily or keeps it for an exceedingly long time and in the meantime her status changes and she becomes a monk — what results? It becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

Venerable one, if a monk seeks a rains-retreat cloth that is held in common very hastily or keeps it for an exceedingly long time — what results? It is a minor offense.

Venerable one, if a rains-retreat cloth is sought before full ordination, obtained before full ordination, and kept for an exceedingly long time — what results? It is a minor offense.

If it is sought before full ordination and obtained at the moment of full ordination and kept for an exceedingly long time — what results? It is a minor offense.

If it is sought before full ordination and obtained after full ordination and kept for an exceedingly long time — what results? It is a minor offense.

If it is sought at the moment of full ordination and obtained at the moment of full ordination and kept for an exceedingly long time — what results? It is a minor offense.

If it is sought at the moment of full ordination and obtained after full ordination and kept for an exceedingly long time — what results? It is a minor offense.

If it is sought after full ordination and obtained after full ordination and kept for an exceedingly long time — what results? It becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

If it is sought at the time of full ordination and obtained before full ordination and kept for an exceedingly long time — what results? It is a minor offense.

Venerable one, if a monk seeks a rains-retreat cloth that was not requested very hastily or keeps it for an exceedingly long time — what results? It is a minor offense.

Venerable one, if a monk seeks a rains-retreat cloth made of cotton very hastily or keeps it for an exceedingly long time — what results? It is a minor offense.

Venerable one, if a monk perceives a human being as a human being and seeks a rains-retreat cloth from that person very hastily and obtains the cloth — what results? It becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. If he keeps it for a long time, it is likewise. If he perceives a human being as a non-human being and obtains it from that person, it is a minor offense. If he perceives a non-human being as a human being and obtains it from that person, it is a minor offense. If he perceives a non-human being as a non-human being and obtains it from that person, it is a minor offense.

Venerable one, if a monk, after the rains-retreat cloth has properly arisen, perceives that half a month has passed when it has indeed passed and keeps it — what results? It becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. If he perceives that it has not passed when in fact it has passed, there is no offense. If he perceives that it has passed when it has not passed, it is a minor offense. If he perceives that it has not passed when in fact it has not passed, there is no offense.

Venerable one, if monks who have entered the rains retreat are expelled by the king — how should those monks, having entered the rains retreat in the proper manner, conclude it? Just as they properly entered it, so too should they conclude it. And how should they keep the rains-retreat cloth? Just as it properly arose, so should they keep it.

Venerable one, if one who has been given the training seeks a rains-retreat cloth very hastily or keeps it for an exceedingly long time — what results? It becomes an offense entailing forfeiture.

Venerable one, if a novice seeks a rains-retreat cloth very hastily or keeps it for an exceedingly long time — what results? It is a minor offense.

Venerable one, if a nun seeks a rains-retreat cloth — what results? It is a minor offense. If she keeps it beyond ten days, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. If a nun or a female novice seeks a rains-retreat cloth or keeps it beyond ten days, it is a minor offense.

In brief:
Through a messenger, a letter, a hand-signal,
Having another speak, or passing word from one to the next —
Through one who has become mad, or whose mind is disturbed,
Or one who is ill, newly recovered, or simple-minded.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk, while intending to dedicate his gain to the Saṅgha, dedicates it to himself instead, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture. Venerable one, if a monk, while intending to dedicate his gain to the Saṅgha, has it dedicated to himself through a messenger, and the gain is thereby actually obtained — what results? It is a minor offense. The same applies when done through a letter, a hand-signal, having another speak, or passing word from one to the next.

Venerable one, if a mad monk, while intending to dedicate his gain to the Saṅgha, dedicates it to himself and the gain is thereby actually obtained — what results? It is a minor offense. The same applies in the case of one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness,

one who is stupefied, one who is mute, and one who is deaf — all of these result in a minor offense.

In brief:
Those whose reception is impermissible or whose kind is unsuitable,
The seventh category and those characterized as the fourth,
Laypeople and the like,
Wanderers, trainees, and nuns.

Venerable one, if a monk, intending to dedicate a robe of less than one cubit to the Saṅgha, dedicates it to himself and the robe is thereby actually obtained — what results? It is a minor offense. However, if it is a robe of a full square cubit or larger, it entails a defeat.

Venerable one, is there a case where a monk, intending to dedicate a gain to the Saṅgha yet dedicating it to himself, does not incur a defeat? Upāli: Yes, there is. Namely, when the material of the robe is suitable but the seam is not; when the seam is suitable but the material is not; or when both are unsuitable. As for both being unsuitable — wool from a she-goat, wool from a cow, wool from a goat, wool from a wild animal, mixed wool, or wool that has not been woven: if one dedicates such a robe to oneself and it is actually obtained, it is a minor offense.

Venerable one, does it entail a defeat if a monk receives a robe from his father and mother? Upāli: Yes, it does — specifically, if the father and mother knowingly dedicated it to the Saṅgha and the monk then dedicates it to himself, that entails a defeat.

Venerable one, if a robe is solicited before full ordination and obtained before full ordination — what results? It is a minor offense. If solicited before full ordination and obtained in the course of receiving full ordination — what results? It is a minor offense. If solicited before full ordination and obtained after full ordination — what results? It is a minor offense. If solicited in the course of receiving full ordination and obtained in the course of receiving full ordination — what results? It is a minor offense. If solicited in the course of receiving full ordination and obtained after full ordination — what results? It is a minor offense. If solicited after full ordination and obtained after full ordination — what results? It entails a defeat. If solicited after full ordination and obtained before full ordination — what results? It is a minor offense.

Venerable one, if a monk, intending to dedicate a gain to the Saṅgha, perceives it as dedicated and yet dedicates it to himself — what results? It entails a defeat. If he perceives something dedicated as not dedicated, there is no offense. If he perceives something not dedicated as dedicated, it is a minor offense. If he perceives something not dedicated as not dedicated and then obtains it, there is no offense.

Venerable one, if a monk, intending to dedicate a gain to the Saṅgha, dedicates it to himself, and then changes his ordination status and becomes a nun, and only then obtains it — what results? It entails a defeat. Venerable one, if a nun, intending to dedicate a gain to the Saṅgha, dedicates it to herself, and then changes her ordination status and becomes a monk, and only then obtains it — what results? It entails a defeat.

Venerable one, if a monk dedicates a gain to a layman for himself, and that gain is thereby actually obtained — what results? It is a minor offense. Likewise, the same applies in the following cases: a eunuch, an androgyne, a nun who has been expelled, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who with malicious intent has drawn the blood of a Tathāgata, a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika), one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, a thief, one dwelling separately, one not residing in the community, one who has drawn near to departure, one who has previously committed an offense, one who has previously caused conflict, and one to whom the precepts have been administered — if a monk dedicates a gain to any of these for himself and that gain is actually obtained, it is a minor offense.

Venerable one, if a monk dedicates a gain belonging to beings residing elsewhere to himself, and that gain is thereby actually obtained — what results? It is a minor offense.

Venerable one, if a monk dedicates a gain belonging to the Saṅgha to himself — intending to dedicate it to the Saṅgha yet dedicating it to himself — and that gain is actually obtained, what results? It is to be relinquished.

Venerable one, if a monk dedicates to himself a gain that was dedicated to two monks or to many monks, and that gain is actually obtained, what results? It is a minor offense.

If a monk dedicates to himself a gain that was dedicated to the community of monks, or to the community of nuns, or to both communities, and that gain is actually obtained, what results? It is to be relinquished.

Venerable one, if a monk dedicates to himself a gain that was dedicated to a nun, or to a nun in probationary training, or to a female novice, or to male novices, and that gain is actually obtained, what results? It is a minor offense.

Likewise, if a nun in probationary training dedicates to herself a gain that was dedicated to a monk, or to a nun, or to a nun in probationary training, or to a female novice, or to male novices, and that gain is actually obtained, what results? It is a minor offense.

In the same way, for a nun in probationary training, a male novice, and a female novice, the minor offense should also be set forth in full.

In summary, as with the improper and the fourth —
seeking what is lost, in just that same way —
that itself and the seventh arise:
unconsecrated and consecrated.

Then the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if medicine kept beyond seven days is to be relinquished. But, venerable one, is there a case in which medicine kept beyond seven days is not to be relinquished?"

Upāli, there is. It is medicine that has become improper — that is, medicine mixed with what is improper, or medicine that monks are not permitted to use.

"Venerable one, if a monk obtains medicine, and once seven days have passed he perceives that seven days have passed, and then dawn breaks, what results?" It is to be relinquished.

"If seven days have passed and he perceives them as not yet passed, there is no offense. If seven days have not yet passed and he perceives them as seven days, it is a minor offense. If seven days have not yet passed and he perceives them as not yet passed, and dawn breaks, there is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk loses medicine that is to be relinquished, should he confess the transgression or not?"

Upāli, he should confess it.

"If after confessing the transgression he again obtains it, should it be relinquished?"

Upāli, it should not.

"Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk may keep medicine for as long as he lives without it needing to be relinquished?"

Upāli, there is — when it has been timed before the seven days are complete.

"Venerable one, if a monk obtains medicine and seven days pass, or more than seven days pass, and in that interval he changes status and becomes a nun, what results?" It is to be relinquished.

"Venerable one, if a nun obtains medicine and seven days pass, or more than seven days pass, and in that interval she changes status and becomes a monk, what results?" It is to be relinquished.

"Venerable one, is there a case in which that same medicine is to be relinquished and yet that same medicine is also actually relinquished?"

Upāli, there is — as when a monk's medicine has exceeded seven days and the time too has elapsed.

"Venerable one, if medicine is obtained before full ordination and seven days pass before full ordination, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If obtained before full ordination and seven days pass at the moment of full ordination, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If obtained before full ordination and seven days pass after full ordination, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If obtained at the moment of full ordination and seven days pass at the moment of full ordination, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If obtained at the moment of full ordination and seven days pass after full ordination, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If obtained after full ordination and seven days pass after full ordination, what results?" It is to be relinquished.

"If obtained at the moment of full ordination and seven days pass before full ordination, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk obtains medicine and seven days have passed and he then becomes mentally disturbed, from what point should the seven days be counted?" From the moment when his mind returns to normal.

"Venerable one, is it permitted for a monk to take medicine that has not been received and blessed — whether it is medicine for the morning period, medicine for the afternoon period, medicine for seven days, or medicine for as long as life lasts — and, claiming it as his own, to use it freely?" Upāli answered: "It is not permitted."

"In any case, if a monk has received that medicine at the time of the morning period, he may use it during the morning period. If he has received it at the time of the afternoon period, he may use it during the afternoon period. If the allotted time has passed, he may not use it."

"If it goes past the time, what results?" It is to be relinquished.

"Venerable one, if a monk seeks out or blesses medicine that has already been relinquished, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk has received and blessed medicine that is for the morning period, the afternoon period, for seven days, or for as long as life lasts — is he permitted to use it?" Upāli answered: "He is permitted. Morning medicine is to be used in the morning; if the morning period has passed, it may not be used. Afternoon medicine is to be used in the afternoon; if the afternoon period has passed, it may not be used. Seven-day medicine is to be used within seven days; if seven days have passed, it may not be used. Medicine for as long as life lasts may be used for as long as life lasts."

"If he uses it beyond those limits, what results?" Using what has been relinquished incurs a downfall.

"Venerable one, if he blesses it anew after that, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if, having been given a training rule, a monk lets medicine pass the seven-day limit, what results?" It is to be relinquished.

"Venerable one, if a fully ordained nun lets medicine pass the seven-day limit, what results?" It is to be relinquished.

"For female probationers, female novices, and male novices, it should be stated that they incur a minor offense."

The offenses entailing relinquishment are complete.

In summary: conveying a message by messenger, letter, hand gesture, by having another say it, from one to the next, becoming insane, mental disturbance, affliction by illness, being deaf, being mentally impaired, fallen asleep, struck dumb, intoxicated, in meditative absorption — those in transit are the last.

The venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that lying knowingly incurs a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk lies through a messenger, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Likewise through a letter, through a hand gesture, by having another say it, and by passing it from one to the next — what results in each case?" The same applies to all of these.

"Venerable one, if a monk lies to a madman, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Likewise, if he lies to one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is mentally impaired, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one who is struck dumb, one who is intoxicated, one in meditative absorption, or one who is residing elsewhere — in all such cases it is a minor offense."

In summary: solitude, language, the fourth case, a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika), one who does not speak, nighttime, the seventh case — likewise: the body, a student, and a nun.

"Venerable one, if a monk lies to a person in solitude, taking them for someone not in solitude, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a noble monk lies to a border-dweller in the noble language, and that border-dweller does not understand the noble language, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"If a noble monk lies to another noble person in the language of the border-dwellers, and that noble person does not understand the language of the border-dwellers, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"If a border-dweller lies to a noble person in the language of the border-dwellers, and that noble person does not understand the language of the border-dwellers, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"If a border-dweller lies to another border-dweller in the noble language, and that border-dweller does not understand the noble language, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a human being as a human being and lies to them, what results?" It is a downfall. "If he perceives a human being as a non-human, it becomes a minor offense. If he perceives a non-human as a human being, it becomes a minor offense. If he perceives a non-human as a non-human and lies, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk asks another monk, 'Who are you?' and that monk replies, 'I am a non-Buddhist adherent' — is this to be counted as relinquishing the training?" "No, Upāli. Because he knowingly spoke a lie, it becomes a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk asks another monk, 'Are you a non-Buddhist adherent?' and the other, by not speaking, acknowledges it by silence — what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk, while lying, undergoes a change of sex and becomes a nun, what results?" It becomes a downfall. "Venerable one, if a nun, while lying, undergoes a change of sex and becomes a monk, what results?" It is a downfall.

"Venerable one, if one who has not received full ordination intends to lie and speaks to one who has not received full ordination, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one who has not received full ordination intends to lie and speaks to one who is in the process of receiving full ordination, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one who has not received full ordination intends to lie, and then, upon becoming fully ordained, speaks, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one who is in the process of receiving full ordination intends to lie and speaks to one in the process of receiving full ordination, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one who is in the process of receiving full ordination intends to lie and speaks to one who is fully ordained, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one who is fully ordained intends to lie and speaks while fully ordained, what results?" It is a downfall. "If one who is fully ordained intends to lie and speaks before full ordination is complete, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk asks another monk, 'Did you see such-and-such a thing?' and that monk, though not having seen it, says, 'I saw it by means of a bodily sign' — what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if one who has given up the training lies, what results?" It becomes a downfall. "Venerable one, if a nun lies, what results?" It is a downfall. For female trainees (śikṣamāṇā), novice nuns, and male novices, it is a minor offense.

In brief:
By messenger, letter, gesture,
by quoting another, by relay from one to the next,
one who has become insane, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is ill, one who is mute, one who is simple-minded,
one who is asleep, one who is hiccupping,
one who is intoxicated, one who is in meditative absorption — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that speaking a human's fault incurs a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk speaks words of a human's fault by messenger, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Just as it is through a messenger, so too through a written letter, a hand-gesture, quoting another, and transmission from one to the next — all of these become minor offenses."

"Venerable one, if a monk speaks words of a human's fault to a madman, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Likewise, speaking words of a human's fault to one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is simple-minded, one who is mute, one who is dumb, one who is asleep, one who is hiccupping, one who is intoxicated, and one who is in meditative absorption — what results in all these cases?" In all cases it is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk speaks words of a human's fault to someone dwelling in another destiny, what results?" It is a minor offense.

In brief:
Speech, body, and similarly solitude,
characteristics, the fourth and the seventh,
laypeople and the rest —
giving up the training, and the nun.

"Venerable one, if a noble monk speaks words of a human's fault to a border-dweller in the noble language, and that border-dweller does not understand the noble language, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a noble monk speaks words of a human's fault to a noble one in the border-dweller's language, and that noble one does not understand the border-dweller's language, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"If a border-dweller speaks words of a human's fault to a noble one in the border-dweller's language, and that noble one also does not understand the border-dweller's language, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"If a border-dweller speaks words of a human's fault to another border-dweller in the noble language, and that border-dweller also does not understand the noble language, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk speaks words of a human's fault while directing his attention through the body, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a secluded place as unsecluded and speaks words of a human's fault, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk speaks words of a human's fault to another monk, and in the midst of speaking undergoes a change of gender and becomes a nun, what results?" It is a downfall.

"Venerable one, if a nun speaks words of a human's fault to another nun, and in the midst of speaking undergoes a change of gender and becomes a monk, what results?" It is a downfall.

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a fully ordained person as fully ordained and speaks words of a human's fault, what results?" It is a downfall. "If he perceives a fully ordained person as not fully ordained, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If he perceives a not fully ordained person as fully ordained, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If he perceives a not fully ordained person as not fully ordained, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a human as a human and speaks words of a human's fault, what results?" It is a downfall. "If he perceives a human as a non-human, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If he perceives a non-human as a human, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If he perceives a non-human as a non-human, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk intends to speak words of a human's fault to someone not fully ordained and speaks to someone not fully ordained, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If he intends to speak to someone not fully ordained and speaks to someone in the process of receiving full ordination, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If he intends to speak to someone not fully ordained and speaks to someone who has just completed full ordination, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If he intends to speak to someone in the process of receiving full ordination and speaks to someone in the process of receiving full ordination, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If he intends to speak to someone in the process of receiving full ordination and speaks to someone who has just completed full ordination, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If he intends to speak to a fully ordained person and speaks to one who has just completed full ordination, what results?" It is a downfall. "If he intends to speak to a fully ordained person and speaks to someone not fully ordained, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk speaks words of a human's fault to a layperson, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Venerable one, if a monk speaks words of a human's fault to a paṇḍaka, what results?" It is a minor offense.
