Likewise, if words of a human's fault are spoken to any of the following — a nun who has been expelled, one who has killed her father, one who has killed her mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a non-Buddhist adherent, one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, one who dwells as a thief, one who is unsettled in conduct, one who does not abide, one who dwells separately, one who was previously in dispute, or one against whom an offense was previously brought — in all such cases it is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk speaks words of a human's fault to monks who have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, who have taken their side, or to monks who have been given a formal ruling, what results?" It is a downfall. "Venerable one, if one who has been given a formal ruling speaks words of a human's fault, what results?" It is a downfall.

"Venerable one, if a monk speaks words of a human's fault to a nun, a female probationer, a female novice, or male novices, what results?"

In all such cases it is a minor offense. "Venerable one, if a nun speaks words of a human's fault to another nun, what results?" It is a downfall. "If a nun speaks words of a human's fault to a monk, a female probationer, a male novice, or a female novice, in all such cases it is a minor offense."

The minor offenses pertaining to a female probationer, a female novice, and male novices should be stated in full in the same way. Just as the full treatment was given for speaking words of a human's fault, so too should the full treatment be given for slander.

In brief:

By voice, by body, by isolation,
by the marks, by the fourth, and by the seventh,
and in relation to laypeople and others —
the last of the trainings given is this.

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk who has sought to settle a dispute in the Saṅgha in accordance with the rule is subsequently subjected to a formal act, it is a downfall. Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk who has properly settled a dispute in accordance with the rule and is then subjected to a formal act does not incur a downfall?" Upāli, there is. In any case where those who previously committed an offense, or who were previously parties to a dispute, or who are not in good standing, settle a dispute in accordance with the rule and are subsequently subjected to a formal act — that is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, when a dispute has been properly settled in accordance with the rule, and a noble monk subsequently subjects the one who settled it to a formal act using the language of a noble one, and that monk who subjected him to the act did not seek to use the language of a noble one, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"When a dispute has been properly settled in accordance with the rule, and a noble monk subjects the one who settled it to a formal act using the language of a border monk, and that noble monk likewise did not seek to use the language of a border monk, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"When a dispute has been properly settled in accordance with the rule, and a border monk subjects the noble one who settled it to a formal act using the language of a border monk, and that noble monk likewise did not seek to use the language of a border monk, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"When a dispute has been properly settled in accordance with the rule, and a border monk is subsequently subjected to a formal act by another border monk using the language of a noble one, and that border monk likewise did not seek to use the language of a noble one, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, when a monk has properly settled a dispute in accordance with the rule and is subsequently subjected to a formal act based on a charge, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, when a monk who has sought to settle a dispute in the Saṅgha in accordance with the rule is subjected to a formal act, perceiving what is settled as unsettled, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, when a monk is in the process of enacting a formal act against one who has properly settled a dispute in accordance with the rule, and in the meanwhile that monk changes his status and becomes a nun, what results?" It is a downfall.

"Venerable one, when a nun is in the process of enacting a formal act against one who is in the process of properly settling a dispute in accordance with the rule, and in the meanwhile that nun changes her status and becomes a monk, what results?" It is a downfall.

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a properly settled dispute as properly settled, and the one who settled it is subsequently subjected to a formal act, what results?" It is a downfall. "If what was properly settled is perceived as not properly settled, and the one who settled it is subsequently subjected to a formal act, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If what was not properly settled is perceived as properly settled, and the one who settled it is subsequently subjected to a formal act, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If what was not properly settled is perceived as not properly settled, and the one who settled it is subsequently subjected to a formal act, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives one who has received full ordination as fully ordained, and that monk is subsequently subjected to a formal act for settling a dispute in accordance with the rule, what results?" It is a downfall. "If one who has received full ordination is perceived as not fully ordained, and that monk is subsequently subjected to a formal act for settling a dispute in accordance with the rule, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"If one who has not received full ordination is perceived as fully ordained, and a dispute settled in accordance with the rule is subsequently subjected to a formal act, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one who has not received full ordination is perceived as not fully ordained, and a dispute settled in accordance with the rule is subsequently subjected to a formal act, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Venerable one, if a monk prepares to subject to a formal act one who has not received full ordination and who has settled a dispute in accordance with the rule, and then makes that person out to be not fully ordained, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one is prepared as not fully ordained but turns out to be fully ordained, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one is prepared as not fully ordained and one is indeed not fully ordained, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one is prepared as fully ordained and turns out to be fully ordained, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one is prepared as fully ordained and one is indeed fully ordained, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one who is fully ordained is prepared as such and is indeed fully ordained, what results?" It is a downfall. "If one who is fully ordained is prepared as such but turns out not to be fully ordained, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk subjects to a formal act the properly settled dispute of a layperson, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Venerable one, if a monk subjects to a formal act the properly settled dispute of one who is any of the following: a hermaphrodite, a person of indeterminate sex, a person of dual sex, a nun who has been expelled, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent drew blood from a Tathāgata, one who is a non-Buddhist adherent, one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, one who dwells in a forbidden place, one who is not a resident, one who was previously the cause of a dispute, or one who previously committed an offense — if the dispute of any such person has been properly settled in accordance with the rule and is then subjected to a formal act, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk subjects to a formal act a dispute that has been properly settled in accordance with the rule involving those who have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, those who have sided with schismatics, or those who have relinquished their training, what results?" It is a downfall.

In brief:
By message, by letter, by gesture,
by having another speak, or from one to another,
by one disturbed in mind, by the sick,
by the deaf-mute, and by travelers.

"Venerable one, if a monk subjects to a formal act a monk's dispute that has been properly settled in accordance with the rule, doing so through a message, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Likewise, by letter, by gesture, by having another speak, or by relaying from one to another — all of these are minor offenses."

"Venerable one, if a monk subjects to a formal act a dispute that has been properly settled in accordance with the rule and that involved a mad person, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Likewise, if settled disputes involving one disturbed in mind, one afflicted by illness, one who is stupid, one who is mute, one who is deaf-mute, or one who dwells elsewhere — if any of these are subsequently subjected to a formal act, all constitute minor offenses."

"Venerable one, if a monk subjects to a formal act a dispute among nuns that has been properly settled in accordance with the rule, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If it is done by a probationer nun, a novice nun, or male novices, all constitute minor offenses. If a nun subjects another nun to a formal act of the nuns' assembly, it is a downfall. If a nun subjects to such an act male novices, probationer nuns, or novice nuns, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if one who has relinquished the training subjects to a formal act a dispute that has been properly settled in accordance with the rule, what results?" It is a downfall. "As for probationer nuns, novice nuns, and male novices, each case should be explained in full as a minor offense."

In brief:
By message, by letter, by gesture,
by having another speak, or from one to another,
by one who has become mad, by one disturbed in mind,
by the sick, the deaf-mute, the stupid,
by one asleep, by one stupefied, by one intoxicated,
by one in meditative absorption, by a traveler — these are the last.

Thus did the venerable Upāli ask the Blessed One, the Buddha.

"Venerable one, the Blessed One declared that if a monk teaches Dharma to a woman without a knowledgeable man present, speaking more than five or six words, it becomes a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk teaches Dharma to a woman by message, without a knowledgeable man present, speaking more than five or six words, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Likewise for letter, for gesture, for having another speak, and for one to another in relay."

"Venerable one, if a monk teaches Dharma to a mad woman without a knowledgeable man present, speaking more than five or six words, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Likewise for one disturbed in mind, one afflicted by illness, a foolish woman, a mute woman, a deaf woman, one lying asleep, one stupefied, one intoxicated, one in meditative absorption, and one dwelling in a distant place — in all such cases it becomes a minor offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk teaches Dharma to a woman with a knowledgeable man who is mad present, speaking more than five or six words, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Likewise for a man disturbed in mind, one afflicted by illness, a foolish man, a mute man, a deaf man, one lying asleep, one intoxicated, one in meditative absorption, a blind man, a border-dweller, and one dwelling in a distant place — in all such cases, with such a knowledgeable man present, teaching Dharma to a woman becomes a minor offense in every case."

In brief:
By speech, by body, by seclusion,
and likewise with a eunuch or an intersex attendant,
the third point and the fourth in the same way —
these apply to the probationer nun and to the fully ordained nun.

"Venerable one, if a noble monk teaches Dharma to a woman in the noble language, speaking more than five or six words without a knowledgeable man present, and that woman too does not know the noble language, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If a noble monk teaches Dharma to a woman in a border language without a knowledgeable man present, speaking more than five or six words, and that woman too does not know the border language, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If a border-dweller teaches Dharma to a woman in a border language without a knowledgeable man present, speaking more than five or six words, and that woman too does not know the border language, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If a border-dweller teaches Dharma to a woman in the noble language without a knowledgeable man present, speaking more than five or six words, and that woman too does not know the noble language, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a noble monk, together with an attendant who is a border-dweller, teaches Dharma to a woman in the noble language, speaking more than five or six words, and that attendant too does not know the noble language, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Likewise, if a noble monk teaches Dharma in the noble language with a border-dwelling attendant present, it becomes a minor offense. If a border-dweller teaches Dharma in a border language together with a noble attendant, it becomes a minor offense. If a border-dweller teaches Dharma to a woman in the noble language with a border-dwelling attendant present, speaking more than five or six words, and that attendant too does not know the noble language, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk teaches Dharma to a woman, speaking more than five or six words, with only a bodily gesture as the means of indication, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a secluded place as secluded, teaches Dharma to a woman, speaking more than five or six words, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Venerable one, if a monk teaches Dharma to a woman together with an attendant who is an intersex person, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Likewise, if he teaches Dharma to a woman together with a eunuch attendant or a two-gendered attendant, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Venerable one, if a monk teaches Dharma to an intersex person without a knowledgeable man present, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk is teaching Dharma to a woman, speaking more than five or six words, and his sex changes so that he becomes a nun, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Venerable one, if a nun is teaching Dharma to a man, speaking more than five or six words, and her sex changes so that she becomes a monk, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a woman as a woman and teaches her Dharma speaking more than five or six words, what results?" It is a transgression (āpatti). "If he perceives a woman as not a woman, there is no offense." "If he perceives a non-woman as a woman, it is a minor offense." "If he perceives a non-woman as a non-woman and teaches Dharma speaking more than five or six words, there is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a human woman as a human woman and teaches her Dharma speaking more than five or six words, what results?" It is a transgression. "If he perceives a human as a non-human, it is a minor offense." "If he perceives a non-human as a human, it is a minor offense." "If he perceives a non-human as a non-human, it is a minor offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives the attendant man as a man and teaches Dharma to the woman, what results?" There is no offense. "If he perceives the man as not a man and teaches Dharma, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If he perceives a non-man as a man and teaches Dharma, what results?" There is no offense. "If he perceives a non-man as a non-man and teaches Dharma, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if one who has been given a training rule teaches Dharma to a woman speaking more than five or six words, what results?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, if a nun teaches Dharma to a man speaking more than five or six words, what results?" It is a transgression. For female probationers (śikṣamāṇā), novice nuns, and novice monks, the offense is to be explained as a minor offense in each case.

In summary, as verse:

One who has gone mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is ill, one who is deaf and mute, and one journeying away —
likewise a layman in the matter of words,
and the same applies to a nun.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk reads Dharma in unison, word for word, with a person not fully ordained, it becomes a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk reads Dharma in unison, word for word, with a mad person, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Likewise, with one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is simple-minded, one who is mute, one who is deaf, and in the same way with one residing elsewhere" — reading Dharma in unison with all of these is a minor offense in each case.

"Venerable one, if a monk reads Dharma in unison, word for word, with a layman, what results?" It is a transgression. "If he reads Dharma in unison with an intersex person or a eunuch, what results?" It is a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk reads Dharma in unison, word for word, with a nun who has been expelled, or with one who has killed her father or mother, or has killed an arhat, or with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata, or with a tīrthika or with one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, or with one suspended from the community or formally separated, or with one who has previously committed offenses, or with those who had previously caused a dispute — what results?" It is a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk reads Dharma in unison, word for word, with one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, or with one who has sided with such a person, or with one who has been given a training rule, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"If a noble one reads Dharma in the noble language in unison with a monk, and that monk has not mastered the noble language, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If a noble one reads Dharma in a border language in unison with a monk, and that monk has not mastered the border language, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If a border person reads Dharma in a border language in unison with a monk, and —"

that monk too has not mastered the border language, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If a border person reads Dharma in the noble language in unison with a monk, and that monk too has not mastered the noble language, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk reads Dharma in unison with a person who has not received full ordination, and during that recitation that person's name changes and they become a nun, what results?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, if a nun reads Dharma in unison with a person who has not received full ordination, and during that recitation that person's name changes and they become a monk, what results?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk or a nun reads Dharma in unison with a person who has not received full ordination, and that unordained person also changes their name during the recitation, what results?" It is a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives an unordained person as unordained and reads Dharma in unison with them, what results?" It is a transgression. "If one perceives an unordained person as fully ordained, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one perceives a fully ordained person as unordained, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one perceives a fully ordained person as fully ordained and reads with them, what results?" There is no offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a human as a human and reads with them, what results?" It is a transgression. "If one perceives a human as a non-human and reads with them, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one perceives a non-human as a human, what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one perceives a non-human as a non-human, what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if one reads Dharma in unison with a nun, what results?" It is a minor offense. If one reads Dharma in unison with a female trainee or a female novice, in every case it is a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a nun reads Dharma in unison with a person who has not received full ordination, what results?" It is a transgression. If a nun and a monk read Dharma in unison, it is a minor offense. If she reads in unison with a female trainee, a female novice, male novices, a female trainee, or female novices, it is a transgression. If she reads with a female trainee, a female novice, or male novices, it is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if one who has been given a training rule reads Dharma in unison with a person who has not received full ordination, what results?" It is a transgression.

The sacred Vinaya text, the sixth fascicle. In brief:

By messenger, by letter, by gesture,
by having another say it, by relay from one to the next —
one who has become mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is deaf or dull-witted, one who is asleep,
one who is in a swoon, one who is intoxicated,
one who has entered absorption, one who is traveling — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that a monk who, apart from one who has been granted a vow by the Saṅgha, communicates a serious transgression to a person who has not received full ordination incurs a transgression. If a monk communicates a serious transgression to an unordained person by means of a messenger, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Likewise, if it is communicated by letter, by gesture, by having another convey it, or by relay from one to the next — in every case it is a minor offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk communicates a serious transgression to a madperson, what results?" It is a minor offense. "Likewise, if it is communicated to one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is deaf, one who is in a swoon, one who is asleep, one who is in a stupor, one who is intoxicated, one who has entered absorption, or one who resides in another abode — in every case it is a minor offense."

In brief:

By word, by body, and by solitude, in just that way;
the fourth — the name — likewise;
the appointed one and the seventh — oneself;
laypeople and nuns.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha:

"Venerable one, if a fully ordained monk speaks of a transgression involving a defeat to a borderer in the noble language, and that borderer does not understand the noble language — what results?" It is a minor offense. "If a noble one speaks to a noble one in the language of the borderer, and that noble one does not understand the language of the borderers — what results?" It is a minor offense. "If a borderer speaks to a noble one in the language of the borderers, and that noble one does not understand the language of the borderers — what results?" It is a minor offense. "If a borderer speaks to a borderer in the noble language, and that borderer does not understand the noble language — what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk communicates a transgression involving a defeat through a bodily gesture — what results?" It is a minor offense. "Venerable one, if one who is in solitude is perceived as not being in solitude, and a transgression involving a defeat is communicated — what results?" It is a minor offense. "Venerable one, if a monk speaks of a transgression involving a defeat to one who is not fully ordained, perceiving that person as not fully ordained — what results?" It is a downfall. "If one speaks perceiving one who is not fully ordained as fully ordained — what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one speaks perceiving one who is fully ordained as fully ordained — there is no offense." "If one speaks perceiving one who is fully ordained as not fully ordained — what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk speaks of a transgression involving a defeat to a human being, perceiving that person as a human being — what results?" It will be a downfall. "If one speaks perceiving a human being as not a human being — what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one speaks perceiving a non-human being as a human being — what results?" It is a minor offense. "If one speaks perceiving a non-human being as a non-human being — what results?" It is a minor offense.

"Venerable one, if a monk is in the midst of communicating a transgression involving a defeat to one who is not fully ordained, and in the interval that person becomes a fully ordained nun — what results?" It will be a downfall. "Venerable one, if a fully ordained nun is in the midst of communicating a transgression involving a defeat to a person who is not fully ordained, and in the interval that person becomes a fully ordained monk — what results?" It will be a downfall.

"Venerable one, since the Blessed One has declared that if a monk speaks of a transgression involving a defeat to one who is not fully ordained, except when authorized by the Saṅgha, it becomes a downfall — venerable one, is it possible that a monk not appointed by the Saṅgha might speak of a transgression involving a defeat to one who is not fully ordained without incurring an offense?" Upāli replied: "Yes, there is such a case. There are four such persons. They are as follows.

"There is a person with respect to whom giving that reaches the end of transgression and also reaches the end of what is fitting is appropriate. There is a person with respect to whom giving that reaches the end of transgression but does not reach the end of what is fitting is appropriate. There is a person with respect to whom giving that reaches the end of what is fitting but does not reach the end of transgression is appropriate. And there is a person with respect to whom giving that reaches neither the end of transgression nor the end of what is fitting is appropriate.

"What is the giving that reaches the end of transgression and reaches the end of what is fitting? It is the case of one who, by means of a minor offense, has defiled many of the family line. What is the giving that reaches the end of transgression but does not reach the end of what is fitting? It is the case of one who, by means of a minor offense, has defiled the family line in numerous ways. What is the giving that reaches the end of what is fitting but does not reach the end of transgression? It is the case of one who, by means of a grave offense, has defiled only a few of the family line. And what is the giving that reaches neither the end of transgression nor the end of what is fitting? It is the case of one who, by means of a grave offense, has defiled many of the family line.

"With regard to a person for whom giving that reaches the end of transgression and the end of what is fitting is appropriate, one should inform that person individually of each transgression as many as there are and of each line of the family as many as there are. To inform beyond that will be a downfall. With regard to a person for whom giving reaches the end of transgression but does not reach the end of what is fitting, one should inform that person of the transgressions as many as there are, and

one should inform that person individually of each line of the family as many as there are. To inform beyond that will be a downfall. With regard to a person for whom giving reaches the end of what is fitting in the family line but does not reach the end of transgression, one should not inform that person of all the transgressions one by one according to each line of the family as many as there are. To inform beyond that will be a downfall. With regard to a person for whom giving reaches neither the end of transgression nor the end of what is fitting in the family line, one should inform that person of all the transgressions and of each line of the family as many as there are individually, and in so doing there is no downfall.

Venerable one, if one who has not received full ordination prepares to speak of a matter involving a base offense to a person who has not received full ordination, and it is accomplished without full ordination, what results? A wrongdoing. If one prepares to speak to one who has not received full ordination and it is accomplished just as full ordination is being conferred, what results? A wrongdoing. If one prepares to speak to one who has not received full ordination and it is accomplished after full ordination has been received, what results? A wrongdoing. If one prepares to speak just as full ordination is being conferred and it is accomplished just as full ordination is being conferred, what results? A wrongdoing. If one prepares to speak just as full ordination is being conferred and it is accomplished after full ordination has been received, what results? A wrongdoing. If one prepares to speak after full ordination has been received and it is accomplished after full ordination has been received, what results? A downfall. If one prepares to speak after full ordination has been received and it is accomplished before full ordination is complete, what results? A wrongdoing.

Venerable one, if a monk speaks of his own matter involving a base offense to one who has not received full ordination, what results? A wrongdoing. If a monk speaks of a monk's matter involving a base offense to a nun, what results? A wrongdoing. Likewise, if one speaks to a paṇḍaka, a female paṇḍaka, or a hermaphrodite, all of these are wrongdoings. If a monk speaks of a monk's matter involving a base offense to a nun who has been expelled, what results? A downfall. Likewise, if one speaks to one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has shed blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent, a non-Buddhist adherent, one who has gone over to the non-Buddhist adherents, one who is abiding as a thief, one who has no standing in the community, one who is abiding separately, one who has previously caused a schism, or one who has previously committed an offense, all of these are downfalls. If a monk speaks of a monk's matter involving a base offense to a monk or nun who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, who has sided with the schism, or who has relinquished the training, all of these are wrongdoings. If one speaks to a probationer nun, a novice nun, or a male novice, all of these are downfalls.

If a fully ordained nun speaks of a nun's matter involving a base offense to one who has not received full ordination, what results? A downfall. If a monk speaks of it to a fully ordained nun, what results? A wrongdoing. If one speaks to a probationer nun, a novice nun, or a male novice, all of these are downfalls.

Venerable one, if one who has given the training speaks of a matter involving a base offense to one who has not received full ordination, what results? A downfall. Likewise, with regard to a probationer nun, a novice nun, and male novices, all should be stated extensively as wrongdoings.

If one states rightly the Dharma of one who has become a teacher surpassing human beings, excepting only the declaration "The Buddha is the Teacher," this is to be distinguished progressively from the statement of a root defeat.

In summary:

By message, letter, gesture,
and through another, or from one to the next,
one who has become mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is ill, one who is possessed, one who is confused,
one who is asleep, one who is rambling, one who is intoxicated,
one who is entering absorption, one who is in the final destiny —

This was asked of the Blessed One, the Buddha, by the venerable Upāli.

The Blessed One declared: if a monk who had previously given his consent later says, "Venerable one, the Saṅgha's gain has been dedicated to such and such a dear person," that constitutes a transgression.

The venerable Upāli asked: if a monk conveys by messenger the words "Venerable one, the Saṅgha's gain has been dedicated to such and such a dear person," what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if done by letter, by gesture, through another's words, or passed along from one to the next — all of these are wrongdoings.

If a monk says to one who is mad, "Venerable one, the Saṅgha's gain has been dedicated to such and such a dear person," what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if said to one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is bewildered, one who is possessed, one who is dull, one who is asleep, one who is intoxicated, one who has entered absorption, or one who abides in another destiny — if to any of these one says, "Venerable one, the Saṅgha's gain has been dedicated to such and such a dear person," all of these are wrongdoings.

In summary:

By voice and body, by solitude,
by mark and the fourth and the seventh,
a householder who is unfit, one of minor status,
and a nun — these are the last as regards gain.

If a noble monk speaks to another monk in the noble language, saying, "Venerable one, the Saṅgha's gain has been dedicated to such and such a dear person," and that monk does not understand the noble language, what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing. If a noble monk speaks to another monk in a border language, saying the same, and that monk does not understand the border language, what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing. If one who speaks a border language speaks to another monk in a border language, and that noble monk does not understand the border language, what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing. If one who speaks a border language speaks to another monk in the noble language, saying the same, and that monk does not understand the noble language, what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing.

If a monk makes the words "Venerable one, the Saṅgha's gain has been dedicated to such and such a dear person" understood through a bodily indication, what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing. If a monk, perceiving what is not secluded as secluded, says, "Venerable one, the Saṅgha's gain has been dedicated to such and such a dear person," what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing.

If a monk says, "Venerable one, the Saṅgha's gain has been dedicated to such and such a dear person," and in the course of his speaking his status changes and he becomes a nun, what is the outcome? It is a transgression. If a nun says the same, and in the course of her speaking her status changes and she becomes a monk, what is the outcome? It is a transgression.

If a monk, perceiving a fully ordained person as fully ordained, says, "Venerable one, the Saṅgha's gain has been dedicated to such and such a dear person," what is the outcome? It is a transgression. If he perceives a fully ordained person as not fully ordained and says the same, what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing. If he perceives a person who is not fully ordained as fully ordained and says the same, what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing. If he perceives a person who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained and says the same, what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing.

If a person who is not fully ordained perceives another who is not fully ordained as such, and says, "Venerable one, the Saṅgha's gain has been dedicated to such and such a dear person," what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing. If a person who is not fully ordained perceives a fully ordained person as such and says the same, what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing. If a person who is not fully ordained perceives a fully ordained person as such and then says the same after full ordination, what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing. If one who perceives a fully ordained person as fully ordained says the same while not yet fully ordained, what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing. If one who perceives a fully ordained person as fully ordained says the same after becoming fully ordained, what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing. If a fully ordained person perceives a fully ordained person as such and says those words, what is the outcome? It is a transgression. If a fully ordained person perceives a fully ordained person as such but the words are spoken by one not fully ordained, what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing.

If a monk says to a layperson, "Venerable one, the Saṅgha's gain has been dedicated to such and such a dear person," what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing.

Likewise, if such words are said with regard to a woman, a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, one who has killed a father, one who has killed a mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused a schism among nuns, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a non-Buddhist adherent, one who has gone over to non-Buddhist adherents, one who remains in a state of theft, one who does not remain in good standing, one who resides separately, one who has previously committed an offense, or one who has previously caused a dispute — in all such cases, what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing.

If a monk says to those who are drawing near to the training and to those who have been given the precepts, "Venerable one, the Saṅgha's gain has been dedicated to such and such a dear person," what is the outcome? It is a transgression.

Is there any case in which a monk may say, "Venerable one, the Saṅgha's gain has been dedicated to such and such a dear person," and yet it does not become a transgression? Upāli, there is. In any case in which the material for a robe is suitable but the distribution is not suitable, or the distribution is suitable but the material is not suitable, or both are not suitable — and unsuitability means cloth made from the wool of a female sheep, wool of a cow, wool of a goat, wool of a deer, mixed wool, unspun fiber, or similar materials not fit to be robe material — if those words are spoken on account of such goods, it becomes a wrongdoing.

If the Saṅgha obtains a robe of unmeasured length that has not yet been requested, and then a monk, having first obtained consent, subsequently says, "Venerable one, the Saṅgha's gain has been dedicated to such and such a dear person," what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing.

If a monk speaks those words with regard to gains other than gains of robes, what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing.

If the Saṅgha has given a robe to a certain monk without his being present, and he subsequently comes forward and says, "Venerable one, the Saṅgha's gain has been dedicated to such and such a dear person," what is the outcome? It is a wrongdoing.

If one who has been given the precepts speaks those words, what is the outcome? It is a transgression. If a nun speaks those words, it is likewise a transgression. If a female trainee, a male novice, or a female novice says, "Venerable one, the Saṅgha's gain has been dedicated to such and such a dear person," it becomes a wrongdoing.

In brief:

By messenger, letter, or sign,
through another's voice, or one by one,
one who has gone mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is ill or incapacitated, one who is dull-witted,
one who is asleep, one who is delirious, one who is intoxicated,
one who has entered meditative absorption — these are the exceptions at the end.

Thus did the venerable Upāli present his questions to the Buddha, the Blessed One.

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that to mock a training rule is a downfall. If a monk mocks a training rule through a messenger, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. Likewise, through a letter, through a sign, through another's voice, or through transmission from one to another — all of these become wrongdoings.

"Venerable one, if a monk mocks a training rule in the presence of one who is mad, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. Likewise, in the presence of one whose mind is disturbed, one who is tormented by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is deaf, one who is mute, one who is asleep, one who is delirious, one who is intoxicated, one who has entered meditative absorption, or one who is dwelling elsewhere — if one mocks a training rule in the presence of any of these, it becomes a wrongdoing in every case.

In brief:

By voice, by body, in private,
likewise by sign, and the fourth case,
before a layperson and so forth, before an emanation,
before a training rule, and before a nun.

"Venerable one, if a noble monk (ārya) mocks a training rule before another monk in the noble language, and that monk does not understand the noble language, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. If a noble monk mocks a training rule before a monk in a border language, and that monk does not understand the border language, what does that become? It becomes a wrongdoing. If a border-region person mocks a training rule before a monk in a border language, and that monk does not understand the border language, what does that become? It becomes a wrongdoing. If a border-region person mocks a training rule before a monk in the noble language, and that monk does not understand the noble language, what does that become? It becomes a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk mocks a training rule by means of a bodily gesture, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk mocks a training rule by perceiving what is private as not private, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk, while mocking a training rule, changes his status and becomes a nun, what does that become?" It becomes a downfall. "Venerable one, if a nun, while mocking a training rule, changes her status and becomes a monk, what does that become?" It becomes a downfall.

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a fully ordained person as fully ordained and mocks a training rule in that person's presence, what does that become?" It becomes a downfall. If he perceives a fully ordained person as not fully ordained and mocks a training rule in that person's presence, what does that become? It becomes a wrongdoing. If he perceives a not-fully-ordained person as fully ordained and mocks a training rule in that person's presence, what does that become? It becomes a wrongdoing. If he perceives a not-fully-ordained person as not fully ordained and mocks a training rule in that person's presence, what does that become? It becomes a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk mocks a training rule in the presence of a layperson, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. In the presence of a pandaka, a person of indeterminate sex, a suspended nun, one who has killed his father or mother or an arhat, one who has shed the Tathāgata's blood with malicious intent, a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika), one who has gone over to non-Buddhist adherents, a thief in hiding, one who is not dwelling in the community, one who is dwelling separately, one against whom a prior offence has arisen, or one with whom there was prior conflict — if one mocks a training rule in the presence of any of these, it becomes a wrongdoing in every case.

"Venerable one, if a monk mocks a training rule in the presence of one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has sided with such a person, or one who has had training rules promulgated against him, what does that become?" All of these become wrongdoings.

"Venerable one, if a monk mocks a training rule in the presence of an emanation, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk mocks a training rule in the presence of a nun, a female trainee, a female novice, or a male novice, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. If a nun mocks a training rule in the presence of another nun, what does that become? It becomes a downfall. If a nun mocks a training rule in the presence of a monk, a female trainee, a female novice, or a male novice, what does that become? It becomes a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a female trainee mocks a training rule, what does that become?" It becomes a downfall. "In the presence of a male novice, a female novice, and a novice nun" — these become wrongdoings.

In brief:

An emanation body, stone dust,
roots, flowers, fish scales,
dwellings, mushrooms, old things,
flowers, fruits, bark,
signs, the fourth, the seventh,
and lastly, the fruit.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, you have taught that if one causes the destruction of a village of seeds or a village of living creatures, it is a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk fells a tree by means of supernormal power, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk fells a tree through bodily intention alone, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk chips away stone, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk pulls out a seed-substance that has not yet taken root, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk washes something mossy or something with mold on it, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk pulls fish scales from the mud and tosses them onto dry ground, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk destroys the dwelling of a living creature, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "If he burns it or renders it unfit, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk tears open, removes, or destroys a bird's nest, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk breaks off a mushroom or pulls up a mushroom, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk peels the bark from an old tree, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk plucks flowers, fruits, or old leaves, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk is cutting down a tree and it changes sex in the process and becomes a nun, what does that become?" It becomes a downfall. "Venerable one, if a nun is cutting down a tree and it changes sex in the process and becomes a monk, what does that become?" It becomes a downfall.

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a seed as a seed and makes it unfit by destroying it, what does that become?" It becomes a downfall. "If one perceives a seed as not a seed and makes it unfit, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "If one perceives what is not a seed as a seed, it becomes a wrongdoing. If one perceives what is not a seed as not a seed and destroys it, there is no transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who is not yet fully ordained prepares something intending to cut it, and cuts it while not yet fully ordained, what does that become?" There is no transgression. "If one who is not yet fully ordained prepares it, and cuts it just as full ordination occurs, what does that become?" There is no transgression. "If one who is not yet fully ordained prepares it, and cuts it after becoming fully ordained, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "If the preparation was done just at the time of full ordination, and the cutting is done just at the time of full ordination, what does that become?" There is no transgression. "If the preparation is done just at full ordination and the cutting is done after full ordination, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing. "If the preparation is done after full ordination and the cutting is done after full ordination, what does that become?" It becomes a downfall. "If the preparation is done at the time of full ordination and the cutting is done before full ordination, what does that become?" It becomes a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, is it possible for a monk to eat fruit that has not been made allowable and yet incur no transgression?" Upāli, yes — it is possible: if one thinks that an unripened seed is not a seed-substance and eats it.

"Venerable one, is it possible for a monk to make the five kinds of seeds allowable by fire and yet still incur a downfall?" Upāli, yes — it is possible: if one has made the five kinds of seeds allowable, but then places them in soil, or places them in a vessel, or lays them on a germinating board, and they sprout. If one then eats them, what does that become? It becomes a cause of downfall.

In brief:

A message, a letter, a hand-sign,

Relayed by another, passed from one to the next —
the mad, the mentally disturbed, the sick,
the mute, those who are absent,
and laypeople and the like:
those who have given up the training, and nuns.

Venerable one, if a monk orders a tree to be felled by means of a message, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Likewise, ordering it by a letter, a hand-sign, relay through another, or passing word from one to the next — all of these become offenses. Venerable one, if a monk orders a madman to fell a tree, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Likewise, causing one who is mentally disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is foolish, one who is mute, one who is deaf-mute, one who is absent, or one staying elsewhere to cut a tree — all of these become offenses. Venerable one, if a monk directly orders a layperson to fell a tree, what does that become? It becomes a downfall. Likewise, causing a woman of ambiguous gender, a hermaphrodite, a nun who has been expelled, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika), one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, a thief, one who does not belong to the community, one who belongs to a different community, one against whom an offense has previously arisen, one who was previously in dispute, one who has taken sides, or one who has given up the training — if any of these, directly and in person, is caused to fell a tree, all become offenses.

Venerable one, if one who has given up the training causes a green shoot to be destroyed or orders it to be destroyed, what does that become? It becomes a downfall. Venerable one, if a nun destroys a green shoot or orders it to be destroyed, what does that become? It becomes a downfall. Venerable one, if a nun causes a green shoot to be destroyed or orders it to be destroyed, what does that become? It becomes an offense. For novice monks and novice nuns there is no offense.

In brief:

By voice, by body, by private communication,
by sign, the fourth, and the seventh,
laypeople and the like —
those who are appointed and those who are not.

Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if one confesses an offense and imposes a penalty, one thereby incurs a downfall. Then is it possible for a monk to confess an offense and impose a penalty and yet not incur a downfall? Upāli, yes — it is possible: if one has gone forth from and received full ordination among non-humans and one confesses an offense, it becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a noble monk confesses an offense to a monk in the noble language and imposes a penalty, and that monk does not know the noble language, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If a noble monk confesses an offense to a monk in a border-region language and imposes a penalty, and that monk does not know the border-region language, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If a border-region monk confesses an offense to a monk in a border-region language and imposes a penalty, and that monk does not know the border-region language, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If a border-region monk confesses an offense to a monk in the noble language and imposes a penalty, and that monk does not know the noble language, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a monk confesses an offense and imposes a penalty by means of a bodily gesture, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a monk perceives a non-secluded place as secluded and then confesses an offense and imposes a penalty, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a monk is in the midst of confessing an offense and imposing a penalty, and in the interim his status changes and he becomes a nun, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a nun is in the midst of confessing an offense and imposing a penalty, and in the interim her status changes and she becomes a monk, what does that become? It becomes an offense.

Venerable one, if a monk perceives one who has received full ordination as fully ordained, and confesses an offense and imposes a penalty in that person's presence, what does that become? It becomes a transgression. If he perceives one who has received full ordination as not fully ordained, it becomes an offense. If he perceives one who has not received full ordination as fully ordained, it becomes an offense. If he perceives one who has not received full ordination as not fully ordained, it becomes an offense.

Venerable one, if one who has not received full ordination is counted by the Saṅgha as one before whom an offense may be confessed and a penalty imposed, and then an offense is confessed and a penalty imposed before that unordained person, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If one counted as not fully ordained is treated as fully ordained when the offense is confessed and the penalty imposed, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If one counted as not fully ordained is actually fully ordained when the offense is confessed and the penalty imposed, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If one counted as almost fully ordained is treated as almost fully ordained when the offense is confessed and the penalty imposed, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If one counted as almost fully ordained is actually fully ordained when the offense is confessed and the penalty imposed, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If one who is fully ordained is counted as such, and is actually fully ordained when the offense is confessed and the penalty imposed, what does that become? It becomes a transgression. If one counted as fully ordained is not yet fully ordained when the offense is confessed and the penalty imposed, what does that become? It becomes an offense.

Venerable one, if a monk confesses an offense and imposes a penalty before a layperson, what does that become? It becomes an offense.

Venerable one, if a monk confesses an offense and imposes a penalty before one who has committed any of the following: a monk who has caused a nun to disrobe, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent, a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika), one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, one who is living as a thief, one who is not in good standing, one who is in a separate standing, one before whom an offense has already occurred, or one before whom there has already been conflict — in all such cases it becomes an offense.

Venerable one, if a monk confesses an offense and imposes a penalty before one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has sided with such a schismatic, or one who has been given a formal training measure — in all such cases it becomes a transgression.

Venerable one, whether a monk has been appointed or not, if apart from one who is attending to the Saṅgha's affairs he confesses an offense and imposes a penalty before someone other than such a person, what does that become? It becomes an offense.

In brief:

Through messenger, written message, gesture,
through the word of another, or passed from one to the next,
before the mad, the mentally disturbed, the ailing,
the mute, the deaf, the sleeping,
the intoxicated from alcohol, the drunk,
or those in meditative absorption — these are the last cases.

Venerable one, if a monk confesses an offense and imposes a penalty through a messenger, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Likewise, through a written message, through a gesture, through the word of another, or passed from one to the next — all of these become offenses.

Venerable one, if a monk confesses an offense and imposes a penalty before a mad person, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Likewise, before one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is dumb, one who is asleep, one who is intoxicated from fermented drink, one who is drunk, one who is in meditative absorption, or one who has gone to dwell elsewhere — confessing an offense before any such person becomes an offense.

Venerable one, if a monk confesses an offense and imposes a penalty before a nun, a female probationer (śikṣamāṇā), a female novice, or male novices, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a nun confesses an offense and imposes a penalty before a monk, a male novice, a female novice, or a female probationer, what does that become? It becomes an offense.

Venerable one, if one who has been given a formal training measure confesses an offense and imposes a penalty, what does that become? It becomes a transgression. If the offense is confessed and the penalty imposed before a female probationer, a female novice, or male novices, what does that become?

It becomes an offense.

In brief:
Offenses arise likewise in all these ways —
through body, speech, and silence's mark,
with laypeople and the rest among them,
the fourth being last in the sequence.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that failing to act in accordance with an instruction is a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk fails to act in accordance with instructions other than those concerning a monk's own offense, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a monk fails to act in accordance with an instruction given through a physical indication, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a noble monk gives an instruction in the noble language and the monk receiving it fails to carry it out, and that monk has not sought to learn the noble language, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If a noble monk gives an instruction in the border language, the monk fails to carry it out, and that monk has not sought to learn the border language, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If a border monk gives an instruction to a monk in the border language, the monk fails to carry it out, and that monk has not sought to learn the border language, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If a border monk gives an instruction to a monk in the noble language, the monk fails to carry it out, and that monk has not sought to learn the noble language, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a monk fails to act in accordance with an instruction given through a monk's silence, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a monk fails to act in accordance with a monk's instruction, and then that monk's status changes and he becomes a nun, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a nun fails to act in accordance with a nun's instruction, and then that nun's status changes and she becomes a monk, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a monk fails to act in accordance with an instruction given by a layman, what does that become? It becomes an offense.

Similarly, if a monk fails to act in accordance with instructions given by a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, a nun who has been expelled, one who has killed his father or mother or an arhat, one who with malicious intent has shed the blood of a Tathāgata, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, a thief in hiding, one dwelling separately, one who is not a resident, one who has previously caused a schism, or one who has previously committed an offense — in all such cases it becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a monk fails to act in accordance with instructions given by one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has taken sides in a schism, or one who has been given a formal training measure, what does that become? In all cases it becomes a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk perceives one who has received full ordination as having received full ordination and then fails to act in accordance with that person's instruction, what does that become? It becomes a transgression. If a monk perceives one who has received full ordination as not having received full ordination and fails to act in accordance with that person's instruction, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If a monk perceives one who has not received full ordination as having received full ordination and fails to act in accordance with that person's instruction, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If a monk perceives one who has not received full ordination as not having received full ordination and fails to act in accordance with that person's instruction, what does that become? It becomes an offense.

In brief:
Through messenger, written letter, gesture,
through a third party, and from one to another —
through one gone mad, through disturbed mind,
through illness, through being mute, deaf, or dull.

Venerable one, if a monk fails to act in accordance with an instruction conveyed by a messenger, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Similarly, if a monk fails to act in accordance with instructions conveyed by written letter, by gesture, through a third party, or passed along from one to another, in all such cases it becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a monk fails to act in accordance with an instruction given by a mad monk, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Similarly, if a monk fails to act in accordance with instructions given by one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, one who is deaf, or one dwelling in another place — in all such cases it becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a monk fails to act in accordance with instructions given by a female probationer, a female novice, or male novices, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Venerable one, if one who has been given a formal training measure fails to act in accordance with an instruction, what does that become?

It becomes a transgression. Venerable one, if one fails to act in accordance with instructions given by female trainees, female novices, or male novices, what does that become? It becomes an offense.

In brief:
The unsuitable, the person, the excess beyond the permitted, the seventh,
The sign, the fourth likewise,
Body, speech, and seclusion the same —
Laypeople and others are the last of the interruptions.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable Blessed One, you have said that if a monk lays down a Saṅgha bed or sets one down, or is in the act of setting one down, and then departs without entrusting it to another monk, a transgression arises. Venerable one, are there cases in which a monk who has laid down a Saṅgha bed and departs without entrusting it to another does not incur a transgression?

Upāli, there are. It depends on whether the bed is fit in material but unfit in construction, fit in construction but unfit in material, or unfit in both respects. As for being unfit in material: if a bed has been laid down or set down that is made with a mixture of she-ass wool, ox wool, goat wool, or deer-hair wool, or that has not been woven — if one departs from such a bed without entrusting it, it becomes an offense.

Venerable one, if a monk has laid down or set down a personal bed and departs without entrusting it to another, what does that become? It becomes an offense.

Venerable one, are there cases in which a monk who has spread out a Saṅgha chair or stool and departs without entrusting it to another does not incur a transgression? Upāli, there are. If the leg-height exceeds eight finger-widths of the Sugata, it becomes an offense.

Venerable one, if one who has not received full ordination lays down a bed, and then one who has not received full ordination goes beyond the boundary of the vicinity, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If one who has not received full ordination lays it down, and then one who is about to receive full ordination goes beyond the boundary of the vicinity, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If one who has not received full ordination lays it down, and then one who is in the act of receiving full ordination goes beyond the boundary of the vicinity, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If one who is about to receive full ordination lays it down, and then one who is about to receive full ordination goes beyond the boundary of the vicinity, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If one who is about to receive full ordination lays it down, and then one who has fully received ordination goes beyond the boundary of the vicinity, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If one who is in the act of receiving full ordination lays it down, and then one who has fully received ordination goes beyond the boundary of the vicinity, what does that become? It becomes a transgression. If one who is in the act of receiving full ordination lays it down, and then one who has not received full ordination goes beyond the boundary of the vicinity, what does that become? It becomes an offense.

Venerable one, if a monk has laid down a Saṅgha bed and, without entrusting it and without any other monk being present, departs elsewhere — and during that journey his sex changes and he becomes a nun — what does that become? It becomes a transgression.

Venerable one, if a nun has laid down a Saṅgha bed and, without entrusting it and without any other nun being present, departs elsewhere — and during that journey her sex changes and she becomes a monk — what does that become? It becomes a transgression.

Venerable one, if a monk has laid down a Saṅgha bed and, without entrusting it and without any other monk being present, perceives himself to be on the far side of the boundary when in fact he is on the far side of the boundary and departs, what does that become? It becomes a transgression. If he is on the far side of the boundary but perceives himself to be on the near side, there is no offense. If he is on the near side of the boundary but perceives himself to be on the far side, it becomes an offense. If he is on the near side of the boundary and perceives himself to be on the near side, there is no offense.

Venerable one, if a noble monk entrusts a Saṅgha bed to another monk using the noble language and then departs, but that other monk does not seek the noble language, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If a noble monk entrusts a Saṅgha bed to another monk using a regional language and then departs —

and that monk also does not seek the regional language, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If a monk of the border regions entrusts a Saṅgha bed to another monk using the regional language and then departs, and that monk also does not seek the regional language, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If a monk of the border regions entrusts a Saṅgha bed to another monk using the noble language and then departs, and that monk also does not seek the noble language, what does that become? It becomes an offense.

Venerable one, if a monk sets out a Saṅgha bed and entrusts it to a present monk by a physical sign and then departs elsewhere, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a monk sets out a Saṅgha bed and, perceiving a secluded place to be non-secluded, entrusts it and then departs elsewhere, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a monk sets out a Saṅgha bed and, without entrusting it to a present monk, entrusts it to a layman and then departs elsewhere, what does that become? It becomes an offense.

Likewise, if it is entrusted to a female novice; to one who has expelled a nun; to a parricide or matricide; to one who has slain an arhat; to one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata; to a tīrthika or one who has gone over to the tīrthikas; to one who dwells as a thief; to one who does not reside in the community; to one who resides separately; to one who has previously committed an offense; or to one who has previously caused a dispute — if it is entrusted to any of these and one then departs elsewhere, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a monk sets out a Saṅgha bed and entrusts it to one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, to one who has sided with such a schismatic, or to one who has been given a training rule — and then departs elsewhere, what does that become? It becomes an offense.

Venerable one, are there circumstances in which a monk who has set out a Saṅgha bed may pass beyond the boundary without entrusting it, even though a monk is present, without incurring an offense? Upāli, yes there are. This is the case when that monk departs without abandoning the bed and one of the eight kinds of obstruction arises at that assembly hall.

In brief:
One who is mad, mentally disturbed, or ill,
one who is deaf, simple-minded, or asleep,
one who is stammering, or intoxicated,
and one departing into meditative absorption — these are the last.

Venerable one, if a monk sets out a Saṅgha bed without entrusting it to a mad monk and then departs elsewhere, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Likewise, if it is entrusted — without proper entrustment — to one who is mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, simple-minded, mute, deaf, asleep, stammering, intoxicated, or abiding elsewhere in another capacity, and one then departs, what does that become? It becomes an offense.

Venerable one, if a monk entrusts a Saṅgha bed to a nun and then departs elsewhere, what does that become? It becomes an offense. If it is entrusted to a female trainee, a female novice, or a male novice and one then departs, what does that become? It becomes an offense. Venerable one, if a nun entrusts a bed to a female trainee, a female novice, or a male novice and then departs elsewhere, what does that become? It becomes an offense.

Venerable one, if one who has been given a training rule departs elsewhere without entrusting a Saṅgha bed even though a monk is present, what does that become? It is a downfall. With respect to a female trainee, a female novice, and a male novice, it becomes an offense.

What has been said here concerning the bed applies in full equally to the sitting mat. However, mats that are smaller or larger than eight finger-breadths of the Sugata are excepted, as they are not suitable.

In brief:
Sending a message, a letter, a hand-sign,
speaking through another, or from one to another;
one who is mad, mentally disturbed, or ill,
one who is deaf, simple-minded, or asleep,
one who is stammering, or intoxicated,
and one departing into meditative absorption — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that whichever monk expels or causes to be expelled another monk from a Saṅgha assembly hall while that monk is seeking it — that monk incurs a downfall. Now —

Venerable one, if a monk expels or causes to be expelled another monk from a Saṅgha assembly hall by means of a message, what does that incur? It is a downfall. Likewise, by a letter, a hand-sign, speaking through another, or passing word from one to another — all of these incur a downfall.

Venerable one, if a monk expels or causes to be expelled a mad monk, what does that incur? It is a downfall. Likewise, if he expels or causes to be expelled one who is mentally disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is simple-minded, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one who is stammering, one who is intoxicated, one who has entered meditative absorption, or one who has departed and is residing elsewhere — all of these incur a downfall.

The Noble Vinaya, the seventh fascicle. In brief:

The fourth with characteristics, the seventh,
and likewise laymen and the rest —
these are the last of the Saṅgha.

Venerable one, if a monk expels or causes to be expelled a monk from a Saṅgha assembly hall and, during the act, that monk's status has shifted and he has become a nun, what does that incur? It is a downfall. Venerable one, if a nun expels or causes to be expelled a nun from a Saṅgha assembly hall and, during the act, her status has shifted and she has become a monk, what does that incur? It is a downfall.

Venerable one, if a monk perceives one who is fully ordained as fully ordained and expels or causes to be expelled that person, what does that incur? It is a transgression. If he perceives one who is fully ordained as not fully ordained, it incurs a downfall. If he perceives one who is not fully ordained as fully ordained, it incurs a downfall. If he perceives one who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained, it incurs a downfall.

Venerable one, if a monk prepares to expel someone during the ceremony of full ordination and the act is completed while the ceremony is still in progress, what does that incur? It is a downfall. If he prepared the expulsion before full ordination and carries it out just as full ordination is being completed, what does that incur? It is a downfall. If he prepared the expulsion before full ordination and carries it out after full ordination is complete, what does that incur? It is a downfall. If he prepared the expulsion just as full ordination was being completed and carries it out just as full ordination is being completed, what does that incur? It is a downfall. If he prepared the expulsion just as full ordination was being completed and carries it out after full ordination is complete, what does that incur? It is a downfall. If he prepared the expulsion after full ordination was complete and carries it out while the ordination is still in progress, what does that incur? It is a transgression. If he prepared the expulsion after full ordination was complete and carries it out before full ordination is complete, what does that incur? It is a downfall.

Venerable one, if a monk expels or causes to be expelled a layman, what does that incur? It is a downfall.

Venerable one, if a monk expels or causes to be expelled a hermaphrodite, an androgyne, one who has expelled a nun, one who has killed his father or mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn the blood of a Tathāgata, a non-Buddhist adherent, one who has gone over to non-Buddhist adherents, one who is a spy, one who has previously committed an offense, or one who has previously caused a schism — all of these incur a downfall.

Venerable one, if a monk expels or causes to be expelled one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has taken sides in a schism, or one who has been given a training rule — what does that incur? All of these incur a transgression.

Venerable one, if a monk directly and openly causes a layman to be expelled, what does that incur? It is a transgression. Likewise, directly and openly causing to be expelled a hermaphrodite, an androgyne, one who has expelled a nun, one who has killed his father or mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn the blood of a Tathāgata, a non-Buddhist adherent, one who has gone over to non-Buddhist adherents, a spy, one who is residing separately, one who is not residing there, one who has previously caused a schism, one who has previously committed an offense, one who has taken sides in a schism, one who has been given a training rule, a nun, a female trainee novice, a female novice, or a male novice whom one has expelled — all of these incur a transgression.

Venerable one, if a nun expels or causes to be expelled another nun, what does that incur? It is a transgression.

Venerable one, if a nun expels or causes to be expelled a female trainee novice, a female novice, or male novices, what does that incur? It is a transgression.

Venerable one, if one who has been given a training rule expels or causes to be expelled a nun, what does that incur? It is a downfall. With respect to a female trainee novice, a female novice, or male novices, it is a transgression.

In summary:

One who is mad, mentally disturbed,
one who is deaf, dull-witted, or asleep,
one who is delirious, intoxicated,
and one who has entered meditative absorption — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk, approaching a monk who was there first and then coming afterward, causes him great harm by lying down or sleeping there — that is a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk causes great harm to a mad monk by lying down or sleeping there, what does that incur? It is a transgression. Likewise, if he does so toward one who is mentally disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one who is delirious, one who is intoxicated, one who has entered meditative absorption, or one who is residing elsewhere — causing him great harm by lying down or sleeping there — what does that incur? It is a transgression.

In summary:

Whether it concerns an individual or the Saṅgha,
likewise the third case and the fourth,
laypeople and the like —
the improper ones come last.

Venerable one, if a monk causes great harm by lying down or sleeping before monks who were already present in a temple belonging to a private individual, what does that incur? It is a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk causes great harm by lying down or sleeping before monks who were already present in a place other than a Saṅgha temple, what does that incur? It is a transgression. Venerable one, if while causing great harm by lying down or sleeping before monks in this way, one's sex changes and one becomes a nun, what does that incur? It is a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving one who has not received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, lies down or sleeps there, what does that incur? It is a transgression. If he perceives one who has not received full ordination as one who has received full ordination, it is a transgression. If he perceives one who has received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, it is a transgression. If he perceives one who has received full ordination as one who has received full ordination, and causes him great harm by lying down or sleeping there, what does that incur? It is a downfall.

Venerable one, if a monk causes great harm to a layman by lying down or sleeping there, what does that incur? It is a transgression. Likewise, if he does so toward a hermaphrodite, a pandaka, or those who have previously committed an offense — in all cases it is a transgression.
