Venerable one, if a monk causes great harm by lying down or sleeping there in relation to one who has previously caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has taken sides in a schism, or one who has been given a training rule, what does that incur? In all cases it is a downfall.

Venerable one, is there a case where a monk causes great harm by lying down or sleeping before monks already present in a Saṅgha temple and yet does not incur a downfall? Upāli, yes there is — it is an improper sleeping place, one that monks are not permitted to use.

Venerable one, if a monk causes great harm by lying down or sleeping in relation to a nun, a female trainee novice, a female novice, or male novices, what does that incur? It is a transgression. Venerable one, if a nun causes great harm by lying down or sleeping in relation to a monk, a female trainee novice, a female novice, or male novices, what does that incur? It is a transgression. Venerable one, if one who has been given a training rule causes great harm by lying down or sleeping before monks who were already present, what does that incur? It is a downfall. With respect to a female trainee novice, a female novice, and

male novices, it is a misdeed.

In brief:
Those of an individual and those of the Saṅgha,
Likewise the night and the fourth,
The unsuitable and likewise the seventh,
And the canopy of sky — these are the last.

Then the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has also declared that if a monk, without a leg-rest, sits down or lies down heavily upon a seat or chair — whether large or small — within a multi-storied building erected over a temple of the Saṅgha, it is a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk sits down or lies down without a leg-rest upon a seat or chair — large or small — within a multi-storied building erected over a temple belonging to an individual, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. Venerable one, if a monk — in a place other than a temple of the Saṅgha — sits down or lies down without a leg-rest upon a seat or chair lacking a leg-rest within a multi-storied building at some other location, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. Venerable one, if a monk causes great harm and sits down or lies down in the uppermost room of an upper story, and in the course of doing so changes sex and becomes a nun, what does that incur? It is a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving the uppermost room of an upper story as an upper story, lowers himself heavily onto a seat or chair without a leg-rest and sits down or lies down, what does that incur? It is a downfall. If one perceives an upper story as not an upper story, there is no offence. If one perceives what is not an upper story as an upper story, it becomes a misdeed. If one perceives what is not an upper story as not being an upper story, there is no offence. Venerable one, are there cases in which a monk may lower himself heavily onto a seat or chair without a leg-rest within the uppermost room of an upper story — sitting or lying down — and yet not incur a downfall?" Upāli, there are. When the surface of the temple has been covered with flat stone slabs, or wherever there is solid ground — sitting or lying down upon it, there is no offence. "Venerable one, if one who has been given a training rule lowers himself heavily onto a seat or chair without a leg-rest within the uppermost room of an upper story and sits down or lies down, what does that incur? It is a downfall. If a nun lowers herself heavily and sits down or lies down, what does that incur? It is a downfall. If a female trainee novice, a female novice, or male novices lower themselves heavily and sit down or lie down, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. The Blessed One has also declared that pouring water containing living creatures onto grass, earth, or cattle dung is a downfall — this too should be stated in full as it has been taught."

In brief:
Messages, letters, hand signals,

Relayed by another, passed from one to the next,
By one who is mad, mentally disturbed,
By one who is mute, or by one residing elsewhere —

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk builds a great monastery, he should spread mud and plaster and build up to two or three stories; if he builds beyond that, it is a downfall. If a monk, through a messenger, builds beyond two or three stories, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. Likewise, all cases conveyed through a letter, a hand signal, relaying through another, or passing the instruction from one person to the next — all are misdeeds. If a monk who is mad builds beyond two or three stories, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. Likewise, one who is mentally disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, one who is mute, or one who is residing in another place — if such a person is commissioned to build, what does that incur? All of these are misdeeds."

In brief:
A great building, one made of stone,
One begun by another — it is the same;
The fourth category with its mark is likewise so;
One under training, and the nun as well.

"If a monk builds something other than a great monastery — some other property of the Saṅgha — and builds it beyond two or three stories, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. If a monk builds a monastery for an individual and builds beyond the limit, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. Is there a case where a monk who builds a Saṅgha monastery beyond two or three stories does not incur a downfall? Upāli, yes, there is. It is as follows: if the monastery is built of stone alone, or if the donor has said 'I have already given what is needed — do as you see fit,' then there is no offense. If a monk completes work that another had begun at two or three stories, or completes work that another had built, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. If a monk spreads mud and plaster and builds beyond two or three stories but another does not complete it, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. One who has become mentally disturbed, or one who has died — it is the same. If a monk spreads mud and plaster and builds beyond two or three stories, and then changes status and becomes a nun, and then completes it, what does that incur? It is a downfall. If a nun spreads mud and plaster and builds beyond two or three stories, and then changes status and becomes a monk, and then completes it, what does that incur? It is a downfall. If a monk spreads mud and plaster and builds beyond two or three stories — perceiving it as beyond the limit and then building it — what does that incur? It is a downfall. If one perceives something that is beyond the limit as not beyond the limit, there is no offense. If one perceives something that is not beyond the limit as beyond the limit, it is a misdeed. If one perceives something that is not beyond the limit as not beyond the limit, there is no offense. If one under training builds beyond two or three stories, what does that incur? It is a downfall. If a nun builds beyond two or three stories, what does that incur? It is a downfall. For a female trainee, a female novice, and male novices, it is a misdeed."

In brief:
Messages, letters, hand signals,
Relayed by another, passed from one to the next,
By one who is mad, mentally disturbed,
By one who is mute, dull-witted, or fallen asleep,
By one who is in agony, intoxicated,
Or in meditative absorption — the last is residing elsewhere.

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has also declared that if a monk teaches a nun without being appointed by the Saṅgha, it is a downfall. If a monk, without being appointed by the Saṅgha, teaches a nun through a messenger, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. Likewise, through a letter, a hand signal,

— relayed by another, passed from one to the next — all of these are misdeeds.

Venerable one, if a monk, without being appointed by the Saṅgha, teaches an insane nun, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. Likewise, teaching one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is deaf, one who is mute, one who is asleep, one who is in agony, one who is intoxicated, one who is in meditative absorption, or one residing elsewhere — all of these are misdeeds.

In brief:

Through word, through body, through privacy,
Through signals, the fourth and fifth,
Through a sent messenger, through one who approaches —
Appointed to teach another, appointed twice.

Venerable one, if a monk who is a noble one teaches a nun in the noble language, and that nun does not understand the noble language, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. If a noble one teaches a nun in a border language, and that nun does not understand the border language, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. If one from the borderlands teaches a nun in the noble language, and that nun does not understand the noble language, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. If one from the borderlands teaches a nun in a border language, and that nun does not understand the border language, what does that incur? It is a misdeed.

Venerable one, if a monk teaches a nun through a bodily gesture, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. Venerable one, if a monk teaches in a secluded place while perceiving it as not secluded, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. Venerable one, if a monk is in the middle of teaching a nun and during that teaching her status changes and she becomes a nun of the other sex, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. Venerable one, if a monk is in the middle of teaching a nun and during that teaching her status changes and she becomes a monk, what does that incur? It is a misdeed.

Venerable one, if a monk perceives one who has not received full ordination as not having received full ordination, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. If he perceives one who has not received full ordination as having received full ordination, it is a misdeed. If he perceives one who has received full ordination as not having received full ordination, it is a misdeed. If he perceives one who has received full ordination as having received full ordination and teaches her, what does that incur? It is a downfall.

Venerable one, if a monk teaches a nun who is a hermaphrodite, one who has remained by stealth, one who lives separately, one who has previously committed an offense, or one who has previously caused a dispute — what does that incur for all of these? They are all misdeeds.

Venerable one, if a monk teaches a nun who is one who causes schism in the Saṅgha, one who is a partisan, or one who has been given training precepts, what does that incur? All of these are downfalls. If he teaches a female trainee or female novices, all of these are misdeeds.

Venerable one, if one who has been appointed to teach nuns has lapsed in that appointment — is he to be appointed a second time? Upāli, that is not necessary. Let him teach by virtue of the original authorization itself.

Venerable one, if a monk who is not a partisan teaches a nun who is a partisan, what does that incur? It is a misdeed. Venerable one, if a monk who is a partisan teaches a nun who is not a partisan, what does that incur? It is a misdeed.

Venerable one, if a monk who has been given training precepts was previously appointed to teach nuns and that appointment has lapsed — is he to be appointed a second time? Upāli, that is not necessary. Let him teach by virtue of the original authorization itself.

Venerable one, a monk appointed to teach nuns has been appointed to a different residence; he goes to that other residence and teaches — should he teach nuns by virtue of that same original authorization, or should he not? Upāli, he should teach.

Venerable one, if while teaching nuns a monk becomes mentally disturbed, and then recovers his own mind — is he to be appointed a second time? Upāli, that is not necessary.

If a monk endowed with five qualities is appointed to teach nuns, is that called an appointment or is it called not an appointment?

Upāli, that is called an appointment, and the Saṅgha does not thereby incur a transgression.

Venerable one, can it happen that a monk appointed by the Saṅgha to teach nuns nonetheless incurs a transgression? Upāli, it can — namely, when he has ceased to be endowed with the five qualities.

Venerable one, can it happen that a monk teaches nuns without having been appointed by the Saṅgha and yet incurs no transgression? Upāli, it can — namely, when it is an arhat who teaches.

Venerable one, if one who has been granted the training teaches nuns without having been appointed by the Saṅgha, what does that become? A transgression.

Venerable one, if a novice monk teaches nuns, what does that become? A misdeed.

In brief:
By message, by letter, by sign,
through another's words, from one to the next,
when mad, when mentally disturbed, when ill,
when mute, when simple-minded, when asleep,
when hiccupping, when intoxicated,
when in meditative absorption — the last of all.

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One Buddha: Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that a monk is appointed to teach nuns for the duration of one umbrella's worth of shade, and that if he teaches beyond that, it becomes a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk teaches beyond the duration of one messenger's errand, what does that become? A misdeed. Likewise, by letter, by sign, through another's words, or transmitted from one to the next — all of these become misdeeds.

Venerable one, if a monk teaches a mad nun beyond the appointed duration of shade, what does that become? A misdeed. Likewise, if he teaches one who is mentally disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is simple-minded, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is blind, one who is asleep, one who is hiccupping, one who is intoxicated, one who has entered meditative absorption, or one who is residing elsewhere — all of these become misdeeds.

In brief:
By voice, by body, in seclusion,
by night — the fourth is the same;
the neuter sex, and obstruction,
and the rains retreat — the last of all.

Venerable one, if a noble monk teaches a nun beyond the appointed duration of shade in the noble language, and that nun does not request it in the noble language, what does that become? A misdeed. If a noble one teaches a nun in a regional language, and that nun does not request it in a regional language, what does that become? A misdeed. If one from the borderlands teaches a nun in a regional language, and that nun does not request it in a regional language, what does that become? A misdeed. If one from the borderlands teaches a nun beyond the appointed duration of shade in the noble language, and that nun does not request it in the noble language, what does that become? A misdeed.

Venerable one, if a monk teaches a nun beyond the appointed duration of shade while directing attention through the body, what does that become? A misdeed.

Venerable one, if a monk perceives a secluded place as non-secluded and teaches a nun beyond the appointed duration of shade, what does that become? A misdeed.

Venerable one, if while a monk is teaching a nun beyond the appointed duration of shade her status changes and she becomes a fully ordained nun, what does that become? A misdeed.

Venerable one, if while a monk is teaching a nun beyond the appointed duration of shade that nun's status also changes and she becomes a fully ordained monk, what does that become? A misdeed.

Venerable one, if a monk perceives one who has not received full ordination as not having received full ordination and teaches her beyond the appointed duration of shade, what does that become? A misdeed. If he perceives one who has not received full ordination as having received full ordination, what does that become? A misdeed. If he perceives one who has received full ordination as not having received full ordination, what does that become? A misdeed.

If he perceives one who has received full ordination as having received full ordination and teaches her beyond the appointed duration of shade, what does that become? A misdeed. Venerable one, if a monk perceives the shade as being within the appointed duration and teaches a nun, what does that become? A misdeed. If the sun has set and he perceives it as having set and teaches, there is no offense. If the sun has not set and he perceives it as having set and teaches, that is a misdeed. If the sun has not set and he perceives it as not having set and teaches, there is no offense. Venerable one, if a monk teaches a nun who is a hermaphrodite, who is in a stolen place, who is not in a proper place, who is dwelling apart, who has previously committed an offense, or who was previously involved in a dispute, what does that become? In every case, a misdeed. Venerable one, if a monk teaches beyond the appointed duration of shade to nuns who have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, who have taken sides, or who have been given training precepts, what does that become? A misdeed.

Venerable one, is there a case where a monk teaches a nun beyond the appointed duration of shade and yet it does not become a transgression? Upāli, there is. If any one of eight interrupting obstacles arises while the nuns are on their way, there is no offense. Venerable one, is there another case where a monk teaches a nun beyond the appointed duration of shade and yet it does not become a transgression? Upāli, there is. If he goes to the nuns' residence and teaches there, there is no offense.

In brief:
Voice, body, solitude,
the night, and the fourth likewise —
the seventh, the hermaphrodite, likewise too —
the one given training precepts, and the nun.

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk says to another monk, "The venerable monk teaches a fully ordained nun for the sake of even a little food," that monk incurs a transgression. Venerable one, if a noble monk says to a monk in the noble tongue, "Venerable one, you teach a nun for the sake of even a little food," and that monk does not respond in the noble tongue, what does that become? A misdeed. If a noble one says this to a monk in the tongue of a border region, and that monk does not respond in the tongue of that border region, what does that become? A misdeed. If a person of a border region says this to a monk in the tongue of a border region, and that monk does not respond in the tongue of that border region, what does that become? A misdeed. If a person of a border region says this to a monk in the noble tongue — "Venerable one, you teach a nun for the sake of even a little food" — and that monk does not respond in the noble tongue, what does that become? A misdeed.

Venerable one, if a monk conveys to another monk — by means of a bodily gesture — "The venerable one teaches a nun for the sake of even a little food," what does that become? A misdeed. Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving what is a solitary place as not being a solitary place, says, "Venerable one, you teach a nun for the sake of even a little food," what does that become? A misdeed. Venerable one, if a monk says to another monk, "Venerable one, you teach Dharma to a nun for the sake of even a little food," and in the meantime the status of the monk spoken to changes and he becomes a nun, what does that become? A misdeed. Venerable one, if a nun says to a monk, "Noble one, you teach a nun for the sake of even a little food," and that very nun's status then changes and she becomes a monk, what does that become? A transgression.

Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a fully ordained person as fully ordained, says to that person, "Venerable one, you teach a nun for the sake of even a little food," what does that become? A transgression. If he perceives a fully ordained person as not fully ordained, it becomes a misdeed. If he perceives a not-fully-ordained person as fully ordained, it becomes a misdeed. If he perceives a not-fully-ordained person as not fully ordained, it becomes a misdeed.

Venerable one, if a not-fully-ordained person, upon seeing another not-fully-ordained person, says to that person, "Venerable one, you teach a nun for the sake of even a little food," what does that become? A misdeed. If one sees a not-fully-ordained person but speaks thus to someone fully ordained, what does that become? A misdeed. If one sees a not-fully-ordained person but the person spoken to is in fact fully ordained, what does that become? A misdeed. If one sees a fully-ordained person but speaks thus to someone not fully ordained, what does that become? A misdeed. If one sees a fully-ordained person and the person is in the process of becoming fully ordained, what does that become? A misdeed. If one sees a fully-ordained person and the person spoken to is fully ordained, what does that become? A transgression. If one sees a fully-ordained person but the person spoken to is not fully ordained, what does that become? A misdeed.

If a monk says thus to those ranging from a novice nun up through a nun who has been expelled, all the way up to one who has previously caused a dispute, what does that become? A misdeed. Venerable one, if a monk says thus to one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, to a partisan, or to one who has been given training, what does that become? All become transgressions. If one who has been given training says, "Venerable one, you teach a nun for the sake of even a little food," what does that become? A transgression.

Venerable one, if a nun says thus to a female probationer, or to a female novice, or to male novices, "Venerable one, you teach a nun for the sake of even a little food," what does that become? A misdeed.

In brief:

By message, by letter, by hand-sign,
through the words of another, from one to another,
when one is mad, mentally disturbed,
deaf, dull-witted, or asleep,
in a state of excitement, drunk,
or in meditative absorption — these are the last.

Venerable one, if a monk conveys by message to a monk the words, "Venerable one, you teach a nun for the sake of even a little food," what does that become? A misdeed. Likewise, whether by letter, by hand-sign, through the words of another, relayed from one to another, whether the speaker is mad, mentally disturbed, dull-witted, mute, deaf, asleep, excited, drunk, in meditative absorption, or residing elsewhere — in all cases it becomes a misdeed.

In brief:

The improper, and the seventh,
likewise the nocturnal and the fourth,
begun by another, not completed,
the greater not permitted — likewise so.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable Blessed One, you have declared that a monk who makes robes for a nun who is not a relative incurs a transgression. Is there any case, venerable one, in which a monk makes robes for a nun who is not a relative and yet does not incur a transgression?" Upāli, there is. It is as follows: where the material is suitable but the kinship-relation is unsuitable; where the kinship-relation is suitable but the material is unsuitable; and where both are unsuitable. Now, unsuitable material refers to that which is mixed with the wool of a female deer, the wool of cattle, the wool of a wild animal, or the wool of a goat, or that which has not been woven on a loom,

if one makes a robe of that sort, it is a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk begins making a robe for a nun who is not a relative and she has not yet received full ordination, and she remains without full ordination throughout, what does that entail?" It is a transgression. "If he begins while she has not received full ordination and she receives full ordination in the course of the work, what does that entail?" It is a transgression. "If he begins while she has not yet received full ordination and she has received full ordination by the time it is completed, what does that entail?" It is a transgression. "If he begins while she has just received full ordination and she remains one who has just received full ordination, what does that entail?" It is a transgression. "If he begins while she has just received full ordination and she has received full ordination, what does that entail?" It is a transgression. "If he begins when she is fully ordained and she is fully ordained, what does that entail?" It is a downfall. "If he begins when she is fully ordained and she is not fully ordained, what does that entail?" It is a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk is making a robe for a nun who is not a relative and in the course of the work a change of sex occurs and she becomes a fully ordained monk, what does that entail?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, if a nun is making a robe for a monk who is not a relative and in the course of the work a change of sex occurs and he becomes a fully ordained nun, what does that entail?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk is making a robe for a nun who is not a relative and in the course of the work a change of sex occurs and she becomes a fully ordained nun, what does that entail?" It is a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk makes a robe for a nun who is not a relative, perceiving her as one who is not a relative, what does that entail?" It is a downfall. "If he perceives one who is not a relative as a relative, what does that entail?" There is no offence. "Venerable one, if a monk perceives a relative as one who is not a relative, what does that entail?" It is a transgression. "If he perceives a relative as a relative and makes the robe, what does that entail?" There is no offence.

"Venerable one, if a monk makes a robe for a nun who is not a relative, perceiving a fully ordained nun as fully ordained, what does that entail?" It is a downfall. "If he perceives one who is fully ordained as not fully ordained, it becomes a transgression. If he perceives one who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained, what does that entail?" It is a transgression. "If he perceives one who is not fully ordained as fully ordained, what does that entail?" It is a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk has another make a robe for a nun who is not a relative, what does that entail?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk completes a robe for a nun who is not a relative that was begun by another, what does that entail?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk abandons in an unsuitable way a robe he was making for a nun who is not a relative, what does that entail?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk makes a robe for a nun who is not a relative that is smaller than the prescribed measure and it is not fit for consecration, what does that entail?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk makes a robe for a nun who is not a relative that is larger than the prescribed measure and it is not fit for consecration, what does that entail?" It is a transgression.

The Vinaya, the Sacred Fundamental Text. The eighth fascicle.

In brief:

The mad woman, the mentally disturbed, the sick,
the mute, the foolish, the neuter — likewise these —
those who have received the precepts, and the fully ordained nun.

"Venerable one, if a monk makes a robe for a mad nun, what does that entail?" It is a transgression. Likewise, making a robe for a nun who is mentally disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is foolish, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is blind, one who is a neuter, one who has taken refuge in theft, one who has no fixed abode, one who lives apart, one who has previously caused a dispute, one who has previously incurred an offence, and one who has gone to live elsewhere — all of these entail a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk makes a robe for nuns who have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, those who have sided with them, or those who have renounced the training, what does that entail?" All of these entail a downfall.

"Venerable one, if a monk makes a robe for a female novice in training or for a novice nun, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a nun makes a robe for monks or male novices who are not her relatives, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression.

"Venerable one, if one who gives the training makes a robe for a fully ordained nun who is not her relative, what does that entail?" That is a downfall.

In brief, the exceptions are as follows:
By messenger, written letter, hand gesture,
through another's words, from one to another,
one who is mad, one mentally disturbed,
one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is asleep,
one who is a neuter, one who is intoxicated,
and one who has entered meditative absorption — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that a monk who gives a robe to a fully ordained nun who is not his relative incurs a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a fully ordained nun who is not his relative by means of a messenger, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. Likewise, sending it by written letter, by hand gesture, through another's words, relayed from one person to another — and similarly, giving a robe to a nun who is mad, or one who is mentally disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one who is a neuter, one who is intoxicated, one who has entered meditative absorption, and likewise one who has gone to live elsewhere — all of these entail a transgression.

In brief:
The unsuitable, the fourth category,
likewise the measure, not more than that excess,
thus the seventh, the precious,
the shared, and the neuter.

"Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk gives a robe to a fully ordained nun who is not his relative and yet does not incur a downfall?" Upāli, there is. Such is the case when the material of the robe is suitable but the relative connection is not suitable; or when the relative connection is suitable but the material is not suitable; or when both are not suitable. What is meant by unsuitable material? It is material mixed with the wool of a female camel, the wool of cattle, the wool of goats, or the wool of wild animals, or material that has not been woven on a loom. If one gives a robe of such a kind, what does that entail? That entails a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a fully ordained nun as fully ordained and gives her a robe, what does that entail?" That is a downfall. "If he perceives a fully ordained nun as not fully ordained, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "If he perceives one who is not fully ordained as fully ordained, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "If he perceives one who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a fully ordained nun who is not his relative as not being his relative, and gives her a robe, what does that entail?" That is a downfall. "If he perceives one who is not his relative as his relative, what does that entail?" There is no offence. "If he perceives one who is his relative as not his relative, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "If he perceives a relative as his relative, what does that entail?" There is no offence.

"Venerable one, if a monk is in the process of giving a robe to a fully ordained nun who is not his relative, and in the interim she changes status and becomes a fully ordained nun — that is to say, she was not yet fully ordained when he began — what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, if a nun is in the process of giving a robe to a monk who is not her relative, and in the interim he changes status and becomes a fully ordained monk, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression.

"Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk gives a robe to a fully ordained nun who is not his relative and yet does not incur an offence?" Upāli, there is: a robe that is smaller than a cubit in measure, and one that has reached the measure of the Sugata's Dharma robe.

"Venerable one, if a robe is dedicated while the recipient is not yet fully ordained, and then given while she is still not fully ordained, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "If it is dedicated before full ordination and given at the time of full ordination, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "If it is dedicated before full ordination and then given after full ordination has been conferred, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "If it is stored at the time of full ordination and given at the time of full ordination, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "If it is dedicated at the time of full ordination and then given after full ordination has been conferred, what does that entail?"

That entails a transgression. "If it is dedicated at the time of full ordination and given at the time of full ordination, what does that entail?" That entails a downfall. "If it is dedicated at the time of full ordination and given before full ordination has been conferred, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a valuable robe to a nun who is not a relative, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk gives a robe to a nun who is not a relative and yet incurs no fault?" Upāli, there is: if it is sold and then bought back with the proceeds. "Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe held in common to a nun who is not a relative, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a layman, what does that entail?" If he gives a monastic robe, it entails a transgression. If he gives a lay robe, there is no fault. "Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a female probationer or a novice nun, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. Likewise, if he gives a robe to a paṇḍaka, a woman who has stolen entry into the order, one who has no valid standing, one who dwells separately, one who has previously committed a fault, or one who was previously involved in a dispute — in all such cases it entails a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a nun who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, or to one who has taken sides in a schism, or to one who has been given a formal training rule, what does that entail?" In all such cases it entails a downfall.

"Venerable one, if a nun gives a robe to a layman, what does that entail?" If she gives a monastic robe, it entails a downfall. If she gives a lay robe, there is no fault. "Venerable one, if a nun gives a robe to a fully ordained monk or to a novice monk, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, if one who has been given a formal training rule gives a robe to a nun who is not a relative, what does that entail?" That entails a downfall. To a female probationer or a novice nun, it entails a transgression.

In brief:
Mantras and the fourth, supernatural powers,
marks and time, and the seventh,
wrong paths, households, and so forth —
sound and body and solitude likewise.

Venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk joins himself to a large escort of nuns and then falls in behind them, it entails a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk joins himself to such an escort and then renders himself invisible by means of a mantra or medicine and travels on, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving an unordained woman as fully ordained, joins himself to her escort and travels on, what does that entail?" That entails a downfall. If he perceives an unordained woman as not fully ordained, it entails a transgression. If he perceives a fully ordained woman as not fully ordained, it entails a transgression. If he perceives a fully ordained woman as fully ordained, it entails a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk joins himself to a nun's escort and travels on together with her by means of supernatural powers, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk joins himself to a large escort of nuns and travels along together with them, and in the course of the journey his sex changes so that he becomes a nun, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, if a nun joins herself to a large escort of monks and falls in behind them, and in the course of the journey her sex changes so that she becomes a monk, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression.

"Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk joins himself to a nun's escort and falls in behind her and yet incurs no fault?" Upāli, there is: that is the case where, among the eight obstructions on the path, any one obstruction has arisen. "Venerable one, if one who is not fully ordained joins an escort of those not fully ordained and travels on, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "If one who is not fully ordained joins an escort of those not fully ordained and travels on as a fully ordained person, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "If one who is not fully ordained joins an escort of those not fully ordained and travels on at the time of full ordination, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression.

"If one who is at the point of full ordination joins an escort of those at the point of full ordination and travels on, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "If one who is at the point of full ordination joins an escort of those who are fully ordained and travels on, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "If one who is fully ordained joins an escort of those who are fully ordained and travels on, what does that entail?" That entails a downfall. "If one who is fully ordained joins an escort of those who are not fully ordained and travels on, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk joins an escort and travels on ahead, leaving the rear unguarded, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk joins a laywoman in escort and travels on together with her up to the point of a prior quarrel, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk joins in escort and travels together with a woman who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha and with a woman who has been given the training precepts, what does that entail?" That entails a downfall. "Venerable one, if a noble monk joins a nun in escort using the noble language, and that nun does not seek out the noble language, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "If one using the border language joins in escort, and that nun does not seek out the border language, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "If one of the borderlands using the border language joins in escort, and that nun does not seek out the border language, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "If one of the borderlands using the noble language joins in escort, and that nun does not seek out the noble language, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk joins a nun in escort with a bodily gesture as the signal and then falls in behind, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk perceives a solitary place as not solitary and joins in escort, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression.

In brief:

By message, by letter, by hand-sign,
by another's word, from one to the next,
one who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is deaf, one who is dull, one who is asleep,
one who stammers, one who is intoxicated,
and one who has entered absorption — these are the last.

"Venerable one, if a monk sends a message to join a nun in escort and then falls in behind, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. Likewise, by letter, by hand-sign, by another's word, and all cases of transmission from one to the next — all entail a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk joins a mad nun in escort, travels along together with her, and falls in behind, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. Likewise, one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is blind, one who is asleep, one who stammers, one who is intoxicated, one who has entered meditative absorption, and similarly nuns residing elsewhere — if a monk joins any of these in escort, travels the road together with them, and goes on, all of these entail a transgression. "Venerable one, if one who has been given the training precepts joins a nun in escort and falls in behind, what does that entail?" That entails a downfall. "Venerable one, if a monk joins a female trainee or a novice nun in escort and travels on together, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, if a nun joins in escort and travels on together with monks, male novices, or laymen, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "If she travels on together with female trainees, novice nuns, or male novices, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression.

Whatever has been understood with regard to travelling on the road should be understood in the same way with regard to crossing a river — excepting only those with supernatural powers and those who travel by a route other than the road; all remaining cases are to be expounded in the same way in full.

In brief:

One who has become mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is ill, one who is deaf, one who is dull,
one who is asleep, one who stammers, one who is intoxicated,
and one who has entered absorption — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk approaches a secluded place alone together with a woman, that entails a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk approaches a secluded place alone together with a mad woman, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Likewise, one whose mind is disturbed" —

"What of approaching a secluded place alone together with an ill woman, a dull woman, a mute woman, a deaf woman, a blind woman, one who is asleep, one who stammers, one who is intoxicated, one who has entered absorption, and likewise one who is abiding elsewhere going about her own way?" That entails a transgression.

In brief:
A young woman, the sky,
mantra and marks — the fourth —
and a hermaphrodite in seclusion likewise:
these are the trainings given to nuns.

"Venerable one, if a monk approaches a secluded place alone together with a young woman, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, if a woman is on the ground and the monk is in the sky, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk renders himself invisible by mantra or medicine and approaches her, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk approaches a secluded place alone together with a woman and then undergoes a change of marks and becomes a nun, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, if a nun approaches a secluded place alone together with a man, and then undergoes a change of marks and becomes a monk, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk perceives a human woman as human and the two of them approach a secluded place alone, what does that entail?" That is a downfall. "If one perceives a human as a non-human, that entails a transgression. If one perceives a non-human as a human, that entails a transgression. If one perceives a non-human as a non-human, that entails a transgression." "Venerable one, if a nun approaches a secluded place alone together with a hermaphrodite, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. The second category of marks is likewise the same. "Venerable one, if a monk approaches a secluded place alone together with a hermaphrodite, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk approaches a secluded place alone together with a nun who has been expelled, what does that entail?" That is a downfall. Likewise, if he approaches a secluded place alone together with a woman who has killed her father, a woman who has killed her mother, a woman who has killed an arhat, a woman who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a tīrthika woman, or a woman who has gone over to the tīrthikas — all of those entail a downfall. "Venerable one, if a monk approaches a secluded place alone together with a nun, what does that entail?" That is a downfall. Likewise, if he approaches together with a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā), a female novice, a female thief who has taken refuge in the Saṅgha, a woman who has been suspended, a woman who has been expelled from the community, a woman who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, a woman against whom an offense has previously arisen, or a woman who has been given the training — if any of those sit together with him alone in a secluded place, all of those entail a downfall. "Venerable one, if a nun approaches a secluded place alone together with a man, what does that entail?" That is a downfall. "If she approaches a secluded place alone together with a monk, what does that entail?" That is a downfall. "If a male novice approaches a secluded place alone together with him, what does that entail?" That is a downfall. "Venerable one, if a woman who has been given the training approaches a secluded place alone together with a woman, what does that entail?" That is a downfall.

"Venerable one, if a monk approaches together with a woman, the two of them alone, perceiving a non-secluded place as secluded, what does that entail?" That entails a transgression. For a female trainee, a female novice, and male novices, it likewise entails a transgression. Just as the full explanation is given for sitting together with a woman, so too it should be set forth in full for sitting together with a nun.

In brief:
Sending a messenger, a written message, a hand-signal,
having another convey it, and from one to another —
one who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed, one who is ill,
one who is deaf, one who is dull, one who is asleep,
one who stammers, one who is intoxicated,
one who has entered absorption, and one going elsewhere — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha:

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk eats food that has been arranged by nuns, he incurs a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk solicits and eats food that has been arranged through a messenger by a nun, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Likewise, if it is arranged by means of a written message, a hand-signal, by having another convey it, or by passing it from one to another — all of these are wrongdoings."

"Venerable one, if a monk solicits food that has been arranged by a mad nun, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Likewise, if food is arranged by a nun whose mind is disturbed, by one afflicted by illness, by one who is dull, by one who is mute, by one who is deaf, or by one who is staying elsewhere, and he eats it — all of these are wrongdoings."

"Venerable one, if a householder or a householder's wife who is mad has arranged food, and a monk solicits and eats it while doing so knowingly, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Likewise, if such food is arranged by one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is dull, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one who stammers, one who is intoxicated, one who has entered meditative absorption, or one who is staying elsewhere — if the monk eats it knowingly, all of these are wrongdoings."

In brief:
For another's sake, and likewise for the body,
for the third case and for the fourth and seventh,
for one of other discipline, for a monk,
for a layman, and for a trainee — these are the last.

"Venerable one, if a nun has arranged food for the sake of another with that very intention and gives it to another, and the monk solicits and eats it knowingly, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a nun arranges food by means of a bodily indication and the monk solicits and eats it, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if while a monk is soliciting food arranged by a nun his status changes and he becomes a nun, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if while a nun is soliciting food arranged by a monk her status changes and she becomes a monk, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives food arranged by a nun as food that has been arranged and solicits it, what is that?"

"It is a downfall."

"If one perceives food that has been arranged as not arranged and eats it, there is no offence."

"If one perceives food that has not been arranged as having been arranged and eats it, it is a wrongdoing."

"If one perceives food that has not been arranged as not having been arranged and eats it, there is no offence."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a fully ordained nun as fully ordained and solicits food she has arranged, what is that?"

"It is a downfall."

"If one perceives a fully ordained nun as not fully ordained, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If one perceives one who is not fully ordained as fully ordained, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If one perceives one who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If food was arranged when she was not yet fully ordained, and one solicits it when she is not yet fully ordained, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If food was arranged when she was not yet fully ordained, and one solicits it just as she is becoming fully ordained, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If food was arranged when she was not yet fully ordained, and one solicits it after she is fully ordained, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If food was arranged just as she was becoming fully ordained, and one solicits it just as she is becoming fully ordained, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If food was arranged when she was fully ordained, and one solicits it after she is fully ordained, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If food was arranged when she was fully ordained, and one solicits it when she is fully ordained, what is that?"

"It is a downfall."

"If food was arranged when she was fully ordained, and one solicits it when she is not fully ordained, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk, aside from what is arranged for the sake of one endowed with moral discipline and learning, solicits food arranged for the sake of some other quality, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk solicits roots, fruits, and the like — things other than food — that have been arranged, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk solicits food arranged for another monk, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

Likewise, if one eats food arranged by a novice monk, a male probationer, a hermaphrodite monastic, a nun who has been expelled, or one who has received the training precepts — in all such cases it is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a nun solicits food arranged for a śikṣamāṇā, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

Likewise, if one eats food arranged by a novice nun, a hermaphrodite female monastic, an expelled nun, one who has killed a father, one who has killed a mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata, one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), one dwelling as a thief, one not properly dwelling, one dwelling separately, one in whom a prior offense has arisen, one previously in a state of conflict, or laywomen — in all such cases it is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk solicits food arranged by one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has taken sides in a schism, or one who has received training precepts — what is that?"

"In all cases it is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun solicits food arranged for her by a monk, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

Likewise, if one eats food arranged by a novice nun, a śikṣamāṇā, a novice monk, a laywoman, a hermaphrodite laywoman, or those who have received training precepts — in all such cases it is a wrongdoing. This should be applied in full.

"Venerable one, if one who has received training precepts solicits food arranged by a nun, what is that?"

"It is a downfall."

"If one solicits food arranged by a śikṣamāṇā, a novice nun, or novice monks, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

In brief:
Food and other provisions are the same in this regard:
the two matching cases, the improper ones,
those soliciting the remainder due to kin,
the fourth, seventh, and second.

The venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that repeatedly soliciting outside the proper time is a downfall. Is it possible for a monk to invite guests on two occasions and yet incur no downfall?"

"Upāli, it is possible. That is the case where a monk first invited someone for solid food, prepared food, drink, soft food, and things to lick and so forth, and then afterward invited them again for a meal."

"Venerable one, if a monk intends harm toward another monk, invites him, and after that monk has accepted the later invitation and solicited on that basis — what is that?"

"There is no offense."

"Venerable one, is it possible for a monk who invites a second or third time and solicits to incur no transgression?"

"Upāli, it is possible. That is the case where a monk was invited without a robe, and then after eating, was invited again with a robe included, making it a double invitation."

"Venerable one, is it possible for a monk to solicit twice with a robe included and yet incur no transgression?"

"Upāli, it is possible — when the robe is an improper one."

"And if the monk knows this and solicits, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk is invited for improper food, and afterward seeks and solicits proper food — what is that?"

"There is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk is invited for a meal in the morning, and afterward solicits again from a further invitation — what is that?"

"There is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a nun who had not yet solicited food for the sake of a robe undergoes sex-change and becomes a monk, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk who had not yet solicited food for the sake of a robe undergoes sex-change and becomes a nun, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives that there is no robe when in fact there is no robe, accepts an invitation on that basis, and afterward does not solicit — what is that?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives that there is no robe when in fact there is no robe, and eats — there is no offense."

"If one perceives that there is a robe when in fact there is no robe, and eats — it is a wrongdoing."

"If one perceives that there is a robe when in fact there is a robe, and eats — there is no offense."

"Venerable one, if before full ordination one accepts an invitation on the grounds that there is no robe, and solicits while still not fully ordained — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If before full ordination one accepts and solicits at the point of full ordination — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If before full ordination one accepts and solicits after having become fully ordained — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If at the point of full ordination one accepts and solicits at the point of full ordination — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If at the point of full ordination one accepts and solicits while still at the point of full ordination — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If after full ordination one accepts and solicits after full ordination — what is that?"

"It is a transgression."

"If after full ordination one accepts and solicits while not yet fully ordained — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk may solicit in a single place without committing an offense?"

"Upāli, there is. It is as follows: when both a monk and a householder have been invited together to a meal."

"Venerable one, if one who has received a training rule solicits food again and again — what is that?"

"It is a transgression."

In summary:

One who has gone mad, and one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is ill, one who is mute, one who is dumb,
one who is a paṇḍaka — and likewise
a fully ordained nun — these are the last cases.

"Venerable one, if a monk accepts an invitation for a robe-less meal from a madman and solicits — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

One whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, one who is dumb, a paṇḍaka, a female paṇḍaka — and likewise, non-Buddhist wanderers outside this tradition, other ascetics, brahmins, the virtuous, and those who roam about — these cases are the same.

Likewise, if a monk, a nun, a probationer nun (śikṣamāṇā), a male novice, a female novice, or those who have gone to another destination — if any of these solicit and eat a subsequent invitation for which there is no robe, all of them commit a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a nun solicits food again and again — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If a probationer nun or female novices solicit — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

In summary:

Mantra and the fourth — and sky,
mark and food likewise —
the seventh, the second, and the others,
and the changed — these are the last cases.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, when the Blessed One, intending the case of a non-Buddhist establishment, declared that a monk who has not requested a meal should eat one serving and that eating beyond that is a transgression — venerable one, if a monk renders himself imperceptible by mantra or medicine and solicits a second serving, what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a non-Buddhist establishment as a non-Buddhist establishment and solicits a second serving — what is that?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives a non-Buddhist establishment as not a non-Buddhist establishment — there is no offense."

"If one perceives what is not a non-Buddhist establishment as a non-Buddhist establishment — it is a wrongdoing."

"If one perceives what is not a non-Buddhist establishment as not a non-Buddhist establishment — there is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk solicits a second serving while situated in the sky — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk solicits a second serving of food at a non-Buddhist establishment and, in the midst of doing so, changes sex and becomes a nun — what is that?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun solicits a second serving of food at a non-Buddhist establishment and, in the midst of doing so, changes sex and becomes a monk — what is that?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk solicits, apart from cooked food, other things to eat — solid food, beverages, or items to lick — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if one who has not yet received full ordination, intending a non-Buddhist establishment, solicits as one who has not yet received full ordination — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If one who has not yet received full ordination solicits at an establishment, treating it as if full ordination had been received — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If one who has not yet received full ordination solicits at an establishment after having received full ordination — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If one in the process of receiving full ordination solicits at an establishment while in the process of receiving full ordination — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If one in the process of receiving full ordination solicits at an establishment after full ordination has been completed — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If one who has received full ordination solicits at an establishment while having received full ordination — what is that?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one who has received full ordination solicits at an establishment as one who has not received full ordination — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk takes food from elsewhere, then goes to a non-Buddhist establishment and solicits there — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk takes food from a non-Buddhist establishment and then goes elsewhere and solicits — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk, apart from a non-Buddhist establishment, solicits at a different establishment of ascetics or brahmins — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

In summary:

One gone mad, or with a disturbed mind,
One who is sick, one who has gone elsewhere,
A woman, a hermaphrodite — the same applies.
One under training, and a female novice.

"Venerable one, if a monk solicits a second serving of food at the dwelling of one who has gone mad — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

Likewise, at the dwelling of one with a disturbed mind, one afflicted by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, one who has gone elsewhere, a woman, a hermaphrodite — and similarly at the dwelling of others who reside in a different place — if one eats a second serving, all of these are wrongdoings.

"Venerable one, if one who has taken the training precepts, intending a non-Buddhist establishment, solicits a second serving of food — what is that?"

"It is a transgression."

"If a female probationer, a male novice, or a female novice solicits — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

The Noble Vinaya. The Ninth Fascicle.

In summary:

By messenger, by letter, by hand-signal,
By having another say it, and passing it from one to another,
One gone mad, one with a disturbed mind,
One who is sick, one who has gone elsewhere.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that when monks go to a village in a group and brahmins and householders give them large quantities of food and clarified butter, those monks, if they wish, may take two or three full almsbowls, but if they take more than that it is a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk, by sending a messenger, takes more than three full almsbowls — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Likewise, by letter, by hand-signal, by having another convey the request, or by passing it from one to another — if one takes more, all of these are wrongdoings."

"Venerable one, if a monk takes more than three full almsbowls from a person who has gone mad — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

Likewise, from one with a disturbed mind, one afflicted by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, one who has gone elsewhere — if one takes more than three full almsbowls from any of these, all are wrongdoings.

In summary:

From another to another, and beyond this:
Food, improper things,
By night, the fourth, the seventh,
And hermaphrodites — the same applies.

"Venerable one, if a monk gives more than three full almsbowls to another to take — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk takes on behalf of another — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk takes more than three full almsbowls from other non-Buddhist wanderers (tīrthikas) outside this community — from other ascetics, brahmins, wanderers, or mendicants — what is that?"

"All are wrongdoings."

"Venerable one, are there cases in which a monk takes more than three full almsbowls and yet incurs no transgression?"

"Upāli, there are. If one takes improper food, it is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk takes more than three full almsbowls of things other than food — such as things to be eaten as a snack, things to be prepared, things to be drunk, or things to be tasted — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if, while a monk is taking more than three full almsbowls, his status changes and he becomes a nun — what is that?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if, while a nun is taking more than three full almsbowls, her status changes and she becomes a monk — what is that?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a human as a human and takes more than three full almsbowls — what is that?"

"It is a downfall."

If he perceives a human as a non-human, it is a wrongdoing. If he perceives a non-human as a human, it is a wrongdoing. If he perceives a non-human as a non-human, it is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives that what exceeds six and a half measures is in excess and then takes it — what is that?"

"It is a downfall."

If he perceives what is in excess as not in excess, there is no offence. If he perceives what is not in excess as being in excess, it is a wrongdoing. If he perceives what is not in excess as not in excess, there is no offence.

"Venerable one, if one who has not received full ordination obtains something and takes it in the state of not having received full ordination — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If one who has not received full ordination obtains something and takes it at the moment of receiving full ordination — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If one who has not received full ordination obtains something and takes it after having received full ordination — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If one who is in the act of receiving full ordination obtains something and takes it at that moment — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If one who is in the act of receiving full ordination obtains something and takes it after having received full ordination — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If one who has received full ordination obtains something and takes it after having received full ordination — what is that?"

"It is a downfall."

"If one who has received full ordination obtains something and takes it without having received full ordination — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, are there cases in which a monk takes more than three full almsbowls and yet incurs no transgression?"

"Upāli, there are. When one remains in that very household and eats there."

"Venerable one, if a monk takes more than three full almsbowls from a hermaphrodite — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

Likewise, taking from a female intermediary and from hermaphrodites — all are wrongdoings.

"Venerable one, if one who has been given a training takes more than three full almsbowls — what is that?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun takes more than three full almsbowls — what is that?"

"It is a downfall."

If a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā), a novice nun, or novice monks take them — it is a wrongdoing.

In summary:

Time and night — the same applies;
Things to be eaten and things to be tasted,
The improper seventh — likewise;
All ordinations: not done and done.

Then the venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has said: 'Any monk who, without having made it a remainder, seeks or takes food or prepared foods that have not been left over, will incur a downfall.' Venerable one, are there cases in which a monk seeks or takes prepared or raw foods that have not been made into a remainder and yet incurs no transgression?"

"Upāli, there are. When one is ill and it is blessed and then eaten."

"Venerable one, if, after setting aside what has been sought and not sought, he seeks something prepared or raw that has not been made into a remainder, and in the meantime his status changes and he becomes a nun — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a nun, having set aside what was sought and what was not sought, seeks prepared or raw food that has not been made into a remainder, and in the meantime her status changes and she becomes a monk — what is that?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, when a monk is making something into a remainder and his status changes, is it said to be 'made into a remainder' or 'not made into a remainder'?"

"It is said to be 'not made into a remainder.'"

"Venerable one, if a monk seeks, without first making it a remainder, other edible things apart from cooked food — namely prepared foods, beverages, things to be licked, things to be tasted, and so forth — which count as foodstuffs but are not medicines — what is that?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk sets aside other edible things apart from cooked food — prepared foods, beverages, things to be licked, things to be tasted, and so forth — is that said to be 'setting aside'?"

"Upāli, it is not."

"Why is that?"

"Upāli, there is no such thing as setting aside in relation to prepared foods, beverages, things to be licked, things to be tasted, and so forth."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives what has been set aside as having been set aside, and then seeks food and drink that has not been made into a remainder — what is that?"

"It is a downfall."

"If he perceives what has been set aside as not having been set aside, and seeks it — what is that?"

"There is no transgression."

"If he perceives what has not been set aside as having been set aside, and eats it — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If he perceives what has not been set aside as not having been set aside, and eats it — what is that?"

"There is no transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives what has not been made into a remainder as not having been made into a remainder, and seeks prepared or raw food — what is that?"

"It is a downfall."

"If he perceives what has not been made into a remainder as having been made into a remainder, and eats prepared or raw food — what is that?"

"There is no transgression."

"If he perceives what has been made into a remainder as not having been made into a remainder, and eats it — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If he perceives what has been made into a remainder as having been made into a remainder, and eats it — what is that?"

"There is no transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk seeks food that is improper and sets it aside — is that said to be 'setting aside' or 'not setting aside'?"

"Upāli, it is said to be 'setting aside.'"

"Venerable one, if before full ordination one sets something aside, and before full ordination one seeks something that has not been made into a remainder — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If before full ordination one sets something aside, and at the moment of full ordination one seeks it — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If before full ordination one sets something aside, and after full ordination one seeks it — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If at the moment of full ordination one sets something aside, and at the moment of full ordination one seeks it — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If at the moment of full ordination one sets something aside, and after full ordination one seeks it — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If after full ordination one sets something aside, and after full ordination one seeks it — what is that?"

"It is a downfall."

"If after full ordination one sets something aside, and before full ordination one seeks it — what is that?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk sets aside something that has not been properly distributed in full — is that said to be 'setting aside' or 'not setting aside'?"

"Upāli, it is said to be 'not setting aside.'"

"Why is that?"

"Upāli, there is no setting aside in relation to what has not been properly distributed in full."

"Venerable one, in how many cases is something said to be 'not made into a remainder'?"

"Upāli, there are five: when it has not been received from another; when prepared or raw food has not been presented before one; when the act of receiving it has not been performed; when one has not yet received full ordination; and when what has been made a remainder was not established in its natural condition — in these cases what was made a remainder is nonetheless said to be 'not made into a remainder.'"

"Upāli, there are five cases in which something is said to be 'made into a remainder': when it has been received from another; when prepared or raw food has been presented before one; when the act of receiving it has been performed; when one has received full ordination; and when what was made a remainder was established in its natural condition — in these cases it is said to be 'made into a remainder.'"

"Venerable one, before whom does one make something into a remainder?"

"Upāli, a monk makes it into a remainder before a monk, not before a nun. A nun makes it before a nun. A male novice makes it before a monk. A female trainee (śikṣamāṇā) makes it before a nun, a female trainee, or a female novice."

"Venerable one, may one make it into a remainder before a nun —"

"Upāli, no."

"Venerable one, if a monk makes something into a remainder before a nun, is it said to be 'made into a remainder,' or may one also confess before her?"

"Upāli, no."

In brief:
By messenger, letter, gesture,
Through another, or from one to another —
A madman, one mentally disturbed, one who is ill,
A deaf-mute, one who is dull-witted, one who is asleep,
One who is delirious, one who is intoxicated,
One in meditative absorption, a wanderer, a eunuch —

"Venerable one, if a monk makes something into a remainder through a messenger, is it said to be 'made into a remainder'?"

"Upāli, no. Likewise, if it is made through a letter, a gesture, through another person, or passed from one to another, it is said to be 'not made into a remainder.'"

"Venerable one, if a monk makes something into a remainder before a madman, is it said to be 'made into a remainder' or 'not made into a remainder'?"

"It is said to be 'not made into a remainder.' Likewise, before a mentally disturbed monk, one afflicted by illness, one who is dull-witted, a mute, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one who is delirious, one who is intoxicated, one who has entered meditative absorption, or one who is residing elsewhere — if something is made into a remainder before any of these, is it said to be 'made into a remainder'?"

"Upāli, no."

"Venerable one, if a monk makes something into a remainder before a eunuch, is it said to be 'made into a remainder'?"

"Upāli, no. Likewise, before a nun who has been expelled, one who has killed her father, one who has killed her mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent, a non-Buddhist adherent, one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, one dwelling as a thief, one who is not residing in the community, one who is living apart, one who has previously committed an offense, or one who has previously caused a disruption — if something is made into a remainder before any of these, is it said to be 'made into a remainder'?"

"Upāli, that is not so."

"Venerable one, if a monk makes something into a remainder before a monk who is a glutton, is it said to be 'made into a remainder'?"

"It is not to be called 'made into a remainder' — it is 'made into a remainder' with an extreme transgression accompanying it."

"Venerable one, if a monk makes something into a remainder before one who has split the Saṅgha, one who has taken sides, or one who has given training — is it said to be 'made into a remainder' or 'not made into a remainder'?"

"Upāli, if it is called 'made into a remainder,' the act of making it into a remainder entails an extreme transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who has given training requests food and provisions without having made the remainder, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun requests food and then, after having renounced it, requests food and provisions again, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Venerable one, if a female trainee, a female novice, or a male novice requests food and provisions without having made the remainder, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."

In brief:
By voice, body, and seclusion likewise,
Food, improper matters,
The sign, and the fourth in the same way —
Schism of the Saṅgha, and a nun.

Then the venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that a monk incurs a transgression if, while seeking to renounce something that another monk has or has not requested, he offers food at a wrong time before making the remainder. Venerable one, if a noble monk offers a monk food and provisions without the remainder being made, speaking in the noble language, and that receiving monk does not respond in the noble language, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."

"If a noble monk offers it speaking in a border language, and that monk does not respond in the border language, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."

"If a border person offers it in a border language, and that monk does not respond in the border language, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."

"If a border person offers it in the noble language, and that monk does not respond in the noble language, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives food and provisions that have not been formally offered to the Saṅgha to another monk by means of a physical gesture, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a secluded place as non-secluded, gives food and provisions that have not been formally offered to the Saṅgha, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk, apart from food, gives other eatables, provisions, beverages, lickables, and tastables and so forth at an improper time, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression (āpatti)."

"Venerable one, if a monk, while seeking food in the proper manner of seeking, gives food and provisions set aside as not allowable at an improper time, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk, while seeking food in the proper manner of seeking, gives food and provisions that have not been formally offered to the Saṅgha at an improper time, and in the meantime a change of status occurs and that person has become a nun, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a nun, while seeking food in the proper manner of seeking, gives another nun food and provisions that have not been formally offered to the Saṅgha at an improper time, and in the meantime a change of status occurs and that person has become a monk, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives one who is fully ordained as fully ordained and gives food and provisions at an improper time, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"If one perceives a fully ordained person as not fully ordained and gives, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."

"If one perceives a person who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained and gives, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."

"If one perceives a person who is not fully ordained as fully ordained and gives, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."
