"Venerable one, if a monk, while a monk is seeking food in the proper manner of seeking, perceives one who has been suspended as suspended and gives food and provisions to that person directly, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"If one perceives a suspended person as not suspended and gives, what is the consequence?"

"No offence."

"If one perceives an unsuspended person as suspended, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."

"If one perceives an unsuspended person as unsuspended and gives, there is no offence."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives food and provisions directly to a hermaphrodite or a person of indeterminate sex who has been suspended, while that person is seeking food in the proper manner, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."

"Likewise, giving directly to a suspended nun, to one who has killed father or mother, to one who has killed an arhat, to one who has maliciously drawn blood from a Tathāgata, to a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika), to one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, to one who is staying as a thief in the community, to one who is not remaining in the community, to one who is living apart, and to those who have previously committed offences — if one gives to all such persons at an improper time, all become wrongdoings."

"Venerable one, if those who have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, those who have sided with the schismatics, and those who have relinquished the trainings seek food and receive it, and one gives directly to them who have been suspended at an improper time, what is the consequence?"

"All become transgressions."

"Venerable one, if a monk, while nuns, female trainees, and male novices seek food in the proper manner and wish to be suspended, gives to them at an improper time, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a nun gives directly to female trainees, female novices, and male novices — those who have not been formally offered to the Saṅgha — at an improper time, what is the consequence?"

"A wrongdoing."

"For female trainees, female novices, and male novices as well it is a wrongdoing; and these cases are to be applied to one another in their full elaboration."

"Venerable one, if one who has relinquished the trainings, while a monk is seeking food in the proper manner and having been suspended, gives food and provisions that have not been formally offered to the Saṅgha at an improper time, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun, while seeking food in the proper manner and wishing to be suspended, gives the five types of eatables and provisions at an improper time, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"For female trainees, female novices, and male novices, it is a wrongdoing."

In brief:

By messenger, letter, sign,
through an intermediary, or from one to another;
when insane, of disturbed mind, or afflicted;
when mute, simple-minded, asleep;
when babbling, or intoxicated —

one in meditative absorption, and one dwelling elsewhere — these are the final cases.

"Venerable one, if a monk, while seeking food and wishing to be suspended, has not made the five types of eatables and provisions into a formal offer to the Saṅgha, and these are then delivered by a messenger at an improper time, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Likewise, whether by letter, by sign, by word of another, passed from one to another, when insane, of disturbed mind, afflicted by illness, simple-minded, mute, deaf, asleep, babbling, intoxicated, in meditative absorption, or dwelling elsewhere — in all such cases, if the five types of eatables and provisions that have not been formally offered to the Saṅgha are delivered to a monk at an improper time, it is a transgression in every instance."

In brief:

By spell or boundary-space,
at an improper time, or with food,
in the same place or in another,
in great number, by night, and the fourth.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has taught that if a monk gathers in a large group and eats at a time other than the permitted occasion, it is a downfall. If a monk uses spells or medicine to render himself invisible and then seeks to gather in a large group, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk goes up into the sky and seeks food where the food-container is on the ground, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk is on the ground and seeks food where the food-container is in the sky, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk is outside the boundary and seeks food that is inside the boundary, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk is inside the boundary and seeks food that is outside the boundary, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gathers a large amount of improper food and seeks to receive it, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk gathers in a large group and seeks food without incurring a downfall?"

"Upāli, there is: when any one of the six permitted occasions has arisen."

"Venerable one, if a monk gathers in a large group and seeks things other than food — namely eatables, drinks, soft foods, and things to taste — what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Venerable one, if another person takes food from outside the boundary and brings it inside the boundary, and a monk then gathers in a large group and seeks it, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Venerable one, if food is taken from inside the boundary and brought elsewhere, and a monk then gathers in a large group and seeks it, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Venerable one, is there a case in which several monks from different boundaries, each gathering separately, may eat without incurring a downfall?"

"Upāli, there is: if they gather in groups of three within three separate locations and eat, provided they do not complete a group of four."

"Venerable one, if while a monk is gathering in a large group and seeking food the night passes and he becomes a monk again, what is the consequence?"

"A downfall."

"Venerable one, if while several nuns are gathering in a large group and seeking food the night passes and they become monks, what is the consequence?"

"A downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives what is inside the boundary as inside the boundary, gathers a large group, and eats, what is the consequence?"

"A downfall."

"If one perceives what is inside the boundary as outside the boundary and eats, there is no fault."

"If one perceives what is outside the boundary as inside the boundary and eats, it is a transgression."

"If one perceives what is outside the boundary as outside the boundary and eats, there is no fault."

In brief:

One who has become insane, of disturbed mind,
one who is ill, deaf, or simple-minded —
and likewise a paṇḍaka and one who has gone away:
these are the nuns censured for gathering in large groups.

"Venerable one, if a monk is counted among the large group by an insane person, and then together with them gathers inside the boundary in a large group and seeks food, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"One of disturbed mind, one tormented by illness, one who is deaf, and one who is simple-minded — likewise in all those cases."

"Venerable one, if a monk, with food —"

"Venerable one, if a paṇḍaka counts among the large group and together with them gathers inside the boundary in a large group and seeks food, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Likewise in the case of a nun who has been expelled, one who has slain father or mother, one who has slain an arhat, one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, one who is staying as a thief, one who is not staying, one who is staying separately, one in whom a transgression has previously arisen, and one who was previously in schism — if any of these count among the large group and together gather inside the boundary in a large group and seek food, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk who has schismed the Saṅgha, one who has taken sides, or one who has relinquished the training count among the large group and together gather in a large group and seek food, what is the consequence?"

"In all those cases there is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk dwelling in another district counts among the large group and together with them gathers inside the boundary in a large group and seeks food, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk counts nuns, female trainees, female novices, and male novices among the large group and together with them gathers inside the boundary in a large group and seeks food, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk gathers in a large group and seeks food yet incurs no fault?"

"Upāli, there is. It is as follows: when food has become utterly finished in that very place, or when food has been sent back and forth between them."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a solitary place as crowded and then seeks food, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who has relinquished the training gathers in a large group and seeks food, what is the consequence?"

"A downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun gathers in a large group and seeks food, what is the consequence?"

"A downfall."

"Venerable one, if female trainees, female novices, and male novices gather in a large group and seeks food, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

In brief:

The fourth topic, divine food, follows likewise —
the continents, the gods, and the marks,
food that is not food and its transgressions,
the wicked ones, and nuns.

The venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that any monk who prepares and eats food at an improper time incurs a downfall. Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk seeks food at an improper time yet incurs no fault?"

"Upāli, there is. It is when one has consumed divine food."

"Venerable one, what is the nature of divine food?"

"Upāli, it is like the nature of butter."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving an improper time as an improper time, seeks food at that time, what is the consequence?"

"A downfall."

"If one perceives an improper time as a proper time and seeks food at that time, what is the consequence?"

"No fault."

"If one perceives a proper time as an improper time and seeks food, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"If one perceives a proper time as a proper time and seeks food, what is the consequence?"

"No fault."

"If one perceives food as food and seeks to eat it, what is the consequence?"

"A downfall."

"If one perceives food as not food and eats it, what is the consequence?"

"No fault."

"If one perceives what is not food as food and seeks to eat it, what is the consequence?"

"A transgression."

"If one perceives what is not food as not food and seeks to eat it, what is the consequence?"

"No fault."

"Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk prepares and eats food at an improper time yet incurs no fault?"

"Upāli, there is. It is when one eats in the three other continents or in the realm of the gods according to the proper time of Jambudvīpa."

"Venerable one, if a monk is seeking to prepare and eat food at an improper time and his sex changes so that he becomes a nun, what is the consequence?"

"A downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun is seeking to prepare and eat food at an improper time and her sex changes so that she becomes a monk, what is the consequence?"

"A downfall."

"Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk prepares and eats food at an improper time yet incurs no fault?"

"Upāli, there is."

Except for those edible preparations that are made along with food, all other eatables apart from these may be taken for medicinal purposes — not as food.

"Venerable one, can a monk incur a single moment's transgression that amounts to four downfalls?"

"Upāli, there is such a case: not giving, being improper, being set aside, and eating at an improper time."

"Venerable one, what the Blessed One taught as 'give bad food to the sick' — what are those? Ash, earth, bran, and urine."

"Venerable one, is it permissible for all of these to be taken at an improper time?"

"Except for bran, all the others are permissible at an improper time."

"Venerable one, if one who has been given a training seeks to prepare and eat food at an improper time, what is the consequence?"

"A downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun seeks to prepare and eat food at an improper time, what is the consequence?"

"A downfall."

"If a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā), a novice nun, or male novices seek to prepare and eat such food, what is the consequence?"

"A misdeed."

In brief:
One who has become mad, and one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is sick, a hermaphrodite, a traveler,
one eating at night, and a fourth time of eating,
divine food, the other continents, and a nun.

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that any monk who eats food that has been set aside incurs a downfall. If a monk who has gone mad eats food that was set aside, what is the consequence?"

"A misdeed."

"Likewise, one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one afflicted by a demon, a hermaphrodite, a nun who has been expelled, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to tīrthikas, one dwelling in a thieves' encampment, one dwelling in a separate residence, one for whom a prior offense has arisen, one involved in a prior dispute — and likewise monks dwelling in another district who eat what has been set aside: all these cases result in a misdeed."

"Venerable one, if a monk who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, or who has taken sides in a dispute, or who has been given a training rule, seeks to eat food that has been set aside, what is the consequence?"

"A downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk who is seeking to eat food set aside undergoes a sex change and becomes a nun, what is the consequence?"

"A downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun who is seeking to eat food set aside undergoes a sex change and becomes a monk, what is the consequence?"

"A downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives food that has been set aside as having been set aside and eats it, what is the consequence?"

"A downfall."

"If he perceives food that has been set aside as not having been set aside and eats it, what is the consequence?"

"No offense."

"If he perceives food that has not been set aside as having been set aside and eats it, what is the consequence?"

"A misdeed."

"If he perceives food that has not been set aside as not having been set aside and eats it, what is the consequence?"

"No offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk takes medicines other than food and drink — such as things to be licked, things to be swallowed, ash, salt, lac, and the like — that have been set aside, what is the consequence?"

"A misdeed."

"Venerable one, if a monk eats bad food that has been set aside, what is the consequence?"

"A misdeed."

"Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk eats food that has been set aside without incurring an offense?"

"Upāli, there is: if he eats divine food, it becomes a misdeed."

"Venerable one, if a monk eats food set aside in the Eastern Continent of Videha, the Western Continent of Godānīya, or the Northern Continent of Uttarakuru, what is the consequence?"

"Upāli, if he makes use of and eats food that has exceeded its proper time according to the time of Jambudvīpa, it becomes a downfall. However, if he eats it at what counts as an improper time according to the time of those continents themselves, there is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk eats food set aside by a nun, what is the consequence?"

"No offense."

"Venerable one, if a nun eats food set aside by a monk, what is the consequence?"

"No offense."

"If a monk and a nun have both set aside food and a trainee nun eats it, there is no offense."

"Venerable one, if one who has received the training rules requests prepared food and edibles that have been set aside, what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk requests food that has been set aside by a nun, what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk requests food that has been set aside by a trainee nun, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If male novices and female novices have set aside food and one eats it, there is no offense."

The Vinaya Text Proper, the Tenth Fascicle.

In summary:

From one who is mad, one receives; from drunk, two kinds and purposeless;
By night and the fourth with the continents — conjured, not manifest, one goes.

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that whatever food a monk takes into his mouth without it having been given to him — water and tooth-cleaning sticks excepted — constitutes a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk receives food from a madman, is it said to have been received?"

"Upāli, if he has the perception that it is being given away, it is said to have been received. If he does not have the perception that it is being given away, it is said not to have been received."

"One whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is delirious, and one who is drunk — the same is to be said of all these."

"Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk who requests food or edibles without having received them commits no downfall?"

"Upāli, there is. When many people who are filled with contempt have completely abandoned their intent and rendered the food fit to be discarded, and one eats it — that is such a case."

"Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk who requests food or edibles that have been received commits a downfall?"

"Upāli, there is. When he receives it with the perception that it belongs to someone else, and then eats it — that is such a case."

"Venerable one, if a monk, apart from food and edibles, requests other things that have not been received — medicine set aside, drinks, what is ground fine, what is smeared on, ash, salt, honey, buttermilk, and the like — what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk requests inferior food without having received it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a drunk person pours food and edibles into a monk's alms-bowl, is it said to have been received?"

"Upāli, it has not been received properly. Have it received again afterwards."

"Venerable one, whether it is two monks or many, if one deputized person receives on their behalf, is it said to have been received?"

"Upāli, it is said to have been received."

"Venerable one, if a monk receives food without intending to want it, is it said to have been received?"

"Upāli, it is not. Why is that? Because there is no receiving on the part of a monk who does not wish it. Have him receive it again afterward."

"Venerable one, if a monk who has not received food and edibles requests them, and in the meantime his gender changes so that he becomes a nun, what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun who has not received food and edibles requests them, and in the meantime her gender changes so that she becomes a monk, what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk eats food he has not received, with the perception that he has not received it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"If he eats food he has not received, with the perception that he has received it, what is the consequence?"

"No offense."

"If he eats food he has received, with the perception that he has not received it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If he eats food he has received, with the perception that he has received it, what is the consequence?"

"No offense."

"Venerable one, may one eat without having received food in the Northern Continent of Uttarakuru, or may one not?"

"Upāli, one may eat."

"Venerable one, may one eat without having received food in the other continents?"

"Upāli, no."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes an emanation — one that does not count as a sentient being — to receive food on his behalf, is it considered received?"

"Upāli, no. He must receive it again afterwards."

"Venerable one, if a monk, while no one suitable is present, is nonetheless permitted to receive food and does so, is it considered received?"

"It is considered received, but it becomes a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said, 'Receive food from those dwelling in other destinies,' from what sort of beings dwelling in other destinies should one receive food?"

"Upāli, from those in whom there is the appearance of offering and who also have the perception of giving completely — from such beings one should receive food and eat it."

"Venerable one, if one who has been given a training precept eats without having received food, what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun eats without having received food, what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a female novice in training eats without having received food, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a female novice or a male novice eats without having received food, what is the consequence?"

"No offense."

In brief:
By messenger, by letter, by gesture,
by having another say it, by transmission from one to another,
by the mad, the mentally disturbed, the sick,
the deaf, the dull-witted, one who is asleep,
one who is delirious, one who is intoxicated,
one in meditative absorption, and one dwelling in another destiny — these are the last.

Then the venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has further said, 'If a monk, for his own sake, takes alms-food obtained from another clan without having begged it properly for himself, and then eats it, it becomes a downfall.' Venerable one, if a monk takes alms-food by sending a messenger to have it brought and then eats it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Likewise, if it is brought through a letter, through a gesture, through having another say it, or through being passed along from one to another and then eaten — in all such cases it becomes a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk takes alms-food from a mad person and then eats it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Likewise, from one whose mind is disturbed, from one tormented by illness, from one who is dull-witted, from one who is mute, from one who is deaf, from one who is asleep, from one who is delirious, from one who is intoxicated, from one who is in meditative absorption, and from one dwelling in another destiny — if one takes alms-food from any of these and eats it, it becomes a wrongdoing."

In brief:
By voice, by body, by solitude,
for another's sake, when improper,
at night, as the fourth for attendance,
and alms-food — seven — it is the same.
From householders and the like,
from those given the training precept, and from nuns.

"Venerable one, if a monk who is a noble one requests alms-food in the noble language, and the householder does not respond in the noble language, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If a noble one requests alms-food in a frontier language, and the householder does not respond in the frontier language, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If a frontier person requests alms-food in a frontier language, and the householder does not respond in the frontier language, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If a frontier person requests alms-food in the noble language, and the householder does not respond in the noble language, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk receives alms-food using a gesture of the body and then eats it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a secluded place as not secluded, takes alms-food there, and then eats it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk takes alms-food on another's behalf and then eats it himself, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk takes and eats meat or milk that is not permissible, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk receives alms-food and eats it, and in the meantime undergoes a change of sex and becomes a nun, what is the consequence?"

"It is to be confessed individually."

"Venerable one, if a nun receives alms-food and eats it, and in the meantime undergoes a change of sex and becomes a monk, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a human being as a human being, receives alms-food from that person, and then eats it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives a human being as not a human being and receives food from that person, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If one perceives a non-human as a human being and receives food from that being and eats it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If one perceives a non-human as a non-human and receives food from that being and eats it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives an almsgiver as an almsgiver, receives alms-food from that person, and eats it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives an almsgiver as not an almsgiver, receives food, and eats it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If one perceives one who is not an almsgiver as an almsgiver, receives food, and eats it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If one perceives one who is not an almsgiver as not an almsgiver, receives food, and eats it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if food is received when it is offered with the hand and eaten when it is offered with the hand, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If food is received when it is offered with the hand and eaten when offered without the hand, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If food is received when offered without the hand and eaten when offered with the hand, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If food is received when offered without the hand and eaten when offered without the hand, what is the consequence?"

"There is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk receives alms-food from a relative and eats it, what is the consequence?"

"There is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk receives and eats not alms-food but other things such as prepared food, beverages, soft foods, or things to be licked, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if alms-food is received before full ordination and eaten before full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If it is received before full ordination and eaten at the moment of full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If it is received before full ordination and eaten after full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If it is received at the moment of full ordination and eaten at the moment of full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If it is received at the moment of full ordination and eaten after full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If it is received after full ordination and eaten after full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If it is received after full ordination and eaten before full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk directs a layperson to seek alms-food and then eats it himself, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

Likewise, all of the following cases are wrongdoings: eating food received from a hermaphrodite; from one who has disrobed a nun by force; from one who has killed his father; from one who has killed his mother; from one who has killed an arhat; from one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata; from one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists; from one who lives as a thief; from one who is dwelling alone; from one who is not a resident; from one in whom a prior offense has arisen; from one who was previously involved in a dispute; from one who has taken a side in a dispute; from one who has surrendered the training; and from food received from a fully ordained nun, a probationer nun, a novice nun, or male novices — all such cases are wrongdoings.

"Venerable one, if one who has surrendered the training receives alms-food and eats it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun receives alms-food and eats it, what is the consequence?"

"It is to be confessed."

"Venerable one, if a probationer nun, a novice nun, or a male novice receives alms-food and eats it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

The detailed explanation of the transgression of drinking water containing living creatures should be set forth in full.

In brief:

Secluded places, and spells of the sky,
The night, the fourth case, hermaphrodites,
Female hermaphrodites, attendants,
Young women, and wandering ascetics.

This was asked of the Blessed One, the Buddha, by the Venerable Upāli.

"Venerable one, if the Blessed One has declared that a monk who forcibly enters a village containing a dangerous woman while seeking alms commits a transgression, then if a monk, while seeking alms, perceives a deserted village containing a dangerous woman as deserted and forcibly enters it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk, while seeking alms, forcibly enters a village containing a dangerous woman through the sky, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk, while seeking alms, renders himself invisible by means of a mantra or a medicine and enters a village containing a dangerous woman, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk, while forcibly entering a village containing a dangerous woman, undergoes a change of sex and becomes a nun, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun, while forcibly entering a village containing a dangerous woman, undergoes a change of sex and becomes a monk, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk forcibly enters a village perceiving a human being as a human being, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives a human being as not a human being and forcibly enters, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If he perceives a non-human being as a human being and forcibly enters, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If he perceives a non-human being as a non-human being and forcibly enters, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a dangerous woman as a dangerous woman, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives a dangerous woman as not a dangerous woman, what is the consequence?"

"There is no offence."

"If he perceives one who is not a dangerous woman as a dangerous woman, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"If he perceives one who is not a dangerous woman as not a dangerous woman, there is no offence."

"Venerable one, if a monk, while seeking alms, forcibly enters a hermaphrodite's village that contains a dangerous woman, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk forcibly enters together with a hermaphrodite, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk forcibly enters a village containing a dangerous woman seeking refuge, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if monks forcibly approach a young bride, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk, while seeking alms, enters and forcibly stays in the vicinity of a village containing a dangerous woman to the extent of merely hearing distance, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

In brief:

The mad, the mentally disturbed,
The deaf, the dull-witted, the drowsy,
Those in pain, the intoxicated,
Those in absorption, and travelers to other places — these are the final cases.

"Venerable one, if a monk forcibly enters a village of the mad, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrongdoing."

Likewise, forcibly sitting together with the mentally disturbed, those afflicted by illness, the dull-witted, the mute, the deaf, the drowsy, those in pain, the intoxicated, those in meditative absorption, and those dwelling elsewhere — all of these are wrongdoings.

"Venerable one, if one who has been given the training, while seeking alms, forcibly enters a village containing a dangerous woman, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun, while seeking alms, forcibly enters a village containing a dangerous woman, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

As set forth in the chapter on a probationer nun, a novice nun, or a male novice sitting in concealment in a place containing a dangerous woman, the case of sitting concealed in a place containing a dangerous woman is also to be stated.

In brief:

Messages, letters, hand-signals, and —

"— another's word, and passing from one to another, a madman, one whose mind is disturbed, one who is afflicted, a fool, one who is asleep, one who is intoxicated with alcohol, one who is inebriated, one who has entered meditative absorption, one who has gone elsewhere — these are the final cases."

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk gives food and drink with his own hand to one who is naked — whether a naked man or naked woman, a male wanderer or female wanderer — it is a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk, through a messenger, gives food and drink with his own hand to one who is naked — whether a naked man or naked woman, a male wanderer or female wanderer — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If he gives it likewise through a written message, a hand-signal, another's word, or passing it from one to another, what is the consequence in each case?"

"All of these are transgressions."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives food and drink with his own hand to a madman who is naked — whether a naked man or naked woman, a male wanderer or female wanderer — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Likewise, one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, a fool, a mute, one who is afflicted, one who is asleep, one who is intoxicated with alcohol, one who is inebriated, one who has entered meditative absorption, and one who dwells elsewhere — if a monk gives food and drink, whether to a naked man or naked woman, a male wanderer or female wanderer, among all such persons, what is the consequence in each case?"

"All of these are transgressions."

In brief:

Improper food and the naked,
vessels and characteristics, the seventh,
the fourth, mantras (Skt. mantra),
and through another — another's non-Buddhist renunciant.

"Venerable one, if a monk gives food and drink to one who is naked or to a wanderer, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives to such a person, apart from food, other things to eat or drink, to taste, or to lick and so forth, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives food and drink with his own hand to ascetics (Skt. śramaṇa) and brahmins other than the naked and the wanderers, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, are there cases in which a monk gives food and drink to one who is naked or a wanderer and yet incurs no fault?"

"Upāli, there are. These are: placing the vessel on the ground and pouring into it before giving; wishing to be free from an evil view held by that person; and giving to a relative."

"Venerable one, if a monk is in the act of giving food and drink with his own hand to one who is naked or a wanderer, and in the course of that act his status changes and he becomes a nun, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun is in the act of giving food and drink with her own hand to one who is naked or a wanderer, and in the course of that act her status changes and she becomes a monk, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who has not yet received full ordination dedicates food and drink with her own hand to one who is naked or a wanderer, and then gives it before receiving full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one dedicates it before full ordination and gives it at the very moment of receiving full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one dedicates it before full ordination and gives it after having received full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one dedicates it at the very moment of receiving full ordination and gives it at that same moment, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one dedicates it at the very moment of receiving full ordination and gives it after having received full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one who has fully received ordination dedicates it and gives it after having fully received ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one who has fully received ordination dedicates it and gives it before full ordination has been received, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a human as human, gives food and drink to one who is naked or a wanderer, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives that human as not human, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives a non-human as human, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives a non-human as non-human, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk makes himself invisible by means of a mantra or medicine, and then gives food and drink to one who is naked or a wanderer, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives food and drink to one who is naked or a wanderer, receiving it from another, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives food and drink to one who is naked or a wanderer on behalf of another, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives food and drink to one who is naked or a wanderer who is a hermaphrodite, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives food and drink to one who is naked or a wanderer who is a female hermaphrodite, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who has given the precepts gives food and drink to one who is naked or a wanderer, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a fully ordained nun gives food and drink from her own hand to one who is naked or a wanderer, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a female probationer, a novice nun, or a male novice gives food and drink from their own hand to one who is naked or a wanderer, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

In brief:

The mad one and the mentally disturbed,
the deaf, the wanderers, and their kinds,
the king who holds the seventh view,
the fourth ones, and the hermaphrodites.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that whatever monk goes to watch a battle array incurs a downfall. If a monk goes to watch a battle array where there are mad combatants, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Likewise, if those who are mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, dull-witted, mute, or deaf go to watch a battle array in the same way, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk goes to watch a battle array that is stationed in another region, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if, while a monk is going to watch a battle array, he undergoes a change of marks and becomes a nun, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if, while a nun is going to watch a battle array, she undergoes a change of marks and becomes a monk, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk, when looking at a battle array, goes only as far as the surrounding area, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk may go to watch a battle array without incurring an offense?"
"Upāli, there is: namely, when a monk has been summoned by a royal messenger."

"Venerable one, if one who has not received full ordination goes there in body, and while not yet fully ordained looks on, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one who has not received full ordination goes there and looks on at the time of full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one who has not received full ordination goes there and looks on after full ordination has been received, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one who is at the time of receiving full ordination goes there and looks on at the time of full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one who is at the time of receiving full ordination goes there and looks on after full ordination has been received, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one who has fully received ordination goes there and looks on while fully ordained, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If one who has fully received ordination goes there and looks on before full ordination has been received, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a human battle array as a human battle array and goes to watch it, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If one perceives a human battle array as a non-human battle array, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives a non-human battle array as a human battle array, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives a non-human battle array as a non-human battle array, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk goes to watch a battle array of neither-male-nor-female beings, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who has been given a training rule goes to watch a battle array, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a fully ordained nun goes to watch a battle array, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if female probationers, female novices, and male novices go to watch a battle array, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

As for watching a battle array — in the same way as the chapter on the training rules, all the cases of staying no more than two nights should be stated in full.

In brief:

By message, by letter, by gesture,
by having another say it, or relayed from one to the next;
one who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed, one who is ill,
one who is deaf, one who is foolish, one who is asleep,
one who is delirious, one who is intoxicated,
one who has entered meditative absorption — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli asked the buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that whatever monk strikes a monk incurs a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk sends a strike to a monk by message, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Likewise, if one causes a strike to be delivered by letter, by gesture, by having another say it, or relayed from one to the next — all of these are transgressions."

"Venerable one, if a monk strikes a monk who is insane, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Likewise, if one strikes a monk whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one who is delirious, one who is intoxicated, one who has entered meditative absorption, or — in the same manner — a monk who abides elsewhere in another destiny: all of these are transgressions."

In brief:

By mantra, by medicine, by another's means,
the fourth and seventh done by another,
householders and those like them,
by night likewise, and a fully ordained nun.

"Venerable one, if a monk renders himself invisible by means of a mantra or medicine and then strikes a monk, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, is there a case where one strikes a monk and yet the fault does not become a downfall?"
"Upāli, there is: if one strikes thinking it to be play, or if one strikes thinking it to be accidental."

"Venerable one, if a monk strikes a monk on behalf of another, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes another to be struck, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a human as a human and strikes, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If one perceives a human as a non-human, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives a non-human as a human, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives a non-human as a non-human, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives one who is fully ordained as fully ordained and strikes, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If one perceives one who is fully ordained as not fully ordained, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives one who is not fully ordained as fully ordained, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives one who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one prepares to strike before full ordination has been received and then strikes before full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one prepares to strike before full ordination and then strikes at the moment of full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one prepares to strike before full ordination and then strikes after full ordination has been received, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one prepares to strike at the moment of full ordination and then strikes at the moment of full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one prepares to strike at the moment of full ordination and then strikes after full ordination has been received, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one prepares to strike after full ordination has been received and then strikes after full ordination has been received, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If one prepares to strike after full ordination has been received and then strikes before full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if a monk strikes a layman, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Similarly, if one strikes a woman, a eunuch, a nun who has been expelled, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has maliciously shed the blood of a Tathāgata, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, one who dwells as a thief, one who does not dwell in the community, one who dwells separately, one against whom an earlier offense has arisen, or one with whom there has been an earlier dispute — in all such cases it is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if a monk strikes one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has sided with the schism, or one who has been given a formal act of instruction — what is the consequence in all such cases?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable ones, if a monk is striking another monk and that other's sex changes so that he becomes a nun, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if a nun is striking another nun and that other's sex changes so that she becomes a monk, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if a monk strikes a nun, a probationer, a female novice, or a male novice, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if a nun strikes a monk, a probationer, a female novice, or a male novice, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if one who has been given a formal act of instruction strikes a monk, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"Venerable ones, if a nun strikes a nun, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If she strikes a probationer, a female novice, or a male novice, it is a transgression."

Just as the chapter on striking has been set forth, so too the chapter on threatening to strike is to be stated in the same way.

In brief:
By message, letter, or gesture,
by having another say it, or by passing word from one to another —
if one is mad, mentally disturbed, or afflicted by illness,
or is mute, deaf, or asleep,
or is in delirium, drunk,
in meditative absorption, or gone elsewhere — these are the last cases.

The venerable Upāli asked the buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that whichever monk confronts a monk with a charge of a grave offense is guilty of a downfall. If a monk confronts a monk with a charge of a grave offense by means of a messenger, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Likewise, if such a charge is conveyed by letter, by gesture, by having another say it, or by passing it from one to another — in all such cases it is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if a monk confronts a monk with a charge of a grave offense by conveying it through a madman, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Likewise, if conveyed through one who is mentally disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is simple-minded, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one in delirium, one who is drunk, one in meditative absorption, or one who has gone to dwell elsewhere — in all such cases it is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if a monk confronts a monk who is mad with a charge of a grave offense, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Likewise, monks who are mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, simple-minded, mute, deaf, asleep, delirious, drunk, in meditative absorption, or dwelling elsewhere — if a monk confronts such monks with a charge of a grave offense, in all such cases it is a transgression."

In brief:
By voice, by body, by solitude,
by the fourth and seventh offense categories,
against laymen and the rest —
such is the confronting with charges, and so too for nuns.

"Venerable ones, if a monk, having been questioned, confronts a monk with a charge of a grave offense in the noble language, and that monk does not acknowledge it in the noble language, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If someone from the borderlands confronts a monk with a charge of a grave offense in the borderlands language, and that monk does not acknowledge it in the borderlands language, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If someone from the borderlands confronts a monk with a charge of a grave offense in the borderlands language—"

"—and that monk does not acknowledge it in the borderlands language, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If someone from the borderlands confronts a monk with a charge of a grave offense in the noble language, and that monk does not acknowledge it in the noble language, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if a monk, having been questioned, confronts a monk with a charge of a grave offense by means of a physical gesture, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, is there a case in which a monk confronts a monk with a charge of a grave offense, and yet it does not constitute an offense?" "Upāli, there is. It is when, on account of that charge, a monk's livelihood is disrupted, his life as a renunciant is disrupted, or his practice of the holy life is disrupted."

"Venerable ones, is there a case in which a monk confronts a monk with a charge, and yet it does not constitute a downfall?" "Upāli, there is. It is when he confronts him with a charge of an offense other than a grave offense."

"Venerable ones, if a monk confronts a monk with a charge of a grave offense, and then a change of status occurs so that the monk becomes a nun, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if a nun confronts a nun with a charge of a grave offense, and then a change of status occurs so that the nun becomes a monk, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if a monk perceives a grave offense as a grave offense and confronts the monk with a charge accordingly, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If he perceives a grave offense as not a grave offense and confronts him with a charge, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives something that is not a grave offense as not a grave offense and confronts him with a charge, what is the consequence?" "There is no offense."

"If he perceives something that is not a grave offense as a grave offense and confronts him with a charge, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if a monk perceives a fully ordained person as fully ordained and confronts him with a charge of a grave offense, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If he perceives a fully ordained person as not fully ordained and confronts the monk with a charge of a grave offense, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If he perceives a person who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained and confronts him with a charge, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If he perceives a person who is not fully ordained as fully ordained and confronts him with a charge, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if, at the time of full ordination, one sees a grave offense by a monk and then confronts him with a charge when he is not yet fully ordained, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one sees it at a time when he is not yet fully ordained and confronts him with a charge when the ordination is in progress, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one sees it at a time when he is not yet fully ordained and confronts him with a charge when he is fully ordained, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one sees it when the ordination is in progress and confronts him with a charge while the ordination is in progress, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one sees it when the ordination is in progress and confronts him with a charge after ordination is complete, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one sees it at the time of full ordination and confronts him with a charge at the time of full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If one sees it at the time of full ordination and confronts him with a charge when he is not yet fully ordained, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if a monk confronts a layman with a charge of a grave offense, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

Likewise, if one confronts any of the following with a charge of a grave offense — a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, a suspended nun, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a robber who has remained in the order, one who has not remained in the order, one who dwells apart, a non-Buddhist adherent, one who has gone over to non-Buddhist adherents, one who previously caused a schism, or one against whom a prior offense has arisen — in all such cases it constitutes a transgression.

"Venerable ones, if a monk confronts with a charge of a grave offense those who have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, those who have sided with them, or those to whom a rule of training has been administered, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable ones, if a monk confronts a layperson with a charge of a grave monastic offense, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Likewise, if he confronts any of them — from a female trainee down to one against whom a prior offense has arisen — in all such cases it is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if a monk confronts those who have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, those who have sided with them, or those to whom a rule of training has been administered with a charge of a grave monastic offense, what is the consequence?" "In every case it is a downfall."

"Venerable ones, if a monk speaks of a grave monastic offense to a layperson, does that count as having formally confronted him with it?" "Upāli, it does not."

"Likewise, if he speaks of it to any of them — from a female trainee down to one to whom a rule of training has been administered — does that count as having formally confronted them?" "Upāli, it does not."

"Venerable ones, if a monk confronts a fully ordained nun, a female trainee, a female novice, or a male novice with a charge of a grave monastic offense, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if a fully ordained nun confronts a monk, a female trainee, a female novice, or a male novice with a charge of a grave monastic offense, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if one to whom a rule of training has been administered confronts another with a charge of a grave monastic offense, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable ones, if a fully ordained nun confronts another fully ordained nun with a charge of a grave monastic offense, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"And if she confronts a female trainee, a female novice, or a male novice with such a charge, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

This is the noble Vinaya, the eleventh fascicle.

In summary:

By message, by letter, by gesture,
through another's words, or relayed from one to the next,
through madness, mental disturbance, illness,
deafness, dullness, sleep,
incoherence, intoxication,
and one in meditative absorption going elsewhere — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable Blessed One, you have declared that if a monk says to another monk, intending to have him separated from his food, 'Venerable, whether you speak with me or keep my company, things will not go well for you — you should leave,' and thereby causes that monk to be separated from his food even for a single moment, it becomes a downfall. Now, venerable one, if a monk causes another monk to be separated from his food by a personal message, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Likewise, if it is done by a written letter, by a gesture, through another's words, or relayed from one to the next and he is thereby separated from his food, in all such cases it is a transgression."

"Venerable ones, if a monk causes a mad monk to be separated from his food, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Likewise, if he causes any of the following to be separated from their food — one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is dull-witted, one who is asleep, one who is incoherent, one who is intoxicated, one who has entered meditative absorption, or a monk who is residing elsewhere — in all such cases it is a transgression."

In summary:

By voice, by body, in private,
by one using another's name,
laypersons and so forth —
the fourth and seventh concern food.

"Venerable ones, if a noble monk separates another monk from food using the noble language, and that monk does not understand the noble language, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a noble monk separates another from food using a regional border language, and that monk does not understand the regional border language, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one from the border regions separates another from food using a border language, and that monk does not understand the border language, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one from the border regions separates another from food using the noble language, and that monk does not understand the noble language, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a noble monk separates another monk from food using a physical gesture as the indicator, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If a noble monk perceives a secluded place as not secluded and separates another from food, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If a noble monk instructs another to separate someone else from food, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If a noble monk separates another from food on behalf of a third party, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If a noble monk is in the process of separating another monk from food, and in the course of that act the monk changes gender and becomes a nun, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a noble nun is in the process of separating another nun from food, and in the course of that act the nun changes gender and becomes a monk, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a noble monk separates a layman from food, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

Likewise, in all the following cases — separating a laywoman from food, separating an intersex person from food, separating one who has been expelled from the nuns' order, separating one who has killed a father, one who has killed a mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent, a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika), one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, one who has taken up a life of theft, one who is not residing in the community, one who is residing separately, one against whom an offence was previously committed, and one with whom a dispute previously arose — in all such cases the consequence is a transgression.

"If a noble monk separates from food one who has schismed the Saṅgha, one who has sided with a schism, or one who has given training rules, what is the consequence?" "In every case it is a downfall."

"If a noble monk perceives a human being as a human being and separates that person from food, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If a monk perceives a human being as not a human being and separates that person from food, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If a monk perceives a non-human being as not a human being and separates that being from food, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a monk perceives a non-human being as a human being and separates that being from food, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If a noble monk perceives one who is fully ordained as fully ordained and separates that person from food, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If a monk perceives one who is fully ordained as not fully ordained and separates that person from food, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a monk perceives one who is not fully ordained as fully ordained and separates that person from food, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a monk perceives one who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained and separates that person from food, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Noble one, if a monk who is not yet fully ordained invites a guest, and that guest is also not yet fully ordained at the time of being separated from food, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a monk who is not yet fully ordained invites a guest, and that guest has since received full ordination at the time of being separated from food, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a monk who is not yet fully ordained invites a guest, and that guest is in the very act of receiving full ordination at the time of being separated from food, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a monk who is in the very act of receiving full ordination invites a guest, and that guest is also in the very act of receiving full ordination at the time of being separated from food, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a monk who is in the very act of receiving full ordination invites a guest, and that guest has already received full ordination at the time of being separated from food, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a monk who is fully ordained invites a guest, and that guest is also fully ordained at the time of being separated from food, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If a monk who is fully ordained invites a guest, and that guest is not yet fully ordained at the time of being separated from food, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Noble one, are there cases in which a monk separates another monk from food and yet incurs no offence or downfall?"
"Upāli, there are. It is the case of one who is separated from food on the prescription of a physician."

"Noble one, are there cases in which a monk is separated from food and yet it does not constitute a downfall?" "Upāli, there are. If, apart from food proper, one is separated from other kinds of provisions — namely things to be eaten, things to be drunk, things to be tasted, things to be licked, and the like — the consequence is a transgression, not a downfall."

"If a noble monk separates a nun, a female probationer, a female novice, or male novices from food, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a noble nun separates a monk, a female probationer, a female novice, or male novices from food, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If a noble monk, applying a precept, separates a fully ordained monk from food, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If a noble nun separates a fully ordained nun from food, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If a female probationer, a female novice, or male novices separate a fully ordained monk, a fully ordained nun, a female probationer, a female novice, or male novices from food, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

In summary:
By messenger, by letter, by gesture,
by having another convey it, from one to another,
whether one has become mad, is mentally disturbed,
is ill, is disabled, or is traveling.

Venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, if the Blessed One has declared that whichever monk, without having requested permission, causes another to enter or exit a fire on his own behalf, incurs a downfall — if a monk causes another to enter or exit by means of a messenger, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "Likewise, if he causes another to enter or exit a fire by means of a letter, by gesture, by having another convey it, or by passing it from one to another, all such cases are transgressions."

"If a noble monk causes a madman to enter or exit a fire, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "Likewise, if he causes someone mentally disturbed, someone tormented by illness, a simpleton, a mute, a disabled person, or one who has gone to dwell in another place to enter or exit — all such cases are transgressions."

In summary:
By voice, by body, by a secluded place,
and in the same manner one reveals another's marks to others —
whether to householders and the like:
the fourth and seventh rules are the same.

"If a noble monk causes someone to enter or exit using the noble language, and that monk does not know the noble language, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If a noble one causes someone to enter or exit using a border language, and that monk does not know the border language, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If a border person causes someone to enter or exit using a border language, and that monk does not know the border language, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If a border person causes someone to enter or exit using the noble language, and that monk does not know the noble language, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a noble monk causes someone to enter or exit by means of a physical gesture, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If a noble monk, perceiving a place of solitude as not being solitary, causes someone to enter or exit, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a noble monk causes another person to enter or exit, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If a noble monk causes someone to enter or exit on behalf of another person, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If, while a noble monk is causing someone to enter or exit, that person's gender changes and he becomes a nun, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If, while a noble nun is causing someone to enter or exit, that person's gender changes and she becomes a monk, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If a noble monk causes a householder who is visibly present to enter or exit, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall." "Likewise, if he causes a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, a nun who has been expelled, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a non-Buddhist adherent, one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, one who has remained among thieves, one who has previously caused strife, or one against whom a previous offense has arisen, to enter or exit — in all such cases it is a downfall."

"If a noble monk causes those who have schismatized the Saṅgha, those who have sided with schismatics, or those upon whom a disciplinary measure has been imposed to enter or exit, what is the consequence?" "In all such cases it is a downfall."

"If a noble monk, perceiving a human being as a human being, causes that person to enter or exit, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall." "If he perceives a human being as not a human being and causes that person to enter or exit, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If he perceives a non-human being as a human being and causes that person to enter or exit, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If he perceives a non-human being as a non-human being and causes that person to enter or exit, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a noble monk, when a person has not yet received full ordination, arranges for a candidate who has not yet received full ordination, and causes that person to enter or exit, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If he arranges for a candidate who has not yet received full ordination, and causes someone who is in the process of receiving full ordination to enter or exit, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If he arranges for a candidate who has not yet received full ordination, and causes someone who has fully received ordination to enter or exit, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If he arranges for someone who is in the process of receiving full ordination, and causes someone who is in the process of receiving full ordination to enter or exit, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If he arranges for someone who is in the process of receiving full ordination, and causes someone who has fully received ordination to enter or exit, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If he arranges for someone who has fully received ordination, and causes someone who has fully received ordination to enter or exit, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall." "If he arranges for someone who has fully received ordination, and causes someone who has not yet received full ordination to enter or exit, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If a noble monk causes someone to enter or exit by means of giving a training precept, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall." "If a noble monk causes this through a fully ordained nun, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall." "If probationary nuns, novice nuns, or male novices cause someone to enter or exit, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

In brief:

By message, by letter, by gesture,
through another's words, or passed along from one to the next,
through a madman, one mentally disturbed, one who is ill,
one who is mute, one who is an idiot, one who is asleep,
one who is about to sneeze, one who is intoxicated,
and one who has entered meditative absorption — these are the last cases.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One taught that if a monk, having received a gift of faith for a deed in conformity with the Dharma of the Saṅgha, thereafter performs a deed of entanglement with respect to that same matter, and then says, 'Monk, I will not give you the gift of faith — relinquish it!' — he incurs a downfall." The venerable one then asked: "If a monk, having received a gift of faith for a deed in conformity with the Dharma of the Saṅgha, thereafter performs a deed of entanglement through a message, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "Likewise, if he performs a deed of entanglement through a letter, through a gesture, through another's words, or by passing it along from one to the next, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If a monk, having received a gift of faith for a deed in conformity with the Dharma of the Saṅgha, thereafter performs a deed of entanglement with respect to a madman, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "Likewise, if the deed of entanglement is performed with respect to one who is mentally disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is mute, one who is an idiot, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one about to sneeze, one who is intoxicated, one who has entered meditative absorption, or one who is dwelling elsewhere — in all such cases it is a transgression."

In brief:

By voice, by body, by solitude,
likewise, by one person indicating another's mark,
with respect to householders and others of that kind —
the fourth and seventh cases are likewise so.

"If a noble monk performs a deed of entanglement with a monk using the refined language of the noble ones, and that monk does not understand the refined language of the noble ones, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If a noble one performs a deed of entanglement with a monk using the language of the borderlands, and that monk does not understand the language of the borderlands, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If a borderlander performs a deed of entanglement with a monk using the language of the borderlands, and that monk does not understand the language of the borderlands, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If a borderlander performs a deed of entanglement with a monk using the refined language of the noble ones, and that monk does not understand the refined language of the noble ones, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If a monk performs a deed of entanglement by means of a bodily sign, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If a monk performs a deed of entanglement perceiving a secluded place as non-secluded, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If a monk instructs another to perform a deed of entanglement, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If a monk performs a deed of entanglement on behalf of another, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If a monk, while performing a deed of entanglement, changes his status and becomes a nun, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If a nun, while performing a deed of entanglement, changes her status and becomes a monk, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If a monk performs a deed of entanglement with a layman, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

Likewise, if a deed of entanglement is performed with a hermaphrodite, with a paṇḍaka, with an expelled nun, with one who has killed his father, with one who has killed his mother, with one who has killed an arhat, with one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent, with a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika), with one who has gone over to the non-Buddhist adherents, with one who is dwelling as a thief, with one who is not dwelling in proper standing, with one who is dwelling apart, with one against whom a prior offence has arisen, or with one involved in a prior dispute — in all such cases it becomes a transgression.

"If a monk performs a deed of entanglement with one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, with one who has sided with that schism, or with one who has been given a training — what is the consequence?" "In every case it becomes a downfall."

"If a monk perceives a Dharma-conformant act as a Dharma-conformant act and, granting consent, performs a deed of entanglement, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If a monk perceives a Dharma-conformant act as one that is not Dharma-conformant and performs a deed of entanglement, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a monk perceives a non-Dharma-conformant act as a Dharma-conformant act and performs a deed of entanglement, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a monk perceives a non-Dharma-conformant act as a non-Dharma-conformant act and performs a deed of entanglement, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a monk perceives one who has received full ordination as one who has received full ordination and performs a deed of entanglement, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If a monk perceives one who has received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination and performs a deed of entanglement, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a monk perceives one who has not received full ordination as one who has received full ordination and performs a deed of entanglement, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a monk perceives one who has not received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination and performs a deed of entanglement, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."
