"If consent is given during the period before full ordination and a deed of entanglement is performed during that same pre-ordination period, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If consent is given during the period before full ordination and a deed of entanglement is performed at the very moment of full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If consent is given during the period before full ordination and a deed of entanglement is performed after full ordination has been received, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If consent is given at the very moment of full ordination and a deed of entanglement is performed at that same moment of full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If consent is given at the very moment of full ordination and a deed of entanglement is performed after full ordination has been completed, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If consent is given after full ordination has been completed and a deed of entanglement is performed by one who has completed full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If consent is given at the time of full ordination and a deed of entanglement is performed in the pre-ordination period, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a monk grants consent to a Dharma-conformant act of the Saṅgha and then performs a deed of entanglement with a nun, a probationer nun (śikṣamāṇā), a female novice, or male novices, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a nun performs a deed of entanglement with a monk, a probationer nun, a female novice, or male novices, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one who has been given a training grants consent to a Dharma-conformant act of the Saṅgha and performs a deed of entanglement, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If a monk performs a deed of entanglement apart from having granted consent to a Dharma-conformant act of the Saṅgha, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"For a nun, a probationer nun, a female novice, and male novices, it becomes a transgression."

In brief:
One who has become mad, or whose mind is disturbed,
one who is sick, or one who walks while casting a spell,
at the middle watch of the night and at the fourth watch,
likewise an emanation, a paṇḍaka,
one who is veiled, one who is surrounded, and a nun —

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable Blessed One, you have declared that if a monk sleeps in the same dwelling together with an unordained person for more than two nights, it becomes a downfall. Venerable One, if a monk sleeps together with a mad person in a dwelling for two nights, and then on the third night sleeps together with one who is in their natural state of mind, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable One, if a monk sleeps for two nights with one who is in their natural state of mind, and then on the third night sleeps together with a mad person, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Likewise, if he sleeps together with one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, a deaf person, a mute, or one who dwells in another place of existence — all of these become transgressions."

"Venerable One, if a monk, having made himself invisible through a spell or medicine, sleeps in the same dwelling together with an unordained person for more than two nights, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable One, if a monk sleeps in the open sky together with an unordained person for more than two nights, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable One, if a monk sleeps with an unordained person for two nights in the same dwelling, and then on the third night sleeps together with a woman, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable One, if a monk perceives an unordained person as unordained and sleeps with that person for more than two nights, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If he perceives an unordained person as fully ordained and sleeps with that person, what is the consequence?"
"There is no offense."

"If he perceives a fully ordained person as unordained and sleeps with that person, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives a fully ordained person as fully ordained and sleeps with that person, what is the consequence?"
"There is no offense."

"Venerable One, if a monk perceives a human as human and sleeps for more than two nights with that person, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If he perceives a human as a non-human and sleeps with that being, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives a non-human as human and sleeps with that being, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives a non-human as a non-human and sleeps with that being, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable One, if a monk is sleeping with an unordained person for more than two nights and during that time changes status by receiving full ordination as a monk, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable One, if a nun is sleeping with an unordained person for more than two nights and during that time changes status by receiving full ordination as a nun, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable One, if a monk sleeps together with an emanation for more than two nights in the same dwelling, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable One, if a monk sleeps with an unordained person for two nights, and then on the third night sleeps together with a paṇḍaka, what is the consequence?" "It becomes both a downfall and a transgression."

"Venerable One, is there any case in which a monk might sleep in the same dwelling together with an unordained person without incurring an offense?" "Upāli, there is. If it is a place where every side is uncovered, or surrounded by a fence, or half-surrounded, or not surrounded at all, or unenclosed, or half-unenclosed — if one sleeps in such a place, there is no offense."

"Venerable One, if a monk sleeps with an unordained person for more than two nights in a mountain cave, a hollow tree, or a dense thicket, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable One, if one who has been given a training rule sleeps together with an unordained person for more than two nights, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable One, if a fully ordained nun sleeps together with an unordained person in the same dwelling for more than two nights, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression. For a female probationer, a novice nun, or male novices, it is a wrongdoing. The case of the monk Ariṣṭa, who was silenced three times and then declared to be in the remainder of the Saṅgha's judgment, applies here as well."

In brief:
By message, letter, gesture,
Or through another, from one to the next —
One who has become mad or mentally disturbed,
One who is ill or deaf — these are the categories.

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, if the Blessed One has declared that a monk who, while seeking to speak with a person who speaks in such a way and has not been followed in the Dharma, who has not abandoned the view of that wrongdoing, speaks with him, speaks with him repeatedly, seeks food from him, or sleeps together with him in the same dwelling — it becomes a transgression. Venerable One, if a monk who is seeking to speak with such a person as one who speaks in that way speaks by sending a message, or speaks repeatedly, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, sending a letter, using a gesture, having another convey the message, or passing it along from one to the next — all of these become wrongdoings."

"Venerable One, if a monk speaks with, speaks repeatedly with, seeks food from, or sleeps together in the same dwelling with a monk who is mad and has not been followed in the Dharma, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is simple-minded, or a monk who resides elsewhere and has not been followed in the Dharma — if one speaks with such a person, speaks repeatedly, eats with them, or sleeps together in the same dwelling, all of it becomes a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if a monk, while seeking to speak with a person who speaks in that way and has not been followed in the Dharma, renders himself invisible by means of a mantra or a medicine, and then speaks with that person, speaks repeatedly, seeks food, or sleeps together with that person in the same dwelling, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

In brief:
Mantra, utterances of the sky,
Body, seclusion, and eating —
The seventh and the fourth are likewise —
And so too with the female and the neuter.

"Venerable One, if a monk, while seeking to speak with a person who speaks in that way and has not been followed in the Dharma, renders himself invisible by means of a mantra or a medicine, and then speaks with that person, speaks repeatedly, seeks food, and sleeps together with that person in the same dwelling, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if a monk, while seeking to speak with such a person, they both go up into the sky and sleep there, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if a noble one who is a monk addresses such a person who speaks in that way using the noble language, and that person does not respond in the noble language, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if a noble one addresses that person who speaks in that way and has not been followed in the Dharma using a border language, and that person does not respond in a border language, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if one who speaks a border language addresses such a person who speaks in that way using a border language, and that person does not respond in a border language, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if one who speaks a border language addresses such a person who speaks in that way using the noble language, and that person does not respond in the noble language, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if a monk, while seeking to speak with such a person, makes himself understood through bodily signs, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if a monk, perceiving a secluded place as not secluded, speaks with or sleeps near such a person who speaks in that way, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if a monk, while seeking to speak with a person who speaks in that way, shares a meal together with that person, and beyond that meal also shares other provisions —"

drinks, lickables, and tastables, and the like — what is the consequence?"
"It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if a monk, seeking to speak with a person who speaks in that way while still not yet fully ordained, speaks to that person while both are not yet fully ordained, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"If the monk seeks that person out while not yet fully ordained, and speaks to them at the moment of full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"If the monk seeks that person out while not yet fully ordained, and speaks to them after full ordination has been completed, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"If the monk seeks that person out at the moment of full ordination and speaks to them at the moment of full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"If the monk seeks that person out at the moment of full ordination and speaks to them after full ordination has been completed, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"If the monk seeks that person out after full ordination has been completed and speaks to them after full ordination has been completed, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If the monk seeks that person out after full ordination has been completed and speaks to them while not yet fully ordained, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if a monk speaks to a person who speaks in that way, perceiving a fully ordained person as fully ordained, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If the monk speaks to a fully ordained person, perceiving that person as not fully ordained, what is the consequence?"
"It is a wrongdoing."

"If the monk speaks to a person who is not fully ordained, perceiving that person as fully ordained, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"If the monk speaks to a person who is not fully ordained, perceiving that person as not fully ordained, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if a monk, while seeking to speak with a person who speaks in that way, speaks to one who has not been consented to, perceiving that person as not consented to, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If the monk speaks to one who has not been consented to, perceiving that person as consented to, what is the consequence?" "There is no offense."

"If the monk speaks to one who has been consented to, perceiving that person as not consented to, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"If the monk speaks to one who has been consented to, perceiving that person as consented to, what is the consequence?"
"There is no offense."

"Venerable One, if a monk speaks with a person who speaks in that way and in the course of speaking that person changes sex and becomes a nun, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if a nun, while seeking to speak with a nun who speaks in that way, speaks with that nun and in the course of speaking that person changes sex and becomes a monk, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if a monk, while seeking to speak with a person who speaks in that way, speaks with a pandaka, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"Likewise, if the monk speaks with a nun who has been expelled, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, one who abides as a thief, one who does not abide in good standing, one who abides in a separate station, one who has previously caused a schism, or persons against whom a prior offense has arisen — in all such cases it is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if a monk, while seeking to speak in that way with such a person, speaks with one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has taken sides, or one to whom a training has been administered, what is the consequence?" "In all cases it is a downfall."

"Venerable One, if a monk speaks with a person who speaks in that way while that person is asleep, delirious, or intoxicated, and has not conformed to the Dharma, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if a monk speaks with a nun who speaks in that way, a female probationer, a female novice, or male novices, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if one to whom a training has been administered, while seeking to speak with a person who speaks in that way and has not conformed to the Dharma, speaks with that person, speaks constantly with that person, seeks food together with that person, or sleeps near that person, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable One, if a nun, while seeking to speak with a nun who speaks in that way, speaks with that nun, speaks constantly with her, or sleeps together with her in the same dwelling, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable One, a nun and —"

"Venerable One, if one speaks with a novice monk who speaks in that way and has not conformed to the Dharma, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"With a probationer nun, a novice nun, and novice monks — it is a downfall. Just as with a person who speaks in that way, one must also declare that such a person has been shown to be unfit as a renunciant. When asked what the difference is, one must also explain the matter of service and veneration apart from work and provisions."

In brief:
The unfit, the marks, and so forth —
the fourth and the seventh are as stated —
all prohibitions, their nature,
the dyes, the training, and the nuns.

The venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, the Blessed One has declared that when a monk obtains a robe, he must discolor it by one of three means of discoloring; if he distributes a robe without having discolored it by any one of those three means, it becomes a downfall. Venerable One, is there a case where a monk distributes a robe without having discolored it by any one of the three means of discoloring, yet it does not become a downfall?"

"Upāli, there is: the use of a prohibited robe. A prohibited robe is one made of she-camel's wool, ox wool, goat's wool, wild animal's wool, a mixture of these, or cloth that has not been woven. If such a robe is used, it becomes an offense."

"Venerable One, if a monk uses a robe without having discolored it by any one of the three means of discoloring, and in the meantime his status changes and he becomes a nun, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If a nun uses a robe without having discolored it by any one of the three means of discoloring, and in the meantime her status changes and she becomes a monk, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable One, if a monk perceives a robe that has been properly discolored as not having been discolored, and uses it, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If one perceives a robe that has not been discolored as having been discolored, and uses it, there is no offense."

"If one perceives a robe that has been discolored as not having been discolored, and uses it, what is the consequence?"
"It is an offense."

"If one perceives a robe that has been discolored as having been discolored, and uses it, what is the consequence?"
"There is no offense."

"Venerable One, if a robe was obtained before full ordination and one of the three means of discoloring was applicable to it, and one uses it without having discolored it after full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is an offense."

"If a robe was obtained before full ordination and one uses it as if still before full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is an offense."

"If a robe was obtained before full ordination and one uses it after having received full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If a robe was obtained at the time of full ordination and one uses it at the time of full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is an offense."

"If a robe was obtained at the time of full ordination and one uses it after full ordination, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If a robe was obtained after full ordination and one uses it after full ordination, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If a robe was obtained after full ordination and one uses it without full ordination, what is the consequence?"
"It is an offense."

"Venerable One, if a monk uses a robe smaller than one cubit, or a piece of cloth the size of the Sugata's Dharma robe, without having discolored it by any one of the three means, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable One, is there a case where a monk uses a robe that has been discolored by one of the three means of discoloring, yet it nonetheless constitutes an offense?"

"Upāli, there is: when a monk uses a robe that is entirely blue, entirely yellow, or entirely red."

"Venerable One, is there a case where a monk uses a robe without having discolored it by any one of the three means of discoloring, and yet it does not constitute an offense?"

"Upāli, there is: namely, when that monk has divided up the cloth that is the nature of a robe."

"Venerable One, is there a case where a monk uses a robe that has been discolored by one of the three means of discoloring, and yet it nonetheless constitutes an offense?"

"Upāli, there is: when it has been dyed with a major dye. The major dyes are saffron, yellow orpiment, lac, madder, heartwood of the ra tree, and similar substances. If one uses a robe dyed with such dyes, it becomes a transgression."

"Venerable One, if one who has received the training uses a robe not discolored by any one of the three means of discoloring, what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable One, if a nun uses a robe not discolored by any one of the three means of discoloring, what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable One, if female probationers, novice nuns, and male novices use a robe not discolored by any one of the three means of discoloring, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

In summary:
The rule on women and precious things is likewise so.
The fourth, on touching, is the same.
The rule for others, and the seventh, illustrates this.
Musical instruments and magical creations — bear this in mind.

The venerable Upāli then questioned the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, the Blessed One has said that if a monk takes up with his own hand, or causes another to take up, a precious thing or something counted as precious, it becomes a downfall — except when he is within a boundary enclosure or within a residence. Venerable One, is there a case where a monk takes up with his own hand a precious thing or something counted as precious, and yet the offense does not become a downfall?"

"Upāli, there is: if one takes up one of the five precious things such as a precious woman and so forth, it is an offense proportionate to the actual act. However, if one takes up a precious jewel or a precious wheel, it is a downfall."

"Venerable One, if a monk takes up a precious thing or something counted as precious, and then undergoes a change of sex and becomes a nun, what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable One, if a nun takes up a precious thing or something counted as precious, and then undergoes a change of sex and becomes a monk, what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable One, if a monk takes up a precious thing perceiving it as precious, what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"If one takes up a precious thing perceiving it as not precious, what is the consequence?"

"There is no offense."

"If one takes up something that is not precious perceiving it as precious, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one takes up something that is not precious perceiving it as not precious, what is the consequence?"

"There is no offense."

"Likewise, perceiving something as being counted as precious is also to be applied in these four ways."

"Venerable One, if a monk hands over a precious thing or something counted as precious to another, what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable One, if a monk causes another to take up a precious thing or something counted as precious, what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable One, if, before full ordination, one sets out a precious thing or something counted as precious intending to take it, and takes it before full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one sets it out before full ordination and takes it at the moment of full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one sets it out before full ordination and takes it after full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one sets it out at the moment of full ordination and takes it at the moment of full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one sets it out at the moment of full ordination and takes it after full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one sets it out at the moment of full ordination and takes it at the moment of full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one sets it out at the moment of full ordination and takes it before full ordination, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk may take a precious object or something equivalent to a precious object and yet not incur a transgression through a downfall?"

"Upāli, there is. If one takes a divine precious object or something equivalent to a precious object, it becomes a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk may take something equivalent to a precious object and yet not incur a transgression through a downfall?"

"Upāli, there is. It is a case of taking something that is damaged."

"Venerable one, if a monk takes an emanated precious object or something equivalent to a precious object, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk may use a precious object or something equivalent to a precious object and yet not incur a transgression through a downfall?"

"Upāli, there is: in a dwelling place of gods, or a dwelling place of nāgas, or a dwelling place of yakṣas, or in a royal palace, or in the residence of a great minister of the king, where no seat or other receptacle is available."

"Venerable one, if one to whom a training has been given takes a precious object or something equivalent to a precious object, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun takes a precious object or something equivalent to a precious object, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a female trainee takes a precious object or something equivalent to a precious object, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a female novice or a male novice takes a precious object or something equivalent to a precious object, what is the consequence?"

"There is no offense."

The Sacred Vinaya Text, the Twelfth Fascicle.

In brief, the four factors of time are thus explained,
along with preparation and likewise the night,
as well as water and rain,
the giving of training, and the nun.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that bathing twice a month is a transgression except when the occasion for it has arisen. Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk may bathe constantly without incurring an offense?"

"Upāli, there is: bathing when any one of seven legitimate occasions has arisen."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives that the half-month has not yet elapsed when it actually has not elapsed, and bathes, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives that the half-month has elapsed when it actually has not elapsed, and bathes, what is the consequence?"

"There is no offense."

"If one perceives that the half-month has not elapsed when it actually has elapsed, and bathes, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one perceives that the half-month has elapsed when it actually has elapsed, and bathes, what is the consequence?"

"There is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives water as water and bathes in it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives water as something that is not water and bathes in it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one perceives something that is not water as water and bathes in it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one perceives something that is not water as not water and bathes in it, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk bathes at the proper time, with the blessing conferred, and yet incurs an offense?"

"Upāli, there is: one who, having sent away the bather, creeps in like a small bird."

"Venerable one, if a monk who has bathed within the half-month without having received the blessing has his sex changed and becomes a nun, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun who has bathed without having received the blessing has her sex changed and becomes a monk, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk bathes using something other than water, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk may bathe constantly and yet not incur an offense?"

"Upāli, there is."

"Swimming across water, or bathing when rain falls."

"Venerable one, if one who has received the precept bathes within the half-month without having received the blessing, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun bathes within the half-month without having received the blessing, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if female probationers (śikṣamāṇā), female novices, and male novices bathe within the half-month without having received the blessing, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

The case of knowingly depriving a living animal that has fallen into the animal realm of its life is to be distinguished as explained in the section on root defeats.

In brief:
A message, a letter, a gesture,
through an intermediary, from one to another,
a madman, one mentally disturbed, one afflicted by illness,
one who is deaf, one who is dull-witted, one who is asleep,
one who has a speech impediment, one who is intoxicated,
one who is in meditative absorption, and one who has gone elsewhere — these are the last.

Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that if a monk, while being solicited, causes another monk to feel regret, it is a transgression. If a monk causes a monk to feel regret by means of a message, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if he causes regret through a letter, a gesture, through an intermediary, or passed from one to another — all of these are wrong deeds."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes a mad monk to feel regret, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if he causes regret in a monk who is mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, dull-witted, mute, deaf, asleep, with a speech impediment, intoxicated, in meditative absorption, or residing in another destination — all of these are wrong deeds."

In brief:
Voice, body, and solitude, mantra,
a sign, the fourth, the seventh,
householders and the like,
and the remainder — these apply to nuns.

"Venerable one, if a noble monk causes regret in the noble language, and that monk does not understand the noble language, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a noble monk causes regret in a frontier language, and that monk does not understand the frontier language, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one from the frontier causes regret in a frontier language, and that monk does not understand the frontier language, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one from the frontier causes regret in the noble language, and that monk does not understand the noble language, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes a monk to feel regret by directing his attention toward his body, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a secluded place as non-secluded and causes regret, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk renders himself invisible by means of a mantra or medicine and thereby causes a monk to feel regret, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if, while a monk is causing a monk to feel regret, his sex changes and he becomes a nun, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if, while a nun is causing regret, her sex changes and she becomes a monk, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives one who is fully ordained as fully ordained and causes regret, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives one who is fully ordained as not fully ordained and causes regret, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If he perceives one who is fully ordained as not fully ordained, it is a wrong deed."

"If he perceives one who is not fully ordained as fully ordained and causes regret, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk intends to cause regret to one who is not fully ordained, perceiving him as not fully ordained, and it is accomplished, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If he intends it toward one who is not fully ordained, perceiving him as fully ordained, and it is accomplished, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If he intends it toward one who is not fully ordained, and it is accomplished with one who is fully ordained, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If he intends it toward one who is fully ordained, perceiving him as fully ordained, and it is accomplished, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If he intends it toward one who is fully ordained, and it is accomplished with one who has become fully ordained, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If he intends it toward one who is fully ordained, perceiving him as fully ordained, and it is accomplished with one who is fully ordained, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If he intends it toward one who is fully ordained, perceiving him as not fully ordained, and it is accomplished, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes regret to a layman, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

Likewise, causing regret to a woman, a paṇḍaka (a person of indeterminate sex), an expelled nun, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has, with malicious intent, drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, one abiding as a thief, one dwelling in isolation, one not dwelling in the community, one against whom an offense had previously arisen, and those who had previously been in conflict — causing regret to all of these constitutes a wrong deed in every case.

"Venerable one, if a monk causes regret to those who have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, to those who have sided with them, and to those who have administered a training rule — what is the consequence?"

"All of these are transgressions."

"Venerable one, is there a case where a monk causes regret to a monk and yet the offense of causing regret does not constitute a transgression?"

"Upāli, there is. If the offense in question is one accompanied by a residual factor, and he causes regret with respect to it."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes regret on behalf of others, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes regret to a nun, a probationer nun, a novice nun, or to the community of monks, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a nun causes regret to a nun, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If she causes regret to a monk, a probationer nun, a novice nun, or to male novices, all of these are wrong deeds."

Likewise, if a probationer nun, a novice nun, or male novices cause regret to one another, it is a wrong deed in every case.

"Venerable one, if one who administers a training rule causes regret to monks, what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

In brief:
One who is mad, mentally disturbed,
one who is senseless, foolish, or asleep,
one who is delirious, one who is intoxicated,
one in meditative absorption — these last are the exceptions.

Then the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that touching another with a finger is a transgression. If a monk touches a mad monk with a finger, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

Likewise, touching one who is mentally disturbed, foolish, mute, senseless, asleep, delirious, intoxicated, in meditative absorption, or a monk dwelling in another place — touching all of these is a wrong deed in every case.

In brief:
The body, a tooth, a fingernail,
hair, a covering, a wound — likewise —
laymen and others of that kind:
the marks, and then the fourth and the seventh.

"Venerable one, apart from touching with a finger, if a monk touches another using another part of the body — the head, the shoulder, the elbow, the knee, the heel — or using a stick, a stone, or a clod of earth — what is the consequence?"

"All of these are wrong deeds."

"Venerable one, if a monk whose bodily faculties are impaired touches one whose bodily faculties are not impaired, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk whose bodily faculties are not impaired touches one whose bodily faculties are impaired — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk touches using a tooth — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk touches using a fingernail — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk touches using a hair, or touches a hair — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk touches one who is covered — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk touches a wound, or touches at a wound — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk touches a layman — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

Likewise, if one touches in such a manner: a woman, a eunuch, a suspended nun, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika), one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, one who dwells among thieves, one dwelling apart, one who does not dwell in the community, one who has previously committed an offense, or one who has previously caused a schism — all of these are wrong deeds.

"Venerable one, if a monk touches one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has taken sides in a schism, or one who has administered a training rule — what is the consequence?"

"All of these are transgressions."

"Venerable one, if a monk touches a fully ordained nun, or a nun in training, or a female novice, or male novices — what is the consequence?"

"All of these are wrong deeds."

"Venerable one, if a fully ordained nun touches a monk, a nun in training, a female novice, or male novices — what is the consequence?"

"All of these are wrong deeds."

"Venerable one, if a monk, while touching a monk, has a sex change and becomes a nun — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a fully ordained nun, while touching a nun, has a sex change and becomes a monk — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a fully ordained person as fully ordained and touches that person — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives a fully ordained person as not fully ordained and touches that person — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one perceives a person who is not fully ordained as fully ordained and touches that person — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one perceives a person who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained and touches that person — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

Likewise, the fourfold matrix is to be applied also to the case of perceiving a human being as a human being.

"Venerable one, if one intends to touch a person who is not fully ordained and touches one who is not fully ordained — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one intends to touch a person who is not fully ordained and touches one who is in the course of receiving full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one intends to touch a person who is not fully ordained and touches one who is fully ordained — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one intends to touch one who is in the course of receiving full ordination and touches one who is in the course of receiving full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one intends to touch one who is in the course of receiving full ordination and touches one who is fully ordained — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If one intends to touch one who is fully ordained and touches one who is fully ordained — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one intends to touch one who is fully ordained and touches one who is not fully ordained — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if one who has administered a training rule touches a monk — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a fully ordained nun touches a fully ordained nun — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"With regard to a nun in training, a female novice, and male novices — it is a wrong deed."

In brief:
A message, a letter, a hand-signal,
speaking through another, and from one to another —
a mad person, one whose mind is disturbed, one who is ill,

one who is deaf-mute, one who is simple-minded, one who is asleep,
one who is vomiting, one who is intoxicated,
one who has entered meditative absorption, and one traveling elsewhere — these are the last.

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if one causes satisfaction with water it becomes a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk causes satisfaction with water by means of a message — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if one causes satisfaction with water by means of a letter, a hand-signal, speaking through another, or passing the message from one to another — all of these become wrong deeds."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes satisfaction to a mad woman with water — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if one causes satisfaction to one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is simple-minded, one who is mute, one who is deaf-mute, one who is asleep, one who is vomiting, one who is intoxicated, one who has entered meditative absorption, or one who is dwelling elsewhere — all of these become wrong deeds."

Just as the manner in which one causes satisfaction is elaborated, so too playing, expression of desire, laughing, running, and physical striking are to be set forth in full.

In brief:
Water, two, and likewise mantra,
another through another's characteristics,
seclusion, the fourth, a hermaphrodite,
one who has administered a training rule, and a fully ordained nun.

"Venerable one, if a monk causes satisfaction by means of something other than water — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes satisfaction with drops of falling rain, or with drops of snow, or with drops of dew — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk renders himself invisible by means of mantra or medicine and then causes satisfaction — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes another monk to bring about satisfaction — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes satisfaction on behalf of others — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if while a monk is causing satisfaction with water his characteristics change and he becomes a fully ordained nun — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if while a fully ordained nun is causing satisfaction with water her characteristics change and she becomes a fully ordained monk — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a secluded place as not secluded and causes satisfaction — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives water as not water, it becomes a wrong deed."

"If he perceives what is not water as not water and causes satisfaction — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if one perceives a human as a human, this too is to be applied in four ways."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes a hermaphrodite to experience satisfaction — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if one causes a female hermaphrodite or a person of dual characteristics to experience satisfaction, all of these become wrong deeds."

Just as the manner of causing satisfaction is elaborated, so too playing, desire, laughing, running, and physical striking are likewise to be set forth in full.

"Venerable one, if one who has administered a training rule causes satisfaction — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a fully ordained nun causes satisfaction with water or causes another to do so — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

With regard to a nun in training, a female novice, and male novices — it is a wrong deed.

In brief:
A mad person, one whose mind is disturbed,
a female hermaphrodite, one traveling in an emanated form,
space, mantra, characteristics,
the fourth — and likewise a hermaphrodite.

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk sleeps together with a woman in the same dwelling it becomes a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk sleeps together with a mad woman in the same dwelling — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if one sleeps together with one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, or one dwelling elsewhere, in the same dwelling — it is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk sleeps together with an emanated woman in the same dwelling — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk sleeps together with a woman in the same dwelling, up in the open sky — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk renders himself invisible by means of mantra or medicine and sleeps together with a woman in the same dwelling — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk is sleeping together with a woman in the same dwelling and his sex changes so that he becomes a nun — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a nun is sleeping together with a man in the same dwelling and her sex changes so that she becomes a monk — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a woman as a woman and sleeps with her — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives a woman as not a woman — there is no offense."

"If he perceives a non-woman as a woman — it is a wrong deed."

"If he perceives a non-woman as a non-woman — there is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a human woman as human and sleeps together with her in the same dwelling — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives a human as non-human — it is a wrong deed."

"If he perceives a non-human as human — it is a wrong deed."

"If he perceives a non-human as non-human — it is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk sleeps together with a hermaphrodite in the same dwelling — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

In summary:

A mountain ravine, dense forest,
Surrounded, covered, a large one,
Grasped, likewise by day,
Giving the training, and a nun.

"Venerable one, if a monk sleeps together with a woman in a mountain ravine, a dense forest, or the hollow of a tree — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk sleeps together with a woman wholly covered, or half-encircled, or not encircled — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk sleeps together with a woman encircled by a boundary, uncovered, half-covered, or half-uncovered — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if one sleeps in the same dwelling as a being born in an animal rebirth it is a wrong deed. Of what kind is that?"

"Upāli, it is a great female animal."

"Of what kind, great one?"

He declared: "Among birds — a hen, or another like a hen. Among four-footed animals — a female monkey, or another like a female monkey."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk sleeps in the same dwelling together with a non-human woman it is a wrong deed. Of what kind is a non-human?"

"One who possesses and displays all her limbs."

"Venerable one, if a monk sleeps together with a woman in the same dwelling during the daytime — what is the consequence?"

"Upāli, up until dawn it is a wrong deed. From dawn onward it becomes a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who has been given the training sleeps together with a woman in the same dwelling — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun sleeps together with a man in the same dwelling — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

For a female probationer, a novice nun, and male novices — it is a wrong deed.

In summary:

Sending a message, a letter, a hand-signal,
Another saying it, from one to another,
Mad, mentally disturbed, ill,
Mute, foolish, asleep,
Delirious, intoxicated,
In meditative absorption, and finally the one departing.

Thus did the venerable Upāli petition the Blessed One, the Buddha.

"Venerable one, if the Blessed One has declared that blaming or causing to be blamed incurs a transgression — then, venerable one, if a monk causes a monk to be blamed by means of a messenger, what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if it is done through a letter, a hand-signal, through another person speaking, or passed along from one to another causing blame — all of these are wrong deeds."

"Likewise, if a monk who is mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, foolish, mute, deaf, asleep, delirious, intoxicated, in meditative absorption, or one who has gone to dwell elsewhere — if such a one causes blame or is caused to blame another — all of these are wrong deeds."

In summary:

By voice, by body, and by a secluded place's signal,
Another blamed by another's seventh,
Laymen and the rest,
The fourth case — including the night — is likewise.

"Venerable one, if a noble monk causes a monk to be blamed in the noble language, and that monk does not know the noble language — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If a noble monk causes a monk to be blamed in a frontier language, and that monk does not know the frontier language — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If a frontier monk causes a monk to be blamed in a frontier language, and that monk does not know the frontier language — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If a frontier monk causes a monk to be blamed in the noble language, and that monk does not know the noble language — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk blames a monk using a physical gesture — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a secluded place as non-secluded, blames a monk — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk renders himself invisible by means of a mantra or a drug and then blames a monk — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes another to be blamed — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk blames a monk on behalf of another monk — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if the blame was prepared before full ordination and completed before full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If it was prepared before full ordination and completed during the act of full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If it was prepared before full ordination and completed after full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If it was prepared during the act of full ordination and completed during the act of full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If it was prepared during the act of full ordination and completed after full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"If it was prepared after full ordination and completed after full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If it was prepared after full ordination and completed before full ordination — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Venerable one, if a monk blames a layman — what is the consequence?"

"It is a wrong deed."

"Likewise, if it concerns a eunuch, an expelled nun, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn the blood of a Tathāgata, a non-Buddhist adherent, one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, one who dwells among thieves, one who dwells apart, one who does not dwell in the community, one against whom an earlier offence has occurred, or one against whom there was a prior dispute — if blame is given or caused to be given to any of these, all such acts are wrong deeds."

"Venerable one, if a monk directly blames or causes to be blamed a monk who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has sided with the schismatic faction, or a monk who has been given a formal instruction — what is the consequence?"

"All of these are transgressions."

"Venerable one, if a monk directly causes a monk to blame a layman — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Likewise, a eunuch, an expelled nun, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, and one who with malicious intent has drawn the blood of a Tathāgata —"

one who holds non-Buddhist views, one who has gone over to non-Buddhist views, one who is dwelling illicitly, one who is living separately, one who is not residing in the community, one against whom a prior offense has arisen, one who was previously involved in a dispute, one who has sided with a faction, a monk who has been given a formal instruction, a nun, a female probationer, a female novice, or male novices — if a monk directly blames or causes any of these to be blamed, all of these are transgressions.

"Venerable one, if a monk directly blames or causes to be blamed a nun, a female probationer, a female novice, or male novices — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun directly blames or causes to be blamed a monk, a female probationer, a female novice, or male novices — what is the consequence?"

"All of these are transgressions."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving one who is fully ordained as fully ordained, directly blames or causes him to be blamed — what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"If he perceives one who is fully ordained as not fully ordained, it is a transgression. If he perceives one who is not fully ordained as fully ordained, it is a transgression. If he perceives one who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained and directly blames or causes him to be blamed, it is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk directly blames or causes a monk to be blamed and, while this is occurring, that monk changes his status and becomes a nun — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun directly blames or causes a nun to be blamed and, while this is occurring, that nun changes her status and becomes a monk — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who has been given a formal instruction directly blames or causes a monk to be blamed — what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun directly blames or causes a nun to be blamed — what is the consequence?"

"It is a downfall."

As for a female probationer, a female novice, and male novices, these are to be explained extensively as transgressions.

In brief:

By messenger, by letter, by hand-signal,
through another's words, and from one to another;
one who is mad, mentally disturbed, or ill,
one who is mute, simpleminded, or asleep,
one who is intoxicated, one who is drunk,
one in meditative absorption, and one who has gone elsewhere — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk conceals or causes to be concealed the alms bowl, the robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to another monk, it is a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk causes such concealment by means of a messenger — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Likewise, if it is done by letter, by hand-signal, through another's words, or by passing it from one to another and causing the concealment — all of these are transgressions."

"Venerable one, if a monk conceals or causes to be concealed the alms bowl, the robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to a monk who is mad — what is the consequence?"

"All of these are transgressions."

"Likewise, if it involves the alms bowl, the robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to a monk who is mentally disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is simpleminded, one who is mute, one who is blind, one who is asleep, one who is intoxicated, one who is drunk, one who is in meditative absorption, or one who has gone to dwell elsewhere — if anyone conceals or causes the concealment of such items, all of these are transgressions."

In brief:

Unsuitable items and likewise mantras,
small and large, and also robes;
laypeople and so forth;
with marks, and the fourth, and the seventh;
one Saṅgha acting on behalf of another Saṅgha,
giving a training precept, and a nun.

"Venerable one, if a monk conceals or causes to be concealed the alms bowl, the robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to another monk by hiding something that is unsuitable — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk, by means of a mantra or medicine, renders a monk invisible and conceals his alms bowl —"

"— or a robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk by means of a mantra, or medicine, or supernatural power conceals a monk's alms bowl, or robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes to be concealed a robe smaller than a cubit, or a small alms bowl, or an alms bowl larger than the standard measure — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk conceals or causes to be concealed, not the alms bowl, or robe, or any other requisite of a monk proper, but rather some other item belonging to a layperson — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes to be concealed a layperson's vessel, or robe, or any other such item — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

Likewise in all the following cases: one who has eaten a meal with a hermaphrodite; one who has expelled a nun; one who has killed his father; one who has killed his mother; one who has killed an arhat; one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent; a tīrthika; one who has gone over to the tīrthikas; one who is a thief living among the community; one who is living separately; one who is not residing properly; one who was previously involved in a schism; one who has previously incurred an offense — if the alms bowl, or robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to such a person is concealed or caused to be concealed, all cases constitute a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk conceals or causes to be concealed the alms bowl or robe of a monk who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, or who has taken sides in a schism, or who has received a training precept — what is the consequence?" "All are downfalls."

"Venerable one, if a monk conceals or causes to be concealed the alms bowl, or robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to a nun, a female probationer, a female novice, or a male novice — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun conceals or causes to be concealed the alms bowl, or robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to a monk, a female probationer, a female novice, or a male novice — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk causes a layperson to conceal in plain sight a monk's alms bowl, or robe, or any other requisite of a monk — what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

Likewise, in all the following cases: one who has eaten a meal with a hermaphrodite; one who has expelled a nun; one who has killed his father; one who has killed his mother; one who has killed an arhat; one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent; a tīrthika; one who has gone over to the tīrthikas; one who is a thief living among the community; one who is living separately; one who is not residing properly; one who has previously incurred an offense; one who was previously involved in a schism; one who has taken sides in a schism; one who has received a training precept — and likewise a monk, a nun, a female probationer, a female novice, or a male novice — if any of them are caused to conceal such requisites in plain sight, it is a downfall.

"Venerable one, if a monk conceals or causes to be concealed the alms bowl, or robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to a monk, and in the meantime that monk changes his status and becomes a nun — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun conceals or causes to be concealed the alms bowl, or robe, or any other requisite of an ascetic belonging to a nun, and in the meantime that nun changes her status and becomes a monk — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk conceals — perceiving a fully ordained person as fully ordained — what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

"If he perceives a fully ordained person as not fully ordained, it is a transgression. If he perceives one who is not fully ordained as fully ordained, it is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who is not fully ordained is concealed while being perceived as not fully ordained — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one sets out to conceal while the other is not fully ordained, and the concealment is accomplished while the other is still not fully ordained — what is the consequence?"

"It is a transgression."

"If one sets out to conceal while the other is not fully ordained, and the concealment is accomplished just as the other becomes fully ordained — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one sets out to conceal while the other is not fully ordained, and the concealment is accomplished after the other has been fully ordained — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one sets out to conceal just as the other is becoming fully ordained, and the concealment is accomplished just as the other is becoming fully ordained — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one sets out to conceal just as the other is becoming fully ordained, and the concealment is accomplished after the other has been fully ordained — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If one sets out to conceal while the other is fully ordained, and the concealment is accomplished after the other has been fully ordained — what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If one sets out to conceal while the other is fully ordained, and the concealment is accomplished while the other is not fully ordained — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives another person the bowl or robe of a monk, or any other requisite of a renunciant, to be hidden — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk hides the property of the Saṅgha, or gives it to another to be hidden — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk hides the bowl or robe of a monk, or any other requisite for the livelihood of a renunciant, on behalf of another — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who gives the training hides or gives to another to be hidden the bowl or robe of a monk, or any other requisite of a renunciant — what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun hides or gives to another to be hidden the bowl or robe of a nun, or any other requisite of a renunciant — what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

For novice nuns, novice nuns, and male novices it is a transgression.

In summary, the categories are:
by messenger, written message, gesture,
through another's word, or passed from one to the next,
in the case of one who is mad, mentally disturbed, or ill,
a mute, a deaf person, one who is asleep,
one who has lockjaw, one who is intoxicated,
one who has entered absorption, or one dwelling elsewhere — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has taught that if a monk gives a robe and it is used without being reclaimed, it becomes a downfall. If a monk gives a robe to a monk by messenger and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Likewise, if a robe given by written message, gesture, through another's word, or passed from one to the next is used without being returned — all of these are transgressions."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a mad monk and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

Likewise, if a robe is given to a monk who is mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, confused, mute, deaf, asleep, suffering from lockjaw, intoxicated, in meditative absorption, or dwelling in another place, and it is used without being returned — all of these are transgressions.

In summary:
improper cloth, and likewise mantras,
small and large robes,
householders and the like,
by night, and the fourth, and the seventh,
another's property and given to another,
given as training, and a nun.

"Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk gives a robe to a monk, and even though it is used without being reclaimed, the offense does not become a downfall?" "Upāli, there is. It is when the cloth has become improper. Improper cloth is: wool from a female yak, wool from an ox, wool from a deer, wool from a goat, mixed wool, or wool that has not been woven. If a robe of such material is given and used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives something produced by mantra, medicine, or miraculous transformation, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe that is smaller than a cubit in measure, or of the size of a robe of the Sugata (the Well-Gone One, an epithet of the Buddha), and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives items of a recluse's requisites other than robes, and they are used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a layman, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a female monk who eats together with the community, or to a hermaphrodite, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

Likewise, if a robe is given to one who has killed a father, or a mother, or an arhat; to one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent; to a non-Buddhist adherent; to one who has gone over to non-Buddhist adherents; to one who is in hiding; to one who does not remain in the community; to one who dwells in seclusion; to one against whom a prior offence has arisen; or to one who was previously in dispute — and in each case it is used without being reclaimed — all such cases are transgressions.

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a monk who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, or to one who sides with such a person, or to a monk who confers the training precepts, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a nun, a probationary nun, a female novice, or a male novice, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a nun, a probationary nun, a female novice, or a male novice, and while it is being used without being reclaimed, a change of status occurs and the recipient becomes a fully ordained nun — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to a monk, and while it is being used without being reclaimed, a change of status occurs and the recipient becomes a fully ordained nun — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a fully ordained nun gives a robe to a fully ordained nun, and while it is being used without being reclaimed, a change of status occurs and the recipient becomes a fully ordained monk — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe to one who has received full ordination, perceiving that person as fully ordained, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If one perceives a fully ordained person as not fully ordained — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives a person who has not received full ordination as fully ordained — what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If one perceives a person who has not received full ordination as not fully ordained, gives a robe, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if while one has not yet received full ordination a robe is given, and before full ordination has been received it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If it is given before full ordination, and is used without being reclaimed while full ordination is in the process of being conferred — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If it is given before full ordination, and is used without being reclaimed after full ordination has been completed — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a robe is given while full ordination is in the process of being conferred, and it is used without being reclaimed while full ordination is still in the process of being conferred — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a robe is given while full ordination is in the process of being conferred, and it is used without being reclaimed after full ordination has been completed — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If a robe is given after full ordination has been completed, and it is used without being reclaimed after full ordination has been completed — what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If a robe is given after full ordination has been completed, and it is used without being reclaimed before full ordination was completed — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a robe away that he received from another monk, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a monk a robe that is held in common, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk gives a monk a robe on another's behalf, and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who confers the training precepts gives a robe to a monk and it is used without being reclaimed — what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

For a probationary nun, a female novice, and male novices, all such cases are to be stated as transgressions.

As for giving the surplus property of the Saṅgha with malicious intent — the distinctions are to be set forth in the same manner as what has been described regarding malicious intent toward a root downfall.

The Noble Vinaya Text, the Thirteenth Fascicle.

In brief:
One who is insane, one whose mind is disturbed,
One who is ill, and likewise one who uses mantra,
The sky, the fourth case with its counterpart,
Youths and those of indeterminate sex,
And likewise an emanated being of indeterminate sex.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that any monk who, without a man present, enters into a secluded place together with a woman — that is a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk enters into a secluded place together with a woman who is insane — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "And likewise with a woman whose mind is disturbed, a woman afflicted by illness, a foolish woman, a mute woman, a deaf woman, and a woman who is dwelling elsewhere but is traveling on the road together with him — all such cases are transgressions."

"Venerable one, if a monk enters into a secluded place together with an insane man and a woman — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "And likewise with a man whose mind is disturbed, a man afflicted by illness, a foolish man, a mute man, a deaf man, and a man dwelling elsewhere — if he enters the secluded place together with such a man and also with a woman, all such cases are transgressions."

"If a monk enters into a secluded place together with a woman and a person of indeterminate sex — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk makes himself invisible through mantra or medicine and then, without a man present, enters into a secluded place together with a woman — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk, without a man present, travels through the sky together with a woman — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk who has entered into a secluded place together with a woman, without a man present, then undergoes a change of sex-mark and becomes a nun — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a nun who has entered into a secluded place together with a man then undergoes a change of sex-mark and becomes a monk — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a human woman as a human, enters into a secluded place with her — what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall." "If he perceives a human as not human — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If he perceives a non-human as human — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If he perceives a non-human as non-human — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a human woman as a woman, enters into a secluded place with her — what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall." "If he perceives a human woman as a man and enters into a secluded place — what is the consequence?" "There is no offence." "If he perceives a man as a woman and enters into a secluded place — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression." "If he perceives a man as a man and enters into a secluded place — what is the consequence?" "There is no offence."

"Venerable one, if a monk enters into a secluded place together with a young woman, without a man present — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk enters into a secluded place together with a person of indeterminate sex — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk, without a man present, enters into a secluded place together with a woman — what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk enters into a secluded place together with a person of indeterminate sex — what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if one who confers training precepts enters into a secluded place together with a woman, without a man present — what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun, without a woman present, enters into a secluded place together with a man — what is the consequence?" "It is as the matter stands."

For a probationary nun, a female novice, and male novices, all such cases are to be stated as transgressions.

In brief:
One who has become insane, one whose mind is disturbed,
One who is ill, one who is deaf, one who is a traveler —
The sky, the sex-change case, the fourth case,
An emanated being, and the path of one of indeterminate sex.

the wrong path, and the case of the nun.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk travels along a road together with a large band of thieves, it is a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk travels along a road together with a single thief who is insane, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Likewise, if he travels along a road together with a large band of thieves who are mentally disturbed, who are tormented by illness, who are foolish, who are mute, who are deaf, or who are staying in another destination — in all such cases, what is the consequence?" "In all such cases it is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk, having made himself invisible by means of a mantra or a medicine, travels in the company of a large band of thieves, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk travels through the sky together with a large band of thieves, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk is traveling together with a large band of thieves and along the way his sex changes and he becomes a nun, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun is traveling along a road together with a large band of thieves and along the way her sex changes and she becomes a monk, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a large band of thieves as a large band of thieves and then travels along a road with them, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If he perceives a large band of thieves as not a large band of thieves and travels with them, what is the consequence?" "There is no offense."

"If he perceives those who are not a large band of thieves as a large band of thieves and travels with them, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"If he perceives those who are not a large band of thieves as not a large band of thieves, what is the consequence?"
"There is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk perceives a person as a person and then travels along a road together with a large band of thieves, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."
