"If he perceives a person as not a person, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives one who is not a person as a person, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"If he perceives one who is not a person as not a person, what is the consequence?"
"It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk travels along a road together with an emanated likeness of a large band of thieves, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, if a monk travels along a road together with a thief who is a person of indeterminate sex, what is the consequence?" "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, are there cases in which a monk travels along a road together with a large band of thieves and yet incurs no offense?" "Upāli, there are. If within the distance of one league he turns back, or if the thieves seize the monk and lead him away, or if they themselves disperse, or if he loses the road and someone shows him the way."

"Venerable one, if a monk travels along a road that is not the same road as that taken by a large band of thieves, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if one who has been given a training rule travels along a road together with a large band of thieves, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun travels along a road together with a large band of thieves, what is the consequence?"
"It is a downfall."

For a probationary nun, a female novice, and male novices, it is a transgression.

In brief:
The prior disturbance, full ordination, and the sex-change case,
The fourth: one insane, one mentally disturbed,
One ill, one deaf, one who is traveling,
A layman and so forth, a laywoman,
One given a training rule, and a nun.

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk confers full ordination as a monk upon a person who has not yet reached the age of twenty, it is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk confers full ordination upon a person who has not yet reached the age of twenty, perceiving them to be of that age, does that constitute a valid full ordination?"

"Upāli, these four are prior disturbances. The first: the candidate has not yet reached the age of twenty, the monk perceives them as not having reached twenty, and when the monk asks whether they have reached the age of twenty, the candidate says, 'I know and am aware that I have not reached twenty — I have no doubt about this.' If that person is then given full ordination as a monk by the monk, this is the first prior disturbance. The second: the candidate has not yet reached the age of twenty, the monk perceives them as not having reached twenty, and when the monk asks whether they have reached twenty, the candidate says, 'I do not know, I do not recall.' If that person is then given full ordination as a monk by the monks, this is the second prior disturbance. The third: the candidate has not yet reached the age of twenty, the monk perceives them as not having reached twenty, and when the monk asks whether they have reached twenty, the candidate says, 'I am uncertain.' If that person is then given full ordination as a monk by the monk, this is the third prior disturbance. The fourth: the candidate has not yet reached the age of twenty, the monk perceives them as not having reached twenty, and when the monk asks the question, the candidate gives no answer. If that person is then given full ordination as a monk by the monks, this is the fourth prior disturbance. Upāli, apart from these four prior disturbances, all remaining cases constitute a valid full ordination."

"Venerable one, if a monk confers full ordination as a monk upon a person who has not yet reached the age of twenty, and that person then undergoes a sex change and becomes a nun, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a nun confers full ordination as a nun upon someone who has not yet reached the age of twenty, or who has not yet reached the age of twelve, and that person undergoes a sex change and becomes a monk, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving someone who has not yet reached the age of twenty as not having reached that age, confers full ordination upon them, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

"If one has not yet reached the age of twenty but is perceived as having done so, and full ordination is conferred, there is no fault."

"If one has reached the age of twenty but is perceived as not having done so, and full ordination is conferred, it becomes a wrongdoing."

"If one has reached the age of twenty and is perceived as having done so, and full ordination is conferred, there is no fault."

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving an insane person as not having reached the age of twenty, confers full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

Likewise, if one perceives a mentally disturbed person, one afflicted by illness, a simpleton, a mute, a deaf person, or one who is traveling elsewhere as not having reached the age of twenty and confers full ordination upon any of them, in every case it becomes a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a layman as not having reached the age of twenty, confers full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is a downfall."

A male novice is likewise the same.

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a sexually indeterminate person as not having reached the age of twenty, confers full ordination, what is the consequence?" "It is a wrongdoing."

Likewise, if one perceives as not having reached twenty any of the following and confers full ordination upon them: a nun who has been expelled, one who has killed their father, one who has killed their mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has maliciously drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, one who is a thief by position, one who is not a resident, one who is dwelling separately, one in whom a prior disturbance has occurred, or one in whom a prior fault has arisen — in every case it becomes a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, can it occur that a monk confers full ordination perceiving the candidate as not having reached the age of twenty, yet it neither constitutes a fault nor a downfall, and the full ordination is properly conferred?" "Upāli, it can."

"Go to a person who has not yet reached the age of twenty and confer full ordination upon them." "Venerable one, if one confers full ordination by means of giving the training upon a person who has not yet reached the age of twenty, what does that become?" "It becomes a downfall." "Venerable one, if a nun confers full ordination upon a young woman who has not yet reached the age of twenty, or upon a married woman who has not yet reached the age of twelve, what does that become?" "It becomes a downfall. For a female probationer, a female novice, and male novices, there is no fault."

In brief:
By messenger, letter, gesture,
through another's word, or passing it from one to another,
while insane, while mentally disturbed,
while ill, while mute, or while traveling — these are the categories.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk digs the earth or has it dug with his own hand, it becomes a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk has earth dug by means of a messenger, what does that become?" "It becomes a wrongdoing." "Likewise, if one causes earth to be dug by means of a letter, by a gesture, through another's word, or relayed from one to another — all of these become wrongdoings." "Venerable one, if a monk has a madman dig the earth, what does that become?" "It becomes a wrongdoing. Likewise, having one who is mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, dull-witted, mute, incapable of speech, or residing in another place dig the earth — all of these become wrongdoings."

In brief:
At dawn, on the fourth and seventh,
in the presence of householders and others,
without sound, without body, without intervention,
a stake, a clod, the burning of earth.

"Venerable one, if a monk, while digging the earth with his own hand, undergoes a change of sex and becomes a nun, what does that become?" "It becomes a downfall." "Venerable one, if a nun, while digging the earth with her own hand, undergoes a change of sex and becomes a monk, what does that become?" "It becomes a downfall." "Venerable one, if a monk perceives earth to be earth and digs it or has it dug, what does that become?" "It becomes a downfall." "If he perceives earth as not being earth, there is no fault." "If he causes what is not earth to be dug while perceiving it as earth, it becomes a wrongdoing." "If he perceives what is not earth as not being earth, there is no fault." "Venerable one, if a monk causes another to dig the earth, what does that become?" "It becomes a wrongdoing." "Venerable one, if a monk digs for the sake of another, what does that become?" "It becomes a downfall." "Venerable one, if one prepares to dig before full ordination and completes it before full ordination, what does that become?" "It becomes a wrongdoing." "If one prepares before full ordination and completes it at the moment of full ordination, what does that become?" "It becomes a wrongdoing." "If one prepares before full ordination and completes it after full ordination, what does that become?" "It becomes a wrongdoing." "If one prepares at the moment of full ordination and completes it at the moment of full ordination, what does that become?" "It becomes a wrongdoing." "If one prepares at the moment of full ordination and completes it after full ordination, what does that become?" "It becomes a wrongdoing." "If one prepares after full ordination and completes it after full ordination, what does that become?" "It becomes a downfall." "If one prepares after full ordination and completes it before full ordination, what does that become?" "It becomes a wrongdoing." "Venerable one, if a monk directly causes a householder to dig the earth, what does that become?" "It becomes a downfall." Likewise for a woman, a hermaphrodite, an expelled nun, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has maliciously drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, a thief by position, one who is dwelling separately, one who is not a resident, one in whom a prior disturbance has occurred, one in whom a prior fault has arisen, one who has drawn near to disrobing, one who has given back the training, a monk, a nun, a female probationer, a female novice, and male novices — if he directly causes any of them to dig the earth, all of these become downfalls.

Venerable ones, if a noble monk invites someone to dig earth using the noble language, and that person does not seek permission in the noble language, what does this become? It is a misdeed. If a noble one invites someone to dig earth using the border language, and that person does not seek permission in the border language, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Venerable ones, if a border monk invites someone to dig earth using the border language, and that person does not seek permission in the border language, what does this become? It is a misdeed. If a border person invites someone to dig earth using the noble language, and that person does not seek permission in the noble language, what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a monk causes earth to be dug by means of a bodily gesture, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Venerable ones, if a monk causes unsettled earth to be dug, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Venerable ones, if a monk drives a peg into the earth, what does this become? It is a downfall. Venerable ones, if he then pulls it out, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Venerable ones, if a monk scrapes mud from the earth, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Venerable ones, if a monk presses down on the earth, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Venerable ones, if a monk digs earth that contains ox dung or has become sodden and clumped, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Venerable ones, if a monk digs burnt earth, what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if one who has given the training digs or causes the digging of earth with his own fingernail, what does this become? It is a downfall. Venerable ones, if a nun digs or causes the digging of earth with her own fingernail, what does this become? It is a downfall. For a female probationer it is a misdeed. For a female novice and a male novice there is no fault.

In brief:

By message, by letter, by hand signal,
by word of another, relayed from one to the next,
by one who is mad, whose mind is disturbed, who is ill,
by one who is mute, who is foolish, who is asleep,
by one who is stammering, who is intoxicated,
and one who is in meditative absorption — these are the last.

Then the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable Blessed One, you have declared that a monk should accept an invitation within four months, and that accepting beyond that becomes a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk, for however long and for however many times he has been invited, accepts and seeks food beyond that limit by means of a message, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Likewise, if he accepts and eats beyond that limit by means of a letter, a hand signal, the word of another, or by relay from one to the next, all of these become misdeeds.

Venerable ones, if a monk is invited by a madman, and he accepts and seeks food beyond that limit, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Likewise, if one whose mind is disturbed, one who is afflicted by illness, one who is foolish, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one who is stammering, one who is intoxicated, one who is in meditative absorption, or one who is dwelling elsewhere — if any of these invite for however long, and the monk accepts and eats beyond that limit, all of these become misdeeds.

In brief:

What is unsuitable and what is excluded,
what pertains to the name, and likewise the fourth —
what is appointed, and again the interruption,
and another's on behalf of another — these are the seventh.

Venerable ones, if a monk is invited for however long and for however much food and drink, and he accepts food and drink that is suitable beyond that limit, what does this become? It is a downfall. Venerable ones, if a monk is invited for however long and however much food and drink, and setting aside that food and drink, he seeks other things — medicines — intending to use them as medicine, and accepts and receives those things that are not food, what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a monk is invited for however long and for however much, and while accepting beyond that limit his status changes and he becomes a nun, what does this become? It is a downfall. Venerable ones, if a nun is invited for however long and for however much, and while accepting beyond that limit her status changes and she becomes a monk, what does this become? It is a downfall.

Venerable ones, if a monk, perceiving a human being as a human being, solicits and accepts from him, what does this become? It is a downfall. If he perceives a human being as a non-human, it becomes a misdeed. If he perceives a non-human as a human being, it becomes a misdeed. If he perceives a non-human as a non-human and accepts beyond that limit and receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, is there any case in which a monk, however long and for however much he has been invited, accepts within that limit and yet incurs no offense? Upāli, there is. It is as a monk hears when invited to a village where the training precepts are given. Venerable ones, is there any case in which a monk, however long and for however much he has been invited, accepts beyond that limit and yet incurs no offense? Upāli, there is. It is when that monk, while still there, flees and goes elsewhere, and any one of the eight interruptions arises.

Venerable ones, if a monk, invited for however long and for however much, accepts beyond that limit on behalf of another and receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed. Venerable ones, if a monk, invited for however long, accepts beyond that limit and gives the invitation to another who then receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if one who has not received full ordination accepts, and one who has not received full ordination receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one who has not received full ordination accepts, and one who is in the act of receiving full ordination receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one who has not received full ordination accepts, and one who has fully received ordination receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one who is in the act of receiving full ordination accepts, and one who is in the act of receiving full ordination receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one who is in the act of receiving full ordination accepts, and one who has fully received ordination receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one who has fully received ordination accepts, and one who has fully received ordination receives, what does this become? It is a downfall. If one who has fully received ordination accepts, and one who has not received full ordination receives, what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if one accepts more than what the training precepts allow and then receives, what does this become? It is a downfall. Venerable ones, if a nun accepts more than that limit and receives, what does this become? It is a downfall. If a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā), a novice nun, or male novices accept more than that limit and receive, what does this become? It is a misdeed.

In brief:
Through messenger, letter, gesture,
through the word of another, through relay from one to the next,
through one who is mad, mentally disturbed, or ill,
through one who is deaf, dull-witted, asleep,
through one with cleft palate, one who is intoxicated,
and one entering meditative absorption — these are the final cases.

Then the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: Venerable one, the Blessed One has also declared that if a monk is instructed by another monk — "Venerable one, train in this precept" — and that monk says, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable one has instructed me," this becomes a downfall. Venerable one, if a monk instructs another monk, and through a messenger that monk says, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable ones have instructed me," what does this become? It is a misdeed. Likewise, if he says so through a letter, through a gesture, through the word of another, or through relay from one to the next — all of these become misdeeds.

Venerable ones, if the monks instruct a monk and a mad monk says, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable ones have instructed me," what does this become? It is a misdeed. Likewise, one who is mentally disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one with a cleft palate,

one who is intoxicated, one in meditative absorption, and monks dwelling in another region — if any of these say, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable ones have instructed me," all of these become misdeeds.

In brief:

By voice, by body, by solitude,
by a seventh party acting for another,
by laypeople and the like —
these are the mark: the fourth and the seventh.

Venerable ones, if a monk instructs a monk in the noble language saying, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable one has instructed me," and that monk does not understand the noble language — what does this become? It is a misdeed. If a noble one says this in the language of the border regions, and the monk does not understand the language of the border regions — what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one from the border regions says this in the language of the border regions, and the monk does not understand the language of the border regions — what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one from the border regions says this in the noble language, and the monk does not understand the noble language — what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a monk conveys this meaning through a bodily gesture — namely, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable one has instructed me" — what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a monk, perceiving one who is present alone as though he were not present alone, says, "I do not train in accordance with the words of the venerable one — train as you will" — what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a monk has another person say, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable one has instructed me" — what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a monk says on behalf of another, "The venerable one will not train in this precept as instructed" — what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if one who has not yet received full ordination gives the instruction, and one who has not yet received full ordination says, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable one has instructed me" — what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one who has not yet received full ordination gives the instruction, and one in the act of receiving full ordination says this — what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one who has not yet received full ordination gives the instruction, and one who has fully received ordination says this — what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one in the act of receiving full ordination gives the instruction, and one in the act of receiving full ordination says this — what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one in the act of receiving full ordination gives the instruction, and one who has fully received ordination says this — what does this become? It is a misdeed. If one who has fully received ordination gives the instruction, and one who has fully received ordination says this — what does this become? It is a transgression. If one who has fully received ordination gives the instruction, and one who has not yet received full ordination says this — what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a layperson instructs a monk, and the monk says, "I will not train in this precept as the venerable one has instructed me" — what does this become? It is a misdeed.

Likewise, if the instruction is given by a woman, by a eunuch, by an expelled nun, by one who has slain his father or mother, by one who has killed an arhat, by one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent, by a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika), by one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, by one who is a thief living in hiding, by one who is not residing, by one who is residing apart, by one who has previously committed an offense, or by one who has previously caused a schism — if the instruction is given by any of these and that declaration is made, all cases become misdeeds.

Venerable ones, if a monk who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, or who has sided with that schism, or monks who have given the training — if they give the instruction and that declaration is made, all cases become misdeeds.

Venerable ones, if a monk is instructed by a fully ordained nun, by a probationary nun, by a female novice,

by male novices — if the instruction is given by them and that declaration is made, all cases become misdeeds.

Venerable ones, if a monk says, "I will not train in this training as instructed by the venerable one," and his gender then changes and he becomes a nun, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a nun says the same, and her gender then changes and she becomes a monk, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

Venerable ones, if a monk, perceiving someone who has received full ordination as one who has received full ordination, says, "I will not train in this training as instructed by the venerable one," what becomes of it? It is a transgression. If he perceives someone who has received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, it becomes a misdeed. If he perceives someone who has not received full ordination as one who has received full ordination, it becomes a misdeed. If he perceives someone who has not received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, it becomes a misdeed.

Just as a monk incurs a transgression by speaking in that way, so too does one who has given the training, and likewise a nun incurs a transgression. In the cases of a probationary nun, a female novice, and male novices, it becomes a misdeed.

In brief:
One who has gone mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is ill, one who is unable to speak, one who departs —
these are the same as the fourth, namely the characteristic;
with mantra and the other, these seven,
householders and the like,
the pacification, and the nun.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable Blessed One, you have declared that if monks are quarreling and a monk is present, and he listens without speaking, he incurs a transgression. Venerable one, if monks who are mad are quarreling and a monk is present, and he listens without speaking, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

"Likewise, in the cases of monks whose minds are disturbed, those afflicted by illness, those who are dull-witted, those who are mute, those unable to speak, and those who have gone to dwell elsewhere — if one listens without saying anything to them, all cases become misdeeds.

"Venerable one, if monks are quarreling and a monk is present listening without speaking, and his gender then changes and he becomes a nun, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

"Venerable one, if a nun is present listening without speaking, and her gender then changes and she becomes a monk, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving one who has received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, is present listening without speaking, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

"Venerable one, if a monk has made himself inconspicuous through mantra or medicine and is present listening without speaking, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

"Venerable one, if monks are quarreling and a monk causes another to listen to it, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

"Venerable one, if monks are quarreling and a monk listens on behalf of others, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

"Venerable one, if one seats a person who has not received full ordination in a place not for those who have not received full ordination, and that person listens there, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed. If one seats a person who has not received full ordination in a place for those who have received full ordination, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed. If one seats a person who has not received full ordination in a place for those who have received full ordination, and that person listens there, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed. If one seats a person who has received full ordination in a place for those who have received full ordination, and that person listens there, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed. If one seats a person who has received full ordination in a place for those who have received full ordination, and that person listens in a place for those who have received full ordination, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed. If one seats a person who has received full ordination in a place for those who have received full ordination, and that person listens in a place for those who have received full ordination, what becomes of it? It is a transgression. If one seats a person who has received full ordination in a place for those who have received full ordination, and that person listens in a place for those who have not received full ordination, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

"Venerable one, if laypeople are quarreling and a monk is present listening without speaking, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

"Likewise with respect to a woman, a paṇḍaka, a nun who has been expelled, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat,

one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, one who is dwelling as a thief, one who is not residing in the community, one who is living separately, one who previously committed an offense, and one who was previously in a dispute — if a monk listens to all of these without saying anything, it is a misdeed in every case.

"Venerable one, if a monk has caused a schism in the Saṅgha and another monk, without taking leave, listens while staying on without saying anything, what becomes of it? It is a transgression. If one listens without taking leave among those who are siding with a party and among those who have been given training precepts, what becomes of it? It is a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk listens without taking leave among nuns, probationary nuns, novice nuns, and male novices, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed in every case.

"Venerable one, is there a case where monks who have come together and are quarreling — a monk listens without taking leave yet commits no offense?" "Upāli, there is. It is as follows: that monk listens having thought to pacify the situation.

"Venerable one, if one who has been given training precepts listens without taking leave, what becomes of it? It is a transgression. Venerable one, if a nun listens without taking leave, what becomes of it? It is a transgression. If probationary nuns, novice nuns, and male novices listen without taking leave, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed.

In brief: through messenger, letter, gesture,
through hearsay and from one to another,
through one who is mad, mentally disturbed,
through one who is deaf, dull-witted, or sleeping,
through one who is mute, intoxicated,
or one who has entered meditative absorption — these are the last.

"The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: 'Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that any monk who, while the Saṅgha is reciting a definitive statement of Dharma, rises from his seat and departs without having taken leave and without saying anything — such a monk commits a transgression. If a monk, while the Saṅgha is reciting a definitive statement of Dharma, sends a message granting approval and then departs, what becomes of it?' It is a misdeed. 'Likewise, if approval is sent and one departs by letter, by gesture, through hearsay, or relayed from one to another, what becomes of it in every case?' It is a misdeed in every case.

"Venerable one, if a monk, while the Saṅgha is reciting a definitive statement of Dharma, grants approval to a mad monk and then departs, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed. Likewise, if approval is granted and one departs to a monk who is mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, dull-witted, deaf, mute, sleeping, mute, intoxicated, in meditative absorption, or residing elsewhere — it is a misdeed in every case.

In brief: to paṇḍakas and the like,
to one bearing marks, and likewise the fourth,
to śramaṇas, and those who perform sky-mantras,
to one acting by body, one acting by voice, and a nun.

"Venerable one, if a monk grants approval to a paṇḍaka and then departs, what becomes of it? It is a misdeed. Likewise, to a female paṇḍaka, to an expelled nun, to one who has killed his father, to one who has killed his mother, to one who has killed an arhat, to one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent, to a tīrthika, to one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, to one who is dwelling as a thief, to one who is not residing in the community, to one who is living separately, to one who was previously in a dispute, to one who previously committed an offense, to one who is siding with a party, and to those who have been given training precepts — if approval is granted and one departs to any of these, it is a misdeed in every case.

"Venerable one, if a monk, while the Saṅgha is reciting a definitive statement of Dharma, rises from his seat and departs without saying anything and without granting approval, and in the meantime his status changes and he has become a nun, what becomes of it? It is a transgression. Venerable one, if a nun, while a definitive statement of Dharma is being recited, rises from her seat and departs without saying anything and without granting approval, and in the meantime her status changes and she has become a monk, what becomes of it? It is a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a Dharma-act as a Dharma-act, departs without granting approval, what becomes of it?"

It is a transgression. If one perceives a Dharma-act as not a Dharma-act, it is a wrongdoing. If one perceives a non-Dharma-act as a Dharma-act, it is a wrongdoing. If one perceives a non-Dharma-act as a non-Dharma-act and yet departs without granting approval, what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk, while a definitive statement of Dharma is being recited by the Saṅgha, rises from his seat and departs without saying anything, and yet no transgression or downfall occurs?" Upāli, there is: when one is sitting merely at the edge of hearing range, and the recitation does not reach one's ears with its meaning understood.

"Venerable one, if a monk, while a definitive statement of Dharma is being recited by the Saṅgha, departs without granting approval by going up into the sky, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk, while a definitive statement of Dharma is being recited by the Saṅgha, makes himself invisible by means of a mantra or medicine and then departs, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk, while a definitive statement of Dharma is being recited by the Saṅgha, grants approval by means of a bodily gesture and then departs, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, during the recitation of a definitive Dharma-statement by the Saṅgha, if a noble monk grants approval in the noble language, but the monk in question has not sought out the noble language, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If a noble monk grants approval in a border dialect, but the monk in question has not sought out that border dialect, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If a border-dweller grants approval in a border dialect, but the monk in question has not sought out that border dialect, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If a border-dweller grants approval in the noble language, but the monk in question has not sought out the noble language, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk who has given up his training, while a definitive statement of Dharma is being recited by the Saṅgha, rises from his seat and departs without saying anything, what becomes of it?" It is a downfall. "Venerable one, if a nun, while a definitive statement of Dharma is being recited by the Saṅgha, rises from her seat and departs without saying anything, what becomes of it?" It is a downfall. For a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā), a novice nun, and novice monks, it is a wrongdoing.

In summary:

By message, letter, hand-sign,
through an intermediary, and from one to another,
through madness, mental disturbance,
illness, stupidity, and sleep,
through being deaf, through intoxication,
and through meditative absorption — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that if one plugs one's ears when an instruction is being given, it is a downfall. If a monk, when an instruction is given by the Saṅgha's spokesman, turns back the message and does not heed it, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if one turns back and does not heed an instruction conveyed by letter, by hand-sign, through an intermediary, or passed from one to another, all of these are wrongdoings.

"Venerable one, if a monk, when an instruction is given by the Saṅgha's spokesman through a madman, turns it back and does not heed it, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if one turns back and does not heed an instruction conveyed through one who is mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, stupid, mute, or deaf, all of these are wrongdoings.

"Venerable one, if a monk, when an instruction is given by the Saṅgha's spokesman, fails to heed it because he is asleep, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if one fails to heed it because one is yawning, intoxicated, or in meditative absorption, all of these are wrongdoings.

"Venerable one, if a monk turns back and does not heed an instruction given by the Saṅgha's spokesman of a Saṅgha residing in a different place, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

The Noble Vinaya, the fourteenth fascicle.

In summary:

Language, body, seclusion, and mantra,
marks, the fourth and the seventh,
counting and the seventh, not-speaking,
giving up training, and the nun.

"Venerable one, when the Saṅgha's spokesman conveys an instruction and a noble monk turns back and does not heed it in the noble language, and that monk has also not sought the noble language, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "When a noble monk turns back and does not heed it in the border language, and that monk has also not sought the border language, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "When a border monk turns back and does not heed it in the border language, and that monk has also not sought the border language, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "When a border monk turns back and does not heed it in the noble language, and that monk has also not sought the noble language, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, when the Saṅgha's spokesman conveys an instruction and a monk turns back and does not heed it on account of a bodily fixation, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, when the Saṅgha's spokesman conveys an instruction and a monk, perceiving a secluded place as non-secluded, turns back and does not heed it, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, when the Saṅgha's spokesman conveys an instruction and a monk renders himself invisible through mantra or medicine, then turns back and does not heed it, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, when a monk turns back and does not heed the Saṅgha's instruction and then changes his status and becomes a nun, what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, when a nun turns back and does not heed the Saṅgha's instruction and then changes her status and becomes a monk, what becomes of it?" It is a transgression.

"Venerable one, when the Saṅgha's spokesman conveys an instruction and a monk, perceiving what is Dharma as Dharma, turns back and does not heed it, what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "If one perceives what is Dharma as not Dharma, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one perceives what is not Dharma as Dharma, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one perceives what is not Dharma as not Dharma, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, is there a case in which one turns back and does not heed the Saṅgha's spokesman's instruction and yet the offense does not constitute a transgression?" Upāli, there is: when the Saṅgha has counted one without respect. Even so, to transgress what the Saṅgha has established to be done is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if one who has not received full ordination has been counted by the Saṅgha without respect, and one who has not received full ordination turns back and does not heed it, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one who has not received full ordination has been counted and, at the time of receiving full ordination, turns back and does not heed it, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one who has not received full ordination has been counted and, after receiving full ordination, turns back and does not heed it, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one counted at the time of receiving full ordination turns back and does not heed it at the time of receiving full ordination, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one counted at the time of receiving full ordination turns back and does not heed it after receiving full ordination, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one counted after receiving full ordination turns back and does not heed it after receiving full ordination, what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "If one counted after receiving full ordination turns back and does not heed it when one has not received full ordination, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, when the Saṅgha's spokesman conveys an instruction to a monk and he does not heed it by remaining altogether silent, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if one who has given up the training does not heed the Saṅgha's spokesman's instruction by turning back, what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, when the Saṅgha's spokesman conveys an instruction to a nun and she turns back and does not heed it, what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. For female trainees, novice nuns, and male novices, it is a wrongdoing.

In summary:

Two fruits, and likewise mantra,
the fallen, salt, and one carrying liquor,
root, trunk, and bearing fruit,
the seventh, mixed with the rootless,
what was instructed, the deity, the fourth, and the mark.

This was asked of the Blessed One, the Buddha, by the Venerable Upāli.

"Venerable one, the Blessed One declared that if one seeks liquor or fruit-liquor that would cause intoxication, it is a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk seeks roots, trunks, leaves, flowers, or fruits that would cause intoxication, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk seeks roots, trunks, leaves, flowers, or fruits, or other such things placed inside liquor, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk, having received liquor or fruit-liquor that would cause intoxication from someone in his vicinity by means of a mantra or medicine, then seeks it, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk seeks the dregs, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, may one seek liquor that has turned to salt?" Upāli, in such a case: if the substance of the liquor is much and the substance of the salt is little, one may not drink it. But if the substance of the salt is clearly predominant and the substance of the liquor is little, one may drink it, diluted with water using a straining cloth. Upāli, why so? Because in that case it cannot perform the function of liquor. "Venerable one, is it permitted to seek liquor that has turned to salt at an irregular time?" Upāli, in such a case: if it has become clear and clarified and does not cause intoxication, dilute it with water, strain it through a water-straining cloth, and drink it in the company of the community. "Venerable one, if a monk, while carrying liquor, seeks it from the one holding it, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, is it permitted to seek the juice of these roots, trunks, leaves, flowers, and fruits at an irregular time?" Upāli, in such a case: if it has become clear and thoroughly transparent, strain it through a water-straining cloth, dilute it with water, and drink it. But if, from its own substance, it has transformed into the substance of liquor, may one seek it? Upāli, one may not. "Venerable one, if a monk, apart from intoxicating liquor, seeks the smell of liquor, the taste of liquor, the colour of liquor, and the fragrance of liquor that are other than that, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. Salt that resembles the colour of liquor incurs no offence. "Venerable one, if a monk, from a mixture of liquor and rice grains, strains out the liquor and then seeks the rice, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if one who has not yet received full ordination takes it and seeks it before receiving full ordination, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one who has not yet received full ordination takes it and seeks it just as one is receiving full ordination, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one who has not yet received full ordination takes it and seeks it after having received full ordination, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one who is in the process of receiving full ordination takes it and seeks it in the process of receiving full ordination, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one who is in the process of receiving full ordination takes it and seeks it before full ordination, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one who has received full ordination takes it and seeks it after having received full ordination, what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "If one who has received full ordination takes it and seeks it before full ordination, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk seeks the foam of grape-liquor, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk seeks something that has been poured into liquor, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk seeks something fumigated by the steam of liquor so as to carry the fragrance, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk may seek an intoxicating drink and yet the offence does not become a transgression?" Upāli, there is: if one drinks the liquor of the gods, it becomes a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving liquor as liquor, seeks it, what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "If, perceiving liquor as not being liquor, one seeks it, what becomes of it?" There is no offence. "If, perceiving what is not liquor as liquor, one seeks it, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If, perceiving what is not liquor as not being liquor, one seeks it, what becomes of it?" There is no offence. "Venerable one, if a monk, in the course of seeking liquor or fruit-liquor, undergoes a change of marks and becomes a nun, what becomes of it?" It is a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a nun, in the course of seeking liquor or fruit-liquor, undergoes a change of marks and becomes a monk, what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, if one who has been given the training seeks liquor or fruit-liquor, what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, if a nun seeks liquor or fruit-liquor, what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. For a female trainee, a novice nun, or a male novice, it becomes a wrongdoing.

In brief:
By messenger, letter, or sign,
through another's word, or passed from one to the next,
one who is mad, disturbed in mind, or afflicted by illness,
one who is deaf, dull-witted, or asleep,
one who is delirious, one who is intoxicated,
one who has entered meditative absorption — these are the final cases.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk goes to the midday meal in a village without having sought permission from a monk who is present, it is a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk seeks permission from another monk by sending a messenger and then goes, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "In the same way, if one sends a letter, a sign, a word through another, or has word relayed from one to the next and then goes, all of these become wrongdoings."

"Venerable one, if a monk seeks permission from a mad monk and then enters the village for the midday meal, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "In the same way, if one seeks permission from a monk who is mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, dull-witted, mute, deaf, asleep, delirious, one who has entered meditative absorption, or a monk who is staying in another place, and then goes — all of these become wrongdoings."

In brief:
By mantra, through the sky, or by means of the body,
a remote place, or a place where there is no monk,
a temple, a circumambulation circuit,
a boundary, the night, and the fourth case,
a householder, an interruption, the Saṅgha,
one who has been given the training, and a nun.

"Venerable one, if a monk renders himself invisible by means of a mantra or medicine and goes, having failed to seek permission from a monk who is present, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk goes to the midday meal in a village through the sky, having failed to seek permission from a monk who is present, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a noble monk seeks permission from another monk using the noble language and goes, but that other monk did not seek it in the noble language, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If a noble monk seeks permission using a border-region language and goes, but that other monk did not seek it in the border-region language, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If a border-region monk seeks permission using a border-region language and goes, but that other monk did not seek it in the border-region language, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If a border-region monk seeks permission using the noble language and goes, but that other monk did not seek it in the noble language, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk signals his intention to go to a monk who is present by means of a bodily gesture and then goes, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk perceives a remote place as not being remote, seeks permission, and goes to a village, what becomes of it?" There is no offence.

"Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk goes to the midday meal in a village without having sought permission from a monk who is present and yet incurs no transgression?" Upāli, there is. It is the case in which that monk is dwelling in a place where there are no monks.

"Venerable one, if there is a temple inside a village, or a circumambulation circuit, and one goes from there without having sought permission, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk goes through the sky, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if permission is sought from a monk who is travelling through the sky, is that considered to be having sought permission?" Upāli, it is considered to be having made it known. In the same way, when one who is on the ground does so in regard to one who is in the sky,

and when one who is within a boundary seeks permission from one who is outside the boundary, is that considered to be having sought permission? Upāli, it is considered to be having made it known.

Venerable one, if a monk goes to a village in the afternoon without having sought permission from a monk who is present, and then the night passes and he has become a nun, what becomes of it? It is a transgression. Venerable one, if a nun goes from a nuns' residence to a village in the afternoon without having sought permission from a nun who is present, and then the night passes and she has become a monk, what becomes of it? It is a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving the afternoon to be afternoon, goes to a village in the afternoon while a monk is present and without having sought permission, what becomes of it? It is a transgression. If one goes at an improper time while perceiving it to be the proper time, what becomes of it? There is no offence. If one perceives the proper time to be an improper time, what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. If one perceives the proper time as the proper time, what becomes of it? There is no offence.

Venerable one, if a monk seeks permission from a layman, what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if one makes it known to a woman, to a eunuch, to an expelled nun, to a father, to a mother, to one who has slain an arhat, to one who with malicious intent has shed the blood of a Tathāgata, to a tīrthika, to one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, to a thief, to one who does not reside in the community, to one who lives separately, to one who has drawn near to apostasy, to one who has previously committed an offence, to one who has previously caused a schism, or to one who has surrendered the training — in all these cases it is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk may go to a village in the afternoon without incurring a fault? Upāli, there is. For instance, if one of the eight impediments has arisen for that monk in the monastery. Venerable one, what if the entire Saṅgha, or a preceptor, or an abbot, or any other learned individual who leads a holy life, should go to the village in the afternoon at an improper time without having sought permission from a monk — should they too seek permission? Upāli, they too should make it known.

Venerable one, if one who has surrendered the training goes to a village in the afternoon while a monk is present and without having sought permission, what becomes of it? It is a transgression. Venerable one, if a nun goes from a nuns' residence to a village while nuns are present and having sought permission, what becomes of it? It is a transgression. For a female trainee and female novices, it is a wrongdoing; for male novices, it is a wrongdoing.

In summary, the exemptions are as follows:

By messenger, by letter, by hand-signal,
by having another say it, by relay from one to the next —
for the mad, the mentally disturbed, the ill,
the deaf, the dull-witted, those asleep,
those who cry out in pain, the intoxicated,
and those departing from meditative absorption — these are the last.

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the buddha: Venerable one, the Blessed One has also declared that if a monk has been invited as a meal-guest to a village, whether for a meal before noon or after, and he goes to another village without having sought permission from that householder, it is a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk who has been invited as a meal-guest makes it known to the householder by messenger and then goes to another village, what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if he makes it known by letter, by hand-signal, by having another say it, or by relay from one to the next, and then goes to another village — in all these cases it is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one, if a monk has been invited as a meal-guest to another village, whether for a meal before noon or after, and he goes to another village without having sought permission from the householder — who is mad — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. Likewise in the case of one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one who cries out in pain, one who is intoxicated, and

one going to stay elsewhere — in all these cases, going to another village without having sought permission is a wrongdoing.

In brief:
Voice and body and solitude,
mantra and mark and the fourth,
food and the two kinds of invitation —
these apply to eunuchs, to those under training, and to nuns.

Venerable one: if a monk has sought permission from the householder in the noble language (Sanskrit), and has come to the village, but the householder did not seek permission in the noble language — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. If the monk sought permission in the language of the frontier regions, and came to the village, but the householder did not seek permission in the language of the frontier regions — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. If a person of the frontier regions sought permission in the language of the frontier regions, and came to the village, but the householder did not seek permission in the language of the frontier regions — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. If a person of the frontier regions sought permission from the householder in the noble language, and went to another village, but the householder did not seek permission in the noble language — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one: if a monk sought permission from the householder by means of a bodily sign, and came to the village — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. Venerable one: if a monk, perceiving a secluded place as not secluded, sought permission and came to the village — what becomes of it? There is no fault. Venerable one: if a monk, having made himself invisible by mantra or medicine, sought permission and came to the village — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one: if a monk went to the village without having sought permission from the householder, and in the meantime changed his status and became a nun — what becomes of it? It is a transgression. Venerable one: if a nun went to the village without having sought permission from the householder, and in the meantime changed her status and became a monk — what becomes of it? It is a transgression.

Venerable one: if a monk, perceiving a person as a person, went to the village without having sought permission — what becomes of it? It is a transgression. If he perceived a person as a non-human being, it is a wrongdoing. If he perceived a non-human being as a person, it is a wrongdoing. If he perceived a non-human being as a non-human being, it is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one: if a monk was invited as a meal-guest to a village for things other than food — namely for drink, for delicacies, or for licking-foods and so forth — and went to the village without having sought permission from the householder — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one: are there cases where a monk goes to a single village without having sought permission from the householder and yet does not incur a fault or transgression? Upāli, yes there are: entering a village and passing the time until the shadow has moved.

Venerable one: if a monk is invited as a meal-guest by a woman, a eunuch, or a hermaphrodite, and goes to the village without having sought permission — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. Venerable one: if one who has received the training precepts is invited as a meal-guest to a village for food, and goes to the village without having sought permission from the householder — what becomes of it? It is a transgression. Venerable one: if a nun is invited as a meal-guest to a village for food, and goes to the village without having sought permission from the householder — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. For female probationers, novice nuns, and male novices it is a wrongdoing.

In brief:
Mantra and sky — likewise —
mark and likewise the fourth,
village and wandering in open space,
the not-having-stayed and the having-stayed.

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable Blessed One, you have said that if a monk, in the home of a royal-clan king — one consecrated by having the royal water poured upon his head — has not gathered together the jewels or things that count as jewels before dawn has broken and the sky has brightened, and then passes beyond the threshold or its immediate vicinity, he incurs a transgression. Venerable one: if a monk, before dawn has broken and the sky has brightened, has not gathered the jewels or things that count as jewels, but has made himself invisible by mantra or medicine, and then passes beyond the near vicinity of the threshold — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one: if a monk, before dawn has broken and the sky has brightened, has not gathered the jewels or things that count as jewels, and then passes through the sky beyond the threshold or its immediate vicinity — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one: if a monk, before dawn has broken and the sky has brightened, has not gathered the jewels or things that count as jewels, and while in the act of passing beyond the threshold or its immediate vicinity the night-watch changes and he becomes a nun — what becomes of it? It is a transgression.

Venerable one: if a nun, while in the act of passing beyond the threshold or its immediate vicinity, the night-watch changes and she becomes a monk — what becomes of it? It is a transgression.

Venerable one: if a monk perceives that the dawn, which has not yet broken, has not yet broken, and without gathering the jewels or things that count as jewels passes beyond the threshold or its immediate vicinity — what becomes of it? It is a transgression. If he perceives that the dawn, which has not yet broken, has already broken, and then passes beyond — what becomes of it? There is no offense. If he perceives that the dawn, which has already broken, has not yet broken, and then passes beyond — it is a wrongdoing. If he perceives that the dawn, which has already broken, has already broken, and then passes beyond — there is no offense.

Venerable one: if a monk perceives that the jewels or things that count as jewels, which have not been gathered, have not been gathered, and passes beyond the threshold or its immediate vicinity — what becomes of it? It is a transgression. If he perceives that what has not been gathered has been gathered, and then passes beyond — what becomes of it? There is no offense. If he perceives that what has been gathered has not been gathered, and then passes beyond — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. If he perceives that what has been gathered has been gathered, and then passes beyond — what becomes of it? There is no offense.

Venerable one: if a monk perceives a human being as a human being and passes beyond the threshold or its immediate vicinity — what becomes of it? It is a transgression. If he perceives a human being as a non-human being — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. If he perceives a non-human being as a human being — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. If he perceives a non-human being as a non-human being — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one: if a monk, in a village other than Rājagṛha, before dawn has broken and the sky has brightened, without having gathered the jewels or things that count as jewels, passes beyond the threshold or its immediate vicinity — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one: is there a case in which a monk passes beyond the threshold or its immediate vicinity before dawn has broken and the sky has brightened, without having gathered the jewels or things that count as jewels, and yet incurs no offense? Upāli, there is — namely, when that monk departs while Rājagṛha is empty.

Venerable one: if all the royal palaces of Rājagṛha are surrounded and whether they are curtained off or not, and that monk, before dawn has broken and the sky has brightened, without gathering the jewels or things that count as jewels, passes beyond the threshold or its immediate vicinity — what becomes of it? It is a transgression.

Venerable one: if all of Rājagṛha is curtained off and only half of it is surrounded, and the monk, before dawn has broken and the sky has brightened, without gathering the jewels or things that count as jewels, passes beyond the threshold or its immediate vicinity — what becomes of it? It is a transgression.

Venerable one: if a monk, after dawn has broken and the sky has brightened, gathers the jewels or things that count as jewels and then passes beyond the threshold or its immediate vicinity — what becomes of it? There is no offense.

Venerable one: if a monk, before dawn has broken and the sky has brightened, gathers the jewels or things that count as jewels and then passes beyond the threshold or its immediate vicinity — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one: is there a case in which a monk passes beyond the threshold or its immediate vicinity before dawn has broken and the sky has brightened, without having gathered the jewels or things that count as jewels, and yet the offense does not become a transgression? Upāli, there is — namely, those dwelling in a destiny other than the human destiny: if one passes beyond a single threshold of theirs, it becomes a wrongdoing.

Venerable one: if one who has been given the training precepts passes beyond the threshold or its immediate vicinity before dawn has broken and the sky has brightened, without having gathered the jewels or things that count as jewels — what becomes of it? It is a transgression.

Venerable one: if a nun, before dawn has broken and the sky has brightened, without having gathered the jewels or things that count as jewels, passes beyond the threshold or its immediate vicinity — what becomes of it? It is a transgression.

What of a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā), a novice nun,

a novice monk — for all of them it becomes a wrongdoing.

In summary:

By messenger, by letter, by gesture,
by having another speak, or from one to another,
by one who is mad, mentally disordered, or ill,
by one who is mute, simple-minded, or asleep,
by one who is intoxicated, drunk, or in deep meditative absorption —
these are the final cases.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has also declared that when a monk, at the recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra every half-month, says the following words — 'Venerable one, I now request that these Dharma teachings be included in the sūtra collection and gathered into the sūtra collection' — it becomes a transgression." "Yes," declared the Blessed One. "Venerable one, if a monk sends a messenger saying, 'Venerable one, I now request that these Dharma teachings be included in the sūtra collection and gathered into the sūtra collection' — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if one sends a letter, a gesture, has another speak the words, or conveys the message from one person to another — in all such cases it becomes a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk says to a mad monk: 'Venerable one, I now request that these Dharma teachings be included in the sūtra collection and gathered into the sūtra collection' — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if one says this to a mentally disordered monk, one afflicted by illness, one who is simple-minded, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is asleep, one who is intoxicated, one who is drunk, or a monk dwelling in another realm of existence — in all such cases it becomes a wrongdoing.

In summary:

By voice, by body, in private,
by mantra, by sign — the fourth case —
to laypeople and the like,
for the sake of another, and to a nun.

"Venerable one, if a monk who knows the noble language says in that noble language, 'I now request, venerable one, that these Dharma teachings be included in the sūtra collection and gathered into the sūtra collection,' and the monk to whom it is said does not know the noble language — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one who knows the noble language says these words in a border dialect, and the monk to whom it is said does not know the border dialect — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one who speaks a border dialect says these words in a border dialect, and the monk does not know that border dialect — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one who speaks a border dialect says these words in the noble language — 'I now request, venerable one, that these Dharma teachings be included in the sūtra collection and gathered into the sūtra collection' — and the monk does not know the noble language — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk conveys this meaning through bodily gesture — making it understood that 'I request, venerable one, that these Dharma teachings be included in the sūtra collection and gathered into the sūtra collection' — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a private place as not private, says, 'I now request, venerable one, that these Dharma teachings be included in the sūtra collection and gathered into the sūtra collection' — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk renders himself invisible through mantra or medicine, and says, 'I now request, venerable one, that this be done' — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if while such words are being spoken the sex changes and the monk becomes a nun — what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, if while such words are being spoken the sex changes and the nun becomes a monk — what becomes of it?" It is a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving one who has received full ordination as one who has received full ordination, says, 'Venerable one, I now request that these teachings be included in the sūtra collection and gathered into the sūtra collection' — what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "If one perceives one who has received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, it is a wrongdoing. If one perceives one who has not received full ordination as one who has received full ordination, it is a wrongdoing. If one perceives one who has not received full ordination as one who has not received full ordination, it is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if a monk says to a layman, 'Venerable one, I now request that these teachings be included in the sūtra collection and gathered into the sūtra collection' — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Likewise, if such words are spoken to a woman, to a hermaphrodite, to an expelled nun, to a father, to a mother, to one who has killed an arhat, to one who with malicious intent has drawn the blood of a Tathāgata, to a non-Buddhist adherent, to one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, to one who is dwelling in a place of thieves, to one who is without a dwelling, to one dwelling separately, to one who has previously caused a dispute, or to one in whom a previous offense has arisen — in all cases it is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, if such words are spoken to those who have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, to those who have taken sides in such a schism, or to those who are being given training — what becomes of it?" In all cases it is a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk says to nuns, to probationary nuns, to female novices, or to male novices: 'Venerable one, I now request that these teachings be included in the sūtra collection and gathered into the sūtra collection' — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

In brief:
By message, letter, hand-signal,
speaking through another, one to another,
one who has gone mad, one mentally disturbed,
one who is ill, going on a journey —

The noble Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that a monk who makes a needle-case from bone, tooth, or horn commits a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk has another make a needle-case from bone, tooth, or horn on his behalf — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Likewise, if he causes it to be made by sending a message, by letter, by hand-signal, speaking through another, or relayed one to another — it is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if he causes a madman to make it, or one mentally disturbed, or one tormented by illness, or one who is foolish, or one who is mute, or one who is dumb, or one dwelling in another region — in all cases it is a wrongdoing."

In brief:
Caught by another, for another's sake —
the fourth is improper, as is the seventh;
likewise excepted is the last.

"Venerable one, if a monk approves of a needle-case from bone, tooth, or horn that was begun by another — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk makes a needle-case for the sake of another — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk makes one improperly and then discards it — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if while a monk is making a needle-case from bone, tooth, or horn the sex changes and he becomes a nun — what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, if while a nun is making a needle-case from bone, tooth, or horn the sex changes and she becomes a monk — what becomes of it?" It is a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving a human being as a human being, has a needle-case made — what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "If one perceives a human being as a non-human being, it is a wrongdoing. If one perceives a non-human being as a human being, it is a wrongdoing. If one perceives a non-human being as a non-human being, it is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk who has a needle-case made from bone, tooth, or horn commits no transgression thereby?" Upāli, there is: when it is made from what is improper.

"Venerable one, if one begins while not yet fully ordained and it is completed while not yet fully ordained — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one begins while not yet fully ordained and it is completed at the moment of full ordination — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one begins while not yet fully ordained and it is completed after full ordination — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one begins at the moment of full ordination and it is completed at the moment of full ordination — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one begins after full ordination and it is completed after full ordination — what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "If one begins after full ordination and it is completed while not yet fully ordained — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk has other implements besides a needle-case made from bone, tooth, or horn — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if one who has given the training has a needle-case made from bone, tooth, or horn — what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "If a nun has it made, it becomes a transgression. If a female trainee, a female novice, or a male novice has it made — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

In brief:
Made by another, for another, not held,
with the marks, likewise the fourth,
laypeople and the like —
these are what is improper, and the seventh.

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that if a monk makes a seat or bench for the Saṅgha more than eight finger-breadths of the Sugata in height — except for mortise work in the legs — and retains it, it becomes a transgression. Venerable one, if a monk finishes off something begun by another that exceeds eight Sugata finger-breadths in height — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if a monk has it made for another's sake — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable one, if one makes it improperly and then discards it — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable one, if a monk who was having a seat or bench for the Saṅgha made in excess of eight Sugata finger-breadths undergoes a change of marks and becomes a nun — what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, if a nun who was having a seat or bench for the Saṅgha made in excess of eight Sugata finger-breadths undergoes a change of marks and becomes a monk — what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "Venerable one, if a monk, perceiving that a seat or bench for the Saṅgha is in excess of eight Sugata finger-breadths and knowing it to be in excess, has it made — what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "If it is in excess and one does not perceive it as in excess, and has it made — there is no offense." "If it is not in excess and one perceives it as in excess, and has it made — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If it is not in excess and one does not perceive it as in excess — there is no offense."

"Venerable one, if a monk has a seat or bench for the Saṅgha made for a layperson in excess of eight Sugata finger-breadths — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Likewise, if it is made for a female trainee, a hermaphrodite, an expelled nun" — and so on through to having it made for one who has been given the full training — "in all cases it becomes a wrongdoing."

"Venerable one, is there any case in which a monk who has a seat or bench for the Saṅgha made in excess of eight Sugata finger-breadths commits no transgression thereby?" Upāli, there is: when it is made from what is improper.

"Venerable one, if one begins making a seat or bench for the Saṅgha exceeding eight Sugata finger-breadths while not yet fully ordained and it is completed while not yet fully ordained — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one begins while not yet fully ordained and it is completed at the moment of full ordination — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one begins while not yet fully ordained and it is completed after full ordination — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one begins at the moment of full ordination and it is completed at the moment of full ordination — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one begins at the moment of full ordination and it is completed after full ordination — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"If one begins at the moment of full ordination and it is completed at the moment of full ordination — what becomes of it?" It is a transgression. "If one begins at the moment of full ordination and it is completed before full ordination — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

In brief:

By messenger, by letter, by gesture,
Through an intermediary, from one to another,
Through one who has gone mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
One who is ill, one who is mute, one who has gone elsewhere.

Venerable monks: if a monk causes the Saṅgha's chair or small chair to be used as a messenger for an amount exceeding eight of the Sugata's finger-breadths — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if one causes it to be done by written letter, by gesture, through an intermediary, or relayed from one to another, all of these become wrongdoings. Venerable monks: if a monk causes one who has gone mad to act using the Saṅgha's chair or small chair for an amount exceeding eight of the Sugata's finger-breadths — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, if one causes it to be done by one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is stupid, one who is dumb, one who is mute, or one who is dwelling elsewhere — all of these become wrongdoings.

Venerable monks: if one who has been given a training rule causes an act to be done involving the Saṅgha's chair or small chair for an amount exceeding eight of the Sugata's finger-breadths — what becomes of it? It is a transgression. If a fully ordained nun causes it to be done — what becomes of it? It is a transgression. If a female trainee, a female novice, or male novices cause it to be done — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing.

Just as this chapter on the basis of training has been set forth, so too the same is to be stated in the same manner concerning the alms bowl, the sitting mat, the blanket cover, the cloth of the summer rains, and the Sugata's robe of Dharma.

Here ends the section on transgressions from the noble Vinaya scripture.

The noble Vinaya scripture, the fifteenth fascicle. In brief:

One who has gone mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
One who is ill, one who is mute, one who has gone elsewhere,
The improper, the sign, and likewise
The fourth and the seventh are the same.
