The venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, you have declared that if a monk lifts and receives alms food from a fully ordained nun who is not a relative while she is on her alms round, it constitutes an offense requiring individual confession. Venerable One, if a monk lifts and receives alms food from a mad fully ordained nun while she is present on her alms round — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Likewise, if he receives it from a nun whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is stupid, one who is dumb, one who is mute, or one who is dwelling elsewhere, and eats it — all of these become wrongdoings."

"Venerable One, can it be that a monk who lifts and receives alms food from a fully ordained nun who is not a relative while she is present on her alms round would not incur a transgression as a downfall?" Upāli, if one eats what is improper food it becomes a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, if a monk receives staple and non-staple food from a fully ordained nun who is not a relative, one who is on her alms round and is present, and in the midst of receiving it a change of gender occurs and she becomes a fully ordained monk — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable One, if a fully ordained nun receives alms food from a fully ordained monk who is not a relative, one who is on his alms round and is present, and in the midst of receiving it a change of gender occurs and he becomes a fully ordained monk — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, if a monk perceives a fully ordained person as fully ordained and receives and lifts alms food from that person — what becomes of it?" It requires individual confession. "If one perceives a fully ordained person as not fully ordained — it is a wrongdoing. If one perceives a person who is not fully ordained as fully ordained — it is a wrongdoing. If one perceives a person who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained — it is a wrongdoing." Likewise, with regard to perceiving a human as a human, the same fourfold treatment applies.

"Venerable One, if one receives and lifts food while not yet fully ordained, and accepts it while not yet fully ordained — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, if one receives and lifts food while not yet fully ordained, and accepts it at the moment of full ordination — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one receives and lifts food while not yet fully ordained, and accepts it after full ordination — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one receives and lifts food at the moment of full ordination, and accepts it at the moment of full ordination — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one receives and lifts food at the moment of full ordination, and accepts it as a fully ordained person — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one receives and lifts food after full ordination, and accepts it after full ordination — what becomes of it?" It requires individual confession. "If one receives and lifts food after full ordination, and accepts it while not yet fully ordained — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

In brief:
Food and mantra likewise,
One person receiving for another's female paṇḍaka,
Paṇḍaka women and the like,
One who has surrendered training, and nuns.

Venerable One, if a monk receives and accepts things other than food — namely prepared provisions, drinks, things to be licked, and things to be tasted — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. Venerable One, if a monk, having taken almsfood from a nun who is not a relative while she stands in the alleyway, on behalf of someone else, and then consumes it himself — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. Venerable One, if a monk takes almsfood from a nun who is not a relative and consumes it, is there a case in which the individual wrongdoing need not be confessed? Upāli, there is. It is like this: if that monk is standing in the alleyway and a nun is sitting in a summer retreat house or in a village and gives it — it becomes a wrongdoing. Venerable One, if a nun takes almsfood from a nun who is a female paṇḍaka standing in the alleyway and then accepts it — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. Venerable One, if a monk takes almsfood from a nun who is a female paṇḍaka standing in the alleyway and then accepts it — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. Likewise, from a nun who has been expelled, and so on through all the cases up to one previously embroiled in disputes: if one has taken almsfood from any of these and eaten it, all of them become wrongdoings. Venerable One, if a monk takes almsfood from a nun who has created a schism in the Saṅgha, or who has taken a partisan side, or who has surrendered her training, while she stands in the alleyway, and then accepts it — what becomes of it? It requires individual confession. Venerable One, if a monk takes almsfood from a female probationer or a novice nun and then accepts it — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. Venerable One, if one who has surrendered training takes almsfood from a monk who is not a relative while he stands in the alleyway, and then accepts it — what becomes of it? It requires individual confession. Venerable One, if a nun takes almsfood from a monk who is not a relative while he stands in the alleyway, and then accepts it — what becomes of it? It requires individual confession. If one takes almsfood from a novice monk and accepts it — what becomes of it? It is a wrongdoing. Just as a monk must make individual confession, so too in the case of female probationers, novice nuns, and novice monks it becomes a wrongdoing.

In brief:
Verbal message, written letter, hand-signal,
Quoting another's words, and passing from one to another;
One who is mad, whose mind is disturbed, one who is ill,
One who is senseless, a fool, one overcome by sleep,
One who is delirious, one who is intoxicated,
And one who is entering meditative absorption — these are the final cases.

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, Blessed One, if the Blessed One had instructed those monks to say this to that nun, 'Sister nun, stay here until the meal is finished' — and if some monks did not dare to say this to that nun, they must make individual confession. That being so, Venerable One, if a monk conveys the instruction through a messenger and thereby has her accept it — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Likewise, if one conveys and has her accept it through a written letter, through a hand-signal, through quoting another's words, or through passing the message from one to another — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, if a nun who is insane and wandering is present and those monks have eaten without conveying the instruction to her — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Likewise, if monks eat without conveying the instruction to a nun who is mentally disturbed, or afflicted by illness, or mentally dull, or mute, or deaf, or who has gone to stay elsewhere — all of these are wrongdoings."

"Venerable One, if a nun is waiting for the sake of the monks and falls asleep, and those monks convey the instruction to her while she is sleeping and then eat — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Likewise, if the instruction is conveyed to a nun who is snoring, or intoxicated, or in meditative absorption, and they then eat — all of these are wrongdoings."

In brief:

By voice and body, by a private place,
by mantra and sign — these being the fourth —
by improper food, by the layman,
by the training given, and by the nun.

"Venerable One, if a monk who is a noble one conveys the instruction to a nun in the noble language, and that nun does not accept it in the noble language — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If a noble one conveys the instruction in the language of the frontier regions, and that nun does not accept it in the language of the frontier regions — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one from the frontier regions conveys the instruction in the language of the frontier regions, and that nun does not accept it in that language — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "If one from the frontier regions conveys the instruction in the noble language, and that nun does not accept it in the noble language — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, if a monk conveys the instruction by means of a bodily gesture and she accepts it — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, if monks, with the perception that a nun who is waiting is not in a secluded place when she actually is, convey the instruction to her and eat — what becomes of it?" There is no transgression.

"Venerable One, if a monk makes himself invisible by means of a mantra or medicine and eats without conveying the instruction to a nun — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, if a monk eats without conveying the instruction while a nun is waiting, and in the meantime his sex changes and he becomes a nun — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable One, if a nun eats without conveying the instruction while she is waiting for the sake of monks, and in the meantime her sex changes and she becomes a monk — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, if a monk, perceiving a fully ordained nun as a fully ordained nun, eats without conveying the instruction to her — what becomes of it?" Individual confession is required. "If he perceives a fully ordained nun as not fully ordained and eats without conveying the instruction — it is a wrongdoing." "If he perceives a not-fully-ordained woman as fully ordained — it is a wrongdoing." "If he perceives a not-fully-ordained woman as not fully ordained — it is a wrongdoing."

"Venerable One, if a nun is waiting while serving a single dish of improper food, and monks eat without conveying the instruction to her — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Venerable One, if a nun is waiting while serving, apart from cooked grain, other kinds of prepared food — drinks, eatables, lickables, and the like — and monks eat without conveying the instruction to her — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, if a monk eats without conveying the instruction while a laywoman is waiting — what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing. "Likewise, if he eats without conveying the instruction while waiting is being done by an expelled nun, or a woman who has killed her father, or one who has killed her mother, or one who has killed an arhat, or one who with malicious intent has drawn the blood of a Tathāgata, or a tīrthika, or one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, or one dwelling as a thief, or one living separately, or one who has left the community, or one against whom a prior offense has arisen, or one who was previously involved in a schism — all of these are wrongdoings."

"Venerable One, if a monk receives the instruction conveyed by a nun who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, or one who has taken sides in a schism, or one who has been given a training — what becomes of it?"

It is to be confessed individually.

"Venerable One, what becomes of it if a monk receives instruction conveyed by a nun, a female trainee, or a novice nun?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, what becomes of it if a nun conveys food that has been received from one who has been given a training?" It is to be confessed individually.

"Venerable One, what becomes of it if a nun conveys food that she has received and then seeks it?" It is to be confessed individually. For a female trainee, a novice nun, and male novices, it becomes a wrongdoing.

In brief:
By messenger, by written letter, by hand signal,
By speaking through another, from one to another,
By the mad, the mentally disturbed, the afflicted,
The deaf, and the foolish.

The venerable Upāli then put a further question to the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable One, the Blessed One has also declared to the Saṅgha that regarding one who has become a student-village — one upon whom a training vow has been conferred — if a monk who has accepted a training vow with respect to such a student-village makes an arrangement and accepts food through his own lay supporter and seeks it, that is to be confessed individually." In that case, "Venerable One, if a monk, from a village upon which a training vow has been conferred, makes an arrangement and accepts food through a messenger and seeks it, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

Similarly, if he accepts and eats it through a written letter, through a hand signal, through speaking via another, or through transmission from one person to another — all of these become wrongdoings.

"Venerable One, if a monk accepts food and provisions from a mad person's village upon which a training vow has been conferred and seeks it, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

Similarly, if he accepts and eats food and provisions from one who is mentally disturbed, one afflicted by illness, a foolish person, a mute, a deaf person, a person of intermediate sex (paṇḍaka), a female of intermediate sex, or one who has gone to dwell elsewhere — all of these become wrongdoings.

In brief:
By another for another's sake, likewise;
By mantra and medicine, by food unfit,
And by a guest at night — likewise;
Thus the fourth case: the nun.

"Venerable One, if another person accepts food and provisions from a village upon which a training vow has been conferred by a monk and then seeks it, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, if a monk accepts food and provisions from a village upon which a training vow has been conferred, on behalf of another, and seeks them for himself, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, if a monk, having concealed his own identity by means of mantra or medicine, accepts food and provisions from a village upon which a training vow has been conferred and seeks them, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, if a monk seeks from a village upon which a training vow has been conferred — other than cooked grain — other kinds of provisions, drinks, things to taste, things to lick, and the like, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, if a monk accepts unfit food from a village upon which a training vow has been conferred and seeks it, what becomes of it?" It is a wrongdoing.

"Venerable One, is there a case in which a monk who accepts food and provisions from a village upon which a training vow has been conferred through his own lay supporter and seeks them does not incur a downfall?" Upāli, there is. It is as follows: a monk was previously invited to a village as a guest, and after that the Saṅgha conferred a training vow upon it.

"Venerable One, if a monk seeks food and provisions from a village upon which a training vow has been conferred, and then changes status and becomes a nun, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually.

"Venerable One, if a nun seeks food and provisions from a village upon which a training vow has been conferred, and then changes status and becomes a monk, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually.

"Venerable One, if a monk accepts and seeks food and provisions from a village upon which a training vow has been conferred, perceiving it as having been given, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually.

"Venerable One, if a monk accepts and seeks food and provisions from a village upon which a training vow has been conferred, perceiving what has been given as not having been given, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. "If he perceives what has not been given as having been given and seeks it, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. "If he perceives what has not been given as not having been given, what becomes of it?" There is no offence.

"Venerable One, if a monk accepts and seeks food and provisions from the people of a village upon which a training vow has been conferred, perceiving those people as human beings, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. "If he perceives human beings as non-human beings, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. "If he perceives non-human beings as human beings, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. "If he perceives non-human beings as non-human beings, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually.

"Venerable One, if one who has conferred training vows accepts and seeks food and provisions from a village upon which a training vow has been conferred, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. "Venerable One, if a nun accepts and seeks food and provisions from a village upon which a training vow has been conferred, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. "If a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā), a female novice, or male novices seek it, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually.

In brief:
By messenger, by letter, by gesture,
by having another say it, from one to another,
one who has become mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is sick, a deaf-mute — these are the cases.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, the Blessed One has taught that when the Saṅgha is dwelling in a monastery, one should seek food and provisions with apprehension, with fear, and while being frightened and alarmed. If a monk, while dwelling in such a monastery with apprehension, fear, and while being frightened and alarmed, takes food and provisions from beyond the boundary of the monastery courtyard and then seeks food and provisions within the monastery courtyard, it is to be confessed individually." To this the Blessed One declared: "Venerable One, if a monk, while dwelling in such a monastery, takes food and provisions from beyond the boundary of the monastery courtyard and seeks food and provisions within the monastery courtyard through a messenger, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. "Likewise, if he does so by letter, by gesture, by having another say it, or by passing it from one to another, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually.

"Venerable One, if a monk dwelling in such a monastery takes food and provisions from a madman beyond the boundary of the monastery courtyard and seeks them, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. "Likewise, if he takes and consumes food and provisions from beyond the boundary of the monastery courtyard from one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is mentally deficient, one who is mute, one who is deaf-mute, a hermaphrodite, a female hermaphrodite, one with both characteristics, or one dwelling elsewhere — in all such cases it is to be confessed individually."

In brief:
When another acts on behalf of another in the same way,
by mantra and medicine, and what is unsuitable,
by full understanding, and likewise
the thief, the characteristics, and the fourth.

"Venerable One, if a monk dwelling in such a monastery, while within the monastery courtyard, seeks food and provisions that another person has taken, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. "Venerable One, if a monk dwelling in such a monastery himself takes food and provisions intended for others and seeks them within the monastery courtyard, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. "Venerable One, if a monk dwelling in such a monastery disguises himself through mantra and medicine so as not to be recognizable, and then accepts and seeks food and provisions within the monastery courtyard, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. "Venerable One, if a monk dwelling in such a monastery accepts and seeks things other than food — such as provisions, drinks, soft foodstuffs, and things to be licked — what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually.

"Venerable One, if a monk dwelling in such a monastery accepts and seeks improper food within the monastery courtyard, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. "Venerable One, is there any case in which a monk dwelling in such a monastery might accept and seek provisions and foodstuffs within the monastery courtyard without incurring an offense?" Upāli, there is: if he eats in a properly designated forest, there is no offense. "Venerable One, is there any case in which a monk dwelling in such a monastery might accept and seek provisions and foodstuffs both in a properly designated forest and within the monastery courtyard without incurring an offense?" Upāli, there is: if that monk eats while staying in close proximity to a band of thieves. "Venerable One, if a monk is in the act of accepting and seeking provisions and foodstuffs within the monastery courtyard and his sex changes so that he becomes a nun, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. "Venerable One, if a nun is in the act of accepting and seeking foodstuffs and provisions within the monastery courtyard and her sex changes so that she becomes a monk, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually.

"Venerable One, if a monk perceives a properly designated place as properly designated and then accepts and seeks provisions and foodstuffs there, what becomes of it?" There is no offense. If he perceives a properly designated place as not properly designated, it becomes a transgression. "If he perceives a place that is not properly designated as properly designated and seeks food there, what becomes of it?" There is no offense. "If he perceives a place that is not properly designated as not properly designated and seeks food there, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. Likewise, the same analysis is to be applied regarding perceiving a person as a person.

"Venerable One, if one who has been given a training rule accepts and seeks provisions and foodstuffs in a forest that is not properly designated, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. "Venerable One, if a nun accepts and seeks provisions and foodstuffs within the courtyard of a monastery that is not properly designated, what becomes of it?" It is to be confessed individually. For female probationers (śikṣāmāṇā), novice nuns, and novice monks, it becomes a transgression.

This completes the training rule on individual liberation as found in the section on full ordination within the noble Vinaya.

In brief:
Shape and color, impediment,
Two preceptors, expulsion,
Place and person, the island groups,
Ground and boundary, and full ordination.
The fifth, and the three acts,
Householder, border regions, and the last.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable One, the Blessed One has said that one who resembles a woman in bodily appearance should not be ordained and given full ordination. Now, if a man whose complexion resembles a woman's, whose physical marks resemble a woman's, whose voice resembles a woman's, and whose bodily shape resembles a woman's were given full ordination as a monk in proper form, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, it would be called a full ordination, and the act of ordination would be valid. "Venerable One, if a woman whose complexion resembles a man's, whose physical marks resemble a man's, whose voice resembles a man's, and whose bodily shape resembles a man's were given full ordination, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, it would be called a full ordination, and the act of ordination would be valid.

"Venerable One, if a person who possesses the qualities of an impediment declares, 'I possess the qualities of an impediment,' and the monks then give that person full ordination as a monk in proper form, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, it would not be called a full ordination, yet the act of ordination would be valid.

"Venerable One, if a person who possesses the qualities of an impediment declares, 'I do not possess the qualities of an impediment,' and the monks then give that person full ordination as a monk in proper form, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, it would not be called a full ordination, and those who perform the ordination also incur a transgression.

"If a person who does not possess the qualities of an impediment declares, 'I do possess them,' and the monks give that person full ordination as a monk in proper form, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, it would be called a full ordination, and those who perform the ordination incur a transgression.

"If a person who does not possess the qualities of an impediment declares, 'I do not possess them,' and the monks give that person full ordination as a monk in proper form, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, it would be called a full ordination, and those who perform the ordination would not incur a transgression.

"Venerable One, if one who is conferring full ordination does so without having asked about the qualities of an impediment, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, it would be called a full ordination, yet those who perform the ordination incur a transgression.

"Venerable One, if someone who has not reached the age of twenty is given full ordination, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, with the exception of one who is able to know, all others would be called fully ordained.

"Venerable One, if full ordination is given without a bowl being present, or without robes being present, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, it would be called a full ordination, and those who perform the ordination incur a transgression.

"Venerable One, if full ordination is given without the permission of one's father and mother, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, it would be called a full ordination, and those who perform the ordination incur a transgression.

"Venerable One, are there cases where one ordained without the permission of one's father and mother would not incur wrongdoing?" Upāli, there are. These are: where the father and mother have passed away, where they have taken rebirth as animals, or where the permission of a master has been granted.

"Venerable One, if a child is in such a situation, to whom should one apply? One should apply to the person acknowledged as his parent."

"Venerable One, if a slave is given full ordination, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, it would be called a full ordination, and those who perform the ordination incur a transgression.

"Venerable One, if someone who is a thief, a debt-evader, one cherished by a king, one at enmity with a king, or one who performs acts harmful to a king is given full ordination, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, it would be called a full ordination, and those who perform the ordination incur a transgression.

"Venerable One, if a eunuch is given full ordination, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, it would not be called a full ordination, and those who perform the ordination also incur a transgression.

"Venerable One, if a hermaphrodite is given full ordination, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, it would not be called a full ordination, and those who perform the ordination incur a transgression.

"Venerable One, if someone who has been expelled from the community of nuns is given full ordination, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, in some cases it would be called a full ordination, and in some cases it would not. One who has been expelled from the community of nuns on account of unchaste conduct — this would not be called a full ordination; even if such a person is nearby, one should treat them as though they are invisible to the eye. One who has been expelled from the community of nuns merely because of physical contact — this would be called a full ordination; do not drive such a person away.

"Venerable one, if a person who has not killed their mother is given full ordination, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, in some cases it would be called a full ordination, and in some cases it would not. One who has separated from their mother's livelihood under the mistaken perception that she belongs to another — or even one who has merely contracted such a relationship — this would be called a full ordination; even if such a person is nearby, do not treat them as invisible to the eye. One who has knowingly separated from their mother's livelihood — this would not be called a full ordination; even if such a person is nearby, do not let them be visible to the eye. Just as this has been stated regarding one who has not killed their mother, the same should be said regarding one who has killed their father and one who has killed an arhat.

"Venerable one, if a person who caused a schism in the Saṅgha then relinquished their training and fell away, and who thereafter, with faith in the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, went forth into renunciation, received full ordination, and sought the status of a fully ordained monk — if a monk were to give such a person full ordination, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, in some cases it would be called a full ordination, and in some cases it would not. One who split the Saṅgha under the perception that it was not in accordance with the Dharma — this would not be called a full ordination; even if such a person is nearby, treat them as invisible to the eye. One who split the Saṅgha under the perception that it was in accordance with the Dharma — this would be called a full ordination; even if such a person is nearby, do not treat them as invisible to the eye.

"Venerable one, if a person who drew blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent is given full ordination, would that be called a full ordination?" Upāli, in some cases it would be called a full ordination, and in some cases it would not. One who knowingly drew blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent — this would not be called a full ordination; even if such a person is nearby, treat them as invisible to the eye. One who drew blood without knowing, without malicious intent — this would be called a full ordination; even if such a person is nearby, do not treat them as invisible to the eye.

"Venerable one, if a tīrthika is given full ordination, would that be called a full ordination?" In some cases it would be called a full ordination, and in some cases it would not. One who has not abandoned their tīrthika views — this would not be called a full ordination; even if such a person is nearby, treat them as invisible to the eye. But if they have abandoned those views, it would be called a full ordination; even if such a person is nearby, do not treat them as invisible to the eye.

"Venerable one, if a person who has gone over to the tīrthikas is given full ordination, would that be called a full ordination?" In some cases it would be called a full ordination, and in some cases it would not. One who, without having relinquished their training, took up the banner of the tīrthikas and delights in their views — this would not be called a full ordination; even if such a person is nearby, treat them as invisible to the eye. One who relinquished their training, then took up the banner of the tīrthikas but does not delight in their views — this would be called a full ordination; even if such a person is nearby, do not treat them as invisible to the eye.

"Venerable one, if a person who abides as a thief is given full ordination, would that be called a full ordination?" In some cases it would not be called a full ordination, and in some cases it would be. One who, with a thieving mind, received their insignia and then participated in the restoration ceremony two or three times — this would not be called a full ordination; even if such a person is nearby, treat them as invisible to the eye. One who, with a thieving mind, had not yet gone forth and had participated in the restoration ceremony once, or had not yet participated at all — this would be called a full ordination; even if such a person is nearby, do not treat them as invisible to the eye.

"Venerable one, if a person who has been restrained by the training surrenders the training, becomes a layman, and then receives full ordination again in this well-taught Dharma and Vinaya — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is called a full ordination, and the one who confers full ordination has also transgressed."

"Venerable one, if one who has previously committed an offense receives full ordination — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is not called a full ordination, and the one who confers full ordination has also transgressed."

"Venerable one, how much is required for one to be called a person who has previously committed an offense?" Upāli replied: "One who previously went forth without surrendering the training and then incurred any one of the four defeats, and who, without having surrendered the training, went and became a layman, and who then again goes forth and receives full ordination in this well-taught Dharma and Vinaya and wishes to be established as a monk — this is called a person who has previously committed an offense."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One declared that a person who has previously committed an offense must not be given ordination or full ordination. If such a person is given full ordination — does a valid full ordination result?" Upāli replied: "There is a case where it does. It is like this: one who has incurred a defeat that is not shared with nuns, and who then surrenders the training and becomes a layman, and in that state undergoes a change of sex and is reborn as a man, and then goes forth and receives full ordination in this well-taught Dharma and Vinaya and wishes to be established as a monk, and monks confer full ordination upon that person — this is called a full ordination."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One declared that a nun who has once fallen back must not be given the going-forth or full ordination. If full ordination is nonetheless conferred — is this called a full ordination or not?" It is not called a full ordination, and the one who confers full ordination has also transgressed.

"Venerable one, if a person who has previously caused a schism receives full ordination — is this called a full ordination or is it not?" In some cases it is called a full ordination, and in some cases it is not. One who knowingly ordains a person who has not yet reached twenty years of age and who accepted such a candidate on the claim that they fulfill this Dharma and Vinaya — if monks confer full ordination on such a person, this is called a full ordination, and the one who confers full ordination does not thereby transgress.

"Venerable one, if one who has drawn near, surrendered the training, become a layman, and then receives full ordination in this well-taught Dharma and Vinaya — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is not called a full ordination, and the one who confers full ordination has also transgressed."

"Venerable one, one who was given the training, then surrendered the training and became a layman — if such a person again goes forth and receives full ordination in this well-taught Dharma and Vinaya, wishing to be established as a monk, and monks confer full ordination upon them — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is called a full ordination, and the one who confers full ordination has also transgressed."

"Venerable one, if a debtor receives full ordination — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is called a full ordination, and the one who confers full ordination has also transgressed."

"Venerable one, if a sick person receives full ordination — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is called a full ordination, and the one who confers full ordination has also transgressed."

"Venerable one, if full ordination is conferred without an abbot being present — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is called a full ordination."

the one who confers full ordination has also transgressed.

"Venerable one, if a full ordination is conferred while dismissing the abbot — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "In some cases it is called a full ordination, and in some cases it is not called a full ordination. If someone abuses and dismisses the abbot, saying of the candidate himself, 'He is unworthy, he is shameless, he is without restraint' — that is not called a full ordination. But if someone abuses the abbot, saying 'He is unworthy, he is shameless,' and dismisses as abbot one who is not himself a monastic — that is called a full ordination."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that a person who disrupts the assembly should not be given going forth or full ordination. If that person is given full ordination, is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "There are four kinds of assembly-disrupters. Apart from the first kind, those who have caused disturbance in the past, the rest are called fully ordained, and the one who confers full ordination has also transgressed."

"Venerable one, is it permitted for the officiating monk to be on one side and for four persons in four locations to be given full ordination?" It is permitted. And this is how it is done: the officiating monk, standing at the boundary of all four locations — whether leaning against a post, a pillar, or a door-frame — confers full ordination on them one by one, two by two, or three by three, so long as the full four are not incomplete.

"Venerable one, is it permitted for a single act of karma to give full ordination to two or three persons?" Upāli replied: "It is permitted."

"Venerable one, if the officiating monk is on one side, and four persons are given full ordination by a single motion and a single act of karma — is the karma valid, and will those monks not have transgressed?" Upāli replied: "There is such a case. This is how it is done: the officiating monk, standing at the boundary, whether lying, standing, or sitting at the boundary — places two within the boundary and two outside the boundary and performs the act."

"Venerable one, if a person from the western land of the Cow-Conduct, or from the eastern continent of Superior Body, is given full ordination — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is called a full ordination, and the one who confers full ordination has also transgressed."

"Venerable one, if a person from the northern land of Unpleasant Sound is given full ordination — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is not called a full ordination, and the one who confers full ordination has also transgressed."

"Venerable one, is it permitted for those who are present on enclosed ground to count numbers and confer full ordination on those who are in open sky?" Upāli replied: "It is not permitted."

"Venerable one, is it permitted for those who are present in open sky to count numbers and confer full ordination on those who are on enclosed ground?" Upāli replied: "It is not permitted."

"Venerable one, is it permitted for one performing the act on enclosed ground to perform the act for those in open sky?" Upāli replied: "It is not permitted."

"Venerable one, is it permitted for one performing the act in open sky to perform the act for those on enclosed ground?" Upāli replied: "It is not permitted."

Likewise, those sitting inside the boundary and those sitting outside the boundary — the same four cases apply.

The Noble Vinaya, the sixteenth fascicle.

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that in border regions, full ordination may be conferred by five monks including one who holds the Vinaya. If ten are present but full ordination is conferred by four including a Vinaya-holder — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have all transgressed."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that in central regions, full ordination may be conferred by ten or more monks including one who holds the Vinaya. If twenty or more are present, but full ordination is conferred by fewer than twenty — is this called a full ordination or not a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have all transgressed."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that full ordination is recognized in five ways: from the naming of the candidate who seeks full ordination up to the point at which the act is performed without flaw. If, when performing full ordination, the name of the one seeking full ordination is not stated, but the name of the preceptor is stated, the name of the Saṅgha is stated, the formal request is made, and the act is performed without flaw — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is not called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have all transgressed."

"If the name of the one seeking full ordination is stated, the name of the Saṅgha is stated, but the name of the preceptor is not stated, the formal request is made, and the act is performed without flaw — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is not called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have all transgressed."

"If the name of the one seeking full ordination is stated, the name of the preceptor is stated, but the name of the Saṅgha is not stated, the formal request is made, and the act is performed without flaw — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is not called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have all transgressed."

"If the name of the one seeking full ordination is stated, the name of the preceptor is stated, the name of the Saṅgha is also stated, but the formal request is not made, and the act is performed without flaw — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is not called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have all transgressed."

"If the name of the one seeking full ordination is stated, the name of the preceptor is stated, the name of the Saṅgha is stated, the formal request is made, but the act is flawed — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is not called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have all transgressed."

"Venerable one, if a male novice is fully ordained by the act of a community of fully ordained nuns — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have all transgressed."

"Venerable one, if a female probationer is fully ordained by the act of a community of fully ordained monks — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have all transgressed."

"Venerable one, if, while the act of conferring full ordination is being performed, the time lapses — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "If in that case the act has been performed in its greater part, it is called a full ordination."

"Venerable one, if during full ordination the ceremony is interrupted and one speaks back, saying, 'Do not confer full ordination upon me' — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli replied: "It is not called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have all transgressed."

"Venerable one, if during full ordination one declares a wish to be a layman — is this called a full ordination or not a full ordination?" It is not called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have all transgressed.

"Venerable one, if full ordination is conferred upon a border-region person in the noble language, and that border-region person does not understand the noble language — is this called a full ordination?" If that person possesses and fully commands this scriptural tradition and has the intention to accept it, it is called a full ordination.

Those who confer full ordination upon such a person have engaged in what ought not to be done and incur a transgression by conferring that full ordination.

In brief:

One who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is mute, one who is dull, one who is asleep,
one who stammers, one who is intoxicated,
one in meditative absorption, and one in the act of departing — these are the marks.

"Venerable one, if full ordination is conferred upon a madman — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli, if that person has the perception of full ordination and accepts it with body or speech through an intentional act, it is called a full ordination. Just as in the case of the madman, the same should be stated in full for one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is dull, and one who is mute or deaf.

"Venerable one, if full ordination is conferred upon one who is asleep — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli, if that person's body and speech are present and directed toward the request, and the rite is being performed while the person has fallen asleep, it is nonetheless called a full ordination. Just as in the case of one who is asleep, the same should likewise be stated for one who stammers and one in meditative absorption.

"Venerable one, if full ordination is conferred upon one who is in the act of departing to another place — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli, it is not called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have incurred a transgression.

"Venerable one, if the ordination name is changed in the very midst of the full ordination ceremony — is this called a full ordination?" It is called a full ordination. Count it among those of nuns.

In brief:

One who has become mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is ill, one who is deaf, one who is dull,
and laymen and the like —
give the training and note these as the marks.

"Venerable one, if a madman who is capable of performing acts confers full ordination — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli, if the monk performing the act possesses the perception of Saṅgha, has made the request, and the rite has not broken down, it is called a full ordination, though those who have conferred the full ordination have all incurred a transgression. The same is to be stated in full for one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is mute, one who is deaf, and likewise for one who stammers.

"Venerable one, if a layman who is performing the act confers full ordination — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli, it is not called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have all incurred a transgression. Likewise, a paṇḍaka, a nun who has been expelled, one who has killed a father or mother or an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn the blood of a Tathāgata, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, one who resides in a stolen place, one who does not reside permanently, one who dwells in a separate abode, one in whom a prior offense has arisen, or one who performs the act on the basis of a prior dispute — is this called a full ordination? Upāli, it is not called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have all incurred a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a person who is acting as celebrant while under vows of the laity confers full ordination — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli, it is not called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have all incurred a transgression.

"Venerable one, if those acting as celebrant who have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, who have aligned themselves with a schismatic faction, or who have given the training, confer full ordination — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli, it is not called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have incurred a transgression.

"Venerable one, if the celebrant is one who has gone to dwell in another realm and confers full ordination — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli, it is not called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have incurred a transgression.

"Venerable one, if during the performance of the rite the ordination name of the celebrant is changed — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli, it is called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have incurred a transgression.

In brief:

One who is mad or mentally disturbed, one who is mute, foolish, or asleep, one who is intoxicated, one who is in meditative absorption, one who is a being of ill omen, laypeople, and the like — giving precepts to these is the lowest of transgressions.

"Venerable one, if a celebrant who is mad confers full ordination — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli, it is called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have incurred a transgression. Likewise, from a celebrant who is mentally disturbed, through one who is ill, down to one who is in meditative absorption — all the same applies.

"Venerable one, if a celebrant who has gone to dwell in another realm confers full ordination — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli, it is called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have incurred a transgression.

"Venerable one, if, while a novice is being given full ordination, the ordination name of the celebrant is changed — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli, it is called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have incurred a transgression.

"Venerable one, if a layman acts as celebrant and confers full ordination — is this called a full ordination?" Upāli, it is called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have incurred a transgression. Likewise, from a celebrant who is a woman, through a hermaphrodite, down to one who gives the extended training — if any of these confer full ordination, is this called a full ordination? Upāli, it is called a full ordination, and those who confer full ordination have incurred a transgression.

Here ends the section on the essentials of full ordination from the noble Vinaya.

In brief:

Half, three, encirclement,
the fourth, the boundary, and the night mark,
the broken, the prior boundary, and the tree,
exclusion, the ineligible, the layman,
and finally exclusion was declared.

The venerable Upāli then put a question to the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has taught that a great boundary should be established — venerable one, what is the measure of a great boundary?" Upāli, it is three and a half leagues. Anything less than that is a small one, namely a maṇḍala that can contain a circle of forty assembled monks. "Venerable one, if a boundary is established that exceeds three and a half leagues — is that called a boundary?" Upāli, it is not. Three and a half leagues is the boundary; beyond that it is not a boundary. If such a boundary has been established, it is still to be called not established, and the monks too have incurred a transgression. Likewise, all should be understood in the same way.

"Venerable one, what constitutes the lower boundary?" Upāli, it extends as far as there is water.

"Venerable one, if there is water at a distance exceeding three and a half leagues, is that called a boundary?" Upāli, it is not. Three and a half leagues is the boundary; below that it is not a boundary.

"Venerable one, what constitutes the boundary of the upper sky?" Upāli, it extends as far as there is a rooftop or a treetop.

"Venerable one, if there is a rooftop or treetop at a distance exceeding three and a half leagues, is that called a boundary?" Upāli, it is not. Three and a half leagues is called the boundary; beyond that it is not a boundary.

"Venerable one, what constitutes the boundary of a mountain peak?" Upāli, it extends as far as there is a spring.

"Venerable one, if there is a spring at a distance exceeding three and a half leagues, is that called a boundary?" Upāli, it is not. Three and a half leagues is the boundary; beyond that it is not a boundary.

"Venerable one, is it permitted for a boundary to be encircled by another boundary?" Upāli, it is not permitted — except for a boundary of earshot, a boundary of a wall, or a maṇḍala encircled by water.

"Venerable one, if a noble one performing a rite has pronounced the establishing of a boundary in the noble language —

— but those monks have not mastered the noble language, is that called nullifying the boundary?" Upāli, it is called cutting the boundary; the act, however, is accomplished and has passed.

"Venerable one, if a noble one has established a boundary using the language of the borderlands, and those monks have not mastered the language of the borderlands, is that called nullifying the boundary?" Upāli, it is called cutting it; the act, however, is accomplished and has passed.

"Venerable one, if a person of the borderlands has established a boundary using the language of the borderlands, and those monks have not mastered the language of the borderlands, is that called nullifying the boundary?" Upāli, it is called cutting the boundary; the act, however, is accomplished and has passed.

"Venerable one, if a person of the borderlands has established a boundary using the noble language, and those monks have not mastered the noble language, is that called nullifying the boundary?" Upāli, it is called cutting the boundary; the act, however, is accomplished and has passed.

"Venerable one, is it permissible to establish a boundary in the open sky above?" Upāli, it is not permissible. And why is that, Upāli? Because a boundary cannot be indicated there.

"Venerable one, is it permissible to establish a boundary using the sun, the moon, or the stars?" Upāli, it is not permissible. And why is that, Upāli? Because the sun, the moon, and the stars are unstable and in motion.

"Venerable one, is it permissible to establish a boundary using waves, a succession of waves, or a riverbank?" Upāli, it is not permissible. And why is that, Upāli? Because waves, a succession of waves, and a riverbank are shifting and unstable.

"Venerable one, if a riverbank were to become stable, would it then be permissible to establish a boundary there?" Upāli, it is not permissible.

"Venerable one, is it permissible to establish a boundary by means of supernormal powers or illusion?" Upāli, it is not permissible. And why is that, Upāli? Because supernormal powers and illusions cannot serve as conventional designations.

"Venerable one, is it permissible to fix a boundary from a river or a dry watercourse?" Upāli, it is not permissible, for such a river or dry watercourse does not flow without ceasing.

"Venerable one, is it permissible to fix a boundary from water that flows constantly and runs deep?" Upāli, it is permissible — provided that such a river or dry watercourse has been covered over with planks of wood, a wall, or boards.

"Venerable one, if wood or boards come to be subject to decay, is that called destruction?" If the intention to repair them has been abandoned, it is called destruction. But if the intention to cover them again has not been abandoned, it is not called destruction.

"Venerable one, if night falls while a monastic act for cutting a boundary is being performed, is that called cutting the boundary?" Upāli, it is called cutting the boundary.

"Venerable one, is it permissible to release a boundary by means of a boundary?" Upāli, it is permissible only for a boundary of earshot and a boundary of a wall; for all others it is not permissible.

"Venerable one, in how many ways is a boundary destroyed?" Upāli, in five: by there being no boundary marker, by there being no monk, by there being no expectation, by a motion, and by a formal act — five in all.

"Venerable one, is it permissible to establish another boundary without first dissolving the previous one?" Upāli, it is not permissible, except for a boundary of earshot, a boundary of a wall, and a maṇḍala boundary.

And why is that, Upāli? A boundary is cut by a motion and a formal act; and it is released by a motion and a formal act.

"Venerable one, can it happen that establishing a boundary dissolves another, or that dissolving a boundary establishes another?" Upāli, it can. If a boundary is cut by a formal act, a boundary of earshot and a boundary of a wall are released. And if a boundary is released by a formal act, a boundary of earshot and a boundary of a wall are cut.

"Venerable one, what follows upon going?" Upāli, a boundary. "Venerable one, what follows upon having gone?" Upāli, a boundary.

"Venerable one, is it permissible for a single person to establish a boundary where there are four, five, or even more residences?" Upāli, it is permissible.

"As long as it can be proclaimed and established, that is the extent of a boundary.

"Venerable one, is it permissible to move a boundary from one place to another?" Upāli, it is not permissible — except for a boundary of earshot and a boundary of a wall.

"Venerable one, how many kinds of boundaries that cannot be moved are there?" Upāli, there is one: a boundary of a formal act, a spring, or a well.

"Venerable one, what is meant by a suitable place and an unsuitable place?" "Venerable one, what is a suitable place?" Upāli, whatever residence within a boundary has been consecrated as a suitable residence — that is called a suitable place. "Venerable one, what is an unsuitable place?" Upāli, whatever residence within a boundary has not been consecrated as a suitable residence — that is called an unsuitable place. Upāli, as long as the holy Dharma exists, an unsuitable place may also exist. Upāli, if the holy Dharma were to disappear, all would become suitable places.

"Venerable one, by what measure does the holy Dharma exist?" Upāli, so long as those who undertake training do undertake training and also perform formal acts — that is, so long as they undertake training by means of what is to be undertaken through training, and also perform formal acts — for that long the holy Dharma is said to exist.

"Venerable one, by what measure has the holy Dharma ceased to exist?" Upāli, when those who undertake training do not undertake training and do not perform formal acts — that is, when through what should be undertaken as training they do not undertake training, and do not perform formal acts — at that time, the holy Dharma is said to have ceased to exist.

"Venerable one, if a layman who is performing a formal act collapses a boundary, is it called collapsing a boundary?" Upāli, it is not. Likewise, if one who is performing a formal act is a paṇḍaka, or a hermaphrodite, or one who has expelled a nun, or a patricide, or a matricide, or one who has killed an arhat, or one who with malicious intent has shed the blood of a Tathāgata, or a tīrthika, or one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, or a thief, or one who has no [legitimate] residence, or one who resides separately, or one who previously caused a schism — if such a person collapses a boundary, is it called collapsing a boundary?" Upāli, it is not.

"Venerable one, if one who is performing a formal act has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, or has sided with the schism, or has been given a probationary penalty — if such a person collapses a boundary, is it called collapsing a boundary?" Upāli, it is called cutting a boundary, and the Saṅgha is bound up with transgression.

"Venerable one, if a madman who is performing a formal act collapses a boundary, is it called collapsing a boundary?" Upāli, if he has the perception of a monk, is able to state the marks, and has made a formal request, and the formal act has not been impaired, then it is called cutting a boundary. Likewise, one who is performing a formal act and is mentally disturbed, tormented by illness, deranged, or mute — all of these should be stated in the same manner.

"Venerable one, if one who is performing a formal act collapses a boundary while residing elsewhere, in another place, is it called collapsing a boundary?" Upāli, it is not.

"Venerable one, when a boundary is collapsing, if the monk performing the formal act is late — is that called collapsing a boundary?" Upāli, if he understands that the boundary has been proclaimed, and the formal act has been performed many times, then it is called cutting a boundary. Upāli, if he neither understands that the boundary has been proclaimed, nor has the formal act been performed many times, then it is called not cutting a boundary.

Likewise, knowing that one is a layman, knowing that one is a paṇḍaka, knowing that one has expelled a nun, knowing that one has killed one's father or mother, knowing that one has killed an arhat, knowing that one has with malicious intent shed the blood of a Tathāgata, knowing that one is a tīrthika, knowing that one has gone over to the tīrthikas, knowing that one is a thief, knowing that one has no legitimate residence, knowing that one resides separately, knowing that one has previously committed an offence, knowing that one was previously a schismatic — and in the same way, knowing that one is oneself residing elsewhere in another place — all of these should be stated in full.

"Venerable one, when a boundary is about to collapse, if one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, or sided with the schism, or been given a probationary penalty, wishes to do so — is that called collapsing a boundary?" Upāli, it is called cutting a boundary, and the Saṅgha is bound up with transgression.

"Venerable one, if a boundary is collapsed by a layperson making up the number, is that called collapsing a boundary?" Upāli, it is not. And in the same way, from the hermaphrodites through to those who previously caused a schism — if those persons make up the number and a boundary is collapsed, is that called collapsing a boundary? Upāli, it is not.

"Venerable one, if a boundary is collapsed by a monk who is a glutton making up the number, is that called collapsing a boundary?" Upāli, one should not say 'cut'; yet the Saṅgha is bound up with transgression. "If those who have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, sided with the schism, or been given a probationary penalty make up the number and collapse a boundary, is that called collapsing a boundary?" Upāli, it is called cutting a boundary, and the Saṅgha is bound up with transgression.

In brief:

Boundaries and suitable dwellings,
and likewise the single-act recitation zone;
collapse and the three islands,
and the village — the third is likewise so.

"Venerable one, if the marker of a boundary has ceased to exist, is that called a boundary having collapsed?" Upāli, it is called having collapsed. "Venerable one, if a boundary has collapsed, is the suitable dwelling also called collapsed?" Upāli, it is called collapsed.

"Venerable one, is it permissible to collapse boundaries for a place with four residences, when the formal act is done with a single motion and a single recitation, in a single area?" Upāli, it is permissible; and in whichever way the monk performing the act cuts the boundary of the four residences, he presses upon a piece of wood, a stick, or a key.

"Venerable one, if a river or water from a stream floods and submerges the marker of a boundary that was being collapsed, is that called a boundary having collapsed?" Upāli, if the marker of the boundary is firm and stable, it is not called collapsed. If the marker of the boundary has ceased to exist, it is called collapsed.

"Venerable one, if a boundary has collapsed, is the vow of not parting from one's robes also absent?" Or is it present? Upāli, it is said to be present.

"If the venerable one has said that a vow of not parting from one's robes should be established for a boundary intended for formal acts — should a vow of not parting from one's robes also be established for a call-distance boundary and for a wall boundary?" If the need arises, establish it.

"Venerable one, if a village and a monastery are adjacent and the boundaries are connected, how far should the vow of not parting from one's robes be established for that?" Up to the village's immediate surroundings, but not including them.

"Venerable one, if the Blessed One has taught the vow of not parting from one's robes as not extending to the village or its immediate surroundings — if a village is established within a place for which a vow of not parting from one's robes has been set, does the vow of not parting from one's robes collapse in that direction?" Upāli, it is called collapsed.

"Venerable one, if the village moves away from a place for which a vow of not parting from one's robes has been established, why should a vow of not parting from one's robes be established again in that direction?" Upāli, there is no need; restoring the previous vow is sufficient.

In brief:

The fourth mindfulness, the third,
the fifth, and the two characteristics;
two offences and the division of occasions;
intention, sitting, arising;
laypeople and so forth,
the insane, the explanation, and the many.

"Venerable one, if the Saṅgha has mentally noted 'today is our restoration ceremony' at the time of dawn breaking — how should those monks perform the restoration ceremony? They should express from the mind in words 'today is our restoration ceremony,' and then if the Prātimokṣa is recited there, it is called having been recited. Those monks will indeed have performed the restoration ceremony, but it will be bound up with transgression."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has taught that the formal act of the restoration ceremony has four aspects: performing it improperly and without assembly; assembling but doing so improperly; assembled properly but without the proper procedure; and assembled properly with the proper procedure." —

What is meant by performing it improperly and without assembly? It is when, at the time the Prātimokṣa should be recited, it is not recited at that time; it is not recited by the one who should recite it; it is not recited in the manner in which it should be recited; it is not recited for as long as it should be recited; and the assembly has not gathered.

What is meant by assembling but doing so improperly? It is when, at the time the Prātimokṣa should be recited, it is not recited at that time — and so on in full through: it is not recited for as long as it should be recited — yet the assembly has gathered.

What is meant by assembled properly but without the proper procedure? It is when, at the time the Prātimokṣa should be recited, it is recited at that time; it is recited by the one who should recite it; it is recited in the manner in which it should be recited; it is recited for as long as it should be recited — yet the assembly has not gathered.

What is meant by assembled properly with the proper procedure? It is from the time the Prātimokṣa is recited at the proper time, recited through to completion for as long as it should be recited, all the way until the assembly has gathered.

"Venerable one, if a noble one recites the Prātimokṣa in the noble language, and those monks do not understand the noble language, may it be said that they have performed the restoration ceremony?" "Upāli, it may not. The recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra, too, will be bound up with transgression."

"If a borderlander recites the Prātimokṣa in the border language, and those monks do not understand the border language, may it be said that they have performed the restoration ceremony?" "Upāli, it may not. The recitation of the Prātimokṣa, too, will be bound up with transgression."

"If a noble one recites the Prātimokṣa in the border language, and those monks do not understand the border language, may it be said that they have performed the restoration ceremony?" "Upāli, it may be said that they have. The recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra, too, will be bound up with transgression."

"If a borderlander recites the Prātimokṣa sūtra in the border language, and those monks do not understand the border language, may it be said that they have performed the restoration ceremony?" "Upāli, it may not be said that they have. The recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra, too, will be bound up with transgression."

"Venerable one, if the number of those dwelling on the ground is made up by those dwelling in the sky, and they recite the Prātimokṣa sūtra, may it be said that they have performed the restoration ceremony?" "Upāli, it may not. Those monks, too, will be bound up with transgression."

"Venerable one, if the number of those dwelling in the sky is made up by those dwelling on the ground, and they recite the Prātimokṣa sūtra, may it be said that they have performed the restoration ceremony?" "Upāli, it may not. Those monks, too, will be bound up with transgression."

"Venerable one, if one dwelling in the sky recites the Prātimokṣa sūtra and performs the restoration ceremony for those dwelling on the ground, may it be said that they have performed the restoration ceremony?" "Upāli, it may not. Those members of the Saṅgha, too, will be bound up with transgression."

"Venerable one, if one dwelling on the ground recites the Prātimokṣa sūtra and performs the restoration ceremony for those dwelling in the sky, may it be said that they have performed the restoration ceremony?" "Upāli, it may not. Those monks, too, will be bound up with transgression."

In the same way, the four cases of those who sit inside the boundary and those who sit outside the boundary should be elaborated in full.

"Venerable one, in how many ways may the Prātimokṣa be recited?" "Upāli, in five ways. The first way of reciting the Prātimokṣa sūtra is this: a request is made, the occasion is recited, and then it is announced that the remainder has been heard. The second way of reciting the Prātimokṣa sūtra is this: a request is made, the occasion is recited, the four defeats are recited, and then it is announced that the remainder has been heard. The third way of reciting the Prātimokṣa sūtra is this: a request is made, the occasion is recited, the four defeats are recited, the thirteen remainders of the Saṅgha are recited, and then it is announced that the remainder has been heard. The fourth way of reciting the Prātimokṣa sūtra is this: a request is made, the occasion is recited, the four defeats, the thirteen remainders of the Saṅgha, and —

the two indeterminate offenses are recited, and then it is announced that the remainder has been heard. This is the fourth way of reciting the Prātimokṣa sūtra. Together with the full recitation, these make five.

Venerable one, in how many ways is the act of the restoration ceremony performed? Upāli, there are five: by recitation, by mental resolve without recitation, by consecration, by complete purity, and by the opening of a boundary. These are the five ways.

Venerable one, if, while a monk is reciting the Prātimokṣa sūtra, night should fall during the recitation, may one say that the restoration ceremony has been performed? Upāli, one should say it has been performed.

Venerable one, if monks who are assembled in one direction recite the Prātimokṣa sūtra in four separate groups and also perform the restoration ceremony, may those monks be said to have performed it without transgression? Upāli, yes. In such a case, the monk who is reciting the Prātimokṣa sūtra presses down a stick, a piece of cane, or a key at the boundary at which he stands, and thus recites the Prātimokṣa sūtra.

Venerable one, if monks who share a single boundary perform the restoration ceremony separately in four directions within that single boundary, may the ceremony be said to have been performed and may those monks be said to have done so without transgression? Upāli, yes. They have granted consent to one another.

Venerable one, if a monk who is reciting the Prātimokṣa sūtra is present on one side, and some monks are residing within the boundary while others are residing beyond the boundary, and the Prātimokṣa is recited for them, may the ceremony be said to have been performed and may those monks be said to have done so without transgression? Upāli, yes. In such a case, the monk reciting the Prātimokṣa sūtra presses down and marks the boundary, and while standing or sitting at the boundary line, he recites the Prātimokṣa sūtra for those who are both within and outside the boundary.

Venerable one, among the five ways of reciting the Prātimokṣa sūtra, may the restoration ceremony be considered performed even without any one of the five methods of recitation being recited? Upāli, yes. When the boundary is opened, it is opened by the opening of the boundary.

Venerable one, may the restoration ceremony be considered performed even without a word being spoken? Upāli, yes. By mental resolve alone.

Venerable one, if you were to say that the assembly has not risen and that the monks have not departed, what is the measure by which one would say the assembly has not risen? Upāli, wherever four or more monks are seated, that is called not having risen. If fewer than four are present, it is called having risen.

Venerable one, if a monk, having recited the Prātimokṣa sūtra, rises from his seat and departs, and even though monks are still present does not take leave of them, will he necessarily have committed a general transgression? Upāli, not necessarily. If he has gone to a place for the purpose of relieving himself, and has not gone beyond the range of hearing from that place, he has not transgressed.

If a layman recites the Prātimokṣa sūtra and the restoration ceremony is performed, may it be said that the restoration ceremony has been duly performed? Upāli, it should be said that the restoration ceremony has not been performed, and the Saṅgha has transgressed along with it.

Likewise, if a eunuch performs it, or a paṇḍaka, or one who has been expelled from the order of nuns, or one who is not abiding in it, or one who is residing separately, or one who has gone to dwell elsewhere — up to and including one who previously was in conflict — in all such cases, Upāli, it should be said that the restoration ceremony has not been performed, and the Saṅgha has transgressed along with it.

Venerable one, if those who have created a schism in the Saṅgha, those who have taken one side, or those who have been given a disciplinary training measure, recite the Prātimokṣa sūtra and perform the restoration ceremony, may it be said that it has been performed? Upāli, it should be said that it has been performed, and the Saṅgha has not transgressed.

Venerable one, if a mad person recites the Prātimokṣa sūtra and the restoration ceremony is performed, may it be said that the restoration ceremony has been performed? Upāli, it should be said that it has been performed, and the Saṅgha has not transgressed.

Venerable one, similarly, if one whose mind is disturbed, or one tormented by illness —

If a person with paralysis recites the Prātimokṣa sūtra and the restoration ceremony is performed, may it be said that the restoration ceremony has been performed? It should be said that it has been performed, and the Saṅgha has not transgressed. Just as it is with the recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra, so too the extensive forms of restoration are to be applied in the same way.

In brief:

What has not been offered, the Saṅgha,
The fourth and the second designated,
Transmitted from one to another,
Given, the path, and likewise the many.

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: Venerable one, if a monk, having taken up faith and complete purity, travels beyond reach of the sky above and arrives on the other side of a boundary, may it be said that faith and complete purity have not been offered? Upāli, it should be said that they have not been offered.

Venerable one, but if one travels there with hope, may it be said that faith and complete purity have not been offered? Upāli, no, it may not be so said.

Venerable one, is it permissible for one standing on the ground to give faith and complete purity to those who are stationed in the sky? Upāli, it is not permissible. Is it permissible to receive it? Upāli, it is not permissible.

Venerable one, is it permissible for one stationed in the sky to give faith and complete purity to those standing on the ground? Upāli, it is not permissible. Is it permissible to receive it? Upāli, it is not permissible.

Similarly, regarding one who is inside a boundary and one who is outside a boundary, these four cases apply in the same way.

Venerable one, if a monk offers faith and complete purity to the entire Saṅgha assembled and gathered together, may it be said that faith and complete purity have been offered? Upāli, it should be said that they have been offered. Who might be harmed by this? No one at all.

Venerable one, if a noble monk offers faith and complete purity in the noble language, and the receiving monk does not understand the noble language, may it be said that faith and complete purity have been offered? Upāli, no. If a noble monk offers faith and complete purity in a border language, and the receiving monk does not understand the border language, may it be said that faith and complete purity have been offered? Upāli, no. If a border person offers faith and complete purity in a border language, and the receiving monk does not understand the border language, may it be said that faith and complete purity have been offered? Upāli, no. If a border person offers faith and complete purity in the noble language, and the receiving monk does not understand the noble language, may it be said that faith and complete purity have been offered? Upāli, no.

Venerable one, if a monk indicates it through a physical gesture without uttering a word, may it be said that faith and complete purity have been offered? Upāli, it should be said that they have been offered. If it is expressed verbally without any physical gesture, may it be said that faith and complete purity have been offered? Upāli, it should be said that they have been offered. If it is expressed by both body and speech, may it be said that faith and complete purity have been offered? Upāli, it should be said that they have been offered. If it is expressed by neither body nor speech, may it be said that faith and complete purity have been offered? Upāli, no.

Venerable one, if the monk who is to receive faith and complete purity from the one giving them changes his name in the interval, may it be said that it has not been offered? Upāli, no.

Venerable one, if faith and complete purity are offered by transmission from one to another, may it be said that faith and complete purity have been offered? Upāli, it should be said that they have been offered, and those monks have not transgressed.

Venerable one, if faith and complete purity are offered by one who is under a suspension that has lapsed, may it be said that faith and complete purity have been offered? Upāli, it should be said that they have been offered, and those monks have not transgressed.

Venerable one, if a monk, having offered faith and complete purity, then declares himself a layman, may it be said that the offering has been made?

Upāli, it should be said that they have not been offered. Likewise, in full detail, from declaring oneself a pandaka up through declaring oneself previously in a state of conflict — in all those cases, may it be said that faith and complete purity have not been offered? Upāli, it should be said that they have not been offered.

Venerable one, if a monk, having offered faith and complete purity, then declares himself a eunuch, may it be said that faith and complete purity have not been offered? Upāli, it should be said that they have not been offered.
