If those who have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, who have taken sides, or who have relinquished the training declare this, may it be said that faith and complete purity have not been offered? Upāli, it should not be said so.

Venerable one, if a monk, having received faith and complete purity, then declares himself a layman, may it be said that faith and complete purity have not been offered? Upāli, it should be said that they have not been offered. Likewise, in full detail, from declaring oneself a pandaka up through declaring oneself previously in a state of conflict — in all those cases, may it be said that faith and complete purity have not been offered? Upāli, it should be said that they have not been offered.

Venerable one, if a monk, having received faith and complete purity, declares himself a eunuch, a layman, one who has departed, or one who dwells apart — may it be said that faith and complete purity have not been offered? Upāli, it should be said that they have not been offered.

Venerable one, if a monk, having received faith and complete purity, declares himself one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has taken sides, or one who has relinquished the training — may it be said that faith and complete purity have not been offered? Upāli, it should not be said so.

Venerable one, if a monk, having received faith and complete purity, enters the midst of the Saṅgha and then declares himself a layman — may it be said that faith and complete purity have not been offered? Upāli, it should be said that they have been offered. Likewise, from a pandaka up through declaring oneself previously in a state of conflict — in all those cases, may it be said that faith and complete purity have not been offered? Upāli, it should be said that they have been offered.

Venerable one, if a monk, having received faith and complete purity and entered into the midst of the Saṅgha, then declares himself a eunuch — may it be said that faith and complete purity have not been offered? Upāli, it should not be said so. Likewise, one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has departed, one who dwells apart, one who has taken sides, and one who has relinquished the training — if any of these declares this, venerable one, may it be said that faith and complete purity have not been offered? Upāli, it should not be said so.

This completes the substance of the restoration ceremony.

The Noble Vinaya. The seventeenth fascicle.

In brief: the fourth type with its four aspects, and the two kinds of substance, likewise; mindfulness, walking and refraining, sitting and standing as marks; laymen and the like; the mad, and the enumeration of the suspended.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable one, the act of opening an opportunity has many aspects. How many, Upāli? Four: opening an opportunity in a non-Dharmic way without a quorum; assembling in a non-Dharmic way; not assembling in a Dharmic way; and assembling in a Dharmic way.

What is opening an opportunity in a non-Dharmic way? It is when one does not open the opportunity at the time it should be opened; does not open it in the manner in which it should be opened; does not open it to the extent to which it should be opened; and is not opened by the one by whom it should be opened — and a quorum has not been formed.

What is assembling in a non-Dharmic way? In full detail, from not opening it at the time it should be opened up through not being opened by the one by whom it should be opened — stated in full — and a quorum has been formed.

What is not assembling in a Dharmic way? It is when one does open the opportunity at the time it should be opened, and

opens it in the manner in which it should be opened; opens it to the extent to which it should be opened; and is opened by the one by whom it should be opened — and a quorum has been formed.

What is assembling in a Dharmic way? It is when one opens the opportunity at the time it should be opened, from that point all the way through to being opened by the one by whom it should be opened — stated in full — and a quorum has also been formed.

Venerable one, if a noble one (ārya) opens the opportunity in the noble language, and those monks do not understand the noble language, should we say that the opportunity has been opened? Upāli, it is said that the opportunity has not been opened, and those monks too have committed a transgression.

If a noble one opens the opportunity in a border dialect, and those monks do not understand the border dialect, should we say that the opportunity has been opened? Upāli, it is said that the opportunity has not been opened, and those monks too have committed a transgression.

If a border person opens the opportunity in a border dialect, and those monks do not understand the border dialect, should we say that the opportunity has been opened? Upāli, it is said that the opportunity has not been opened, and those monks too have committed a transgression.

If a border person opens the opportunity in the noble language, and those monks do not understand the noble language, should we say that the opportunity has been opened? Upāli, it is said that the opportunity has not been opened, and those monks too have committed a transgression.

Venerable one, if the number of those present on the ground is completed by those dwelling in the sky, and the opportunity is opened, should we say that the opportunity has been opened? Upāli, it is said that the opportunity has not been opened, and those monks too have committed a transgression.

Venerable one, if the number of those present in the sky is completed by those dwelling on the ground, and the opportunity is opened, should we say that the opportunity has been opened? Upāli, it is said that the opportunity has not been opened, and those monks too have committed a transgression.

Venerable one, if those dwelling on the ground open the opportunity to those dwelling in the sky, should we say that the opportunity has been opened? Upāli, it is said that the opportunity has not been opened, and those monks too have committed a transgression.

Venerable one, if those dwelling in the sky open the opportunity to those dwelling on the ground, should we say that the opportunity has been opened? Upāli, it is said that the opportunity has not been opened, and those monks too have committed a transgression.

In the same way, those situated within the boundary and those situated outside the boundary together make four cases to be treated accordingly.

Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that at the time one opens the opportunity, the act itself exists, but the person does not. Venerable one, what then is the act, and what is the person? The transgression is the act. The one who commits the transgression is called the person.

Venerable one, can the opportunity be opened without any words being spoken? Upāli, yes it can. In such a case, the monk opens the opportunity by means of a letter or a hand signal.

Venerable one, if a monk stands off to one side and opens the opportunity to those in the four directions, does the opportunity thereby become opened? Upāli, yes. In such a case, that monk who opens the opportunity presses a stick or a key at the boundary-point of the four directions and thereby opens the opportunity.

Venerable one, if monks who share a single dwelling and a single boundary open the opportunity in the four directions, can it come about that the opportunity is opened and yet those communities have not assembled? Upāli, yes — when each has granted consent to the other.

Venerable one, if the entire Saṅgha recalls at dawn having already opened the opportunity, how should the monks proceed with the opening? They should say the words: "We are now opening the opportunity." Alternatively, if the opportunity is opened with the third utterance, it is said to be opened, and those monks have committed a transgression.

Venerable one, if the Blessed One declared, "Open the opportunity during the rains retreat for the sake of relatives,"

Venerable one, by what means should it be granted? Upāli: to one who dwells at a distance and cannot come at the time of opening the opportunity.

Venerable one, if a monk, having opened the opportunity during the rains retreat for the sake of relatives and having gone with the blessing for seven days or forty days, returns at the very moment of the fifteenth-day opening of the opportunity — should he also open the opportunity then? Upāli: No. The opening that was already performed is sufficient for him.

Venerable one, if a monk who is to open the opportunity has abandoned his vows on the very day of the fifteenth, should the opportunity be opened together with him? Upāli: No.

Venerable one, the Blessed One declared, "The retinue of monks has not risen, has not departed." Venerable one, how many does it take for the retinue to be considered as not having risen? Upāli: wherever four monks, or five, or more than that are seated, it is called "not having risen." If fewer than four, it is called "having risen."

Venerable one, if on that very fifteenth day one rises from one's seat and departs without seeking out the monks who are present — is there no transgression in that? Upāli: There is none, provided one has gone to relieve oneself and has not gone beyond earshot of those who have heard.

Venerable one, if someone is in the process of opening the opportunity and during the opening of the opportunity the night passes and he has become a nun and then opens the opportunity — is it considered opened? Upāli: It is considered opened.

Venerable one, if a layperson opens the opportunity, is it considered opened? Upāli: It is not considered opened, and the Saṅgha too has incurred a transgression.

Likewise, if it is opened by a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, an unsettled person, or one who has gone to dwell elsewhere — all the way through, in detail, to those who were previously in dispute — it is not considered opened, and those Saṅghas too have incurred a transgression.

Venerable one, if the opportunity is opened by one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, or who has taken sides in a schism, or who has been given a training — is it considered opened? Upāli: It is considered opened, but the Saṅgha has incurred a transgression.

Venerable one, if a madman opens the opportunity, is it considered opened? Upāli: It is considered opened, and the Saṅgha has incurred a transgression. Likewise, if the opportunity is opened by one who is mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, an imbecile, a mute, or one who is deaf — is it considered opened? Upāli: It is considered opened, and the Saṅgha has incurred a transgression.

Venerable one, if the opportunity is opened by messenger, is it considered opened? Upāli: It is considered opened, and the Saṅgha has incurred a transgression. Likewise, if opened by written message, by hand signal, or by transmission from one person to another — is it considered opened? Upāli: It is considered opened, and the Saṅgha has incurred a transgression.

Venerable one, if it is opened with the words "Another says so" — is it considered opened? Upāli: No.

Venerable one, if a layperson completes the number and opens the opportunity — is it considered opened? Upāli: It is not considered opened, and the Saṅgha has incurred a transgression. Likewise, the same should be applied to a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, an unsettled person, one dwelling separately, and one who has gone to dwell elsewhere, all the way through to those who were previously in dispute.

Venerable one, if those who have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, or who have taken sides, or who have been given a training, complete the number and open the opportunity — is it considered opened? Upāli: It is considered opened, and the Saṅgha has incurred a transgression.

Venerable one, likewise if those who are mentally disturbed, afflicted by illness, an imbecile, a mute, a deaf person, one who is asleep, one who is intoxicated, one who is rambling in speech, one who has entered meditative absorption, or one who has gone to dwell elsewhere, complete the number and open the opportunity — is it considered opened? Upāli: It is not considered opened —

— and the Saṅgha has incurred a transgression.

In brief:

The offering and the acceptance, the Saṅgha,
The fourth and the second, the boundary sign,
Penalty and expulsion, one to another,
The path and the many — likewise so.

Venerable one, if a monk takes the consent and the opening of the opportunity and, going to the sky above, arrives beyond the boundary without there being any expectation — is it said that the consent and the opening of the opportunity have not been offered? Upāli: It is said they have not been offered.

Venerable one, but if one arrives with expectation — is it said they have not been offered? Upāli: Not so; it will count as having transgressed.

Venerable one, is it permissible for those dwelling on the ground to offer consent and the opening of the opportunity to those dwelling in the sky? Upāli: It is not. Venerable one, is it permissible to accept it? Upāli: It is not.

Venerable one, is it permissible for those dwelling in the sky to offer consent and the opening of the opportunity to those dwelling on the ground? Upāli: It is not.

Likewise, those assembled within the boundary and those assembled outside the boundary are also to be stated in four ways.

Venerable one, if a monk, when the entire Saṅgha has assembled and gathered, offers consent and the opening of the opportunity — is it said that consent and the opening of the opportunity have been offered? Upāli: It is said they have been offered. By whom should it be proclaimed? By no one in particular.

Venerable one, if a noble monk offers consent and the opening of the opportunity in the noble language, but those monks have not sought it in the noble language — is it said that consent and the opening of the opportunity have been offered? Upāli: It is not.

If a noble monk offers consent and the opening of the opportunity in a border language, but those monks have not sought it in a border language — is it said they have been offered? Upāli: It is not.

Venerable one, if a border monk offers consent and the opening of the opportunity in a border language, but those monks have not sought it in a border language — is it said they have been offered? Upāli: It is not.

Venerable one, if a border monk offers consent and the opening of the opportunity in the noble language, but those monks have not sought it in the noble language — is it said they have been offered? Upāli: It is not.

Venerable one, if the monk who is offering consent and the opening of the opportunity indicates it by body but not by speech — is it said that consent and the opening of the opportunity have been offered? Upāli: It is said they have been offered. Likewise, if by speech but not by body — is it said they have been offered? Upāli: It is said they have been offered. And if indicated by both speech and body — is it said they have been offered? Upāli: It is said they have been offered.

Venerable one, but if not indicated by body and not spoken by speech — is it said that consent and the opening of the opportunity have been offered? Upāli: It is not.

Venerable one, if the monk who is offering consent and the opening of the opportunity falls asleep during the night — is it said they have been offered? Upāli: It is not.

Venerable one, if consent and the opening of the opportunity are offered by one who has incurred a penalty or been expelled — is it said they have been offered? Upāli: It is said they have been offered, but those monks have incurred a transgression.

Venerable one, if consent and the opening of the opportunity are conveyed by transmission from one to another — is it said they have been offered? Upāli: It is said they have been offered, but those monks have incurred a transgression.

If, after offering consent and the opening of the opportunity, one acknowledges oneself to be a layman — is it said that consent and the opening of the opportunity have not been offered? Upāli: It is said they have not been offered.

Likewise, if one acknowledges oneself to be a eunuch, and so forth up through acknowledging oneself to have previously been in a dispute — is it said that consent and the opening of the opportunity have not been offered? Upāli: It is said they have not been offered.

If, when a monk is offering consent and the opening of the opportunity, he acknowledges himself to be a eunuch — is it said that consent and the opening of the opportunity have not been offered? Upāli: It is said they have not been offered.

If one acknowledges oneself to have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, to be a partisan, or to have been given a training rule — is it said that consent and the opening of the opportunity have not been offered? Upāli: No, it is not.

If a monk who has received consent and the opening of the opportunity, having accepted them, enters into the midst of the Saṅgha and then acknowledges himself to be a layman — is it said that consent and the opening of the opportunity have not been offered? Upāli: It is not said that they have not been offered.

Likewise, if one acknowledges oneself to be a eunuch, and so forth up through acknowledging oneself to have previously been in a dispute — is it said that consent and the opening of the opportunity have not been offered? Upāli: It is not said that they have not been offered.

If one acknowledges oneself to be a eunuch — is it said that consent and the opening of the opportunity have not been offered? Upāli: No, it is not.

Likewise, from acknowledging that one has caused a schism in the Saṅgha up through acknowledging that one has been given a training rule — is it said that consent and the opening of the opportunity have not been offered? Upāli: No, it is not.

The subject of the opening of the opportunity is complete.

In brief:

A boat, the sky as a third, and the domain of movement with doubt arisen,
marks with a third, places, and the rains retreat as a third — or likewise so.

If a monk enters the rains retreat properly in a boat moored to a peg — is it said that he has entered properly? Upāli: It is said that he has entered properly.

If during the rains retreat the boat is sent off elsewhere — is it said that the rains retreat is broken? Upāli: No, it is not.

If a monk who has properly entered the rains retreat is granted the seven-day leave and travels beyond the boundary through the sky above — is it said that the rains retreat is broken, or that it is not broken? Upāli: It is said that it is not broken.

If a monk enters the rains retreat properly in the sky above — is it said that he has entered properly? Upāli: No, it is not.

If a monk enters the rains retreat properly in a palace suspended in the sky above — is it said that he has entered properly? Upāli: It is said that he has entered properly.

If he then departs from that palace to another dwelling — is it said that the rains retreat is broken? Upāli: No, it is not.

The Blessed One (the Buddha) said, "Enter the rains retreat in dependence on a domain of movement." If a monk enters the rains retreat properly without having a domain of movement — is it said that he has entered properly? Upāli: It is said that he has entered properly.

If a monk has entered the rains retreat in dependence on a domain of movement, may he then go from it to that domain of movement with the seven-day leave? Upāli: No, because he has entered the rains retreat in dependence on that very place.

If a monk, having entered the rains retreat, is in doubt and uncertainty as to whether he has entered properly or not — is it said that he has entered properly? Upāli: It is said that he has entered properly.

If he is unable to resolve that doubt and uncertainty, should he enter the rains retreat again? Upāli: He should enter again.

What then is the status of that rains retreat? Upāli: It is the earlier one.

If a monk sets his intention on dwelling in a certain place for the rains retreat, travels there, and when dawn breaks it has become the latter rains retreat period — is it said that he has entered the rains retreat properly? Upāli: It is said that he has entered properly, because he had the intention of entering properly there.

If a monk goes to a temple, thinks to himself "I shall enter the rains retreat here," and then places one foot inside the boundary —

— and one foot outside the boundary, and then dawn breaks and it has become the latter rains retreat period — is it said that he has entered the rains retreat properly? Upāli: It is said that he has entered properly, because he had the intention of entering properly there.

Venerable one, if a monk enters the rains retreat properly and night falls — is it said that he has entered properly? Upāli: It is said that he has entered properly. But should he remain in that very place? Upāli: No. He should go to the nuns' rains retreat quarters and remain there.

Venerable one, can it be that a monk enters the rains retreat properly in four residences and yet it counts as a proper entry? Upāli: Yes, it can. This is how: that monk pressed down the boundary-marker of four residences — whether a piece of wood, a slab of slate, or a key — and thereby entered the rains retreat properly. Where then should he reside? Wherever he pleases.

Venerable one, if that piece of wood, slate slab, or key becomes subject to destruction — is it said that his rains retreat is broken? Upāli: No. Where should he then reside for the rains retreat? In whichever single place he pleases. To which of those residences does his rains retreat belong? To whichever one his mind intended. As for the remaining ones, they are said to be relinquished.

Venerable one, if from that point on he goes to the second of those residences within the seven-day period without having received a blessing — is it said that his rains retreat is broken? Upāli: It is said that his rains retreat is broken.

Venerable one, if a monk makes four residences — or more than four — share a single boundary and then enters the rains retreat properly — is it said that he has entered the rains retreat properly in all those residences? Upāli: It is said that he has entered properly. Where should he then reside? Wherever he pleases.

Venerable one, if a monk enters the rains retreat properly in one residence and thereafter enters the rains retreat properly in a second, a third, and a fourth residence — is it said that he has entered properly? Upāli: It is said that he has entered properly. In which residence? The latter one.

Venerable one, if someone has neither an earlier nor a latter rains retreat — what is the term for that? Upāli: It is said that his rains retreat is broken.

Venerable one, if someone has both an earlier and a latter rains retreat, and yet, without having received a blessing for the seven-day period, goes beyond the boundary on some business with the intention of returning — is it said that his rains retreat is broken? Upāli: It is said that his rains retreat is broken. Can he then re-enter the rains retreat properly? Upāli: No. Since he has transgressed his commitment, let him be made to incur the penalty.

Venerable one, for how long does one enter the rains retreat? Upāli: Three months.

Venerable one, how does one who entered the rains retreat for the latter period properly conclude the retreat? Either by completing the count of three months from the time of entry, or else because some circumstance has arisen.

In brief:

At dawn, abandoning intention —
a residence, a carriage house, a home,
a tree, a cave, likewise;
even if broken, it is the same.
The five classes, and intention,
the seven, and not remaining.

Venerable one, if a dispute arises within the Saṅgha during the rains retreat, and a monk, while fully aware, takes the side of the Dharma or the side of what is not the Dharma — is it said that his rains retreat is broken? Upāli: If he aligns with a party that is still deliberating the matter and dawn then breaks, it is said that his rains retreat is broken.

Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said to a monk "Enter the rains retreat properly before me," and that monk then sets his intention and enters the rains retreat properly in the presence of a nun — is it said that he has entered the rains retreat properly? Upāli: It is said that he has entered properly. However, if a monk was present, then it counts as a transgression.

Venerable one, may one reside together with a monk who has been expelled from within the rains retreat during that same rains retreat? Upāli: One may reside with him, but only after the matter has been opened for deliberation. One should not remain without that.

Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said to a monk: "Enter the rains retreat properly in this place among monks who are sūtra-holders and who are like me — that is, monks of such a kind who neither generate doubts that have not yet arisen nor fail to remove doubts that have arisen — whether such a thing is possible or not," then, venerable one, is it permissible to enter the rains retreat in the absence of sūtra-holders and those who are like me? Upāli: It is permissible. Venerable one, is it permissible to enter the rains retreat in the absence of a Vinaya-holder? Upāli: It is not permissible. In that case, venerable one, if there is no Vinaya-holder, should one seek a monk who can recite the Prātimokṣa sūtra? If there is no one who can recite the Prātimokṣa, then it is not permitted to enter the rains retreat.

Venerable one, is it permissible to reside in a house where carriages pass or in a cowherd's house and there enter the rains retreat? Upāli: If one has resolved in one's mind that one will not depart from that rains retreat location, then it is permissible. Venerable one, if one departs from a place where the rains retreat has been properly entered, is it said that the rains retreat is broken? Upāli: It is not.

Venerable one, is it permissible to enter the rains retreat at the foot of a tree, or on a mountain slope, or in a cave, or in a makeshift shelter? Upāli: It is not permissible.

Venerable one, if a monk has gone out with a seven-day or forty-day permission for a particular purpose, and that time runs out — is it said that the seven-day or forty-day permission is broken? Upāli: It is not. Let it be exhausted by the other purpose.

Venerable one, if a monk has gone out with a seven-day permission, thinking "I will open a matter for deliberation," is it said that the rains retreat is broken? Upāli: It is said that the rains retreat is broken. Venerable one, if he has gone out with a six-day, five-day, four-day, or one-day permission, thinking "I will depart from the retreat by such-and-such means," is it said that the rains retreat is broken? Upāli: It is said that the rains retreat is broken.

Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said "Go with a seven-day permission," to whom should the permission be granted? Upāli: To the five groups. Where should the permission be granted? Within the boundary. How should the permission be granted? One should form the intention and speak the words: "I, of such-and-such a name, having properly entered the former rains retreat here in this place within the boundary, and having been granted permission to go beyond the boundary for such-and-such a purpose, I, of such-and-such a name — this is my rains retreat; I remain in this same rains retreat." For whose sake should the permission be granted? Upāli: For the sake of the seven groups.

Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said "Confer the forty-day vow," upon whom should it be conferred? Upāli: Upon the five groups. Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said "Give the forty-day vow for the sake of the Saṅgha," may the forty-day vow be conferred upon monks, nuns, female probationers, female novices, male novices, laywomen, laymen, those with family connections, and beyond these upon other non-Buddhist renunciants, brahmins, wanderers, and mendicants? Upāli: It is not permissible.

Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said "The instructions should be given for forty days," is it permissible to give the instructions for thirty-nine days, for thirty days, or for twenty days? Upāli: It is permissible. Venerable one, is it permissible to give the instructions for thirty-nine days, thirty days, twenty days, ten days, or seven days in addition to the forty days?

Upāli: It is not permissible. Venerable one, is it permissible to give the instructions for thirty days, twenty days, ten days, or seven days in addition to thirty-nine days? Upāli: It is not permissible. Venerable one, is it permissible to consecrate for seven days in addition to forty days? Upāli: It is not permissible. And why is that, Upāli? Within the boundary one should remain for more days; outside the boundary one should remain for fewer days. Venerable one, is it permissible to consecrate for seven days in addition to thirty-nine days? Upāli: It is not permissible. Venerable one, is it permissible to consecrate for seven days in addition to thirty days, twenty days, or seven days? Upāli: It is permissible. Venerable one, is it permissible to give the instructions for forty days in addition to seven days? Upāli: It is not permissible. And why is that, Upāli? Within the boundary one should remain for more days; outside the boundary one should remain for fewer days. Venerable one, is it permissible to give the instructions for thirty-nine days, thirty days, twenty days, ten days, or seven days in addition to seven days? Upāli: It is permissible. Venerable one, is it permissible to give the instructions for yet another seven days in addition to seven days? Upāli: It is permissible. Venerable one, if a monk has entered the rains retreat and his preceptor and abbot have passed away, and he then cannot find a place to reside, is he called one whose rains retreat has been broken? Upāli: He is called one whose rains retreat has been broken.

The substantive matters of the rains retreat are complete.

In brief:
Sandals of two kinds of leather,
bear-hide or those with a tail,
a high bed and a large bed,
sandals with an upper, and wooden sandals.

Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said "Do not keep the five kinds of impermissible sandals," are there also other wild animals, bad woollen oxen, bad horses, and the like, such that sandals made of their hides should also not be kept? Upāli: Those sandals too should not be kept. Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said "Accept sandals given by householders that have not had medicine applied to them," if a monk keeps sandals given by a householder that have had medicine applied to them, does he incur an offense? Upāli: He does. For instance, if the monk has kept ones that are entirely decorated with designs, or adorned with gold, or adorned with silver. Venerable one, are there cases where a monk keeps five impermissible kinds and yet does not incur an offense? Upāli: There are. For instance, if he is frightened by a small wild animal or by a nāga. Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said "A monk should not keep a hide; he should not sit on a hide," venerable one, how much contact with a hide counts as sitting on it? Upāli: As much as is settled by resting the buttocks upon it. Venerable one, how much contact counts as lying down? Upāli: As much as the body is stretched out upon it. Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said "A monk should not keep a hide," are there cases where a monk keeps a hide and yet does not incur an offense? Upāli: There are. One who is ill may keep a hide; one who is not ill may not. Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said "Bear-hide may be used," should only the sick keep it, or may the healthy also keep it? Upāli: Both the sick and the healthy may use it. If the Blessed One has said "Take five tail-hairs and use them as a ford-crosser," venerable one, if there are other four-footed animals, may one cross with those as well? Upāli: One may cross. Venerable one, if the male is not present, may one cross with the female? Upāli: If an obstacle has arisen, one may cross with that. Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said "A monk should not sit on a high bed," what is the measure of a high bed?

A high bed is one that exceeds eight finger-breadths of the Sugata's measure. Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said to the monks "Do not sit on a bed that is both high and large," are there cases in which a monk may sit on a bed that is both high and large without incurring a transgression? Upāli: There are. When there is no other seat available in the dwelling of a god (deva), the dwelling of a nāga, the dwelling of a yakṣa, the dwelling of a king, or the dwelling of a minister.

Venerable one, are there cases in which a monk's mounting a vehicle would result in three transgressions? Upāli: There are. Namely, when the vehicle is female, and when it is adorned with gold.

Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said "In a snowy region, wear boots," are there cases in which a monk may keep boots even in a region other than that without incurring a transgression? Upāli: There are. In a place where one cannot survive without boots.

Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said "Monks should not keep wooden sandals," are there cases in which a monk may keep wooden sandals without incurring a transgression? Upāli: There are. In a place where there is water and the ground is flooded, so that one cannot travel without wooden sandals.

The section on leather goods is complete.

In brief:

Two medicines, two kinds of salt,
two kinds of butter — likewise so.
Raw and cooked, and molasses,
grain-oil is the last that profits.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: Venerable one, can that very same medicine be a morning medicine, that same one an afternoon medicine, that same one a seven-day medicine, and that same one a medicine to be kept for the duration of one's life? Upāli: There can be. Sugar-cane is for the morning. Its juice is for the afternoon. Molasses is for seven days. Burnt ash is for the duration of one's life.

Upāli: Curd is for the morning. Water is for the afternoon. Butter is for seven days. Burnt ash is for the duration of one's life.

Upāli: Meat is for the morning. Fat is for seven days. Burnt ash is for the duration of one's life.

Upāli: Grain is for the morning. Grain-oil is for seven days. Burnt ash is for the duration of one's life.

Venerable one, if the morning medicines, the afternoon medicines, the seven-day medicines, and the lifetime medicines are mixed together, may they be consumed? Upāli: They may not.

Venerable one, may medicines that have been taken up but not yet received as a gift, or that have been taken up and received as a gift, or that have been stored inside, or that have been cooked inside, or that one has cooked oneself — may these be consumed? Upāli: They may not.

Venerable one, if a monk consumes whatever morning, afternoon, seven-day, or lifetime medicines he has taken up but not received as a gift, or taken up and received as a gift, or stored inside, or cooked inside, or cooked himself, or cooked by a monk — what does that become? It becomes a wrongdoing.

Venerable one, if a nun consumes whatever morning, afternoon, seven-day, or lifetime medicines she has taken up but not received as a gift, or taken up and received as a gift, or stored inside, or cooked inside, or cooked herself, or cooked by a nun — what does that become? It becomes a wrongdoing.

Venerable one, if a monk has taken up medicines and received them as a gift, or stored them inside, or cooked them inside, or cooked them himself, or had them cooked by a monk, and while consuming them he changes his ordination status and becomes a nun — what does that become? It becomes a wrongdoing.

Venerable one, if a nun has taken up medicines and received them as a gift, or stored them inside, or cooked them inside,

cooked herself, or had them cooked by a nun — and while consuming them she changes her ordination status and becomes a monk: what does that become? It becomes a wrongdoing.

Venerable one, with respect to medicines that are suitable for the morning period, those that are suitable for the afternoon period, those that are suitable for seven days, and those that are suitable for life — if these are mixed together and not separated, may those mixed medicines be consecrated for use throughout one's lifetime? Upāli: That is not permissible. The morning-suitable, afternoon-suitable, and seven-day-suitable medicines cannot be put to the purpose of medicines for life, and they cannot be consecrated as such.

However, if one is able to separate out those morning-suitable, afternoon-suitable, and seven-day-suitable medicines, then consecration is permissible.

Venerable one, may one consume salt cooked on an impermissible day? Upāli: The sick may not eat it.

What of food cooked with meat, or cooked with butter, or cooked with oil? The same applies.

Venerable one, may one consume grain-oil or butter cooked with impermissible salt? Upāli: That is not permissible.

Venerable one, may one consume butter or grain-oil cooked together with beer? Upāli: That may be eaten.

Venerable one, may one consume butter or grain-oil that has become mixed together with beer? Upāli: That is not permissible.

Venerable one, may one consume medicine that has been rejected by reason of beer? Upāli: For the sick it is permissible; for those who are not sick it is not.

Venerable one, if a tree has grown in an impermissible place and a fruit falls in an impermissible place, may that fruit be consumed? Upāli: That is not permissible.

If a tree has grown in an impermissible place and a fruit falls in a permissible place, may that fruit be consumed? Upāli: That is not permissible.

If a tree has grown in a permissible place and a fruit falls in an impermissible place, may that fruit be consumed? If it has not yet been there for a full day, it may be eaten.

If a tree has grown in a permissible place and a fruit falls in a permissible place, may that fruit be consumed? Upāli: That may be eaten.

Venerable one, if a tree is rooted in permissible ground and it leans over impermissible ground — if one in impermissible ground grafts it, or grafts a branch, or by cutting a branch renders it permissible, can one say "it has been rendered permissible," or say "it has been done," or consume it? Upāli: That is not permissible.

Venerable one, if a tree is rooted in permissible ground and one who is in impermissible ground causes it to be grafted — can one say "it is permissible," or say "it has been done," or consume it? Upāli: That is not.

If a tree is rooted in impermissible ground and one who is in permissible ground grafts it, or grafts a branch, or by cutting a branch renders it permissible — can one say "it has been rendered permissible"? Upāli: One may say "it has been rendered permissible," and it may be eaten.

If a tree is rooted in impermissible ground and one who is in permissible ground causes it to be grafted — can one say "it has been rendered permissible"? One may say "it has been rendered permissible." May it be consumed? Upāli: It may be eaten.

Venerable one, if three stumps are in impermissible ground and a grafting branch from a tree that is in permissible ground bridges them — may that be consumed? Upāli: That is not permissible.

Venerable one, if a tree is rooted in impermissible ground and two stumps are in permissible ground and one stump is in impermissible ground, and a grafting branch bridges them — may that be consumed? Upāli: That is not permissible.

Venerable one, if one stump is in impermissible ground and a tree is rooted in permissible ground and its grafting branch bridges them — may that be consumed? Upāli: That is not permissible.

Venerable one, if a tree is rooted in permissible ground and two stumps are in permissible ground and one stump is in impermissible ground, and a grafting branch bridges them — may that be consumed? Upāli: That may be eaten.

If three stumps are in permissible ground and a tree is rooted in permissible ground, and a grafting branch bridges them — may that be consumed? Upāli: That is permissible.

Venerable one, if a monk renders any of the five classes of seeds permissible — by piercing, cutting, or scratching with a fingernail — may one say "it has been made permissible," or "it is permissible"? And having been made permissible, may it be eaten? Upāli: It may be eaten. All except those made permissible by fire may be eaten.

Venerable one, the Blessed One declared, "Drink these eight kinds of drink." Are roots, trunks, leaves, fruits, and those mixed with something strained — are these permissible to receive? Upāli: They are permissible.

Venerable one, may sugar-cane water consecrated seven times by sky be received? Upāli: It is permissible. For how long may it be drunk? Until it has transformed into something else.

Venerable one, may a medicine that is impermissible be had dissolved in sugar-cane water? Upāli: No.

Venerable one, how should one attend upon a sick person? One should attend upon them with the attitude of a teacher, with medicines that are beneficial and appropriate.

Venerable one, what should one give to a sick person? Upāli: Except for what is intrinsically blameworthy, give whatever will bring about the recovery of the sick person.

In summary:
The owl, the vulture, and the crow,
the heron, the kite, the cormorant —
birds that eat human corpses,
and those possessed of powerful claws and beaks.

Venerable one, may the flesh of an owl be received? Upāli: It is not permissible. May the flesh of a vulture, the flesh of a crow, the flesh of a heron, the flesh of a kite, the flesh of a cormorant, and likewise other carrion-eating birds, and the flesh of those possessed of powerful claws and beaks — may these be received? Upāli: They are not permissible.

In summary:
Animals with stripes, flesh and lotus,
insects and frogs likewise —
the mongoose, the snake, the monitor lizard,
the white frog, the she-donkey, the otter.

Venerable one, may the flesh of a striped animal be received? Upāli: It is not permissible. Venerable one, may the flesh of a lotus-dweller, the flesh of a frog, the flesh of a mongoose, the flesh of a snake, the flesh of a monitor lizard, the flesh of a white frog, the flesh of an otter, the flesh of a crow, and likewise those that dwell in water, those possessed of powerful claws and fangs, and other carrion-eaters — may the flesh of these be received? Upāli: They are not permissible.

In summary:
The yak, the fox, and the horse,
the monkey and the human likewise —
the lion, the tiger, and the bear,
and those possessed of powerful claws and fangs.

Venerable one, may the flesh of a yak be received? Upāli: It is not permissible. Venerable one, may the flesh of a horse, the flesh of a fox, the flesh of a monkey, the flesh of a human, the flesh of a lion, the flesh of a tiger, the flesh of a bear, and likewise other four-footed animals possessed of powerful claws and fangs — may the flesh of these be received? Upāli: They are not permissible.

Venerable one, as for that whose flesh is not permissible — may its fat and its milk be received? Upāli: They are not permissible. Upāli, why is that? Upāli: All that pertains to one whose flesh is impermissible is likewise impermissible.

Venerable one, may raw flesh be received? Upāli: It is not permissible. May the flesh of one slain on one's own behalf be received? Upāli: It is not permissible.

The section on medicinal substances is complete.

The Noble Vinaya, the eighteenth chapter.

In summary:
The place where the rains retreat is divided in two,
the two of gain and the Saṅgha —
the madman, the suspension, these three —
the preparation, the many guests during the rains.

Venerable one, a householder approaches one who has entered the rains retreat properly and says, "I offer this Dharma robe." If a Dharma robe is offered to those observing the rains retreat, but the final month of the rains retreat has not yet come and no resolution has been set — who receives it? Upāli: Those observing the rains retreat receive it.

Venerable one, a householder approaches and says, "I offer this Dharma robe to those who have entered the rains retreat properly." If it is offered to the Saṅgha who have entered the rains retreat properly, and the final month of the rains has arrived and a resolution has been set at that place — who receives it?

Those observing the rains retreat receive it.

Venerable one, a householder approaches the Saṅgha and says, "I offer this Dharma robe to whatever monks are residing here at this place." If a robe is offered in this way, who receives it? Whoever it was given to receives it. And likewise for the second, and expanding in the same way from the third up through the tenth — if offered to those monks, who receives it? Whoever it was given to receives it.

Venerable one, a householder offers a robe to the Saṅgha and says, "I offer this robe to the monks who will be residing here at this place tomorrow." Who receives it? Whoever it was given to receives it. And likewise from the second up through monks residing for ten years — if he says, "I offer it to those who have resided here," who receives it? Whoever it was given to receives it. But if it happens that those monks are no longer residing at that place, may those monks divide those robes? Upāli: They should divide them.

Venerable one, if the Saṅgha separates during the rains retreat, should those gains of the rains retreat be given out? Upāli: No. Venerable one, if the Saṅgha separates from those who have resided long at the rains retreat residence, should those gains of the rains retreat be given out? Give them. To whom? To both sides equally.

Venerable one, if during the rains retreat a monk goes out seeking a bowl and Dharma robe, should the gains of that rains retreat be given to him? Upāli: No. Venerable one, if he has resided long at the rains retreat residence, should the gains of the rains retreat be given to him? Upāli: Give them. To whom? To whoever the gift was dedicated or assigned.

Venerable one, if during the rains retreat a monk passes away, should the gains of that rains retreat be given to him? Do not give them. If he has resided long at the rains retreat residence and then passes away after his time, should the gains of the rains retreat be given? Upāli: Give them. To whom? To whoever it was dedicated. But if it was not dedicated to anyone, to whom should it be given? To the Saṅgha.

Venerable one, if during the rains retreat a monk acknowledges having been a novice's father — should he receive the gains of the rains retreat? He should be given them. How much should be given to him? A novice-father's share. If he has resided long at the rains retreat residence and then acknowledges having been a novice's father, how much should be given? A monk's full share.

Venerable one, if during the rains retreat a monk acknowledges having been a layman — should he receive the gains of the rains retreat? He should not be given them. If he has resided long at the rains retreat residence and then acknowledges having been a layman, should he receive the gains of the rains retreat? Give them. To whom? To whoever it was dedicated.

Venerable one, if during the rains retreat a monk acknowledges having been a eunuch, or having expelled a nun, or having killed his father, or having killed his mother, or having killed an arhat, or having created a schism in the Saṅgha, or having drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent, or having been a non-Buddhist, or having gone over to non-Buddhists, or having been a thief who entered the order under false pretenses, or having previously committed an offense, or having previously been a troublemaker — should those persons receive the gains of the rains retreat? Upāli: They should not be given them.

Venerable one, if someone who has resided long at the rains retreat residence then comes to full understanding — should he receive the gains of the rains retreat? Upāli: He should be given them.

Venerable one, if during the rains retreat a monk acknowledges having been a nun, or having been non-resident, or having dwelt separately, or having sided with one party, or having relinquished the training — should those persons receive the gains of the rains retreat? Upāli: They should not be given them.

Venerable one, if monks have resided long at the rains retreat residence, or have resided through the full rains period — if they acknowledge this, should those persons receive the gains of the rains retreat? Upāli: They should be given them.

Venerable one, can there be a case where a monk appropriates robe-cloth from any of the four residences without thereby incurring an offense? Upāli: There can. This is the case where that monk, having made all four residences into a single boundary, then entered the rains retreat in proper form.

Venerable one, by what measure does one speak of a monk having obtained robe-cloth? Upāli: It is like this: thinking "this is my robe-cloth," it has come into view with the eye, or has been placed in one's hand, on one's shoulder, or in one's lap.

Venerable one, can there be a case where a single monk appropriates the gains of the Saṅgha without thereby incurring an offense? Upāli: There can. This is the case where that monk was residing alone, and people offered robes there on behalf of the Saṅgha.

Venerable one, can there be a case where a monk who has received an allocation of the Saṅgha's gains appropriates them and thereby incurs an offense? Upāli: There can. When those gains had been dedicated to the Saṅgha.

Venerable one, may a monk who has gone mad be appointed to distribute robe-cloth? Upāli: No. One whose mind is disturbed, one oppressed by illness, one who is mentally deficient, one who is mute, and one who is deaf — these are likewise.

Venerable one, may a blind monk be appointed to distribute robe-cloth? Upāli: No.

Venerable one, from when are the robes of a mad monk to be held and dedicated? Up until the time when his own mind is restored.

Venerable one, should robes be received from a mad monk, or should they not? From some they should be received; from others they should not. From whom should they be received? From one who has a living father, mother, brother, or sister, or who has made a gift from his own home and with the intention of relinquishing it.

Venerable one, should the gains of the rains retreat be given to one who has broken the rains retreat? To some they should be given; to others they should not. To whom should they not be given? To one who is known to have neither the manner of the earlier rains period nor the manner of the later rains period. To whom should they be given? To one who is known to have the manner of the earlier rains period and also of the later.

Venerable one, if a nurse sent out an attendant to assist another, and the patient then passed away — to which nurse should the robe be given? To the latter one.

Venerable one, if a nurse who has gone beyond the boundary for a reason returns, and the patient then passes away — should that nurse be given the robe? If the nurse went for the sake of the patient, that nurse should be given the robe. But if the nurse went for some other purpose, the robe should not be given.

Venerable one, if a nurse entered the rains retreat at a different residence — should that nurse be given the robe or not? The robe should be given.

Venerable one, if a novice served as a nurse and the patient passed away — should that novice be given the nurse's robe? Upāli: It should be given.

Venerable one, if a fully ordained nun served as nurse and the patient passed away — should that nurse be given the robe? It should not be given. Probationary nuns and novice nuns are likewise.

Venerable one, if robes obtained from robbing many travelers are encountered — should they be received or not? Upāli: If a merchant has given them, they may be received. But if a thief has given them, they should not be received at that time.

Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that a monk should not set aside rains retreat gains inside the rains retreat itself. If a householder, having invited monks from many residences and gathered them in one place — whether that place was sought out or not — then presented robes directly to those members of the Saṅgha, should those monks divide the robes?

Upāli: Those robes may be divided as robes occasioned by circumstance.

Venerable one, if during the rains retreat a monk passes away, may those monks divide his robes? They may be divided as the goods of the deceased.

In brief:
The outer boundary between two villages,
and likewise that of a stūpa —
dedicated from the boundary,
and finally lapsed.

Venerable one, if there is a temple within a village and the Saṅgha that has entered the rains retreat there goes beyond the boundary for some purpose, and monks stationed at the edge of that boundary are within the boundary of the town, and people there then offer rains-retreat gains to the Saṅgha — who receives them? The Saṅgha of the town.

Venerable one, if the Saṅgha has entered the rains retreat in a town and is dispersed within the rains retreat period — who receives the rains-retreat gains? Upāli: Those who have inclined toward the Dharma.

Venerable one, if a monk consecrates wool as the three Dharma robes — is that considered to be consecrated? If there is other cloth available, it should not be consecrated. If it is consecrated, a transgression is incurred.

Venerable one, if a monk goes beyond the boundary and takes the Saṅgha's gains for himself — what becomes of that? It is a wrongdoing.

Venerable one, can it happen that a Saṅgha that has entered the rains retreat divides the gains of a stūpa during the rains retreat without incurring a fault, and that it is allowable? Upāli: There is such a case. Gains dedicated to a stūpa of a hearer may be divided as the goods of the deceased.

Venerable one, when the Blessed One has said "let those within the boundary divide the goods of the deceased" — if a monk consecrates the goods of the deceased and then goes beyond the boundary, is a share of the goods of the deceased given? Upāli: It is given. But if he has gone without consecrating them? Upāli: It is not.

Venerable one, if other monks are present and the goods of the deceased and the robes have not been consecrated — should those monks be given a share of the goods of the deceased? Upāli: They should be given. Venerable one, if they have come after consecrating them? Upāli: No.

Venerable one, when the Blessed One has said "consecrate the goods of the deceased by petition and by formal act" — if a monk is alone in a residence, how should he consecrate them? Upāli: That monk should arouse the intention and speak the words aloud: "This article, obtained through division, I shall take up as this Dharma robe. I shall make it my own. This I shall consecrate." Thus he should consecrate it. If two or three monks are staying in a place, they should say this to one another.

Venerable one, may cloth that has not been examined be consecrated? Upāli: It may not. Venerable one, if a circumstance similar to that arises, may it be done? Upāli: It may.

The section on robes is complete.

In brief:
Two old ones, and what is laid aside,
a new permanent one, a damaged one,
one received and one not received,
gains at the right time and undivided —
the impermissible, beyond the boundary,
and the undesignated person: these too are ten.

Venerable one, if an old robe is permanently set aside — is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside, and the Saṅgha incurs a transgression. What is an old robe? It is one that the Saṅgha has previously set aside permanently.

Venerable one, if a held old robe is permanently set aside — is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside, and the Saṅgha incurs a transgression. What is a held old robe? It is one that has been used by a monk.

Venerable one, if a set-aside robe is permanently set aside — is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside, and the Saṅgha incurs a transgression. What is a set-aside robe? It is one that has been relinquished.

Venerable one, if a new robe is permanently set aside — is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside, and the Saṅgha does not incur a transgression. What is a new robe? It is one that the Saṅgha has permanently set aside for the first time.

Venerable one, if a permanent robe is permanently set aside — is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside, and the Saṅgha incurs a transgression. What is a permanent robe? It is a robe obtained in the final month of the rains retreat.

Venerable one, if a worn-out robe is permanently set aside — is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside, and the Saṅgha incurs a transgression. What is a worn-out robe? It is a robe that has rotted.

Venerable one, if an unsuitable robe is permanently set aside — is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside, and the Saṅgha incurs a transgression.

Venerable one, if a suitable robe is permanently set aside — is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside, and the Saṅgha does not incur a transgression.

Venerable one, when the Blessed One declared that a robe obtained at the right time should be permanently set aside — if a robe obtained at the right time is permanently set aside, is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside. What is a robe obtained at the right time? It is a robe obtained on the very same lunar day, one day after three months have passed.

Venerable one, when the Blessed One declared that an unworn robe should be permanently set aside — what is an unworn robe? It is one on which the dye has just been applied.

Venerable one, when the Blessed One declared that a suitable unworn robe should be permanently set aside — is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside. What is a suitable unworn robe? It is one that is of a permissible color.

Venerable one, if an impermissible robe is permanently set aside — is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside, and the Saṅgha incurs a transgression. What is an impermissible robe? It is one that is impermissible by reason of its own nature.

Venerable one, if a robe or the one appointed for permanent setting aside has not been distributed, and yet a permanent setting aside takes place — is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside, and the Saṅgha incurs a transgression.

Venerable one, if a Dharma robe appointed beyond the boundary is permanently set aside — is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside, and the Saṅgha incurs a transgression.

Venerable one, if a permanent setting aside takes place that has been interrupted by one who is carrying out a forfeiture — is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside, and the Saṅgha incurs a transgression.

Venerable one, likewise, if the permanent setting aside is carried out by one undergoing forfeiture, by one who is content to undergo it, by one who conducts himself contentedly, by one who has acted in such contentment, by one who has surrendered the training, by one who has not entered the rains retreat, by one who has broken it, by one who has entered the later rains retreat in the proper manner, by one residing elsewhere for the rains retreat, or by those who are insane — is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside, and the Saṅgha incurs a transgression.

In summary:
Two fives, two minds,
two leavings-over, and likewise —
women, the mark, the permanent, and the place:
these are to be understood in six aspects.

Venerable one, the Blessed One declared that five types of persons should not be appointed for permanent setting aside: namely, those carrying out a forfeiture, those undergoing a forfeiture, those who conduct themselves contentedly, those who have acted in such contentment, and those who have surrendered the training. If a person carrying out a forfeiture permanently sets aside a robe — is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside, and the Saṅgha incurs a transgression.

Venerable one, likewise, if those undergoing a forfeiture, those who conduct themselves contentedly, those who have acted in such contentment, and those who have surrendered the training permanently set aside a robe — is it considered set aside? Upāli: It is considered set aside, and the Saṅgha incurs a transgression.

The Saṅgha includes both those who have passed away and those still living. Furthermore, there are five classes of person who are not appointed to preside over the invitation ceremony: those who have observed no rains retreat, those whose rains retreat has been broken, those who have entered the later rains retreat in the proper manner, those who have spent the rains retreat elsewhere, and those who have surrendered the training.

Venerable one, the Blessed One has further declared that if those same five classes of person — those who have observed no rains retreat, those whose rains retreat has been broken, those who have entered the later rains retreat in the proper manner, those who have spent the rains retreat elsewhere, and those who have surrendered the training — conduct an invitation ceremony, it is to be considered conducted. In that case, venerable one, if a person who observed no rains retreat conducts an invitation ceremony, is it considered conducted? Upāli: In some cases it is considered conducted; in some cases it is not. Venerable one, in which case is it considered conducted, and in which case is it not? Upāli: Here is how it is: a novice who has entered the rains retreat properly, and who, within that same later rains retreat period, receives full ordination, and then three months pass — if such a person conducts an invitation ceremony, it is considered conducted for that person. Why is that? Upāli: Because one who has passed three months is called one who has completed the rains, and this too is manifest in three months. But as for one who, having gone forth from the later rains retreat and received full ordination, stays together with monks for three months and then conducts the invitation ceremony — that is not considered conducted. Upāli: Three months of staying is what is called the rains, and this has not been completed in three months.

Venerable one, if a person whose rains retreat has been broken conducts an invitation ceremony, is it considered conducted? Upāli: In some cases it is considered conducted; in some cases it is not. Venerable one, in which case is it considered conducted, and in which case is it not? Upāli: Here is how it is: a person who has no knowledge of the earlier rains retreat and no connection to the later rains retreat either — if that person stays together with monks for three months and simultaneously conducts the invitation ceremony, it is not considered conducted for that person. Upāli: Three months of staying is what is called the rains, and for such a person there is no recognition of three months. But as for one who has stayed in the earlier rains retreat, or who also knows the later one, and who, having gone beyond the boundary with the seven-day or forty-day authorization, and the dawn has risen outside the boundary — if that person, having stayed three months, conducts the invitation ceremony, it is considered conducted for that person. Upāli: Three months of staying is what is called the rains, and for that person too it is manifest in three months. But if one violates the commitment, it becomes an offense.

Venerable one, if a person who has entered the later rains retreat in the proper manner conducts an invitation ceremony, is it considered conducted? Upāli: In some cases it is considered conducted; in some cases it is not. Venerable one, in which case is it considered conducted? Upāli: When the monks of a Saṅgha who entered the earlier rains retreat properly — those conducting an invitation ceremony together — and those who entered the later rains retreat properly all conduct the invitation together, it is considered conducted for those persons. Upāli: Three months of staying is what is called the rains, and for them there is no recognition of three months. But if the entire Saṅgha has entered the later rains retreat in the proper manner, stays for three months, and then conducts the invitation ceremony, it is considered conducted for all of them. Upāli: Three months of staying is what is called the rains, and for them it is manifest in three months.

Venerable one, if a person who has spent the rains retreat elsewhere conducts an invitation ceremony, is it considered conducted? Upāli: In some cases it is considered conducted; in some cases it is not. Venerable one, in which case is it considered conducted, and in which case is it not? Upāli: Monks who reside in a place where the boundaries have been separately established, and who, having spent the rains retreat elsewhere, go somewhere else and then conduct the invitation ceremony — for those persons it is not considered conducted. Upāli: What, then, is the invitation ceremony? The invitation ceremony that is conducted after staying three months — for those persons there is no recognition of three months.

Upāli: When the Saṅgha of monks who have resided through the three months of the rains retreat — once the three rains months have passed and, on that very last day of the additional period, they dissolve the great boundary and consolidate four or five separate boundaries into a single one and then perform the invitation ceremony — it is to be called the invitation ceremony conducted for all of those residences. Likewise, for those who were residing in one place and perform the invitation ceremony in another, it is to be called the invitation ceremony conducted in another residence.

Venerable one: If the invitation ceremony is conducted after a dismissal, is it to be called conducted?

Upāli: In some cases it is called conducted; in some cases, not conducted.

Venerable one: In which case is it not called conducted?

Upāli: When a monk who entered the rains retreat has had a formal act of suspension performed against him by an assembled Saṅgha — and those monks who are residing through the rains also perform the invitation ceremony together with him without his having sought their consent — in that case it is not called conducted.

And in which case is it called conducted?

Upāli: When a monk who entered the rains retreat has had an act of suspension from association imposed upon him by an assembled Saṅgha, or has had a formal act of censure performed against him, and he then seeks consent — and the Saṅgha of monks residing through the rains performs the invitation ceremony together with him — in that case it is called conducted.

Venerable one: The Blessed One has declared that a monk who performs the invitation ceremony, having taken up the invitation-robe, should go first to washing it, straightening it, mending it, and sewing it — right up to the final needle-stitch — and should generate a threefold mental resolve: "With this Dharma-robe I shall establish the invitation ceremony for the Saṅgha; I am establishing it; I am performing it." Even if the threefold mental resolve is generated, if with this Dharma-robe one establishes the invitation ceremony for the Saṅgha and generates the twofold mental resolve — "I am performing it" — then it is called conducted.

Venerable one: Is it sufficient to perform the invitation ceremony with a single mental resolve?

Upāli: It is sufficient. It is as follows: when a monk who is performing the invitation ceremony generates the mental resolve — "I, called such-and-such by name, am performing the invitation ceremony for the Saṅgha with this robe" — it is called the performing of the invitation ceremony.

Venerable one: When monks are expelled by a king after leaving the monastic life, how are those monks to perform the invitation ceremony?

Just as when one has gone forth in the proper way.

Venerable one: Can that very invitation ceremony be both valid and invalid?

Upāli: Yes. It is as follows: if among those monks some have been expelled by the king and some have not, and they go forth in the proper manner — and on that very last day of the additional period a householder of the place where those who were not expelled reside provides a meal for both groups of Saṅgha and offers a robe for the invitation ceremony — that robe is valid for those who were not expelled by the king, and it is not valid for those who were expelled.

Venerable one: By which of these eight phrases does one come forth from the invitation ceremony? And which among them are shared, and which are not shared?

Upāli: All of them except the first and the last are shared.

Venerable one: If night falls while a monk is performing the invitation ceremony, is it called conducted?

Upāli: It is called conducted. Take that monk who is concealing the invitation-robe as a believer.

Venerable one: We speak of the invitation-robe, we speak of performing the invitation ceremony, and we speak of coming forth from the invitation ceremony. Venerable one, what then is the invitation-robe, what is performing the invitation ceremony, and what is coming forth from it?

Upāli: The robe is the invitation-robe. The generating of the mental resolve is the performing of the invitation ceremony. The eight phrases are the coming forth from the invitation ceremony.

Venerable one: If monks entered the rains retreat within four or five boundary areas, and then departed from the retreat and performed the invitation ceremony, is it called performed in all of those residences?

Upāli: It is called performed in all of them.

Venerable one: If, having performed the invitation ceremony, one dissolves the great shared boundary and then draws up individual boundaries separately, is it called the invitation ceremony having been withdrawn?

Upāli: It is not. It is called the invitation ceremony having been performed in all of those residences.

Venerable one: If one draws up separate individual boundaries and then withdraws the invitation ceremony, is it called the invitation ceremony having been withdrawn from all of those residences?

Upāli: It is not. Those from which it is withdrawn, it is called the invitation ceremony having been withdrawn. Those from which it is not withdrawn, it is called the invitation ceremony not having been withdrawn.

Venerable one: If those who have come forth from the ceremony and the monks took four or five boundary areas and merged them into one and then performed the invitation ceremony, is it called the invitation ceremony having been performed in all of those residences?

Upāli: It is called the invitation ceremony having been performed in all of them.

Venerable one: If, having performed the invitation ceremony, one dissolves the great shared boundary and draws up separate individual boundaries, is it called the invitation ceremony not having been performed?

Upāli: It is not. It is called the invitation ceremony having been performed in all of them.

Venerable one: If one draws up separate individual boundaries and then withdraws the invitation ceremony, is it called the invitation ceremony having been withdrawn from all of those residences?

Upāli: It is not. Those from which it is withdrawn are called the invitation ceremony having been withdrawn. Those from which it is not withdrawn are called the invitation ceremony not having been withdrawn.

In brief:

The third and fifth months, and the five and three limits of the restoration ceremony,
the robe and the large cloth as conditions,
two withdrawals and two separations,
the second measure likewise,
and laypeople and the rest —
last is the giving of the precepts.

Venerable one: For how long may one hold the invitation ceremony open?

Upāli: Three months — just as one dwells for three months having entered the rains retreat.

Venerable one: For how long may one keep the invitation ceremony?

Upāli: Five months.

Venerable one: For those who perform the invitation ceremony at the end of the later rains retreat, does that also count as keeping it for five months?

Upāli: However many there are among those who thus perform the invitation ceremony, they should each keep it according to that number of months, up to five months.

Venerable one: Should the invitation ceremony be held open until the end of the restoration ceremony?

Upāli: It should be done at the end of the restoration ceremony.

Venerable one: Should the invitation ceremony be withdrawn at the end of the restoration ceremony?

Upāli: It should be done at the end of the restoration ceremony.

Venerable one: On what causes and conditions did the Blessed One declare that an unsuitable rains retreat should be set aside?

Upāli: The Blessed One declared five causes and five conditions, and those five are these: a residence that has monks together with doors and shutters; a locale that has danger and that has cause for suspicion; when it rains or there is reason to suspect rain; when one wishes to go at an improper time to another village; when one has taken up the invitation ceremony at one's residence; and last is the petition and the formal act.

Venerable one: On what causes and conditions did the Blessed One declare that the large cloth of the rains season is permissible?

Upāli: Three: when it does not rain and there is no reason to suspect rain; when one wishes to go at an improper time to another village, another town, or to cross a river; and when one is not staying at the bank of a river or by a well.

Venerable one: For how long may one keep the large cloth of the rains season?

Upāli: A month and a half.

Venerable one: How many are the conditions that disqualify a residence for performing the invitation ceremony?

Upāli: Ten: not being separated for even a single day; not exceeding ten days; not exceeding one month; keeping robes that have not been stitched together; going about using both the upper and lower robes without a third robe; not eating in excess; not eating repeatedly; going without having been invited; seeking robes as one pleases; and from the last month of autumn up to the beginning of spring — whatever gains are obtained in that period should be distributed by the Saṅgha of those who have dwelt in the rains retreat.

Venerable one: Is this a matter of training or —

Venerable one: Will those who have received the kathina robe be deprived of it?

Upāli: No. These are qualities.

Venerable one: Is there a case in which the established ground can be revoked without a formal request and without a Saṅgha act having been performed?

Upāli: There is. For example, if the resident monks have established their ground on the very last day of the month of Kārttika, and then a large number of monks arrive unexpectedly, so that that very day is the fifteenth for those newcomers, and they perform the restoration ceremony and recite the code of individual liberation — if the resident monks too join in after them and perform the restoration ceremony, this is called revoking the established ground without a formal request and without a Saṅgha act.

Venerable one: If the resident monks have established their ground and gone beyond the boundary, and monks arrive unexpectedly and revoke the established ground, is that called a revocation?

Upāli: No. And why? Because it is only the one who established the ground who can revoke the established ground.

Venerable one: When the Saṅgha has separated in a proper rains retreat, who presides?

Those who speak in accordance with the Dharma.

Venerable one: When the Saṅgha has separated in the place where the ground was established, who receives the gains of the rains retreat?

Both parties.

Venerable one: If gains are obtained directly and in person, who receives them?

The Dharma-side receives them.

Venerable one: If cloth that is below the required size is stitched together in pieces and sewn into a robe, and then established as the kathina ground, is it called the establishing of the kathina ground?

Upāli: It is not called establishing.

Venerable one: If something below the required size is established as the kathina ground, is it called establishing?

Upāli: It is not called establishing.

Venerable one: With what kind of robe is the kathina ground to be established?

Upāli: One that is five spans in length and three spans in width.

Venerable one: If a layperson establishes the robe for the purpose of establishing the kathina ground, is it called establishing?

Upāli: It is not called establishing, and the Saṅgha act too is void.

Likewise, when the robe for establishing the kathina ground is laid down by one who is no longer in good standing, or who is no longer residing, or who is dwelling separately, up until the point of the preceding dispute — if they establish the kathina ground, is it called establishing?

Upāli: It is not called establishing, and the Saṅgha act too is void.

Venerable one: If a novice establishes the robe for the kathina ground and establishes the kathina ground, is it called establishing?

Upāli: It is not called establishing, and the Saṅgha act too is void.

Venerable one: If those who establish the kathina ground have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, have taken a partisan position, or have given up their training, and they establish the kathina ground, is it called establishing?

Upāli: It is called establishing, and the Saṅgha act too is void.

Venerable one: If a mad person establishes the robe for the kathina ground and establishes the kathina ground, is it called establishing?

Upāli: It is not called establishing.

If one has the perception of a monk, and, thinking "I who am called such-and-such am establishing the kathina ground for the Saṅgha; I am establishing it," arouses that intention — it is called establishing. Likewise, it should be understood the same way for those with distracted minds and those tormented by illness.

Venerable one: If a fool, a mute, or a deaf person establishes the robe for the kathina ground and establishes the kathina ground, is it called establishing?

Upāli: It is called establishing, and the Saṅgha act too is void.

Venerable one: If one dwelling elsewhere establishes the kathina ground, is it called establishing?

Upāli: It is called establishing, and the Saṅgha act too is void.

The topic of the kathina ground is complete.

In summary:

Where, by whom, the four boundaries,
assigning, robe, and four restorations,
four kathinas, separation, and the individual —

Venerable one: In the region of Kauśāmbī, when the Saṅgha separates, if one who dwells alone within the boundary performs the restoration ceremony, and the affairs of the Saṅgha and the purposes of the Saṅgha are conducted separately —

Venerable one: In the region of Kauśāmbī, which faction of the Saṅgha first caused the division? It was those who spoke contrary to the Dharma — they were the first to perform the restoration ceremony separately within the boundary, and to conduct the affairs of the Saṅgha and the purposes of the Saṅgha separately.

Venerable one: If one who broke the boundary at Kauśāmbī breaks it again, is it called breaking the boundary?

Upāli: No.

Venerable one: If one dwelling at Vaiśālī breaks it, is it called breaking the boundary?

Upāli: No.
