Venerable one: When the community of nuns has separated and dwells in different quarters, should one recite and teach the fortnightly confession to them half by half, announcing: "Sisters, be more harmonious with one another"?

Venerable one: May the nuns who dwell in a separate quarter, the community of nuns having divided, seek the fortnightly recitation and teaching?

They should seek it. From whom should they seek it? From those who incline toward the Dharma.

Venerable one: May those monks who dwell in the two separate quarters, the community of monks having divided, give the recitation and teaching to the nuns? Give it, in order that the community of nuns not be split.

Venerable one: In the region of Kauśāmbī, when both factions assemble and are gathered together, where shall the individual monk recite to the nuns? Outside the boundary.

Venerable one: In the region of Kauśāmbī, when both factions have assembled and gathered together, and the individual monks have also gone outside the boundary, and a householder comes and offers a robe to the Saṅgha — who receives it? Both factions.

If one dwelling in Kauśāmbī performs the restoration ceremony together with those dwelling in Vaiśālī, is it called having performed the restoration ceremony?

Upāli: No.

If one dwelling in Vaiśālī performs the restoration ceremony together with those dwelling in Kauśāmbī, is it called having performed the restoration ceremony?

Upāli: No.

If individual monks perform the restoration ceremony together with those dwelling in Kauśāmbī, is it called having performed the restoration ceremony?

Upāli: No.

If individual monks perform the restoration ceremony together with those dwelling in Vaiśālī, is it called having performed the restoration ceremony?

Upāli: No.

If they do so, the individual's matter comes to nothing.

Venerable one: When the Saṅgha divides in a place where a sentence of suspension has been pronounced, by whom is the suspension to be imposed? By those who speak in accordance with the Dharma.

Venerable one: When the Saṅgha divides in a place where a sentence of suspension has been pronounced, by whom is it to be lifted? By those who speak in accordance with the Dharma.

Venerable one: Does every case of partial alignment entail separate standing?

There is partial alignment without separate standing; there is separate standing without partial alignment; there is both partial alignment and separate standing; and there is neither partial alignment nor separate standing.

Partial alignment without separate standing is this: a monk who has become partially aligned on five matters but has not been expelled by the Saṅgha because he has not been seen, or has not been expelled because the act has not been repeated, or has not been expelled because his view of wrongdoing has not been abandoned.

Separate standing without partial alignment is this: a monk who has been expelled by the Saṅgha because he has not been seen, or because the act has not been repeated, or because his view of wrongdoing has not been abandoned — but who has not become partially aligned on the five matters.

Both partial alignment and separate standing is this: a monk who has become partially aligned on the five matters and has also been expelled by the Saṅgha because he has not been seen, or because the act has not been repeated, or because his view of wrongdoing has not been abandoned.

Neither partial alignment nor separate standing is this: all cases other than those described above.

Is it the case that everything that is partial alignment is also non-standing? There is partial alignment that is not non-standing; there is non-standing that is not partial alignment; there is that which is both partial alignment and non-standing; and there is that which is neither partial alignment nor non-standing.

Partial alignment that is not non-standing is this: a monk who has become partially aligned on the five matters, but in whom none of the offenses of the four defeats has arisen.

Non-standing that is not partial alignment is this: a monk in whom one or another of the offenses of the four defeats has arisen, but who has not become partially aligned on the five matters.

That which is both partial alignment and non-standing is this: a monk who has become partially aligned on the five matters and in whom one or another of the offenses of the four defeats has arisen.

That which is neither partial alignment nor non-standing is this: all cases other than those described above.

Is it the case that everything that is separate standing is also non-standing? There is separate standing that is not non-standing; there is non-standing that is not separate standing; there is that which is both separate standing and non-standing; and there is that which is neither non-standing nor separate standing.

Separate standing that is not non-standing is this: a monk who has been expelled by the Saṅgha because he has not been seen, or because the act has not been repeated, or because his view of wrongdoing has not been abandoned, but in whom none of the offenses of the four defeats has arisen.

Non-standing that is not separate standing is this: a monk in whom one or another of the offenses of the four defeats has arisen, but who has not been expelled by the Saṅgha because he has not been seen, or because the act has not been repeated, or because his view of wrongdoing has not been abandoned.

That which is both non-standing and separate standing is this: a monk who has been expelled because he has not been seen, and in whom one or another of the offenses of the four defeats has arisen.

That which is neither non-standing nor separate standing is this: all cases other than those described above.

Venerable one, is it only a monk who can split the monastic Saṅgha of monks — not a nun, not a female trainee, not a female novice, not a male novice?

Upāli, it is indeed only a monk who splits the monastic Saṅgha of monks — not a nun, not a female trainee, not a female novice, not a male novice. Nevertheless, nuns do strive to bring about schism in the Saṅgha.

Venerable one, is it only a nun who can split the monastic Saṅgha of nuns — not a monk, not a female trainee, not a female novice, not a male novice?

Upāli, it is indeed only a nun who splits the monastic Saṅgha of nuns — not a monk, not a female trainee, not a female novice, not a male novice. Nevertheless, monks do strive to bring about schism in the Saṅgha.

Venerable one, what is schism, and what constitutes blameworthy conduct?

Schism is the Saṅgha itself. Blameworthy conduct belongs to the one who creates the division.

Venerable one, when the Saṅgha is split, what results? It is a grave matter. If the summons and the act are not heeded, then the remainder constitutes the Saṅgha.

Venerable one, how much is required for there to be said to be a split Saṅgha?

Upāli, when however many monks are within the boundary and are required to be present, when all of them have assembled and are face to face, when they have accepted adherence by means of a valid form of accepting adherence, and when those monks, perceiving what is within the boundary to be within the boundary, perform the restoration ceremony and formal acts separately — that is what is called a split Saṅgha.

What transgression should one who has split the Saṅgha confess? It is a grave offense.

Venerable one, the Blessed One has said: do not speak about a person of that kind.

"Do not speak of such a person." What sort of person is that? It is a person who holds the sūtras differently from how the sūtras should be held, who has great merit, many attendants and followers, and great renown. If one were to expel such a person, what would result? It would become a grave offense. Here ends the matter of Kauśāmbī.

The Vinaya, the Sacred Texts. The nineteenth fascicle.

In brief:

Language, and the boundary of space and earth,
The two factors, and the non-assembled,
Lapsing, the group, and one by one,
The non-assembled person, and the place accordingly.

Venerable one, if a noble one performs an act in the noble language, and those monks do not understand the noble language, should it be said that the act has been performed? Upāli, it is called an act performed, and the monk who performed it is included among those who have passed over.

Venerable one, if a noble one performs an act in the border language, and those monks do not understand the border language, should it be said that the act has been performed? Upāli, it is called an act performed, and the monk who performed it is included among those who have passed over.

Venerable one, if a border person performs an act in the border language, and those monks do not understand the border language, should it be said that the act has been performed? Upāli, it is called an act performed, and the monk who performed it is included among those who have passed over.

Venerable one, if a border person performs an act in the noble language, and those monks do not understand the noble language, should it be said that the act has been performed? Upāli, it is called an act performed, and the monk who performed it is included among those who have passed over.

Venerable one, if one standing on the ground is counted in the number of those standing in the sky, may an act be performed? Upāli, it may not. Venerable one, if one standing in the sky is counted in the number of those standing on the ground, may an act be performed? Upāli, it may not. Venerable one, may one who has performed an act while standing on the ground perform an act for those standing in the sky? Upāli, it may not. Venerable one, may one who performs an act while standing in the sky perform an act for those standing on the ground? Upāli, it may not. In the same way, these four cases apply equally to those dwelling within the boundary and those dwelling outside the boundary.

Venerable one, may those standing on the ground perform an act together with those standing on the ground? Upāli, they may. Moreover, in such a case, those standing on the ground complete the count and accept the consent from those standing on the ground.

Just as those standing on the ground may act together with those standing on the ground, so too: those standing on the ground with those standing on a wall; those standing on the ground with those standing in a tree; those standing on a wall with those standing on a wall; those standing on a wall with those standing on the ground; those standing on a wall with those standing in a tree; those standing in a tree with those standing in a tree; those standing in a tree with those standing on the ground; and those standing in a tree together with those standing on a wall — may an act be performed? Upāli, it may, for in whatever combination those standing in trees complete the count and accept the consent from those standing on the ground.

There are four kinds of acts: one performed contrary to the Dharma and without assembly; one performed contrary to the Dharma but with assembly; one performed in accordance with the Dharma but without assembly; and one performed in accordance with the Dharma and with assembly.

What is an act performed contrary to the Dharma and without assembly? It is when a motion has been made but the act has not been announced and the assembly has also not gathered. What is an act performed contrary to the Dharma but with assembly? It is when a motion has been made but the act has not been announced, yet the assembly has gathered. What is an act performed in accordance with the Dharma but without assembly? It is when a motion has been made and the act has been announced, but the assembly has not gathered. What is an act performed in accordance with the Dharma and with assembly? It is when a motion has been made, the act has been announced, and the assembly has gathered.

Furthermore, there are four kinds of acts: one performed contrary to the Dharma, in harmony, and without assembly; one performed contrary to the Dharma, in harmony, and with assembly; one performed in accordance with the Dharma, in harmony, and without assembly; and one performed in accordance with the Dharma, in harmony, and with assembly.

What is an act performed contrary to the Dharma, in harmony, and without assembly?

It is when the motion was announced first and the appeal comes afterward, and the assembly has not gathered.

What is an act performed contrary to the Dharma, in harmony, and with assembly? It is when the motion was announced first and the appeal comes afterward, and the assembly has also gathered.

What is an act performed in accordance with the Dharma, in harmony, and without assembly? It is when the motion itself has been proposed and a different act has been announced, but the assembly has not gathered.

What is an act performed in accordance with the Dharma, in harmony, and with assembly? It is when the motion itself has been proposed and a different act has been announced, and the assembly has also gathered.

Venerable One, we speak of an act performed without assembly and an act performed with assembly. What, Venerable One, is an act performed without assembly?

Upāli, when all the monks who are within the boundary have come to the boundary, have come to be present for the act, have all assembled in person, and those who are eligible to give consent have given their consent — if the monks then turn back and wander off, and the act is performed while they are turning back and wandering off in that way, that is called an act performed without assembly.

What is an act performed with assembly? When all the monks within the boundary have come to the boundary, have come to be present for the act, have all assembled in person, and those who are eligible to give consent have given their consent — if the monks do not turn back or wander off, and the act is performed while they remain without turning back and without wandering off, that is called an act performed with assembly.

Venerable One, is it possible that even when the entire Saṅgha has assembled and gathered and an act has been performed, that act could become an act performed without assembly?

Upāli, yes, it is possible — namely when, in the course of making the motion and performing the act, monks turn back and wander off, and the act is performed while they are turning back and wandering off in that way.

Venerable One, if an act is performed by one who has been interrupted and whose turn has passed, can it be said that the act has been performed?

Upāli, it can be said that the act has been performed, and the members of the Saṅgha are included in what has passed.

Venerable One, if one who has been interrupted and whose turn has passed gives consent and then an act is performed, can it be said that the act has been performed?

Upāli, it can be said that the act has been performed, and those monks are included in what has passed.

Venerable One, if consent is given by one in place of another and an act is performed, can it be said that the act has been performed?

Upāli, it can be said that the act has been performed, and the members of the Saṅgha are included in what has passed.

Venerable One, if an act is performed without the assembly having gathered, can it be said that the act has been performed?

Upāli, it cannot be said that the act has been performed, and the Saṅgha too is included in what has passed.

Venerable One, is it proper for one to perform acts for one, for two, for three, or for many?

Upāli, it is not proper.

Venerable One, is it proper for two to perform acts for one, for two, for three, or for many?

Upāli, it is not proper.

Venerable One, is it proper for three to perform acts for one, for two, for three, or for many?

Upāli, it is not proper.

Venerable One, is it proper for many to perform acts for many?

Upāli, it is not proper.

Venerable One, if those who perform the act are in one location, is it proper to perform all acts for four locations?

Upāli, it is proper — provided that the monk performing the act does so by marking the boundary of all four locations with a wall, a fence, or a latch.

Venerable One, if one who performs an act, in a single boundary, with a single motion and a single announcement, performs an act for four individuals, can it be said that the act has been performed?

Upāli, it cannot. And why? Because it is not proper for many to perform acts for many in a single boundary.

Venerable One, is it possible that a monk might perform an act for monks who share the same boundary and co-reside there, and yet no transgression occurs and the Saṅgha is not considered to have failed to assemble?

Upāli, yes, it is possible — by means of consent that has been duly given.

Venerable One, is it possible that a monk who is present in a single boundary performs an act for four individuals, and yet the act is considered performed, and those monks are not considered to have incurred a transgression?

Upāli, yes, it is possible — when the monk performing the act stands or sits astride the boundary, touching it and holding it, so that two persons are inside the boundary and two are outside the boundary when the act is performed.

In brief:

Those present, those who gave consent before,
Three kinds of acts, death,
The boundary of comfort where none can serve,
Transgressions — so too with these.

Venerable One, when the Blessed One says "Acts must be performed for those who are present," is it possible that the Saṅgha performs acts for those who are not present and yet the acts are considered performed?

Upāli, yes, it is possible — as when the assembly of nuns confers a vow of non-salutation or a vow of deprivation of requisites, and when the assembly of monks confers a vow of insanity upon a monk.

Venerable One, if the announcement is made first and the motion is made afterward, is it called performed?

Upāli, it is called performed, but those monks have incurred a transgression.

Venerable One, if one abandons oneself, is it called abandoned?

Upāli, it is called abandoned.

Venerable One, if one has abandoned oneself and then consents to oneself on one's own behalf, is it called consenting?

Upāli, it is called consented.

Venerable One, if a censure act has been performed and one performs a censure act again upon it, is it called performed?

Upāli, it is not.

Likewise, if upon one who has had a rebuke act performed one performs a rebuke act; or if one performs an expulsion act, a reconciliation act, an act of suspension for not seeing a transgression, an act of not restoring, an act of suspension for not abandoning a wrong view, an act of punishment, an act of probation, or an act of removal — is it called performed?

Upāli, it is not.

Venerable One, if upon one who has had a censure act performed one performs a rebuke act, an expulsion act, a reconciliation act, an act of suspension for not seeing a transgression, an act of not restoring, an act of suspension for not abandoning a wrong view, an act of punishment, an act of probation, or an act of removal — is it called performed?

Upāli, it is called performed. And so it is for all acts, to be understood in sequence like the turning of a wheel.

Venerable One, if upon one who deserves a censure act one performs a rebuke act, an expulsion act, or a reconciliation act, is it called performed?

Upāli, it is called performed, but it is an act of degradation.

Venerable One, if upon one who deserves a censure act one performs an act of suspension for not seeing a transgression, an act of not restoring, or an act of suspension for not abandoning a wrong view, is it called performed?

Upāli, it is not called performed. And why? Because an act of degradation is one thing, and an act of suspension is another.

Venerable One, if upon one who deserves a censure act one performs an act of punishment, an act of probation, or an act of removal, is it called performed?

Upāli, it is not called performed. And why? Because an act of degradation is one thing, and an act of purification is another.

Venerable One, if upon one who deserves an act of suspension for not seeing a transgression one performs an act of not restoring or an act of suspension for not abandoning a wrong view, is it called performed?

Upāli, it is called performed.

And why? Because all of those are acts of suspension.

Venerable One, if upon one who deserves an act of suspension for not seeing a transgression one performs an act of censure, an act of rebuke, an act of banishment, or an act of reconciliation, is it called performed?

Upāli, it is not called performed. And why? Because an act of suspension is one thing, and an act of degradation is another.

Venerable One, if upon one who deserves an act of suspension for not seeing a transgression one performs an act of punishment, an act of satisfaction, or an act of removal, is it called performed?

Upāli, it is not called performed. And why? Because an act of suspension is one thing, and an act of purification is another.

Venerable One, if upon one who deserves an act of punishment one performs an act of satisfaction or an act of removal, is it called performed?

Upāli, it is called performed. And why? Because all of these are acts of purification.

Venerable One, if upon one who deserves an act of punishment one performs an act of censure, an act of rebuke, an act of banishment, or an act of reconciliation, is it called performed?

Upāli, it is not called performed. And why? Because an act of purification is one thing, and an act of degradation is another.

Venerable One, if upon one who deserves an act of punishment one performs an act of suspension for not seeing a transgression, or an act of suspension for not restoring, or an act of suspension for not abandoning a wrong view, is it called performed?

Upāli, it is not called performed. And why? Because an act of purification is one thing, and an act of suspension is another.

Venerable One, if a motion is made by one party and the proclamation is made by another, is it called performed?

Upāli, it is not called performed — and those monks also have committed an offense.

Venerable One, the Blessed One has said that a person who is childish, foolish, unclear, unskillful, shameless, unstable in speech, fallen from his commitments, who has previously committed offenses, who has previously caused disruption, or who is deranged — that even when disturbed by such ten types of persons, no disruption counts. Venerable One, if they act contrary to the Dharma and those persons nonetheless obstruct and cause disruption again, does their repeated obstruction and disruption count?

Upāli, it does count. Because I said that with reference to a Dharma-conforming act, the obstruction and disruption by those persons does not count when one is performing a Dharma-conforming act.

Venerable One, when assigning an act to twelve persons, or when performing full ordination for one who is fit for full ordination, or when granting removal to one who is fit for removal, if they obstruct and cause disruption, saying "Do not perform this act against us" — does their obstruction and disruption count?

Upāli, it does count. I spoke with reference to acts of punishment.

Venerable One, if one who is performing an act does so when the time has passed, is it called performed?

Upāli, if the act has been performed many times over and the time has also passed, it is called performed.

Venerable One, should one associate and live together with one who has been suspended, or not?

Upāli, one should not associate or live together with one who has been suspended.

Venerable One, is one who has been suspended called a companion, or not a companion?

Upāli, all who have been suspended are to be called not companions.

Venerable One, when the Blessed One has said that one should grant consent to one upon whom a censure act has been performed — Venerable One, where should consent be granted?

Within the boundary.

How should consent be requested?

One who has been given a probationary penality should, while lying down as if with hair bristling, make an effort to rise and present oneself prostrating to the Saṅgha, and should sit within the appointed session, request forgiveness, and acknowledge one's fault.

Venerable One, if one against whom the Saṅgha has announced the matter three times within the community does not send back a reply — do all of them incur a fault? And should the announcement be made three times within the community to all of those against whom a fault has occurred? All who, having been announced to three times within the community, do not send back a reply incur a fault.

Venerable One, can it happen that even though a fault has occurred, one would not have the announcement made three times within the community?

Upāli, it can. If the announcement is of a kind that would be fitting to announce, but a different fault from that one has arisen, then one is exempt from that other fault.

Venerable One, the Blessed One has said that for a monk possessed of certain qualities, acts of censure, acts of removal, and acts of purification should be performed. Venerable One, if a nun likewise comes to possess such qualities, should those acts also be performed upon her?

Upāli, they should.

Venerable One, if female trainees (śikṣamāṇās), female novices, and male novices come to possess those qualities, should those acts also be performed upon them?

Upāli, all the acts other than the act of purification should be performed.

In brief:

One who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is dull, one who is asleep, one who babbles,
one who is intoxicated, one in meditative absorption, one who has departed,
those who are pandakas, and so forth,
and finally one who has been given a training — these are the last.

Venerable One, if an act is performed upon one who is mad, is it called a performed act?

Upāli, for one who is mad — apart from the act of granting a vow — for the remaining acts: if one still has the perception of being a monk and knows that this act is being performed upon oneself, it is called a performed act.

The same applies to one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is dull, one who is mute, and one who is deaf.

Venerable One, if an act is performed upon one who is asleep, is it called a performed act?

Upāli, if at the time when one is addressed in body or speech and the act is to be performed one falls asleep, it is called a performed act.

The same should be said concerning one who is intoxicated, one who babbles, and one who is in meditative absorption.

Venerable One, if an act is performed upon one who has gone and is dwelling elsewhere, is it called a performed act?

Upāli, apart from the presenting of the bowl, the remaining acts are called performed.

Venerable One, if the one upon whom an act is to be performed has died in the meantime, is it called a performed act?

Upāli, it is called a performed act.

Venerable One, if an act is performed upon a pandaka, is it called a performed act?

Upāli, it is not called a performed act.

The same should be said from the case of a nun who has been expelled through to the case of one who was previously in dispute.

Venerable One, if an act is performed upon a hermaphrodite (ubhatovyañjanaka), is it called a performed act?

Upāli, it is not called a performed act.

Venerable One, if an act is performed upon one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who has taken sides in a dispute, or one who has been given a training, is it called a performed act?

Upāli, it is called a performed act — and the Saṅgha includes both those who are present and those who are deceased.

In brief:

One who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one who is ill, one who is deaf, one who is dull,
laypeople and the like,
one who has been given a training, and one who has died in the same way —

Venerable One, if one who is mad has performed an act, is it called a performed act or not a performed act?

Upāli, if one has regained the perception of being a monk and has made the request and the act is not impaired, it is called a performed act.

The same applies to one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is dull, one who is mute, and one who is deaf.

Venerable One, if one who is dwelling elsewhere has performed an act, is it called a performed act?

Upāli, it is so.

The same should be said concerning a layman who has performed an act, a hermaphrodite, and

a neuter person — and, from "not dwelling together" and "dwelling separately" up through "the previously disputed matter" — if those individuals perform an act, is it called a performed act?

Upāli: it is not.

Venerable One, if those who have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, those who have taken sides, and those who have been given a training — if those perform an act, is it called a performed act?

Upāli: it is called performed, and the Saṅgha includes the departed.

Venerable One, if while performing an act it is called a performed act, and then the name changes, is it called a performed act?

Upāli: it is called performed. And just as one says it of the one performing the act, so too should one say it of the one who completes the number.

Here ends the substance of acts — the substance of the red-yellow section.

In summary:

Suspension is made in seven kinds —
the three abodes and the tīrthika case,
proclamation, and offense,
and mark, and not a gift.

Venerable One, could it be that the very same person who imposes the suspension is himself the one around whom it turns, and the very same person who performs the invitation ceremony is himself the one by whom the invitation ceremony is performed?

Upāli: Yes, it can be. For instance, a person performed the invitation ceremony, and from that there arose for him a further Saṅgha offense. He requested the invitation ceremony from the Saṅgha, and the Saṅgha granted him the invitation ceremony. While he was performing the invitation ceremony, two further Saṅgha offenses arose for him — one incurred on the first day, and one incurred on the second day. He then requested suspension from the Saṅgha on account of those offenses, and the Saṅgha granted him the suspension. He carried out the suspension for one day; the suspension for one of his offenses was completed. He is carrying out the second suspension; thirdly he performs the invitation ceremony; and fourthly the invitation ceremony has been performed.

Venerable One, if the invitation ceremony is granted to a person who is fit for suspension, is it called granted?

Upāli: it is called granted, and the Saṅgha includes the departed.

Venerable One, if one individual who is fit for suspension is expelled, is it called expulsion?

Upāli: it is called expulsion, and the Saṅgha includes the departed.

Venerable One, if suspension is granted to a person who is fit for the invitation ceremony, is it called granted?

Upāli: it is not, and the same applies to the Saṅgha — it includes the departed.

Venerable One, if one individual who is fit for the invitation ceremony is expelled, is it called expulsion?

Upāli: it is called expulsion, and the Saṅgha includes the departed.

Venerable One, if suspension is granted to a person who is fit for expulsion, is it called granted?

Upāli: it is not, and the same applies to the Saṅgha — it includes the departed.

Venerable One, if the invitation ceremony is granted to one individual who is fit for expulsion, is it called granted?

Upāli: it is not, and the same applies to the Saṅgha — it includes the departed.

Venerable One, if those performing the act are stationed at one boundary and are at the four positions, may they perform the acts of suspension, granting the invitation ceremony, and expulsion?

Upāli: It is permissible if the monk performing the act is pressed at the junctures of the four positions by a stick, a staff, or a key.

Venerable One, if at the junctures of the four positions for performing the act, pressed with a stick, a staff, or a key, they perform with a single motion and a single act the acts of suspension, invitation ceremony, and expulsion for four persons, is it called a performed act?

Upāli: it is not.

Why is that? Upāli: at a single boundary it is not proper for many to perform acts for many with one act.

Venerable One, if a monk who dwells within a single boundary performs the acts of suspension, invitation ceremony, and expulsion while the monks who are assembled there together are not present — without there being a failing on his part — could it be that there is also no non-concordance with the Saṅgha?

Upāli: There is such a case — it is one where consent has been duly submitted.

Venerable One, if a monk who performs an act stands to one side and performs the acts of suspension and invitation ceremony for four persons, is it both the case that the act is performed and that those monks do not incur a transgression?

Upāli: There is such a case. It is as follows: that monk who performs the act presses the boundary, seizes the boundary, and then — whether standing or sitting at the boundary — places two within the boundary and two outside the boundary, and so performs it.

Venerable One, the Blessed One has declared that two persons under suspension must not dwell in the same lodging. Is there a case where two persons under suspension dwelling in the same lodging do not thereby incur a transgression?

Upāli: There is such a case — it is when one dwells together with a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).

Venerable One, could one for whom no transgression whatsoever has arisen also be placed under suspension?

Upāli: There is such a case — it is a non-Buddhist.

Venerable One, could one who has not incurred a Saṅgha remainder offence be given a suspension without that constituting a transgression?

Upāli: There is such a case — it is a non-Buddhist.

Venerable One, if a monk has not announced the category and name of the offence, is it called a concealment?

Upāli: It is called a concealment.

Venerable One, if the category has been announced but the name has not been announced, is it called a concealment?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, from how many sources does a Saṅgha remainder arise?

Upāli: From thirteen.

Venerable One, is there a case where a monk incurs a Saṅgha remainder offence and, without having confessed it and without having restored it, is nonetheless purified of it?

Upāli: There is such a case. It is as follows: that monk has incurred a non-shared Saṅgha remainder offence, and then his status has changed and he has become a nun — for him the Saṅgha remainder offence has arisen, but the wrongdoing transgression must be confessed.

Venerable One, is there a case where a nun incurs a Saṅgha remainder offence and, without having confessed it and without having restored it, is nonetheless purified of it?

Upāli: There is such a case. It is as follows: that nun has incurred a non-shared Saṅgha remainder offence, and then her status has changed and she has become a monk — the Saṅgha remainder offence has arisen, but the wrongdoing transgression must be confessed.

Venerable One, is there a case where one who has incurred a Saṅgha remainder offence is again required to confess that same offence a second time?

Upāli: There is such a case. It is as follows: that monk has incurred a non-shared Saṅgha remainder offence, and then his status has changed and he has become a nun, and the Saṅgha remainder has arisen; and then once again his status changes and he becomes a monk — that offence must be confessed.

Venerable One, if a monk who is undergoing a suspension changes status and becomes a nun, is it called being released from suspension?

Upāli: It is not. The suspension must be applied to the nun.

Venerable One, if that monk who is undergoing the invitation ceremony changes status and becomes a nun, is it called being released from suspension?

Upāli: It is not. For as many days as have been observed, that number must be completed before both communities for a half-month.

Venerable One, if a nun who is undergoing a suspension changes status and becomes a monk, is it called being released from suspension?

Upāli: It is not. Let the suspension be applied to the monk.

Venerable One, if a nun who is undergoing the invitation ceremony changes status and becomes a monk, is it called being released from suspension?

Upāli: It is not. Six days shall be surrendered and a fresh start made.

Venerable One, is it proper to impose a suspension and an invitation ceremony on a monk who has been given training?

Upāli: It is not proper.

Venerable One, is it proper to impose a suspension and an invitation ceremony on one who has been given training?

Upāli: It is not proper.

In brief:
Offences, and likewise the nighttime,
Utterances, and also the fourth —

Body, seclusion, and likewise mantra,
The fourth two, and trained —

Venerable One, is it proper to impose a suspension and an invitation ceremony on a monk by one who is himself under offense?

Upāli: It is not proper.

Venerable One, is it proper to carry out a suspension or an invitation ceremony from a state of offense?

Upāli: It is not proper.

Likewise, the completion of the count should be stated in the same way.

Venerable One, when those who are imposing a suspension are dwelling in one place, is it proper to carry out a suspension or an invitation ceremony?

Upāli: It is not proper. Many should carry out the suspension or invitation ceremony for many.

Venerable One, if the Blessed One has said that one who is imposing a suspension should not remain in another dwelling-place, and that monk does remain in another dwelling-place, shall the days be counted?

Upāli: They shall not.

Venerable One, if a noble one (ārya) speaks an offense to a monk in the noble language, and that monk does not know the noble language, is it considered as having been spoken?

Upāli: It is not.

Is it considered as having been received?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if a noble one speaks an offense to a monk in a border dialect, and that monk does not know the border dialect, is it considered as having been spoken?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if a border person speaks an offense to a monk in a border dialect, and that monk does not know the border dialect, is it considered as having been spoken?

Upāli: It is not.

Is it considered as having been received?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if a border person speaks an offense to a monk in the noble language, and that monk does not know the noble language, is it considered as having been spoken?

Upāli: It is not.

Is it considered as having been received?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if an offense is indicated and shown by means of body alone, is it considered as having been spoken?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if one speaks while perceiving a secluded place as non-secluded, is it considered as having been spoken?

Upāli: It is not.

Is it considered as having been received?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if a monk has made himself invisible by medicine or by mantra and then speaks an offense, is it considered as having been spoken?

Upāli: It is not.

Is it considered as having been received?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if those dwelling on the ground impose a suspension, an invitation ceremony, or even a lifting act on those dwelling in the sky, is it considered as having performed the act?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if those dwelling in the sky impose a suspension, an invitation ceremony, or even a lifting act on those dwelling on the ground, is it considered as having performed the act?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if those dwelling on the ground complete the count of those dwelling in the sky and then impose a suspension, an invitation ceremony, or even a lifting act, is it considered as having performed the act?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if those dwelling in the sky complete the count of those dwelling on the ground and then impose a suspension, an invitation ceremony, or even a lifting act, is it considered as having performed the act?

Upāli: It is not.

Likewise, for those dwelling within the boundary and those dwelling outside the boundary together, this should be set out in four ways.

The Sacred Text of the Vinaya, the Twentieth Fascicle.

Upāli addressed the Buddha, the Blessed One: Venerable One, of these thirteen remaining rules of the Saṅgha — from the one-day suspension arising from an emission of semen up to and including the thirteen-day suspension arising from words that cause mental distress — is it proper that those thirteen offenses, having been received at different and dissimilar times, be dealt with by a single motion and a single act?

Upāli: It is proper.

Venerable One, is it proper to grant the satisfaction of the suspension from the beginning of the penalty period?

Upāli: It is proper.

Is it proper to grant release from the satisfaction period?

Upāli: It is proper.

Venerable One, is it proper that, by a single motion and a single act, the Saṅgha's many remaining offenses arising from different and dissimilar sources be dealt with simultaneously — imposing a suspension on one person, granting satisfaction to another, and granting release to yet another?

Upāli: It is not proper.

Venerable One, is it proper that, by a single motion and a single act, the Saṅgha impose upon a single person, simultaneously, both the suspension and the satisfaction and the release for many remaining offenses arising from different and dissimilar sources?

Upāli: It is not proper.

In brief:

One who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness,
One who is dull-witted, mute, sleeping, delirious,
One who is intoxicated, one who has entered meditative absorption, one in transit,
Householders and the like,
And lastly, one who has relinquished the training.

Venerable One, if a mad person confesses an offense, is that considered a spoken confession?

Upāli: It is not.

Will it count as having been registered?

Upāli: It will not.

The same applies to one whose mind is disturbed and to one tormented by illness.

Venerable One, if an offense is spoken in the presence of a mad person, is that considered spoken?

Upāli: It is not.

Is it considered registered?

Upāli: It is not.

The same applies likewise to one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is sleeping, one who is delirious, one who is intoxicated, and one who has entered meditative absorption: if an offense is confessed to any of them, it is not considered spoken, and it will not be registered.

Venerable One, if a monk confesses an offense to someone who is staying in a different locality, is that considered spoken?

Upāli: It is to be considered spoken.

Will it be registered?

Upāli: It will be registered.

Likewise, from the case of a paṇḍaka down to that of a nun who has been expelled, and up through the case of one who was formerly in dispute — if an offense is confessed to any of these, it is considered spoken.

Will it be registered?

Upāli: It will not be registered.

Venerable One, if a monk confesses an offense to a novice, is that considered spoken?

Upāli: It is to be considered spoken.

Will it be registered?

Upāli: It will not be registered.

The same applies likewise to one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who is not residing, one who is residing separately, one who has taken sides, and one who has been given the training: if an offense is confessed to any of these, it is considered spoken, but it will not be registered.

Venerable One, if a monk confesses an offense while changing his name, is that considered spoken?

Upāli: It is to be considered spoken.

Will it be registered?

Upāli: It will not.

Venerable One, is there a remaining offense of a monk for which it would never be proper to grant release as long as he lives?

Upāli: There is. It is as follows: if a monk has committed any one of the four root defeats, and thereafter a remaining offense of the Saṅgha arises subsequent to that, release is not to be granted for it as long as he lives.

In brief:

One who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed, one who is ill,
One who is dull-witted, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is sleeping, one who is delirious,
One who is intoxicated, one who has entered meditative absorption, one in transit,
Paṇḍakas and the like,
And lastly, one who has relinquished the training.

Venerable One, if the acts of suspension, satisfaction, and release are performed in the presence of a mad person, are they considered performed?

Upāli: They are considered performed if that person still perceives himself as a monk, and if he is aware, through body or speech, of being the object of the act and understands that this act is being done to him. The same is to be stated for one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, and one who is deaf.

Venerable One, if the acts of suspension, satisfaction, and release are performed in the presence of one who is sleeping or one who is delirious, are they considered performed?

Upāli: They are considered performed if, at the time the motion is made — having been perceived through body or speech — he then falls asleep. The same applies likewise to one who is delirious, one who is intoxicated, and

The same is also to be stated for those in meditative absorption.

Venerable One, if the acts of suspension, satisfaction, and release are performed in the presence of a monk who is residing in another district, are they considered performed?

Upāli: They are not.

Likewise, the same is to be stated from the case of a paṇḍaka through to one whose mind was previously disturbed.

Venerable One, if a monk performs an act of suspension, satisfaction, or release in the presence of a eunuch, are they considered performed?

Upāli: They are not considered performed.

Venerable One, if the acts of suspension, satisfaction, or release are performed in the presence of a monk who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, or one who has sided with such a monk, or one who has been given training precepts, are they considered performed?

Upāli: They are not considered performed, and the Saṅgha too has transgressed.

The section on persons and the section on the subjects of suspension are complete.

In summary:
Through messenger, letter, gesture,
through another's words, and one from another —
one who is mad, one whose mind is disturbed, one who is ill,
one who is mute, and one who is dull-witted,
and a paṇḍaka and so forth,
and last of all, one given training precepts.

Venerable One, if a monk obstructs the restoration ceremony by messenger, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is not.

Likewise, if the restoration ceremony is obstructed by letter, by gesture, by another's words, or by being passed from one to another, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is not.

One whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, one who is deaf, a paṇḍaka, a nun who has been expelled, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, one who dwells as a thief, one who is not residing, one residing separately, one who has sided with a schismatic, one who has previously committed an offense, and one whose mind was previously disturbed — for all of these it is likewise the same.

Venerable One, if one who has been given training precepts obstructs the restoration ceremony, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if a eunuch obstructs the restoration ceremony, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is not.

In summary:
One who has become mad, one whose mind is disturbed,
one tormented by illness, one who is deaf, one who is dull-witted,
one who is sleeping, one who is delirious, one who is intoxicated,
one in meditative absorption, one residing in another district,
a paṇḍaka and so forth,
and last of all, one given training precepts.

Venerable One, if a mad monk obstructs the restoration ceremony, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is not.

Likewise, the same is to be stated for one whose mind is disturbed, one tormented by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, one who is deaf, one who is sleeping, one who is delirious, one who is intoxicated, and one in meditative absorption.

Venerable One, if a monk who is residing in another district obstructs the restoration ceremony, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is considered obstructed.

Venerable One, likewise, from the case of a paṇḍaka through to those who have been given training precepts — if they obstruct the restoration ceremony, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is considered obstructed.

Venerable One, if a eunuch obstructs the restoration ceremony, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is considered obstructed.

In summary:
Voice and body, a secluded place and mantra,
eye and ear likewise —
boundary, ground, and those dwelling there —
these constitute the restoration ceremony; that is the last.

Venerable One, if a noble one obstructs the restoration ceremony by speaking in the noble language, and that monk does not understand the noble language, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is not.

Likewise, it is to be elaborated in four ways.

Venerable One, if a monk obstructs the restoration ceremony by means of a bodily gesture, and the other monk does not perceive it, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if one perceives a secluded place as not secluded and obstructs the restoration ceremony, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if a monk renders himself invisible by means of a spell or medicine and thereby obstructs the restoration ceremony, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if one sees by means of divine sight and obstructs the restoration ceremony, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is not considered obstructed, and the Saṅgha has also transgressed.

Venerable One, if one hears by means of divine hearing and obstructs the restoration ceremony, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is, and the Saṅgha has also transgressed.

Venerable One, if one who is within a boundary obstructs the restoration ceremony for those who are beyond the boundary, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if one who is beyond a boundary obstructs the restoration ceremony for those within the boundary, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if one standing on the ground obstructs the restoration ceremony of those standing in the sky, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, if one standing in the sky obstructs the restoration ceremony of those standing on the ground, is it considered obstructed?

Upāli: It is not.

Venerable One, is it possible for a single monk, situated in one direction, to obstruct the restoration ceremony of four persons in four locations?

Upāli: It is. If that monk presses a stick, a clod of mud, or a key against the boundary at the boundary points of the four locations and thereby obstructs the restoration ceremony, it is considered obstructed.

Venerable One, is it possible for a monk to obstruct the restoration ceremony of a monk and yet it not constitute obstruction?

Upāli: It is. This is the recitation of an auspicious restoration ceremony.

In brief:
Recall the raising of the subject, and likewise
the opening of the occasion and the speaking;
the citing of scripture and the objection,
the restoration ceremonies and the division of occasions.

Venerable One, the Blessed One has said, "One should speak having opened the occasion; one should recall." Venerable One, if one speaks and recalls having opened the occasion, can a transgression result?

Upāli: It can. This occurs when one speaks and recalls after having let the opened occasion pass.

Venerable One, where should one speak in accordance with the Dharma? Within the Saṅgha.

Venerable One, where should one recall in accordance with the Dharma? Within the Saṅgha.

Venerable One, where should one open an occasion in accordance with the Dharma? Within the Saṅgha.

Venerable One, where should one speak out in accordance with the Dharma? Within the Saṅgha.

Venerable One, where in accordance with the Dharma should one object to the citing of scripture? Within the Saṅgha.

Venerable One, where in accordance with the Dharma should one object to the opening of an occasion? Within the Saṅgha.

Venerable One, where should one request the opening of an occasion? Within the Saṅgha.

Venerable One, where should one open an occasion? Within the Saṅgha.

Venerable One, where should one perform the procedure in accordance with the Dharma? Within the Saṅgha.

Venerable One, where should one debate in accordance with the Dharma? Within the Saṅgha.

Venerable One, where should one make a lawful agreement? Within the Saṅgha.

Venerable One, how many ways are there of obstructing the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma, and how many ways not in accordance with the Dharma?

Obstructing the restoration ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma: one. In accordance with the Dharma: one.
Not in accordance with the Dharma: two. In accordance with the Dharma: two.
Not in accordance with the Dharma: three. In accordance with the Dharma: three.
Not in accordance with the Dharma: four. In accordance with the Dharma: four.
Not in accordance with the Dharma: five. In accordance with the Dharma: five.
Not in accordance with the Dharma: six. In accordance with the Dharma: six.
Not in accordance with the Dharma: seven. In accordance with the Dharma: seven.
Not in accordance with the Dharma: eight. In accordance with the Dharma: eight.
Not in accordance with the Dharma: nine. In accordance with the Dharma: nine.

Not in accordance with the Dharma: ten. In accordance with the Dharma: ten.

What is the one way that is not in accordance with the Dharma of blocking the restoration ceremony? Blocking the restoration ceremony on the grounds that there is no basis in something that was done is blocking the restoration ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma. Blocking the restoration ceremony on the grounds that there is a basis in something that was done is blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma. These, then, are one way of blocking the restoration ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma and one way in accordance with the Dharma.

What are the two ways not in accordance with the Dharma and the two ways of blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma? In whatever manner a monk blocks the restoration ceremony against a monk — blocking it without a basis in something done and without a basis in something not done — that is blocking the restoration ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma. Blocking it with a basis in something done and with a basis in something not done is blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

What are the three ways not in accordance with the Dharma and the three ways of blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma? In whatever manner a monk blocks the restoration ceremony against a monk — blocking it without a basis in something done, without a basis in something not done, and without a basis in something both done and not done — that is blocking the restoration ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma. Blocking it with a basis in something done, with a basis in something not done, and with a basis in something both done and not done is blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

What are the four ways not in accordance with the Dharma and the four ways of blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma? Blocking the restoration ceremony without a basis in any of the four — degeneration in moral discipline, degeneration in view, degeneration in conduct, and degeneration in livelihood — is blocking the restoration ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma. Blocking the restoration ceremony with a basis in the four — degeneration in moral discipline, degeneration in view, degeneration in conduct, and degeneration in livelihood — is blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

What are the five ways not in accordance with the Dharma and the five ways of blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma? Blocking the restoration ceremony without a basis in any of the five — a defeat, a Saṅgha remainder offense, a transgression, a confessable offense, and a wrong act — is blocking the restoration ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma. Blocking the restoration ceremony with a basis in any of the five — a defeat, a Saṅgha remainder offense, a transgression, a confessable offense, and a wrong act — is blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

What are the six ways not in accordance with the Dharma and the six ways of blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma? Blocking the restoration ceremony without a basis in something done where there is a remainder, without a basis in something not done where there is a remainder, without a basis in something both done and not done where there is a remainder, without a basis in something done where there is no remainder, without a basis in something not done where there is no remainder, and without a basis in something both done and not done where there is no remainder — that is blocking the restoration ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma. What are the six ways of blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma? Blocking it with a basis in something done where there is a remainder, with a basis in something not done where there is a remainder, with a basis in something both done and not done where there is a remainder, with a basis in something done where there is no remainder, with a basis in something not done where there is no remainder, and with a basis in something both done and not done where there is no remainder — that is blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

What are the seven ways not in accordance with the Dharma and the seven ways of blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma? Blocking the restoration ceremony without a basis in any of the seven — a defeat, a Saṅgha remainder offense, a transgression, a confessable offense, a wrong act, degeneration in view, and degeneration in livelihood — is blocking the restoration ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma.

Blocking the restoration ceremony with a basis in degeneration in livelihood is blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

What are the eight ways not in accordance with the Dharma and the eight ways of blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma? Blocking the restoration ceremony without a basis in degeneration in moral discipline, degeneration in conduct, degeneration in view, or having brought about degeneration in livelihood — and without a basis in degeneration in moral discipline, degeneration in view, degeneration in conduct, or not having brought about degeneration in livelihood — is blocking the restoration ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma. Blocking the restoration ceremony with a basis in degeneration in moral discipline, degeneration in conduct, degeneration in view, or having brought about degeneration in livelihood — and with a basis in degeneration in moral discipline, degeneration in view, degeneration in conduct, or not having brought about degeneration in livelihood — is blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

What are the nine ways not in accordance with the Dharma and the nine ways of blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma? Blocking the restoration ceremony without a basis in: something done where there is a remainder; something not done where there is a remainder; something both done and not done where there is a remainder; something done where there is no remainder; something not done where there is no remainder; something both done and not done where there is no remainder; something done where there is both a remainder and no remainder; something not done where there is both a remainder and no remainder; or something both done and not done where there is both a remainder and no remainder — is blocking the restoration ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma. Blocking the restoration ceremony with a basis in: something done where there is a remainder; something not done where there is a remainder; something both done and not done where there is a remainder; something done where there is no remainder; something not done where there is no remainder; something both done and not done where there is no remainder; something done where there is both a remainder and no remainder; something not done where there is both a remainder and no remainder; or something both done and not done where there is both a remainder and no remainder — is blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

What are the ten ways not in accordance with the Dharma and the ten ways of blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma? They are: he has committed a defeat; he has entered into discussion of a defeat; he has degenerated in moral discipline; he has degenerated in view; he has degenerated in conduct; he has degenerated in livelihood; he has relinquished the training; he has entered into discussion of relinquishing the training; he has incurred a liability to the Saṅgha; or he has entered into discussion of a liability to the Saṅgha.

As to how he has committed a defeat: whatever the aspect, whatever the manner, and whatever the characteristic mark by which a monk has incurred an offense involving defeat — when a monk is seen to have incurred an offense involving defeat by that same aspect, that same manner, and that same characteristic mark, then blocking the restoration ceremony on the basis of having so seen him is blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma. That is how he has committed a defeat.

As to how he has entered into discussion of a defeat: in whatever way — whether inside a monastic hall or outside it — when many monks are assembled and gathered together, he has entered into discussion of matters arising from that and in conformity with it, of that very nature; whether one has heard this from a believer or whether one has oneself formed a suspicion — blocking the restoration ceremony on the basis of having heard it or having formed that suspicion is blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

As to how he has degenerated in moral discipline: he has thoroughly transgressed any one of the four defeats.

As to how he has degenerated in view: he has come to hold and thoroughly adopted any one of the sixty-two views.

As to how he has degenerated in conduct: he engages in what ought not to be done and does not train in the trainings of a monk.

As to how he has degenerated in livelihood: his livelihood is thoroughly impure.

As to how he has returned the training: one sees a monk returning the training in such a form, in such a manner, and with such marks, and in that very form, that very manner, and those very marks one recognizes him as a monk — and having seen him thus, blocking the restoration ceremony on that basis is blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

As to how he has entered into discussion of matters relating to the return of the training: in whatever way — whether in the temple or outside the temple — monks have assembled and gathered, and he has entered into discussion of matters arising from that and in conformity with it, of that very nature; whether one has heard this from a believer or whether one has oneself formed a suspicion — blocking the restoration ceremony on the basis of having heard it or having formed that suspicion is blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

As to how he has imputed a grievance against the Saṅgha: one sees a monk reviling the Saṅgha in such a form, in such a manner, and with such marks — and having seen him thus reviling the Saṅgha in just such a form, just such a manner, and just such marks, blocking the restoration ceremony on that basis is blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

As to how he has entered into discussion of matters relating to a grievance imputed against the Saṅgha: in whatever way — whether in the temple or outside the temple — monks have assembled and gathered, and he has entered into discussion of matters arising from that and in conformity with it, of that very nature; whether one has heard this from a believer or whether one has oneself formed a suspicion — blocking the restoration ceremony on the basis of having heard it or having formed such a suspicion is blocking the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

The reversal of these ten things that accord with the Dharma is to be applied as not in accordance with the Dharma. The subject of blocking the restoration ceremony is complete.

In brief, as a verse:

One who has not completed a novice's years,
one of bad color, and likewise one who dwells there,
one who has not been appointed, and one who makes obeisance,
one seen in person, and one without food —

"Venerable Upāli, if novice monks enter the rains retreat in a brief manner, may they distribute sleeping places?" — "No." — "May they receive sleeping places?" — "Upāli, they may receive them."

"Venerable one, if those who have not completed their years enter the rains retreat in a brief manner, may they distribute sleeping places?" — "No." — "May they receive sleeping places?" — "Upāli, they may receive them."

"Venerable one, if one, two, three, or four monks enter the rains retreat, may they distribute sleeping places?" — "No." — "May they receive sleeping places?" — "Upāli, they may receive them."

"Upāli, if five or more monks are residing somewhere, they should make a request and appoint someone to distribute sleeping places; and let the one appointed distribute them."

"Venerable one, is there a case where using that very sleeping place would constitute an offense, and a case where using that very sleeping place would not?" — "Upāli, there is. If one uses a sleeping place that has not been rendered of bad color for a particular person, or if one uses an end-piece that is too long, that constitutes an offense. Using one belonging to the Saṅgha does not constitute an offense."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that a monk should not take a Saṅgha sleeping place to another location and use it there. If a monk seeks out a Saṅgha sleeping place and uses it at another location, what does that entail?" — "It is a transgression." — "Unless it happens that any one of the eight obstacles has arisen, and one is unable to protect the sleeping place in that very location, and one who has taken a vow not to remain in that location — in such cases there is no offense."

"Venerable one, may one who has not been appointed distribute sleeping places?" — "No."

"Venerable one, is there a case where a monk using that very Saṅgha sleeping place would constitute an offense,

and where using that very sleeping place would constitute no offense?" — "Upāli, there is such a case: if one wears it with the fur turned outward, that is an offense; if one lies down on it, there is no offense. If one wears it without a sweat-cloth, that is an offense; if one wears it with a sweat-cloth, there is no offense."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that one must not draw near to and remain in all places. Does it follow that one who has not drawn near should bow to an elder who has drawn near?" — "No, Upāli. All those who have drawn near must bow to those who have not drawn near. They are placed last among the monks."

"Venerable one, are those monks also given sleeping places last?" — "Upāli, those who have drawn near are given neither gains nor sleeping places."

"Venerable one, may a sleeping place be given to one who is not present? Give it to some and not to others? To whom should it be given?" — "Give it to one who has gone and will return. To whom should it not be given? Do not give it to one who has gone and will not return."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that a monk must not use Saṅgha property without a sweat-cloth. Is there a case where a monk uses Saṅgha property without a sweat-cloth and yet commits no offense?" — "Upāli, there is. This is when a householder has presented to the Saṅgha a servant or a share to be used without a sweat-cloth."

In brief:
Ānanda, and individuals,
and those who have drawn near, and those who are fitting,
and lastly, those residing during the rains,
and the writing of one-third — likewise;
householders and others,
and those who have given back their training — these are last.

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has said, 'Ānanda, you must distribute the surplus sleeping places.' What constitutes a surplus?" — "Whatever exceeds the allocation of one and of two."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that a monk must not use a Saṅgha sleeping place without a sweat-cloth. If a monk uses an individual's sleeping place, what does that entail?" — "It is a transgression."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has said: 'Monks who have just arrived and those who are resident should bow according to seniority.' Does it follow that one bows even to an elder monk who is inflicting a penalty?" — "No, Upāli." — "Why is that?" — "Upāli, one must not bow to all those for whom it is improper to bow — except in a case where there is bad feeling."

"Upāli, who are the individuals within the Saṅgha for whom it is improper to bow? One against whom a censure act has been carried out; one against whom a degradation act has been carried out; one against whom a banishment act has been carried out; one against whom a reconciliation act has been carried out; one against whom an act of suspension for not seeing a fault has been carried out; one against whom an act of suspension for not redressing a transgression has been carried out; one against whom an act of suspension for not relinquishing a wrong view has been carried out; one who inflicts a penalty; one who inflicts a penalty by rising from the seat; one who is accompanied by those inflicting a penalty; one who engages in conduct requiring appeasement; one who engages in conduct requiring appeasement by rising from the seat; a layman; a eunuch; one who has expelled a nun; one who has killed his father; one who has killed his mother; one who has killed an arhat; one who, with malicious intent, has drawn blood from a Tathāgata; a tīrthika; one who has gone over to the tīrthikas; a corrupter; one who is not a resident; one who lives apart; one who has previously committed an offense; one who was previously in dispute; one who has drawn near; one who has given back the training; a fully ordained nun; a probationer nun; a novice nun; a novice monk; and one who is very young — do not bow to these. One must not bow to a person who is defecating; one who is defecating must not bow. One must not bow to a person who is urinating; one who is urinating must not bow. One must not bow to a person chewing a tooth-wood; one who is chewing a tooth-wood must not bow. One must not bow to a person who is eating;

one who is eating must not bow. One must not bow to a person who is drinking; one who is drinking must not bow. One must not bow to a person who is hungry; one who is hungry must not bow. One must not bow to a person wearing only a single garment; one wearing only a single garment must not bow. One must not bow to a person sitting in the dark; one sitting in the dark must not bow. One must not bow to a person sitting in discomfort; one sitting in discomfort must not bow. One must not bow to a person engaged in reciting scripture, in reflection, or in listening to Dharma; one engaged in reciting scripture, in reflection, or in listening to Dharma must not bow. One must not bow to a person who is distracted. One must not bow to a person who has entered a household. These are the individuals to whom it is not fitting to bow.

Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk who sits or lies down on a seat or bench belonging to the Saṅgha does not incur an offense? Upāli, there is: when it is improper to do otherwise, when one sits or lies down there — that which monks may not properly use.

Venerable one, when the Blessed One said that a monk who carries out a penalty shall be placed last among the monks, is that so? Upāli, it is not so — he is placed there gradually.

Venerable one, when the Blessed One said, "Give the sleeping mat first to those who have not yet entered the rains retreat and to those who are dwelling according to their natural seniority, and thereafter to those who have renounced," if more mats then remain, are they given together with those who are dwelling by natural seniority? Upāli, they are not given; they are given separately.

Venerable one, is there a case in which a monk who takes a sleeping mat from one of the four residences does not incur an offense? Upāli, there is: when a monk has marked the boundaries of the four residences with a stake, mud, or a peg, and has properly entered the rains retreat.

Venerable one, when the Blessed One said, "Give novices a third of the gains," does that also apply to sleeping mats? Upāli, it does not — they are to be given an equal share.

Venerable one, when the Blessed One said, "Let the newly ordained monks not take sleeping mats before the senior monks," is there a case in which a young monk who takes a sleeping mat before a senior monk does not incur an offense? Upāli, there is: one who has received the Saṅgha's permission for a residence, one who has received permission as an attendant, and one who has fled and come from a place of danger.

Venerable one, may a layman be appointed to arrange the sleeping mats? Upāli, he may not. Likewise, from a probationer nun up through one who has been given the training — may any of them be appointed to arrange the sleeping mats in an extensive manner? Upāli, they may not. Venerable one, may a madman be appointed to arrange the sleeping mats? Upāli, he may not. Likewise, this applies also to one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, and one who is deaf.

Venerable one, may those dwelling in another destination be appointed to arrange the sleeping mats? Upāli, they may not. Venerable one, may a hermaphrodite be given a sleeping mat? Upāli, he may not. Likewise, from a suspended nun through one previously in dispute — may sleeping mats be given to these? Upāli, they may not.

Venerable one, may sleeping mats be given to one who has divided the Saṅgha and to one who has been given the training? Upāli, they may be given. Venerable one, may a sleeping mat be given to a madman? Upāli, if he does not use it as it ought to be used, do not give it. Likewise, this should be said also of one whose mind is disturbed, one afflicted by illness, one who is dull-witted, one who is mute, and one who is deaf.

Venerable one, if the night passes while a monk has been appointed to arrange sleeping mats, is he still called "appointed"? Upāli, he is still called "appointed." Does he then distribute the sleeping mats? Upāli, he does not.

This concludes the section on sleeping mats.

The Vinaya Pitaka. The twenty-first fascicle. In brief.

Done thrice, the gravitas,
and likewise the mark of full quiescence —
the direct perceptions of the restoration ceremonies,
and the occurrences as well are just the same.

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, possessing how many qualities of gravitas is a holder of the Vinaya able to quell disputes?"

Upāli, eleven. And what are the eleven? He knows a dispute. He knows from what a dispute has arisen. He knows how to summarize a dispute. He knows how to quell a dispute. He knows how to quell a dispute so thoroughly that it does not arise again afterward. He knows what has arisen. He knows what has been established. He knows what has been subsequently established. He knows what has been blocked. He knows what has been expressly permitted. He knows what actions have been done and what have not been done. Upāli, a person of gravitas endowed with these eleven qualities is one who, as a holder of the Vinaya, is able to quell disputes.

Furthermore, another eleven qualities. And what are the eleven? He knows an offense. He knows a non-offense. He knows a grave offense. He knows a light offense. He knows how an offense has arisen. He knows from what an offense has arisen. He does not go astray out of desire. He does not go astray out of aversion, fear, or delusion. He knows what punitive actions are to be done and what are not to be done. Upāli, these eleven are an elaboration up to the point of quelling.

Furthermore, another eleven qualities up to that point. And what are the eleven? He is learned in the sūtras. He is learned in the Vinaya. He is learned in the analysis. He is versed in scripture. He is one who opens up the sūtras. He does not hold to mistakes. He does not hold to secret words. He holds without fail to what is certain. He does not hold to many words. He holds to what has been agreed upon. He refutes up to three times. Upāli, a person of gravitas endowed with these eleven qualities is one who, as a holder of the Vinaya, is able to quell disputes.

"Venerable one, does one endowed with these qualities thoroughly quell a dispute?"

Upāli, twenty-one. And what are the twenty-one? He gives instructions to the Saṅgha. He accords with the Dharma and is in harmony with the Victor's teaching. He makes the monks of both sides understand. He proceeds in accordance with the Dharma toward monks who argue and monks who counter-argue, and he ensures that monks who argue and counter-argue do not violate the Vinaya. He does not cover up the offense of an impure person. He does not distort what has arisen. He does not distort what has been established. He does not distort what has been subsequently established. He does not distort what has been blocked. He does not distort what has been expressly permitted. He does not distort an offense. He holds very firmly to the commitment of the arguing monk. He holds very firmly to the commitment of the replying monk. He also teaches the words of the sūtras. He accords with the Vinaya. He follows the eye of the Dharma. Having been appointed, he quells the matter. He points out the offense. He applies the punitive action that is called for. He shows the way to purification. He quells the dispute by means of the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher's teaching. Upāli, one who is endowed with these twenty-one qualities is said to quell disputes.

"Venerable one, if a monk who is arguing or counter-arguing has changed his affiliation, is the dispute said to be quelled?"

Upāli, it is said to be quelled.

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that when a dispute arises, immediately upon its arising one should quell it by means of the seven Dharmas for quelling disputes.
