Venerable one, if any one of the four kinds of dispute arises — when a dispute has arisen — is it possible that without quelling it by means of whichever of the seven Dharmas for quelling disputes is the appropriate one for quelling it, it is nonetheless quelled?"

Upāli, there is such a case: it is the consensual restoration ceremony (poṣadha).

"Venerable one, if any one of the four kinds of dispute —

when a dispute arises, whose words among the monks who bring the charge and the monks who respond to the charge should be taken? One takes according to seniority of ordination.

"Venerable one, if their years of ordination are equal, whose words should be taken?" Whichever of them is more learned.

"Venerable one, if both are equally grounded in the texts, whose words should be taken?" Whichever of them is of purer conduct.

"If both are of pure conduct, whose words should be taken?" Whichever of them is more substantially pure of conduct — and by that person's words the disputes should be quelled.

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that when a dispute is to be quelled by means of many voting sticks, if one side gains even a single voting stick more, the dispute should be quelled in favor of that side. Venerable one, if the voting sticks of both sides turn out to be equal, by whose authority is the dispute quelled?" Upāli, whichever side has the greater majority of monks of purer conduct.

"Venerable one, if monks are unable to quell a dispute among monks, may nuns quell it?" Upāli, they may. And likewise the five groups should each be applied to the others in turn.

In brief:

By messenger, letter, gesture,
by hearsay and by transmission from one to another,
by the mad, the disturbed, the sick,
by the dull-witted, laypeople, and the like —
the giving of the training is the last.

"Venerable one, if a dispute has been quelled by means of a messenger, is it said to be quelled?" Upāli, it is called quelled, and the Saṅgha's act has been performed. Likewise if it has been quelled by means of a letter, or a gesture, or hearsay, or transmission from one to another — is it called quelled? Upāli, it is called quelled, and the Saṅgha's act has been performed.

"Venerable one, if a madman has quelled a dispute, is the dispute said to be quelled?" Upāli, it is called quelled, and the Saṅgha's act has been performed. Likewise, if it has been quelled by one who is mentally disturbed, by one afflicted by illness, by one who is dull, by one who is mute, or by one who is deaf — is it called quelled? Upāli, it is called quelled, and the Saṅgha's act has been performed.

"Venerable one, if a layman has quelled a dispute, is it called quelled?" Upāli, it is called quelled, and the Saṅgha's act has been performed.

"Venerable one, likewise from the intermediate beings down to those upon whom the training has been bestowed — if these have quelled a dispute in full, is it called quelled?" Upāli, it is called quelled, and the Saṅgha's act has been performed.

"Venerable one, if the one who brought the charge or the one who responded to the charge acted at an improper time, is the dispute said to be quelled?" Upāli, it is called quelled. Likewise, from the case of one accepted as a layman down to the case of one duly accepted as a recipient of the training — if one who has been fully accepted in this way has quelled a dispute, is it called quelled? Upāli, it is called quelled.

"Venerable one, if a monk who brought the charge or responded to the charge has changed his name, is the dispute said to be quelled?" Upāli, it is called quelled.

The section on the substance of disputes is complete.

In brief:

Schism, uproar in the Saṅgha,
separation, proper procedure,
kalpas, wrongdoing and perversion,
schism of the Saṅgha, and the unskilled.

"Venerable one, one speaks also of the Saṅgha being split, and one speaks also of the Saṅgha being assembled. Venerable one, what is the splitting of the Saṅgha?" Upāli, when one who creates a schism perceives what is not Dharma as not Dharma, and perceives what is not Vinaya as not Vinaya — yet that person suppresses this perception, suppresses assent, suppresses confidence — and with intelligence

and views and thoughts suppressed — and then declares, "This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is what the Teacher taught" — and having said this, he instructs the monks, properly instructs them, trains them, and leads them to accept it, and he carries out and follows the five bases of the rules of conduct; and those among you, venerable ones, who have faith and acceptance and conviction in him — let them take the wooden rule; let them proclaim the five bases of the rules of conduct and make the formal motion; and having properly enacted the wooden rule, he leads away a great many — this is called a splitting of the Saṅgha.

What is the assembling of the Saṅgha? However many monks are dwelling within the boundary, when they are performing an act, all of them have come together, have come into each other's presence, and those from whom acceptance is to be received have given their acceptance; and the monks are without quarrel, without dispute; they perceive things as Dharma, they perceive them as Vinaya, and they perform the restoration ceremony — this is called the assembling of the Saṅgha.

Venerable one, when one splits the Saṅgha, what is it that constitutes an unpardonable wrongdoing and becomes an act of immediate retribution?

Upāli, when one who creates a schism perceives what is not Dharma as not Dharma — and with respect to the schism also perceives it as not Dharma — yet suppresses this perception, suppresses assent, suppresses faith, suppresses intelligence, suppresses views and thoughts, and then declares, "This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is what the Teacher taught" — and having said this, he instructs the monks, properly instructs them, trains them, and leads them to accept it, and he carries out and proclaims the five bases of the rules of conduct — when this schism-maker proclaims the five bases of the rules of conduct and makes the formal motion, properly enacts the wooden rule, and leads away a great many — this is indeed a splitting of the Saṅgha. An unpardonable wrongdoing is incurred, and by properly instructing others, by accepting and leading them to receive it, it further becomes an act of immediate retribution.

When one splits the Saṅgha, what is it that constitutes an unpardonable wrongdoing yet does not become an act of immediate retribution?

Upāli, when one who creates a schism perceives what is not Dharma as not Dharma, and with respect to the schism also perceives it as Dharma; or perceives what is not Dharma as not Dharma, and with respect to the schism also perceives it as not Dharma; or perceives what is not Dharma as not Dharma, and with respect to the schism is uncertain; or perceives what is not Dharma as Dharma, and with respect to the schism perceives it as not Dharma; or perceives what is not Dharma as Dharma, and with respect to the schism also perceives it as Dharma; or perceives what is not Dharma as Dharma, and with respect to the schism is uncertain; or perceives what is Dharma as Dharma, and with respect to the schism perceives it as not Dharma; or perceives what is Dharma as not Dharma, and with respect to the schism perceives it as Dharma; or perceives what is Dharma as not Dharma, and with respect to the schism is uncertain; or perceives what is Dharma as not Dharma, and with respect to the schism also perceives it as not Dharma; or perceives what is Dharma as not Dharma, and with respect to the schism perceives it as Dharma; or perceives what is Dharma as not Dharma, and with respect to the schism is uncertain; or is uncertain about both Dharma and what is not Dharma, and with respect to the schism perceives it as not Dharma; or is uncertain about what is not Dharma, and with respect to the schism perceives it as Dharma; or is uncertain about what is not Dharma, and with respect to the schism is also uncertain; or is uncertain about Dharma, and with respect to the schism perceives it as not Dharma; or is uncertain about Dharma, and with respect to the schism perceives it as Dharma; or is uncertain about Dharma, and with respect to the schism is also uncertain — and suppresses this perception, suppresses assent, suppresses faith, suppresses intelligence, suppresses views and

thoughts — and having suppressed these thoughts, says the following: "This is Dharma. This is Vinaya. This is what the Teacher taught." And then he instructs the monks, properly instructs them, trains them, and draws them in toward it. Striving in this way for the sake of splitting the Saṅgha — that is what causes a schism in the Saṅgha. An offense without remainder is incurred, yet it does not become an act without interval.

"Venerable one, does it follow that in every case where the Saṅgha is split there is also a Saṅgha in dispute? There is splitting of the Saṅgha without a Saṅgha dispute; there is a Saṅgha dispute that does not lead to a split; there is both a split and a dispute; and there is neither a split nor a dispute.

"What is splitting without a dispute? It is when one splits the Saṅgha while perceiving it as Dharma. What is a dispute without a split? It is when any one of the fourteen matters giving rise to schism has been firmly and definitively taken hold of, yet the Saṅgha has not been divided. What is both a split and a dispute? It is when the Saṅgha has been divided and any one of the fourteen matters giving rise to schism has been firmly and definitively taken hold of. What is neither a split nor a dispute? It is all cases other than these.

"Venerable one, does it follow that in every case where the Saṅgha is split there is also a differentiated Saṅgha? There is a differentiated Saṅgha that does not entail a split; there is a split that does not result in a differentiated Saṅgha; there is both a split and a differentiated Saṅgha; and there is neither a split nor a differentiated Saṅgha.

"What is a differentiated Saṅgha without a split? It is when the two sections of the Saṅgha abide in separate localities, with separate support, separate dwelling, and separate boundaries, yet the Saṅgha has not been divided. What is a split without a differentiated Saṅgha? It is when one splits the Saṅgha while perceiving it as Dharma. What is both a split and a differentiated Saṅgha? It is when the Saṅgha has been divided and the two sections abide separately in their own localities, with separate support, separate dwelling, and separate boundaries. What is neither a split nor a differentiated Saṅgha? It is all cases other than these.

"Just as four cases arise in connection with a differentiated Saṅgha, so too four cases should be stated in connection with the conduct of the Saṅgha.

"Venerable one, does it follow that those who perform the act of schism in the Saṅgha remain thus for an aeon? There are those who have caused a Saṅgha schism yet do not remain for an aeon; there are those who remain for an aeon yet have not caused a Saṅgha schism; there are those who have caused a Saṅgha schism and remain for an aeon; and there are those who have neither caused a Saṅgha schism nor remain for an aeon.

"Those who have caused a Saṅgha schism yet do not remain for an aeon are those who have divided the Saṅgha while perceiving it as Dharma. Those who remain for an aeon yet have not caused a Saṅgha schism are the elephant king Airāvaṇa, the elephant king Most Steadfast, the elephant king Pleasing, the elephant king Yama, and the gods of the Brahma heaven who are Brahmā's close helpers. Those who have divided the Saṅgha and remain for an aeon are Devadatta. Those who have neither divided the Saṅgha nor remain for an aeon are all cases other than these.

"When the Saṅgha has been split by such an act, the offense of remaining for an aeon is likewise to be stated in four cases, and these too are to be distinguished in the same way."

"Are all those who have performed the act of dividing the Saṅgha necessarily destined to fall into the lower realms? No — there are those who divide the Saṅgha yet are not destined to fall, those who are destined to fall yet do not divide the Saṅgha, those who both divide the Saṅgha and are destined to fall, and those who neither divide the Saṅgha nor are destined to fall. One who divides the Saṅgha yet is not destined to fall is one who divides the Saṅgha believing it to be Dharma. One who is destined to fall yet does not divide the Saṅgha is one who has committed one of the four acts of immediate retribution. One who both divides the Saṅgha and is destined to fall is Devadatta. One who neither divides the Saṅgha nor is destined to fall is anyone not falling into these categories.

"Are all those who have performed the act of dividing the Saṅgha unskilled and ignorant? No — there are those who divide the Saṅgha yet are neither unskilled nor ignorant, those who are unskilled and ignorant yet do not divide the Saṅgha, those who divide the Saṅgha and are unskilled and ignorant, and those who neither divide the Saṅgha nor are unskilled nor ignorant. One who divides the Saṅgha yet is neither unskilled nor ignorant is one who divides the Saṅgha believing it to be Dharma. One who is unskilled and ignorant yet does not divide the Saṅgha is the six teachers. One who divides the Saṅgha and is unskilled and ignorant is Devadatta. One who neither divides the Saṅgha nor is unskilled nor ignorant is anyone not falling into these categories."

In brief, the division is made in six aspects:
The challenger in four cases, the restoration ceremony,
The four cases of immediacy, a third of the same,
Remaining for an aeon or not — likewise —
Then those such as householders and so on,
And lastly those who have relinquished the training.

"Venerable Upāli, what possesses the quality of schism? What is a fault? Schism in the Saṅgha possesses the quality of division. Creating the schism is the fault."

"Venerable one, if the Saṅgha is divided, into what does one fall? One falls into a grave offense."

"Venerable one, if the Saṅgha is divided, what transgression is to be confessed? A grave offense."

"Venerable one, monks can divide the monks' Saṅgha, but not nuns, not probationary nuns, not novice nuns, not novice monks — is that so?" "Upāli, that is so. Monks can divide the Saṅgha, but not nuns, not probationary nuns, not novice nuns, not novice monks."

"Upāli, likewise nuns can divide the nuns' Saṅgha, but not monks, not probationary nuns, not novice nuns, not novice monks — yet they do strive to bring about a schism."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that the Saṅgha is divided in two ways: by proclamation and by taking up the procedural staff. Now, venerable one, if someone who is seeking amusement or not seeking it makes a proclamation and takes up the procedural staff, is that called dividing the Saṅgha?" "Upāli, it is not." "Then what is it?" "It is an offense."

"If a monk who is dividing the Saṅgha changes his precept category while in the act of dividing it, is that called dividing the Saṅgha?" "Upāli, it is not."

"Venerable one, if the nuns' Saṅgha has been split and abides in two factions on opposite sides, and a nun requests instruction every fortnight, should that be given?" "Upāli, without giving it, say this: 'Sisters, be harmonious with one another.'"

"Venerable one, if the monks' Saṅgha has been split and abides in two factions on opposite sides, may a nun request instruction every fortnight?" "Upāli, she may request it." "From whom should she request it?" "From those who have not yet taken sides."

"Venerable one, if the monks' Saṅgha has been split and abides in two factions on opposite sides, should the instruction be given to nuns?" "Upāli, it should be given, so that nuns too will not cause a split."

"Venerable one, if the nuns' Saṅgha has been split and abides in two factions on opposite sides, who should give instruction to the nuns?" "Those who have not yet taken sides should give it."

"Venerable one, if the monks' Saṅgha has been split and abides in two factions on opposite sides, should nuns perform the restoration ceremony?" "Upāli, they should."

"Venerable one, if the monks' Saṅgha has been split and abides in two factions on opposite sides, should the monks who have taken sides perform the restoration ceremony?" "Upāli, they should not." "For what reason?" "The restoration ceremony is to be performed by an assembled Saṅgha."

"Venerable one, if those who have taken sides break the boundary of those who have not taken sides, is that called breaking a boundary?" "Upāli, it is not."

"Venerable one, if those who have not taken sides break the boundary of those who have taken sides, is that called breaking a boundary?" "It is called breaking a boundary."

"Venerable one, if some of those who have taken sides abide separately, each on their own — is that so stated?" "It is stated in full in four modes."

"Venerable one, if some have taken sides and all of them do not abide — is that so stated?" "It is stated in full in four modes."

"Venerable one, if some abide separately each on their own, and all of them do not abide — is that so stated?" "It is stated in full in four modes."

"Venerable one, if the Blessed One has said that one should seek out even a fragment of iron shattered into a hundred pieces, what does 'a fragment of iron' mean?" "One should seek out faith, one should seek out conviction, one should seek out reconciliation, and one should seek out an assembled Saṅgha — but one should not seek it out for the sake of dividing the Saṅgha."

"Venerable one, if the Saṅgha has been split and abides in two factions on opposite sides, by whom should the resolution be raised?" "By those who have not taken sides."

"Venerable one, if a paṇḍaka splits the Saṅgha, is that called a split?" "Upāli, it is not."

"Venerable one, likewise, beginning from the expulsion of a nun down to the giving of the training — if throughout all of that they split the Saṅgha, is that called a split?" "Upāli, it is not."

"Venerable one, if a madman splits the Saṅgha, is that called a split?" "Upāli, it is not."

"Venerable one, likewise, if those who are mentally disturbed, tormented by illness, deranged, mute, or paralyzed split the Saṅgha, is that called a split?" "Upāli, it is not." "For what reason?" "Upāli, one who does not abide in a natural state of mind is unable to split the Saṅgha." Just as is said of one who splits the Saṅgha, so too it should be stated that they do not count in the same way.

The chapter on the substance of schism in the Saṅgha is complete. The questions of Upāli are complete.

In brief: Supriya, Vajrasaṃjñā, the female buffalo, the female camel, the female yak, the mare, the female deer, the female donkey, the female sheep, the female dog, and the female pig.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling in Vaiśālī, in the Gabled Hall beside the Monkey Pool. Supriya, son of Kalandaka, had not had a rule of training laid down for him, and so when there is no offence for a first offender, he began to wonder: "When the training had not yet been laid down, and I on many occasions engaged in sexual misconduct — what was my first such act?" Doubt arose in his mind, and from it came apprehension and remorse. He spoke of his condition to the monks, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, before the rule of training had been laid down, all acts of Supriya, son of Kalandaka, that had already passed — all of those were first offences.

There is no offence for a first offender. The monk known as Vajraputra did not formally relinquish his training, and without confessing a lapse in his training he became a layman. Having then engaged in sexual misconduct, the act of intercourse, he thought to himself: "For now, let me ask the monks whether I am eligible to go forth and receive full ordination — if I am, I will go forth; if I am not, I will simply remain as I am." Thinking this, he reported everything that had happened, from beginning to the declaration of the Blessed One, in full detail. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, one who has not relinquished his training and not confessed a lapse in his training, and who has then taken on the status of a layman and engaged in sexual misconduct, the act of intercourse — such a person is no longer eligible to go forth and receive full ordination again. Accordingly, the case of training is to be explained in full." Furthermore, the Blessed One declared: "Whatever monk, without having relinquished his training and without having confessed a lapse in his training, engages in sexual misconduct, the act of intercourse — that monk too has incurred a defeat and must not remain in the community."

A certain monk was dwelling alone in a hermitage. Not far from there, a female yak gave birth, and from that female yak a calf was born. The mother went off in search of food, and the monk took some grass and gave it to the calf, and poured water for it. As he sat there, he saw the calf's female parts, and seeing them he became attached and penetrated her. He then felt shame, and he thought: "I wonder whether I have incurred an offence of defeat." Doubt arose in him, and he reported what had happened in full to the monks. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, since there was no contact, there is no offence of defeat, but a grave offence does arise."

When the calf of the female yak had grown large, the monk saw her female parts; seeing them he became attached, and intending to penetrate her he inserted his member into her opening. She gave him a slight kick and he became frightened. He thought: "I wonder if I have not incurred an offence of defeat." He reported everything in full detail. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, since when she was frightened there was no attachment on his part, there is no offence of defeat, but a grave offence does arise."

Just as in the case of a female yak, so too is it with a female camel, a female mare, a female deer, a female donkey, a female sheep, a female dog, and a female pig.

In brief:

One who has become insane, one whose mind is disturbed,
one tormented by illness, those who are human,
one who mistakes what is not the path for the path —
these three cases have been clearly proclaimed.

Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that there is no offence for one who is insane. How much insanity qualifies one as insane? One becomes insane by five means: the exhaustion of one's kinsmen and friends; the exhaustion of one's enjoyments; the exhaustion of one's wealth; the imbalance of the bodily elements; and being afflicted by non-human beings; and the karmic maturation of past karma. By these five means one becomes insane. If one knows that it is the property of a monk, the matter stands as it is. If one does not know that it is the property of a monk, there is no offence for the insane person.

Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that there is no offence for one whose mind is disturbed. How much disturbance qualifies one as having a disturbed mind? One is said to have a disturbed mind by five means: a non-human being disturbs that person's mind; a non-human being afflicts that person; a non-human being steals that person's vitality; imbalance of the bodily elements; and the karmic maturation of past karma. By these five means one is said to have a disturbed mind — and this is to be explained in full.

Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that there is no offence for one tormented by illness. How much illness qualifies one as being tormented by illness?

One is said to be tormented by illness by five means: disturbance by wind, by bile, by phlegm, by a combination of these, and by a change of season. These five means constitute being tormented by illness.

A monk, perceiving a path where there is no path, engaged in unchaste conduct — the act of sexual intercourse. That monk then wondered whether a defeat offense had arisen for him, and, with doubt having arisen, he related in full what had occurred. The Blessed One declared: If one perceives a path where there is no path, it is a defeat. If one perceives a path where there is no path with doubt, it is also a defeat. If one perceives what is not a path as a path, it is a grave offense. If one has doubt about what is not a path, it is a grave offense. The three paths are the defecation passage, the urination passage, and the mouth.

If a monk inserts the tip of his member beyond the foreskin into the urination passage, it is a defeat. If a monk inserts the tip of his member beyond the buttocks into the defecation passage, it is a defeat. If a monk inserts his member beyond the teeth into the mouth, it is a defeat.

In brief:

The female monkey, the lioness, the female crane,
the peahen, and the domestic hen — likewise these.
Longmark and Backdoor-Kin,
Nandikā, and the two orifices.

The four grave offenses are: the female monkey, Longmark — these are as they arise in their full analysis. The Blessed One declared: it is a defeat. Backdoor-Kin is also a defeat. Regarding Nandikā, the training is given as set forth in the Vinaya.

A monk, sitting without cover, was bathing naked. Four men were attending him, and through contact with his body his male member became functional, with attachment pervading it. Another monk who happened to be sitting before him took that monk's member into his own mouth, and that monk also bent his body and emitted semen. That monk, with doubt having arisen, wondered whether a defeat offense had arisen for him. He related the matter in full from what had occurred up to the declaration of the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: there is no defeat offense in this. However, whether standing or sitting without cover, one should not allow what another does to be taken as one's own doing.

A monk was tormented by attachment pervading him entirely. He had a fellow monk who was his close friend. He went to that friend and said: "Venerable one, I am overwhelmed and tormented by attachment." The other said: "Go and engage in unchaste conduct," and he indeed went and engaged in unchaste conduct. Doubt then arose in him about whether a defeat offense had arisen for him, since he had been instructed. The Blessed One declared: there is no defeat offense, but it is a grave offense.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable one, how should a grave offense be confessed? Upāli, there are four kinds of grave offense: the heavy kind arising from a defeat, the light kind arising from a defeat, the heavy kind arising from a Saṅgha remainder offense, and the light kind arising from a Saṅgha remainder offense. Upāli, a heavy grave offense arising from a defeat is to be confessed before the entire Saṅgha within the boundary. A light one arising from a defeat is to be confessed before four monks outside the boundary. A heavy grave offense arising from a Saṅgha remainder offense is to be confessed before four monks outside the boundary. A light one arising from a Saṅgha remainder offense is to be confessed before a single monk within the boundary.

In brief:

One who has become functional, the mother, and the charnel-ground dwellers,
Odbzang and Bzangskyes,
the supremely good one who plunges in,
and the one called Rab-tu-bzang.

A monk who, without having been restrained, lay down, and another monk tormented and utterly oppressed by attachment was sitting in front of him, placed his male organ into that monk's mouth, and the monk, having bent his body, drew out the seminal fluid — and then that monk arose in doubt, wondering whether a defeat had come upon him or not. The Blessed One declared: "A defeat has not occurred; however, from this time forward a monk must not lie down without being restrained. If he does so, it will become an offense requiring confession."

A monk, while his male organ was erect and functional, thought to himself that even if he were to insert it into a woman's organ it would not become an offense. He then inserted it into a woman's organ, and arose in doubt, wondering whether a defeat had come upon him or not. The Blessed One declared: "The moment of insertion, it becomes a defeat."

A monk was completely covered and tormented by attachment, and went to his mother and said to her: "I am tormented, oppressed by attachment that pervades me entirely." The mother replied: "Son, you came forth from this very place — let it return to this very place." He, thinking to insert it there, placed it at the wound, but then he felt shame, and that monk arose in doubt, wondering whether a defeat had come upon him or not. The Blessed One declared: "Because of the shame, there was no attachment, and so there is no defeat; however, it will become a grave offense."

A monk went to a charnel ground to examine a human corpse, and there he saw the corpse of a woman that had been cast away still adorned with ornaments. Upon seeing it, a state of attachment arose in him. Thinking to insert into it, he placed himself at the wound, but the inside was filled with worms. That monk arose in doubt, wondering whether a defeat had come upon him or not. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, that transgression is of two kinds: inner transgression and outer transgression. A defeat has not occurred, but it will become a grave offense."

A laywoman by the name of Ödzangmo died in the evening and was cast into the charnel ground still adorned with her ornaments. A monk who had gone to the charnel ground to examine a human corpse saw her, and a state of attachment arose in him toward her. Thinking to insert into her, he placed himself at the wound — and she then rose up and sat upright, and that monk was filled with terror. He arose in doubt, wondering whether a defeat had come upon him or not. The Blessed One declared: "Because of the terror, there was no attachment, and so there is no defeat; however, it will become a grave offense."

The wife of a householder named Bzangskyes was walking near his village, and a monk who was there went to her and said to her: "The householder's wife is tormented, oppressed by attachment." She replied: "Thrust in from below and release the seminal fluid from above; thrust in from above and release the seminal fluid from below." And she said that she herself did not know how to engage in unchaste conduct. He, for his part, thought: "This is good, this is excellent, this is fitting and proper." He thrust in from below and released the seminal fluid from above, and that monk arose in doubt. The Blessed One declared: "The moment of insertion, it becomes a defeat."

The narrative occasion of Śintubzangmo is as it appears in the full analysis of the Vinaya.

A monk named Rabtubzang was dwelling alone in a solitary hermitage. Not far from there was a brahmin's field, and he observed that the brahmin came there regularly.

Upon seeing him, faith arose in the brahmin. He invited the monk to a meal, and the monk accepted. The next morning the brahmin prepared food in advance and sent a small girl to summon the monk. The monk caught sight of the girl's genitals. Upon seeing them, attachment arose in him, and he performed the act. When the girl's genitals were torn, doubt arose in him. The Blessed One declared: "If pleasure is felt through unchaste conduct, it becomes a defeat. If no pleasure is felt, it becomes a grave offence."

In brief, what is unfit to receive does not apply to the sleeping, the pressed down, the mad, the afflicted by disease, the unwilling, males, and those of indeterminate sex.

A monk whose male organ is by nature unfit to receive — if it is inserted into one that is fit to receive, it becomes a defeat offence. Thinking that if it is inserted into one unfit to receive, no offence would result, he inserted it while it was not erect. Doubt arose, and the Blessed One declared: "There is no defeat offence, but it becomes a grave offence."

A monk performed the act with a sleeping woman, and doubt arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: "If hand meets hand, foot meets foot, thigh meets thigh, and body presses against body, it becomes a defeat. If there is no such contact, it becomes a grave offence." Exactly as with the sleeping woman, so too with the mad, the disease-afflicted, and the unwilling. Just as it is stated in four ways with respect to a woman, so too it is the same with respect to males and those of indeterminate sex.

The Vinaya: the Noble Fundamental Text, the twenty-second fascicle.

In brief: the four modes, the fifth, all actions, and the sleeping woman, performed once and a third time, woman, man, and one of indeterminate sex.

A woman performed the act with a sleeping monk, and remorse arose in him. The Blessed One declared: "O monk, did you feel pleasure?" He replied: "I felt pleasure." The Blessed One declared: "Did you know?" He said: "I was not aware of it; I had only moved slightly." The Blessed One declared: "For a monk who was sleeping and merely moved slightly, there is no defeat offence, but it becomes a grave offence."

A monk was sleeping and a woman performed the act with him, and remorse arose in him. The Blessed One declared: "O monk, did you feel pleasure?" He replied: "I did not feel pleasure." The Blessed One declared: "If no pleasure was felt, there is no offence."

A monk was lying down and sitting up when a woman performed the act with him, and remorse arose in him. The Blessed One declared: "O monk, did you know?" He replied: "I was not aware." The Blessed One declared: "If there was no awareness, there is no offence."

A monk who was lying down and then sitting up when a woman performed the act with him, and remorse arose in him. The Blessed One declared: "O monk, did you know, or did you feel pleasure?" He replied: "I was not aware, and I did not feel pleasure." The Blessed One declared: "Where there is no awareness and no pleasure felt, there is no offence."

What applies to a monk applies equally to a nun (bhikṣuṇī), a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā), a female novice (śrāmaṇerikā), and a male novice (śrāmaṇera).

Three evil ascetics said: "Even if one seizes a woman and performs the act throughout the journey, no offence will result," and they did so throughout the journey. Doubt arose in them, and the Blessed One declared: "The moment of insertion, it becomes a defeat." What applies to a woman applies in the same way to all men and those of indeterminate sex.

In brief: woman, man, and one of indeterminate sex,

expelled for sensing pleasure, no offence;
three for the wilderness, five for the renunciant.

A woman performed the act upon a monk who was asleep. When that monk arose with remorse, the Blessed One declared: "Monk, did you know?" He replied: "I did not notice, Lord." The Blessed One declared: "For one who did not know, there is no offence."

What applies to a woman applies in the same way to a man and to one of indeterminate sex.

An evil monk of a forest dwelling deceived a female trainee and said to her: "Since you have not received full ordination, if unchaste conduct is performed, no offence will result for either of us." She consented. Having consented, she then felt remorse; yet he performed the act without her assent, and the female trainee felt remorse thinking: "Perhaps I have not become disqualified as a female trainee." The Blessed One declared: "The training has been broken; let it be restored. It becomes a transgression."

An evil monk of the forest dwelling deceived a male novice, saying: "Since you have not received full ordination, even if unchaste conduct is performed it will not result in an offence for either of us." And at length the Blessed One declared: "It becomes a transgression for the male novice." What applies to the male novice applies in the same way to the female novice.

An evil nun of a forest dwelling said to one whose time had not yet come: "You have already received full ordination; it will not be long now — even if unchaste conduct is performed, no offence will result for us." That one consented. Having consented, she then felt remorse again; yet he performed the act upon her without her assent, and that monk felt remorse thinking: "Perhaps the offence of defeat has not arisen for me." The Blessed One declared: "For one who does not experience pleasure, there is no defeat; yet it becomes a grave offence."

A monk performed the act upon a monk who was asleep. If that sleeping monk did not know at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end, the monk who performed the act should be dealt with as unfit. The full detail is as it appears in the Vinaya analysis.

In brief:

Fourth: an image, a female nāga,
a female yakṣa, a goddess, a female gandharva,
a female asura, a female hungry ghost, a cannibal ogress —
these too are the same.

A monk made a wooden image — well-formed, pleasant to behold, beautiful. Upon seeing it, desire arose in him, thinking he would insert himself into it, and he thrust into its wound. It opened, and the monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "If he made contact with all the limbs and thereby incurred a defeat, yet if it was merely the insertion of the organ, it becomes a grave offence."

Just as with one made of wood, so too with one made of earth, made of stone, or made of cloth — it is the same.

A daughter of the nāgas came to a monk and said: "Venerable one, come and engage in unchaste conduct with me." He consented. He inserted himself into her, thrusting into her aperture. She then expanded her body to great length, and the monk, filled with terror, felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "Because there was no attachment in the monk's terror, there is no offence of defeat; yet it becomes a grave offence."

Likewise in detail up to the daughter of the yakṣas: she too became invisible, and that monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offence of defeat; it becomes a grave offence."

Daughters of the gods, daughters of the gandharvas, and daughters of the asuras — in all these cases it is the same, explained at length: just as with the daughter of the nāgas, each expanded her body to great size, and the monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "Because there is no desire in one who is terrified, there is no offence of defeat; it becomes a grave offence."

Likewise, the daughter of the hungry ghosts grew her female organ to great size, and she planted it upon the monk. The monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offence of defeat; it becomes a grave offence."

A monk who was dwelling alone in a forest hermitage was visited by a human woman. She said: "Venerable one, come and engage in unchaste conduct with me." The monk, being virtuous, felt no arousal. She said: "Venerable one, be aroused — you have been made unworthy. Let him do to me whatever he wishes." "I will not be aroused," he replied. She then wrapped the monk in her outer garment while he lay sleeping and placed him in the bedchamber where the king slept together with his queen. The king saw the monk and said: "What are you doing here?" The monk replied: "I was dwelling alone in a forest hermitage, and a human woman came to me and said, 'Venerable one, come and engage in unchaste conduct with me.' When I did not become aroused, she said, 'Venerable one, be aroused — you have been made unworthy. Let me do to him whatever I wish. I will not become aroused,' I said. And while I lay sleeping she wrapped me in her garment and placed me here." The king said: "Venerable one, why do you dwell in such a hermitage where such frightening things can happen?" and expelled the monk. The monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offence of defeat. From now on, do not dwell in a hermitage in which such frightening things can happen."

Likewise, a flesh-eating demoness did the same — she too wrapped the monk in her garment while he lay sleeping and placed him in the shop of a liquor-seller. The liquor-seller looked into his shop, saw the monk, and the rest proceeds in detail just as in the case of the human woman.

In brief, here is a summary verse:

The blue-lotus complexion, and the joyful one,
two young children, blood and flesh,
a female dog, a vixen, a female crow,
a non-human being, a water-crosser,
a fish, a shrew, and a piece of wood.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī. The nun Upālavarṇā, early in the morning, having put on her lower robe, entered Śrāvastī for alms. She washed her feet thoroughly and, entering her dwelling to enter into meditation, she opened the door and went inside. The hot season had arrived, and she fell asleep lying down. Some rogues who were wandering and walking along a lane saw her, did what they did to her as she lay there, then went away. She awoke, and the nun felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offence. From now on, a nun must not lie down without having bolted the door. If she does, it becomes a wrongdoing."

Likewise, if it was done to her while she was in meditative absorption, there is no offence; but from now on, a nun must not enter meditative absorption without having bolted the door. If she does enter absorption, it becomes a wrongdoing.

A monk was on his alms round at Śrāvastī and entered the home of a householder. A piglet belonging to that householder had been tied to a stake and was circling around the stake. The monk, feeling compassion, released it from the stake and sent it off. The householder saw the monk, ran after him, grabbed him by the neck, and said: "You have let loose my piglet — you are a thief! You are a fool! You are a wicked ascetic!" The monk thought: "I have let the piglet go, therefore I am a thief, I am a fool,

I am a wicked ascetic — I shall go and engage in unchaste conduct." Having thought thus, he went and engaged in unchaste conduct. He then thought: "Let me ask the monks about this: if, after I have gone forth and received full ordination, I can still be accepted back, then I shall go forth again; if not, I shall remain as I am." Having thought this, he told the monks what had happened, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense for the former act; the latter has become a wrongdoing." The case of the chick of a crow is the same.

A householder was carrying a piece of raw meat and going on his way, when a vulture snatched it and flew off with it. The piece of raw meat slipped from the vulture's beak and fell into the alms bowl of a monk who was on his alms round. The householder, seeing the meat sitting in that monk's alms bowl, grabbed the monk by the scruff of the neck and said: "That vulture snatched my piece of raw meat, and it was caught by your alms bowl — you are a thief! You are a fool! You are a wicked ascetic!" The monk thought: "His piece of raw meat was caught by my alms bowl, therefore I am a thief, I am a fool, I am a wicked ascetic — I shall go and engage in unchaste conduct." He thought thus. The full account is just as in the case of the piglet.

A monk urinated in front of a female dog. She inserted his member into her mouth, and he discharged semen; his body became flaccid as well. The monk was seized with remorse, and the Blessed One declared: "There is no offense of defeat. Henceforth, monks must not urinate in front of a female dog; or else drive her away, or move aside."

While a monk was walking, a female fox made a sound and tore the cloth from his rag pile. He then thought: "Who is it that has torn the cloth from my rag pile? I shall go and look." He went and found himself wrapped up in the rag-pile cloth, and the female fox then came and mounted on top of the monk. He wrapped the fox in the rag-pile cloth and held her, thinking: "Let me look and see whether this fox is male or female." He thus saw her female organ. Seeing it, a lustful thought arose in him, and he thought: "I shall insert myself right into that." He pushed into the wound, and she withdrew, pulled back, and escaped. The monk was frightened, and the Blessed One declared: "There is no offense of defeat for the frightened monk, but it becomes a grave wrongdoing."

A monk was dwelling alone in a dense forest. A female spirit of some sort led him from there into a cave and did to him whatever perception arose in her. She then changed his perception and went off to her domain, and the monk, having regained his perception, rose from that place and fled. The monk was seized with remorse, and the Blessed One declared: "There is no offense. Henceforth, monks must not dwell in a wilderness that is frightening in such a way."

A monk was crossing a river in the cold of winter, and his member was seized by a fish. His body too became flaccid and he discharged semen. The monk was seized with remorse, and the Blessed One declared: "There is no offense. Henceforth, do not cross in the cold of winter any river where such a danger may occur."

A woman was crouching in a thicket of wood, relieving herself, when a monk, peering through the branches of the thicket, saw her private parts. Having seen them, he was overcome by desire, and he touched her private parts with his own member. The Blessed One declared: "There is no root defeat, but it becomes a grave offense."

The Blessed One was dwelling in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. Some monks, having completed their duties and gone to a place for walking and taking the day's ease, one of them spread out his mat there, sat cross-legged, and rested. As the hot season had come, he grew drowsy in that spot, lay down, and fell asleep. As he slept, his lower robe became disordered and his member became responsive. A woman who had come to that place to gather firewood saw the monk lying there in an unsightly state. She was seized by intense desire and performed the sexual act upon him as he slept. Having done so, she departed. The monk awoke and, regaining his senses, she said: "Noble one, I have a household here, and if you should ever wish it again, come there." The monk was seized with remorse. The Blessed One declared: "Monk, were you aware of it?" He replied: "I was not, Blessed One." "If one was unaware, there is no offense. Henceforth, do not lie down to sleep alone, uncovered and unguarded. If one does so, it becomes a wrongdoing."

In brief:
The five grasses of Śāketā,
the five ingredients of Campā,
the medical treatments of Rājagṛha,
and the courtesan of Bharukaccha.

The Blessed One was dwelling in the forest of Ketā's woodsman. Then, in the case of another monk, a grass called "the five grasses," in its elaborate form, works just as with the firewood gatherer. In the city of Campā, when one is afflicted by a festering disease, through five causes and five conditions the member becomes responsive — as is set forth in the Vibhaṅga.

The Blessed One was dwelling in Rājagṛha. A monk was tormented by a disease of the member. His life-sustaining member was also tormented by disease. He had it placed in a woman's mouth. He then heard that one is thereby freed from such a disease. He thought: "The Blessed One has permitted this as a medical treatment for the sick," and, thinking so, he placed it in a woman's mouth and was freed from that disease. The monk was seized with remorse. The Blessed One declared: "The moment of insertion constitutes a root defeat."

In the land of Bharukaccha, a thief had taken up residence in the house of a courtesan. He went out from there and was harming the people of that place. They appealed to the king, and the king summoned the courtesan and asked: "Is a thief living in your house?" She replied: "There is no one, Sire." "If he is found upon search, you will be convicted of having harbored and concealed him, and you shall be put to death by that penalty. If he is still alive, you will be given to the dogs." The people seized the thief, brought him, and presented him to the king. The king commanded: "Go, bind this courtesan by her ankles, drag her along the ground, tie her face downward, and throw her in the charnel ground. Whoever releases her shall be put to death by this same penalty. If she survives, she shall be given to the dogs." They bound her by her ankles, dragged her along, tied her face down, and threw her into the charnel ground. A monk who was sitting in the charnel ground contemplating a corpse saw her, and a thought of desire arose in him. He thought: "I will insert right then and there," and placed his member in her wound. She rose and sat up, and said: "Venerable one, please give me some water first." He poured water over her. She said: "Venerable one, what use is this impure body and womb of mine?" He held her from that moment onward. When her relatives and friends came, the monk saw them from a distance and, ashamed, departed off to one side.

She said to her relatives and friends: "Whatever little life remains in me is entirely due to the power of this monk. Please call him." When they called him, he said: "Venerable lady, whatever little life remains in you is entirely due to your own merit. These are your relatives and friends — let them nurse you back to health. And if there is anything I can do for you, I am at this house; come there." The monk then felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no root downfall; however, it becomes a gross offense."

In brief:
Inside a wool-bull pen and a pit,
by touch, and a sunken boat as well,
men — both lay and ordained —
women, girls, and nuns,
a noble-born wealthy man tending a palace,
a monk tending a palace retinue —

A monk entered a pen containing an unruly bull. The bull, being unruly, tossed him and he fell on top of a woman. The monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense. Be mindful, and enter the bull pen." A monk looked into a broken pit and fell in, and there grasped around the neck a woman who had previously fallen in as well. Householders took a rope and pulled the monk out, and seeing a woman grasping him around the neck, they said: "Woman, where have you come from?" The monk said: "This is the woman who fell in before me; she grabbed me around the neck." The monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense. Be mindful, and watch out for pits." A monk who was going on alms-round came out through a narrow doorway, and a woman who was also entering brushed her female member against his male member. The monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense. Be mindful, and go on alms-round in the village." A monk was crossing a river by boat when the boat capsized. A woman was also there, and she grasped him around the neck. The monk swam across, and then felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense. Be mindful, and cross rivers." A layman called Blessedly Born went to a nun and said: "Noble lady, please ordain me." Without examining the matter, they ordained him, and he touched a nun. They felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense. Examine very carefully before ordaining." The nun Śomā Gāndhinī abandoned a child in the same manner as others abandon a child. The Blessed One declared: "Nuns should not abandon a child. If one does, it becomes a gross offense." The incident of the laywoman Blessedly Good was told at length, and the Blessed One asked: "Blessedly Good, did you feel pleasure?" She replied: "Venerable one, how could I have felt pleasure? It was like burning iron tongs." The Blessed One declared: "The region of a woman's female member arises from the ripening of karma; there is no offense when something is done by force." The nun called Blessedly Born Supriyā was seized by wrongdoers who covered her mouth, led her into a dense forest, defiled her, and released her; the nuns then expelled her from the residence. She said: "Noble ladies, I did not experience pleasure." They replied: "You were seized by wrongdoers, led into a dense forest, defiled, and released — why then did you not feel pleasure?"

The nuns reported what had happened to the monks, and the monks in turn informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One asked: "Did you experience pleasure?" She replied: "Blessed One, when someone is waving a handful of grass and thorns at you, how could you possibly experience pleasure?" The Blessed One then declared: "Monks, the region of a woman's female member arises from the ripening of karma. Coming and going, and the waving of a hand, constitute being taken by force, and for one taken by force there is no offense."

There was a nun in Śrāvastī named Norchen who, while going on her alms round, was seized by wrongdoers, led into a dense forest, defiled, and released. The nuns expelled her from the residence, and she said: "Noble ladies, I did not experience pleasure." They replied: "You were seized by wrongdoers, led into a dense forest, defiled, and released — why then did you not feel pleasure?" The nuns reported what had happened to the monks, and the monks in turn informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One asked: "Did you experience pleasure?" She replied: "Blessed One, I wept and cried out loud, saying 'Do not seize me!' — how could I have felt pleasure?" The Blessed One declared: "The region of a woman's female member arises from the ripening of karma. Weeping constitutes being taken by force; crying aloud and saying 'Do not seize me!' constitutes being taken by force; and for one taken by force there is no offense."

There was a nun in Śrāvastī named Phorang Kyong who, while going on her alms round, was seized by wrongdoers, led into a dense forest, defiled, and released. The nuns expelled her from the residence. She said: "I did not experience pleasure." They replied: "Then go to Ānanda." She went to him, but when the elder saw her he did not speak to her respectfully, and he too sent her away. She then thought to herself: "It is better for me to leave than to go on living like this." She thought to fill a clay pot with sand, tie it around her neck, and leap into the Ajiravatī river. She did just that — she tied the sand-filled pot around her neck and leapt into the Ajiravatī — but a rotten rope broke and she floated and sank, and the wrongdoers, seeing this, pulled her out and laid her down. When she regained consciousness, they defiled her again. The nuns, who had been searching for her, arrived at that place and saw them defiling her. She said: "Was I not already a nun before? Am I still a nun even now?" She reported what had happened to the monks, and the Blessed One asked: "Did you experience pleasure?" She replied: "Blessed One, when someone waves grass and thorns at you and you say 'Do not seize me!' — how could you feel pleasure?" The Blessed One declared: "Monks, the region of a woman's female member arises from the ripening of karma. From the point of 'walking constitutes being taken by force' down through 'saying "Do not seize me!" constitutes being taken by force' — in full — for one taken by force there is no offense."

In brief:
The Norchen monastery, the perception and going-forth,
The ten alms rounds and ten thieves —
And likewise the ten of the gambling board and the residence —
The buddha, the Blessed One, dwelt in Rājagṛha.

Previously, the monk Norchen the potter had not established the training rules, so there is no offense for a novice beginner. He thought: "If I take a good many pieces of wood without permission and bring them back, who will hold me to account for being a first offender?" His mind was tormented by this and he came to regret it; he became remorseful. The Blessed One then declared:

Monks, because the training rules had not yet been established, the former potter, the monk Norchen, had already passed beyond them all, and since he was a first offender in every respect, there is no offense for a first offender.

A monk who perceived ownerless monastery supplies as having an owner and took them without being given them — that monk came to feel remorse. The Blessed One then declared: If one perceives what has an owner as having an owner and takes it, it incurs defeat. If one is in doubt about what has an owner and takes it, it incurs defeat. If one perceives what has no owner as having an owner and takes it, it incurs a grave offense. If one perceives what has no owner as having no owner and takes it, there is no offense.

A monk took alms-food bearing grain without being given it. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense of defeat; it incurs a grave offense. With regard to alms-food bearing grain — in the same way, alms of flour, alms of cooked grain-porridge, alms of meat, and alms of cooked food: all of these likewise incur a grave offense.

A monk ate food without being invited. That monk came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense of defeat; it incurs a wrongdoing.

When the Saṅgha's food distribution was taking place in the province of Kosala, a resident monk had gone to another village. There were two monks who lived together, and the two of them had each accepted the preceptor's food separately. The two of them thought: "You accepted it, and I accepted it — in which case, neither of us knows who took it without permission, so perhaps it has not incurred the offense of defeat." The Blessed One declared: There is no offense in having taken it. Let it be regarded as belonging to someone else.

When the Saṅgha's food distribution was taking place in the province of Kosala, a resident monk had gone to another village. A friend of that monk accepted his food on his behalf. When he returned, that friend said: "Venerable one, did you accept my food?" He replied: "I accepted it." The monk said: "Why did you accept it without my having commissioned you?" That monk came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense. What was not commissioned — do not accept it.

When the Saṅgha's food distribution was taking place in the province of Kosala, there was a sick monk. His nurse accepted food on his behalf and then departed. The monk's meal time had passed, and he did not know what to do. The Blessed One declared: If the meal time had not yet passed before and the food was accepted afterward, then return it then and there. But if it was accepted before and the meal time passed afterward, handle it as one would any other requisite in the appropriate manner.

A monk said to another monk: "Come here, venerable one — let us go to the thieves." The two of them set out and had gone halfway along the road, when they thought: "We have gone forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, and if we commit theft it would be unseemly and improper for us." Being possessed of a sense of shame, the two of them did not go there. They came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense of defeat; it incurs a wrongdoing.

A monk said to several monks: "Come here, venerable ones — let us go to the thieves." They set out and had gone halfway along the road, when they thought: "This would be unseemly for us," and being possessed of a sense of shame they did not go there. Those monks came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense of defeat; it incurs a wrongdoing.

Among those who acted in the same manner, one of them, being possessed of a sense of shame, thought: "If I do not go, they will deprive me of my livelihood. Yet I shall go, and I shall not take what is not given, nor shall I accept my share." Thinking thus, he went there, and he neither took what was not given nor carried off his share. That monk came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense of defeat; it incurs a wrongdoing.

Some monks said to other monks: "Come here, venerable ones — let us go to the thieves." They set out, and of them, half carried out the deed while the other half stood guard on the road. Those who were standing guard on the road thought: "We have not taken anything and have not stolen, so we will not incur an offense." When the other monks heard what had occurred, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: If the full constituent elements are present, it incurs defeat. If the constituent elements are not complete, it incurs a grave offense.

A monk said to another monk: "Come here, venerable one — let us go to the thieves." They took what was not given, but in some other instance the constituent elements were not complete; yet from the very location where they had taken the goods, the full constituent elements were subsequently present there, and both those monks came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: The value is to be reckoned from the place from which it was moved.

A monk said to several monks: "Come here, venerable ones — let us go to the thieves. Whatever each one obtains, that shall be his own to keep." They set out and went there, and of them some obtained something while others obtained nothing. They came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense of defeat; it incurs a grave offense.

As for those monks, if the thieves gave them a share and the guards also gave them something, yet they came to feel remorse and did not take it, the Blessed One declared: When permission is granted, regard the giver with the mind of a donor and accept it.

A companion of a certain monk was carried off by thieves. That companion escaped and came back, and the monk came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: It is permissible for a monk to rescue himself; there is no offense.

If a monk has in hand an object used for playing dice, and if it passes beyond the boundary of the gaming place, it incurs defeat. But if he thinks: "This belongs to my mother, this to my father, this to my son, this to my sister, to my preceptor, to my teacher, to a stūpa, or to the Saṅgha" — and he dedicates it to many and it passes beyond, it incurs a grave offense. If it passes beyond into the sky, there is no offense.

In brief:
A stool, a book, a bolt of linen cloth,
Alcohol, meat, clothing, and the interior;
A funeral streamer, a charnel ground,
And the two locations of a charnel ground.

A monk stole a stool and carried it off, thinking that its owner would not give it back. That monk came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense of defeat; it incurs a grave offense.

A monk stole a book and carried it off; that case too is elaborated in the same way.

A monk took a bolt of linen cloth without it being given, and having stolen it he tore it apart. From inside it there emerged a piece of silk of great value. That monk came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: The value of the linen cloth is to be reckoned.

Some thieves took some alcohol and went to a monastery. Some of the alcohol they drank, and some they concealed and departed.

Some monks also went out to that place to take their morning exercise. They saw it and said, "Before those turn sour, take them to the monastery," and they carried it to the monastery. The thieves, growing thirsty, went back there and searched for it, and not finding it they saw those monks and asked them: "Venerable ones, did you not take some alcohol?" The monks replied, "We took it." The thieves said, "We had hidden that alcohol, so you are thieves." Those monks came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense. One should examine carefully whether there is an owner or not, and then take it. Likewise with meat, it is the same.

Some thieves sacked a village and were chased away by arrows. They went to a monastery and, out of fear, entered it; they gave their garments to the monks and fled to a hermitage. The householders surrounded the monastery and entered it, and seeing those garments in the hands of the monks they said, "These garments are ours." The monks replied, "The thieves gave them to us." Those monks came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense. Do not accept goods that have been stolen and not yet settled. However, if a thief bearing a victory banner gives something, one may accept it from him; wash the garment, change its color, and use it. If even after changing its color someone comes back to claim it again, give it back to that person as well.

A launderer put a garment into the washing water and then forgot it and went into the village. He later remembered the garment and turned back to go and retrieve it. In the meantime a monk who was searching for rag-robes went to that place, saw the garment, took it, and left. The launderer saw this and said, "Venerable one, do not steal the garment!" The monk replied, "I was searching for rag-robes and found this — what do you need it for?" The launderer said, "Venerable one, I put this garment in the wash water and forgot it; it is my garment, do not steal it. You have taken it without it being given." That monk came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense. One should examine carefully whether there is another owner or not, and then take it.

A launderer washed a garment and left it by a tree. A rag-robe seeker, searching for rag-robes, came to that place, saw the garment, took it, and left. The launderer saw this and said, "Venerable one, this is my garment; do not steal it. If it is yours, take it back." That monk came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: One should examine most carefully — and this is elaborated at length.

A householder set down his garment while attending to the call of nature. A rag-robe seeker, searching for rag-robes, came to that place, saw the garment, took it, and left. The householder stood up and said, "Venerable one, this is my clothing; do not steal it. If it is yours, take it back." That monk came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense. Examine it thoroughly and take it.

Not far from the Jeta Grove, a field laborer set down his garments and was working the field. A monk who was a rag-robe seeker, searching for rag-robes, came to that place, saw the garment, took it, and left. The field laborer saw this and said, "Venerable one, do not steal the garment!" But the monk did not listen to him, and —

He ran after him, caught him, and said, "Venerable one, do not take the garment without it being given. I saw it when I was searching for rag-robe cloths. What need do you have of this? Venerable one, I left the garment there and went off to till the field. This garment is mine." And he added, "If it is yours, take it back." That monk came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense. Examine it thoroughly and take it.

A householder had heard that the monks, the sons of the Śākyan ascetic, take whatever fallen garments they find, calling them rag-robe cloths. He therefore took a fine piece of cloth worth eight kārṣāpaṇas, buried it deep in a heap of discarded rags, and left it with just a corner showing, then went away. A monk who was searching for rag-robe cloths came to that place, saw the corner, pulled the cloth out from there, and took it. The householder saw this and said, "Venerable one, do not steal the cloth!" The monk replied, "I found this while searching for rag-robe cloths — what concern is it of yours?" The householder said, "Venerable one, I heard that the monks, the sons of the Śākyan ascetic, take whatever fallen garments they find, calling them rag-robe cloths. So I buried the cloth in the heap of rags, having paid eight kārṣāpaṇas for it." Upon hearing this, the monk saw the eight kārṣāpaṇas and said, "If they are yours, take them." That monk came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense. Examine it carefully and treat it with respect.

A householder's boy set down his garment in the street and went off to play. After he had finished playing and gone home, a monk who was searching for rag-robe cloths came to that place, saw the garment, took it, and left. A woman came out from that house and, seeing the monk, said, "Venerable one, do not steal the garment!" He replied, "I found it while searching for rag-robe cloths." She said, "Venerable one, her boy was playing and forgot the garment and went home." He replied, "If it is yours, take it." That monk came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense. Examine it thoroughly and take it.

A monk hid a rag-robe cloth and then went into Śrāvastī on alms round. Another monk, also searching for rag-robe cloths, came to that place, saw it, and washed it. The first monk, having searched for his rag-robe cloth and not found it, then saw that other monk washing it, and said to him, "Venerable one, a root defeat has occurred for you." The other monk asked why. "Because you took my rag-robe cloth without it being given." The first monk added, "I did not know that this had an owner." That monk came to feel remorse. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense. Examine it carefully and take it.

Those monks were carrying rag-robe cloths that had been touched by unclean things, and the lesser gods (devas) were mocking them. The Blessed One declared: Rag-robe cloths should be washed, properly dried, and then carried. Therefore monks must not carry rag-robe cloths that have been touched by unclean things. Whoever does so commits a wrongdoing.

Those monks took garments from a charnel ground that had an owner. People of low birth, whatever work they did, did it on account of these monks, and they began to spread disagreeable talk, saying, "Do not steal garments from here."

The Blessed One declared: Do not take garments from a charnel ground that has an owner. If one does take them, a serious offense results.

Not far from a certain charnel ground there was a temple that was facing the wrong direction. A piece of cloth had been blown by the wind into the charnel ground, and a monk who was searching through the charnel ground for rag-robe cloths came there, found that piece of cloth, took it, and carried it away. Those who dwelt in the wrongly-facing temple saw this and said: "Venerable one, this cloth of ours fell from the temple into the charnel ground — do not steal this cloth." He replied: "If it is yours, then take it back." That monk became remorseful. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense. Inquire very carefully and with an open mind as to whether or not there is another owner.

Here ends the Vinaya section.

The Noble Vinaya. The twenty-third fascicle.

In brief: two boys crossing a third, missions and the Saṅgha's field, requisites and pegs, wood and two kinds of bird's nest.

The great Mahāmaudgalyāyana freed the boys of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada in the Jeta Grove from wrongdoers, and this is to be understood in detail as it appears in the extended explanation.

A householder had invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha at the time of midday. The Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha was coming, but one monk remained in the monastery and missed the meal. Meanwhile the boys of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada were playing in the Jeta Grove when wrongdoers stole them. That monk heard of this, and having learned a mantra, before long he thought to himself: "With this mantra I shall awaken my mother." He recited the mantra, and those wrongdoers found themselves surrounded by four armies, whereupon they abandoned the boys and fled.

When the monks heard what had happened, they said to that monk: "A root defeat has occurred." The monk became remorseful. The Blessed One declared: "Monk, what was your intention when you freed the boys?" He replied: "My intention was to awaken her with the mantra." The Blessed One declared: There is no offense in reciting a mantra.

In the province of Kosala, when the Saṅgha distributed robes, a resident monk went to another village, and two companions of his who lived together there each collected the portion owed to the preceptor separately. After collecting and returning, each asked the other: "Did you collect the preceptor's robe?" When both said they had, they said: "Since both of us collected it, we do not know whose collecting caused a root defeat." The Blessed One declared: There is no offense in the collecting, but one should inform the other party.

In the province of Kosala, when the Saṅgha distributed robes, a resident monk went to another village. A friend of that monk collected his robe and came back, saying: "Venerable one, this is your robe — I collected it and have brought it." The monk replied: "I did not entrust you with that." The monk became remorseful. The Blessed One declared: There is no root defeat. Do not accept what is found without being entrusted with it; if one does accept it, it becomes a wrongdoing.

In the province of Kosala, at the time of distributing robes, a monk was ill, and his attendant collected his robe and took it away.

That monk too had passed away, and the attendant monk did not know what to do. The Blessed One declared: If the robe was distributed before the time had passed but was given to the attendant only after the time had passed, then it must be returned to the Saṅgha right then. If it was given to the attendant before the time had passed but the time then passed afterward, handle it as one would any other requisite. A monk said to another monk: "Come here, venerable one — taking something small by small amounts without its being given does not become a wrongdoing." The monks heard this and reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: It is to be assessed by a single combined valuation.

A layman was plowing a field belonging to the Saṅgha, and a resident monk came to him and said: "Layman, either give a share or stop plowing." The man did not comply and continued plowing. The monk then lay down at the tip of the furrow. The layman then abandoned the furrow and said: "May this one such as this śramaṇa be parted from it," and cursed and dismissed him with unkind words. The monk became remorseful. The Blessed One declared: There is no wrongdoing. But from now on, monks should not make themselves a bodily nuisance in this way.

A monk said to another monk: "Come here, venerable one — even if we were to steal the wealth of a stūpa, no wrongdoing would arise for the two of us." The Blessed One declared: Monks, from stūpa property that has no guardian, if the full value is present, it becomes a root defeat.

A resident monk caused a field belonging to the Saṅgha to be plowed, and not long after, a layman also plowed that field. The layman came and said: "Venerable one, do not plow my field." The monk replied: "This is not yours — it is the Saṅgha's field." "Venerable one, let me be shown what is not under my authority," said the layman, and he dug up the boundary stake that had previously been planted. Having dug it up and been shown this, the layman abandoned the furrow and left. After the layman had gone, the monk pushed his stake back in and plowed the field. The layman returned and said: "Venerable one, even though I won just now, why are you plowing again?" The monk became remorseful. The Blessed One declared: If the thing is present in full, it becomes a root defeat.

A monk took without permission a flowering tree belonging to a layman. The monk became remorseful. The Blessed One declared: If the thing is present in full, it becomes a root defeat. A fruit tree is likewise.

A tree grew in a monk's walking-meditation path, and sparrows built their nest in it. As the monk walked, it caused him to drop the tree and make a noise. He destroyed the nest, and the bird cried out. The Blessed One asked: "Why is the beloved one causing the beloved one to cry out?" The monks replied: "It was because of destroying the sparrows' nest." The Blessed One declared: Do not destroy sparrows' nests. Whoever destroys one incurs a wrongdoing. A monk who destroyed a sparrows' nest and then boiled the dye — that case is also detailed in the same way.

In brief:
A hollow tree, a trunk, and fruit,
and leaves and flowers — these make three;
stealing a horse and a horse-rider,
crossing by boat, and a jewel.

At Śrāvastī a certain layman had a hollow tree, and a monk went there and said: "Give me the hollow tree." The layman replied: "Venerable one, please pay for it." "There is nothing to pay." "If there is no payment, how can I give it?" "Give it without payment for the sake of the Dharma." The layman said: "Venerable one, if we were to give everything to all who come here without payment, we would have not even a little food and clothing."

"Will you not give even a little? I am not asking for much." Having said this, he dried out the roots of the hollow tree by means of mantras. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense of defeat, but it becomes a grave offense."

Just as with the roots of a hollow tree, so too it is the same with the roots of a trunk, the roots of leaves, and the roots of fruit.

A horse was standing and grazing on grass, and a monk took a bundle of grass and held it up in front of the horse, and the horse followed along behind him. Then that monk, thinking, "I shall steal it in this way," moved his body aside, and then remorse arose in him. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense of defeat, but it becomes a grave offense."

A monk was traveling together with many merchant travelers, and they went down into a ravine in Kosala, passing through a road beset with danger. The merchants, riding on horseback, said to the venerable one: "This road is dangerous — mount a horse and pass through quickly." The monks mounted horses, and thinking, "We shall steal in this manner," they moved their bodies. Remorse then arose in those monks. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense of defeat, but it becomes a grave offense."

A monk who was crossing over on a boat laden with jewels thought, "I shall steal in this manner," and moved his body. Remorse then arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense of defeat, but it becomes a grave offense."

A merchant's boat laden with jewels sank in the water. He was in distress, and a box of jewels was carried away by the current. Some monks who were washing below in the water saw the box of jewels and retrieved it. The merchant saw this and said: "Venerable ones, this box of jewels is mine." They replied: "We found it, carried here by the current." He said: "Venerable ones, my boat laden with jewels sank in the water, and I was thrown into distress, and this small box of jewels was carried away by the current. This box of jewels is mine." They answered: "If it is yours, then take it." Remorse then arose in those monks. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense."

A resident monk, with a mind of theft, transferred the property of the Saṅgha of the four quarters from place to place. Remorse arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense of defeat, but it becomes a grave offense."

Some thieves led a cow up to a forest dwelling, tied it there, and departed. Some monks came to that place for their daytime sojourn, and seeing the cow, they took pity on it and let it go. Remorse then arose in them. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense of defeat, but it becomes a minor offense."

In brief:
A corpse, a golden garland,
a finger, and two kinds of rat,
three wild animals, and two empty vessels,
a pestle, a bird, and a bird's nest.

At Śrāvastī, some people petitioned others regarding a corpse, and a certain householder, having requested something, had his request fulfilled. He then laid out for the other a piece of white cloth as a covering. A monk named Nāgapīta went there and took that cloth. The monks said to him: "A root defeat has come upon you. For what thing? Because you took without permission the cloth belonging to the corpse." Remorse arose in him. The Blessed One declared:

There is no root defeat. It becomes a grave offense.
