At Vaiśālī, a corpse had been adorned with a golden garland and was being kept under guard. A monk by the name of Nāgapīta Gāvaya heard of this and went there. He struck the corpse, and the corpse spoke. Because he was brave and capable, he seized the golden garland and made off with it. When the monks heard of this, it too was reported in the same way at length.

A number of women had left their clothes and ornaments on the bank of the river Vaggumudā and were bathing. A monkey came down from a tree, took the ornaments, and climbed back up into the tree. The women came out of the water, divided the clothes among themselves, and were told to each take their own ornaments. When one woman's pearl necklace was nowhere to be found, she wept at not having found it. Thereupon the monkey dropped that pearl necklace back down in that very spot. Some monks who were walking nearby saw the pearl necklace, picked it up, and gave it to the women. The women said, "You have stolen this pearl necklace." The monks replied, "We did not steal it. While you were bathing, a monkey came down from a tree, took this pearl necklace, and climbed back up. When you searched and could not find it and wept, it came back down and placed it in that very spot." Remorse arose in the monks. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense.

A monk dismantled a nest in a window frame and took the eggs, whereupon the window frame made a sound. It too was then reported in the same way at length.

A number of monks were staying in a temple when some rats came out of their holes, stole valuables and food, and returned to their holes. The monks thought to themselves, "Who is it that is stealing from us?" They had gone out on alms rounds and were sitting out at midday, when a rat again emerged from its hole, carried off food, and returned to its hole in the same manner. The monks then thought, "This is the one that has been stealing from us." They caught it and showed it to the other monks, saying, "This is the one that has been stealing from us." Those other monks said, "A root defeat has come upon you, for you seized without permission, on account of the rat." Remorse arose in them. The Blessed One declared: There is no offense. Whatever belongs to the monks, that may be reclaimed. Whatever belongs to the rat, that must not be taken.

A rat brought provisions and food and placed them under the sleeping mat of a certain monk. The next morning, that monk first cleaned his teeth and washed his face, then performed the collection of alms and ate what had been placed there. When he had eaten, the other monks said to him, "Venerable one, though you always wash your hands and feet well, you do not enter the village for alms rounds. Why is that?" He replied, "A rat brought provisions and food, placed them under my sleeping mat, and I performed the collection and ate them in the morning." They said, "Venerable one, a root defeat has come upon you, for you took without permission the provisions and food belonging to the rat." When the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: That monk in a former life was the rat's father. Because of the paternal love the rat bears him, it brought food and gave it to the monk. There is no offense.

A wild deer, having been chased by hunters, came into the monastery. The hunters said, "Our deer has been chased and gone into the monastery — give it back." When the monks did not hand it over at that point, they let it go and departed. The monks then felt remorse, and the Blessed One declared: There is no offense. The case of a deer struck by a hunter's arrow is to be elaborated in the same way.

A hunter struck a deer with a poisoned arrow, and the deer came into the monastery. The hunters said, "Our deer has been shot with a poisoned arrow and will certainly die — give it back." The monks did not return it, and the hunters let the matter go and left. After they had gone, the deer passed away in due course. The monks did not know what to do, and the Blessed One declared: Give it back to those hunters. If a monk cuts the throat of a deer in order to harm it, it becomes a grave offense. If it is done out of compassion, it becomes a minor offense. Likewise, if a monk cuts the wing of a bird in order to harm it, it becomes a grave offense. If it is done with compassionate intent, it becomes a minor offense. A bird's nest is likewise the same.

In brief: a cloth merchant, a market trader, a triangular cake and thick soup, a bag, goods and robes.

A monk took a piece of cloth from a cloth-selling tanner and carried it off. The cloth merchant saw this and said, "You have stolen the cloth." The monk replied, "I took it openly and am bringing it." The monk felt remorse, and the Blessed One declared: There is no root defeat; it becomes a grave offense.

A monk borrowed a great quantity of goods on credit from a market trader. Before he repaid the debt, the monk thought, "I will not give this back to him." Remorse then arose, and the Blessed One declared: There is no root defeat; it becomes a grave offense.

There was a sick monk who entrusted another monk with a triangular cake and thick soup, thinking, "Let him offer it to the Saṅgha and let me also eat some." He told his attendants, "Prepare a triangular cake and thick soup — offer it to the Saṅgha, and I too will eat." He gave payment for this, and the attendants thought, "Why do we need to give this monk alone a triangular cake and thick soup? Let us give it to him alone and divide the payment among ourselves." So they gave him the triangular cake and thick soup and divided the payment, and remorse arose among the monks. The Blessed One declared: There is no root defeat; it becomes a grave offense.

There was a sick monk who had a great many provisions. He thought, "When I die, these will be divided among the Saṅgha." He told his attendants, "Venerable ones, prepare a small pea-broth for me." They prepared a small pea-broth and gave it to him. While the attendants were busy, he mixed the provisions into the pea-broth and drank it. Because the food was heavy, he passed away in due time, and the monks gathered and carried him to the charnel ground. After leaving him there, they told the attendants, "Bring a large share of that monk's provisions to be distributed." When the monks searched, they could not find them; they rose from their seats and departed. The monk had been disemboweled by a predatory animal, and his entrails had been dragged out. As the entrails were drawn out, the provisions came spilling out onto the ground and were found lying there.

A monk who had gone to the charnel ground to inspect a corpse found the provisions there, took them, and offered them to the Saṅgha. When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared, "There is no offense."

There was a sick monk who had many material goods. He said to his attendants, "Venerable ones, summon the monks. I will give to the Saṅgha, I will give to the stūpa, I will give to individuals." But the attendants thought, "If it is given to the Saṅgha and the stūpa, we ourselves will receive nothing at all." So they did not call the monks. That monk then passed away, and remorse arose in those attendants. The Blessed One declared, "There is no offense for the attendants. However, attendants should not act contrary to the wishes of the sick. Whatever the sick person directs, that is what they should carry out. Even if the account is set down in a different way, let it be done just as the sick person instructs."

There was another sick monk who had many alms bowls and robes. He said to his attendants, "Summon the monks. I will give to the stūpa, I will give to the Saṅgha, I will give to individuals." That case too should be related in full in the same way.

In brief, the following summary verse applies:

Candalaka, Sodaya,
Sphyarma and Branyaba,
Sushima and Zangzhyin,
who took an alms bowl thinking it their own;
Ajita and Śaśigupta
who stole their own robes.

This summary verse is as it appears in the detailed analysis of the sūtra.

In brief, the following verse applies:

Two nuns with two things,
and Maudgalyāyana, and two more besides;
the two of Pilindavatsa,
and Nandaka, and the Abandoner.

For the two nuns and the two things, it is as in the Vinaya.

Some merchants from Śrāvastī boarded a great ship and set sail across the ocean. While they were out on the open sea, a great nāga seized the ship and, though the divine servants pleaded, would not release it. At that time there was a lay practitioner from a village near the elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana who thought, "If the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana were to direct his attention here, may it be auspicious." The elder, too, turned his attention to the matter, and entered into meditative absorption of such a kind that, through his absorption, he became the king of birds, Garuḍa, alighting on the prow of the ship. The nāgas were terrified, released the great ship, and the merchants sailed safely back to Śrāvastī. All proclaimed, "This was the power of the noble Maudgalyāyana." The monks asked what had happened, and he related it in full. Then those monks declared that a root defeat offense had arisen for the elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana on account of the property, saying that the nāga had seized the ship and he had caused it to be released without having been given it. Remorse arose in that monk, and the Blessed One declared, "Maudgalyāyana, with what intention did you release it?" He replied, "I had in mind the manifestation of a miraculous display." The Blessed One then declared, "For Maudgalyāyana's releasing it through miraculous power, there is no offense."

Some merchants from Śrāvastī had taken their goods and set out traveling through a region, and they entered a narrow defile. Many of those travelers were surrounded by bandits, and though they prayed to the gods, the gods did not release them. Among them was a merchant from the village near the elder Maudgalyāyana, who thought, "If the elder were to direct his attention here, may it be auspicious."

The elder too, directing his attention there, entered into meditative equipoise of such a kind that the bandits found themselves surrounded by a fourfold army. Terrified, the bandits released the many travelers and fled, and the merchants went safely and auspiciously to Śrāvastī. The merchants told the monks in full what had happened, just as before. The two sons of Pilindavatsa are as described at length in the Vinaya.

Ānanda, son of the Śākyas, during the final month of the summer rains retreat, was moving about and staying in the monastery asking how many monks had entered the rains retreat in such and such a place, and how much gain the Saṅgha had obtained there. When he arrived at whichever residence those monks came from, they greeted him with pleasant words and asked, "Are you well?" and, having been seated, said, "Venerable one, take whatever Saṅgha gains are here; divide them and take my share of the robe cloth." The monks brought the robes, set them before him, and after he had divided them he took the portion of robe cloth belonging to the elder of the Saṅgha of that residence and rose to leave. The elder said to him, "Venerable one, stay yet a while longer." Ānanda, being eloquent and gifted in various pleasing speech, confident in right reasoning and in liberation, taught Dharma in such a way as to inspire faith in the elder. The elder then said, "Venerable Ānanda, please accept whatever is my share of the robe cloth." Likewise the second elder, the third elder, and many among those monks gave him their robes. Carrying all those robes in a bundle, he entered the Jeta Grove.

The monks asked the venerable Ānanda, "Venerable one, where did you obtain all these robes?" and he recounted to them at length what had occurred. Although such events had transpired, the Blessed One, the Buddha, had not yet laid down a rule of training. The two concerning entering the rains retreat late are as they appear at length in the Vinaya.

A monk must not take another's rains-retreat robe allocation. Whoever takes it commits a transgression.

There was one called the Abandoner, a companion of the venerable Ānanda, who was a person of moral discipline. He used to visit the village of another householder, and that householder had two sons. That householder fell ill, and the Abandoner went to inquire after his illness. The householder gave him wealth. One of the two sons received nothing and, harboring resentment toward the venerable Ānanda, the venerable Ānanda had the Abandoner penalized. Now, since the Abandoner had previously gone forth from among students, he rallied about five hundred of those students and said, "Ask my preceptor to forgive me." They replied, "How should we ask your preceptor to forgive you? Take the boys and bring them to the preceptor. He will teach you all the Dharma. When the teaching of Dharma is finished, then abandon the boys and girls and leave. When they weep, take those boys and girls and go, saying such and such to him. And then say to him, 'And will you forgive the Abandoner as well?'" They did just as they had been instructed. When the teaching of Dharma was finished, the boys and girls were abandoned and departed, and they wept bitterly. The venerable Ānanda said, "Bring these boys and girls here — why have they been sent away?" They replied, "Will you also forgive the Abandoner?" He said, "He is forgiven. Let him confess his transgression." In brief:

The pig, the sugarcane stalk,
and Nāgapriya's Dharma robe —

a half-measure of butter and aloe wood —
the pig, the sugarcane stalk, and Nāgapriya's Dharma robe, being the fifth —

all of these are to be understood in their full detail as they appear in the Vinaya.

There was a monk of great merit who was well known among merchants. Another merchant said to him, "Whatever you need or require, I will provide it for you." The monk's attendant thought to himself, "If that merchant keeps offering things again and again, will he do so wholeheartedly, or is he just offering it out of politeness?" Thinking this, he went to the merchant and said, "The preceptor needs some butter." The merchant gave a half-measure of butter, and then said, "Also, venerable one, whatever you need — lentil broth, or meat broth — take it from here." The attendant said, "Very well," and the monk poured a little of that butter into the monk's lentil broth and meat broth.

After some time the merchant sent word to the monk, saying, "Noble one, I sent you the butter before. If you still need lentil broth, or meat broth, or whatever else is needed, please take those things." The monk asked the attendant, "Did you receive butter from this merchant?" and the attendant replied, "I did." The monk said, "Then a pārājika offence has occurred." The attendant said, "It was because the merchant kept offering things again and again that I took it and tested whether he was sincere, and then I gave it to the preceptor." The monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared, "There is no offence. He went asking for such and such. Go."

In brief:

Sukhavat and a perception,
two wives and five wrongdoers,
ten cases of remaining in the womb,
and ten more involving non-monks and others.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Vṛji, in a place among the trees of the plain. Because no rule of training had yet been laid down for the monks on the bank of the river Sukhāvatī, those who were first offenders were without fault. The monks then felt doubt, uncertainty, and remorse, thinking, "We told many monks they would die, without any rule of training yet having been established — what then counts as a first offence for us?" The Blessed One declared, "For the monks who were dwelling beside the Sukhāvatī river when no rule had yet been established, everything — past as well as present — is entirely a first offence, and for a first offender there is no fault."

A monk perceived a human being as not human and deprived him of his life. That monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared, "If one perceives a human as not human, a grave offence is incurred. If one perceives a non-human as not human, a grave offence is incurred. If one is uncertain about whether something is non-human, a grave offence is incurred."

A monk had long been tormented by illness, and thinking to himself, "What is the point of this for me?" he went to a friend and said, "Give me a knife." The friend said, "What do you need a knife for? Here, take it for now," and gave it to him. The monk entered his cell, shut the door, fastened the latch, sat cross-legged, and cut his own throat. He passed away still holding the knife. After two or three days another monk thought, "That monk took the knife and went away — let me go and check on him." He went to the monk's cell and found him seated cross-legged, his throat cut, dead, still holding the knife. That monk felt remorse. Whatever had happened — everything that had passed away at that time had arisen through what had been set in motion —

He thought, "If I had not given him the knife, he would not have been separated from his life." The Blessed One declared: "There is no transgression. From now on, give knives to the sick without hesitation, as the occasion demands."

A monk had gone near another village and entered that village. The woman of that household said to the venerable one, "Come here — he has been behaving unchastely." The monk replied, "Your husband is fierce and hard to restrain." The woman said, "I will do whatever it takes to prevent the venerable one from being restrained by his fierceness," and she gave him poison. That householder passed away from this life. A day later the monk went to that house, and the woman said again, "Come here, venerable one — he has been behaving unchastely." He replied, "Sister, do not say such things. I am one who lives in chastity." She said, "Were you truly living in chastity at the very time when, by my doing, your husband was separated from his life?" He replied, "Did I say to you, 'Separate your husband from his life'? Did I not say, 'Your husband is fierce and hard to restrain'? I said that your husband is fierce and hard to restrain — I did not say, 'Separate your husband from his life.'" Remorse arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: "There is no transgression." That a monk went near another village, entered it, and acted — "Your husband is ill" — the full account is as found in the Vinaya.

A monk intended to kill, and having beaten someone: if that person passes away, it is a defeat. If that person does not pass away, it is a grave offense. A monk, through negligence, crushed a being in the womb and the being in the womb died — it is a defeat. If it did not die, it is a grave offense. If both died, it is a defeat. If both did not die, it is a grave offense. If a living human in the womb is extracted, it is a grave offense. If a being of the animal realm in the womb is extracted, it is likewise a grave offense. If a nun did the same, it is the same in like manner.

Thus is the noble Vinaya text, the twenty-fourth fascicle.

In brief: the five kinds of fierce drink, fresh actions, stones, the horns of an ox, the vixen, the seat, and the one who has become mad.

A monk administered a fierce drink to the Saṅgha, and many monks thereupon passed away from this life. Remorse arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: "There is no transgression."

Two monk friends were staying together; one fell ill and lay down. He said to his attendant in illness: "If you, venerable one, could find a fierce drink, I would be well." The full account is as it appears in the Vinaya.

A brahmin was tormented by an ailment of convulsions and went to a monk, saying: "Venerable one, if I could find a fierce drink, I would be well." The monk replied, "You are a brahmin of wrong views — what need do you have of a fierce drink?" The venerable one continued: "In the past, when I was struck by illness, I drank a fierce drink and became well." That monk poured out a fierce drink for him, and he passed away from this life. Remorse arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: "There is no transgression."

A monk went to a charnel ground to examine a human corpse. There a man was sitting having driven in a sharpened stake. He said to the monk: "Venerable one, if you pour me a fierce drink, I will be well." That monk poured out a fierce drink for him, and he passed away from this life. Remorse arose in that monk.

The Blessed One declared: "There is no transgression." A certain nun poured a fierce drink for five hundred thieves, and they too passed away from this life. The details are as they appear in the Vinaya at length.

In a place called the New Hermitage, a plank was being laid for a building, and a fragment fell from a monk's hand onto a worker below, who passed away from this life. Remorse arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: "There is no transgression. Be heedful and work with a helper."

In a hermitage, while the Saṅgha was building a structure for a building, a monk on an unguarded surface let a brick slip from his hand for placing, and it fell onto a plasterer working below, who passed away from this life. Remorse arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: "There is no transgression. Be heedful and work with a helper."

In a hermitage, while building a structure for shade, when monks were hauling a beam up, there were too few monks for such a heavy and weighty load, and they let it go; it fell onto a carpenter who was setting timber below, and he passed away from this life. Remorse arose in those monks. The Blessed One declared: "There is no transgression. Do not let a small number lift a heavy load." The same applies likewise to raising ladders.

In a hermitage, while building a structure for shade, a monk was lifting wet clay up inside a scaffold, when the rope was poor and snapped, and the clay in its scaffold fell onto a mason working below, and he passed away from this life. Remorse arose in those monks. The Blessed One declared: "There is no transgression. Be heedful and work with a helper."

The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha. A monk was sitting cross-legged at the foot of a mountain, and another monk rolled a boulder from the mountain's peak, which fell upon that monk, who passed away from this life. Remorse arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: "Understand this thoroughly, be heedful, and roll boulders with care."

A monk entered among cattle. An untamed bull struck him and he fell upon a boy, and the boy passed away from this life. Remorse arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: "Be heedful when entering among cattle."

A monk had become bent over from prolonged illness, and he thought to himself: "What is the point of my living on like this? Let me jump from a precipice myself." He leapt from a precipice, and there was a vixen below eating a human corpse; the monk fell upon her, and that vixen passed away from this life. The monk himself was straightened. Remorse arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: "There is no transgression. Do not in that way bring harm upon your body."

A sick monk was sitting on his seat, and his attendant said to him: "Venerable one, please rise." The monk replied: "Do not rouse me; I will come when ready." Still the attendant kept saying: "Venerable one, please rise." When the monk rose, he passed away from this life. Remorse arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: "There is no root downfall. However, a grave offense is incurred."

A monk struck a madman with the intent to kill. If he passes away from this life, it is a root downfall. If he does not pass away, it is a grave offense.

In summary:

Many things and what was not requested,
presumptuous sight and improper food,
medicine and fine provisions, conduct —
there is no transgression; apply these likewise to others.

A monk had been afflicted by a long illness, and his attendant, grown weary, said to him: "You will soon die anyway, so I will no longer nurse you." Because the attendant ceased nursing him, the monk passed away from this life. Remorse arose in that monk's attendant. The Blessed One declared: "There is no root downfall. However, a grave offense is incurred."

A monk said to a sick man's attendant: "Do not nurse him — when he dies, there will be a great deal of property from the Saṅgha's distribution." The attendant then ceased nursing the sick monk, and that monk passed away from this life. Remorse arose in that monk's attendant. The Blessed One declared: "There is no root downfall. However, a grave offense is incurred."

A monk was lying ill and not yet digesting his food. His attendant said: "Venerable one, please lie down straight." The monk said to the attendant: "I am going to die — do not straighten me." The attendant then said again: "Venerable one, please lie straight," and straightened him. The monk passed away from this life. Remorse arose in that monk's attendant. The Blessed One declared: "There is no root downfall. However, a grave offense is incurred."

If a monk squeezes an unripe boil and the person passes away from this life as a result, a grave offense is incurred. If the boil is ripe when he squeezes it, there is no offense.

If a nun squeezes an unripe boil and the person passes away from this life as a result, a grave offense is incurred. If the boil is ripe when she squeezes it, there is no offense.

A monk was ill and suitable food for him could not be found. His attendant gave him unsuitable food and said: "Venerable one, eat whatever there is." The monk ate it and passed away from this life. A grave offense is incurred. If suitable food had been given and the monk passed away from it, there is no offense.

If a monk who is ill cannot obtain medicine suitable for him, the same applies to his attendant as well.

A sick monk said to his attendant: "Venerable one, attendant — bring me out of my room, wash me, dry me, bring me back inside, and let me sit." The attendant brought him out, and also let him sit and lie down. If the monk then passed away from this life, there is no offense for anyone.

In summary:

Striking with a stick, a thunder-bolt, or water,
two wilderness places, sleeping on a high bed,
anger, and striking the palms together.

A monk was sitting when someone nearby fainted. A monk struck that person to rouse him, and that person passed away from this life. Remorse arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense. At that time, a wind known as 'sword-like' had arisen in that person."

Furthermore, cases in which someone is struck by lightning and passes away from this life, and cases in which someone is struck by water and passes away from this life — all these are likewise to be explained in full. The seventeen groups are also to be analyzed in detail, just as they appear in the Vibhāṅga.

Another householder, newly faithful, offered the Saṅgha fresh seasonal grain and fresh seasonal fruit of various kinds, and afterward ate some himself. Another monk living in a forest hermitage went to that householder's house. The householder thought: "From now on, instead of offering to the Saṅgha, I will offer to this forest monk," and gave accordingly. Those monks then told that householder: "Previously, when you offered fresh seasonal grain and fresh seasonal fruit to the Saṅgha and then ate afterward yourself, that was given by you — yet now a forest monk came to your house and you have been turned away from giving. Go, and call that monk here." The others then called out, and that forest monk told the householder about the fresh seasonal grain and fresh seasonal fruit —

that those fresh seasonal grain and fresh seasonal fruit had been offered first to the Saṅgha and that one ate afterward — "You went to that householder's house and caused him to be turned away." The forest monk replied, "Reverend ones, I did not turn him away. I did not instruct him to do so." The monks then said, "This cannot be settled by words here; bring him and let him be taken to court." They took him to court, and at that point his time had passed. The monks were seized with remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense of defeat; however, a grave offense is incurred."

Another householder, who had been in the custom of offering robes to the monks of the Saṅgha during their rains retreat, had a forest monk come to his house. The householder thought: "From now on, rather than offering to the Saṅgha, I will offer to this forest monk," and gave accordingly. The monks then thought: "That householder, who used to offer robes to the monks of the Saṅgha during their rains retreat, has now stopped offering because a forest monk went there and turned him away." They went and called that monk, and when they had called him, they asked the forest monk: "Has that householder, who previously offered robes to the monks of the Saṅgha during their rains retreat, now stopped offering because you went to his house and turned him away?" He replied, "Reverend ones, I did not turn him away. I did not instruct him to do so." The monks then said, "This cannot be settled by words here; bring him and press him as far as the door panel." They pressed him as far as the door panel, and at that point his time had passed. Those monks were seized with remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense of defeat; however, a grave offense is incurred."

A monk who was practicing almsround was standing near a house with a closed door, leaning a bed-post against it, when his monastic robe's hem flipped outward and fell upon a child, and that child's time passed. That monk was seized with remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense of defeat. Be heedful and practice the almsround."

A brahmin, having performed auspicious rites and taken omens early in the morning, was sitting inside his house. A monk who came to that house on almsround — the brahmin grew angry and pushed him away, and that monk fell upon a child, and the child died. That monk was seized with remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense."

A monk who was striking ashes with a mantra and smearing them with his hand sneezed a handful of ash, and at that point someone's time passed. Those monks were seized with remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense; be heedful and sneeze."

A monk who had been hiccupping reached the point of near death, and another monk pressed a fist against him, causing blood to come along with the hiccup — and that monk's time passed. That monk was seized with remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offense of defeat. Take every care to press in such a way that the hiccup is relieved while no passing of time occurs."

In brief:

A second seat and a second pair of parents,
and likewise a second act of throwing,
comparable cases with monkeys,
and threatening thieves — these are set out.

The case of the venerable one who sat on a seat without checking it for black insects is to be understood in full as it appears in the Vinaya. The case of Bhikṣuṇī Gālinī is to be applied in the same manner. The case of a monk who offered on the road and at whose point time passed is likewise to be understood as it appears in the Vinaya.

Two senior monks — a father and a son who had gone forth — went together to the Jeta Grove, and they reached the monastery village.

The father said to the son, "Inside here, leopards are likely to cause fright — stay within the enclosure." The son replied, "You are elderly. If you stay together with the laypeople, what difference is there between them and us?" The father said, "Son, keep the fire-watch; I will sleep." Then the elderly man lay down, and the monk too lay down. The elderly man snored, and at the sound of this, a leopard came. The leopard seized him by the head, and he cried out. Startled by the cry, the leopard released him and fled. The monk took a lamp and examined the situation, and saw that the time had passed. He thought: "Even though he said to stay inside, I did not heed his words, and so whatever has come to pass that is beyond the time — all of it is my fault." The monk fell into remorse, and the Blessed One declared: "There is no offence. Keep the fire-watch."

A monk who sent another monk, with intent to kill, to a place of danger: if the other monk's time passed as a result, this constitutes a root downfall. If the time did not pass, it constitutes a grave offence.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Vaiśālī, and some monks went into a great forest by day to walk about. One of them killed a monkey there, and another monk said to him, "A root downfall has occurred for you. On what grounds? What difference is there between being deprived of a human livelihood and this one who resembles a human?" The monk fell into remorse, and the Blessed One declared: "There is no root downfall. It does entail a downfall."

The case of threatening a thief is to be understood in full as it appears in the Vinaya.

In brief:
The case of Mgo-ldan, the physician of old,
the one who was obstructed and died,
the residence at Vaiśālī,
the cutting of a life-cord, and the one who fled.

At Śrāvastī, a certain householder's wife gave birth to a boy child who grew up. Because a crowd burned his scalp as a treatment for scabies, his name was given as Mgo-ldan, "the Head-marked one." In time he went forth from home life, and once, having entered a village for some purpose, another householder's wife arrived, leading a boy child, following just behind him while looking about to left and right. A ram came and butted her, and the monk, walking with his head bowed down, also became aware that he had been struck against her, and as the ram butted him from behind, the monk fell on top of the boy child, and the boy's time passed. The monk fell into remorse, and the Blessed One declared: "There is no offence. Henceforth, monks, do not walk in such a manner — look ahead as far as a yoke-length."

Another monk who had formerly been a physician came to a sick monk and said to him, "You should get a bloodletting." He then inserted a needle into him, and when he drew the needle back out, the monk's time passed. The monk fell into remorse, and the Blessed One declared: "There is no offence. Henceforth, monks, do not practice medicine without training."

Another sick monk, whose illness was not getting better, thought: "I am alive and lingering on — I may as well die by whatever means." He said to his nursing attendant, "Venerable one, give me a cord." The attendant gave it to him, he tied it around his throat, and his time passed. The monk who had given the cord fell into remorse, and the Blessed One declared: "There is no offence. Henceforth, monks, do not give a cord to a sick patient indiscriminately."

While a monk was on his alms round in the city of Vaiśālī, some residents who were carrying bows and arrows approached him, and the monk said, "Good sirs, rather than kill me, let fly at that one there!" They shot an arrow and killed that other person on the spot. The monk fell into remorse, and the Blessed One declared: "There is no offence. Henceforth, monks, do not give such instructions."

Another sick monk, in the manner already described in detail, took a rope and went into a great forest. There he climbed a tree, tied the rope to a branch, put his neck through the noose, and leapt from the tree. The rope snapped, and beneath him lay a dog that had just given birth; the monk fell on top of it, and the dog together with her pups passed away. The monks who heard of this reported it in full to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "The former monk incurs an offence; the latter incurs no offence. Monks, do not strive for death by such bodily means. If one does so, a grave offence is incurred."

Another monk needed to go to a village on some business. He led along a monk who had recently recovered from illness and had not yet regained his strength. On the road, they were alarmed by a robber, and the first monk said to the other, "Venerable one, run ahead!" The other replied, "I cannot." The monk then said, "Come here then — hold on to me," and led him along in that way, bringing him toward the village, but that monk passed away. The first monk thought: "Had I not led him, he would not have died." Remorse arose in him, and the Blessed One declared: "There is no offence. Henceforth, monks, do not take a patient who is as frail as that out on the road."

In summary, the following topics have been covered in verse:

Telling one with a pleasant feeling to seek death,
an arhat, a brahmin, a lord among the senses,
robes and alms round,
and the two forms of going to the village.

The Blessed One, the Buddha (Skt. buddha), was dwelling in the forest grove of the village of Bṛjī's Light. As no rule of training had yet been laid down for the monks dwelling on the bank of the Suvastu river, they were all first offenders and thus incurred no offence. When, although no rule of training had been laid down, a superhuman quality was claimed in the presence of many people from various clans, doubt arose among them: "Who among us would be a first offender?" Scruple and remorse arose. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, when no rule of training has been laid down, all the monks — including those of the past — who dwelt on the bank of the Suvastu river were first offenders. Therefore, no offence is incurred by first offenders."

A monk, perceiving a person as non-human, claimed to that person a superhuman quality that did not exist. Remorse arose in that monk, and the Blessed One declared: "If one perceives a human as a human and makes such a claim, it constitutes a root defeat. If one has doubt as to whether the other is non-human, a grave offence is incurred. If one perceives a non-human as a human, a grave offence is incurred."

A monk claimed a non-existent superhuman quality to a householder. The householder was distracted and simply said, "Whatever you say, Venerable One." Remorse arose in the monk, and the Blessed One declared: "It does not constitute a root defeat, but a grave offence is incurred."

A householder said to a monk, "Venerable One, as you are an arhat, you are worthy of the finest robes, alms food, lodging, medicines for illness, and requisites." Since the monk said nothing and thereby accepted this, a grave offence is incurred.

If a householder asks a monk, "Are you possessed of the blameless, brahma-like Dharma?" and the monk says nothing and thereby accepts this, a grave offence is incurred.

If a householder says, "Venerable One, if you are an arhat, please accept my alms," and the monk says nothing and thereby accepts this, a grave offence is incurred.

A monk intending to go on alms round in a nearby village puts on his lower robe in the early morning and goes to the village. A householder says to him, "Venerable One, if you are an arhat, please come inside," and the monk says nothing and enters — a grave offence is incurred. Likewise, if the householder says, "Please be seated, take your meal, express your rejoicing, and come again," and the monk says nothing and thereby accepts this, a grave offence is incurred.

A monk intending to go on alms round in another village puts on his lower robe in the early morning and goes to that village. A householder says, "Venerable One, if you are an arhat, please come inside the house." If the monk replies, "I am not in the slightest an arhat — but if you will permit it, I shall come in," there is no offence. If the householder then says, "Please be seated, take your meal and refreshments and the rest, and rejoice; please come again," and the monk replies, "I am not in the slightest an arhat — but if you permit it, I shall withdraw," there is no offence.

If a householder says to a monk, "Venerable One, your sense faculties are supremely restrained and well guarded," and the monk says nothing and thereby accepts this, a grave offence is incurred. But if the householder says, "Please come out again," and the monk says, "I am not in the slightest an arhat," and then comes out, there is no offence.

In brief, the two sūtra verses on the cases of the group of six, of supernormal knowledge, of the absence of a mass of fire, of voices not yet transcended, of gandharvas and asuras, of beating the pool and the outcry of Bā-la-ha, the two lower austerities practised continuously, the two who quarrelled and the child who came in peace, the beautiful one, and these two — all of these should be understood in detail.

In brief: the large curtain, the sky, anointing the head with both hands, the small chamber, intoxication from bathing, and what is improper in conduct and place — these too should be known.

The setting is at Śrāvastī. Before the training rule had been laid down, when there was as yet no offence for a first offender, the venerable Chaṅka thought to himself repeatedly, "The training rule has not yet been laid down," and while thinking this many times ejaculated semen. He then became uncertain, thinking, "Have I committed a first offence or not?" The Blessed One declared: "Before the training rule was laid down, Chaṅka and all cases like his count entirely as first offenders, and a first offender incurs no offence."

A monk who ejaculated semen by blowing upon himself, or practised in open space, or ejaculated into the sky, or touched his own member, or pressed it and experienced pleasure, or pressed it and emitted, or emitted while awake, or began and then emitted again — in all these cases a grave offence is incurred.

A monk who ejaculated semen by rubbing his thigh felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offence."

A woman prostrated with both hands at a monk's two feet, and he thereupon ejaculated semen. The monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offence."

The doe Mṛgāra's mother bowed at the feet of the monks. She prostrated her head at the feet of the venerable Nandika. He ejaculated semen, and it fell upon the head of the doe Mṛgāra's mother.

She went off to one side, placed both hands upon her head, and said: "Those who practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One practice it under great affliction. As for me, I have made a fine find indeed." And so she uttered words of self-congratulation. The venerable monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offence."

A leaping monkey. A monk touched a monkey and ejaculated semen. The monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offence."

A monk was working in a steam house and semen arose. The monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offence."

A monk was walking from lodging to lodging, and semen arose. The monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offence with respect to the Saṅgha's residue, yet a grave offence is incurred." It is the same when there is unwise attention.

In brief:

In five ways with a woman, and five ways with harm,
Five ways with taking hold, and six with a charnel ground dweller.

A monk's mother, sister, daughter, wife, and female friend drew close to him, and before long embraced him around the neck, whereupon semen arose. The monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offence."

A monk rescued a woman from fire, from water, from a precipice, from a weapon, from a wild beast, from a non-human being, and semen arose. The monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offence."

A woman seized a monk by the foot, or by the shin, or by the knee, or by the thigh, or by the toes, and semen arose. The monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "There is no offence."

When a monk ejaculated semen through discoloration, or through being bloated, or swollen, or reddened, or decayed, or when semen was drawn from a skeleton — in all these cases a Saṅgha residue offence is incurred.

In brief:

Through scratching, dragging, with the finger,
Through being chilled by water,
And through making it an internal vessel —
These are the twenty modes of conduct.

If a monk ejaculates semen through scratching, there is no offence. It is the same through dragging. But if that monk grasped his own member and semen arose, the Blessed One declared: "A grave offence is incurred."

A monk who was on his alms round encountered a young girl who was lying stretched out, and she said to the noble one: "Come here — do such-and-such to me," and he inserted his finger into her. The monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "A grave offence is incurred."

A monk who was bathing let his member rest in the current of water, and through the chill semen arose. The monk felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: "A grave offence is incurred."

If a monk ejaculates semen into his own head, or into his ear, or into his nose — in all these cases a Saṅgha residue offence is incurred.

If a monk ejaculates semen into his armpit, his back, his chest, his navel, or into his hair — in all these cases a Saṅgha residue offence is incurred.

If a monk ejaculates semen into his hand, his shoulder, or his upper arm — in all these cases a Saṅgha residue offence is incurred.

If a monk ejaculates semen into his waist, his shin, his foot, or his thighs — in all these cases a Saṅgha residue offence is incurred.

If a monk ejaculates semen into his palm, his sole of the foot, or —

— or into his palms and similar places, in all these cases a Saṅgha residue offence is incurred.

If a monk ejaculates semen onto a throne, a small seat, a wooden stool, or between seat cushions — in all these cases a Saṅgha residue offence is incurred.

If a monk ejaculates semen onto a pot, a small vessel, a ladle, or into the interior of a pot — in all these cases a Saṅgha residue offence is incurred.

If a monk ejaculates semen onto a stone, onto something cracked, into the interior of something cracked, onto a door-threshold, or onto soft flesh — in all these cases a Saṅgha residue offence is incurred.

In summary, the foregoing is set forth in verse:

Ejaculating with the perception of a woman — between the thighs and the shoulder,
away from the hand and fingers;
grasping with the foot and so forth;
and embracing from a green or similar state onward.

When the Venerable Charka had not yet established a rule of training and thought, "I have come into full bodily contact with many women — what was my first such act?" — the Blessed One declared: Where no rule of training has yet been established, everything that occurred before Charka, including that occasion, is a first offence; and for one who commits a first offence there is no transgression.

A monk grasped a human woman with the perception that she was not human. When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: If one perceives a human being as a human being, it is a Saṅgha residue offence. The fuller account is to be understood under four aspects.

If a monk pushes a woman with his foot, it is a minor offence. If a woman pushes a monk with her foot, there is no offence. If a monk pushes a woman with his shoulder, it is a minor offence. If a woman pushes a monk with her shoulder, there is no offence.

A monk embraced a woman around the neck. When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: There is no offence.

A woman grasped a monk with her fingers. When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: There is no offence.

A monk rescued a woman from fire, water, a precipice, weapons, wild beasts, and non-human beings. When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: There is no offence.

A woman grasped a monk with her foot, her arm, her knee, her thigh, or her fingers. When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: There is no offence.

If a monk embraces a woman's corpse that has turned blue-green around the neck, or one that is swollen, putrefied, turned red, scattered, or reduced to bones — in all these cases a Saṅgha residue offence is incurred.

In summary, this is set forth in verse:

Lifting a woman who has fallen and is rolling about;
meeting a woman in the dark;
a young woman calling out from a village —
these are the fifth and thirteenth rules.

If a woman has fallen and is rolling about and a monk lifts her up, it is a minor offence. If a woman lifts a monk who has fallen and is rolling about, there is no offence.

An elderly monk went to look after a girl and sat down on her lap. When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: There is no offence.

A monk was sitting urinating at midnight. A woman came out from inside and in the darkness they met face to face; she knocked him down and fell on top of him. When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: There is no offence.

A monk entered a village for alms. A young girl was seated, calling out from the village. She said to the noble monk, "Come here — please do this and that for me." He approached her; she put alms in his bowl; then she smeared him with excrement and struck him — in all these cases a Saṅgha residue offence is incurred.

A monk was teaching the Dharma to a woman, and she offered him her seat-post, her thigh, her upper arm, her waist, her ribs, her back, her hand, her shoulder, and her head — all of these constitute a wrongdoing.

In brief, the verses run:

Charka's pleasure and his perception,
the bee that receives what is vile,
the sister engaged in bad conduct —
"I have seen it," and "before you,"
"that one," "this one," "that one pleases me" —
these are the cases.

Where no rule of training had yet been laid down, the first offender incurs no offence. The venerable Charka thought to himself, "I have spoken words of indecency to quite a number of women — what is my status as a first offender?" and doubt arose in him. This is elaborated fully. When he reported what had happened to the monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: Where no rule of training has been laid down, one who has acted together with Charka and those like him is in every case a first offender, and a first offender incurs no offence.

A monk perceived a human woman as a non-human and spoke words of indecency to her. When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: When one perceives a human as a human, it becomes a Saṅgha residue offence. The full details should be inquired into. If one speaks of it as a matter involving supernormal power and miraculous display, a grave offence is incurred. If one speaks of it as a matter not involving miraculous display, it becomes a Saṅgha residue offence.

A monk went to a woman and said, "Sister, please give me a silk ear-ornament." She replied, "Noble one, what silk ear-ornament can I give you? But I heard you, noble one — I had prepared a silk ear-ornament in advance." When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: A grave offence is incurred.

A monk was going around a village for alms when a woman approached him and said, "Noble one, do it like this," and then said, "A body of yours with such fortune as this accords with a donkey — do it like that, in that way." When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: There is no Saṅgha residue offence, but a grave offence is incurred.

A monk who was naturally given to speaking words of indecency spoke such words to a woman. When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: There is no Saṅgha residue offence, but a grave offence is incurred.

A nun rose early in the morning, bathed, applied eye-ointment, combed her hair, put on a worn-out old Dharma robe, and went to Śrāvastī. A monk who was out collecting alms saw her and said to her, "Sister, you mount upon men and conduct yourself accordingly." When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: A grave offence is incurred.

An elderly monk went in the manner of a girl — that is, he went about like one. She was a girl of loose conduct. He said to the girl, "Do not destroy two households like this." She replied, "If I cannot refrain, what am I to do?" He said, "If you cannot refrain, then have yourself cut apart with a sickle." When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: There is no Saṅgha residue offence, but a grave offence is incurred.

A monk was one who would go frequently to a nearby village. Early one morning he put on his lower robe and went to that village. There he said to the householder's wife, "Sister, give me some." She said, "Noble one, what shall I offer you?" He said, "Sister, give me that." She consented and said, "Noble one, I have prepared it in advance." He said —

When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: A grave offence is incurred. "Sister, give me whatever pleases you." She said, "Noble one, what could please me?" He said, "Sister, give me whatever pleases you." She understood and said, "Noble one, I have prepared it in advance." When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: A grave offence is incurred. "Sister, give me whatever is before you." She said, "Venerable one, what is before me? What is before me, noble one?" He said, "Sister, give me whatever is before you." She understood and said, "Noble one, I have prepared it in advance." When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: A grave offence is incurred.

A monk was one who would go frequently to another nearby village. One early morning he put on his lower robe and outer robe, took his bowl, and went to that village. He said to the householder's wife, "Sister, give me whatever is pleasing to you." She said, "Noble one, what could be pleasing to me?" He said, "Sister, give me whatever is pleasing to you." She understood and said, "Noble one, I have prepared it in advance." When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: There is no Saṅgha residue offence, but a grave offence is incurred.

The same applies to the expression "whatever is pleasing."

A monk was one who would go frequently to another nearby village. One early morning he put on his lower robe, took his bowl, and went to that village. A householder said to his wife, "Give the monk whatever he wishes," and departed. That monk also, in the early morning, having put on his lower robe and outer robe and taken his bowl, went to that house. The woman said, "Noble one, the householder has instructed me to give the monk whatever he desires." He said, "Sister, I desire you yourself." She also understood and said, "Noble one, I have prepared it in advance." That monk, thinking, "Perhaps no Saṅgha residue offence has arisen for me," felt remorse. The Blessed One declared: There is no Saṅgha residue offence, but a grave offence is incurred.

A monk was one who would go frequently to another nearby village. One early morning he put on his lower robe and went to that village. He said to the householder's wife, "Sister, give me some water to drink." She said, "Venerable one, please wait while I draw water." He said, "Sister, you yourself are the water." She also understood and said, "Noble one, I have prepared it in advance." When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: A grave offence is incurred. "Sister, give me some food." She said, "Venerable one, please wait while I prepare it." He said, "Sister, you yourself are my food." She said, "Noble one, I have prepared it in advance." When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: A grave offence is incurred. "Sister, give me some porridge." She said, "Venerable one, please wait while I cook it." He said, "Sister, you yourself are my porridge." She said, "Noble one, I have prepared it in advance." When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: A grave offence is incurred.

A monk was one who would go frequently to another nearby village. One early morning he put on his lower robe and went to that village. He said to the householder's wife, "Sister, give me some food."

This is the twenty-fifth fascicle of the Noble Vinaya Text. In brief:

Things pleasing and delightful,
water and food set out,
porridge and things to eat —
what was spoken is the same in each case.

"Noble one, wait here a moment. Sister, you yourself are my porridge." When she understood, she said, "Noble one, I will prepare it in advance." When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: A grave offence is incurred.

If a monk were to speak lewd words to a woman and she did not understand, that virtuous woman asked, "What did the noble one say?" When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: There is no Saṅgha remainder offence, but a grave offence is incurred.

In brief:

A doe's young and a messenger,
a name and three wives of nobles,
two prostitutes and a woman,
a young man — these form a cluster.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove (Jetavana), in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, at Śrāvastī. The rule not yet having been laid down, there is no offence for one who acts for the first time. The one who is like a doe's young — that dark-complexioned youth — thought to himself: the rule not yet having been laid down, if I were to speak lewdly to a considerable number of people, what would that make of my being one who acts for the first time? Doubt, suspicion, and remorse arose in his mind. He reported what had happened to the monks, and the Blessed One declared: Before the rule was laid down, that dark-complexioned youth who is like a doe's young, and all others together with him who transgressed, are ones who acted for the first time — and for one who acts for the first time there is no offence.

A monk was one who would go frequently to a nearby village in another district. He went to that village, and the householder said to him, "Noble one, would you be willing to carry a message to the woman called such-and-such, saying, 'Come here'?" He replied, "I can go, but I cannot bring back a reply." The householder said, "Well then, how shall it be known that the matter has been remembered and accomplished? I will station a monk at a place called such-and-such." He sent that monk to another house. When he saw that monk return, he said to him, "Venerable one, stay here for just a moment." That monk stayed there, and then the householder came back out and said to the monk, "Reverend one, excellent, excellent — the matter has been accomplished." The monk said, "What was the signal?" When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: There is no offence.

A monk was one who would go frequently to a nearby village in another district. He went to that village, and the householder said to him, "Noble one, would you be willing to carry this message to the woman called such-and-such: 'Come here in this manner'?" He said, "I can," and went and delivered the message. That woman replied, "Reverend one, I do not wish it," and the matter was not accomplished. When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: There is no Saṅgha remainder offence, but a grave offence is incurred.

A householder's wife had committed a slight fault, and he beat her with his fist and drove her away. Meanwhile, a monk was one who would go frequently to a nearby village in another district. He brought those two together, and those two were reconciled. When remorse arose in that monk, the Blessed One declared: If they were thrown together as though casting three stones, or clapped together like cymbals, and it was proclaimed that they were not husband and wife, then if one acts as a go-between in such a case a grave offence is incurred.

A monk was one who would go frequently to a nearby village in another district. He went to that village, and the householder said to him, "Noble one, would you be willing to carry a message to this woman called such-and-such, a prostitute, saying, 'Come here'?" He said, "I can," went there, and delivered the message to her.

She thought, "He cannot come to sleep on the far side; I shall sleep here," and with that thought she lay down. When dawn came, the purpose of those two had not been fulfilled.

Remorse arose in that monk, and the Blessed One declared: There is no offence entailing suspension for the Saṅgha, but a grave offence is incurred.

A monk was one who would go frequently to a nearby village in another district. He went to that village, and the householder said to him, "Noble one, would you be willing to carry this message to the woman called such-and-such, saying, 'Come here'?" He said, "I can," went there, and delivered the message to her. She was on her way there when another person intercepted and carried her off, and so the purpose of those two was not fulfilled.

Remorse arose in that monk, and the Blessed One declared: A grave offence is incurred.

A monk was one who would go frequently to a nearby village in another district. He went to that village, and the householder said to him, "Noble one, would you be willing to carry this message to the woman called such-and-such?" He said, "I can," went, and delivered the message to her. She, however, adorned herself and dressed at once, but her husband arrived, and so the purpose of those two was not fulfilled.

Remorse arose in that monk, and the Blessed One declared: A grave offence is incurred.

Two householders were friends, and both their wives became pregnant. They agreed: "If you bear a daughter and I bear a son, give your daughter to my son; and if I bear a daughter and you bear a son, I will give my daughter to your son." In due course one of them bore a son and the other bore a daughter, but that householder passed away. When he had passed away the household affairs fell into decline, and that householder's family resolved not to give the girl in marriage. When the young man heard of this, there was a monk who would go frequently to a nearby village, and when he arrived in that village the young man said to him, "Noble one, would you be willing to carry this message to the girl called such-and-such: 'If your parents have not given you to me, and if you would come to me on your own, then I too, through the ripening of my karma, have fallen into hardship; yet even so, my resources may yet be found again — so for now do not send me away'?" He said, "I can," went, and delivered the message. The girl fled from her mother and father, went to him, and those two came together.

Remorse arose in that monk, and the Blessed One declared: There is no offence entailing suspension for the Saṅgha, but a grave offence is incurred.

A householder said to a woman, "Arrange an opportunity for me with her." She replied, "I am unable to do so." He said, "How shall I know when you are able? Tell that monk who goes frequently to the village: when you strike a fist against the householder's back, she should take note." When that monk came to the village, the woman said to him, "Noble one, would you be willing to strike a fist against the back of the householder called such-and-such?" He said, "I can," went, and struck a fist against that householder's back. Then the noble one said, "Excellent, excellent!" — and when asked, "What is this?" he replied, "It is a signal." Remorse arose in that monk, and the Blessed One declared: There is no offence entailing suspension for the Saṅgha, but a grave offence is incurred.

In brief:

The two who go to the nearby village,
and two others of the Saṅgha as well,
the one in robes and the one who is sick,
the young woman — these make five cases.

A certain monk was one who went to a nearby village. He arrived at that village, and the woman said to him, "Noble one, would you be willing to carry a message to the householder called such-and-such, saying, 'Come here'?" He replied, "I can, if I may also arrange a meal for the Saṅgha." She provided the funds, the monk arranged the meal, summoned the householder, and the two of them met. Remorse arose in that monk, and the Blessed One declared: There is no offence entailing suspension for the Saṅgha, but a grave offence is incurred.

Likewise, the same applies in the case of the householder himself.

The wife of a householder was beautiful, attractive, and lovely. A certain great minister named Gzhongs Gyad desired her and sent many messages to her, yet the woman would not yield. Then the householder passed away. After he had passed away, the great minister said on account of some slight grievance: "Is there truly no means at all by which, even now, things might work out well for us without difficulty?" Someone said, "There is a way." The great minister went to her and sent many messages, but she would not yield, it is said. Then he was told, "Well then, dear girl, be willing. Through your efforts alone these people will come to be at ease." She asked him, "Then who shall be sent as a messenger?" and he said, "We have a monk who goes to the nearby village — let us send him as the messenger." That monk also went to that village, and the householder's wife said to him: "Noble one, would you be willing to carry this message to the great minister called such-and-such, offering him this house of mine, these goods of mine, and all these possessions of mine, and saying, 'Come here'?" He said, "I can," went, and conveyed the message to him. The two of them met, and remorse arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: A grave offence is incurred.

A certain householder's wife built a temple for the Saṅgha, and she was in the practice of offering robes and medicinal supplies to it. Then that householder's wife passed away. After she passed away, there was no one to continue offering robes and medicinal supplies to that temple. The monks went to the householder and said: "Householder, just as your wife established this temple, would you not also offer a little in the way of robes, supplies, and medicine for the sick?" He replied, "Venerable ones, that wife was a woman of great merit and great power. Whatever she said, everything was done because of her. But if the householder called such-and-such's wife would send meals to me, then perhaps I might still be inclined to give." The monks went to that householder's wife and said: "Householder's wife, are you able to send meals to the householder called such-and-such?" She replied, "Venerable ones, I am not able. Here in my own household there is much to be done; I am unable even for that, so what need is there to speak of sending to another?" They then urged the householder's wife to be willing, saying, "It will be an offering to the stūpa; it will be offered to the Saṅgha." Now the householder's wife was a person of faith, and she said, "I have faith," and agreed. The two of them met again and again, and they came together. Remorse arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: There is no offence.

A certain householder built a monastery for the Saṅgha, and made offerings there of robes and medicines for the sick, rendering benefit in various ways. That householder then passed away. The fuller account follows in the same manner as before. His widow said, "If you send such-and-such works to be done for the householder so-and-so, then I will be able to continue making offerings in the same way." The fuller account follows. The Blessed One declared: There is no offence.

A monk was going to visit a nearby village in another district. Having arrived there, a householder said to him, "Venerable one, can you carry the message to the wife called such-and-such, telling her to come here?" The monk replied that he could, went and delivered the message. But that woman fell ill, and the householder too fell ill, and since both were struck down by illness, the matter was not accomplished. The Blessed One declared: A grave offence is incurred.

A monk was going to visit a nearby village in another district. Having arrived there, a woman said to him, "Venerable one, can you carry the message to the householder called such-and-such, telling him to come here?" He replied that he could, went there, and delivered the message. But that householder fell ill, and the woman too fell ill. Since both were struck down by illness, the matter was not accomplished. Remorse arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: A grave offence is incurred.

A monk was going to visit a nearby village in another district. In the morning he dressed in his robes and lower garment, took up his alms bowl, and went to that village. A householder there said to him, "Can you carry the message to the householder called such-and-such, asking him to give his daughter or sister in marriage to my son?" He replied that he could, went and delivered the message. But the boy had passed away, or the girl had become hunchbacked, or had gone mad, or had been given to another. Remorse arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: A grave offence is incurred.

A monk was going to visit a nearby village in another district. In the morning he dressed in his robes and lower garment and took up his alms bowl, and went to that village. The fuller account is to be given in the same way here too. Whether the boy fell ill or the girl fell ill, or became hunchbacked, or was given to another, in any of these cases the result is the same. Remorse arose in that monk. The Blessed One declared: A grave offence is incurred.

The Vinaya section on the Disciplinarian is concluded.

The sūtra collection of the Vinaya from a single rule upward, comprised under three doors: the first exposition and the second, and the third likewise — having striven to the last, this summary was definitively stated.

The summary of the first door of sūtras: the inexpert one who was addressed, and the entangled one from whom an offence arose likewise; the learned one and the one who was instructed, and the one greatly learned who abandoned the Dharma.

The second: the abridged exposition, the one who disparaged, and the two who formed views from sifting; and likewise those four who denigrated; and the two of the restoration ceremony.

This is to say: by that single cause of being possessed of the vow, all offences are to be declared. This is to say: by that single cause of not being possessed of the vow, all offences are not to be declared. This is to say: by that single cause of not being possessed of the vow, all offences are not brought together into one. This is to say: by that single cause of being possessed of the vow, all offences are brought together into one.

Among all verbal wrongs, the single gravest is to slander a Tathāgata by attributing to him what does not exist. Among all physical wrongs, the single gravest is to draw blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent.

Among all wrongs, the single gravest is to divide the Saṅgha. Among all wrongs arising from a multitude, the single gravest is to side with one who is dividing the Saṅgha. Among all wrongs arising from slander, the single gravest is to cause a schism in the Saṅgha of the śrāvakas of a Tathāgata. Among all wrongs arising from persons, the single gravest is to falsely attribute what does not exist. Among all wrongs arising from taking life, the single gravest is to deprive a pratyekabuddha of his life. Among all wrongs arising from taking what is not given, the single gravest is to steal from what belongs to the Saṅgha of the śrāvakas of a Tathāgata. Among all wrongs arising from unchaste conduct, the single gravest is to engage in unchaste conduct with one who is both an arhat and a woman. Among all wrongs arising from false speech, the single gravest is to claim, in the absence of any such attainment, a superhuman quality before another person.

One kind of properly conducted restoration ceremony is this: one without a valid basis. One kind of properly conducted restoration ceremony is this: one with a valid basis. The first section is complete.

In brief: with one who is unskilled, act in three ways; and also, together with the remainder, three. With bodily action that is entirely complete, and with verbal action, do not cite scripture.

Transgressions are of two kinds: non-virtuous, and not cited in scripture. Non-virtuous transgressions are also of two kinds: those with a remainder, and those without remainder. Those not cited in scripture are also of two kinds: those with a remainder, and those without remainder. Transgressions too are of two kinds: those with a remainder, and those without remainder. Those with a remainder are of two kinds: non-virtuous, and not cited in scripture. Those without remainder are also of two kinds: non-virtuous, and not cited in scripture.

Transgressions are also of two kinds: those arising from body, and those arising from speech. Those arising from body are of two kinds: those with a remainder, and those without remainder. Furthermore, those arising from body are of two kinds: non-virtuous, and not cited in scripture. Furthermore, those arising from body are of two kinds: those that have an object, and those without an object. Those arising from speech are also of two kinds: those with a remainder, and those without remainder. Furthermore, those arising from speech are of two kinds: non-virtuous, and not cited in scripture. Furthermore, those arising from speech are of two kinds: those that have an object, and those without an object.

Transgressions are of two kinds: those cited in scripture, and those not cited in scripture. Transgressions are also of two kinds: those that are concealed, and those that are not concealed.

In brief:

What is fit to be confessed, and
what has not been confessed and is to be raised again —
having made a fivefold division,
one speaks to an intimate who is pure.

Transgressions are of two kinds: those requiring confession, and those not requiring confession. Transgressions are also of two kinds: those that are fit to be set down, and those that are not fit to be set down. Transgressions are also of two kinds: permitted offences, and non-permitted offences. Transgressions are also of two kinds: those that can be raised again, and those that cannot be raised again. Transgressions are also of two kinds: those that cause division, and those that do not cause division. Those that cause division are of two kinds: those with a remainder, and those without remainder. Those that do not cause division are of two kinds: non-virtuous, and not cited in scripture. Furthermore, those that do not cause division are of two kinds: those with a remainder, and those without remainder.

Transgressions are also of two kinds: those that are grave, and those that are momentary. Transgressions are also of two kinds: those that are spoken, and those that are not spoken.

In brief:

Utterly entangled and without concealment —

common and the sevenfold, the time of a buddha and the localities, extreme attachment and the directions.

Transgressions are of two kinds: those that are utterly entangled, and those that are not entangled. Those that lead to concealment, and those that do not lead to concealment. Those that are common, and those that are not common. Those common to nuns and those common to monks. Those common to monks and those common to probationary nuns. Those common to monks and those common to novice nuns. Those common to monks and those common to novice monks. Those common to monks and those common to male lay practitioners. Those common to monks and those common to female lay practitioners. Those at the time of a buddha, and those in an intermediate period. Those permitted by the locality, and those not permitted by the locality. Those with extreme attachment, and those without extreme attachment. Those on one side, and those on all sides.

In brief:

Departing from voluminous reading in other ways,
weighty in ripening — likewise so;
the fourfold arousing of confession,
and subsequent reliance on disclosure.

Those with karmic ripening, and those without karmic ripening. Those that may be raised again, and those that may not be raised again. Of those that may be raised again there are two: through confession, and through the giving of vows from the outset. Furthermore, those that may be raised again are of two kinds: imputed, and ultimate. Those that may not be raised again are of two kinds: not seen, and not amenable to settlement. Reliance is of two kinds: reliance on the Saṅgha, and reliance on an individual person. Confession is of two kinds: to the Saṅgha, and to an individual.

In brief:

The learned should be understood threefold:
those with conscience, of two kinds,
the challenger and what is declared in words,
the steadfast and the petitioner.

Being skilled in recognizing when no transgression has occurred as no transgression, and being skilled in recognizing when a transgression has occurred. Furthermore, skill is of two kinds: being skilled in raising again a transgression that has occurred, and being skilled in purifying that which has not become a transgression. Conscience is of two kinds: those with carefulness, and those without carefulness. The two transgressions that arise for those who act as challengers: from the Saṅgha, and from an individual. The two transgressions arising from speech: what is declared in words, and what is explained. Furthermore, speech-arising transgressions are of two kinds: steady, and unsteady. Furthermore, speech-arising transgressions are of two kinds: those who make petition, and those who do not make petition.

In brief:

Appointed and bound by vows, having examined,
listening, and being very attentive,
fully knowing, conciliatory, discordant,
abiding in one's nature, speaking with certainty, and wisdom.

Of those who preside over the Saṅgha, there are two: the appointed and the unappointed; those bound by vows and those not bound by vows; those who speak after having examined and those who speak without having examined; those who listen and those who proclaim; those who are attentive and those who are not attentive; those who know fully and those who do not know fully; those who are conciliatory and those who are not conciliatory; those who are discordant and those who are concordant; those who abide in their nature and those who do not abide in their nature; those who speak with certainty and those who speak without certainty; those with wisdom and those with faulty wisdom.

In brief:

Much learning and mastery of recitation,
complete and definite,
rendering service, having acted badly,
knowing the Dharma — these are the seven.

Of those who preside over the Saṅgha, there are two: those with much learning and those with little learning; those who have mastered the recitation of scripture and those who have not mastered the recitation of scripture; those with complete scriptural transmission and those with incomplete scriptural transmission; those who are certain and those who are not certain; those who render service and those who do not render service; those who know the Dharma and those who do not know the Dharma; those who know the meaning and those who do not know the meaning; those who know the time and those who do not know the time; those who know measure and those who do not know measure; those who know themselves and those who do not know themselves;

those who do not know themselves; those who know the retinue and those who do not know the retinue; those who know noble persons and those who do not know noble persons; those who know noble persons and those who do not know noble persons.

In brief:

In Dharma and Vinaya, when one who has erred,
With surplus rules, with weighty matters too,
Speaks of what to practice, speaking boldly,
Bound yet heedless, one falls into wrongdoing.

There are two kinds of servants of the Saṅgha.
