The first kind: those who slander the Tathāgata and act in extreme transgression, who do not speak as has been taught, who do not speak in accordance with Dharma, who do not act in accordance with the Dharma that those who seek Dharma should follow — who declare what is not Dharma to be Dharma, and what is Dharma to be not Dharma. When challenged in response to what they have said, such persons become an object of censure among those who accord with Dharma.

The second kind of servants of the Saṅgha: those who do not slander the Tathāgata, who do not act in extreme transgression, who speak as has been taught, who act in accordance with Dharma, following the Dharma that those who seek Dharma should follow — who declare what is Dharma to be Dharma, and what is not Dharma to be not Dharma. When challenged in response to what they have said, such persons do not become an object of censure among those who accord with Dharma.

In the intermediate summary:

One who slanders, who is censured and at fault,
Blameworthy through childishness and sin,
Is rightly gathered in this middle summary.

A servant of the Saṅgha who declares what is not Dharma to be Dharma, and what is Dharma to be not Dharma — one possessed of these two qualities — is to be censured, condemned, expelled, abandoned, left without allies, made to shrink in shame, humbled, and caused to generate doubt, uncertainty, and remorse. They are to be pressed hard, struck to the vital point, and shown to be at fault.

A servant of the Saṅgha who declares what is Dharma to be Dharma, and what is not Dharma to be not Dharma — one possessed of these two qualities — is not to be censured, not to be condemned, not to be expelled, not to be abandoned, not to be left without allies, not to be made to shrink in shame, not to be humbled, and not to be caused to generate doubt, uncertainty, or remorse. They are not to be pressed hard, not to be struck to the vital point, and not to be shown to be at fault.

A servant of the Saṅgha who declares what is not Dharma to be Dharma, and what is Dharma to be not Dharma — one possessed of these two qualities — incurs a transgression. They are accompanied by doubt, accompanied by uncertainty, accompanied by remorse, accompanied by an obligation to be discharged, they are impure and unfit to be reinstated.

A servant of the Saṅgha who declares what is Dharma to be Dharma, and what is not Dharma to be not Dharma — one possessed of these two qualities — does not incur a transgression. They are not accompanied by doubt, not accompanied by uncertainty, not accompanied by remorse, not accompanied by an obligation to be discharged; they are pure and fit to be reinstated.

A servant of the Saṅgha who declares what is not Dharma to be Dharma, and what is Dharma to be not Dharma — one possessed of these two qualities — is accompanied by blame. They are accompanied by proximate blame, accompanied by harm, accompanied by subsequent torment, and accompanied by that which deserves to torment them.

A servant of the Saṅgha who declares what is Dharma to be Dharma, and what is not Dharma to be not Dharma — one possessed of these two qualities — is not accompanied by blame. They are not accompanied by proximate blame, not accompanied by harm, not accompanied by subsequent torment, and not accompanied by that which deserves to torment them.

A servant of the Saṅgha who declares what is not Dharma to be Dharma, and what is Dharma to be not Dharma — one possessed of these two qualities — is to be recognized as childish, foolish, unclear in understanding, unskilled, and not a noble person.

One who has not abandoned personal arrogance becomes accompanied by blame. Even in the slightest matter involving proximate blame, the wise will censure such a person; and demerit, immeasurable and uncountable, will increase without bound. Then, just as an arrow once released brings down its target, after the body falls in death, such a person falls downward into the lower realms, the evil destinies, the states of ruin, and is born in the hells. They are born in the lower realms, born in the evil destinies, born in the states of ruin. They go to the lower realms, they go to the evil destinies, they fall into the states of ruin. Again and again they are born in the lower realms, born in the evil destinies, born in the states of ruin. Wandering and tumbling about for a long, long time, they do not turn back from cyclic existence.

A servant of the Saṅgha who declares what is Dharma to be Dharma, and what is not Dharma to be not Dharma — one possessed of these two qualities — is to be recognized as wise, clear in understanding, keen in mind, possessed of discernment, and a true and noble person. By having abandoned personal arrogance, such a one is not accompanied by blame, not accompanied even in the slightest by proximate blame; the wise will praise them. Merit, immeasurable and uncountable, will increase without bound. Then, just as an arrow once released finds its mark, even when the body falls here, such a one goes to happiness, and is born in the world of the gods of the higher realms. They are not born in the lower realms, not born in the evil destinies, not born in the states of ruin. They do not go to the lower realms, they do not go to the evil destinies, they do not fall into the states of ruin. They do not come to be born in the lower realms, do not come to be born in the evil destinies, do not come to fall into the states of ruin. While dwelling within cyclic existence for a long time, they do not wander lost; they turn back from cyclic existence.

Just as Dharma and not-Dharma have been set forth in five categories, under both the dark side and the bright side, so too Vinaya and not-Vinaya are to be set forth in five categories under both the dark side and the bright side. Likewise, offenses with a remainder and offenses without a remainder are to be set forth in five categories under both the dark side and the bright side. Likewise, grave offenses and light offenses are to be set forth in five categories under both the dark side and the bright side. Likewise, what has been spoken and what has not been spoken are to be set forth in five categories under both the dark side and the bright side. Likewise, what has been established through resolution and what has not been so established are to be set forth in five categories under both the dark side and the bright side. Likewise, what has been determined and what has not been determined are to be set forth in five categories under both the dark side and the bright side. Likewise, what has been expelled and what has not been expelled are to be set forth in five categories under both the dark side and the bright side. Those who have deteriorated in moral discipline and those who have deteriorated in view — these too, in full, are to be set forth in five categories under both the dark side and the bright side.

In brief:

From admonishment to be abandoned, pressed with urgency,
up to and including expulsion —
all such acts are to be carried out in two ways;
and likewise the identification of faults and disputes.

What is to be admonished is of two kinds: the act of forfeiture, and assignment by the Saṅgha. What is to be abandoned is likewise of two kinds: the act of forfeiture, and assignment by the Saṅgha. What is further to be abandoned is of two kinds: the act of forfeiture, and abandonment by the Saṅgha. Service and attendance are of two kinds: the act of forfeiture, and service and attendance rendered by tīrthikas. Further service and attendance are of two kinds: the act of forfeiture, and making use of material things. What is to be approved is of two kinds: the act of forfeiture, and the abandonment of conceit. Further approval is of two kinds: the act of forfeiture, and the use of material things. Approval granted from the very foundation is of two kinds: the act of forfeiture, and censure. Censure is likewise of two kinds: the act of forfeiture, and censure directed at the Prātimokṣa.

Expulsion is of two kinds: the act of forfeiture, and being placed under the rule of the Saṅgha. Reconciliation is of two kinds: the act of forfeiture, and being placed under the rule of the Saṅgha. Reinstatement is of two kinds: the act of forfeiture, and acknowledgment by the Saṅgha. Celibate conduct is of two kinds: the act of forfeiture, and the arising of a virtuous mind. Further celibate conduct is of two kinds: the act of forfeiture, and the complete fulfillment of the training.

The formal acts to be performed as censure against two persons are as follows: censure, expulsion, reconciliation, exclusion for failure to acknowledge an offense, exclusion for failure to cease an act, and exclusion for failure to relinquish a wrong view — together with forfeiture, forfeiture from the very foundation, approval, approval from the very foundation, approval granted from the very foundation, and the acts pertaining to the celibate life.

The formal acts to be performed as censure against both monks and nuns are: censure, expulsion, reconciliation, exclusion for failure to acknowledge an offense, exclusion for failure to cease an act, and exclusion for failure to relinquish a wrong view.

For those who are fully ordained and those who are not yet fully ordained, the following acts apply: forfeiture, forfeiture from the very foundation, approval, approval from the very foundation, approval granted from the very foundation, and the act of expulsion.

The same applies to female trainees and male novices.

Transgressions that arise from offenses are of two kinds: those that are intentional and those that are unintentional. The expulsion of offenses is of two kinds: intentional and unintentional. Disputes are of two kinds: those involving monks and those involving nuns. Further, disputes are of two kinds: those involving monks and those involving female trainees. Further, disputes are of two kinds: those involving monks and those involving female novices. Further, disputes are of two kinds: those involving monks and those involving male novices.

Here ends the first gate of the Vinaya alone, treating of forfeiture.

The Noble Vinaya Text, the twenty-sixth fascicle.

Now follows the summary of the second gate:

Three offenses, and what is improper,
What has been legislated and what has been transgressed,
Forfeiture likewise, and the two acts,
Instruction and expulsion in the same way.

In brief: the three dust-like offenses,
The Vinaya codes and the three gates,
The two collections and the two acts,
And the training in its two aspects.

The three dusts are the dust of attachment, the dust of aversion, and the dust of delusion.

The three offenses arising from body are: those arising from attachment, those arising from aversion, and those arising from delusion. The three offenses arising from speech are: those arising from attachment, those arising from aversion, and those arising from delusion. The three offenses arising from non-Vinaya conduct are: those arising from attachment, those arising from aversion, and those arising from delusion. The Vinaya is of three kinds: the Vinaya of attachment, the Vinaya of aversion, and the Vinaya of delusion.

All offenses are gathered under three headings: arising, legislated, and distinguished. All offenses are entered into through three kinds of formal act: the act of a single motion, the act of a motion and one proclamation, and the act of a motion and three proclamations. Three kinds of formal act serve as the basis of authority: the act of the Saṅgha, the act of individual liberation, and the act of forfeiture. The training is of three kinds: training in higher moral discipline, training in higher mind, and training in higher wisdom. Furthermore, the training is also of three kinds: training in general conduct, training in higher Vinaya, and training in higher individual liberation.

In brief: the three kinds of what becomes an offense,
And disputes likewise of three kinds —

acts, schism of the Saṅgha, and what is prescribed — these are likewise three. One incurs offense through three kinds of action that lead to offense: bodily action, verbal action, and mental action. Disputes are of three kinds: virtuous, non-virtuous, and indeterminate. Formal acts are of three kinds: a lawful act, an unlawful act, and a concordant act. Schism of the Saṅgha is of three kinds: virtuous, non-virtuous, and indeterminate. One is not absolved of what has been prescribed by virtue of three conditions: the arising, the prescription, and the subsequent prescription.

In brief: dwelling improperly, not dwelling,
And dwelling separately — likewise so;
Offerings, honor, prostration,
Rising up and joining the palms.

Through three conditions one becomes unworthy of dwelling: together with an offense, and without an offense. Through three kinds one comes not to dwell: together with an offense, and without an offense. Through three kinds one comes to dwell separately: together with an offense, and without an offense. There are three who are worthy of offerings: a Tathāgata, arhat, and perfectly complete buddha; one in training; and those who are beyond training. Furthermore, there are another three who are worthy of offerings: a preceptor, an abbot, and those very senior in holy conduct. Just as these are worthy of offerings, so too should one understand who is fitting to be honored, prostrated to, risen before, and greeted with palms joined.

In brief: prescription of two kinds,
And the four categories of occasion,
Vows, and fellowship,
And setting aside — that is the last.

Prescription is of three kinds: prescription arising from an occurrence, prescription arising from an offense, and prescription made by way of differentiation. Furthermore, prescription is of three other kinds: prescription for the sake of guarding henceforth, prescription for the sake of teaching henceforth, and prescription for the sake of benefiting henceforth. Categories of occasion are of three kinds: occasion, and individual occasion. Furthermore, there are three other categories of occasion: occasion through faith, occasion through complete purity, and occasion through wealth. There are yet another three categories of occasion: occasion for the alms bowl, occasion for the monastic robe, and occasion for material goods. And there are three further categories of occasion: occasion for medicine, occasion at the proper time, and occasion of indefinite kind. Vows are of three kinds: the vow of the Saṅgha, the vow of a donor, and the vow of a physician. Fellowship is of three kinds: inferior, middling, and excellent. Setting aside is of three kinds: setting aside of what has been obtained, setting aside of a boundary, and setting aside of a person.

In brief: the past-and-prescribed are fourfold,
Offenses are of two kinds,
Delegation also fourfold,
And attendants are of two kinds.

Three kinds of person are rendered past-and-prescribed when one performs a prostration before them: one in whom a prior offense has arisen, one who is a resident in hiding, and one who dwells in separation. Furthermore, three other kinds are rendered past-and-prescribed when a prostration is performed: one who is shameless, one who is resentful, and one who takes sides. Three kinds of person, when no prostration is performed before them, are rendered past-and-prescribed: a Tathāgata, arhat, and perfectly complete buddha; those who are venerable; and those who are very senior in holy conduct. Furthermore, three other kinds, when no prostration is performed, are rendered past-and-prescribed: a Tathāgata, arhat, and perfectly complete buddha; an abbot; and those who are very senior in holy conduct. Three kinds for whom no prostration is performed yet no offense is incurred:

one who previously committed an offense, one who is in hiding, and one who is dwelling apart. Furthermore, three other kinds for whom no prostration is performed yet no offense is incurred: one who is shameless, one who is resentful, and one who takes sides.

Three kinds of assignment: assignment by the Saṅgha, assignment by an individual, and assignment by the Prātimokṣa. Furthermore, three other kinds of assignment: assignment by the Saṅgha, assignment by a group, and assignment by the elders of the Saṅgha. Furthermore, three other kinds of assignment: assignment by a preceptor, assignment by an abbot, and assignment by the Saṅgha. Furthermore, three other kinds of assignment: assignment by a king, assignment by a thief, and assignment by the reasoning class.

Three kinds of Saṅgha steward: one who is skilled, one who is more skilled than skilled, and one who is even more skilled than the more skilled.

Furthermore, three other kinds of Saṅgha steward: one who is appointed, one who is not appointed, and one who is permitted.

In brief, in verse:

Knowing the penalty, removing it,
relying on the abbot, gathering the assembly,
relinquishing the two remedies,
and permissions — the place and the act —

A monk who, on four grounds of cause, performs the act of penalty and conducts himself to the satisfaction of the penalty, should count the days of penalty: those together with whom a straightforward monk has spent the night at the break of dawn; those who have gone to a place without monks and the break of dawn has come; those for whom the penalty is incomplete and there is no penalty; and those who are unwilling to be told of the penalty by monks who are satisfied with the penalty.

Four kinds of knowledge: knowing what has arisen, knowing the offense, knowing the absence of offense, and knowing what has been raised.

Four kinds of raising: raised by seeing, raised by confession, raised by not having acted previously, and raised by disclosure.

Four things to rely upon: rely on the meaning, not the letter; rely on the Dharma, not the person; rely on sūtras of definitive meaning, not those of interpretable meaning; and rely on gnosis, not on consciousness.

Four kinds of abbot: there is an abbot who gathers by the Dharma and not by material goods; there is an abbot who gathers by material goods and not by the Dharma; there is an abbot who gathers both by the Dharma and by material goods; and there is an abbot who gathers neither by the Dharma nor by material goods. Among these, an abbot who gathers by the Dharma and not by material goods — one should recognize such an abbot and remain with him. An abbot who gathers by material goods and not by the Dharma — from such an abbot one should take leave with a respectful glance and depart. An abbot who gathers both by the Dharma and by material goods — even though it is uncomfortable, one should remain with him for as long as one lives. An abbot who gathers neither by the Dharma nor by material goods — even if one is instructed not to go, one should depart without a backward glance.

The four means of gathering: generosity, kind words, acting for the benefit of others, and consistency of purpose.

Four kinds of remedy: there is a remedy that is improper in itself and whose secondary application is also improper; there is a remedy improper in itself but whose secondary application is proper; there is a remedy proper in itself but whose secondary application is improper; and there is a remedy both proper in itself and proper in its secondary application.

Relying on four kinds of power of purpose, the Blessed One granted remedies to the monks: the power of season, the power of place, the power of the person, and the power of circumstance.

Four kinds of relinquishment: that which is blameworthy, that which is cut by penalty, that which is beneficial, and abiding in the holy Dharma.

Four kinds of permission: that which is not blameworthy, that which is not cut by penalty, that which is beneficial, and that which conduces to ease.

The training of the śrāvakas of the Tathāgata is established in four domains: the domain of gnosis,

the domain of Dharma, the domain of persons, and the domain of miracles.

There are four kinds of formal act. There is the act of conferring benefit, the act of formal censure, the act of penalty, and the act of establishing one in the rules of conduct.

In brief, the five acts are:
Formal acceptance with faith, and the act with admonition,
Pure acts and Vinaya acts,
And the act of formal censure — these are likewise.

The five kinds of formal acceptance are: performing an act on one's own behalf; accepting after having come into the presence of the assembly; presenting a declaration of faith; making an oral statement of one's own view; and accepting by remaining silent.

When five are not openly present within the boundary, the act of presenting faith may be performed; but not within a gathering of many who are openly present. The five cases are: the spy, one who abides separately, one who does not abide, one who is partisan, and one who has expelled a nun.

The five acts that are not permitted unless performed are: "You are to do this in this place," "You are to do this within this Saṅgha," "You are to do this within the Saṅgha of another place," "Such-and-such a transgression shall be imposed upon you" — and with those words having charged him with the transgression, the transgression is formally established, and he is dismissed having been bound, admonished, made to undergo rehabilitation, and sanctioned accordingly.

There is the act of confession, the act of blessing, the act of assignment, the act of permission, and the act of establishing in the rules of conduct.

The five kinds of purifying acts are: penalty, the raising of a penalty from its basis, satisfaction, the raising of satisfaction from its basis, and rehabilitation.

The five instruments of discipline are: censure, reproof, dismissal, reconciliation, and rejection.

The five objects of reproof are: censure, reproof, dismissal, reconciliation, and rejection.

The five kinds of act of penalty: one should proclaim them until abandonment of each of those has been achieved.

In brief, two ways of conduct within the Saṅgha,
Two modes of the elder's heedlessness,
Becoming inferior and falling into dispute,
And self and the notion of self — these are likewise.

A monk who conducts himself within the Saṅgha, when going before the Saṅgha, should set these five Dharma-factors inwardly in mindfulness and then enter into the Saṅgha. What are the five? Being composed in proper order, being composed in respectful comportment, being composed under the sway of caution, being composed with a humble mind, and being skilled in sitting on the seat with a mind equal to one who is a broom-sweeper.

A monk who conducts himself within the Saṅgha should further set these other five Dharma-factors inwardly in mindfulness and then enter into the Saṅgha. What are the five? A mind of loving-kindness, a mind of beneficence, a mind of tenderness, speaking kindly, and not speaking harsh words.

Now there are also those who dispute in ways that are not in accordance with the Dharma within the Saṅgha. In that case, a monk who conducts himself within the Saṅgha should take the side that accords with the Dharma. Or else, having stated his own view, he should rise from his seat and depart, and without stirring up that occasion for dispute, he should remain devoted to meditative practice.

A senior monk who is endowed with five Dharma-factors should be censured, subjected to formal punishment, rejected, rendered without a side, silenced, and humiliated; doubt, uncertainty, and regret should be caused to arise in him; and he should be bound, admonished, and subjected to rehabilitation. What are the five? He is of bad moral discipline; transgressions of moral discipline have occurred in him and he holds wrong views; he views things in a perverted way and is without shame; he is without shame before his peers and incites monks who dispute and counter-dispute to quarrelling, fault-finding, ill-will, and conflict; and he is contentious and —

— leads monks who dispute and counter-dispute into what is contrary to Dharma.

A monk possessing five qualities is one whom laywomen (upāsikā) are right to regard with a feeling of distrust. What are the five? He speaks ill of laypeople; he speaks unpleasantly about laypeople; he speaks of laypeople by pointing out their faults; he does what is neither beneficial nor purposeful toward laypeople; and he engages in the pursuit of gains that bring them no benefit.

Furthermore, a monk possessing five qualities is one whom laymen (upāsaka) are right to regard with a feeling of distrust. What are the five? He speaks ill of the Buddha; he speaks ill of the Dharma; he speaks ill of the Saṅgha; he engages in conduct that should not be engaged in; and he has no respect for the training of monks.

A layman possessing five qualities is one who deserves to have the Saṅgha's alms-bowl turned upside down before him. What are the five? He speaks ill of monks; he speaks unpleasantly about monks; he speaks badly of monks; he is one who harms monks, acts contrary to their benefit and purpose, desires gains from them, and pursues such gains.

Furthermore, a layman possessing five qualities is one who deserves to have the Saṅgha's alms-bowl turned upside down before him. What are the five? He speaks ill of the Buddha; he speaks ill of the Dharma; he speaks ill of the Saṅgha; he engages in conduct that should not be engaged in; and he does not train in the training of a layman.

A Vinaya-holder possessing five qualities is incapable of settling a dispute. What are the five? He has become hostile and contemptuous toward others; he goes astray; he has become one who speaks a great deal; he speaks with scattered and careless words; and he has become one who gathers what is harmful. The reversal of these five into their wholesome counterparts should also be stated.

Furthermore, a Vinaya-holder possessing five qualities is incapable of settling a dispute. What are the five? He retains confused accounts; he retains secret words; he retains many words; he retains them without definiteness; and he renders service without having caused a commitment to be made within three repetitions. The reversal into five wholesome counterparts should also be stated.

Furthermore, a Vinaya-holder possessing five qualities is incapable of settling a dispute. What are the five? He does not know the full extent of what he himself has said; he does not bring the words of others to their conclusion; he does not listen; and he does not make things clear and known. The reversal into five wholesome counterparts should also be stated.

Furthermore, a Vinaya-holder possessing five qualities is wholly incapable of settling a dispute: he does not give instructions to one who has not been instructed; he does not give correct instructions to one who has not been correctly instructed; he does not bring to attention what has not been attended to; he incites monks who dispute and counter-dispute into quarrelling, fault-finding, ill-will, and conflict; and he leads monks who dispute and counter-dispute to side with what is contrary to Dharma. The reversal of these five into their wholesome counterparts should also be stated.

In brief:

Guidance, dispute, formal act, taking up a case,
what is contrary to Dharma — the sūtras and Vinaya regulate these;
the unappointed who arise, and the transgression likewise —

A Vinaya-holder possessing five qualities is incapable of giving guidance. What are the five? He does not know the five modes of speech for giving guidance; he does not know how to counter-argue; he does not know how to connect things to what is Dharma; he does not know how to connect things to what is contrary to Dharma; and he makes no resolution. Again, the reversal into five wholesome counterparts should be stated.

A Vinaya-holder possessing five qualities is incapable of settling a dispute.

What are the five? He does not know disputes; he does not know from what a dispute has arisen; he does not know how to contain a dispute; he does not know how to bring a dispute to peace; and even when a dispute has been brought to peace, he is not skilled in preventing transgressions from arising again. Again, the reversal into five wholesome counterparts should be stated.

A Vinaya-holder possessing five qualities is incapable of performing formal acts. What are the five? His giving of the meaning is thoroughly impure and he does not convey it step by step — he instructs, Ānanda, using the words of a novice, and does not know the words of the sūtra. He does not know the formal act of a single motion. He does not know the formal act of motion-and-one proclamation. He does not know the formal act of motion-and-three proclamations. He does not know the formal act of conveyance; and he does not know the formal act of consecration. Again, the reversal into five wholesome counterparts should be stated.

A monk possessing five qualities should not have his words accepted when he acts as the proposing party. What are the five? His giving of the meaning is thoroughly impure and he does not convey it step by step; he teaches, in the manner of Ānanda, using the words of a novice; he does not know the basis in the sūtra; he does not know how to teach what was spoken from the position of what is not manifest as it was spoken; and he does not purify by resting in whatever is required. Again, the reversal into five wholesome counterparts should be stated.

A monk possessing five qualities is unfit to have his words accepted as the responding party. What are the five? When the proposing monk asks about one thing, he attacks another; he spreads false rumor; he harms a pure monk; standing on a partisan side, though knowing a transgression, he says he does not know the transgression. Again, the reversal into five wholesome counterparts should be stated.

A Vinaya-holder possessing five qualities is incapable of settling a dispute. What are the five? He causes the proposing and the responding monks to draw near to a side contrary to Dharma; he incites the proposing and responding monks to quarrel, to expose faults, to bear grudges, and to provoke disputes; he does not listen to the sūtra words of the respected monks; he slanders the senior monks; and he is unskilled in the beginning, middle, and end of a dispute. Again, the reversal into five wholesome counterparts should be stated.

A Vinaya-holder possessing five qualities is incapable of knowing the qualities of the sūtra. What are the five? He is unskilled in the sūtra; he is unskilled in the Vinaya; he is unskilled in the mātṛkā; he is unskilled in analysis; and he has not trained in the oral recitation of scripture. Again, the reversal into five wholesome counterparts should be stated.

Furthermore, a Vinaya-holder possessing five qualities is incapable of knowing the qualities of the sūtra. What are the five? He does not know the Vinaya that is temporary and the Vinaya that is complete in every case; he does not know the Vinaya that is provisional and the Vinaya that applies at all times; he does not know the Vinaya of transgressions; he does not know the Vinaya of disputes; and he does not know the Vinaya of afflictions. Again, the reversal into five wholesome counterparts should be stated.

A Vinaya-holder possessing five qualities is incapable of knowing the qualities of the sūtra. What are the five? He is undecided with respect to the Vinaya of transgressions, the Vinaya of disputes, the temporary and the complete, and the provisional and the perpetual.

A Vinaya-holder possessing five qualities is incapable of settling a dispute. What are the five?

He settles disputes without having been appointed to do so; he does not show transgressions; he does not cut short proceedings for punishment; he does not demonstrate purification; and in this way what was entrusted to him by the Saṅgha is left undone. Again, the reversal into five wholesome counterparts should be stated.

A Vinaya-holder possessing five qualities is incapable of showing transgressions. What are the five? He does not know what constitutes a transgression; he does not know what does not constitute a transgression; he does not know what is heavy; he does not know what is light; and he has not learned to recite the Prātimokṣa sūtra by heart. Again, the reversal into five wholesome counterparts should be stated.

Furthermore, a Vinaya-holder possessing five qualities is incapable of showing transgressions. What are the five? He does not know the arising of a transgression; he does not know what is accompanied by it; he does not know what follows from it; he does not know its abandonment; and he does not know what is permitted regarding it. Again, the reversal into five wholesome counterparts should be stated.

In brief:

Rising, formal acts, covering over,
fire-giving, and the sleeping place;
mental disturbance, the male organ, semen,
the wooden sounding board, and appointment.

The five kinds of rising from a transgression are these. What are the five? Rising by request; rising without need of a request; rising by sign; rising in the ultimate sense; and that which goes beyond what nuns share in common and has become manifest.

By five causes, what is done becomes an act contrary to the Dharma and an act contrary to the Vinaya. What are the five? Performing it without it having come before the assembly; without deliberation; without having brought it to mind; without the matter being present; and without having established a resolution.

A monk who acts when such characteristics have passed away falls like an arrow that has been shot, and immediately upon death falls into the lower realms, the bad destinations, the wrong course, and is reborn in the hells. What are the five? He goes out of desire; he goes out of aversion; he goes out of delusion; he goes out of fear; and he does not know what was done and what was not done.

By five causes, if a monk takes what has not been given from another's side, it becomes the transgression of defeat. What are the five? He takes it without the perception that it belongs to another; he takes it without the perception of seizing it for even a moment; he takes it without the perception of borrowing it; when taking it he lets another know and then does not take it; and the intention to steal remains present. Again, the reversal into five wholesome counterparts should be stated.

The improper use of sleeping places is to be understood under five headings. What are the five? By smoke; by dust; by water; by dragging; and by hauling — these are the five.

By five causes mental disturbance arises. What are the five? Exhaustion of friends and companions; exhaustion of resources; imbalance of the elements; affliction by non-human beings; and the ripening of past karma.

Furthermore, mental disturbance arises from five causes. What are the five? Agitation of the wind element; bile; phlegm; a combination of these; and the ripening of past karma.

Furthermore, mental disturbance arises from five causes. What are the five? Being struck by a non-human being; having the mind disturbed by a non-human being; having one's vitality seized by a non-human being; imbalance of the elements; and the ripening of past karma.

By five causes the male organ becomes functional while not free from attachment. What are the five? Blockage of defecation; blockage of urination; blockage of wind; being seized by a creature called ucca-tiṅka; and being thoroughly bound by attachment to desired objects — these are the five.

Semen is of five kinds: blue-black; yellow; red; hot; and thin — these are the five.

The striking of the wooden sounding board is of five kinds: the sounding board of the entire Saṅgha; the sounding board for a formal act; the sounding board for a death; the sounding board for a transgression; and the sounding board for abandonment — these are the five.

The sounding board of the entire Saṅgha comprises three series and three urgent strikes.

The sounding board for a formal act comprises two series and one urgent strike. The sounding board for a death comprises one series. The sounding board for a transgression is sounded until the matter is resolved. The sounding board for abandonment is struck at the throat of the board.

A monk who possesses five qualities may transmit scriptural instruction to nuns. What are the five? He is one who is endowed with moral discipline; he is one who is learned; he is one who is like a king among elders; he is one who is conversant with the language of the city; and he is one who has not caused offense to nuns through physical conduct. How is he endowed with moral discipline? He has not transgressed any of the four root defeats. How is he learned? He has recited or given oral teaching on the Sūtra of Individual Liberation. How is he one who is like a king among elders? He has reached twenty years since his full ordination, or has passed beyond that. And as for causing offense to nuns through physical conduct — either he has not done so, or any such transgression has been handled by him in accordance with the Dharma.

The two sections are complete.

A summary verse for the three sections:

Dispute and satisfaction,
wealth found and the person likewise,
Upāli's completion of discipline,
and the going forth and giving — likewise.

In brief: the six transmissions on the root of strife,
formal acts and teaching likewise,
what is to be assigned and what is impaired,
and what is to be reversed — likewise.

Monks, in this regard the roots of strife are six. There exists a monk who is wrathful and holds grudges. Monks, a monk who is wrathful and holds grudges does not treat the Teacher as a superior, does not show him respect, does not bow down before him, and does not honor him. Because he has not treated the Teacher with deference, not treated him as a superior, not shown him respect, not bowed down before him, and not honored him, he does not see the Dharma. Not seeing the Dharma, he does not conduct himself with proper regard toward the Saṅgha. Acting without proper regard toward the Saṅgha, he acts heedlessly toward the very life of renunciation. Acting heedlessly toward the life of renunciation, he comes to generate strife in the Saṅgha, mud-slinging, grudge-holding, and quarreling of that sort. Strife, mud-slinging, grudge-holding, and quarreling are not of benefit to the many, are not for the welfare of the many, but bring suffering to the many. They are neither of benefit nor of help to gods and humans, and bring suffering. Monks, should you observe such a root of strife present within or without, and see that it has not yet been abandoned by oneself, then, harmonizing together with one another with great joy, generate faith, diligence, effort, and enthusiasm. Having generated enthusiasm, strive without releasing mindfulness and awareness until that root of strife has been relinquished. Likewise, monks, if you observe a root of strife present within or without that has not been abandoned, then harmonizing together with one another in joy, strive with mindfulness that guards the mind with great care until the fault of that root of strife is exhausted. Then that root of strife of yours, having been utterly destroyed, will not arise again in the future.

Just as with grudge-holding, so too with concealment, spite, envy, arrogance, deceit, fraud, shamelessness, lack of conscience, and holding one's own views in high esteem — these are all to be set forth at length as words that are hard to abandon because they are grasped at again and again.

The transmissions are of six kinds: transmission by a buddha; transmission by the Saṅgha; transmission by a preceptor;

transmission by a preceptor; transmission by a king; and transmission by a thief.

There are six kinds of livelihood that are improper for a male lay practitioner to pursue: trading in sentient beings; trading in weapons; trading in alcohol; trading in poison; work involving lacquer; and the work of making oil from grain.

The six cases of something being shown to be spurious are as follows.

When a monk says to other monks, "Venerable ones, I myself heard directly from the Blessed One and received directly from him: 'This is the Dharma; this is the Vinaya; this is what the Teacher taught,'" the monk who hears this should neither express enthusiasm for what that monk has said nor condemn it. Without either expressing enthusiasm or condemning it, taking the words, the meaning, and the syllables together, he should compare them against the sūtras and examine them against the Vinaya. If, upon comparing them against the sūtras and examining them against the Vinaya, they are found to be inconsistent with the sūtras, to be absent from the Vinaya, and to contradict the nature of reality, then he should address that monk thus: "Venerable one, what you claim the Blessed One said — he did not say it. Or else, venerable one, you have grasped this teaching wrongly. For when I compared this teaching against the sūtras and examined it against the Vinaya, it was inconsistent with the sūtras, absent from the Vinaya, and contradictory to the nature of reality. Therefore know that this is not the Dharma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the teaching of the Teacher — and set it aside."

Furthermore, when a monk says to other monks, "Venerable ones, in such-and-such a place there resides a great community of monks, elders with full individual liberation, and I myself heard directly from that community of monks and received it directly: 'This is the Dharma; this is the Vinaya; this is what the Teacher taught,'" the monk who hears this should neither express enthusiasm nor condemn it. Without expressing enthusiasm or condemning it, taking the words, the meaning, and the syllables together, he should compare them against the sūtras and examine them against the Vinaya. If, upon comparing them against the sūtras and examining them against the Vinaya, they are found to be inconsistent with the sūtras, absent from the Vinaya, and contradictory to the nature of reality, then he should address that monk thus: "Venerable one, you have perceived what you heard from that community of elders with full individual liberation as Dharma, as Vinaya, and have spoken what is not Dharma and not Vinaya. Or else, venerable one, you yourself have grasped this teaching wrongly. For when these teachings are compared against the sūtras and examined against the Vinaya, they are inconsistent with the sūtras, absent from the Vinaya, and contradictory to the nature of reality. Therefore know that this is not the Dharma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the teaching of the Teacher — and set it aside."

Furthermore, when a monk says to other monks, "In such-and-such a place there reside many monks who are holders of sūtras, holders of Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkā. I myself heard directly from those monks and received it directly: 'This is the Dharma; this is the Vinaya; this is what the Teacher taught'" — from that point onward to the words "address that monk as follows," everything proceeds exactly as before: "Venerable one, those monks have perceived it as Dharma, as Vinaya, and have spoken what is not Dharma and not Vinaya. Or else, venerable one, you yourself have grasped these teachings wrongly. For when this teaching is compared against the sūtras and examined against the Vinaya, it is inconsistent with the sūtras, absent from the Vinaya, and contradictory to the nature of reality. This is not the Dharma; this is not the Vinaya;

this is not what the Teacher taught — know it to be so, and set it aside."

Furthermore, if a monk says to other monks: "Venerable ones, in such-and-such a place, among the resident senior monks of that monastery, and among the presiding officers of that monastery, there dwell certain monks. From those venerable monks I have heard directly and received directly: 'This is the Dharma; this is the Vinaya; this is what the Teacher taught'" — from that point onward to the words "address that monk as follows," everything proceeds exactly as before: "Just as the venerable one, being any senior monk among the senior monks and any presiding officer among the presiding officers, has perceived this as Dharma and as Vinaya and has spoken what is not Dharma and not Vinaya — or else, venerable one, you yourself have grasped these teachings wrongly" — from that point onward to "know it to be so, and set it aside," everything proceeds exactly as before.

Furthermore, if one monk says to another monk: "Venerable one, in such-and-such a place there is a faithful and believing layman. From that layman I have heard directly and received directly: 'This is the Dharma; this is the Vinaya; this is what the Teacher taught'" — from that point onward to the words "address that monk as follows," everything proceeds exactly as before: "Just as the venerable one, having heard from a layman what he perceived as Dharma and as Vinaya, has spoken what is not Dharma and not Vinaya — or else, venerable one, you yourself have grasped these teachings wrongly" — from that point onward to "know it to be so, and set it aside," everything proceeds exactly as before.

Furthermore, if a monk says to other monks: "Venerable ones, I have heard directly from gods: 'This is the Dharma; this is the Vinaya; this is what the Teacher taught'" — from that point onward to the words "address that monk as follows," everything proceeds exactly as before: "Just as the gods have spoken to the venerable one what they perceived as Dharma and as Vinaya, yet have spoken what is not Dharma and not Vinaya — or else, venerable one, you yourself have grasped these teachings wrongly" — from that point onward to "know it to be so, and set it aside," everything proceeds exactly as before.

Now, what is called the Six Great Pronouncements is this: If a monk says to other monks, "Venerable ones, I have heard directly from the Blessed One and received directly: 'This is the Dharma; this is the Vinaya; this is what the Teacher taught'" — one should neither rejoice in nor disparage what that monk has said. Without either rejoicing or disparaging, one should take hold of the words, the meaning, and the syllables, compare them against the sūtras, and examine them against the Vinaya. If, upon comparing them against the sūtras and examining them against the Vinaya, they are consistent with the sūtras, present in the Vinaya, and not contradictory to the nature of reality, then address that monk as follows: "Venerable one, these teachings were indeed spoken by the Blessed One, and the venerable one has grasped them well. Therefore, since these teachings, when compared against the sūtras and examined against the Vinaya, are consistent with the sūtras, present in the Vinaya, and not contradictory to the nature of reality, know this to be the Dharma, know this to be the Vinaya, know this to be what the Teacher taught — and hold it fast."

These six great pronouncements in their extended form are to be recited in the same way for the positive side as well.

The six modes of transmission are: transmission from a monk,

transmission from a nun, transmission from both, individual transmission, transmission from a person, and transmission through one who has aroused the awakening mind.

There are also a further six modes of transmission: transmission through faith, transmission through complete purity, transmission of material goods, transmission of requisites, transmission of medicine, and transmission at the proper time.

The six kinds of degradation are: degradation of oneself, degradation of others, degradation of moral discipline, degradation of view, degradation of conduct, and degradation of livelihood.

The six kinds of excellence are: excellence of oneself, excellence of others, excellence of moral discipline, excellence of view, excellence of conduct, and excellence of livelihood.

The Noble Vinaya, the twenty-seventh fascicle. In brief:

Pleasing, stealing,
What has become manifest in the same way —
Degraded and not degraded,
Six kinds of action are taught.

What is meant by "pleasing": the Dharma that reads, "May I dwell nearby with love toward my own body for those who are skilled practitioners of the holy life equal to the Teacher's" — this is what is pleasing, what is delightful. Proceeding with love toward the venerable preceptor — it should be delighted in, regarded as a superior, honored, venerated, cultivated, upheld, accorded with, not resented, not disputed; and to the end of becoming one, loving action of speech and loving action of mind are set forth.

Whatever gain has been obtained in accordance with the Dharma, if it is small and has come within the begging bowl or falls within the bowl's compass — such gain should be shared in common with those who are skilled practitioners of the holy life equal to the Teacher's. This Dharma is what is pleasing. And as before, up to and including "in order to become one, it is set forth."

As before, up to the same point: whatever moral disciplines are not torn, not broken, not mixed, not become turbid, not degraded, without fault, perfectly complete, perfectly held, praised by the wise — such moral discipline: "May I share moral discipline in common together with those skilled practitioners of the holy life equal to the Teacher's." This Dharma is what is pleasing, and as before up to and including "in order to become one, it is set forth."

As before, up to the same point: the view of definite emergence that leads the noble ones to arise toward the complete exhaustion of suffering and toward passing to the end of suffering — "May I share that view in common together with those skilled practitioners of the holy life equal to the Teacher's." This Dharma is what is pleasing. As before, up to and including "in order to become one, it is set forth."

The six kinds of stealing are: stealing by stealth, stealing by deception, stealing by force, stealing after promising to return it, stealing by snatching, and stealing through an accomplice.

The six cases in which one who has become manifest may receive full ordination: when the Teacher is manifest, when the Dharma is manifest, when the Saṅgha is manifest, when purity is manifest, when the preceptor is manifest, and when the abbot is manifest.

The six Dharma factors that become causes for the degeneration of what the Teacher has taught: delighting in work, delighting in talk, delighting in sleep, delighting in gossip, delighting in gain, honor, and fame and being unable to relinquish them — being devoted to not relinquishing them and therefore taking no delight in renunciation and not engaging in yogic practice, and not delighting in meditation and having no interest in it, so that one takes no delight in meditation and does not engage in yogic practice.

The six Dharma factors that become causes for the non-degeneration of what the Teacher has taught: not delighting in work, not delighting in talk, not delighting in sleep, not delighting in gossip, not delighting in gain and honor — and instead delighting in renunciation, being devoted to renunciation, and therefore delighting in renunciation and engaging in yogic practice; and delighting in meditation, being devoted to meditation, and therefore delighting in meditation, being devoted to it, and engaging in yogic practice. These six Dharma factors become causes for what the Teacher has taught. Monks, you should know this.

Those Dharma factors that become causes for universal attachment, universal aversion, universal delusion, universal engagement in afflictions, and abundant conceptual elaboration — these are not the Dharma, these are not the Vinaya, these are not what the Teacher has taught. You should understand and know this.

Those six Dharma factors that become causes for what the Teacher has taught — monks, you should know these. Those Dharma factors that do not become causes for universal attachment, that do not become causes for universal aversion, that do not become causes for universal delusion, that do not become causes for universal engagement, but rather become causes for thorough purification and non-elaboration — these are the Dharma. These are the Vinaya. These are what the Teacher has taught. You should understand this.

Furthermore, those six Dharma factors that become causes for what the Teacher has taught — monks, you should know these. Those Dharma factors that become causes for not knowing contentment — causes for not experiencing satisfaction, for being hard to fill, for being difficult to sustain, for having many desires — these are not the Dharma, these are not the Vinaya, these are not what the Teacher has taught. You should understand and know this.

Those six Dharma factors that become causes for what the Teacher has taught — monks, you should know these. Those Dharma factors that become causes for knowing contentment — causes for being easy to please, easy to sustain, easy to satisfy, and for having few desires — these are the Dharma. These are the Vinaya. These are what the Teacher has taught. You should determine and know this.

In brief:

Wealth and strength and calm abiding,
degenerations, and robes as well,
not allowing qualities to decline —
such is the Saṅgha's conduct in accordance with the Dharma.

The seven wealths are: the wealth of faith, the wealth of moral discipline, the wealth of a sense of propriety, the wealth of conscientiousness, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, and the wealth of wisdom — these seven.

The seven powers are: the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of meditative absorption, the power of wisdom, the power of a sense of propriety, and the power of conscientiousness.

The seven factors that resolve disputes are: resolution in the presence of those concerned, resolution through mindfulness, resolution through the absence of confusion, decision by majority vote, inquiry into the matter itself, proceeding by agreement, and that which is like spreading grass.

The seven factors of degeneration are: conducting oneself without veneration toward the Buddha, without veneration toward the Dharma, toward the Saṅgha, toward the trainings, toward heedfulness, toward the settled mind, and toward meditative absorption.

The seven factors of non-degeneration are: conducting oneself with veneration toward the Buddha, with veneration toward the Dharma, toward the Saṅgha, toward the trainings, toward heedfulness, toward the settled mind, and toward meditative absorption.

The seven things suitable as robes are: wool, a linen garment of śāṇaka fiber, cotton wool cloth, a coarse fabric, a grass-cloth of dugulaka, a grass-cloth of koṭavaka, and —

and spider silk. The seven things unsuitable as robes are: the wool of a female yak, the wool of a bull, goat's wool, the wool of a wild deer, the wool of a female deer, blended fiber, and fiber that has not been woven into cloth.

A person who holds the Vinaya possesses seven qualities: they are the guardian of the treasury within the Victor's dispensation; they guard and carefully conceal their own aggregate of moral discipline; they possess inexhaustible resources of scripture for transmission and teaching; they attract the fourfold assembly; they become a refuge for those who have fallen into doubt; they conduct themselves fearlessly within the Saṅgha; and they act with great clarity of mind.

The seven spheres of conduct that a monk should not frequent are: the household of a partisan, the household of one who distributes gifts, the household of a prostitute, the household of a liquor-seller, the household of a musician, the royal palace, and the household of a person of low caste.

The seven things that are not noble Dharma are: not knowing the Dharma, not knowing the meaning, not knowing the proper time, not knowing the proper measure, not knowing oneself, not knowing the assembly, and not knowing how to distinguish persons — those who are superior and those who are inferior.

A monk conducting himself within the Saṅgha who possesses seven qualities should not conduct himself within the Saṅgha: being impatient and ungrateful; speaking too much; speaking in a garbled and rambling way; speaking without circumspection; and not knowing what is within bounds.

The seven qualities of noble Dharma are: knowing the Dharma, knowing the meaning, knowing the proper time, knowing the proper measure, knowing oneself, knowing the assembly, knowing whether many people are unfriendly, not being skilled in the beginning, middle, and end of a dispute, and not knowing what is similar and what is dissimilar. This completes the groups of seven.

In brief:

Stable gains and their relinquishment,
and likewise sandals as well;
the eight worldly dharmas,
and equally the absence of schism and its roots;
the middle of the eight kinds of gains —
boundary occasions, duties, residence,
the rains retreat, the five matters of the Saṅgha,
persons who are manifest,
and the eighth — each one's own domain.

The eight kinds of gains are: offerings made within a boundary; offerings made at the time of an act; offerings made at the time of residence; gains of the rains retreat; gains designated to the Saṅgha; gains designated to a particular person; gains that have become manifest; and gains that have become separate — these eight.

The eight causes that lead to relinquishing gains from a situation resembling a mother are: departure, taking hold, thinking one will not return, having secretly heard, having heard openly, going beyond the boundary, having given up hope, and the deed of request — these eight.

The eight kinds of sandals that a monk should not wear are: sandals made of kuśa grass, sandals made of muñja grass, sandals made of balbaja grass, sandals made of rice straw, sandals made of bamboo, sandals made of palm leaves, and sandals of wheat straw.

Furthermore, the eight other kinds of sandals that a monk should not wear are: sandals made of cord, sandals fitted with bells, sandals made of hide, wooden sandals, sandals made of bone, sandals made of iron, sandals made of precious jewels, and sandals made of tree bark.

The eight worldly dharmas are: gain, no gain, fame, no fame, blame, praise, pleasure, and suffering.

Among the eight dharmas that cause division in the Saṅgha, these are: declaring "this is Dharma" and declaring "this is not Dharma"; declaring "this is Vinaya" and declaring "this is not Vinaya";

declaring "this is a transgression" and declaring "this is not a transgression"; declaring "this is serious" and declaring "this is light"; declaring "there is a remainder" and declaring "there is no remainder whatsoever"; declaring "it should be confessed" and declaring "it should be restrained"; declaring "this goes beyond the Vinaya" and declaring "this is to be explained wrongly"; declaring "this is non-virtuous" and declaring "this is not supported by scripture."

There are eight ways by which one who is without a basis is condemned: resentment, despondency, anger, contrariness, displeasure, being hard to please, envy, and miserliness.

In summary:

Examining a person,
objecting and counter-objecting,
the dust-like factors of the Vinaya and the eight modes,
and the laying down of individual liberation.

The eight ways of examining a person are: conduct, domain of activity, friendships, companionship, livelihood, learning, bodily actions, and verbal actions. Just as a person is, so too should their objecting and counter-objecting be understood.

The eight factors by which one arrives at complete mastery in taming attachment are the noble eightfold path: right view, right thought, right speech, right action in its entirety, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right meditative absorption. Just as one arrives at complete mastery in taming attachment, so too does one arrive at complete mastery in taming aversion and complete mastery in taming delusion — it is the same in each case.

The eight dust-like factors are: dust-like in housing, dust-like in food, dust-like in drink, dust-like in licking, dust-like in tasting, dust-like in medicine, dust that is dust itself — these are the eight.

The eight improper grounds for laying down individual liberation are: degradation of moral discipline performed as though one has a basis, when one does not; degradation of view; degradation of conduct; degradation of livelihood — and again, degradation of moral discipline not performed on a basis, when one genuinely lacks a basis; degradation of view; degradation of conduct; and degradation of livelihood.

The eight proper grounds for a restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma are: degradation of moral discipline performed with a genuine basis; degradation of view; degradation of conduct; degradation of livelihood — and again, degradation of moral discipline not performed when a genuine basis exists; degradation of view; degradation of conduct; and degradation of livelihood.

In summary:

Upāli, the unobstructed one,
and Gautamī — Gautama's lineage;
what is not fitting to abide in,
harm, and the Vinaya.

The venerable Upāli then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, it would be good if you would briefly explain to me the teaching by which I may seek the Dharma and the Vinaya." The Blessed One then spoke to the venerable Upāli as follows:

"Upāli, whatever Dharma leads to quarreling, to fault-finding, to resentment, to dispute, to speaking separately, to discordant speech, to disunity, to loss of mindfulness, to proliferation — with regard to such things, understand clearly: this is not Dharma, this is not Vinaya, this is not the teaching of the Teacher.

"Upāli, whatever Dharma leads to non-quarreling, to not finding fault, to non-resentment, to non-dispute, to not speaking separately, to concordant speech, to unity, to not losing mindfulness, to becoming one — with regard to such things, understand clearly: this is Dharma, this is Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Teacher.

"Upāli, the eight are just as has been said."

As for what has not yet been covered, those should be stated as eight in the dark and light modes.

The occasion: it was in Śrāvastī. At that time, Gautamī, the great lady, mother of the people, went to where the Blessed One was and, having arrived, bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. Seated to one side, Gautamī, the great lady, mother of the people, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it would be well if you would teach me the Dharma in such a way that I might know how to seek Dharma and Vinaya."

And when she had said that, the Blessed One spoke thus to Gautamī, the great lady, mother of the people: "Gautamī, whatever Dharma serves as a cause for universal attachment, but not as a cause for freedom from universal attachment; serves as a cause for universal aversion, but not as a cause for freedom from universal aversion; serves as a cause for universal delusion, but not as a cause for freedom from universal delusion; serves as a cause for universal engagement, but not as a cause for non-engagement; serves as a cause for universal affliction, but not as a cause for purification; serves as a cause for great desire, but not as a cause for the diminishment of great desire; serves as a cause for not knowing contentment, but not as a cause for knowing contentment; serves as a cause for being hard to satisfy, but not as a cause for being easy to satisfy; serves as a cause for being hard to support, but not as a cause for being easy to support — with regard to such things, understand clearly: this is not Dharma, this is not Vinaya, this is not the teaching of the Teacher.

"Gautamī, whatever Dharma serves as a cause for freedom from universal attachment, but not as a cause for universal attachment; serves as a cause for freedom from universal aversion, but not as a cause for universal aversion; serves as a cause for freedom from universal delusion, but not as a cause for universal delusion; serves as a cause for non-engagement, but not as a cause for universal engagement; serves as a cause for purification, but not as a cause for universal affliction; serves as a cause for the diminishment of great desire, but not as a cause for great desire; serves as a cause for knowing contentment, but not as a cause for not knowing contentment; serves as a cause for being easy to satisfy, but not as a cause for being hard to satisfy; serves as a cause for being easy to support, but not as a cause for being hard to support — with regard to such things, understand clearly: this is Dharma, this is Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Teacher.

"As has been said to Gautamī, the great lady, mother of the people, so shall the sūtra be recited."

The eighth is complete.

The nine are as follows: abiding in the Teacher, abiding in the Dharma, abiding in the Saṅgha, abiding in one's ācārya, abiding in one's upādhyāya, abiding in one's senior master, abiding in one's dwelling, abiding in a person, and abiding in a domain.

The nine instances of what is improper: it is improper for an arhat in whom the defilements are exhausted knowingly to deprive a living being of life; to take what is not given; to engage in unchaste conduct, in the sexual act; knowingly to speak falsehood; to wish to partake of and consume what is stored away; knowingly to transgress the training; to hand over the training and fall away; to seek another teacher outside of this; and to trust in divination and omens for purification rather than in deeds of faith. These are what is improper.

The nine objects of desire: "This one wishes to harm me. This one wishes to bring me no benefit. This one wishes me to be unhappy. This one does not wish me to have happiness. This one wishes me to be without ease." And: "This one has harmed me. This one does harm me. This one will do harm to me." Thinking thus, one does harm to that person.

"Whoever wishes to harm me, wishes me no benefit, wishes me to be unhappy, does not wish me to have happiness, and does not wish me to have ease — this one does not wish me harm, wishes me benefit, wishes me happiness, wishes me to have happiness, and wishes me ease; this one has not done me harm, does not do me harm, and will not do me harm." Thinking thus, one does harm to that person.

"Whoever wishes me no harm, wishes me benefit, wishes me happiness, wishes me to have happiness, and wishes me to have ease — this one wishes that person harm, wishes that person no benefit, wishes that person unhappiness, does not wish that person happiness, and does not wish that person ease." And so one does harm to that person.

The nine objects of desire that are to be subdued: "This one wishes to harm me, wishes me no benefit, wishes me unhappy, does not wish me happiness, and does not wish me ease. This one has done me harm, does do me harm, and will do me harm." Thinking thus, one repays that person by generating harm toward them.

"Whoever wishes to harm me, wishes me no benefit, wishes me unhappy, does not wish me happiness, and does not wish me ease — this one does not wish that person harm, wishes that person benefit, wishes that person happiness, wishes that person happiness, and wishes that person ease; and this one has not done harm to that person, does not do harm, and will not do harm." Thinking thus, one reflects: "Would that I might be thus — how could I receive from another what I have not become?" And so, thinking in this way, one repays that person by generating harm toward them.

And again, "Whoever wishes me no harm, wishes me benefit, wishes me happiness, and wishes me ease — this one wishes that person harm, wishes that person no benefit, does not wish that person happiness, and does not wish that person ease. This one has done harm to that person, does harm, and will do harm." Thinking thus, one further reflects: "Would that I might be thus and not be otherwise — how could I receive from another what I have not become?" And so, thinking in this way, one repays that person by generating harm toward them.

The ninth is complete.

In brief:

What is not discipline is of two kinds,
And what is discipline is of three:
Generosity, and what is to be gathered in,
And virtuous qualities are the last.

The ten that are not discipline are the ten paths of non-virtuous action: killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, malice, covetousness, and wrong view.

Further, another ten that are not discipline are the ten limbs of the wrong path: wrong view, wrong thought, wrong speech, wrong end of action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong meditative absorption, wrong liberation, and wrong gnosis.

The ten that are discipline are the ten paths of virtuous action: refraining from killing, refraining from taking what is not given, refraining from sexual misconduct, refraining from lying, refraining from divisive speech, refraining from harsh speech, refraining from idle chatter, and refraining from malice, covetousness, and wrong view.

Further, another ten that are discipline are the ten limbs of the right path: right view, right thought, right speech, right end of action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right meditative absorption, right liberation, and right gnosis.

Still further, another ten that are discipline: arising in the age of a buddha,

arising at all times, arising in an age of decline, going everywhere, discipline of time, discipline of place, discipline of persons, discipline of dwelling, discipline of effort, and discipline of afflictions.

Ten that are the gathering of things: gathering of the alms bowl, gathering of robes, gathering of medicine, gathering of material goods, gathering of bedding and seats, gathering of sūtras, gathering of Vinaya, gathering of the Mātṛkā, gathering of complete purification, and gathering of rising from transgression.

Ten that are generosity: giving of the alms bowl, giving of robes, giving of medicine, giving of material goods, giving of bedding and seats, giving of sūtras, giving of Vinaya, giving of the Mātṛkā, giving of complete purification, and giving of rising from transgression. These likewise are to be understood as the ten objects of gathering.

Ten qualities of the person who upholds the Vinaya: knowing what has arisen, knowing what is accompanied by conditions, knowing what is subsequently accompanied by conditions, knowing what is not permitted, knowing what is permitted, being renowned as one who is manifest on my side, having become manifest, having become fully manifest, being renowned as one who has not emptied my side, and the Tathāgata having less activity to perform in whatever region that person who upholds the Vinaya in such a manner dwells.

In brief, as verse:

The ten acts of penalty and, directly,
ordination with its obstacles,
the discussions, the fourth, the pleasing,
and the sixfold — these are the categories.

Ten acts of penalty: censure, reproach, expulsion, suspension, the penalty levied on the basis called "unseen," removal from residence, withholding of the restoration ceremony, withholding of the invitation ceremony, withholding of the statement of request, and satisfaction — these are the ten.

Ten things by which, upon being made directly present, one undergoes full ordination: the Teacher being directly present and one undergoing full ordination, a buddha being directly present, the Dharma being directly present, the preceptor being directly present, the instructor being directly present, the one wishing full ordination being directly present, the requisites of one wishing full ordination being directly present, complete purification being directly present, the request being directly present, and the formal act being directly present.

Ten things that become obstacles to full ordination: having become a hermaphrodite, having expelled a nun, having killed one's father, having killed one's mother, having killed an arhat, having caused a schism in the Saṅgha, having drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent, being a thief who has entered the robes through deception, having previously committed a transgression, having previously caused disruption, and having gone over to the non-Buddhists.

Ten forms of full ordination: full ordination from a Tathāgata without a preceptor, the five forms of full ordination following the direct realization of gnosis, full ordination by Mahā-Kāśyapa's self-declaration before the Teacher, full ordination by knowing that one has received the reply to Soḍāya's question, full ordination of Gautamī, the Great Mistress of Beings, by her acceptance of the precepts of her guru, full ordination of Dharmadinnā who had not crossed over, full ordination in the borderlands by a holder of the Vinaya together with five persons, full ordination without a preceptor and without an instructor, full ordination by the utterance "Come here, monk," and full ordination through the formal act with the request and the four motions.

Ten discussions: timely and untimely, true and untrue, with meaning and without meaning, pleasant and harsh, and loving and hateful.

One who possesses ten qualities may discuss matters with others: one who has become endowed with moral discipline; who is learned through extensive hearing; who has applied diligence; who abides in close mindfulness; who is endowed with wisdom; who speaks in a timely way and does not exceed the proper moment for discussion; who speaks truthfully and not untruthfully; who speaks with meaning and not without meaning; who speaks pleasantly and not with harsh words; and who speaks with loving-kindness and not with aversion.

Furthermore, one who possesses ten qualities may discuss matters with others: one who has become endowed with moral discipline; who is learned through extensive hearing; who has applied diligence; who is undistracted; who is endowed with wisdom; who speaks in a timely way and does not exceed the proper moment for discussion; who speaks truthfully and not untruthfully; who speaks with meaning and not without meaning; who speaks pleasantly and not with harsh words; and who speaks with loving-kindness and not with aversion.

Furthermore, one who possesses ten qualities may discuss matters with others: one who is endowed with moral discipline; who is learned through extensive hearing; who has applied diligence; who abides in close mindfulness; who has become possessed of the power of individual analysis; who speaks in a timely way and does not exceed the proper moment for discussion; who speaks truthfully and not untruthfully; who speaks with meaning and not without meaning; who speaks pleasantly with agreeable words and not with harsh words; and who speaks with loving-kindness and not with aversion.

A monk who possesses ten qualities will be beloved by those of brahma-like conduct. Those qualities are: being endowed with moral discipline; being learned through extensive hearing; having applied diligence; abiding in close mindfulness; being endowed with wisdom; having become possessed of the aggregate of moral discipline belonging to one who is beyond training; the aggregate of wisdom; the aggregate of meditative absorption; the aggregate of liberation; and the aggregate of the wisdom that sees liberation.

Just as such a one is beloved, so too the ten qualities are to be enumerated for the second category, those who are agreeable. For the third category, those made into a preceptor, the ten qualities are likewise to be enumerated. For the fourth category, those to be shown confidence in, the ten are likewise to be enumerated. For the fifth category, those worthy of veneration, the ten are likewise to be enumerated. For the sixth category, those worthy of praise, the ten are likewise to be enumerated.

In summary:

Going forth and the four,
liberation and excellence,
qualities and likewise giving,
and the restoration ceremony — these are their foundations.

One who possesses ten qualities may perform the going forth, confer full ordination, and grant residence: one who has completed ten years since full ordination, or more than that; who is capable of setting one's companions in practice and one's attendants to nursing the sick; who is capable of resolving or causing to be resolved any remorse that arises in companions and attendants; who is capable of sending away or causing to be sent away companions and attendants who have come to display a blameworthy manner; who is capable of sending to another locality companions and attendants who are unwilling to remain in that region; who is endowed with moral discipline; who is learned through extensive hearing; who has applied diligence; who abides in close mindfulness; and who is endowed with wisdom.

Furthermore, one who possesses ten qualities may perform the going forth, confer full ordination, and grant residence. What are the ten? Knowing what constitutes a transgression; knowing what does not constitute a transgression; knowing what is weighty; knowing what is light; having learned the sūtra of individual liberation by heart so as to be able to recite it; the aggregate of moral discipline belonging to one in training; the aggregate of meditative absorption; the aggregate of wisdom; the aggregate of liberation;

and the aggregate of the gnosis that sees liberation. One who possesses these ten qualities may perform the going forth, confer full ordination, and grant residence.

Furthermore, one who possesses ten qualities may perform the going forth, confer full ordination, and grant residence. What are the ten? Knowing what has arisen; knowing what is prescribed; knowing what is subsequently prescribed; knowing what is not permitted; knowing what is permitted; knowing what constitutes an obstacle; knowing what does not constitute an obstacle; being one who transmits the scriptures; being one who gives instruction; and being capable of introducing others to the ten topics of practice.

Furthermore, one who possesses ten qualities may perform the going forth, confer full ordination, and grant residence. What are the ten? Excellence in faith; excellence in moral discipline; excellence in learning; excellence in generosity; excellence in wisdom; excellence in moral discipline; excellence in meditative absorption; excellence in wisdom; excellence in liberation; and excellence in the gnosis that sees liberation.

By means of ten qualities one becomes a cause for entering perfectly into liberation: the aggregate of moral discipline belonging to one in training; the aggregate of meditative absorption; the aggregate of wisdom; the aggregate of liberation; the aggregate of the gnosis that sees liberation; the aggregate of moral discipline belonging to one beyond training; the aggregate of meditative absorption; the aggregate of wisdom; the aggregate of liberation; and the aggregate of the gnosis that sees liberation.

The ten excellences are: excellence in the Teacher; excellence in the Dharma; excellence in the Saṅgha; excellence in the preceptor-teacher; excellence in the abbot; excellence in moral discipline; excellence in learning; excellence in wisdom; excellence in liberation; and excellence in the gnosis that sees liberation.
