The ten qualities are: gathering the Saṅgha together; bringing virtue to the Saṅgha; enabling the Saṅgha to live at ease; dealing strictly with those individuals who are shameless; letting those who have a sense of shame live at ease; causing those who have not yet gained trust to gain trust; causing those who have gained trust to increase their trust still further; restraining the defilements of the present life; thoroughly overcoming those that would arise in future lives; and, by means of the holy life, bringing benefit to others and causing the holy life to endure long in harmony with the holy life, so that it may be of benefit to the many and, spreading wide, be rightly proclaimed to gods and humans alike. Having seen these ten qualities, the Tathāgata established this rule of training for the śrāvakas.

The ten cases in which giving is improper: if any person whatsoever gives a gift to one person and then gives the same to another as well, it has been given contrary to the Dharma and received contrary to the Dharma, and that is improper conduct. If a gift has been given to one person and is then also offered to the Saṅgha, it has been given contrary to the Dharma and received contrary to the Dharma, and that is improper conduct. Likewise, if a gift has been given to two persons and is then given to one person, or to many, or to two communities, it has been given contrary to the Dharma and received contrary to the Dharma, and that is improper conduct. In the same way, whether given to one person, to two, to many, or offered to the Saṅgha, if it has been given contrary to the Dharma and received contrary to the Dharma, that is improper conduct. Likewise, if a gift has been given to the Saṅgha and is then given to one, or to two, or to many, or offered to the Saṅgha again, it has been given contrary to the Dharma and received contrary to the Dharma, and that is improper conduct. Likewise, if a gift has been given to the community of monks and is then given to the community of nuns,

or given to both communities of monks and nuns; if a gift has been given to the community of nuns and then offered to the community of monks, or offered to both communities; if a gift has been given to both communities and then offered to the other two communities in exchange; or if the Saṅgha dwells separately in two different directions and a gift given to one group is then offered to the group in the other direction — in all such cases, it has been given contrary to the Dharma and received contrary to the Dharma, and that is improper conduct. When the reverse of all these applies, the gift is proper, and it should be declared as belonging to the virtuous side. There are ten cases in which the restoration ceremony conducted in accordance with the Dharma is set aside: one who has incurred a root defeat; one who has entered into talk of incurring a root defeat; one who has relinquished the training; one who has entered into talk of relinquishing the training; one who has reviled the Saṅgha; one who has entered into talk of reviling the Saṅgha; one whose moral discipline has deteriorated; one whose view has deteriorated; one whose conduct has deteriorated; and one whose livelihood has deteriorated.

In brief:

Those who raise objections, the analysis of circumstance,
the taking up of the matter, and the twofold pacification;
the one who presses the charge, the offense,
and what has directly arisen — these are to be cut off.

If the monk who raises the charge wishes to take up the matter, he should think very carefully about the ten grounds, examine them very carefully, and investigate them very carefully, and then take up the matter. What are the ten? Does the matter I wish to take up rest on truth, or would I be taking it up on the basis of something untrue? Is the time right to take up this matter, or is it not the right time? Is the taking up of this matter opportune, or is it not opportune? Does the taking up of this matter serve a purpose, or does it not? Is there something I have seen, heard, suspected, or some offense of body or speech, about which I should speak? And have I thought, "Am I able to lead this venerable one away from an unwholesome state and establish him in a wholesome state?" The monk who replies should likewise think very carefully about the ten grounds, examine them very carefully, and investigate them very carefully, and then analyze the circumstances with respect to the monk who raised the charge. What are the ten? Is this venerable one endowed with moral discipline or not? Does he have a sense of shame? Does he have remorse? Does he have restraint? Does he have a desire for the training? Is he learned? Does he retain what he has heard? Does he uphold it? Is he highly skilled in the Vinaya and the higher Vinaya? Has he mastered the recitation of the scriptural transmissions? And does this venerable one have the substance of a senior?

Then, Upāli, a senior Vinaya-holder who wishes to take up a dispute should also think very carefully about the ten grounds, examine them very carefully, and investigate them very carefully, and then take up the dispute. What are the ten? Am I skilled in the origin of this dispute I am taking up? Does this dispute I am taking up fall within what I have mastered of its origins? Do I have the substance of a senior? Can I get these monks — the one who raised the charge and the one who replied — to listen to me? Can I instruct these monks who raised the charge and who replied in accordance with the Dharma? Can I purify these monks who raised the charge and who replied of transgressions? Can I admonish these monks who raised the charge and who replied? Can I bring this dispute to a resolution in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Teacher taught? Can I lead these monks who raised the charge and who replied away from unwholesome states and firmly establish them in wholesome states? And can I bring this dispute to rest in such a way that it will not arise again in the future? With these thoughts in mind, the matter should be undertaken.

Then, Upāli, if a senior Vinaya-holder wishes to take up a dispute, he should think very carefully about the ten grounds, examine them very carefully,

and examine them very carefully, and then bring the dispute to rest. What are the ten? He should think: Will there be monks in this Saṅgha who hold the sūtras, hold the Vinaya, and hold the matrices — monks like myself who have mastered what I am about to teach? Is there a companion of mine within this Saṅgha who will bring this dispute among monks to rest in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Teacher taught? Is there a companion of mine within this Saṅgha who will prevent this dispute among monks from spreading further? Is there a companion of mine within this Saṅgha who will bring this dispute among monks to rest in accordance with the Dharma, in such a way that it will not arise again in the future? Is there someone in this Saṅgha who intends to scatter this dispute — together with the monks who raised the charge and who replied — into the royal court, and to scatter it into its proper category there, and who should therefore be properly restrained in accordance with the Dharma? Can I bring this dispute to rest within this Saṅgha? Will it be the case that I need not seek the resolution of this dispute outside? Will it be possible for me to manage the matter so that the monks who raised the charge and who replied need not go from place to place? Can I bring this dispute to rest in such a way that it will not arise again in the future? These are the thoughts he should hold in mind.

Upāli, a Vinaya-holder who is endowed with ten qualities is capable of resolving a dispute that has arisen. What are the ten? He is able to teach the sūtras spoken by the Buddha; he is able to explain the sūtras taught by the śrāvakas; he is able to explain the sūtras that arose at the time of the Buddha; he is able to explain the sūtras that arose at all times; he is able to explain the sūtras that belong to one school; he is able to explain the sūtras that were taught as dark and as bright; he is able to explain the sūtras that are spoken everywhere, having sought out the sūtra tradition according to sūtra; he is able to explain the harmonious sūtras; and he is able to explain the sūtras that are in accord with the Vinaya.

Upāli, a Vinaya-holder who is steady and composed, having taken up a dispute, should bring it to rest by means of ten methods. What are the ten? He should know the monk who raised the charge. He should know the monk who replied. He should examine the monk who raised the charge. He should examine the monk who replied. He should have the monk who raised the charge take an oath. He should have the monk who replied take an oath. He should bring the monk who raised the charge to a determination. He should bring the monk who replied to a determination. He should cause the monk who raised the charge to rise. He should cause the monk who replied to rise.

A Vinaya-holder endowed with ten qualities is able to set forth offenses. What are the ten? He knows what is a grave offense. He knows what is a light offense. He knows what has a remainder. He knows what has no remainder. He knows what is a case of bad conduct. He knows what is not a case of bad conduct. He knows what was laid down. He knows what was not laid down. He knows what has been confessed. He knows what requires restraint.

A Vinaya-holder endowed with ten qualities is capable of performing formal acts. What are the ten? He knows a formal act that is manifest. He knows a formal act that is not manifest. He knows a formal act performed in the wrong context. He knows a formal act performed in the right context. He knows what is fitting to bring up for discussion. He knows what is not fitting to bring up for discussion. He knows what is fitting to recall. He knows what is not fitting to recall. He knows what is fitting as a basis for adjudication. He knows what is not fitting as a basis for adjudication.

A Vinaya-holder endowed with ten qualities is capable of resolving disputes. What are the ten? He does not err regarding what occurred. He does not err regarding what was laid down. He does not err regarding what was subsequently laid down. He does not err regarding what was not permitted. He does not err regarding what was subsequently permitted. He does not set forth an offense in a manner that is improper for a monk. He administers oaths to the monks who raised the charge and to those who replied.

He presents the words of the sūtras in their proper sense. He does not impair what has been subsequently established. He is in accordance with the Vinaya. He resolves disputes in accordance with the Dharma.

A Vinaya-holder endowed with ten qualities is capable of adjudicating by means of acts of penalty. What are the ten? He knows the act of brahmatic penalty. He knows the act of causing displeasure. He knows the act of causing non-association. He knows the act of making one unfit. He knows the act of causing one to seek one's own essential nature. He knows the act of reversal. He knows the act of expulsion. He knows the act of purification. He knows the act of consecration. He knows the act of reproof.

This completes the ascent from one section of the text of the holy Vinaya.

The holy text of the Vinaya, the twenty-eighth fascicle. This is a summary of the fifth among the five sūtras of the Vinaya: the twenty-four topics, the dispelling of fears, accepting and taking by stealth, full ordination, the boundary sections, food likewise with the division of occasions, the assembly hall, and the final topic. In summary:

The twenty-four, moral discipline and truth,
What is to be spoken, the defeats,
The two offenses, and the views,
Transgressions and weighty matters,
And how it is fitting, O son of good family,
These and the rest are set forth in order.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Reverend One, if a monk who is an accuser wishes to bring a charge against another, where should he stand and speak? And should he cause the monk to undergo a division of occasions?"

The Buddha replied: "Upāli, a monk who wishes to bring a charge against another monk should stand in five positions and then speak. And he should cause the monk to undergo a division of occasions."

"What are the five in which one causes a monk to undergo a division of occasions? One bares one shoulder of the upper robe, removes one's sandals, sits in order of seniority, joins one's palms in añjali toward the community of monks, and with a mind of loving-kindness, one causes the monk who is the subject of the charge to undergo a division of occasions."

"A monk who brings a charge and wishes to speak against another should keep these five things inwardly in mind and then speak against the other. What are the five? He should reflect: 'Am I possessed of moral discipline and have I completed prior training? Am I endowed with a sense of shame and the capacity to distinguish? Am I restrained by my vows and do I wish to train? Am I widely learned and do I retain what I have heard — am I trained in the recitation of scriptural transmissions and so forth? Am I utterly unassailable in the Vinaya and in the higher Vinaya?' Having thus reflected, the monk who brings the charge and wishes to speak against another should, keeping those five things inwardly in mind, then speak against the other."

"Furthermore, a monk who is an accuser and who wishes to bring a charge should keep these five things inwardly in mind before speaking. What are the five? He should think: 'Is it with truth or with untruth that I, wishing to bring this charge against another, am taking up this matter? Is this a timely matter or untimely? Is the matter I am raising fitting to the occasion or unfitting? Is the matter I am raising one that is meaningful or not meaningful? And am I speaking from what I have seen, from what I have heard, or from what I suspect?' The monk who brings charges and wishes to speak against another should keep those five things inwardly in mind and then speak against the other."

"A monk who speaks a charge should cause the monk who is being charged to undergo a division of occasions in five ways. What are the five? As follows: 'Know that a charge is being brought against you. Venerable One, a statement is being made to you. Venerable One, a charge is being brought against you. Venerable One, you are to be reminded. Venerable One, you are to open an occasion for me.' Whichever among defeats, the remainder pertaining to the Saṅgha, transgressions, confessable offenses, and wrongdoings is being stated to you, expressed to you, charged against you, recalled to you, and opened as an occasion against you — if it has become a wrongdoing, whether it arose from a defeat or from the remainder pertaining to the Saṅgha, or —"

— or arising from a confessable offense, or arising from a training: whatever is to be stated to you, confessed, restrained, whatever has gone far beyond the Vinaya, or arising from wrong speech, or from misconduct — whatever wrongdoing is to be stated to you, whatever is to be stated to you as seen, heard, or suspected; whatever transgression of body or transgression of speech is to be stated to you; whether a grave downfall or a light one, with remainder or completely without remainder, or having gone beyond all — whatever downfall is to be stated to you; whether a breach of moral discipline, a breach of view, or a breach of livelihood — whatever breach in its entirety is to be stated to you; whether while walking, standing, sitting, lying down, or pacing — whatever mode of conduct is to be stated to you; whether done in a village, at a hermitage, on a road, gone astray from a road, or done in a secluded place — in whatever place it was done: the charging monk makes this statement, saying, "It shall be raised with you." Having opened the occasion in these five respects and having taken an oath, only then should the charge be brought.

If the one being charged does not acknowledge the charge, the charging monk should bring it with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of compassion, a mind of wishing benefit, a mind of affection, and a mind of wishing to uplift him.

The monk who answers the charge, for his part, when the one bringing the charge does so, should stand in five modes and open an occasion for the charging monk. What are the five? He should rise from his seat, remove his sandals, arrange his outer robe over one shoulder, bow with palms joined in deference to those senior in the order, remain in a respectful posture, and — bringing himself under the sway of a sense of reverence — open an occasion for the charging monk.

When the monk who has answered the charge wishes to open an occasion for the charging monk, he should first examine the charging monk in these five respects. What are the five? First, whether this venerable one is possessed of moral discipline and is formerly complete in it; whether he is possessed of conscience and remorse; whether he holds his vow and wishes to hold it. Second, whether the venerable one has heard much, retains what he has heard, has accumulated what he has heard, and has learned the recitation of texts by heart; and whether he is thoroughly and unquestionably versed in the Vinaya, the Higher Vinaya, and the sūtras. It is after the answering monk has examined the charging monk in these five respects that he should thereafter open an occasion for him.

When the answering monk wishes to open an occasion for the charging monk, he should settle within himself mindfulness of these five things, and then open the occasion. What are the five? "The charge brought against me is brought on the basis of truth, not on the basis of falsehood; it is brought at the right time, not at the wrong time; it is brought with meaningful purpose, not without purpose; it is brought in gentle words, not in harsh ones; it is brought with loving-kindness, not with aversion — where else would I find such a thing from another?" Having reflected in this way, the answering monk who wishes to open an occasion for the charging monk should settle these five things inwardly in mindfulness, and then address the charging monk with these words: "O venerable charging one, take note and speak to me. Venerable One, open an occasion for me. Venerable One, bring your charge against me. As to what you have stated by way of opening an occasion for the venerable one — what you have stated to me, what you have charged me with, what you have recalled to me, what you have opened as an occasion against me — and for what reason you open an occasion for me: of the offenses, whether it be a defeat, a remainder pertaining to the Saṅgha, a downfall, or a confessable offense — which of these do you raise?"

Of all such offenses — whether arising from a defeat, from what remains pertaining to the Saṅgha, from a downfall, or from a confessable offense, or from a training — I shall open an occasion. Whether it is something to be confessed, something to be restrained, a transgression of the Vinaya, something arising from slander, or something arising from manifest conduct: state which offense it is that opens an occasion. Was it something I saw, heard, suspected, transgressed in body, or transgressed in speech? State what manifest conduct you speak of against me. State whether what you bring against me is grave or light, whether it comes with a remainder or without remainder, or whether it has entirely passed. State what fault you speak of against me. Whether it is a fault in moral discipline, a fault in view, a fault in conduct, a fault in livelihood, or a fault in all of these — state which fault you name. Speak from whatever deportment was observed: walking, standing, sitting, lying down, or not lying down. Speak from what was done in a village, what was done in a monastery, what was done on a road, what was done off the road, what was done at night, or what was done by day — state where I did it.

The charging monk, having opened an occasion for the charged monk in these five ways, should cause him to make a pledge and should say these words: "State the offense in accordance with the pledge made by the charging monk."

In brief:

Those relating to fear and confusion,
brahmic penalties and non-observance of proper conduct,
censure penalties and direct confrontation,
and those relating to truths — all are to be handled accordingly.

When the charging monk has opened an occasion, the charged monk should at that time be steadfast in five points: "O venerable one, do not be frightened. Do not make yourself afraid. Do not make yourself terrified. Do not be altogether terrified. Do not make yourself altogether terrified. Do not be alarmed. Do not make yourself alarmed. Do not shrink back. Do not make yourself shrink back."

The charging monk should further be steadfast in five points toward the charged monk: "O venerable one, I do not take hold of your confusion. I do not take hold of the occasion of your alarm. O venerable one, I hold you to a definitive position. O venerable one, I place the matter in a pledge to be made up to three times."

The charging monk should further be steadfast in yet another five points toward the charged monk: "If you, venerable one, are to be rightly subject to a brahmic penalty, then a brahmic penalty shall be pronounced upon you. If you are to be rightly subject to an act of censure, then an act of censure shall be performed. If you, venerable one, act without proper conduct, then you shall be counted among those who act without proper conduct. If you, venerable one, speak face-to-face of a fault, then you shall be counted among those who speak face-to-face of a fault. If you lay hands on another saying 'He is the one who said it,' then you shall be counted among those who lay hands on another saying 'He is the one who said it.' If you do not heed the pronouncement, then you shall be counted among those who do not heed pronouncements. If by remaining silent you do not heed the pronouncement, then you shall be counted among those who remain altogether silent."

The charging monk should further be steadfast in yet another five points toward the charged monk: "If you, venerable one, are to be rightly subject to a censure act, then a censure act shall be performed upon you. If you are to be rightly subject to an act of separate enjoyment of requisites, then an act of separate enjoyment shall be performed. If you are to be rightly subject to an act of not appearing in sight, then an act of not appearing in sight shall be performed upon you. If you are to be rightly subject to expulsion, then an act of expulsion shall be performed. If you are to be rightly subject to an act of reproach, then an act of reproach shall be performed. If you are to be rightly subject to reconciliation, then an act of reconciliation shall be performed upon you. If you are to be rightly subject to abandonment, then an act of abandonment shall be performed upon you."

Furthermore, the monk who raises the matter shall, in five further respects, be confident before the monk who has been addressed. If it is right that you, Venerable, be punished with a penalty, then you shall be punished with a penalty. If it is right that you be dismissed from the root and punished with a penalty, then you shall be dismissed from the root and punished with a penalty. If it is right that you be made to carry out a probationary penance, then you shall be made to carry out a probationary penance. If it is right that you be dismissed from the root and made to carry out a probationary penance, then you shall be dismissed from the root and made to carry out a probationary penance. If it is right that you be again dismissed from the root and made to carry out a penalty, then the formal act of again dismissing you from the root and making you carry out a penalty shall be performed upon you. If it is right that you be again dismissed from the root and made to carry out a probationary penance, then you shall be again dismissed from the root and made to carry out a probationary penance.

Furthermore, the monk who raises the matter shall, in five further respects, be confident before the monk who has been addressed. If it is right that you, Venerable, be disciplined by direct acknowledgment, then you shall be disciplined by direct acknowledgment. If it is right that you be disciplined by recollection, then you shall be disciplined by recollection. If it is right that you be disciplined through a declaration of non-confusion, then you shall be disciplined through a declaration of non-confusion. If it is right that you be disciplined by an inquiry into the nature of the matter, then you shall be disciplined by an inquiry into the nature of the matter. If it is right that multiple blades of grass be given to you, then multiple blades of grass shall be given to you.

Furthermore, the monk who raises the matter shall, in five further respects, be confident before the monk who has been addressed. You who have been addressed, hear this. Concerning whatever has been asked of you, speak accordingly. Do so in such a way that you do not disgrace yourself, that you do not harm others, that you do not oppress those monks who are without fault, that you do not openly revile those monks who have come forward openly, and that you do not bring what you say into conflict with the words of the sūtras in the presence of authoritative monks. If you act in this way, it will be virtuous and exceedingly wholesome.

In brief:
The offense alleged is to be admitted accordingly —
acknowledgment, view, the restoration ceremony,
the teacher and what is practiced,
the fall of status, and expulsion.

The five ways in which an offense is committed: an offense arising from shamelessness, an offense arising from doubt, an offense arising from not knowing, an offense arising from weakness of mind, and an offense arising from failure of mindfulness.

The five things to be abandoned: making a request, making an inquiry, giving an instruction, speaking to some, and making a declaration.

What is meant by making a request? One requests of you, Venerable, saying: "Do not, even in the slightest, do what would prevent you, Venerable, from becoming an ascetic." What is meant by making an inquiry? One asks you, Venerable: "Have you, Venerable, done even the slightest thing that would prevent you from becoming an ascetic?" What is meant by giving an instruction? One gives you the instruction: "Do not, Venerable, do what would prevent you from becoming an ascetic." What is meant by speaking to some? One urges: "Venerable, be careful not to act as certain others do in preventing themselves from becoming ascetics." What is meant by making a declaration? One declares again and again to you, Venerable, for the sake of preventing you from ceasing to be an ascetic.

The five ways of making an acknowledgment that is not in accordance with the Dharma: making an acknowledgment out of fear of the king, making an acknowledgment out of fear of a thief, making an acknowledgment out of fear of the intimidation of the village community, making an acknowledgment out of fear of punishment, and making an acknowledgment without regard for the ascetic life itself.

The five ways of making an acknowledgment in accordance with the Dharma are the reversal of the above in five modes toward the white side.

The five ways of declaring a view that is not in accordance with the Dharma: declaring a view with respect to an object, omitting nothing that remains —

declaring a view with respect to the object of what is being acknowledged, declaring a view with respect to the object of the offence when a different offence has arisen, declaring a view with respect to an object that is not fit to be acknowledged, and declaring a view while wishing not to rise. The five ways of declaring a view in accordance with the Dharma are likewise those that arise from virtue and method, reversed toward the white side in five modes.

The five preceptors of a novice are: the preceptor of the novice's training, the preceptor who instructs in secret, the preceptor who performs the act, the preceptor who assigns the residence, and the preceptor who reads aloud. Who is the preceptor of the novice's training? The one who has given the basis of training for a novice. Who is the preceptor who instructs in secret? The one who gives the secret instruction at the time of full ordination. Who is the preceptor who performs the act? The one who has carried out the act of full ordination. Who is the preceptor who assigns the residence? The one from whom one has earnestly requested a residence up to three times, and by whom it has been assigned. Who is the preceptor who reads aloud? The one from whom even a single word has been received with the intention of taking it up.

The five kinds of exclusion are: being forbidden to speak, not being shown scriptural transmission, not being kept company, cutting off the virtuous side, and dissolving the assigned residence — these are the five. What is being forbidden to speak? Not being spoken to at all, in any way whatsoever. What is not being shown scriptural transmission? Not transmitting scriptural texts to that person, nor giving subsequent instruction. Not showing teachings. What is not being kept company? Not making one's own whatever service that person has rendered. What is cutting off the virtuous side? Not teaching that person recitation, yoga, or mental application. What is dissolving the assigned residence? Not allowing entry into the residence.

By five factors the assigned residence is broken: being expelled, rising up and leaving, falling back, going from one's own side to a different side, and giving rise to the thought of hopelessness — these are the five.

If one is endowed with five qualities, one may be given a residence assignment. What are the five? One has faith, one is accompanied by respect, one has applied diligence, one is receptive to speech, and one is a spiritual friend of virtue.

If one is endowed with five qualities, the residence assignment is to be dissolved. What are the five? One lacks faith, one has no respect, one is lazy, one is unreceptive to speech, and one is a companion in wrongdoing.

If a companion and attendant are endowed with five qualities, they are to be expelled. What are the five? Lack of faith, absence of respect, laziness, unreceptiveness to speech, and companionship in wrongdoing.

If a companion and attendant are endowed with five qualities, they are not to be expelled. These five, reversed toward the white side in five modes, are to be stated.

If a companion and attendant are endowed with five qualities, they are not to be tolerated: lack of faith, absence of respect, laziness, unreceptiveness to speech, and companionship in wrongdoing.

If a companion and attendant are endowed with five qualities, they are to be tolerated: these are to be stated reversed toward the white side in five modes.

In brief: the three types of receiving, destruction, the nāga and the acknowledgment of offences, the paṇḍaka of male and female types, the suitable residence, and the two kinds of dust.

The five types of receiving are: giving with the body to the body, receiving with the body in the body, giving with what is held by the body to the body, giving with what is held by the body to what is held by the body, and receiving by placement — these are the five. How is the giving with the body to the body? Something passes from the hand and is received in the hand. How is the receiving with the body in the body? Something is given from the hand and received into the alms bowl. How is the giving with what is held by the body to the body? Something is given by means of a vessel and received in the hand. How is the giving with what is held by the body to what is held by the body? Something is given from a vessel and received into a vessel.

How is the receiving by placement? There are people known as the reviled — even their fathers and brothers revile them, to say nothing of others. One places an alms bowl before them and says: "Good-looking one, if you would give, pour it into this alms bowl." If they then pour into that bowl, this is called receiving by placement.

Furthermore, there are five kinds of giving and receiving: on a seat, on a small seat, on a low stool, on a mat, and at the base of an alms bowl.

There are five ways in which, even though giving and receiving occur, no valid giving and receiving has taken place: taking without it having been given; taking without intending to eat it; taking it while perceiving it as belonging to someone else; taking it when one is not present before the giver; and taking from someone who is not a proper person.

There are five ways in which giving and receiving, though completed, become invalidated. What are the five? It is seized away; it is lost; it is discarded; it returns; or the time has passed.

The five natures of nāgas: the remainder are emanations. By nature they are born; by nature they die; by nature they sleep; by nature they become angry; and by nature they engage in unchaste conduct, that is, they engage in sexual behavior.

The five transgressions are: defeat, that which belongs as a remainder to the Saṅgha, downfall, individual confession, and wrongdoing.

Five modes in which a transgression arises: there are transgressions that arise from body but not from speech; transgressions that arise from speech but not from body; transgressions that arise from body and mind but not from speech; transgressions that arise from speech and mind but not from body; and transgressions that arise from body, mind, and speech together.

Five modes in which one is cleared of a transgression: by being seen; by being proclaimed; by not having done it from the beginning; by consecration; and by confession — these are the five.

Five types of pandaka of the male kind: the pandaka by nature, the half-monthly pandaka, the pandaka of jealousy, the pandaka of attachment, and the impaired pandaka.

What is the pandaka by nature? One who has become a pandaka by nature. What is the half-monthly pandaka? For half the month they become male, and for half the month they become female. What is the pandaka of jealousy? One who, upon seeing another engaged in misconduct, thereupon commits misconduct himself. What is the pandaka of attachment? One who, when another acts upon him and presses him, thereupon does it. What is the impaired pandaka? One whose male organ has been eaten by an animal or severed by a weapon.

There are also five types of pandaka of the female kind: one who has both sets of marks; one who is connected at both openings; one who flows continuously; one who lacks a monthly mark; and one who has only the appearance of a mark.

Five suitable sites: one where an object has been obtained; one where an object has not yet been obtained; one where an object has been abandoned; one where there was already something beforehand; and one that is unoccupied — these are the five.

What is a suitable site where an object has been obtained? It is one where all those objects are fully complete. Whatever has been consecrated is consecrated by three means: by generating the intention, by declaring it to one another, and by making a request.

What is a suitable site where an object has not yet been obtained? Even if it is small, it is one where even a foundation stone has been laid. This too is consecrated in that same threefold manner of consecration.

What is a suitable site where an object has been abandoned? One that has been consecrated as a formally suitable site but then abandoned, and then consecrated again as a suitable site by that same threefold consecration.

What is a suitable site that existed beforehand? It is one that has been shared in common by various remarkable tīrthikas (non-Buddhist adherents), such that

consecrated by the Saṅgha through that same threefold consecration.

What is a suitable site where none has yet been established? It is a place where previously there was no suitable site, but which has been enclosed by a wall, enclosed by a fence, or enclosed by a ditch — and within that enclosure the Saṅgha has drawn a line on the ground, or driven in a stake, or enclosed it with a wall, or erected any other marker whatsoever. Through that threefold consecration it is consecrated as a suitable site.

The five kinds of dust are: dust of food, dust of drink, dust of fragrance, dust of medicine, and dust that is dust itself — these are the five. Furthermore, there is another set of five kinds of dust: dust of what is chewed, dust of what is placed in the mouth, dust of porridge, dust of what is licked, and dust of what is tasted — these are the five.

In brief:

Theft, and the opening of an opportunity,
gifts, and the place of the restoration ceremony,
the recitation of a scriptural ruling,
and the two kinds of going near a village.

The five kinds of theft are: stealing by deception, stealing by force, stealing while saying "I am returning it," stealing by snatching, and stealing after having dedicated it — these are the five.

The five kinds of persons one must not admit into an assembly are: one who is shameless, one who has an impediment, one whose word is unreliable, one who does not remain in their natural state, and one who has incurred a root defeat — these are the five.

The five kinds of giving that are counted as non-meritorious are: giving a weapon, giving alcohol, giving poison, giving a woman, and giving what is contrary to Dharma — these are the five.

Five causes and conditions whereby not attending the restoration ceremony does not constitute an offense: being impeded by a king, being carried away by water, being burned by fire, being impeded by non-human beings — these are the five.

The five kinds of recitation of a scriptural ruling are: reciting it while being mad, with a disturbed mind, afflicted by illness; reciting it while pretending to be disciplined, out of devotion to wrongdoing; reciting it while being foolish, being stupid, lowly, and confused; reciting it out of manifest arrogance; and reciting it while being genuinely and fully liberated — these are the five.

When a monk who goes near a village enters that village, five occasions of fault are to be recognized. What are the five? Going into the village at an improper time without having informed the monks who are present; sitting down on a seat without having examined it properly; teaching the Dharma to a woman in more than five statements; sitting together with a woman alone on the same seat; and insistently sitting down on a seat in a village that has a bad reputation — these are the five.

When a monk who goes near a village enters the village with heedlessness, these further five occasions of fault are also to be recognized: looking at a woman continually; looking at her and then engaging in conversation; becoming familiar through conversation; once familiar, entertaining improper thoughts; and having entertained improper thoughts, coming to dislike the celibate life — up to the point of committing a grave offense, or surrendering the training, or falling back to the lower state.

In brief:

Full ordination and individual liberation,
admission, Vinaya, liberation,
the five permanent ones and the lesser,
the unborn, and the suspected.

Full ordination is spoken of for five reasons: the name is drawn from the preceptor, the name is drawn from the Saṅgha, the name comes from the one who wishes to be fully ordained, a request is made, and the act is not impaired — these are the five.

In the age when a buddha has appeared, the five kinds of full ordination are: direct penetration of gnosis, acceptance of what one will teach, acceptance of the pure code of conduct, being addressed by the words "Come, monk," and the absence of a master and preceptor — thus these are the five.

The five kinds of recitation of the individual liberation:

a request having been made, the origin-statement is recited, and then "the remainder has been heard" is proclaimed — this is the first recitation of the individual liberation. A request having been made, and the origin-statement and the four defeats having been read, and "the remainder has been heard" proclaimed — this is the second reading of the sūtra of individual liberation. A request having been made, and the origin-statement, the four defeats, and the thirteen remainders of the Saṅgha having been read, and "the remainders have been heard" proclaimed — this is the third reading of the sūtra of individual liberation. A request having been made, and the origin-statement, the four defeats, the thirteen remainders of the Saṅgha, and the two indeterminate cases having been read, and "the remainder has been heard" proclaimed — this is the fourth reading of the sūtra of individual liberation. And the fifth is the complete reading of the sūtra.

The five ways of taking something to heart: it is dear, in that it is pleasing; it is patient, in that there is no opposition; it is a teacher, in that it is to be revered; it is accepted, in that it acts according to one's wishes; and it provides lodging and sustenance — thinking of it in that way. And upon hearing that it has been taken up, one becomes glad.

The five kinds of discipline: during the lifetime of a buddha, constantly, one-sidedly, universally, and taming the afflictions.

Further, another five kinds of discipline: taming through objects, taming through time, taming through place, taming through persons, and taming through conflict.

The Vinaya is not expounded to five kinds of persons: one who questions while seeking an opportunity to cause harm, one who questions with the intention of injuring, one who questions with the intention of finding fault, one who questions with the intention of defeating in argument, and one who questions with the desire to speak of faults.

The five qualities of a permanent robe: it does not become obligatory after one day, it does not become obligatory after ten days, it does not become obligatory even beyond ten days, one may keep a surplus robe without dedicating it, and one may travel and move about wearing an upper and lower garment.

Further, another five qualities of a permanent robe: there is no communal eating, no repeated eating, one may go without being invited, one may seek a Dharma robe as one pleases, and from the last month of autumn until the beginning of the first month of spring, whatever is obtained is divided equally with the Saṅgha that has kept the rains retreat together.

Five kinds of persons are not appointed to assign a permanent robe: one who has not kept the rains retreat, one whose rains retreat was interrupted, one who entered the later rains retreat, one who entered the rains retreat elsewhere as is the custom, and one who has been expelled.

Further, another five kinds of persons are not appointed to assign a permanent robe: one who remains separately, one who does not remain, one who has sided with a faction, one who has surrendered the training, and one who has disrobed.

Further, another five kinds of persons are not appointed to assign a permanent robe: one who has been suspended for not seeing a fault, one who has been suspended so as not to repeat the act, one who has been suspended for not relinquishing a wrongful view, one who has sided with a faction, and one who does not remain.

Further, another five kinds of persons are not appointed to assign a permanent robe: one who imposes penalties, one who imposes penalties on the basis of a root matter, one who acts to please, one who acts to please on the basis of a root matter, and one who has behaved in a manner aimed at pleasing.

Five kinds of persons have no authority over gains: one who has not kept the rains retreat, one whose rains retreat was interrupted, one who entered the later rains retreat as is the custom, a novice monk's father, and one who has surrendered the training.

Further, another five kinds of persons have no authority over gains: one who has been suspended for not seeing a fault, one who has been suspended for not repeating the act, one who has been suspended for not relinquishing a wrongful view, one who has drawn near to a faction, and one who does not remain.

Five kinds of persons are neither in authority over gains nor have any quality in relation to them: one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, and one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent.

Further, another five kinds of persons are neither in authority over gains nor have any quality in relation to them: a hermaphrodite, one who has expelled a nun,

one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), one who is a thief-dweller, and one who had previously committed an offense.

Five qualities render a monk incapable of being made a preceptor: he is without faith, he is of bad moral discipline, he has heard little, he is miserly, and he is of defective wisdom.

Five kinds of persons are of such a nature that they cannot be born from within this Dharma and Vinaya: one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, and one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent.

Further, another five kinds of persons are of such a nature that they cannot be born from within this Dharma and Vinaya: a hermaphrodite, one who has expelled a nun, one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, one who is a thief-dweller, and one who had previously committed an offense.

A monk possessing five qualities is one who is suspected of wrongdoing: one who consorts with a female yakṣa, one who consorts with a prostitute, one who consorts with a widow, one who consorts with a young woman of high station, and one who consorts with a female hermaphrodite.

In brief:
More than three intervals remaining,
one who moves to a swift residence,
robes and suitable medicines,
and a needle-case likewise the same.

A boundary is dissolved again in five ways: the entire Saṅgha departs, the entire Saṅgha disperses, the entire Saṅgha dies and passes away, the entire Saṅgha scatters in all directions and is cut off, and a fifth is that a formal request and act have been performed.

Further, a boundary is dissolved again in five other ways: there is no marker, there is no monk, there is no expectation, another boundary is encircled, and a fifth is that a formal request and act have been performed.

In five ways it is said that no surplus has been made: one makes a surplus of food and drink without it having come into direct presence, one makes a surplus of food and drink without receiving it, one makes a surplus without directing another, one makes a surplus in the presence of one not fully ordained, and one makes a surplus in the presence of one who does not remain by nature. The making of a surplus is to be stated as reversed in five ways on the side of the wholesome.

For a person who speaks rapidly, five objects of fault are to be known. What are the five? The body will become weary, mindfulness will decline, the mind will be harmed, the throat will be obstructed, and one will not reach a clear understanding at the margins. These are the objects of fault for a person who speaks rapidly. For a person who does not speak rapidly, five virtues arise — to be stated reversed in five ways on the side of the wholesome.

For a person who remains long in one place, five objects of fault arise: what has not been absorbed will not become absorbed, what has been absorbed will decline, even what Dharma has been heard will be forgotten, one will experience great harm, and one will not be accompanied by friends. For a person who does not remain long in one place, five virtues arise — these are to be stated reversed in five ways on the side of the wholesome.

For one who is constantly on the move, five objects of fault arise: what has not been absorbed will not become absorbed, what has been absorbed will decline, even what Dharma has been heard will be forgotten, one will experience great harm, and one will not be accompanied by friends. For one who is not constantly on the move, five virtues arise — these are to be stated reversed in five ways on the side of the wholesome.

Permissible robes are of five kinds: wool, cotton-wool, silk-wool, kambala-hemp cloth, and linen cloth.

In five ways a Dharma-robe that has been consecrated is dissolved back: it is seized away, it is given away, it is retrieved back, it lapses, and the owner has died.

In five ways, what has been consecrated is likewise dissolved back: it is seized away, it is given away, it is retrieved back, it lapses, and the owner has died. The same is to be stated for a consecrated alms-bowl. Likewise, the same is to be stated for consecrated medicine and dedicated medicine.

A needle-case is not to be entrusted to five kinds of persons: one without shame, one who harbors resentment, one who does not know moderation, one whose mindfulness has weakened, and one who is naturally unstable.

In brief:

The wandering ascetic who eats in the prescribed manner,
the layman, the sick person — two —
the five who have gone forth,
and the many virtues — all are likewise to be understood.

Five are the objects of fault in one who eats without measure: the body becomes heavy; one becomes unfit for work and unable to endure exertion; breathing in and out becomes uncomfortable; excrement and urine increase greatly; and the mind becomes entirely overcome by torpor and sleep, so that it does not become one-pointed but becomes distracted. For one who observes measure in eating, five virtues arise — these are to be stated reversed in five ways on the side of the wholesome.

If possessed of five qualities, a wandering ascetic who follows along behind need not be led: he goes far too much ahead, he comes dawdling far behind, he walks jostling others, he interrupts conversations, and he is unable to receive what is obtained in a fitting and appropriate manner. The same reversed in five ways on the side of the wholesome is likewise to be stated for receiving what is found when one has two alms-bowls or finds something while carrying an alms-bowl.

A layman possessed of five qualities is a defiled layman, a deceiving layman, a corrupt layman — he is to be known as a layman of ignoble kind: he is one of bad moral discipline who does not fulfill the training completely; he relies on omens and auspicious signs, trusting in omens and auspicious signs to purify rather than through the activity of faith in the Dharma; he holds wrong views, and with wrong views he is one who extensively disparages monks; he dominates the Saṅgha of elders, middle-standing monks, and novices, and thereby reviles the monks residing there.

A layman possessed of five qualities is a layman like a lotus, a layman like a white lotus — he is to be regarded as an excellent layman. These are to be stated reversed in five ways on the side of the wholesome.

A sick person possessed of five qualities is difficult to attend upon as a patient: he possesses the qualities of being unamenable to instruction, being unamenable to what is instructed; he does not act as directed by the attendant; he does not know what is beneficial and what is not; he does not rely on medicine; and whatever provisions come to him he distributes them all to others for their sustenance, while not knowing when ailments are exhausted or not exhausted. These same are to be stated reversed in five ways on the side of the wholesome.

If possessed of five qualities, it is inappropriate to appoint someone as an attendant for a sick patient: he is unamenable to instruction and possesses the qualities of being unamenable; he does not act toward the patient as directed; he does not know what is beneficial and what is not beneficial for the patient; he is unable to prepare medicine for the patient; and he attends the patient for the sake of food rather than for the sake of Dharma, and he is one who reviles — having thoroughly abused the patient, he is unwilling and contemptuous when it comes to disposing of the patient's excrement, urine, saliva, vomit, and pus. These are to be stated reversed in five ways on the side of the wholesome.

One who is possessed of five qualities and has completed ten years may bestow going forth, may bestow full ordination, and may bestow residence. What are the five? Being endowed with moral discipline, being learned, holding the sūtra collections, holding the Vinaya, and holding what resembles a mother.

Furthermore, stated in another set of five: being endowed with moral discipline, being learned, being skilled in the sūtra collections,

being skilled in the Vinaya, and being skilled in what resembles a mother.

Furthermore, stated in another set of five: being endowed with moral discipline, being greatly learned, knowing the sūtra collections, knowing the Vinaya, and knowing what resembles a mother.

Furthermore, stated in another set of five: being endowed with moral discipline, being greatly learned, being clear in the sūtra collections, being clear in the Vinaya, and being clear in what resembles a mother.

Furthermore, stated in another set of five: being possessed of moral discipline, being greatly learned, being able to introduce a companion or a personal attendant to the sūtra collections, the Vinaya, and what resembles a mother.

Furthermore, stated in another set of five: being possessed of moral discipline, being greatly learned, and having trained in the higher moral discipline, the higher mind, and the higher Vinaya.

Furthermore, stated in another set of five: being possessed of moral discipline, being greatly learned, training in the training that goes beyond the training, the higher Vinaya, and the higher individual liberation.

Furthermore, stated in another set of five: being endowed with faith, being endowed with moral discipline, being endowed with learning, being endowed with generosity, and being endowed with wisdom.

Furthermore, stated in another set of five: being endowed with moral discipline, being endowed with wisdom, being endowed with meditative absorption, being endowed with liberation, and being endowed with the gnosis that sees liberation.

Furthermore, stated in another set of five: being possessed of moral discipline, being greatly learned, undertaking diligence, establishing mindfulness, and being possessed of wisdom.

Furthermore, stated in another set of five: being possessed of moral discipline, being greatly learned, having undertaken diligence, abiding in meditative equipoise, and being possessed of wisdom.

Furthermore, stated in another set of five: being possessed of moral discipline, being greatly learned, having undertaken diligence, striving to place the mind correctly within, and being possessed of wisdom.

Furthermore, stated in another set of five: being endowed with the aggregate of moral discipline belonging to one still in training, the aggregate of meditative absorption, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the gnosis that sees liberation.

Furthermore, stated in another set of five: being endowed with the aggregate of moral discipline belonging to one beyond training, the aggregate of meditative absorption, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the gnosis that sees liberation.

Furthermore, stated in another set of five: knowing what constitutes a transgression, knowing what has been instituted, knowing what has been subsequently instituted, knowing what is permitted, and knowing what has been subsequently permitted.

Furthermore, stated in another set of five: knowing what is an impediment, knowing what is not an impediment, being able to instruct, to give supplementary instruction, and to assign residence.

Furthermore, stated in another set of five: knowing what is a transgression, knowing what is not a transgression, knowing what is heavy, knowing what is light, and being thoroughly versed in the sūtra of individual liberation and able to recite it by heart.

One who is possessed of these five qualities may bestow going forth, may bestow full ordination, may bestow residence, and may himself sit without taking up residence. Of the first group of five, there are two deficient cases: after having received full ordination, whether ten years have passed or more, and whether one is a companion or a personal attendant — if one is able to nurse a sick person or to cause another to nurse them; and whether one is a companion or a personal attendant — if, when a doubt arises, one is able to resolve it or cause it to be resolved; and whether one is a companion or a personal attendant — if, when the companion or attendant has fallen to looking upon what is blameworthy, one is able to send them away or cause them to be sent away; and whether one is a companion or a personal attendant — if the companion or attendant has become discontented in this residence,

one is able to bring them to accept a different location. If one possesses these five qualities, one may confer the going forth, confer full ordination, grant residence, and dwell without setting oneself up as their preceptor.

The noble text of the Vinaya, the twenty-ninth fascicle. The middle verses of the Sūtra of the Five are to be recited.

Ten years: the fourth sūtra collection,
and the remaining: the conduct and the complete —
these two are made, and diligence is begun.
Yet another, the third: the aggregates,
and likewise the arising — in two;
the interruptions and the offenses,
and finally, gathered into categories.

The five objects of fault for one who does not uphold the Vinaya are: it is profound; one lacks confidence; one's intentions are many; it is expressed in worldly script; and it is difficult to understand.

The five qualities of a person who upholds the Vinaya are: one becomes the guardian of the treasury within the Victor's domain; one conceals and utterly conceals the heap of one's own moral discipline; one transmits the scripture to others; the teaching does not come to depend on another; one becomes a refuge for the four assemblies gathered together; and one becomes a refuge for the wise, for those leading the holy life equal to Brahmā, when remorse arises in them.

Furthermore, the five qualities of a person who upholds the Vinaya are: one dwells fearlessly in the midst of the Saṅgha; one comes to have thoroughly mastered the topics of training; one causes the teaching of the Teacher to increase; one proclaims the Dharma; and, having made this training the governing principle, one stands established at the crown of those outside this — the non-Buddhists.

Furthermore, the five qualities of a person who upholds the Vinaya are: in whatever direction a person who upholds the Vinaya resides, that direction becomes illumined, becomes clearly illumined, becomes brilliantly illumined; that direction is not left empty by me; and in whatever direction a person who upholds the Vinaya dwells, the Tathāgata's activity in that direction is lessened.

Furthermore, the five qualities of a person who upholds the Vinaya are: knowing what has arisen; knowing what has been laid down; knowing what has been subsequently laid down; knowing what has been abandoned; and knowing what has been permitted.

Furthermore, the five qualities of a person who upholds the Vinaya are: knowing what is an offense; knowing what is not an offense; knowing what is heavy; knowing what is light; and one recites the Prātimokṣa sūtra and proclaims it in full.

Furthermore, the five qualities of a person who upholds the Vinaya are: knowing what constitutes an interruption; knowing what does not constitute an interruption; transmitting the scripture; giving subsequent instruction; and being able to establish one in a residence.

In brief:

What has been abandoned and the second,
and the bowing there — make these two;
the second permitted: the food,
and the lodging allowance — likewise.

The five ways in which one is said to have abandoned: manifestly eating; manifestly appearing to give food; manifestly receiving food; manifestly appearing to renounce food; and manifestly rising from one's seat.

How does one manifestly eat? One abandons again the five kinds of food and the five kinds of lodging allowance.

How does one manifestly appear to give food? One manifests to a man, a woman, or a neuter person.

How does one manifestly receive food? The five foods and the five lodging allowances have been brought to accord.

How does one manifestly appear to renounce food? One declares, "I do not want the five foods and the five lodging allowances," and abandons them.

What is meant by manifestly rising from one's seat? It is simply rising from one's seat.

The five ways in which one is said to have not abandoned: the reverse of such, expressed in five ways.

Furthermore, the five reasons why one is said to have not abandoned are:

One abandons by mixing what is unsuitable to eat with food, and what is unsuitable to lodge with lodging. One abandons by setting it down or mixing it with what has been set down. One abandons by what is not beneficial, or by mixing it with what is not beneficial. One abandons by what is not wanted, or by mixing it with what is not wanted. And there is the case of not having been satisfied, or of not having become complete.

These are called the five ways of abandoning. The reverse of those, expressed as five, is to be stated as not having abandoned.

Furthermore, the five ways in which abandonment expressed in words that include a remainder is called not having abandoned are these: saying "That will do for now," saying "Set it aside for now," saying "I will eat it later," saying "I do not need it for now," and saying "I will see whether I am satisfied or not." These five are called not having abandoned.

The five ways of abandoning expressed in words that include no remainder are: saying "That is enough," saying "Set it aside," saying "I have finished eating," saying "I do not need it," and saying "I am satisfied." These five words, free from any remainder, are called having abandoned.

The five kinds of rag-robes are: the rag-robe from a market, one carried away by water, one that has been used as a rag, one found lying in a wilderness, and one taken from an old storehouse — these are the five.

Furthermore, the five kinds of rag-robes are: one eaten by cattle, one eaten by rats, one eaten by birds, one scorched by fire, and one discarded by a mother — these are the five.

The five ways of making something suitable for use are: making it suitable by fire, making it suitable by a blade, making it suitable by a fingernail, making it suitable by a needle, and making it suitable by wringing — these are the five.

Furthermore, the five ways of making suitable are: extracting, picking out, cutting, scraping off, and rendering it into a non-seed state — these are the five.

The five foods are: grain that has been husked, flour that has been cooked, meat, fish, and dry provisions.

The five medicinal lodging allowances are: root preparations, trunk preparations, leaf preparations, flower preparations, and grain preparations.

Furthermore, the five additional lodging allowances are: preparations of flour cakes, preparations of fermented foods, preparations of dried provisions, preparations of sugar, and preparations of ale.

One who is weakened in five ways may take consecrated sugar as a lodging allowance: one who has eaten only a small amount of food, one who has not eaten at all, one who is afflicted by illness, one who has set out on a journey, and one who is beginning new work.

In brief:

The bath-house, moral discipline one cannot bear,
Many friends who are not of the true Dharma,
The begging bowl, food, and likewise
Clothing and alms-rounds — these are the same.

The five qualities of the bath-house are: it removes impurity from the body, it brightens the skin and complexion, it draws out diseases present within the skin, it counteracts wind and phlegm that have become imbalanced, and the many illnesses of monks are eliminated by the bath-house — these are the five.

If a monk possesses these five qualities, the Saṅgha will dwell in ease.

The five are: being restrained by the vow of individual liberation (prātimokṣa), being endowed with conduct and the path of conduct, taking fear even in the slightest fault that is blameworthy and training firmly in the bases of training, looking after oneself without looking after others, and having few companions, with knowledge and understanding being extremely limited.

Now, having few companions means that one will be free from the suffering of longing to meet with others, that one dwells at ease and is happy in that one does no harm to others; and when others speak disagreeable words or speak harshly, one will not be tormented by others and will not become unable to bear it.

The five faults perceived in a person who lacks patience are: one is unsuitable, one is fierce, one is disliked by many people, one is disagreeable, and one will be remorseful afterward.

The five qualities of a person endowed with patience are to be stated as the reverse, expressed in the five ways of the virtuous side.

The five faults perceived in a person who lacks patience are: one will come to have many enemies; one will have much suffering and mental discomfort; one will come to have many separations; one will pass one's time in a state of constant remorse; and, upon leaving the body at death, one will be reborn in a lower realm, in the continuum of a being in hell. The five qualities of a person endowed with patience are to be stated as the reverse, expressed in the five ways of the virtuous side.

When the holy Dharma is in decline — when the world has come to be at odds with the holy Dharma — five things that are not the holy Dharma will arise in the world. What are those five?

When the holy Dharma is in decline and the world has come to be at odds with the holy Dharma, monks will be without faith, without a sense of shame, without a sense of conscience, will be lazy, and their mindfulness will deteriorate; they will be unable to unify the mind and their minds will become disturbed. Thus, when the holy Dharma is in decline and the world has come to be at odds with the holy Dharma, this is the first arising of what is not the holy Dharma in the world.

When the holy Dharma is in decline and the world has come to be at odds with the holy Dharma, monks will engage in fighting, in fault-finding, in grudges, and in quarreling. Thus, when the holy Dharma is in decline and the world has come to be at odds with the holy Dharma, this is the second arising of what is not the holy Dharma in the world.

When the holy Dharma is in decline and the world has come to be at odds with the holy Dharma, certain monks who feign good conduct while holding to a view of evil will rely on mere calm abiding and will cite scriptural authority for their words. Thus, when the holy Dharma is in decline and the world has come to be at odds with the holy Dharma, this is the third arising of what is not the holy Dharma in the world.

When the holy Dharma is in decline and the world has come to be at odds with the holy Dharma, monks will pass their time in death while their moral discipline is in decline, and they will denigrate those who are endowed with moral discipline. Thus, when the holy Dharma is in decline and the world has come to be at odds with the holy Dharma, this is the fourth arising of what is not the holy Dharma in the world.

When the holy Dharma is in decline and the world has come to be at odds with the holy Dharma, householders will have done service to the renunciants, yet those householders, upon leaving the body at death, will be reborn as gods of the higher realms in a happy existence, while the renunciants will in large numbers fall into the lower realms. Thus, when the holy Dharma is in decline and the world has come to be at odds with the holy Dharma, this is the fifth arising of what is not the holy Dharma in the world.

One should not associate with, and should not rely upon, a companion endowed with these five qualities: one who has entered into worldly affairs, one who has entered into quarreling, one who is given to wandering about continuously, one who fraternizes with cherished ones, and one who dwells in the retinue of a king. These are to be stated as the reverse on the virtuous side, expressed in the five ways. The five distinctions are: a distinct Teacher, a distinct Dharma, a distinct Saṅgha, a distinct karma, and a distinct path.

Even if one does not have these five alms bowls, one should not seek them; and even if one has them, one should not keep them. What are the five? A crystal alms bowl, a stone alms bowl, a wooden alms bowl, a jeweled alms bowl, and a lidded alms bowl.

A monk who eats food in five ways incurs a transgression. These are: eating from a bowl made of leaves, eating with cupped hands, eating by extending the tongue, eating by drawing food in with the lips, and eating with food pushed in by the hand.

The five kinds of torn robes are: one given because it is worn out from walking, one given for the purpose of walking,

one given to a sick person, one given on account of sickness, and one given when something has been torn.

The five who receive long-stored provisions are: one who is traveling, one who is ill, one who is caring for the sick, one who is doing work, and one who is maintaining a residence.

One should not sit on five kinds of seats: the seat of a Tathāgata, the seat of an elder of the Saṅgha, the seat of a preceptor, the seat of an abbot, and the seat of one who is teaching the Dharma.

Here ends the fifth chapter of the noble text of the Vinaya.

The Vinaya in sixteen sections — in brief:

What is to be stated, and the counter-argument,
The reply, two: keeping composed and responding in turn,
The suitable, and the qualities,
The basis and the exposition, likewise —
Two transgressions and the act of penalty,
Two pacifications and abundant merit,
And finally, gathered into sections.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, when a monk who wishes to raise a counter-argument desires to argue a matter on its merits, he should think it through very carefully, examine it very thoroughly, and investigate it very searchingly — and then raise the counter-argument on its merits."

"Upāli, when a monk who wishes to raise a counter-argument desires to argue a matter on its merits, he should think it through very carefully in the sixteen bases, examine it very thoroughly, and investigate it very searchingly — and then raise the counter-argument on its merits."

"What are the sixteen? He should ask himself: Is this matter about which I wish to raise a counter-argument true or false? Has the time come for raising this counter-argument on its merits, or has the time not come? Is this the appropriate occasion for raising this matter, or is it not the appropriate occasion? Is this counter-argument meaningful, or is it without meaning? Beyond this, he should investigate further: On the basis of what has been seen, heard, or suspected should he speak? Was it done in body, or done in speech? Was it done in a village, or done in a hermitage? Was it done at night, or done in the daytime? Was there a remainder, or was there no remainder? Is this venerable one capable of being raised from a wholesome ground and established on a wholesome ground? Upāli, a monk who wishes to raise a counter-argument should think through these sixteen bases very carefully, examine them very thoroughly, and investigate them very searchingly — and then raise the counter-argument on its merits."

"If a monk who raises counter-arguments possesses these five qualities, one should not accept his words. What are the five? The counter-argument he raises is not thoroughly pure; he raises counter-arguments based on what one person told another; he proceeds from a place of ill-will; he raises counter-arguments against the words of his novice-master; and he does not know the words of the sūtras as they were definitively taught, nor does he know the basis on which purification is to be undertaken. Upāli, if a monk who raises counter-arguments possesses these five qualities, one should not accept his words."

"Upāli, if a monk who raises counter-arguments possesses five qualities, one should accept his words. The counter-argument he raises is thoroughly pure; he does not raise counter-arguments based on what one person told another; he proceeds from a place of good will; he does not raise counter-arguments against the words of his novice-master; he knows the words of the sūtras as they were definitively taught; and he knows the basis on which purification is to be undertaken. Upāli, if a monk who raises counter-arguments possesses these five qualities, one should accept his words."

"Upāli, a monk who gives a reply should think through these sixteen bases very carefully, examine them very thoroughly, and investigate them very searchingly — and then give room to the monk who is being challenged. What are the sixteen? He should ask: Is this venerable one one who possesses moral discipline? Has he been fully ordained from the very beginning? Does he have a sense of shame? Does he have remorse? Does he have restraint? Does he desire to train? Is he one of great learning? Does he retain what he has heard?

Has he accumulated learning? Does he know the Vinaya? Does he understand the higher Vinaya with certainty? Has he mastered the recitation of the scriptures? And further, beneath all of that, he should also investigate: Is it by what he himself has seen, or by what he has heard, or by what he suspects, or by a physical transgression, or by a verbal transgression, that he speaks? Was it committed in a village or in a forest? Was it done at night or by day? Was it done with a remainder or without a remainder? And is this venerable one capable of lifting the monk from an unwholesome state and establishing him in a wholesome state? Upāli, having very carefully thought through, very thoroughly examined, and very searchingly investigated all sixteen of these bases, the monk who is giving a reply should give room to the monk who is being challenged.

Upāli, if a monk who is giving a reply possesses these five qualities, his words should not be accepted. What are the five? He does not answer according to what the challenging monk asked; after being asked, he reveals something that was not what was intended; he speaks of one thing in terms of another; he introduces extraneous talk; he puts the monk who has been cleared in an unfavorable position; he relies on taking sides; and he does not know what is a transgression and does not know what is not a transgression. Upāli, if a monk who is giving a reply possesses these five qualities, his words should not be accepted.

Upāli, if a monk who is giving a reply possesses these five qualities, his words should be accepted. What are the five? He answers according to what the challenging monk asked; he does not speak of the matter asked about in one way and then another; he does not introduce other extraneous talk; he does not put the monk who has been cleared in an unfavorable position; he does not rely on taking sides; and he knows what is a transgression and knows what is not a transgression. Upāli, if a monk who is giving a reply possesses these five qualities, his words should be accepted.

Upāli, when the monks on both sides — the challenger and the one giving the reply — wish to settle a dispute, they should seek out an impartial holder of the Vinaya who possesses sixteen qualities. What are the sixteen? He possesses moral discipline; he was fully ordained from the very beginning; he has a sense of shame; he has remorse; he has restraint; he desires to train; he is one of great learning; he retains what he has heard; he has accumulated learning; he knows the Vinaya; he understands the higher Vinaya with certainty; he knows the sūtras; he has mastered the recitation of the scriptures. And further, beneath all of that, one should also investigate: Does this venerable one actually possess the qualities of an impartial arbiter? Has this venerable one not been previously entangled with the matter? Is this venerable one skilled in disputes that have arisen before? Is this venerable one perhaps acting for the sake of a bowl, or for the sake of robes, or for the sake of some small material gain? Is he perhaps acting out of desire, or out of aversion, or out of delusion, or out of fear? Is this venerable one afflicted by attachment? Is he afflicted by aversion? Is he afflicted by delusion? Does he transgress the word of the Victor? Does this venerable one fail to treat what is reasonable as reasonable, or does he cut down what is reasonable? Does this venerable one pacify matters through the Dharma and Vinaya as taught by the Teacher? And does this venerable one lift this venerable one from an unwholesome state and establish him in a wholesome state? Upāli, when the monks on both sides — the challenger and the one giving the reply — wish to settle a dispute, they should seek out an impartial holder of the Vinaya who possesses those sixteen qualities.

Upāli, if an impartial holder of the Vinaya possesses these five qualities, he will be unable to settle a dispute. What are the five? He leads the challenging monk and the monk giving the reply toward an unlawful side; he causes conflict between the challenging monk and the monk giving the reply;

he exposes faults, he foments resentment, he incites further conflict, he causes the monks who hold the sūtras to refrain from reciting the scriptural text, he imputes blame to the elder monks, and he is not skilled in the beginning, middle, and end of a dispute.

Upāli, an impartial holder of the Vinaya who possesses these five qualities will be able to settle a dispute. What are the five? He guides the challenging monk and the monk giving the reply toward the side of the Dharma; he prevents conflict between the challenging monk and the monk giving the reply; he does not expose faults, does not foment resentment, and does not incite further conflict; he causes the monks who hold the sūtras to recite the scriptural text; he does not impute blame to the elder monks; and he is skilled in the beginning, middle, and end of a dispute.

Upāli, if that impartial holder of the Vinaya wishes to take up the settling of a dispute, he should first examine himself and others thoroughly in those sixteen respects, and only then take up the dispute. He should examine himself thoroughly by eight criteria, and he should examine others thoroughly by eight criteria.

What are the eight criteria for examining oneself? He reflects: Am I skilled in the beginning, middle, and end of this dispute? Have I been uninvolved in this dispute from the very start? Have I grasped the words of the challenging monk and the monk giving the reply? Have I listened to the words of the challenging monk and the monk giving the reply? Am I able to purify the faults of the challenging monk and the monk giving the reply? Am I able to instruct each side in accordance with the Dharma? Am I able to settle this dispute in accordance with the Vinaya and as the Teacher has taught?
