Am I able to lift the challenging monk and the monk giving the reply from an unwholesome state and establish them in a wholesome state? By these eight criteria he should examine himself thoroughly.

What are the eight criteria for examining others? He reflects: Among those members of the Saṅgha, are there monks who hold the sūtras, who hold the Vinaya, and who hold the summaries, who will support what I say in proclaiming the word of the Victor? At that time, are there monks who hold the sūtras, who hold the Vinaya, and who hold the summaries who intend to settle this dispute in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Teacher has taught? Among those members of the Saṅgha, are there senior monks, middling monks, and junior monks who intend to properly turn back the monks on either side in accordance with the Dharma? Will this dispute be spread to the royal court, or will it not be spread among those of proper reasoning? Do the venerable ones not seek to settle this dispute outside this very Saṅgha? Do the venerable ones seek to settle the dispute within this very Saṅgha? By these eight criteria he should examine others.

Upāli, having thus examined oneself and others by sixteen criteria, one should take up the settling of the dispute.

Upāli, an impartial holder of the Vinaya who possesses these five qualities will be unable to settle a dispute. What are the five? He does not know disputes, he does not know how disputes arise, he does not know how to properly take up a dispute, he does not know how to settle a dispute, and he does not know how to ensure that once a dispute is settled it does not arise again. Upāli, an impartial holder of the Vinaya who possesses those five qualities will be unable to settle a dispute.

Upāli, an impartial holder of the Vinaya who possesses these five qualities will be able to settle a dispute.

What are the five? He knows disputes, he knows how disputes arise, he knows how to properly take up a dispute, he knows how to settle a dispute, and he knows how to ensure that once a dispute is settled it does not arise again. Upāli, an impartial holder of the Vinaya who possesses those five qualities will be able to settle a dispute.

Now, Upāli, when an impartial holder of the Vinaya has taken up a dispute, he should examine the monk who brings an accusation by sixteen points, and he should examine the monk who responds to the accusation by eight characteristics.

What are the eight characteristics by which the accusing monk is to be examined? His conduct, his resort, his friendships, his companions, his bodily actions, his verbal actions, his livelihood, and his learning.

If the impartial holder of the Vinaya thinks: "This venerable one is of bad character — he conducts himself badly, his resort is bad, his friends are bad, his companions are bad, his bodily actions are bad, his verbal actions are bad, his livelihood is bad, his learning is bad — and this venerable one is capable of bringing disrepute upon a pure monk and of bringing such a dispute into the Saṅgha," then he should instruct him: "Do not speak in that way."

But if the impartial holder of the Vinaya thinks: "This venerable one is of good character — he conducts himself well, his resort is good, his friends are good, his companions are good, his bodily actions are good, his verbal actions are good, his livelihood is good, his learning is good — and this venerable one is not capable of bringing disrepute upon a pure monk, nor of bringing such a dispute into the Saṅgha," then he should instruct him: "You may speak."

Upāli, it is by these eight characteristics that the accusing monk is to be examined.

The monk who responds to the accusation is likewise to be examined by these same eight characteristics: his conduct, his resort, his friendships, his companions, his bodily actions, his verbal actions, his livelihood, and his learning.

If the impartial holder of the Vinaya thinks: "This venerable one is of bad character — he conducts himself badly, his resort is bad, his friends are bad, his companions are bad, his bodily actions are bad, his verbal actions are bad, his livelihood is bad, his learning is bad — and this venerable one is capable of entering into such conduct," then he should speak gently to the responding monk and say the following to him: "Venerable one, at that time, how were your bodily formations? How were your verbal formations? How were your mental formations? Whatever you admit to, let it be done accordingly."

Upāli, if the impartial holder of the Vinaya thinks: "This venerable one is of good character — he conducts himself well, his resort is good, his friends are good, his companions are good, his bodily actions are good, his verbal actions are good, his livelihood is good, his learning is good — and this venerable one would not engage in such conduct," then he should speak gently to the responding monk and instruct the accusing monk to understand the matter according to the Dharma, and examine the other by these eight characteristics.

Upāli, an impartial holder of the Vinaya who possesses these five qualities will be unable to settle a dispute. What are the five? He seizes upon errors, he seizes upon words spoken in confidence, he seizes upon many words, he seizes upon what is uncertain, and he does not proceed to a formal charge up to the third time. An impartial holder of the Vinaya who possesses these five qualities will be unable to settle a dispute.

Upāli, an impartial holder of the Vinaya who possesses these five qualities will be able to settle a dispute. What are the five?

He does not seize upon errors, he does not seize upon words spoken in confidence, he does not seize upon many words, he does not seize upon what is uncertain, and he does proceed to a formal charge up to the third time. Upāli, an impartial holder of the Vinaya who possesses these five qualities will be able to settle a dispute.

Now, Upāli, an impartial holder of the Vinaya must examine the monks who make a charge and those who respond to it according to sixteen points, and must settle the matter by reasoning in sixteen points. What are the sixteen? He must reason with the monk who makes the charge; he must examine the monk who makes the charge; he must reason with the monk who responds; he must examine the monk who responds; he must request forbearance from the monk who makes the charge; he must request forbearance from the monk who responds; he must cause the monk who makes the charge to withdraw; he must cause the monk who responds to withdraw; he must question the monk who makes the charge; he must question the monk who responds; he must cause the monk who makes the charge to act; he must cause the monk who responds to act; he must cause the monk who makes the charge to affirm his position; he must cause the monk who responds to affirm his position; he must cause the monk who makes the charge to make a formal declaration; he must cause the monk who responds to make a formal declaration. He must then recite the relevant sūtra, and having recited it, he must settle that dispute in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Teacher taught. Upāli, this is how an impartial monk must settle matters by reasoning in these sixteen points.

Upāli, an impartial holder of the Vinaya who possesses the following five qualities will be unable to establish a matter by reasoning. What are the five? He does not know the five qualities to be followed. What are those five? He does not know how to make a charge, he does not know how to respond, he does not know what is in accordance with the Dharma, he does not know what is not in accordance with the Dharma, and he has not made a formal declaration. Upāli, an impartial holder of the Vinaya who possesses these five qualities will be unable to establish a matter by reasoning.

Upāli, an impartial holder of the Vinaya who possesses the following five qualities will be able to establish a matter by reasoning. He will know the five qualities to be followed. What are those five? He knows how to make a charge, he knows how to respond, he knows what is in accordance with the Dharma, he knows what is not in accordance with the Dharma, and he has made a formal declaration. An impartial holder of the Vinaya who possesses these five qualities will be able to establish a matter by reasoning.

Now, Upāli, when an impartial holder of the Vinaya settles a matter by reasoning in sixteen points, he should proclaim the sūtra having seen sixteen benefits. What are the sixteen? He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "I will teach the sūtra." He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "I will analyze the sūtra." He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "I will come to follow the Vinaya." He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "My words will be well composed." He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "I will cut off the shameless party by means of a penalty." He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "I will be able to convey the words of the Omniscient One." He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "The Saṅgha will be shown to be in harmony." He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "I will convey it to others." He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "My words will be taken up by others." He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "I will instruct the monks." He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "I will lead the faithless to faith." He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "Those with faith will increase further in faith." He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "I will cut off the shameless party by means of a penalty."

He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "I will take up the position of those who know shame." He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "Disputes that are arising will not arise." He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "Disputes will be pacified." He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "Once disputes have been pacified, they will not arise again later." He should proclaim the sūtra thinking, "I will long abide in the holy life."

Upāli, if a conscientious Vinaya-holder sees these sixteen qualities, he should proclaim the sūtra.

Upāli, if a conscientious Vinaya-holder possesses the following five qualities, he will not understand the virtues of the sūtra. What are the five? Not being skilled in sūtra, not being skilled in Vinaya, not being skilled in what is analogous, not being skilled in analysis, and not having recited the scriptures. Upāli, if a conscientious Vinaya-holder possesses those five qualities, he will not understand the virtues of the sūtra.

Upāli, if a conscientious Vinaya-holder possesses the following five qualities, he will understand the virtues of the sūtra. What are the five? Being skilled in sūtra, being skilled in Vinaya, being skilled in what is analogous, being skilled in analysis, and having trained in scriptural recitation. Upāli, if a conscientious Vinaya-holder possesses those five qualities, he will understand the virtues of the sūtra.

Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who is able to understand the sūtra, having seen these sixteen virtues in this sūtra, should recite the sūtra.

Moreover, the sūtra should be recited in sixteen contexts. What are those sixteen? The sūtra spoken by a buddha should be recited. The sūtra taught by a śrāvaka should be recited. The sūtra from the time when a buddha appeared should be recited. The sūtra of a single direction should be recited. The sūtra that exists everywhere should be recited. The sūtra that resembles that very thing should be recited. The sūtra that accords with Vinaya should be recited. The sūtra that goes beyond Vinaya should be recited. Having sought the virtues of the sūtra, the sūtra should be recited. Having sought the ornament of the sūtra, the sūtra should be recited. Having sought the narrative occasion of the sūtra, the sūtra should be recited. Having sought even a portion of the sūtra, the sūtra should be recited. Having sought the words of the sūtra, the sūtra should be recited. Upāli, if a conscientious Vinaya-holder sees those sixteen virtues, he should recite the sūtra.

Upāli, if a conscientious Vinaya-holder possesses the following five qualities, he will be unable to recite the sūtra. What are the five? Not knowing the Vinaya of monks, not knowing the Vinaya of nuns, not knowing the Vinaya of offenses, not knowing the Vinaya of disputes, and not knowing the Vinaya of afflictions. Upāli, if a conscientious Vinaya-holder possesses those five qualities, he will be unable to recite the sūtra.

Upāli, if a conscientious Vinaya-holder possesses the following five qualities, he will be able to recite the sūtra. What are the five? Knowing the Vinaya of monks, knowing the Vinaya of nuns, knowing the Vinaya of offenses, knowing the Vinaya of disputes, and knowing the Vinaya of afflictions. Upāli, if a conscientious Vinaya-holder possesses those five qualities, he will be able to recite the sūtra.

The Noble Vinaya, the thirtieth fascicle.

Now, Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder, having recited in the sixteen contexts, should examine the Vinaya in sixteen contexts. What are the sixteen? Scripture, the transmission of scripture, the substance of the matter, analysis, conduct, the domain of conduct, desiring little, desiring much, contentment, discontentment, difficulty in satisfying, ease in satisfying, difficulty in maintaining, ease in maintaining, what is most precious, and knowing sufficiency. Upāli, by these sixteen points one should examine the Vinaya.

Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses five qualities will be unable to expel a transgression. What are the five? Not knowing what arose, not knowing what was established, not knowing what was subsequently established, not knowing what was permitted, and not knowing what was subsequently permitted. Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses those five qualities will be unable to expel a transgression.

Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses five qualities will be able to expel a transgression. What are the five? Knowing what arose, knowing what was established, knowing what was subsequently established, knowing what was permitted, and knowing what was subsequently permitted. Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses those five qualities will be able to expel a transgression.

Now, Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder, having examined the Vinaya in the sixteen contexts, should declare transgressions in sixteen contexts. What are the sixteen? Grave, light, with remainder, without remainder, one involving habitual acquisition, one of body, one of speech, non-virtuous, not shown by scripture, established, not established, leading to confession, leading to restraint, leading to transgression of the Vinaya, leading to ill speech, and — Upāli, by these sixteen contexts one should examine the Vinaya, and by these sixteen contexts declare transgressions.

Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses five qualities will be unable to declare a transgression. What are the five? Not knowing what is a transgression, not knowing what is not a transgression, not knowing what is grave, not knowing what is light, and not being able to recite the scriptural text. Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses those five qualities will be unable to declare a transgression.

Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses five qualities will be able to declare a transgression. What are the five? Knowing what is a transgression, knowing what is not a transgression, knowing what is grave, knowing what is light, and being able to recite the scriptural text. Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses those five qualities will be able to declare a transgression.

Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder, having declared a transgression by these sixteen contexts, should admonish with a punitive act in sixteen contexts. What are the sixteen? Declaring the transgression to one's face, imposing a probationary penalty, not heeding the instruction given, neither speaking nor heeding, threatening, approving, expelling, reconciling again, setting aside on account of not seeing, setting aside on account of not making amends, setting aside on account of not abandoning a wrong view, imposing a punitive act, imposing a punitive act starting from the basis, making one satisfied, making one satisfied starting from the basis, and declaring starting from the basis. Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder, having declared the Vinaya by these sixteen contexts, should admonish with a punitive act in these sixteen contexts.

Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses five qualities will be unable to admonish with a punitive act. What are the five? Acting out of attachment, acting out of aversion, acting out of delusion, acting out of fear, and not knowing whether a punitive act has been performed or not performed. Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses those five qualities will be unable to admonish with a punitive act.

Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses five qualities will be able to admonish by means of a punitive act. What are the five? Not proceeding where attachment would lead, not proceeding where aversion would lead, not proceeding where delusion would lead, not proceeding where fear would lead, and knowing whether a punitive act has been performed or not performed.

Regarding this matter, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who has admonished by means of a punitive act applied through sixteen grounds should further admonish by means of a punitive act through those same sixteen grounds. What are the sixteen? Reproaching with a brahma-penalty; causing one to perform an act of reconciliation so that faith will not be lost; causing one to perform an act of reconciliation so that enjoyments are not experienced; causing one to perform an act of absence from sight; causing one's character to be investigated; harming; disparaging; rejecting; making partyless; humiliating; cowing; producing regret; complete remorse; renewed remorse; being placed under censure; being brought to a critical point; and being declared at fault. Thus, Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder should admonish by means of a punitive act through these sixteen grounds.

Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses five qualities will be unable to admonish by means of a punitive act. What are the five? Not knowing the five Vinaya matters. What are the five? Reproach, disparagement, expulsion, reconciliation, and rejection — these are the five.

Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses five qualities will be able to admonish by means of a punitive act. What are the five? Knowing the five Vinaya matters. What are the five? Reproach, disparagement, expulsion, reconciliation, and rejection — these are the five. Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses those five qualities will be able to admonish by means of a punitive act applied through penalty.

Thus, Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder, having admonished by means of a punitive act applied through penalty using these sixteen grounds, should then perform the formal act through sixteen grounds. What are the sixteen? Performing the act when the matter is manifest; performing the act even when it is not manifest; performing the act when an opportunity is given; performing the act even when no opportunity is given; performing the act when reminded; performing the act even without being reminded; performing the act when one's memory is invoked; performing the act even without one's memory being invoked; performing the act when questioned; performing the act even without being questioned; performing the act when applied; performing the act even when not applied; performing the act when individually known; performing the act even when not individually known; performing the act when settled; and performing the act even when not yet settled. These are the sixteen grounds on which the act should be performed.

Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses these five qualities will be unable to perform the formal act. What are the five? Not knowing the single-motion act; not knowing the motion-and-one-proclamation act; not knowing the motion-and-three-proclamations act; not knowing the act of assignment; and not knowing the act of consecration. Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses those five qualities will be unable to perform the formal act.

Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses these five qualities will be able to perform the formal act. What are the five? Knowing the single-motion act; knowing the motion-and-one-proclamation act; knowing the motion-and-three-proclamations act; knowing the act of assignment; and knowing the act of consecration. Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who possesses those five qualities will be able to perform the formal act.

Upāli, a conscientious Vinaya-holder who has performed the formal act through those sixteen grounds and then settles a dispute through sixteen grounds — that is a faulty settlement. What are the sixteen? It has occurred without a motion being put to the Saṅgha; it has occurred in discord with the word of the Victor; it has occurred without assignment being made to the monks of both sides and neither side; the Vinaya of the objecting monk has been violated; a fault has been covered by an impure monk; what has arisen has become improper; what has been enacted has become improper; what has been subsequently enacted has become improper;

what has been permitted has become improper; what has been subsequently permitted has become improper; the objecting monk has not been allowed to state his position; the responding monk has not been allowed to state his position; the wording of the sūtra has become improper; it has occurred in discord with the Vinaya; the eye of the Dharma has not been opened wide; and the dispute has not been settled in the manner consistent with the Dharma, consistent with the Vinaya, consistent with the teaching of the Teacher. Upāli, a settlement of a dispute carried out through these sixteen grounds is a faulty settlement.

Upāli, if a settlement of a dispute is carried out while possessing these five qualities, that settlement of a dispute is faulty — what are the five? One settles without having assigned the matter; one does not state the fault; one does not bring down a censure through a formal act of penalty; one does not demonstrate purification; and it has occurred without his having petitioned the Saṅgha. Upāli, even if one settles a dispute while possessing these five qualities, it has not truly been settled.

Upāli, if a settlement of a dispute possesses these sixteen qualities, it is a proper settlement — what are the sixteen? He has petitioned the Saṅgha; it has occurred in accord with the word of the Victor; assignment has been made to the monks of both sides and neither side; the Vinaya of the objecting monks has not been violated; a fault has not been covered by an impure monk; what has arisen has not become improper; what has been enacted has not become improper; what has been subsequently enacted has not become improper; what has been permitted has not become improper; what has been subsequently permitted has not become improper; the objecting monk has been fully allowed to state his position; the responding monk has been fully allowed to state his position; the wording of the sūtra has become proper; it has occurred in accord with the Vinaya; the eye of the Dharma has been opened wide; and the dispute has been settled in the manner consistent with the Dharma, consistent with the Vinaya, consistent with the teaching of the Teacher. Upāli, if a settlement of a dispute possesses these sixteen qualities, it is a proper settlement.

Upāli, if one settles a dispute while possessing these five qualities, it is a proper settlement — what are the five? One settles having first assigned the matter; one states the fault; one does not bring censure down through a formal act of penalty; one demonstrates purification; and it has occurred with his having petitioned the Saṅgha. Upāli, if one settles a dispute while possessing these five qualities, it is a proper settlement.

Now in that regard, Upāli, if a conscientious upholder of the Vinaya settles a dispute through sixteen grounds, merit will greatly increase — what are the sixteen? He has endowed himself with many heaps of merit; he has likewise endowed others with great heaps of merit; the objecting and responding monks have purified their faults; the faults of those who object and respond have been extinguished; the afflictive streams of the four factions have been stilled; one has entered for the purpose of gathering the Saṅgha together; the eye of the Dharma has been opened wide for the purpose of maintaining the sacred Dharma; one has pressed hard against those who are without conscience; one has properly gathered together those who do have conscience; what is not the sacred Dharma has been turned back; what is the sacred Dharma has been fully grasped; the nature of reality has been proclaimed; illumination has been extended to people of future generations; and one has entered for the purpose of the sacred Dharma's enduring and for the benefit of the many. Upāli, if a conscientious upholder of the Vinaya settles a dispute through these sixteen grounds, merit will greatly increase.

Upāli, if a conscientious upholder of the Vinaya settles a dispute while endowed with these five qualities, merit will greatly increase. What are the five? Declaring what constitutes a transgression to be a transgression, and declaring what does not constitute a transgression to be no transgression; declaring what is weighty to be weighty, and declaring what is light to be light; declaring what carries a remainder to carry a remainder, and declaring what carries no remainder to carry no remainder; declaring that a person who has no transgression has no transgression, and declaring that a person who has a transgression has a transgression; and investigating a person who has no transgression as having no transgression, and investigating a person who has a transgression as having a transgression. Upāli, if a conscientious upholder of the Vinaya settles a dispute while endowed with these five qualities of Dharma, merit will greatly increase.

Upāli, therefore train in just this way, thinking: whenever a dispute has arisen and occurred, I shall settle it in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Teacher has taught. Upāli, train yourself in exactly this way.

This concludes the text called The Sixteen Qualities Arising from the Vinaya.

A summary verse of the chapters: Full ordination first, then the separate sections, the maṇḍala, likewise the flat door and the awakening mind — the grounds for instruction are here summarized.

A further summary: Full ordination, the superior, the completely pure, and the encircling; the half, the three, the various groups, and likewise the transgressions; the accepted, the bare flesh, and the collected — this is the brief account of the summaries.

In brief: At the time of conferring full ordination, a woman is present as a man; full ordination without prior going forth; and the impediments are of four kinds — no preceptor, the crow, and these are also stated in the first group.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One: "Venerable One, if during full ordination the name is changed, should that be called full ordination or not full ordination?"

The Blessed One declared: "Upāli, it is indeed full ordination — but count it among the nuns."

"Venerable One, if monks confer full ordination on someone born from a woman resembling a man — having a male voice, speaking in a male manner, possessing a male sound, and appearing in a male form — should that be called full ordination or not full ordination?"

"Upāli, it is indeed full ordination, but the one who conferred full ordination incurs a transgression."

"Venerable One, if someone born as a man resembles a woman — having a female voice, speaking in a female manner, possessing a female sound, and appearing in a female form — and monks confer full ordination on that person, should it be called full ordination or not full ordination?"

"Upāli, it is indeed full ordination, but the one who conferred full ordination incurs a transgression."

"Venerable One, if monks confer full ordination on someone who has not gone forth, should that be called full ordination or not full ordination?"

"Upāli, it is indeed full ordination, but the one who conferred full ordination incurs a transgression."

"Venerable One, if someone who has not received full ordination is made a preceptor and monks thereby confer full ordination, should that be called full ordination or not full ordination?"

"Upāli, it is indeed full ordination, but the one who conferred full ordination incurs a transgression."

"Venerable One, if someone who has an impediment declares 'I have an impediment' and monks nonetheless confer full ordination on that person, should that be called full ordination or not full ordination?"

"Upāli, it is not full ordination, and the ones who conferred full ordination also incur a transgression."

"Venerable One, if someone who does not have an impediment declares 'I have an impediment' and monks confer full ordination on that person, should that be called full ordination or not full ordination?"

"Upāli, it is indeed full ordination, but those who conferred full ordination incur a transgression."

"Venerable One, if someone who neither has an impediment nor declares having one, and monks confer full ordination on that person, should that be called full ordination or not full ordination?"

"Upāli, it is full ordination, and those who conferred full ordination do not incur a transgression."

"Venerable One, if monks confer full ordination without a preceptor present, should that be called full ordination or not full ordination?"

"Upāli, it is indeed full ordination, but those who conferred full ordination incur a transgression."

"Venerable One, if monks confer full ordination with a preceptor present, should that be called full ordination or not full ordination?"

"Upāli, it is full ordination, and those who conferred full ordination do not incur a transgression."

Then the venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable One, the Blessed One has said, 'If one who has reached the age of seven can chase away crows, let him go forth.' Venerable One, if one who has reached the age of six can chase away crows at the monastery gate, should that person be given going forth or not?"

"Upāli, do not give going forth to one who has not yet reached seven years of age."

"Venerable One, if one has indeed reached seven years of age but cannot chase away crows from the monastery gate, should that person also be given going forth?"

"Upāli, do not give going forth until one is able to chase away crows."

This is the first sūtra verse of the introductory section on the opening of the gateway.

In summary:

For brahmins, days of the fortnight,
the date-count, and likewise for others,
the remainder, six years, making six,
fourteen, added with the intercalary month —
the same is to be done with those who are questioned.
In a place where monks are present,
let the precepts given be recited.

When the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove (Jetavana), the park of Anāthapiṇḍada, in Śrāvastī, brahmins and householders came before the monks and asked, "Noble ones, what is today's date?" The monks replied, "Alas, we do not know." The brahmins and householders said, "Even non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) know the date, the day, the stars, and the very moment — can it be that you who have gone forth do not even know the date?" The monks had no answer and said nothing.

The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Therefore, I hereby permit the counting of dates." And so all the monks took up the counting. The monks then again reported this matter to the Blessed One,

The Blessed One declared, "Rather than everyone counting individually, let the elder of the Saṅgha and the keeper of the monastery do the counting together." But when even the elder of the Saṅgha and the keeper of the monastery lost track, those monks became subject to censure. When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, he declared, "Make fifteen clay balls, thread them on a string, and set them out, then remove one each day." When the string became tangled, the Blessed One declared, "Make fifteen discs of felt, thread them on a string, and set them out, removing one each day." All the monks did so, but they still lost track. The Blessed One then declared, "Let the elder of the Saṅgha do the counting."

Then brahmins and householders came to the monastery and asked, "Noble ones, what is today's date?" The monks replied that the elder of the Saṅgha and the keeper of the monastery knew, and referred them to those two. But those two said, "Noble ones, are we the treasurers of your date-count? When you are asked, why do you refer the question to others? You yourselves must answer." And those two had no reply and said nothing. The brahmins and householders mocked them and departed from the monastery.

When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One reflected: "The mockery of the brahmins and householders is a grave matter. Therefore, the date should be announced within the Saṅgha." He then declared to the monks, "Since the mockery of the brahmins and householders is a grave matter, you must announce the date within the Saṅgha." When the Blessed One had thus declared that the date should be announced within the Saṅgha, the monks announced the date but did not take hold of the fortnight of the month. The householders and brahmins then said, "Noble ones, you do not even know how to grasp the fortnight of the month — if you do not grasp the fortnight, how will you know the waxing half and the waning half of the month?" And those monks had no reply and said nothing.

When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared, "You must take hold of the fortnights and announce the dates. The announcement is to be made as follows: when the entire Saṅgha has assembled and is seated, one monk, sitting first in order of seniority, should press his palms together with all due ceremony and speak these words: 'Today is the first day of the waning fortnight of the month. For the sake of the patron of the monastery and of the gods, let each recite a verse.' "

The monks then announced the date but did not mention the name of the patron of the monastery. The Blessed One declared, "The name of the patron of the monastery must also be stated." The announcement is to be made in this way: "The donor named such-and-such has invited the community of monks for a meal tomorrow. May the venerable ones regard him with a mind of virtue and affection. Since the patron of the monastery gives in various other ways as well, may the venerable ones regard the generous donor too with a mind of virtue and affection. For when you regard someone with a mind of virtue and affection, that person's virtuous qualities will increase and will not diminish." Similarly, all the sentient beings present there are to be named individually. After all these words are complete, let each monk recite a verse in turn.

Then brahmins and householders came there as well, and

The noble ones were asked what the date was, and they replied, "Today is the fifteenth." The brahmins and householders said, "Noble ones, for all the world it is the fourteenth today — how then can it be the fifteenth for you? Do you not reckon the days by halves of the month?" When this matter was reported to the Blessed One by the monks, the Blessed One declared, "You should reckon the days by halves of the month." When the Blessed One had declared that they should do so, the monks began dividing the month into two halves and reckoning the days accordingly.

Brahmins and householders came there again and asked, "Noble ones, what is today's date?" The monks replied, "Today is our fourteenth." They said, "Noble ones, for all the world it is the fifteenth today — how then can it be the fourteenth for you? Do you really reckon the days by halves of the month, one day at a time?" The monks said that they did. When the brahmins and householders had raised this objection and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared, "Monks, the brahmins and householders are causing embarrassment, and so you should not reckon the days by halves of the month one day at a time. Instead, let a half-month and two days together pass, and then reckon the intercalary day. In this way, in one year there will be six restoration ceremonies on the fourteenth, and the remainder will be on the fifteenth."

Then brahmins and householders came there again and asked, "Noble ones, which month of the year is this current month for you?" The monks replied, "For us this is the last month of the rains season." They said, "Noble ones, for all the world this current month is the middle month of the rains season — how then can it be the last month of the rains season for you? Have you dropped an intercalary month?" The monks replied that they had not. The brahmins and householders, having raised this objection, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Monks, the brahmins and householders are causing embarrassment, and so you should add in an intercalary month." When the Blessed One had declared that they should add an intercalary month, the monks began inserting an extra month every single year. Brahmins and householders came there again and asked, "Noble ones, what is this current month for you?" The monks replied, "For us it is now the middle month of the rains season." They said, "Noble ones, for all the world this month is the last month of the rains season — how then is it the middle month for you? Do you insert an intercalary month every single year?" The monks replied that they did. The brahmins and householders raised this objection, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Monks, the brahmins and householders are causing embarrassment, and so you should not add an intercalary month every year, but rather every six years. Six times six is thirty, and when calculated thus against days, half-months, months, and years, everything will balance out, and non-Buddhists who seek a pretext will find none." When the Blessed One had declared that an intercalary month should be added every six years, the monks began inserting an intercalary month every six years. Kings insert an intercalary month every three years.

When the monks failed to do likewise, the ministers raised objections, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Monks, the ministers are causing embarrassment, and so you should follow the royal calendar as well."

The stars fell out of alignment, and when the monks did not adjust for this, the astronomers mocked the monks about what had occurred. The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Monks, the astronomers are causing embarrassment, and so you should follow the astronomical reckoning as well."

This is the second verse of the first section within the origin story.

In summary:

The two purifications are to be performed,
and the boundary is to be set in four ways;
likewise, faith received from the sky
remains, like before, unreleased.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One: "Venerable One, may one who is inside the boundary grant purification to those who are outside the boundary?" "Upāli, one may not." "Venerable One, may one who is outside the boundary grant purification to those who are inside the boundary?" "Upāli, one may not." "Venerable One, may one who is inside the boundary perform a formal act for those who are outside the boundary?" "Upāli, one may not." "Venerable One, may one who is outside the boundary perform a formal act for those who are inside the boundary?" "Upāli, one may not." "Venerable One, while performing a formal act and being inside the boundary, may one perform that act for those who are outside the boundary?" "Upāli, one may not." "Venerable One, while performing a formal act and being outside the boundary, may one perform that act for those who are inside the boundary?" "Upāli, one may not."

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable One, if a monk who is receiving an offering of faith has taken that offering and then goes up into the sky, is it considered received or not received?" "Upāli, it is not received — go back and look again." "Venerable One, may a later boundary be annulled while a prior boundary has not been dissolved?" "Upāli, one may not."

This is the third verse of the first section's sūtra within the origin story.

The noble Vinaya text. The thirty-first fascicle.

In summary:

Encircling and destruction,
the arising of trees and earth,
non-arising and arising,
and death — it is likewise so.

When the Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada, the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One: "Venerable One, may a boundary be enclosed by another boundary?" "Upāli, a maṇḍala boundary, a water boundary, and the rains-retreat building of the bhikṣuṇīs are permissible; other cases are not." "May a boundary be annulled by another boundary?" "Upāli, one may not." "Venerable One, in how many ways may a boundary be annulled?" "Upāli, five: when the entire Saṅgha abandons it and departs; when the entire Saṅgha transfers to a night lodging elsewhere; when the entire Saṅgha returns; when the entire Saṅgha has died; and with a formal act of petition — those are the five." "Venerable One, may a single tree serve to annul the boundary of two assembly halls?" "Upāli, it may — and likewise for three or four assembly halls; only the tree itself should be divided."

While the Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling in Campā practicing the practice there, he smiled in another place. By the very nature of things, whenever the Blessed One smiled, rays of blue, yellow, red, and white light would issue from his mouth. Some went downward and some went upward. Those that went downward reached into the hells for sentient beings — the Arbuda hell, the Aṭaṭa hell, the Mahāvīci hell, the Raurava hell,

the Loud Cries hell, the Burning hell, the Greatly Burning hell, the Unrelenting hell, the Blister hell, the Repeated Blister hell, the Aṭaṭa hell, the Hahāpa hell, the Huhūpa hell, the Blue-Lotus-like hell, the Lotus-like hell, and the Great-Lotus-like hell. When those rays fell upon the hot hells, they became cool. When they fell upon the cold hells, they became warm. The pain of those sentient beings was transformed into a distinction of ease, and they thought: "Oh — have we passed away from here, or have we been born elsewhere?" Then, in order to arouse faith in them, the Blessed One sent forth an emanation. When they saw the emanation, they thought: "We have not passed away from here, nor have we been born elsewhere — yet by the power of this sentient being we had never seen before, our pain has been transformed into a distinction of ease." Having reflected thus, they turned their minds in faith toward the emanation, and the karmic action driving their suffering in the hells was exhausted. They were reborn among gods and humans in a place fit to receive the noble truths.

The rays that went upward reached the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Heaven of Delight in Transformation, the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations, and then the Brahmā Heaven, the Heaven of Brahmā's Ministers, the Great Brahmā Heaven, the Heaven of Minor Light, the Heaven of Limitless Light, the Heaven of Radiant Light, the Heaven of Minor Virtue, the Heaven of Limitless Virtue, the Heaven of Abundant Virtue, the Cloudless Heaven, the Heaven of Increasing Merit, the Heaven of Great Fruit, the Heaven of Non-Ideation, the Untroubled Heaven, the Heaven of Clear Vision, the Heaven of Beautiful Appearance, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven and the rest. There they proclaimed impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness, and spoke two verses as well:

Strive to arise!
Be diligent in the Buddha's teaching!
Like a great elephant in a swamp,
vanquish the armies of the lord of death!

Whoever with great heedfulness
walks this path of training and restraint
will, having thoroughly abandoned the wandering of rebirth,
bring suffering to its final end.

Then those rays circled the great three-thousandfold world-system and returned, tracing their way back to the Blessed One, and disappeared.

Now, if the Blessed One intended to prophesy concerning past karma, the rays would vanish at his back. If he intended to prophesy concerning future karma, they would vanish at his front. If he intended to prophesy rebirth in the hells, they would vanish at the sole of his foot. If he intended to prophesy rebirth as an animal, they would vanish at his heel. If he intended to prophesy rebirth as a hungry ghost, they would vanish at his great toe. If he intended to prophesy rebirth as a human, they would vanish at his two knees. If he intended to prophesy that someone would become a wheel-turning king of power, they would vanish at the palm of his left hand. If he intended to prophesy that someone would become a wheel-turning monarch, they would vanish at the palm of his right hand. If he intended to prophesy rebirth as a god, they would vanish at his navel. If he intended to prophesy awakening as a śrāvaka, they would vanish at his mouth. If he intended to prophesy solitary awakening, they would vanish at his hair between the brows. If he intended to prophesy the unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening, they would vanish at his crown protrusion.

Then those rays circled the Blessed One three times and vanished into his crown protrusion. Thereupon the venerable Ānanda joined his palms together and —

addressed the Blessed One in verse:

Many thousands of rays of diverse hues
have issued forth from his mouth in abundance,
illuminating every direction all around
just as the sun rises in the east.

And then he spoke these further verses:

Free from agitation and despondency, having abandoned pride,
the cause for beings to attain the highest — the buddha —
white as a conch or lotus root, without any cause or condition,
the Victor, subduer of foes, does not display a smile in vain.

At such a time, those who are themselves aware and resolute,
those who hope and long to hear the speech of the sovereign of victors —
by the firm and excellent words of the chief of sages,
may those in whom doubt has arisen have it removed through virtue.

As a king of mountains stands firm above the ocean,
so the true Protector does not lightly rest in a causeless smile.
Since in his steadfastness he has displayed a smile,
may the many beings hear why he has done so.

Then the venerable Ānanda declared in prose: "Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly and completely awakened buddhas do not smile without cause and without condition. O Venerable One, for what cause and for what condition did he smile?" And the Blessed One spoke: "Ānanda, it is so, it is so. A Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and completely awakened buddha does not smile without cause and without condition. Ānanda, in this very direction there dwells the perfectly and completely awakened buddha Kāśyapa, who has been teaching the Dharma there."

Thereupon the venerable Ānanda swiftly and without delay folded his upper robe into four layers and spread it as a seat, then said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, I beg you to be seated on this seat I have spread. If you sit here, this place will have been graced by two perfectly and completely awakened buddhas — Kāśyapa and the present Blessed One."

The Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Excellent, Ānanda! It is excellent that you understood this without my having to say it." So saying, the Blessed One sat down upon that seat.

Having sat, the Blessed One then said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, this direction is the temple of the perfectly and completely awakened buddha Kāśyapa. This is the walking-meditation ground. This is the dais. This is the gatehouse. This is the foot-washing place. This is the warming house. This is the dwelling house. This is the latrine."

The venerable Upāli then put a question to the Blessed One, the bhagavān: "Venerable One, one may speak of a 'permitted place' and of a 'non-permitted place.' Venerable One, by what criterion does one recognize a permitted place?" The Blessed One answered: "Upāli, so long as the true Dharma exists, there are permitted and non-permitted places. When the true Dharma has perished, all places become permitted."

Upāli asked: "Venerable One, by what criterion does one say the true Dharma is present? And by what criterion does one say it has perished?"

The Blessed One answered: "Upāli, for as long as formal acts are performed and those who make effort in performing them are present — that is to say, so long as formal acts are carried out and those who engage in them with diligence also exist — one should say the true Dharma is present. When formal acts are no longer performed and those who engage in them with diligence are also absent, then one should say the true Dharma has perished."

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the bhagavān: "Venerable One, is it permitted to perform a formal act within a boundary while the Victor is in residence?" The Blessed One answered: "Upāli, it is permitted." "Is it permitted to perform a formal act after the Victor has been counted among the number?" The Blessed One answered: "Upāli, it is not permitted." "Why is that?" "Upāli, the Jewel of the Buddha is one thing; the Jewel of the Saṅgha is another."

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the bhagavān: "Venerable One, is it permitted to establish a new boundary where no boundary previously existed?" The Blessed One answered: "Upāli, it is not permitted." "Venerable One, by what criterion is one to know that it is not permitted to establish a boundary?" The Blessed One answered: "Upāli, by three: a maṇḍala boundary, a water-encircled boundary, and the interior of an already existing boundary."

The venerable Upāli asked: "Venerable One, is it permitted to establish a boundary on the far bank of a flowing river?" "Upāli, it is not permitted." "What if there is a sturdy bridge?" "In that case it is permitted." "Venerable One, if the bridge should break or be destroyed, for how long does it remain unbroken?" "Upāli, if there is the intention to repair it, it will not be considered destroyed for seven days."

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the bhagavān: "Venerable One, when a monk performs an act at the same time as a boundary is being dissolved, and the boundary dissolves while the act is being performed — is that act considered completed or not completed?" The Blessed One answered: "Upāli, if the marks have been announced and the act has been performed in full, it is called completed. If it was stopped, it is not completed." "Venerable One, when a nun performs an act at the same time as a boundary is being dissolved, and the boundary dissolves while the act is being performed — is that act considered completed or not completed?" "Upāli, if the marks have been announced and the act has been performed in full, it is called completed. If it was stopped, it is not completed."

These are the four verses of the first sūtra within the section on the opening cases.

In brief:
Acts performed on land or in the sky —
the boundary, and the question of full purity,
and monks dwelling in one place:
these are what one must examine in all acts.

When the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada, the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the bhagavān: "Venerable One, is it permitted for those on the ground to perform an act together with those on the ground?" "Upāli, it is not permitted. However, giving consent is permitted. If those dwelling on the ground are complete in number and consent has also been received from those on the ground, that is permissible."

"Venerable One, is it permitted for those on the ground to perform an act together with those on a wall?" "Upāli, it is not permitted. However, giving consent is permitted. If those dwelling on the ground are complete in number and consent has also been received from those on the wall, that is permissible."

"Is it permitted for those on the ground to perform an act together with those on a tree?" "Upāli, it is not permitted. However, giving consent is permitted. If those dwelling on the ground are complete in number and consent has also been received from those on the tree, that is permissible."

"Venerable One, is it permitted for those on the ground to perform an act together with those in the sky?" "Upāli, it is not permitted."

"Venerable One, is it permitted for those on top of a wall to perform an act together with those on top of a wall?" "Upāli, it is not permitted. However, giving consent is permitted. If those dwelling on top of the wall are complete in number and consent has also been received from those on top of the wall, that is permissible."

"Venerable One, is it permitted for those on top of a wall to perform an act together with those on the ground?" "Upāli, it is not permitted. However, giving consent is permitted. If those on top of the wall are complete in number and consent has also been received from those dwelling on the ground, that is permissible."

"Venerable One, is it permitted for those on top of a wall to perform an act together with those on top of a tree?" "Upāli, it is not permitted. However, giving consent is permitted. If those dwelling on the wall are complete in number and consent has also been received from those dwelling on top of the tree, that is permissible."

"Venerable One, is it permitted for those on top of a wall to perform an act together with those in the sky?" "Upāli, it is not permitted."

"Venerable One, is it permitted for those on a tree to perform an act together with those on a tree?" "Upāli, it is not permitted. However, giving consent is permitted. If those dwelling on the tree are complete in number and consent has also been received from those dwelling on the tree, that is permissible."

"Is it permitted for those on a tree to perform an act together with those on the ground?" "Upāli, it is not permitted."

giving consent is permitted. If those dwelling on the tree are complete in number and consent has also been received from those dwelling on the ground, that is permissible."

"Venerable One, is it permitted for those on a tree to perform an act together with those on a wall?" "Upāli, it is not permitted. However, if those dwelling on the tree are complete in number and consent has also been received from those dwelling on the ground, that is permissible."

"Venerable One, is it permitted for those on a tree to perform an act together with those in the sky?" "Upāli, it is not permitted."

"Venerable One, is it permitted for those in the sky to perform an act together with those in the sky?" "Upāli, it is not permitted."

"Venerable One, is it permitted for those in the sky to perform an act together with those on the ground?" "Upāli, it is not permitted."

"Venerable One, is it permitted for those in the sky to perform an act together with those on a wall?" "Upāli, it is not permitted."

"Venerable One, is it permitted for those in the sky to perform an act together with those on a tree?" "Upāli, it is not permitted."

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, the Blessed One has taught one hundred and one acts within the scope of this Vinaya. Among those one hundred and one acts, Venerable One, which acts require consent and which do not require consent?" "Upāli, all of them require consent — except for those in which the boundary has been nullified."

"Venerable One, is it permitted to nullify a boundary by means of supernatural power or illusion?" "Upāli, it is not permitted. Why is that? Because supernatural power and illusion cannot be designated by conventional expression."

"Venerable One, is it permitted to nullify a boundary by means of a planet, a ray of light, the sun, the moon, or stars?" "Upāli, it is not permitted. Why is that? Because planets, rays of light, the sun, the moon, and stars are unstable."

"Venerable One, is it permitted to nullify a boundary by means of a wave of water?" "Upāli, it is not permitted. Why is that? Because waves of water are unstable."

The venerable Upāli then asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, if a monk who is receiving a formal declaration of purity has received that declaration and is then above in the sky, is that considered to be a received declaration of purity?" "Upāli, it has not been received — it must be received again from the beginning."

"Venerable One, is it permitted for a single performer of the act, a single reciter of the act's formula, and a single supplicant to perform an act for four assemblies in four locations?" "Upāli, it is permitted — provided that in each of the four locations there are three monks present, and that the supplication and the act are manifest there; and that the monk performing the supplication, stationed at the juncture of the four locations, presses down with a board, a door-bar, a throne, or any other such thing at the boundary of the four locations, and sits upon it and performs the act. That performer of the act himself thereby completes the count for each of those groups."

"Venerable One, is it permitted for a single monk present in a single location to perform an act for four locations?" "Upāli, it is permitted — and those four-location acts are as follows: an act of censure, an act of rebuke, an act of banishment, an act of reconciliation, an act of suspension for not seeing a fault, an act of suspension for not rectifying conduct, an act of suspension for not relinquishing a wrong view, and an act of penalty — when these are manifestly present, the monk performing the act sits upon a board or door-bar pressed into the juncture of the four locations."

This concludes the fifth verse-set of the first section of the root narrative.

In summary:
Beyond a half and three, and at a half and three, on the slopes of a mountain,
A Saṅgha of ten million — at dawn, blessed within the boundary.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Then the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha:

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that a great boundary should be established. Venerable one, what is the measure of such a great boundary?"

"Upāli, it is a yojana and a half."

"Venerable one, does something beyond a yojana and a half also count as a boundary?"

"Upāli, no. Up to a yojana and a half is a boundary."

"Venerable one, what is the boundary of the lower realm?"

"Upāli, it extends as far as the water is reached."

"Venerable one, if one goes beyond a yojana and a half and reaches the water, does that also count as a boundary?"

"Upāli, no. Up to a yojana and a half is a boundary; beyond that is not."

"Venerable one, what is the boundary of the upper realm?"

"Upāli, it extends as far as the top of a tree or the top of a wall is reached."

"Venerable one, if the top of a tree or the top of a wall lies beyond a yojana and a half, does that also count as a boundary?"

"Upāli, no. Up to a yojana and a half is a boundary; beyond that is not."

"Venerable one, what is the boundary of a mountain?"

"Upāli, it extends as far as it is encircled by water."

"Venerable one, if beyond a yojana and a half it is entirely encircled by water, does that also count as a boundary?"

"Upāli, no. Up to a yojana and a half is a boundary; beyond that is not."

"Venerable one, during the rains retreat, when the Saṅgha is divided, if a monk has been blessed for seven days and, intending to go to the proper side, goes instead to the improper side, is his rains retreat broken or is it unbroken?"

"Upāli, if he is confident in his view and goes there, and dawn rises, his rains retreat is broken. But if he is not confident in his view and goes there, and dawn has not yet risen, his rains retreat is not broken."

"Venerable one, during the rains retreat, when the Blessed One declares 'Go beyond the boundary for seven days, blessed with leave,' where is the blessing to be given?"

"Upāli, within the boundary."

"How is it to be done?"

"Sit before the monk, join one's palms, and speak these words: 'Please attend, venerable one. I, so-and-so by name, having entered the rains retreat properly — either the first or the final — within this dwelling inside the boundary, I, so-and-so by name, have been blessed with seven days' leave to go beyond the boundary for the sake of the Saṅgha. I keep this rains retreat here. I dwell in this rains retreat here.' This is to be declared in full, as before."

This concludes the sixth verse-set of the sūtra of the first gateway of the root narrative.

In summary: The five groups — deliberately, and likewise when going to relatives — when doubt has arisen concerning scripture, and when going again because one has not obtained what was needed.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha:

"Venerable one, when the Blessed One has declared 'Enter the rains retreat,' who are those who are to enter it?"

"Upāli, there are five: fully ordained monks, fully ordained nuns, female probationers, male novices, and female novices."

"How are they to enter?"

"All of them in the same manner as before."

"Venerable one, when the Blessed One has given seven days' leave, declaring 'Go beyond the boundary for the sake of a layman,' if there is a non-Buddhist present, should one go for his sake as well?"

"Upāli, if one wishes to free him from that wrong view, one may go."

"Venerable one, if there is a relative present, should one go for his sake as well?"

"One may go."

"Venerable one, if a monk has a doubt or suspicion regarding the rule, may one go for his sake as well?"

"Upāli, one may go for his sake as well."

"Venerable one, if a monk has a doubt or suspicion regarding what has not been attained — so that it may be attained — regarding what has not been understood — so that it may be understood — regarding what has not been realized — so that it may be realized, may one go for his sake as well?"

"Upāli, one may go for his sake as well."

These are the seven verses of the sūtra of the first topic of the opening section.

In summary:

Unwashed cloth is the same in this regard;
yet going into the village,
wandering about, and the like —
when settled, follow the former rule.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, is it permissible to consecrate unwashed cloth?"

"Upāli, it is not permissible in general, yet it is permissible under such circumstances."

"Venerable one, is it permissible to receive unwashed cloth and then go into the village?"

"Upāli, it is not permissible in general, yet it is permissible under such circumstances."

"Venerable one, is it permissible to receive unwashed cloth and go to a layman's house?"

"Upāli, it is not permissible in general, yet it is permissible under such circumstances."

"Venerable one, is it permissible to receive unwashed cloth and stay at a layman's house?"

"Upāli, it is not permissible in general, yet it is permissible under such circumstances."

"Venerable one, is it permissible to receive unwashed cloth and go to a wanderer's house?"

"Upāli, it is not permissible in general, yet it is permissible under such circumstances."

"Venerable one, is it permissible to receive unwashed cloth and stay at a wanderer's dwelling?"

"Upāli, it is not permissible in general, yet it is permissible under such circumstances."

"Venerable one, is it permissible to receive unwashed cloth and go beyond the boundary?"

"Upāli, it is not permissible in general, yet it is permissible under such circumstances."

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that a robe should be made of the measure of a cubit. If a particular monk's arm is short and his body is tall, should he too make it to the measure of a cubit?"

"Upāli, it is not to be made to the measure of a cubit; rather, make it to the measure of his body."

"Venerable one, what should one do if one cannot afford to have a robe made?"

"Upāli, follow the former rule and make do."

These are the eight verses of the sūtra of the first topic of the opening section.

In summary:

Footwear is to be made in five ways.
That of lion, wild beast, and unfit animals —
sitting in them is also not permissible,
and one must not lie upon such hides.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that sandals made from the hide of a yak should not be worn. Venerable one, then is it also not permissible to make and wear sandals from the hide of an ordinary ox?"

"Upāli, sandals from the hide of those animals also must not be made and worn."

"Upāli, why is that? Because they too possess powerful noses, powerful teeth, and powerful legs."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that sandals made from the hide of a horse should not be worn. Venerable one, is it also not permissible to wear sandals made from the hide of an ordinary horse?"

"Upāli, sandals made from the hide of such animals also must not be worn."

"Why is that? Upāli, because they are possessed of speed and strength."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that sandals made from the hides of lions, tigers, and leopards should not be worn. Venerable one, are there other wild and unfit animals as well? Should sandals made from their hides also not be worn?"

"Upāli, sandals made from their hides must also not be worn."

"Why is that? Upāli, because they too are possessed of the power of claws and the power of fangs."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that one must not sit on hide. Venerable one, how much of one does it take to count as sitting on hide?"

"Upāli, it is however much of one's haunches are placed upon it."

"Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that one must not lie on hide. Venerable one, how much of one does it take to count as lying on hide?"

"Upāli, it is however much of one's body is stretched out upon it."

This is the ninth verse of the first section of the origin stories.

In brief:
Raw meat, and sour whey,
And what has been thoroughly pressed out,
Feces and abscesses must not be treated —
These apply in a temple setting.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upāli put this question to the Blessed One: "Venerable one, the Blessed One has declared that one should give raw meat to the monk who is convalescing. Venerable one, from whom should it be obtained?"

"Upāli, it is from among the five kinds of meat-sellers. And what are those five kinds? They are: butchers, those who slaughter domestic fowl, those who slaughter wild fowl, those who slaughter pigs, and those who slaughter game."

"Well then, venerable one, from whom should one receive and accept it?"

"Upāli, from a faithful layman."

The origin story is set at Śrāvastī. At that time a certain monk fell ill and went to a physician. He said, "Good sir, I am ill. I suffer from such-and-such an ailment — please diagnose it and prescribe a treatment." The physician said, "Noble one, you should drink butter — that will sustain you." The monk replied, "Good sir, the Blessed One has not permitted it," and the physician said, "Noble one, your Teacher is compassionate; he will certainly permit it." The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "If the physician has prescribed that butter will sustain him, then he may drink it."

When that monk drank the butter, he was afflicted by thirst. He went to the physician and said, "Good sir, I am tormented by thirst." The physician said, "Noble one, drink sour whey." The monk replied, "Since the Blessed One has not permitted food at improper times, how can I drink it?" The physician said, "Noble one, your Teacher is compassionate; he will certainly give permission." The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Then he may drink sour whey," and gave permission accordingly. But the monks did not know how sour whey was to be drunk. They reported this again to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Monks, sour whey is of five kinds. What are the five? These: the lees of fruit wine, the lees of grain ale, whey water, strained whey liquid, and whey itself.

"The lees of fruit wine are what has been made from fruits and has gone sour by turning bad. The lees of grain ale are what has been prepared from grains, gone bad, and turned sour. Whey water is the liquid that has come out of curd. Strained whey liquid is whey that has become like whey water. Whey itself is just whey.

"When any of these has been diluted with water and strained through a cloth until it has taken on the colour of arrow-shaft pigment, it may be drunk by monks both in season and out of season, both by the sick and by the healthy — let there be no doubt about this."

The origin story is set at Śrāvastī.

At that time, another monk was afflicted with a fistula of the anus. He had cut the boil with his fingernail, and as a result it became painful, raw, hot, harmful, and aching. Tormented by this suffering, he thought to himself: "The Blessed One has not looked upon me with compassion, even though I have been oppressed by pain and am in a wretched state."

Then the Blessed One, moved by his great compassion, came to where the monk was staying. "Monk, what ails you?" he asked. The monk, feeling sorrow and unhappiness, his eyes brimming with tears and his mouth trembling, spoke with difficulty and reported to the Blessed One in full detail what had happened. The Blessed One then declared: "Monks, did I not instruct you previously not to cut an anal fistula?" "You did, Blessed One." "Then why did you do so?" "Blessed One, I was tormented by suffering." The Blessed One then addressed the monks: "Monks, because this monk was tormented by suffering, there is no offence. Yet I now give this further instruction: Monks, when afflicted by the disease of an anal fistula, do not cut it yourselves with a fingernail or any such thing, and do not cause others to cut it. Two kinds of treatment should be applied to it: medicinal and mantra-based. If a monk who is afflicted by the disease of an anal fistula cuts it with a fingernail or any such thing, or causes another to cut it, he incurs a transgression along with what has passed."

The Blessed One, the awakened Bhagavān, was residing in the Śākya border-town called Merchant Gourd-Leaf. At that time, a certain householder, of his own accord, with his own faith, and with his own joy, constructed a shrine-hall and offered it to the single individual of the venerable Śāraṇa. Then the venerable Śāraṇa, for as long as he stayed in that shrine-hall, took his bowl and robes and went to use it as a place of resort. The householder heard that the noble Śāraṇa had stayed in the shrine-hall for a certain time, then taken his bowl and robes and departed to use it as a place of resort elsewhere. Upon hearing this, the householder offered the shrine-hall to the Saṅgha.

Then the venerable Śāraṇa, for as long as he wished, used it as a place of resort elsewhere, then took his bowl and robes and, going to the Śākya border-town called Merchant Gourd-Leaf, travelled along using it as a place of resort in stages, until he arrived at the place called Merchant Gourd-Leaf. There the venerable Śāraṇa heard that the householder had offered that shrine-hall to the Saṅgha. Upon hearing this, he went to where the Blessed One was staying. He bowed with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Śāraṇa addressed the Blessed One thus:

"Venerable One, a certain householder, of his own accord, with his own faith, and with his own joy, built a shrine-hall and offered it to me as a single individual. I stayed in that shrine-hall for a certain time, then took my bowl and robes and went to use it as a place of resort. Then that householder heard that the noble Śāraṇa had stayed in that shrine-hall for a certain time, had taken his bowl and robes, and had gone to use it as a place of resort. Upon hearing this, the householder offered the shrine-hall to the Saṅgha. Now, Venerable One, what am I to do?" "Let Śāraṇa come here." The householder went to where the Blessed One was and came into his presence, and the Blessed One said to him:

"Householder, ask whether I have committed any offense in body, speech, or mind." The venerable Śāraṇa replied, "Very well, Venerable One," and having received this instruction from the Blessed One, he went to where that householder was. When he arrived, he said to the householder: "Householder, have I committed any offense in body, speech, or mind?" The householder replied: "The noble Śāraṇa has not committed even the slightest offense in body, speech, or mind." Thereupon the venerable Śāraṇa examined the matter carefully with that householder and then went to where the Blessed One was. Coming into his presence, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet and said to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, when I said to that householder, 'Householder, have I committed even the slightest offense in body, speech, or mind?', he replied: 'The noble Śāraṇa, you have not committed even the slightest offense in body, speech, or mind.'"

At that time, the venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Blessed One, holding a fan and fanning him. The Blessed One then said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and gather all the monks who are staying and residing in the Śākyan border-town called Merchant-of-Gourds into the assembly hall." Ānanda replied, "As you command, Venerable One," and having received this instruction from the Blessed One, he gathered all the monks who were staying and residing in the Śākyan border-town called Merchant-of-Gourds into the assembly hall. He then went to where the Blessed One was and, having prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet, said to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, Blessed One, if it please you, the time has come: all the monks who are staying and residing in the Śākyan border-town called Merchant-of-Gourds have assembled in the assembly hall." The Blessed One then went to where the assembly hall was. Having arrived, he took a seat on the appointed throne in front of the Saṅgha of monks. Seated there, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

"Monks, when a gift has been given to a single individual and is then given to another, it is given contrary to Dharma, received contrary to Dharma, and wrongly used. When given to more than two, or to the Saṅgha, it is likewise given contrary to Dharma, received contrary to Dharma, and wrongly used. Monks, when a gift has been given to two individuals and is then given to one, or to another, or to two, or to many, or to the Saṅgha, it is given contrary to Dharma, received contrary to Dharma, and wrongly used. Monks, when a gift has been given to many individuals and is then given to one, or to two, or to other many, or to the Saṅgha, it is given contrary to Dharma, received contrary to Dharma, and wrongly used. When a gift has been given to the Saṅgha and is then given to a single individual, or to two, or to many, or to another Saṅgha, it is given contrary to Dharma, received contrary to Dharma, and wrongly used. When the Saṅgha of śrāvakas of the Tathāgata is divided, residing in factions and non-factions, and a gift given to one faction is then given to the other, it is given contrary to Dharma, received contrary to Dharma, and wrongly used. Monks, when a gift has been given to a single individual and is not given to another, it is given in accordance with Dharma, received in accordance with Dharma, and rightly used. When it is not given to two, not given to many, not given to the Saṅgha, it is given in accordance with Dharma and rightly used."

Monks, when a gift has been given to two persons, it is not given to one, not given to others, not given to many, and not given to the Saṅgha — it is given in accordance with Dharma, received in accordance with Dharma, and rightly used. Monks, when a gift has been given to many persons, it is not given to one, not given to two or to other many, and not given to the Saṅgha — it is given in accordance with Dharma, received in accordance with Dharma, and rightly used. Monks, when a gift has been given to the Saṅgha, it is not given to a single person, not to two, not to many, and not to another Saṅgha — it is given in accordance with Dharma, received in accordance with Dharma, and rightly used. And when the Saṅgha of śrāvakas of the Tathāgata is divided, residing in factions and non-factions, and a gift given to one faction is not then given to the other — it is given in accordance with Dharma, received in accordance with Dharma, and rightly used.

Monks, a king has authority over the land. An owner has authority over the bedding. A monk has authority over his bowl and robes. One who gives a gift, and the master of a gift, should not redirect to another those things that have been given — it is not fitting to give them to another. Why so? Because, monks, the giving is the former act, not the latter. Therefore the monastery should be returned to Śroṇakaraṇin.

Monks, if someone gives a gift to another and that same person then gives it again to yet another, then — except in a case of such a condition — it becomes something of the past. The monks also returned the monastery to the venerable Śroṇakaraṇin.

The Sacred Vinaya Text, the thirty-second bundle. The occasion is at Śrāvastī, when the Blessed One said, "Hold the fifth-year festival, the sixth-year festival, the monastery's seasonal festivals, and the great seasonal festivals," and the brahmins and householders did likewise. Monks who dwelt in various regions also assembled, and the faithful brahmins and householders gave them abundant provisions. Having eaten a little, those monks gave the remainder to their novice fathers. The next day those same monks were given the same in return, and they asked their novice fathers, "Where did this food of yours come from?" They replied, "It is precisely what you yourselves gave us yesterday." The monks said, "We gave this to you," but they fell into doubt and did not accept it.
