The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: If he gave with expectation and they ate again with expectation, then both the giving and the eating were transgressions — the giving was a wrongdoing, and the eating was a downfall. If he gave with expectation and they ate again without expectation, then the giving was a wrongdoing, but the eating was without fault. If he gave without expectation and they ate with expectation, then the giving was without fault, but the eating was a downfall. If he gave without expectation and they ate without expectation, then the giving was without fault and the eating was also without fault.

The tenth sūtra of the first section of the occasion is complete. The first section is complete.

In summary:

Dispatching and re-announcing,
and likewise not receiving the deposit;
giving instruction, performing the act,
being patient, and expelling;
conducting in accordance with Dharma,
cutting off by cutting the wall —
this is the second of the collected sūtras.

In brief:

The monk who answered questions by invitation
and transgressed the time —
at Śrāvastī: the dispute,
the two Saṅghas, and the robe.

The Blessed One (the Buddha) was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there lived a certain householder who took a wife from a family of equal rank and enjoyed himself with her in sport and pleasure. From that sport and pleasure, his wife conceived a child; after eight or nine months she gave birth to a son. Within twenty-one days — seven times three — a great birth-feast was held on a lavish scale, and the child was given a name in keeping with his family lineage.

Then at a later time that son went forth into the teaching of the Blessed One, and again at a later time he was struck by illness. He passed away, and the monks, taking his alms-bowl and robes together, discarded them in the charnel ground. Some brahmins and householders who happened to be passing along that road came upon them and, speaking among themselves as they went, said: "We householders, dwelling at home, acquire wealth and goods by many means, and yet we do not discard our vessels and utensils or our clothing. These sons of the Śākya renunciant — though they beg for their food with great difficulty, going past a hundred thresholds — why do they discard alms-bowls and robes?" The monks were coming toward them from that direction, and those people said to them: "Noble ones, we householders dwell at home; we acquire wealth and goods by many means and yet we do not discard our vessels or clothing. You, who with great difficulty fill your bellies by going for alms past a hundred thresholds — whence then come your alms-bowls and robes? Why do you discard this monk's alms-bowl and robes together in the charnel ground?" The monks replied that the Blessed One had not permitted otherwise, and those people went away without another word.

The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Do not discard them together with the alms-bowl and the robes." When the Blessed One had said, "Do not discard them together with the alms-bowl and the robes," the monks discarded the body naked. The Blessed One declared: "Do not discard it naked; wrap it in a lower garment and a sweat-cloth and then discard it." Thereupon the monks discarded it with fine robes, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not discard it with fine ones." So they discarded it with poor ones. The Blessed One declared: "Do not discard it with poor ones either; discard it with middling ones." The Blessed One had declared, "Do not discard them together with the alms-bowl and the robes," but the monks did not know what to do. The Blessed One then declared: "Give them to whatever monk is in need." The group of six monks habitually feigned poverty, so the Blessed One declared: "Do not give to the group of six; give in order of seniority." The junior monks then went without receiving anything, and the Blessed One declared to the monk who answered questions by invitation: "Announce it to the Saṅgha, and when the entire assembly of the monks has gathered and is seated, let the monastery-keeper cause an appraisal to be made within the Saṅgha."

The occasion of origin is at Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī another monk had passed away, and his alms-bowl and robes were placed in the hands of a certain nun. After the monks had cremated his body and returned to the monastery, they searched for the alms-bowl and robes but could not find them. Learning that they were in the possession of a certain nun — known by such-and-such a name — in the nuns' winter quarters, the monks went to those winter quarters.

They said to her, "Noble nun known by such-and-such a name, the alms-bowl and robes of the recently deceased monk are stored here. Please hand them over." She replied, "Noble ones, where did that monk pass away? He passed away in our monastery. What is present there belongs to you; what is present here belongs to us. How so? Our Dharma-brother by such-and-such a name also passed away here." The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "The alms-bowl and robes of a monk belong to the monks. Nuns must not retain them."

The occasion of origin is at Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī another nun had passed away, and her alms-bowl and robes were placed in the hands of a certain monk. After the nuns had cremated her body, they went to the monks' monastery in search of the alms-bowl and robes, but could not find them. Learning that they were with a monk known by such-and-such a name in another monastery, they went to that monastery, paid homage at the feet of the monks, and said, "Noble ones, a nun known by such-and-such a name has passed away, and if her alms-bowl and robes are here, we ask that you please return them to us." He replied, "Where did that nun pass away? She passed away in our winter quarters. Noble ones, what is staying there — that is yours to keep; but what is here with us belongs to us, for she was our Dharma-sister." The nuns reported this to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "If those are the alms-bowl and robes of a nun, they belong to the nuns. Since they belong to the nuns, monks must not retain them."

The occasion of origin is at Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī, a certain monk was travelling on alms-rounds when he went to another village in the rocky hills and passed away in the house of a householder there. That householder brought him to the charnel ground, then concealed and set aside his alms-bowl and robes. Some time later, a number of nuns, while travelling on alms-rounds, went to that village in the rocky hills, and the householder, seeing them, said, "Noble ones, here are the alms-bowl and robes of a monk who passed away in my house. Please take them." They replied, "Householder, the Blessed One has not granted this. These belong to the monks." The nuns thus reported the matter to the monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "In places where there are no monks, nuns may take them. Have no hesitation about this."

The occasion of origin is at Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī, while a number of nuns were travelling on alms-rounds, one nun among them fell ill. As she walked slowly and came back late, she lost the way and reached another village in the rocky hills, where she passed away in the house of a householder there. That householder brought her to the charnel ground, then concealed and set aside her alms-bowl and robes. Some time later, a number of monks, while travelling on alms-rounds, went to that village in the rocky hills, and the householder, seeing them, said, "Noble ones, a nun passed away in my house; here are her alms-bowl and robes. Please take them." They replied, "Householder, the Blessed One has not granted this. These belong to the nuns."

The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Where there are no nuns present, the monks may take the robes and bowl. Have no doubt about this."

The occasion for the next ruling arose at Śrāvastī. The venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable one, when a monk passes away, and his alms-bowl and robes are in the possession of a layman there, who has the right to them?" The Blessed One declared: "Upāli, whoever came first to claim them has the right." "If two come, who has the right?" "Whoever picked them up first." "If both picked them up at the same time, who has the right?" "Whoever received them first." "If both received them at the same time, both have the right." "And if both received them at the same time, then whoever the householder has faith in and gives them to has the right."

The occasion for the next ruling arose at Śrāvastī. At that time, in the Jeta Grove, two monks came to quarrel, and they stood there surrounded by other monks. Some brahmins and householders, seeing this, said: "Noble ones, when we laypeople quarrel, you yourselves intervene to stop us — so why do you stand here surrounding these monks and not intervene?" Others among those present replied: "These monks are the very ones who are quarreling — what is the point of intervening?" Having no answer to that, those people fell silent and remained standing there.

The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "You should intervene and not stand around watching." They did intervene, but they were unable to stop the fight. The monks again reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If intervention does not work, then carry out the act of censure."

The Blessed One declared that the act of censure should be carried out, and some time later two monks got into a dispute, arguing, "This belongs to you," and "This belongs to me." In the course of that dispute they spoke roughly to each other. The Saṅgha then imposed the act of censure on both of them. The two monks said: "Venerable ones, all we did was speak roughly to each other while arguing over a matter — why have you cut us off with the act of censure?" The others replied: "Because the Blessed One said to carry out the act of censure against those who quarrel — that is why we have imposed it on you two." The two monks said nothing further and stood in silence.

The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Rather than imposing the act of censure on those two, you should intervene and separate them. If one of them is a newcomer, his preceptor and teacher should admonish him. If one of them is an elder, let him gather the entire Saṅgha and settle the dispute. If even that fails to bring reconciliation, then and only then impose the act of censure on both."

The occasion for the next ruling arose at Śrāvastī. The venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable one, if a monk passes away in a border region, who gains the right to the possessions of the deceased?" The Blessed One replied: "Upāli, whoever is on that side." "Venerable one, if both sides are equidistant?" "Upāli, then both."

Here ends the second section of the body of occasions, the first verse section.

In summary:
What is to be proclaimed, and the vehicle,
then the garland, and the robes,
and likewise the robes belonging to the Saṅgha —
doubt is a matter for the individual.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada (the Benefactor of the Destitute), at Śrāvastī, and many remarkable things occurred and were set down there.

During that time when the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, the non-Buddhist adherents (tīrthikas) were losing their influence and receiving fewer offerings. Accordingly, they took whatever they wanted and began to carry on their non-Buddhist activities. Meanwhile, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, the Benefactor of the Destitute, who had become a Buddhist, would rise early in the morning and go to see the Blessed One. Then one day, having risen early in the morning and gone to the Jeta Grove, he was approached by the non-Buddhist adherents, who took from him whatever they wished and urged him vigorously. He then thought to himself: "These are non-Buddhist adherents of bad doctrine and bad discipline. They take whatever they want and carry on their non-Buddhist activities. The Blessed One himself has also said, in such and such sūtras, that those who lack faith should be properly urged, introduced, and established in perfect faith. If the Blessed One gives his permission, I shall also establish many people in the practice of making offerings to the Saṅgha." With this in mind, he went to where the Blessed One was, arrived, prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable one, these non-Buddhist adherents of bad doctrine and bad discipline take whatever they want and carry on their non-Buddhist activities. If the Blessed One gives his permission, then — from the point of doing such and such — I shall establish people in the practice of making offerings to the Saṅgha." And the rest proceeds as before, up to those words. The Blessed One then declared: "In that case, householder, I give you permission. Take whatever you want and carry out activities for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha." After the Blessed One had given this command — "Take whatever you want and carry out activities for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha" — and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada began to urge people properly, some brahmins and householders said: "If noble ones are also properly urged, we shall gain even more merit than that." The Blessed One then declared: "Monks, too, should assist. The brahmins and householders then said: "If it is announced in our names, that would be excellent." The Blessed One declared: "It should be announced when the donor has given." Then the householder had it announced accordingly, and the brahmins and householders said: "If noble ones also announce it, we shall gain even more merit than that." The Blessed One declared: "Monks should also announce it. When brahmins and householders come to the assembly hall and make an offering, the Blessed One declared: "It should be announced in the assembly hall as well." When the one making the announcement was surrounded by a great many people and could not be seen, the Blessed One declared: "Mount a chariot and make the announcement." Then heat, rain, and wind arose, and the Blessed One declared: "Erect a high pavilion." When many people blocked the doorways, the Blessed One declared: "Place four announcers at the four gates." Thereupon the householder Anāthapiṇḍada took what he wanted and gathered a great many pairs of robes — many hundreds and thousands of pairs of robes. He then thought to himself: "Now that a great many robes have been assembled, I shall serve a meal to the monastic Saṅgha of monks beginning with the Buddha, and then offer the robes to the monastic Saṅgha of monks beginning with the Buddha, in order of seniority."

He adorned the Jeta Grove with robes of every kind, stringing garlands of robes throughout, and posted guards as well. He invited friends, relatives, and kinsmen as guests. Then, having prepared clean and abundant food and drink, he invited the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of monks to a meal in the Jeta Grove.

The next morning he rose early, arranged the seats, filled the water vessels and set them out, and then served the meal to the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of śrāvakas. He addressed the Blessed One, saying: "Venerable One, these are worthy recipients of offerings in the world."

Now there are two kinds of householder: those who are still in training and those who are beyond training. Among these, the householder in training is of eighteen kinds, and the one beyond training is of nine kinds.

What are the eighteen kinds of one in training? One who has entered the path for the purpose of realizing the fruit of stream-entry; one who has attained stream-entry; one who has entered the path for the purpose of realizing the fruit of once-returning; one who has attained once-returning; one who has entered the path for the purpose of realizing the fruit of non-returning; one who has attained non-returning; one who has entered the path for the purpose of realizing the fruit of arhatship; one who follows through faith; one who follows through the Dharma; one who is liberated through faith; one who is attained through view; one who proceeds ever higher; one who is bound for one more life; one who passes into nirvāṇa in the intermediate state; one who passes into nirvāṇa immediately upon birth, with mental formation; one who passes into complete nirvāṇa without mental formation; and those who are ascending upward — these are called the eighteen kinds in training.

What are the nine kinds beyond training? One whose Dharma has faded; one whose Dharma has not faded; one who has the hidden Dharma; one who is protected by subsequent mindfulness; one who dwells unmoved; one who, having realized individually, does not become a person of fortune; one who has the Dharma of the immovable; one who is liberated through wisdom; and one who is liberated on both sides — these are called the nine kinds beyond training.

The Blessed One spoke these words. Having spoken them, the Sugata, the Teacher, then declared in verse:

Those in training and beyond training who dwell in this world
with body, speech, and mind made straight —
they are worthy of gifts, worthy of veneration;
that supreme field of merit — great is the fruit of giving there.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada sat before the assembly in order of seniority and appointed an announcer. When the noble announcer proclaimed this, he said: "Let the Blessed One's Saṅgha of śrāvakas — those worthy of giving, worthy of abundant giving, worthy of joined palms, worthy of homage, the unsurpassed field of merit, the world's worthy recipients of offerings — receive these robes and accept them at their pleasure."

Then the monk acting as announcer sat before the assembly in order of seniority and proclaimed: "Listen, venerable members of the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's śrāvakas — worthy of giving, worthy of abundant giving, worthy of joined palms, worthy of homage, the unsurpassed field of merit, the world's worthy recipients of offerings — let them receive these robes that have been obtained and accept them at their pleasure."

Then those monks who were free from attachment, free from aversion, free from delusion thought to themselves: "The householder Anāthapiṇḍada has proclaimed this: 'Let those of the Blessed One's Saṅgha of śrāvakas who are worthy of giving, worthy of abundant giving, worthy of joined palms —"

worthy of joined palms, worthy of homage, the unsurpassed field of merit, the world's worthy recipients of offerings — let them receive these robes that have been obtained and accept them at their pleasure." We are the unsurpassed, and so this acquisition is within our power — yet the Blessed One has said, "Monks, you should proclaim your virtues and declare your faults." How then could we bring ourselves to speak of ourselves merely for the sake of obtaining robes? We are free from attachment, free from aversion, free from delusion." And so they remained, saying nothing.

Those who still had the remainder of fetters also thought to themselves: "The offering has been dedicated to the unsurpassed; we still have the remainder of fetters, and so we are not our own masters." And they too remained, saying nothing.

Those who were bound by every kind of bondage thought to themselves: "That is being offered to the unsurpassed." And they too said nothing and remained still. Those with the remainder of fetters likewise remained silent, thinking: "We are bound by every kind of bondage, and so in all respects and at all times we are not our own masters." And they too said nothing and remained still.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having offered those robes, found that not a single monk had accepted them. He thought to himself: "I wonder whether I have caused the noble Saṅgha to upend their bowls." His body became pale and gaunt, and he grew thin and wasted with distress. He went to where the Blessed One was, approached him, prostrated himself at the Blessed One's feet with his head, and sat down to one side.

Sitting to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Buddha, though already knowing, asked: the Blessed One asked the venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada arranged and gave robes to the monks — why did they not accept them?" Thereupon the venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One that the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had said: "Those of the Blessed One's Saṅgha of śrāvakas who are worthy of giving, worthy of abundant giving, worthy of joined palms —" and he recited everything just as before, up to the point of "— and let them say nothing." And so he reported: "The Blessed One's householder Anāthapiṇḍada gave, and not a single monk accepted."

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and gather in the assembly hall every single monk, however many are residing and staying in Śrāvastī." The venerable Ānanda replied, "Blessed One, I shall do so," and having heard the Blessed One's instruction, he gathered together every single monk residing and staying in Śrāvastī into the assembly hall. He then went to where the Blessed One was, approached him, prostrated himself at the Blessed One's feet with his head, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, may the Blessed One know that the time has come. Every monk residing and staying in Śrāvastī has assembled and gathered in the assembly hall."

Then the Blessed One went to where the assembly hall was and, upon arriving, sat down on the seat that had been prepared. Having taken his seat, the Blessed One addressed the monks in these words: "Monks, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada gathered many robes and gave them — why did you not accept them?"

The monks remained silent, saying nothing. The Blessed One, though already knowing, asked nonetheless. When the Blessed One questioned the venerable Ānanda, asking, "Ānanda, why are the monks sitting in silence without speaking?" Ānanda reported the whole matter to the Blessed One in full detail.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, did you go forth under me with the thought of passing beyond sorrow into nirvāṇa?"

"Venerable One, it is so," they replied.

"Monks, if that is the case, then for one who has gone forth under me with the thought of passing beyond sorrow into nirvāṇa, I permit: fine robes of a thousand threads, multi-storied dwellings with five hundred windows, and foods possessing a hundred flavors. However, monks, those who have broken their moral discipline are not permitted to make use even of a single heel-step of the Saṅgha's pleasure grove.

"Why is that? Because for a person who has broken moral discipline, there are these ten objects of reproach. What are the ten? Being reviled by one's own moral conscience; being reviled by others, by the gods, and by the Teacher; being censured by those who are skilled in the holy life of pure conduct; being condemned by the very nature of reality; becoming known in all directions through the ugly sound and verse of an ill reputation; those who have not realized coming to no realization; those who have realized suffering decline; what was previously heard being forgotten; spending one's time in continual remorse; and, upon being separated from the body and dying, falling downward into an evil destiny, an evil path, and being reborn in a hell among sentient beings.

"Nevertheless, monks, there are four modes of using things. Enjoying what has no owner; enjoying what has been given; enjoying by permission; and enjoying through debt. Among these, those monks who are free from attachment, free from aversion, and free from delusion — these enjoy what has no owner. Those who still have the residue of active engagement enjoy what has been given. Ordinary persons of virtue who are engaged in meditative concentration and in recitation enjoy by permission. Those who are lazy enjoy through debt. As for those who have broken their moral discipline, none of the four modes of use is permitted to them.

"Therefore, if there are any gains, they should be divided equally by the Saṅgha."

This is the second verse of the sūtra of the second occasion for the rule.

In summary:

Accepted and not accepted,
Withdrawn and likewise not withdrawn,
And so too, staying outside the boundary —
These are to be understood through learning and reflection.

The Blessed One was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One: "Venerable One, is it possible that a monk might not come to a vote while the Saṅgha is casting a vote, even though he has been fully present?"

"Upāli, it is possible. When the Saṅgha is casting a vote, if that monk has not given his consent and lies down asleep, the Saṅgha's vote will still be carried."

"Upāli, in that case, a monk does not come to cast a vote even though he has been fully present.

"Venerable One, is it possible that a monk who has not been present at all would come to have the Saṅgha's vote cast?"

"Upāli, it is possible. If at the time the Saṅgha is casting a vote, a monk gives his consent and then lies down — the Saṅgha's vote will still be carried. In that way, even one who was not fully present would have the vote cast.

"Upāli, likewise, when the Saṅgha is casting a vote, if a monk who has given consent lies down in sleep or enters meditative absorption —"

the vote will still be carried. In that way, even one who was not present at all would have the vote cast.

"Venerable One, is it possible that a monk, even though he was present when the Saṅgha was casting a vote, would not have the vote carried?"

"Upāli, it is possible. This is the case: when the Saṅgha is casting its vote, a monk has not given his consent and then lies down in sleep or enters meditative absorption. In that way, Upāli, even though a monk was present when the Saṅgha was casting a vote, the vote would not be carried for him."

"Venerable One, is it possible that a monk, even though he was not present when the Saṅgha was casting a vote, would have the vote carried?"

"Upāli, it is possible. This is the case: when the Saṅgha is casting its vote, a monk gives his consent and then lies down in sleep, or enters meditative absorption, or goes outside the boundary — and yet he hears that the Saṅgha has carried the vote, and upon hearing it he rejoices, saying, 'It has been carried well — excellent!' In that way the vote is carried."

This is the third verse of the sūtra of the second section on the ruling case.

In brief:
One who has given a training rule, and the ceremonial wood,
And those for whom acts are to be performed,
And reversal of the twelve, and impurity,
And non-validity.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, when a training rule has been given, is it proper that the ceremonial wood be prepared and the act performed?"

"Upāli, it is not proper."

"A paṇḍaka, a eunuch, a woman, one who has caused a nun to be expelled, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika), one who has gone over to the non-Buddhists, one who dwells in a stolen place, one who dwells separately, and one who does not dwell properly — is it proper that the ceremonial wood be prepared and the act performed?"

"Upāli, it is not proper."

"Venerable One, the Blessed One has said that an act performed for one for whom it was reversed is not valid. If an act is performed for such a one in a way that does not accord with the Dharma and is then reversed in that manner, will it still not be valid?"

"Upāli, it is valid."

"Venerable One, when the twelve acts have been assigned to a person and those persons say, 'Do not assign these to us' — is that reversal also not valid?"

"Upāli, it is valid. That was said by me out of consideration for those who abide by the penalty."

"Venerable One, the Blessed One has said that if those who are impure reverse an act, it is not valid. Venerable One, how much impurity makes one 'impure'?"

"Upāli, that is the case in which any one of the four defeats has occurred for the person in question. That much makes one impure."

This is the fourth verse of the sūtra of the second section on the ruling case.

In brief:
One who has given a training rule and one who performs acts,
And likewise one who dwells in a stolen place,
Outside the boundary of full ordination,
And sending by proxy — these are not to be done.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, when one who performs an act has been given a training rule and then performs an act, is it considered done, or is it considered not done?"

"Upāli, it is to be called not done, and it must be done again."

"Likewise for a paṇḍaka, a eunuch, and all cases up through 'one who does not dwell properly' — it is to be done as before."

The ruling case took place at Śrāvastī. A certain monk, wishing to give full ordination to another monk, gathered the monks who were to perform the full ordination. In order to perform the full ordination, he brought along the preceptor's novice, entered the assembly area, and went into the assembly area together with the monks.

He was sent outside the boundary, and his relatives took him and departed. The impediment arose for those venerable ones between the time of their going forth and their receiving full ordination and becoming established as monks. When this occurred, the monks reported it to the Buddha, the Blessed One, and the Buddha, the Blessed One, declared: "Therefore, monks, a novice who desires full ordination should not be sent outside the boundary. Consider this, monks: just as a prince who is eligible to receive the consecration of a wheel-turning king, if he has not yet received the consecration, must be carefully protected and guarded until he obtains the regency, in the same way it is fitting that a novice who desires full ordination should likewise be carefully protected and guarded. Therefore, monks, those novices who desire full ordination should be placed outside the range of hearing but within the range of sight, their palms joined in reverence, visibly present. In this way no transgression will arise." This is the fifth verse of the sūtra of the second chapter of the ruling case.

In summary:
Requesting forbearance, and the boundary —
shaving hair too is the same.
Overturning the latrine-stand and threatening,
rebuking, and condemning the lineage.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Blessed One, you have said that monks against whom a censure act has been performed should ask for forbearance. Where should they ask for forbearance?"

"Upāli, within the boundary."

"How should they ask for forbearance?"

"Having stood up with hair erect and having risen fully, let them communicate to the Saṅgha that they lay their hair down. Let them demonstrate prostration openly, and they should also restore the overturned latrine-stand."

"Blessed One, if you have said that a censure act should be performed upon monks who overturn the latrine-stand, and if at that time the venerable one becomes displeased when the censure act is being performed upon him, what is to be done in that case?"

"Upāli, among his goods and belongings, some should take away his bowl and robes; others should take away his water vessels and throw them outside and discard them. If he seizes hold of a pillar, cut the pillar. If he seizes hold of a door-post, remove the door-post. And do not fail to turn him away even if he cannot be made to comply. Who should then repair things afterward?"

"The Saṅgha."

"Whose task is it to gather the repaired goods? Request them from the donors. If they are not forthcoming, have them provided from the common wealth of the entire Saṅgha. Do not be in doubt about this."

"If it is a venerable nun who overturns the latrine-stand, should a censure act also be performed upon her?"

"Upāli, a censure act should indeed be performed upon her also." From "if she becomes displeased" up through "do not be in doubt about this," it is as before.

"Blessed One, and if a female trainee, a male novice, or a female novice overturns the latrine-stand, should a censure act also be performed upon them?"

From "do not be in doubt about this," it is as before.

"Blessed One, you have said that a banishment act should be performed upon a monk who condemns the lineage. If at that time the venerable one becomes displeased when the banishment act is being performed upon him, what is to be done?"

"Upāli, from 'his goods and belongings' up through 'do not be in doubt about this,' it is as before." Likewise, if it is a nun who condemns the lineage, or a female trainee, a male novice, or a female novice — a banishment act should also be performed upon them — up through "do not be in doubt about this," it is as before. This is the sixth verse of the sūtra of the second chapter of the ruling case.

The Noble Vinaya, the thirty-third fascicle.

The venerable Blessed One declared: "Expel a monk who has transgressed the moral discipline." By whom should he be expelled? He should be expelled by the Saṅgha. As for his belongings, some should take his bowl and robe; others should take his various miscellaneous vessels, carry them outside, and set them down. If he clings to a pillar, the pillar should be cut. If he clings to a doorpost, the doorpost too should be removed — but do not refrain from dismissing him on account of it. By whom should repairs subsequently be made? By the Saṅgha. To whom should the materials for repair be solicited? The patrons (upāsakas) should be urged. If they too are unable to provide, repairs should be made with the wealth of the entire Saṅgha — do not be in doubt about this. Just as in the case of a monk who has transgressed the moral discipline, so too it is the same for a nun, a female trainee, a male novice, and a female novice.

The venerable Blessed One declared: "Perform a reconciliation act upon a monk who speaks ill of laypeople." Then if a nun also speaks ill of laypeople, should a reconciliation act be performed upon her as well? Upāli, let a reconciliation act be performed upon her too. And so it is likewise for a female trainee, a male novice, and a female novice.

The venerable Blessed One declared: "Let a reconciliation act be performed upon a monk who speaks ill of laypeople." If a monk speaks ill of a monk, should a reconciliation act be performed upon him as well? Upāli, a reconciliation act should be performed upon him too. And a monk who speaks ill of a nun, a female trainee, a male novice, or a female novice — it is the same likewise. A female trainee who speaks ill of a nun, a monk, a female trainee, a male novice, or a female novice — it is the same likewise. A female trainee who speaks ill of another female trainee, a monk, a nun, a male novice, or a female novice — it is the same likewise. A male novice who speaks ill of another male novice, a monk, a nun, a female trainee, or a female novice — it is the same likewise. A female novice who speaks ill of another female novice, a monk, a nun, a female trainee, or a male novice — it is the same likewise. And so it is elaborated extensively, turning like a wheel. This is the seventh verse of the sūtra of the ruling case of the second chapter.

In brief:

Novices, and the censure act,
those unable to remain because fewer than five —
as Upāli inquired about these,
five evenings' worth of answers were given.

The buddha, the Blessed One, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One: "Venerable one, if a male novice upon whom a monk has performed a censure act is then given full ordination, is he to be called fully ordained, or not fully ordained?" Upāli, the ordination itself is completed, but the one who performed the ordination has acted in a manner that is past and done. The approval is called the motion.

The venerable Blessed One declared: "If one has completed five years and possesses five qualities, one may be permitted to use a mentor's requisites without a fixed residence." If one has completed four years and possesses five qualities, would such a one also be permitted to use a mentor's requisites without a fixed residence? Upāli, that is not permitted. Why is that? Because five years not yet completed is not fitting. If one has completed six or nine years but does not possess the five qualities, would that one be permitted to use a mentor's requisites without a fixed residence? Upāli, that is not permitted. Why is that? Because one must possess the five qualities.

The venerable one asked: if a monk has completed three years since full ordination and also possesses the three scriptural collections —

and is also endowed with the three kinds of knowledge and free from the three defilements — would such a one also be permitted to use a mentor's requisites without a fixed residence? Upāli, the same applies in that case as well. Why is that? Because it must be done in the prescribed manner. For how long may requisites be given to one without a fixed residence? Upāli, even if they are many, it is for up to five days — and even then only while that one is seeking a fixed residence and has not abandoned the effort.

This is the eighth verse of the sūtra of the second section on the grounds for narrative.

In brief:
Concordant and discordant,
with and without measure,
suspended and not suspended,
likewise name and class.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable One, there is said to be a transgression that is concordant and also one that is discordant — what, Venerable One, is a concordant transgression, and what is a discordant one? Upāli, defeats (pārājika) are concordant with defeats and discordant with the others. A remainder offense with the Saṅgha is concordant with a remainder offense with the Saṅgha. A downfall is concordant with a downfall. A transgression requiring individual confession is concordant with a transgression requiring individual confession. A wrong act is concordant with a wrong act.

Venerable One, there is also said to be a transgression that has measure and one that does not have measure — what, Venerable One, is a transgression with measure, and what is one without measure? Upāli, whatever one remembers the boundaries of the person and the boundaries of the offense, that is called having measure. Whatever one does not remember the boundaries of the person and the offense, that is called not having measure.

Venerable One, there is also said to be a transgression that is suspended and one that is not suspended — what, Venerable One, is a suspended transgression, and what is one that is not suspended? Upāli, suspension is of two kinds: suspension by intention and suspension by days. Of these, what is suspended by days is not suspended. What is suspended by intention is called suspended.

Venerable One, regarding the name and class of transgressions — what, Venerable One, is the name, and what is the class? Upāli, defeats are the name; what arises from them is the class. What is called a remainder offense with the Saṅgha is the name; what arises from it is the class. Downfalls, individually confessed transgressions, and wrong acts are the names; what arises from them are the classes.

This is the ninth verse of the sūtra of the second section on the grounds for narrative.

In brief:
Expelled by a penalty,
surrendering the training and not practicing —
to such ones faith is not given;
one either performs or does not accept the role of monk.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The group of six monks had incurred remainder offenses with the Saṅgha, and having been penalized, they formed a circle within the enclosure and enacted the penalty. The monks said to them: "Venerable Ones, what are you doing?" They replied: "We are enacting the penalty." The monks said: "This is one who has been restored — it is not a penalty." Then those monks sat there without saying anything further.

When this had occurred, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not enact a penalty act where only a single monk resides. Monks, do not enact a penalty act where two or three monks reside. Where four monks or more than four reside, monks should enact the penalty, the penalty raised from the basis, restoration from the basis, appeasement, appeasement raised from the basis, and raise from the basis and perform appeasement."

After the Blessed One had declared that monks should enact the penalty, the penalty raised from the basis, restoration from the basis, appeasement, appeasement raised from the basis, and raise from the basis and perform appeasement in places where four or more than four monks reside — monks then enacted a penalty against four monks who had relinquished their training. The Blessed One declared: "I do not permit enacting a penalty against four monks who have relinquished their training." After the Blessed One had declared that he did not permit enacting a penalty against four monks who have relinquished their training, monks enacted it against three who had relinquished their training and one who was dwelling in proper accordance with it; then against two who had relinquished their training and two who were dwelling in proper accordance; then against one who had relinquished their training and three who were dwelling in proper accordance. When this had occurred, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not enact a penalty against four who have relinquished their training. Do not enact it against three who have relinquished their training and one who is dwelling in proper accordance. Do not enact it against two who have relinquished their training and two who are dwelling in proper accordance. Do not enact it against one who has relinquished their training and three who are dwelling in proper accordance. Rather, enact the penalty against a complete four — or more than four — who are all fully pure. And just as this applies to enacting a penalty, the same holds likewise for the penalty raised from the basis, restoration from the basis, performing appeasement, raising from the basis and performing appeasement, and performing appeasement raised from the basis."

Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "May faith be taken from one who has relinquished the training?" Upāli replied: "That is not permitted. But if one has come into contact with the Dharma itself, then it is permitted." "Venerable one, may the going-forth be received from one who has relinquished the training?" "Upāli, if the perception of that person as a monk is maintained, then from the very beginning it is permitted."

The tenth verse-section of the second chapter on the base-case has been completed. The second chapter is complete.

The summary verse:

The maṇḍala, the alms-bowl, the parasol and shelter,
Drinking smoke, and the small cup,
An iron comb, the nave of a chariot,
The stretcher-pole, the lamp, and the stūpa.

In brief: the maṇḍala, the abode of the gods,
A half, a third, and an undesignated spot;
Going forth without an alms-bowl,
And not diminishing the alms-bowl.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Monks were washing their alms-bowls here and there wherever they happened to be, and when that area became filled with bees and turned unsightly, brahmins and householders saw this and said: "Have the noble ones been relieving themselves and urinating here?" The monks said: "Good sirs, no one has done that here. We have been washing our alms-bowls." The householders said: "Noble ones, you must have been performing a maṇḍala rite here." And they sat there without saying anything further. Then they mocked the monks, saying: "The ascetics, the sons of the Śākyas, are unclean — they wash their alms-bowls wherever they happen to be." When this had occurred, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Since brahmins and householders mock you, henceforth monks must not wash alms-bowls here and there wherever they happen to be. Monks should make a maṇḍala in the very place where the alms-bowls are washed."

When the Blessed One had said "Make a maṇḍala," the monks made a round maṇḍala in the place where they had washed the alms-bowls. Then brahmins and householders came to the monastery, and seeing the maṇḍala on the ground in the middle of the courtyard, asked: "What on earth is this?" Some of them said: "Oh, what is there to know about looking at this? The ascetics, the sons of the Śākyas, worship the sun." Others said: "Yes, that is so — the ascetics, the sons of the Śākyas, truly do worship the sun." When this had occurred, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, do not make a maṇḍala that resembles the sun." When the Blessed One had said not to make a maṇḍala resembling the sun, the monks made a maṇḍala shaped like a crescent moon. Again brahmins and householders came to the monastery and said: "The ascetics, the sons of the Śākyas, worship the moon." When this had occurred, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, do not make a maṇḍala resembling the moon either." The monks then set about making a square one, and again brahmins and householders came to that monastery and said: "The ascetics, the sons of the Śākyas, worship the cow." When this had occurred, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, do not make the maṇḍala square, and do not make it in either of those two shapes. Make it resembling a lance-tip or a drum." The monks did not know how to go about this, and the Blessed One declared: "Smear it with cow dung, or with earth, or with water." The Blessed One then said: "Make the maṇḍala in these two ways." The monks made such a maṇḍala in two forms for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and those present were pleased. When this had occurred, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "For the Three Jewels, whether in the form of the sun or the moon, or in whatever way one has faith, do it in every manner — have no doubt about it."

The occasion is in Śrāvastī. The Blessed One then declared to the monks: "Monks, those who give alms and the patrons who give offerings should from time to time properly please, properly honor, and properly bring happiness to the gods who receive the food offerings, in three ways. What are the three? From time to time sweep the area clean; from time to time also perform the task of setting out the food offerings; and from time to time dedicate the merit of what has been given. Monks, when those who give alms and the patrons properly please, properly honor, and properly bring happiness to the gods who receive the food offerings in this way, those gods in turn regard the givers and patrons with affection and goodwill."

When the Blessed One had said these words, the Sugata having spoken, the Teacher then declared further in verse:

Those faithful persons who
honor the gods,
who act in accordance with the Teacher's word —
even the buddhas praise them.

In whatever place there dwell
the wise, the learned, the morally disciplined —
proclaim there the giving of food and make it known;
through gaining such ones, one will be honored.

Through making offerings, one becomes worthy of offering.
After that, with tender heart,
as a mother toward her child,
those who are cherished by the gods
will behold happiness and all that is good.

When faithful persons honor the gods, the Blessed One declared, they are acting in accordance with the Teacher's word.

— buddhas too have praised them — thus did the Blessed One speak.

Now the group of six monks began making offerings to the gods of the fence, the gods of the forest, the gods of the crossroads, the gods of the triple junction, and the gods of the world, and so forth, making offerings to all of them. Then faithful brahmins and faithful householders, having heard this noble teaching declared as wholesome by the Blessed One, thought: if one who has gone forth under the Dharma and Vinaya declared virtuous by these noble ones were to make offerings to those who harm beings by eating flesh and blood, by consuming fat and sinew, and by taking the lives of others — while we lay practitioners must long abandon such things — then this is what it means to make offerings. They spoke thus to censure them with blame and to speak ill of them, and the monks drove those of the group of six away.

Then some of the monks said: "Venerable ones, did the Blessed One not declare: 'When faithful persons — men and women — make offerings to the gods, they are acting in accordance with the Teacher's word, and buddhas too have praised them'? Are we not also persons of faith? Why, then, should we not make offerings?" So they spoke.

When this had come to pass, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, I spoke that with laypeople in mind — not for monks. Therefore, monks, do not make offerings to the gods."

After the Blessed One had declared that monks should not make offerings to the gods, the group of six monks set out to interfere with those who did make such offerings and to harm them. Then gods appeared in the dreams of those monks, saying: "What wrong have we done to you that you should harm us?" And brahmins and householders who had no faith mocked the noble ones, saying: "What harm have these noble ones done to you that you should treat them so badly?"

When this had come to pass, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then declared: "Do not make offerings to them, but do not harm them either."

Then the group of six monks set out on a road, and when they passed by shrines of the gods they turned off the road and went by way of uneven paths full of thorns. Some monks were trodden down by mud; some were pierced by thorns; some tumbled into ditches. When this had come to pass, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not turn off the road. Keep to the straight path. When you come to a shrine of the gods, make a snapping sound with the fingers and recite aloud the verse spoken from the Blessed One's own mouth. Do not hesitate in this."

The occasion for the next rule arose at Śrāvastī. The venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, you have declared that a monk of the same community and a personal attendant monk should attend upon his preceptor and teacher three times a day, and also that they should remain within a major boundary of two and a half yojanas. Venerable One, if the teacher and preceptor are two and a half yojanas away, how often should they attend on him?" "Upāli, they should attend every half month. If those persons dwell within the range of a yojana, they should attend every seven or eight days. Within that distance, they should attend at the proper times. If they dwell within five hundred fathoms, they should attend three times a day. If they fail to attend accordingly, it becomes a transgression."

Another occasion arose at Śrāvastī. A person who wished to take full ordination under the venerable Ānanda came and Ānanda ordained him without an alms-bowl. At that time the monks washed their own bowls, set them in their proper places, made prostrations to the stūpa, each took up his own bowl, and went to the place for taking the meal. When the monks, while eating their meal, washed their bowls and then proceeded to make prostrations to the stūpa —

That newly ordained monk also made prostrations together with the others. At the moment when the monks, having made prostrations to the stūpa, washed their hands, that newly ordained monk took up the alms-bowl of the elder Kauṇḍinya, who was known to all, and Kauṇḍinya took it back. Then he reached for the bowls of Gavāṃpati, Mahānāma, Aśvajit, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Ānanda, Revata, and the others, and each of them likewise took their bowls back. He sat off to one side with tears filling his eyes. The monks who had not yet abandoned attachment made the accusation: "Who ordained someone without an alms-bowl?" Some said it was the venerable Ānanda, and then remarked: "Who else but one who behaves in grossly improper ways would do such a thing?" The monks who had become aware of what happened reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, such accusations are frivolous. Therefore, monks, before conferring full ordination on someone who has no alms-bowl, first seek an alms-bowl for him and only then confer ordination. If none is available, I myself shall provide a small bowl. If a monk confers full ordination without an alms-bowl, there will be an offense."

The occasion for the next rule arose at Śrāvastī. The venerable Aśvajit had a young attendant who carried his alms-bowl. This attendant washed both his own and Aśvajit's bowl, but since the two bowls were alike he could not tell which was his and which was his preceptor's. Some time later he wrote "Preceptor Aśvajit's bowl" on the bottom of the venerable Aśvajit's bowl.

Later, another householder invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, to a meal at his home. This householder had a former courtesan whom he had previously kept. He sent word to her: "My dear, I have invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha to a meal; come and serve with your own hands." But as it happened, something else came up and she did not go. The Blessed One and the community of monk-hearers were fed, the gift-dedication was spoken, and they departed. The young attendant carrying the venerable Aśvajit's bowl remained there, planning to wash the bowl before leaving. The householder said to him: "Noble one, lend me the bowl for a moment — I shall send some leftover food to a certain friend." The attendant replied that his own he could not give, but offered the venerable Aśvajit's bowl. The householder filled it with pure food and drink, and sent it to the courtesan with the message: "My dear, I have satisfied the community of monks headed by the Buddha with food such as this; please rejoice on their behalf." When she received the food and was about to eat it, she saw an inscription on the bottom of the bowl. Now, women are skilled in all eighteen scripts. She read it and saw the name of the venerable Aśvajit. She thought to herself: "It is improper of me to have sent back in this way the bowl of the noble Aśvajit, who is venerated by gods and men." She inquired about the bowl, then filled it with fragrant, beautiful flowers, placed it upon a painted stand, and sat before it, bowing down and worshipping it with incense.

Then another man arrived bearing five hundred kārṣāpaṇa coins along with perfumes and garlands, and said to her: "Good woman, whatever you are doing, come away with me." She replied: "Wait a moment — I am making an offering to this bowl." He then asked: "Where did this bowl come from, and to whom does it belong?" She told him everything in detail, exactly as it had occurred. He said: "You give generously even to all sorts of remarkable beings, yet you have let the renunciants slip away." At that she covered her ears and said: "Do not do such a wicked thing as that — it would be the cause of going to hell." Though she spoke thus, he would not desist from his improper behavior, and she did not yield to him.

The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One considered it. He reflected that a monk who inscribes what ought not to be inscribed thereby incurs an offense, and therefore declared: "Monks, do not inscribe what ought not to be inscribed." And further: "Monks, do not engrave what ought not to be engraved." The monks, not knowing what ought not to be engraved, asked, and the Blessed One declared: "There are five kinds of what ought not to be engraved: all the codes of individual liberation, anything pertaining to individual liberation, all the Vinaya, anything pertaining throughout the Vinaya, and individual persons. Marking something with an identifying sign, however, is without offense." This is the first verse of the sūtra of the third topic of the origin narrative.

In brief:
A novice broke an alms bowl.
How should an alms bowl be burned?
The use of a fire cover is to be permitted.
The Great Sage authorized it.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain monk caused the novice who was holding his senior monk's alms bowl to carry it by the strap, and since that novice lacked proper mindfulness it slipped from his hands and broke. The monk was distraught. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One considered it. He reflected that a monk who causes a novice to carry an alms bowl by the strap thereby incurs an offense, and declared: "Monks, do not cause novices to carry the alms bowl by the strap."

After the Blessed One had given this training rule — "Monks, do not cause novices to carry the alms bowl by the strap" — the novice disciple of the venerable Śāriputra named Cundaka was holding his preceptor's alms bowl. When his preceptor said to him, "Hand over the bowl — I will wash it myself," Cundaka replied: "The Blessed One has established a training rule that a monk must not cause novices to carry the alms bowl by the strap, so I myself will wash it; you go elsewhere." The preceptor then asked: "Will I myself also incur an offense?" Cundaka replied: "The Blessed Buddha is the master of the Dharma — what am I to do?" The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Those novices who are possessed of mindfulness may indeed carry the bowl by the strap. Have no doubt about this."

The origin narrative is at Śrāvastī. Monks ate food from the alms bowl and then, without cleaning it, covered it and carried it away, whereupon it split open. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Burn the alms bowl." After the Blessed One had said "Burn the alms bowl," the monks burned the bowl with wood, and the bowl was ruined. The Blessed One then declared: "Do not burn it with wood."

The monks wrapped the bowl in grass and chaff and fired it, and this very act became the occasion for a transgression. The Blessed One then declared: "Do not fire it wrapped in grass and chaff." Since the monks did not know how else to fire it, the Blessed One declared: "Prepare a firing cover for the alms bowl." Since the monks did not know how to prepare a firing cover for the alms bowl, the Blessed One declared: "There are two kinds of firing cover: one made by a craftsman, and one made by oneself. The kind made by a craftsman is like a pot. The kind made by oneself may be either a tube or a clay vessel — fill it with ash, and coat the outside of the clay vessel to whatever depth is fitting." When the monks then fired the bowl inside a cooking pot in the same way, this too became the occasion for a transgression. The Blessed One declared: "On the outside, smear it with a mixture of clay and chaff to a solid coat, and on the inside coat it with sesame residue or cow dung; let it dry. Sweep the ground clean, and beneath it lay a bed of chaff, sesame residue, and other materials that will improve the firing. Cover it over with grass, dung, and chaff, and take care that no smoke escapes, and fire it. Tend to it on both sides, turning it and smothering it carefully, so that the living creatures inside may be at ease. When the firing is finished and it has cooled, take out the alms bowl, rinse it, and continue to fire it until it takes on a sky-blue color." Therefore the alms bowl firing cover and the implements for firing are hereby permitted. This concludes the second verse-summary of the third origin narrative of the sūtra.

In brief: the first narrative, the bath house, the third concerning the layman — likewise, the suspension cord and then hair, and all things made with dung — all these have been heard.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī a certain householder constructed a bath house for the Saṅgha. Thereupon the Group of Six monks, covering themselves below with a single garment, engaged in manual work together in close proximity. Some brahmins and householders arrived at that place and, seeing this, said: "Now who are these who behave in such a manner?" Some among them said: "They are non-Buddhists (tīrthikas)." Others said: "No, they are not non-Buddhists — they are the ascetics (śramaṇas), sons of the Śākya." And they began to mock them, saying: "If the Teacher himself is possessed of shame, why are these ones without shame or modesty?" The monks reported this state of affairs to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is indeed improper that brahmins and householders should mock you. Therefore, monks, do not perform manual work together in a bath house wearing only a single garment. If monks perform work in a bath house while wearing only a single garment, they incur a transgression together with its past instances."

The origin narrative is at Śrāvastī. A certain householder at Śrāvastī constructed a bath house for the Saṅgha, and the monks there anointed themselves with grain ghee, touching the feet and then touching the head, touching the head and then touching the mouth, touching the mouth and then touching the hands and feet, touching the hands and feet and then touching the mouth again, and sat there with a poor, worn garment covering them below. Then a certain faithless householder came to that place and, seeing the monks, began to mock them, saying: "These ascetic sons of the Śākya are impure! They touch what they have touched with their feet to their mouths, and they sit there with a poor garment covering them."

"You are sitting naked in the midst of householders!" At this, the monks who were present reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is shameful to mock brahmins and householders. Therefore, do not allow laypeople into the bathhouse, and do not allow the faithless to work there. Assign monks as doorkeepers of the bathhouse, and have them not let householders inside." The Blessed One had declared: "Do not send laypeople into the bathhouse, and do not allow them to work there."

Then, at a later time, when the monks had gone into the bathhouse, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada came there, and the monk who was doorkeeper said to him: "Householder, do not go inside. The Blessed One has declared that laypeople are not to be sent into the bathhouse." The householder replied: "O noble ones, would I too become someone else? I will certainly perform service for the noble ones!" The monks who were present reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Those who have faith, let them into the bathhouse and allow them to work. Do not be uncertain about this." The Blessed One had declared: "Those who have faith, let them into the bathhouse and allow them to work."

Then, when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went inside, a brahmin came along with him and was not admitted. The brahmin said: "O noble ones, why is the householder Anāthapiṇḍada sent inside while I am not?" The monk said to him: "Brahmin, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was sent in because of his faith." The brahmin replied: "Well then, if I too were to become faithful, would you send me in?" The monks who were present reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If he has indeed become faithful, let him in." Then the monks gave him the three refuges and let him inside.

Once inside, he too saw the monks touching their feet and then touching their mouths and heads, and sitting with a poor, worn garment covering them below. He became faithless and launched into mockery, saying: "These ascetic sons of the Śākya are impure! They touch what they have touched with their feet to their mouths and heads, and they sit with a poor garment covering them!" The monks who were present reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, let only those of firm faith inside the bathhouse, and do not admit those of weak faith."

The Vinaya, the Supreme Text. The thirty-fourth fascicle.

The occasion is at Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī, a certain other householder invited the buddha together with the monastic Saṅgha of monks to his bathhouse, and the monks went inside. There, a monk who was an arhat was performing a service for a monk of broken moral discipline. The Blessed One also entered and, seeing him performing this service, declared to the monks: "Monks, did you see this monk performing a service for that monk?" "Venerable One, we saw it," they replied. "The monk performing this service is an arhat, one whose defilements are exhausted. But the one for whom the service is being performed has broken moral discipline; he is one of evil character, rotten, corrupt, festering, behaving like a hidden enemy, not a true ascetic though claiming to be one, not a practitioner of the holy life though claiming to be one. Therefore, monks, let not one who is like a lion perform the service of one who is like a jackal. If he does so, he comes to be one who has transgressed." The Blessed One had declared: "Let not one who is like a lion perform the service of one like a jackal."

Now in Śrāvastī there was another householder who took a wife from a family of equal standing, and together with her he enjoyed himself in pleasure and delight. From that pleasurable enjoyment, in the course of time his wife became with child, and after eight or nine months had passed she gave birth, and a son was born. He was fine in form, beautiful and lovely to behold, endowed with all his limbs — and upon his birth a great birth-celebration was held, and a name was given to him. He was nursed and raised until he grew up, and then in the course of time he went to the Jeta Grove and went forth into the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya. He came to possess the three collections of scripture. He reflected thus: "The Blessed One has said that a son's parents are those who toil with difficulty, who give benefit, who nourish, who raise him, who suckle him at the breast, and who reveal to him the diverse world of Jambudvīpa. And yet even if a son were to carry his mother on one shoulder and his father on the other for a full hundred years, or even if he were to install them as lords and sovereigns over a great realm filled with jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch, crystal, gold, silver, agate, and red coral, and things such as right-coiling conches of the like — not even by such means would a son have repaid or fully repaid his father and mother. But whoever establishes parents who have no faith in full and perfect faith, who rouses them, tames them, leads them in, and settles them; who from poor moral discipline establishes them in perfect moral discipline, from miserliness establishes them in perfect generosity, and from confused wisdom establishes them in perfect wisdom — rousing them, taming them, leading them in, and settling them aright: in such a way does a son repay and fully repay his father and mother." So having reflected in this way, he thought: "Let me too do something, however small, to be of benefit to my parents." And so he enjoyed the pleasures of youth for as long as he wished while living in Śrāvastī, then departed from there enjoying those pleasures as he went, gradually enjoying them as he traveled, and finally arrived at Śrāvastī. He then established those two in taking refuge and set them thoroughly in the training precepts.

Then in the course of time he recounted to his father in full the qualities of those seven goods through which merit is made from wealth. The noble one said: "Father, I too shall make some merit through the seven kinds of noble wealth." His father replied: "Old man, well then — do so!" "What shall I do?" "Build a rest-house." So he built a rest-house, and the householder himself entered upon his own work in his own rest-house. He labored greatly, and when it was done, much washing water, oil, flour, and the like remained. Then the father said: "Son, I am very tired — scratch my back a little." The son replied: "Father, the Blessed One declared, 'Let not one who is like a lion perform service for those who are like jackals,' and has not permitted it."

The father said: "Son, who is the lion and who is the jackal?" The son replied: "Father, I am like the lion; you are like the jackal." The father said: "Son, why is that?" The son replied: "Father, you possess moral discipline; you are not endowed with poor moral discipline." "Son," said the father, "is it so that from one like a jackal, such as I, one like a lion, such as you, was born?"

When this had come to pass, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, that family in which the parents are properly pleased, properly honored, and properly maintained in happiness — that family is one that dwells together with Brahmā. And why is this so?

"Monks, that family in which a son acts rightly toward his parents in accordance with the Dharma — one who acts thus in accordance with the Dharma is called a Brahmā. Monks, that family in which the parents are properly pleased, properly honored, and properly maintained in happiness — that family is one that dwells together with a teacher. And why is this so? Because when a son acts rightly toward his parents in accordance with the Dharma, he becomes like a teacher. Monks, that family in which the parents are properly pleased, properly honored, and properly maintained in happiness — that family is one worthy of generosity. And why is this so? Because when a son acts rightly toward his parents in accordance with the Dharma, that family is worthy of generosity. Monks, that family in which the parents are properly pleased, properly honored, and properly maintained in happiness — that family is one that dwells together with fire. And why is this so? Because when a son acts rightly toward his parents in accordance with the Dharma, they are like fire. Monks, that family in which the parents are properly pleased, properly honored, and properly maintained in happiness — that family is one that dwells together with the gods. And why is this so? Because when a son acts rightly toward his parents in accordance with the Dharma, they become like gods."

When the Blessed One had so declared, and after the Sugata had thus spoken, the Teacher spoke again in verse:

Father and mother are Brahmā;
they are likewise teacher and god.
As a servant tends the fire-god,
so the parents are worthy of a son's offerings.

Therefore one should bow to them with reverence,
honor them, bathe them,
wash their very feet as well —
so should the wise attend upon them.

With food and drink,
with clothing and bedding likewise,
if the wise one serves with such care
both father and mother —
here in this life no grief shall come,
and having gone hence, one shall rejoice in the heavens.

When the Blessed One had taught this sūtra, the monks were filled with doubt, and having been filled with doubt, they asked the Blessed One, the buddha, who cuts through all doubt: "Revered Blessed One, it is wonderful that you have spoken of the virtue of attending upon father, mother, and teacher."

The Blessed One then declared: "Monks, what is so wonderful about this? Now, while the Tathāgata is free from attachment, free from aversion, free from delusion — free from birth, old age, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, displeasure, and distress — he nevertheless speaks of the virtue of attending upon one's parents. In times long past, when I had not yet been freed from attachment, aversion, and delusion, from birth, old age, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, displeasure, and distress, I once did a small harm to my mother and in consequence experienced great suffering; and having done a small good for her, I experienced great happiness in consequence. Hold these events well in mind, for I shall tell them to you.

What happened in the past: Monks, in times long past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a caravan-leader named Mitra, who was wealthy, of great possessions, and of great fortune, whose estate was vast and wide — comparable to the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa, a rival to the riches of Vaiśravaṇa. He took a wife of equal birth, and together with her he lived in enjoyment and delight. Though sons were born to him from that life of enjoyment together, they all died, and so he was without a son; and desiring a son, he prayed to a thousand gods — Agulāng, Varuṇa, Vaiśravaṇa, Vāsava, and others — yet no living son came to him.

Someone else had told him: "If a son is born to you, give him a girl's name, and he will live long." Then, in later days, he lived together with his wife in enjoyment and delight. Through that enjoyment together, his wife conceived a child, and after eight or nine months she gave birth to a boy. He was handsome and beautiful to behold, fair and lovely, with a complexion like golden hue, a head like a parasol, long arms, a broad forehead, a long neck, even eyebrows, a high nose — endowed with all the major and minor marks of a fine form. Upon his birth they held a great birth-feast and then set about giving him a name. Since a friend had instructed that the boy be given a girl's name, the child was named Priyā — "Dear Girl." And as the child called Priyā grew up, his father ventured into the great ocean — and there he died.

Then Priyā said to his mother: "Mother, by what fruit of my father's former karma do we live? I too will do likewise in time to come." The mother thought: "If I tell him that his father was a merchant who entered the great ocean, then he too will enter the great ocean and die there." So she said to him: "Son, your father used to trade in grain. If you wish, you may trade in grain." So he built a grain stall, and on the first day he earned four kārṣāpaṇas, and he gave them to his mother.

Then, in later days, someone else told him: "Your father used to trade in perfumes." Thereupon he abandoned the grain trade and set up a perfume stall. On the very first day he earned eight kārṣāpaṇas, and again he gave them to his mother.

Then, in later days, someone else told him: "Your father was a gold trader." So he abandoned the perfume trade and took up dealing in gold. On the first day he earned sixteen kārṣāpaṇas, and again he gave them all to his mother. The next day he earned thirty-two kārṣāpaṇas, and gave those to his mother as well.

Then the gold traders, who were full of jealousy, thought: "This one is going to corner all the gold in every city." And so they said to Priyā: "What kind of life is this for you, going on like this? Your father was a merchant who entered the great ocean — who has let you fall into such a wretched livelihood as this?"

Stirred by the words of those gold traders, Priyā went to his mother and said: "Mother, I have now heard that my father was indeed a merchant of the great ocean in former times. Do not grieve. I too will enter the great ocean." The mother said to him: "Son, that is true — but you are young and my only child. Do not abandon me and go to the great ocean." But Priyā did not heed his mother's words. He proclaimed himself a caravan-leader and announced: "Let all those in the city who wish to enter the great ocean come with me."

Then, accompanied by five hundred merchants, he set out. His mother, overwhelmed with grief and heartache, weeping and streaming with tears, seized him by both feet and cried: "Son, do not abandon me and enter the great ocean!" But he — feeling neither compassion nor joy at her quiet pleading — flew into a rage and kicked his mother on the head with his foot. Then he went on his way in the company of many travelers.

His mother said: "May this karma not ripen upon you, my son."

Then he passed through villages and towns and —

He looked upon the retinue in the royal palace and made his way to the shore of the great ocean. There he bought a large ship with five hundred old coins, and he hired men to load and unload the vessel, to bail it, to handle the ropes, and to navigate by the stars. He struck a great bell three times in proclamation, then set out and sailed into the great ocean. But after a time, water-monsters and sea creatures made the ship unnavigable. He clung to a plank of wood together with his beloved and reached the far shore. Then he came to dry land.

He saw a city called Joyful and went to it. There he was met by four divine maidens of fine form and lovely to behold, who said to him: "Dear beloved, have you come safely? These are our houses of food and drink, our houses of clothing, our houses of rest — all full of jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli (vaiḍūrya), conch, crystal, coral, gold, and silver. Take all of this. Come inside and dwell with us." And so he dwelt with them for many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, many hundreds of thousands of years, enjoying pleasures just as a sentient being who has accumulated merit, performed virtue, and who through great miraculous power and great force comes to enjoy the fruits of that merit. They instructed him: "Do not take the road to the south." Yet even as they forbade him, he felt ever more drawn in that direction. After some time he went along the southern road, and he saw a city called Ever Joyous and came to its gate. There he was met by eight divine maidens more beautiful than the first, lovelier to behold, more radiant than those before, who said: "Dear beloved, have you come safely? Come inside, dear beloved. These are our houses of food and drink, our houses of clothing, our houses of rest — all filled with jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch, crystal, coral, gold, and silver. Come inside and dwell with us." And so he dwelt with them for many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, many hundreds of thousands of years, enjoying pleasures just as a sentient being who has accumulated merit and virtue, and who through great miraculous power and great force comes to enjoy such fruits. They too instructed him: "Do not take the road to the south." Yet even as they forbade him, he felt all the more drawn that way and wished to go, and after some time he went along the southern road. He saw a city called Full of Joy and came to its gate.
