There again sixteen divine maidens appeared, more beautiful than those before, lovelier to behold, more radiant than any yet, who said: "Dear beloved, have you come safely? Dear beloved, come inside. These are our houses of food and drink, our houses of clothing, our houses of rest — all filled with jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch, crystal, coral, gold, and silver. Come inside and dwell with us." And so he dwelt with them for many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, many hundreds of thousands of years, enjoying pleasures just as a sentient being who has accumulated merit and virtue and who through great miraculous power and great force comes to enjoy such fruits. They too instructed him: "Do not take the road to the south." Yet even as they forbade him, he felt ever more pulled in that direction and wished to go, and after some time he set out along the southern road. He saw a fine mansion called the Brahma Dwelling of the Teacher and came to its gate. Inside he found a divine maiden more beautiful than all those before —

Even more beautiful than she — thirty-two of them appeared, and they said to her: "Welcome, dear friend. Are you well arrived? We have here a hall of food, a hall of drink, a hall of robes, a hall for sleeping, filled with all manner of things — jewels, pearls, beryl, conch, crystal, coral, gold, silver, and the rest in great variety. Come, and dwell here with us." And so he enjoyed things together with them for many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, many hundreds of thousands of years, just as a sentient being who has accumulated merit and virtue and who through great miraculous power and great force comes to enjoy such fruits. They too instructed him: "Do not take the road to the south." Yet even as they forbade him, he felt ever more pulled in that direction and wished to go, and after some time he set out along the southern road. As he traveled further south, devotion arose in him, and he continued gradually southward until he saw a city built entirely of iron and entered it. The moment he entered, the gate was shut behind him. He went further inside, and that gate too was shut in the same way. He went still further inside, and again the gate was shut. Then there emerged from within a man of enormous stature, on whose head a burning iron wheel was spinning — blazing, fiercely ablaze, its flames all merged into one — and from his head, pus and blood flowed down, and these were being eaten as food. Then the dear maiden asked that man: "Why have you come to be in this state?" The man replied: "Because I harmed my mother." The instant the man uttered those words, the karma of the dear maiden also ripened openly before her. She thought: "I too harmed my mother, and by that karma I have been brought here and have arrived at this place." And at that very moment a voice from the sky declared: "Whoever is bound is freed; whoever is not bound is bound." The instant that voice arose, the wheel that had been on the man's head was there no more, and a wheel appeared on the head of the dear maiden. Then the man, seeing the dear maiden suffering terribly, spoke these verses:

Always rejoicing and proud,
abandoning delight and happiness,
from the mansion of Brahmā the supreme teacher —
why have you come here?

The dear maiden replied:
Always rejoicing and proud,
abandoning delight and happiness,
from the mansion of Brahmā the supreme teacher —
desiring to come here,
fetched by karma accumulated over a long time.
By karma long accumulated,
wherever karma leads,
there too karma ripens.
By that karma now ripened,
the blazing, fiercely burning wheel
has come to afflict my very life,
and on my head the wheel now burns.

The man spoke:
With a wicked mind you raised your hand
and struck your mother, who was in distress, upon the head —
this is the fruit of that karma.

The dear maiden spoke:
The blazing, fiercely burning wheel
that afflicts my very life —
for how many thousands of years
will it spin upon my head?

The man spoke:
For sixty times a thousand years,
and up to a hundred years beyond,
the blazing iron wheel
will be placed upon your head.

Then the dear maiden said to that man: "Is there yet a prospect that others will come here?" And the man replied:

"Those who have performed such karma as this will come here."

Then the dear maiden, though tormented and afflicted by suffering, roused compassion for all sentient beings and spoke these words to the man: "Good sir, for the sake of all sentient beings I have endured this wheel upon my head. May those others who have performed karma such as this not come here." The moment she had spoken these words, the wheel rose up from the head of that bodhisattva into the sky to the height of seven tāla palms and remained there — and in that same instant she passed away and was born in the realm of the gods of Tuṣita Heaven. So declared the Blessed One.

"Monks, what do you think? She who was called the dear maiden at that time was none other than myself. At that time I was engaged in trade, and through the karmic maturation of the gift I gave — a single copper coin — I experienced supreme happiness in four great cities. But then, through the karmic maturation of the small harm I did to my mother, I experienced suffering such as this. Therefore, monks, train yourselves accordingly. Benefit your father and your mother; do not harm them. One who does not experience such harm as this is like the dear maiden, who experienced it in her life as an ordinary person. She also became endowed with many good qualities, and today she is a Tathāgata. Monks, train yourselves accordingly.

Monks, for this reason, even when one's moral discipline has seriously deteriorated, service is permitted to these five: one's father, one's mother, one's preceptor, one's teacher, and those who are sick."

The occasion for what follows is at Śrāvastī. The Blessed One declared to the monks: "Monks, the sun has risen; the crow caws; the farmer tills the field; and all thieves have gone to their dens."

"Monks, I have used this as a simile; but because its meaning is not understood, that meaning too must be explained. Monks, 'the sun has risen' is a noble utterance of the Tathāgata, the perfectly accomplished buddha. 'The crow caws' is a noble utterance of those persons who are vessels of the Dharma. 'The farmer tills the field' is a noble utterance of those who give and those who are donors. 'All thieves have gone to their dens' is a noble utterance of the retinue of Māra.

Therefore, monks, the Teacher, with affection and out of compassionate purpose, looking to the benefit of his hearers, acting out of compassion, has performed this service for you — and it is now fitting that you act accordingly. Therefore, monks, dwell in solitary places: in forests, at the foot of trees, in empty houses, on hillsides, in ravines, in mountain caves, among piles of straw, in open spaces without shelter, in charnel grounds, in woodland retreats, and at the outermost edges. Monks, do not be heedless. Regret comes later. This instruction I have given is what I have taught you by way of guidance."

Because the Blessed One had spoken of dwelling in solitude — from "regret comes later" and "this is what I have taught" onward, it is as before.

The monks at Śrāvastī then entered into solitary and forested retreats and took up meditative concentration.

At Śrāvastī there was another householder who built a house in the wilderness for monks who dwelt in solitary retreat. After some time another monk who was living off alms, following an ascetic practice, came to Śrāvastī and then returned to the house and stayed there. As time passed his hair and beard grew long, and one early morning he put on his lower robe, took up his bowl and outer robe, and set out.

The householder said to the noble one, "Your hair and beard are long." The monk replied, "There is no one to shave them." The householder then said, "Noble one, please wait here — I will send a barber." The monk set out to collect alms and then returned, and the householder sent a barber as well. Now that monk on his alms round was exceedingly lazy. He had been sitting on a mat while his hair was being shaved, and the cut hair had fallen onto the mat, but he was too indolent to throw it away. The householder thought to send the barber back with the message: "Go and check whether that monk's hair and beard have been shaved or not." The barber went there, found the monk sitting on the mat, and saw that hairs were clinging to his robe. The householder, having been pleased with the monk on his alms round, returned home. His wife said, "My lord's son, were you at the barber's house?" He looked at his robe and saw that hairs were sticking to it, and he thought, "That monk on his alms round must not have had his hair shaved while sitting on the mat — I should go and see." He went and looked, and saw that the mat was full of hair. He then rebuked the monk to his face, saying, "Noble one, do you not even know enough to sweep the hair off the mat after shaving?" The monk on his alms round was mortified, his face burning with shame, and he sat there saying nothing at all.

When this came about, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Monks, those householders are right to reproach him. Therefore, monks, do not shave hair while sitting on a mat." When the Blessed One had declared that monks should not shave hair while sitting on a mat, some monks then shaved in the dwelling hall, in the storage area, and in the gatehouse, and this itself became a matter of offense. The Blessed One then declared, "Do not shave hair in any place used by the Saṅgha for hanging up cloths. If you do, you incur a transgression."

When the Blessed One had declared that hair should not be shaved in places used by the Saṅgha for hanging cloths, some monks were old, feeble, and shivering, and were unable to go outside. Others fell ill, and those who were not ill found it hot and rainy and were also unable to come out, and so they were harmed. When this came about, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Those monks who are old, feeble, and shivering, and those who are sick and uncomfortable, may shave their hair wherever they are. Those who are not sick but for whom it is hot and rainy so that going outside is uncomfortable may also shave their hair wherever they are. In all places, the ground should be swept clean, or it may be swept by someone else. The cut hair should be gathered up and thrown into the midst of the refuse cloths. The cutting of nails follows the same procedure. As for those who are not unwell, they should not do it in that manner — if they do, they incur a transgression."

The occasion for the next rule is as follows. At Śrāvastī a monk fell ill, and though he was treated with medicines made from roots, stems, leaves, and fruits, his illness did not recover. After some time a physician came to the monastery, and the monks said to him, "Good physician, a monk such as this has fallen ill — please prescribe a medical treatment." The physician said, "Noble one, if he eats ground wheat in the evening, he will recover." The monks then said, "Good physician, the Blessed One has not permitted the eating of ground wheat in the evening — how then are we to give him ground wheat to eat in the evening?"

The physician said, "Noble ones, your Teacher is compassionate — he will permit it." The monks then reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, there is such a thing as barley that old oxen without teeth have chewed — therefore I permit it: take ground wheat from barley that an old ox has chewed and give it to him. Have no hesitation about this." But even after they gave him that ground wheat, the monk did not recover. The monks then described the matter in detail to the physician, who said, "Noble ones, that has lost its flavour and is of no benefit — grind other barley and give it to him." The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "In that case, grind barley that has not been eaten by another and give it to the assembly by means of a sieve." Yet even when the monks did so the monk did not recover. The monks described the matter in detail to the physician, who said, "Noble ones, make it into a thick porridge and give it to him, and he will recover." They reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If the physician so prescribes, make the ground wheat into a thick porridge and give it to him — and similarly whatever is made from ground wheat is also permitted; give all of it. Have no hesitation about this."

The narrative setting is at Śrāvastī. At that time at Śrāvastī another monk fell ill. Medicines made from roots, stems, leaves, and fruits were used to treat him, but he did not recover. After some time a physician came to the monastery, and the monks asked him, "Good physician, please prescribe a medical treatment for a monk who is ill in this way." The physician said, "Noble ones, give him broth in the evening and he will recover." The monks said, "Good physician, since the Blessed One has not permitted eating in the evening, how can he eat broth in the evening?" The physician replied, "Noble ones, your Teacher is compassionate — he will permit it." The monks then reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, there is a creature called the she-bear — the meat she has chewed comes out in such a way that I permit it. Therefore take the meat that a she-bear has chewed, make it into broth, and give it to him. Have no hesitation about this." They made broth from the meat a she-bear had chewed and gave it to him, but the monk did not recover. The monks described the matter in detail to the physician, who said, "Noble ones, that has already lost its flavour — give him broth made from fresh meat, and he will recover." The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If the physician so prescribes to make broth from fresh meat, then I permit it: make broth from fresh meat, strain it through cloth, and give it to him." Yet even when the monks did so the monk did not recover. The monks described the matter in detail to the physician, who said, "Noble ones, prepare a compound medicine and give it to him." The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If the physician so prescribes to give him a compound medicine, then give it — and similarly everything that has been cooked down, and all dry things, give them as well. Have no hesitation about this."

This is the third sūtra verse of the third part of the narrative setting.

In summary:

Smoking inhalation and cotton cloth,
nasal irrigation and a small bowl,
needle and lancet and eye ointment —
all these the Great Sage has permitted.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upāli put a question to the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable Blessed One, you have said, 'Keep a tube for smoking inhalation.' Of what kind should one keep it?" "Upāli, of anything except precious materials." "Venerable Blessed One, you have said, 'Keep a cotton cloth.' Of what kind should one keep it?" "Made of wool, of hemp fibre, of woven cloth." "Venerable Blessed One, you have said, 'Keep a vessel for nasal irrigation.' Of what kind should one keep it?" "Upāli, of anything except precious materials." "Venerable Blessed One, you have said, 'Keep a small bowl for drinking in sequence.' Of what kind should one keep it?" "Upāli, of anything except precious materials." "Venerable Blessed One, you have said, 'Keep a lancet.' Of what kind should one keep it?" "Upāli, of anything except precious materials." "Venerable Blessed One, you have said, 'Keep a container for eye ointment.' Of what kind should one keep it?" "Upāli, of anything except precious materials."

This is the fourth sūtra verse of the third part of the narrative setting.

In summary:

A medicine bowl and a yarn winder,
a footrest and a foot support,
medicinal washes and a fee,
and the robe of one who has died.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upāli put a question to the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable Blessed One, you have said, 'Keep a medicine bowl.' Of what kind should one keep it?" "Upāli, of anything except precious materials." "Venerable Blessed One, you have said, 'Keep a yarn winder.' Of what kind should one keep it?" "Upāli, it is made of seven kinds of thread: wool, hemp fibre, cotton wool, nettle fibre, coarse grass fibre, jute fibre, and silk thread." "Venerable Blessed One, you have said, 'Keep a foot support.' Of what kind should one keep it?" "Upāli, of anything except precious materials." "Venerable Blessed One, you have said, 'Keep a couch and a foot support.' Of what kind should one keep it?" "Upāli, of anything except precious materials."

Now the narrative setting is at Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī, a certain householder fell ill and consulted a physician, saying, "Good sir, I am afflicted with such-and-such a disease; please show me a means of medical treatment." The physician said to him, "Householder, first eat an oily preparation, and afterwards undergo a medicinal wash." So the householder began eating the oily preparation. After some time, a monk who was going near to that village came to him, and said, "Householder, what are you doing?" The householder told him in detail how things stood. The monk said, "Householder, I am skilled at administering medicinal washes — give me the fee you would give the physician, and I will give you a medicinal wash." The householder replied, "Excellent, I will do exactly so," and the monk administered the medicinal wash to him and then rose and went to the monastery. After the householder's medicinal wash had been completed, his relatives went and asked the physician, "What is to be done when that householder has had his medicinal wash?" The physician said, "Who administered the wash?" They replied, "A noble one of such-and-such a name administered it." He was angered and said, "Go and ask that very person." They reported that the man had nearly died but had recovered, and the monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, accept the fee but do not administer the medicine. And if you have administered a medicinal wash, do not go off in secret. If a situation of that kind arises, go and show the patient to a physician. If you go off without having done so, you will incur an offense with remainder."

The narrative occasion for this is at Śrāvastī. A creditor seized a debtor and fixed a term, saying, "Pay me at such-and-such a time," and then released him. The debtor thought: "Though the term has been fixed, I cannot repay him on time; I will flee when the time comes." Later he thought again: "To go away and leave this place will be very painful. I will kill that creditor." And thinking so, he killed him on the road to the Jeta Grove. Before long the group of six monks saw the body and thought: "We have found a charnel-ground robe!" and began stripping it. The man's relatives came to that place, saw what was happening, burst into tears, and said, "You have killed him!" The monks replied, "We certainly did not kill him; he was undoubtedly killed by an enemy." The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the suspicion that arose in the relatives was natural. Therefore, monks, do not pick up a robe of that kind from a charnel ground. Wait until the moment when many people have recognized it for what it is, and only then take it. If you do not do so, you will incur an offense with remainder."

This is the fifth verse of the third subsidiary topic's sūtra.

The Noble Vinaya. The thirty-fifth fascicle.

In brief:
A iron bowl with a carrying cord,
a back-, waist-, and head-load,
robes and food for mother and father,
the woolly robe is the third.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Reverend Blessed One, it was said, 'Monks should hang an iron bowl from an iron cord.' How is the iron cord to be attached?" "Upāli, everything except one made of precious materials." "Reverend Blessed One, it was said, 'Monks should carry a medicinal scraper.' How is one to be carried?" "Upāli, everything except one made of precious materials." "Reverend Blessed One, it was said, 'Monks should not carry loads on their backs, waists, or heads.' Should nuns also not carry loads on their backs, waists, or heads?" "Upāli, nuns too should not carry loads on their backs, waists, or heads. If they do, they will incur an offense with remainder."

The narrative occasion for this is at Śrāvastī. A certain householder there took a wife from among his own kind and enjoyed himself with her in happiness. After they had enjoyed themselves together in happiness, in later times his wife became pregnant. When eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth to a boy who was handsome, beautiful, and endowed with all his limbs. They held a great naming ceremony for the newborn and gave him a name. They raised him and he grew up, and then in later times, without asking his parents, he went forth into the teaching of the Blessed One. One morning he put on his lower robe, took his bowl and monastic robe, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. His elderly father saw him and said: "Son, if you have gone forth, who will take care of us?"

He stood there without saying a word. When the monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is parents who endure hardship for the sake of their children. Therefore, even after a son has gone forth, he is permitted to provide his parents with food and clothing." After the Blessed One had said "Even though he has gone forth, provide his parents with food and clothing," the monks did not know how to do so. The Blessed One then declared: "Whatever surplus he has from his bowl and monastic robes, let him provide from that. If there is none, let him seek it from a donor and provide it. If he belongs to the Saṅgha and has access to the Saṅgha's material gains, let him give half of that. If he is one who goes on alms round, let him give half of what he receives on alms round. If he does not do so, he incurs an offense together with the past."

The setting for the next matter is Śrāvastī. Not far from Śrāvastī there was a village called Cliff Village, and in that village there was a temple. Within it there dwelt an elderly monk. In later times he went to Śrāvastī in order to pay homage at a stūpa. Now among the Group of Six monks, one of them was guarding the gate of the Jeta Grove. The venerable Ānanda, who was sitting at the gate, saw from a distance an old white-haired monk with long eyebrows approaching and thought to himself: "Shall I go out to meet this senior monk who is coming?" He went out ahead, and said: "Elder, have you come comfortably?" The monk paid homage to him, saying: "I pay homage." When he said "I pay homage," the venerable Ānanda thought: "This elderly monk does not know who is a teacher and who is an abbot," and realizing this, he said: "Elder, come here. Come along to the temple." He led him to the temple and had him rest. After the elder had sat for a short while, he said: "Teacher, I have come to pay homage at the stūpa." Ānanda said: "Stay. Wait until the time of the assembly and then go." The elder replied: "Teacher, I will take all three of my monastic robes and leave now, before the assembly." Ānanda said: "Elder, stay. I will perform the consecration of the three monastic robes here." When the time for the assembly had come, Ānanda consecrated the rectangular cloth as the lower robe, the upper cloth as the upper garment, and the small piece of cloth as the combined robe. Then he placed the upper cloth and the small cloth over the elder's shoulder, wrapped them with the rectangular cloth over that, fastened the waist-cloth firmly, and then sent him into the assembly. When the monks saw this they were troubled. Some monks confessed it as an offense. Others said: "Why is the elderly monk pretending to be mad?" The elder said: "Venerable ones, these are my three monastic robes. If I am suddenly called away, where would I put them?" They asked: "Are those really three monastic robes?" He replied: "What would one who lacks them do?"

When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "That which has become the object of the offense is: monks performed the consecration of three monastic robes from a long hair. Therefore, wishing to rule that monks should not perform the consecration of three monastic robes from a long hair, the Blessed One declared: 'Monks, it is good that monks confess offenses. But that which has become the object of the offense is that one performed the consecration of three monastic robes from a long hair.'"

"Therefore, monks, do not perform the consecration of three monastic robes from a long hair. If one does perform such a consecration, it will result in a transgression." When the Blessed One had declared, "Monks, do not perform the consecration of three monastic robes from a long hair," faithful brahmins and householders then offered wool cloth, blanket material, and cotton cloth. The monks, arising in doubt, did not accept these. Thereupon those donors said: "When a buddha, the Blessed One, had not appeared in the world, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) were our merit-field. Now that a buddha, the Blessed One, has appeared in the world, you are our merit-field. If you do not accept now, how shall we pass to the next world without any store of virtue?" But the monks said nothing at all.

The monks then reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, what the faithful brahmins and householders say is true. Therefore I permit this: accept the wool; short hairs may be consecrated as extra cloth, and long hairs should be consecrated as the property of the donor and kept accordingly."

This is the sixth verse of the sūtra of the third section of the narrative basis.

In brief, the verse runs:

A stūpa of head-hair and nail clippings,
a white-colored lamp,
a house, a lamp-vessel,
wool, an ox, a noble lady, and a horse-race.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, faithful by disposition, rose early and went to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One and the monastic Saṅgha. After some time had passed, the Blessed One, wishing to demonstrate the practice of acquiring merit for sentient beings, summoned a barber and had his hair and beard shaved. Thereupon the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to the Jeta Grove, prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and said: "Blessed One, if the Blessed One permits, I should like to build a stūpa enshrining the Blessed One's head-hair and nail clippings." The Blessed One declared: "Then, householder, I permit it — build one." He chose a broad and spacious site, made great preparations together with friends, brothers, and relatives, and built a stūpa enshrining the Blessed One's head-hair and nail clippings that was beautiful to behold by all people. But because it had not yet been plastered with lime, it was not beautiful in appearance. So he went again into the presence of the Blessed One, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet, and said: "Blessed One, I have built a stūpa enshrining the Blessed One's head-hair and nail clippings that is beautiful to behold by all people, but until it is plastered with lime it is not beautiful in appearance. May the Blessed One permit me to plaster it with lime." The Blessed One declared: "Then, householder, I permit it — plaster it with lime." He plastered it with lime and made offerings of incense, perfume, and flowers. Then, because there was no lamp at night, it was not beautiful in appearance. Again he went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet, and addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, I have plastered the stūpa enshrining the Blessed One's head-hair and nail clippings with lime and made offerings of incense, ointment, and flowers; but at night there is no lamp within, and it is not beautiful in appearance. May the Blessed One permit this" —

"I have made offerings at the stūpa enshrining the Blessed One's head-hair and nail clippings, and I wish to hang a garland of butter-lamps there at night," he said. The Blessed One declared, "Very well, householder. I permit it. Make offerings there, and in the evening hang a garland of butter-lamps above the stūpa of head-hair and nail clippings." He did so, but the butter dripped down and spoiled the white surface of the stūpa. He went again to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at the Blessed One's feet, and reported this. The Blessed One declared, "Place the garland of butter-lamps lower down." He placed the garland of butter-lamps lower down, but then dogs drank the butter and carried off the vessels as well.

Again he went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at the Blessed One's feet, and addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, when I place a garland of butter-lamps beneath the stūpa enshrining the Blessed One's head-hair and nail clippings, dogs drink the butter and carry off the lamp-vessels too. May the Blessed One permit me to build a small lamp-house." The Blessed One declared, "Very well, householder. I permit it. Do so." He built the small lamp-houses.

Then oxen fouled the stūpa of head-hair and nail clippings. Again he went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at the Blessed One's feet, and said these words: "Blessed One, oxen have fouled the stūpa of the Blessed One's head-hair and nail clippings that I erected. May the Blessed One permit me to enclose it with a railing." The Blessed One declared, "Very well, householder. I permit it. Enclose it with a railing." When he enclosed it with a railing, there was no stairway and it was not beautiful in appearance. Again he went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at the Blessed One's feet, and said: "Blessed One, I have enclosed the stūpa of the Blessed One's head-hair and nail clippings all around with a railing, but this railing has no stairway and it is not beautiful. May the Blessed One permit me to add a stairway to the railing." The Blessed One declared, "Very well, householder. I permit it. Build one." He built the stairway, and then having assembled all the requisite materials, he gathered his friends, brothers, and kinsmen and made a great offering at the stūpa of the Blessed One's head-hair and nail clippings.

Many people seeing this were filled with deep admiration. Faith arose in them, and they too, in just the same manner, erected stūpas enshrining the Blessed One's head-hair and nail clippings in place after place.

Then the Blessed One, having dwelt at Śrāvastī as long as he was pleased to stay, set out to travel toward Rājagṛha and arrived at Rājagṛha. He took up residence in the Bamboo Grove of Kalandaka at Rājagṛha. King Bimbisāra, hearing that the Blessed One had arrived and was staying in the Bamboo Grove of Kalandaka at Rājagṛha, took his great royal retinue and, accompanied by his queens of the inner court, young attendants, ministers, and members of his household, went to where the Blessed One was. He bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat to one side.

The Blessed One, knowing the king's disposition, his latent tendencies, his temperament, and his character, then taught him the Dharma in such a way as would lead him to realize the Four Noble Truths of the noble ones, speaking thus:

Upon hearing this teaching, King Bimbisāra, together with eighty thousand gods, shattered the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection with the vajra of primordial wisdom, and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry. Having thus seen the truth, he together with those eighty thousand gods went to pay homage to the Blessed One three times each day.

Then one day, as spring had come and the trees were in full bloom, and in a dense forest where geese, cranes, peacocks, parrots, cuckoos, the kokila birds, and the jīvañjīvaka birds and others were all calling out, the king was seated together with the queens of his inner court. The queens of the inner court spoke to him, saying: "Your Majesty, since we are unable to go each day to behold the face of the Blessed One, please have a stūpa of the Tathāgata's hair and nails erected in the midst of us, the queens of the inner court, so that we may pay it honor and worship it with flowers, perfumes, unguents, incense, parasols, victory banners, and pennants."

He then made request to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One grant us his hair and nails, so that we may erect a stūpa of the Tathāgata's hair and nails in the midst of the queens of the inner court."

The Blessed One granted his hair and nails. The king made great reverence and honor, and then, together with the queens of the inner court, erected a stūpa of the Tathāgata's hair and nails in the midst of the queens of the inner court. The queens of the inner court then made excellent offerings to it with lamps, incense, flowers, perfumes, and unguents.

Then at a time when King Ajātaśatru, incited by his evil friend the god Devadatta, had deprived his father, the Dharma-king Bimbisāra who ruled righteously according to the Dharma, of his life and his kingdom, and had himself ascended to the throne, he then made it law that all offerings of Dharma to the Blessed One's teaching were cut off, so that no one would perform any act of devotion at the stūpa of the Tathāgata's hair and nails. And when the occasion of the fifteenth day arrived for the opening of the fortnight, still no one offered silken pennants, lamps, or flowers at the stūpa of the hair and nails.

Then the queens, seeing the stūpa of the hair and nails in such a state, remembered King Bimbisāra. Unhappy and grieving, weeping, they said: "We have become separated from Bimbisāra, the Dharma-king, and our merit too has been exhausted."

Among them was a queen named Śrīmatibuddhi. Heedless of her own life, with her thoughts fixed upon the qualities of the Buddha, she swept the stūpa of the hair and nails with a silken pennant and offered a garland of lamps.

At that moment Ajātaśatru appeared on the rooftop of the palace and, looking out, saw a great radiance blazing forth. He asked what it was. Someone told him that Queen Śrīmatibuddhi had offered a garland of lamps at the stūpa of the hair and nails. Ajātaśatru then summoned Śrīmatibuddhi and said: "Why have you acted against the king's law?" The queen replied: "I have indeed acted against the king's law, yet I have not acted against the law of the Dharma-king Bimbisāra."

Enraged at this, he hurled a wheel at her, separating her from her life. Yet she, as she died, with her mind filled with reverent faith in the Blessed One, departed this life and was reborn in the good abode of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

At that time the gods assembled in their meeting place. Then the goddess Śrīmatibuddhi, her body encircled by a radiant light shining for a full league in every direction, went to the assembly of the gods. Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, seeing a vast and brilliant light radiating a full league in every direction, asked:

Who has anointed your body with gold?
You who resemble a blue lotus in bloom —
matchless and glorious, from what have you come?
This light that shines from you —
why does your face resemble an opening lotus?
You who are like the radiance of gold —
tell me, goddess, what is the fruit of your deeds,
and by whose karma have you come to act thus?

The goddess replied:

The protector of the three worlds,
the lamp for all living beings —
seeing the excellent marks of the supreme Buddha,
the dispeller of darkness, to him I offered a lamp.
I offered it to dispel the darkness of afflictions.
Seeing the light like the rays of the moon,
the sage who illuminates, who is a being of clarity —
seeing the power and light of the Teacher,
I paid homage to his most excellent speech.
By that karma I am born here,
luminous and beautiful to myself.
My face when looked upon is lovely,
pure as a lotus, pure as the moon.

Śakra said:

How wonderful — this world is endowed with virtue!
Having abandoned all faults,
you have planted the seed for birth in the high realms.
Who would not honor the supreme form,
white and heaped like gold?
The Buddha, like a lotus opening wide,
lotus eyes born from the pure waters of transcendence,
his finest limbs blazing with light,
his eyes like the flower of the lotus (kamala).

It is the nature of reality that whether a son or daughter of the gods is born in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, before much time has passed three thoughts naturally arise concerning: from where they died and transmigrated, where they have been born, and by what karma they were born. The goddess Śrīmatibuddhi, upon examining from where she had died and transmigrated, saw that it was from among humans. Upon wondering where she had been born, she saw that she had been born in the excellent realm of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. As for the karma, she recalled: "I had sincere faith in the Blessed One."

Then Śrīmatibuddhi thought: "It would not be proper for me to go and see the face of the Blessed One when I have only just been born. By all means let me go to see the Blessed One before my newborn time has passed." And so the goddess Śrīmatibuddhi put on luminous, stainless, flashing earrings and adorned her body with necklaces and ornaments. She filled her arms with divine flowers — blue lotus, lotus, white lotus, great white lotus, coral tree blossoms, and other such flowers — and with that great brilliance she illuminated the entire Kalandaka Bird Forest of the Grove of Light. She scattered flowers before the Blessed One and went to hear the Dharma. The Blessed One, knowing her intention, her latent disposition, her constitution, and her nature, taught the Dharma in such a way that she would fully realize the Four Noble Truths of the noble ones. Upon hearing it, the goddess Śrīmatibuddhi shattered the twenty-peak mountain of the view of the transitory collection (the belief in a personal self) with the vajra of wisdom, and manifestly attained the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truth, she proclaimed three utterances of true words:

"Reverend One, this was not done for me by my father, nor by my mother, nor by the king, nor by a god, nor by a beloved one, nor by brother, sister, or relative, nor was it done in previous lives, nor by brahmin or ascetic — it is the Blessed One who has dried up for me the ocean of tears and blood, who has freed me from the mountain of bones, who has closed the door to the lower realms, who has opened the door to the high realms and liberation, and who has established me in the abode of gods and humans."

Then she spoke:

Brilliantly illumined by your power,
the path to the lower realms, with its many faults —

the door to high realms and merit I have opened as well.
The path to nirvāṇa, too, have I attained.
Relying on you, I have abandoned all faults.
I have obtained forever a purified eye.
I have gained the path that is joyful and peaceful to the noble ones.
Having crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering,
even while wandering among the destinies, gods and humans honor me.
Free from the faults of birth, aging, and death —
even in a thousand existences, this is exceedingly hard to behold.
Today, having seen the face of the Sage, I have obtained the fruit.
Bowing low, my hair loosened and hanging freely,
I touched my hands to your two feet and joy arose.
Circumambulating the Victor from the right,
I went forth into the realm of the gods.

Then the goddess Śrīmati, like a merchant who has found profit, like a farmer who has had a good harvest, like a hero who has won a battle, like a sick person who has been freed from all illness, departed with those same riches with which she had come to the Blessed One's presence, and went to her own abode.

Now the monks, having remained without sleeping through the night and at dawn, diligently attending on the Sage, saw a great radiance shining in that place of the Blessed One. Upon seeing this, they inquired of the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, was it Brahma, lord of the assembly, or Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, or one of the four world-guardians, or who was it that came to look upon the face of the Blessed One?"

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, it was not Brahma, lord of the assembly; it was not Śakra, lord of the gods; nor did the four world-guardians or others come. Rather, it was a being called Śrīmati, wife of King Rūpasāraṃ, who, without regard for her own life, offered a garland of lamps to the reliquary stupa of the Tathāgata's hair and nails. Thereafter King Ajātaśatru hurled a wheel-weapon and separated her from her life. She, with a mind of manifest faith toward me, at the time of her passing was born as a god in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. That very night she came to my presence; I taught her the Dharma, she saw the truth, and then departed to her own abode.

Therefore, monks, do not be afraid of merit. Why so? Merit is a word of happiness — desirable, pleasant, supremely pleasant, agreeable. That, monks, is merit. Monks, you should be afraid of non-merit. Why so? Non-merit is a word of suffering — undesirable, unpleasant, supremely unpleasant, disagreeable. That, monks, is non-merit.

Monks, I myself directly perceive from long ago that merit accumulated long ago, at the time of its ripening, is experienced as desirable, pleasant, supremely pleasant, and agreeable.

Monks, because I cultivated the mind of loving-kindness for seven years, for seven aeons of destruction and re-formation I did not come to this world. At the time of the world's destruction I was born in the heaven of the gods of universal light. At the time of re-formation I was born in an empty Brahmā palace, and there too I became the master of Brahmā and Mahābrahmā, prevailing by my own superior power and not by another's. I exercised sovereignty over a thousand hundreds of sentient beings and was praised as supreme among beings. For thirty-six thousand aeons I became Śakra, lord of the gods. For a countless number of hundreds of aeons I became a wheel-turning king who had subdued the four quarters and was endowed with the seven precious things. The seven precious things are of the following kinds, namely:

the precious wheel, the precious elephant, the precious horse, the precious jewel, the precious queen, the precious minister of the household, and the precious general — these are the seven. I had a full complement of a thousand sons, all of them courageous, capable, and handsome, capable of vanquishing enemy forces. And I subdued this great earth as far as the ocean's shore by Dharma alone, without recourse to the rod or the sword, and dwelt there free from all discomfort. At that time I reflected: "By what karma has its ripening made me so mighty and so possessed of great supernatural power?" And then I thought: "It is by three fruits of this karma and three maturations of this karma that I have become so mighty and so possessed of great supernatural power. What are these three? They are: generosity, taming, and self-restraint." Having so reflected, the Blessed One spoke those words, and then the Teacher spoke further as follows.

You who desire virtue and happiness,
look to the ripening of merit.
For seven years the monks
cultivated a mind of loving-kindness,
and for seven aeons of formation and dissolution
they did not return to this world.
At the time of dissolution I remained
illuminating all the world in the intermediate state.
After reformation, dwelling in the Brahmā realm,
I abided there as the ruler of great Brahmā
for seven successive times.
For thirty-six periods
I became king of the gods.
For countless hundreds of aeons
I became a king of fearsome renown,
anointed on the crown with the royal consecration of the warrior lineage,
sovereign over Jambudvīpa.
Not by the rod or the sword
did I subdue this world,
but by the very nature of reality, without constraint,
I trained beings in the correct way.
Having turned the wheel of Dharma
throughout these circles of the earth,
in that place of wealth and great abundance
I too was born into such a lineage.
Every manner of wealth was perfectly complete,
and likewise the seven precious things.
Endowed with riches and many resources,
I became a king of fame and awe.
By the cause of that great power,
wherever I was born I became supreme.
This is what was taught by the Buddha,
the Blessed One who benefits the world.
Those who know this great wonder —
and it is no small supernatural feat —
what wise person would not have faith?
Therefore, even if one's birth is humble,
one who wishes to bring benefit to others
and sincerely aspires to great power
should take the sacred Dharma as one's teacher
and keep the Buddha's teaching in mind.

When the Blessed One had spoken these words, the monks were pleased and rejoiced in what the Blessed One had declared.

This was the seventh verse section of the sūtra of the three doors, from within the narrative framework.

In summary: a house with a foundation and a stairway, a bride with a terrace, pillars plastered with red lac, and walls painted with patterns of resin.

The Blessed One, the Buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada in Śrāvastī. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One thus: "If the Blessed One grants permission, I will build a circumambulatory perfume chamber around the reliquary shrine of the Blessed One's hair and nails, and will also construct a stairway for it." The Blessed One declared: "Then, householder, proceed with my permission."

Again the householder addressed the Blessed One thus: "If the Blessed One grants permission, I will build a surrounding wall around the reliquary shrine of the Blessed One's hair and nails." And the Blessed One declared:

"Then, householder, proceed with my permission."

Again, when the Blessed One had granted permission, the householder addressed him thus: "I will encircle it with a railing." And the Blessed One declared: "Then, householder, proceed with my permission."

Again, when the Blessed One had granted permission, the householder addressed him thus: "I will paint the pillars with red lacquer." And the Blessed One declared: "Householder, then proceed with my permission."

Again, when the Blessed One had granted permission, the householder addressed him thus: "I will paint the wall surfaces with lac dye." And the Blessed One declared: "Householder, then proceed and paint them with my permission."

This is the eighth verse of the sūtra of the three gates within the introductory narrative.

To summarize in verse:

The tooth of a bull, and thread,
a garland, one adorned with precious garlands,
an attendant, and the essence,
and also the gate of the essence.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One said: "Monks, offer worship and pay honor to the reliquary shrine of my hair and nails." When the monks were making offerings at the reliquary shrine, they drove in pegs and hung garlands of flowers. Brahmin householders who were devotees, upon seeing this, raised a complaint: "Why are the monks driving pegs into the Teacher's reliquary shrine, which had no pegs?" When matters stood thus, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Setting aside the criticism of the brahmins and householders — do not drive pegs into the reliquary shrine; instead, obtain something small, like the tooth of a bull."

When the Blessed One had declared, "Obtain something small, like the tooth of a bull," the monks began digging a hole in the reliquary shrine and inserting something shaped like a bull's tooth. The Blessed One then declared: "Do not dig a hole in the reliquary shrine and insert something shaped like a bull's tooth; rather, affix it at the time of building the reliquary shrine's wall, before it is erected."

When the monks were making offerings, they climbed up onto the reliquary shrine and hung the flower garlands on the rim of the water-spout trough. Brahmin householders, upon seeing this, raised a complaint: "Why are the monks climbing onto and trampling the Teacher's reliquary shrine in this way, and wandering about upon it?" When matters stood thus, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Setting aside the criticism of the brahmins and householders — monks must not trample and wander upon the Teacher's reliquary shrine. If it is for the purpose of making offerings, a layman may climb up. If there is no layman, a novice who has washed both feet and either anointed them with perfume or wrapped them in cloth may climb up. If none of these is available, a monk, bearing in mind that this is the Teacher's shrine and reflecting on the occasion as it presents itself, may climb up in just that way and make decorative patterns with perfume."

When the reliquary shrine was large and it was not possible to climb it, the Blessed One declared: "One may climb by holding a rope."

Flower garlands were offered at the reliquary shrine of hair and nails, but they wilted and became unsightly. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada said to the Blessed One: "I offered flower garlands at the Blessed One's reliquary shrine of hair and nails, but they wilted and became unsightly. If the Blessed One grants permission, I will offer a garland of precious jewels at the Blessed One's reliquary shrine of hair and nails." And the Blessed One declared:

"Therefore, householder, since it is permitted, you may offer it."

Crows and other birds perched on the reliquary shrine of hair and nails, and their droppings made the shrine unsightly. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada said to the Blessed One: "Crows and other birds have come to the Blessed One's reliquary shrine of hair and nails, and their droppings have made the shrine unsightly. If the Blessed One grants permission, I will wrap it in fine cloth." And the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, householder, since it is permitted, wrap it in fine cloth." And so he wrapped it in fine cloth.

That wrapping rotted in the rains and became dark and invisible. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada said to the Blessed One: "The fine cloth with which I wrapped the Blessed One's reliquary shrine of hair and nails has now been rotted by the rains of summer, grown dark, and is no longer visible. If the Blessed One grants permission, I will put a drainage spout on it." And the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, householder, since it is permitted, put a canopy on it."

This is the ninth verse-summary of the third-gateway sūtra within the accounts of origin.

In brief:
Make a reliquary shrine from copper and the like,
From gold and silver and so forth,
Encircle it with victory banners,
And apply seals of grain and butter.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the pleasure garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to where the Blessed One was, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, and said to the Blessed One: "If the Blessed One grants permission, I will build a copper reliquary shrine for the Blessed One." And the Blessed One declared: "Householder, therefore, since it is permitted, build it." Again he said: "If the Blessed One grants permission, I will build a golden reliquary shrine." And the Blessed One declared: "Householder, therefore, since it is permitted, build it." And likewise for one made of silver — build it on a grand scale; for one made of vaiḍūrya — build it on a grand scale; for one made of crystal — build it on a grand scale.

Again he said: "If the Blessed One grants permission, I will offer victory banners at the Blessed One's reliquary shrine of hair and nails." And the Blessed One declared: "Householder, therefore, since it is permitted, offer them." When the Blessed One said to offer victory banners, Anāthapiṇḍada did not know what kind to offer. The Blessed One declared: "There are four kinds of victory banner: the lion victory banner, the makara victory banner, the nāga victory banner, and the garuḍa victory banner."

Again he said: "If the Blessed One grants permission, I will apply seals of grain and butter to the Blessed One's reliquary shrine of hair and nails." And the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, householder, since it is permitted, apply the seals." Again he said: "If the Blessed One grants permission, I will anoint the Blessed One's reliquary shrine of hair and nails with red ochre." And the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, householder, since it is permitted, anoint it. And just as you anoint with red ochre, likewise anoint with sandalwood on a grand scale."

This is the tenth verse-summary of the third-gateway sūtra within the accounts of origin. Herewith the third gateway within the accounts of origin is complete.

In brief:
The flat door-slab, and likewise in summer,
The six groups and the cook,
The bowl-stand and the permanent stand likewise,
The wanderer and the loan,
The application of seals as is fitting —
Thus are the sūtras summarized in brief.

In brief:
The flat door-slab and the knee-embrace,

The net, and likewise the frame of the net,
The field, the crop, and the birth,
What arises from wealth, and garments —
These are the sūtras summarized in brief.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Reverend Blessed One, when you say 'Let a monk take hold of a flat door-slab,' from what material should it be made?" "Upāli, from anything except precious substances."

He asked again: "Reverend Blessed One, when you say 'Let a monk make a knee-embrace,' how should it be made?" "Upāli, from seven kinds of cord: wool, flax stalk fiber, cotton thread, silk, kuśa grass, koṭambaka fiber, and hair-cloth."

He asked again: "Reverend Blessed One, when you say 'Make a net,' of what kind should it be made?" "Upāli, of four kinds: from muñja grass, balvaja grass, silk, and cotton thread."

He asked again: "Reverend Blessed One, when you say 'Make a frame for the net,' of what kind should it be made?" "Upāli, from anything except precious substances."

The account of origin for this takes place in Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī there lived a certain householder who had faith and a virtuous mind. He had married the daughter of a lay follower who was a Jain, and he instructed her: "My dear, the Buddha is our teacher, the Dharma is our banner, and the monks are our field of offerings — make offerings to them." She, being deceitful and accustomed to acting dishonestly, replied just as the master's son Legs would have done honestly: "I will do so." Accordingly, each day the Saṅgha's appointed monks were served the midday meal at that householder's home.

Then, some time later, the householder had a small matter of business in another rocky mountain village. He instructed his wife: "My dear, I have a small matter of business in the rocky mountain village called such-and-such — I am going there. You, in the same way, continue serving the midday meal to those worthy of offerings." She, deceitful as she was, replied just as the master's son Legs would have done honestly: "I will serve the midday meal."

After he left, he thought: "I have given instructions to my wife; I should also give instructions to the monks." He went to the monastery, paid homage at the feet of the monk in charge of the schedule, and said: "Noble one, I have a small matter of business in that rocky mountain village called such-and-such — I am going there. Please, noble one, send the monks appointed by the Saṅgha as before." The monk replied graciously: "Householder, they will be well sent as before."

The householder then paid homage to the Teacher, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and departed for that rocky mountain village.

The Saṅgha's appointed monks spoke among themselves, saying: "That householder's wife has no faith; she will send us away before noon." So they arrived before noon. When the householder's wife saw them she accused them, saying: "Noble ones, you have come far too early — is there no one more important among you?" They said not a word in response, but remained there from that time until noon, ate their meal, and departed.

The next day she prepared the food early, set out the seats, and sat there ready, waiting. When the monks arrived at noon she looked them over, and then she taunted them — she taunted them both on both sides together, one by one, saying: "However it may be, after eating and going, tell those who practice celibacy that henceforth the monks need not come here either." Having said this, she ate the food herself and went to the monastery.

Those monks then recited everything that had happened, and from then on the monks did not go there again. Some time later, when that householder came back and asked the Lady Bzang mo, who was in charge of the offerings, "Has the porridge been served?", she replied: "Master, it has been two days now — the monks came, had their porridge, and then stopped coming." Hearing this, he went to the monastery and said to the noble ones: "Why did the Saṅgha not send the assigned monks?" They recited back to him everything that had happened. He said to the noble ones: "In that case, please accept the produce of my fields and take your meal here." The monks replied: "Householder, we cannot do that. Why not? The Blessed One has not permitted receiving uncooked grain." With that, the man said nothing more.

The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Very well then — for the sake of the Saṅgha, go and receive that produce of the fields, and have no hesitation about it."

The origin story is set in Śrāvastī. In Śrāvastī, a certain householder built a dwelling for another person, furnished it with many beds and seats, and had it placed there. The monks gathered them all together and stored them in a large storeroom. A monk then told that householder about it, and the householder mocked him. The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the householder's mockery is of no consequence. Therefore the beds and seats should be used exactly as they were dedicated. Whoever resides there has authority over them."

Then that same householder offered a large amount of cloth provisions to that dwelling, and a monk spread it out as bedding and put it together with the Saṅgha's provisions. The monk told the householder, and the householder mocked him again. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the householder's mockery is of no consequence. Put it under the donor's authority, and as for those cloth provisions of the household — authority over them belongs to those who reside there. When they did not give the monk his individual share, the Blessed One declared: "Give from those provisions that belong to the Saṅgha as well — let him enjoy the use of that too, and have no hesitation about it."

This is the first verse of the sūtra of the fourth door within the origin story.

The holy Vinaya, the thirty-sixth fascicle.

In brief:

Whoever resides in a given place —
that monk too is entitled to what suits it:
the implements for the work of plastering,
food and lamps — he is entitled to these.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. In Śrāvastī, a certain householder built dwelling rooms in a monastery, offered beds and seats there, and provided provisions as well. The monks then put those beds and seats into the Saṅgha's general pool and distributed the provisions commonly. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not move things from where they are assigned. Whatever is definitely established in a particular place should be used by those who are definitely residing there, and the provisions too are to be regarded as theirs." When the monks did not give him a share of other provisions, the Blessed One declared: "Give both, and he may use them as he pleases. However, monks are to be assigned according to seniority."

The origin story is set in Śrāvastī.

In Śrāvastī there lived another householder, and another alms-wanderer went to him, took refuge with him, and was established in the training precepts. Later, when the alms-wanderer expounded the merits of the seven kinds of meritorious objects to be accomplished with wealth, the householder became deeply inspired and said, "I too, noble one, will perform some meritorious acts with wealth as their basis." The alms-wanderer replied, "Householder, do so." The householder said, "Noble one, what shall I do?" The alms-wanderer replied, "Build a Dharma hall for the Saṅgha." The householder said, "Noble one, I have the kārṣāpaṇas, but I lack helpers to accomplish the merit." The alms-wanderer said, "Householder, bring the kārṣāpaṇas; I will be your helper in merit." The householder gave him the kārṣāpaṇas and also appointed a building supervisor. But the supervisor stored the kārṣāpaṇas inside a storeroom and did not begin even the slightest work.

When the householder came there wondering how far the construction of his Dharma hall had progressed, he found that not even the least bit of work had been done. He asked the alms-wanderer, "Noble one, why has the work not been started?" The building supervisor replied, "The necessary materials are needed here." The householder said, "The kārṣāpaṇas I donated — why are they not being used to procure the building materials?" The supervisor replied, "Householder, how could I improperly use the possessions of the Saṅgha of the four quarters?" The householder said, "Noble one, there is no fault in doing so — please proceed." The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If the householder has given instructions, use those funds for the building materials and do not have any doubts about it."

The supervisor then applied the funds to the building materials, and the alms-wanderer, after overseeing the building work, went out for alms. The householder saw him and said, "Noble one, while you are going for alms, who is doing the building work on my Dharma hall?" The alms-wanderer replied, "Householder, since all sentient beings depend on food for their existence, would you have me work on your Dharma hall while I go hungry? Please allow me to engage in almsgoing at least." The householder said, "Noble one, in that case, please take the building funds to cover your meals." The alms-wanderer said, "Why should I eat what I have dedicated to the Saṅgha of the four quarters?" The householder said, "Noble one, there is no harm in it — please eat." The monks reported this in turn to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If the householder has given instructions, eat from those very funds without any doubt."

Then, because the alms-wanderer had eaten poor food, he fell ill. The Blessed One said, "Do not eat poor food." So he began eating good food. The Blessed One then declared: "Do not eat the finest food either; eat in the same manner as the provisions customary for other Dharma halls." When he could not obtain clarified butter, the Blessed One declared: "Obtain it in the same way that clarified butter is obtained in other Dharma halls, and have no doubts about it."

When the alms-wanderer took grain-oil for alms in order to care for the building materials, the Blessed One declared: "Purchase the grain-oil from the building funds. Other necessary materials too should be procured from those funds, and you need have no doubts about it."

This is the second verse of the sūtra of the fourth door within the origin story.

In brief, as for the sleeping mats of the monks —

Do not distribute without a cover, do not distribute for use in dyeing work or for alms-bowl maintenance work, and do not distribute sleeping mats in the middle of the night.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The group of six monks, having divided up the Saṅgha's sleeping mats, used them for dyeing work, washing and wringing out dyed cloth, and for alms-bowl maintenance work, scorching robes over fire so that the robes became soiled and ruined by the dye. When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Do not use the Saṅgha's robes for dyeing work, for alms-bowl maintenance work, or moreover for any wood-splitting work. If you do so, you will incur a transgression."

The origin story is set at Śrāvastī. Again, the group of six monks, having put on the Saṅgha's robes, sat out in the rain without a cover while doing dyeing work, and the robes were ruined. When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Do not sit in the rain without a cover while wearing the Saṅgha's robes. If you do so, you will incur a transgression."

The origin story is set at Śrāvastī. The group of six monks, while wandering about in the countryside, went in the middle of the night — after midnight — to another village in the hills. They arrived at a Dharma hall that was there and settled in to rest, each in whatever lodging he chose. They then said: "Venerable ones, let us rest a little while first. Then call the one who distributes sleeping mats and have the sleeping mats and lodgings distributed according to seniority." Those monks, once some of them had lain down and even as midnight turned, disturbed them and said: "Venerable ones, go and sleep wherever you like, as lodging-companions. Tomorrow at dawn the lodgings and sleeping mats will be distributed." The monks then said: "Venerable ones, would you have the Teacher's teachings destroyed while the Teacher still lives? Distribute the lodgings and sleeping mats to us according to seniority." The sleeping-mat distributor then set about distributing the lodgings and sleeping mats, but without distributing them to the junior monks, waited until dawn; the group of six slept a short while, then rose before dawn, returned the sleeping mats, and departed. When the monks asked why they had returned the sleeping mats, those monks replied: "Venerable ones, we came to pay homage at a stūpa and now we are leaving again." The others said: "Venerable ones, in that case, why did you harass the monks in the middle of the night?" They replied: "Venerable ones, we did it in order to make the teaching firm — what fault is there in that?" The monks imposed a penalty on them.

When the monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, from midnight onward, mats are not to be distributed. If someone unexpectedly arrives in the evening, let him stay in whatever lodging he finds convenient. And if he is still there at dawn, then a lodging and a sleeping mat should be assigned to him."

The origin story is set at Śrāvastī. The group of six monks, wandering about in the countryside, went to another village in the hills. They arrived at a Dharma hall that was there and were seated by the monks each in whatever lodging they chose. Then, when the sleeping mats were being distributed according to seniority, those monks forcibly sat down on the seniority seats and could not be moved from them even according to seniority. When the sleeping mats were distributed, those monks occupied the senior monks' seats together with the others at the same time, and —

given to the attendants, and those who had not received sleeping mats were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is wrong to mock the newly ordained monks. Therefore, let the seniority seats and the junior sleeping mats alike be distributed according to seniority."

This is the third verse of the sūtra on the fourth gate within the origin story.

In summary:

The latrine ground, the washing ground,
The urination ground, and the foot-washing place,
The scraper vessel, the scraping tool,
And the various other such things are the same.

The awakened one, the Blessed One, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The group of six were walking about at the door of the latrine, talking and sitting, and in this way they troubled the monks. They said: "Venerable ones, wait a moment — we are senior and must proceed by seniority." Then, right there in that vicinity, they taught, recited aloud, and cooked food, so that monks who needed to go to the latrine were too embarrassed to go, and they could not relieve themselves of excrement, urine, and the like at ease. Just as they came, they were blocked from entering inside, and all of them fell ill. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, monks, do not sit at the door of the latrine talking. Do not teach in that vicinity. Do not read there. Do not recite there. Do not cook food there. If monks sit at the latrine talking, proceed according to seniority there, teach in that vicinity, recite aloud, read, or cook food, there will be a transgression with expiation."

When monks were at the washing place still engaged in washing, the group of six said "We are senior," and drove them away. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not drive away a monk from the washing place while he has not yet finished washing. If one does drive him away, there will be a transgression with expiation."

When monks went to the urination area, the group of six came there afterward and said: "We elders will proceed by seniority," and the monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, at the urination area, do not proceed by seniority. Enter in the order in which one has arrived. If monks proceed by seniority at the urination area, there will be a transgression with expiation."

When monks were sitting washing their feet, the group of six, before they had finished washing, said "We are senior," and took away the foot-washing stand, assigning it by seniority, and those monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not take away the foot-washing stand from monks who have not yet finished washing their feet and distribute it according to seniority. If a monk takes away the foot-washing stand from a monk who has not yet finished washing his feet and distributes it by seniority, there will be a transgression with expiation."

When the group of six saw monks using the face-scraper, they said "We are senior," and before those monks had finished, took away the face-scraper and distributed it by seniority, and those monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not take away the face-scraper from monks who have not yet finished using it and distribute it by seniority."

If a monk takes away the face-scraper from monks who have not yet finished using it and distributes it by seniority, there will be a transgression with expiation. Likewise, the same rule is to be applied in full to the basin, the razor, and the nail-cutter, and so forth.

This is the fourth verse of the fourth-gate sūtra within the body of the canonical occasion.

In summary:

The water pot and the wash-basin,
The black iron bowl and the drinking cup,
The sharpening of the razor and the cutting of nails,
The medicinal thorns and the foot-stand.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The group of six said to monks who had not yet finished the Saṅgha's dyeing work, "We are senior," took away the Saṅgha's dye pot, and those monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not take away the Saṅgha's dye pots by seniority from monks who have not yet finished the dyeing work. If a monk takes away the Saṅgha's dye pots by seniority from monks who have not yet finished the dyeing work, there will be a transgression with expiation. As it is with the dye pot, so too it is with the wash-basin."

The group of six said to monks who had not yet finished eating, "We are senior," took away the black iron bowl, and those monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not take away the black iron bowl by seniority from monks who have not yet finished eating. If a monk takes away the black iron bowl by seniority from monks who have not yet finished eating, there will be a transgression with expiation."

The group of six said to monks who were eating and had drunk only half their fill of liquid, "We are senior," took away the drinking cup, and those monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not distribute the drinking cup by seniority to monks who are eating and have drunk only half their fill of liquid. If monks take away the drinking cup by seniority from monks who are eating and have drunk only half their fill of liquid, there will be a transgression with expiation."

The group of six said to monks who had only half-finished shaving their hair and beard, "We are senior," took away the razor, and those monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not distribute the razor by seniority to monks who have only half-finished shaving their head-hair and facial hair. If monks take away the razor by seniority from monks who have only half-finished shaving their head-hair and facial hair, there will be a transgression with expiation."

The group of six said to monks who were having their razor for shaving head-hair and facial hair sharpened and had only half-finished the sharpening, "We are senior," took away the whetstone, and those monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not distribute the whetstone by seniority when monks have only half-finished sharpening the razor used for shaving head-hair and facial hair. If monks take away by seniority the whetstone for a razor used for shaving head-hair and facial hair when it has only been half-sharpened, there will be a transgression with expiation."

The group of six said to monks who had only half-finished cutting their nails, "We are senior," took away the nail-cutter, and those monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not distribute the nail-cutter by seniority to monks who have only half-finished cutting their nails."

If monks take away by seniority the nail-cutter from monks who have only half-finished cutting their nails, there will be a transgression with expiation.

The group of six said to monks who had only half-finished plucking their nose-hairs, "We are senior," took away the nose-hair tweezers, and those monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not distribute the nose-hair tweezers by seniority to monks who have only half-finished plucking their nose-hairs. If monks take away the nose-hair tweezers from monks who have only half-finished plucking their nose-hairs, there will be a transgression with expiation."

The group of six said to monks who were lying and sitting on Saṅgha couches with legs, "We are senior," and took them away, and those monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not distribute by seniority the couch with legs on which a monk is lying. If monks take away the legs of a couch from monks who are lying or sitting upon a Saṅgha couch with legs, there will be a transgression with expiation."

This is the fifth verse of the sūtra of the fourth gate within the introductory narrative section.

In summary:
The permanent thread, the second,
The knife, the needle, the taking away,
And likewise other things not yet finished —
These are not to be taken away.

The buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The group of six placed robes, upper garments, and lower garments on a Saṅgha plank-board when those robes were only half laid out there, said "We are senior," and took them away, and those monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not distribute by seniority the Saṅgha plank-board when robes, upper garments, and lower garments have been only half laid out upon it. If monks take away by seniority the Saṅgha plank-board from monks who have only half laid out their robes, upper garments, and lower garments upon it, there will be a transgression with expiation."

The group of six said, "We are senior," and took away the Dharma robes of monks that had been only half-sewn with Saṅgha thread, and those monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not distribute by seniority the Dharma robes of monks that have been only half-sewn with Saṅgha thread. If monks take away by seniority Dharma robes of monks that have been only half-sewn with Saṅgha thread, there will be a transgression with expiation."

The group of six half-dyed the Dharma robes of monks in dye and then soaked them in the Saṅgha's dyeing solution, said "It is to be done by seniority," and took them away. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not distribute by seniority robes of monks that have been half-dyed and then soaked in the Saṅgha's dyeing solution. If monks take away by seniority robes of monks that have been half-dyed and soaked in the Saṅgha's dyeing solution, there will be a transgression with expiation."

The group of six said, "We are senior," and took away the Dharma robes of monks that had been only half-cut with the Saṅgha's scissors, and those monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,

The Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not distribute by seniority Dharma robes of monks that have been only half-cut with the Saṅgha's scissors. If monks take away by seniority the Dharma robes of monks that have been half-cut with the Saṅgha's scissors, there will be a transgression with expiation."

The group of six said, "We are senior," and took away the Dharma robes of monks that had been only half-sewn with the Saṅgha's needle, and those monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not distribute by seniority the Dharma robes of monks that have been only half-sewn with the Saṅgha's needle.
