If monks take away by seniority the Dharma robes of monks that have been half-sewn with the Saṅgha's needle, there will be a transgression with expiation."

The group of six then said, "We are senior," regarding monks whose hair had been only half-shaved, and took away the cloth used by the Saṅgha for collecting hair, and those monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not distribute by seniority the cloth for collecting hair from monks whose hair has been only half-shaved, and the Saṅgha's hair-collecting cloth. If monks take away by seniority the hair-collecting cloth of monks whose hair has been only half-shaved, there will be a transgression with expiation."

The group of six then caused monks who were seated on the Saṅgha's mats in various places, while still engaged in various tasks that were not yet finished, to be told "Yield your seat in order of seniority," and had them rise and sent them away, and those monks were mocked. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not tell monks who are seated on the Saṅgha's mats in various places, while still engaged in various tasks that are not yet finished, to yield their seats in order of seniority, causing them to rise and go. If monks tell monks who are seated on the Saṅgha's mats in various places, while their various tasks are still unfinished, to yield in order of seniority, causing them to rise and go, there will be a transgression with expiation."

This is the sixth verse of the sūtra of the fourth section within the root narrative.

In brief:
A wandering tīrthika,
one bearing a name but not giving the self at death,
five to be received with trust —
a nun who is a keeper, for the sake of the allowance.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Grove of the Veṇuvana. At that time, the Blessed One had tamed the king of Kosala named Prasenajit with a sūtra teaching likened to falling silk, and when the Blessed One had at another time been dwelling there, the king of the land of Samaka, a wise and capable man named Rūpasāra, together with eighty thousand devas of the land of Samaka, along with brahmin and householder assemblies numbering a hundred thousand, had been established by the Blessed One in the truth. At that time a proclamation was made at Rājagṛha as follows: "Listen, you many people dwelling in Rājagṛha and those who have come from various lands — let no one in my realm commit theft. Whoever does so I will banish from the land. To the owners of property, I shall give recompense from my own treasury and storehouses."

And at the time when the Blessed One had tamed Prasenajit, king of the land of Kosala, with the sūtra teaching likened to falling silk, that king likewise had a proclamation made in Śrāvastī as follows: "Let no one in my realm commit theft. Whoever commits theft in my realm shall be put to death as punishment, and to the owners of the property I myself shall give recompense from my own storehouses and treasury."

At that time, the thieves who were dwelling in the land of Samaka and those dwelling in the land of Kosala went and gathered together up to the border between those two territories.

The word spread far and wide that many travelers were gathering there. Hearing this, many travelers from Samaka set out together for the land of Kosala. From Kosala as well, travelers similarly set out toward Samaka. Then, at a later time, when many travelers from Samaka set out together for the land of Kosala, and when they had crossed the border and entered Kosala, the caravan leader spoke: "It is well known that Prasenajit, king of Kosala, is fierce and wrathful toward those who defy him, and that he is brave and mighty. If we attack this large caravan, we shall yet be able to profit by it. Send those escorts back." The many travelers said, "Very well, so be it," and the escorts were sent back.

The thieves had posted a lookout and kept watch. When the lookout saw the escorts turn back, he called out, "The escorts have gone back — fall upon the caravan!" The caravan then entered a grove of sāl trees, and they fell upon it. Some of the merchants were killed, and some fled.

Those who fled, with heads covered in dust, went before King Prasenajit and said, "Sire, we were merchants. Having entered your realm, we are merchants no longer. Why? Sire, we have been set upon by thieves." King Prasenajit commanded the officer Ārya-Janman: "Young man, go swiftly in pursuit, seize the thieves together with the goods, and return." The officer replied, "Sire, so be it," and having received this command from Prasenajit, king of Kosala, he swiftly set out in pursuit with the fourfold army — troops of war elephants, troops of cavalry, troops of chariots, and troops of infantry — all armored, heading for the sāl grove. By that time the thieves were within the grove, deep among the dense sāl trees, at their ease, dividing up the goods and taking their rest. Ārya-Janman fell upon them from above. Some of the thieves were killed, some fled, and some were captured alive. Having won the battle against the thieves, he took the thieves and the plundered goods and went before the king, prostrated at his feet, and said, "Sire, these are the goods of the thieves." The king then commanded the merchants, "Come, identify your own goods and take them back."

Now among those captured were also wandering tīrthikas (non-Buddhist ascetics), and monks as well. The king returned all of the plundered goods to everyone, but a wandering tīrthika had hidden some within his own robe bundle, and some belonging to the monks he took as well. The monks, not knowing that goods had been concealed within their own robe bundles, went about together with those who were wandering thieves, and a dispute broke out. The many wandering tīrthikas seized those goods and went before the king, saying, "Sire, goods hidden within our robe bundles were taken by those wandering tīrthikas and they will not return them." The king summoned those wandering tīrthikas and commanded, "Why did you take the robes of these noble ones? Return them at once." They replied, "Sire, these things concealed within the bundle are our own robes." The king said to the monks, "Noble ones, identify what belongs to you and take it." The monks drew the items out one by one and examined them.

Some of the monks recognized their items and said, "Sire, these are our robes." The king then said to the wandering tīrthikas, "Shame on you, wandering tīrthikas! If you are thieves who steal by stealth, then you are great thieves indeed." Having no reply, they stood there in silence. The king then said, "Noble ones, from this day forward it would be fitting to mark your Dharma robes with a distinguishing sign." When the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared, "Monks, what the king said is right. Therefore, obtain a distinguishing mark for the Dharma robes. Stitch a border or patch-seam around them, and attach a corner tab as well." When the Blessed One said "obtain a distinguishing mark," the monks did not know how to do so. The Blessed One then declared, "Apply dots of ink along the edges of the Dharma robes."

The background story takes place in Śrāvastī. In Śrāvastī, a certain householder took a wife from a family of equal rank and enjoyed himself with her in pleasure and sport. From that pleasurable union, after some time the wife became with child, and when eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth to a boy. For a period of seven days, fourteen days, or twenty-one days after the birth, a great birth-celebration was held. The child was given a name in keeping with his family lineage, and he was nurtured and raised until he grew up. Then after some time the boy's mother passed away. The householder took another wife and enjoyed himself with her in pleasure and sport. From that union, in time three sons were born, and they too were given names in keeping with their family lineage.

Now within this family a great quarrel broke out between the elder and younger children. The older son, whose mother had died, was persistently harassed, and feeling unremembered and disheartened, he went to another region, where he went forth into the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya.

Then after some time the householder fell ill, and though he was treated with medicines made of roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits, his illness was not alleviated. Knowing that, tormented by the suffering of sickness, he would soon pass away, the householder gathered his household members together. In their assembly he said to his sons, "Children, your elder brother has gone forth into the community of the renunciant sons of the Śākyas. You must give him his share of the inheritance." After saying this, he recited:

All that is gathered will be exhausted.
All that is high will fall.
All that is assembled will disperse.
The end of all phenomena is peace.
He had come to accord with the nature of time.

Now the younger son who was away enjoying himself in the countryside heard that his father had passed away. He thought to himself, "I shall go and console my stepmother and younger brothers in their grief, and then go to hear the Dharma." So, after enjoying himself for as long as he pleased, he traveled on, making his way through the countryside toward where Śrāvastī was located. Traveling gradually along the road, he arrived at Śrāvastī and, resting from the weariness of the journey, came to his own home. When those within the household saw him, they wept, and the sound of their weeping was heard by the neighbors, who gathered together. Some of them cried aloud, while others sat with their eyes filled with tears. Ordinary people, bound by attachment and now separated from a kinsman, had their eyes filled with tears of grief. He too sat there carried away by weeping.

Then an elderly woman said, "Child, your father gave his share of the inheritance — we all heard him. Do not weep. If there is birth, there will be death." Hearing this, the young man sat quietly for a short while in reflection. He then taught the Dharma to his stepmother and his younger brothers. When their grief had somewhat subsided,

They said to him, "Receive your share of the inheritance." He reflected: "The Blessed One has said that after he passes away he will not give anything — how then should I accept it?" He thought further: "Venerable ones, for one who has gone forth, there is no use for material wealth. Furthermore, the Blessed One has declared that after he passes away he will give nothing. You yourselves take it." At this, they acknowledged their fault, saying: "Give a gift to the noble one who has gone forth. Accumulate merit too. What fault is there in that?" When the monks were informed of what had occurred, they reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, laypeople have hopes of inheritance, whereas those who have gone forth do not. Therefore, what a layperson wishes to give after death is the business of the householder — it is firmly established as such. For one who has gone forth, there is nothing of that kind. Therefore let the layperson's bequest be received by the laity in that spirit, for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Let there be no doubt about this."

The occasion arose in Śrāvastī. Monks were going out on walks and wandering in the walkway, the courtyard, and the gatehouse, and they left behind heavy stone-rollers, tooth-cleaning sticks, bathing implements, and cattle dung. The monks developed doubt and did not make use of them. When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "You may make use of five kinds of trustworthy items: what belongs to a friend, what is mixed together, what belongs to a teacher, what is unchanging, and what would cause joy upon hearing. You may make use of those five kinds of trustworthy items. Have no doubt about this."

The occasion arose in Śrāvastī. In Śrāvastī there was a certain householder who took a wife of equal clan and enjoyed himself fully together with her. In the course of his enjoyment, after some time the wife became with child, and when eight or nine months had passed she gave birth to a daughter. Within seven days — and within the twenty-one days after birth — he held a great birth-celebration for her, gave her a name befitting her lineage, raised and nurtured her, and when she had grown, another householder proposed for her, she was given in marriage, and she was sent off. Some time later the householder died, and she, tormented by grief over the loss of her husband, went forth into the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya. Then, some time later, when a famine arose and she was out wandering for alms, her father encountered her on a street while she was making her alms round. He said to her: "Daughter, where are you living and how are you getting by?" She replied: "Father, a famine has come and I am very hungry." He said: "Daughter, if you have not yet fully gone forth, then even against my wishes I would give to you whatever you want. Now, rather than going on alms round, come eat meals at my house and go to the winter quarters." She agreed, and in the company of one or two companions she ate there and went to the winter quarters. When several days had passed and she had been eating there, he said: "I cannot feed the two monastic alms-goers; you alone should eat here and stay." She replied: "Father, the Blessed One has not permitted me to go into the town alone." He said nothing more to that. When the nuns were informed of what had occurred, they told the monks, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "In such a case as this, I permit the nun to approach the nuns' Saṅgha together with a companion, and —"

— and request the vow of associating together with a companion. The request is to be made as follows. The gong is struck while the seats are being laid out, and when the nuns' Saṅgha has assembled and is seated, one pays homage in order of seniority. Then, in front of the senior members, one sits on a mat or a clean seat with palms joined and speaks these words:

"Hearken, venerable members of the Saṅgha of nuns. I, who am called such-and-such, having come upon a time of famine such that I am unable even to go on alms-rounds, request of the venerable Saṅgha of nuns that I, called such-and-such, be granted by the venerable Saṅgha of nuns the vow of associating together with a companion. May the venerable Saṅgha of nuns grant me, called such-and-such, the vow of associating together with a companion — out of compassion, for the sake of compassion."

This is to be repeated a second and a third time.

After that, a single nun is to make the formal motion and perform the act. She speaks thus:

"Hearken, venerable members of the Saṅgha of nuns. This nun called such-and-such has come upon a time of famine and requests of the venerable Saṅgha of nuns the vow of associating together with a companion. If the time is right and the venerable Saṅgha of nuns consents, let the venerable Saṅgha of nuns remain silent. Let those who do not consent speak."

This is the motion. The formal act is likewise performed:

"Hearken, venerable members of the Saṅgha of nuns. This nun called such-and-such has come upon a time of famine and requests of the venerable Saṅgha of nuns the vow of associating together with a companion. Those among the venerable ones for whom it is acceptable to grant the nun called such-and-such, who has come upon a time of famine, the vow of associating together with a companion — let them remain silent. Those for whom it is not acceptable — let them speak. The venerable Saṅgha of nuns has granted the nun called such-and-such the vow of associating together with a companion, and so it is upheld."

When the vow of associating together with a companion has been granted to a nun by the Saṅgha of nuns, she may go alone to eat food at a companion's household — let her have no scruple about that. It is permitted only during a time of famine; outside that time she should not remain thus. If she continues in this way when no famine has arisen, it becomes an offence together with expiation.

This is the seventh verse of the fourth-door sūtra within the opening narrative.

In summary:

Of borrowing there are two types;
of cloth, again, there are three kinds;
of purchasing, there is what is desired;
and all are subsumed in the compendium.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

A certain monk had borrowed a kārṣāpaṇa coin from a householder, and then at some point in time he passed away from one cause or another. That householder heard how that monk had passed away. Having heard this, he went to the monastery and, knowing the situation, asked the monks: "Where is the monk called such-and-such, the noble one?" They replied: "Good sir, he has passed away." "That noble one borrowed a kārṣāpaṇa of mine and I am seeking it. Good sir, take him to the charnel ground — go there and retrieve it. If you distribute his bowl and his robes, I will go to the charnel ground and lay claim to it."

"Give it to him," they said. The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, that householder has spoken rightly. Whatever of his wealth the monk borrowed, the monks shall give it back." Not knowing from where they should give it, the Blessed One declared: "Give it from his bowl and robes." The monks gave the bowl and robes, but the householder did not want them. The Blessed One then declared: "Sell them and give him the proceeds." The monks gave all of it. The Blessed One declared: "Give the amount that was borrowed, and distribute the remainder."

At Śrāvastī, another monk borrowed a kārṣāpaṇa coin from a householder, and at some point in time he passed away from one cause or another. Those monks sold the bowl and robes as before and gave the householder what was owed. The householder said: "That noble one owed me only so much — do not give me anything more than that, but do give the rest as well." When the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Tell him that there are no more bowl and robes of that monk's to give. If he does not believe it, make him understand. If he still cannot be made to understand even after explanation, do not render him any service from the Saṅgha's resources or from any other individual's. Have men of good family explain the matter to him and let him go."

The occasion at Śrāvastī was this: a monk had taken a piece of cloth from a cloth merchant without paying the price. That monk then passed away, and when the cloth merchant heard that the monk had died, he came to the monastery. Knowing the situation, he asked the monks: "Where is the monk who goes by the name of such-and-such, the noble one?" They replied: "Good sir, he has passed away." "That noble one took a piece of cloth from me and carried it off, saying he would pay the price. Good sir, take him to the charnel ground and go retrieve it there. If you are distributing that noble one's robes and bowl among yourselves, why should I go all the way to the charnel ground to claim it? You give it to me." The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, what this cloth merchant says is true — give it to him." The monks gave him the very piece of cloth, and he said: "Noble ones, that monk owed me such-and-such a price for it." The Blessed One then declared: "Sell that cloth and give him the proceeds." The monks began to sell it but did not obtain its original price. The Blessed One declared: "For the remainder, sell the robes and bowl and give him that."

The occasion at Śrāvastī was this: a monk had given thread and a fee to a weaver in order to have a piece of cloth woven, and that monk then passed away. The monks summoned the weaver and said: "Good sir, the monk called such-and-such gave you thread and a fee to weave a piece of cloth — please return them." The weaver replied: "Noble ones, I have already woven the cloth for him — the thread and the fee are not available to return." The monks did not know what to do, and they reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared to the monks: "What the weaver says is true — receive the cloth."

The monks summoned a fine-cloth seller, and that person said to the noble ones: "I have given him a coarser piece in exchange." The Blessed One declared: "Since that monk has passed away, receive what was given accordingly."

The occasion for the next ruling was also at Śrāvastī. A monk gave a cloth merchant a kārṣāpaṇa and said: "Please give me a piece of cloth." That monk then passed away. The monks summoned the cloth merchant and said: "Good sir, a monk by the name of such-and-such gave you the price of a piece of cloth — please return it." The merchant replied: "Noble ones, I gave him cloth in exchange." The monks did not know what to do. They reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared to the monks: "What that cloth merchant says is true — receive the cloth."

The monks then summoned a fine-cloth seller, and that person said to the noble ones: "I gave him a coarser piece in place of it." The Blessed One declared: "Since that monk has passed away, receive what was given accordingly."

The Noble Vinaya, the thirty-seventh fascicle.

The occasion for the next ruling was at Śrāvastī. The group of six monks became well known among worldly people, and whenever anyone was buying or selling something, those people would go to them and ask: "Noble one, what is this thing worth?" Now at Śrāvastī there were two householders — one who bought cloth and one who sold it. While the two of them were talking and haggling over a price, the venerable Nandaka happened to come to that spot. Both of them urged the noble Nandaka to arbitrate. One of them said: "Yes, let him arbitrate." So the two of them asked the venerable Nandaka: "Noble one, what is the price of this cloth?" He pulled each one aside separately: first he asked the buyer privately, "Good sir, are you buying or selling?" The man replied: "I am buying." Nandaka said to him: "This is worth twenty kārṣāpaṇas." Then he drew the other aside and asked him privately: "Good sir, are you buying or selling?" That man replied: "Noble one, I am selling." Nandaka told him: "This is worth forty kārṣāpaṇas." Having deceived them both separately, he then said to them together in front of both: "Do between yourselves as seems best to you." At this, the seller said: "This is worth forty kārṣāpaṇas," while the buyer said: "Out of faith and trust in him, I say it is worth twenty kārṣāpaṇas." The seller replied: "Who is this person you placed your faith and trust in? It is the noble Nandaka. He deliberately cheated the two of us — he told me it was worth forty kārṣāpaṇas." The buyer answered: "He deliberately deceived us both as well — in short, he has behaved in a manner befitting a scoundrel. From now on, even if I have need of something, I will not ask him." The monks heard what had happened, reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, those two householders spoke rightly in rebuking him. Therefore, monks, do not appraise the price of any goods whatsoever, and do not sit in the presence of laypeople who are in dispute. Any monk who appraises the price of goods or sits in the presence of laypeople in dispute shall incur a transgression." Since the Blessed One had declared that monks must not appraise the price of any goods whatsoever, a monk who wished to buy a monastic robe went to the market at the time of trading, and —

there he walked alongside a householder, haggling over a single kāṛṣāpaṇa, or one paṇa, or four paṇas, or a quarter of a paṇa, or an eighth of a quarter. The householder grew angry and said: "Noble ones, we ourselves are merchants — and yet you are the greater hagglers by far!" When the monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Monks, those people were right to say what they said. Therefore, monks, do not make purchases yourselves." When the Blessed One had said that monks must not make purchases themselves, the monks did not know how they were to make a purchase. The Blessed One then declared: "Seek out a male lay practitioner residing at the monastery. If the lay practitioner residing there has no faith, or if one truly wishes to make a purchase, speak the determined word two or three times, but do not negotiate by way of kāṛṣāpaṇas and the like." Whether the monk wishes to buy or does not wish to buy, if he goes beyond speaking the determined word two or three times by negotiating in terms of kāṛṣāpaṇas and the like, he shall incur a transgression. There is no fault, however, in negotiating a price for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

This is the eighth verse of the sūtra of the fourth section of the introductory narrative.

In brief:

One must not make a living by trade as one's root livelihood.
The four kinds are not to be divided.
What is to be guarded should be guarded, and done in abundance.
It brings forth a great deal of clamor.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing at Rājagṛha in the bamboo grove, the Kalandaka garden. At that time, King Bimbisāra offered the community of monks a pleasure grove furnished with a thousand fruit trees. The monks ate the fruit and carelessly threw the seeds about, and the grove became like a thicket of arrows. Later, at some point, the king passed by that way and saw what had happened. He asked his ministers whose pleasure grove it was that had become like a thicket of arrows. A minister replied: "Sire, this very grove, furnished with a thousand fruit trees, was the one offered by Your Majesty to the noble ones. They ate the fruit and cast the seeds about carelessly, and so it has now become like a thicket of arrows." The king said: "Do these noble ones not perform tasks and duties here?" The minister replied: "Sire, they are engaged in meditation and recitation, and so they do not perform tasks or duties here." The king said nothing further.

When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, do not neglect duties in the grove that is your source of livelihood — attend to the work." The monks did not know who was to do the work. The Blessed One declared: "Let those who are resident there do it." But those monks were old, and so they were unable to do the work. The Blessed One declared: "Let the entire Saṅgha do the work." Some among them were bent with age; others were unable to work because of illness. The group of six, being unsuitable for such work, did not do it. The Blessed One then declared: "Divide the assembly into portions, and in groups, taking turns, do the work." The monks occupied themselves with receiving scriptural transmission, reading, recitation, and proper mental contemplation, and they entered into that group. The Blessed One declared: "One must not be limited to that alone. Some should eat the tooth-cleaning twigs. Some should wash their faces. Some should wash their feet."

Those monks did the work accordingly, and the fruit ripened and became ready to harvest. Now at some point a group of monks arrived unexpectedly. Seeing the ripened fruit, they said to the venerable ones, "May we also eat ripe mango fruit? Are we permitted?" The monks replied, "These have already been portioned out among us — how could there be any left?" Those new arrivals became disgruntled. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Give some to those who have arrived unexpectedly as well." After the monks had given from what remained after the portioning, the Blessed One declared: "There are four categories that monks must not apportion among themselves. What are the four? They are as follows: whatever belongs to the Saṅgha of all four directions, whatever belongs to all stūpas, whatever is appropriate for all the sick, and all food with monetary value. Therefore, monks may make use of roots, fruit, flowers, and the like — just as individual persons use them for their own purposes — provided that those things fall within their direct purview. As for the flowers and fruit: take care of the trees, and distribute those flowers and fruit to the Saṅgha." The Blessed One said, "Since it falls within their direct purview, each should tend to his own tree, and the flowers and fruit should be distributed to the Saṅgha."

The monks tended the trees accordingly. As the flowers and fruit ripened, the monks abandoned their posts, and thieves carried the flowers and fruit away. The Blessed One then declared: "Post guards." The monks posted only a small number, and that itself became the object of a fault. The Blessed One declared: "Let half of those in the retinue eat first, in rotation." The Blessed One then declared: "Distribute the ripe fruit on the trees to the Saṅgha." But when the fruit ripened, insects had eaten it. The Blessed One declared: "Let those who are resident in the monastery inspect them individually." When those who were inspecting did so, they made a great commotion, and though the monks tried to dissuade them, those inspectors could not be stopped. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "The inspection should be carried out in noble silence — do not make a clamor. If one speaks, there will be an offence."

This is the ninth verse-summary of the fourth narrative episode of the sūtra.

In brief: making fit for use, and a novice's father,
one who has been blessed by me,
one who receives and accepts,
or one who has been instructed accordingly,
bounded and empty,
and a stove — these are complete.

The Blessed One was dwelling in the bamboo grove called Veṇuvana in Rājagṛha, at the place of the Kalandakas.

The Blessed One had declared: "Distribute the ripe fruit on the trees." The monks did not know who was to distribute it. The Blessed One declared: "Let the one who makes things fit for use distribute it. If there is no one to make things fit for use, let the father-novice do it. If there is no father-novice, let the monk himself wash his hands, receive the offering, make it individually fit, and then distribute it." The Blessed One declared, "Let the monk wash his own hands, receive the offering, make it individually fit, and then distribute it." When a single branch was laden with much fruit and could not be borne, the Blessed One declared: "A layman may also assist, and the two together shall distribute it. Whatever the layman has distributed, that is to be received."

Whatever has been made fit for use by a monk need not be received again. If there were some other mangoes known as sweet, these were mixed together and made fit for use one by one, and all had been received. The Blessed One then declared, "Make those fit for use separately." When the Blessed One declared that the mangoes known as sweet were to be made fit for use separately, the group of six went to the pleasure garden and took those mangoes known as sweet themselves, then came to the monastery, received them, and ate them. The monks said, "Venerable ones, if those sweet mangoes were not made fit for use, why have they been consumed?" The attendants replied, "How could they have been made fit for use? The group of six took them, went to the monastery, received them, and ate them." The monks were displeased. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One reflected: if a monk receives something later that he had already taken up earlier, he becomes an object of blame. Therefore a monk should not receive later what he has already taken up earlier. Knowing this, the Blessed One declared, "Monks, the group of six has acted improperly. Therefore, monks, do not receive later what you have already taken up earlier. If one receives later what was already taken up earlier, it becomes an offense."

The origin story is from Śrāvastī. The monks, by pointing with a finger at flowers, fruits, prepared foods, and other foods and drinks that had been made fit for use, said, "Give this," and "Give these." When all of it had been eaten up and the making-fit-for-use had not been equalized, some monks who had not yet parted from attachment were displeased. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Monks, being displeased is pointless. Therefore a monk shall not eat while pointing with a finger and saying, 'Give this,' and 'Give these.' If a monk eats while pointing with a finger and saying, 'Give this,' and 'Give these,' it becomes an offense." As for drinks, those lacking warmth are sought when one desires something ripened, while those with great warmth are sought when one desires something unripened.

The origin story is from Śrāvastī. When the group of six were going about on their tour of the region, they arrived at the monastery of another village in the rocky hills, and the monks of that monastery had gone out for their daytime activity, leaving the monastery empty. The members of the group of six said among themselves happily and joyfully, "This monastery is empty and has no boundary established. If we were to stay here, how should we reside? Let us establish a boundary and then come back." They said, "Very well, let it be done just so." And immediately after they had established the boundary, the monks who had previously been residing there arrived. The group of six said to them, "Rest here." Those monks replied, "Venerable ones, you have only just arrived unexpectedly. We have been residing here from before, so it is fitting that we should say to you, 'Please rest.'" The group of six said, "Venerable ones, we too have established a boundary here." Those monks replied, "We too established a boundary here earlier." And so those monks became uncertain, wondering whether the earlier boundary or the later one should prevail. The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared:

Monks who arrive unexpectedly at a monastery, even if they see it empty upon entering, must not establish a boundary. They should rest from the journey, and only after making careful inquiry, if no one was residing there before, may they then establish a boundary for the first time. Otherwise, they may not establish one.

The basis for the next rule arose in Śrāvastī. At the gate of the Jeta Grove, a quarrel broke out between two laymen. One of the monks who had assembled there took sides with one of them, and acting on his behalf, brought a lawsuit against the other before the king's court. When the other party was condemned and fined, the second layman then abused him. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is improper for a layman to abuse another. Therefore, monks must not sit near people who are quarreling, and must not take sides in lawsuits — leave and go elsewhere. If a monk sits near those who are quarreling and takes sides in a lawsuit, he incurs a transgression."

This concludes the tenth set of verses of the fourth group of rules in the sūtra.

The fourth group of rules is complete.

Now the summary verse. Statues of bodhisattvas, going on circuit, vessels for offerings, assemblies and platforms, and the great drum and wheel — these are last.

In brief, what the great sage declared as permitted: images of bodhisattvas, platforms, victory banners, pennants, and iron pillars.

The basis for the next rule arose in Śrāvastī. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada (Anāthapiṇḍika) made a request to the Blessed One: "If the Blessed One will permit it, I should like to make an image of the Blessed One as a bodhisattva." The Blessed One declared, "Householder, you may make it." Then the householder said, "If the Blessed One permits it, I should like to surround the bodhisattva image with victory banners." The Blessed One declared, "Householder, you may surround it." Then the householder said, "If the Blessed One permits it, I should like to surround the image with a platform." The Blessed One declared, "Householder, you may surround it with a platform." Then the householder said, "If the Blessed One permits it, I should like to surround the image with an iron railing." The Blessed One declared, "Householder, you may surround it." Then the householder said, "If the Blessed One permits it, I should like to place pennants atop the iron railing." The Blessed One declared, "Householder, you may hang them."

This is the first set of verses of the fifth group of rules in the sūtra.

Now the summary verse. A bodhisattva image taken on circuit, likewise adorned with ornaments and anointing substances, with a palanquin and a chariot, a pennant, a parasol, a victory banner, and ear-ornaments.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍika. The householder Anāthapiṇḍika made a request to the Blessed One: "If the Blessed One permits it, I should like to take a bodhisattva image on circuit through the town." The Blessed One declared, "Householder, you may take it on circuit." Since the bodhisattva image had no ornaments and was not beautiful, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika then said, "If the Blessed One permits it, I should like to offer ornaments to the bodhisattva image." The Blessed One declared, "Householder, you may offer them — offer ankle ornaments, ear ornaments, and the like as well." Then the householder said, "If the Blessed One permits it, I should like to adorn the bodhisattva image with perfumed ornaments." The Blessed One declared, "Householder, you may adorn it."

The bodhisattva image was carried on foot through the town,

The householder Anāthapiṇḍika then said, "If the Blessed One permits it, I should like to carry the bodhisattva image from the side road into the city." The Blessed One declared, "Householder, you may — carry it." But when it was carried along the side road, it did not look beautiful. So the householder Anāthapiṇḍika said, "If the Blessed One permits it, I should like to carry the bodhisattva image on a chariot." The Blessed One declared, "Householder, you may — do so." But the chariot, having neither banners nor a parasol, did not look beautiful. So the householder Anāthapiṇḍika said, "If the Blessed One permits it, I should like to adorn the top of the chariot with banners, a parasol, victory standards, and the like." The Blessed One declared, "Householder, you may — adorn it." But when the bodhisattva image's ear ornament above the head was adorned with flowers, it did not look beautiful. So the householder Anāthapiṇḍika said, "If the Blessed One permits it, I should like to offer a flower garland ornament for the ear ornament above the head of the bodhisattva image." The Blessed One declared, "Householder, you may — offer it."

This is the second verse of the fifth section of the sūtra dealing with the narrative occasion.

In brief:

Offerings given and offerings made,
likewise the garland-vessels,
and the musical instruments as well — none of these shall be stopped,
and none of the assembled ornaments shall be removed.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍika's park at Śrāvastī. The householder Anāthapiṇḍika then said, "If the Blessed One permits it, I should like to offer a gift at the feet of the bodhisattva image." The Blessed One declared, "Householder, you may — offer it."

At the time of that festival offering, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen from various regions, and also the great majority who had come wishing to view it, made many offerings to the image. The monks who were carrying it did not know into whose care the offerings received should be entrusted. The Blessed One then declared, "Monks shall take charge of it." But the elder monks were displeased at having to carry it. The Blessed One declared, "Those who arrange the lodgings — and also both the junior and senior monks — shall take charge of it. As for the elder monks, the elders themselves shall guard it."

Offerings given — flowers, garments, and the like — were placed on top of the chariot, and some things that had fallen were taken without having been given. People then carried it away in the folds of their robes. The householder Anāthapiṇḍika then said, "If the Blessed One permits it, I should like to place garland-vessels on top of the chariot." The Blessed One declared, "Householder, you may — do so."

The monks did not stop the music, and without dispersing the crowd they concealed the material ornaments. Brahmin and householder devotees then said of the noble ones, "They have the same faith as we do, and yet some have no faith at all — how wrong it is of you to stop the music, to disperse the many people, and to remove the material ornaments!" When things had reached this point, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Monks, to rebuke the brahmins and householders is inappropriate. Therefore the monks shall not stop the music, shall not disperse the crowd, and shall not remove the material ornaments."

If one observes them, one incurs a transgression along with the corresponding offence. This concludes the third set of verses of the sūtra of the fifth ground of the narrative basis.

In brief:

The great assembly, and the festival,
the warming of the face in the last month of spring,
and those performed every five or six years —
these culminate in the great offering feast.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada in Śrāvastī. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada saw monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who had come from various districts, and joy arose in him, and he thought: "The Blessed One has declared that timely giving is of five kinds. What are these five? Giving to those who have arrived unexpectedly — this is the first occasion of giving. Giving to the sick and to those who care for the sick — this is the second occasion of giving. Giving when the harvest has failed and there is poverty and distress — this is the third occasion of giving. When new grain and new fruit have come in, first offering them to one who is endowed with moral discipline and endowed with virtue, and only thereafter eating oneself — this is the fourth occasion of giving. When the wind rises, or the region is overcast, or rain falls, or there is cold, and by reason of wind, overcast sky, rain, or cold, cooked rice, gruel, porridge, drink, or the like is brought out and offered to the Saṅgha, thinking: 'If the noble ones eat this, their bodies will not be chilled, their Dharma-robes will not be wetted by the rain, and they will dwell in comfort and ease' — this giving is the fifth occasion of giving.

"Since it is so, if the Blessed One permits me, I will prepare a gathered meal for the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen and others who are weary from the road and dwelling in various districts."

He then went to where the Blessed One was, approached him, prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, he addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable Blessed One, giving to those who have arrived unexpectedly from various districts is called the first occasion of giving — and so on through to the fifth occasion, the giving in due season, which enables them to dwell in comfort and ease, as described before. These five occasions of giving in due season have been taught. Now, here, at this great offering for the bodhisattva, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen and others who have come unexpectedly from various districts and are thoroughly worn out by the journey — if the Blessed One permits, I will prepare a gathered meal for that assembly."

The Blessed One replied: "Householder, you have permission — make the preparations."

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada then asked the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, in which month was the Blessed One born?" The Blessed One replied: "Householder, in the last month of spring." "Then, if the Blessed One permits, I will prepare a warming of the face at the Blessed One's palace." The Blessed One replied: "Householder, you have permission — make the preparations."

He then asked again: "Venerable Blessed One, after how many years should the head be shaved?" The Blessed One replied: "Householder, after five years have passed." "Then, if the Blessed One permits, I will prepare a great feast for the Blessed One once every five years."

The Blessed One replied: "Householder, you have permission — make the preparations."

He then asked again: "Venerable Blessed One, after how many years is the topknot left in place?" The Blessed One replied: "Householder, after six years." "Then, if the Blessed One permits, I will prepare a feast for the topknot ceremony." The Blessed One replied: "Householder, you have permission — make the preparations."

He then asked: "In which month did the Blessed One attain the supreme wisdom face to face?" The Blessed One replied: "Householder, in the last month of spring." "Then, if the Blessed One permits, I will prepare a great feast in honour of the Blessed One, who dwells in the shadow of the rose-apple tree of Jambudvīpa." The Blessed One replied: "Householder, you have permission — make the preparations."

This is the fourth verse of the sūtra of the fifth section of the nidāna.

In brief:

The grass-mat, and the doubt,
sitting at different times,
the commotion and the roads,
the wooden plank, the conch, and the beating of the drum.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One instructed that a communal meal be prepared. When many monks had no seat, the Blessed One declared: "Arrange grass-mats and sit there to eat." When the Blessed One had said that they were to sit on grass-mats, the monks, having eaten, became uncertain and carried off the grass-mats and departed. The Blessed One declared: "Do not carry the mats away and leave; instead, gather them into bundles and stack them there, and when the feast is fully concluded, everyone take them at that time."

Because the monks sat at various times, both early and late, for the feast, some finished eating and left while others had not yet arrived, and confusion arose. The Blessed One declared: "Sit in proper order."

When many monks gathered and fell into commotion, not knowing what the time was, the Blessed One declared: "Let the time be announced." They announced it then and there: "The time has come, the time has come." When they announced "the time has come," the Blessed One declared: "Strike the wooden plank." Yet even so, it was not clear to those in other places. The Blessed One then said: "First strike the small wooden plank, and afterwards strike the large wooden plank." Still, those who were dwelling in other quarters during the day did not hear it. The Blessed One then declared: "Press the conch to the mouth and blow it, and also beat the drum."

This is the fifth verse of the sūtra of the fifth section of the nidāna.

In brief:

Then the drum too shall be beaten.
After that, sending out a vehicle,
the arrival of goods and provisions —
these shall be announced in proper fashion.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. When the Blessed One gave the instruction to strike the wooden plank, press the conch, and beat the drum, they struck them one after another in immediate succession, and this caused harm to those who were sick and to those engaged in work. The Blessed One then declared: "When the sick have finished taking their food and those doing work have also finished eating, at that point strike the wooden plank, press the conch, and beat the drum."

Even when the feast was concluded, certain monks, nuns, male lay practitioners, female lay practitioners, and others dwelling in their own quarters had not yet departed. The Blessed One declared: "Send out a vehicle, and once that has gone, everyone depart on their own."

At that time of the feast, the monks did not know how to divide what had been obtained. The Blessed One declared: "Distribute it equally in order of seniority."

When a large gathering of monks made an uproar, the Blessed One declared: "Divide it in groups of ten as one, then in groups of a hundred as one, and after that divide the gains in groups of a thousand as one."

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if within a group of ten one person passes away before the time of distribution, who has rights over the belongings of the deceased?"

The Blessed One declared: "Upāli, if someone dies before the time of distribution, the belongings of the deceased pass by right to the assembled Saṅgha as a whole. However, if one has already distributed and someone then passes away after the time of distribution, the remaining nine receive that person's share. The same principle is to be applied likewise to the groups of eight, of a thousand, and so on."

This is the sixth verse of the sūtra of the fifth section of the case-narratives. The fifth section of the case-narratives is complete. The case-narratives are complete.

A summary of the section on individual matters: first there is salutation; second, the vessels are undetermined; third, there are also the requisites — these are designated as individual. In brief summary: salutation and the strainer, likewise placing down, lying down, and the dog; likewise the drinking bowl and sugarcane; likewise butter, roots, and tree-trunks — these are said to be gathered together in the sūtras.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time two monks who had been speaking harsh and contentious words fell into a quarrel, each speaking harshly to the other, until the younger one rebuked the elder. The elder then withdrew to his dwelling and remained there. The younger monk thought to himself: "I have rebuked the elder; I should go and ask his forgiveness." He went to the elder's dwelling, touched his feet with both hands, and said: "Venerable one, please forgive me for having rebuked you." But the elder, greatly angered, struck and harmed him, saying: "You have done me harm."

When the other monks heard this they ran up and asked the venerable one why he was crying out. He said: "Venerable ones, look — such-and-such a one came to my dwelling and is harming me." They said to him: "Venerable one, why did you strike that elder monk?" And he explained what had happened, whereupon they said nothing and sat in silence.

He then reflected on this, and so the Blessed One had declared that one should pay homage, saying: "That my śrāvakas may accomplish their own aims with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of beneficence, and a mind of affection." With this in mind, he had thought: "When I see this one and feel displeasure and anger, I shall forgive him and depart in whatever manner is fitting." But after he had gone, if later he does not even pay homage to the other person, how much less would he offer forgiveness.

Then at a later time the elder monk was walking and conversing alongside another monk. That monk, coming from the direction where monks were paying homage, arrived there. The monk who was the elder's walking companion said to him: "Why did you not forgive a monk of such virtue, a monk endowed with moral discipline?" The elder replied: "This one has a wicked and wrathful mind — look here, even now he pays homage to you but does not pay homage to me." Just then that monk did pay homage, and the elder said: "Venerable one, do you see that wicked-minded being?" The monk replied: "Venerable one, I do see him."

Then that monk said to him: "Venerable one, if I were to hear elsewhere what I have heard here — that you are one who feels shame and remorse, one devoted to the training — and were to see it confirmed elsewhere, and someone were to say, 'Why are you not like that?' — what then?" The other replied: "Venerable one, what am I to do?" The first then said: "Why do you not forgive a monk such as this, a monk who is fully endowed with moral discipline?" The elder then recounted at length everything that had happened. The monks mocked that elder, and the matter was reported by the monks to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then declared: "Monks, the monk who mocked him should, by all means, ask forgiveness of the one who holds the grudge." When the Blessed One had said that the one who holds the grudge should be asked for forgiveness, a certain monk tried to ask forgiveness but was refused. The Blessed One then declared: "The one who will not forgive should go to the cell of the one who will not be approached, and bow down. That monk need only say 'Be well,' or else simply bow down. If neither is done, a transgression will accrue to both." The Blessed One having said that one should seek forgiveness from a monk who holds a grudge, two monks then fell into a quarrel arising from sharp and unpleasant words, and from that into mutual fault-finding, fighting, and disputing. Of the two, the younger monk addressed the elder monk with harsh and offensive words, then, growing utterly enraged, went into his dwelling, shut the door, and sat there brooding on those very abusive words he had spoken. Yet throughout all of this there was nothing that the blessed Buddha did not know, did not see, did not comprehend, or did not cognize fully. For the blessed buddhas, by the very nature of reality, are possessed of great compassion, and have entered upon the task of benefiting the world; they are guardians, solitary and courageous; they abide alone in calm abiding and insight; they are skilled in the three aspects of those who are to be tamed; they have crossed the four rivers; they stand utterly firm on the base of the four legs of miraculous power; they are fearless, made free from fear by the four fearlessnesses; they have utterly abandoned the five limbs; they have passed completely beyond the five destinies; they are endowed with the six limbs; they have fully completed the six perfections; they ever abide in the six; they are adorned with the flowers of the seven limbs of awakening; they teach the noble eightfold path; they are skilled in the nine successive abiding meditative absorptions; they are endowed with the power of the ten powers; they are renowned in the ten directions; they are supreme in holding sway over the thousand hundreds. They observe who is declining, who is advancing, who has fallen into suffering, who is afflicted, who is being harmed, who has fallen into suffering and affliction and harm, who is inclining toward the lower realms, who is falling into the lower realms, who is heading straight to the lower realms — and they resolve: "Those whom I shall draw out of the lower realms I shall place individually upon the fruit of liberation in the higher realms. Those who have not yet generated roots of virtue, I shall cause them to generate them. Those who have generated them, I shall bring them to full maturation. Those who have fully matured, I shall bring them to complete liberation." Three times by day and three times by night, the Buddha surveys the world with his buddha-eye and enters into the illumination of gnosis.

It has also been said:

Even the ocean that is home to sea monsters
may in time be crossed and passed beyond,
but for the children who are to be tamed,
a buddha will never fail to come at the right moment.

Then the Blessed One, in another place, produced a smile. By the very nature of reality, whenever the blessed buddhas produce a smile, rays of light — blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth — issue from their mouths. Some of these rays descend downward, and some ascend upward. Those that descend downward pass through the realms of the reviving, the black-line, the crushing, the crying, the great crying, the burning, the great burning, the without-respite, the blister realm,

the continuous-blister, the Aṭaṭa, the Hahava, the Huhuva, the Utpala, the Padma, and the Mahāpadma — and so forth — the realms of hell-beings. Wherever those rays descended upon the hot hells, they became cool; wherever they descended upon the cold hells, they became warm. In this way, those beings were relieved of their particular torments and made comfortable. Then, as those beings began to wonder, "Might we have died and passed on from here, or have we been reborn elsewhere?" — in order to generate in them deep faith, the Blessed One sent forth an emanation. When they saw that emanation, they thought: "We have not died and passed on from here, nor have we been reborn elsewhere. It is by the power of seeing this being who has come before us that our torments have been relieved." Their minds rejoiced in the emanation, and the karmic force of the torments of hell being exhausted, they were established wherever the right vessel for truth existed, taking rebirth among gods and humans at the border of those realms.

Those rays that went upward then visited the gods of the realm of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-Three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the gods who delight in creation, the gods who lord over others' creations, and the gods of the Brahmā realm: Brahmā's Company, the Ministers of Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Minor Radiance, the Immeasurable Radiance, the Utter Radiance, the Minor Virtue, the Immeasurable Virtue, the Abundant Virtue, the Cloudless, the Born of Merit, the Great Fruit, the Not-Great, the Not-Tormented, the Clear-Sighted, the Resplendent, and the gods of Akaniṣṭha. There the rays proclaimed impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness, and also recited two verses:

Strive to take birth in a fortunate state.
Apply yourselves diligently to the Buddha's teaching.
Like a great elephant in a house of mud,
vanquish the armies of the Lord of Death.

Whoever, with true and careful heedfulness,
shall practice this Dharma of discipline,
having utterly abandoned the wandering of birth,
shall in the end draw forth suffering by the root.

Then those rays encircled the great trichiliocosm — the world-system of one billion worlds — and returned to attend upon the Blessed One. If the Blessed One intended to give a prophecy concerning a past event, they dissolved at his back. If he intended to give a prophecy concerning the future, they dissolved before him. If he intended to give a prophecy of birth in hell, they dissolved at the soles of his feet. If he intended to give a prophecy of birth as an animal, they dissolved at his heels. If he intended to give a prophecy of birth as a hungry ghost, they dissolved at his toes. If he intended to give a prophecy of birth as a human being, they dissolved at his knees. If he intended to give a prophecy of becoming a wheel-turning monarch of power, they dissolved at the palm of his left hand. If he intended to give a prophecy of becoming a wheel-turning monarch, they dissolved at the palm of his right hand. If he intended to give a prophecy of birth as a god, they dissolved at his navel. If he intended to give a prophecy of awakening as a śrāvaka, they dissolved at his mouth. If he intended to give a prophecy of solitary awakening, they dissolved at the space between his brows. If he intended to give a prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, they dissolved at the crown of his head.

Then those rays circled the Blessed One three times and dissolved at the back of the Blessed One's feet. Thereupon the venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, the Blessed One, in verse:

Like the rising of the sun that illumines all,
the many rays that issued from within your mouth,
blazing in a thousand hues of varied color,
have filled the ten directions with their light.

And then he spoke again in verse:

Free from excitement and dejection, released from pride,
the Buddha, the very cause for all beings —
the Victor, conqueror of foes, white as a conch and as a lotus —

does not smile without cause. You who possess a steady mind, may you yourself know the right moment. Let those who hear and follow the sovereign Victor, the noble supreme herd-leader of the steadfast Sages, have their doubts cleared away by virtue. Without a purpose, the ocean or the king of mountains he would not reveal. A fully awakened buddha does not display a smile. Because he who is steadfast shows a smile for a reason, all these many people long to hear it.

Then the Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, it is so. It is indeed so. Ānanda, a Tathāgata, an arhat, a fully and perfectly awakened buddha does not smile without cause and without condition.

"Ānanda, did you see that young monk? He spoke harsh words to a monk, slandering and abusing him, and that monk became angry." The Blessed One said: "Yes." "That monk entered his room, shut the door, and sat there contemplating inwardly those harsh words that had been spoken to him. Overwhelmed by anger, he dwelt upon them again and again. As a result of that, he fully gave rise to all ten roots of aversion. When his time passed and he died, he will be reborn as a venomous serpent in that very room of his."

The noble Vinaya, the thirty-eighth fascicle.

Thus, while the Blessed One was conversing with the venerable Ānanda, that same monk — he who had spoken the harsh words — had contemplated them many times over, and being utterly consumed by anger, had multiplied and intensified it greatly. Having thereby attained all ten roots of aversion, he died and passed away, and was reborn as a venomous serpent in that very room of his.

Then the Blessed One declared to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, that deluded man has been reborn as a venomous serpent in that same room. Go to him, approach him, and in my name say: 'May you be free from illness.' Say to him: 'You went forth into my teaching, and from the four fruits of the contemplative life you were due to realize any one of those fruits. But now, because of the power of your anger, you have been reborn here as a venomous serpent. Forgive that monk. If further time passes without that, you will be born among hell-beings.'"

"Reverend, I will do as commanded," said the venerable Ānanda. He heard this from the Blessed One, and then, taking the monk along, he went to that monk's room and knocked gently at the door and said: "Good sir, the Blessed One sends you his greeting: May you be free from illness. He says: You went forth into my teaching, and from the four fruits of the contemplative life you were due to realize any one of those fruits. But now, because of the power of your anger, you have been reborn here as a venomous serpent. Forgive this monk. And even now, when your time here is done, you risk being born among hell-beings."

At that very moment the serpent released its venom in anger and remained inside the room, not coming out.

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana: "Maudgalyāyana, come here. Go to where the venomous serpent is, and when you have gone, say to it: 'Forgive that monk.'" And so he too went there and spoke those words. The serpent showed only its head through the keyhole, then withdrew back inside.

The news spread everywhere, becoming widely known throughout the land, that a monk had harmed a fellow monk in mind and had as a result been reborn as a serpent in his own room. When King Prasenajit of Kośala, together with his inner court ladies, young attendants, ministers, townspeople, and

retinue, having heard the news and wishing to see this wonder, were moved by curiosity and set out for the Jeta Grove.

Then the Blessed One too, accompanied by his great śrāvaka disciples — the all-knowing Kauṇḍinya, Vāṣpa, Mahānāman, Acyuta, Śāriputra, the great Maudgalyāyana, Ābhāsvara, Ānanda, Nāgasamāla, and others — entered together with King Prasenajit into that room. When the Blessed One spoke to the serpent in its own tongue, it immediately came out of the room.

Then the Blessed One led it out of the building, and at the gateway of the Jeta Grove, before an assembly of many hundreds of thousands and before the Saṅgha of monks, a seat was arranged and the Blessed One took his place upon it. The venomous serpent then looked all around at the great multitude of people and, seized with fear, came to the side of the Blessed One's seat. Moving to the far end of the row in order of seniority, it coiled there, gazing steadily at the Blessed One.

The Blessed One addressed it: "Fair-faced one — having gone forth into my teaching and having the opportunity to realize any one of the four fruits of the contemplative life, you instead allowed yourself to be utterly overcome by violent anger, which you dwelt upon again and again, and you even generated a malicious mind toward a monk. Because of this, you are now reborn as a venomous serpent — a being that is attached to harming and killing, that takes the lives of others and lives by depriving other creatures of their lives. When you die and pass on from here, into what lineage of birth will you be born? Where will you take birth? Where will you come to be reborn?"

When the Blessed One called to mind the serpent's former existence, it broke into weeping.

Then the Blessed One at that moment spoke these verses:

You have taken birth in the animal realm,
born too without leisure.
Why weep to no purpose?
What is there now that you can do?

The Victor is endowed with compassion —
arouse from your heart sincere faith in him.
Then, abandoning this animal birth,
you will go from here to the higher realms.

Because the Dharma taught by the buddha, the Blessed One, is unfailing, the habitual dwelling that the serpent had in that place came to an end.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monk: "Come here, monk. Grant forgiveness to that venomous serpent." The monk said, "Blessed One, how am I to grant forgiveness? Am I to touch its feet?" The Blessed One then made it manifest that it had indeed been a monk in a former life and said: "Have no doubt — touch its feet." In accordance with the Teacher's word, the monk touched its feet, and the serpent in turn touched its head to him. The two of them were seen by the great multitude, who were filled with profound wonder. And so the Blessed One, on account of this event, taught the Dharma to that great multitude in a manner befitting the occasion. Upon hearing it, many hundreds of thousands of living beings came to great realization. The venomous serpent itself, with a mind of sincere faith in the Blessed One, passed away at that moment and was reborn in a fine celestial dwelling among the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Therefore, monks, if this or any other monk is utterly overcome by anger, that is a matter warranting censure. Therefore, when one monk has been angered by another and that other remains still engulfed in anger, let the first monk appeal to him in whatever manner will cause his anger to subside and allow him to dwell in purity. Let that monk also resolve the matter in mind with patience. If someone was angered in the morning, let the other seek his forgiveness in the afternoon. If it was in the afternoon, then let it be in the evening. If it was in the evening, let the other seek his forgiveness the following day."

The Blessed One rose from his seat and went to the assembly hall to enter into inner meditative stillness. Now, by the very nature of things, a certain son of the gods or daughter of the gods, however long or short their life had been, passes away from one place and is reborn in another, and three kinds of thought arise: where did they come from, where have they been reborn, and what karma brought this about? This particular being had died from the bite of a venomous snake and was reborn in the excellent divine realm of the Thirty-Three Gods, where he beheld the Blessed One and, filled with manifest faith toward him, saw clearly. Then that former son of the gods, who had once been bitten by a venomous snake, thought to himself: "I have been here long enough. It would not be fitting for me to go to the Blessed One's presence as I am now. I have not yet been here long enough — I will go to the Blessed One." And so, wearing spotless earrings and a garland, adorned with bracelets and jeweled ornaments, that same evening he gathered armfuls of divine flowers — utpala, padma, kumuda, puṇḍarīka, māndārava, and the like — and illuminated the entirety of the Jeta Grove with a great radiance. He then scattered flowers before the Blessed One and sat in the Blessed One's presence to hear the Dharma. The Blessed One, knowing his intention, his underlying disposition, his temperament, and his nature, taught the Dharma in such a way that he would come to realize the Four Noble Truths of the noble ones in their fullness. Upon hearing this, the son of the gods who had formerly been bitten by the venomous snake shattered the twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection (the belief in a personal self) with the vajra of wisdom and directly actualized the fruit of stream-entry. Seeing the truth, he uttered three words of rejoicing:

"Such benefit as this the Venerable One has given — my mother never gave it, my father never gave it, no king ever gave it, no god ever gave it, no beloved ever gave it, no multitude of my own relatives ever gave it, none of my former ancestors ever gave it, no ascetic or brahmin ever gave it. The Blessed One has dried up my ocean of blood and tears, led me beyond the mountain of bones, closed the door to the lower realms, and opened the door to the higher realms and to liberation, placing me in the abode of gods and humans.

Through your power, you have cut the roads of the lower realms,
those paths teeming with manifold faults and intolerable suffering.
The supreme merit — the path leading to the higher realms —
and the path beyond sorrow I have attained this very day.
Relying on you, free from fault,
today I am utterly pure, with eyes perfectly cleansed.
I have attained the noble, pleasing calm abiding of insight.
I have crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering.
I am worthy of worship by humans, gods, and asuras.
Released from birth, old age, sickness, and death,
an outcome so difficult to see even in a thousand existences —
O Sage, today, having seen you, I have attained the fruit."

Then, with his ornaments still hanging, he prostrated at the Blessed One's two feet with joy arising in him. He circumambulated to the right around the Foe-Subduer and departed to the divine world, the realm of the gods.

Afterward, the son of the gods who had formerly been bitten by the venomous snake departed with such joy as a merchant who has found his profit, as a farmer rejoicing in a fine harvest year, as a hero who has won the victory in battle, as a sick man released from every illness — he came to the Blessed One with such joy and abundance, and having gone to his own abode, he was seen by the monks who strove diligently without sleeping in the early evening and at dawn. Seeing a great radiance blazing in the Blessed One's presence, they became uncertain and asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, did Brahmā, lord of the Brahmā assembly, come to visit the Blessed One last night? Did Śakra, Lord of Gods (Indra), come? Did the four World-Protectors come to pay their respects?" And the monks replied: "It was not Brahmā, lord of the Brahmā assembly —

nor was it Śakra, Lord of Gods — nor did the four World-Protectors and the like come to pay their respects to me. Rather, the one who was bitten by the deadly snake and endured it through the patience practiced by the monk — he, with open faith arising toward me in his mind, passed away from this life and was reborn in a fair and pleasant abode among the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. And so last night he came to my presence, I taught him the Dharma, he saw the truth, and then he went to his own abode." Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves in this way: one should practice patience, and one should speak of the virtues of patience. Train yourselves, monks, in precisely that way. When the Blessed One had so declared, those monks rejoiced and took delight in what the Blessed One had spoken.

The setting is in Śrāvastī. The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One: "Venerable one, when one performs a full ordination, while saying to those to be fully ordained 'Do not ordain me,' if monks nonetheless perform the full ordination, does that count as a full ordination or not?" The Blessed One replied: "Upāli, it does not count as a full ordination; moreover, those who perform the ordination incur a transgression." "But why, Blessed One?" "Because even a fully ordained monk who surrenders his training is called 'not fully ordained' — how much more so at the time of actually conferring full ordination."

Again, the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, you have said that novice monks who have reached the age of twenty should be given full ordination. If other novice monks whose own ages are not known to them — because their bodies are large — and the monks, being uncertain about their age, are unwilling to ordain them, how should one proceed with them?" The Blessed One declared: "Upāli, in such a case, determine it from the physical marks and then confer full ordination. Do not be uncertain about this." When the Blessed One had said, "Determine it from the physical marks and confer full ordination," the monks stripped the candidate bare and proceeded to examine the marks. The candidate was intensely embarrassed, and thereupon the Blessed One declared: "Do not strip him bare. Instead, tell him to place his alms bowl or a vessel covered with a robe or a Dharma robe on the space under his armpit and upon the armpit itself — and examine it there. If those marks are present, confer full ordination; if they are absent, do not."

He asked again: "Venerable one, if monks confer full ordination upon a monk using the procedure for ordaining a nun, does that count as a full ordination or not?" "Upāli, it does count as a full ordination; however, those who perform the ordination incur a transgression." "Venerable one, if monks and nuns together confer full ordination upon a nun using the procedure for ordaining a monk, does it count as a full ordination or not?" "Upāli, it does count as a full ordination; however, both assemblies incur a transgression."

These are the opening verses of the first sūtra of the Single Chapter:

In brief: a gathering place, a village with its surrounds,
with the arising of mind — the restoration ceremony —
and also the three killings in the same way:
analysis and the remainder of the Saṅgha.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. Some monks set out to travel about the region together with many guests. At that time the restoration ceremony (poṣadha) fell due for them, and they saw a direction where the ground was strewn with living creatures. They said to one another: "Venerable ones, come this way."

"Let us perform the restoration ceremony on the side where the ground is clear of living creatures." And so they undertook to perform the restoration ceremony there. Meanwhile, many of the guests had gone on ahead, and those monks followed behind them. Along the way they were waylaid by bandits and arrived at the temple. The monks saw them and said: "Have you come safely? Venerable ones, have you come safely? Did you travel well?" They replied: "How could we have traveled well? What is the trouble? We were waylaid by bandits." They told the monks what had happened to them, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Do not perform the restoration ceremony out of attachment to a place free of living creatures. Perform the restoration ceremony in the village and its surrounds." The Blessed One said this, and then half of the monks entered the village while the other half remained outside, so they did not assemble together and the ceremony was not performed. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Those who reside in the village should perform the restoration ceremony in the village. Likewise, monks should perform the restoration ceremony and not remain sitting through the ceremony without performing it. If they do remain, it becomes a transgression."

Some monks set out on the road together with many merchant travelers. A monk said to the merchants: "Friends, we are going to perform the restoration ceremony — please wait just a moment." The merchants replied: "Noble ones, there is danger from bandits in this direction; please keep moving and stay together." The monks thought: "Shall we stay here? Shall we stay here?" and they followed behind those travelers until dawn came upon them as they went. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, when it is time for the restoration ceremony, do not go without having performed it. Or else perform the ceremony while traveling."

When the monks undertook to perform the ceremony while traveling, the merchants said: "Noble ones, we are saying nothing and moving along out of fear of bandits — why are you making such noise?" The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not perform the restoration ceremony in an elaborate way — do it in brief."

When the monks undertook to do it in brief, the merchants still found fault with them. The Blessed One then declared: "By the mere arising of mind, consecrate it." Therefore there are these four things — the consecration of the monastic robe, the dedication of the robe, the restoration ceremony, and arising from the proper procedure — that are all accomplished by the mere arising of mind. This is how it should be done: fixing mindfulness with the Buddha as its object, one should generate the mind and consecrate the restoration ceremony. Then one should also recite the words aloud: "Today is the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony of the Saṅgha. I, the monk named such-and-such, likewise perform the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony. I, named such-and-such, declare my own purification from all impediment-creating phenomena." Having thus consecrated the restoration ceremony by one's own recitation, when the time comes to meet with an assembled Saṅgha, one should perform the restoration ceremony together with the Saṅgha. One should recite this twice, then three times, and perform the ceremony accordingly. It is not the case that the ceremony need not be performed. If it is not performed, a transgression occurs.

The occasion for the next rule is in Śrāvastī. Some monks were traveling through a ravine when bandits seized them. The bandits said among themselves: "Come now, what shall we do with them? Let us strike their heads — kill these ones." The monks thought to themselves:

"We are surely going to be killed and cut down," they thought, and so they said to the bandits: "Why do you wish to kill us?" The bandits replied: "Kings, wealthy men, merchants, and caravan leaders hold great faith in you, and if you were to speak to them, they would harm us." At that point a young monk committed a transgression arising from deliberate false speech. He then said to the venerable ones: "Will it be permitted for me to remain here until I have confessed this transgression to the venerable ones?" The others said: "Very well, then stay right here."
