He came forward before the monks and knelt down, and said: "Please hear me, venerable ones. I, who am called such-and-such, have committed the transgression of deliberate false speech knowingly. I confess this fault before the venerable ones. I acknowledge it. I disclose it. I do not conceal it. If I confess and acknowledge it, it will be well with me; if I do not confess and acknowledge it, it will not be." He replied to him: "Do you see it clearly?" "I see it." "Do you vow henceforth to restrain yourself?" "I vow." This was said twice, and then three times. When all the bandits heard this, they said: "Do the noble ones not speak falsehood? Truly, they do not speak falsehood." Filled with manifest faith in the noble ones, they then said: "In that case, do not say anything to anyone today." "Certainly, we will say nothing to anyone," the monks said, and departed. They went to the monastery, and when doubt arose among them, the monks who were in that situation reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the lord of the forest confessed before the bandits — do not have any doubt in that regard."

The occasion for the next rule is also in Śrāvastī. Another monk who was traveling on tour was seized by bandits. The bandits deliberated amongst themselves and said: "Come now, what shall we do? Strike their heads — kill these ones." The monks thought: "We are surely going to be killed and cut down." They said to the bandits: "Why do you wish to kill us?" The bandits replied: "Kings, wealthy men, merchants, and caravan leaders hold great faith in you, and if you were to speak to them, they would do us harm and render our efforts fruitless." The monks said: "Release us and we will say nothing to anyone." The bandits said: "Then if you vow to us that at the time of the fifteenth — when you gather together and recite — you will speak at length before us, we will let you go." At that point one monk, who knew the text well by heart, fearing that they would be killed, was frightened, and quickly recited the Prātimokṣa individually on his own. When the bandits heard this with manifest faith, they said: "Noble ones, do you truly uphold and protect all of this?" He replied: "This is the teaching of the Teacher — why would we not uphold and protect it properly?" The bandits then said: "Noble ones, please depart in peace and do not speak of this to anyone." "Certainly, we will not speak of it," the monks said, and departed. They went to the monastery. When doubt arose among them, the monks in that situation reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the lord of the forest recited the Prātimokṣa before the bandits — it was well recited. Do not have any doubt in that regard."

The occasion for the next rule is also in Śrāvastī. Some monks who were touring through a district called Beu set out on their way, and —

The bandits seized them. The bandits said among themselves: "These men are useless — what are they good for? Let's cut off their heads and kill them." Now among the bandits there was one who knew about monks. He saw them, and compassion arose in him. Unable to free them, he said out of sympathy: "Kill these men and be done with it — it is better that way. Tie them to some uncut grass, take their belongings, and go. As for me, I am tortured by hunger and cold and shall likely die." At that, one of the others said: "If he speaks like that, what are we to do?" Some said: "It is good that he does so." So they stripped the monks of their belongings, bound them to some uncut grass, and departed.

Now the king of the district of Beu, named Cārpa, had gone out with a fourfold army in pursuit of a wild animal that had strayed. His troops spotted the monks from a great distance. The king asked his minister: "Look there — are those not wild animals?" The minister shielded his eyes to look, then drew closer to the king and saw that they were human beings. The king said: "Are they naked non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), or what?" One of those with him said: "Your Majesty, it would seem so." But one among them who knew about monks said: "Your Majesty, they are not naked tīrthikas — they are monks, sons of the Śākyans." "How do you know?" "Your Majesty, on the one side they are dark, on the other they are white." Then the king went and asked them: "Noble ones, why are you in this state?" "Your Majesty, we were overpowered by bandits." "Noble ones, but then why are you bound like this?" "Your Majesty, we have been bound with the bonds of the training, for the Blessed One has laid down as our training: 'To demolish a village of seeds or a village of living creatures, or to cause it to be demolished, is a transgression.'" The king was filled with faith and rejoicing, and he released them. He then presented each one with three robes.

They went to the monastery. Since they had spoken of the transgression in that manner before the king, doubt arose among them. They described at length what had happened to the other monks, and the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "This king is a consecrated monarch, head-anointed from the kṣatriya lineage, and he is the foremost among all worldly people. Therefore what was spoken was well spoken — do not have any doubt in that regard."

The occasion for the next rule is also in Śrāvastī. The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable One, when a person who has committed a transgression is in the presence of another who has likewise committed that same transgression, may that person confess the transgression? Upāli, is that permissible?" "It is not permissible. However, if the offenses are of different kinds, then it is permissible."

The occasion for the next rule is also in Śrāvastī. A certain monk committed an offense against the Saṅgha that exceeded the ordinary, and remorse arose in him. He became pale, emaciated, and despondent, lay down on a bed, and stopped caring for his body. Other monks said to him: "Venerable one, why have you become so pale, so emaciated and despondent — lying in bed and neglecting your body? Tell us what your illness is." He said nothing. Then a monk who was a close friend of his noticed him and asked him, and he told him everything in detail. The friend said: "Venerable one, in that case, you should report it to the monks." "If that is what must be done, I will come," he said. Then the friend said: "In that case, come here — or go to another place and confess it there."

He agreed, and the two of them set out together for another place. But halfway along the road, the time had passed, and that monk thought: "The purpose for which I set out — the time for it has already passed. Why go on?" So he turned back. When he returned, the other monks greeted him: "Welcome, venerable one. Did you have a comfortable journey? Did you make good use of your time?" At that he burst into tears. The monks asked him: "Venerable one, why are you weeping?" He said: "Because the monk who was traveling with me has passed away." They said to him: "Venerable one, why weep? All conditioned things are just so by their very nature." He replied: "It is because he passed away while still bearing a transgression." At this the monks said: "In that case, weeping is appropriate, for he will dwell for a long time in hell."

The monks reported all of this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, that son of good family has been cleared of that transgression. I have taught that a transgression is cleared through intention, not through punitive action. Therefore, one who has natural shame may be permitted to confess before a single person. Let him confess before one person alone, and have no doubt about this."

Now, certain individuals who had not yet been freed from attachment — those who held the sūtras, those who held the Vinaya, those who held the matrices, some elder members of the Saṅgha, those of great renown, and those of great merit — without examining the matter properly, incurred a secondary Saṅgha transgression. They associated with those who were practicing the penalized acts, lived alongside them, and criticized even those monks who had learned little — including attendants, brahmins, householders, and others. Some became displeased. The monks reported this as it had occurred to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "They too, having resolved firmly not to act that way again in the future, should confess before a single person. Have no doubt about this."

This is the second verse of the first sūtra within the section of individual cases.

In summary:
What is to be settled, let it be settled.
Though seven years have passed, one may still proceed.
What was not concluded together remains just so.
It is the case of one whose hide is unsuitable.

The blessed buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. It fell to the venerable Ānanda to look after the monastery. Prasenajit, king of Kośala, came to the Jeta Grove, paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One, and then went to where the venerable Ānanda was staying, approached him, paid homage at his feet, and sat down before him to hear the Dharma. The venerable Ānanda then entered into the sūtra collection, drew from it, and began to explain it at some length before moving on to an abridged explanation. The king said: "Noble Ānanda, I am busy — please do not give the abridged version." He said this two and three times. The venerable Ānanda replied: "Great king, even if you are busy, I am occupied." The king asked: "Noble Ānanda, what are you occupied with?" He said: "I must look after the monastery." The king said: "Noble Ānanda, could someone else take the turn? I belong to the Saṅgha, so I wish to do the work." The king thought: "This is something I can do," and went to where the Blessed One was staying.

He prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and spoke these words: "Venerable One, I am King Prasenajit, consecrated with the royal diadem upon my head. Whatever work is mine to do, I do it myself. Whatever is fitting for the ladies of the inner court to do, the ladies of the inner court do it. Whatever is fitting for the young attendants to do, the young attendants do it. Whether minister, chief minister, military commander, townsman, or villager — each does their own work. The Blessed One is the unsurpassed king of Dharma. Ah, Blessed One! Surely the compassionate one too ought to leave in place those who are fit to remain, and not assign them to work duties — why would he do otherwise?" When King Prasenajit had spoken thus, the Blessed One said nothing in reply, and so his silence was taken as consent. King Prasenajit, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that he had accepted, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence.

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and gather all the monks residing and staying in Śrāvastī into the assembly hall." The venerable one replied: "Venerable One, as you command." And so the venerable Ānanda, having received the instruction from the Blessed One, gathered together all the monks residing in Śrāvastī into the assembly hall, then went to where the Blessed One was, approached, and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

The venerable Ānanda then said to the Blessed One: "Venerable One, all the monks residing and staying in Śrāvastī have assembled in the assembly hall. Blessed One, may you now consider this the right moment."

Thereupon the Blessed One proceeded to where the assembly hall was, entered, and took his seat on a prepared throne before the community of monks. Seated there, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, today Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, came to me and said: 'Ah, Blessed One! Those who are fit to remain — let them be set aside; it is not right to assign them to work duties.' He says this on your behalf. So from this day forth, do not assign to work duties those who are fit to remain."

When the Blessed One had said, "Those who are fit to remain, set them aside from work duties," the monks did not know who was fit to remain. The Blessed One then declared: "Those who are masters of the sūtras, masters of the Vinaya, masters of the mātṛkā (Skt. mātṛkā — the proto-Abhidharma matrices), those who teach many, and the elders of the Saṅgha — these are the ones fit to remain. As for a master of sūtras, it is just that alone. Similarly, a master of the Vinaya, a master of the mātṛkā, one who teaches many, and the elders of the Saṅgha — these too are by reason of that very qualification."

When the Blessed One had declared, "A master of sūtras, a master of the Vinaya, and a master of the mātṛkā — these are so by reason of that very qualification," the group of six monks, having read one or two chapters of a sūtra collection, said: "We are masters of sūtras — therefore, do not assign us to work duties." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "One who holds all the sūtras — that one is a master of sūtras, and should not be assigned to work. In the same way, those who have committed one or two pārājika offenses said: 'We too are masters of the Vinaya.'" Similarly, those who had read two chapters of the Vibhaṅga said: "I am a master of the mātṛkā, so do not assign me to work duties." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "One who holds all the Vinaya and —

— all the mātṛkā — that one should not be assigned to work duties."

The setting for the following rule is at Śrāvastī. At that time, King Prasenajit of Kosala, returning from a certain village in the hills, sent out a company of soldiers. They were defeated and came back. He sent them a second and a third time, and each time they were defeated and came back. The ministers said to the king: "Sire, the power of those hill villages is very great. Now that your majesty's power has waned, if your majesty himself were to march there in person, those hill villages would inevitably fall; otherwise it cannot be done." The king then had a great drum sounded, proclaiming: "Let every person in my realm who lives by the power of arms come, without exception, and assemble." Then the king, together with a great army, marched to those villages and surrounded them on all sides. Yet the villagers took refuge in a dense forest and could not be reached.

A minister then said: "The householder Anāthapiṇḍada is of boundless merit and is encompassed entirely by the gods. If he comes here, those hill villages will without doubt submit; no one else can achieve this." The king, showing great respect to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, sent him a letter saying: "Householder, I wish to look upon your face." The moment Anāthapiṇḍada heard this letter read, he set out directly and traveled to those hill villages. But before he reached the villages, he was held up for a long time. Not having seen any monks, he grew thin and pale, his body had wasted away, and when the king saw him he asked: "Householder, do you miss your children?" He replied: "Sire, it is not that I miss my children — it is that I long to see the noble ones." The king then sent a letter to his ministers saying: "Without letting it be known that it is my command, arrange by every means for the noble ones to come here."

The ministers read the letter and entered into consultation. "Now then, how shall this be accomplished?" they asked. Another, elder minister said: "I see a way; let me devise a means and present it." At the gate of the Jeta Grove there was an old orchard belonging to Ārdha-Brahmadatta, which had become overgrown like an arrow-thicket. He had it properly repaired and restored. Then, from the courtyard of the stūpa of hair and nail relics, he stretched a cord to that orchard, saying that by disturbing them — the relics themselves — the gods would come to look and walk there. The workers then began to restore that old orchard. He said: "Stretch a cord through the center of the stūpa of hair and nail relics, and dig irrigation channels following that cord to draw water there."

The monks who were dwelling in the monastery, as well as those who had gone out on their daytime rounds, gathered together and went to that minister. "Good sir," they said, "what are you undertaking here?" He replied: "Noble ones, the gods have sent us a letter saying: 'Restore my father's old orchard, and I shall come there.' And so we ourselves are clearing it on the outside and digging irrigation channels to bring water there." The monks said: "Are you demolishing the stūpa of the Blessed One's hair and nail relics? Do not do that." He replied: "Noble ones, it would not be right for us to disobey the command of the god. Since we do not have two heads, it would not be right for us to break the god's command." The senior monk said: "Good sir, we shall petition the god about it. Wait until then." "Noble ones, we will wait — please make the petition." "Good sir, how long will the god be present there?" "Noble ones, the road is long."

"Good sir, will he return in one to seven days, or will he not return at all?" "Noble ones, he may or may not return." The monks reported what had occurred to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "In that case, monks, for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, I grant the blessing of forty days and permit going beyond the boundary.

Since the monks did not know how to perform the blessing, the Blessed One declared: "Spread out the seats, strike the board, appoint a monk to answer questions that are put, and assemble the entire Saṅgha together. Then, one, two, or three monks — whichever you prefer — should announce: 'Buddhaguptra, Dharmadatta, and the community of Saṅgha — you who have entered the proper early or late rains retreat within this boundary — for the sake of the Saṅgha you have been blessed with forty days and are permitted to go beyond the boundary. Do you consent to remain in this rains retreat, at this rains residence?' If they consent, then following that, one monk should make the motion and perform the formal act.

"'Hear me, venerable Saṅgha. Buddhaguptra, Dharmadatta, and this community of Saṅgha — having entered the early or late rains retreat in this place within the boundary — have been blessed with forty days for the sake of the Saṅgha and will go beyond the boundary. This is their rains residence; they will remain in this rains retreat. If the Saṅgha approves and the time is right, let the Saṅgha grant permission and appoint Buddhaguptra, Dharmadatta, and the Saṅgha community for forty days. That is the motion. The formal act is likewise:

"'Hear me, venerable Saṅgha. Buddhaguptra, Dharmadatta, and this community of Saṅgha have been blessed with forty days for the sake of the Saṅgha and will go beyond the boundary. This is their rains residence; they will remain in this rains retreat. Those among the venerable ones who consent to Buddhaguptra, Dharmadatta, and the Saṅgha community being appointed forty days for the sake of the Saṅgha — let them remain silent. Those who do not consent — let them speak.'

"The Saṅgha has consented to Buddhaguptra, Dharmadatta, and this community of Saṅgha being blessed with forty days for the sake of the Saṅgha, going beyond the boundary, with this as their rains residence, remaining in this rains retreat. The Saṅgha has approved and granted this by its silence, and so it is taken.

"Those whom the Saṅgha has appointed for forty days — let them receive the blessing and go beyond the boundary. Do not be uncertain about it.

"The blessing itself should be performed as follows. One should sit before a monk with palms joined and speak these words:

"'I, whose name is such-and-such, having entered the early or late rains retreat — three months equal — within the boundary, I whose name is such-and-such, for the sake of the Saṅgha, have been blessed with forty days and will go beyond the boundary. This is my rains retreat; I remain in this rains retreat.'

"Say this twice and three times."

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, if one has received the blessing for one day, is it permissible to go beyond the boundary?" "Upāli, it is permissible."

"In the same way, if one has been blessed for two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, seven days, eight days, nine days, ten days, twenty days, or thirty days, it is permissible to go beyond the boundary up to forty days."

"Venerable one, is it permissible to be blessed for more than forty days?" "Upāli, it is not permissible. Why not? Upāli, one should dwell many days within the boundary and few days beyond the boundary."

He asked again: "Venerable one, when the Blessed One has said that one should be blessed for one day — before whom should one be blessed?" "Upāli, that is to be done before a single monk. In the same way, one may be blessed for two days, three days, four days, five days, or up to six days. From six days up to forty days, one should request it from the Saṅgha, and once appointed, one may be blessed before either the Saṅgha or an individual, as one wishes."

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable one, if the skin of something is not permissible, is the flesh of it also not permissible?" "Upāli, if the skin of it is not permissible, then the flesh of it is also not permissible. And the sinews and bones of it are also not permissible."

This is the third verse of the opening sūtra of the first section on the Prātimokṣa.

The Noble Vinaya, the thirty-ninth bundle.

In brief:

Forms with essence, bedding and robes,
And the deceased in the same way —
Crow, owl, and vulture:
These shall not be eaten.

When the Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove of Kalandaka, at the time when King Ajātaśatru had been deceived by the god Devadatta and had removed his father Bimbisāra — who governed his kingdom righteously according to the Dharma — from his throne, depriving him of his life, at that time the king saw the bedding and robes and began to weep. The ministers said: "Your Majesty, the old divine king took delight in the noble ones; it would be fitting to donate these furnishings to the Saṅgha as well." At that the king offered those robes and bedding to the monastery. The monks stored them by placing them in the gatehouse. Then on a later occasion the king came to the monastery and upon seeing them, began to weep. The ministers said: "These were placed in the gatehouse so that the noble ones' gift to you would not be visible — this has become a matter of blame." The monks said nothing. The monks reported this situation to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not store things in the gatehouse." Then they were stored on the upper floor, and that too became a cause for blame. The Blessed One declared: "Do not store things on the upper floor." So they were stored in a dwelling room. Those of little faith said: "The royal robes and bedding — the monks have certainly sold and consumed them; that is why they were visible before and are no longer visible now." They made this reproach. The Blessed One then declared: "On the eighth or fourteenth day, display them on the upper floor." Those of little faith, upon seeing them, said: "The divine bedding and cushions have been sold and consumed by the monks and are gone." The monks reported this situation to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Write and affix a label at the end stating: 'These donated articles belong to King Bimbisāra.'"

The narrative context is at Śrāvastī. At that time a beloved and pleasant-looking grandmother of Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, passed away. She was carried out, cremated, and the funeral rites performed. The next morning, with robes still damp and hair still wet, he went to where the Blessed One was, arrived there, and prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One.

He sat to one side. As he sat there, the Blessed One spoke to Prasenajit, the king of Kosala, saying: "Great king, why have you come here this morning with your hair still wet and your robes still damp?"

"Venerable One, my grandmother, who was so very dear to me and so pleasant to look upon, has passed away. She was carried out, cremated, and the funeral rites were performed. That is why I have come here this morning with robes still damp and hair still wet."

"Great king, was your grandmother truly so dear to you?"

"Venerable One, she was exceedingly dear and pleasant to me. Venerable One, if someone could have kept my grandmother alive in exchange for many draft oxen, I would have given many draft oxen. In the same way, for many horses, for many carriages — even if half my kingdom were asked in exchange for her recovery, and she could thereby have been saved, I would have been able to give even half my kingdom. Yet, Venerable One, though I was gripped by grief such as that, afflicted in such a way, stricken and oppressed by sorrow in such a way, still my grandmother who was so dear and pleasant to me passed on. And I thought to myself: how wonderful is the well-spoken teaching of the Blessed One — that all sentient beings, all living creatures, all born beings reach the end of their life in death. Because it comes to death in the end, the Blessed One's teaching that whatever is born will die — how wonderful that is!"

The Blessed One replied: "Great king, it is indeed so. It is exactly so. All sentient beings, all living creatures, all born beings reach the end of their life in death. Because it comes to death in the end, there is none who, once born, does not die.

"Great king, those of great and high royal lineage, those of great and high brahmin lineage, those of great and high householder lineage — they too reach the end of their life in death. Because it comes to death in the end, there is none who, once born, does not die.

"Furthermore, great king, even those who have received empowerment as rulers, who wield power over many people and have attained dominion, who thoroughly subdue and govern the expanse of great territories — even such beings reach the end of their life in death. Because it comes to death in the end, there is none who, once born, does not die.

"Great king, likewise those who, having gone forth from kingship to dwell as sages, live in such a way that they eat the fruits that fall of themselves, sustaining themselves on roots and fruits — even they reach the end of their life in death. Because it comes to death in the end, there is none who, once born, does not die.

"Great king, likewise even the long-lived gods (devas), resplendent with color in their lofty celestial mansions — even they are subject to dying and passing away from that state of existence.

"Moreover, great king, even the arhats whose defilements are exhausted, who have accomplished what had to be done, who have laid down the burden, who have attained their own goal, whose bond to further existence is destroyed, who are fully liberated in mind through the true teaching — even their bodies are subject to being cast off.

"Further, great king, even the pratyekabuddhas, those solitary awakened ones like a rhinoceros horn, who have tamed themselves alone, who have pacified themselves alone, who have passed beyond sorrow by themselves alone — even they are subject to casting off the body.

"And further, great king, even the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha, endowed with the ten powers, unafraid by virtue of the four fearlessnesses, supreme among the great herd, who roars the lion's roar — even such a body is subject to being cast off.

"Great king, know that all things of that nature are likewise so. Of all sentient beings, of all living creatures, of all born beings —

all beings without exception will come to the end of their life in death. Since death is the final terminus, there is none born who does not die. All sentient beings will come to the end of their life in death.

According as the actions one has done —
so one goes to the fruit of merit or of sin.
Sinful action falls into the hells,
meritorious action goes to the higher realms.
Some, by cultivating the path,
pass beyond sorrow without any defilement.
When even buddhas, solitary buddhas,
and the śrāvakas of the buddhas
must cast off the body,
what need is there to speak of common folk?

Then Prasenajit, king of the land of Kosala, rejoiced at the words of the Blessed One and expressed his delight. He bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, took his leave, and went to his own home. There, seeing the bedding of his late queen lying empty, his mind was overcome by the grief of bereavement, and he said to his ministers: "I have seen this bedding and deep sorrow has arisen in me. Go and offer it to the noble Saṅgha." They took it and offered it to the noble Saṅgha in the Jeta Grove, and the monks stored it by placing it in a gatehouse.

Then at a later time the king came to the temple, saw it there, and wept. His ministers said to him: "Because the noble ones kept it and did not display it when it was offered to you, the act of placing it in the gatehouse itself has become a cause for reproach." The ministers said nothing further and sat in silence.

When the monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Do not store it in the gatehouse — hang it upstairs in an upper room." That too became a cause for reproach, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not hang it in the upper room — store it in a dwelling room." When it was placed in the dwelling room, some people of little faith spread the slander that the monks had sold the queen's bedding and eaten the proceeds: "It was visible before; now it is not." The Blessed One then declared: "On the eighth or fourteenth day of the month, hang it in the upper room for display." People of little faith, seeing it, said: "This is not the queen's bedding — the monks have certainly sold it and eaten the money." The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Write an inscription stating that it is the robe offered by Prasenajit, king of Kosala, and display it thus."

Now the occasion for what follows arose in Śrāvastī. At that time a fierce hailstorm struck Śrāvastī, and many animals and birds died there. Many people rose early and gathered the carcasses of animals and birds fit to eat and carried them away, while those not fit to eat — such as those belonging to crows and the like — were discarded. The Group of Six monks ate abundantly of the meat and slept long. They woke up late and, having heard of it, went off in haste, and they returned bringing crows, owls, vultures, and herons. Brahmins and householders saw them and asked: "What do these noble ones intend to do with those?" The monks replied: "To eat them." The people said: "These noble ones should discard what is not fit to eat. Even if other kinds of meat are obtained, why would one eat this?" The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not eat flesh that is not fit to eat — such as that of crows and the like. If one does eat it, one incurs an offense with remainder."

This has been the fourth verse-section of the first chapter on the Single-Pronged Scepter sūtra.

In summary:

Dogs, hawks, owls,
and birds that eat human flesh,
horses, mules, and foxes,
and monkeys — these you shall not eat.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

A famine arose, and the householders fell into the habit of eating dog flesh. The group of six went on their alms round in Śrāvastī, and at whichever house they arrived, the people there said, "There is not even a little something worthy." Then they arrived at another householder's home, where inside the cooking pot a piece of dog flesh was boiling away. The householder's wife said, "There is nothing worthy here whatsoever — please move on." The monks said, "What is that boiling in the pot?" She replied, "Venerable ones, this is dog flesh." "Do you eat dog flesh?" "Venerable ones, a famine has come upon us, and so we seek what we can." "In that case, give us some as well." "Venerable ones, will you eat it too?" "Indeed — if our lives depend on you, and you are eating it, why should we not eat it as well?" They gave it to them. Having received it, the monks took it and departed. The dogs, catching the scent of what was being carried, surrounded them, barking and biting, and followed along close behind. Brahmins and householders saw this and said to the monks, "Venerable ones, why are you walking along harassed by dogs?" The monks replied, "We obtained a little dog flesh on our alms round." The brahmins and householders said, "Do you venerable ones eat dog flesh?" And the monks replied, "At a time like this, when one cannot obtain alms, should we simply die of hunger?" The monks then reported what had happened to the Blessed One. The Blessed One considered the matter and declared: "Monks, eating dog flesh incurs a fault with an object. Therefore, monks, do not eat dog flesh. If monks eat dog flesh, it becomes an offense with remainder."

The setting is in Śrāvastī. The group of six also ate the flesh of hawks, owls, and flesh-eating birds. Brahmins and householders who lacked faith criticized them. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not eat the flesh of hawks, owls, and flesh-eating birds. If monks eat the flesh of hawks, owls, and flesh-eating birds, it becomes an offense with remainder."

The setting is in Śrāvastī. Thieves stole a young mule belonging to King Prasenajit of the kingdom of Kosala, led it away into a dense forest, slaughtered it there, carried off the flesh, and cast away the head and hooves before departing.

Now the group of six had a custom: they would rise early in the morning, go up to the roof, look out in all four directions to see where smoke was heaviest and where vultures were circling, and then set out in that direction. Seeing vultures circling over the dense forest, they ran toward the forest and went a long way in, and there in the dense forest they found the head, legs, and tail of the mule. They said among themselves, "Friends, dear friends, if something fit to take is found in a refuse heap, may one take it?" "Yes indeed, take it," they agreed, and gathered it all together. The keeper of the mule then came searching up and down and, seeing them, said: "Venerable ones, you who bear the victory banner of the sages — why do you behave so badly? What wrong have we done?" They replied, "You have slaughtered the king's mule." The monks said, "May this evil be pacified — we did not kill it." "Then who did kill it?" "Thieves killed it, and we simply consecrated the head, the feet, and the tail by taking them from the refuse heap." The mule keeper then asked, "Venerable ones, did you take and carry mule flesh?" When the monks said, "We ate it," he criticized them. The monks then reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

"Monks, eating the flesh of a mule constitutes a fault. Therefore, monks, do not eat the flesh of hoofed animals. If monks eat it, they incur a transgression."

The next occasion arose at Śrāvastī. The group of six monks ate fox meat, and brahmins and householders who saw them said, "Venerable ones, what is that?" "It is fox meat." "Do noble ones also carry and eat fox meat?" When the monks said they did, the brahmins and householders criticized them. The monks then reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, for brahmins and householders to criticize is natural. Therefore, monks, do not eat fox meat. If monks eat fox meat, they incur a transgression."

The next occasion arose at Śrāvastī. In the Jeta Grove, a monkey was leaping from branch to branch and fell and died. The group of six monks placed it in a pot and were boiling it. A woman who had lost her small child was searching for him and came into the Jeta Grove, where she saw the group of six boiling something in the pot. She saw this, and thinking, "Could they have boiled my child here?" she became alarmed and drew near. After a while the pot bubbled and boiled, and the monkey's hand rose to the surface. She beat her breast and cried out, "Kyi hud, my child! Kyi hud, my child!" Then its foot rose up as well, and she cried out again, "Kyi hud, my child! Kyi hud, my child!" The group of six asked her, "Why are you doing that?" She said, "These hands and feet that have risen up — this is my child!" Then after a moment the tail appeared as well. The group of six asked, "Does your child have a tail?" Startled, she said, "Noble ones, is this a monkey?" They replied, "It is a monkey." "Do noble ones also carry and eat monkey flesh?" She said they did, and then criticized them. The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the monkey resembles a human being. Therefore, monks, do not eat monkey flesh. If monks eat monkey flesh, they incur a transgression."

This is the fifth verse of the first sūtra of the single section.

In brief:

A bowl, a robe, and a hide,
and no giving with a leaf-bowl.
Save only for an iron funnel,
gemstones are to be passed by mouth.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time in Śrāvastī there was another monk who was severely afflicted by illness. He went to a physician and said, "Please, good sir, I am ill in such-and-such a manner — show me a remedy so that I may be cured." The physician said, "Noble one, take medicine administered from below." The monk replied, "Good sir, the Blessed One has not permitted that." The physician said, "Noble one, your Teacher is compassionate — he will come to permit it." When things stood thus, the monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If the physician prescribes it and the monk will recover by it, then administer the medicine from below — have no hesitation in this." The Blessed One declared, "Administer the medicine from below," and they poured it using a bowl, but it was messy and unsuitable. The Blessed One declared, "Do not pour it with a bowl." They then poured it using the corner of a robe, but that too proved to be a source of fault. The Blessed One declared, "Do not pour it with the corner of a robe." They then poured it from inside a leather bag, and that also proved to be a source of fault. The Blessed One then declared:

"Do not pour it from inside a leather bag," and they poured it from inside a leaf bowl. That too proved to be a source of fault. The Blessed One declared, "Do not pour it from inside a leaf bowl — instead, administer it from inside a tube." They then administered it from a metal tube, but when it was inserted it was exceedingly hot and rough. The Blessed One declared, "Rather than a metal tube, administer it through a tube of crystal or a tube of ivory."

This is the sixth verse of the first chapter of the Sūtra on Individual Liberation.

In brief:

Sugar cane and yogurt, grain, butter,
broth, scorched porridge, and ghee,
roots, fruits, stems, and leaves —
all manner of broths may be administered.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove (Jetavana) of Anāthapiṇḍada at Śrāvastī. The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One: "Venerable One, is it possible that from a single medicine the very same one is suitable in the morning, that very same one suitable in the afternoon, that very same one suitable for seven days, and that very same one suitable for the duration of one's life?"

"Upāli, sugar cane is for morning use. Its juice is for afternoon use. Molasses is for seven-day use. Sugar cane and the ash of burnt sugar cane are for use for the duration of life. Upāli, yogurt is for morning use. Whey is for afternoon use. Butter is for seven-day use. The ash of burnt yogurt is for use for the duration of life. Upāli, meat is for morning use. Fat drippings are for seven-day use. The ash of burnt meat is for use for the duration of life. Upāli, sesame is for morning use. Sesame oil is for seven-day use. The ash of burnt sesame is for use for the duration of life."

The occasion was at Śrāvastī. A certain monk fell ill, and a physician who examined him said, "Noble one, prepare a broth of medicinal herbs and drink it." The monk reported this to the other monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Do as the physician has prescribed — have no hesitation in this."

The occasion was at Śrāvastī. Some other monks also fell ill, and for some of them the physician prescribed, "Drink a broth of mustard seed." For some, "Drink a broth of roots." For some, "Drink a broth of stems." For some, "Drink a broth of fruits." The monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Therefore, I permit this: whenever a physician prescribes it for a sick monk, drink whatever broth is prescribed — have no hesitation in this."

This is the seventh verse of the first chapter of the Sūtra on Individual Liberation.

In brief:

Molasses dissolved in water and the like,
what is stored for seven days,
what is dedicated for the sake of others —
all should be taken up with benefit in mind.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada at Śrāvastī. The Blessed One, accompanied by the Saṅgha of hearers, was going on tour through the countryside. They arrived at another village in the rocky hill country. Knowing that the time had come to tame another householder who dwelt in that village, the Blessed One went to that rocky hill village. When the householder saw the Blessed One, faith arose in him and he came into the presence of the Blessed One. The Blessed One, knowing his intention, his latent dispositions, his constitution, and his nature, taught him the kind of Dharma through which one comes to realize the four noble truths. Hearing this, the householder shattered the twenty-peaked mountain of the view of the transitory collection (the belief in a real self among the heaps) with the vajra of gnosis, and directly realized the fruit of stream-entry.

As the monks were wearied by the fatigue of the road, they arrived at a certain ruined temple, a charnel ground, and —

they laid down their outer robes and settled to sleep in the pleasure grove and at the foot of the trees. The householder, filled with profound faith, went in turn to pay his respects to the monks at the charnel ground, the shrine room, and the roots of the trees. When he saw that the monks were lying down and sitting where they had taken up lodging, he said, "Why are you sleeping and resting, you noble ones who are so very diligent in the teaching?" They replied, "Householder, we are oppressed by the weariness of the road and too exhausted to engage in wholesome activity." He then said to the noble ones, "In that case, if the Blessed One would permit it, please ask him whether you might take some molasses this afternoon, and I shall go and bring it." Some among them said, "That householder will provide it." Others said, "The venerable householder Ambāṭhika — owing to his eating molasses — directly realized arhatship. If the Blessed One likewise permits it, those among us who are oppressed by the weariness of the road: unbelieving people in the village will find fault, saying we are eating while settled in the town." These ones said they were displeased and would decline. Others said, "If the venerable one goes ahead in that way, we shall request it of the Blessed One." The monks then reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Molasses may be eaten at any time. Do not have any doubt about this." After the Blessed One had declared that molasses might be eaten at any time, the monks ate. Then, tormented by thirst from the weariness of the road, the Blessed One declared, "Drink molasses-water as a drink."

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, "Venerable one, may one bless molasses-water and drink it after seven days?" "Upāli, that is not permitted." "Venerable one, for how long may one store it and drink it?" "Upāli, for as long as it remains clear and has not turned sour nor lost its natural quality."

The occasion was at Śrāvastī. The Blessed One declared that the restoration ceremony, a matter arising from the rules, the blessing of robes, the dedication of robes, and the invitation of a single person as a guest — these five things are accomplished by one's own intention alone.

If monks are invited as guests at a certain place, they may also be invited elsewhere in addition or even beyond that place. In the first case, one goes oneself; in the second, one sends another after setting aside one's own wish.

A time of famine came, and the monks fell into great want in their alms round. Faithful brahmins and householders invited the senior monks to a meal. A monk accepted the invitation of one householder and then sent others in his place. The Blessed One declared, "Therefore, when I permit it — in a time of famine, of suffering, and of scarce provisions — you may take as guests wherever you are invited, as many as are invited: regard it all as your own, and you yourself eat there too, and share it with the monks as well." The monks went to another brahmin's or householder's place, and those hosts said, "We did not invite you noble ones; it is this elder, So-and-so, whom we invited." The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Go yourselves, accept what is offered, eat two or three portions, and then say this: 'Householder, these monks are occupied with their food; please rejoice in giving it to them.' Likewise, whether two, three, or however many were invited, do this for all of them. Having done all that, whatever the last host invited — eat until you are satisfied. Have no doubt about this."

This is the eighth verse-section of the sūtra of the first chapter with a single door.

In brief:
Either butter or grain-butter —

Furthermore: what was set aside, the concealment of eye-medicine, Vaiśālī, and a suitable place.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain monk was afflicted with a wind ailment. He went to a physician and said, "Good sir, I am afflicted with such an illness; please prescribe medicine for me." The physician said, "Noble one, if you drink this much butter, you will recover." The monk reported the matter to the other monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "If the physician prescribes that butter be drunk, then drink it." The monk drank it and felt well during the day, but at night the wind ailment flared up again. The monks asked the physician, and he said, "Drink it at night as well." The monks informed the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Drink it at night as well." The monk accumulated a supply of it, consecrated it over seven days, and recovered.

The occasion for the next rule was likewise at Śrāvastī. Another monk fell ill and went to a physician. After the customary greeting he said, "Good sir, I am afflicted with such an illness; please show me the means of medicine." The physician prescribed, "Noble one, if you drink this much grain-butter, you will recover." The monk reported this to the other monks, and the monks informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "If the physician prescribes that grain-butter be drunk, then drink grain-butter." The monk drank it and recovered during the day, but at night the wind ailment flared up again. The monks asked the physician, and he prescribed, "Drink it at night as well." The monks informed the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Drink it at night as well." The monk accumulated grain-butter, consecrated it over seven days, drank it, and recovered.

The occasion for the next rule was likewise at Śrāvastī. Another monk fell ill. He also went to a physician, spoke the customary greeting, and said, "Good sir, I am afflicted with such an illness; please show me the means of medicine." The physician said, "If you drink this much butter or grain-butter, you will recover." The monk sought it among his few acquaintances but could not find any, and so he went again to the physician and said, "Good sir, even though you prescribed it, I could not find grain-butter anywhere — how could I find butter? Please show me something else, whatever is suitable." The physician said, "There is a monk named so-and-so who has combined grain-butter with another substance, and a monk named so-and-so who has combined butter; go to them. It is also possible that there may be some of what was mixed remaining." The monk went to them and asked, but they said, "The venerable one's seven days have passed and it has all been used up — there is none left." The monk reported the matter to the other monks in this way, and the monks informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "When one understands the situation of a sick monk, whether butter or grain-butter or anything else whatsoever that has been set aside, that too may be eaten on the basis of prior acceptance. Have no doubt about this." When the Blessed One declared, "Whether butter or grain-butter or anything else whatsoever that has been set aside, eat it on the basis of prior acceptance — have no doubt about this," there was no one to make the acceptance. The Blessed One then declared, "If there is no one to make the acceptance, even without formal acceptance, eat it nonetheless. When permission has been granted to a sick person and that person recovers, let it not be used further. If it is used, it becomes an offense." The occasion for this rule was at Śrāvastī.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable Blessed One, you have declared, 'Fill an eye-medicine container to the brim.' What may be put in it?" "Upāli, anything except that which is made from precious materials."

He asked again: "Venerable Blessed One, you have declared, 'In the city of Vaiśālī, abandon the ten improper things, and consecrate a proper dwelling.' Venerable One, if the lower part of a dwelling has been consecrated as proper, does the upper part also become consecrated as proper?" "Upāli, just as one says of the upper, so too one may say of the side."

This is the ninth verse of the first section of the Ekaśataka.

In summary:

Roots, trunks, leaves, and fruits,
all steeped in fermented liquor,
or washed without food,
or of bad food — it is the same.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodhārāma. At that time King Śuddhodana offered five hundred Śākyas, one Śākya from each Śākya family, to serve the Blessed One, and the Blessed One ordained them all. Since their bodies had previously been sustained by liquor, once they were without it they fell ill.

The Blessed One, seeing this, said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, why have the Śākyas become so gaunt and thin?" Ānanda reported the matter in detail to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Then this is what I permit: roots, trunks, and the like that would become liquor — dry them and grind them into powder; wrap the powder in bundles inside white cloth; soak these bundles in a vessel of earthenware not yet full, which has the strength and potency of liquor; then draw the bundles out again, wash the hands, mix it with water that has no food value, and drink it in sufficient quantity as a group. If they are thirsty, whether in the morning or in the afternoon, drink it without hesitation. Do this, and they will be separated from their craving for liquor. Monks, if you have me your Teacher in mind, do not drink liquor; do not press it out; and do not touch it even with the tip of the finger."

The occasion for this was at Śrāvastī. When another monk fell ill and a physician instructed that he be given bad food, some monks knew what to do and some did not, and those who did not asked the venerable Upāli, who explained it to them in detail.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable Blessed One, when you said, 'Give bad food to the monk Svāti' — does that too require formal acceptance?" "Upāli, that too should be accepted by formal acceptance." "From whom should the acceptance be made?" "Upāli, from a lay devotee of faith."

This is the tenth verse of the first section of the Ekaśataka. The first section is complete.

In brief:

Vessels and robes both together,
and Kosala and likewise Sarpa,
proclamations and various robes,
and companions too — for nuns
these are taught last and gathered in summary.

In brief:

Vessels and furnishings, a temple,
many guests, cloth beaten out,
cloth and parasols and likewise wood,
charnel-ground dwellers — likewise abandoned.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time a certain householder constructed a temple fully equipped with all furnishings in a different village in the rocky hills, and offered it to the Saṅgha of the four quarters. In it there were many beds and utensils, but only a few monks were residing there. Among them some said, "The venerable ones are not using the beds, utensils, and furnishings — they will go to waste."

From among these, they said, "Let us keep as much as we need for our own use, and send the remainder to another temple." And they did so accordingly.

Now, after some time had passed, a wandering alms-seeker came to that temple, using the road as his customary practice. The monks had him rest there. Among them was an elder of that Saṅgha who, having rested from the weariness of the road in the temple, said to them, "Venerable ones, are there beds here?" They replied, "There are none." Then the monks told him in detail exactly how things stood. Without any bedding, he lay down on the bare ground just as it was, and rose early the next morning. There was a crooked key and a key, and taking them he went to the householder's home. The householder greeted him with words of welcome and, bringing out a mat, emerged to meet him. The alms-seeker sat in a posture of peaceful composure.

The alms-seeker then spoke at length of the merit-qualities of the seven objects that constitute the bases for making merit from one's wealth. The householder said, "Noble one, I have done all of that." The alms-seeker replied, "Householder, as for whether there are beds in your temple — last night I too lay down just as I was on the bare ground without any bedding, and came here this morning. And yet you say you have done all of this — what fault is there in that?" The householder said, "Noble one, I had provided many beds, utensils, and furnishings there; those noble ones must certainly have sent them off to another temple." The alms-seeker then asked, "Is the householder himself familiar with the temple's crooked key and its key?" The noble one graciously assented. He showed it to him, and then said, "Noble one, please proceed — I shall come as well."

The alms-seeker went collecting alms, and the householder followed behind and arrived there. He assembled the monks and asked, "Noble ones, I provided many beds, utensils, and furnishings here — where have they gone?" Then everything that had happened was reported to the householder in full. The householder declared the wrong openly and said, "You have not acted well. Given that it has already come to this, is it now possible to retrieve them or not?" They said, "It is not possible. Noble one, we did not offer them there — go and take them back." The monks then reported what had occurred to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Do not send things to another temple. Use them in accordance with the intended purpose. Otherwise, place a valuation on whatever someone has donated, as though it were a price."

The narrative occasion is at Śrāvastī. The group of six monks were going about using the road as their habitual practice, together with many travelers. Being afraid of the dust raised by the Dharma, they walked either ahead of the travelers or behind them. After a time, many of the travelers were attacked by bandits, and many people fled abandoning their goods. The bandits, unable to carry off all the wealth, selected the best things and went off with them. The group of six monks, having followed along behind the many travelers, reached that place and saw the great quantity of goods that had been cast aside. Then, delighted and overjoyed, Nandaka said, "Cloth beaten out — let us take the finds!" And so they selected garments from among those things and carried them away.

The many travelers, together with their escorts of archers and road-guards, turned back and recognized what the group of six had taken. And they thought, "What even the bandits discarded — those have been stolen by the shaven-headed ascetics."

They reproached the group of six, saying, "Those who bear the standard of the ascetics — noble ones — conduct themselves in such a perverse manner!" and denounced them to their faces. The group of six replied, "The many travelers were attacked by bandits — that was not our doing. We found cloth from a charnel ground." The travelers said, "These are not charnel-ground cloths." The six had no answer and fell silent.

When this had come to pass, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, to revile the many travelers is a grave matter. Therefore, monks, do not accept garments taken from travelers who have been attacked. If monks carry off garments from travelers who have been attacked, there will be a transgression along with a downfall. Furthermore, if those who have gained faith say to the noble ones, 'Please take whatever you like,' the monks fall into doubt and do not take. The Blessed One declared: 'If they say, "Take freely," take without hesitation.'"

The setting is at Rājagṛha. The group of six monks went to the charnel ground of the Cool Grove, and seeing the great many funerary requisites — parasols, wooden implements, and cloths — that had been left there, one of them said to Nandaka, "How wonderful, dear Nandaka! A find — charnel-ground cloth! Let us take it." Nandaka said, "Excellent! Well done! Take it." And they took the things and went.

Now a low-caste guardian of the charnel ground came and thought to himself, "There is not a scrap left in this charnel ground. Surely someone has robbed it. And whoever did so may well come back again, having marked the place." Thinking thus, he hid himself and stayed there day by day within a dense thicket.

After seven or eight days, the group of six said, "Nandaka, dear Nandaka — since we have not gone to the charnel ground in quite a while, let us go again today; there may well be a few things to find." And so they went. Just as they began picking up the cloths, parasols, and wooden implements that had been left there, the low-caste man who had been hiding in the dense thicket saw them, ran out, and said to them: "The noble ones cause our family — our brothers, kin, and friends — to carry out the king's decrees, and all on account of these charnel-ground cloths. So why do you take funerary requisites from a charnel ground that has an owner?" They replied, "Good sir, we took cloth from an unowned charnel ground." He said to the noble ones, "If they are truly charnel-ground cloths, well and good." They had no answer and fell silent.

When this had come to pass, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, to revile a low-caste person is a grave matter. Therefore, monks, do not take charnel-ground cloth from a charnel ground that has an owner. If monks take charnel-ground cloth from a charnel ground that has an owner, there will be a transgression along with a downfall. Furthermore, if the faithful say, 'Noble ones, please take freely,' the monks fall into doubt and do not take. The Blessed One declared: 'If they say, "Take freely," then take — do not be in doubt about that.'"

This is the first verse of the sūtra on the second gate of the Single One.

The Glorious Vinaya Compendium, the fortieth fascicle. In brief:

Cloth, wood-wool, and the like,
and likewise what is seized from a shrine —

The three Dharma robes of the Saṅgha
must not be taken from individuals.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The group of six monks set out on the road together with many riders in carriages. When they had traveled halfway, the axle-pole of one carriage broke. The merchant replaced it with a new axle-pole and, abandoning the broken one, went on his way. Ānanda picked up the broken carriage axle-pole and placed it at a crossroads on the main road, saying: "Friend, dear Ānanda, we have placed this axle-pole here so that it may serve as the support of a deity named Īśvara." As word spread, other householders too built a platform there. Someone else made a prayer at it, saying: "If such-and-such a purpose of mine is accomplished, I will build a house here and hold a feast for one hundred and eight brahmins." And indeed, through dependent origination, that too came to pass. He fulfilled every vow he had made, and the place became a temple for a heterodox deity, and the temple-keeper consecrated it. Thereafter many merchant travelers entered that road and made many offerings of cloth, wool, and wood-wool there. When the group of six monks returned and saw that the temple had become greatly prosperous, they said: "Friend, dear Ānanda, the carriage axle-pole of Īśvara has received abundant and splendid cloth, wool, and wood-wool — let us take it." And just as they were about to take these things, the temple-keepers came forward and said to the noble ones: "This temple is ours — we maintain and care for it. Why are you taking and using the deity's cloth? Have you not abandoned taking what is not given?" The monks replied: "Poor man, how is this your temple? We placed a broken carriage axle-pole here as a support and left it." The temple-keeper cried out in protest. Then Ānanda, angered, kicked him once and knocked him down. Thereupon, puffed up with pride and arrogance, the temple-keeper said: "Whether it was you noble ones or someone else who did this, we live in dependence on this place and look to it for our livelihood — why then do you, noble ones, do what is not in accord with the Dharma of the noble ones?" The monks were abashed and said nothing. The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, to revile those who dwell in a temple of wrong view is unseemly. Therefore monks must not take cloth and the like from a temple that has an owner. If monks take cloth and the like from a temple that has an owner, there will be a transgression along with a downfall. If a keeper of a temple of wrong view, being of a different faith, says, 'Use freely,' —" and at that, the monks fell into doubt and did not take. The Blessed One declared: "If they say, 'Use freely,' then take — do not be in doubt about that."

The setting for this rule is Śrāvastī. The Blessed One had instructed that the sick be attended to. A certain monk fell ill, and his attendant said to the venerable Saṅgha: "Please give a little something." And that monk replied: "I have nothing whatsoever of my own — I offer my three Dharma robes." No one said anything. He presented his three Dharma robes, and the others sold them and divided the proceeds. When the monk recovered and rose from his sickness, he found himself destitute of his three Dharma robes. The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

"Monks, do not take the three Dharma robes from a monk on behalf of the Saṅgha. If they are taken, a transgression is incurred. The Saṅgha likewise should not take them. Even if taken, do not divide them. If they are divided, a transgression is incurred." These are the two verses of the sūtra of the paired chapter.

In summary:

Both are permitted,
and permission is given in different forms.
A third share applies, and also to the novice,
the female probationer, and the nun.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Sixty monks were wandering on tour, and they arrived at a certain mountain village. A faithful householder living there invited them to his home for a meal, intending to offer each monk one bolt of cloth. While they were seated eating, sixty nuns who were also wandering on tour arrived at that same mountain village and began going from house to house for alms. Someone told them: "The monks are being hosted for a meal at this householder's house — go there." They went, and they too ate. Then the householder set out sixty bolts of cloth before the assembly in order of seniority. The monks did not know how to divide them. The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Both communities of the Saṅgha are entitled to it — divide the cloth between the two communities of the Saṅgha."

The setting for this rule is Śrāvastī. At Śrāvastī a certain householder built a temple, then hosted both communities of the Saṅgha for a meal, offered abundant gifts, and the monks divided them. Then the monks said tauntingly: "We need three Dharma robes, yet for you novices even an upper robe and a lower robe are sufficient — why should you share equally with us?" The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks and nuns are to receive an equal share. To male novices, female novices, and female probationers, give one third."

When the Blessed One had declared that male novices were to be given one third, a certain other male novice who was fully twenty years of age and wished to receive full ordination was told by a monk: "Venerable one, you are fully twenty years of age — why do you not take full ordination?" He replied: "With our gains fixed as they are by the Blessed One, even an upper robe and a lower robe do not arise — to say nothing of the three Dharma robes. How am I to take full ordination?" The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "To a male novice who wishes to receive full ordination and to a female probationer, give two thirds. Other male novices and female novices are to receive only a one-third share." This is the third verse of the sūtra of the paired chapter.

In summary:

In Kosala: sixty,
one hundred fifty-three,
Śabdāgata, Śrīvṛddha,
the temple, and the stūpa likewise,
the parasol and the painting — apply them similarly.
Invited as guests for a meal.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, while wandering on tour through Kosala, arrived at another mountain village. A householder living in that mountain village invited the Blessed One together with the community of śrāvaka monks to his home for a meal.

Sixty nuns who were wandering on tour through that region arrived at that same mountain village and took their meal there. The Blessed One, together with a retinue of one hundred and fifty-three, had received the meal offering, and that householder then placed one hundred and fifty-three lengths of cloth in order before the elders.

The monks, not knowing how to divide these, heard the nuns say to them: "What else is there to be done here? Previously, when the two communities of the Saṅgha were invited for a meal together, we received half of whatever gains were obtained. So now too, give us half of the gains." When the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Wherever nuns are many and monks are few, divide the gains between both communities. Wherever monks are many and nuns are few, divide according to individual head-count."

The account of the origin is set in Śrāvastī. A householder invited the buddha and the community of monks to a meal. The community of monks went, but the Blessed One remained in the temple and accepted the meal brought to him there. The Blessed One remained in the temple and accepted the meal brought to him for five reasons. What are the five? He wished to teach the Dharma to the gods. He wished to look upon the sick. He wished to look upon the sleeping mats and seats. He wished to enter into inner meditative composure. And he wished to establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the śrāvakas. It was for this last reason — wishing to establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the śrāvakas — that the Blessed One remained in the temple and accepted the meal brought to him.

That householder, having deep faith in the elders, dispensed to the elders in order butter and dishes prepared from butter; to those of middle seniority he dispensed sesame oil and dishes prepared from sesame oil; and to the young he dispensed the dregs of sesame oil.

At that time, the venerable Śabdāgata accepted the meal offerings on behalf of the Blessed One. Having done so, he returned, and the Blessed One asked Śabdāgata: "Were the community of monks satisfied with the food at the meal?" He replied: "Venerable One, the elders were satisfied." The Blessed One said: "Śabdāgata, why do you look so downcast and diminished? Speak and tell me what you mean." He then spoke in verse:

Sesame oil makes one plump,
and butter makes one radiant.
With only the thin dregs of sesame oil,
where is there any radiance — what of strength?

The Blessed One declared: "Śabdāgata, tell me exactly what happened." Śabdāgata then reported the matter to the Blessed One in detail. The Blessed One asked Śabdāgata who among the senior resident monks had been present, and Śabdāgata replied: "Venerable One, the abbot was present." The Blessed One told Śabdāgata: "It is because the monk Śāriputra did not inspect the lower portions that they were eaten improperly." Because such a thing had occurred, the Blessed One assembled the community of monks, seated himself on a seat laid out before the community, and — in order to establish a rule of training in the Vinaya for the śrāvakas — declared: "I am laying down a rule of conduct for the practice equal to that of the senior resident monk of the community. Instruct him thus: when the senior resident monk of the community distributes food, let him distribute it evenly." He spoke this to each condiment as well. The Blessed One then declared: "Speak of it at the time when salt, or whichever item was distributed first, is being served — not at the time of all the others." If the senior resident monk of the community did not act in accordance with the rule of equal practice, he would incur a transgression together with whatever had already passed.

When the venerable Śāriputra heard that the Blessed One had rebuked him for the manner in which the food had been eaten,

he thought to himself, "It is improper for me to remain here when the Teacher has rebuked me for the manner in which I ate," and he vomited up what he had eaten and expelled it.

The monks were filled with doubt, and presenting all their doubts to the Buddha, the Blessed One, they said, "Venerable Blessed One, please look upon the rebuke given by the Blessed One to the venerable Śāriputra for the manner in which he ate, and upon his subsequent vomiting."

The Blessed One declared, "Monks, this is not the only time. In the past as well I rebuked him for the manner in which he ate, and because of that rebuke he vomited. Monks, listen. Long ago, in another city there lived a brahmin who was widely learned and renowned as a teacher. While he was wandering and traveling about together with his brahmin's son, they came to a village at the foot of a cliff. There, beside a pond, the brahmin left the brahmin's son, saying, 'Stay here a while. I will go into the village to fetch flour and other provisions and return.' While the son was sitting there, a dog with mange came to the pond to drink. The brahmin's son said to it, 'Friend, please give me a drink of water as well.' The dog replied, 'Make a vessel out of leaves,' and the boy did so. The dog then took some flour from inside a small bag made from a dog's hide and gave it to him. When the boy kneaded it, he asked, 'What is this that has become so oily?' The dog replied, 'That is the property of the hide from which the bag was made,' and when the brahmin's son inquired more closely about what exactly the bag was made from, he did not understand.

When the brahmin returned he said to his son, 'Go and request some drinking water.' The son replied, 'I have already obtained drinking water.' The brahmin asked who had given it, and the boy said, 'A companion gave it to me — that companion being the mangy dog — and if he gave you flour, you would be defiled by it.' The brahmin then thoroughly rebuked him, and at that the boy vomited up what he had eaten.

Monks, do you not know? The brahmin who was learned and renowned as a teacher at that time was none other than myself as I am now. And the brahmin's son of that time is none other than the monk Śāriputra as he is now. At that time too I thoroughly rebuked him regarding his eating, and he vomited. Now here too I have thoroughly rebuked him regarding what he ate, and here again he has vomited."

The original occasion was in Rājagṛha. At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a Nirgrantha lay practitioner named Śrī-bhadra who was the husband of the sister of the householder Agnidatta. The faithful householder Agnidatta thought to himself, "I shall encourage Śrī-bhadra to make offerings and present gifts to the Saṅgha," and so he said to him, "Śrī-bhadra, make offerings and present gifts to the Saṅgha — it will become merit for you."

Śrī-bhadra replied, "I too shall make offerings and present gifts to the Saṅgha. You as well should make offerings and serve a meal to the Saṅgha of those who have gone forth, headed by Gaṅgā and the others."

Agnidatta thought to himself, "If I do not agree, Śrī-bhadra may well become an obstacle to making offerings to the Saṅgha. Since there is no fault in giving to all sentient beings, I shall give food to the Nirgrantha community and thereby ensure that he creates no obstacle to my making offerings and presenting gifts to the Saṅgha." Having agreed to provide the food, he accepted the offer.

Śrī-bhadra then thought, "If I first serve a meal to the Saṅgha of monks beginning with the buddhas, Agnidatta will afterward not give food to me. So let me first serve the meal to the Saṅgha of those who have gone forth, headed by Gaṅgā and the others, and afterward I shall give the food." And so he said to Agnidatta, "Agnidatta, you give the food first, and I will afterward give food to the śramaṇa Gautama and the Saṅgha of his hearers."

He agreed, and then the householder Agnidatta went to where the Gaṅgā ascetics were staying. He exchanged many words of delight and pleasure with them and then sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Agnidatta said this to Gaṅgā: "Gaṅgā, tomorrow please accept the invitation to take a meal at my home together with the many naked ascetics and the Saṅgha."

Gaṅgā thought, "This householder has, without fail, grown disenchanted with the śramaṇa Gautama and has come to have great faith in us — that is truly a fine gain for us. Gaṅgā, he has come to have faith in the community of our kind." And so he accepted.

Then the householder Agnidatta issued the invitation and departed.

That evening, Agnidatta prepared fine, pure food and provisions for the meal. Rising early the next morning, he set out seats, filled bowls with water and set them in place, and then sent word to the Gaṅgā ascetics that the meal was ready: "Come, Gaṅgā — the food is prepared; please know that the time has come."

They set out. Now Śrī-bhadra came to that very place and said, "Noble Gaṅgā, the śramaṇa Gautama has entered the householder's home, and just as he stepped over the threshold at the door, he smiled. Then the hearer named Ānanda drew his outer robe to one side, knelt his right knee on the ground, pressed his palms together, and asked: 'Venerable one, a Tathāgata and the hearers of a Tathāgata do not smile without cause or condition. For what cause and what condition, sir, did you smile?' The Tathāgata replied to Ānanda, 'That is so, Ānanda, that is so. Ānanda, a Tathāgata and the hearers of a Tathāgata do not smile without cause or condition. He smiled in accordance with a prophetic vision he holds.' Having said this, many people were filled with faith. You too, when you go to the householder Agnidatta's home, should do something of that kind — and indeed many people will be filled with faith." Gaṅgā agreed.

Then Gaṅgā, surrounded by many naked ascetics, went to the home of the householder Agnidatta. As he stepped over the threshold at the door of Agnidatta's house, he broke wind loudly. From within, one of the naked ascetics fell at his feet and asked, "Blessed one, O holy man, why is it that someone such as you does not smile without cause or condition?"

He replied: "Listen — on the bank of a river with a gentle current, a male monkey caught sight of a female monkey and, overcome with intense desire for her, thought to mount her and rushed toward her. He slipped and fell from the treetop, and he died on the spot. At that moment I thought to myself: 'This sentient being has come to great suffering on account of desire.' That is what came from my mouth."

The moment he said this aloud, the householder Agnidatta heard it and thought: "This Gaṅgā, son of Buzanmo, is like a needle-seller who returns to the home of a needle-maker to sell needles — I must find some way to humiliate him." All those who carried staffs were sitting comfortably, and the householder filled their bowls with clean, fine food and provisions, then poured soup on top and gave it to them. To Gaṅgā alone, he poured the soup into the base of the bowl, covered the top with cooked rice, and gave it to him.

While the naked ascetics were eating, Gaṅgā thought, "Surely he intends to make a show for me — he must have put tasty soup and fine food in mine." And just as he finished scooping up all the soup, he thought to himself:

He thought, "He must have forgotten out of distraction — I reminded him of it myself," and so he called out: "Householder, only cooked rice came into mine; there is no soup." The other then replied in verse:

One sees what is not to be seen,
and fails to see what should be seen.
He sees the monkey on the Gaṅgā's bank,
but not the soup inside the bowl.

When Gaṅgā looked at the other man's face, the man showed him that soup was sitting in the base of his bowl, and said: "Gaṅgā, you saw the monkey sitting on the bank of the river Gaṅgā, but you did not see the soup inside the bowl."

At that, the man thought to himself: "This fellow has shamed me. I shall now recite the virtues of generosity in such a way that it will be of benefit neither in this world nor in the next." And as Fireborn became aware that the man intended to shame him, and began to recite the virtues of generosity, Gaṅgā did not stay in his presence. Fireborn finished his meal and then recited the virtues of generosity in verse:

When the donor gives, it is the time of giving.
When other ascetics are eating, it is the time of eating.
When the remainder comes to others, it is the time of remainder.
Merit and non-virtue have no fixed time.
