A gatekeeper who had been listening and heard this recitation of the virtues of generosity grew angry, thinking: "A sinner of this kind ate the food but could not even restrain himself. What virtues of generosity could there be from such a one? I shall play a trick on this son of a needle-maker's wife." He filled a jar with the water in which rice had been boiled and hurled it at the doorway. The lintel of the gate was raised up halfway, and as the naked ascetic came out, he slipped on the rice-water and his head struck the lintel, drawing blood.

The gatekeeper then saw this and spoke in verse:

The moment has come when the gate-bolt was drawn.
The moment has come when the rice-water was hurled.
This is indeed the moment for the head to be struck —
there is no fixed time for virtue and non-virtue.

And with blood dripping from his head, Gaṅgā went to where the householder Śrībhadra was and came before him. When Śrībhadra saw him, he asked: "Venerable Gaṅgā, what is wrong?" Gaṅgā replied: "Fireborn has harmed me like this." Then Śrībhadra said: "Be glad you escaped with your life. But please do not do anything that would cause the ascetic Gautama with his community of monks to leave my home alive no more than this." Śrībhadra thought to himself: "I shall go as an invitation to settle the score against his enemy. If the ascetic Gautama is omniscient, he will not accept even when invited. But if he is not omniscient, he will accept." With this thought, he went to where the Blessed One was.

He exchanged various pleasant words with the Blessed One and then sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Śrībhadra addressed the Blessed One thus: "O Gautama, please accept my invitation to come tomorrow to my home for the meal together with the community of monks." The Blessed One reflected: "One who will come to see truth from me acts in just such a way. If I do not accept, it will become an obstacle to truth — I must accept." And so he accepted the invitation to come.

Śrībhadra thought: "This one is not omniscient. If he were omniscient, he would be right not to accept in this way. However I must now settle the score against his enemy by making sure he does not become omniscient at all." With that he went home, and at the gateway of his house he dug a great pit, filled it inside with smouldering charcoal of the tree called kādira where there were no flames, covered it on top with grass, and set soil over it to conceal it. He also laced food and drink with potent poison.

Then Śrībhadra's sister Meṣkī asked her brother what he intended to do, and he replied: "I am going to kill my enemy." She asked: "Who is your enemy, elder brother?" He answered: "The ascetic Gautama." She then said: "If your enemy is the Blessed One, then consider well — whoever might be a friend of yours should think it wrong for you, a person of such standing, to perform an act unworthy of a noble one." Śrībhadra then thought: "This one will come as an ally of Meṣkī, and out of faith in the ascetic Gautama she will let the secret out." With that, he put her inside a storage chest, fastened the lock, and left her there.

He called together Gaṃpa and all the other naked ascetics and said: "Come and watch me kill my enemy! For the sake of killing the ascetic Gautama I have dug a great pit at the gateway, filled it inside with smouldering charcoal of kādira wood, and set it there. And into the food and drink I have blended a fierce and potent poison." Those men were overjoyed. They went quickly and in great number, climbed up and stationed themselves on top of the upper story, thinking: "Today we are well placed. Let us watch how the ascetic Gautama burns in the fire pit, how he writhes under the fierce poison, and how he tumbles and falls to the ground."

Śrībhadra had a seat laid out and, summoning the Blessed One to come, announced the hour: "Gautama, the food is prepared and ready. Come, Gautama — please be mindful that the time has arrived."

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and tell the monks this: let no monk go ahead to Śrībhadra's house before the Tathāgata arrives." The venerable Ānanda, having heard this from the Blessed One, conveyed it to the monks: "The Blessed One has commanded: let no monk go ahead to Śrībhadra's house before the Tathāgata arrives." Thus he relayed the instruction.

Then the Blessed One, in the early morning hour, wrapped his waist-cloth, took up his alms bowl and outer robe, and set out, surrounded by many monks with the monastic Saṅgha before him, toward the place where Śrībhadra's house stood.

Now the servant-deities dwelling in the Ambavana grove were afflicted and stricken with distress and sorrow of mind. They hastened quickly and in great number to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there and touching their heads to his feet, they spoke these words of compassion: "Blessed One, it is not fitting that you should go to Śrībhadra's house." The Blessed One replied: "Deity, what harm is there?" They said: "Blessed One, Śrībhadra has made preparations to do the Blessed One harm." The Blessed One said: "Deity, the Tathāgata is free from all harm — what harm could he possibly do to me?" The servant-deities replied: "Blessed One, for the sake of killing the Blessed One he has filled a great pit with smouldering charcoal of kādira wood." The Blessed One said: "Deity, even the fire of attachment, the fire of aversion, and the fire of delusion are extinguished when doused with the water of gnosis — what then can that lesser fire do? Do not be troubled; be at ease." The servant-deities said: "That is not all — others, too, have taken measures to kill the Blessed One: they have blended into the food and drink a fierce, unbearable poison." The Blessed One replied: "Deity, through gnosis as the antidote, the poison of attachment, the poison of aversion, and the poison of delusion have already been utterly expelled, thoroughly purged.

What then can the least of all poisons do once those have been utterly expelled? Go back and attend diligently to your own work."

Then the Blessed One arrived in Rājagṛha, and the deities who dwelt in Rājagṛha reported to him as before, and the Blessed One instructed those deities as he had the earlier ones and sent them back. Then he arrived at the door of the house of Śrīgupta, and the household deities of Śrīgupta's home reported to him as before, and the Blessed One likewise instructed those deities as he had the earlier ones and sent them back.

Now Śrīgupta's wife thought to herself: "The Blessed One has now passed through the first door — at any moment he will be stepping over the pit. At any moment he will fall in from above the pit whose mouth is covered over with grass — at any moment the Blessed One will tumble into the fire, and smoke will billow up, tears will flow, smoke will rise from the robes burned by the flames." With such dismay she admitted him inside the house, and as he entered, grief arose in her; her eyes filled with tears, her face crumpled and twisted, and she sat weeping, overcome with anguish, brooding on the unwholesome act.

Then the Blessed One, his mind fully engaged in bringing benefit to all sentient beings, came to the middle of the door and stepped down over the fire-pit. The moment his feet touched the surface of the fire-pit, the whole of it was transformed into a lotus pond — covered with blue lotuses, red lotuses, white night-blooming lotuses, and white day-blooming lotuses — and adorned with water-birds such as geese, kāraṇḍa ducks, ospreys, and the like, all uttering varied calls, just like the divine lake Mandāka of the gods. And the deities dwelling in the sky showered down from above divine night-blooming lotuses and divine lotuses of many colors.

Then the Blessed One stepped across the lotus hearts and arrived at Śrīgupta's house. The householder Śrīgupta stared with wide, wonder-filled eyes and said: "Noble Gaṅgopa, look at the miraculous powers and marvels of the Blessed One!" Gaṅgopa turned his face into a scowl and replied: "Householder, is your faith in the ascetic Gautama, or in these illusions of his?" Śrīgupta answered: "Noble Gaṅgopa, if one could accomplish such things as these, then you too, since you are omniscient, should produce and display such illusions. By means like these, accomplish the same for me and my friends and brothers." Gaṅgopa, realizing his aim had not been achieved and thinking he would leave, spat at Śrīgupta, leapt down from the roof of the house, and — terrified and ashamed — was unable to come face to face with the Blessed One. He departed with slow, shuffling steps, eyes cast down at the ground, slipping out of Śrīgupta's house and fleeing away.

Then the householder Śrīgupta went to where his sister, the sister of the householder Agniprabhā, was staying, and opening the door said: "Bhadra, come here. Prostrate at the feet of the Tathāgata." She thought to herself: "This man is trying to deceive me," and with a sorrowful voice said slowly: "If I am to be killed, betrayed by an evil companion, what refuge is there left for me?" He replied: "Bhadra, you speak truly, and there is no deception — it was not possible to harm the Blessed One. Since it was not possible to kill the Blessed One, and since now you cannot come before him, come, let him take you to the Blessed One." Then Śrīgupta's wife, filled with joy and with a gladdened mind, led Śrīgupta and went to where the Blessed One was. Arriving there, she prostrated with her head at the feet of the Blessed One and addressed him with these words: "Venerable one, please forgive us."

She said: "This householder was deceived by an evil companion, and on that account performed these unwholesome acts toward the Blessed One." At that, the Blessed One extended his hand — which resembled the trunk of a great elephant — and said: "Householder, come, and be forgiven. The Tathāgata makes no distinction between friend and foe. The Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha makes no distinction between friend and foe. He is like sandalwood and the cassia tree alike."

Then, upon hearing this, the householder Śrīgupta gave rise to great joy toward the Tathāgata, and with a mind full of devotion addressed the Blessed One: "Please accept a little from me — I have now prepared a meal." The Blessed One replied: "Householder, the proper way to invite the Tathāgata is to invite him in order, according to seniority. Say, 'Gautama, the meal is also ready; Gautama, please know it is time.' Why then do you speak otherwise?" Śrīgupta answered: "Venerable one, my mind, having looked upon an evil companion, went astray into three wrong views — through the sins of one who tends toward all that is hateful and pleasant, and having blocked both kinds of beings who go about endearing themselves to all, I undertook to harm the Blessed One."

The Blessed One then declared: "Householder, since the Tathāgata is free from all harm, how could he be harmed by me?" Śrīgupta said: "Venerable one, I mixed potent poison into the food and drink, and had it prepared first for the men." The Blessed One replied: "Householder, one who has thoroughly expelled and cast off the poison of attachment, the poison of aversion, and the poison of delusion — what could such a poor poison as this do? Bring what you have prepared and come."

Then the Blessed One had a seat laid out before the community of monks and took his place there. Seated, he addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go and tell the monks this: 'Assemble in order of seniority. Let no one eat food until the signal is given.'" The venerable Ānanda then conveyed the Blessed One's instruction to the monks: "The venerable ones are commanded by the Blessed One: 'Assemble in order of seniority, and let no one eat food until the signal is given.'"

Then that community of monks, settling themselves comfortably, were served food and drink, and with miraculous power, wonder-working, and display of spiritual marvels, gave the signal: "Assemble at Śrīgupta's home in order of seniority." At that moment the food and drink became free of poison.

All the while Śrīgupta, still anxious, was serving and attending to the food and drink, watching as those who came first — the senior monks — arrived before the younger ones, and he thought to himself: "Just now the senior monks might fall stricken by the potent poison." Then the younger monks came after the elders, and he thought likewise. But the thought arose in him: "The Blessed One has abandoned the poisons of attachment, aversion, and delusion — this is not so for all hearers." Yet when all the monks ate the meal, not even one was harmed. Even the young attendants who ate the remainders were not harmed.

Then the householder Śrīgupta gave rise to faith from without and within. He and his wife, having served the Blessed One the meal, knowing that the bowl had been lifted and set aside, took a low seat and sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma. Then the Blessed One, perceiving the intention, the disposition, the character, and

the natural dispositions of beings, he then taught the Dharma in such a way that they would thoroughly realize the Four Noble Truths of the noble ones (āryasatya). When the householder Śrīgupta heard this teaching, the twenty mountain-peaks of the view of the transitory collection were shattered by the vajra of gnosis, and he actualized the fruit of stream-entry. Having seen the truth, he three times joyfully exclaimed these words:

"Venerable Blessed One, such benefit as this has never been done for me by my father, nor by my mother, nor by loved ones, friends, relatives, and retinue, nor by a king, nor by the gods, nor by people of former times, nor by renunciants and brahmins. The Blessed One has dried up for me the ocean of tears and blood, delivered me from the mountain of bones, cut off the door to the lower realms, opened the door to higher states of existence, and established me in the abode of gods and humans."

Then he spoke again in verse:

The many faults, the paths that lead to lower realms —
by your power all of these have been cut through.
You of merit, you have opened the door to higher birth.
The path to passing beyond sorrow I too have now attained.

Faultless, gained through relying upon you,
my eyes are pure, utterly purified.
I have reached the four abodes that gladden the noble ones,
and crossed to the far shore of the ocean of suffering.

Honored by ordinary beings, asuras, gods, and humans —
it is exceedingly rare, in even a thousand existences, to meet you.
Free from birth, aging, and death:
O Sage, today, having seen you, I bear the fruit.

"Venerable one, I have passed beyond, I have truly passed beyond! Now I take refuge in the Blessed One, in the Dharma, and in the Saṅgha of monks. From this day forth, for as long as the sky endures, I take refuge with my life at stake, and with manifest faith. Please accept me as a layman. Venerable one, from this day forth I close the door to the naked tīrthikas, to naked women of that sect, and to the hearers of the naked ones; and I open the door to the hearers of the Blessed One, to monks, to nuns, to male lay practitioners, and to female lay practitioners."

Then the Blessed One instructed the householder Śrīgupta thoroughly with a discourse on the Dharma, thoroughly trained him, thoroughly praised him, and filled him with great joy. Then the Blessed One rose from his seat and departed. The Blessed One then proceeded to the assembly hall, spread out a seat in front of the community of monks, and sat down. Seated there, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

"Monks, at the householder Śrīgupta's house, where such harm was intended, had the Tathāgata not known of it, a great many monks would have died from the poison without escape. That householder, through his evil conduct, would have fallen into the avīci hell. Therefore a rule of conduct (prātimokṣa) is hereby established concerning the elder monk of the Saṅgha's residence. When the elder monk of the Saṅgha is seated in order of seniority and food is brought and offered, not even a pinch of salt should be taken in advance as before. If, without calling out 'Come, be served in order of seniority,' it is taken, one incurs a transgression."

The ground for this ruling is as follows: at Śrāvastī, at that time, a certain householder had undertaken the construction of a great assembly hall, but after he had built about half of it, he passed away. His son then became head of the household. The monks went to him and said: "Good man, your father undertook the construction of an assembly hall, and he completed about half of it before he passed away. It is fitting for you to bring it to completion." When they said this,

He had little faith, and because the assembly hall was large, he said: "Who could complete such a structure? If the Blessed One permits it, I will demolish that large one and build a smaller one instead." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "If it cannot be completed as it stands, then demolish it and build a smaller one. Have no doubt about this."

The ground for the next ruling is as follows: at Śrāvastī, another householder undertook the construction of a small assembly hall, but after he had built about half of it, he passed away. His son then became head of the household. The monks said to him: "Good man, your father began building an assembly hall and completed about half of it before he passed away. It is fitting for you to bring it to completion." He was a person of great faith, and he replied: "Noble ones, I would gladly build a large one. If the Blessed One permits it, I will demolish what was built before and build a large one instead." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "If it can be done, permission is granted to demolish the smaller one and build a larger one. Have no doubt about this."

Likewise, another householder undertook the construction of a great stūpa, but after he had built about half of it, he passed away. His son then became head of the household. The monks said to him: "Good man, your father began building a stūpa and had it about half completed. It is fitting for you to bring it to completion." He was a person of little faith, and he said: "Noble one, if at the present time it cannot be completed by those who follow the Dharma, and if the Blessed One permits it, I will demolish what is there and build a smaller one." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Monks, an assembly hall may be converted from a larger to a smaller one or enlarged — either is permissible. But a stūpa must not be reduced from a larger to a smaller one. If it is made smaller, one incurs a transgression involving the deceased."

Yet another householder undertook the construction of a small stūpa, but after he had built about half of it, he passed away. His son then became head of the household. The monks said to him: "Good man, your father began constructing a stūpa and had it about half completed, and he passed away before finishing it. Now it is fitting for you to bring it to completion." He was a person of great faith, and he said: "I am a man of great faith. If the Blessed One permits it, I will make it larger." When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "If the smaller one can be demolished and a larger one built in its place, permission is granted to do so. Have no doubt about this."

The same ruling applies to old and deteriorating stūpa canopies. The Blessed One issued a ruling, and when someone took down a canopy but then passed away before restoring it, the Blessed One declared: "Do not take down what is earlier until the later one is in hand."

Similarly, clay buddha images that had grown old — the monks, uncertain what to do, left them untouched. The Blessed One declared: "Make one the same size or larger. Do not make it smaller."

In the same way, when painted murals had become worn — the monks, uncertain what to do, left them unpainted. The Blessed One declared: "If you paint, paint them again following the same design."

In the same way, when scriptural volumes of the Buddha's word had become worn — the monks, uncertain, left them uncopied. The Blessed One declared:

"If you copy it, copy the Buddha's word again. Do not be uncertain about it."

This is the fourth verse of the sūtra of the Second Door of the Single Section.

The noble Vinaya. The forty-first bundle.

In brief:

The admission of newcomers, and
The five aspects of the retinue,
Offerings, vessels, and music,
And the proclamation of lay practitioners.

The occasion was at Śrāvastī. The Blessed One declared: "Arrange the image of the Buddha residing in the shade of the jambu tree together with a great reliquary shrine befitting the occasion, and carry it in honor through the city." The monks, not knowing who should carry it, were uncertain. The Blessed One declared: "Let the young monks carry it." When the Blessed One had said that the young monks should carry it, the procession became disorderly and unseemly. The Blessed One then declared: "Let the elder monks give guidance and oversight, and let others carry it." When the monks went without music, a lay householder named Anāthapiṇḍada said: "If the Blessed One permits it, when the image is being taken in procession I will arrange music." The Blessed One declared: "Householder, do so — make the arrangements." Then the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One: "Reverend sir, is it permissible for monks to perform music?" The Blessed One replied: "Upāli, it is not permissible. At the time of offerings, announce at the door: 'Come and make offerings to the Teacher of the beautiful countenance.'"

This is the fifth verse of the sūtra of the Second Door of the Single Section.

In brief:

Making proclamations, covering vessels,
Providing separate conveyances,
Distributing the vessels in faith —
These are expressed as the verses of the sūtra.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One declared: "Organize a great seasonal festival, and arrange for the image of the Buddha residing in the shade of the jambu tree to be carried in grand procession through the city." The monks went without informing the brahmins and householders. Those people said: "Oh, noble ones! If you had informed us in advance, we would have prepared our offerings." The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Seven or eight days before the time, announce in the city, in the marketplace, in the bazaars, on the roads, and at crossroads that a great seasonal festival will be held on such a day." They announced it, calling out: "Festival! Festival!" The Blessed One declared: "When the day has come, announce: 'On this very day, in so many days' time, the festival will be held.'" Even when that was done, not everyone throughout the world heard it. The Blessed One declared: "Write it on a board, place it on the back of a woolen ox, and proclaim it in the marketplaces, bazaars, on the roads, and at crossroads." On the day of the Blessed One's great seasonal festival, the Blessed One declared: "Let the elder monks give oversight, and let the elders guard the offerings while the younger monks carry them."

When the offerings were carried off and scattered here and there, and when they were stolen by those who took what was not given, the Blessed One declared: "Appoint a monk to watch over the Saṅgha's vessels and supplies." The appointment is to be made as follows. A monk is to be appointed who, after the sitting mat is spread and the wooden sounding board struck, will answer questions that are asked. Then, when the monks of the Saṅgha have assembled and are seated, first ask his consent: "You, whose name is such-and-such — do you consent to being appointed as the Saṅgha's keeper of vessels?" If he consents, he should say, "I consent." After that, let one monk make the motion and perform the formal act. "Hearken, venerable members of the Saṅgha. If this one, named such-and-such, consents to serve the Saṅgha as keeper of vessels, and if the occasion is fitting and the Saṅgha approves, let the Saṅgha grant it — and let this one, named such-and-such, be appointed as keeper of vessels. This one, named such-and-such, serves the Saṅgha as keeper of vessels. This is the motion." The formal act is likewise to be performed thus: "Hearken, venerable members of the Saṅgha. This one, named such-and-such, consents to serve the Saṅgha as keeper of vessels. The Saṅgha appoints this one, named such-and-such, as keeper of vessels. Of those of you who are the venerable ones, whoever consents to the appointment of this one, named such-and-such, as keeper of vessels, let them remain silent. Whoever does not consent, let them speak. The Saṅgha has appointed this one, named such-and-such, as keeper of vessels. The Saṅgha has consented and approved; therefore none spoke, and so it is accepted."

After that, when many offerings had come in, the nuns said to the noble monks: "Noble ones, grant us a share of these offerings" — yet the monks did not give any. The following day, the nuns set out a separate cart, and when the brahmins and householders asked the noble nuns, "Is this the same cart or a different one?" — the nuns too received many offerings. When the monks saw that the nuns had grown satisfied with offerings and honors, they said: "Noble ones, you did not give us a share of the offerings — yet we too have now received many offerings by setting out a separate cart." When the monks then reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One deliberated: "What is blameworthy here is that at the time of the seasonal festival the nuns set out a cart apart from the monks' cart. Therefore, bearing in mind that monks and nuns should not set out their carts separately," the Blessed One declared: "Monks, the nun has acted improperly. Therefore a nun must not set out a cart separately at the time of the seasonal festival. If nuns set out a cart separately at the time of the seasonal festival, it constitutes a schism and will become a grave proximate offense."

Now those vessels remained as they were, and the monks, not knowing what to do with them, reported it to the Blessed One, who said: "Divide them." And when they did not know how to divide them, the Blessed One declared: "Appoint a monk to divide the vessels." The appointment is to be made as follows. After the sitting mat is spread and the wooden sounding board struck, a monk who will answer questions is to be appointed. Then, when all the Saṅgha has assembled and is seated, first ask his consent: "Do you consent to being appointed as the Saṅgha's divider of vessels?" If he says "I consent," then after that let one monk make the motion and perform the formal act. "Hearken, venerable monks. If this one, named such-and-such, consents to serve the Saṅgha as divider of vessels, and if the occasion is fitting and the Saṅgha approves —

— the Saṅgha approves and the Saṅgha appoints this one, named such-and-such, as divider of vessels. This one, named such-and-such, is hereby appointed by the Saṅgha as divider of vessels. This is the motion. And the formal act is to be performed as follows. Hearken, venerable monks. This one, named such-and-such, consents to divide vessels and is hereby appointed by the Saṅgha as divider of vessels. Let the venerable ones who consent to the Saṅgha's appointing this one, named such-and-such, as divider of vessels remain silent. Let those who do not consent speak. The Saṅgha has appointed this one, named such-and-such, as divider of vessels. Since the Saṅgha consents and approves, it remains silent, and so this is held to be the case."

This is the sixth verse of the sūtra of the Two-Part Vinaya.

The middle sūtra:

When things are divided and shares given,
if at some point one exceeds the rest,
if at some point of two one takes,
it is not fitting to claim it as one's own.

The Blessed One, the buddha Śākyamuni, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove (Jetavana) in Śrāvastī, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. On an occasion when a great festival took place, many gains were received, and the monks did not know how to proceed. The Blessed One declared: "A monk in charge of storing robes shall strike the wooden sounding board, appoint a monk to answer questions, and then sell the goods in the presence of the fully assembled Saṅgha." When those monks did not know how to set a price, the Blessed One declared: "Let the senior monk of the Saṅgha set it." When that same item was caused to be bought by himself, the Blessed One declared: "Do not cause that same monk to buy it himself; do not make the buyer the same person who set the price." When the senior monk of the Saṅgha set a high price and no one bought it, the Blessed One declared: "Do not set the price too high." Then it was set very low. The Blessed One declared: "Do not set it too low either; let it be obtained at an appropriate price. Whoever first raised the price should be the one permitted to buy. If, after being told he may buy it, the item is not sold to him, and then no one else raises the price, sell it to him first." When the Group of Six set a high price and then raised it higher, saying, "We raised the price for the sake of the Saṅgha," the Blessed One declared: "The one who is buying should raise the price. If another raises it, a transgression is incurred." The Group of Six raised the price, bought the item, washed it, and distributed it. The price was returned to the seller. The Blessed One declared: "Do not give it back to the seller until the price has been received. If distribution is made before the price is paid, a transgression is incurred."

This is the seventh verse of the sūtra of the Two-Part Vinaya.

In summary:

When a temple is in disrepair
or heavy, let it be made secluded.
When at some point danger arises
and the Saṅgha has been alerted for an instant —

The Blessed One was dwelling in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, let dwelling rooms be built with five stories, bathrooms with seven stories, and gatehouse buildings also with seven stories." The dwelling rooms of nuns are to be three stories. Their bathrooms are to be five stories. Their gatehouses are also to be five stories. The weight of the upper stories was causing the walls to crumble. When this happened, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Remove the top story." But it continued to crumble, and the Blessed One declared: "In the same way, remove stories down from the second to the fourth, leaving only the ground floor." The occasion for this ruling arose in Śrāvastī, where dangers had arisen for the monks and they had left the temple empty.

The Saṅgha's bedding had been abandoned and left behind when they fled, and thieves — those who take what is not given — stole it. Because it was stolen, the monks were left destitute. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not abandon the Saṅgha's bedding and go off. Wherever you go, take it with you." When the Blessed One declared that it should be taken wherever one goes, one monk took his portion of the bedding and fled together with the other monks. That evening, another monk said, "Among this Saṅgha, I am the senior one — it is right that I should have authority according to seniority," and so the bedding was given to him. Having received it, when dawn came he said, "Take this portion away." The other replied, "At the time when the bedding was shared out and you were the elder, you said I should take it — but now, when it is a burden, are you giving it to me, or should you carry it yourself?" The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "The one who carried it away when there was danger is the rightful holder of it." When the danger had passed, however, the bedding was not returned to the Blessed One with the declaration "The Blessed One has given permission." The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, for the present I have given the Saṅgha's bedding as a concession — it is not given permanently. Once the danger has passed, return it and distribute it according to seniority."

This is the eighth verse-summary of the sūtra of the two-leaved gate.

In summary:

When a great feast is held in the Jeta Grove,
let the great drum summon the assembly.
When they are arranged in separate rows,
appoint a monk as table-server.

The Blessed One, the awakened one, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove at the pleasure garden of Anāthapiṇḍada in Śrāvastī. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the Blessed One, saying: "Blessed One, if the Blessed One permits, I will hold a great feast." The Blessed One declared: "Householder, I permit it — proceed." A great feast was held in the Jeta Grove, but the monks had not assembled. The Blessed One then declared: "When a great feast is being held, summon the monks with a wooden sounding board, a drum, and a conch. When the monks are notified that the time has come and that it falls at the hour of noon, they will know to come promptly." When the monks were struck by the sound of the drum and conch, they assembled in scattered disorder. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Appoint a monk as table-server to ensure that they are arranged in order of seniority." When they were arranged in order of seniority, the food was distributed from the most senior down, but by the time it reached the youngest, the noon hour had already passed, and the monks were obstructed from taking their meal. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Form a line of five hundred and place the food before those of highest seniority." When the monks did so, the householder found that the distribution of food was too slow. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Appoint monks as supervisors of the distribution." But those too became an obstruction to the meal. The Blessed One then declared: "Let those supervisors be given food first, and afterwards let them perform their table-serving duty."

This is the ninth verse-summary of the sūtra of the second two-leaved gate.

In summary:

The nuns had become many,
and the first monk was content with them.
One, two, and many —
and the young children grew exceedingly delighted.

The Blessed One was dwelling in the Jeta Grove (Jetavana), in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. In a certain other village of Rājagṛha, a householder was residing there, and he invited a large number of nuns for a meal. After some time, a single monk was wandering about traveling together with many guests, and when he arrived in that village of Rājagṛha and entered upon alms-round, someone there said to him: "Noble one, in this house the nuns have been invited and their meal is being served — please go there." He then went there and found the senior nun of the nuns' community, Gahaladā, sitting pleasantly. She said to him: "Noble one, if you are able to speak in praise of generosity, then please take your seat in order of seniority. But if you are not able, then go off to one side and partake of the meal." He was embarrassed by this, and he thought: "If I sit here until I have spoken in praise of generosity, the many guests too will have gone, so I will eat my meal off to one side and leave." Thinking this, he ate his meal off to one side and departed. He then went on in due course to Śrāvastī. The monks asked him: "Venerable one, did you arrive comfortably? Was your journey comfortable?" He replied: "How could it have been comfortable? The nuns acted with contempt." They asked: "How did this happen?" and he related the whole matter in detail to the monks. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Wherever there is a single monk and a single nun in residence, that monk shall receive the seat first, the water first, and the food first. If a single monk arrives where there are two or three nuns, or more than three, that single monk shall receive the seat first, the water first, and the food first. Even where there are only nuns, always set aside the first seat at the head of the row, and have it prepared. If a male novice arrives, he too shall sit there and eat. If he is unable to do so, the nun shall speak in praise of generosity. If a nun does not act accordingly, there shall be an offense with expiation."

The occasion for this is in Śrāvastī. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada arranged a great seasonal festival in the Jeta Grove and offered his wife and son to the Saṅgha as servants. The monks, not knowing what to do, reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Ask the householder." When asked, the father said: "Noble ones, have them appraised, and I will pay the ransom." The group of six monks thereupon entered into a rivalry with one another and began to bid against each other. Among them, the wife who had a young child prostrated at the feet of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and said: "Master, do not send me away because of my small child." The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, among sentient beings there is none more faint-hearted than a woman — do not cause her to be afraid. Therefore monks must not assign a price to a woman. If one does so, there shall be an offense with expiation. Let each one enjoy the gift as the donor is pleased and delighted to give it."

This is the tenth verse-summary of the individual sūtra. It is complete.

In summary:

Household goods packed away in stupidity,
and whose cow and whose —
in that way a child is not to be taken away.
Anāthapiṇḍada likewise:
the razor, the attendants,
and water — these are taught together.

In brief:

Household goods and permissions,
and the questions of Upāli —
how blessings are to be conferred:
the verses on focusing the mind are briefly taught.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. While monks were traveling on tour, some fell ill. Having no medicine, they tried to sell their alms bowls, yet no householder would buy them, and time passed without relief. The monks reported this situation to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore I permit you to sew robes from cloth scraps." When the Blessed One had said "Sew robes from cloth scraps," the monks washed the scraps, turned them over, and stitched them together, yet the resulting cloth was of little value. The Blessed One then declared: "Do not wash them, do not turn them over. Stitch them together straightway, as soon as the needle is threaded."

The venerable Upāli then put a question to the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Reverend Blessed One, when you have declared that monks are to consecrate the thirteen requisites, how is that consecration to be done?" The Blessed One replied: "Upāli, it is to be consecrated separately. This robe is consecrated as an inner garment and is to be used for the purpose for which it is meant." In the same way, the upper covering, the bathcloth, the lower robe, the lining of the lower robe, the upper garment, the lining of the upper garment, the face cloth, the body-wiping cloth, the woolen cloth, the hair-wrap, the blanket, and the large cloth — this cloth is consecrated as a requisite cloth, being needed for the sick, and it is consecrated for the purpose of maintaining the life of purity equally with oneself.

The venerable Upāli again put a question to the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Reverend Blessed One, when you have declared that monks should consecrate the thirteen requisites, what is to be done with robes that are in excess of these?" The Blessed One declared: "Upāli, those are to be dedicated and kept for one's teacher, one's preceptor, and one's intimates, and the dedication is to be done in the following way. Sitting before a single monk, one should say these words: 'Please attend, venerable one. I, so-and-so by name, hereby specially dedicate this robe. Since it is appropriate to dedicate it, I dedicate it to the preceptor. With the preceptor's consent, it is to be kept.' In the same way, this should be said two and three times."

This is the first verse-summary of the individual sūtra with three doors.

In summary:

Knowing the packed goods and the rest,
and persons of the twelve kinds —
likewise the distinctions among them,
and what is proper: this is the third.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upāli put a question to the Blessed One: "Reverend one, how many kinds of persons cannot be corrected in turn?" The Blessed One declared: "Upāli, there are twelve: one who is deluded, one who is stupid, one who is unclear, one who is unskilled, one who is shameless, one who bears grudges, one who dwells outside the boundary, one who has been expelled, one who is unsteady of word, one who transgresses the code of conduct, one who does not abide in what is proper, and one to whom the training has been given." Upāli then asked again: "Reverend one, from what point does one count as childlike, and up to what point as one to whom the training has been given?" The Blessed One replied: "Upāli, one who conceives wrong thoughts and thinks wrong thoughts, who speaks wrongly and speaks wrongly, who is corrected only with difficulty when corrected — Upāli, that is the present-day understanding. As for how long one counts as stupid: one who does not grasp the sūtras, does not grasp the Vinaya, does not grasp the Abhidharma — to that extent, Upāli, one is stupid. As for how long one counts as unclear: Upāli, one who grasps the sūtras, grasps the Vinaya, grasps the Abhidharma, yet does not know the meaning that is to be brought into direct understanding from the sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Dharma — to that extent, Upāli, one is unclear. As for how long one counts as unskilled: Upāli, one who grasps the sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma,

and knows their meaning as well, yet is unable to make others understand — to that extent, Upāli, one is unskilled. That much, Upāli, constitutes being unskilled.

"Venerable One, to what extent is one counted as shameless?"

"Upāli, one who has incurred a transgression in any one of the four defeats — that one, Upāli, has become shameless. To that extent, Upāli, one is shameless."

"Venerable One, to what extent is one counted as resentful?"

"Upāli, one who is wrathful, contentious, and who moreover becomes a doorway to quarrels in whatever circumstances — to that extent, Upāli, one is resentful."

"Venerable One, to what extent is one counted as dwelling beyond the boundary?"

"That is one, Upāli, who dwells outside the monk's boundary. To that extent, Upāli, one is counted as dwelling outside the boundary."

"Venerable One, to what extent is one counted as expelled?"

"Upāli, one who has been expelled by the Saṅgha through the act of formal request followed by three proclamations — to that extent, Upāli, one is said to have been expelled."

"Venerable One, to what extent is one counted as unreliable in speech?"

"Upāli, one who is unreliable in speech, who speaks falsehood, who engages in divisive talk, who speaks harshly, and who speaks idle chatter — to that extent, Upāli, one is counted as unreliable in speech."

"Venerable One, to what extent is one counted as having departed from proper conduct?"

"Upāli, that is one who has risen and departed from the midst of the Saṅgha. To that extent, Upāli, one is counted as having departed from proper conduct."

"Venerable One, what does it mean to be said not to abide by proper standards?"

"Upāli, that is one who practices what should not be practiced, and who does not train in the training of a monk. To that extent, Upāli, one is said not to abide by proper standards."

"Venerable One, what does it mean to be said that training has been granted?"

"Upāli, that is when the Saṅgha, through a formal request followed by three proclamations, has granted training to a monk for the duration of his life. Such, Upāli, is what is called granting training."

Then Upāli asked further: "Venerable One, to what extent does a person earnestly attempt to turn back?"

The Blessed One declared: "Upāli, there are three aspects: abiding by proper standards, being reliable in speech, and not having departed from proper conduct."

This is the second verse of the sūtra of the third section of the Ekaṃsaka.

In brief:

Because of the actions and
The twelve persons as well —
Those who undergo full ordination
And those who claim to be laymen.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One, the buddha: "Venerable Blessed One, when you have declared that one should not be earnest in reversing an act performed against a particular person, and when the twelve persons are each addressed individually and they say, 'Venerable ones, do not address us!' — does their earnestness in reversal then also not apply?"

"Upāli, it does apply. I said that with regard to the act of punishment in mind."

"Venerable One, if one who undergoes full ordination declares himself to be a layman, is he to be called fully ordained or not fully ordained?"

"Upāli, even if one has received full ordination, if one declares oneself to be a layman, then that person is said to be not fully ordained. If that is so even for one who has received full ordination, what need is there even to speak of the case of one who is in the process of being fully ordained?"

This is the third verse of the sūtra of the third section of the Ekaṃsaka.

In brief:

The five kinds of sandals that are improper,
By which the feet are not to be anointed —
Sovereignty is to be proclaimed,
And the field's property belongs to the Saṅgha.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One, the buddha, declared that sandals of five improper kinds should not be worn, and —

The group of six went and anointed their feet with the fat of those five improper kinds of sandals, and then approached King Prasenajit of Kosala, where his bull-elephants were stationed. The elephant handlers were standing to one side. The bull-elephants caught the scent and bolted. The handlers said to them, "Venerable ones, please restrain them!" They replied, "We cannot restrain them. Good sirs, shall we restrain them? Noble ones, restrain them yourselves — what will you give us?" "We will give a fee for the task." One of them went before the elephants and sat in a position from which the herdsman would not have to rise, and the bull-elephants too settled down. They then said, "Noble ones, do you perhaps know the science of this?" The monks replied, "Good sirs, we know nothing of the science — it is simply that our bull-elephants happened to recognize the fat with which our feet were anointed." The handlers then said, "Noble ones, when the king's finest bull-elephants bolted, did you not cause harm to the king?" And with that they accused them of wrongdoing, derided them, and spoke of it disparagingly.

The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not anoint the feet with the fat of bull-elephants that happen to recognize. Should a monk anoint his feet with the fat of a bull-elephant that happens to recognize, he incurs an offense. Just as in the case of bull-elephants that happen to recognize, so too the same should be stated at length for horses, lions, tigers, leopards, and the like."

The occasion for the next rule arose in Rājagṛha. King Bimbisāra went to where the venerable Ānanda was staying and approached him. He bowed his head to the venerable Ānanda's feet and sat to one side. Seated to one side, King Bimbisāra said this to the venerable Ānanda: "Noble Ānanda, this lion-throne that has been set out — what is it for? Is the Dharma to be proclaimed today?" At that time it happened to be the day of the restoration ceremony. "Great king, it has been taken up by the monks — it has not been taken up by householders." The king then bowed to his feet and departed.

Now, the one who asked while already knowing was the blessed buddha. The blessed buddha said to the venerable Ānanda, "Why did the king depart without hearing the Dharma?" Ānanda reported what had happened to the Blessed One in full detail. The Blessed One declared, "Ānanda, you have acted wrongly. Had King Bimbisāra come to hear the individual liberation teaching, he would certainly have been delighted even by the mere recitation of its opening, and being delighted, by the power of that delight he would surely have done what is to be done. Therefore I permit this: let those faithful men of good standing listen to it. Furthermore, there are those who, though wealthy, have no faith, and those who, though poor, have great faith." The Blessed One declared, "Let those of that kind also listen to it."

Now at that time the venerable monk known as Twenty-Million-Grain was pale, emaciated, dried out, gaunt, wasting away, and had become feeble in body. The Blessed One observed him and said to the venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, why has the one known as Twenty-Million-Grain become pale, emaciated, dried out, gaunt, wasting away, and feeble?" Ānanda replied, "Blessed One, since first entering the monastic life under the Blessed One, he has sustained his body on porridge alone." The Blessed One declared, "Ānanda, that being so, I permit: let porridge be given to Twenty-Million-Grain."

Then the venerable Ānanda conveyed the message to the venerable Twenty-Million-Grain, saying, "The Blessed One has granted you permission to drink porridge." Twenty-Million-Grain asked, "Venerable Ānanda, is this permission for me alone, or for the entire Saṅgha?" Ānanda replied, "For you alone." Twenty-Million-Grain said, "Venerable Ānanda, since this matter has been raised, the other celibate practitioners have also been saying this: 'Twenty-Million-Grain went forth under the Teaching, and in former times, when the harvest was good in the city of Campā, he gave up even a cart drawn by seven bulls when he went forth — and now he has grown attached to mere porridge.' Since people are saying such things, I ask that if the Blessed One would grant the permission to drink porridge for my sake to the entire Saṅgha as well, then I too would be willing to accept it." The monks then reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Very well. For the sake of Twenty-Million-Grain, let the entire Saṅgha also drink porridge."

When King Bimbisāra heard that the Blessed One had granted the Saṅgha permission to drink porridge, he offered to the Saṅgha fields that had been planted with a thousand seed-jars. The monks declined to accept them. The Blessed One then declared, "Accept them for the sake of the Saṅgha; do not be uncertain in this matter. Therefore let the Saṅgha make use of the yield from those fields."

This is the fourth verse of the sūtra of the third gate of the single section.

In summary:
Ordination candidate, and full ordination too,
A novice's spiritual father, and a newcomer,
One in meditative absorption, and those not permitted —
The second training given, these two make it complete.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, "Venerable one, is it proper for a monk and a layman together to attend a single formal legal proceeding?" The Blessed One replied, "Upāli, that is not proper as a rule; however, if such a circumstance arises, it is permitted."

"Venerable one, is it proper for a novice's spiritual father, a newly ordained monk, a paṇḍaka, a eunuch, a suspended nun, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata, a follower of a non-Buddhist school, one who has gone over to a non-Buddhist school, one who is a thief by nature, one who dwells separately, and one whose status is unsettled — is it proper for all such persons together at a single formal legal proceeding?" The Blessed One replied, "Upāli, that is not proper as a rule; however, if such a circumstance arises, it is permitted." Likewise, in the same way, sharing a single seat, a single throne, a single low seat, or a single mat — it is not proper as a rule, but if such a circumstance arises, it is permitted.

"Venerable one, is it proper for a layman and a monk to be together on a seat that has been placed upon a platform?" The Blessed One replied, "That is not proper as a rule; however, if such a circumstance arises, it is permitted." As for placing mats, that too is not proper as a rule, but if such a circumstance arises and mats have been placed, the same applies.

Likewise, from a novice's spiritual father and a newly ordained monk down through those dwelling separately — if they sit together and no occasion for an offence has arisen in that place, it becomes associated with what is past.

"Venerable one, is it proper for two persons who have been given the trainings to be together on a single seat?" The Blessed One replied, "Upāli, that is not proper."

This is the fifth verse of the sūtra of the third gate of the single section.

The Sacred Vinaya Text, the forty-second fascicle.

In summary:
One not to be invited, and a single low seat,
And one who has become entangled — it is the same;
Even one who has become slightly entangled,
And grass and wood too belong to the Saṅgha.

When the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada —

Some monks were sitting and attending to cooking duties on small seats, and the group of six came to that very place and sat there causing disturbance. While those monks were busy and occupied, the group of six roused them, and harm came to those monks. The other monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Monks must not rouse monks who are busy attending to cooking duties. If they do rouse them, it will be an offense."

The occasion was at Śrāvastī. The group of six roused monks who were sitting eating and were occupied, telling them to rise according to seniority. The monks were unable to stand. The Blessed One declared, "Let them sit according to seniority as they are." When the Blessed One had declared, "Let them sit according to seniority as they are," the group of six arrived later and roused the earlier monks who were busy eating. The Blessed One declared, "Monks must not rouse monks who are busy eating; instead they should sit aside. If they rouse them, it is an offense."

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, "Venerable one, up to what point is it said that monks are busy eating?" The Blessed One replied, "Even so much as a little salt, or something to dip in, or a small morsel that has been tasted."

When the Blessed One had declared that monks who are busy eating must not be roused, the group of six sat down first according to seniority and then deliberately kept themselves occupied with eating. The Blessed One declared, "Monks must not sit out of order and keep themselves busy with eating. If they do, it is an offense. Monks, be skilled in the order of seating. If one departs from this, it is an offense."

Some monks took the Saṅgha's cooking vessels and bowls and attended to the cooking duties. The group of six said to the venerable ones, "Since we are senior, we have prior right," and then took the dye-solutions and carried them off, leaving the monks in disarray. The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Monks must hold the vessels and bowls so they cannot be seized by those who are preoccupied, and then face forward." When the Blessed One had declared that monks must not let the vessels and bowls be taken by those who are preoccupied, the group of six deliberately smeared the vessels with just a little dye and left them set aside. The Blessed One declared, "All the dye-solutions should be poured into a single vessel, and when one needs them, they may be taken from there. A monk must not smear the inside of vessels with a small amount of dye-solution and then leave them. If one does, it is an offense."

The occasion was at Śrāvastī. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada had the Jeta Grove surrounded with a fence of dense wood. Householders were breaking pieces off and taking them away. The Blessed One declared, "Have word sent not to take them." When word was sent, they abandoned even the wood and grass and departed. When this wood and grass had deteriorated, the Blessed One declared, "Whatever is unfit for use should be sent off in large quantities. What remains should be offered to those engaged in new construction." The group of six took wood that was fit for new construction, burned it as fuel, and attended to cooking. The Blessed One declared, "Wood fit for new construction must not be burned. If it is burned, it is an offense."

This is the sixth verse of the sūtra of the third gate of the single section.

In summary:

The ornament of Anāthapiṇḍada's grove —
Occupied seats must not be taken.
Vessels in use and things held in hand,
And shoes too are to be set outside.

The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada's park. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada then requested of the Blessed One: "If you would grant your permission, I will also donate the Jeta Grove itself." The Blessed One declared, "Householder, I grant permission — make the offering."

Anāthapiṇḍada then offered trees that bore masculine names adorned with masculine ornaments, and trees that bore feminine names adorned with feminine ornaments. The monks, not knowing how to proceed, reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Ask the householder himself." When they asked the householder, he said, "Do as the noble ones have dedicated it."

They again reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Gather up the ornaments of the trees bearing masculine names and the trees bearing feminine names separately, bundle them, and store them. Whenever festival occasions come, adorn them in the same way again. Use the ornaments of the walls as decorative implements for the walls. For the walls and pillars of the warming hall, use them as new construction; on that site, have them serve as the lamps of the Saṅgha. For the walls and pillars of the infirmary, use them as new construction; on that site, fashion them into medical implements. For the walls and pillars of the latrine block, use them as new construction; on that site, make them into food offered to the Saṅgha. For the walls and pillars of the water structure, use them as new construction; on that site, make them into drinking provisions. For the walls and pillars of the storehouse, use them as new construction; on that site, make them into the storehouse. For the walls and pillars of the greasy-goods room, use them as new construction; on that site, make them into an oil storage vessel. For the walls and pillars of the corridors, platforms, walking areas, gatehouse, and upper storey, use them as new construction; on that site, distribute them in common among the Saṅgha. Whatever accrues from the pond should be placed in common for the Saṅgha of monks of the four directions."

A monk was sitting in his private dwelling, cultivating virtue, when the group of six arrived and, claiming seniority, drove him from his seat and sent him away. The Blessed One declared, "A monk must not drive away a monk who is seated on the grounds of seniority. If he does drive him away, it constitutes an offense."

Then some monks had finished their affairs, risen from their seats, and were walking about, when others took their seats and would not return them, and the monks became troubled. They reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "When one has finished one's affairs and risen from one's seat, one should reserve the seat." After monks had sat for a long time on their seats, risen, and gone to walk, the group of six took those spots, and the monks again reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared, "Do not sit in that spot. If you are rising to go for a walk, leave your robe or your outer wrap on that seat to mark it."

The occasion arose at Śrāvastī. Monks came to the assembly hall while carrying vessels, and one monk, with his hands thus occupied, made a prostration, and his bowl broke. Another struck a fine pillar with his shoe, and the monks were reproached. They reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "I shall establish a rule of proper conduct for monks entering a path."

When a monk entering a path sees water, he should set his bowl and robe aside in one place. Then he should shake out his clothes and wash. Then his feet and —

hands with water — water that has collected through the natural seeping of moisture should be wiped off with a damp cloth, and then one should dry the hands after that, put on the upper and lower robes properly, and proceed to the assembly hall with composed deportment. To do otherwise entails a transgression.

This is the seventh verse of the sūtra of the Three-Door Solitary Chapter.

In summary:

The razor's stropping and the cutting of nails,
ointment, thorns, and foot supports,
the place for defecation and the place for urination —
what has been used there one should not retain.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Blessed One declared to the Saṅgha, "A razor case should be procured for the Saṅgha." The group of six monks, however, would take the Saṅgha's razor, use it, and then, picking it back up, claim there was still a use for it, and would not return it. When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared, "After using the razor, one should not retain it. If it is retained, there is a transgression." The same rule applies to the stropping cloth, the nail-cutter, the medicinal lancet, and the foot support.

Those same group of six monks would enter the place for urination, do their business, and yet say they would enter again shortly, and so would not yield the place to monks who came after them needing to use it. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "When a monk has entered the place for urination and finished his business, he should not be blocked from leaving. If he is blocked, there is a transgression." The same applies equally to the place for defecation.

This is the eighth verse of the sūtra of the Three-Door Solitary Chapter.

In summary:

Attendants and the great festival,
turbid water,
scattering from powder, a strainer,
a drain-cover — likewise what has been proclaimed.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if you would grant permission, I would hold a great festival in honor of the stūpa of the nails and hair." The Blessed One declared, "Very well, do so." And so the Blessed One instructed that a festival be held at the stūpa of the hair and nails.

At the time of the great festival, the monks assembled and washed their bowls in the pond, and lay practitioners also washed their jars of butter, oil, curds, and honey in the pond. As a result, the grease from those bowls and jars formed a film on the surface of the water. The monks became uncertain on account of this and would not drink the water. They reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Since it cannot function as food, stir it and drink. Do not be uncertain about it."

Now the water in that area was stirred by a great many people on all sides, until everything became thoroughly turbid, and one could no longer see one's own reflection in it. Moreover the water-filter was clogged by the turbidity, so that water would not flow through, and this caused them difficulty.

They reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "In water so turbid that one cannot see one's reflection, drop a fruit of the kataka tree into a small bowl or other vessel of water, wait a moment, and observe — the reflection of one's face will assuredly become visible. If no such fruit is available, use a ball of cooked grain. Because that has no grease, it will break apart." And the Blessed One declared —

"Grind it into a powder and pour it in." The water then became salty, and the monks became uncertain. The Blessed One declared, "If it is able to perform the function of salt, accept it and drink it. If it is unable to perform that function, drink it as plain water. Have no doubt about this."

This is the ninth verse of the sūtra on the triple gateway of the sole.

In summary:

Water separated from milk, and what becomes water from curds —
likewise the vessel and the little vessel —
drinking after rinsing with one's hand —
these four ways apply to novices as well.
The alms-bowl and the washing of one's face —
two modes for those who are on alms-round.
Fruits, roots, and flowers —
when one is in need, these may indeed be eaten.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The monks drew water from a well and, when they strained it, bits of fruit-laden aquatic weed and pieces of stem emerged. Being uncertain, they were unwilling to use them, and the bits of clinging matter and pieces had been washed away. The monks reported this situation to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Since these cannot serve as food, take them out, discard them, and then assemble. Have no doubt about this."

The monks were drawing water from a pond, and there they washed the water-vessel and the honey-vessel. The monks also washed their greasy alms-bowls. The grease from these clung to the surface of the water in a film, and droplets of curds also appeared. The monks became uncertain and did not scoop up the water. The Blessed One declared, "Since that cannot serve as food, drink it as water."

When they did not drink in the afternoon, the Blessed One declared, "Drink it. Do not be fastidious about the vessels and the balls."

The Blessed One declared, "Pour it off." Some monks who were traveling along a road found that there was no water there. A householder gave water to many travelers from a vessel, and the monks were unable to drink it. The Blessed One declared, "If there is no alternative, understand the situation and drink. Do not be fastidious about vessels and balls." The Blessed One declared, "That too, pour it off." When they did not drink in the afternoon, the Blessed One declared, "Drink it."

Along the road there was a stone water-trough, and the monks became uncertain and did not take water from it. The Blessed One declared, "Monks, a stone water-trough is something that is washed repeatedly — understand the situation and drink it. Do not be fastidious about balls and vessels." The Blessed One declared, "That too, pour it off." When they did not drink in the afternoon, the Blessed One declared, "Drink it. Have no doubt about this."

Likewise, water that stands in a wooden trough or in a hollow — understand the situation and drink it. Regarding afternoon drinking, balls, and the interior of vessels, pour them off as well. Have no doubt about this.

The monks presented water to the Saṅgha, and then the monks said to the venerable one, "We have left it in the alms-bowl because the stream of water had not been cut off." But they did not take it. The monks reported this situation to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Monks, all liquid naturally flows downward and does not rise upward — drink it, and have no doubt about this." In the same way, he went on to speak at length about milk, curds, whey, butter, thick cream, salt, and so forth.

The setting of the following is Śrāvastī. While monks were wandering and moving about on their rounds, they came upon a cattle shed,

There was no water there, and so the herdsmen gave them whey. But the monks felt doubt and did not wash with it. The monks reported this situation to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Where there is no water, wash with whey, with thin gruel, or with dough-water. Have no doubt about this."

The monks searched through the jars belonging to a cattle herder and found among them jars of butter and jars of milk. They felt doubt and did not take them. The monks reported this situation to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Monks, there are five kinds of jar: a jar for excrement, a jar for urine, a jar for fermented drink, a jar for oil, and a jar for butter. Of these, do not store the first three — and if they are found stored, cast them far away. As for the oil jar and the butter jar, burn them in a fire; then, using solid cow-dung or fresh cow-dung as appropriate, scrub them with water, and they may be used both in the morning and in the afternoon. Have no doubt about this."

The setting of this rule is Śrāvastī. A certain monk drank water from inside a water-pot, and insects had gotten into it. The monks reported this situation to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Monks, do not drink water from inside a water-pot in that way — if you do, a transgression is incurred. First, extend your hand, rinse your mouth, and then drink the water. Do not leave the mouth of the water-pot uncovered." And so the Blessed One declared, "I permit you to fit a cover to the mouth of the water-pot." When the monks did not know what kind of cover to make, the Blessed One declared, "One made of wood, one made of stone, or one made of clay."

When the Blessed One declared, "Extend your hand and drink the water," it happened on a journey that one monk had very little water. The Blessed One declared, "Look for a naturally hollow leaf and drink from that." When that too was unavailable, the Blessed One declared, "Carefully take water from where it clings to a branch and drink it." When that too was unavailable, the Blessed One declared, "Sit in a secluded spot and drink directly from the water-pot itself, in a way that is seemly and not observed by others."

"Monks, what I have permitted when you are in want, do not use when you are not in want. If you do, a transgression is incurred."

The setting of this rule is Śrāvastī. While monks were wandering and traveling on their rounds, the novices' fathers sent loads of goods to them, but the monks did not carry them. The fathers said, "Please carry them," but the monks felt doubt and would not pick them up. The monks reported this situation to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Pick them up." When the novice fathers, being tired, said, "We are exhausted — please carry some," the monks did not carry them. The monks reported this situation to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Carry them." When they carried the loads while the novice fathers had not yet taken hold of them, setting them down and raising them, the Blessed One declared, "Do not set down and raise loads while the novice fathers have not yet taken hold of them." When the novice fathers said, "We have gone some distance and are tired — take a little of this," the monks did not carry it. The Blessed One declared, "Tie a cord to it, have the novice fathers hold the end of the cord, and let them follow behind while the monk carries the load."

When the monks felt doubt and would not eat what was on the load, the Blessed One declared, "Have no doubt — eat of it."

A monk was traveling together with a large group of lay travelers when many of those travelers were set upon by bandits,

The novices threw down their loads and fled. The monks, not having carried the novice fathers' loads, remained right there with them set aside. When the many travelers said, "Venerable ones, your loads were not taken by the bandits," the monks said to the novice fathers, "Come now, take your loads and let us be off." The novice fathers, being frightened, were unable to set out, and said, "Why will you not go? We were not killed by the bandits." When the monks reported this situation to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared, "Take the loads, and only then have the novice fathers give them to you."

When the monks felt doubt and would not eat what was on the loads, the Blessed One declared, "Have no doubt — eat of it."

When they came to a river crossing, the Blessed One declared, "Ask the novice fathers, 'Are you able to carry these across yourselves?' If they say they can, excellent. If they say they cannot, carry the loads across and let them wade." When monks needed to get loads to the other side, they were to have the novice fathers carry them across and assess the situation. If the novice fathers too were unable to manage, the monks were to convey the loads to the other side and then afterwards bring the novice fathers across as well. If both could be managed at once, the monks were to take the novice fathers and the loads across together. When they had brought both across together, the monks felt doubt and did not eat. When they reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared, "Have no doubt — eat of it."

The Blessed One then declared to the monks, "Eat from your begging bowls." A monk washed his bowl, tapped it with his thumb, and it did not ring clearly. That monk felt doubt. The Blessed One declared, "Wash it straightforwardly two or three times, and if when you tap the clean bowl with your thumb it rings clearly, have no doubt — eat from it."

Another monk washed his bowl and found inside it a fragment of a joint of food. He felt doubt. The Blessed One declared, "Scrape it out with a wooden skewer, wash it thoroughly up to three times, and have no doubt about it."

Another monk took some warm broth inside a cracked bowl, and from it oil seeped out, rose to the top, and formed a film of grease. That monk felt doubt. The Blessed One declared, "Skim off the film of grease on top and drink the remainder."

A monk was afflicted with a wind ailment and in the afternoon drank some broth. Toward evening he called for drinking water into that same bowl, and inside the bowl the oil had risen and a layer of grease had settled on top of it. That monk felt doubt and did not drink even the water. When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared, "Wash your hands and mouth, skim off and pour away the grease, and then drink without doubt."

When the Blessed One declared, "Rinse the mouth," the monks did not know with what to rinse it. The Blessed One declared, "With clay, or earth, or strips of tree bark, or other such things."

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Bhagavān, "Blessed One, how much rinsing constitutes having rinsed the mouth?" The Blessed One declared, "The mouth and a wound are alike — one can never prevent them from continually seeping. Nevertheless, rinsing the mouth three times and spitting out the water: that is called rinsing the mouth."

A certain monk had collected his alms-round food, left it in his cell, and gone outside. Another householder then poured some additional food on top of it and left. When the monk who had been on alms-round returned, he saw other food poured on top of his alms food, and doubt arose in him, so he did not eat. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "If there is someone to receive it formally, have it formally received and then eat. If there is no such person, simply turn the top layer over and, without any doubt, eat."

Another monk had collected his alms food, left it in his cell, and gone outside. A householder then touched it. The monk saw this, doubt arose in him, and he did not eat. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Ask that householder why he touched it. If he says he touched it to remove grass or insects, have it formally received and eat. If he says he touched it out of desire, in that case too, take off half and have the rest formally received; eat it without doubt."

When the Blessed One declared, "Monks, carry a travel provision with you," there were no householders or novice fathers available. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared, "Have the donor prepare it with delight. If there is no donor, carry it back yourself and eat it after a layman. If even that is not possible, divide it into two portions, give one to a layman, and if he takes it, receive back his portion and have it formally received; then eat. Give him your own portion. If that arrangement too cannot be made, on the first day remain fasting. If on the following day there is no one to formally receive it, eat one mouthful of tiger-paw bread. If on the day after that there is still no one to formally receive it, eat two mouthfuls of tiger-paw bread. If on the fourth day as well there is still no one to formally receive it, eat as much as you need. Do not be doubtful about this."

"If there is no travel provision and there is fallen fruit, take it and carry it with you until the shadow reaches midday. If you meet a layman, divide it into two, give one portion to him, then receive back his share and make it allowable, and eat. Give him your own share. If you meet no one, whether it is morning or afternoon, as there is no fire to make it allowable and one would perish without it, eat without doubt. If there is likewise no fallen fruit, climb a tree and pluck some. Or shake the tree, dedicate it toward the north, and eat. Similarly with roots and the like: dig them up from the ground yourself and eat without doubt. The permission I have granted you for times of destitution is not to be used when you are not destitute. If you use it then, it will be accompanied by a transgression."

These are the ten verses of the third sūtra of the Ekottarika, and the third sūtra is complete.

The summary verse:

Seeds, a jar, a thief who steals,
and touching with the body likewise;
fruits, brine that has been used,
sugarcane, grapes,
what arrives unexpectedly, and what already abides.

In brief:

Seeds in portions, a cart, a boat,
a load, and a milk-seller too;
from crow, bee, and what is cooked and scooped —
Upāli's four allowances: all is known.

The Blessed One, the Bhagavān and buddha, was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Grove. At the time when King Bimbisāra (Skt. Bimbisāra) offered a gift of seeds sown in a thousand jars, the monks ate from the crop and abandoned the fields, which then became overgrown with kuśa grass. When King Bimbisāra came outside and saw this,

He asked his minister: "Who has abandoned all the fields in this way and left them to become a place of kuśa grass?" The minister replied: "It was when seeds sown in a thousand jars were offered to the noble ones — one may see for oneself how well they received them." The king said: "Did those noble ones not even give a portion share?" The minister conveyed this to the monks, and the monks in turn reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Release the Saṅgha's fields as a portion share." The monks gave them as a portion share.
