The farmers said: "All the harvested crops — you may take them entirely," but the monks did not accept their allotted portion. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Accept your portion share of the fields." The monks accepted it but left it right there on the spot. The Blessed One declared: "Have the portion share carried into the monastery." A farmer then carried it in. The Blessed One then declared: "Henceforth let the field-owner have it carried in." But when it was being grown, it was stolen. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Appoint guardian monks." While the crops were growing in a cart, the cart broke and a monk did not offer help. A householder became displeased and said: "Noble one, this is yours — why do you not help?" The monk replied: "The Blessed One has not permitted it." The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Except for the place where the oxen are harnessed to the cart, help there and assist the farmer." Another monk fell ill, and the cart-drivers said: "Mount the cart," but he was in doubt and did not mount. The Blessed One declared: "When ill, mount the cart — have no doubt about it." While a boat was transporting portion-share crops along a river, the boat broke, and the monks did not offer assistance. A householder became displeased and said: "This is yours — why do you not help?" They replied: "The Blessed One has not permitted it." The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Except for the hull of the boat, help with it and assist the farmer." Another monk who was walking along a riverbank fell ill, and someone said: "Noble one, board this vessel here," but he was in doubt and did not board. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Except for the hull, have no doubt about boarding." Furthermore, a load being carried broke, and the carrier said: "Noble one, lower this down here," but the monks were in doubt and did not lower it. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Lower it." The monks lowered it but then did not pick it up again. The Blessed One declared: "Pick it up again just as you set it down." A deity at whose gate some of the crops had been thrown out — those who take what is not given stole them, and the Blessed One declared: "Carry them inside." The monks did not know who should carry them inside, and the Blessed One declared: "A layman should. If no layman is present, a novice's father may. If no novice's father is available either," the Blessed One declared, "carry them inside yourselves." The monks carried them in, but thinking "I am the one who carried them in," they did not eat.

When things had turned out in this way, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not be doubtful about it — eat it." When milk and the like was being boiled in the Saṅgha's bronze vessels over a great fire, someone who was making it suitable went out at the gate and spat, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not let that go outside." If by some circumstance it did go outside, the Blessed One declared: "Drive back in whatever has not been contaminated." Yet it was spat out again just the same, and the Blessed One declared: "Remove the spittle." The spittle was removed, but it was spat again, and the Blessed One declared: "Fan it off with the hem of the outer robe." Still it was spat, and the Blessed One then declared: "Stir it yourself with a ladle." "Monks, what I have permitted for the needy is not to be used when one is not in need. If it is used then, a transgression will have occurred." Likewise, medicines too — if a novice's father or a deity dwelling in the vicinity stirs them, and they then go outside, the earlier methods apply.

The occasion arose in Śrāvastī. A number of merchants together invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha of monks, among others, to a cooked meal. They prepared the cooked food, set it out early in the morning, and before the invitation had come, a fire broke out in the trading hall and they went to extinguish it. The midday mark had passed by the time they returned. The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Since the merchants had surrendered it with their minds, monks, do not be doubtful about it — you may eat it." After eating, offer a blessing dedication at the time of the northern sound of the ill-omened drum.

The Saṅgha's food was touched by a crow's beak early in the morning, and the monks, having grown doubtful, did not eat the rice. When things had turned out in this way, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Just stir around the area the beak has been, and do not be doubtful about it — eat it." The monks did not eat the food in their almsbowls because a crow had touched it, and the Blessed One declared: "Just stir around the area the beak has been, and do not be doubtful about it — eat it." The venerable Namgru was doubtful about everything, and so he came to be known by the name "Doubtful Namgru, Doubtful Namgru." When he went to the toilet he saw a bee. Later, when another one just like it was appointed, he saw it sitting on the food. He then said: "The bee I saw in the toilet has come here and has settled on the food and rendered it improper." Upon hearing this, a number of monks did not eat the food. When things had turned out in this way, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, bees travel everywhere throughout high and low places, and wherever one has touched, simply stir that spot, and do not be doubtful — eat it."

Monks who were doing painting work became confused in their minds, thinking "these are paint jars," and lifted up and carried off the Saṅgha's jars of sesame oil and jars of butter. Then, at the moment they recognized what they had done, they dropped them where they stood and the jars broke. When things had turned out in this way, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If one has ascended only a little way up a full ladder and one has to descend further, lean back and set oneself down comfortably in a stable place without falling. If one has ascended a full ladder many times and then must ascend a short one, ascend and set oneself down comfortably in a stable place without falling." The monks grew doubtful and did not eat. When things had turned out in this way, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared:

"Eat it without hesitation." The venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable One, in how many ways may setting down be permitted?" "Upāli, in two ways: one who has no shame and is not devoted to the training, and one who has shame but whose mindfulness has lapsed. By these two it is permitted to set down. Eat both." The Blessed One declared: "If one gives to a sentient being born in an animal existence, one may expect a hundredfold karmic maturation. If one gives to a person seized by bad moral discipline, one may expect a thousandfold karmic maturation. If one gives to a person endowed with moral discipline, one may expect a hundred-thousandfold karmic maturation. If one gives to external sages (ṛṣis) who are free from the attachment of desire, one may expect a tenfold hundred-thousandfold karmic maturation. For one who has entered upon the path toward the direct realization of the fruit of stream-entry, it is immeasurable. For a stream-enterer, it is even more immeasurable than that. For one who has entered upon the path toward the direct realization of the fruit of once-returning, it is even more immeasurable than that. For a once-returner who has entered the stream, it is even more immeasurable than that. For one who has entered upon the path toward the direct realization of the fruit of non-returning, it is even more immeasurable than that. For a non-returner who has entered the stream, it is even more immeasurable than that. For one who has entered upon the path toward the direct realization of the fruit of arhathood, it is even more immeasurable than that. If for an arhat it is even more immeasurable than that, then what need is there even to speak of a pratyekabuddha or a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha?

"Now, when believing brahmins and householders sent monks to go and pay homage at a stūpa, sending parasols, victory banners, and pennants, and when such circumstances arose for the monks, they were unable to deliver them to the place they had been sent to deliver them. Among them, some said: 'Venerable ones, the Blessed One has declared that one should dedicate things in one direction and not distribute them in another direction.' Others again said: 'What else is there to do? Let us ask the Blessed One.' When things had turned out in this way, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: 'Monks, there are four occasions to which one must certainly deliver: the awakening, the wheel of Dharma, the great miracle, and the descent from the divine realm. Having dedicated to these, do not redirect to another direction. If, apart from these, dedication has been made in one direction but circumstances of such a kind arise, it is permissible to redirect to another, and about that you need have no doubt.

"Monks, do not make use in times of abundance of what I have permitted in times of scarcity. If one acts in that way, one incurs an offense along with what is past."

The venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable One, if two monks quarrel, dispute, and come to blows, which one should be upheld?" The Blessed One declared: "Whichever one is endowed with moral discipline. If both are endowed with moral discipline, whichever one is learned. If both are learned, whichever one is content. If both are content, whichever one is more content. If both are more content, Upāli, there is no such thing as and it is impossible that, of two who are both more content, one could be yet more content. There is no basis for it. In the case of two such as these, there is no basis for quarrel, dispute, or coming to blows to arise."

This is the first verse section of the fourth sūtra of the Single-Door Gate.

The sacred text of the Vinaya, the forty-third volume, in summary:

The thief's abode and food,
and prior quarrels — in four ways:
giving the training, the willow branch applied accordingly —
these shall not divide the Saṅgha.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, if one applies the willow branch in a thief's abode, does that divide the Saṅgha?" "Upāli, it does not."

"Venerable One, if a eunuch, a person born of a mixed union, one who has expelled a nun, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who with malicious intent has drawn the blood of a Tathāgata, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, one who dwells separately, or one who does not dwell — if such persons apply the willow branch, does that divide the Saṅgha?" "Upāli, it does not."

"Venerable One, if the willow branch is applied by means of the four prior quarrels, does that divide the Saṅgha?" "Upāli, it does not."

"Venerable One, if the willow branch is applied by one who has given up the training, does that divide the Saṅgha?" "Upāli, it does not."

This is the second verse section of the fourth sūtra of the Single-Door Gate.

In summary:

Contact with the body, and a sweat-cloth —
one must not interrupt the fall of rain.
A latrine and a privy —
what is improper shall not be discarded.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

The group of six divided up the Saṅgha's bedding among themselves, distributing it according to bodily contact from the feet to the head, until they were exhausted. The monks then reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not divide the Saṅgha's bedding by bodily contact. If you do, you incur a transgression."

When the Blessed One had declared that monks should not divide the Saṅgha's bedding by bodily contact, the monks did not know how to divide it. They reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Divide it deliberately, with due care, placing one piece upon another on the sweat-cloth."

The group of six divided up the Saṅgha's robes and then sat without any covering during the summer rains, and they were exposed to the rain and became uncomfortable. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not sit without any covering during the summer rains while wearing the Saṅgha's robes. If you do, you incur a transgression."

The group of six divided up the Saṅgha's robes and then went to a latrine, and the smoke made it uncomfortable. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not go to a latrine wearing the Saṅgha's robes. If you do, you incur a transgression."

The group of six divided up the Saṅgha's bedding and went to the privy, and the privy's planks injured them and caused discomfort. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not go to the privy wearing the Saṅgha's bedding. If you do, you incur a transgression."

The occasion for the following rule was at Śrāvastī: monks were discarding worn-out and torn pieces of the Saṅgha's bedding wherever they happened to fall, leaving them unused, and this became a matter of impropriety. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If a piece of the Saṅgha's bedding is somewhat worn or torn, do not discard it. If it is worn, mend it by patching it; if it is torn, have it repaired again. As for the old stuffing inside, take it out and beat the new stuffing. If what is old is still serviceable, use it as the inner core. If even that is not serviceable, mix it with cow dung and earth for the plaster of a pillar base, or —"

use it as plaster in the joints of a wall." This will serve both the donor and the patron for long use. This is the third verse of the Sūtra of the Single Gate of the Four.

In brief:
Food, and then oil for lamps,
ointment for the body, and shoes,
cloth and an umbrella, wood,
and root medicines — these are the last.

The Blessed One the Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī there lived another householder. He had built a temple fully furnished with all the necessary requisites and offered it, together with its large retinue, to a community of monks. The community entered the rains retreat there — sixty monks together with their companions. When the retreat ended, those monks who were practicing together, along with their attendants, came from various districts and quarters, wherever they had been residing, to pay homage at his feet. After they had done so and departed, he said to the venerable ones: "This householder, so-and-so, has invited me; please stay right here." They replied: "We accept your invitation, Preceptor." He said: "Very well then, come and take your meal today." They said: "We will come bringing food and requisites — that is what we seek." He said: "Very well, do just so." And they departed carrying food and requisites.

In the same way, some brought butter-oil for the lamps, some brought ointment for the feet, some brought shoes, some brought cloth, some brought umbrellas, some brought wood, and some brought medicines of roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits. Before long the temple became cluttered with requisites. The monk then went to where the householder was and said: "Your requisites are exhausted." The householder replied: "Noble one, if the monks there are few but a great many requisites have been offered, why were they consumed so quickly?" They explained in detail, and the householder said in acknowledgment of the fault: "Noble one, I offered those things for those who were resident there; those others are residing elsewhere — why should they be used elsewhere?"

The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, it is improper to reproach that patron. Therefore, monks, do not use elsewhere what is brought from elsewhere while residing elsewhere. Monks, if you reside elsewhere and use what belongs to elsewhere, reckon up the full value of whatever amount was used." This is the fourth verse of the Sūtra of the Single Gate of the Four.

In brief:
Insignia, and again clear insignia,
with partition screens and those that bear designs,
stool legs with designs,
the so-called "ragged stitching" — a summer dwelling.

The Blessed One the Buddha was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At Śrāvastī, two men who were brothers had gone forth into the monastic life. One of them was staying in the winter residence, the other in the Jeta Grove. At a certain time the one staying in the winter residence went to the cliff village on some matter. The monk went, dividing the shares, in order to visit his younger brother, and having divided the shares, he went to where he was. He placed one person's share among the Saṅgha's distributed shares, and stayed there engaged in conversation. Then by mistake he put on a share belonging to the Saṅgha and departed. Thereafter the one from the winter residence returned and noticed a small share there. He said: "Venerable one, have the Saṅgha's receipts been settled?" The other replied: "The Saṅgha has no receipts. What are these shares here? They belong to the Saṅgha." He replied:

"Ours is the larger share; this one is small. Did anyone come here and put on a share and leave? A younger brother of mine came here." The other was told to go and ask. He went and asked, and upon looking, the brother found that it was the Saṅgha's. He said: "I made a mistake — it was the Saṅgha's that I took away, and mine is presumably the one lying there." He took that one and came back.

When this matter arose, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Let a mark be obtained for the Saṅgha's share." The monks, not knowing how to affix a mark, asked the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Write in characters: 'Offered by the monk so-and-so.'" A monk wrote this both for the Saṅgha's share and for the individual's share alike. When this matter arose, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Let a personal mark be obtained for the individual's share."

The origin of this ruling is at Śrāvastī. The Blessed One declared: "Whether it belongs to the Saṅgha or to an individual, a decorated sitting-cloth is not to be used until it has been marked." The monks, embarking on the making of sitting-cloths for individuals, began to disagree among themselves. Some said: "The Blessed One has permitted receiving a decorated sitting-cloth; he did not say one must make it oneself." Others said: "Abandon the ready-made article."

When this matter arose, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Therefore, even if a decorated sitting-cloth belonging to the Saṅgha is found or made, it is permitted. As for an individual's, if it has been given by another and dedicated to that very donor, it is permitted to keep; but making it oneself is not permitted." After the Blessed One had declared this, another monk said: "I have a decorated chair-leg that I did not make myself but that was given to me by another — I shall keep it." When this matter arose, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, my instruction concerned decorated sitting-cloths; it does not apply to decorated chair-legs. Therefore it is permitted for the Saṅgha to keep a decorated chair-leg whether found or made, but for an individual it is not permitted."

The Blessed One instructed that nuns who had entered the rains retreat should go out and walk about after the rains retreat had ended. Some then departed having left the repairs of the building unfinished, and because the repairs were left undone, damage resulted. When this matter arose, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If a nun who has entered the rains retreat departs without having made the repairs, she incurs a transgression."

This is the fifth verse of the sūtra of the fourth gateway of the single door.

In brief:

What went out and came back without being given,
what was given and then returned again,
the Saṅgha too shall give —
and that from which one was provisioned.

The Blessed One, the buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. A certain layman's relative had died, and for the sake of performing the funeral honors, he led a procession with victory banners and pennants to the charnel ground and conveyed the body there. On returning, he brought these back and offered them to the monks, but the monks did not accept them. When this matter arose, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "What has gone out and come back — let that be called 'returned' and take it." Some, however, were poor, and when they had offered what had been returned and were again looked down upon —

The monks did not give it. The Blessed One declared: "If it is offered back, take it." He was looked down upon again, and that person, feeling regret, offered it once more, and again the monks did not accept it. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Think of it as having come back again, and take it. Do not be doubtful or resentful toward him."

The occasion for the next rule arose in Śrāvastī. A monk who served as steward had lent something of value to a layman on behalf of the Saṅgha. In due time that monk passed away. When word spread that he had passed away, a certain man came to the monastery and inquired about him. He said: "What of the monk known by such-and-such a name?" The monks replied: "He has passed away." The man said: "Reverend ones, he had lent me something of value." The monks said: "Go and return it directly to him." He replied: "He carried it for the sake of the Saṅgha, not for his own sake, nor for his parents — therefore, please, you must give it over." The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If it is known that he lent it on behalf of the Saṅgha, then let the Saṅgha give the loan." The Blessed One then said: "Monks, I shall establish a rule of monastic conduct for steward monks. A steward monk, when making loans, should consult the senior monks and then collect. If those who act as steward do not follow the rule of conduct as established for their peers in service, they shall incur a transgression."

This is the sixth verse of the sūtra of the fourth section of the single chapter.

In summary:

Sugarcane and monks —
what is eaten and shared brings benefit.
The unsplit portion and the fourth share,
and the star — these should not be shown.

The Blessed One, the buddha (Śākyamuni), was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Saṅgha had obtained a sugarcane allotment, and the Blessed One declared: "Give the novice fathers a third each." So each of those was given a third of the sugarcane. The monks, arranged in order of seniority, had formed two rows, and the distribution came around again from the top of the seniority order. The Venerable Śabdadhara was seated before the Blessed One, eating a piece of sugarcane while gazing up at the Blessed One's face. The Blessed One declared: "Venerable Śabdadhara, do you wish for more sugarcane?" He replied: "Blessed One, I desire it." Then the Blessed One cut a piece from his own portion and gave it to him. When the monastic community of monks had finished with the sugarcane and returned to the monastery, the Venerable Śabdadhara came into the presence of the Blessed One to pay homage at the Blessed One's feet, and the Blessed One declared: "Venerable Śabdadhara, were you satisfied by eating the sugarcane?" He replied: "Blessed One, how could I have been satisfied when you declared 'Give one third of our gains'? Yet because the Blessed One declared it, I was satisfied from the very start." The Blessed One then assembled the monastic community of monks and addressed them thus: "When I said 'Give the novice fathers a third of the cloth allowances,' that applies to cloth. As for food allowances, divide them equally. Even if it is as little as a leaf from a small tree, divide it equally. If it is divided unequally — whether more or less — a transgression shall be incurred."

The occasion for the next rule arose in Śrāvastī.

There was a householder residing in Śrāvastī who used to go regularly to the Jeta Grove. A monk there spoke to him at length about the seven meritorious objects that arise from wealth, and the householder, having thus generated faith, built a monastery. He regularly provided food for the monks residing there, and for this purpose he gave them some kārṣāpaṇa coins. The monks said to him, "Venerable sir, we go on alms round, so what troubles us is robes, not food. The kārṣāpaṇas shall therefore be distributed for robes." The monks then resolved among themselves: "None of us shall ever go to that householder's house."

Then after some time, a wandering mendicant monk made his way through various districts and arrived in Śrāvastī. He came to the monastery belonging to that householder, and the monks there offered him rest, gave him a place and bedding, and he settled in thinking: "Today I will rest and eat a meal together with the community, and tomorrow morning I will set out on alms round." Meanwhile the resident monks took their bowls and robes and went out to beg alms. The visiting mendicant thought: "The resident monks appear so destitute — I too shall end up like that, so I had better go and beg alms." He took his bowl, his robes, his key, his bent key, and the door-latch along with him, and as he proceeded gradually on alms round through Śrāvastī he arrived at the house of that householder. He greeted him with a word of welcome, spread out a mat, made obeisance at his feet, and sat down before him. As he sat before him, he extolled to him the seven meritorious objects that arise from wealth. The householder then said, "Noble one, I have accomplished all of that." The mendicant replied, "Householder, you have done nothing whatsoever — there is no food at all in your monastery to begin with." He said, "Noble one, what do you mean? I have offered much there — perhaps the noble one went somewhere else in error?" The mendicant said, "Householder, do you know the keys and bent keys of the monastery?" He replied, "I do, noble one, please ask." The householder then showed him the keys and bent keys, and the monk said, "The noble one has grasped the heart of the matter." With that, the mendicant took them and went back. The householder followed after him and sat in the monastery, and as he waited, he saw the monks returning with their alms. When he saw them he said, "Noble ones, where have you come from?" They replied, "Householder, we went in order to generate faith among the patrons in our circuit. As for the kārṣāpaṇas — we thought they were in the dwelling-room, noble one." They brought them out and gave them to him. He said, "Very well then, now please proceed to generate faith among the patrons in your circuit." But they were embarrassed and sat there without saying a word.

The monks then reported all that had happened to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, to disparage that householder is pointless. Therefore, do not divide in four ways what belongs to all the stūpas, to all the Saṅgha of the four directions, to all the fees for the care of the sick, and to all the food funds."

The occasion for the next rule arose in Śrāvastī. The group of six monks were wandering through districts, and around the time when the stars were just rising they arrived at a certain monastery. The monks there let them rest and lodged them in a place dear to them.

They said: "Venerable ones, why are you sitting there? While the Teacher is still present, shall we let the teaching be ruined? Why not divide things in order of seniority?" And so, as they proceeded to divide according to seniority, the juniors received nothing, and dawn came.

When dawn broke they rose and said: "Venerable ones, we are leaving — clear away the bedding." The monks replied: "Venerable ones, because you stayed only for a moment you have caused harm to the entire Saṅgha." They said: "That is in accordance with the Teacher's instruction."

The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, do not divide bedding after the stars have risen. If you do, there shall be a transgression. And do not divide bedding already assigned. If you do, there shall be a transgression."

This is the seventh verse of the Sūtra of the Four-Part Single Section.

In summary:

Grapes and rice and other garments,
and likewise what is suitable for fire,
cooking hearths, lamps, and tree trunks —
all these the Great Sage has permitted.

The buddha, the Blessed One, was wandering through various districts and came to Rohitaka, where he stayed at the shrine of the yakṣa of Rohitaka named Woolly-Bull. The yakṣa Woolly-Bull went to where the Blessed One was, and having bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One he spoke these words: "Blessed One, would you be so kind as to spend this evening together with the Saṅgha of monks at my abode?" The Blessed One accepted the invitation of the yakṣa Woolly-Bull in silence. Then, knowing that the Blessed One had accepted in silence, the yakṣa conjured five hundred temples, and within them conjured five hundred seats covered with cushions and square seats as well, and also conjured five hundred lamps filled with smokeless fire. He assigned the great temple to the Blessed One, and the remaining temples he assigned to the monks. Having assigned the remaining temples to the monks, he went to where the Blessed One was, bowed his head to the feet of the Blessed One, and addressed him: "Blessed One, would you be so kind as to accept a meal together with the Saṅgha of monks at my home tomorrow?" The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent, giving his consent. Now the yakṣa Woolly-Bull had a friend, a yakṣa named Uṇika who dwelt in the land of Kāśmīra. He sent word to that yakṣa: "I am inviting the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of hearers to a meal tomorrow — please send fruits from the forests of the northern regions." And that one filled vessels with grapes, pomegranates from Nepal, rice, and so forth, and sent them by the hand of a yakṣa. The yakṣa piled them up and set them in the courtyard of the temple.

The monks reported this to the Blessed One and asked: "Blessed One, what is this?" The Blessed One declared: "Monks, these are fruits from the forests of the northern regions." The monks asked what they should do with them, and the Blessed One declared: "Make them suitable by fire and eat them." The monks made them suitable one by one, but the Blessed One then declared: "If you pile them in a heap and touch them with fire two, three, or four times, they will become suitable." The monks made them suitable and distributed them to the Saṅgha, and there was a remainder. The monks did not know how to proceed. The Blessed One declared: "Squeeze all of them and strain the juice inside with water, then gather the whole assembly together and drink it in the afternoon as a thirst-quencher." When they were drinking it as an afternoon thirst-quencher,

There was a remainder, however, and the Blessed One declared: "Boil it and set it aside, then drink it the following day as an afternoon thirst-quencher."

The setting is Śrāvastī. When the cold season arrived, the monks were cold. They lit fires on the ground-spreads, and the ground-spreads were rendered unsuitable. The Blessed One declared: "Do not light fires on the ground-spreads; light them on a fire-screen instead." When they lit fires on the fire-screen, it became smoky. The Blessed One declared: "Light the fire outside, and blow it into the fire-screen from outside so there is no smoke, and use the hearth-screen as you like."

The setting is Śrāvastī. A craftsman gave the monks a lampstand with a single branch, but they did not accept it. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A single-branched lampstand, if it is made for the Saṅgha, is permitted; it is permitted for an individual as well. A two-branched or many-branched lampstand is permitted for the Saṅgha but not for an individual."

This is the eighth verse-summary of the sūtra of the fourth gate of the Bare Section:

Regarding the two sudden arrivals, the two far banks of the river,
rendering many things unsuitable,
the measure for the body is the monastic robe.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada. Some monks who had arrived unexpectedly went to the assembly hall, and a monk who was residing there allowed them to rest. Once they had rested, those monks stole whatever was there and left. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not allow those you do not recognize to rest."

After the Blessed One had declared that those who are unrecognized should not be allowed to rest, a monk who was recognized was allowed to rest. Later, a monk who was unrecognized arrived. When that monk went outside, he began to take the other's bowl and robe. The monk residing there thought, "This is surely his companion," and so did not stop him, and the unrecognized monk took them and fled.

Later, when the first monk returned and found his robe and bowl gone, he said: "Venerable one, who took my bowl and robe?" The resident monk said: "Your companion took them." The first monk replied: "I have no acquaintance here. Return my bowl and robe; you owe me the loan." They began quarreling with one another. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "When a monk arrives unexpectedly, ask him who he is. If that monk says, 'I am known to you,' then ask that monk whether he will give or not give the bowl and robe — or indeed anything of yours — that he requests. If he says he will not give it, pursue the matter as one of monetary value. If he takes something by saying he will give it, it is simply a matter of taking."

The setting is Śrāvastī. Another monk who had arrived unexpectedly was allowed to rest by a monk residing there. After that, just as before, an unrecognized monk arrived. While the resident monk had gone outside to dispose of tooth-wood, that monk took his bowl and robe and left. The monks who had arrived unexpectedly thought to themselves:

"He must be one who used to live in this dwelling," they thought, and so they said nothing at all. He took the bowl and robe and fled.

When the resident monk returned and found his bowl and robe missing, he said, "Venerable ones, who took my bowl and robe?" They replied, "Someone staying in the dwelling took them." He said, "Whoever is staying in my dwelling — you have taken my bowl and robe; give me compensation." The two of them fell into a dispute, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "The monk who arrived unexpectedly should ask the resident monk, 'Will you give or not give this monk here anything of yours that he requests?' If he says he will not give it, pursue the matter as one of monetary value. If he takes something by saying he will give it, it is simply a matter of taking."

The setting is Śrāvastī. A monk left his robe with a resident monk as a deposit, with these parting instructions: "If, after I am gone, my disciples come and ask for it, give it to them," and then he departed. One of his disciples took the robe and fled. When the resident monk demanded it back, a dispute arose between the two. The monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "If he said to give it to a disciple, then although the disciple's taking it is simply a matter of taking, if there is a credential, give it. If the Blessed One has said to give it when there is a credential, and the credential becomes known and spoken of publicly, so that others hear of it and steal it, the Blessed One declares: Give the credential in secret. Instruct the recipient that if someone comes who knows the credential as it truly is, then give it to them."

Some monks set out on a journey, went to the bank of a river, and boarded a boat. Another monk was already in the boat. The monk who had boarded said, "Please pass me my bailing scoop." When the other passed the bailing scoop, he lurched in the act of doing so and fell overboard and was swept away by the current. The other then said, "You dropped my bailing scoop, so you must give me compensation." The two fell into dispute, and the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Ask him, 'Did it come into your hands?' If he says it did, give it to him at once. If not, settle it and apportion according to its monetary value. The same rule applies to other articles. Just as in the case of a river, the same rule applies to climbing a mountain, crossing a marsh, and the like: if one says 'It has come into your hands, release it,' and then it is handed over and lost in the handover, it is simply a matter of loss."

The setting is Śrāvastī. In a certain temple, the keeper of the temple had not secured the door and had not checked it properly, so thieves found their opportunity and stole from it. The monks mocked him, saying, "The compensation for that field should be charged to the temple keeper." The monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Monks, there are five means of securing a door, and they are these: a bar-bolt, a door-bolt, a wheel-lock, a door-chain, and a bent key. If all of these are present in the temple and the temple keeper employs four but omits one, charge him for one part. If he employs three but omits two, charge him for three parts. If he employs two but omits three, charge him for three parts. If he employs one but omits four, charge him for four parts. If he employs none of them, charge him for the entirety of whatever is lost."

If all five means of securing a door are employed and something is nonetheless lost, then that is simply a loss. Do not charge the temple keeper for it.

The basis of the following rule is at Śrāvastī. The venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Blessed One, you have declared that monks' Dharma robes should be made to the measure of a cubit. But if a monk's cubit is short yet his body is tall, should he too make his Dharma robe to a cubit's measure?" The Blessed One replied: "Upāli, make it to the measure of the body. And if the body is short yet the cubit is long, should he likewise make it to the measure of the body?" The Blessed One declared: "Upāli, if the body is short yet the cubit is long, make it to the measure of the body. If both body and cubit are large, make it to the measure of the cubit." Otherwise it constitutes an excess. If something beyond what the rule prescribes is found, it need not be consecrated, but if it has been consecrated and rendered serviceable, it should be assigned and used as belonging to one's preceptor, abbot, or close friend.

This is the ninth verse of the Sūtra of the Four Bare Doors.

In summary:

The lower robe is permitted, and the same holds for its inner lining.
The upper robe is to be used for acts of offering, and likewise when not formally received.
The topic of sweat and what is bare is explained.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada's garden. When the spring season arrived, the monks' lower robes became soiled and foul-smelling with dust. The Blessed One declared: "Sew a lining for the lower robe." The lining too became dusty and foul-smelling. The Blessed One declared: "Make an upper robe." This likewise became foul-smelling. The Blessed One declared: "Make a lining for the upper robe, and wash it from time to time."

The basis of the following rule is at Śrāvastī. When monks wore their Dharma robes to perform the work of making offerings, and those robes became unsuitable on account of fragrances, flour, and oil, the Blessed One declared: "Whoever has become unsuitable due to fragrances should wash the robe and put it on. Whoever has become unsuitable due to flour should shake it out and put it on. Whoever has become unsuitable due to oil should wash the robe with whatever degreasing agent is available and then put it on."

The basis of the following rule is at Śrāvastī. When monks were eating their meal without having formally received it, food fell into their alms-bowls and they became doubtful and refrained from eating. The Blessed One declared: "Receive it formally and eat." When there was no one present to perform the formal reception, the Blessed One declared: "Turn the bowl upside down, right it again, and eat without entertaining doubt about it." When food fell into a pot of broth, the Blessed One declared: "Likewise turn the bowl upside down, right it, and eat." And he added: "What I have permitted for monks in times of scarcity should not be practiced in times of abundance. If it is practiced, it constitutes a transgression."

When monks were on their alms round and wind and rain fell so that dust entered their alms-bowls, they became doubtful and would not eat. The same thing also occurred while eating together in a row. The Blessed One declared: "Monks, dust is of five kinds: acceptable dust, unacceptable dust, settled dust, unsettled dust, and dust that is merely dust. There is also another set of five kinds of dust: dust from food, dust from drink, dust from cloth, dust from flowers, and dust from fruit. When there is no evident contamination, all of these are acceptable. Eat without entertaining doubt."

This is the tenth verse of the Sūtra of the Four Bare Doors.

The Bare Doors are now complete.

This is the sacred text of the Vinaya, the forty-fourth fascicle.

"Is a transgression something that is observed, or would you say it is not observed?" He declared: "A transgression is not observed."

"Is a transgression something that has form, or would you say it is formless?" He declared: "A transgression is formless."

"Is a transgression something that can be pointed out, or would you say it cannot be pointed out?" He declared: "A transgression cannot be pointed out."

"Is a transgression something that is accompanied by obstruction, or would you say it is not accompanied by obstruction?" He declared: "A transgression is not to be called accompanied by obstruction."

"Is a transgression something that is accompanied by defilement, or would you say it is without defilement?" He declared: "A transgression is accompanied by defilement."

"Is a transgression something conditioned, or would you say it is unconditioned?" He declared: "A transgression is conditioned."

"Is a transgression something worldly, or would you say it is supramundane?" He declared: "A transgression is worldly."

"Is a transgression something belonging to the aggregates, or would you say it does not belong to the aggregates?" He declared: "A transgression belongs to the aggregates."

"Is a transgression something belonging to the elements, or would you say it does not belong to the elements?" He declared: "A transgression belongs to the elements."

"Is a transgression something apprehended, or would you say it is not apprehended?" He declared: "A transgression is not apprehended."

"Is a transgression something foretold, or would you say it is not foretold?" He declared: "A transgression may be called foretold, and it may also be called not foretold."

What is that which is foretold? That which one knowingly transgresses against a training rule laid down by the Blessed One — this is called foretold. What is that which is not foretold? That which one transgresses against a training rule laid down by the Blessed One without having reflected — this is called not foretold.

"Is a transgression something foretold with respect to the great elements, or would you say it is not foretold with respect to the great elements?" He declared: "A transgression is foretold with respect to the great elements."

"Is a transgression something fully engaged in, or would you say it is not engaged in?" He declared: "A transgression is fully engaged in."

"Is a transgression something that is obscured, or would you say it is not obscured?" A transgression is obscured.

"Is a transgression something afflicted, or would you say it is not afflicted?" He declared: "It may be called afflicted, and it may also be called not afflicted."

What is afflicted? That in which one knowingly transgresses against a training rule laid down by the Buddha — this is afflicted. What is not afflicted? That in which one transgresses against a training rule laid down by the Buddha without having reflected — this is not afflicted.

"Is a transgression something accompanied by a material object, or would you say it has no material object?" He declared: "A transgression is accompanied by a material object."

"Is a transgression something that abides in attachment, or would you say it abides in renunciation?" He declared: "A transgression abides in attachment."

"Is a transgression something that has an adversary, or would you say it has no adversary?" He declared: "It has an adversary."

"Is a transgression something that is observed, or would you say it is not observed?" He declared: "It is not observed."

"Is a transgression something with mind, or would you say it is without mind?" He declared: "A transgression is without mind."

"Is a transgression something that has ripened, or would you say it has not ripened?" He declared: "It may be called ripened, and it may also be called not ripened."

What is ripened? That which one has knowingly transgressed against a training rule laid down by the Buddha — this is called ripened. What is not ripened? That which one has transgressed against a training rule laid down by the Buddha without having reflected — this is not ripened.

"Is a transgression something called karma, or would you say it is not karma?" He declared: "A transgression is karma."

"Is a transgression something belonging to the inner sense bases, or would you say —"

it belongs to the outer sense bases." He declared: "It is to be called belonging to the outer sense bases."

"Would you say a transgression is past, or future, or present?" He declared: "A transgression may be called past, it may also be called future, and it may also be called present."

What is past? When a transgression has occurred and one has confessed it and been restored from it — one has risen out of that transgression. That is also called past. What is future? When a transgression has not yet occurred but is certain to arise — that is also called future. What is present? When a transgression has occurred — that is the present one.

"Would you say a transgression is virtuous, or non-virtuous, or morally indeterminate?" He declared: "A transgression is to be called non-virtuous, and also to be called morally indeterminate."

What is non-virtuous? That which one has knowingly transgressed against a training rule laid down by the Buddha — this is non-virtuous. What is morally indeterminate? That which one has transgressed against a training rule laid down by the Buddha without having reflected — this is morally indeterminate.

"Does a transgression belong to the desire realm, or to the form realm, or to the formless realm?" He declared: "A transgression is to be called belonging to the desire realm."

"Would you say a transgression belongs to the path of one in training, or to the path of one beyond training, or neither?" He declared: "A transgression is to be called neither belonging to the path of one in training nor to the path of one beyond training."

"Would you say a transgression is abandoned by seeing, or abandoned by cultivation?" He declared: "It is to be called abandoned by cultivation."

"Is a transgression something that arises from body, or from speech, or from mind?" He declared: "There are transgressions that arise from body, there are those that arise from speech, and there are those that arise from mind."

What are those that arise from body? Engaging in unchaste conduct; taking what is not given; depriving a human being of life; intentionally causing an emission of semen; making physical contact; cutting green grass; eating in the afternoon; and drinking fermented drink — these are those that arise from body.

What are those that arise from speech? Claiming for oneself, falsely and before the assembled community, the status of one who is foremost in Dharma, when in fact one has no such quality; addressing a woman with words that speak of a serious offence; extolling to a woman the merits of one's own bodily conduct; and teaching Dharma to a woman in more than five or six words — these are those that arise from speech.

What are those that arise from mind? Take the case of a monk who dwells alone in a wilderness hermitage: he does not generate the thought for the restoration ceremony there, nor does he even say the words. The transgression that arises from his mind is not cleared. Nevertheless, it is said thus: though a transgression arising from mind is not cleared, still this is a failure to connect with roots of virtue.

"Is there a case where, with respect to the very thing on account of which a transgression would occur, if one fails to perform a certain act one incurs a transgression, and yet if one does perform that very act one does not incur a transgression?" He declared: "There is indeed a case where, if one fails to perform the act in question one incurs a transgression, while if one does perform it one does not incur a transgression."

What is that? That in which a monk, without having spread his sitting mat, carries his monastic robe however he likes and, without a companion, enters a village; or enters a village without having been invited; or eats in company; or eats repeatedly — these are transgressions.

And what is the case where one does that very same thing and yet does not incur a transgression? Take this: a monk who has spread his sitting mat and carries his monastic robe however he likes and, without a companion, enters a village; or

enters a village without having been invited; or eats repeatedly; or eats in company — in these cases there is no transgression. Thus the very same thing on account of which, when done with a certain basis, a transgression arises, can be done with that very same basis and yet no transgression arises.

It was asked: "Can that very same action, the performance of which incurs a fault, be performed and yet no fault arise?" It was answered: "There is indeed a case where that very same action, the performance of which incurs a transgression, is performed and yet no transgression arises."

What, then, is the action which, though performed, incurs no transgression? It is this: when the monks, having decided "We have not seen the nun," have formally abandoned her, have resolved not to act with her again, and have renounced gazing upon her in wrongdoing — they make this presentation to the monks: to shave the head, to join the palms, and to demonstrate reverence by prostration. If she is then expelled to outside the boundary, a transgression arises. As for that very same action performed without transgression: it is this — when the monks, having decided "We have not seen the nun," have formally abandoned her, have resolved not to act with her again, and have renounced gazing upon her in wrongdoing, and she herself makes this presentation to the monks: to shave the head, to join the palms, and to demonstrate reverence by prostration — and if she is then expelled to within the boundary, there is no transgression. Thus the very same action that incurs a transgression when performed can also be performed without incurring a transgression.

It was then asked: "Can that very same action, when sought or requested, incur a fault, while that same action, when sought, incurs no fault?" It was answered: "There is indeed a case where knowing of that action leads to a transgression, and knowing of that very same action leads to no transgression."

How, then, is it that the very same action, when sought, incurs a fault, while that same action, when sought, incurs no fault? It is like this: the monks, having decided "We have not seen the nun," have abandoned her, have resolved not to act with her again, and have renounced gazing upon her in wrongdoing — they make this presentation to the monks: to shave the head, to join the palms together and to demonstrate reverence by prostration. She is expelled to outside the boundary, and the monks then assemble with her, dwell together, and sleep together in the same dwelling. Then other monks say: "O venerable ones, this monk has been formally expelled by the assembled Saṅgha in accordance with the Dharma on grounds that she was not seen — do the monks support him in this?" And those monks speak thus: "That is true; this monk should be expelled" — and he shaves the head, joins the palms, and demonstrates reverence by prostration, and is expelled. When one says "to outside the boundary," a transgression has arisen.

And in this further case: the monks, having decided "We have not seen the nun," have abandoned her, have resolved not to act with her again, and having renounced gazing upon her in wrongdoing, have abandoned all of this — they make this presentation to the monks: to shave the head, to join the palms, and to demonstrate reverence by prostration. She is expelled to within the boundary, and the monks assemble with her, dwell together, and sleep together in the same dwelling. Other monks then say: "O venerable ones, this monk has been formally expelled by the assembled Saṅgha in accordance with the Dharma on grounds that she was not seen — do the monks support him?" And those monks say: "That is true; this monk should be expelled." He shaves the head, joins the palms together, and demonstrates reverence by prostration, and is expelled — and when one says "to within the boundary," there is no transgression. Thus it is that knowing of an action leads to a transgression, while knowing of that very same action leads to no transgression.

It was then asked: "Can there be a transgression arising from one's own pledge, and a transgression arising from another's pledge?" It was answered: "There is indeed transgression arising from one's own pledge and transgression arising from another's pledge."

"And how does transgression arise from one's own pledge?" It was answered thus: when a monk has incurred any one of the transgressions within the five classes of transgressions, and he himself is aware of it — that is transgression arising from one's own pledge.

"And what is transgression arising from another's pledge?" It was answered thus: when a monk has incurred any one of the transgressions within the five classes of transgressions, and he performs the disclosure of that transgression in proper form in accordance with the word of a faithful layman — that is transgression arising from another's pledge.

Thus there is transgression arising from one's own pledge and transgression arising from another's pledge.

It was then asked: "Can there be a transgression arising from remembering, and a transgression arising from not remembering?" It was answered: "There is indeed."

"And how does transgression arise from remembering?" It was answered thus: when a monk remembers that he has incurred any one of the transgressions within the five classes of transgressions — that is transgression arising from remembering.

"And how does transgression arise from not remembering?" It was answered thus: when a monk, having incurred any one of the transgressions within the five classes of transgressions, does not remember it — even though he has forgotten it entirely, it is still a transgression. Thus it is that whether one remembers, it is a transgression, and whether one does not remember, it is equally a transgression.

It was then asked: "Can there be a transgression arising from something manifest, and a transgression arising from something not yet manifest?" It was answered: "There is indeed."

"And how does transgression arise from something manifest?" It was answered thus: when a monk has incurred any one of the transgressions within the five classes of transgressions and it has become manifest — that is transgression arising from something manifest.

"And how does transgression arise from something not yet manifest?" It was answered thus: when a monk has not yet incurred any one of the transgressions within the five classes of transgressions, yet it is absolutely certain that he will incur it — that is transgression arising from something not yet manifest.

Thus, whether the matter is not yet manifest it is a transgression, and whether it is manifest it is equally a transgression.

It was then asked: "Can there be a matter by which one is not reinstated, and that very same matter by which one is reinstated individually?" It was answered: "There is indeed."

"And how is it that the very matter by which one is not reinstated is also the matter by which one is reinstated individually?" It was answered thus: when the monks have expelled a monk on the grounds of not having seen the transgression, and he undertakes not to repeat the offense, and he relinquishes the wrong view without abandoning it anew — such a case is one where the matter by which one is not reinstated is the very same matter by which one is reinstated individually.

It was then asked: "Can there be an act by which one is not reinstated, and that very same act by which one is reinstated individually?" It was answered: "There is indeed an act by which one is not reinstated, and that very same act by which one is reinstated individually."

"And how is it that the act by which one is not reinstated is also the act by which one is reinstated individually?" It was answered thus: when the monks have expelled a monk on the grounds of not having seen the transgression, and he undertakes not to repeat the offense, and he is expelled having relinquished the wrong view — such a case is one where the very act that brings about non-reinstatement is also, when that same act is performed, the act by which one is reinstated individually.

It was then asked: "Can there be an act whose disclosure leads to non-reinstatement, and that very same act whose disclosure leads to individual reinstatement?" It was answered: "There is indeed an act which, when disclosed, leads to non-reinstatement, and that very same act which, when disclosed, leads to individual reinstatement."

"And how is it that the act which when disclosed leads to non-reinstatement is also, when that very same act is disclosed, what leads to individual reinstatement?" It was answered thus: when the monks have expelled a monk on the grounds of not having seen the transgression, and he undertakes not to repeat the offense, but has not been expelled because he has not relinquished the wrong view — such a case is one where, even though the act is disclosed, there is no reinstatement, and yet the disclosure of that very same act is what leads to individual reinstatement.

It was then asked: "Can there be one's own pledge by which one is not reinstated, and one's own pledge by which one is reinstated individually?" It was answered: "There is indeed one's own pledge by which one is not reinstated, and one's own pledge by which one is reinstated individually."

"And how is it that one's own pledge brings about non-reinstatement, and that very same pledge of one's own brings about individual reinstatement?" It was answered thus: when the monks have expelled a monk on the grounds of not having seen the transgression, and he undertakes not to repeat the offense, and

— he has been expelled on account of not repeating the view toward the offense. Such a case as that is one's own pledge bringing about non-reinstatement, and one's own pledge bringing about individual reinstatement.

It was then asked: "Can there be another's pledge by which one is not reinstated, and another's pledge by which one is reinstated individually?" It was answered: "There is indeed another's pledge by which one is not reinstated, and another's pledge by which one is reinstated individually."

"And how is it that another's pledge brings about non-reinstatement, and that same other's pledge brings about individual reinstatement?" It was answered thus: when the monks have expelled a monk on the grounds of not having seen the transgression, and in accordance with the word of a believing layman, and he undertakes not to repeat the offense, and he has been expelled on account of not repeating the view toward the offense — such a case as that is another's pledge bringing about non-reinstatement, and another's pledge bringing about individual reinstatement.

It was then asked: "Can there be non-reinstatement even when it is recollected, and individual reinstatement even when it is recollected?" It was answered: "There is indeed non-reinstatement even when it is recollected, and individual reinstatement even when it is recollected."

"And how does non-reinstatement even when recollected, and individual reinstatement even when recollected, come about?" It was answered thus: when the monks have expelled a monk on the grounds of not having seen the transgression, and he undertakes not to repeat the offense, and he has been expelled on account of not repeating the view toward the offense — such a case as that is non-reinstatement even when recollected, and individual reinstatement even when recollected.

It was then asked: "Can there be non-reinstatement even when it is not recollected, and individual reinstatement even when it is not recollected?" It was answered: "There is indeed non-reinstatement even when it is not recollected, and individual reinstatement even when it is not recollected." It was answered thus: when the monks have expelled a monk on the grounds of not having seen the transgression, and he undertakes not to repeat the offense, and he has been expelled on account of not repeating the view toward the offense — such a case as that is non-reinstatement even when it is not recollected, and individual reinstatement even when it is not recollected.

It was then asked: "Can there be non-reinstatement in the case of what is directly present, and individual reinstatement in the case of what is directly present?" It was answered: "There is indeed non-reinstatement in the case of what is directly present, and individual reinstatement in the case of what is directly present."

"And how does non-reinstatement in the case of what is directly present, and so forth, come about?" It was answered thus: when the monks have expelled a monk on the grounds of not having seen the transgression, and he undertakes not to repeat the offense, and he has been expelled on account of not repeating the view toward the offense — such a case as that is non-reinstatement in the case of what is directly present, and individual reinstatement in the case of what is directly present.

It was then asked: "Can there be non-reinstatement even when it is not directly present, and individual reinstatement even when it is not directly present?" It was declared: "There is indeed such." "And how does non-reinstatement even when not directly present, and individual reinstatement even when not directly present, come about?" It was answered thus: when the monks have expelled a monk on the grounds of not having seen the transgression, and he undertakes not to repeat the offense, and he has been expelled on account of not repeating the view toward the offense — such a case as that is non-reinstatement even when it is not directly present, and individual reinstatement even when it is not directly present.

It was then asked: "Is the matter on account of which the Saṅgha carries out an act something that is many, or two, or one?" It was declared: "The matter on account of which the Saṅgha carries out an act can indeed be many, or two, or one."

"And how can one matter be the matter on account of which the Saṅgha's act is carried out, yet that matter be many, or two, or one?" It was answered thus: when the nuns have been instructed by a resolution stipulating that they shall not pay homage to a monk, that they shall not speak with him, and that they shall not share the same use of resources — a case such as that is one in which the matter on account of which the Saṅgha carries out the act can be many, or two, or one.

As for the act that the Saṅgha carries out as an act, that act can be many, or two —

or one — and the same holds for one as well. It was answered thus: just as before, when monks have instructed a monk by stipulating that the nuns shall not pay homage to him, shall not speak with him, and shall not share the same use of resources with him — in such a case the act that the Saṅgha carries out as an act can indeed be many, or two, or one.

"And when the Saṅgha carries out the very act that is sought after as an act to be sought, can that too be many, or two, or one?" It was answered: yes, it can be many, or two, or one. "And the act that the Saṅgha is to carry out knowingly — even though it is known as such, can it also be carried out by many, or by two, or by one?" Yes, it can be so. "And how is it that the very act which the Saṅgha carries out as an act to be sought after can be performed by many, or by two, or by one?" It is as follows: when monks have instructed a monk by stipulating that the monks shall not pay homage to him, shall not speak with him, and shall not share the same use of resources with him — a case such as that is one in which the act the Saṅgha is to carry out knowingly, even though it is known as such, can be carried out by many, or by two, or by one. And the same holds as before.

"When the Saṅgha carries out an act in accordance with its own resolution, can it also be that such an act is carried out by many, or by two, or by one?" It was answered: yes, even when the Saṅgha carries out an act in accordance with its own resolution, it can indeed be done by many, or by two, or by one. "And how is it that the Saṅgha carrying out an act in accordance with its own resolution can be performed by many, or by two, or by one?" It is as follows: when monks have instructed a monk by stipulating that the monks shall not pay homage to him, shall not speak with him, and shall not share the same use of resources with him — a case such as that is one in which even when the Saṅgha carries out an act in accordance with its own resolution, it can be done by many, or by two, or by one.

"And when the Saṅgha carries out an act in accordance with another's resolution, can it also be that such an act is done by many, or by two, or by one?" It was answered: yes, it can be so. When monks have instructed a monk by stipulating that the monks shall not pay homage to him, shall not speak with him, and shall not share the same use of resources with him — a case such as that is one in which even when the Saṅgha carries out an act in accordance with another's resolution, it can be done by many, or by two, or by one, just as before.

"And when the Saṅgha carries out an act while being mindful, can it also be that such an act is done by many, or by two, or by one?" It was declared: yes, even when the Saṅgha carries out an act while being mindful, it can be done by many, or by two, or by one. It is as follows: when monks have instructed a monk by stipulating that the monks shall not pay homage to him, shall not speak with him, and shall not share the same use of resources with him — a case such as that is one in which even when the Saṅgha carries out an act while being mindful, it can be done by many, or by two, or by one, just as before. And the same holds for the case of not being mindful — even without mindfulness, it extends up to the point of being many, or two, or one, in the same way as before.

"And when a matter is directly present and the Saṅgha carries out an act concerning it, can that also be done by many, or by two, or by one?" It was answered: yes, even when a matter is directly present, it can be done by many, or by two, or by one. It is as follows: when monks have instructed a monk by stipulating that the monks shall not pay homage to him, shall not speak with him, and shall not share the same use of resources with him — a case such as that is one in which even when the matter is directly present and the Saṅgha carries out the act, it can be done by many, or by two, or by one, just as before.

It was asked whether, even when a matter is not directly present and the Saṅgha carries out an act concerning it, that too becomes valid in the same way. It was answered: yes. It is as follows: a case in which monks have instructed a monk by stipulating that the monks shall not pay homage to him, shall not speak with him, and shall not share the same use of resources with him — a case such as that is one in which even when the matter is not directly present and the Saṅgha carries out the act, it can be done by many, or by two, or by one, just as before.

The four acts concerning a disciplinary proceeding (Skt. tajjanīyakarman) are: the act of censure, the act of reprimand, the act of banishment, and the act of reconciliation. It was asked: if, in a case that properly calls for the act of censure, the acts of reprimand, banishment, and reconciliation are performed instead, is that considered done? The Blessed One declared: if it was done for the purpose of those three or those five factors, it is considered done. But if it was done merely on the basis of the sūtra text, it is considered not done. Why? Because censure is one thing, reprimand another, banishment another, and reconciliation yet another.

Venerable sir, it was asked: if, in a case that properly calls for the act of reprimand, the acts of banishment, reconciliation, and censure are performed instead, is that considered done? The Blessed One declared: if it was done for the purpose of those three or those five factors, it is considered done. But if it was done merely on the basis of the sūtra text, it is considered not done. Why? Because reprimand is one thing, banishment another, reconciliation another, and censure yet another.

Venerable sir, it was asked: if, in a case that properly calls for the act of banishment, the acts of reconciliation, censure, and reprimand are performed instead, is that considered done? The Blessed One declared: if it was done for the purpose of those three or those five factors, it is considered done. But if it was done on the basis of the sūtra text, it is considered not done. Why? Because banishment is one thing, reconciliation another, censure another, and reprimand yet another.

Venerable sir, it was asked: if, in a case that properly calls for the act of reconciliation, the acts of censure, reprimand, and banishment are performed instead, is that considered done? The Blessed One declared: if it was done for the purpose of those three or those five factors, it is considered done. But if it was done on the basis of the sūtra text, it is considered not done. Why? Because reconciliation is one thing, and censure and the rest are each something different.

It was asked: can the same grounds on which one performs the act of banishment serve as the grounds for reprimand, censure, and reconciliation? The Blessed One declared: if done for the purpose of that matter, it is permissible.

It was asked: can the same grounds on which one performs the act of reprimand serve as the grounds for banishment, censure, and reconciliation? The Blessed One declared: if done for the purpose of that matter, it is permissible.

It was asked: can the same grounds on which one performs the act of censure serve as the grounds for reconciliation, banishment, and reprimand? The Blessed One declared: if done for the purpose of that matter, it is permissible.

It was asked: can the same grounds on which one performs the act of reconciliation serve as the grounds for banishment, censure, and reprimand? The Blessed One declared: if done for the purpose of that matter, it is permissible.

It was asked: can one for whom an offense results in there being no remainder come to have a remainder by means of the same grounds? The Blessed One declared: yes. It is as follows: a nun who commits the four root defeats (Skt. pārājika) that are not shared in common comes to have no remainder. A monk, however, comes to have a remainder.

It was asked: can the very grounds by which a pārājika offense results in a transgression come to constitute a remainder within the Saṅgha? The Blessed One declared: yes. When a nun engages in bodily contact, it constitutes a root defeat for her. For a monk, it constitutes a remainder within the Saṅgha.

It was asked: can the very grounds by which a root defeat offense arises come to constitute a transgression? The Blessed One declared: yes. If a nun knowingly conceals a serious offense committed by another nun until dawn breaks, it constitutes a root defeat for her. If monks conceal an offense committed by a monk, it constitutes a transgression.

It was asked: can the very grounds by which a root defeat offense arises come to constitute a wrongdoing? The Blessed One declared: yes. If a nun, in the following manner — when the Saṅgha is assembled and acting in accordance with the Dharma, she has been dismissed from it after it was proclaimed that such-and-such monk's parents have been seen, and then she enters again — and even though she is admonished up to three times within the Saṅgha she does not leave, it constitutes a root defeat for her. If a monk has been admonished and does not leave, it constitutes a wrongdoing.

It was asked: can that very ground by which something constitutes a remainder within the Saṅgha also constitute a transgression? The Blessed One declared: yes. If a monk intentionally emits semen, it constitutes a remainder within the Saṅgha. If a nun emits semen, it constitutes a transgression.

It was asked: can that very ground by which something constitutes a remainder within the Saṅgha also constitute a wrongdoing? The Blessed One declared: yes. If a nun goes outside at an improper time for the sake of some matter, it constitutes a remainder within the Saṅgha. For a monk, it constitutes a wrongdoing.

It was asked: can the very grounds by which something constitutes a transgression also constitute an offense requiring individual confession? The Blessed One declared: yes. If a monk accepts food solicited from one who is not a relative, it constitutes a transgression. If a nun accepts it, it constitutes an offense requiring individual confession.

It was asked: can those very grounds by which something constitutes a transgression also constitute a wrongdoing? The Blessed One declared: yes. If a nun defecates or urinates on green grass, it constitutes a transgression. If a monk does so, it constitutes a wrongdoing.

It was asked: can those very grounds by which something constitutes an offense requiring individual confession also constitute a wrongdoing? The Blessed One declared: yes. Among the rules of the training that have been formally undertaken — if one has accepted food and drink with one's own hand by spreading it out, it constitutes an offense requiring individual confession. If a nun accepts it, it constitutes a wrongdoing.

It was asked: is it possible that one who has sworn an oath in a place of theft, not yet having received full ordination, will not be given full ordination; that one who has received full ordination will be expelled again; that one who has not yet received full ordination will be given full ordination; and that one who has received full ordination will not be expelled? The Blessed One declared: if one has participated in the restoration ceremony two or three times, that person, not yet having received full ordination, shall not be given full ordination; and if already fully ordained, shall be expelled once more. But if one has participated in the restoration ceremony only once, that person, even without having received full ordination, shall be given full ordination; and even if already fully ordained, shall not be expelled.

It was asked: is it possible, in the case of a nun who has been expelled by oath, that even without having received full ordination she will not be given full ordination; that even if fully ordained she will be expelled again; that even without having received full ordination she will be given full ordination; and that even if fully ordained she will not be expelled? The Blessed One declared: yes. A nun who has been expelled on account of engaging in impure conduct — even if she has not yet received full ordination, she shall not be given full ordination; and even if she has received full ordination, she shall be expelled once more.

A nun who has been expelled on account of bodily contact — even if she has not yet received full ordination, she shall be given full ordination; and even if she has received full ordination, she shall not be expelled again.

Concerning a nun who has been expelled by oath on account of having split the Saṅgha: are there cases where, even without having received full ordination she will not be given full ordination, and even if fully ordained she will be expelled again; where even without having received full ordination she will be given full ordination, and even if fully ordained she will not be expelled? The Blessed One declared: yes. One who perceives what is not in accord with the Dharma as not being in accord with the Dharma, and who, seeing the split as contrary to the Dharma, has nonetheless divided the Saṅgha; and one who perceives what is not in accord with the Dharma as being in accord with the Dharma, and who, seeing the split as contrary to the Dharma, has divided the Saṅgha; and one who is uncertain about what is not in accord with the Dharma, and who, seeing the split as contrary to the Dharma, has divided the Saṅgha — such a person, if not yet fully ordained, shall not be given full ordination, and if already fully ordained shall be expelled again. One who, perceiving what is not in accord with the Dharma as being in accord with the Dharma, has caused a split in the Saṅgha, and who regards that split as well to be in accord with the Dharma — such a person, even if not yet fully ordained, shall be given full ordination, and even if fully ordained shall not be expelled.

Concerning a nun who is under oath regarding not having killed her mother: are there cases where, even without having received full ordination she will not be given full ordination, and even if fully ordained she will be expelled again; where even without having received full ordination she will be given full ordination, and even if fully ordained she will not be expelled? The Blessed One declared: yes.
