One who has deliberately, with her own hand, deprived her mother of life — if not yet fully ordained, she shall not be given full ordination, and if already fully ordained she shall be expelled again. One who has deprived her mother of life while mistaking her for someone else — even if not yet fully ordained, she shall be given full ordination, and even if fully ordained she shall not be expelled. The same applies in the case of a father, an arhat, and a śrāvaka as well.

Venerable one, does a monk deprive his mother of life with a wholesome mind, or with an unwholesome mind, or with a mind that is neither?

The Blessed One declared: Upāli, a monk deprives his mother of life with a wholesome mind, with an unwholesome mind, and with a mind that is neither.

Venerable one, if a monk deprives his mother of life with a wholesome mind, does that entail a defeat and does it also become a boundless act?

The Blessed One declared: Upāli, if a monk deprives his mother of life with an unwholesome mind, it does entail a defeat, and it does also become a boundless act. There are also cases where, if he deprives his mother of life with a wholesome mind, it does not entail a defeat and it does not become a boundless act.

Venerable one, if a monk deprives his mother of life with an unwholesome mind, does it in all cases entail a defeat and become a boundless act? Or are there cases where, even with an unwholesome mind, it does not entail a defeat and does not become a boundless act?

The Blessed One declared: Upāli, there are cases where depriving one's mother of life with an unwholesome mind entails a defeat and also becomes a boundless act. And there are also cases where depriving one's mother of life with an unwholesome mind does not entail a defeat and does not become a boundless act.

Venerable one, if a monk deprives his mother of life with a mind that is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, does that in all cases entail a defeat and become a boundless act? Or are there cases where, even with such a mind, it does not entail a defeat and does not become a boundless act?

The Blessed One declared:

Upāli, there are cases where a monk who deprives his mother of life with a mind that is neither wholesome nor unwholesome incurs a defeat and also commits a boundless act. And there are also cases where a monk who deprives his mother of life with a mind that is neither wholesome nor unwholesome does not incur a defeat and does not commit a boundless act.

Venerable one, in what cases does a monk who deprives his mother of life with a wholesome mind incur the transgression of defeat and also commit a boundless act? And in what cases does a monk who deprives his mother of life with a wholesome mind not incur the transgression of defeat and not commit a boundless act?

The Blessed One declared:

Upāli, consider this case: a monk's mother has been ill for a long time, suffering and in severe pain, experiencing great distress; and it is under such a circumstance that he deprives her of life. Then he incurs the transgression of defeat and also commits a boundless act. But consider this case: that same monk, while nursing his ailing mother, gives her cooked rice, barley gruel, broth, meat, or game, and she subsequently passes away due to that very condition. Then he does not incur the transgression of defeat, nor does he commit a boundless act. Thus it is that in one case a monk who deprives his mother of life with a wholesome mind incurs the transgression of defeat and commits a boundless act, and in the other case a monk who deprives his mother of life with a wholesome mind does not incur the transgression of defeat and does not commit a boundless act.

Venerable one, in what cases does a monk who deprives his mother of life with an unwholesome mind incur the transgression of defeat and also commit a boundless act? And in what cases does a monk who deprives his mother of life with an unwholesome mind not incur the transgression of defeat and not commit a boundless act?

The Blessed One declared:

Upāli, consider this case: a monk deprives his mother of life for the sake of wealth or for the sake of an inheritance. Then he incurs the transgression of defeat and also commits a boundless act. But consider this case: a monk with an unwholesome mind intends to beat a yak, or to beat a sheep or a goat, and instead strikes his mother, and she subsequently passes away on account of that. Then he does not incur the transgression of defeat, nor does he commit a boundless act. Thus it is that in one case, when a monk with an unwholesome mind deprives his mother of life, he incurs the transgression of defeat and commits a boundless act, and in the other case, when a monk with an unwholesome mind deprives his mother of life, he does not incur the transgression of defeat and does not commit a boundless act.

In what cases does a monk who deprives his mother of life with a mind that is neither wholesome nor unwholesome incur the transgression of defeat and also commit a boundless act? And in what cases does he not incur the transgression of defeat and not commit a boundless act?

The Blessed One declared:

Consider this case: a monk employs a means so that his mother lies down in order for his karma to be pacified, and she dies while lying there beneath him. Then he incurs the transgression of defeat and also commits a boundless act. But consider this case: a monk with a mind that is neither wholesome nor unwholesome strikes the ground, intending to strike the earth or the leaves of a tree, and instead strikes his mother, and she subsequently passes away on account of that. Then he does not incur the transgression of defeat, nor does he commit a boundless act. Thus it is that in one case, when a monk with a mind that is neither wholesome nor unwholesome kills his mother, he incurs the downfall of defeat and commits a boundless act, and in the other case, when a monk with a mind that is neither wholesome nor unwholesome kills his mother, he does not incur the transgression of defeat and does not commit a boundless act.

The same applies to a father and to a śrāvaka arhat — it is just the same.

The Noble Vinaya, the forty-fifth fascicle.

A venerable monk who has been dwelling within a boundary from the very beginning without having withdrawn, and when the Saṅgha has not yet assembled — is it possible that if he performs all the acts by word alone, it counts as having performed them, and yet no transgression is incurred?

The Blessed One declared: It is possible. The Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened Buddha — therefore I directed the son of Maudgala: "You, recite the Prātimokṣa sūtra for them; do not have the Tathāgata stand reading the Prātimokṣa sūtra." That is what I instructed.

Again — is it possible that if a certain monk has never experienced any one of the five kinds of restoration ceremony, and yet the restoration ceremony is performed, no transgression is incurred?

The Blessed One declared: It is possible. It is a consecrated restoration ceremony.

Venerable one, the Blessed One has said that the restoration ceremony is not to be performed in the presence of a householder, and that the Prātimokṣa is not to be recited. If the Saṅgha performs the restoration ceremony and recites the Prātimokṣa sūtra while a householder is present — does it count as having recited it, and yet no transgression is incurred?

The Blessed One declared: Such a case exists as well. This is what I directed: "Monks, assemble before Prasenajit, king of Kosala, without any other retinue, and recite the Prātimokṣa sūtra — and he will come to have deep faith in it." That is what I instructed.

Blessed One, does a monk incur a transgression through a wholesome mind, or does he incur a transgression through a non-virtuous mind, or through a mind that is not in accordance with scripture?

The Blessed One declared: There are cases in which a monk incurs a transgression through a wholesome mind, through a non-virtuous mind, and through a mind that is not in accordance with scripture. As for how a transgression is incurred through a wholesome mind: a newly ordained monk, unskilled in the training rules he has vowed to uphold, who cuts the grass or plants around a stūpa, or the grass or plants of a walking path or courtyard, or picks flowers — this is done with a wholesome mind. As for how a transgression is incurred through a non-virtuous mind: knowingly transgressing the training rules laid down by the Buddha — this is done with a non-virtuous mind. As for how a transgression is incurred through a mind that is not in accordance with scripture: knowingly transgressing the training rules laid down by the Buddha — such an act is done with a mind that is not in accordance with scripture.

Venerable one, do arhat monks incur transgressions through a wholesome mind, or do they incur transgressions through a mind that is not in accordance with scripture?

The Blessed One declared: Upāli, when an arhat commits any such act, it is to be said that all of them are done with a mind that is not in accordance with scripture.

Venerable one, how is it that when a monk who is an arhat incurs a transgression, all such acts are said to be done with a mind that is not in accordance with scripture?

Upāli, it is like this: a monk who is an arhat, having lost mindfulness at this or that moment and at this or that juncture, wears his monastic robes however he pleases, enters a village without having fastened them, eats repeatedly, eats in company, when lying down to sleep is placed upon a great high seat, when lying down to sleep reclines in a woman's bed, lies down when those who have not yet received full ordination are departing, and when those who have not yet received full ordination arrive, confesses according to the Dharma to whoever is sitting with him when he rises. All such acts, when committed as transgressions by a monk who is an arhat, are said to be done entirely with a mind that is not in accordance with scripture.

Is it "the Saṅgha in its entirety is disrupted" that one says, or is it "all the disruptions of the Saṅgha"? The Saṅgha in its entirety — the Saṅgha is not disrupted; there is also a disrupted Saṅgha that is not in its entirety. There is a Saṅgha in its entirety that is not disrupted. There is also a Saṅgha in its entirety that is disrupted.

There is also a Saṅgha that is not in its entirety yet is not disrupted. What is a Saṅgha that is in its entirety yet not disrupted? It is as follows: the Saṅgha has indeed become divided, and the fourteen factors that bring about the division of the Saṅgha have been fully cultivated and set in motion, yet they have not been grasped and acted upon. In that case, the Saṅgha, though divided, is not disrupted. What is a Saṅgha that is disrupted yet not in its entirety? It is as follows: the fourteen factors that bring about the division of the Saṅgha have been fully cultivated, set in motion, and grasped, yet the Saṅgha has not actually become divided. That is a Saṅgha that is disrupted yet has not become divided. What is a Saṅgha that is in its entirety and has also become disrupted? It is as follows: the Saṅgha has become divided, and the fourteen factors that bring about division have also been fully cultivated, set in motion, and grasped — that is a Saṅgha that is in its entirety and is disrupted. What is something that is neither a disrupted Saṅgha nor a Saṅgha that is not in its entirety? It is everything apart from these categories.

Is it "every Saṅgha that is divided is a separate Saṅgha" that one says, or "every separate Saṅgha is a divided one"? There is also a Saṅgha that is divided yet has not become a separate Saṅgha. There is also a Saṅgha that is separate yet not divided. There is also one that is both divided and has become a separate Saṅgha. And there is also one that is neither divided nor has become a separate Saṅgha. What is a Saṅgha that is divided yet has not become separate? It is as follows: the Saṅgha has become divided, but the two Saṅghas do not abide as separate — they are not divided by purpose, not divided by boundary, not divided by material gain, and not divided by food. That is a Saṅgha that is divided yet has not become a separate Saṅgha. What is a Saṅgha that is separate yet not divided? It is as follows: the two Saṅghas abide as separate — divided by purpose, divided by boundary, divided by material gain, divided by food — yet the Saṅgha has not actually been divided. That is a Saṅgha that abides as separate yet is not divided; that is a separate Saṅgha that is not a divided one. What is a Saṅgha that is divided and has become a separate Saṅgha? It is as follows: the Saṅgha has become divided and the two Saṅghas abide as separate — divided by purpose, divided by boundary, divided by material gain, divided by food. That is a Saṅgha that is divided and has become a separate Saṅgha. What is something that is neither a divided Saṅgha nor a separate Saṅgha? It is everything apart from these categories.

Is it "every divided Saṅgha abides as a separate Saṅgha" that one says, or "every Saṅgha abiding as separate is a divided Saṅgha"? There is also a Saṅgha that is divided yet does not abide as separate. There is also one that abides as separate yet is not divided. There is also one that is both divided and abides as separate. And there is also one that is not divided and does not abide as separate. What is a Saṅgha that is divided yet does not abide as separate? It is as follows: those Saṅghas have become divided, but the two Saṅghas do not abide as separate — not separate in purpose, not separate in boundary, not separate in material gain, not separate in food. That is a Saṅgha that is divided yet does not abide as separate. What is a Saṅgha that abides as separate yet is not divided? It is as follows: the two Saṅghas have become separate — separate in purpose, separate in boundary, separate in material gain, separate in food — yet the Saṅgha has not been divided. That is one that abides as separate yet is not divided; that is a Saṅgha that abides as separate yet is not divided. What is a Saṅgha that is divided and abides as separate? It is as follows: the Saṅgha has become divided, and the two Saṅghas have come to abide as separate — separate in purpose, separate in boundary, separate in material gain, separate in food. That is a Saṅgha that is divided and abides as separate.

What is that which is neither a divided Saṅgha nor a Saṅgha that abides as separate? It is as follows: anything other than these forms just described.

Then a question was posed: Are all those divisions of the Saṅgha such that they persist for an eon? And does everything that persists for an eon constitute a schism in the Saṅgha?

It was declared: There is that which has divided the Saṅgha yet does not persist for an eon. There is that which persists for an eon and has also divided the Saṅgha and persists for an eon. And there is that which neither divides the Saṅgha nor persists for an eon.

What is that which has divided the Saṅgha yet does not persist for an eon? One who has divided the Saṅgha while perceiving that one is acting in accordance with the Dharma — that is a division of the Saṅgha that does not persist for an eon.

What is that which persists for an eon yet has not divided the Saṅgha? The nāga king Śaktin, the nāga king Sthira, the nāga king Manāpa, the nāga king Priya, the nāga king Priyadarśin, the nāga king Lābhin, the nāga king Suvarṇāśva, the king of Yama, and the gods of the Brahma realm — these persist for an eon, yet they have not divided the Saṅgha.

What is that which both divides the Saṅgha and persists for an eon? Devadatta. He both divides the Saṅgha and persists for an eon.

What is that which neither divides the Saṅgha nor persists for an eon? Anything other than these forms just described.

Then a further question was posed: Does everything that has divided the Saṅgha thereby incur a fault that persists for an eon? And does everything that incurs a fault that persists for an eon constitute a division of the Saṅgha?

It was declared: There is that which has divided the Saṅgha yet does not incur a fault that persists for an eon. There is that which incurs a fault that persists for an eon yet has not divided the Saṅgha. There is that which both divides the Saṅgha and incurs a fault that persists for an eon. And there is that which neither divides the Saṅgha nor incurs a fault that persists for an eon.

What is that which has divided the Saṅgha yet does not incur a fault that persists for an eon? One who has divided the Saṅgha while perceiving that one is acting in accordance with the Dharma — this is a division of the Saṅgha that does not incur a fault that persists for an eon.

What is that which incurs a fault that persists for an eon yet has not divided the Saṅgha? The nāga king Śaktin, the nāga king Sthira, the nāga king Manāpa, the nāga king Priya, the nāga king Priyadarśin, the nāga king Lābhin, the nāga king Suvarṇāśva, the king of Yama, and the gods of the Brahma realm — these incur a fault that persists for an eon, yet they have not divided the Saṅgha.

What is that which both divides the Saṅgha and incurs a fault that persists for an eon? Devadatta. He both divides the Saṅgha and incurs a fault that persists for an eon.

What is that which neither divides the Saṅgha nor incurs a fault that persists for an eon? Anything other than these forms just described.

Then a question was posed: Is everything that has divided the Saṅgha thereby definitely going wrong? And is everything that is definitely going wrong a division of the Saṅgha?

It was declared: There is that which divides the Saṅgha yet is not definitely going wrong. There is that which is definitely going wrong yet does not divide the Saṅgha. There is that which both divides the Saṅgha and is definitely going wrong. And there is that which neither divides the Saṅgha nor is definitely going wrong.

What is that which divides the Saṅgha yet is not definitely going wrong? One who has divided the Saṅgha while perceiving that one is acting in accordance with the Dharma — that one divides the Saṅgha yet is not definitely going wrong.

What is that which is definitely going wrong yet does not divide the Saṅgha? One who has killed one's father, one who has killed one's mother, one who has killed an arhat,

one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent — these are cases of definitely going wrong, yet they do not divide the Saṅgha.

What is that which both divides the Saṅgha and is definitely going wrong? It is Devadatta. He both divided the Saṅgha and is definitely going wrong.

What is that which neither divides the Saṅgha nor is definitely going wrong? It is all those apart from the cases mentioned.

Now, is everyone who divides the Saṅgha unskilled, and does everyone who is unskilled speak in an unskilled manner? And is everyone who is unskilled and speaks in an unskilled manner thereby one who divides the Saṅgha?

The Blessed One declared: There are those who divide the Saṅgha and yet are neither unskilled nor speaking in an unskilled manner. There are those who are unskilled and speak in an unskilled manner and yet do not bring about a division of the Saṅgha. There are those who both divide the Saṅgha and are unskilled and speak in an unskilled manner. And there are those who neither divide the Saṅgha, nor are unskilled, nor speak in an unskilled manner.

What is it to divide the Saṅgha and yet be neither unskilled nor speaking in an unskilled manner? Whoever divides the Saṅgha while perceiving that one is acting in accordance with the Dharma — such a one divides the Saṅgha and yet is neither unskilled nor speaking in an unskilled manner.

What is it to be unskilled and to speak in an unskilled manner, and yet not bring about a division of the Saṅgha? It is one who is committed to the six teachers. Such a one is unskilled and speaks in an unskilled manner, and yet does not bring about a division of the Saṅgha.

What is it to both divide the Saṅgha and to be unskilled and speak in an unskilled manner? It is Devadatta. He both divided the Saṅgha and was unskilled and spoke in an unskilled manner.

What is it to neither divide the Saṅgha, nor be unskilled, nor speak in an unskilled manner? It is all those apart from the cases mentioned.

The venerable one then asked: Can a monk bring about a schism in the monks' Saṅgha? Or can a nun, a female trainee, a male novice, or a female novice bring about a schism in the Saṅgha?

The Blessed One declared: A monk can bring about a schism in the Saṅgha. A nun, a female trainee, a male novice, and a female novice cannot bring about a schism in the Saṅgha.

The venerable one asked: Can a nun bring about a schism in the nuns' Saṅgha? Or can a monk, a female trainee, a male novice, or a female novice bring about a schism in the nuns' Saṅgha?

The Blessed One declared: A nun can bring about a schism in the nuns' Saṅgha. A monk, a female trainee, a male novice, and a female novice cannot bring about a schism in the nuns' Saṅgha.

The venerable one asked: Does blame accrue to the Saṅgha, or does blame accrue to the one who causes the division?

The Blessed One declared: The Saṅgha acquires merit, while blame accrues to the individual who causes the division.

The venerable one asked: If one has divided the Saṅgha, what transgression does one incur?

The Blessed One declared: It becomes a grave offense.

The venerable one asked: When the Saṅgha has been divided, what transgression should be confessed?

The Blessed One declared: It is a grave offense.

The venerable one asked: Does every one who sides with a faction thereby cease to reside, and does every one who ceases to reside thereby side with a faction?

The Blessed One declared: There are those who side with a faction and yet do not cease to reside. There are those who cease to reside and yet do not side with a faction. There are those who side with a faction and do come to cease residing. And there are those who neither side with a faction nor cease to reside.

What is it to side with a faction and yet not cease to reside? Whoever has sided with one of the five matters and yet has not incurred any of the four categories of transgression — that one sides with a faction and yet does not come to cease residing.

What is it to cease residing and yet not side with a faction? Whoever has incurred any one of the four categories of transgression and yet has not sided with any of the five matters — that one ceases to reside and yet does not side with a faction.

What is it to side with a faction and come to cease residing? Whoever has sided with the five matters and has also incurred any one of the four categories of transgression — that one both sides with a faction and ceases to reside.

What is it to neither side with a faction nor cease to reside? That is anyone who does not fall into any of the foregoing cases.

Then it was asked: Does everyone who ceases to reside thereupon separately abide? And does everyone who separately abides cease to reside?

The Blessed One declared: There are those who cease to reside and yet do not separately abide. There are those who separately abide and yet do not cease to reside. There are those who both cease to reside and separately abide. And there are those who neither cease to reside nor separately abide.

What is it to cease to reside and yet not separately abide? It is this: one has incurred any one of the four categories of transgression, and has been suspended by the Saṅgha on account of not seeing a fault, or for not making amends, or for not relinquishing a wrong view — and yet the suspension has not been lifted. That one ceases to reside but does not separately abide.

What is it to separately abide and yet not cease to reside? It is this: one has been suspended by the Saṅgha on account of not seeing a fault, or for not making amends, or for not relinquishing a wrong view, and that suspension has indeed been lifted — and yet one has not incurred any of the four categories of transgression. That one separately abides but does not cease to reside.

What is it to both cease to reside and separately abide? One has incurred any one of the four categories of transgression, has been suspended on account of not seeing a fault, or for not making amends, or for not relinquishing a wrong view, and that suspension has also been lifted — and one has still incurred any one of the four categories of transgression. That one both ceases to reside and separately abides.

What is it to neither cease to reside nor separately abide? It is anyone who does not fall into any of those cases. Those who fall outside all those cases are neither ceasing to reside nor separately abiding.

Then it was asked: Is what one is made to relinquish also called a penalty?

The Blessed One declared: What one relinquishes — that is identical to the penalty itself.

It was asked: What is the act? What is the object? The act is the action that extracts the transgression. The object is what has not been confessed.

It was asked: What is a sanction? What is imposing a sanction? What is lifting a sanction?

The Blessed One declared: Upāli, the name of that very thing is a sanction. Giving rise to the intention regarding it is imposing the sanction. Deliberating upon it in its eight aspects is lifting the sanction.

It was asked: If a transgression occurred while one was a nun and one has since become a monk, can there be purification? If a transgression occurred while one was a monk and one has since become a nun, can there be purification?

The Blessed One declared: Yes. How is it that a transgression that occurred while one was not yet a monk can be purified once one has become a monk? It is this: a transgression of the Saṅgha's residual offenses belonging exclusively to the order of nuns arose during the time when one was a nun; one then changed status; and having changed status, if one comes within the order of monk-fathers, that transgression is called a pure transgression.

How is it that a transgression that arose during the time of being a monk can be called pure during the time of being a nun? It is this: a transgression of the Saṅgha's residual offenses belonging to a different category arose during the time of being a monk; one then changed status; and having changed status, if one has become a nun, that transgression is called a pure transgression.

It was asked: Can there be purification in a case where a transgression was incurred without knowing, when one subsequently acts with knowing? Can there be purification where a transgression was incurred with knowing, when one subsequently acts without knowing?

The Blessed One declared: Yes. How is it that a transgression incurred without knowing can be purified when one acts with knowing? It is this: a monk, lifted from sleep, was placed upon a large, high bed; or, while lying in sleep, was placed in a woman's bed; or someone not fully ordained was brought out and slept alongside him; or

that person not fully ordained then came back, sat down, and when the monk awoke and proceeded to carry out again that same transgression in the lawful manner — this is a case in which a transgression was incurred without knowing, and purification came about with knowing.

It was asked: What is a case in which a transgression was incurred with knowing and purification comes about without knowing? It is this: a monk incurred a saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression within the Saṅgha. The formal acts of speech were being performed to remove it; the preliminary recitation had been done; he then fell asleep, and the three formal acts of speech were completed to the end; and when he rose — such a case as this is one in which a transgression was incurred with knowing and purification came about without knowing.

It was asked: Can there be a case where a transgression arose during sleep and purification comes about upon waking? And can there be a case where a transgression arose upon waking and purification comes about during sleep? The Blessed One declared: Yes. What is a case in which a transgression arose during sleep and purification comes about upon waking? It is this: a monk, lifted from sleep, was placed in the vicinity of a high and large bed; or, while lying in sleep, was placed in a woman's bed; or someone not fully ordained was brought out; and that person not fully ordained then came back beneath where he was lying, sat down, and when the monk awoke and proceeded to carry out that same transgression again in the lawful manner — this is a case in which a transgression arose during sleep and purification came about upon waking.

What is a case in which a transgression arose upon waking and purification comes about during sleep? It is this: a monk incurred a saṅghāvaśeṣa transgression within the Saṅgha. The formal acts of speech were being performed to remove it; the preliminary recitation had been done; he then fell asleep, and the three formal acts of speech were completed to the end; and when he rose — such a case as this is one in which a transgression arose upon waking and purification came about during sleep.

It was asked: Can it happen that a monk, by speaking a single utterance to its conclusion, thereby incurs three defeats? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: a monk, together with a nun, says the following: "Whenever I saw the householder so-and-so, he took something of great value without it being given, was cut off from his livelihood, and you should know that I too have attained arhatship" — and all of that is spoken to completion by the nun. Such a case produces three defeats for the monk.

It was asked: Can it happen that a monk, by speaking a single utterance to its conclusion, incurs four defeats? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: a monk, together with a nun, declares: "Whenever you saw me, the householder so-and-so took something without it being given, was separated from his livelihood, and the object referred to as such-and-such was taken by theft, and you should know that I have attained arhatship" — and the monk speaks all of this as a boast.

It was asked: Can it happen that a monk, while dwelling in a single place, incurs five heaps of transgression? The Blessed One declared: Yes. Using just the amount of the Teacher's robes is a misdeed. If, from a village bound by the training precepts and its code of restraint, one takes food and provisions with one's own hand, it becomes a matter for individual confession. Teaching the Dharma to a woman beyond five or six sentences is a downfall. Speaking words of corrupt conduct to a woman becomes a saṅghāvaśeṣa matter. Claiming for oneself, falsely, a state superior to human beings before a woman becomes a defeat.

It was asked: Can a monk, through a single act, incur a hundred transgressions, or a thousand, or even more than that? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: a monk, consumed by burning anger, his mind agitated and disturbed, scatters — whether by throwing cooked peas or by throwing flour — upon a large crowd of people assembled and gathered together; and however many are struck by it, that many transgressions does he incur.

It was asked: Can there be a case in which a monk carries an item of great value from one place to another, and yet it does not become a defeat? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: an item belonging to a non-human being that is of great value, that is, one which does not reach the value of five māṣas.

It was asked: Can a monk incur a defeat by stealing three māṣas? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: when three māṣas constitute a thing of great value.

It was asked: Can a monk steal five māṣas and yet it not become a defeat? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: when a kārṣāpaṇa constitutes a thing of little value.

It was asked: Can there be a case in which taking something small without it being given constitutes a transgression, and yet taking that very same small thing without it being given does not constitute a transgression? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: taking even a small amount from white wool becomes an offense. Taking even a small amount from black wool does not become an offense.

It was asked: Can there be a case in which doing more than what is equal constitutes a transgression, and yet doing more than what is equal does not constitute a transgression? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: doing more than the equal measure of black cloth becomes an offense. Doing more than what is equal with white wool does not become an offense.

It was asked: Can there be a case in which not doing what should be done constitutes a transgression, and in which doing it constitutes no transgression? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: a monk who has obtained a new robe is required to perform one of the three color-alterations; not having performed any of the three color-alterations is the offense. Having done so, there is no offense.

It was asked: Can there be a case in which making something to the proper measure constitutes a transgression, and in which making something to the proper measure does not constitute a transgression? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: making a robe to the measure of the Tathāgata's robe constitutes an offense. Making it to the measure of a maṇḍala does not constitute an offense.

It was asked: Can there be a case in which, with the very same object with which a monk enters into the first meditative concentration and that object thereby becomes a remainder belonging to the Saṅgha, he also enters into the second, third, and fourth meditative concentrations with that very same object, and it likewise becomes a remainder belonging to the Saṅgha? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: when that monk, about to enter the first meditative concentration, gives the instruction, "Let a house be built for me," and immediately upon giving that instruction he enters the first meditative concentration, and while he is in meditative equipoise in the first concentration the house is completed — then that house becomes a remainder belonging to the Saṅgha. And if, on account of that very same object, he again gives the instruction, "Let a house be built for me," immediately before entering the second, third, or fourth meditative concentration, and immediately upon giving that instruction he enters the second, third, or fourth concentration, and while in that state the house is again completed — then it likewise becomes a remainder belonging to the Saṅgha.

It was asked: Can there be a monk who has committed no transgression anywhere, who has committed not even the slightest misdeed, and yet who is unfit to be a monk? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: one who has undergone a change of sex.

It was asked: Can there be a nun who has committed no transgression anywhere, who has committed not even the slightest misdeed — not so much as having shaken and worn the lower robe below the waist — and yet who is unfit to be a nun? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: one who has undergone a change of sex.

It was asked: Can there be a monk who has entered a temple, and within that very temple has his robe with him, and yet may be called one who has let the rains retreat lapse, and also be called one who is separated from his robe, and who has moreover violated his commitment? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: when the final seventh day of the rains retreat which the monk entered has arrived, and he has left his robe — without having consecrated it — lying on a chair, a small chair, or a support, open to the sky above, and then dawn breaks — he is called one who has let the rains retreat lapse, and is also called one who is separated from his robe.

And one may also be called one who has violated his commitment.

Is it possible that a monk alone who has entered a temple may incur a root defeat? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is sexual misconduct — namely, a long pillow and a bolster.

And what of taking what is not given, and taking life? A monk who uses a device and enters inside may have both stolen and taken a life.

And what is the cause of lying? It is this: saying "I am an arhat" or "I am a buddha."

Is it possible that a monk who is separated from the livelihood of a monk — though he is neither a monk nor an arhat — may yet incur a root defeat, and that it may further become a crime without interval? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: when the mother of that monk has gone forth and received full ordination, and then changes her sex, and having changed her sex is separated from her livelihood — that is a root defeat, and it also becomes a crime without interval.

Is it possible that a nun who is separated from the livelihood of a nun — though she is neither a nun nor an arhat — may yet incur a root defeat and that it may further become a crime without interval? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: when the father of that nun has gone forth and received full ordination, and then changes his sex, and having changed his sex is separated from her livelihood — that is a root defeat, and it also becomes a crime without interval.

Is it possible that another speaks, and by reason of what that one has said another may incur a root defeat? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: a nun who sides with a monk assembly that has not been restrained by the Saṅgha, and who, even after being instructed up to three times in the midst of the Saṅgha to desist, does not desist — that is a root defeat.

Is it possible that another speaks, and by reason of what that one has said, another may become one who has gone beyond what is proper for the Saṅgha? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: whoever has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, and who sides with that cause, and who, even after being instructed up to three times within the Saṅgha to desist from words of divisiveness that are difficult to hear, does not desist — that one becomes one who has gone beyond what is proper for the Saṅgha.

Is it possible that another speaks, and by reason of what that one has said, another may commit a transgression? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: whatever monk has taken up and firmly held a wrong view, and who, even after being instructed up to three times within the Saṅgha to desist, does not desist — that is a transgression.

Is it possible that another speaks, and by reason of what that one has said, another must confess? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: a monk who, when invited to a home and eating a meal there, a nun who is directing the serving is present and says, "Give this one rice, give this one legumes, give this one as well" — if he eats what is served without having signaled her, he must confess.

Is it possible that another speaks, and by reason of what that one has said, another commits a fault? The Blessed One declared: Yes. It is this: whatever monk, when the Prātimokṣa sūtra (the code of individual liberation) is being recited, is aware of an offense and yet, even after it has been proclaimed up to three times within the Saṅgha, does not rise to confess — that becomes a fault committed.

Venerable Blessed One, it has been said that once a nun has surrendered her training, she may not again be fully ordained into the state of being a nun, and that any nuns who readmit her to going forth or to full ordination are themselves at fault.

Venerable Blessed One, if from that nun who has surrendered her training and disrobed, those other nuns admit her to going forth and grant her full ordination, and the full ordination is valid — is there a case in which they would incur no fault? The Blessed One declared: There is. It is this: if that nun who has surrendered her training and disrobed has undergone a change of marks, and having changed marks has become male, and she is then admitted to going forth and granted full ordination, no fault is incurred.

Venerable Blessed One, if you have previously said, "Do not admit that former disruptive one to going forth; do not grant her full ordination" — and yet that formerly disruptive one is admitted to going forth and granted full ordination — can there be a case in which the full ordination is nonetheless valid and no fault is incurred? There is. It is this: if that nun has incurred a defeat offense of a kind not shared in common, and having surrendered her training has disrobed, and she has then undergone a change of marks and been born male, and she is admitted to going forth and granted full ordination — no fault is incurred.

What are all the types that formal acts may comprise? The Blessed One declared: Three kinds: the act by motion, the act by motion with two proclamations, and the act by motion with four proclamations.

Venerable Blessed One, you have declared that there are one hundred and one formal acts. Of these, how many are subsumed by the act by motion, how many by the act with two proclamations, and how many by the act with four proclamations? The Blessed One declared: Twenty-four are by motion alone. Forty-seven are by motion with two proclamations. Thirty are by motion with four proclamations.

Is there a case in which, though no word is spoken and no physical gesture is made, one is nonetheless disqualified from being a monk? The Blessed One declared: There is. It is this: if a nun, having seen a nun commit a defeat offense, conceals it, and then dawn breaks, she herself incurs defeat.

Is there a case in which a monk incurs four groups of offenses, does not confess them, and has not had the formal act of rehabilitation performed, and yet when he departs he is without fault? The Blessed One declared: There is. One who has changed marks.

Is there a case in which a nun incurs five groups of offenses, does not confess them, and has not had the formal act of rehabilitation performed, and yet when she departs she is without fault? The Blessed One declared: There is. One who has changed marks.

Is there a case in which a monk who takes a human life does not incur a defeat? The Blessed One declared: There is. It is this: when two are dwelling together and one intends to kill the other but instead kills someone else.

Can there be a case in which sexual misconduct is committed by another, and yet defeat is incurred? The Blessed One declared: There is. It is this: if a nun sees sexual misconduct being committed and conceals it, and then dawn breaks, defeat is incurred.

Is there a case in which a monk incurs a defeat through sexual misconduct, and also a case in which he engages in sexual misconduct yet does not incur a defeat? The Blessed One declared: There is. If one who is unwounded engages in sexual misconduct together with another, defeat is incurred. If one who is wounded engages in it together with another, defeat is not incurred.

Is there a case in which taking what is not given results in defeat, and also a case in which taking what is not given does not result in defeat? The Blessed One declared: There is. If one takes without permission an article of value belonging to a human being, that is defeat. If one takes an article of value belonging to a non-human being without permission, it does not become a defeat offense.

Is there a case in which a monk incurs defeat through depriving a human being of life, and also a case in which he deprives a human being of life yet does not incur defeat? There is. If one deprives a human being of life with one's own hand, that is defeat.

If one deprives a human being of life through a misapplied perception directed toward someone else, that does not result in defeat.

Is there a case in which a monk incurs defeat by personally declaring to a human being a superhuman quality that he himself does not possess, and also a case in which he declares to a human being a superhuman quality that does not exist, yet does not incur defeat? The Blessed One declared: There is. If one declares it with a fabricated perception, directing it as a pronouncement of authorization, that is defeat. But if there is such a declaration and it is given as a pronouncement of authorization straightforwardly, without fabrication, then it is not defeat.

Is there a case in which the very same thing that constitutes a defeat offense does not constitute a defeat offense? The Blessed One declared: There is. If a nun allows her body to be touched all over, that is defeat. If a monk does the same, it is not a defeat offense. If a nun knowingly conceals a grave offense of another nun until dawn breaks, that is a defeat offense. If a monk conceals it, it is not a defeat offense. If the Saṅgha, perceiving a monk's conduct to be in accordance with the Dharma, expels him for something unseen, and a nun knowingly takes his side and, though instructed up to three times in the midst of the Saṅgha, refuses to release that position, that is defeat. If she instructs a monk and he refuses to release it, that is not a defeat offense.

Is there a case in which the very same thing that constitutes a Saṅgha remainder offense does not constitute a Saṅgha remainder offense? The Blessed One declared: There is. If a monk intentionally causes emission of semen, that is a Saṅgha remainder offense. If a nun causes emission of semen, that is not a Saṅgha remainder offense for her. If a monk touches a body all over, that is a Saṅgha remainder offense. If a nun touches, that is not a Saṅgha remainder offense for her. If a nun, having abandoned her proper station, touches in that way, that is a Saṅgha remainder offense. If a monk does so, that is not a Saṅgha remainder offense.

Is there a case in which the very same thing that constitutes a transgression does not constitute a transgression? The Blessed One declared: There is. If a nun intentionally causes emission of semen, that is a transgression. If a monk causes emission, that is not a transgression. If a monk accepts cooked food and provisions solicited from someone who is not a relative, that is a transgression. If a nun accepts it, that is not a transgression. If a nun defecates or urinates on green grass, that is a transgression. If a monk does so, that is not a transgression.

Is there a case in which the very same thing that constitutes an offense requiring confession does not constitute an offense requiring confession? The Blessed One declared: If a monk accepts cooked food and provisions solicited from someone who is not a relative, that is an offense requiring confession. If a nun accepts it, that is not an offense requiring confession. If a monk, in a village bound by the training rules, takes food and provisions with his own hand, that is an offense requiring confession. If a nun takes it, that is not an offense requiring confession.

Is there a case in which the very same thing that constitutes a wrongdoing does not constitute a wrongdoing? The Blessed One declared: If a monk defecates or urinates on green grass, that is a wrongdoing. If a nun does so, that is not a wrongdoing. If a nun wraps her lower robe so that it extends past the waist, that is a wrongdoing. If a monk wraps his lower robe past the waist, there is no offense.

Is there a case in which what counts as having gone beyond an offense does not constitute a transgression, and what counts as a transgression does nonetheless constitute having gone beyond it? The Blessed One declared: There is. It is as follows. When a formal act of suspension is being carried out against a monk on account of an offense that is a remainder for the Saṅgha, if during that act he is sitting with shoes on, or sitting with both knees clasped in his arms, or with his head covered, or cutting green grass, or drawing lines in the earth, offenses arising from such conduct arise as offenses from what one thought was going beyond it. What then is the case of having gone beyond on account of thinking an offense has occurred? It is as follows. When that monk, thinking an offense incompatible with the Saṅgha's remainder has occurred, has his name transferred on that account, and the transfer of name is to a nun, then in that way it constitutes having gone beyond on account of thinking an offense has occurred.

Is there a case in which what one takes to be a dissolution of a boundary is in fact an interruption of an act? The Blessed One declared: There is. The boundary of the formal act may be dissolved while the boundary of the village remains undissolved. What is it that follows in the wake of what has gone? The Blessed One declared: It is the boundary.

Is there a case in which five categories of offense arise for a monk? The Blessed One declared: There is. If he makes a woman's robe, that is a wrongdoing. If he takes food and provisions with his own hand from a village bound by the training rules, that is an offense requiring confession. If he teaches the Dharma to a woman in more than five or six sentences, that is a downfall. If he speaks words of reproach to a woman, that is a gross offense that is a remainder for the Saṅgha. If he speaks falsely to a woman claiming to have realized a superhuman Dharma, that is a defeat.

Venerable sir, if we have a question about the Vinaya, where should we seek the answer? The Blessed One declared: From the two codes of individual liberation, from the division texts, and from the accompanying texts; from the eighteen topics of Vinaya and the two introductory narratives that stand alone; from the continuation texts that go beyond the one Vinaya; from what is common and what is not common; and from the transfer of names on the ground and in the intermediate space.

Blessed One, there is one who does not belong to any of the destinies of existence, who is not included within what has been taught, who has not passed into nirvāṇa, and who will not pass into nirvāṇa — what is that? The Blessed One declared: Upāli, it is an emanation body. If it is killed, what offense is incurred? The Blessed One declared: A gross offense. If it is killed, what offense is to be confessed? The Blessed One declared: A gross offense.

Thus is the subject matter of the noble Vinaya complete.

The noble Vinaya, the forty-sixth fascicle, being a summary of the Mānavikā Sūtra:

Suitable mixtures, two kinds — molasses-water and the like,
Five types — meat, insects, and lotus;
Morning consumption, and what has been received,
Intoxication, laymen, novices, and monks.

In brief:
Those who are assembled, and those who are infants,
The blind, and also those with birthmarks,
Excepting the young ones,
The rest are suitable.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: Venerable sir, when the Blessed One declared that full ordination is permissible in a border region with a Vinaya master and five, if ten are present and full ordination is conferred with a Vinaya master and five, should it be called full ordination or not full ordination? Upāli, it is to be called fully ordained as a monk, and the members of the Saṅgha are included in those who are present and accounted for.

Venerable sir, when the Blessed One declared that if a Dharma robe is obtained and held beyond ten days it becomes an offense involving forfeiture, how much time must elapse before one is able to obtain a Dharma robe?

At the moment when one finds it and sees it, and has touched it with the hand or taken it into one's lap, and has generated the perception "this is my robe" — that is how a robe is obtained by a sighted person. By how much does a blind person obtain a robe? At the moment when one has heard of it and taken it in hand or taken it into one's lap, and has generated the perception "this is my robe" — that is how a robe is obtained by a blind person.

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One the Buddha: "Is it permissible for a robe that is half-marked with lines and half-unmarked?" "Upāli, it is not permissible. Is there another supporting hem on top of it?" "If it has become worn out, then it is permissible."

"Venerable sir, the Blessed One declared: 'Hold onto the tail and cross the river.' Is it permissible to cross a river by holding onto something other than a mount?" "It is permissible. If one holds onto an ox, or a horse, or a buffalo, or a yak, and crosses a river, there is no offense."

In brief:
Sugar cane, and seven-day fat,
salt and grain-oil are permitted.
Whatever the monk has made permissible,
where it is not permissible, it remains impermissible.

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One the Buddha: "Venerable sir, is it permissible to bless sugarcane beer for seven days?" "Upāli, it is permissible." "For how long may one drink it?" "So long as one does not become intoxicated, it is not mixed with food, it has not turned turbid, it has not become oppressive, and it has not come from one's own brewing."

Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One the Buddha: "Venerable sir, is it permissible to eat salt boiled from impermissible fat?" "Upāli, it is not permissible. If it has been reduced to ash, then eating it is no offense."

"Venerable sir, is it permissible to eat grain-oil cooked from impermissible medicine?" "Upāli, it is not permissible. But if it is applied to the eye, the ear, or the nose, there is no offense."

If a monk himself, by fire, by knife, or by nail, renders permissible the five kinds of seeds that would germinate — is that called having rendered them permissible? May they be eaten? They may, except for whatever is rendered permissible by fire; whoever renders them permissible by fire incurs the offense of destroying seeds not yet made impermissible.

If a tree has grown in an impermissible place and its fruit falls in a permissible place, may it be eaten? "Upāli, it is not permissible." If a tree has grown in a permissible place and its fruit falls in an impermissible place, may it be eaten? "Upāli, it is permissible, as the days have not elapsed."

In brief:
Two cases in which they become permissible:
that which is not food,
what is known as human milk,
and what has turned into sour whey.

When the five kinds of seeds are in a permissible place and are absent, yet they are rendered permissible in an impermissible place by fire, by knife, or by nail — is that called having rendered them permissible or not? It is called having been done. May they be eaten? "Upāli, they may not be eaten."

When a monk is in a permissible place and renders the five kinds of seeds in a permissible place permissible by fire, by knife, or by nail — is that called having been done or not? It is called having been done. May they be eaten? "Upāli, they may not, except where they have been rendered impermissible by fire. Whoever renders them permissible incurs the offense of destroying seeds."

May one take them away, or leave them unburned, or put them in a nest or inside a basket and eat them? "Upāli, that is permissible." May human milk be eaten? "Upāli, it may not, except when needed as eye medicine." May sour whey be eaten at an improper time? "Upāli, it is permissible."

In brief:
Human flesh, and what is known
as having been killed intentionally,
and the flesh of impermissible animals —
all of these must not be eaten.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "Venerable One, may human flesh be sought?" "Upāli, it may not." "Venerable One, what offense does one who transgresses this incur?" "A grave offense."

"Apart from human flesh, may the flesh of other permissible animals that were killed intentionally on one's behalf be sought?" "Upāli, it may not." "May the flesh of impermissible animals be sought?" "Upāli, it may not."

In brief:
Insects, lotuses, and horses,
and frogs as well — one must not eat them.
All those creatures without exception
are not to be eaten.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "May the flesh of insects and lotuses be sought?" "Upāli, it may not." "May the flesh of birds and woodpeckers be sought?" "Upāli, it may not." "May the flesh of frogs be sought?" "Upāli, it may not." "May the flesh of creatures of that kind be sought?" "Upāli, it may not."

In brief:
Mixed together with what is permissible,
it may not be eaten even for seven days.
The same applies to fat —
combined with molasses tree and the earlier-stage product.

The venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "If the early-stage medicine is mixed with the afternoon medicine, may it be taken?" "Upāli, it may not." "If the afternoon medicine is mixed with the seven-day medicine, may it be taken?" "Upāli, it may not." "If the seven-day medicine is mixed with the life-long medicine, is it permissible?" "Upāli, it may not." "Venerable One, if that same substance is the early-stage form, may it also serve as the afternoon medicine, the seven-day medicine, and the life-long medicine?" "Upāli, it is permissible. The molasses tree in its early stage is the early-stage medicine; the juice pressed from it thereafter is the afternoon medicine; the juice boiled down into molasses from that is the seven-day medicine; and that seven-day substance burned to ash is the life-long medicine."

"May that same substance serve simultaneously as the early-stage, the seven-day, and the life-long medicine for that very same thing?" "It is permissible. Flesh is the early-stage form; the fat rendered by cooking it thereafter is the seven-day medicine; and the ash of that seven-day substance burned thereafter is the life-long medicine."

In brief:
Received in the proper manner,
yet not consecrated —
a sick person tormented by illness,
and the eighth kind of medicinal drink.

"May these early-stage medicines be consecrated for storage?" "Upāli, they may not — and likewise for the afternoon medicines, the seven-day medicines, and the life-long medicines." "Similarly, may what has not been properly received, what has been cooked indoors, what has been fetched, and what is of impermissible kinds be sought?" "Upāli, they may not." "May what has been properly received yet not consecrated be sought?" "Upāli, it may not." "May what has been received again and not consecrated be sought by one who is well?" "Upāli, it may not." "May what has been received again and not consecrated be sought by a sick person?" "Upāli, it is permissible."

Then the venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One, the Buddha: "What should be given to a sick person?" "Whatever is accompanied by an offense that would result in the sick person recovering — that should be given to the sick person."

The Blessed One permitted drinks of eight kinds. If the medicinal drink in question is mixed with root medicines, stem medicines, leaf medicines, or flower medicines, may it be taken? "Upāli, it is permissible." For how long is it permissible? "As long as one does not become intoxicated, as long as it is not mixed with food and does not become turbid, and as long as it remains a medicinal drink."

In brief:
If one becomes drunk, it must be consecrated.
If one is sitting alone,
and it is not consecrated upon one's robe —
that belongs to the Saṅgha beyond the boundary.

"May robes be taken from a mad person?" It was declared: "From some they may be taken; from others they may not." "From whom may they be taken?" "From one who has a father, or a mother, or an elder or younger brother, or a sister, or one who gave them from a household — from such a person they may be taken." "From whom may they not be taken?"

"From one who has no father, no mother, no elder or younger brother, no sister, and no one from a household who gave it — from such a person it may not be taken."

"From what point onward may a mad person's robe be consecrated?" "From the moment that person's mind returns to its proper state."

"Venerable monks, if there is a single monk staying alone, and laypeople have offered a robe for the sake of the Saṅgha — a robe that the Saṅgha is to distribute in open assembly — how should that monk proceed upon receiving the robe?" It was declared: "Upāli, for that reason, let that monk generate this intention and also pronounce these words aloud: 'I am staying here alone. This robe has been given for the sake of the Saṅgha and is to be properly distributed by the Saṅgha in open assembly. I therefore take it under my own authority on account of illness, and I shall use it.' " He may do so. He should then consecrate it. Having used it, having set it aside, and having consecrated it, if he has done all this, it is said that the act has been performed. Even if other monks arrive, shares should not be given to them. If he does not proceed in this way, that monk alone must not carry off that robe — if he takes it, a transgression with remainder will result. If those other monks are equally entitled, and one of them, having consecrated it alone for the sake of the Saṅgha, then goes beyond the boundary and takes it, that becomes an offense. If it is done with the intention to steal, a transgression with remainder will result.

In brief:
A layman's son,
the rains retreat having become manifest,
and monks of the past and future —
thus has the rains retreat been broken.

"If a layman's son has fallen ill, may a robe be taken from him or not?" The Blessed One declared: "It may not be taken."

"If this robe has been offered to a Saṅgha observing the rains retreat, yet it is not yet the final month of the rains, and no fixed residence has been established there — even though it is not the final month and no fixed residence has been established — those who are observing the rains retreat shall have the right to that robe. If it is said that this robe belongs to those of the Saṅgha who are present in open assembly, then also, even if it has become the final month and a fixed residence has been established there, those who did not observe the rains there shall also have the right to that robe."

"If this robe has been offered to the Saṅgha assembled in open meeting, and a monk stays at that place the following year, then stays again, stays a third time, and in the same manner continues to stay for up to ten subsequent years, and it is said that the robe is offered to them — then it has come to be the final month of the rains, and a fixed residence has also been established. Even though it has become the final month, those to whom it is given have the right to it, and the matter is explained in full from the earlier first and second months up through the tenth."

"If a monk observing the rains retreat goes beyond the boundary for some business of the Saṅgha, from where shall his share of the rains retreat be granted?" "From the place for whose sake he went, and where he stayed for a long time."

"Should a share of robes be given to one who has broken the rains retreat?" "To some it should be given; to others it should not." "To whom should it be given?" "To one for whom there is both a prior period and a subsequent period, and who stayed for a long time at that place." "To whom should it not be given?" "To one for whom there is neither a prior period nor a subsequent period, and who did not stay for a long time."

In brief:
For the sake of one who is sick,
having become a nurse,
having made it suitable and given the training —
how should one properly use those goods?

"When a monk who is acting as a nurse goes beyond the boundary for some purpose, and..."

...after going beyond that boundary, if the sick person then passes away, should the nurse's robes be given to him or not? To some it should be given; to others it should not. To whom should it be given? To one who was engaged in attending upon the sick person, that one should receive them. To one who was engaged in attending upon his own affairs or the affairs of others, that one should not receive them.

If a layman acts as nurse to the sick person, should robes be given to him or not? It was declared: they should not be given. Likewise, a fully ordained nun, a probationary nun, and a novice nun — to these also they should not be given. If a novice monk acts as nurse, should nursing robes be given to him? It was declared: they should be given. How much should be given? Equal to everyone else's share.

If a nurse entered the rains retreat elsewhere and falls ill, should nursing robes be given to that person? The Blessed One declared: they should be given.

Who is to act as nurse? The preceptor, the teacher, one who shares the same preceptor, one who shares the same teacher, a fellow-speaker, a co-reciter, an instructor, a companion in practice, or a pupil. If none of these are present, the Saṅgha should appoint a nurse. If the Saṅgha also does not appoint a nurse, there is an offense and wrongdoing. If the nurse also fails to nurse the sick person, that too becomes a wrongdoing. If the sick person does not heed the nurse when the nurse instructs him in accordance with Dharma, that becomes a wrongdoing. And the same applies to the sick person in return.

For how long should one act as nurse to a sick person? Until the sick person either dies or recovers. One abandons what is not beneficial; one accomplishes what is beneficial; and the training is given so that one does not cause matters to deteriorate. From when does one consecrate the robes once they are found? From the time they are obtained. How should the goods be used properly? With the thought: "By means of whatever is unsuitable, I shall accomplish what is suitable, and I shall set aside medicine for the sick."

In brief, the four residences for a monk are: permission, cloth, the departure-and-return, and three — the thick cloth of non-Buddhist mendicants. Can a monk who neither [intends it to be a prior period] nor [a subsequent period] enter the rains retreat at all four residences simultaneously in a proper manner, and yet not commit an offense? Yes, it is possible. It is like this: that monk presses down on the boundary of all four residences — whether it be a throne, a door-latch, or a fence — and enters the rains retreat in a proper manner; it is still called a proper entry, and there is no offense. From where does he receive his share of robes? From all of them. If one holds a rains cloth smaller than the prescribed measure, what offense is that? It was declared: it becomes a wrongdoing. Likewise it is the same for covering the back and fastening the edges. If one fastens the edges with the departure-and-return robe, is that called "fastening" or "not fastening"? It was declared: it should be called "not fastened." What is that robe? One obtained from a journey onward. If one distributes the robes that were set aside, what transgression is that? It was declared: it is a wrongdoing. If one carries the three things of a non-Buddhist standard — no robe, peacock feathers, and a hair-charm — what is the transgression? It becomes a grave offense. If one takes hold of a non-Buddhist standard other than those three, what does it become? The Blessed One declared: it is a wrongdoing.

This is the first section on discipline from the noble Vinaya text, dealing with the opening of the section on nuns. It is complete.

In brief: the three — old cloth, the departure cloth, and the long cloth — with how many wrongdoings for the base offense; how the action is performed with kauśāmbī cloth; action and base offense were then proclaimed. What was gathered up and summarized has now been proclaimed.

In brief: the old and the second, the fresh; the colored and the unstored; the unsuitable — likewise; the distributed and the permissibly undistributed.

The Blessed One declared: if one stores worn cloth, it is stored; if one does not store it, it is not stored. When asked, "What is worn cloth?" — it is any cloth that has already been stored. The Blessed One declared: if one stores fresh cloth, it is stored. When asked, "What is fresh cloth?" — it is any cloth not previously stored.

The Blessed One declared: when a monk who has stored cloth comes to receive cloth, he must generate three mental intentions. He must go first. When he reaches the end, even if only three threads of edging remain, he must still generate the three mental intentions. He must wash it, match it, dye it, and also make the half-and-third of the circle.

When asked: if one who has stored cloth generates the three mental intentions, does one call it stored? — or rather: "This cloth I dedicate as a stored robe for the Saṅgha — by me," generating two mental intentions? If one generates those two mental intentions and then stores it, in that case of storing, it becomes a wrongdoing. If one stores a robe that is to be abandoned, it is not considered stored. When asked, "What is a robe to be abandoned?" — it is one that has exceeded ten days or has been separated from one for a single night.

If one stores an unsuitable robe, it is not considered stored. When asked, "What is an unsuitable robe?" — it is any robe whose material is unsuitable. If one stores a divided old robe, it is not considered stored. When asked, "What is a divided old robe?" — it is any robe that a monk has permanently divided. If one stores an undivided robe, it is considered stored. When asked, "What is an undivided robe?" — it is any robe newly made from its material. If one stores an undivided but permissible robe, it is considered stored. When asked, "What is an undivided but permissible robe?" — if it possesses a border, and one stores it, it is called stored.

In brief:

Without having stored it, the Saṅgha divides it;
Having stored it, one then divides it —
what one person does with a single portion
is what becomes obtained.

The Blessed One was asked: in a place where the cloth has not been stored, if the Saṅgha divides it and one person takes one portion or two portions and then stores it, is that called stored? Upāli replied: it is called stored. Is everything then called stored? Upāli replied: no — those for which it was stored are called stored; those for which it was not stored are called not stored.

The Blessed One was asked: in a place where the cloth has been stored, if the Saṅgha divides it and whether one person with one portion or with two portions stores it, is that called having removed the stored robe? Upāli replied: it is removed. Is everything then called removed? Upāli replied: no — those who removed the stored robe are called removed; those who did not remove it are not called having removed the stored robe.

When the Saṅgha has divided into those of one side and those of the other, and has separated, who then may store? The Blessed One declared: those who speak in accordance with the Dharma.

The Blessed One was asked: if cloth has not been obtained and one stores it for the Saṅgha, is it called stored or not stored? Upāli replied: it is called not stored. The Blessed One was asked: if cloth has been obtained and one then stores it, is it called stored? Upāli replied: it is called stored.

In brief:

Generating the three intentions, being diligent,
the conditions and the meaning of storage —
Upāli finds this matter intricate.

The Blessed One declared: when a monk who has stored cloth finally draws the needle through at the end, he must generate the three mental intentions. When asked what these are, one declares: "This cloth I shall dedicate as stored for the Saṅgha. This cloth is being dedicated. This cloth is being stored." If one who is dedicating storage generates the three mental intentions in this way, is it called stored?

Is it called not stored, or is it called stored? It is called stored. However, the two mental intentions that were generated previously must be generated again as before. If those two intentions are not generated, what happens? It is called definitively stored. Definitively dedicating it without generating those two intentions becomes a transgression. Regarding the occasions for carelessness in a place where cloth is definitively stored, there are five: wearing whatever cloth one finds; entering a village without having put on the patch-robe; eating in a group; eating repeatedly; making use of things without having assigned them; and going to the provinces wearing the upper and lower robes as traveling garments.

Venerable one, there are five conditions of time when, even if the patch-robe has not been set aside, separation does not occur: just as those who come together during the rains retreat as described in the Vinaya, so too is the setting aside of the great rains-retreat cloth.

What is the meaning of the term "definitively stored"? "Definitively stored" refers to cloth — specifically, cloth that has been dedicated as a permanent store for the Saṅgha.

Venerable one, what is the meaning of what the Blessed One said to Upāli: "You are someone whose place is entangled"? A place where cloth has been obtained is called "entangled."

In brief:

Examined cloth, the third month,
timing, that which has been worn out,
five persons, and one like a mother —
the third category is dedication by three persons, and that concludes the matter.

When the Blessed One declared, "If one stores examined cloth as a permanent store, it is called definitively stored" — what is examined cloth? It is cloth obtained at a time when an opportunity for distribution is about to arise within a certain number of days.

When the Blessed One declared, "If cloth obtained after three months have passed is stored as a permanent store, it is called definitively stored" — what is cloth obtained after three months have passed? The resident monks numbered fifteen. Then suddenly a large number of monks arrived, and these newcomers were of pure view and harmony. Their count came to fourteen days. Now, if those who arrived suddenly acted as the resident monks did, then whatever cloth was obtained at that time is cloth obtained after three months have passed; and if it is stored as a permanent store, it is called definitively stored.

When the Blessed One declared, "If the timely cloth is stored as a permanent store, it is called definitively stored" — what is timely cloth? It is cloth obtained in the final month of the rains retreat.

When the Blessed One declared, "If worn-out cloth is stored as a permanent store, it is not definitively stored" — what is worn-out cloth? It is whatever has fallen away from the body of a monk.

When five kinds of persons store cloth as a permanent store, it is not definitively stored. What are the five? One who has not entered the rains retreat; one who has broken the rains retreat; one who entered the later rains retreat; one who has abandoned the training; and one who has sided against the Saṅgha.

From the basis that is like a mother, storage is released by eight such factors. What is reckoned as compatible? All the remainder, excluding the final two categories, are not reckoned as compatible.

If storage is dedicated with fewer than four, is it called definitively stored, or not stored? It is called not stored. Likewise, if the four — such as a householder, or one who has drawn blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent — were to dedicate storage, it would not be stored.

Can there be a case where, on the very day that a permanent store is dedicated, the store is released without a request having been made and without the act having been performed? Yes, there can. This is how it is: the resident monks dedicated the permanent store on the sixteenth day of the month, and suddenly a large number of monks arrived. These monks too were of pure view, in harmony of place and view, and for them that day was the fifteenth. If the resident monks then acted in accordance with these newcomers and performed the restoration ceremony on that day, the permanent store would be released without a request having been made and without the act having been performed.

In brief:

In what measure, and for the Saṅgha —
three aspects of that rule —
another bringing comfort to another,
and the restoration ceremony of the monks.

To what extent is a person one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha? When the Saṅgha — the assembly of śrāvakas of the Tathāgata — is split, that person incurs a transgression entailing the Avīci hell, and it also becomes an act of immediate karmic consequence. Upāli, this is as follows: when a monk, through a perception that what is not Dharma is not Dharma, elaborates upon it in the eighteen modes exactly as they arise in the Vinaya.

Is every case of causing a schism in the Saṅgha a case of the Saṅgha being in strife? And is every case of the Saṅgha being in strife a case of a schism in the Saṅgha? There are also four cases in which there is schism in the Saṅgha yet no strife in the Saṅgha. What is a case of schism in the Saṅgha yet no strife? It is as follows: the Saṅgha has indeed been split, but the fourteen factors that would constitute a schism in the Saṅgha have not been grasped. That is a split Saṅgha, but it is not a Saṅgha in strife. What is a case of the Saṅgha being in strife yet not a split Saṅgha? It is as follows: the fourteen factors that would constitute a schism in the Saṅgha have been grasped — that is the Saṅgha being in strife, but it is not yet a schism of the Saṅgha. What is a case of the Saṅgha being in strife and also the Saṅgha being split? It is as follows: the Saṅgha has also been split, and the fourteen factors that would constitute a schism have been definitively and completely grasped — that is both the Saṅgha being split and the Saṅgha being in strife. What is neither a schism of the Saṅgha nor a state of strife? It is every case other than those just described.

Is every case of the Saṅgha being split a case of the Saṅgha becoming separate? And is every case of the Saṅgha becoming separate a case of the Saṅgha being split? There are also cases in which the Saṅgha is split yet the Saṅgha has not become separate, and these too are applied in four modes.

A question is posed: what is a case of the Saṅgha being split yet the Saṅgha not having become separate? It is as follows: the Saṅgha has indeed been split, but no separation has arisen with respect to the Saṅgha's residence or robes — that is a split Saṅgha, yet the Saṅgha has not become separate. What is a case of the Saṅgha having become separate yet the Saṅgha not being split? It is as follows: from the time when two Saṅghas become separate and onward, right up to the point at which the Saṅgha has not yet split — the Saṅgha has become separate, but it has not split. What is a case of the Saṅgha being split and the Saṅgha also having become separate? It is as follows: that Saṅgha has been split, and the two Saṅghas have come to live separately by reason of residence or boundary or gains or robes — that is a case of the Saṅgha being split and also the Saṅgha having become separate. What is a case of there being neither a split Saṅgha nor a Saṅgha that has become separate? It is every case other than those just described.

Is every case of the Saṅgha being split a case of the Saṅgha having become individually distinct? And is every case of the Saṅgha having become individually distinct a case of the Saṅgha being split? There are also cases in which the Saṅgha is split yet the Saṅgha has not become separate, and these too are applied in four modes.

What is a case of the Saṅgha being split yet not having become individually distinct? It is as follows: even though the Saṅgha has been split, the two Saṅghas dwell mostly in separate residences and make use of separate robes — that is indeed a split Saṅgha, but the Saṅgha has not come to abide separately. What is a case of the Saṅgha having become separate yet the Saṅgha not being split? It is as follows: the two Saṅghas have come to have separate residences, separate boundaries, and separate gains — that is the Saṅgha having become separate, yet the Saṅgha is not split.
