What is a case of the Saṅgha being split and also the Saṅgha having become separate? It is as follows: the Saṅgha has been split, and the two reside in separate residences and so forth, as described before. What is a case of the Saṅgha neither being split nor abiding separately?

It is everything except a case of that kind. When the Saṅgha has become separate and is acting in a divided manner, if one side or both sides dissolve it, is that called a dissolution? If it is dissolved by one who speaks in accordance with the Dharma, then yes, it is called a dissolution.

When the Saṅgha has been divided and abides settled in separate factions, may the nuns perform the restoration ceremony? They may. Why is that? Because the nuns and the monks are residing separately.

In brief:

From the original, two are to be made.
The one who has been expelled is without a companion.
If one does not know that another has been expelled,
then following that side, associating with them,
and following along in causing the schism.

When the Saṅgha has been divided and abides in both factions and in neither faction, what should the neutral members do? They should go outside the boundary and perform the restoration ceremony.

When the Saṅgha has been divided and abides settled on both sides of the boundary, who should instruct the nuns? One who speaks in accordance with the Dharma. If those neutral members who speak in accordance with the Dharma are on this side of the boundary, they should give instruction there today.

If one has followed the side of the expelled, what offense does it become? In relation to two it is a wrong act, and in relation to one it is a transgression.

As for "the expelled" and "the expelled with companions" — is it said "with companions" or "without companions"? All those who have been expelled are solitary, that is, not two — they are said to be without companions.

As for associating together with the expelled — should one associate with them or not? One should not associate with the expelled at all. If one does not know that someone has been expelled, one may remain and associate with that person, and there is no offense.

If someone who is on one side and someone who is not on that side associate together, it becomes a wrong act. If someone who is not aligned with a faction and someone who is aligned with a faction associate together, it becomes a wrong act.

If there are four individuals who follow along in causing a schism, it is called a divided Saṅgha. How many does it take for a schism of the Saṅgha to occur? When four persons have come to side with the schism-makers.

In brief:

Similar, and faithful, and
in accord with the Dharma and similar to the Dharma,
expelling from an offense, expelling,
seeing the schism and the limb.

If the Blessed One has said, "Do not expel a monk who is such-and-such," which monk is that? A monk who is reputable, has great merit, is learned, holds the sūtras, holds the Vinaya, holds what is like a mother, has many attendants, and has a large retinue — such is called a monk who is such-and-such.

If a monk who is such-and-such is expelled, what offense does it become? A wrong act.

As for the distinction in that — what is it? When I have spoken with the intention of "a monk who is faithful," let the offense be dealt with in accordance with the Dharma, as the words "a monk who is faithful" suggest — just as one says a brahmin is faithful. If a monk does not deal with the offense in accordance with the Dharma, it becomes a wrong act.

If it has been said, "Let the monk who speaks in accordance with the Dharma remain until the seat is finished" — what is it to speak in accordance with the Dharma? It is one who, regarding a single offense, confesses to the other one alone, and offers to reveal it, and shows deference.

When the Saṅgha has been divided and abides in a non-factionalized manner, who should lift the penalty that has been imposed? Those who speak in accordance with the Dharma should lift it.

If the expelled monks shave their heads, are ready to receive the lifting of the penalty, and show deference, who should be asked to consent on their behalf? Those who have followed the side of the expelled.

When Śāriputra said, "Arrange the seats and mats in a suitable manner" — what is that suitable arrangement? It is having arranged them together on one side.

When he said, "Seek out the pieces of limbs scattered into a hundred hairs and join them together, but do not separate them individually" — what is the meaning of those words?

"Pieces of limbs" means taking up the taking of faith. One should seek out the limbs; one should seek out the pieces; one should seek out the assembled Saṅgha — but one should not enter into what would cause schism.

In brief:

The two factions of Kauśāmbī,
the restoration ceremony, the Dharma-robe,
and the one faction of Kauśāmbī,
the elders of Vaiśālī —
and the elders too, in both factions,
are the elders of Vaiśālī.

If the two factions of Kauśāmbī gather together and enter the restoration ceremony, how should the elders proceed? "Perform today's restoration ceremony outside the boundary."

When both factions of Kauśāmbī have gathered and assembled together in one place, and someone there offers a robe to the Saṅgha, who has authority over it? The authority belongs to whichever elder is present there.

If elders are present on one side and junior monks on the other side, who has authority? Of those two, authority belongs to whichever one the stream of water has reached.

How are all to divide it? In order of seniority among those who have received it.

If the community of Vaiśālī and the community of Kauśāmbī perform the restoration ceremony together, is it said to be performed? Upāli answered: No, it is not.

If the elders perform the restoration ceremony together with the people of Kauśāmbī, is it said to be performed? No, it is not.

If the elders perform the restoration ceremony together with the people of Vaiśālī, is it said to be performed? No, it is not.

In brief:

At the time when the schism occurred,
it was also announced to the sisters —
the faction, the community of nuns,
and at the time when the Saṅgha of Kauśāmbī became divided,
when within their boundary a separate restoration ceremony was held.

And at the time when the monks of Kauśāmbī were divided by certain monks — by those who do not speak in accordance with the Dharma — who, while dwelling together within the boundary, held a separate restoration ceremony, the community of nuns too is said to have split and to dwell separately.

"Is the fortnightly recitation and the giving of instruction to the divided community of nuns to be carried out?" The Blessed One declared: It should not be given. Instead, instruct them beforehand thus: "Sisters, be reconciled."

It was said: "For two reasons it is proper to announce the schism of the Saṅgha and for the use of the measuring rod to apply." If one who has initiated the schism and caused harm then undergoes the announcement or submits to the measuring rod, is it said that there is a schism of the Saṅgha? Upāli answered: No, it is not.

What becomes of the acts performed? Because of belonging to the circle of schism, all of the Saṅgha — indeed the entire Saṅgha — incurs transgression along with what is past.

If the community of nuns dwelling outside is established on a side that is both a faction and not a faction, should the fortnightly recitation and the giving of instruction be offered to them? The community of nuns will indeed become divided, so it should be given.

When instruction is being given to the nuns of Vaiśālī, if those of Kauśāmbī are also present there, how should instruction be given to them? Go outside the boundary and give instruction.

In brief:

One abandoning another,
abandoning through having fallen asleep,
and others too acting toward a person
not in the proper manner —

Venerable one, the Blessed One has spoken of acting not in accordance with the Dharma and not assembling, acting not in accordance with the Dharma and assembling, assembling in a manner similar to not acting in accordance with the Dharma, and not assembling in a manner similar to not acting in accordance with the Dharma. What, then, is "acting not in accordance with the Dharma and not assembling"? It is assembling having departed from a proper formal act that ought to be performed, while having done so improperly. That is what is meant by acting not in accordance with the Dharma and not assembling.

Then what is "acting not in accordance with the Dharma and assembling"?

It is having set aside what is proper for a formal act that is to be annulled, and then assembled. That is what is meant by acting not in accordance with the Dharma and assembling.

What, then, is "not assembling in a manner similar to not acting in accordance with the Dharma"? It is when what ought to be set aside is first announced, and thereafter, following that announcement, a motion is made and it is set aside. That is what is meant by not assembling in a manner similar to not acting in accordance with the Dharma.

What is "assembling in a manner similar to not acting in accordance with the Dharma"? It is when what ought to be set aside is first announced, and thereafter, following that announcement, a motion is made, it is set aside, and one has assembled. That is what is meant by assembling in a manner similar to not acting in accordance with the Dharma.

What is "not assembling in accordance with the Dharma"? It is when what ought to be set aside is set aside and one has not assembled. That is what is meant by not assembling in accordance with the Dharma.

If one monk sets aside one other monk, it becomes a wrongdoing. If one monk sets aside two or many, up to four, he is to be encircled and gathered in. If four set aside four, it becomes a grave offence belonging to the category of schism.

When the entire Saṅgha is lying down asleep and a monk sets aside another, is it considered a valid setting aside? If a motion is made and then one lies down and sets aside, it is called a setting aside. But if one has already lain down beforehand and then a motion is made afterward, it is not called a setting aside.

If a formal act is announced in one place and the setting aside occurs in a different place, it is called a setting aside. But if the entire Saṅgha does not know, then for those who perform the formal act while belonging to the schismatic faction, it becomes a grave offence.

If the entire Saṅgha does know, then the matter is concluded together with the entire Saṅgha having passed it.

If fewer than four monks set aside, is it called a setting aside? It is not, Upāli. From a layperson up to one who with malicious intent draws blood from a Tathāgata, when their number is counted among them and a monk sets aside, it is not called a setting aside.

In brief:

One who has departed for the formal act,
one who has turned back,
one who is lying down or has entered meditative equipoise,
one who has been commissioned to a single monk —
by these five, setting aside is not to be done.

The Venerable Blessed One said: However many monks have arrived at the formal act and are present, among those for whom it is proper to take assent, assent has been taken. And among those monks who are present and are resolved to object, even if someone attempts to turn them back, there is neither prohibition nor turning back.

When this was said, Upāli asked: What, then, is a monk who has arrived at the formal act?

When four monks have gathered to perform a formal act, and those four who are gathered are all pure monks who stand on equal footing — that is a formal act being arrived at. When five monks gather to perform an act, or ten gather to perform an act, or twenty gather to perform an act, and those monks who have gathered are all pure and of harmonious view — that is called arriving at the formal act.

What is turning back? When one who is resolved on objecting is standing on the ground, one who is standing in space cannot be effective in turning him back. Likewise, one who is sitting outside the boundary cannot effectively turn back one who is sitting inside the boundary.

Upāli, when someone is resolved — if, when a novice is being instructed in the training rules, he says "Do not teach me the training rules," that is him being resolved on turning back. If, when a novice is to be given full ordination, he says "Do not give me full ordination," that is also him being resolved on turning back. If, when a penalty is being imposed on one subject to penalty, he says "Do not impose a penalty on me," likewise, all cases — arising from the ground, satisfying, elevating, and in the same manner the commissioning of all twelve persons — are counted as being resolved on turning back.

Is one who is lying down considered to have set aside? If one has heard the motion and then lies down, it is called setting aside. If one has already lain down beforehand and the motion is made afterward, it is called not setting aside. The same applies to one who has entered meditative equipoise.

If even a single monk makes a commission, it is called turning back.

When the Saṅgha has dispersed and is residing in various directions — some within the boundary, some outside the boundary — if any one faction sets aside, is it called a setting aside or not a setting aside?

It is said: It is not a setting aside.

In brief:

Filled up by the croupier, proclaimed as Dharma what is not Dharma, commissioned in the midst of the Saṅgha — commissioned together with a joining.

If a monk has set aside when the count has been filled up by the croupier multiple times, is it called setting aside or not setting aside? It is said: It is called setting aside, and the substance of the croupier's act is thereby nullified.

Is every act that is not in accordance with Dharma an incomplete act? Or is every incomplete act an act not in accordance with Dharma? Upāli: No. An act not in accordance with Dharma is one thing, and an incomplete act is another.

What is an act that is not in accordance with Dharma yet is not an incomplete act? That in which the matter has not been made present, has not been announced, has not been recalled by another, or has been performed without allowing a challenge to arise; and all the monks who ought to come to the act have gathered and the matter has been made present, consent has been sought by the proper procedure for taking consent, the monks who are present and dedicated to turning it back do not obstruct or turn it back — this is an act not in accordance with Dharma but is not an incomplete act.

What is an incomplete act that is not an act not in accordance with Dharma? That in which the matter has been made present, announced, recalled, and a challenge has been allowed to arise before performing it; and all the monks who ought to come to the act have not gathered, the matter has not been made present, consent has not been sought by the proper procedure for taking consent; and the monks who are present and dedicated to obstructing and turning it back have made that obstruction and turning back with diligence — this is an incomplete act but is not an act not in accordance with Dharma.

Is every act in accordance with Dharma a complete act? Upāli: No. An act in accordance with Dharma is one thing, and a complete act is another.

What is an act in accordance with Dharma that is not a complete act? It is said: One in which it is performed and announced before the assembly, yet all the monks who ought to come to the act have not assembled and the matter has not been made present, consent has not been sought by the proper procedure, and those monks dedicated to turning it back who are present do obstruct and turn it back — this is an act in accordance with Dharma but is not a complete act.

What is a complete act that is not an act in accordance with Dharma? It is said: One in which it is performed without making the matter present, without announcement, without recall, without the matter being substantiated, without allowing a challenge to arise; yet all the monks who ought to come to the act have assembled and the matter has been made present, consent has been sought by the proper procedure for taking consent, and those monks who are present and dedicated to turning it back do not obstruct or turn it back — this is a complete act but is not an act in accordance with Dharma.

If the commission is made three times within the midst of the Saṅgha to any person, do they all thereby incur a fault? It is said: Some will, and some will not. Those to whom the commission is made three times within the midst of the Saṅgha — all of those will incur an offense. But can it be that among those who do incur an offense there are some to whom the commission within the Saṅgha three times is not applicable? It is said: Apart from the commission itself, another offense has arisen.

How much does it take for what is said to the last one to be called a solemn declaration? It is said: When any one of the four defeats has been incurred as an offense, and one declares it in the midst of the Saṅgha three times, acknowledging the last substantive matter — that is called making a solemn declaration.

If a monk sets aside a commission that has been formalized by a penalty, is it called setting aside? It is said: Apart from the vow that is present and manifest, it is called an act performed on behalf of all the others.

The noble Vinaya. The forty-seventh fascicle.

In brief:

First, the subsequent commission, the solemn self-declaration of consent, giving up the training in the four, taking the probationary stick,

The last of the individual stations.

If a formal act is commissioned first and a request is subsequently made, is it called a case of a monk having relinquished, or of not having relinquished? It is to be called not having relinquished.

What becomes of the one who performs the penalty? If the entire Saṅgha does not know of it, then, through belonging to the circle of schism, the offense is grave. If the entire Saṅgha does know of it, then for the entire Saṅgha as well there will be a transgression that carries a consequent offense.

If one who has performed the penalty takes on faith and relinquishes to a monk, is it called relinquished? Apart from the novice's vow, it is to be called performing all formal acts.

If a formal act is performed on one's own behalf, is it called performed? If there is no doubt, it is to be called performed. If there is doubt, it is to be called not performed.

Performing a formal act again on one's own behalf consists in the following: having performed a penalty act on one's own behalf, requesting pardon from oneself, by oneself.

As for those noble ones against whom a censure act is performed, and against whom an expulsion act is performed, and those to whom assent in accordance with the Dharma is given — if such a one acknowledges before the Saṅgha three consecutive times and, having been given the training, proclaims in the context of the fourfold reasonableness of bestowing the training, is he eligible to have the training bestowed by a single proclamation? The Blessed One declared: Upāli, he is not eligible. Is he eligible to receive full ordination by a single proclamation in the fourfold procedure? Upāli, he is not eligible.

If one relinquishes the training through the probationary stick, is it called relinquishing to a monk with the four, or is it called not relinquishing? It is to be called not relinquishing.

In brief:

A monk freed from censure,
apart from the solitary schismatic,
what does "censure" mean? —
it is a closer examination of the special case.

If a censure act has been performed against one and then a degradation act is performed, is it called performed? The censure act ceases to exist. If a censure act has been performed against one and then an expulsion act and a readmission act are performed, is that called performed or not performed? It is said: It is performed, but the censure ceases to exist. Just as in the case of one against whom a censure act was performed, so too in the cases of one against whom a degradation act was performed, one against whom an expulsion act was performed, and one against whom a readmission act was performed — these are to be set forth in full detail, elaborated in four aspects.

If a censure act is performed against one who has already relinquished, is it called performed? Upāli, it is not, because that one is no longer in the community of practice. Likewise, if a degradation act, an expulsion act, and a readmission act are performed against such a one, is that called performed? Upāli, it is not, because that one is no longer in the community of practice.

If schism is caused against someone other than monks, that becomes a wrongdoing.

What is the meaning of the word "censure"? Upāli, it is merely a name; it means: when a monk has become quarrelsome, instructing him thus: "Until you have turned away from that quarrel, the Saṅgha will conduct a subsequent close examination of you."

What is the meaning of the word "degradation"? Upāli, "degradation" is merely a name; it means: when a monk has subsequently incurred additional transgressions against the Saṅgha, instructing him thus: "Until you have turned away from those subsequent transgressions, you are to abide and remain in restraint."

What is the meaning of the word "expulsion"? Upāli, "expulsion" is merely a name; it means: when a monk has disgraced his family — instructing him: "Do not stay in that dwelling."

What is the meaning of the word "readmission"? Upāli, it is merely a name; it means: when a monk has harmed a layman — instructing him: "You are to request pardon from that householder."

When it is said, "The Saṅgha will conduct a subsequent close examination of you" — what is the meaning of those words? It is said:

"The Saṅgha will act in accordance with the Dharma regarding whatever transgression has arisen on your part" — that is the meaning of those words.

When it is said, "You are to dwell and remain with another" — what is the meaning of those words? It is said: whichever person one is fond of, or treats as a teacher, or feels shame before, or feels embarrassment toward — one is to dwell in stability with that person.

In brief:

He calls a branch offense a branch
when it is not a branch — a monk
thus harms with offense and downfall,
whether inside or outside: this becomes an obstruction.

If one calls what is not a branch offense a branch offense, what results? It is a downfall through knowingly speaking falsehood. If one calls a branch offense a branch offense, it becomes a downfall through speaking of a person's fault.

When it is said, "The harm to a monk is inside or outside" — what is inside and what is outside? What is within the boundary is inside. What is outside the boundary is outside. Alternatively, what is within the shrine hall is inside. What has no roof is outside.

The Blessed One declared that "it is an obstruction in many ways and in many categories." What is the nature of those things that are obstructions? Desire is an obstructive factor. Upāli, I declare desire to be an obstructive factor.

This completes the section on Vinaya of the Vinaya text called the Mānavika.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, was dwelling in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. Then the venerable Upāli went to where the Blessed One, the Buddha, was; having arrived, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One in homage and sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, the venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One, the Buddha, in these words:

"Venerable One, how many aggregates of Vinaya are there?" "Upāli, there are three: the aggregate of full ordination, the aggregate of excellence, and the aggregate of livelihood."

"What is the aggregate of full ordination? It is: those fit for full ordination and those not fit for full ordination; that which is to be fully ordained and that which is not to be fully ordained; full ordination and incomplete ordination; acts and the substance of acts; acts that are to be carried out and acts that are not to be carried out; acts of lifting a penalty; acts of requesting approval; the substance of accusation; the substance of inquiry; the substance of disciplining; the substance of pacifying; the substance of cause; training; non-relinquishment of training; relinquishment of training; declaration of deterioration in training; dispute; bringing together of dispute; settling of dispute; complete settling of dispute; what is to be recited and what is not to be recited; consecration; the vow of the insane; rendering a faithful donation improper; an act and what is not an act; Vinaya; statement of a view; a motion; an act with a motion alone; an act with a motion and one recitation; an act with a motion and three recitations; an act of accusation; an act of censure; an act of expulsion; an act of reinstatement; an act of suspension for non-acknowledgment of an offense; an act of suspension for non-amendment; an act of suspension for non-abandonment of a pernicious view; punishment by sentence; restoration from the basis; causing satisfaction; lifting a penalty; questioning; acting in accordance with the Dharma; what the qualities of a sentence are; repetition from the basis; why satisfaction is to be produced; what the qualities of lifting a penalty are; inquiry into the nature of that — sentencing and punishment; offense and non-offense; heavy offense and light offense; offense with remainder and offense without remainder; offense of a coarse nature and offense not of a coarse nature;

offense with a formal act and offense without a formal act; a formal act that constitutes an offense and a formal act that does not constitute an offense; expulsion of an offense; raising it; bringing it to mind; a formal act involving dispute; a harmful act; not transmitting instruction; prohibiting the transmission of instruction; not completing the transmission of instruction; making an opening; a formal act of making an opening; requesting an opening; suppressing the restoration ceremony; prohibiting an opening; setting aside internally; cooked internally; cooked by oneself; cooked by a monk; accepted; not accepted again; accepted and then reclaimed. Accepting food at the time of the morning meal; carrying away the remainder of that; having wood-ash; having a pond; set down and not set down; brought out and not brought out; costly requisites and inexpensive requisites; requisites to be distributed and requisites not to be distributed; requisites of humans and requisites of non-humans; requisites under one's authority and requisites not under one's authority; requisites fit to be received and requisites not fit to be received; robes of a deceased person; substantial robes; robes from a dust-heap; needle work; work performed by sending it away; work with a blade; cutting; shaving; intentionally prepared food; eating fruit; food of humans; food of non-humans; the Vinaya condensed in five hundred; the Vinaya condensed in seven hundred; the sūtra of the true Vinaya; showing in black; showing in full; mixed; thoroughly mixed; what is suitable for the assembly hall; what is suitable for the forest; what is suitable for the retinue; what is suitable for the region; what is suitable for the quarter; what is suitable for the district; what is suitable for robes; what is suitable as sour liquid.

Who is a fit candidate for full ordination? One who is fully ordained by completing what has been accepted and agreed to — that is full ordination, and there are ten kinds of being a fit candidate for full ordination.

A Tathāgata who is self-arisen, and a pratyekabuddha, receive full ordination without a preceptor, through their own nature. The five receive full ordination by directly realizing gnosis. The venerable Mahākāśyapa received full ordination by the Teacher accepting his declaration. The venerable Śāriputra received full ordination by asking and receiving a prophetic declaration. Some received full ordination by the words "Come here, monk." Some received full ordination by the threefold formula of going for refuge. In a border region, full ordination is from a Saṅgha holding the Vinaya together with a quorum of five. In a central region, full ordination is from an assembly of ten or more. Some received full ordination by accepting the qualities of a preceptor. Some received full ordination through a messenger. Some received full ordination from the dual Saṅgha.

Among these, when one has not been constituted by a formal act of requesting and the four, the full ordination by the threefold formula of going for refuge is called a proper full ordination. However, when one has been constituted by a formal act of requesting and the four, the full ordination by the threefold formula of going for refuge is not full ordination.

As for the formula "Come here, monk" — the beginning and the end being alike, that full ordination is called a proper full ordination. And why is that so? Upāli, the words "Come here, monk" constitute full ordination that I myself directly witnessed, and each and every one to whom the words "Come here, monk" were spoken was in their final existence; those to whom "Come here, monk" was said did not let the time pass while still a student. Therefore those are called properly fully ordained.

As for nuns, they are fit candidates for full ordination in three ways: by accepting the qualities of a preceptor, through a messenger, and from the dual Saṅgha.

Accepting the qualities of a preceptor is as in the case of Mahāprajāpatī and others; for the full account, it is to be stated as it appears in the sūtra.

As for the messenger: any virtuous laywoman who, when she goes to meet someone, might cause an obstacle — in such cases a male messenger is to be employed. The messenger listens to the training precepts and repeats them back to those women, saying, "Excellent! You have been well and fully ordained — like Dharmadattā." The transmission of the authorization is to be given in full, exactly as it appears in the Vinaya.

Those who are fit candidates among these are to be given full ordination by the dual Saṅgha — without withdrawal, without postponement — through the motion-and-three-proclamations procedure. That full ordination is called full ordination. Furthermore, it is said: one who approaches and receives this scriptural tradition, who accepts it with complete commitment, who thereby attains it, who having experienced its well-being, brings it to direct manifestation — such a one is fully ordained.

What then constitutes not being properly fully ordained? If one falls back from it, one is not fully ordained. If one approaches this scriptural tradition without acceptance, and without complete commitment does not attain it, and without having experienced its well-being does not bring it to direct manifestation — this is called not being fully ordained.

Who is to be given full ordination? A human male who is alive and without any disqualifying impediment, and a human female who is alive and without any disqualifying impediment — these are the ones to be given full ordination.

Who is not to be given full ordination? One who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has split the Saṅgha, one who with malicious intent has shed the blood of a Tathāgata, one who has no ācārya, one who has no preceptor, one who has no bowl, one who has no robes, one who would not submit to disciplinary procedures, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, a stolen-lodger, one who lives apart under separate rule, one who is unsettled, a paṇḍaka, a hermaphrodite, one who has expelled a nun, one who has not completed twenty years of age, one who has made a solemn promise, one who has been made unfit for ordination, one who is worthy of being made unfit for ordination, and all non-humans — these are not to be given full ordination. And even if full ordination were conferred on them, it would not constitute full ordination, and the one who conferred it would also be in transgression. Why is that? Because those persons are said to defile the assembly, and they entirely defile the assembly; they are not fit candidates for full ordination.

What then is full ordination? When a person of such-and-such a name, of such-and-such a clan, of such-and-such a lineage, has been given full ordination by a Saṅgha assembled in accordance with the Dharma — without manifest withdrawal, without postponement — through the motion-and-three-proclamations procedure, this is called full ordination. Full ordination given with the appropriate authorization is proper full ordination.

What is not full ordination? One who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has split the Saṅgha, one who with malicious intent has shed the blood of a Tathāgata, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, a stolen-lodger, one who lives apart, a paṇḍaka, a hermaphrodite, one who has expelled a nun, and those who were previously impaired — these are called not fully ordained; they are persons of the character of one who does not arise in this Dharma and Vinaya.

Why are they called not fully ordained? Because they have not obtained the equal training. Therefore they are called not fully ordained.

All persons other than these thirteen are to be given full ordination.

If, however, someone has been given full ordination, they shall not be called fully ordained, and the one who conferred full ordination will likewise have transgressed. Therefore the Blessed One declared them not fully ordained.

What is a formal act? There are three kinds: a formal act by motion, a formal act by motion and one proclamation, and a formal act by motion and three proclamations.

Why are they called formal acts? They are called formal acts because of two aspects: acts that cut by penalty, acts that bring down censure, and acts that bind to the white Dharma by solemn commitment.

What are acts that cut by penalty and acts that bring down censure? They are as follows: censure, reproach, banishment, reconciliation, acts of suspension, penalty, origination from the basis, satisfaction, and origination-from-the-basis satisfaction. Furthermore, there are acts that turn a penalty act into an act of censure.

What are acts that bind to the white Dharma by solemn commitment? They are as follows: the restoration ceremony (poṣadha), the invitation ceremony (pravāraṇā), full ordination, expulsion, the spreading of grass, and whatever other acts bind one by solemn commitment to the white Dharma — these are the formal acts. Therefore they are called formal acts.

What is the subject matter of a formal act? Whatever cause and whatever condition pertain to the subject matter in regard to which a formal act is performed — that cause and that condition in relation to that subject matter is called the subject matter of the formal act.

What is a formal act that is fit to be set aside? A formal act in which the motion is defective, the proclamation is defective, it is not in accordance with Dharma, it has been performed without the Saṅgha being assembled — one that has been invalidated: this is called a formal act that is fit to be set aside.

What is a formal act that is not fit to be set aside? A formal act in which the motion is proper, the proclamation is proper, it is in accordance with Dharma, it has been performed with the Saṅgha properly assembled — one that has not been invalidated: this is called a formal act that is not fit to be set aside.

What is an act of expulsion? Expulsion means exclusion. One who has been excluded does not perform formal acts together with the monks. There is no poṣadha with them, no pravāraṇā, no dwelling together, no communal conduct, no communal conversation, no concord — this is called an act of expulsion. Why is it called an act of expulsion? Because the Saṅgha has expelled that person, therefore it is called an act of expulsion.

What is an act of seeking pardon? Whatever act is performed such that one may again dwell together with the Saṅgha, conduct oneself uniformly with them, share the same boundary, and sit together — this is called an act of seeking pardon.

What is the subject matter of censure? A monk who causes strife, who exposes faults, who causes disruption, who harbors ill will, who creates disputes — this is called the subject matter of censure.

What is the subject matter of reproach? The subject matter of reproach is threefold: what has been seen, what has been heard, and what has been suspected — it has occurred, it is an offense, and moreover it is true and not false; it is timely and not untimely; it is meaningful and not meaningless; it is gentle and not rough; it is spoken with loving-kindness and not with aversion — this is called the subject matter of reproach.

What is the subject matter of discipline? The five acts of diligent application: the act of censure, the act of reproach, and so on up to the act of satisfaction — as before. This is called the subject matter of discipline.

What is the subject matter of pacification? Whatever causes and conditions have given rise to a dispute and which bring about its calming — because of the peace and complete tranquility thereby achieved. That is: the hair standing on end, the bringing about of an arising, a showing through bowing, a showing through prostration — this is called the subject matter of pacification.

What is the subject matter of cause? Whatever cause and whatever condition, in dependence upon which cause, a formal act is performed —

just as it arises in the sūtra Bhadāla. Below this, the conduct to be practiced by the Saṅgha is stated in full, just as it arises in the sūtra Bhadāla. This is called the subject matter of cause.

What is training? There are three trainings: training in the higher moral discipline, training in the higher mind, and training in the higher wisdom. Furthermore, there are three trainings: training in higher conduct, training in higher taming, and training in higher individual liberation.

By what measure is something called an invalid relinquishing of training? Relinquishing one's training in the presence of a madman is called an invalid relinquishing of training. Relinquishing one's training in the presence of one whose mind is disturbed, or one tormented by illness, is called an invalid relinquishing of training. Relinquishing one's training in the presence of one who is foolish, or mute, or deaf, or fallen asleep, or in meditative absorption, or delirious, or severely delirious, or who has entered into anger or agitation, or who does not understand, or who has departed and is dwelling elsewhere — all of these are called an invalid relinquishing of training. Relinquishing one's training through a messenger is also called an invalid relinquishing of training. Relinquishing one's training through a written letter, through hand-signs, through having another speak on one's behalf, through a signal, or through a gesture is also called an invalid relinquishing of training.

If a noble one relinquishes training to a border-dweller using the noble tongue, and that border-dweller does not understand the noble tongue, it is called an invalid relinquishing of training. If a noble one relinquishes training to another noble one using the border-dweller's tongue, and that noble one does not understand the border-dweller's tongue, it is called an invalid relinquishing of training. If a border-dweller relinquishes training to another border-dweller using the noble tongue, and that border-dweller does not understand the noble tongue, it is called an invalid relinquishing of training. If a border-dweller relinquishes training to a noble one using the border-dweller's tongue, and that noble one does not understand the border-dweller's tongue, it is called an invalid relinquishing of training.

If one perceives what is not secluded as secluded and relinquishes training, it is called an invalid relinquishing of training. Even if one perceives what is secluded as secluded and relinquishes training, it is called an invalid relinquishing of training. If one perceives what is secluded as not secluded and relinquishes training, it is called an invalid relinquishing of training. If one perceives what is not secluded as not secluded and relinquishes training, it is called an invalid relinquishing of training.

If one relinquishes training in the midst of uproar, it is called an invalid relinquishing of training. Even if one says the words of relinquishing training to one who is not properly established in the way of the world, it is called an invalid relinquishing of training.

Whether stated briefly or in full: if one does not form the intention of requesting consent, and though one applies the words of relinquishing training while still wishing for the things belonging to a monk and not wishing for the things belonging to a householder, and yet speaks the words while not being in a natural state — even if such words are spoken, the training has not been validly relinquished. This is called an invalid relinquishing of training.

What is a valid relinquishing of training? It is this: when that monk has become attached to the life of a householder, or has grown displeased with it, or desires it, or has become unwilling to continue as an ascetic, or wishes to abandon the monk's estate, or disparages it, or is ashamed, or feels disgrace, or even feels remorse — and then he goes before a monk and says, "I relinquish my training" — that is called a valid relinquishing of training.

If he says, "Regard me as a householder" in relation to: the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, the sūtras, the Vinaya, the matrix, the preceptor, the teachers, oneself; or in relation to a novice, a paṇḍaka, a woman of mixed status, a nun who has been expelled, one's father, one's mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who with malicious intent drew blood from a Tathāgata, a non-Buddhist adherent, one who has gone over to non-Buddhist adherents, a thief in a hiding place, one dwelling apart —

"Hold me as one not residing" — or, in the lesser form, if he says, "It is enough that you share the same Dharma and practice the same celibate life as I do" — that too is called a relinquishing of training. Whether he speaks with attachment, with displeasure, or with a wish to descend, if he declares it through speech, words, utterance, voice, intonation, definitive statement, the path of speech, the sound of speech, the action of speech, or through the intentional use of speech — that is called a relinquishing of training.

What is called declaring the deterioration of one's training? It is as follows. From the point at which the monk has become attached, up to the point of remorse, proceeding as before: he goes to another monk and says, "The celibate life is difficult to practise. True seclusion is extremely difficult. To delight in solitude is difficult. To dwell in forest and woodland, to dwell at the forest's edge and to be present there in full — these too are difficult. For the rest of one's life, to dwell alone in a wilderness together with fierce wild beasts, and to make a bed from grass or leaves — that too is difficult. For the rest of one's life, to depend on others for one's own sustenance and that of others is difficult. For the rest of one's life, to seek from others robes, food, bedding, and medicines and requisites for illness — that is suffering. I miss them. I think of my father, my brothers, and my sisters." Or he says, "Let me be apprenticed to a craft. Let me be set to work. Place me on the side of the reasonable. Release me into the company of the virtuous." From the point of attachment as before, up to and including the declaration by speech — this is called declaring the deterioration of one's training.

What is the distinction between relinquishing training and declaring the deterioration of training? In terms of the words there is no difference; in terms of abandoning the vow there is no difference either, for in each case the vow is released. In both cases it is the same.

What is a dispute? There are four kinds of dispute: dispute through contention, dispute through failure to convey a scriptural transmission, dispute through a transgression, and dispute through a procedural matter. These are called disputes. Why are they called disputes? Because through their force, conflict arises — therefore they are called disputes.

What is the gathering of a dispute? Whatever cause and condition, taken as the governing cause, gives rise to a dispute — that is called the gathering of a dispute.

What is the settling of a dispute? There are seven principles for settling a dispute: settling by direct confrontation, settling by recollection, settling by absence of delusion, settling the dispute according to its own nature, proceeding by majority, introduction of a verdict, and that which is like laying down grass. These are called the means of settling a dispute.

Why are they called the settling of a dispute? Because by means of these seven principles, the four disputes are tamed, quieted, fully pacified, disciplined, abandoned, and brought to cessation — therefore they are called principles for settling a dispute.

What is the non-settling of a dispute? If five qualities are present, a dispute will not be properly settled. What are the five? The matter has not been submitted to the Saṅgha; it is not in accord with the Victor's word; the monks on both sides of the dispute have not been informed; the monks who are arguing in accordance with the Dharma and who are giving responses have not been respectfully restrained; and the monk who has committed a transgression has not purified that transgression. If these five qualities are present, a dispute will not be properly settled.

If five qualities are present, a dispute will be properly settled. What are the five? The matter has been submitted to the Saṅgha; it is in accord with the Victor's word; the monks on both sides of the dispute have been informed; the monks who are arguing in accordance with the Dharma and who are giving responses have been respectfully restrained; and the monk who has committed a transgression has purified the transgression.

If these five qualities are present, a dispute will be properly settled — and that is called a dispute being fully settled.

What is the recitation? It is whichever is longer — the fourth or the thirteenth — that is recited in full; that is called the recitation.

What is non-recitation? In a place where the monk who is supposed to recite the Prātimokṣa sūtra does not recite it, another who comes after him should recite it. If he too has not read it and lacks the confidence to do so, then another who comes after him should give the response. If he too is unable and lacks the confidence, then similarly, going through each successive reciter to the very last, if none of them has the confidence, that is called non-recitation.

What is the consecration of the restoration ceremony? A monk who is dwelling alone: on that very day of the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony (poṣadha), he should rise early, pay reverence to the stūpa and to the vihāra, sweep the courtyard, and sweep the restoration hall as well. He should smear it gently with fresh cow dung, then in due order and at the proper time set out the seats, fill the pure-water vessels and the privy vessels with water, prepare a fire nearby, and place nearby the lamp oil, the lamp vessel, the lamp stand, and the tooth-cleaning sticks. If monks who have not yet performed the restoration ceremony then arrive, he should perform the restoration ceremony together with them and should also announce the recitation of the Prātimokṣa sūtra. If they do not arrive, he should ascend to a high vantage point, stand there, look out in all four directions, and if anyone comes, call out: "Venerable one, come quickly — we are to perform the restoration ceremony!" If no one whatsoever comes, he should descend from there, remain sitting until the end of his time, and recite the triple announcement. He should read the qualities of generosity and arouse the awakening mind. He should also say aloud: "Today is the Saṅgha's fifteenth-day restoration ceremony. I, the monk called such-and-such, today also hold the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony. May all impediment-causing phenomena be completely purified, and may the gods too regard me, the monk called such-and-such, as fully purified. Here the restoration ceremony is to be consecrated for the sake of completely fulfilling the aggregate of moral discipline. Whenever the Saṅgha assembles in harmony, may the full restoration ceremony be experienced and the Prātimokṣa sūtra also be savored." He should say this two and three times. Just as it is for one monk, so too for two or three monks dwelling together — in the same way it should be practiced, the awakening mind aroused, and each should recite it to the other. Having done this, the restoration ceremony has been performed. This is called the consecration.

What is the vow for one who is intoxicated? When a monk has become intoxicated, his mind disturbed and afflicted by illness, one gives him the vow for the intoxicated by means of both the request and the two-person act — to be applied in full just as for the venerable Bimbasāra (Byema-can), in accordance with the Vinaya. That is called the vow for the intoxicated.

What is the vow for one who is not intoxicated? Apart from those vows for the intoxicated, all other vows beyond them are called the vow for one who is not intoxicated.

What is rendering improper a gift given in faith? If something is given to one whose moral discipline has degenerated, that is called rendering improper a gift given in faith. Moreover, if something — even a single portion — is given to one who has entered a wrong path rather than the right path, that too is called having rendered improper a gift given in faith. That, then, is what is called rendering improper a gift given in faith.

What are the acts? The ten acts to be performed before the assembly has formally convened. They are as follows: accepting the bowl by word of mouth; receiving the bowl; the vow pertaining to the training; the release from the vow of the training; the vow pertaining to the temple;

the vow of the novice; the vow of the one acting as if mad; the vow of silence; the vow proper to one for whom prostration is not appropriate; and the vow of one whose conduct is separate. These are what are called the acts.

What are non-acts? When a formal act requires four to be assembled and one performs it without four being assembled, that is a non-act and must not be done in that way. If a layman completes the assembly of four and then performs it, that too is a non-act and must not be done in that way. If it is performed by a novice; by one who has consorted with a woman, a hermaphrodite, or a nun; by one who has killed his father, killed his mother, killed an arhat, divided the Saṅgha, or with malicious intent drawn blood from a Tathāgata; by a tīrthika or one who has gone over to the tīrthikas; by a thief who has entered under false pretenses; by one who previously fell into an offense, or who previously caused a disruption; by one dwelling in a different community; by one who is not present; by one dwelling separately; by one who is not to be counted; by one who has surrendered the training; by one performing a penalty, or who has not completed a penalty, or has not been satisfied, or who will not be satisfied; or when it is performed by those who have surrendered the training — that too is a non-act and must not be done in that way. Just as one should apply in full detail how an act requiring four to be assembled is to be performed, so too for acts requiring five to be assembled, for those requiring ten, and for those requiring twenty. These, then, are what are called non-acts.

What is called the Vinaya? The Vinaya is that which, having arisen from the Vinaya as described, is to be elaborated in full. That is what is called the Vinaya.

What is the stating of a view? The stating of a view encompasses five cases that are not in accordance with the Dharma and five that are in accordance with the Dharma.

What are the five cases of stating a view not in accordance with the Dharma? Stating a view in the presence of one who is not present; stating a view in the presence of one who is dwelling separately; stating a view in the presence of one who has sided with a faction; stating a view in the presence of one who has not received full ordination; and stating a view in the presence of one who is not lacking in the remainder of something. These are the five cases of stating a view not in accordance with the Dharma.

What are the five cases of stating a view in accordance with the Dharma? Not stating a view in the presence of one who is not present; not stating a view in the presence of one who is dwelling separately; not stating a view in the presence of one who has sided with a faction; not stating a view in the presence of one who has not received full ordination; and not stating a view in the presence of one who is not lacking in the full remainder of the matter. These are the five cases of stating a view in accordance with the Dharma.

What is a motion? A motion is a verbal act through which a matter is made known. At the time of performing an act, it is the means by which the matter is made known. Whatever motion states in words the meaning of that particular matter is called a motion.

What is the act of a motion? It is the notification of the Saṅgha by means of a motion together with an act. This applies to such things as the making of an opening, the removal of something, the passing of a bowl, the laying down of grass, and whatever else is to be performed by means of a motion-act. All such things are to be regarded as motion-acts. That is what is called a motion-act.

What is the act of a motion with a second? When, after a motion has been made, a single proclamation follows, that is the second combined with a motion, and this is called the act of a motion with a second.

What is the act of a motion with a fourth? When, after a motion has been made, three proclamations are recited, that is the fourth combined with a motion, and this is called the act of a motion with a fourth.

If, for an act that requires a motion, one performs the act without making the motion, that is an offense. If one makes the proclamation without having made the motion, that is an offense. If, for an act requiring a motion with a second, one makes the proclamation without having made the motion, that is an offense. If the motion has been made but the proclamation has not been made, that is an offense committed. If the proclamation has been made but the motion has not been made, that too is an offense. If, for an act requiring a motion with a fourth, one makes the proclamation without having made the motion, that is an offense. If the motion has been made but the proclamation has not been made, that is an offense. If the proclamation has been made but the motion has not been made, that is an offense. If, for a motion-act, the motion is made, there is no offense.

If the motion has been made and the proclamation has then been made, there is no offense. For a motion-and-one act, if the motion is made and one proclamation is made, there is no offense. If the motion has been made and many proclamations are made, there is no offense. For a motion-and-four act, if the motion has been made and many proclamations are made, there is no offense. These are to be applied in the same manner. Thus, even if many acts are performed, there is no offense. This is called a withdrawn act.

Now, if, when the motion has been made and the proclamation is being announced, certain members of the Saṅgha rise from their seats for some other purpose, and those who have not yet risen wish to do so, one should make the motion again before the remaining members of the retinue in the same way. If it becomes necessary to make the motion differently, one should complete the proclamation without offense. One should also address the Saṅgha verbally, saying: "Venerables, I shall repeat the motion before the Saṅgha, and I shall also repeat the proclamation," and so make the motion. If that motion is not completed, against whom is the act of censure to be performed? It is fitting that monks who are quarrelsome and playful should be subjected to a motion-and-four act without suspension and without postponement. This is called an act of censure.

What is an act of rebuke? When a monk has committed a transgression and it has come out openly, a rebuke act is to be applied to him by means of a motion-and-four act, without suspension and without postponement. This is called an act of rebuke.

What is an act of banishment? When a monk has become a disgrace to his family, a banishment act is to be applied to him by means of a motion-and-four act, without suspension and without postponement. This is called an act of banishment.

What is an act of reconciliation? When a monk has been abusing householders, a reconciliation act is to be applied to him by means of a motion-and-four act, without suspension and without postponement. This is called an act of reconciliation.

What is an act of suspension for not seeing a transgression? When a monk has committed a transgression and says, "I do not see that I have committed a transgression," a suspension act for not seeing a transgression is to be applied to him by means of a motion-and-four act, without suspension and without postponement. This is called an act of suspension for not seeing a transgression.

What is an act of suspension for not doing the work again? When, on account of a transgression that has occurred, one refuses in accordance with the Dharma to do the work again, a suspension act for not doing the work again is to be applied by means of a motion-and-four act, without lifting and without postponement. This is called an act of suspension for not doing the work again.

What is an act of suspension for not abandoning a wrong view? When a monk has come to hold a wrong view and, having seized upon it, persists in holding it firmly and refuses to relinquish it, a suspension act for not abandoning that wrong view is to be applied to him by means of a motion-and-four act, without lifting and without postponement. This is called an act of suspension for not abandoning a wrong view.

What is a probationary act? When a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika) from another tradition, having previously gone forth from among tīrthikas and then entered the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya and received full ordination, desires to be established as a monk, the preceptor first clothes him and imposes a probationary period of four months, applying a motion-and-four act without suspension and without postponement. A probationary act is also to be performed as follows: when a monk has done any one of the thirteen bases and has concealed it, for as long as he is known to have concealed it and remains unrepentant, that probationary act too is to be applied to him by means of a motion-and-four act, without suspension and without postponement. This is called a probationary act.

What is an act of suspension from the beginning? When a monk is undergoing a probationary period, and in the course of that probation an offense occurs such that a suspension-from-the-beginning act is to be performed for that offense, a motion-and-four act is to be applied without suspension and without postponement —

— and without postponement, that monk must undergo the penalty again, because the earlier one had not been carried out. Alternatively, in another category: whether a penalty has been performed or not, that very matter is to be made to start again from the beginning. This is called an act of resuming from the beginning.

What is an act of satisfaction? When a monk has committed any one of the thirteen bases of the Saṅgha's remaining Dharmas and has either not been suspended or has undergone the penalty, a motion-and-four act is applied to him requiring him to perform satisfaction for six days, without suspension and without postponement — and that monk must then perform satisfaction toward all monks. This is called an act performed by satisfaction.

What is rehabilitation? When a monk who has come through a penalty has, in the course of those six days of performing satisfaction, conducted himself in the practice of satisfaction, a motion-and-four act is applied to him without suspension and without postponement. This is called rehabilitation.

Why is it called rehabilitation? Because he is drawn out from an unwholesome state and firmly established in a wholesome state — for this reason it is called rehabilitation.

The word "inquiry" refers to the Dharmas themselves. What is the benefit of performing the penalty? Why is one made to repeat from the beginning? What is the benefit of performing satisfaction? And why is there rehabilitation?

Performing the penalty is the benefit for one who has been suspended on account of the Dharmas. Performing satisfaction is the benefit for one on whom the penalty has been carried out. As for why repeating from the beginning is called intensification — repeating from the beginning is intensification itself. As for why rehabilitation is the benefit of satisfaction — rehabilitation is for the sake of purification.

Why does the fact of having undergone the penalty become a benefit for performing satisfaction? A monk who has been penalized performs satisfaction toward all monks without great difficulty. When satisfaction has been performed, the monks think of him as one to whom satisfaction has been given. For this reason, what has been done through the penalty is the benefit of satisfaction.

Why does repeating from the beginning constitute intensification? When one repeats from the beginning, an intensification has been applied to that person; out of fear he will not act that way again, and the monks too will come to know of it. In this way, a venerable one with great afflictions, out of a sense of shame, will not repeat such conduct thereafter. For this reason, repeating from the beginning constitutes intensification.

Why does performing satisfaction become the benefit of rehabilitation? When a monk is carrying out satisfaction, he performs satisfaction toward all monks without great difficulty. Having performed satisfaction, the monks think of rehabilitating him, thinking: "This venerable one wishes to move forward; this venerable one does not wish for afflictions" — and so they declare, "This venerable one is virtuous; this venerable one is to be rehabilitated." For this reason, performing satisfaction is the benefit of rehabilitation.

Why should rehabilitation be carried out? Rehabilitation is to be performed for the sake of purification. When he is rehabilitated, that monk becomes purified and free of transgression. It is as the saying goes: these two kinds of persons are pure and free of affliction — one in whom no transgression arises, and one who, even if a transgression arises, restores it in accordance with the Dharma. One who is rehabilitated likewise becomes pure. Therefore, rehabilitation too is for the sake of purification.

In search of its essential nature, what is confession? A monk accuses himself of an offense. From accusation he moves to acknowledgment. From acknowledgment he accuses himself again.

Now, regarding confession itself — in search of its essential nature: one should perform the act of petition together with the four acts of pressing, without there being any wearing down or setting aside. This, in search of its essential nature, is called "cutting by means of a penalty."

What is an offense? The five classes of offense are called the aggregate of offenses: defeat (pārājika), formal acts of the Saṅgha (saṃghāvaśeṣa), downfalls, individual confessions, and wrongdoings. When one engages in and commits any of these without restoring oneself, that is called an offense.

What is non-offense? When those same five classes of offense are free of offense, they are called the aggregate of non-offense. One does not act in regard to defeat, formal acts of the Saṅgha, downfalls, individual observances, or wrongdoings — because one has neither engaged in nor committed them, this abstention is called non-offense.

What is a grave offense? That which cannot be lifted. What is a light offense? That which can be lifted.

What is an offense with a remainder? The lower classes of offense: formal acts of the Saṅgha, downfalls, individual confessions, and wrongdoings. What is an offense without a remainder? The first class of offense: the four defeats.

What is a gross offense? Defeat and formal acts of the Saṅgha. Why are these called gross offenses? They are called gross offenses for two reasons: they are called gross offenses because the offense is gross, and they are gross offenses by intrinsic nature — thus they are called gross offenses.

What is an offense that is not gross? The remaining three classes of offense: downfalls, occasions of falling again, and wrongdoings. These are called offenses that are not gross.

What is an offense with an act? That which is to be confessed and that which is to be restrained. What is an offense without an act? The first class of offenses.

Here ends the forty-eighth fascicle of the Noble Vinaya.

What is an offense to be restored? A monk who, having inwardly established mindfulness within the fourth or fifth category of rules, and with faith, restores the offense in accordance with the Dharma — that is an offense to be restored.

What is an offense not to be restored? A monk who lacks the fourth category of rules and also lacks the fifth, yet has inwardly established mindfulness, but does not restore the offense in accordance with the Dharma with faith — that is called an offense not to be restored.

What is the lifting of an offense? In one mode, all offenses are contained — and that is the vow. In another mode, all offenses are not contained — and that is the absence of the vow. That is called the lifting of an offense.

What is a raising of the matter? It is when a monk says to another monk: "Venerable one, such-and-such an offense as this has arisen for you — confess it again, come forward, restore it in accordance with the Dharma." That speaking is called a raising of the matter.

What is a reminder? It is when that monk says to the monk: "Venerable one, do you not remember that such-and-such an offense as this arose?" That speaking is called a reminder.

What is an act with words? It is an act with words. And what is that? It is when a monk says to another monk with words: "Venerable one, there is a matter between us — do not go away from this place until you have spoken with me. Venerable one, there is a dispute between you and me." That is called an act with words.

What is an act of bringing words together? There are five kinds of bringing words together. When a person's matter is opened up, one says: "What you said on this subject, you said such-and-such" — and so the words are brought together. Or: "What you said on this subject, you said it in such-and-such a place" — and so the words are brought together. Or: "What you said on this subject, you said it in this place" — and so the words are brought together. Or: "What you said on this subject, you said it in whatever place you pleased."

— and so the words are brought together — without mentioning it, one raises a fault against that person, points out a fault, brings the words together, and then sends the matter forward with the words having been patched over. It is like, for example, a charioteer whose horse is so unruly that it cannot be brought to a place where it can be tamed, and so that very charioteer ties it up with a rope, fits it with a bit and bridle, harnesses it with these painful restraints, and then abandons it. This is called an act of bringing words together.

What is failing to transmit a scriptural declaration? Whatever one fails to transmit as a scriptural declaration is what is not spoken in words — that is, remaining silent out of having seen, heard, or suspected something. That is called failing to transmit a scriptural declaration.

What is obstructing the transmission of a scriptural declaration? It is striving to ensure that a scriptural declaration is not transmitted.

What is failing to complete the transmission of a scriptural declaration? It is carelessly abandoning the task of ensuring that a scriptural declaration is not transmitted.

What is opening an occasion? One opens an occasion and then speaks to it in a way that is tolerable, and it is to be remembered. This is called opening an occasion.

What is an act of opening an occasion? There are five acts of opening an occasion. One says: "You, open an occasion for me — I will speak to you, I will address you, I will discuss it with you, I will bring it to your remembrance." This is called opening an occasion.

What is an act of opening an occasion together with a petition? It is petitioning another by means of those acts of opening an occasion.

What is obstructing the restoration ceremony (poṣadha)? Ten things that are not in accordance with the Dharma obstruct the restoration ceremony. Ten things that are in accordance with the Dharma also exist.

What are the ten things not in accordance with the Dharma by which the restoration ceremony is obstructed? They are: one who has not incurred a defeat; one who has not been declared in speech to have incurred a defeat; one who has not relinquished the training; one who has not been declared in speech to have relinquished the training; one who has not spoken ill of the Saṅgha; one who has not been declared in speech to have spoken ill of the Saṅgha; one whose moral discipline has not deteriorated; one whose view has not deteriorated; one whose conduct has not deteriorated; one whose livelihood has not deteriorated.

How is it that one has not incurred a defeat? If, by the appearance, the mark, and the sign by which a monk would incur a defeat, one does not see that monk as guilty of a defeat under such an appearance, mark, and sign, then obstructing that monk's restoration ceremony is an obstruction that is not in accordance with the Dharma. Thus that is a case of not having incurred a defeat.

How is it that one has not been declared in speech to have incurred a defeat? If many monks have assembled and gathered together, whether inside or outside the monastery, and neither something arising from that matter, nor a declaration that accords with the nature of that matter, has been spoken; nor has it been heard from a faithful source; nor has it arisen from conceptual thought about one's own circumstances — and yet one obstructs the restoration ceremony without having heard it — then this is an obstruction of the restoration ceremony that is not in accordance with the Dharma. Such is a case of not having been declared in speech to have incurred a defeat.

How is it that one has not relinquished the training? If by the appearance, the mark, and the sign by which a monk would relinquish the training, the monk has not seen such an appearance, such a mark, or such a sign — and yet one says "he has relinquished the training" and, without that monk's having seen it, obstructs the restoration ceremony — then this is not an obstruction of the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma. Thus that is a case of not having relinquished the training.

How is it that one has not been declared in speech to have relinquished the training? If many monks have assembled and gathered together, whether inside or outside the monastery, and neither something arising from that matter, nor a declaration in accordance with its nature, has been spoken; nor has it been heard from a faithful source; nor has it arisen from conceptual thought about one's own circumstances; nor has it been heard —

— yet the restoration ceremony is obstructed without even a suspicion: that is an obstruction of the restoration ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma. Such as this is called not having declared in speech that one has relinquished the training.

How is it that one has not reviled the Saṅgha? If a monk who reviles the Saṅgha does so by means of a certain appearance, a certain sign, and a certain indication — and yet that same appearance, sign, and indication by which that monk would revile the Saṅgha are not seen — then for one who obstructs the restoration ceremony on the basis of those, that is an obstruction of the restoration ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma. Such as this is called not having reviled the Saṅgha.

How is it that one has not been declared in speech to have reviled the Saṅgha? For instance, whether inside or outside the monastery, many monks have assembled and gathered together, and neither something arising from that matter, nor something of that nature, nor a declaration in accordance with it, has been spoken among them; nor has it been heard from a faithful source; nor has it arisen from conceptual thought about one's own circumstances; nor has it been heard; nor is there any suspicion — yet the restoration ceremony is obstructed: that is an obstruction of the restoration ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma. Such as this is called not having been declared in speech to have reviled the Saṅgha.

How is it that moral discipline has not been impaired? If, with respect to any one of the four root defeats, one has not transgressed beyond the rule of root defeat — such as this is called not having impaired moral discipline.

How is it that one's view has not been impaired? If one has not come to hold any view among the sixty-two views — such as this is called one's view not having been impaired.

How is it that one's conduct has not been impaired? If one refrains from improper conduct and trains in the training of a monk — such as this is called one's conduct not having been impaired.

How is it that one's livelihood has not been impaired? If one's livelihood is entirely pure — such as this is called one's livelihood not having been impaired.

These, then, are the ten obstructions of the restoration ceremony that are not in accordance with the Dharma.

What are the ten obstructions of the restoration ceremony that are in accordance with the Dharma? They are: having incurred a root defeat; having been declared in speech to have incurred a root defeat; having relinquished the training; having been declared in speech to have relinquished the training; having reviled the Saṅgha; having been declared in speech to have reviled the Saṅgha; having impaired moral discipline; having impaired one's view; having impaired one's conduct; and having impaired one's livelihood.

How is it that one has incurred a root defeat? If a monk is seen, by means of a certain appearance, a certain sign, and a certain indication — by that same appearance, sign, and indication by which that monk would incur a root defeat — to be committing a root-defeat offense, then for one who obstructs the restoration ceremony on that basis, that is an obstruction of the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma. Such as this is called having incurred a root defeat.

How is it that one has been declared in speech to have incurred a root defeat? This is the case: whether inside or outside the monastery, having assembled and gathered together with many monks, something arising from that matter, or of that nature, or in accordance with it, has been declared in speech among them; it has been heard from a faithful source; it has arisen from one's own conceptual thought; it has been heard; and there is suspicion — and the restoration ceremony is obstructed on another ground: that is an obstruction of the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma. Such as this is called having been declared in speech to have incurred a root defeat.

How is it that one has relinquished the training? If a monk, by means of a certain appearance, a certain sign, and a certain indication by which the training is relinquished — and by that same appearance, sign, and indication — is seen to have relinquished the training, then for one who obstructs the restoration ceremony on that basis, that is an obstruction of the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

Such as this is called having relinquished the training. How is it that one has been declared in speech to have relinquished the training? It is as follows: whether inside or outside a monastery, when many monks have assembled and gathered together, and they have also spoken of something arising from that, or of its nature, or of something consonant with it — whether one has heard it from a trustworthy source, or it has arisen from conceptual thought about one's own appearance — and having heard it, or merely suspecting it, one obstructs the restoration ceremony: such as this is called having been declared in speech to have relinquished the training.

What is it to have become one who reviles the Saṅgha? If a monk, by means of a certain appearance, a certain sign, and a certain indication by which that monk has become one who reviles the Saṅgha — and being seen, by that same appearance, sign, and indication, to be making that monk into one who reviles the Saṅgha — one then obstructs the restoration ceremony on that basis: that is an obstruction of the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma. Such as this is called having become one who reviles the Saṅgha.

What is it to have been declared in speech to be one who reviles the Saṅgha? It is as follows: whether inside or outside a monastery, when many monks have assembled and gathered together, and they have also spoken of something arising from that, or of its nature, or of something consonant with it — whether one has heard it from a trustworthy source, or it has arisen from conceptual thought about one's own appearance, and having heard it, or merely suspecting it, one obstructs the restoration ceremony: such as this is called having been declared in speech to be one who reviles the Saṅgha.

What is it to have a deterioration of moral discipline? When any one of the four root defeats has occurred — such as this is called a deterioration of moral discipline.

What is it to have a deterioration of view? When one has come to hold any view belonging to the sixty-two [wrong] views — such as this is called a deterioration of view.

What is it to have a deterioration of conduct? When one does not conduct oneself properly and does not train in the training of a monk — such as this is called a deterioration of conduct.

What is it to have a deterioration of livelihood? When one's livelihood is utterly impure — such as this is called a deterioration of livelihood. These ten are what obstruct the restoration ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

What are those that obstruct the invitation ceremony? There are four that obstruct the invitation ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma, and four that obstruct the invitation ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

What are the four that obstruct the invitation ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma?
