Obstructing the invitation ceremony when there is no basis for a deterioration of moral discipline — that is obstructing the invitation ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma. Obstructing the invitation ceremony when there is no basis for a deterioration of view, a deterioration of conduct, or a deterioration of livelihood — these four constitute obstructing the invitation ceremony not in accordance with the Dharma.

What are the four that obstruct the invitation ceremony in accordance with the Dharma? Obstructing the invitation ceremony when there is a basis for a deterioration of moral discipline — that is obstructing the invitation ceremony in accordance with the Dharma. Obstructing the invitation ceremony when there is a basis for a deterioration of view, a deterioration of conduct, or a deterioration of livelihood — these four constitute obstructing the invitation ceremony in accordance with the Dharma.

What is food placed inside? Food placed inside a suitable dwelling of Ānanda without having been assigned — that is food which is not to be eaten by fully ordained monks. Food which has been assigned to a suitable place is permissible to eat.

What are food and provisions cooked inside? Whatever provisions and food have been cooked inside are not to be eaten by a fully ordained monk. That which is not to be eaten — that is called having been cooked inside.

What is food cooked by oneself? In the city of Vaiśālī, when a year of misfortune had come and things were scarce and hard to obtain, the brahmins and householders wished to prepare food for the Saṅgha, and they thought to themselves:

If they were to make a commotion at home, they would be obliged to give to many relatives, many friends, and many people. Seeing that this would cause harm to the monks, they went to the monks and said: "Venerable ones, if cooking were done inside the monastery and a meal served there, what offense would result?" When matters had come to this pass, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "I permit cooking to be done outside the monastery and a meal to be served there." When the Blessed One had said, "Cook outside the monastery and serve the meal there," the smoke was great and the place became crowded. Many people came and it grew chaotic, and when the monks distributed food to everyone, the monks' share became very small, and the monks went hungry. The monks reported this state of affairs to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Designate an inspected place inside the monastery, cook there, and serve the meal." When the Blessed One had said, "Designate an inspected place inside the monastery, cook and serve there," the monks did just so. But then the monastery workers and the novices' fathers took from it first for their own benefit, and afterward they gave to the monks assigned to cook whatever little was left over. The monks' share became small and the monks went hungry. The monks reported this state of affairs to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "In such a year of misfortune, when things are scarce and hard to obtain, I permit monks to cook for themselves and eat. Moreover, if a designated inspected place is established, two difficulties are avoided: that of keeping food inside and that of living inside." Except in such a year of misfortune when things are scarce and hard to obtain, whether or not a place has been designated, whatever place it may be — food cooked by oneself is not permissible to eat. That is called food cooked by oneself.

What is the taking back by a monk? Some monks ate a great deal and some ate little. For those who ate a great deal, it was not enough; for those who ate little, there was food left over, and when they gave it to others, the others did not eat it because the Blessed One had not permitted them to eat it. The monks reported this state of affairs to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "In such a year of misfortune when things are scarce and hard to obtain, I permit monks to eat what has been cooked." What, then, is this? It is whatever has been cooked by a fully ordained monk. This is called food cooked by a monk.

What is taking? It is whatever has been taken knowingly by a monk who is ashamed. This is called taking.

What is not receiving? Whether from a woman, a man, a hermaphrodite, a girl, or one of dual characteristics — in any case, food that has not been received is called not receiving.

What is retaking from what was taken? Whatever has been received again by oneself from what one had put down, and afterward received again from another — this is called retaking from what was taken.

What is receiving before the morning meal? It is receiving before one has eaten. The Blessed One permitted this in that very city of Vaiśālī: in such a year of misfortune when things are scarce and hard to obtain, a monk who has satisfied himself, even if he has not done more after having received the morning meal offering, may eat again from what remains. This is called receiving at the time of the morning meal.

What then is carrying away again?

Carrying away again is when a monk, having eaten there, takes food with him as he goes. The Blessed One permitted this too in that very city of Vaiśālī: in such a year of misfortune when things are scarce and hard to obtain, the Blessed One said that a monk who has satisfied himself may carry away what remains and eat from it even without setting aside a surplus. This is called carrying away again.

What then is forest-berry food? Forest-berry food refers to the fruits of forest-shrub plants such as the staghorn sumac, the orumana, the bhatam, and whatever other fruits of forest-berry bushes there may be. The Blessed One is said to have permitted these too at the city of Vaiśālī, saying that in such a year of misfortune when things are scarce and hard to obtain, even if a monk has already satisfied himself, he may eat again from such forest berries without having set aside a surplus.

What then is pond-grown food? The venerable Śāriputra was afflicted with a bile-fever sickness, and a physician indicated a remedy, namely that lotus roots would be fitting as food for him. The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then went to a lotus pond, obtained lotus roots, and gave them to the venerable Śāriputra. Śāriputra ate a little, but not wanting much more, gave the remainder to the monks. The monks, however, said, "We have already satisfied ourselves; we will not eat." When this matter was reported to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "In such a year of misfortune when things are scarce and hard to obtain, even if a monk has already satisfied himself, he may eat from pond-grown things without having set aside a surplus." And what are those things? They are: the rishighati, the kharkatika, the karshingakatala, and whatever other fruits produced within the water there may be. These are called pond-grown food.

Following this, the Blessed One remained in the city of Vaiśālī for as long as he wished during that time of misfortune when things were scarce and hard to obtain, and then set out, travelling gradually, for the city of Śrāvastī. When he had journeyed by stages and arrived at Śrāvastī, he took up residence in the Jeta Grove, in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. There the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, the eight articles I have permitted for monks in that great city of Vaiśālī during the time of misfortune when things are scarce and hard to obtain are these: storing inside, cooking inside, cooking oneself, having a monk cook, receiving at the morning meal time, carrying away again, forest-berry food, and pond-grown food. Are those things still being consumed there as was appropriate?" Some of the monks replied, "Yes, Venerable One," while others said, "No."

Thereupon the Blessed One, for that very same reason, convened the assembly of monks and declared to them: "Monks, out of compassion, the following permission was granted: in the city of Vaiśālī during the time of misfortune when things are scarce and hard to obtain, even if monks had satisfied themselves, these eight articles were permitted. In a year of misfortune, they may be eaten; in a good year, they are not to be eaten. Whoever eats them in a good year incurs a transgression."

What is depositing? Depositing is settled by nine mental acts. What are these? The monk who makes a deposit from the very beginning, in the processes of taking the robe-material, washing it, stretching it, counting the threads, matching them, and sewing, generates three kinds of mental intention: "I, a monk called so-and-so by name, am doing this — this cloth will become a robe-material deposited for the Saṅgha; I shall deposit it; I have deposited it."

In the middle phase as well, three kinds of mental intention are to be generated: "I, a monk called so-and-so by name, this cloth will become a robe-material deposited for the Saṅgha; I shall deposit it; I have deposited it." And at the time of the final stitch completing the sewing, three kinds of mental intention are likewise to be generated: "I, a monk called so-and-so by name, this cloth will become a robe-material deposited for the Saṅgha; I shall deposit it; I have deposited it."

Furthermore, in whatever place the Saṅgha resides, at the time of making the initial deposit, all monks of equally pure stream who are residing within that boundary, upon merely hearing that "the Saṅgha has made a deposit," if they rejoice in it, then it is said that all of them have likewise made the deposit. This is what is called "depositing."

What is non-depositing? The opposite of the above is non-depositing. Specifically, if the Saṅgha makes a deposit when the three months are not yet complete, it is called non-depositing. This is what is called "non-depositing."

What is withdrawal? Withdrawal of the deposit occurs through eight terms resembling the negative. What are these? They are: having withdrawn and departed, having received, having received entirely, having deteriorated, having heard, having passed beyond the boundary, having had one's intention cut off, and having made formal request — these eight terms. This is what is called "withdrawal."

What is non-withdrawal? The opposite of these is non-withdrawal. However, even if any one of the eight interruptions has occurred, if a monk departs from the place of deposit intentionally and then returns, it is still called non-withdrawal of the deposit. This is what is called "non-withdrawal of the deposit."

What are heavy requisites? Those which it is not proper to distribute. What are light requisites? Those which it is proper to distribute. What are requisites that are proper to distribute? The belongings of a deceased monk that are to be distributed — specifically, everything other than the Dharma-robe of the deceased: those remaining items are the light requisites. This is what is called "requisites proper to distribute."

What are requisites not proper to distribute? The belongings of a deceased monk that are not to be distributed — specifically, everything other than the Dharma-robe of the deceased: the heavy items among those remaining. This is what is called "requisites not proper to distribute."

Among these, what is classified as a heavy requisite by being superseded by the Dharma-robe is the sick-attendant's Dharma-robe. Among requisites other than that, the light ones — iron vessels, alms bowls, small bowls, and non-bowl containers — these are requisites proper to distribute. Wooden items, copper pieces, keys, knives, needle-cases, nail-cutters, felt, leather straps, hatchets, brooms, water-strainers — these are requisites proper to distribute. Whatever is even lighter than these is likewise proper to distribute. Whatever heavy requisites are other than these are not proper to distribute; all of those are to be set aside for the Saṅgha of the four directions.

Among wooden vessels, eye-cups, Dharma water-strainers, large bowls, and lacquered bowls — these too are requisites proper to distribute. Whatever light requisites among them are other than these are likewise proper to distribute. Whatever heavy requisites among them are other than these are not proper to distribute; all of those are to be set aside for the Saṅgha of the four directions.

Among earthenware vessels, alms bowls, small bowls, non-bowl containers, clay pots, water-jugs, small jugs, round pouring vessels — these are requisites proper to distribute.

Whatever light requisites among them other than these are likewise proper to distribute. Whatever heavy requisites among them are not proper to distribute; all of those are to be set aside for the Saṅgha of the four directions.

Dye that has been boiled is to be used for washing the robes of the Saṅgha of the four directions. Whatever dye has not been boiled is to be distributed. The five principal dyes are not to be distributed. If there are thrones made of precious materials, they are to be converted and distributed. If something small is made of iron and is fit for use as a requisite, it is to be kept. If it is a heavy requisite of any other kind, it is not proper to distribute it.

Furthermore, there are five kinds of things that are not to be sold, not to be held, not to be needed, not to be distributed, not to be given to others, and not proper to give to anyone at all. What are they? The property of a temple, the property of a residence, the bathing room of the community garden, bedding, and human requisites.

What are human requisites? The Blessed One declared: whether belonging to the Saṅgha or to a stūpa, these are called human requisites.

What are non-human requisites? Yaks, bulls, goats, sheep, and buffalo — these belong either to the Saṅgha or to a stūpa, and the Blessed One declared them to be permitted. These are called non-human requisites.

What are occupied requisites? A village or a forest that is occupied by a woman, a man, a hermaphrodite, a neuter, or a person of both characteristics — that which is occupied by another is called an occupied requisite.

What are unoccupied requisites? A village or a forest that is not occupied by any woman, man, hermaphrodite, neuter, or person of both characteristics — that which is unoccupied is called an unoccupied requisite.

What are requisites that must be received? That which monks receive from others and then eat — what are these? Apart from water and tooth-cleaning wood, everything else that is placed in the mouth and eaten is a requisite that must be received. These are called requisites that must be received.

What are requisites that need not be received? That which monks may eat without having received it from another — what are these? All requisites that are freely used, and what is placed in the mouth, namely water and tooth-cleaning wood. These are called requisites that need not be received.

What is the robe-right of the deceased? The robe-right of the deceased belonging to the five groups is a robe-right of the deceased, and the Blessed One declared that it is to be distributed at all times among the five groups, whether within the rains retreat or outside the rains retreat, without exception. These are called the robe-right of the deceased.

What is the robe-right of the time of signs? The robe obtained in the fifth year, the sixth year, at a great festival, or when examined and received — the Blessed One declared that this too is to be distributed at all times, whether during the rains retreat or outside it. These are called the robe-right of the time of signs.

What are rag robes? Monks are permitted to keep five kinds of rag robes: those scorched by fire, those gnawed by yaks, those gnawed by mice, robes that have been reclaimed, and those that are rotten. These are called rag robes.

What is the enema procedure? The enema procedure that the Blessed One permitted for monks is for those suffering from eye disease, in the same way as it was granted to the venerable Pilindavatsa, in full detail as it appears in the Vinaya. That is called the enema procedure given through the nose.

What is the enema procedure administered through the lower passage? Monks should not administer an enema through the lower passage as long as another means of treatment is available. If they do so, it becomes a serious offense.

The procedure is to be performed only when no other means is available. That is called the enema procedure administered through the lower passage.

What is the surgical procedure? Monks should not perform a surgical procedure on the face as long as another means of treatment is available. If they do so, it becomes a serious offense. The procedure is to be performed only when no other means is available. That is called the surgical procedure.

What is the hair-removal procedure? Monks should not remove bodily hair from limbs other than the hair of the head and the beard. If they do so, it becomes a serious offense. That is called the hair-removal procedure.

What is the hair-cutting procedure? Monks should not cut hair haphazardly in all directions; they should cut it on one side and trim it in order of seniority. Moreover, once hair has been cut with a razor, it should not be raised up again. If it is raised up, it becomes a serious offense. That is called the hair-cutting procedure.

What is the intentional preparation and consumption of food? The five kinds of seeds are to be rendered allowable by the five means of rendering allowable, and then eaten. The eight drinks are to be diluted with water. The ten kinds of cloth are to be rendered of a bad color by one of the three means of discoloring, and then kept. In this way they are to be intentionally prepared and used.

What is the eating of fruit? In the city of Vaiśālī, a great quantity of fruit was prepared for individual use by monks and eaten; whereupon the Blessed One declared: "One should not prepare fruit for individual use and eat it; rather, one should distribute it to the Saṅgha." The Blessed One said, "Let it be distributed to the Saṅgha," and thereupon some monks took one, two, or three portions, some received none at all, and others were left with a surplus. When matters had come to this pass, the monks reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Distribute it evenly to all." They continued selecting and distributing, but while selecting and distributing in accordance with the Blessed One's ruling, they began to pick and choose as they distributed. The Blessed One declared: "One should not pick and choose while distributing." Then they began to indicate portions with their fingers while taking them. The Blessed One declared: "One should not indicate with a finger while taking." Being unable to distribute evenly to all, they fell into dispute. The monks reported this state of affairs to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: "Make a brief formal request: whoever wishes to consume the full portion shall be rendered allowable by the five means by which a monk renders things allowable, and after receiving it, may eat it." That is called the complete use of fruit.

What is the complete use of human goods? Seats made for humans — whether of gold, silver, crystal, or vaidūrya — monks may sit upon but should not use as vessels. That is called the complete use of human goods.

What is the complete use of non-human goods? In a god's dwelling, a nāga's dwelling, or a yakṣa's dwelling — walking on floors, ascending stairs, sitting on seats, and using vessels made of gold, silver, crystal, or vaidūrya — all of these monks are permitted to render allowable and use. That is called the complete use of non-human goods.

What is the Vinaya recension compiled by the five hundred? Not long after the buddha, the Blessed One, had passed into nirvāṇa, five hundred monks assembled in the city of Rājagṛha and compiled all the Sūtras, all the Vinaya, and all the Abhidharma. This is called the Vinaya recension compiled by the five hundred. What is the Vinaya recension compiled by the seven hundred?

One hundred and ten years after the buddha, the Blessed One, had passed into nirvāṇa, the monks dwelling in the city of Vaiśālī brought forth ten improper matters. These were: inferior sūtras, inferior Vinaya, inferior teaching of the Teacher, things contradicting the sūtras, things not arising from the Vinaya, and things discordant with the nature of reality — all of which the monks of Vaiśālī declared allowable, practiced, practiced extensively, and proclaimed widely. Thereupon seven hundred monks assembled together and declared: "This is not the Dharma. This is not the Vinaya. This is not the teaching of the Teacher." Having openly suppressed these matters, this is called the Vinaya recension compiled by the seven hundred.

What is the arising of the Vinaya? The following are called the arising of the Vinaya: the eighteen topics of Vinaya together with the two divisions of individual liberation; the Vinaya surpassing by one; the Vinaya resembling the mother; the fifth Vinaya; the sixteenth Vinaya; the Vinaya called Māṇavakū; the minor Vinaya; the abbreviated Vinaya; the narrative bases; the narrative matter; the Questions of Upāli; the common and the uncommon; the training rules; the five hundred scriptural transmissions; the five hundred sections of birth stories; and the five hundred former deeds — all of these are called the arising of the Vinaya.

What is the dark exposition? There are four dark expositions. What are the four? Here, when a monk comes forward and says, "I myself heard this directly from the Blessed One and received it directly: such and such a Dharma and such and such a Vinaya — this is what the Teacher taught," one should neither rejoice at that nor disparage it. Without either rejoicing or disparaging, one should listen carefully with one's ears, take up the words and letters of the Dharma, and examine them against the sūtras and against the Vinaya. If, upon being examined against the sūtras and against the Vinaya, it is found to be discordant with the sūtras, not in conformity with the Vinaya, and discordant with the nature of reality, then one should speak these words: "Venerable one, such Dharma as this was not taught by the Blessed One, nor was it held as conforming to the nature of reality by the Venerable One. Such Dharma as this, when I examine it against the sūtras and against the Vinaya, is found to be discordant with the sūtras, not in accord with the Vinaya, and contradictory to the nature of reality. Therefore: this is not the Dharma, this is not the Vinaya, and the Teacher did not teach it thus — this is to be understood, and it is to be abandoned."

Furthermore, when another monk comes forward and says, "In such and such a place there dwells a great community of monks, together with elders and together with those bearing individual liberation, and it is from before that assembly of the resident community of monks that I directly heard and directly received the following: this is the Dharma" — and so on, as before — one should speak to him in these words: "Venerable one, that community of monks regards such Dharma as this as Dharma and as Vinaya; but because it has been stated to be non-Dharma and non-Vinaya, you, Venerable one, have received it as non-Dharma" — and so on, as before, it is to be abandoned.

Furthermore, when yet another monk comes forward and those monks say, "In such and such a place there dwells an especially large assembly of monks — monks who hold the sūtras, monks who hold the Vinaya, and monks who hold what resembles the mother — and it is from before those monks that I directly heard and directly received the following: such is the Dharma" —

"This is the Dharma" — and so on as before, having so spoken, one should say to that monk the following: "Venerable one, the monks perceive such teachings as these to be Dharma and to be Vinaya; but because it has been stated to be non-Dharma and non-Vinaya, the Venerable one has received what is contrary to the Dharma" — and so on as before, it is to be abandoned.

Furthermore, when yet another monk comes forward and says the following: "In such and such a place there dwell elder monks, and whatever elder monks there may be, learned monks, and whatever learned monks there may be, and chief monks, and whatever chief monks there may be — it is from before those monks dwelling there that I directly heard and directly received the following" — and so on as before — one should say to him the following: "Venerable one, that monk perceives such things as Dharma and as Vinaya; but because it has been stated to be non-Dharma and non-Vinaya, the Venerable one has in that way received what is non-Dharma" — and so on as before, it is to be abandoned.

Now, why is something called a "dark teaching"? Whatever those are taught darkly, they are taught darkly — that is to say, they are taught as dark. They are taught as non-noble. Therefore they are called "dark teachings."

And why is it that what they have spoken — non-Dharma — is to be cut off, and the Dharma collected, and the individual reflections of the genuine Dharma removed? It is so that one who becomes a śrāvaka without fear will do so through this speech of the Buddha. This is what is called a "dark teaching."

Now, what is a "great teaching"? There are four great teachings. What are the four? Here, when a monk comes forward and says the following: "I directly heard and directly received the following from before the Blessed One himself: this is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is what the Teacher has taught" — when he says this, one should neither rejoice nor criticize. Neither rejoicing nor criticizing, one should listen with one's ears and take up the words and letters of the Dharma, and then compare them with the sūtras and test them against the Vinaya. If, when compared with the sūtras and tested against the Vinaya, they are in accord with the sūtras, appear in the Vinaya, and do not conflict with the nature of reality, then one should say to him the following: "Venerable one, in that case, such Dharma as this was indeed spoken by the Blessed One, and the Venerable one has received that Dharma just as it is. I too, having compared that Dharma with the sūtras and tested it against the Vinaya, found it to be in accord with the sūtras, to arise from the Vinaya, and not to conflict with the nature of reality. This is Dharma, this is Vinaya, this is what the Teacher has taught" — one should understand it to be so and hold it.

Furthermore, when yet another monk comes forward and says the following: "In such and such a place there dwells an assembly of monks together with their elders, possessed of the code of individual liberation, and it is from before that community of monks dwelling there that I directly heard and directly received the following" — and so on as before. Having said that, one should say to him the following: "Venerable one, in that case, that community of monks perceives this Dharma to be Dharma and to be Vinaya, and because Dharma and Vinaya have been stated, the Venerable one has in that way received this Dharma well" — and so on as before, it is to be held.

Furthermore, when yet another monk comes forward and says the following: "In such and such a place there dwell a great many monks — monks who hold the sūtras, monks who hold the Vinaya, monks who hold what resembles the mother — and it is from before those monks dwelling there that I directly heard and directly received the following" —

what was directly received is as follows: "This is the Dharma" — and so on as before. When someone speaks in this way, one should respond with the following words: "Venerable one, in that case, this Dharma is perceived by that monk as Dharma and as Vinaya, and because Dharma and Vinaya have been stated, the Venerable one has also received such Dharma well" — and so on as before, it is to be held.

Furthermore, when yet another monk comes forward and speaks as follows: "In such and such a place there dwell monks who are elders, and whatever elders there may be, and those who are learned, and whoever may be learned, and those who are foremost, and whoever may be foremost — it is from before those monks dwelling there that I directly heard and directly received the following: 'This is the Dharma'" — and so on as before. When someone speaks in this way, one should respond with these words: "Venerable one, in that case, this Dharma is perceived by that monk as Dharma and as Vinaya, and because Dharma and Vinaya have been stated, the Venerable one has also received this Dharma well" — and so on as before, it is to be held.

Now, why are these called "great expositions"? This word means a great exposition — that which has been taught by a great expounder. They teach in the manner of a noble one, and therefore they are called great expositions. And why are these things declared? Fearlessly, in order to cut off what is not Dharma, to gather what is Dharma, and to individually dispel the reflections and images of the true Dharma, one becomes a hearer — that is to say, in order to cut off what is not Dharma and to gather what is Dharma, this is called a great exposition.

Now, monks, the first four great expositions that were stated above should be well and thoroughly examined by monks and properly demonstrated, and having recognized them as "This is not Dharma, this is not Vinaya, this was not taught by the Teacher," they are to be discarded. And the latter four great expositions stated here should be well and thoroughly examined by monks and properly demonstrated, and having recognized them as "This is Dharma, this is Vinaya, this was taught by the Teacher," they are to be held.

What is "mixed"? Whatever, from the cause of being individually established in medicines of roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits, has become mixed together — that is called mixed.

What is "thoroughly mixed"? Having taken from one and from another — that which is for the morning, and that taken for the afternoon, and that for seven days, and that for as long as life lasts — when these are mixed together with one another: what is included in the morning portion should be eaten in the morning; once the morning has passed, it may not be eaten. What is taken and becomes the afternoon portion, or the seven-day portion, or the portion for as long as life lasts — when these are mixed together with one another, it may be eaten in the afternoon; once the afternoon has passed, it may not be eaten. What is taken as the seven-day portion and what is taken as the portion for as long as life lasts, when mixed together, may be eaten as the seven-day portion; once seven days have passed, it may not be eaten. What lasts for as long as life lasts may similarly be eaten for as long as life lasts. This is called "thoroughly mixed."

What is "suitable for the recreation hall"? Whatever a monk takes up while staying in a recreation hall, or staying in the dwelling of a recreation hall, or has caused to be received — saying "This belongs to so-and-so; give this to him" — if received in such a manner, that is called "suitable for the recreation hall."

What is "suitable for a forest"? "Forest" refers to a grove of trees. Whatever branches, leaves, fronds, and —

flowers that spread and cover one another up to the distance of one league — within that boundary, a monk may set down his robes wherever he pleases, and remain until dawn wherever he pleases. This is called "suitable for a forest."

What is "suitable for a circuit"? When there are many surrounding quarters belonging to individual cells in a monastic hall of the Saṅgha, whatever is obtained there is to be divided and used just as it was separately consecrated. This is called "suitable for a circuit."

What is "suitable for a region"? At the time of Jambudvīpa, monks may eat food suitable for the northern continent of Uttarakuru. "Suitable for a region" means: at the time of this continent of Jambudvīpa, the northern continent of Uttarakuru is midday. Just as the correlation is applied across all four continents according to the time of Jambudvīpa, food that is suitable in that region is called "suitable for a region."

What is "suitable for a direction"? Taking and eating what is received in a reviling district is permissible for monks. Monks of great miraculous power and great might who go out to a reviling district to collect alms — when the people of the reviling district, rather than giving directly from hand to hand, toss the food down in front of them — those monks, not knowing how to proceed, reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: receiving is to be understood in five ways. What are the five ways of receiving? Doing so with the body directed toward a body; doing so with the body directed toward something held by a body; doing so with something held by the body directed toward a body; doing so with something held by the body directed toward something held by the body; and doing so with what has been thrown down — receiving what has been cast. These five constitute what is called "suitable for a direction."

What is "suitable for a land"? In a snowy land, sandals with uppers and sandals without uppers are said to be permitted; in other lands they are not permitted. In the land of Uṣmapārantaka, the use of hides and regular bathing are said to be permitted; in other lands they are not. In frontier lands, when ten qualified members of the Saṅgha are not available, full ordination with five, provided one is a Vinaya-holder, is said to be permitted; in other lands it is not. This is called "suitable for a land."

What is "suitable for robes"? Ten types of cloth that have been cut with a weapon and made of inferior color may be kept — these are monk's permissible robes. They are as follows: wool; bark-cloth; hemp; coarse linen grass-cloth; cotton wadding; silk floss; fine soft cloth; Kashmiri silk; grass-cloth of the koṭambhaka grass; and keyūraka. These are the ten. Furthermore, seven types of cloth that, while counted as robes permissible for a monk, need not be formally sanctioned but may simply be kept, are: a loin-cloth; an upper robe; a lower robe; an upper covering; a large summer cloth; a wrapper against the itch; and a cloth for implements. These seven constitute what is called "suitable for robes."

What is "permissible sour liquid"? When monks fell ill and consulted a physician, and the physician said they should drink sour liquid, those monks, not knowing how to prepare it, reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: it is permitted for monks who have a slight fever and whose bile is agitated to prepare and drink sour liquid. How is sour liquid to be prepared? The broth from boiled rice, the rinsing water of washed rice, and the juice of root-joints are to be mixed together in hot water and drunk while it turns sour in the manner of porridge.

This is something that monks may need even at an untimely hour. The Blessed One declared: this too is permitted — that which is light, clear, and free of sediment is to be strained through cloth, diluted with water, and drunk during the daytime and up until the first watch of the night. This is what is called "permissible sour liquid."

Here ends the first aggregate on full ordination, in the manner of the non-like, from the Noble Vinaya.

The Noble Vinaya, the forty-ninth bundle.

What is the aggregate of the pravāraṇā ceremony (the invitation ceremony)? There is the pravāraṇā of opening the occasion, the pravāraṇā of presenting the opened occasion, the pravāraṇā of receiving the opened occasion, and the pravāraṇā of proclaiming the opened occasion. There is the pravāraṇā of the restoration and confession ceremony, the pravāraṇā of presenting the restoration and confession, the pravāraṇā of receiving the restoration and confession, and the pravāraṇā of proclaiming the restoration and confession. There is the pravāraṇā of faith, the pravāraṇā of presenting faith, the pravāraṇā of receiving faith, and the pravāraṇā of proclaiming faith. There is the pravāraṇā of complete purity, the pravāraṇā of presenting complete purity, the pravāraṇā of receiving complete purity, and the pravāraṇā of proclaiming complete purity. There is the pravāraṇā of faith and complete purity together, the pravāraṇā of presenting faith and complete purity, the pravāraṇā of receiving faith and complete purity, and the pravāraṇā of proclaiming faith and complete purity. There is the pravāraṇā of the stūpa, the pravāraṇā of the stūpa's material goods, the pravāraṇā of the garland of the stūpa's cloister, the pravāraṇā of the stūpa's inexhaustible fund, the pravāraṇā of the stūpa's restoration, the pravāraṇā of the stūpa's adornments, and the pravāraṇā of making offerings to the stūpa. There is the pravāraṇā of food, the pravāraṇā of food with accompaniments, the pravāraṇā of porridge, the pravāraṇā of condiments, the pravāraṇā of flavored foods, and the pravāraṇā of solid food. There is the pravāraṇā of the alms bowl, the pravāraṇā of robes, the pravāraṇā of the sitting cloth, the pravāraṇā of needles, and the pravāraṇā of the needle case. There is the pravāraṇā of lodging, the pravāraṇā of receiving lodging, the pravāraṇā of giving lodging, and the pravāraṇā of distributing lodging individually. There is the pravāraṇā of the preceptor, the pravāraṇā of the co-resident, the pravāraṇā of the ācārya, and the pravāraṇā of the attendant. There is the pravāraṇā of the preceptor, ācārya, co-resident, and attendant together. There is the pravāraṇā of monks, the pravāraṇā of novices, the pravāraṇā of material goods, the pravāraṇā of the temple, the pravāraṇā of beds and seats, the pravāraṇā of new construction, and the pravāraṇā of engaging in new construction. There is the pravāraṇā of paying homage, the pravāraṇā of sour liquid, the pravāraṇā of powdered medicine, the pravāraṇā of medicine, and the pravāraṇā of drinks. There is the pravāraṇā of leather goods, the pravāraṇā of sandals, the pravāraṇā of wooden sandals, the pravāraṇā of what is dragged, the pravāraṇā of what is carried on the shoulder, and the pravāraṇā of nets. There is the pravāraṇā of needles and nets, the pravāraṇā of onion sprouts, the pravāraṇā of razors, the pravāraṇā of razor cases, the pravāraṇā of curved keys, the pravāraṇā of door bolts, the pravāraṇā of conveyances, and the pravāraṇā of parasols.

There is the pravāraṇā of fans, the pravāraṇā of fly-whisks with tails, the pravāraṇā of fly-whisk handles, the pravāraṇā of mirrors, the pravāraṇā of garlands, perfumes, and unguents, the pravāraṇā of dancing, singing, and playing music, the pravāraṇā of tooth-cleaning sticks, the pravāraṇā of eye medicine, the pravāraṇā of eye-medicine applicators, the pravāraṇā of eye-medicine containers, the pravāraṇā of mallets, the pravāraṇā of lying down, the pravāraṇā of sitting, the pravāraṇā of knee-clasping, the pravāraṇā of striking-sticks, the pravāraṇā of belts, the pravāraṇā of pebbles, the pravāraṇā of wrapping cloth and tying off knots, the pravāraṇā of earth, the pravāraṇā of supporting trees, the pravāraṇā of material things, the pravāraṇā of groves, the pravāraṇā of disputes, the pravāraṇā of schism, the pravāraṇā of assemblies, and the pravāraṇā of prostrations. This completes the chapter on two matters in the manner of the mother.

What is the pravāraṇā of opening an opportunity? The Blessed One permitted monks to open an opportunity by means of three grounds — seeing, hearing, and suspicion — and declared: the monks who have dwelt through the rains retreat, having come together as one, shall open an opportunity to the Saṅgha on the grounds of seeing, hearing, and suspicion. Why was the opening of an opportunity permitted? Because it serves as a good friend to monks: they speak to one another, remind one another, and point things out, guiding each other; and when, through the force of praise or intimidation by fear, one who is pure and free of fault and blameless comes to be held responsible for something done just then, saying, "I am indeed pure, I am indeed free of fault" — this is called the pravāraṇā of opening an opportunity.

What is the pravāraṇā of tendering a proxy invitation? A monk who is ill and cannot go to the place of the pravāraṇā of opening an opportunity should send a proxy invitation. If one who is not ill fails to go, it becomes a transgression. If there is present before him an evident danger of having his livelihood cut off, or his celibate life cut off, or any one of the eight kinds of obstruction, he too may send a proxy invitation. One who has been seized by another and rendered powerless may likewise send a proxy invitation.

The manner of tendering it is as follows: one rises from one's seat, arranges the upper robe over one shoulder, removes one's sandals, sits in a crouch before a monk, joins the palms together, and speaks these words: "Venerable one, please attend. Today is the pravāraṇā of the fifteenth of the Saṅgha. As for me, the monk called such-and-such, in this pravāraṇā of the fifteenth, I ask the venerable Saṅgha to open an opportunity for me, the monk called such-and-such, on the three grounds of seeing, hearing, and suspicion. Venerable one, please be kind to me. Those who, being compassionate and out of compassion, know and see a fault — let the venerable one speak to me of it. Venerable one, please instruct me, and I shall act in accordance with the Dharma." This is to be said in this way two or three times. The other should respond, "Very well," and the second should say, "Excellent!" If one is able to do so in that way, well and good; if one is unable, one may tender it while seated. If one is unable even seated, one may tender it while lying down. If even lying down one is unable, if one says even briefly, "I am tendering a proxy invitation," the proxy invitation has been tendered. If one says, "Please speak the proxy invitation on my behalf," that too counts as having tendered the proxy invitation. If one is unable by any means to tender the proxy invitation verbally, if it is tendered by a bodily gesture, that too is counted as having tendered the proxy invitation.

If one is unable even by bodily gesture, then if the proxy invitation is tendered by a mere verbal signal, that too is counted as having tendered the proxy invitation. If one is unable by bodily gesture and also unable verbally, then the entire Saṅgha should go to that place, or alternatively that monk should be brought here. If the entire Saṅgha does not go to that place and that monk is not brought there either, then the Saṅgha, by having performed the act without a complete assembly, will have committed a transgression. If the monk who has received the proxy invitation dies after having accepted it, that is counted as the proxy invitation not having been tendered, and the proxy invitation must be tendered to someone else. Likewise, if one acknowledges oneself to be a layman, that too is counted as the proxy invitation not having been tendered, and the proxy invitation must be tendered to someone else. Furthermore, if one acknowledges oneself to be a non-ordained ascetic (śramaṇa), a eunuch, one who has expelled a nun, one who has killed one's father, one who has killed one's mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused schism in the Saṅgha, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from the body of a Tathāgata, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, one who is a habitual thief, one who has previously broken their precepts, one who has previously committed an offense, or one who resides in a different realm — if one acknowledges oneself to be any of these, that too is counted as the proxy invitation not having been tendered, and the proxy invitation must be tendered to someone else. If one acknowledges oneself to be a novice, that too is counted as the proxy invitation not having been properly opened. If one acknowledges oneself to be one who has caused schism in the Saṅgha, one who is not residing in the community, one who is residing separately, one who has taken a partisan position, or one who has returned their training — that too is counted as the proxy invitation not having been tendered. This concludes the section on the proper conduct of tendering the proxy invitation.

What is the proper conduct for receiving the proxy invitation? When a monk receives the proxy invitation from the Saṅgha, he should receive it in the following manner. Whether it is one receiving on behalf of one, one on behalf of two, or one on behalf of many — he should receive it for as many as the names he is able to recite. The monk who has received the proxy invitation must not run, must not leap, must not jump, must not travel underground, and must not travel through the sky. He must not receive the proxy invitation from beyond the boundary. He should receive the proxy invitation mindfully from within the boundary. If he receives it from beyond the boundary, it becomes an offense. However, if, while receiving the invitation from within the boundary, a manifest danger arises that threatens his livelihood, his celibacy, or involves any one of the eight kinds of interruption, and he nevertheless comes from beyond the boundary, there is no offense. This concludes the section on the proper conduct of receiving the proxy invitation.

What is the proper conduct for reciting the proxy invitation? If the monk who is to recite the proxy invitation has not arrived within the Saṅgha and the time has passed, that is counted as the proxy invitation not having been recited. If one acknowledges oneself to be a layman, that too is counted as the proxy invitation not having been recited. If one acknowledges oneself to be a non-ordained ascetic, a eunuch, one who has expelled a nun, one who has killed one's father, one who has killed one's mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused schism in the Saṅgha, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from the body of a Tathāgata, a tīrthika, one who has gone over to the tīrthikas, a habitual thief, one who has previously broken their precepts, one who has previously committed an offense, or one who resides in a different realm — that too is counted as the proxy invitation not having been recited. If one acknowledges oneself to be a novice, that too is counted as the proxy invitation not having been recited. If one acknowledges oneself to be one who has caused schism in the Saṅgha, one who is not residing in the community, one who is residing separately, or one who has taken a partisan position —

— that too is counted as the proxy invitation not having been recited. If one acknowledges oneself to be one who has surrendered the training, that too is counted as the proxy invitation not having been recited.

A monk who has recited the proxy invitation must not, after giving the proxy invitation, lie down to sleep, nor enter into meditative absorption; rather, he must recite the invitation consciously and with full vigilance. And this is how it is to be recited: after the request has been made, one rises from one's seat, arranges the upper robe over one shoulder, sits respectfully in a squatting posture before the monk who is to open the occasion, joins the palms together, and speaks these words:

"Please attend, venerable one. Today is the Saṅgha's fifteenth-day occasion for opening. I, the monk called such-and-such, also have today's fifteenth-day occasion for opening. In the three grounds of what has been seen, what has been heard, and what has been suspected with respect to me, the monk called such-and-such, may the venerable one open the occasion before the noble Saṅgha on my behalf. Please, venerable one, have compassion for me. Out of that compassion, please inform me, venerable one, of my offenses and tell me what has been seen. May the venerable one instruct me accordingly, and I shall restore them in accordance with the Dharma."

This is to be said in this way two and then three times. The other monk should respond: "Very well." To the second repetition he should say: "Good." If it is recited in four modes, it counts as the proxy invitation not having been recited. And what are those four? Shamelessness, heedlessness, lying down in sleep, and having entered meditative absorption. Of these, the two modes of shamelessness and heedlessness entail an offense. The two modes of lying down in sleep and having entered meditative absorption entail no offense. This is called the section on reciting the proxy invitation for opening the occasion.

What is the section on the restoration ceremony (poṣadha)? The Blessed One permitted monks to perform the restoration ceremony twice each month. The monks are to gather together and each one is to examine his own continuum — whether, within that period, any transgressions whatsoever have arisen in the continuum of his nighttime conduct, his daytime conduct, or the conduct of an entire month. If any have arisen, he is to confess them to a trustworthy monk if one can be found. If none can be found, he should dedicate them in his mind. This is called the section on the restoration ceremony. And why is it called the restoration ceremony? Because through it one will decidedly abandon sinful and non-virtuous phenomena, mental afflictions, what has not yet emerged fully, and that which is impure by its very nature, and one will come to obtain the intrinsic nature of purity nearby. For this reason it is called the restoration ceremony. This concludes the section on the restoration ceremony.

What is the section on presenting the restoration ceremony? A monk who is ill and cannot go to the place of the restoration ceremony is said to present the restoration ceremony. If one who is not ill does not go, it becomes a misdeed. If someone who is clearly present and evidently endangered — whether their life is in danger, or their practice of the holy life is in danger, or there is danger from any of the eight kinds of interruptions — that person too may present the restoration ceremony. Even one who has been seized and is without power may present the restoration ceremony.

And it is presented in this manner: rising from one's seat, arranging the upper robe over one shoulder, sitting respectfully in a squatting posture before the monk, joining the palms together, and reciting these words:

"Please attend, venerable one. Today is the Saṅgha's fifteenth-day restoration ceremony. I, the monk called such-and-such, also have the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony. I, the monk called such-and-such, present my faith and complete purity to the restoration ceremony."

Likewise, this is to be recited two and then three times. The other monk should respond: "Very well."

The second monk should respond: "Very well." If one is able to present it in that way, excellent. If one is unable, one should say while seated, "I present my restoration ceremony." That too counts as having presented it. If even sitting is impossible, presenting it while lying down likewise counts as having presented it. If one is too ill even for that and one says, "I am presenting my restoration ceremony," that too counts as having presented it. If one says, "Please speak on my behalf," that also counts as having presented the restoration ceremony. If one toward whom it was not directed indicates it by means of the body, that too counts as having presented the restoration ceremony. If it is not by the body but is declared by speech, that too counts as having presented the restoration ceremony. If it is neither by body nor by speech, then the entire Saṅgha should go to that person's side, or that person should be brought into the midst of the Saṅgha. If the Saṅgha neither goes to that person nor brings that person into the Saṅgha, and the Saṅgha performs the act without being fully assembled, it will have transgressed and the act will be invalidated. This is called the complete procedure for presenting the restoration ceremony.

If the monk who has undertaken to receive the restoration ceremony accepts it and the time then passes on that very day without the restoration having been presented, it counts as not having been presented, and it must be presented to another. If one has acknowledged oneself to be a layperson, the restoration ceremony has not been presented; it must be presented to another. If one has acknowledged oneself to be a śramaṇa, a hermaphrodite, one who has expelled a nun, a parricide, a matricide, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one who with malicious intent has drawn blood from a Tathāgata's body, a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika), one who has gone over to the non-Buddhist adherents, a thief who has entered the order under false pretenses, one who has previously fallen, one who has previously committed an offense, or one who has declared oneself to be residing in another destiny — in any of these cases the restoration ceremony has not been presented, and it must be presented to another. If one has acknowledged oneself to be an icchantica (one who has severed the wholesome roots), that too means the restoration ceremony has not been presented, and it must be presented to another. If one has acknowledged oneself to be non-residing, separately residing, or one who has relinquished the training, that too means the restoration ceremony has not been presented, and it must be presented to another. This is called the complete procedure for presenting the restoration ceremony.

What is the complete procedure for receiving the restoration ceremony? The monk who receives the restoration ceremony, having accepted it, must not run, must not jump, must not leap, must not travel underground, must not travel through the sky, and must not receive the restoration ceremony from outside the boundary. Rather, one should receive it mindfully from within the boundary. If one receives it from outside the boundary, it constitutes an offense. If one who receives it from within the boundary is confronted directly and visibly with a threat to one's life, a threat to one's celibacy, or any one of the eight kinds of threatening obstruction, then receiving it from outside the boundary incurs no offense. This is called the complete procedure for receiving the restoration ceremony.

What is the complete procedure for reciting the restoration ceremony? If the monk who is to recite the restoration ceremony dies after the time has passed without having come to the Saṅgha, it is called not having recited the restoration ceremony. If one has acknowledged oneself to be a layperson, that too is called not having recited the restoration ceremony. The passage from "a śramaṇa, a hermaphrodite, one who has expelled a nun" down to "one who has declared oneself to be residing in another destiny" applies as before — if one has acknowledged oneself to be any of those, it is called not having recited the restoration ceremony. If one has acknowledged oneself to be an icchantica, that too is called not having recited the restoration ceremony. If one has acknowledged oneself to have caused a schism in the Saṅgha, to be non-residing, separately residing, one who has inclined toward a faction, or one who has relinquished the training, that too is called not having recited the restoration ceremony. This is called the complete procedure for reciting the restoration ceremony.

What is the complete procedure for faith? Faith means presenting faith toward those matters that are to be done in accordance with the Saṅgha's Dharma through one's view, one's intelligence, one's wish, and one's thought; rejoicing in those matters that are to be done in accordance with the Saṅgha's Dharma;

approaching, accepting, and undertaking to accept — this is called the complete procedure for presenting faith.

What is the complete procedure for the impoverished presentation of faith? When a monk who is ill is unable to go to the place of the restoration ceremony, he should present faith by proxy. If he does not go while he is not ill, it becomes a transgression. If he is in a situation where he is manifestly threatened by something that would interrupt his livelihood, interrupt his celibate life, or interrupt it through any one of the eight kinds of interruption, he too should present faith by proxy. One who has been seized by those without authority should also present faith by proxy.

This is how the proxy presentation is to be made. Rising from one's seat, arranging the upper robe over one shoulder, one sits respectfully before the monk, joins the palms together, and says the following: "Venerable one, please take note. I, the monk known as so-and-so, present faith toward those matters that are to be done in accordance with the Saṅgha's Dharma. I rejoice in those matters that are to be done in accordance with the Saṅgha's Dharma. I accept them. I undertake to accept them." This is to be said two and three times. The other should say "Appropriate," and the second should say "Excellent."

If one is able to present it in that way, well and good. If one is unable to do so standing, one should present it while seated. If one is unable to do so seated, one should present it while lying down. If one is unable even then, and while gravely ill simply says "I present faith," the faith has been presented. Even if one says "Please recite the faith on my behalf," the faith has been presented. If one is unable to do so by speech but makes a bodily sign, the faith has been presented. If one is unable to use the body but makes a verbal gesture, the faith has been presented. If one makes a gesture with both body and speech, the faith has been given.

If one is unable by body and unable by speech, then let the entire Saṅgha go there, or let the entire Saṅgha bring that monk. If the entire Saṅgha does not go there and that monk is not brought there, it constitutes non-assembly, and those who perform Saṅgha acts will have acted transgressively.

If the monk receiving the faith, having received it, dies in that very place before the time has passed, it is called faith not yet presented, and the faith must be presented to another. If one has acknowledged oneself as a layman, it is called faith not yet presented, and the faith must be presented to another. From the category of one who has been expelled as a wandering ascetic, a eunuch, or as having expelled a bhikṣuṇī — through to one who resides elsewhere — even if one acknowledges it oneself as before, it is called faith not yet presented, and the faith must be presented to another. If one has acknowledged oneself as not being a eunuch, it is called faith not yet presented. If one has acknowledged oneself as having caused a schism in the Saṅgha, as non-residing, as separately residing, as having inclined toward a faction, or as having relinquished the training, even so it is called faith not yet presented. This is called the complete procedure for the impoverished presentation of faith.

What is the complete procedure for receiving faith? A monk who receives faith from another monk should do so as follows: he may receive it for one from one, for two from one, or for many from one — he should receive it for as many as he is able to name by name.

The monk receiving faith, having received it, should not run, should not go quickly, should not jump, should not leap, should not travel underground, should not travel through the sky, and should not receive it from outside the boundary. He should receive faith knowingly from within the boundary. If he receives it from outside the boundary, it becomes a transgression.

If he receives it from within the boundary, and there is an interruption of livelihood, an interruption of celibate life,

any one of the eight interruptions, if a manifest fear of any such interruption has arisen, then even if he receives it from outside the boundary, there is no transgression. This is called the full section on receiving faith.

What is the full section on declaring faith? If the monk who has given faith passes away before coming to the Saṅgha, having let the appointed time go by without declaring the faith — this is called undeclared faith. If he himself avows that he is a layman — this is called undeclared faith. From "called a wanderer, a hermaphrodite, or an expelled nun" up through and including "residing in another destiny" — as before — if he himself makes such an avowal, it is called undeclared faith. If he himself avows that the food is not proper food — this too is called undeclared faith. If he himself avows that he has divided the Saṅgha, or has left it, or is living separately, or has gone over to another side, or has relinquished the training — this too is called undeclared faith.

The monk who declares faith, having received it, should not lie down and should not enter meditative absorption. He should declare the faith with vigilance. He should declare it in the following manner. Rising from his seat, arranging the upper robe over one shoulder, sitting respectfully before the monk with joined palms, he should speak these words: "Attend to me, venerable one. I, the monk called such-and-such, offer faith to you who act in accordance with the Dharma of the Saṅgha. I rejoice in your acting in accordance with the Dharma of the Saṅgha. I approve and follow." He should say this two times and three times. The other should respond the first time with "Very well," and the second time with "Excellent." If performed in four conditions, it is called undeclared faith. What are the four? Shamelessness, heedlessness, lying down in sleep, and being in meditative absorption. Of these, the two conditions of shamelessness and heedlessness incur a transgression. The two conditions of lying down in sleep and being in meditative absorption involve no transgression. This is called the full section on declaring faith.

What is the full section on offering the declaration of purity? A monk who is ill and unable to go to the site of the restoration ceremony should offer the declaration of purity. If he does not go when he is not ill, it becomes a wrongdoing. But if an interruption of his livelihood, or an interruption of his celibate life, or a manifest fear arising from any one of the eight interruptions has occurred, he too should offer the declaration of purity. One who has been seized by a power beyond his control should also offer the declaration of purity.

He should offer it in the following manner. Rising from his seat, arranging the upper robe over one shoulder, sitting respectfully before the monk with joined palms, he should say these words: "Attend to me, venerable one. Today is the Saṅgha's fifteenth-day restoration ceremony. I, the monk called such-and-such — today also being the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony — if my obstructing factors are fully pure, may the venerable one accept the declaration of my purity.

"I, the monk called such-and-such, offer the declaration of purity for the restoration ceremony. Because when the venerable one offers the declaration of purity, he should listen and declare his purity, and by his declaration it will be understood" — he should say this two or three times. The other should respond: "Very well." The second monk should say: "Excellent!"

If he is able to offer it in that manner, well and good. If he is unable to stand, he should offer it seated. If he is unable even seated, he should offer it lying down. If he is unable even lying down, he should say in a soft voice, "I offer the declaration of purity," and this counts as having offered the declaration of purity. If he says, "Please declare my purity," this too counts as having offered the declaration of purity. If he is unable to speak but offers it by a bodily gesture, this counts as having offered the declaration of purity. If he is unable to use his body but gives a verbal indication, this counts as having offered the declaration of purity. If he gives an indication by both body and speech, this likewise counts as having offered the declaration of purity.

If he is unable to give any indication by body or speech, then the entire Saṅgha should go to him, or that monk should be brought here. If the entire Saṅgha does not go to him and that monk is not brought, then the formal act has been performed without a complete assembly, and the Saṅgha members will have committed a transgression.

If the monk who has received the declaration of purity, having taken it, dies that very day before the time has passed, this is called "the declaration of purity not having been offered," and the declaration of purity should be offered to another. If he himself acknowledges that he is a layman, this is called "the declaration of purity not having been offered," and the declaration of purity should be offered to another.

From the case of a novice, a paṇḍaka, or one who has been expelled from the community of nuns, down to the case of one residing in another destiny, it is as stated before: even if he himself acknowledges such a condition, it is called "the declaration of purity not having been offered," and the declaration of purity should be offered to another. Likewise, if he himself acknowledges that he is a paṇḍaka, it is called "the declaration of purity not having been offered."

If he himself acknowledges that the Saṅgha has been split, that he is not residing with the community, that he resides separately, that he has sided with one party, or that he has given up his training, this is called "the declaration of purity not having been offered." This is what is known as the proper procedure for offering the declaration of purity.

Now, what is the proper procedure for receiving the declaration of purity? When a monk receives the declaration of purity from another monk, he should receive it in the following manner: one receiving from one, one receiving from two, one receiving from many — whatever names he is able to pronounce, he should receive that many declarations.

The monk who has received the declaration of purity, having accepted it, should not run, should not go quickly, should not leap, should not jump, should not travel underground, and should not travel through the air. He should not receive the declaration of purity from outside the boundary. If he receives it from outside the boundary, it constitutes a transgression. If he receives it from within the boundary while something that interrupts livelihood, something that interrupts the holy life, or any one of the eight kinds of interruption manifests as a present danger, then even if he has received it from outside the boundary, there is no offense. This is what is known as the proper procedure for receiving the declaration of purity.

Now, what is the proper procedure for declaring the declaration of purity? If the monk who has received the declaration of purity, having accepted it, dies before the time has passed without coming into the Saṅgha's midst, this is called "the declaration of purity not having been declared." If he himself acknowledges that he is a layman, this is called "the declaration of purity not having been declared." From the case of a śrāmaṇera, a paṇḍaka, or one who has been expelled from the nuns' community, down to the case of one residing in another destiny, it is as before: even if he himself acknowledges such a condition, this is called "the declaration of purity not having been declared." If he himself acknowledges that he is a paṇḍaka, this is called "the declaration of purity not having been declared." If the Saṅgha has been split, or

or not residing, or residing separately, or approaching a side party, or having relinquished the training — if he himself acknowledges any such condition, this is called "the declaration of purity not having been declared."

A monk who has declared his purity, having received his declaration of purity, must not lie down to sleep and must not enter into meditative absorption. Rather, with vigilance he should declare his purity. To do so, he should rise from his seat, arrange his outer robe over one shoulder, squat respectfully before a monk, press his palms together, and speak these words: "Venerable sir, please attend. Today is the Saṅgha's fifteenth-day restoration ceremony. I, the monk called such-and-such, likewise observe the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony. Even the obstructing factors pertaining to the monk called such-and-such are purified — so I myself declare. If he offers purity to the restoration ceremony, I shall declare it in his name. Please also accept the tooth-wood." He should speak thus two and three times. The other monk should say, "Very well." The second response is "Excellent!" In four circumstances, however, this is called "the declaration of purity not having been declared." What are the four? Shamelessness, heedlessness, falling asleep, and entering meditative absorption. Of these, shamelessness and heedlessness — these two constitute an offense. Falling asleep and entering meditative absorption — these two incur no offense. This is called "the fully detailed account of declaring purity."

What is the fully detailed account of faith combined with purity? Wherever a restoration ceremony or a Saṅgha act is being performed, one should offer faith and purity combined therein. This is called "the fully detailed account of faith combined with purity."

What is the fully detailed account of offering faith and purity? If a monk is ill and cannot go to the place where the restoration ceremony is held, he should offer faith and purity. If he does not go while he is not yet seriously ill, he incurs an offense. But if it is evident that he is genuinely threatened — whether a threat to his livelihood, a threat to his celibate life, or an evident threat constituting any of the eight kinds of interruption — then he too should offer faith and purity. One who has been seized by a power beyond his control should also offer faith and purity.

This is how it should be offered. He should rise from his seat, arrange his outer robe over one shoulder, remove his sandals, squat respectfully before a monk, press his palms together, and speak these words: "Venerable sir, please attend. Today is the Saṅgha's fifteenth-day restoration ceremony. I, the monk called such-and-such, likewise observe the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony. My obstructing factors too are fully purified. May the venerable one also receive me as fully pure. I, the monk called such-and-such, with faith in acting in accordance with the Saṅgha's rule, offer faith, the restoration ceremony, and purity as well. On my behalf, venerable sir, please accept the tooth-wood and declare my purity. If it is declared, so it shall be understood."

He should speak thus two and three times. The other monk should say, "Very well." The second response is "Excellent!"

If he is able to offer it in that manner, well and good. If he is unable to do so standing, he should sit and offer it. If he is unable to do so sitting, he should lie down and offer it. If he is unable even lying down, then if he says even in a small voice, "I offer faith and purity," this too is considered to be an offering of faith and purity. If he says, "Please declare my faith and purity," this too is called "a declaration of faith and purity."

If it is done not by words but by a bodily gesture, this too is called "a declaration of faith and purity." If it is not by the body but indicated by speech, this too is called "a declaration of faith and purity." If both body and speech are used as signals, this is called "an offering of faith and purity." If neither body nor speech can be used as signals, then the entire Saṅgha should go to that place, or that monk should be brought there. If the entire Saṅgha does not go there and that monk is not brought there, the formal act is rendered incomplete, and the entire Saṅgha incurs a transgression.

If the monk who has received the faith and purity on another's behalf receives it and then time passes and that person dies right there, this is called "faith and purity not offered," and the faith and purity must be offered to someone else. If a person himself has acknowledged that he is a layman, this too is called "faith and purity not offered," and the faith and purity must be offered to someone else. From "one who has been expelled as a novice, a paṇḍaka, or a nun" up to "one who resides in a different destiny," it is as before: even if he himself has acknowledged it, this is called "faith and purity not offered," and the faith and purity must be offered to someone else. If a person himself has acknowledged that he is not a śramaṇa, this too is called "faith and purity not offered." If a person has himself acknowledged that he has split the Saṅgha, or that he does not reside, or that he resides separately, or that he is drawing near to departure, or that he has given up the training, this is called "faith and purity not offered." This is called the proper procedure for offering faith and purity.

What is the proper procedure for receiving faith and purity? A monk who receives purity and faith from another monk should receive it in the following manner: one from one, or one from two, or one from many — as many names as he is able to mention, that many he should receive.

A monk who has received the faith and purity must not run, must not walk swiftly, must not leap, must not jump, must not travel underground, and must not travel through the sky. He must not receive the purity and faith from outside the boundary. He should receive the faith and purity from within the boundary, with mindfulness and vigilance. If he receives the faith and purity from outside the boundary, it becomes a transgression. However, if he is receiving from within the boundary and there is evident before him a danger that would cut short his life, or cut short his celibate life, or any one of the eight kinds of interruption, then even if received from outside the boundary, there is no fault. This is called the proper procedure for receiving purity and faith.

What is the proper procedure for declaring faith and purity? If a monk who is to declare purity and faith has not come into the assembly of the Saṅgha and time passes and he dies, this is called "purity and faith not declared." If a person himself has acknowledged that he is a layman, this too is called "purity and faith not declared." From "one who has been expelled as a female ascetic, or a paṇḍaka, or a nun" up to "one who resides in a different destiny," it is as before: even if he himself has acknowledged it, this is called "purity and faith not declared." If a paṇḍaka himself has acknowledged it, this too is called "purity and faith not declared." If a person has himself acknowledged that he has split the Saṅgha, or that he does not reside, or that he resides separately, or that he is drawing near to departure,

if a person has himself acknowledged that he has given up his training, this too is called "purity and faith not declared."

A monk who has declared purity and faith, having received the declaration of purity and faith, must not lie down, must not enter meditative absorption, but must with vigilance declare purity and faith. And it is to be declared in the following manner. Rising from one's seat, arranging the upper robe over one shoulder, sitting respectfully before the monk, and joining the palms together, one should speak these words: "Venerable one, be so mindful. Today is the Saṅgha's fifteenth-day restoration ceremony, and for the monk called such-and-such it is likewise the fifteenth-day restoration ceremony. I, the monk called such-and-such, declare myself pure, and there are no obstructing factors. I offer faith toward the Saṅgha's Dharma-activities, the restoration ceremony, and the declaration of purity." This should be said in this way two times and three times. The other should respond, "It is fitting." To a second person one says simply "Excellent!"

If these four modes are present, it is called "purity and faith not declared." What are the four? Shamelessness, heedlessness, lying down in sleep, and having entered meditative absorption. Of these four, shamelessness and heedlessness constitute a case involving an offense. Lying down in sleep and having entered meditative absorption constitute a case involving no offense. This is called "the section on declaring purity and faith."

What is the section on stūpas? It is the hair-reliquary stūpa and the nail-reliquary stūpa spoken of by the Blessed One. Just as in the Vinaya it is explained at length in the section on the householder Anāthapiṇḍada's stūpa, so too it should be set forth in full here. The Blessed One declared the hair-reliquary stūpa and the nail-reliquary stūpa for the benefit of sentient beings. In this regard, the stūpa of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is to be complete in every respect. That of a pratyekabuddha is to be made without a vase-drum tier. That of an arhat is to have four tiers. That of a once-returner is to have three tiers. That of a stream-enterer is to have one tier. That of virtuous ordinary persons is to have a finial only.

Now, as for the outer enclosure precinct of a stūpa: the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, being deeply faithful and perfectly devout, went to where the Blessed One was, approached him, and bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, then sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said to the Blessed One: "When, O Blessed One, you departed to travel through the countryside, and I was unable to see the face of the Blessed One, I was utterly tormented. If the Blessed One would grant me his hair and nails, I would venerate them." The Blessed One replied to him, "This shall be your object of veneration," and gave him the hair and nails. Anāthapiṇḍada then spoke these words: "If the Blessed One permits, I shall make a stūpa from the hair and nails." The Blessed One declared: "Householder, I permit it — make both a hair-reliquary stūpa and a nail-reliquary stūpa." This is called "the section on stūpas."

What is the section on the physical objects of a stūpa? One should first establish a stūpa in a stūpa precinct, a grove, or in whatever suitable location. Then the physical objects of the stūpa should be established all around that stūpa, encircling it on all sides.

This is called "the section on the physical objects of a stūpa."

What is the section on the garland of the stūpa's cloister? The stūpa's cloister and its pillars should be described at length just as the Blessed One set them forth in the Vinaya. This is called "the section on the garland of the stūpa's cloister."

What is the section on the inexhaustible fund of the stūpa? Some merchants of the city of Vaiśālī built a stūpa for the Blessed One and constructed a cloister around it, and then offered an inexhaustible fund to the monks for the stūpa's upkeep. The monks, being uncertain, did not receive it individually. The monks in that situation then consulted the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "I permit it. Let the one who dwells in the recreation grove, or a layman, administer that inexhaustible fund of the stūpa. It should be put to use in order to render service to the stūpa. Whatever gains arise from it should be used to make offerings to the stūpa. If there is any surplus beyond that, it should be offered as a gift to the stūpa." This is called "the section on the inexhaustible fund of the stūpa."

What is the section on the restoration of a stūpa? A stūpa should be restored using balls of clay, balls of powdered stone, or balls of mud plaster. This is called "the section on the restoration of a stūpa."
