What is the section on the adornment of a stūpa? The stūpa should be adorned with parasols, victory banners, pennants and other hanging ornaments, bells, wheels, swastika designs, auspicious knot designs, encircling garlands of joy, flower garlands, festoons, strings of pearls, silk, fine silk, brocade, woolen cloth, silk-wool fabric, gold, silver, vaidūrya, crystal, conch, moonstone, coral, silver, sārasabhrama, asmagarbha, musāragalva, red pearls, and what is called "encircled by a rightward-turning spiral" — and, indeed, with all manner of adornments whatsoever that are used as decoration in the world. The stūpa should be adorned with all of these. This is called "the section on the adornment of a stūpa."

What is the section on making offerings to the stūpa? Offerings are to be made to the stūpa using flower garlands, perfume, ointment, incense, flowers, saffron powder, red sandalwood paste, mustard-oil ointment, flower garlands, garlands of lamps, garlands of fragrant substances, powder of āmalaka, powder of agarwood, powder of sandalwood, kalaṅkusāri, golden flowers, silver flowers, jeweled flowers, music, and so forth — and, indeed, using all other articles of worldly offering as well. Offerings are to be made to the stūpa in this way. One should circumambulate it, sweep it with a cloth offering, and prostrate. Hanging a bunch of garlands on a stūpa, or going around the stūpa while presenting it in some other manner, is proper for a monk. This is called "the section on making offerings to the stūpa."

What is the section on food? In whatever monastery it may be, providing food to the monks who dwell there — this is called "the section on food."

What is the section on food accompanied by condiments? If a monk finds something to eat that comes with lawful accompaniments, he should gather and eat it on account of that, and if there is food to eat again and again, he should eat at ease in both places. This is called "the section on food accompanied by condiments."

What is the section on porridge?

The Blessed One taught ten kinds of porridge for monks, as follows: milk porridge, yoghurt porridge, butter porridge, meat porridge, clarified-butter porridge, oil porridge, sesame porridge, pea porridge, fruit porridge, and water porridge. These ten kinds of porridge are to be drunk by monks with vigilance, quietly, without slurping, keeping in mind the perception that one is ill, the perception that it is a remedy, and the perception that it is a condition for practice.

Furthermore, porridge has two qualities: it dispels hunger and it dispels thirst. This is called "the section on porridge."

What is the section on solid food accompanied by condiments? The Blessed One taught nine kinds of solid food for monks, as follows: root food, stalk food, leaf food, flower food, fruit food, grain food, sesame food, meal food, and sugar food. These nine kinds of solid food are to be consumed by monks with vigilance, quietly, without crunching sounds, keeping in mind the perception that one is ill, the perception that it is medicine, the perception that it is for the benefit of others, and the perception that it is a condition for practice. This is called "the section on solid food accompanied by condiments."

What is the section on licking foods? The Blessed One taught five licking foods for monks, as follows: butter, oil, honey, molasses, and fresh butter. These five licking foods are to be licked by monks with vigilance, quietly, without crunching sounds, keeping in mind the perception that one is ill, the perception that it is medicine, the perception that it is for the benefit of others, and the perception that it is a condition for practice. This is called "the section on licking foods."

What is the section on solid foods to be eaten? The Blessed One taught five kinds of food to eat for monks, as follows: cooked rice, cooked barley, ground rice, meat, and flat bread. These five foods are to be eaten by monks with vigilance, quietly, without crunching sounds, keeping in mind the perception that one is ill, the perception that it is medicine, the perception that it is a condition for practice, and the perception that it is for the benefit of others. This is called "the section on solid foods to be eaten."

What is the section on the alms bowl? The Blessed One taught monks two kinds of alms bowl: one made of iron and one made of clay. Eight kinds of bowl are not permitted: those made of gold, silver, beryl, crystal, wood, stone, jackfruit wood, and gourd. This is called "the section on the alms bowl."

What is the section on robes? The Blessed One taught monks thirteen kinds of robes and requisite cloths, as follows: the inner robe, the upper covering cloth, the lower robe, the belt, the bathing cloth, the covering for scabies, the upper garment, the lining of the upper garment, the lower covering, the lining of the lower covering, the body-wiping cloth, the hair-tying cloth, and the great summer cloth. These thirteen Dharma robes are to be used by monks in full simply by virtue of the blessing conferred upon them, without it being necessary to cut them with a blade or alter their colour to make them suitable. This is called "the section on robes."

What is the section on the coverlet? The Blessed One taught monks two kinds of coverlet for covering the bedding: if it is thick, a single layer; if it is thin, a double layer sewn together.

This is called "the section on the coverlet."

What is the section on needles? The Blessed One permitted monks needles of iron, bone, bronze, and horn for the purpose of sewing robes. This is called "the section on needles."

What is the section on the needle case? The Blessed One permitted monks a needle case for the purpose of storing needles. This is called "the section on the needle case."

The Noble Vinaya, the fiftieth fascicle.

What is the section on taking up lodging? The Buddha, the Blessed One, declared: "A monk who has arrived unexpectedly and wishes to take up lodging should, upon entering the assembly's temple, not wipe the dust from his feet and not take up a water vessel until he has been assigned a lodging place." Then it came to pass that another monk who had arrived unexpectedly, wishing to take up lodging and having entered the temple, heard the rule that the Blessed One had laid down — that a monk who arrives unexpectedly and wishes to take up lodging in the assembly's temple should not wipe the dust from his feet nor take up a water vessel until a lodging has been assigned to him — and upon hearing this, he ran back and forth in his effort to be assigned a lodging, his body exhausted, greatly strained, and fatigued, until he collapsed and fell to the ground, and passed away at that very time. When monks reported what had happened to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "Set down your bowl and robe, wipe the dust from your feet, take up a water vessel, and then, right away, take up a lodging. Any one of those monks may take up a lodging as circumstances allow." When suitable circumstances arose and wholesome qualities declined, monks who had found themselves in such a situation again reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "A monk who wishes to take up lodging should not, even when circumstances are suitable, take up lodging immediately wherever things happen to fall, but should deliberate very carefully, investigate very thoroughly, and examine very closely for three days before taking up a lodging. He should inquire into the conduct of the monk from whom he wishes to receive lodging — what that monk's conduct is like, what his companions are like, what those who follow along with him on both sides are like, whether he gives scriptural transmission or not, whether he gives instruction or not — and should reflect: 'Will I come to feel respect and deference toward that monk? Will wholesome qualities arise in me, or will they diminish?' He should deliberate very carefully, investigate very thoroughly, and examine very closely, and only then take up a lodging."

"A monk who wishes to assign lodging, if he wishes to do so, should likewise not assign it to anyone immediately wherever things happen to fall, but should deliberate very carefully, investigate very thoroughly, and examine very closely for three days before assigning a lodging. He should inquire into the conduct of the monk to whom he wishes to assign lodging — what that monk's conduct is like, what his manner of living is like, what his general behaviour is like — and should reflect: 'Will that monk feel respect and deference toward me? Will wholesome qualities arise, or will they diminish? Will that monk come to feel respect toward me or not? Will he feel devotion and show reverence, and will wholesome qualities grow or not grow?' He should deliberate very carefully, investigate very thoroughly, and examine very closely, and only if his mind is satisfied should he then assign lodging to that person." This is called "the section on taking up lodging."

What is the section on receiving a lodging assignment? A monk who wishes to receive a lodging assignment and desires to take up a lodging should do so in the following manner: he should rise from his seat and arrange his upper robe over one shoulder.

He should grasp both feet with both hands, press them twice, and speak these words: "Please give your attention, Venerable One. I, the monk named such-and-such, request a lodging assignment from the Venerable One. May the Venerable One grant me a lodging assignment. I am taking up lodging with the Venerable One." This should be said in the same way a second and a third time. The elder should respond: "Very well." And in return the monk should say: "Excellent!" or "Splendid!" Then: "Practice with care." This is called "the section on receiving a lodging assignment."

What is the section on granting a lodging assignment? A monk who has not completed ten rains retreats may not grant a lodging assignment. Even one who has completed ten rains retreats, if he is known to be ignorant, dull, or without learning, he too should not grant a lodging assignment. A lodging assignment should be granted by a monk who possesses five qualities: he knows what constitutes an offense; he knows what does not constitute an offense; he knows what is serious; he knows what is light; and he has come to know the Prātimokṣa sūtra in full detail. This is called "the section on granting a lodging assignment."

What is the section on revoking a lodging assignment? A lodging assignment should be revoked when a person possesses five qualities: he has no faith; he is lazy; he shows no respect; he speaks harsh words; and he has evil companions. Furthermore, a lodging assignment is revoked by five causes and five conditions: through discharge; through departure; through going in a direction other than one's own; through the lodging assignment being revoked immediately upon seeing one's preceptor; and through revocation by both parties. This is called "the section on revoking a lodging assignment."

What is the section concerning the preceptor? Because certain monks had gone forth and received full ordination without a preceptor, they became undisciplined, poorly trained, not in accordance with the rule: they wore their lower robe improperly, they wore their upper robe improperly, they entered into conduct that was degenerate and improper, they had bad deportment and improper bearing, and as a result no one would attend to them when they were sick. The monks who had become like that reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "There should be a preceptor, and he shall train them, instruct them by assigning scriptural passages, teach them further, and correct them; and if he does so, they will render service to him and attend to him when he is sick." The Blessed One's declaration that service should be rendered is called "the section concerning the preceptor."

What is the section concerning the co-resident? When a monk, having been made to go forth and receive full ordination, does not attend upon his preceptor, and monks who had become that way reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One declared: "The co-resident should attend upon the preceptor, should shave him, should look after him, should please him, should follow in his footsteps, should render him service, and should not do any matter whatsoever without having asked the preceptor — except for three things: attending to one's bodily needs, discarding a tooth-stick, and prostrating to a stūpa within the boundary. The co-resident too should do all things by first asking the preceptor — except for those three things: attending to one's bodily needs, discarding a tooth-stick, and prostrating to a stūpa within the boundary. Co-residents should also show respect to the preceptor of their co-resident, regard him as a superior, venerate him, please him, and whatever task of his there may be, they should not be lazy but should carry it out swiftly and knowingly, with due service, with modesty, and with a sense of deference. They should have a sense of shame, hold themselves with humility, reflect on what will become of their own virtue,

and if he is about to engage in something improper, the preceptor should restrain him. And if the preceptor himself is about to engage in something improper, the co-resident should restrain him. If the preceptor falls ill, the co-resident should attend upon him with care and devotion. To serve in this way without neglecting one's own virtue — this is called being a proper co-resident.

What, then, is being a proper attendant to a teacher (ācārya)? There are monks who went forth and received full ordination without a teacher, and who as a result became untamed, badly disciplined, lacking in proper conduct, wearing the lower robe unsightly, wearing the upper robe improperly, engaging in behavior that is degraded and unseemly, slovenly in appearance, fallen into conduct that is improper in deportment, with no one attending upon them when they are ill. When such a situation arose, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Even when there is a teacher, he should discipline them, assign scriptural recitation, instruct them further, correct them, and when they are ill, attend upon them and care for them." This is what the Blessed One declared when he said, "Render respectful service." This is called being a proper attendant to a teacher.

What is being a proper attendant who dwells nearby? When monks who have been ordained and have received full ordination fail to render respectful service to their teacher, and such a situation arose, the monks reported it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "The attendant should render respectful service to the teacher, shave him, look after him, please him, follow him, and attend upon him. He should not do any task whatsoever without first asking the teacher — except for those three things: attending to one's bodily needs, discarding a tooth-stick, and prostrating to a stūpa within the boundary." The attendant who dwells nearby should also do everything after asking the teacher — except for those three: attending to one's bodily needs, discarding a tooth-stick, and prostrating to a stūpa within the boundary. Those who dwell nearby as attendants should also show respect to the teacher of their own attendant, regard him as a superior, venerate him, please him, and whatever task of his there may be, they should not be lazy but should carry it out swiftly and knowingly, with due service, with modesty, and with a sense of deference. They should have a sense of shame, hold themselves with humility, reflect on what will become of their own virtue, and if the attendant who dwells nearby is about to engage in something improper, the teacher should restrain him. And if the teacher himself is about to do something improper, the attendant should restrain him. If the teacher falls ill, the attendant should care for him devotedly. To serve in this way without neglecting one's own virtue — this is called being a proper attendant who dwells nearby.

What is being a proper preceptor and teacher, co-resident and attendant together? Preceptors and teachers should cultivate openly the perception of co-residents and attendants as being like their own children. Co-residents and attendants, for their part, should gladly cultivate the perception of the preceptor and teacher as being like a father. This is called being a proper preceptor and teacher, co-resident and attendant together.

What is being a proper companion to a monk, in relation to a novice? The Blessed One permitted monks to take a novice who is mature enough — the minimum being one who is seven years old and capable of scaring away crows. If a matter involving an offense arises, the novice should confess and abandon it openly in the presence of a faithful layman. He should not abandon it in private, and should not abandon it wearing only a single robe; rather, he should abandon it while properly dressed in upper and lower robes. This is called being a proper companion to a novice.

What is being a proper companion in terms of material requisites?

The monk who is undertaking new construction work should thoroughly investigate the site where a temple is to be built for the first time. In examining the properties of the existing temple site, he should consider: Does it have light? Does it have trees? Does it have water? Does it have a walking-meditation path? Does it have a neighborhood nearby? Is it free from disputes? Is it free from jealousy? Is it not too far from the alms-round area? Is it also not too close? During the day, are there not too many loiterers? Is there not too much commotion? At night, is there not too much noise? Is there not too much rowdiness? Is there no discomfort from harmful animals, insects, snakes, wind, or heat? Is it peaceful and secluded, and conducive to meditation? Is it, or is it not, a suitable basis for proper internal settlement? Having thoroughly investigated all of this, one should then build the temple. If a monk undertaking new construction builds a temple without proper investigation, a transgression is incurred. This is called being a proper companion in terms of material requisites.

What is being a proper companion in terms of the temple? The Blessed One granted to monks the following types of temple buildings: a building with four verandas, a building with twelve verandas — the gatehouse of which may be four stories or seven stories high — a multi-storied building, a building with a storeroom, a building with many storerooms, a storehouse, a walking-meditation cloister, a toilet building, a foot-washing room, a residence hall, a porch building, a surrounding complex of buildings, and projecting buildings — whether belonging to the Saṅgha or to an individual, whether for one in training or one beyond training — that are suitable for the four modes of comportment. This is called being a proper companion in terms of the temple.

What is being a proper companion in terms of sleeping quarters? The Blessed One granted to monks the following types of sleeping furnishings: a high couch, a low couch, a sitting mat with a border, a mat, a head-rest, and a square seat — whether for the Saṅgha or for an individual — together with coverings and allocations. This is called being a proper companion in terms of sleeping quarters.

What is being a proper companion in terms of new construction? It is as follows. When the Blessed One gave permission for a temple to be built, monks would undertake new construction work as they pleased. Among them, some let the appointed time pass without beginning; some began and then abandoned the work; and some carried it through to completion. Now, the Blessed One, the Buddha, was residing in a certain woodland hermitage, in the finest forest of that hermitage. At that time, he observed that none of the hermitage temples were doing new construction work — that not a single hermitage temple was undertaking new construction. Having observed this, he asked the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, what is the cause, what is the condition, that these hermitages are not undertaking new construction?" The venerable one replied: "Blessed One, it is like this: among the monks of the hermitage, some have let the time pass, some have abandoned the work, and some are doing it properly. It is for such a cause and such a condition as this that the monks of the hermitage are not undertaking new construction." The Blessed One then declared: "Appoint a monk in charge of new construction — but not according to seniority. Rather, appoint as the one to carry out new construction and to act effectively in new construction projects someone who by nature is diligent in virtue, who is free from laziness, who is endowed with the earnestness of joyous effort, and who is capable of carrying out new construction. He should be requested and appointed by a formal act of the two parties."

Thereupon, monks were appointing a monk in charge of new construction even for matters as minor as rebuilding a collapsed wall, or applying ox-dung plaster, or any small task lasting only a single day. The Blessed One declared: "For any task lasting only a single day, do not appoint a monk in charge of new construction. Instead, for the restoration of a stūpa or an old temple —

or if new construction is being carried out — appoint a monk in charge of new construction for that purpose. They were being appointed for the duration of their lives, and they were lodged in the very same smoky room. The Blessed One declared: "Do not appoint them for the duration of their lives, and do not lodge them in the smoky room. For new construction work, appoint a monk in charge of new construction for six years in the case of restoring an old temple, and for twelve years in the case of a new temple. Moreover, the monk endowed with this charge of new construction, in whatever temple he resides, should at all times make regular rounds and inspections of that temple. If he sees that the temple is dilapidated and falling into ruin, then if he himself is capable of restoring it, let him restore it himself. If he himself is unable to do so, let him show the other monks who practise the holy life. Having shown them, let him personally oversee the work and restore it. Let him not simply abandon it. If he abandons it, he incurs an offence. This is what is meant by being endowed with the charge of new construction."

What does it mean to be fully endowed for new construction work? When a monk in charge of new construction undertakes the Saṅgha's new construction work, it may happen that he becomes so absorbed in the Saṅgha's work that the new construction work itself is neglected. When this had occurred, the monks reported the matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "I permit that a monk in charge of new construction not be assigned to Saṅgha work. As for one who is restoring an old temple, he shall not be assigned to Saṅgha work for two years — that is, until the construction, plastering, maintenance, and lime-work are complete. One who builds a temple with four cells shall not be assigned to Saṅgha work for four years — until the construction, plastering, maintenance, and lime-work are complete. One who builds a temple with eight cells shall not be assigned to Saṅgha work for eight years — until the construction, plastering, maintenance, and lime-work are complete. One who builds a temple with twelve surrounding cells shall not be assigned to Saṅgha work for twelve years — until the construction, plastering, maintenance, and lime-work are complete. One who builds a Saṅgha assembly courtyard complete with a stūpa and also provides the furnishings shall not be assigned to Saṅgha work for the duration of his life."

Furthermore, if the monk endowed with the charge of new construction has not been appointed from among monks possessing five qualities, he should not be appointed; and if he has been appointed, he should be removed. What are the five? He is not diligent, he is lazy, he does not apply himself earnestly, he does not act quickly, and he does not know what new construction work has been done and what has not been done.

A monk who possesses the five opposite qualities and has not been appointed to carry out new construction should be appointed, and if he has been appointed, he should not be removed. What are the five? He is diligent, he is not lazy, he applies himself earnestly, he acts quickly, and he knows what new construction work has been done and what has not been done.

The monk in charge of new construction should also make regular rounds of the temple at all times. He must inspire all those who carry out work in the temple in whatever way ensures that new construction done throughout the temple does not fall into disrepair — he should generate that kind of enthusiasm. If he acts in this way, it is excellent. If he does not act in this way, he incurs an offence. Such is what is called being endowed with the charge of new construction.

What does it mean to be fully endowed with the making of prostrations? The Blessed One permitted two kinds of prostration for monks: making prostrations to a fellow monk, and making prostrations to the Teacher. As for making prostrations to a fellow monk — one should, in accordance with seniority, speak pleasant words face to face, make prostration, rise to greet him, press the palms together,

make prostration, and touch the head to the feet. As for taking hold with both hands of the two feet and pressing them — this too is a form of prostration. As for the Tathāgata, one makes prostration with the five-point full prostration. Such is what is called being fully endowed with the making of prostrations.

What does it mean to be fully endowed with sour gruel? Sour gruel is for monks who are ill and for those afflicted with wind disorders, just as it was permitted for the Venerable Śāriputra. From what substances is sour gruel to be made? From roots, stems, leaves, flowers, medicines, and all manner of seeds: these are gathered together and, once they have become sour, at that point one strains them while they are clear and unsettled, filters them through cloth, mixes them with water until clear, and drinks them from morning until evening. Such is what is called being fully endowed with sour gruel.

What does it mean to be fully endowed with powder? The Blessed One fully permitted two kinds of powder for monks: medicinal powder and bathing powder. Medicinal powders were permitted for the relieving of illness. The bathing powder permitted for monks was not for pride, not for arrogance, not for beautification, not for adornment, but for the removal of bodily impurity. From what is bathing powder to be made? From small peas, black beans, large beans, lentils, their outer husks, and from unhusked grain — monks may use these mixed with various fragrances, yet not for the purpose of adornment; they are to be employed fully as bathing powder. If one finds something already mixed with fragrance without having sought it out, there is no offence. If one mixes it oneself with fitting medicines and uses it, the same applies. Such is what is called being fully endowed with powder.

What does it mean to be fully endowed with medicines? The Blessed One, for the sake of relieving illness, permitted medicines for sick monks in accordance with the sequence: to be taken in the morning, in the afternoon, on the seventh day, or for as long as life lasts — medicines made from grass, medicines made from tree trunks, medicines made from leaves, medicines made from flowers, and medicines made from fruits. A monk who is not ill may not make full use of medicines intended for the sick. Such is what is called being fully endowed with medicines.

What does it mean to be fully endowed with drinks? The Blessed One, drawing from the sage known as Kaiṇyaya, permitted eight kinds of drinks for monks. What are they? These: the drink of the jujube fruit, the drink of the rose apple, the drink of the Chinese plum, the drink of the mango, the drink of the rough-skinned fruit, the drink of the Aśvattha fig, the drink of the Udumbara fig, and the drink of grapes. These eight kinds of drink are permitted for monks, provided they do not impair the meal, do not intoxicate, do not produce sourness, are fermented to clarity, are clear and unsettled — filtered through cloth, mixed with water in the assembly, and stored as evening provisions. Such is what is called being fully endowed with drinks.

What does it mean to be fully endowed with leather? A monk may not keep leather, may not store it, may not consecrate it, may not spread it out, may not sit on it, may not spread it as a seat, may not step onto it, and may not mix it with other things. As for footwear — shoes worn-through at the toe, shoes cracked along the side, shoes cut at the top, or short-soled shoes: if such a circumstance arises while one is in a layperson's home, one may then sit on the leather. A sick monk may sit on leather. Such is what is called being fully endowed with leather.

What does it mean to be fully endowed with footwear? The Blessed One permitted two kinds of footwear for monks: single-layered sandals and, if occasion requires, layered sandals of the householder style. A monk should not wear shoes decorated with designs. Such is what is called being fully endowed with footwear.

What does it mean to be fully endowed with wooden sandals? The Blessed One permitted two kinds of wooden sandals for monks: sandals for the lavatory, and sandals for use as a footstool support. A monk should not carry wooden sandals for any purpose other than these; if he does carry them for another purpose, he incurs a transgression. Such is what is called being fully endowed with wooden sandals.

What does it mean to be fully endowed with a walking staff? A monk should not carry a horse-headed staff, a staff topped with a sea-creature's head, or a staff with a foot carved in the shape of a she-crab. Such is what is called being fully endowed with a walking staff.

What does it mean to be fully endowed with a staff? The Blessed One permitted a staff for sick and elderly monks. If it cracks at the base, it should be bound with iron. If it splits at the tip, it should be fitted with a ferrule. Such is what is called being fully endowed with a staff. Now, in the charnel ground of the Cool Grove near the city of Rājagṛha there were snakes, and when monks entered the charnel ground they were struck by snakes, and those who were so afflicted reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One declared: in order to drive off snakes, it is permitted to carry a staff fitted with a noise-making device. Such is what is called being fully endowed with a staff.

What does it mean to be fully endowed with a net? The Blessed One permitted a net for sick and elderly monks. A monk should not carry a net for the purpose of adorning it with many-colored dyes. Such is what is called being fully endowed with a net.

What does it mean to be fully endowed with both a staff and a net? The Blessed One permitted sick and elderly monks to receive the conferral of both staff and net, and to be given both through a single formal act. The fuller account is as it appears in the Vinaya. Such is what is called being fully endowed with both a staff and a net.

What does it mean to be fully endowed with raw garlic? The Blessed One permitted raw garlic for monks who are sick with a wind ailment, just as it was permitted for the Venerable Śāriputra. A monk who is not ill should not eat raw garlic. If he eats it, he incurs a transgression. If he eats it as medicine, it should be used in the proper manner.

The proper manner regarding garlic is as follows. If a monk has eaten raw garlic, he should not go before the Teacher. He should not go into the presence of his preceptor or his teacher. He should not be in the role of a teacher or serve as one who acts in a teacher's place. He should not teach. He should not give recitations. He should not be called to remembrance. He should not be questioned. He should not enter a village. He should not be seated in the row for meals. He should not drink soup. He should not drink sour gruel. He should not listen to the Dharma. He should not sit together with the other monks. He should not gather with them. In short, for any purpose whatsoever, he should not sit alongside others. He should remain dwelling in a secluded dwelling. If he has no bedding or coverings of his own, he should obtain them from the community of the four quarters in a place set apart. He should also designate a separate latrine area. If he has eaten garlic for one day, he should remain apart for seven days. If he has eaten it for seven days, he should likewise remain apart for seven days. When the seven days have passed, he should wash his bedding and coverings. He should also plaster his dwelling. He should wipe down the walls of the dwelling with a cloth. He should clean the floor gently and thoroughly. He should smear it with cow dung. He should also plaster the latrine area. He should wash his Dharma robes. He should bathe. After that, he may at his ease go before the Teacher. He may go to his preceptor, his teacher, and those who serve in a teacher's role. He may teach. He should give recitations, be called to remembrance, and be questioned. He may enter a village. He should be seated in the row for meals. He should be placed in the row for drinking soup and sour gruel. He should listen to the Dharma.

He should sit together with monks.

If a monk who eats garlic does not conduct himself in accordance with the rules of proper conduct that have been laid down, he incurs a transgression. This is called the rule concerning garlic.

What is the rule concerning a razor? The Blessed One permitted monks to use a razor for the purpose of cutting hair. This is called the rule concerning a razor.

What is the rule concerning a razor case? The Blessed One permitted monks to have a razor case for the purpose of protecting the blade of the razor. This is called the rule concerning a razor case.

What is the rule concerning a bent key? The Blessed One permitted monks to have a bent key for the purpose of making up their beds, for the ease of the Saṅgha, and for the Saṅgha to dwell in virtue. This is called the rule concerning a bent key.

What is the rule concerning a door lock? The Blessed One permitted monks to have a door lock — that is, a mechanism opened by a key. This is called the rule concerning a door lock.

What is the rule concerning a mount? The Blessed One permitted monks who are aged, very old, ill, unable to exert themselves, or who have reached old age to use a mount. A monk should not ride a mount adorned with painted decorations. He should not use a female mount as his personal riding animal. This is called the rule concerning a mount.

What is the rule concerning an umbrella? The Blessed One permitted monks to have an umbrella as a remedy against rain and heat. One should not carry a painted umbrella adorned with decorations. One should not carry one with a long handle. One should not walk into a village while carrying an umbrella. This is called the rule concerning an umbrella.

What is the rule concerning a fan? The Blessed One permitted monks to have a fan as a remedy against heat. A monk should not carry a fan adorned with painted decorations. This is called the rule concerning a fan.

What is the rule concerning a fly-whisk made of tail hair? The Blessed One permitted monks to have a fly-whisk made of tail hair for the purpose of driving away harmful creatures and insects. From what should a fly-whisk be made? From the tail of a yak, from a wild animal, from thread, or from felt. A monk should not carry a fly-whisk adorned with painted decorations. A fly-whisk is of two kinds: one is natural in color and one is dark reddish-brown. This is called the rule concerning a fly-whisk made of tail hair.

What is the rule concerning the handle of a fly-whisk? A monk should not carry a fly-whisk with a long handle. If one is found, it should be sold. Upon selling it, the proceeds should be offered to a stūpa of the buddhas or a stūpa of the śrāvakas. This is called the rule concerning the handle of a fly-whisk.

What is the rule concerning a mirror? Monks should not look at their face in a mirror, in the mirror-like surface of a begging bowl, or in water. However, there is no fault if one wishes to look in order to check whether there is a wound on one's face, to see what the face now looks like compared to before, to look at wrinkles and gray hairs on the face, or to reflect that all conditioned things grow old and perish. This is called the rule concerning a mirror.

What is the rule concerning garlands, perfume, and ointment? A monk should not carry garlands, perfume, or ointment on his own person, nor should he give them to others. If any are found, they should be sold, and upon selling them the proceeds should be offered to a stūpa of the buddhas or a stūpa of the śrāvakas. This is called the rule concerning garlands, perfume, and ointment.

What is the rule concerning dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments?

A monk should not himself engage in dancing, singing, or playing musical instruments, nor should he cause others to do so, nor should he go to watch them. In every way, he should abandon dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments. This is called the rule concerning dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments.

What is the rule concerning tooth-wood? The Blessed One permitted monks to use tooth-wood for cleaning the teeth. It should be neither too long nor too short, neither too thick nor too thin, neither bent nor rough, but should be made smooth, straight, and supple, as though it had been permitted by the face. This is called the rule concerning tooth-wood.

What is the rule concerning eye-medicine? The Blessed One permitted five kinds of eye-medicine for monks suffering from eye ailments, namely: eye-medicine made from flowers, powdered eye-medicine, pellet eye-medicine, sap eye-medicine, and black eye-medicine. Monks should not apply eye-medicine for the sake of adornment and vanity. If there is illness, the appropriate medicine should be applied. This is called the rule concerning eye-medicine.

What is the rule concerning the eye-medicine applicator? The Blessed One's permission given to monks regarding the eye-medicine applicator is as it appears in detail in the Vinaya. This is called the rule concerning the eye-medicine applicator.

What is the rule concerning the eye-medicine container? The Blessed One's permission given to monks regarding the eye-medicine container is as it appears in detail in the Vinaya. This is called the rule concerning the eye-medicine container.

What is the rule concerning the mortar? The Blessed One permitted monks a mortar and pestle for pounding medicine. This is called the rule concerning the mortar.

What is the rule concerning lying down? Monks should not lie down during the daytime, nor should they lie down beside a blazing fire. If one is drowsy, one should rise and shake it off. If that is not possible, one should go elsewhere, taking care not to disturb others in doing so. This is called the rule concerning lying down.

What is the rule concerning sitting? During the daytime, while walking or sitting, one should thoroughly purify the mind of obstructing phenomena. Having thus thoroughly purified the mind of obstructing phenomena while walking and sitting during the day, during the first watch of the night one should also, while walking about, thoroughly purify the mind of obstructing phenomena. Having thoroughly purified the mind of obstructing phenomena during the first watch, in the middle watch of the night one should go outside the temple, wash the feet, enter one's dwelling, fold the upper robe into four layers and spread it out, fold the blanket thickly and place it at the head, then lie down on the right side, pressing foot upon foot, limbs not splayed, mind undistracted, robes not disheveled, holding the perception of permission, and keeping in mind mindfulness and vigilance and the perception of rising. Then at dawn, rising quickly and without lingering, one should walk or sit and thoroughly purify the mind of obstructing phenomena. This is called the rule concerning sitting.

What is the rule concerning the knee-support? The Blessed One permitted monks who are ill or suffering from back ailments to use a knee-support, just as he permitted the venerable Śāriputra. A monk should not carry a knee-support decorated with designs for the sake of ornamentation. This is called the rule concerning the knee-support.

What is the rule concerning the back-scratcher?

This is called the rule concerning the beating-block. The Blessed One permitted monks to use a wooden beating-block and mallet for the purpose of beating their robes. This is called the rule concerning the beating-block.

What is the rule concerning the waistband? There are three kinds of waistband. The Blessed One permitted monks the following: a plain waistband, a braided waistband, and a tasseled waistband. A monk should not wear a multicolored waistband for the sake of ornamentation. A monk should not enter a village without a waistband. Even if a single knot has come undone, one should not go into a village; to do so would be an offense. This is called the rule concerning the waistband.

What is the rule concerning the hand-clapper? The Blessed One permitted monks a hand-clapper for the purpose of driving away thieves who come by stealth. However, it must not be used to strike anyone, even by way of any synonym or pretext. This is called the rule concerning the hand-clapper.

What is the rule concerning going about with one's robe loosely tied and a knot undone? Monks should not go about with their robe loosely tied and a knot undone, except when working on a rooftop. This is called the rule concerning going about with one's robe loosely tied and a knot undone.

What is the rule concerning ground? There are two kinds of ground. The Blessed One permitted monks a walking ground and the ground of a shrine hall. This is called the rule concerning ground.

What is the rule concerning planted trees? Monks reported to the Blessed One that at the site of the Vulture Peak on Gṛdhrakūṭa mountain there were no trees and the sky was unshaded, and that when climbing and descending Vulture Peak they were scorched by the heat. The Blessed One thereupon declared: Those that will provide shade, or those that will bear flowers, or those that will bear fruit — these may be planted. And in order to protect the trees planted in those places, enclosing them with a fence of living posts is also permitted. This is called the rule concerning planted trees.

What is the rule concerning properties? The Blessed One permitted monks to have a field for the sake of a garden. A garden the Blessed One permitted for the sake of a temple. The field with its properties, the garden, and the temple — all of these the Blessed One permitted for the benefit of monks. This is called the rule concerning properties.

What is the rule concerning a grove? A grove means a grove of planted trees. How matters of seniority are to be conducted there is set forth in detail in the Vinaya as it arises. This is called the rule concerning a grove.

What is the rule concerning disputes? A dispute means: fighting, fault-finding, quarreling, contention, slander, whispering in ears, words between parties that are incompatible, failure to reconcile, discord, disunity of mind, divisiveness in the Saṅgha, creating a schism in the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha being cut in two, the Saṅgha becoming separate factions, the Saṅgha not being brought back together, taking the lead in keeping the Saṅgha divided, acting at an improper time, acting in a way that causes harm, failing to act in accordance with Dharma when one lacks the power to do so, also failing to act when one has no faction or no allies, also failing to act when one has no following, and not engaging in dispute even when harm comes to oneself — nor engaging in dispute with the other party when it would bring fear and harm to them. Seeing these and other such things as grounds for fault, one should refrain from dispute. This is called the rule concerning disputes.

What is the rule concerning schism? There are two kinds of schism: schism in the Saṅgha and schism in the wheel.

Schism in the wheel is not what is meant here. What, then, is schism in the Saṅgha? It occurs when, among the fourteen things that can cause schism, one takes any single matter whatsoever to be thoroughly good — whether it is in accordance with Dharma or not in accordance with Dharma, whether it is in accordance with the Vinaya or not in accordance with the Vinaya, whether it is a transgression or not a transgression, whether it is grave or light, whether it entails a remainder or leaves no remainder, whether it is something to be confessed or something to be restrained, whether it is a gross violation of the Vinaya, or whether it arises from speaking offensively — and then, with monks who are resident within the same boundary performing communal Saṅgha acts together, they carry out the restoration and confession ceremony, the invitation ceremony, the motion, the motion with a second announcement, and the motion with a fourth announcement. This is called schism of the Saṅgha, and it is not schism of the wheel.

What is schism of the wheel? It occurs when a monk presents himself in this way: having prepared a wooden staff of rule and made a motion, he departs from that assembly. Setting aside the noble eightfold path and establishing another path in its place — this is called schism of the wheel.

When the former — schism of the Saṅgha — and schism of the wheel are combined together as one, that is called the complete set of schism.

What is the complete set of assembly? The assembly means the gathered Saṅgha. All the monks who are resident within the boundary and who have come together for the act are fully assembled and in place. Those who have taken the faith have also received the faith. There are no monks who would be made to leave and then settle, or who would be placed there and then grow firm, so that there is neither one to be moved nor one to be kept in place, and the act is performed. This is called the complete set of assembly.

What is the complete set of salutation? One should pay homage to the Tathāgata in such a manner. Likewise to the preceptor. Likewise to the teacher. Likewise to the guru and to those who stand in the position of guru. Likewise to the elders in order of seniority. Likewise to the junior monks. Being skilled in paying homage to all in this way — this is called the complete set of salutation.

The second volume, called the Collection of Precepts in the Manner of a Mother, is complete.

What is the collection of affairs? There is the affair of expulsion, the affair of separate residence, the affair of suspension, the affair of investigating one's nature, the affair of giving a training, the affair of an elder monk of unbroken boundary, the affair of the assembly hall, the affair of the elder of the assembly hall, the affair of the dwelling, the affair of the elder of the dwelling, the affair of the dwelling with its surrounding compound, the affair of the elder of the dwelling with its surrounding compound, the affair of the forest, the affair of the sleeping mat, the affair of the flat board, the affair of the wheel, the affair of the empty place, the affair of the elder of the empty place, the affair of the alms bowl, the affair of the Dharma robe, the affair of the tent, the affair of the needle, the affair of the needle case, the affair of porridge, the affair of water, the affair of the water vessel, the affair of the filled water vessel, the affair of the cleaning tablet, the affair of food, the affair of what is to be eaten, the affair of what has been entrusted as food, the affair of alms rounds, the affair of the conduct of alms rounds, the affair of receiving cooked food, the affair of the hermitage, the affair of the elder of the hermitage, the affair of the village outskirts, the affair of the elder of the village outskirts, the affair of the new arrival, the affair of the elder for new arrivals, the affair of departure, the affair of the elder for departure, and

the affair of washing the feet, the affair of the elder for washing the feet, the affair of sitting, the affair of the elder for sitting, the affair of teaching the Dharma, the affair of the elder for teaching the Dharma, the affair of the proper time, the affair of an improper time, the affair of the Saṅgha assembling at an improper time, the affair of the elder for the Saṅgha assembling at an improper time, the affair of speaking, the affair of not speaking, the affair of entering the rains retreat in the proper manner, the affair of having entered the rains retreat in the proper manner, the affair of the elder for having entered the rains retreat in the proper manner, the affair of dwelling during the rains retreat, the affair of the assembly, the affair of going into the assembly, the affair of having entered the assembly, the affair of the elder for having entered the assembly, the affair of the restoration ceremony (poṣadha), the affair of performing the restoration ceremony, the affair of the acts of the restoration ceremony, the affair of individual liberation (prātimokṣa), the affair of reciting the individual liberation, the affair of the one who recites the individual liberation, the affair of the elder, the affair of the middle-rank, the affair of the junior, the affair of the elder, middle-rank, and junior together, the affair of the steam house, the affair of bathing in the steam house, the affair of the elder for the steam house, the affair of the preceptor, the affair of the co-resident, the affair of the teacher, the affair of the attendant, the affair of the novice, the affair of what is to be done with diligence, the affair of the śramaṇa who follows close behind, the affair of going near to a village, the affair of the elder for going near to a village, the affair of having gone near to a village, the affair of the elder for having gone near to a village, the affair of dwelling at the base, the affair of resting, the affair of the intermediate space, the affair of the settled place, the affair of the water cistern, the affair of the walking path, the affair of walking, the affair of the cot, the affair of the scraper, the affair of defecating, the affair of the place of defecation, the affair of the pit of the place of defecation, the affair of the elder at the place of defecation, the affair of the surroundings of the place of defecation, the affair of urinating, the affair of the place of urination, the affair of the pit for urination, the affair of the elder at the place of urination, the affair of the area around the place of urination, the affair of washing, the affair of the place of washing, the affair of the opening of the washing place, the affair of the elder at the washing place, the affair of those gathered around the washing place, the affair of spittle, the affair of the spittoon, the affair of the tooth stick, the affair of cleaning the teeth, the affair of scraping the tongue, the affair of cleaning the ears, and what is to be used and what is not to be used. This completes the substance of the three sections of the chapter on the Similitude.

The Noble Vinaya Text, the fifty-first fascicle.

What is meant by the affair of expulsion? Expulsion means dismissal. A dismissed monk must conduct himself in the following manner. A dismissed monk may not perform the going-forth ordination, may not perform the full ordination, may not grant residence, may not give scriptural authorization, may not act as a recollection witness, may not be asked questions, may not be appointed as a companion to a novice, may not be appointed to give scriptural instruction to nuns, may not be appointed to administer vows. Even if previously appointed, he must not teach nuns or perform acts for them. He may not be appointed to perform acts on behalf of that monk, nor may he be commissioned to perform such acts. He must not obstruct a monk who is performing acts. If there is another who holds the Vinaya, he must not expound the Vinaya within the Saṅgha. If there is another who can recite the prātimokṣa sūtra, he must not recite the prātimokṣa sūtra within the Saṅgha. If there is another who can teach the Dharma, he must not teach the Dharma within the Saṅgha. He must not obstruct a monk who is dwelling in accordance with the rule from giving scriptural authorization. He must not be commissioned to administer the restoration ceremony to a monk who is dwelling in accordance with the rule.

He must not obstruct a monk who is dwelling in accordance with the rule from giving scriptural authorization. He must not speak disparagingly of a monk who is dwelling in accordance with the rule. He must not call him to mind with ill intent. He must not associate with such monks. Whatever act the Saṅgha has performed by way of expulsion, and whatever other act is similar to that, he must not commit such an offense again afterward. He must not commit one graver than that. He should conduct himself like one who sweeps away what is behind him as he goes forward. He should engage in the going forth. He should demonstrate reverence through prostration. Even if a monk dwelling in accordance with the rule offers him his alms bowl, he must not accept it. He must not accept his robe either. He must not accept food from him. He must not allow that monk to shave his head. He must not perform acts in the bathhouse. Until he is restored, he must not take up the acts of a monk dwelling in accordance with the rule in any matter whatsoever.

When the entire Saṅgha is assembled and gathered, he must not be appointed by vow to a position requiring careful confidentiality. He must not be appointed by vow to any position of authority. He must not be consecrated by vow for the function of a group of twelve persons. This is called what is to be done by expulsion.

What then is what is to be done by suspension? Suspension is of two kinds: that in which one suspends oneself, and that which has been done in accordance with the Dharma by the Saṅgha.

What is it to suspend oneself? It is when one deliberately turns from the side of Dharma to the side of non-Dharma. That is how one suspends oneself.

What is that which has been done in accordance with the Dharma by the Saṅgha? It is when the Saṅgha, without coercion and without adjournment, abandons one through a motion and a fourfold act performed in accordance with the Dharma by the assembled Saṅgha. That is how one is abandoned in accordance with the Dharma by the Saṅgha.

Likewise, rehabilitation is of two kinds: that in which one rehabilitates oneself, and that which has been done in accordance with the Dharma by the Saṅgha.

What is it to rehabilitate oneself? It is when one deliberately turns from the side of non-Dharma back to the side of Dharma. That is how one rehabilitates oneself.

What is that which has been done in accordance with the Dharma by the Saṅgha? It is when the Saṅgha, finding it improper to leave one without protection, abandons one through a Saṅgha assembled in accordance with the Dharma — having been expelled by a motion made in full assembly and a fourfold act. That is rehabilitation done in accordance with the Dharma by the Saṅgha.

The suspended monk, from the prohibition against his conducting ordination onward, is to be treated as before — that is, just as the Saṅgha has performed an act of expulsion against someone, and similarly against another, so too he must not commit such an offense again, and must not commit one worse than it — up to and including that he must not be appointed by vow for the function of a group of twelve persons.

A suspended monk should bring down upon himself — whether he be a senior monk, a middle monk, or a junior monk — any fellow brahma-farer who knows what he is doing. He must not commit an offense. If he has committed an offense, he should conduct himself in the manner of one returning to the fold. If he does not conduct himself in that manner of returning, he is indeed to be suspended. He is to be addressed with these words:

"The Saṅgha will deal with you as though drawing a line. The Saṅgha will deal with you as though driving in a peg. That offense of yours must be confessed right here within the Saṅgha — it is not to be done outside of it. That act of yours, too, is to be made right again by that very Saṅgha — not outside of it. If you neither confess that offense nor correct it, then those fellow brahma-farers who know will speak of it wherever they wish. And if, even having been treated thus, that person is still not tamed, then he is to be treated as though a line has been drawn and a peg driven in, and he is to be expelled."

It is like this: as with a wild horse, that one is to be kept separate.

What is to be done by a mediator? In order to settle a dispute, one should seek out a mediating monk possessed of twenty-two qualities. And what are those twenty-two? He must be endowed with moral discipline and have previously received full ordination; he must have a sense of shame and remorse; he must be restrained and devoted to the training; he must be learned, retaining and having amassed great learning; he must be versed in the texts by heart; he must thoroughly understand the Vinaya and what surpasses the Vinaya; he must be skilled in dispute, skilled in handling a dispute that has arisen, skilled in settling a dispute, and skilled in ensuring that a settled dispute does not arise again; he must be skilled in treatises; he must be skilled in matters of substance and in how to handle matters of substance; he must be free of anger, he must not speak when in an angry state, and he must not become angered; he must conduct himself gently; he must understand the meaning of what is said through body, speech, and instruction; he must convey it fully and carry it out fully; he must make it understood, and having made it understood, cause it to be taken in; he must speak after reflection and make what has been said upon reflection be understood; he must not go where desire leads; he must not go where aversion leads; he must not go where delusion leads; and he must not go where fear leads. A mediating monk who possesses these twenty-two qualities is one on whom no other depends, and he becomes a source of Dharmic benefit for both sides.

Furthermore, the mediating monk should not regard as his own the pleasant words, the prostrations, the acts of rising first, the pressing of palms together, and the reverences shown him by the monks on the side that makes assertions and those on the side that responds. Even if those monks render him service, he should not accept it. If an alms bowl is offered, he should not take it. If a robe is offered, he should not take it. If food is offered, he should not take it. Whatever other requisites are offered, he should not appropriate them. Nor should he render service to those monks, nor give them an alms bowl, nor give them robes. He should not accept scriptural instruction from them, nor make it an object of mindfulness, nor a topic of yoga, nor something to inquire about mentally. He, too, should not give those monks scriptural instruction; it is not to be an object of mindfulness, not to be asked about altogether, not a topic of yoga, and he should not assign it as a mental object. He should not sit with them on the same seat, should not walk with them in the same walking area, and should not be stationed with them in the same dwelling. He should instead say these words: "Venerable ones, what good can you find in conduct such as this? You who, having so well spoken the Dharma and the Vinaya, having gone forth into such excellent teaching — you have entered into quarreling and have grasped at views and entered into disputation. When two venerable ones dispute, both do not win. When it is settled, one wins and one loses. Therefore, venerable ones, abandon such quarreling, wrangling, and contentious speech as this." That is what is to be done by a mediator.

What is the act of granting investigation into one's identity that is done by giving? If a monk who is guilty of an offense acknowledges it, then retracts the acknowledgment, and then acknowledges it again, the Saṅgha should, by an unobstructed, unpostponed act with a single motion and three declarations, grant that monk investigation into his identity. A monk to whom investigation into his identity has been granted should engage in conduct such as the following. From the point of being granted investigation into his identity, the monk is not to expel — and so on as before. As for the one to whom the Saṅgha has granted investigation into his identity, and likewise any who resemble him: let no such offense as that be committed, and let nothing worse than that be done either, up to that point —

— as before. This, then, is what is called "the conduct of one to whom investigation into his identity has been granted" with respect to the twelve persons whom the vow does not authorize.

What, then, is the conduct of one to whom a training is granted? There is a monk who has engaged in unchaste behavior — the practice of sexual intercourse — and yet in whom not even a thought of touching so much as a blade of grass has arisen with the intent to strike. Toward him, the Saṅgha should, by an unobstructed, unpostponed act with a single motion and four declarations, grant a training. The detailed procedure is to be connected with the Vinaya in the manner of the Venerable Gālyāna. A monk to whom a training has been granted should not expel — and so on as before. As for the one to whom the Saṅgha has granted a training, and likewise any who resemble him, let no such offense as that be committed, and let nothing worse than that be done either, up to that point — as before. This is how the vow does not authorize twelve persons. A monk to whom a training has been granted must train in all the trainings of a monk. He must sit at the end of the Saṅgha's assembly. He should accept offerings from those who have received full ordination. He should accept offerings from those who have not received full ordination. He should change and move out his sleeping arrangement from alongside those who have received full ordination. A monk to whom a training has been granted may perform two kinds of acts: the restoration ceremony and the invitation ceremony. A monk to whom a training has been granted should not perform the restoration ceremony as a way of completing the count. The same applies to other acts of the Saṅgha. If the one to whom a training has been granted comes into the midst of the restoration ceremony, do not summon him. And if he is about to leave, do not restrain him. Why is that? Because the Saṅgha will be neither incomplete nor complete. This is called "the conduct of one to whom a training has been granted."

What is the conduct of an elder who has not broken the boundaries? A monk who is an elder who has not broken the boundaries should engage in conduct such as the following. With respect to newly arrived monks who are staying there, he should know all of them, care for them, instruct them, turn them back from wrongdoing, and bring them into virtue. For those who are engaged in recitation, questioning, relinquishment, practicing seclusion, yoga, and mental application, he should individually assign scriptural transmissions. He should bring them into proper conduct. He should have them examine individually what is to be trained. He should bring about the obtaining of requisites. When individual distributions are made, he should supervise the fair and equal distribution of shares. He should visit the sick. He should encourage monks to serve as attendants to the sick. He should give Dharma teachings to the sick. He should properly proclaim what is the path and what is not the path. He should not allow the thread of observable conduct to be cut. In no way whatsoever should he be negligent toward the sick. Whatever other duties may arise for monks who arrive at the non-boundary-breaking residence — in all of those, the elder monk should take the lead. This is called "the conduct of an elder who has not broken the boundaries."

What is the conduct of the joyful enclosure? The joyful enclosure means the place where the Saṅgha all rejoice together. Since the stipulated duties of the monks who arrive there may differ from one place to another, that monk should examine whether the stipulated duties being undertaken in any given instance are in accordance with the Dharma or not in accordance with the Dharma. If they are in accordance with the Dharma and it is clear that they will not be harmful to oneself or to others, he should leave them as they are without interference. But if they are not in accordance with the Dharma and it is understood that they will be harmful to oneself and harmful to others — and if one's own side has power, has allies, and has a following — and if because of that kind of situation there would arise a schism in the Saṅgha, conflict in the Saṅgha, a split in the Saṅgha, or the Saṅgha would become divided —

then one should remove that unlawful rule one has established and act in accordance with the Dharma. If one has the ability to do so, and to make the Saṅgha understand — "This has not been established in accordance with the Dharma; remove it and establish something else that is in accordance with the Dharma" — one should open that understanding to them. But if our side has little power, has no allies, and has no following, and because of that a schism in the Saṅgha would arise, conflict in the Saṅgha would arise, the Saṅgha would become divided, and one knows that one is unable to remove this unlawful rule one has established and act in accordance with the Dharma — then one should say nothing at all. Or else one should withdraw. One should not, through a condition such as that, take a firm stand and remain there.

As for what is called the monastery grounds: within the monastery grounds are small rooms, large rooms, multi-storied buildings, buildings with surrounding quarters, cells, the furnishings of cells, walking areas, planted trees, and all water channels — all of these should be assigned in order of seniority. Sweeping the outside is called the work of the monastery grounds.

What is the work of the elder monks of the monastery grounds? The elder monk of the monastery grounds should apply himself to such work as this. The elder monk of the monastery should make his appearance bright and clear, without a furrowed brow, smiling before others speak, speaking before others speak. He should speak kindly and say welcoming words such as "Come, be at ease in your coming." He should speak words that are pleasing and not harsh, words that gladden and delight. As for the newly arrived young monks who are there — the procedure is the same as explained before: in every matter the elder monk should take the lead, and this continues up to the point of not abandoning continuity. When quarrels, reproaches, disputes, and contentions arise, one should recognize them in order to tame them; one should recognize them in order to pacify them, for the sake of peace.

In this way too: the elder monk of the monastery should be the first to eat, the first to take his place, the first to be seated on the mat, the first to take porridge, the first to be assigned an inner lodging, the first when the board is struck — he should go first, he should be seated first. He should go before the Saṅgha having established within himself a sense of respect and humility, a sense of being subject to awe, a lowly mind, and a mind like one who sweeps the dust. Having gone, he should bow in order of seniority and sit on his own seat in its proper place.

Toward elders, middle monks, and newcomers alike, he should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benefit, and a mind of affectionate care, regarding them as father, mother, and younger brothers. He should examine the entire assembly: who is well and properly equipped, and who is not — examining who is well provided for and who is not well provided for. Those who are well and properly equipped should be left undisturbed. Those who are not well equipped and are in an unsatisfactory condition should be assigned to tasks and corrected. One who is well provided for should be left undisturbed. One who is not well provided for should be given a signal and a sign. If that one does not notice the sign, one should give the sign to someone seated nearby. If even the one seated nearby does not notice it, then the elder monk himself should instruct that person as gently as possible to dress properly, without making a loud noise.

When the elder monk is going through in order of seniority, holding a ladle, ready to serve food, one should say: "Has it been permitted or not?" Until the occasion for the assembly's gathering is known, one should wait a moment and then say: "Let food be distributed equally to all."

The elder monk of the monastery should be in harmony with the elders, middle monks, and newcomers; and the elders, middle monks, and newcomers should also be in harmony with him.

If faithful brahmins and householders arrive, food should be distributed to them equally in the same way. If the distribution is not done, or if the faithful brahmins and householders are unwilling, the elder monk should teach the Dharma properly, instruct them properly, praise them properly, and gladden them properly, and then say: "We have this available." This is called the duty of the elder monk of Jetavana.

What is the duty of the dwelling-room? A monk who dwells in a dwelling-room should sweep it regularly, wipe it clean with a cloth, dispose of the sweepings, and apply a smooth coat of dung plaster. If any moss or mildew appears, it should be removed. Cracks, damaged areas, and broken places should be repaired. Water pots should be filled with water and set in place — that is, pots for general use, clean round vessels, vessels for wiping the floor, and footwashing vessels, all filled and placed. This is called the duty of the dwelling-room.

What is the duty of the elder monk of the dwelling-room? The duty of the elder monk of the dwelling-room is to set newcomers to work at all these tasks. Whatever newly arrived monks come to reside there should be recognized and made known, as before. The elder monk should set everyone to work from the outset, through and including the duty of not breaking the continuum of practice. This is called the duty of the elder monk of the dwelling-room.

What is the duty of a building with a surrounding enclosure? A monk who dwells in such a building with a surrounding enclosure should sweep it regularly, as before, through and including filling the footwashing vessels and setting them in place. Toward the fellow monks residing in that building with a surrounding enclosure, one should act with equal kindness in body, with equal kindness in speech, and with equal kindness in mind. One should not kindle quarreling there, nor faultfinding, nor strife, nor dispute. If fighting, abuse, strife, or dispute should arise and one is able to calm it, that is well and good. If one is unable to do so, one should withdraw from that place. This is called the duty of a building with a surrounding enclosure.

What is the duty of the elder monk of a building with a surrounding enclosure? The duty of the elder monk of a building with a surrounding enclosure is to set people to work at all these tasks. Whatever newly arrived monks come to reside there should all be recognized, and, as before, the elder monk should set everyone to work from the outset, through and including the duty of not breaking the continuum of practice. This is called the duty of the elder monk of a building with a surrounding enclosure.

What is the duty concerning the grove? "Grove" here refers to a garden grove. The monks residing there should investigate around the perimeter up to a distance of one league to see whether there is anything that might become an obstacle to the livelihoods of those dwelling in that place, or an obstacle to the holy life. If any such thing is found, it should be removed from afar. If none is found and the place is suitable, a boundary should be established up to a distance of one league, a proper site should be designated, and a location for the restoration ceremony should also be designated. There one should cultivate enthusiasm through the sharing of food and the sharing of the Dharma. One should ensure that fighting does not arise there, nor faultfinding, nor resentment, nor dispute. This is called the duty of the grove.

What is the duty concerning bedding? Monks should regularly inspect the bedding, dry it, shake it out, count it, store it. If it becomes soiled, it should be washed.

If the bedding has become torn or worn out, one should mend and patch it to the best of one's ability, and have it stitched and darned. A monk should not take robes belonging to the Saṅgha of the four quarters and go to the place for defecating, nor to the place for urinating, nor into the bathhouse, nor to where feet are washed, nor to the kitchen. One should not sit wearing them in the rain, nor in the strong midday heat, nor leave them in the drying room. In every place where damage might occur, one should not wear, distribute, or store the robes of the Saṅgha of the four quarters. Monks should not treat bedding in any of these five ways: by scorching it with fire, by covering it with dust, by wetting it with water, by soiling it with excrement, or by dragging it.

Monks should not, while distributing the robes of the Saṅgha of the four quarters, strike the main hall with a knocking sound, sweep the floor, discard a broom, fill the mouth with mucus, fill water vessels, use the general-purpose vessel, use the clean-water vessel, use the excrement vessel, fill the foot-washing vessel, make noise with vessels, manage the main hall, do work with alms bowls, or do work with robes. Monks should not wear the robes of the Saṅgha of the four quarters directly against the bare skin of the body, nor wear them without a sweat cloth between.

Monks should not leave the bedding of the Saṅgha of the four quarters outdoors without a cover or shelter, nor abandon it by casting it beyond a distance of forty-nine cubits from the doorway, and then go away. If one must go to the place for defecating or urinating, one should inform the monks who are present and then go. Just as one guards one's own alms bowl, one's Dharma robe, and one's own skin, so should monks fully protect the bedding of the Saṅgha of the four quarters. Monks should by no means allow the bedding of the Saṅgha of the four quarters to be wasted. This is called the duty of bedding.

What is the duty of the door panel? The door panel is the wing of the door. When a monk knocks on it, he should not knock for a long time. He should knock softly and gently with his knuckles, so that those already inside will hear. He should neither open nor close it violently; he should open and close it slowly and gently, mindfully. He should open and close it without dragging it against either side of the doorframe. This is called the duty of the door panel.

What is the duty of the pivot? The pivot refers to the upper and lower hinge supports of the door. These should be well fitted. If a monk goes out of the main hall and leaves both the upper and lower pivots unsecured, the main hall may collapse. If the main hall collapses, it will ruin us ourselves along with our alms bowls, our Dharma robes, and our bedding. This is called the duty of the pivot.

What is the duty of the empty dwelling? A monk should sweep the empty dwelling with a broom, mop the floor, discard the sweeping cloth, and as best he can remove the mucus deposits gently. He should repair cracks, damage, and holes. If any vessels are found scattered about individually and are still serviceable, he should wash and store them; if they are not serviceable, he should discard them. If there is someone able to make them usable again, he should pick out the green grasses. If laypeople arrive, he should give them a talk on the Dharma. Even when a monk has entered an empty dwelling, he should not abandon it heedlessly. If he does not wish to remain there, he should determine where to go from there. He should inspect the vicinity, the place for defecating, the place for urinating, the stairway, and

the stairway, the door fastenings, and the areas of use; having inspected all of these, he should take up residence there. He should see to it that none of these things cause disturbance or harm. This is what is called the duty regarding an empty dwelling.

What is the duty of a senior monk regarding an empty dwelling? The duty of a senior monk who is a monk of an empty dwelling is to engage in the following. From keeping his face clear and free of frowning, as described before, up through taming with diligence, pacifying, and fully quieting any quarrels, disputes, grudges, and conflicts that have arisen — all of this is what is called the duty of a senior monk regarding an empty dwelling.

What is the duty regarding the alms bowl? A monk should not wash his alms bowl without having first applied ash. He should not wash it with gritty soil, nor with earth mixed with sand, nor with balls of gritty soil mixed with sand; rather, he should wash the alms bowl with ground pulse. He should not wash it while standing up, should not dry it while standing up, should not put it into a vessel, should not hide it, should not carry it along the road, should not carry it when crossing water, and should not set down the alms bowl on uneven ground. A monk should not bang his alms bowl against the walls of the dwelling. He should not use it to throw out dust-cloths. He should not smear excrement gently over its face. He should not use it to carry water for washing the hands, nor water for washing the feet, nor water for washing the face, nor water for washing the body. He should not fill water jars with it. A monk should not bring his alms bowl to the place for defecating, nor to the place for urinating, nor into the privy, nor to the place for washing the feet; in short, a monk should not bring the alms bowl to any unclean place whatsoever. A monk who is holding his alms bowl should not make prostrations to a stūpa. When it needs repair, he should not set it aside without repairing it; he should not set it aside while it is still very wet, nor neglect it when it has become very dry. Knowing through careful inspection, he should use it gradually and gently, and should keep it until it finally breaks down completely. A monk should guard his alms bowl as he would guard his very eyes, so that he will never again need to seek one. This is what is called the duty regarding the alms bowl.

What is the duty regarding the robes?
