The Blessed One (the Buddha) permitted monks three robes — not out of arrogance, not to engender pride, not for adornment, not for show — but so that monks might live comfortably: as a remedy against the discomfort of contact with insects, flies, wind, heat, snakes, and so forth, and in order to be clothed in a covering of moral shame and decorum. Moreover, monks should use them in accordance with how they are properly used. The inner robe should be used in accordance with the way of using an inner robe. The upper robe should be used in accordance with the way of using an upper robe. The lower robe should be used in accordance with the way of using a lower robe.

Now, these are the things for which the inner robe should not be used: monks should not bang the walls of the assembly hall while wearing the inner robe; they should not sweep the floors with it; they should not use it to throw out dust-cloths; they should not smear excrement gently over it; they should not use it to fill water vessels; it should not serve as a vessel for use, as a cleaning ball, as a ball for defecating, or at the place for washing the feet; it should not be used to divide vessels, to maintain the assembly hall, for the duties of the alms bowl, or for the duties of the robes; it should not be bathed with. Having taken off the inner robe, one should not carry it to grass, wood, excrement, or earth. Having taken off the inner robe, one should not take it into the place for defecating, the place for urinating, the privy, or the place for washing the feet; in short, having removed the inner robe, one should not go with it to any unclean place whatsoever. One should not divide it as a lower robe, should not use it as a sitting cloth,

One should not wear it constantly. One should not enter into the inner robe to sleep. This is the manner in which the inner robe is not to be used.

The inner robe is to be used in the following way. A nun (bhikṣuṇī), having put on the inner robe, should enter upon alms rounds, enter into the village, enter into her sphere of conduct, go for food, go for gruel and porridge. The inner robe is also to be used in two ways: either it is worn on top, or it is tucked in underneath.

The upper robe (Skt. uttarāsaṅga) is to be used in the following way. Monks (bhikṣus), having put on the upper robe, should not sweep the assembly hall with it, should not use it to sweep the floor, should not cast it aside as a dusting cloth, should not gently smear dung on it, should not use it for the duties of the alms bowl, should not use it for the duties of the robes, and should not bathe with it. Having put on the upper robe, one should not carry it to grass, wood, or earth. Having put on the upper robe, one should not take it into the place for defecating, the place for urinating, the privy, or the place for washing the feet. In short, one should not go to any unclean place whatsoever while wearing the upper robe. One should not wear it as a hip cloth, should not spread it over a sweating body, and should not wear and use it constantly. This is the manner in which the upper robe is not to be used.

The upper robe is to be used in the following way. Having put on the upper robe, one should fill water jars, fill jars for use, fill vessels with pure pills, fill vessels with pills for the privy, and also fill vessels with pills for washing the feet. One should divide vessels, maintain the assembly hall, and indeed for whatever else may be appropriate, one should use the upper robe.

The hip cloth is to be worn everywhere: one should wear it on the hip and use it constantly. A monk should not place his robe in an unclean spot, should not press it down with something heavy. If it is appropriate to mend it, one should mend it. If it is appropriate to wash it, one should wash it. If it is appropriate to turn it over, one should turn it over.

A monk should not retain the five great dyes. What are the five great dyes? They are these: indigo wood, gall-oak extract, lac, saffron, and vermilion. With the exception of bark from the krishna tree, one should seek out colored bark of whatever other kind will produce a reddish-brown hue. If even that is unavailable, then there is no fault.

The inner robe must certainly be marked. For the upper robe there is no definite requirement, and for the hip cloth there is likewise no definite requirement.

If a monk's robe is worn out or scarce, he should patch it on a separate piece of cloth — five, seven, nine, ten, eleven, or more patches as appropriate.

Thus a monk should use what is used as an inner robe as an inner robe, what is used as an upper robe as an upper robe, and what is used as a hip cloth as a hip cloth. A monk should guard his robe just as he guards his own skin, so that there is no need to search for it again afterward. This is called the duty of the robe.

What is the duty of the mat? The Blessed One (the Buddha) permitted monks two kinds of mat for the comfort of the sleeping place. If thick, one should make a single layer; if thin, one should make it two layers. A monk should not sit or lie down before spreading out a mat, should not dedicate a single mat alone, and should not remain for a night without a mat. A monk should take care of his mat properly, so that there is no need to seek another afterward. This is called the duty of the mat.

What is the duty of the needle? The Blessed One permitted monks two kinds of needle for the purpose of mending robes: iron and copper. Monks should not go about on excursions without having a needle.

A monk should store the needle well and take good care of it, so that there is no need to seek another afterward. This is called the duty of the needle.

What is the duty of the needle case? The Blessed One permitted monks needle cases for the purpose of protecting needles. A monk should not entrust a needle case to shameless novices. One should not let it be lost. Even if someone is fully ordained, if they are not trustworthy, one should not do so either. Likewise, there are five kinds of person to whom a needle case should not be entrusted: the shameless, the resentful, the unfriendly, those whose mindfulness has declined, and those who do not abide in proper conduct. A monk should store the needle case well and attend to it diligently, so that there is no need to seek another afterward. This is called the duty of the needle case.

What is the duty of gruel? The Blessed One permitted monks gruel for the purpose of living comfortably and for the purpose of properly consuming what has been given through acts of generosity by donors and benefactors. A monk should not drink gruel while making slurping sounds. One should drink gruel mindfully and with vigilance, suppressing any noise. Not out of arrogance, not out of pride, not out of conceit, not for the sake of taste, but for the sake of healing and sustaining this body. This is called the duty of gruel.

What is the duty of water? A monk should examine water very carefully. Water that is clear, bright, unsettled, unmixed, settled, and pure should be used. This is called the duty of water.

What is the duty of the water vessel? The Blessed One permitted monks water vessels, both for the Saṅgha and for individuals, along with a base to rest on and a lid to cover the mouth. Monks should wash them thoroughly, dry them, keep them clean, and store them. Water should be placed in them by a proper hand and with a proper cloth. One should pour carefully. If brahmins or householders arrive, one should also offer water to them. Monks should store water vessels with great care and attend to them diligently, so that there is no need to seek another afterward. This is called the duty of the water vessel.

What is the duty of the communal water vessel? The Blessed One permitted monks communal water vessels. These should be thoroughly washed, dried, kept clean, and stored. Having been filled, they should be set at the door of the assembly hall. Monks should store that communal vessel with care and attend to it diligently, so that there is no need to seek another afterward. This is called the duty of the communal water vessel.

What is the duty of the cleansing ball? The Blessed One permitted monks cleansing balls. These should not be placed near a stūpa. A monk should inspect them from time to time, dry them, and replenish them. This is called the duty of the cleansing ball.

What is the duty of food? There are five kinds of staple food and five kinds of non-staple food. Monks, when eating any staple or non-staple food, should at the time of eating establish mindfulness clearly: they should examine the food, recognizing it as that which was sought, that which was obtained through effort, that which is similar to other such things, that which is fully to be used, that which is subject to deterioration, and that which is to be discarded. Eating with this understanding in mind, they should eat. Keeping mindfulness close and without distraction of mind, they should eat while cultivating the following perceptions with regard to food: perceiving it as in accordance with its cause, perceiving oneself as an invalid, perceiving oneself as dependent on others, perceiving food as a condition, perceiving it in terms of dependent origination. One should establish these perceptions clearly and then eat. Mindfulness should also be established with regard to eating together with others, eating repeatedly, and eating a sufficient amount. This is called the duty of food.

What is the duty of eating? Whether a monk is eating rice, eating curds, or drinking gruel, when the time is announced or the gong is struck, he should come promptly.

He should come promptly. He should stand with vigilance. He should sit with vigilance. He should eat with vigilance. He should keep mindfulness close at hand and not let the mind wander. He should be well dressed, comport himself with proper bearing, be thoroughly restrained and quite composed. He should make no noise, should not let his eyes wander, and should look only as far as the yoke-beam's length ahead. He should be orderly in his conduct, humble in bearing, and should reflect inwardly on fear and dependence on others, with the thought that he will sweep up the dust, so to speak. He should keep in mind loving-kindness and a warm affectionate heart toward elder monks, monks of middle standing, and novices, perceiving them clearly as father, son, and younger brother, and should sit skillfully on his seat. He should eat skillfully. This is called the duty of eating.

What is the duty of passing on food? A monk should not return food he has received, nor should he pass it on portion by portion. To whom, then, should he give it? He should give it to his mother, to his father, his brothers, and his sisters. He should give it to relatives as well. He should give it to laypeople who have come inside the monastery enclosure. He should give it to those who are of benefit to him, and even to those who are not. He should give it to the sick, to those who are detained, and to those who are occupied with something. Even if a pregnant woman comes, he should keep mindfulness close and give food to her. He should also give a single portion of food to animals. He should give it too to one who wishes to go forth into the monastic life. And he should give after dividing it into portions and setting aside what remains. This is called the duty of passing on food.

What is the duty of alms-going (Skt. piṇḍapāta)? A monk should receive alms respectfully. He should receive them in order — not equal to the broth, not equal to the side-dish. He should be vigilant, keep mindfulness close at hand, keep the mind from wandering, not be hasty, and take only as much as will suffice. This is called the duty of alms-going.

What is the duty of the alms-round practice? A monk who practices the alms-round should enter with vigilance, sit with vigilance, and stand with vigilance. He should keep mindfulness close at hand and not let the mind wander. He should be seemly in appearance, comport himself with proper bearing, be thoroughly restrained, be fully covered, make no sound, not let his eyes wander but look only as far as the yoke-beam's length ahead, restrain his senses, not let the mind stray outward, and maintain awareness of what is before and behind. When he sees a woman who resembles his mother, he should keep the perception of her as his mother close at hand. When he sees a woman who resembles his sister, he should keep the perception of her as his sister close at hand. When he sees a woman who resembles his daughter, he should establish the perception of her as his daughter.

A monk on the alms-round should take note of the landmarks of markets, trading quarters, crossroads, three-way junctions, and gatehouses. When he has reached a householder's doorway, he should gently shake the clapper or knock softly at the door with his fingers. If a woman is asleep, he should jingle the bell-ring to wake her. If she has gone into a place where pounding is being done, he should wait until two or three strokes of the pestle have been made. If she has gone into a place where something is being burned, he should wait until one load has finished burning. If she has been engaged in weaving, he should wait while two or three turns are completed. He should keep mindfulness close at hand and take alms without letting the mind wander. He should take only as much as is sufficient.

If a monk who practices the alms-round wishes, he may eat in the company of the Saṅgha. Even when invited as a guest, he should regard it as his own affair and carry out the practice of the alms-round. This is called the duty of the alms-round practice.

What is the duty of the bowl-carrier? A monk who carries the bowl should know the time and measure, should go on the alms-round, should be knowing, should establish mindfulness, should not let the mind wander, should be undistracted, and should not mingle.

One should by all means keep it clean and neat. One should by no means treat it in the manner of something impure, something broken, something long-used and worn. One should keep it clean and bright. One should bring it in a manner that is well-proportioned and fitting. One should not seek other purposes that are out of place. Having gone to the monastery, one should approach that monk with a pleasant expression, free from frowning, with agreeable words, and with a glad demeanor, and receive the alms-bowl. This is called the duty of the bowl-carrier.

What is the duty of the forest monk? The forest monk should maintain a pleasant expression and should be free from frowning. He should establish mindfulness. First he should offer a kind greeting, welcoming with gentle words such as "Welcome, may you have come comfortably." At the outset he should inquire: "Are you dwelling well? Are you practicing well? Are you doing well in your work?"

The forest monks should take good care of the water and set it out. They should set out the water-vessels as well. They should take care of the food and set it out. They should set out the vessels for food as well. They should take care of the fire and set it out. They should take care of the kindling and set it out. They should take care of the lamps and set them out. They should take care of the vessels for oil and set them out. They should take care of the wick-material and set it out. They should gather together and set out butter, oil of grain, honey, and binding-cords for bundles. They should gather together and set out pieces of leather. They should gather together and set out thread, garlands, and needles for sewing. They should gather together and set out needles, knives, thread, and provisions. They should keep the medicines well stocked. They should keep the carriers for solid goods well stocked.

The forest monks should not show the fire-crystal or the water-crystal to others. The forest monk should know the wells thoroughly. He should be skilled in practical affairs, skilled in the affairs of the night, and skilled in the lay of the land. The forest monk should be skilled in the sūtras, skilled in the Vinaya, and skilled in the Abhidharma. He should be skilled in speech, skilled in teaching the Dharma, skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in what is possible and what is not possible.

The forest monks should know the Dharma and should know its meaning. They should know the time and know the measure, know themselves, know the assembly, know persons, and know the distinctions among persons.

The forest monks should not give rise to pride. They should not behave arrogantly. They should be respectful. They should be dependent upon others' authority. They should not be loose-tongued. Their words should be steady. They should have a sense of shame and a sense of conscience. They should not speak much, and they should not speak in ways that lead to heated argument. They should apply themselves with diligence and should not be indolent. They should act with mindfulness and vigilance. They should keep the sense faculties composed. They should know moderation in food. They should not think of themselves as important. In the evening and at dawn they should apply themselves earnestly to the practice of meditation. They should not pursue the pleasures of sleep, the pleasure of lying on one's side, or the pleasure of the bed. They should know when it is the right time to engage in practice and when it is not. They should be skilled in sitting on seats. They should not revile the elder monks, and they should not revile the junior monks either.

The forest monk should not let his diligence be wasted. He should attain what has not yet been attained, realize what has not yet been realized, and actualize what has not yet been actualized. The monk dwelling in the forest hermitage should, by means of the Dharma-staff, the ball, and the mallet, practice meditation in the evening and at dawn.

If the forest monk does not fulfill the prescribed rules of the holy life in accordance with what has been laid down, he will come to incur a transgression. This is called the duty of the forest monk.

What is the duty of the elder of the forest hermitage? One should engage in all such duties as have been described above.

From knowing all the newly ordained monks dwelling there, everything proceeds as before. In all things, the elder monk of the forest hermitage should be the first to engage, up to and including the point of not abandoning his continuity. He should take hold of the duties of the hermitage and apply himself to the tasks of the hermitage. Those monks, for their part, should listen to the instructions he imparts by way of guidance and carry them out. This is called the duty of the elder of the forest hermitage.

What is the duty of the village-border monk? From maintaining a pleasing appearance, the village-border monk proceeds as before, up to and including dwelling in comfort. He should inquire of monks who have arrived, asking, "Did you travel well?" He should see to it that they rest in accordance with seniority and as is fitting. He should provide whatever sleeping mats and seats are available. If they arrive in the morning, he should divide and distribute whatever food is to be had. Should they come after the meal, he should provide and satisfy them with whatever drink, molasses, sugar, confections, and light refreshments are available. In the evening, he should likewise distribute and provide sleeping mats. He should provide water for washing the feet and oil for anointing them. He should separately show them the way to the park, the entrance inside, the surrounding area, the place for defecating, the place for urinating, the stairways, the steps, the divisions, and the separate sections. He should announce whatever Saṅgha duties have been scheduled. If there is an alms-goer among them, he should also instruct him in the proper domain for his rounds. For those who arrive, he should prepare food and drink. If one decides to stay, he should ask and, if the monk is remaining, provide a dwelling-room or an upper story room, or whatever is suitable for seclusion. If one is departing, he should be given a gracious send-off and escorted on his way. If lay people, brahmins, and householders, arrive, the village-border monk should meet them with a joyful face, free of frowning, welcome them in front, and speak pleasantly to them. He should offer a seat. If food and drink are needed, they should be given. If they wish to sleep, bedding should be provided. If they wish to hear the Dharma, and if he himself is able, he should give a Dharma talk; if he himself is unable, he should appoint another monk to give a Dharma talk. The village-border monk should train those brahmins and householders who come and arrive in generosity, in engaging in acts of giving, in taking refuge, and in undertaking the bases of training. He should also provide them with incense, perfume, and flowers. He should have them circumambulate the stūpa and pay homage. He should instruct them to the best of his ability and then send them on their way. This is called the duty of the village-border monk.

What is the duty of the elder of the village-border community? The elder of the village-border community should engage in duties such as these. From knowing all the newly ordained monks dwelling there, everything proceeds as before, and the elder monk of the village-border community should in all things be the first to engage, up to and including the point of not abandoning his continuity. He should take hold of those monks in the duties of the village-border and instill in them a grasp of the village-border tasks. He should instill in them an engagement with good conduct. He should give them the following instruction: "Venerable ones, keep mindfulness close at hand and dwell at the village border. Toward the park attendants, the novices' fathers, and women, abandon habitual gazing, and even when you must look, keep mindfulness firmly in place, look with care, and speak with care. Do not be arrogant. At due times, give Dharma talks. Turn away from what is outside your proper domain, and hold to what is within your proper domain." Those monks, for their part, should listen to his instructions and

act in accordance with the instructions given. This is called the duty of the resident senior monk at the village border.

What is the duty of a visiting monk? A visiting monk should not simply walk straight into the monastery. At the gate of the monastery, set down the alms bowl and the outer robe. If water is available, wash your feet. If no water is available, wipe off the dust on a mat for wiping dust, or wipe it off with a leaf or a dry leaf. If you need to relieve yourself by way of feces or urine, then do so, and urinate. Then put on the outer robe, take the folds of the outer robe over the left shoulder, pick up the stacked robe-cloth and the alms bowl with the left hand, take a tooth-cleaner in the right hand, and carry your sandals in the left hand. If the monastery is enclosed by a wall, by a wooden fence, or by a hedge, enter mindfully, without dragging the gate, going in with vigilance. Circumambulate the stūpas. With vigilance, keep mindfulness close at hand, and do not let the mind scatter. Comport yourself with beautiful deportment, fully covered, your voice restrained, eyes not wandering, looking only as far ahead as a yoke's length, and enter the main shrine hall. Sit on the side where there is the most open visibility, so that the resident monks, upon seeing you, will know that this monk is a visitor, and they will set about making you comfortable.

When a visiting monk has entered the shrine hall, he should set down, in a suitable place, the robe-cloth, the alms bowl, the water vessel, and the sandals. Then, with respect and reverence, with a sense of awe, bowing down at their feet, pay homage to the senior resident monks. Gladden the younger monks with kind words. Sit on whatever seat you obtain. Whether it is at the time of a meal, the time of drinking, the time of taking gruel, or the time of paying respects, when the signal is given or the wooden sounding board is struck and the Saṅgha assembles, join the assembly. Ask about seniority in years, and sit in the proper order according to where you have come from.

If a bed or mat is being offered, understand the situation fully and look it over carefully. If a dwelling is assigned, ask, "Is it possible to stay here or not?" If it is possible to stay there, say, "What is comfortable?" If it is not possible to stay there, then set the alms bowl and robe off to one side, and look for a broom for sweeping. Look for a water vessel and a wooden seat as well. When you approach the doorway of the dwelling, knock softly and gently. For there may be a snake, a scorpion, a centipede, a house lizard, a chameleon, or some other harmful creature there, and it should be made aware of your presence. Understand what is in the upper and lower parts of the door frame, and understand the door bolt. Then open the door slowly, enter with vigilance, and sit in the middle. From each of the four corners, look for any snake's nesting place, any scorpion's nesting place, or any insects, bees, or other creatures' nesting places. If any are found, cause them to leave in a way that does not harm them.

Then take hold of the broom in the dwelling. Sweep it. Sweep it again. Sprinkle with fine dust and wipe gently and softly. If there are things such as a bed, a chair, a small wooden bench, a stool, a canopied couch, cushions, rectangular seats, or the like, go outside first. If an elderly monk was sitting there before, wait a moment. If not, remove them one by one with care, slowly, enter with vigilance, and wash your feet.

A visiting monk must not perform against the resident monks any act of censure, any act of deprecation, any act of banishment, any act of reconciliation, any act of suspension for not having seen a transgression, any act of suspension for failure to perform a corrective act,

any act of suspension for not having relinquished a wrong view, or any act of penalty, or any act of penalty carried out from the very foundation, or any act of appeasement, or any act of appeasement carried out from the very foundation. Ask whether any such things exist or do not exist. If they do exist, refrain from those and anything of that kind.

Understand and inquire about the exits and entrances of the monastery building, the surrounding areas, the latrine grounds, the urination grounds, the stairs, the steps, and the procedures for opening and closing doors and the like. Ask what kind of Saṅgha business has been arranged. Then enter your lodging, sit cross-legged on a cushion or mat, straighten your body upright, establish mindfulness, and abandon the eight things that this body touches. These are as follows: sickness, tumors, weapons, poison, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness — dwell in these contemplations. If you are able, remain in them for as long as you can. If, however, you are unable, rise, recite three times, recite the praises of the qualities of generosity, and having recited the praises of the qualities of generosity, turn to the right. Pressing foot against foot, having established luminous mindfulness, knowing how to rise, setting up clear perception, attending carefully with the mind, at the end of the night, as the dawn breaks, rise at length and swiftly. Then, sitting cross-legged with body held upright and erect, establish mindfulness in the mind, and abandon by means of this body the eight things that the body touches. These are as follows: sickness, tumors, poison, weapons, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness — dwell in these contemplations. Then when dawn has come, take a tooth-cleaning stick. Then carry out whatever tasks need to be done, and ask: "Today, shall I enter as a guest of the Saṅgha's offering meal, or shall I go on almsround?" If you enter as a guest of the Saṅgha's offering meal, conduct yourself as you please in virtuous activities and carry out the alms duty. If you go on almsround, then ask: "What village, what territory, which families are faithful, which families are not faithful? Have the precepts been given to that family?" Ask: "Has the alms bowl already been accepted?" Ask: "Are there any unruly horses or unruly cattle?" Then in the morning, put on the lower robe, take the alms bowl and the Dharma robe, and go on almsround with clear awareness. Having completed the almsround and performed the meal duties, afterward, having accepted the almsround food, setting aside the meal duties, set down the Dharma robe and alms bowl, and sit in comfort. This is called the duty of a newly arrived monk.

What is the duty of the resident elder monk in regard to newly arrived monks? The resident elder monk of the monastery where one has newly arrived should take note of the monks who have newly arrived. Toward them he should be pleasant of countenance, free from frowning and anger, and with gentle words first bring satisfaction to those monks. For the sake of the monks who have newly arrived, he should search out bedding and seats. From among those sitting, he should designate a host in five ways: informing them as to which is their cell in the monastery and directing them to look at it; informing them as to which bedding and seat is theirs and directing them to look at it; and handing over to them their key — these five constitute what is called the duty of the resident elder monk in regard to newly arrived monks.

The Noble Vinaya, the fifty-second fascicle.

What is the duty of a departing monk? The monk who is departing should investigate the direction and region to which he is going. He should ask the monks who have come from that direction: "In that direction, does any one of the eight obstacles that may arise for monks occur?" "If I go there, will I not be too busy with almsround, medicine for the sick, and rendering service?"

"If I am kept busy and unable to obtain almsround, medicine for the sick, and those who render service to me, will my body not decline and my time not pass in vain? If I go there, will my body and mind be at ease? If I go there, will my wholesome qualities grow? If I go there, will I be together with monks who are endowed with moral discipline, endowed with good qualities, given to wholesome qualities, of the same view, and of the same way of living? Will they prevent doubts I have not yet arisen from arising, and dispel those that have already arisen? Will they prevent wrong views I have not yet arisen from arising, and turn back those that have arisen? Will my body and mind and those venerable ones be at ease together? Will I and those venerable ones grow together in wholesome qualities?" — these are the questions he should ask. In this way he should examine the direction and region.

He should also examine his companions: "Are these venerable ones endowed with moral discipline? Are they endowed with good qualities? Are they given to wholesome qualities? Do they share the same view? Do they share the same way of living? Will they prevent doubts in me that have not yet arisen from arising, and dispel those that have arisen? Will they also prevent wrong views that have not yet arisen from arising? Will my body and mind be at ease together with those venerable ones? Will I together with those venerable ones grow in wholesome qualities? If I fall ill on the road, will those venerable ones not abandon me?" Having examined his companions in this way, he should examine the road: "On that road, will none of the eight obstacles that may arise occur? On that road, will I not be made too busy by almsround, medicine for the sick, and those who render service? And if there are neither almsround nor those who render service, will I not be harmed and my time pass in vain? On that road, will my body and mind be at ease? On that road, will my wholesome qualities grow?" If he will not be excessively occupied, he may go.

Having in this way examined the direction and region, the companions, and the road, if he intends to set out the next day, he should go before his preceptors and teachers, and say: "I am going to such a direction and such a region, to such a town," and request their permission. The preceptors and teachers, for their part, should examine his direction and region, examine the road, and examine his monk companions — what his companion monks are like, what his retinue is like, what those who are to accompany him are like — and, having understood this, if it seems suitable they should grant permission; if it does not seem suitable, they should not grant it. If the departing monk departs without having asked permission, a transgression is incurred. However, if it would lead to growth in wholesome qualities and yet the preceptor and teacher are not acting properly, then to depart without requesting permission is permissible.

The room in which he has been residing he should carefully sweep. He should dust it and sweep out the dust. He should plaster the floor gently with dung. In the evening he should recite the passage on the merits of generosity three times over. At dawn he should make the arrangements for the beds and bedding as they should properly be, then fold them, shake them out, and beat them. Then he should push them back from the wall by about four finger-breadths, stack them, and leave them there. He should shut the door, fasten the inner latch and the upper latch, and before departing inform the monks residing there and the monks of the neighborhood, saying: "Please keep watch over these." The instruction to keep watch over the beds and so forth comprises five parts: this room — "Please watch over this room"; the beds — "Please watch over these beds";

the key — these make the five parts. Once he has left the outer precinct of the monastery, he should check with his fellow monks. Before going far, he should ask anyone he meets: "Has anything been forgotten and left behind?" If something has in fact been forgotten and left, that monk should turn back, retrieve it, and wait until the others arrive. This is called the duty of departing.

What, then, is the duty of the resident elder with respect to departure? The resident elder should rise early in the morning and direct the monks who are setting out. He should instruct those venerable ones to gather their bowls and robes properly, hold them well, and then depart, telling them: "Let no one forget anything." After they have set out, the resident elder himself should check whether anything has been left behind through forgetfulness. Then all should depart from the rear of the group. Before going far, he should say to any one of them: "Is there anything that has been forgotten and left behind?" The resident elder should instruct all those monks, saying: "None of the venerable ones should go ahead and set off first; none should lag behind and straggle. Everyone should assemble together and travel looking after one another." When the resident elder has set out on the road, he should ascertain whether those monks are comfortable or not, and should be aware of whether he himself has gone ahead and set off first, or has lagged behind and been left. If any have gone on ahead, he should urge them on and have them continue. He himself should travel in the midst of the monks. If he is unable to keep pace, he should instruct those monks to see to their bowls, robes, and other things, and have these conveyed to them. If a monk should become entirely unable to travel, the other monks should carry that monk on their shoulders or bear him as a load, bring him out of that monastery, and proceed to the edge of the village. They should provide that monk with an attendant monk, and that attendant monk should seek out food, medicine, and other necessities for him. If the road should prove to be dangerous, they should march along swiftly and without delay, and when past that stretch they should rest. If conditions permit, wherever there is a riverbank, a forest edge, a shaded green meadow, or a pleasant spot of ground, he should identify it and have the monks rest there. After resting, they should continue. The resident elder should then instruct all of them, saying: "Now, all of you, each one recite here a verse on the virtues of generosity." When all the monks have finished reciting verses on the virtues of generosity, the resident elder should conclude by himself reciting a verse on the virtues of giving, and should survey the terrain two or three times before proceeding.

When they arrive at the edge of a village, he should seek lodging for the monks and seek out sleeping places. Alternatively, he should seek out grass and leaves. If these are obtained, he should procure water for washing the feet, oil for anointing the feet, a beverage prepared by steeping, molasses, candy, and so forth. He should also inquire and check for suitable places for urination and defecation, and there they should pass the night. For the sake of the household gods, he should recite three times a single verse and then recite the virtues of generosity. While residing there, the resident elder should seek out and gather rice, gruel, and sour milk for the monks, and distribute them to the monks. There he should speak to the newly arrived monks, speak truthfully, make everything known to them, help them understand, instruct them, and guide them — and by all means turn them away from arrogance, improper conduct, and frivolous behavior.

If the resident elder of the traveling party does not act in accordance with the rules of conduct as established, a transgression with remainder will occur. This is called the duty of the resident elder of the traveling party.

What is the duty of foot-washing? The Blessed One permitted foot-washing for the monks. Monks, if you see the foot-washing vessels empty, fill them yourselves. Or a monk may knock at the doors of those residing in the assembly hall to announce foot-washing. The duty of foot-washing is also this: if a monk wishes to wash his feet, he should go mindfully to the foot-washing area. If an elder is already seated there, he should wait a moment. If no one is present, he should enter mindfully and wash his feet. A monk should not sit for a long time in the foot-washing area. He should not enter into meditative absorption there, nor recite scriptures, nor recite from memory, nor ask questions, nor settle into conversation and sit about. He should quickly wash his feet and mindfully depart. This is called the duty of foot-washing.

What is the duty of the foot-washing elder? The foot-washing elder monk, once a monk has begun washing his feet, should not dismiss or remove him before he has finished. "Has begun washing his feet" means that, at the least, his feet have become wet with water.

If monks behave improperly or settle into conversation and sit about, the resident elder monk should stop them, recite scripture to them, instruct them, and guide them toward proper conduct — leading them to follow the rules of conduct as befits the foot-washing elder. This is called the duty of the foot-washing elder.

What is the duty of the sitting assembly? Monks residing in a monastery or dwelling should gather together on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth days of the month, and speak on the Dharma — whether as taught by the Buddha or as taught by his śrāvakas. On the following morning, as soon as the gate is opened or the wooden sounding board is struck, they should assemble. Having gathered quickly, they should seat themselves mindfully. Having seated themselves mindfully, they should establish close mindfulness. They should keep the mind undistracted. Their conduct should be complete and excellent. They should be thoroughly composed. They should be thoroughly joyful. They should be silent. Without letting the eyes wander, they should gaze as far as a yoke's length ahead. They should be accompanied by reverence, by humility, by deference, and by a sense of awe. They should hold a mind that is lowly, like a broom. Toward elders, those of middle standing, and the newly ordained, they should hold a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benefit, and a mind of affectionate care. They should dwell near to the perception of them as elder brothers and as children. They should be skilled in sitting on their seats, and having sat, they should pass the night until dawn through definitive Dharma talk. If that is not comfortable, they should pass the night through two forms of conduct: walking and standing.

When the monks have assembled and are seated, they should listen to the Dharma at the proper time — with reverence, listening closely, not disparaging it, engaging with it properly, not seeking faults, openly establishing respect for the Dharma, not looking down upon the person who speaks the Dharma, not disparaging oneself, thinking that the mind is unified with the Teacher and with his word, not letting the ears wander, with a reverent mind, gathering all the mind into unity with the Teacher, and so listening to the Dharma.

After that, for the sake of the gods, kings, patrons, and donors, verses on the qualities of generosity should be recited. This is called the duty of the sitting assembly.

What is the duty of the sitting-assembly elder? Whether the gate has been opened or the wooden sounding board has been struck,

One should be the first to go there, the first to stand, and the first to be seated. Having sat, one should not speak even for a moment. Then one should oneself teach the Dharma, or else assign a capable monk to teach it. If one neither teaches the Dharma oneself nor assigns a capable monk to do so, one incurs an offense. Furthermore, if brahmins and householders arrive while the assembly is seated, one should also give them a Dharma talk. And if other wandering non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) arrive seeking an opportunity and looking for a weak point, one should engage them too in a Dharma exchange, saying: "This is unreasonable. This is inconsistent. This is unestablished." One should tame them with the Dharma of reason. One should not give rise to anger, should not be wrathful, and should not be contemptuous. This is called the duty of the sitting-assembly elder.

What is the duty of teaching the Dharma? The monk who teaches the Dharma should be accompanied by respect, should regard himself as lowly, should be subject to reverence and awe, should have a humble mind and a mind like a broom. Having entered into the midst of the assembly, one should teach the Dharma in a way that is reasoned, clear in expression, precise in wording, undisturbed, unmixed, connected, without error, with undistracted mind, and without a mercenary attitude. One should show manifest respect for the Dharma itself and also show manifest respect for those who listen to the Dharma. One should not disparage the Dharma. One should not disparage those who listen to the Dharma. One should not belittle oneself. One should understand all phenomena as being of the nature of reality and as dependent origination. One should act with a spirit of loving-kindness and of affection, so that this Dharma may long endure. One should not teach the Dharma relying on material gain as one's support rather than relying on the nature of reality itself. Beginning with respect, one should act in accordance and in harmony, proceeding in order, and teach the Dharma with delight, with faith, with joy, with enthusiasm, with devotion, with reasonableness, and without agitation. One should remain toward the assembly with a mind of loving-kindness and a mind of affection. It should not be for the sake of gain, honor, or fame. While teaching the Dharma one should not praise oneself or disparage others. This is called the duty of teaching the Dharma.

What is the duty of the Dharma-teaching elder? The elder who oversees the teaching of the Dharma should go to where the Dharma is being taught and listen to whether that monk is teaching in accordance with the Dharma or not in accordance with the Dharma. If he is teaching in accordance with the Dharma, one should generate enthusiasm. If he is teaching contrary to the Dharma, one should have it corrected. If it can be corrected, well and good. If it cannot be corrected, one should, to the best of one's ability and as much as one can, censure him, saying: "This monk's teaching is not the Dharma, it is not the Vinaya, it is not what the Teacher taught. Do not destroy the foundation of the Blessed One's Dharma. Do not scratch out the eye of the Dharma." Having said this, one should rise from one's seat and depart. This is called the duty of the Dharma-teaching elder.

What is the duty concerning proper times? Monks should go at the proper time. This is called the duty concerning proper times.

What is the duty concerning improper times? A monk should not enter a village at an improper time, except when such a circumstance has arisen. Not going without having informed a monk who is present in the residence — this is called the duty concerning improper times.

What is the duty concerning the assembly of the Saṅgha at improper times? Apart from the assembly of the Saṅgha on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth days of the month, assembling the Saṅgha at other times for the purpose of Saṅgha business, Saṅgha duties, and Saṅgha activities — when prior notice has been given or the wooden sounding board has been struck, one should quickly assemble, and should proceed with full awareness, and so forth as before.

One should be skilled in sitting. There, the senior elder of the Saṅgha should bow in order of seniority and take his seat wherever there is space. The second elder likewise should bow to the senior elder of the Saṅgha and take his seat wherever there is space. In the same way, the third elder, the fourth, and so on down to the newly ordained monk — each should bow in order of seniority and take his place wherever there is space. There, monks — whether elders, those of middle standing, or newly ordained — shall conduct Saṅgha business in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Teacher has taught. The senior elder monk shall not revile the monks, shall not disparage them, and shall not treat them with disrespect. This is called the duty concerning the assembly of the Saṅgha at improper times.

What is the duty of the elders concerning the assembly of the Saṅgha at improper times? When the Saṅgha assembles at an improper time and prior notice has been given or the wooden sounding board has been struck, the senior elder monk should be the first to go, the first to rise, and the first to be seated — with reverence, with a humble mind, with a sense of awe and deference, with the mind cast down like a broom, and with such an attitude he should enter into the midst of the Saṅgha. He should bow in order of seniority and take his seat. Toward the elders, those of middle standing, and the newly ordained, he should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of benefit, and a mind of affectionate care, maintaining clearly before him the perception that they are as his father, his younger brothers, and his sons. He should also look over the assembly: which among them is well-attired, which is poorly attired, which is attractive in appearance, which is unattractive, which is well-robed, which is poorly robed. Those who are well and attractively attired he should leave at ease. Those who are poorly and unattractively attired he should approach, instruct, and give guidance. Those who are already well-robed he should leave be. Those who are poorly robed he should signal. If they do not notice the signal, he should signal one seated nearby. If one seated nearby also does not notice, the senior elder monk should approach in a manner that causes no confusion, see that they are properly robed, and not make any loud sound.

The senior elder monk should examine the assembly with this thought: Is this assembly acting in accordance with the Dharma, or is it not? If it is in accordance with the Dharma, let him allow all business to proceed as they see fit. If it is not in accordance with the Dharma, he should take the side of what is in accordance with the Dharma, offer guidance on how to inquire into what is proper, and without saying anything further, rise from his seat and depart, so that disputes and quarrels do not ensue. This is called the duty of the elders concerning the assembly of the Saṅgha at improper times.

What is the duty concerning speaking? In the city of Rājagṛha there were certain wandering non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, would gather together and teach the Dharma, and many people would assemble there to hear them. Those teachers received gains and were shown honor, and their retinues grew large. The wise and capable king of the region of Magadha came to have faith in this excellent teaching and thought to himself: "These wandering non-Buddhists — from the time they are described as teaching the Dharma on the eighth and so forth, up to the point where their retinues have grown large —" and so on as before. "Just so, if the monks likewise were to gather together on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth and teach the Dharma, then I too would go there, and the king too would attend" — thinking thus, many people would also assemble.

The monks too would receive gains, and honor too would come to them, and their retinues would grow large. For the many people as well, merit would increase greatly. The monks would become fearless. The teaching would flourish. The sacred Dharma would endure for a long time. The lamp of the Dharma would blaze. And it would be made to shine for people of future generations.

Thinking thus, the wise and capable king of the region of Magadha, Bimbisāra, went to where the Blessed One was and approached him. He bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Bimbisāra, the wise and capable king of Magadha, addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Venerable One, as for the other wandering non-Buddhists — from the time of the eighth and so forth up to the point where their retinues grew large — it is as before. Now, if the monks likewise, beginning from the eighth, were to make it shine for people of future generations," and so on as before, "what does the Venerable One think of this?"

The Blessed One remained silent, giving his consent to King Bimbisāra, the wise and capable king of Magadha. Then, understanding from the Blessed One's silence that he had given his consent, King Bimbisāra bowed his head at the two feet of the Blessed One and departed from the Blessed One's presence.

Not long after King Bimbisāra the wise had departed, the Blessed One knew it, and declared to the monks: "Therefore, monks, I permit you: on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth, gather together and teach the Dharma. And it is to be taught in this manner: the monk who teaches the Dharma should make his meaning clear to the assembly both in meaning and in words."

Now the monks there spoke in ordinary speech, and because they spoke in ordinary speech, the assembly did not understand. The monks reported this to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "I permit you to teach the Dharma in song, with a melodious voice."

But they taught just as they were seated, and the assembly still could not understand. The Blessed One declared: "I permit you to teach the Dharma from a high seat."

Then they compiled and recited great sūtras at length, and though there was no uncertainty raised, nor any elaboration, the day itself was consumed by this, and the assembly became weary. The Blessed One declared: "I permit you to elaborate as freely as you wish, according to the subject matter."

They then took up only the bare meaning of the sūtra passage in brief and wished to present it as a narrative account, intending to follow the text just as it was spoken. Yet they became uncertain, wondering: would the sūtra not come out properly at its end? The Blessed One declared: "I permit you: take the bare meaning of the sūtra in brief, and intersperse narrative accounts at appropriate moments; also follow the text just as it was spoken; and make the assembly understand by connecting meaning and words together. The sūtras themselves are also to be taken in just this way."

Then two of them taught together before a single assembly. The Blessed One declared: "Do not teach two together within a single assembly. Whoever does so incurs a transgression."

They then taught each to their own separate assembly, and those assemblies fell into dispute. The Blessed One declared: "Do not teach each to separate assemblies. If one does so, it incurs a grave fault."

Then it came about that they were teaching simultaneously to two assemblies, and the Blessed One declared:

"Do not teach simultaneously to two assemblies. Whoever does so incurs a transgression. Teach in such a way that the two assemblies do not fall into dispute from the teaching."

When those monks led their assemblies away on a journey, the Blessed One declared: "Do not lead an assembly away on a journey. Whoever leads an assembly away on a journey incurs a grave fault. As for those who go along with them, there is no fault."

Those monks then sought material gain through the Dharma, living by trading in the Dharma. The Blessed One declared: "Do not seek material gain through the Dharma. Do not make your livelihood by trading in the Dharma."

When there was then no one to speak, the Blessed One declared: "Let one who is capable of reminding do the reminding. If there is also no one able to remind, then speak in order of seniority."

When they composed verse and set it to melody, the Blessed One declared: "Speak it yourself, or else entrust it to another monk. The person entrusted should also be informed. If one does not speak it oneself, and does not entrust it to another monk, and does not inform the person who has been entrusted, one incurs a grave fault."

When monks were being appointed in order of seniority, it came about that simpleminded, hunchbacked, and tongue-tied monks were appointed, and certain wandering non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) began saying of these monks, within the community of the ascetics who are sons of the Śākyans: "This one is an excellent person! This one is a foremost person! This one is a supreme person!" — making false accusations against them, disparaging them, and uttering harsh words against them.

The monks reported the matter as it had occurred to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One declared: "Do not appoint in turn those who teach the Dharma if they do not have the ability. Appoint the one who has the ability. Appoint in such a way that the assembly will not fall into dispute."

As for the duty of speaking at other times: whenever and wherever monks are assembled and gathered together, the settled teachings of the Dharma are to be recited. If one does not know them, one should ask one another, inquire of one another. It should not be done for the sake of argument, not for the sake of finding fault, not for the sake of slander, not for the sake of causing harm. Rather, one should ask and inquire out of reverence and respect for the Dharma alone: "What is virtuous and what is non-virtuous? What is blameworthy and what is blameless? How is one to act so as to be virtuous, and how so as to be sinful?" This is the duty of speaking.

What then is the duty of not speaking? In whatever place monks are speaking yet do not wish to discourse to others, they should cultivate their minds just as they have accomplished the meditative recollection of that kind, and they should enter into the four modes of conduct. The elaboration of entering into mutual silence is as follows: it should be done in the manner of the monks of the Joyful Grove on the banks of the river. This is called the duty of not speaking.

What is the duty of entering the rains retreat (varṣā)? A monk who wishes to enter the rains retreat in the proper manner should reflect thoroughly, examine thoroughly, and analyze thoroughly, and then enter in the proper manner. He should consider: in that dwelling place, how many monks are possessed of moral discipline, possessed of good qualities, possessed of learning, possessed of wholesome qualities? Are their views harmonious, their conduct harmonious, their companionship harmonious? Are there those who are accommodating and agreeable, whether in coming or in going, whether in speaking? In that dwelling place, are there monks who hold the sūtras, who hold the Vinaya, who hold the matrix of teachings — from whom, if doubts have not arisen in me, they will not arise, and if they have arisen, they will be resolved? Are there those who, if something like a wrongdoing has not arisen, will prevent it from arising, and if it has arisen, will subdue it? Will one obtain in that dwelling place medicines suited to illness, food, requisites, and attendants? Will both one's body and one's mind be at ease in that dwelling place?

In that dwelling place, one should also consider whether there are monks who quarrel, who expose one another's faults, who cause conflict, and who engage in disputes — for such a place, it seems, would not be fitting. One should think: would that person not become an obstacle to my obtaining what I have not yet obtained, penetrating what I have not yet penetrated, and realizing what I have not yet realized? And would the Saṅgha not be divided during the rains retreat in that dwelling place? Having thus contemplated thoroughly, examined thoroughly, and investigated thoroughly, one should go to that place that has a companion suited to attending the sick. This is called the act of entering the rains retreat properly.

What then is the act of having entered the rains retreat properly? A monk who has entered the rains retreat properly should not go beyond the boundary even for a single day without purpose. If there is a purpose, one may go, with a blessing granted for seven days or for forty days. And this too is only for the sake of a purpose. What purposes? It may be for the sake of a monk, or a nun, or a male novice, or a female novice, or a male lay practitioner, or a female lay practitioner. It may be for the sake of a relative, or for one's own sake. Or it may be that one has come to doubt, to uncertainty, or to suspicion with regard to the Buddha, or the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, or suffering, or the origin of suffering, or cessation, or the path — and one has the perception that one may obtain what one has not yet obtained, penetrate what one has not yet penetrated, or realize what one has not yet realized. Or it may equally be for the sake of wandering non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Or if that monk would cause a division of the Saṅgha during the rains retreat in that place, or if a stūpa or a temple might be desecrated or burned — then, for the sake of the Buddha, or the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, that monk should go with a blessing granted for seven days or for forty days. If, having gone there, seven days or forty days have elapsed, the monk will incur no offense of breaking the rains retreat. This is called the act of having entered the rains retreat properly.

What then is the act of the elder monk who has entered the rains retreat properly? An elder monk who has entered the rains retreat properly should take note of the condition of the temple buildings and the stūpas — what repairs are needed, and who is willing to carry them out — and should encourage those who are willing, and announce the need publicly. Those who are unwilling should be urged, and reminded. This is called the act of the elder monk who has entered the rains retreat properly.

What then is the act of dwelling in the rains retreat properly? Monks who are dwelling in the rains retreat properly should carry out three kinds of tasks. They should have repaired the buildings of the dwelling where they are spending the rains retreat, those that are broken or deteriorated. They should inspect them, and have them inspected. Whatever robes are found in that dwelling place, those robes should be properly stored, or have them placed in storage. This is called the act of dwelling in the rains retreat properly.

What then is the act of the one who is head of the assembly? The head of the assembly should at regular intervals observe among the members of the assembly who is conducting themselves well and who is not, who is accomplishing what is good and who is not, and examine these things carefully. To one who is conducting themselves well and accomplishing what is good, one should offer full encouragement, saying: "Well done, venerable one, well done! Continue to practice exactly as you are practicing." One should rejoice in them sincerely. And at regular times one should teach them further and instruct them. As for one who is not conducting themselves well or not accomplishing what is good, one should impose upon them whatever penalty is appropriate to the case. This is called the act of the head of the assembly.

What is the act of entering the assembly? A monk, having established mindfulness, should enter the assembly thinking: "This is an assembly of the warrior caste (kṣatriya). This is an assembly of brahmins. This is an assembly of householders. This is an assembly of contemplatives (śramaṇas)." And he should think: "In that assembly I shall walk in such a way, stand in such a way, sit in such a way, speak in such a way, and not speak in such a way." This is called the act of entering the assembly.

What is the act of being present within the assembly? When a monk is present within the assembly, he should not engage in various kinds of chatter, nor in improper talk. He should bring the assembly to a proper state of readiness and then speak words that are in harmony with them. Having spoken, he should rise from his seat. This is called the act of being present within the assembly.

What is the act of the elder monk who is present within the assembly? An elder monk who is present within the assembly should examine the assembly, asking: "Do they prefer talk of such and such a kind, or do they prefer silence?" If there are those who prefer talk, he should speak to them in a manner suited to that. If there are those who prefer silence, he should sit there without saying anything. This is called the act of the elder who is present within the assembly.

What is the act of nourishing restoration? At the time of the restoration ceremony (poṣadha) on the fourteenth or fifteenth day, one should examine one's own mental continuum — the continuum of the night and the continuum of the day — asking: "Has a transgression arisen in me during that period?" If one has arisen, and if one finds a trustworthy monk, one should confess it before him. If one cannot find such a monk, one should purify it by a mental blessing. If no fault has arisen, one should generate the thought and declare aloud: "I am fully purified of such transgressions." The restoration ceremony is what renders moral discipline completely pure. This is called the act of nourishing restoration.

What is the act of performing the restoration ceremony? When the restoration ceremony comes about, even if it is not one's turn, one should still attend in the spirit of faith. And in doing so, one should proceed with full vigilance — from the moment of setting out with awareness, all the way through to the conduct of sitting, including mastery of how to be seated. Once seated, one should cultivate the clear perception that the one reciting is a teacher of the sūtra of individual liberation (Prātimokṣa). One should honor him, listen to him with respect, regard him as a superior, hold him as precious, keep him in mind, unify one's mind, not allow one's ears to wander, and listen with the whole mind focused single-pointedly. Having listened, one should be diligent in practicing accordingly and in accomplishing what was taught. This is called the act of performing the restoration ceremony.

What is the act of the restoration ceremony as a formal act? The act of the restoration ceremony has five aspects: the recitation, the dedication of merit, the complete purification of faith, the setting apart of occasions, and the mental blessing.

Furthermore, the formal act of the restoration ceremony has four types: performing it in a manner contrary to the Dharma and without an assembly, performing it in a manner contrary to the Dharma but with an assembly, performing it in accordance with the Dharma but without an assembly, and performing it in accordance with the Dharma and with an assembly. Of these, the formal act of the restoration ceremony performed in accordance with the Dharma and with an assembly is the one that is properly conducted. This is called the act of the restoration ceremony as a formal act.

What is the act of the individual liberation? At the very time of the restoration ceremony on the fourteenth or fifteenth day, all the monks who have come from the surrounding areas and from within the community should assemble together and be gathered in one place. The elder monk of the Saṅgha should then recite the sūtra of individual liberation. He should cultivate the clear perception that he is a teacher of the Prātimokṣa sūtra. The assembly should listen with honor and respect, regard the reciter as a superior, hold him as precious, keep him in mind, unify one's thoughts,

keep the ears attentive and not let them wander. All other things should be brought to stillness, and one should listen. Having heard, one should likewise apply oneself diligently and put it into practice. This is called the act of individual liberation.

What is the act of reciting the Prātimokṣa? There are five modes of reciting the Prātimokṣa. The first is: after a formal request has been made, the origin story is read, and then it is announced that "the remainder has been heard as before." When the Prātimokṣa is proclaimed in this way, it counts as the Prātimokṣa having been recited. This is the first mode of reciting the Prātimokṣa.

The second mode is: after a formal request has been made, the origin story is read, and then the four root defeats are read, after which it is announced that "the remainder has been heard as before." This too counts as the Prātimokṣa having been recited. This is the second mode of reciting the Prātimokṣa.

The third mode is: after a formal request has been made, the origin story is read, the four root defeats are read, and the thirteen Saṅgha remainders are also read, and then it is announced that "the remainder has been heard as before." This too counts as the Prātimokṣa having been recited. This is the third mode of reciting the Prātimokṣa.

The fourth mode is: after a formal request has been made, the origin story is read, the four root defeats are read, the thirteen Saṅgha remainders are read, and the two classes of indeterminate offenses are also read, and then it is announced that "the remainder has been heard as before." This too counts as the Prātimokṣa having been recited. This is the fourth mode of reciting the Prātimokṣa.

The fifth is: reciting the Prātimokṣa in full. These five constitute the act of reciting the Prātimokṣa.

What is the act of the monk who recites the Prātimokṣa? The monk who recites the Prātimokṣa should recite the Prātimokṣa sūtra clearly and fluently by heart, commit it to memory, and settle it firmly in mind. When the time comes to recite it, he should recite it well, without error. He should also examine his own continuum — examining, from the continuum of the previous night and the continuum of the day, whether at that time a transgression has arisen or not. If a transgression has arisen and there is a trustworthy monk present, he should confess it before that monk. If no such monk is available, he should first perform the restoration ceremony and then, following that, resolve in his mind: "I shall confess my transgressions afterwards in the proper manner as prescribed." He should then consecrate this resolve in his mind. He should apply himself diligently in accordance with what arises from the Prātimokṣa sūtra. This is called the act of the monk who recites the Prātimokṣa.

What is the act of the elder? If monks have been invited to a layman's home for a meal, at that time the elder monk should put on his lower robe early, present himself at a clean and proper place, and take his seat. This is called the act of the elder.

What is the act of the middle monk? The middle monk should, with the elder monk ahead of him, enter the village. If the elder should need to attend to defecation or urination along the way, the middle monk should go a short distance away and wait. If he goes far away, he should go to the edge of the village and wait. If brahmins and householders send an invitation, he should wait until the elder arrives and say, "We shall come presently." If hand-washing water is brought, he should say, "Wait for the elder." When the elder has arrived, all who are seated should rise. This is called the act of the middle monk.

What is the act of the junior monk? The junior monk should sweep the temple, clean the floor, lay out the rugs, and plaster the plastered surfaces gently with dung. Water should be apportioned and set out separately. Mats should be arranged and spread. Food should be directed to a place near the door. Preparations should be made in the kitchen, wood should be gathered there, grain and butter should be set out, earth and flour should be set out, and water should be set out. Whatever monks have accepted as their assigned task, those tasks should be carried out. Any other similar duties that need to be done — all of these are to be performed by the junior monk. Furthermore, the junior monk should regard the elder monks as fathers and elder brothers, hold them close, and show them honor and respect; he should be subject to their authority and yield to them in reverence and awe.

One should keep the mind directed and present with the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha in view. Fulfilling in their entirety the rules of conduct governing the holy life, precisely as they have been established — this is called the duty of a junior monk.

What then are the duties of the elder monk, the middle monk, and the junior monk alike? O monks, all elder monks, middle monks, and junior monks should keep present in mind the thought, "I have gone forth." They should hold the perception that the Blessed One, the buddha who is a guardian, is their protector. They should incline toward nirvāṇa. They should conduct themselves in accordance with the rules of training precisely as established. They should apply themselves with diligence in order to enter thoroughly into the qualities of the teacher. This is called the duty common to elder monks, middle monks, and junior monks.

What is the duty in the bathhouse? A monk who wishes to enter the bathhouse should go inside with full vigilance. He should stand inside with vigilance. He should sit with vigilance. He should establish mindfulness and keep the mind undistracted. He should have good conduct, be exceedingly well composed and thoroughly restrained, speak softly, show honor and respect, and be subject to reverence and awe. He should lower his mind and be like a servant. He should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness toward elder monks, middle monks, and junior monks alike. He should have a mind of benefit and a mind of affectionate care. He should establish the perception of them as fathers, sons, and younger brothers. Once a monk has entered the interior of the bathhouse, he should not engage in various kinds of talk, nor in improper speech. He should engage in one of two kinds of conduct: noble silence, or conversation on the definite Dharma. This is called the duty in the bathhouse.

What is the duty of a monk who bathes in the bathhouse? The Blessed One has permitted monks the use of the bathhouse not for the sake of pride, not for the sake of arrogance, not for the sake of adornment, not for the sake of vanity, but solely for the sake of caring for this body. The bathhouse has five benefits: it washes away sweat and impurities; it brightens the skin and complexion; it draws out diseases present in the skin; it eliminates wind and phlegm; and it makes the bathhouse a place of freedom from illness.

There are also a further five benefits: it washes away sweat and impurities; it brightens the skin and complexion; it draws out diseases present in the skin; it eliminates wind and phlegm; and one should generate a sense of weariness in the bathhouse.

A monk who wishes to bathe in the bathhouse should first request permission from the preceptor and bear with the bathing time patiently. He should enter the interior of the bathhouse with vigilance. He should sit cross-legged and establish the perception that he is a patient in need of care. He should sit facing those who will bathe him and not act in a way that causes discomfort. He should establish mindfulness and do his work. He should also take upon himself the tasks of any monks who are working there. Without having asked his preceptor and teacher, he should not do service for his peers. And he should not appropriate the work as his own. If there is a grievance with either the preceptor or the teacher, he should not be sent around into their presence. If one wishes to pour water, mix it with cold water and pour it. If the water is hot, let him also warn his companion by saying, "It is hot."

Having bathed with vigilance, the small seat, the scrubbing stone, the fish-scraper, the bathing cloth, and all other bathing implements and vessels that are there should be thoroughly washed and placed each in its proper place. This is called the duty of bathing in the bathhouse.

What is the duty of the elder monk in the bathhouse? When an elder monk is in the bathhouse and junior monks are attending to him with the things required, he should not dismiss them. Even if something as small as a particle of dust has fallen from his body there in that bathhouse, he should not dismiss them. If it should happen that the monks there are sitting in postures that are unsightly or improper, or have fallen into conversation, the elder monk should turn them back, close the door, give them instruction, and lead them toward what is beautiful and good.

Just as the practice is conducted in that way, so those monks should be guided in it. Guiding them in Dharma talk — that is called the duty of the elder monk in the bathhouse.

What is the duty of the preceptor? The preceptor should train those who live alongside him, make things clear to them, commission them in their duties, instruct them, turn them back from wrongdoing, guide them toward virtue, remove them from the companionship of the wrongdoer, draw them close to a spiritual friend, gather them through the alms bowl, and set them to work with the robe, the strainer, the bowl, the belt, mindfulness, inquiry, transmission of scripture, and recitation — guiding them into mental application. He should raise them up from faults, attend to them when they are ill, lead them into abandonment, engage them in proper inner settling, and set them to conduct commensurate with coming to understand the distinctive qualities of the teacher. He should remove a co-resident from whatever situation in which he is dwelling in discomfort. That is called the duty of the preceptor.

The Sacred Vinaya Text, the fifty-third fascicle.

What is the duty of the co-resident? The co-resident should bring to mind clearly the thought that the preceptor is his teacher, show him reverence, rise quickly, go quickly, act with respect, and make requests. A co-resident should not perform any duty involving communal service without first asking the preceptor. He should not take his turn in caring for the temple, should not perform duties regarding the alms bowl, should not perform duties regarding the robe, should not do so every morning, every evening, or every month. He should not go to practice at the river, should not practice on a hill, should not practice in a charnel ground, should not wander through parks. He should not wash his feet, should not set out his bedding, should not heat water, should not enter a village, should not go outside the boundary, and should not draw close to an improper person. He should not treat sitting in such a person's presence as something to be appropriated for himself. He should not personally receive offerings made in such a person's presence, should not accept the alms bowl from such a person, should not accept robes, food, medicine, or any other requisite that may be given, and should not treat them as his own. Likewise he should not show reverence to such persons, should not give the alms bowl, should not give food, should not give medicine, and should not treat the giving of any requisite whatsoever as his own affair. He should not accept transmission of scripture from such a person, should not remember him for mindfulness, should not make full inquiry of him, should not ask him about mental application. Nor should he give transmission of scripture to such persons, nor be mindful of them, nor make full inquiry of them, nor instruct them in mental application. All actions whatsoever are not to be performed without first asking the preceptor — with the exception of three kinds of action: going to the toilet, disposing of a tooth-cleaning stick, and within the boundary, paying homage to a stūpa.

Now if it should happen that the preceptor's alms bowl has been washed or has been damaged by fire, the co-resident should quickly arouse enthusiasm, thinking, "By whatever means I shall myself perform the work of the preceptor's alms bowl" — or else thinking, "I shall have another do it." If it should happen that the preceptor's robe has worn out, needs washing, or has been turned inside out, the co-resident should quickly arouse enthusiasm, thinking, "I shall myself perform the work of the preceptor's robe" — or, "I shall have another do it." If it should happen that the preceptor falls ill, the co-resident should quickly arouse enthusiasm, thinking, "I myself shall nurse the preceptor through his illness" — or, "I shall have another nurse him." And if it should happen that a doubt has arisen for the preceptor —

the co-resident should quickly arouse enthusiasm, thinking, "I myself shall dispel whatever doubt has arisen for the preceptor" — or, "I shall have another dispel the preceptor's doubt." If it should happen that the preceptor has come to look favourably upon wrongdoing, the co-resident should quickly arouse enthusiasm, thinking, "I myself shall turn the preceptor away from looking favourably upon wrongdoing" — or, "I shall have another turn him away." If it should happen that a formal act of censure is about to be carried out against the preceptor, or has already been carried out, the co-resident should quickly arouse enthusiasm, thinking, "I shall have the censure act against the preceptor either applied and then lifted, or lifted outright."
