If it should happen that a formal act of suspension is about to be carried out against the preceptor, or has already been carried out, the co-resident should quickly arouse enthusiasm, thinking, "Whether the suspension against the preceptor is being applied or has already been applied, I shall have it lifted." If it should happen that a Saṅgha penalty has been incurred by the preceptor, then if the co-resident arouses enthusiasm, thinking, "I shall have the preceptor given a probationary penalty — whether a formal one from the beginning or a penalty already imposed — and then reconciled; or I shall have him placed under probation from the beginning and then reconciled; or I shall have him, having been reconciled after undergoing probation, given rehabilitation," that is excellent. If he fails to arouse such enthusiasm, he will have committed an offence.

In this way, whatever duties there may be toward the preceptor, the co-resident should arouse enthusiasm for all of them without exception. Likewise, the preceptor too should arouse enthusiasm for whatever duties there may be toward the co-resident — except for the act of formal request.

The co-resident should prepare the preceptor's seat, set out water for washing the feet along with sandals, and place them to one side. He should wash the preceptor's feet, anoint them, and make the bed. He should set out the vessel for urine and the vessel for excrement. If a scriptural recitation needs to be prompted, he should prompt it. If a mental exercise needs to be prompted, he should prompt it. Then he should go apart, sit down, and meditate.

Rising in the morning, he should remove the vessels for urine and excrement. He should bow his head to the preceptor's feet and ask: "Venerable, did you rest comfortably? Did you sleep well? Have you been well?" If the preceptor is ill, the co-resident should arouse enthusiasm for medicine and for nursing. If he is not ill, he should let him rest in comfort.

If there is a Saṅgha meal, or if one has been invited as a guest, he should say to the preceptor: "Venerable preceptor, there is a Saṅgha meal today — please go and partake of it in comfort." If the food is alms food, he should urge the preceptor thus: "Venerable preceptor, please go for alms and receive the Dharma."

The co-resident should offer the preceptor a tooth-stick, water for rinsing, a comb, and tooth powder. When the preceptor has finished with these, the co-resident should wrap up the alms bowl and robe. If they are going for alms together with the Saṅgha, he should send the preceptor ahead and himself proceed from whatever rank has fallen to him. If they are going for the alms of a particular individual, he should offer the preceptor the outer robe, the alms bowl, and a rinsing vessel.

If it is windy, rainy, or cold, he should have the preceptor's outer robe worn beneath and his own worn on top. If the region is warm, he should have his own worn beneath and the preceptor's on top.

The co-resident should walk ahead of the preceptor and clear away mud and similar obstacles. If they are near a river or at some dangerous precipice, he should take the preceptor by the hand and steady him.

When they have come out from the lodgings to the edge of the village, the co-resident should offer the preceptor the outer robe, the alms bowl, and a rinsing vessel. Having offered them, he should send the preceptor ahead and then enter the village himself.

If there is a ladder or a staircase to ascend, the co-resident should go up first and steady the preceptor by the hand. If, in the proper manner, some acquisition is obtained there, the co-resident himself should take it. When the alms-round is complete and they have come back out beyond the edge of the village, he should take the preceptor's outer robe, alms bowl, and rinsing vessel, walk ahead of the preceptor, and set out for the monastery.

On arriving there, he should set down the alms bowl and the Dharma robe, offer water for washing the preceptor's feet together with sandals set out for him, and wash the preceptor's feet. When the appropriate time has come, he should wipe the base of the preceptor's alms bowl and offer it to him. Whatever food is good, tasty, and of the highest quality that he himself has, he should offer it to the preceptor. The preceptor too should be mindful of measure. When the business of eating is done, he should offer the preceptor water for rinsing, and wash the alms bowl with ash and flour, and then put away the alms bowl and the Dharma robe. He should bow to the preceptor and then ask: "Will the preceptor remain here, or does he intend to go on the daytime walk?"

If the preceptor is going on the daytime walk, the co-resident should take the preceptor's small seat, a mat, and a water flask, send the preceptor ahead, and then go wherever the preceptor is going for the daytime walk. On arriving, he should spread out the preceptor's seat. If a scriptural recitation is needed, he should recite it. If contemplation is needed, he should contemplate, and then go off to one side and meditate. When the appropriate time has come, he should take the small seat, the mat, and the water flask, walk ahead of the preceptor, and set out for home.

If the time for the restoration ceremony (poṣadha) has arrived and the assembly has gathered, he should unfold the preceptor's mat and spread it out; once spread, he should arrange it properly. Then, whether the time is announced by signal or by the sounding of the wooden gong, he should take the preceptor's hand with his own left hand, hold a lamp with his right, walk ahead of the preceptor, and proceed to the place of the restoration ceremony. When the individual liberation sūtra has been recited, he should go to the preceptor and ask: "Will the preceptor leave, or will he remain to hear the Dharma?" If the preceptor is leaving, he should hold the preceptor with his left hand, carry a lamp with his right, go ahead of the preceptor, and escort him back to the monastery.

If the preceptor is going to bathe in the bathhouse, the co-resident should rise early in the morning and announce: "Preceptor, today please come to bathe in the bathhouse." The co-resident should carry to the bathhouse on the preceptor's behalf a seat, a small chair, a water flask, a bathing cloth, and whatever other bathing supplies are needed, and should go to the bathhouse with the preceptor ahead of him. On arriving, he should set the Dharma robe to one side and sit neither too close nor too far from the preceptor. Whenever the preceptor perspires, the co-resident should then attend to him in due order, performing his services, and wash him. Having washed him, he should escort the preceptor ahead of him to the monastery. After that, he himself should bathe.

If, while living with a particular preceptor, the co-resident's virtuous qualities (kuśala-dharmas) are not growing, he should say to the preceptor: "Preceptor, I, the monk called such-and-such, request to be assigned to another." The preceptor, for his part, should consider that monk: how is that monk in following along behind and attending closely upon another? Does he teach him the scriptures? If he does not, will he teach them later? If he does not do that either, the matter should be investigated and examined. Having investigated and examined it in this way, if it seems fitting, the co-resident should be assigned to the other.

If it is not fitting, the novice should be assigned to another. If the preceptor himself is not fitting and lacks proper conduct, it is permissible to leave without asking permission. This is called the duty of the co-resident.

What is the duty of the instructor? The instructor should make the attendants understand, as explained before. If the attendant is dwelling in a place where he is afflicted and troubled, the instructor should summon him away from that place, and have him brought back. This is called the duty of the instructor.

What is the duty of the attendant? The attendant should attend upon the instructor with the clear perception that the instructor is the Teacher, and should render service accordingly, as explained before — up to and including the point of leaving without asking permission. This is called the duty of the attendant.

What is the duty of the novice (śrāmaṇera)? The novice should attend upon the preceptor and the instructor with the clear perception that they are the Teacher, and should render service accordingly, as explained before. If either the preceptor or the instructor has come to hold a wicked view, the novice should either dismiss that person himself or have him dismissed. If willingness to do so arises, all is well. If it does not arise, the novice will find himself together with downfall. And in such a case, just as the novice should generate willingness in the preceptor and instructor by saying, "Whatever has occurred with my father novice, please act accordingly," so too the preceptor and instructor should generate willingness in the father novice by saying, "Whatever has occurred with the preceptor and instructor, please act accordingly." Requests, however, are excepted from this. The father novice should arrange the seat for the preceptor and instructor, and so on, as explained before — up to and including washing himself last. In the same way, the father novice should remove green growth, pluck flowers, pick fruit, provide tooth-sticks, provide leaves for the base of the alms bowl, make things suitable, have them given to the monks as an offering, and attend to what is beautifying and what is conducive to care. If the virtuous qualities of the father novice are not growing in the presence of the preceptor and instructor, as explained before, it is permissible for him to leave without asking permission. This is called the duty of the father novice.

What is the duty of diligence? If harm should come to the pleasure grove (upavanaka) of the Saṅgha, a monk should consider how to prevent its loss and secure it. If by no means can it be secured, one should not speak loosely about it to others; rather, one should first inform those who have the king's permission, and after that inform the queen, the young princes, the ministers, the caravan leaders, the royal counselors, and the attendants. The duty of diligence is to ensure that the matter is resolved through verbal instruction alone, without secret acts arising in relation to it. This is called the duty of diligence.

What is the duty of the monk who follows behind? The monk who follows behind should neither walk too far from the monk ahead of him nor press too close. He should not go about with shoulders touching. Even when entering a house, he should not speak to that monk suddenly; he should speak from outside. He should carry out instructions, show respect, hold himself humbly, and become subject to awe and authority. If the elder monk speaks something contrary to the Dharma, he should refute it. If that monk speaks in accordance with the Dharma, he should rejoice. If lawfully obtained requisites come to that monk, he should accept them. This is called the duty of the monk who follows behind.

What is the duty of approaching a village? A monk who teaches by lineage should not be arrogant, should not generate pride, should not be unsteady, should not boast of victories, should not be careless, should know correctly, should be composed, should not let the mind wander, should be gladdened, should make his conduct graceful, should be thoroughly restrained, and

should be thoroughly covered, should speak softly, and should not let the gaze wander beyond a yoke's width. He should be accompanied by respectfulness, should hold himself humbly, should be accompanied by a sense of awe, and should be under self-control. His mind should be humble, and his heart should be like a broom. He should not be desirous of gain and honor. This is called the duty of approaching a village.

What is the duty of going into a village? A monk who wishes to enter a village should go with vigilance, should establish mindfulness close at hand, should not let the mind wander, should restrain the sense faculties, should not let the mind stray, should have a sense of what comes before and after, and should apply attention to what is above and below. If a monk goes to a village with lapsing mindfulness, he should recognize five kinds of occasions for fault. These are: entering at an improper time without informing the resident monks; sitting down on a seat without examining it first; teaching more than five or six words of the Dharma to a woman without a man of understanding present; sitting alone in a secluded place together with just one woman, without a second person to witness; and stubbornly occupying a seat in a household where there is illness and medicine. If a monk goes to a village with lapsing mindfulness, he should further recognize five additional kinds of occasions for fault: repeatedly gazing at women; from gazing, making conversation; from conversation, becoming attached; from having become attached, not applying proper attention; and because of not applying proper attention rightly, engaging in unchaste conduct despite being without faith — and a fault arises, or he returns to the lower state having surrendered his training. If one enters into a village while maintaining mindfulness close at hand, such occasions for fault do not arise. This is called the duty of going into a village.

What is the duty of having gone into a village? A monk who has gone into a village should not speak various idle talk, should not engage in harmful speech, should speak words of Dharma, should not let the stream of discourse be interrupted. He should properly teach words of Dharma to the householders, instruct them, properly inspire them, and thoroughly delight them. He should establish them in the training rules of going for refuge. He should establish them in proper observance of the precepts, in dwelling in the holy life, in generosity, in taming the mind, in restraint, in listening to the Dharma in the company of noble persons, in proper attention, in diligent engagement with practice in accordance with the Dharma, and he should correctly and properly proclaim what is not the path to be not the path. He should purify wisdom and view. This is called the duty of having gone into a village.

What is the duty of the elder who has gone into a village? When a senior monk has gone into a village, he should give instruction to the younger monks there, and should guide them. He should ensure they do not act with arrogance, with conceit, with bodily agitation, or with playfulness. He should lead them to what brings joy, and should establish them in proper observance of conduct in accordance with the precepts. Those younger monks should listen to the words of instruction and guidance he gives. This is called the duty of the elder who has gone into a village.

What is the duty of one who dwells at the residence? A monk dwelling at the residence should have a pleasant expression and be free from frowning. Mindfulness should go first and speech should come first; he should speak pleasing words, agreeable words, and words that bring gladness, such as "Welcome — have you arrived comfortably?" When he sees monks who have arrived unexpectedly, he should come forward to greet them in a friendly manner, should gladden them with pleasant words, and should ask whether they have experienced comfort and whether they have arrived in ease. If that newcomer is an elder, one should pay homage to him, receive his alms bowl and robe, lead him inside the monastery, and have him seated on a seat.

His feet should be washed and anointed with butter. If he is thirsty, cool water should be poured for him. To the best of one's ability, one should act in accordance with whatever Dharma will bring him contentment. Bedding and seats should likewise be offered as is appropriate. For as long as he remains, one should openly regard him and hold him with the perception that he is like a father, a brother, or a son. Even when he is ill, one must not abandon him out of laziness. This is called the duty of the resident monk.

What is the duty of hosting? When a monk who has arrived unexpectedly comes to the monastery, he should not covet the bedding and furnishings of the resident monks or try to dislodge them from their places. He should sit in a visible spot, conduct himself well in his comportment, dress himself properly, and comport himself with proper restraint. This too is the duty of hosting. When the resident monks see a monk who has arrived unexpectedly, and if they recognize him, they should offer him rest. They should live together with him in the manner prescribed by the rules of communal life. If they do not recognize him, they should not simply offer him rest without more ado. They should ask the other monks: "With whom does this venerable one live? What is his conduct like?" If, upon inquiry, his conduct, his domain of practice, his moral discipline, his vows, and his observance of communal life are ascertained, then rest may be offered. One must not entrust the entire monastery to him alone. He must not be given control over the Saṅgha's treasury, storerooms, or beds. Only after one has come to know him thoroughly should one place one's confidence in him. This is called the duty of hosting.

What is the duty regarding open space? Not all open space is of the same boundary. Those who dwell there and those who dwell here cannot work together, nor can a valid act of restraint be effected. Those who dwell here and those who dwell there cannot perform acts together, nor can an act of restraint be valid. A monk must not go out into the open sky before dawn without his robe. If one has entered the rains retreat, one may not go up into the sky and remain there without having obtained authorization for seven days or for forty days. If one were to go and remain there, one would be severed from one's robe and the rains retreat would be broken. This is called the duty regarding open space.

What is the duty of a permanent dwelling? A permanent dwelling has five qualities: one is not separated from it for even a single day; one does not let ten days pass; one does not let a month pass; one may keep as many robes as needed even without having consecrated them; and one may roam about wearing an upper robe and an outer skirt. Furthermore, a permanent dwelling has another five qualities: there is no communal eating; there is no repeated eating; one does not go off without having informed the others; one may freely seek as many robes as needed; and from the last month of autumn through the first month of spring, whatever undivided gains of the Saṅgha remain set aside — accrued by monks who have entered the rains retreat — those who have established a permanent residence may not give them to others if those who have not contributed do not consent. This is called the duty of a permanent dwelling.

What is the duty regarding a water strainer? A monk must not set out and travel a road without a water strainer. If there is a flowing stream that is suitable, is unmixed with other water, or if there is a serviceable well, or if there are monasteries situated continuously at every half-league — except in those cases — this is called the duty regarding a water strainer.

What is the duty regarding a walking ground? The Blessed One (the Buddha) permitted two kinds of walking ground: one for entering into meditative concentration, and one for engaging in recitation. The walking ground for meditative concentration is eighteen cubits in length. The walking ground for recitation is twelve cubits in length. This is called the duty regarding a walking ground.

What is the duty of walking? When a monk wishes to walk, he should walk neither too quickly nor too slowly, but at a measured pace. He should walk with clear awareness and vigilance. He should maintain mindfulness close at hand. He should keep his senses inward. He should not let his mind wander outward. He should not stamp his feet. He should not sway from side to side.

One should walk in a straight line. If one is unable to walk in a straight line, a rope should be stretched taut. A ring should be threaded onto the stretched rope, and one should grasp that ring and walk. This is called the duty of walking.

What is the duty of evacuation? One should not relieve oneself in front of the Teacher, nor before a stūpa, nor before an abbot or preceptor, nor before a spiritual master, nor before those who are to be regarded as a spiritual master, nor in front of ordinary people inside a village. One should not relieve oneself openly outside. However, if one must go outside to relieve oneself, one should go to a secluded spot and do so there, and one must not cause discomfort to others by this means. This is called the duty of evacuation.

What is the duty of cleaning oneself? When a monk wishes to clean himself, he should not do so with a sharp implement, nor with a bundle of grass, nor with leaves, nor with a razor, but with something else that is soft. This is called the duty of cleaning oneself.

What is the duty of defecating? A monk should not defecate just anywhere at random. He should not do so at the foot of a wall, nor at the foot of a tree. With clear awareness and vigilance, he should defecate in a designated place. If one must defecate outside, a defecation vessel should be placed there, or a pit should be dug. This is called the duty of defecating.

What is the duty regarding the latrine? When a monk wishes to go to the latrine, in order to alert anyone who may already be sitting inside, he should snap his fingers. One who entered first should cough to signal his presence. With clear awareness one should enter. One's robe should be properly adjusted before sitting. Having carefully examined both footholds at the opening of the latrine pit, one should sit squarely in the center. When there is no need to defecate, one should not strain by forcing. When there is a need, one should not hold it back. This is called the duty regarding the latrine.

What is the duty regarding the latrine pit? When a monk wishes to defecate, he should do so slowly and deliberately, with clear awareness. He should not allow his robe to brush against and soil the rims of the latrine openings. This is called the duty regarding the latrine pit.

What is the duty of an elder monk regarding the latrine? An elder monk at the latrine should not drive away a younger monk who is sitting there. Not driving away one who is sitting at the latrine means that one should not turn back a younger person who has already entered the inner latrine. This is called the duty of an elder monk regarding the latrine.

What is the duty regarding the area around the latrine? A monk should not stand, sit, or walk in the immediate vicinity of the latrine. He should not recite scripture there, nor receive scriptural transmission there, nor memorize, nor ask questions, nor practice meditation or mental cultivation there, nor enter into conversation there. He should not perform tasks involving his alms bowl or his robes, nor clean his teeth there, nor wash his hands and feet there. Nothing whatsoever is to be done in any direction around the latrine, excepting only those things that are necessarily done in the latrine itself. This is called the duty regarding the area around the latrine.

What is the duty of urinating? A monk should not urinate just anywhere at random. He should not urinate at the foot of a wall, nor at the foot of a tree. With clear awareness and vigilance, he should urinate in a designated place. If urine spills over, a urine vessel should be placed there, or a pit should be dug. This is called the duty of urinating.

What is the duty regarding the place for urinating? When a monk wishes to enter a place for urinating, in order to alert anyone who may already be sitting inside, he should snap his fingers, just as before. He should neither strain when there is no urge, nor hold back when there is. This is called the duty regarding the place for urinating.

What is the duty regarding the urination pit? A monk should urinate at the opening of the urination pit slowly and deliberately, with clear awareness.

He should not scatter or splash at the opening of the urination pit. This is called the duty regarding the urination pit.

What is the duty of a senior monk regarding the urination place? A senior monk at the urination place should not rouse a junior monk who is sitting there urinating. As for not rousing one who is seated there — if a junior monk has entered the urination place, he should not be turned away either. This is called the duty of a senior monk regarding the urination place.

What is the duty regarding the vicinity of the urination place? A monk should not stand about in the vicinity of the urination place — and so forth, as before — up to and excluding what is called the duty regarding the vicinity of the urination place.

What is the duty of washing? A monk should not go before the Teacher without having washed, nor before a stūpa, nor before an abbot, nor before a master, nor before a preceptor, nor before one who acts as a preceptor. He should not pay respects, not recite texts, not transmit scripture, not receive anything, not perform recollection, not enquire of anyone, not enter a town, not sit down to eat food, not sit down to porridge, not sit down to gruel, not sit down to drink, not sit down to a Dharma teaching, and not sit upon the bedding and seats of the Saṅgha of the four directions — unless he is ill, in which case there is no fault. Or if what is available is sacred water, or if water is simply unavailable, or if a medicine that is unsuitable for washing has been applied — these are excepted. This is called the duty of washing.

What is the duty regarding the washing place? A monk going to the washing place should wrap his lower robe around himself and, as before, proceed to sit in the middle of the washing area — up to that point. This is called the duty regarding the washing place.

What is the duty regarding the place for positioning one's feet at the washing place? A monk wishing to bathe should, when washing, neither fill the washing place with saliva nor splash water about. This is called the duty regarding the place for positioning one's feet at the washing place.

What is the duty of a senior monk at the bathing place? A senior monk at the bathing place should not rouse a junior monk who is there. As for not rousing one who has entered the bathing place — if a junior monk has entered the bathing place, he should not be turned away either. This is called the duty of a senior monk at the bathing place.

What is the duty regarding the vicinity of the bathing place? A monk should not stand or sit about in the vicinity of the bathing place — and so forth, as before — up to and excluding what is called the duty regarding activities in the vicinity of the bathing place. This is called the duty regarding the vicinity of the bathing place.

What is the duty regarding spitting? A monk should not spit with a sound. He should not roll his tongue and press it against his teeth. He should not spit in the presence of the Teacher, nor before a stūpa, nor before an abbot or master, nor before a preceptor, nor before one who acts as a preceptor, nor while eating food, nor while drinking, nor in a place where work is being done. A monk should not spit hither and thither. Having spat, he should not leave it — rather, he should either rub it away with his foot or scrape it away with a stone. A monk should not spit outward away from himself. If he must spit outward, then, so that others may not be made uncomfortable by it, he should move to another location. This is called the duty regarding spitting.

What is the duty regarding a spittoon? The Blessed One (the Buddha) permitted monks two kinds of spittoon for the purpose of spitting: one made by a potter, and one made by oneself. A monk should inspect his spittoon at regular intervals, dry it out, set it in a secluded place, and wash it thoroughly, taking care that it not become a cause for searching about outside. This is called the duty regarding a spittoon.

What is the duty regarding a tooth-cleaning stick?

A monk should not fashion a tooth-cleaning stick that is too long, nor one that is too short, nor too thick, nor too thin. He should not use it for an extended period. He should not use it in the presence of the Teacher, nor in front of a stūpa, nor in front of an abbot or a preceptor, nor in front of a teacher, nor beside one who has become a teacher. He should not use it in a fire-room, in a storage area, in a walking-meditation area, in a latrine room, in a foot-washing area, in a residence hall, in a multi-storied building, in a gatehouse, in a toilet area, beside a wall, or beside a tree. He should not use it in the area surrounding a monastery where sweeping is done, nor should he discard a tooth-cleaning stick in any gathering-place of many people. A monk should withdraw to a secluded spot for three purposes: for defecating, for urinating, and for using the tooth-cleaning stick.

After using a tooth-cleaning stick, a monk should rinse it in the same manner with human-free water, or rub it with a lump of earth, and scrub it on the ground. This is called the duty regarding the tooth-cleaning stick.

What is the duty regarding cleaning the teeth? A monk should not clean his teeth with a sharp-ended stick. He should not insert it carelessly into his mouth. He should scrape slowly and with vigilance. He should not scrape the gums hard. This is called the duty regarding cleaning the teeth.

What is the duty regarding scraping the tongue? A monk should not scrape the tongue with a sharp-edged tongue-scraper. He should not insert it carelessly into his mouth. He should scrape slowly and with vigilance. He should not scrape the flesh of the tongue. This is called the duty regarding scraping the tongue.

What is the duty regarding cleaning the earwax? A monk should not clean earwax with a sharp-pointed implement. He should not insert it carelessly into the ear. He should clean it slowly and with vigilance. He should not scrape the flesh of the ear. This is called the duty regarding cleaning the earwax.

What is proper practice? Making use of all the requisites of a mendicant equally and appropriately is proper practice. What is improper practice? The reverse of that is improper practice.

The third aggregate, known as the aggregate of duties that serve as a model, is complete. The section serving as a model is complete.

Reverend one, what is the body of the Vinaya? What is its focus? What is its blessing? What are its characteristics? What is its narrative occasion? What is its essential nature? What is its fruit? Upāli, the body of the Vinaya is its focus. Its focus is diligence. Its blessing is body, speech, and mind. Its characteristic is action. Its narrative occasion is what has been proclaimed. Its essential nature is transgression. Its fruit is the higher realms and liberation.

The noble Vinaya text is complete. The questions of Upāli in their entirety are complete.

Homage to the Omniscient One.

This noble Vinaya text
was requested by the noble Nyewa Khor,
that the misunderstandings and confusions
of future persons might be cleared away,
and the Victor declared in response
the authoritative scripture of definitive meaning,
consisting of commentary on the grounds, the distinctions, and so forth.

What then are those contents? In brief summary:

One inquiry branching from a single source,
groups of five and groups of sixteen,
bare narrative occasions and narrative grounds,
Māṇavikā and the mother,
the body and the rest, and the final Teacher,
all are accepted as chapters in the proper order.

That which was first requested
is accepted as establishing definitively
the distinctions, the four classes of downfall,
and the grounds of those arising spontaneously and so forth.
This is also proclaimed as the questions and answers.

Then come the Vinaya-establishing sections:
from the four root defeats
down to the remaining
downfalls up to the light transgressions,
these establish all matters definitively.

Then come those that branch from one,
ranging from one up to ten,
also proclaimed as "ascending from one."

Then comes the Vinaya in groups of five,
so called because it teaches in sets of five.

Then comes the Vinaya in sixteen sections, so called because it teaches in sixteen sections. The section on the opening narrative has five divisions. In each of the first four, there are ten verses of the vow-formula; in the fifth there are six verses of the vow-formula. Because they rest on their respective narrative foundations, they are designated "openings" or narrative bases.

Each of the four sections on restoration likewise has ten verses each. Within these same passages, what are called "fragments" are the training bases that treat minor points of discordant categories. They are meaningful because they teach such subtle distinctions. The actual substance of the Vinaya narrative arises in the manner of an appendix, and is not subsumed under the vow-formula verses.

The term mūla, meaning "ground" and "root," also applies to the thing itself; since it is used in that way, it also becomes "the ground of the narrative." The first division of the Mānava-pīka contains ten verses; the second contains just over ten. Because it is exceedingly subtle and substantial, it bears the descriptive title "like a brahmin's daughter," a name that is apt to its content.

The Vinaya that is like a mother is to be understood as comprising three aggregates: the aggregate of full ordination, the aggregate of the supplementary, and the aggregate of the procedural. It is called "mother-like" because it resembles a mother. The body, the meditation object, the blessing, the defining characteristic, the narrative base, the essential nature, and the meaning of the result — these are the concluding topics. The questions asked by Upāli complete all of these. Since the sequence of the count of marks and the exposition of those marks is as stated, one should look at it by gathering it together in that way.

Thus it is that the subjects expounded in the sacred text constitute its very body of meaning, while the textual body that expounds them is, in some regions, described as being only around two thousand verses (ślokas) in length in the case of the incomplete petition-text, as commented upon by the Indian master who composed a commentary on the request-text of the noble Upāsaka Nearkin. Although some regions report that the incomplete petition-text amounts to no more than two thousand ślokas, the Tibetan translation of the incomplete petition-text runs to three thousand six hundred ślokas in twelve bampos, while the complete petition-text amounts to fifteen thousand nine hundred ślokas in fifty-three bampos. The combined total therefore comes to nineteen thousand five hundred ślokas in sixty-five bampos.

This work was prepared under the supervision of the venerable Bodhisattvalion, a Vinaya-holder and great scholar of the Dharma-friend tradition, at the time when the great abbot Mchims was present together with his spiritual friend Rgya-'dul-ba-'dzin-pa. The twelve missing bampos of the ancillary scriptural transmission, the twelve bampos of the incomplete petition-text of the root master's tradition, and the twice-incomplete vow-formula texts were sought out from the temples of Ü and Tsang, including Samye Chimphu and others. The elder Dharmasinha then completed and established the full four sections of the scriptural transmission at the temple of La-stod 'Ol-rgod, and this was summoned to the temple of Narthang. A clean copy was made from that exemplar. Furthermore, it was compared with the Vinaya scriptural transmissions of the temples of Chumig Ringmo and Runglungshot Drog, and, after proper prior collation had been carried out, the work was completed. This is thus the four sections of the Vinaya scriptural transmission — the well-proclaimed sacred Dharma that is the very root of the Buddha's teaching.

The pure and refined exemplars of the Kangyur for that edition were then summoned from the glorious Narthang temple, the spring of all learning. Through the combined efforts of one descended in the line of Gar Tongtsen Yulzung — minister of the Dharma-king Songtsen Gampo, who was himself an emanation body of the noble Avalokiteśvara, lord of the world — and of a master of the two traditions of sacred learning,

— one who was never negligent in service to the precious teaching, and who had become a true refuge and protector for countless beings — the glorious Victorious Assembly, for the sake of causing the precious teaching of the Victors, which is the source of all temporary and ultimate benefit and happiness for every single sentient being without exception, to long endure and to spread and flourish in every direction: relying upon the lordly sponsorship of the bodhisattvas who were the powerful aspiration-bearing divine kings of Tibet, together with exceptional and distinguished translators and paṇḍitas, all the sūtra and tantra translations made into Tibetan at various times earlier and later — virtuous from beginning to middle to end, free from the extremes of addition and subtraction, and unsullied by the stain of corrupt textual traditions — were, during the reign of the human sovereign Toghon Temür, at the time when the Tishi Künga Gyeltsen Palsangpo was protecting the teaching, as the seven-hundred-and-fifth-century period of the Victor's teaching drew near its close and the teacher and guide of beings, the guru of wanderers, had shown the manner of passing peacefully into nirvāṇa: in the female Fire-Pig year, three thousand four hundred and eighty years having elapsed since then, begun in the auspicious new-year month on a day of favorable date and stellar conjunction. The Victor's son, the knowledge-holder Changchub Palden, inspired by firm and unwavering faith grounded in understanding of the teaching, accomplished the concordant conditions by providing materials both excellent in quality and ample in quantity and entirely blameless, and properly established a great temple at the magnificent Gungthang monastic complex — the palace shrine of the emanation-king Sechen Gankyi — equal in its being a source of the teaching to the glorious Nālandā. The monk Künga Bum, a senior cleric of great standing who had turned his mind somewhat toward the way of the Tripiṭaka, undertook the initial preparation and the task of collation and correction. Moreover, numerous scholars — excellent monks of great faith and diligence, with brilliant intellects, widely learned and holders of the Tripiṭaka — purified those texts left in their original refined languages such as Sanskrit, relying upon the great individual commentaries composed by the great translators of old and upon the Sgra sbyor bam po gnyis pa and similar works. As for the Tibetan texts, they were purified without error in meaning and expression, unmixed with regional dialects and corrupt contemporary speech, following instead the ancient terminological conventions of the old Tibetan master translators of former times, the old and new terminology of the excellent translators who came at various periods, and the newly fixed orthographic standards — including the presence or absence of the final particles da drag, ma nya, sa, and the like — just as the scholars had established them. These were then written beautifully and in clean, even script on the smooth, firm, white pages of the royal southern palace — gleaming like a conch-shell ground — using ink imported from great China, dark and lustrous as a blue lotus, by scribes expert in the three scripts of raised, running, and upright, who had attained the rank of master in the scriptural art of calligraphy: the scribe Dpon Palsang Rinchen, Sangyé Drak, and other skilled and accomplished calligraphers from Ü and Tsang in central Tibet. These texts, after being written well, were collated and corrected three times over. They were completed in the auspicious new-year month of the female Earth-Ox year, at a time corresponding to the sixth five-hundred-year period of the era of fruition and practice, and to four hundred and eighty-two years having elapsed in the era of scripture and Abhidharma, with eighteen years of the Abhidharma period remaining, and three five-hundred-year periods for the eras of sūtra, Vinaya, and the mere holding of signs — making one thousand five hundred and eighteen years remaining of the teaching. Thus the Kangyur was excellently completed. Of those texts, these are the four sections of the scriptural transmission. Although in the greater part of the Vinaya scriptural transmission the individual liberation codes of monks and nuns, along with certain texts still awaiting collation, have not yet been prepared, nonetheless the two individual liberation texts together with their two analyses constitute the root,

The two analyses are commentaries on the two forms of individual liberation. The texts still awaiting collation, being those most in need of further editorial work, were established as the opening sections of each separate analysis within the scriptural transmission, and the incomplete portions of the Fundamental Treatise were likewise set down as opening sections. The order of the four sections of the scriptural transmission is as follows: first the Root Texts; then the Analyses; then the Fundamental Treatise, which settles through question and answer the difficult passages within those; and finally the Supplements, which fill in whatever is incomplete in those. Although that is the order according to subject matter, scholars have written the Root Texts and the Analyses first, then the Supplements, and then the Fundamental Treatise itself. The title catalogues composed by Kachok and others also present them in exactly that same order, and so here too the Fundamental Treatise has been written at the end. The number of fascicles in these texts, reckoned at three hundred ślokas per fascicle, is as follows: the Root Scriptural Text has one hundred and nine fascicles; the Analysis of the Monks has eighty-three fascicles and one third of a fascicle; the Analysis of the Nuns has twenty-eight fascicles; the Supplements have fifty-nine fascicles; the incomplete portions of the Fundamental Treatise have twelve fascicles; and the Fundamental Treatise in its completed portions has fifty-three fascicles — so that the total for the Fundamental Treatise comes to sixty-five fascicles. Thus, for the four scriptural sections taken together and complete, there are three hundred and forty-four fascicles and one third of a fascicle. The manner in which the previously incomplete texts were completed has already been written down at the end of the Supplements and the incomplete portions, and so one should look there for that account.

Ye dharmā hetuprabhavā hetuṃ teṣāṃ tathāgato hy avadat, teṣāṃ ca yo nirodha evaṃ vādī mahāśramaṇaḥ.

The Hundred-Thousand-Verse Section begins here.

Translator's notes

The opening verse is a mnemonic summary (uddāna) of the topics treated in the section that follows. Its terms are technical shorthand from the Vinaya commentarial tradition: "three of animal kind" refers to the three cases involving animal transformation; "three pathways" to the three bodily orifices; "what is entered and re-entered," "two modes," "what is taken hold of," "what is thrust in again," "the teeth," "what is not touched," and "like a sow" each flag a subsequent case-ruling. These mnemonic verses are intentionally compressed and do not parse as ordinary syntax.

The term rendered "defeat" throughout is the Tibetan mtha' 'gyur, literally "it becomes the end," which is the standard Vinaya idiom for a pārājika, a root downfall entailing expulsion from the monastic community. "Grave offense" renders nyes pa sbom po, a thullullaba or serious (but non-expelling) transgression.

The passage is from the Vinayottaragrantha, a canonical Vinaya text, and the interlocutor is the elder Upāli, the foremost among monks in knowledge of Vinaya. The rulings given here concern the boundaries of the first pārājika rule (the prohibition on sexual intercourse) and its application to extraordinary circumstances. The text is clinical and case-legal in character, which the translation preserves.

The final question — whether a single monk entering union alone for the purpose of unchaste conduct incurs a defeat — is left unanswered in this passage, as the Tibetan ends mid-dialogue. The "group of eighty" refers to a category within the pārājika analysis related to counting or classification of individuals in the Vinaya context. The precise technical meaning of "the eleven dice pieces" in the verse is not entirely transparent from this passage alone; it likely refers to an enumeration scheme in the surrounding Vinaya commentary. The verse is a mnemonic summary and its terms are technical shorthand whose full referents would be clarified in the surrounding commentary.

The final ruling — that stealing an object of no value constitutes a defeat — appears counterintuitive and may reflect a specific Vinaya position that the act itself (the intention and action of taking) rather than the monetary threshold determines the gravity; this is a genuine doctrinal point worth flagging for listeners. The passage distinguishes two senses of "object of no value": one that is intrinsically precious but cannot be given a price (perhaps unique or sacred objects), and one that is simply too small to be priced. The translation follows the Tibetan structure, which presents these as two separate definitions answering the same question, with different legal outcomes.

The dice-throwing section refers to the practice of smuggling goods past toll-checkpoints by throwing them over or around the barrier. The phrase "throws dice in the open sky" likely refers to tossing goods over a toll boundary rather than literal dice-playing; the term for toll-station checkpoint rendered here as "toll-station" is the literal Tibetan for a customs or boundary-check post. The supernatural-power exception reflects Vinaya reasoning that an act accomplished by miraculous means bypasses the ordinary conditions that constitute an offense. The verse summarizing the robe-rack case is a mnemonic stanza embedded in the Vinaya discussion. The line rendered "other continents do not apply to non-humans" reflects a standard Vinaya distinction that the pārājika for theft does not apply in the same way on other continents or with respect to non-human beings — a technical point preserved from the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya tradition.

The currency units māṣa, nāṇaka, kākinī, and kārṣāpaṇa are ancient Indian monetary denominations preserved in the Vinaya as legal thresholds for the theft pārājika. Their exact historical values varied by region and period; the text itself supplies the relative equivalences: four kākinīs equal one māṣaka, and twenty māṣas equal one nāṇaka.

The phrase "Dharma-theft" refers to misappropriating Dharma teachings — for instance, claiming authorship of teachings one has merely heard — and is treated as categorically distinct from ordinary theft, hence excluded from those forms that incur a pārājika defeat. The verse summary in the middle of this passage is a mnemonic gāthā listing the categories of theft just discussed: stūpa, relics, scripture, Saṅgha-dedicated property, individual-to-individual passing, the two perceptions, and so on. The final phrase of the verse, rendered "the last is a household not yet found," is somewhat elliptical; it may indicate that the case of a monk alone entering a household and stealing is the final category about to be treated — serving as a transition into the next question. The rendering follows the most contextually plausible reading.

The phrase rendered "two perceptions" in the verse refers to the paired perception-cases just enumerated: perceiving a human as non-human, a non-human as human, and so forth. The verse summary enumerating cases ("Three animal rebirths, and existence through karma...") is a mnemonic condensation of the preceding casuistry; its terms are deliberately compressed and some correspondences require cross-referencing with the fuller Vinaya discussion. The rendering follows the most defensible structural reading.

The exchange about "father" as karmic existence and "mother" as craving reflects a well-known Mahāyāna Vinaya hermeneutic (paralleled in the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra and Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya commentaries) whereby the killing of these in a spiritual sense — destroying defiled karmic existence and craving — is said not to entail a pārājika or ānantarika offense in the ordinary sense. The passage appears to be presenting this interpretive layer within a Vinaya legal frame. The verse summary near the end is a mnemonic gāthā cataloguing case-types treated in this Vinaya section; its terms are deliberately compressed headings rather than full sentences, and the translation renders them accordingly as a list-in-verse form.

The names in the final case — rendered here as Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa — are the standard list of the six Buddhas preceding Śākyamuni. The Tibetan abbreviated forms correspond to these standard Sanskrit names.

The phrase rendered "announces a prophetic declaration regarding the former abodes" translates a reference to falsely claiming supernormal recollection of past lives associated with those ancient Buddhas, which constitutes a false claim of superhuman attainment and therefore incurs the pārājika defeat. The verse summary near the end is highly compressed and schematic, listing categories of cases discussed in the surrounding prose. The rendering follows the internal logic of the passage — each term in the verse corresponds to a type of case treated above — but the verse itself is formulaic and somewhat elliptical, as is typical of these Vinaya mnemonic summaries.

The phrase rendered "the final offense" translates a term indicating the gravest category of transgression (defeat, pārājika), while "grave offense" renders a distinct lesser category. The passage as a whole operates within Vinaya casuistry on the rule against falsely claiming superhuman attainments, systematically distinguishing which formulations constitute the gravest offense and which constitute a lesser but still serious one. The phrase rendered "noble language" throughout refers to Sanskrit or a prestige liturgical register, contrasted with "border dialect," which refers to vernacular or regional speech. The distinction is between an arya-type speaker and a speaker of a peripheral dialect, and turns on whether the recipient actually comprehends what is said — this affects culpability.

The mountain names Gro-ba, Ri-dgu-pa, Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa), and Öma are Tibetan renderings of specific Indian locations associated with the Buddha's teaching activity. Vulture Peak is identified with Rājagṛha. The others are less certainly identified and are here left in approximate transliteration rather than reconstructed Sanskrit, since the Sanskrit equivalents are uncertain.

The verse summarizing exemptions follows a formulaic Vinaya pattern listing conditions under which the full offense does not apply, and the phrase rendered "the last category" renders a technical Vinaya term indicating that these cases result only in the lesser grave offense, not the root defeat. The verse summary near the middle of the passage lists mnemonic terms for case-types covered in this section of the Vinaya question-and-answer dialogue. The items enumerated — "not asleep, as when asleep, stirring, those without striving, the seventh," and the final verse's "body, doubt, tooth, wound, hair, nail, the fourth, the second, the seventh" — are compressed mnemonics that index specific case-categories discussed in the surrounding text. They resist full transparent rendering in English; the translation preserves their list-form while conveying their function as summaries.

The phrase rendered "change of sex" translates མཚན་འཕོས, literally "the characteristic shifted/transferred," a technical Vinaya term for the phenomenon of sexual transformation, recognized as a distinct legal category in the monastic code. The verse summary presents condensed technical categories that are difficult to render with full precision in verse form. The term rendered "perceiving otherwise" covers the preceding matrix of mistaken perceptions. "A soft one" renders a term for something perceived as soft or pleasant to the touch, a category that in the commentarial tradition covers contact with inert but yielding objects. "Hermaphrodite" renders the term for a person of indeterminate or dual sex characteristics. "Father" and "mother's brother's wife" are interpretations of what the text presents as distinct person-categories in this enumeration; the precise referents of this verse may vary across Vinaya commentaries. The phrase "it is a remainder for the Saṅgha" renders the technical term indicating a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, the second category of grave offense in the Vinaya, lighter than a root defeat. The term rendered "paṇḍaka" (Tib. ma ning) denotes a category of person with ambiguous or non-normative sexual characteristics; the Tibetan distinguishes "ma ning pho" (male paṇḍaka) and further subdivides them as virtuous and wicked, following standard Vinaya taxonomies.

The phrase "Saṅgha remainder offense" renders "dge 'dun gyi lhag ma," the standard Tibetan equivalent of Skt. saṃghāvaśeṣa, a grave offense requiring formal Saṅgha procedure for rehabilitation, as opposed to a root downfall (pārājika) which entails permanent expulsion.

The verse summary (beginning "In summary, by means of voice…") is condensed and somewhat elliptical in the original; the rendering follows the most doctrinally coherent reading within the Vinaya context. The verse summary "The fourth, combined with two, and different perceptions" is a mnemonic condensation of Vinaya case-analysis and its exact referents (which rule is "the fourth," which "two" are combined) depend on the surrounding Vinaya context. The phrase "for the sake of another" as the exception to the Saṅgha remainder offense likely refers to cases where the words are spoken on behalf of a third party rather than as a direct personal solicitation; this is a technical Vinaya distinction that the commentary tradition elaborates. The verse summary near the beginning is a mnemonic colophon-like stanza indexing the content of this section of the Vinaya. Its terse numerical references are difficult to parse without access to the surrounding structural context of the full text, so the translation renders it literally. The precise referents of "two dharmas with a fourth making six aspects," "two faculties to be procured," and so forth cannot be resolved from this passage alone.

The distinction between དབང་བ and མི་དབང་བ is rendered "of sound mind" and "not of sound mind" respectively, following the context of a section that has just discussed madmen. These terms more literally mean "in control of oneself" and "not in control of oneself." The verse in the middle of this passage is difficult and may be a technical mnemonic summarizing categories relevant to the go-between offense. The phrase rendered "comparable to two of these marks" is compressed and somewhat opaque; it likely refers to the two marks or indicators (of male and female) used in Vinaya analysis to classify partners in the go-between rule. The terms "eunuch" (ma ning) and "hermaphrodite" or "female eunuch" (ma ning mo) reflect Vinaya categories of persons with ambiguous or absent sexual characteristics; the distinctions matter for determining offenses.

The repeated permutations concerning "fully ordained" and "not fully ordained" in the message-bearing section closely parallel earlier case matrices in this Vinaya passage; the translation follows the grammar of each case as distinct, though two consecutive cases appear textually very similar and may reflect scribal repetition or a fine legal distinction between agent (the one taking the message) and recipient (to whom it is delivered). The verse summary in the middle is a mnemonic condensing the preceding cases: "without permission," "the measure," "oneself and another," "uncovered," "fallen back after beginning," and "the characteristic being last" — referring to the gender-change scenarios. The verse is deliberately telegraphic.

The phrase rendered "remainder offense" throughout reflects the standard Tibetan Vinaya term for the saṃghāvaśeṣa class of offense, which requires the assembled Saṅgha to deal with the remaining matter — distinct from the pārājika root downfall and from the simple duṣkṛta misdeed. "Serious offense" renders the same term where the Tibetan phrasing indicates a different, heavier offense class distinct from saṃghāvaśeṣa; the two Tibetan terms are kept distinct throughout.

The gender-change scenarios in this passage reflect the classical Vinaya discussion of sexual transformation (Skt. ubhatobyañjanaka or related categories) and their effect on monastic status and culpability during the act of go-between messaging — a genuine doctrinal concern in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya tradition. The verse summary employs a terse mnemonic style typical of Vinaya compendiums; the rendering follows the Tibetan closely, though the exact referent of "seven ways" in the verse is implicit from context and not spelled out in this passage. The distinction between "noble language" (the language of the central region, i.e. Sanskrit or Māgadhī) and "border dialect" reflects standard Vinaya sociolinguistic categorization of śīlasampanna geography. The term rendered "female trainee" (śikṣamāṇā) corresponds to དགེ་སློབ་མ, a woman in the two-year probationary training between novice and full ordination. The term rendered "Saṅgha remainder" translates saṃghāvaśeṣa (Tib. dge 'dun gyi lhag ma), the second class of offense in the Vinaya, less grave than a root defeat but requiring formal Saṅgha procedure for rehabilitation. This is the standard technical Vinaya rendering and is used consistently throughout.

The verse summarizes the rules about borderland and intermediate cases, accusation by letter and by formal grounds, and elaboration of charges. The Tibetan is terse and formulaic; the rendering reflects the standard enumerative style of Vinaya verse summaries.

"Paṇḍaka" (Tib. ma ning) is a category recognized in Vinaya literature referring to persons of ambiguous or indeterminate sex; the term is left in transliterated Sanskrit as there is no neutral single English equivalent in this specialist context.

The repeated question about fully ordained persons perceiving them as fully ordained appears twice in close succession in the Tibetan source itself; this appears to be a textual redundancy in the original, not a translation error. The phrase rendered "a Dharma that is supreme over the human" corresponds to the Vinaya offense of falsely claiming superhuman attainments, one of the four root defeats; the Tibetan follows the standard formula for this pārājika.

The five actions without interval (ānantarya) are the most heinous acts in Buddhist ethics: killing one's mother, killing one's father, killing an arhat, drawing blood from a Tathāgata with malicious intent, and causing a schism in the Saṅgha. The passage discusses how falsely accusing someone of these is classified.

The closing verse is a mnemonic summary verse typical of Vinaya compilations; its compressed syntax makes some terms ambiguous in isolation. The rendering follows the most plausible contextual reading, treating each item as a parallel case for the principle of groundless accusation.

The phrase rendered "one who has drawn near" refers to a novice or probationer (Tibetan: ཉེ་བར་ཕྱོགས་པ), a technical Vinaya category distinct from a layman. The precise identity of this category in context is somewhat uncertain, but the most natural reading in Vinaya literature is a probationary candidate who has been in proximity to the Saṅgha but has not formally gone forth. The western land of "Cow-Conduct" and the eastern "Superior Body" are the Tibetan renderings of two of the four continents in traditional Buddhist cosmology: Aparagodānīya (the western continent, literally associated with cattle) and Pūrvavideha (the eastern continent). The northern continent, Uttarakuru, is rendered here as "Unpleasant Sound" following the Tibetan, though this is an unusual rendering; the standard Tibetan for Uttarakuru is Sgra mi snyan, literally "unpleasant sound," which is the form appearing here. Full ordination there is invalid because its inhabitants are considered incapable of moral discipline. These are standard Vinaya doctrinal positions.

The term rendered "enclosed ground" and "open sky" refers to the distinction between a formally delimited boundary area and open, unroofed space — a standard technical distinction in Vinaya boundary law. The phrase rendered "the noble language" translates "ārya's speech," which in Vinaya context refers to Sanskrit or the language of the canonical ordination formula, as distinct from vernacular border-region languages. The ruling here is that comprehension, or at minimum sincere intent to accept, is what validates the ordination even when the candidate does not fully understand the language of the ceremony.

The "five ways" enumerated for valid full ordination correspond to a standard Vinaya list: correct naming of the candidate, correct naming of the preceptor, correct naming of the Saṅgha, a properly made formal request, and an act free of procedural flaw. The dialogue systematically tests each permutation of omission. The term rendered "paṇḍaka" is a technical Vinaya category. The Tibetan ma ning is the standard equivalent; the term refers to a person of indeterminate or third sex, and in Vinaya law such persons are excluded from full ordination. The term has been left in Sanskrit as it is a recognized Vinaya technical term without a neutral English equivalent.

The phrase "count it among those of nuns" renders a laconic Tibetan instruction meaning the case should be categorized under the corresponding section treating nuns' ordination; the sense is that the ruling applies there as well.

The passage contains a subtle doctrinal asymmetry: when the entire Saṅgha enters only the later rains retreat and remains the full three months, the invitation is valid; but when only some members entered the later rains retreat and others did not, validity depends on whether the early-rains monks are present to lend their three-month standing to the ceremony. This is the governing principle the text is working through case by case. The verse passages in this section are summary verses embedded in what is clearly a Vinaya or proto-Vinaya prose text. The Tibetan verse is terse and elliptical; the rendering attempts to preserve the compressed doctrinal logic while remaining speakable. The repeated phrase rendered "servants of the Saṅgha" translates the Tibetan idiom for those who serve or attend upon the Saṅgha community, here used as a technical category for members subject to Saṅgha discipline and adjudication. The phrase "struck to the vital point" renders a Tibetan idiom meaning to be confronted with the decisive, damaging point of an accusation, a standard term in Vinaya deliberation procedure. The phrase rendered "act of forfeiture" translates ཆད་པའི་ལས, literally "the action of forfeiture/penalty," referring in Vinaya technical usage to a formal saṅgha act of punitive consequence. The list of binary categories in the closing section is a technical Vinaya enumeration whose precise referents belong to a specific scholastic context; the translation follows the literal structure of the Tibetan. The term སྨ་ཕབ་པ (rendered "established through resolution") is a Vinaya procedural term whose exact referent may vary by tradition; the rendering is a reasonable approximation. The term rendered "fascicle" for བམ་པོ follows the standard Tibetan canonical division marker, equivalent to a volumetric or textual unit rather than a doctrinal category.

The phrase གནས་གསུམ་དུ་ཉེས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་འདུས་པར་འགྱུར meaning "all offenses gathered under three headings" with the three terms བྱུང་བ, བཅས་པ, and རྣམ་པར་ཕྱེ་བ — rendered as "arising, legislated, and distinguished" — correspond to technical Vinaya classification categories. The precise rendering of these three is informed by Vinaya commentarial usage; some editors render the third as "differentiated" or "analyzed."

The verse at the end appears to be cut off mid-enumeration, ending on "disputes of three kinds" without completing the stanza. This is a textual boundary marker indicating the passage ends mid-verse. The verse "dwelling improperly, not dwelling, and dwelling separately" and the subsequent prose enumerate Vinaya categories governing where monks may reside and with whom, as well as protocols for salutation. The term rendered "past-and-prescribed" translates a technical Vinaya expression indicating that a formal ecclesiastical act or prescription has already been triggered and is in effect with respect to those persons; the precise technical force is significant in Vinaya jurisprudence.

The phrase "occasion" throughout renders a Vinaya technical term for the granting of permission or dispensation for specific items or situations; the fourfold and threefold enumerations reflect standard Vinaya categorization of such allowances. The verse passage summarizing the four grounds of the penalty procedure is terse and syntactically compressed in the original. The rendering preserves the four items as best the syntax allows, though some Vinaya-technical nuances in the verse may depend on a fuller commentary to resolve definitively.

The phrase rendered "remedy" throughout this section translates a term (sman, literally "medicine") used in the Vinaya as a technical category covering both medicinal substances and, more broadly, remedial or dispensatory allowances. The dual rendering "remedy" is chosen to bridge both senses; a note for specialist readers: some translators render this simply as "medicine" or "medicinal allowance." The passage is a continuous enumerative Vinaya text listing formal acts, procedural categories, and rules of conduct for members of the Saṅgha. The verse summary embedded in the prose follows the standard gāthā format of Tibetan Vinaya literature and has been rendered as verse accordingly.

The phrase rendered "one who is a broom-sweeper" reflects the Tibetan "phyag dar ba," literally one who sweeps or uses a dust-cloth, conveying a sense of lowly, humble station; the instruction is for the monk to sit with a mind as humble as the most menial servant.

The five acts "not permitted unless performed" section is syntactically dense and procedurally elliptical in the Tibetan, as is typical of condensed Vinaya summaries. The rendering follows the most coherent reading of the list, treating each phrase as a formal pronouncement made by the presiding officer in a Saṅgha act. The verse near the end is terse and compressed, as is typical of summary gāthās in the Vinaya literature. The four items listed — "guidance, dispute, formal act, taking up a case" — appear to head categories treated throughout the passage, and the verse trails off as a brief mnemonic rather than a complete grammatical sentence, which is standard for such summaries. The fifth item listed in the final prose set contains only four enumerated qualities in the Tibetan as preserved here, which may reflect a lacuna or textual irregularity in the source. The term མདོ་སྡེའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ཤེས་པ, literally "knowing the qualities of the sūtra," likely refers in this technical Vinaya context to knowing the qualities or merits of the canonical collections as a whole, and may encompass mastery of the entire canonical corpus including the Vinaya; the rendering "qualities of the sūtra" is literal and preserved throughout for consistency.

The term མ་ལྟ་བུ་ (mātṛkā, Skt. mātṛkā) refers to the summary matrices or doctrinal lists fundamental to Abhidharma and Vinaya; rendered here in the body with the Sanskrit retained in parentheses on first occurrence.

The phrase གཅིག་ནས་གཅིག་ཏུ་བསྒོ་བ ("conveying step by step" or "transmitting one to another") is a technical Vinaya expression for the proper relay of procedural meaning through the assembly; the rendering chosen reflects the sequential transmission sense most consistent with the formal act context. The creature named "ucca-tiṅka" (Tibetan: ཨུ་ཙ་ཏིང་ཀ) is a transliteration of an unidentified Sanskrit or Prakrit term for some small organism thought to cause urinary or genital obstruction; no standard Sanskrit equivalent is recoverable, so the transliteration is preserved as a proper term.

The phrase rendered "three series and three urgent strikes" for "རྒྱུད་གསུམ་དང་དྲག་པོ་གསུམ" reflects a technical Vinaya description of the rhythmic pattern used when striking the wooden sounding board to summon the entire Saṅgha; "རྒྱུད་གསུམ" literally means "three sequences" and "དྲག་པོ་གསུམ" means "three forceful beats," together denoting a conventional signal pattern. The term rendered "mud-slinging" is a conventional rendering of the Tibetan for dragging out or exposing faults; the sense is public mutual accusation or reproach within the community. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source text, and the translation reflects that open ending exactly. The term rendered "holders of the Mātṛkā" translates མ་ལྟ་བུ་འཛིན་པ, literally "holders of what is like a mother." This is the standard Tibetan rendering of mātṛkā-dhara, referring to those who hold the Abhidharma matrices or numerical summary lists, essentially masters of the Abhidharma. The reading is reasonably certain in context.

The passage is a classical formulation of the "four great authorities" or "four mahāpadesas" known from Pāli and Sanskrit Vinaya literature, describing how a monk's claim to have received teaching directly from the Buddha, from a community, or from specialist monks should be tested against sūtra, Vinaya, and the nature of reality before acceptance. The six cases described here partially correspond to that framework within a Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya context. The phrase rendered "the Six Great Pronouncements" translates "བསྟན་པ་ཆེན་པོ་དྲུག" — literally "six great teachings/pronouncements." In the Vinaya context this is a technical term corresponding to the Pali "mahāpadesa" (the four great references or authorities). The Tibetan text here presents six rather than the canonical Pali four, which may reflect a distinct recension. The final line introduces a new section on "six modes of transmission" (བསྟབས་པ་རྣམ་པ་དྲུག), the first item of which — transmission from a monk — appears at the passage break. The opening verse is a mnemonic summary stanza in the style common to Vinaya scholastic literature. The four topics it compresses — "pleasing," "stealing," "manifest," and "degraded / not degraded / six actions" — are each then unpacked in the prose that follows, so the verse functions as a chapter-heading rubric rather than a standalone doctrinal statement.

The phrase rendered "practitioners of the holy life equal to the Teacher's" translates a fixed Vinaya technical expression for advanced celibate practitioners whose conduct matches the standard set by the Buddha himself; it recurs formulaically throughout.

The term rendered "fascicle" for the Tibetan chapter-marker is the standard division unit of the Kangyur Vinaya and corresponds to Sanskrit "bāṃpa" (literally "bundle" or volume-section). The verse listing "wealth and strength and calm abiding, degenerations, and robes" is a mnemonic summary verse enumerating the categories that follow. Its meaning is elliptical by design; the translation preserves this as verse.

The seven dispute-resolution procedures correspond closely to the Vinaya's standard saptādhikaraṇaśamatha rules. "Spreading grass" (rtswa 'ding ba lta bu) refers to the specific Vinaya procedure of covering over a dispute by laying grass on it — a formal declaration that past offenses on both sides are set aside, as in a field covered with grass. This is rendered literally since it is a recognized Vinaya technical term.

"Sense of propriety" renders khrel yod pa (shame before others, hri in Sanskrit), and "conscientiousness" renders 'dzem pa (moral dread or shame before oneself, apatrāpya). These are standard but the Tibetan pair is kept consistent throughout.

The passage ends mid-sentence listing the seven suitable robes; the text is incomplete at this point. The list of seven qualities for a monk conducting himself within the Saṅgha appears in the source text to be slightly elliptical — the Tibetan lists only five items explicitly where seven are announced. This likely reflects a lacuna or compression in the manuscript, and the translation renders what the text actually states without supplementing.

The verse section employs a telegraphic mnemonic style typical of Vinaya summary verse, naming topics by brief headings rather than full exposition. The rendering preserves this compressed character.

"Gains from a situation resembling a mother" renders a somewhat opaque Tibetan phrase about gains accruing from a maternal analogue context; the precise Vinaya technical referent would be clarified in a commentary. The summary verse near the end names Upāli, an "unobstructed one," and Gautamī — this appears to be a mnemonic verse referencing the master Upāli, a disciple described as unobstructed in Vinaya matters, and Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the aunt of the Buddha and first bhikṣuṇī, whose ordination story is linked to the bhikṣuṇī Vinaya. The verse is highly compressed and its precise referent for "what is not fitting to abide in" and the remaining items is left implicit in the mnemonic; the rendering above preserves that compression.

The passage's "dust-like" category refers to a Vinaya technical category concerning minute or trace quantities of allowable substances — the exact scope of "dust-like" items is a Vinaya technicality rendered literally here as the text does not elaborate further. The phrase rendered "abiding in one's senior master" translates bla ma la gnas pa, which could also be "abiding in one's lama or guru." In this Vinaya context it most likely refers to a senior monastic preceptor distinct from the ācārya and upādhyāya already listed, so "senior master" is used to preserve the distinction without importing later tantric connotations of "lama."

The nine objects of desire section presents a stock formula of nine grudge-thoughts (three past, present, future acts of harm, plus five ill-wishes) that classically motivate retaliation. The list as it stands in the Tibetan is syntactically compressed; the translation unpacks it faithfully. The passage listing what the nine objects of desire that are to be subdued contains highly recursive and internally mirrored language, tracking who wishes harm to whom and who receives harm from whom. The syntactic inversions are deliberate and represent a structured scholastic enumeration. The logic, though convoluted in texture, has been rendered faithfully according to the Tibetan.

The term rendered "right end of action" translates the Tibetan for the noble eightfold path member usually given as "right action" in Pāli contexts, but the Tibetan literally says "limit" or "culmination of action," which parallels the standard Sanskrit samyakkarmānta. This is retained as "right end of action" to stay close to the literal rendering, consistent with scholastic enumerations found in Āgama-related texts. The term rendered here as "Mātṛkā" refers to the Abhidharma or a proto-Abhidharma matrix text, the third division of the canon alongside sūtras and Vinaya. It is left untranslated as a proper title since "Mātṛkā" (mother-matrix) is the standard technical designation in this Vinaya context.

The phrase "full ordination of Dharmadinnā who had not crossed over" renders Chos-sbyin-ma phrin-pa, referring to a traditional account of the nun Dharmadinnā receiving ordination by messenger, a recognized exception in Vinaya literature. This is one of the canonical special cases of ordination.

The verse summary is terse and enumerative in character; the rendering follows the Tibetan structure closely, as the verse is clearly intended as a mnemonic outline for what follows in the prose. The phrase rendered "those of brahma-like conduct" translates a term meaning those who live the celibate, pure life — the monastic community sharing the same disciplined way of life. The comparison to Brahmā evokes the highest purity.

The five aggregates listed in the passage on the qualities of the beloved monk are the classical five noble aggregates of an arhat: the aggregate of moral discipline beyond training, the aggregate of meditative absorption, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the wisdom that sees liberation. These five appear in Pāli and Sanskrit Vinaya and Abhidharma literature as the distinguishing attainments of one who has reached the fruit of arhatship.

The verse summarizing the categories is terse and schematic; the rendering follows the most natural structural reading. The precise referent of "the four" in the verse is the four categories enumerated just prior, namely the agreeable, the preceptor, those to have confidence in, and those worthy of veneration. The passage lists "excellence in moral discipline" and "excellence in wisdom" twice in the second group of ten. This is not a translation error but reflects what appears in the Tibetan text itself, where the list enumerates the five aggregates of one in training and the five of one beyond training, though the framing here conflates them into a single list of ten. The repetition is rendered faithfully.

The section on improper giving describes a systematic set of cases involving redirecting gifts already designated for a specific recipient or group. The logic is that once a gift is given with a particular intention or designation, redirecting it to another recipient violates the Dharma governing the proper handling of offerings. The translation renders this structure as consistently as the somewhat compressed Tibetan allows. The verse summarizing the section is terse and condensed in the Tibetan original. The rendering captures the six or seven key procedural categories listed: the parties who raise objections, the analysis of circumstance, the taking up of the matter, pacification, the one pressing the charge, the offense, and what has directly arisen resulting in the cutting off of the proceedings. The exact logical relationship between these elements in the verse is compressed and the translation reflects the most doctrinally coherent reading. The passage listing nine qualities of sūtra mastery actually enumerates nine items rather than ten as announced; this is a known textual irregularity in Vinaya lists of this kind, likely reflecting a transmission lacuna or a scribal omission in the Tibetan, and not an error in the translation.

The phrase rendered "matrices" corresponds to Tibetan "ma lta bu 'dzin pa," which likely reflects the Sanskrit mātṛkā-dhara, a holder of the Abhidharma summary matrices, a standard third member of the tripartite canonical classification alongside sūtra and Vinaya.
