The phrase "cause the monk to rise" in the tenfold method refers to a formal procedural step in dispute resolution, probably meaning to bring the party to stand and formally present their position before the assembly; the precise technical sense is debated in the commentarial tradition. The phrase rendered "act of brahmatic penalty" translates tshangs pa'i chad pa, which corresponds to the Sanskrit brahmaghosa-daṇḍa or more likely the brahmadaṇḍa, a formal act of complete social exclusion within the community, consisting of the Saṅgha's refusal to speak with or admonish a monk. This is a recognized category of formal Vinaya act.

The phrase rendered "act of causing one to seek one's own essential nature" translates de'i ngo bo nyid tshol du gzhug pa'i las, referring to a formal act by which a monk is directed to examine or account for his own conduct; this is a somewhat unusual formulation and the precise Vinaya category it corresponds to merits cross-reference with parallel Pāli or Sanskrit Vinaya sources.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source text, and the translation reflects this. No words have been supplied to complete it. The phrase rendered "with remainder or completely without remainder" refers to a technical Vinaya distinction between offenses that carry a residual factor requiring further procedure and those that are fully exhausted by the confession itself. The precise technical valence of "ལྷག་མ་དང་བཅས་པ" and "ལྷག་མ་མ་ལུས་པ" in this context may admit variant interpretations across commentarial traditions, but the rendering given reflects the standard Vinaya usage. The verse rendered in four lines is a summary gāthā that is intentionally terse and somewhat allusive; the translation keeps its compressed quality. The phrase "brahmic penalty" renders tshangs pa'i chad pa, literally "brahma-penalty," a formal Vinaya act of censure or suspension whose name derives from brahmacarya (the holy celibate life); the tradition treats it as a specific category of Saṅgha act. "Act of separate enjoyment of requisites" renders the Vinaya technical term for an act requiring a monk to use his allowances separately from the community. The five-point structure appears three times in the original with slight variation; the translation preserves this deliberately repetitive Vinaya rhetoric, which is characteristic of the genre and intentional rather than inadvertent. The passage deals with formal Vinaya procedure for raising a matter of offense against a monk. Several technical terms here are Vinaya-specific procedural categories with no single standard English equivalent; the renderings used follow the procedural logic of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya context.

The "blades of grass" (Tibetan: ཚུལ་ཤིང་མང་པོར་བྱ་བ) refers to a specific minor disciplinary procedure in which symbolic blades of grass are awarded or distributed as part of a settlement; this is a known Vinaya procedural term.

The verse summary in the middle of the passage is compressed and elliptical; the rendering reflects the compressed enumeration style typical of Vinaya mnemonic verses.

The final sentence is incomplete in the source text as given, ending mid-enumeration; the translation breaks off at the same point accordingly. The term rendered "the nāga" in the verse summary likely refers to a canonical narrative case involving a nāga who took ordination, used in the Vinaya to establish rules about who may be ordained; this is a standard Vinaya technical allusion. The term paṇḍaka (rendered as "paṇḍaka of male and female types," Tibetan ma ning pho and ma ning mo) refers to persons of indeterminate or intermediate sex, a standard Vinaya category; the Tibetan distinguishes a masculine-type and feminine-type paṇḍaka. The phrase "the two kinds of dust" in the verse summary is a Vinaya technical term whose precise referent in this summary verse is not entirely transparent from the immediate context and may refer to categories of impurity or defilement discussed in a surrounding passage not provided here. The term "pandaka" is a technical Vinaya category for individuals of ambiguous or intermediate sex or sexual function. The Tibetan "ma ning" renders the Sanskrit "paṇḍaka." Rather than translate with a modern clinical term — which would be both anachronistic and doctrinally imprecise — I retain "pandaka" throughout, as it is the standard scholarly rendering in Vinaya studies.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source; the translation has been rendered accordingly. The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as it does in the source passage. The classification of "dust" (rdul) likely refers to categories of impure substances or particles relevant to Vinaya rules regarding contamination or offense — the precise Vinaya context is not fully specified in the passage itself, but the listing is faithful to the enumeration as given. The fifth restoration-ceremony impediment appears to be left implicit in the Tibetan as written (the list says "five" but the text as presented gives only four explicit items before the closing formula); this is a feature of the source text and has been rendered faithfully without invention. The term rendered "permanent robe" translates gtan pa, which in Vinaya context refers to the kaṭhina robe, the cloth formally offered to and distributed among monastics following the rains retreat. The enumeration of persons disqualified from administering or receiving a share of this follows standard Vinaya categories. The phrase "father of a novice monk" (dge tshul pha) is slightly unusual; it likely refers to a layman who is the biological father of a novice, and hence has no standing in the monastic distribution of gains. The passage on the five objects of fault for one who remains long in one place and the five for one who is constantly on the move appear to share identical fault-lists in the Tibetan. This may reflect a scribal error or intentional parallel structure in the source; the translation renders each as it stands.

The term rendered "thief-dweller" translates an expression referring to one who takes up residence in a monastic community under false pretenses, without valid ordination — a technical Vinaya category.

The term "kambala-hemp cloth" renders a compound that likely refers to a coarse hempen or plant-fiber cloth; the precise fiber is uncertain and may vary by regional Vinaya tradition. The phrase rendered "holding what resembles a mother" translates a term referring to the Mātṛkā, the proto-Abhidharma matrices or summaries, which function as a "mother" of the Dharma. The rendering preserves the literal sense while alluding to this technical meaning.

The verse beginning "The wandering ascetic who eats in the prescribed manner" is compressed and elliptical in the original, functioning as a mnemonic summary of several categories treated in the surrounding prose; the rendering preserves its condensed character. The phrase rendered "what resembles a mother" follows the standard Vinaya term for the mātikā, the numerical summary-matrix of the Vinaya and Abhidharma. The Tibetan "ma lta bu" literally means "mother-like" and is the standard translation of mātikā in this context; it refers to the summary-matrix that serves as the organisational spine of both Vinaya and Abhidharma literature.

The passage enumerating the "five aggregates" of one in training and one beyond training corresponds to the classical set: the aggregate of moral discipline, meditative absorption, wisdom, liberation, and the gnosis that sees liberation — a standard fivefold schema found in both sūtra and Vinaya literature. The passage is a Vinaya scholastic text, almost certainly from the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya cycle as preserved in the Tibetan canon. The verse section near the beginning (listing the arrangement of the Vinaya collections by sūtra number, aggregates, arising, interruptions, offenses, and categories) is a mnemonic summary of the canon's structure and is rendered as closely as the terse Tibetan allows; the exact referents of each category remain a matter for specialist Vinaya scholars.

The phrase rendered "the Tathāgata's activity in that direction is lessened" is genuinely unusual: the Tibetan states that where a Vinaya-holder dwells, the Tathāgata's commissioned activity (phrin las) is reduced or diminished — meaning that the Vinaya-holder effectively performs the Tathāgata's function there, making direct intervention unnecessary. This reading follows the standard commentarial understanding.

The passage ends mid-sentence, consistent with the continuity format requested. The verse section near the middle of the passage appears to be a mnemonic summary verse listing several subjects treated in the surrounding prose. The connection between "the bath-house, moral discipline one cannot bear, many friends who are not of the true Dharma, the begging bowl, food, and clothing and alms-rounds" is that each of these topics is treated in groups of five in the surrounding text. The verse is terse and somewhat elliptical, and the rendering given is literal; a fuller commentary would be required to unpack each item's precise reference.

The phrase rendered "preparations" for the various lodging allowances follows the Vinaya technical sense of foods processed in specific ways that are permitted as medicines or tonics outside regular meal times. The phrase rendered as "lidded alms bowl" for ལྷག་པའི་ལྷུང་བཟེད is uncertain. The term ལྷག་པ ordinarily means "superior" or "remaining," but in the Vinaya context of a list of prohibited bowl-types, "lidded" or "covered bowl" is a plausible interpretation found in some commentarial traditions; others read it as "a bowl with a surplus" or "an extra bowl." The precise referent may depend on the Sanskrit original, which is not available here for direct comparison.

The closing phrase, beginning with the five kinds of torn robes, is abruptly cut off mid-sentence and the translation necessarily ends there. The summary verse listing the sixteen Vinaya topics is a mnemonic gāthā; the rendering preserves its compressed, list-like character while making it readable aloud. The verse categories correspond to technical Vinaya procedural terms and their pairing is intentional in the original.

The phrase translated as "from a place of ill-will" and "from a place of good will" renders "ཀུན་དགའི་གནས" and "ཀུན་དགའི་གནས" respectively — the first with a negative qualifier, the second without — though the text's exact nuance here (whether this refers to a physical place, an emotional disposition, or an assembly setting) is genuinely ambiguous. The rendering follows the most common commentarial interpretation: disposition or motive. The list of five qualities for rejecting the reply-giver's words contains what appears textually to be six items, not five. This may reflect either a textual inconsistency in the source or a traditional counting that groups some items together. The translation renders the items as they appear in the Tibetan without forcing them into exactly five.

The phrase rendered "with a remainder or without a remainder" refers to a technical Vinaya distinction regarding whether a transgression was committed with an aggravating condition still present or already resolved; the precise referent depends on the specific legal context and commentarial tradition. The term rendered "monks who hold the summaries" translates a Tibetan phrase meaning those who hold a body of material resembling a matrix or compendium. In Indian Vinaya literature this refers to holders of the Mātṛkā, a summary or analytical framework of the Dharma, distinct from the Sūtra and Vinaya collections proper. The rendering "summaries" is approximate; "mātṛkā-holders" would be more precise but is avoided here for TTS fluency.

The phrase about the dispute being spread "among those of proper reasoning" renders a somewhat elliptical expression that may refer to legal or brahmanical assemblies competent to adjudicate. The meaning is that the dispute should be resolved within the Saṅgha rather than taken to outside authorities, whether royal or otherwise. The precise referent of the second category is uncertain. The phrase rendered as "seizes upon words spoken in confidence" translates གསང་བའི་ཚིག་འཛིན་པ, literally "grasping secret words." In the Vinaya commentarial tradition this refers to using private or confidential admissions as the basis for a formal charge, which is procedurally improper. The rendering reflects this technical sense.

The phrase "does not proceed to a formal charge up to the third time" renders ཇི་ཙམ་ལན་གསུམ་གྱི་བར་དུ་དམ་འཆར་མི་འཇུག་པ. The Vinaya procedure requires a formal motion put three times before a binding determination is made; failure to carry this through is the deficiency indicated here. The passage lists sixteen benefits but the enumeration as given in the Tibetan text reaches only thirteen distinct items before ending. This likely reflects either a scribal lacuna in the transmitted text or a compression in this particular version; the parallel Vinaya sources typically give a full sixteen. The translation faithfully renders what is present in the Tibetan without supplying the missing items.

The term rendered "formal declaration" throughout translates a Tibetan expression for a sworn or binding commitment made before the assembly, a technical step in Vinaya procedure; "formal charge" in the same context refers to the act of publicly pressing a case against another monk through the prescribed procedural stages. The phrase "the sūtra of a single direction" and "the sūtra that exists everywhere" are technically compressed formulas likely referring to canonical categories of sūtras by their regional or universal provenance; their precise referents remain debated in commentarial literature and the rendering follows the most natural reading of the Tibetan.

The phrase rendered "what is analogous" for མ་ལྟ་བུ reflects a standard Vinaya hermeneutical category meaning cases not directly legislated but handled by analogical reasoning; this is a technical term of Vinaya interpretation.

The term "fascicle" renders བམ་པོ, a division unit of canonical texts, here marking the thirtieth such division of the Noble Vinaya. The term rendered "expel a transgression" reflects the Tibetan ཉེས་པ་འབྱིན, which in Vinaya technical context means lifting or clearing a monastic offense from its bearer through a formal procedure, distinct from merely identifying or announcing it.

The phrase ཆད་པའི་ལས་ཀྱིས་སྨ་དབབ་པར་བྱ is rendered "admonish with a punitive act," where ཆད་པའི་ལས means a formal act of censure or punishment, and སྨ་དབབ means to push down, subdue, or rebuke; together they describe the formal Vinaya procedure of imposing a disciplinary act. The exact mapping of each of the sixteen sub-categories of this section to known Vinaya technical terms involves some uncertainty, as the list in Tibetan is partially compressed and some terms have multiple plausible referents in the Sanskrit Vinaya tradition. The passage lists sixteen grounds for admonishment, then sixteen grounds for performing a formal Saṅgha act, then five Vinaya matters, then five types of formal acts (single-motion etc.), and finally begins a list of sixteen grounds that constitute a faulty settlement of a dispute. The last sentence is incomplete in the source passage provided and breaks off mid-list.

The term rendered "brahma-penalty" (ཚངས་པའི་ཆད་པ) refers to the brahma-daṇḍa, a specific monastic sanction in which the community refuses all interaction with the offender — a silent shunning. This is a recognized Vinaya technical term and is retained in a descriptive English rendering here.

The term rendered "act of consecration" (བྱིན་གྱིས་བརླབས་པའི་ལས) is literally "the act of blessing/consecration" and in Vinaya context refers to a formally ratified or sanctioned act — one that has been properly validated. This rendering follows standard Vinaya interpretive tradition. The phrase rendered "the eye of the Dharma has been opened wide" translates chos kyi mig rgyas par gyur pa, literally "the eye of the Dharma has become extensive or expanded." This is a recognized idiom in Vinaya literature for the flourishing or promulgation of the Dharma and is rendered consistently throughout.

The phrase "one does not bring down a censure through a formal act of penalty" and its positive counterpart "one does not bring censure down through a formal act of penalty" render chad pa'i las kyis sma mi dbab pa and chad pa'i las kyis sma mi 'bebs pa respectively. The nuance is that a penalizing formal act of the Saṅgha is not used as an instrument to silence or suppress — this is a mark of faulty procedure when absent in the right way and present in the wrong context. The exact procedural sense is preserved as closely as the Tibetan permits. The verse summary section in the middle of this passage is a colophon-like index of chapter topics in highly compressed form. Several terms in these summary verses, such as "the flat door" and "the crow," are technical Vinaya shorthand referring to specific procedural topics whose full context lies in other chapters of this Vinaya collection. "The flat door" likely refers to a specific case or procedural category involving ordination, and "the crow" similarly refers to a Vinaya case, possibly concerning a boundary-determination matter. Their precise referents are established by the surrounding Vinaya commentarial tradition rather than by the verse itself. The note that full ordination "count it among the nuns" in the name-change case is a technical ruling: the ordination is legally valid but is reclassified as a nun's ordination. The verse summary in this passage is a mnemonic condensing the preceding question-and-answer material about age requirements and date-counting. The exact referent of each item in the verse list, particularly "brahmins," "remainder," "making six," and "fourteen," reflects technical Vinaya enumerations of categories of candidates for going forth and their respective age thresholds. The verse is intentionally compressed and formulaic; a fully expanded commentary would be required to unpack each item, but the rendering here preserves the structure as given. The term rendered "keeper of the monastery" translates a compound meaning literally "one who guards or maintains the assembly hall or temple." The phrase "discs of felt" renders a term that could also mean thin pieces of leather or matted fiber; the precise material is uncertain but the function — a counting device on a string — is clear. The passage about "taking hold of the fortnight" refers to the monastic practice of formally registering or declaring which half of the lunar month is in progress, a prerequisite for correctly tracking the lunar calendar. The calendrical arithmetic in this passage reflects an ancient Indian luni-solar intercalation system. The statement "six times six is thirty" is somewhat opaque; it appears to refer to the accumulated discrepancy over thirty years when an intercalary month is added every six years (five intercalations in thirty years), which is the standard Indian cycle for reconciling lunar and solar years. The Tibetan figure as transmitted may reflect a rounded or variant calculation, and the exact arithmetic logic is not spelled out in the text itself. The four hell names at the end of the passage appear in truncated form in the Tibetan and the list is incomplete, as the passage breaks off mid-enumeration. The Tibetan terms rendered as hell names are: སེམས་ཅན་དམྱལ་བ (naraka in general), ཐིག་ནག་པོ (Arbuda, literally "black dot" or "blister," a cold hell), ཀུན་དམྱལ (Avīci or a general hell designation), and འོ་དོད་འབོད་པ (Raurava, "the Screaming"). The identification of ཐིག་ནག་པོ with Arbuda follows standard Vinaya commentarial lists but the Tibetan here is unusual and could denote a different cold hell; this is noted as a genuinely uncertain point.

The phrase གདོད་ལོང་ཤིག rendered as "go back and look again" is an idiomatic expression of mild rebuke or reconsideration directed at Upāli; some traditions read it as "consider it from the beginning." The list of cold hells follows the standard canonical enumeration; "Blue-Lotus-like," "Lotus-like," and "Great-Lotus-like" render the Tibetan comparative forms literally, corresponding to the Sanskrit Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma cold hells. The description of the rays vanishing into different parts of the Blessed One's body as indicators of the type of prophecy to be given is a well-attested formulaic passage in Vinaya and sūtra literature. The term rendered "crown protrusion" is the uṣṇīṣa, one of the thirty-two major marks of a great being. The phrase "wheel-turning king of power" renders a distinction in the Tibetan between a lesser wheel-turning king and a full cakravartin monarch. The phrase rendered "after the Victor has been counted among the number" translates a Vinaya technical idiom meaning after the Buddha has been formally included in the quorum or tally of the Saṅgha for the purpose of a legal act. The doctrinal point being established is that the Buddha, as a distinct Jewel, cannot be counted among the Saṅgha membership for Vinaya procedural purposes, and any act so conducted would be invalid.

The three categories at the close — maṇḍala boundary, water-encircled boundary, and interior of an existing boundary — are standard Vinaya categories for sīmā (boundary) law; the Tibetan is compressed and technical, and the rendering follows the standard commentarial understanding of these three prohibited configurations for new boundary establishment. The phrase rendered "those on the ground performing an act together with those on the ground" and the reply "it is not permitted" followed by "giving consent is permitted" reflects the Vinaya principle that monks in different physical locations or on different levels cannot jointly perform a valid saṅghakamma unless they are within the same boundary and in each other's sight; the exception allowing transmission of consent covers the case where a valid quorum exists in the primary location and absent members formally delegate their agreement. The final incomplete exchange about those on a tree and those on the ground ends without the consent clause, likely because the passage breaks off; this asymmetry is in the source and has not been smoothed over. The opening of the translation continues directly from the preceding rendered passage; the first line beginning "giving consent is permitted" picks up mid-sentence as established in the continuity block.

The verse summary near the end is terse and somewhat elliptical in the Tibetan. The phrase rendered "a Saṅgha of ten million — at dawn, blessed within the boundary" reflects the literal sense: ten million monks (bye ba, koṭi), at dawn (skya rengs), and the boundary being consecrated or blessed (byin gyis brlabs). This appears to be a mnemonic gāthā summarizing the preceding section's key cases rather than a narrative description.

The term rendered "formal declaration of purity" translates yongs su dag pa len pa, which in Vinaya context refers to the pāriśuddhi, the formal declaration of one's purity given by a proxy on behalf of an absent monk. "Received again from the beginning" renders gdod blang dgos, literally "must be taken from the beginning." The term rendered "female probationer" is དགེ་སློབ་མ, which corresponds to Sanskrit śikṣamāṇā, a woman in the two-year probationary period between novice and full ordination. The house glossary does not list this term explicitly; it has been rendered by its standard English equivalent rather than given a Sanskrit gloss in the body, since it appears in a simple list alongside other well-known ordination categories.

The phrase "confident in his view" renders ལྟ་བ་ལ་དད, literally "having faith/confidence in the view," meaning he genuinely believed he was going to the correct side. The contrast with "not confident" determines whether the breach of the rains retreat is culpable. The phrase rendered "unfit animals" translates a term that in the Vinaya context means animals whose hides monks are prohibited from using for footwear, typically because they are fierce, powerful, or spiritually inauspicious. The Tibetan "mi srun" literally means "inappropriate" or "incompatible."

The verse summary in the middle of the passage functions as a mnemonic gāthā recapitulating the preceding topics; its terseness is characteristic of Vinaya mnemonic verse and has been rendered as faithfully as possible while preserving natural English cadence. The verse summary near the opening is a mnemonic gāthā that encapsulates the topics of the section just concluded; the phrase rendered "feces and abscesses must not be treated" reflects a Vinaya regulation about not handling excrement or lancing sores in a temple or monastic hall context, which is the standard commentarial reading. The phrase "arrow-shaft pigment" for the colour standard of properly prepared sour whey follows the Tibetan མདའ་རྒྱུའི་ཁ་དོག, literally "the colour of an arrow-shaft" — this likely refers to the pale yellowish or light brownish hue of a bamboo or wood arrow-shaft, used as a practical visual test for correct dilution. The Śākya border-town name rendered as "Merchant Gourd-Leaf" follows the literal Tibetan tshong pa sbu bu can, a place-name whose Sanskrit original is uncertain; it may represent something like Vaṇijagāma. The rendering is kept literal as a place-name throughout for consistency.

The term gzhongs spyod, here rendered "place of resort" or "using as a place of resort," refers to a monk's using a dwelling as his base for alms-rounds and daily practice — essentially making free use of it as his residence-station. The nuance is that Śāraṇa was not permanently residing there but using it as a roving base, which is doctrinally significant for questions of Saṅgha property. The town name rendered "Merchant-of-Gourds" translates the Tibetan ཚོང་པ་སྦུ་བུ་ཅན, a descriptive toponym that likely corresponds to a Sanskrit place-name such as Tumba-vaṇika or similar; the exact Sanskrit is uncertain. The passage's legal doctrine concerns the Vinaya rule that a gift designated for a specific recipient or category cannot be redirected to a different recipient or category without violating Dharma — a standard principle of Buddhist monastic law governing donations. The term rendered as "novice fathers" translates a compound that literally means "father-novices" or "novice-superiors." In the Vinaya context this refers to the senior monks who serve as preceptors or teachers to novices, and the relationship here is inverted — the full monks are described as giving food to their novice-preceptors — which appears to be the narrative point generating the confusion in the story.

The phrase "cutting off by cutting the wall" in the verse summary is a compressed Vinaya reference, likely referring to a case involving physical separation or enclosure as a disciplinary act; without the full corresponding sūtra this cannot be resolved with certainty.

The proper name Śroṇakaraṇin is a reconstruction from the Tibetan honorific form; the Sanskrit form may vary across recensions. The phrase rendered "the monastery-keeper cause an appraisal to be made within the Saṅgha" (གཙུག་ལག་ཁང་སྐྱོང་གིས་དགེ་འདུན་གྱི་ནང་དུ་རིན་ཐང་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱོས་ཤིག) carries technical Vinaya weight: the "appraisal" or "valuation" (རིན་ཐང་བསྐྱེད་པ) refers to the formal process of assigning monetary or exchange value to the deceased monk's requisites so they may be distributed equitably among the Saṅgha — a standard procedure in Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya contexts. The phrase rendered "Dharma-brother" and "Dharma-sister" translates "chos kyi ming po" and "chos kyi sring mo" literally, referring to a fellow monastic — a member of the same monastic community bound by the same Dharma and Vinaya — rather than a biological sibling. This is standard Vinaya usage. The closing verse is a mnemonic summary of the cases treated in this section. The terms "what is to be proclaimed," "the vehicle," "the garland," and "the robes" are topical headings indexing the individual rulings just given; they are rendered literally as the Tibetan intends them, functioning as a table of contents in verse form rather than as independently meaningful doctrinal statements.

The phrase rendered "whoever is on that side" translates a terse Tibetan idiom meaning whichever community is geographically on that side of the boundary; the intent is that in border zones the Saṅgha whose territory the death occurred in has the right to the belongings. The phrase rendered "from the point of doing such and such" is a summary marker in the text pointing back to an earlier detailed passage; the Tibetan reads literally "from the words such and such" indicating an abbreviated repetition of a previously stated formula, which this translation handles by noting "and the rest proceeds as before."

The phrase "of bad doctrine and bad discipline" translates a stock compound describing certain non-Buddhist groups; the terms rendered "doctrine" and "discipline" could also be understood as "scripture" and "conduct," but the traditional commentarial rendering as "doctrine and discipline" is preserved here. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as the source text itself is incomplete at that point. The eighteen kinds of trainees follow a standard Abhidharma enumeration from the fourfold path-and-fruit schema, expanded with additional categories such as "one who follows through faith" and "one who follows through the Dharma" drawn from canonical classifications. The nine kinds of those beyond training similarly reflect a standard Pāli and Sanskrit Abhidharma list of arhat types, including distinctions such as "Dharma-faded" (one whose liberation can regress), "protected through subsequent mindfulness," "immovable," "liberated through wisdom alone," and "liberated on both sides" (through both meditative absorption and wisdom). These technical enumerations are rendered according to their established doctrinal meaning in the commentarial tradition. The phrase rendered as "upend their bowls" reflects the Tibetan idiom for the Saṅgha's formal act of refusing to receive alms or interact with a layperson — a grave ecclesiastical sanction. Anāthapiṇḍada fears he has somehow provoked this response against himself, which is why he is so distressed.

The expression "those who still had the remainder of fetters" refers to monks who are stream-enterers, once-returners, or non-returners — those who have entered the noble path but have not yet achieved full arhatship and thus still retain some afflictive bonds. "Those bound by every kind of bondage" refers to ordinary monks who have not yet attained any of the noble fruits. The phrase "གཏན་པ་བཏིང་བ" refers to the formal act of casting or proceeding with a Saṅgha resolution or vote. The term "ཤིན་ཏུ་མྱོང་བཞིན་དུ" is rendered as "fully present" or "having fully experienced," but in this Vinaya context it clearly means being present and fully conscious during the proceedings; the contrast with absence or sleep makes this reading secure. The passage ends mid-sentence, consistent with the text's continuation beyond this excerpt. The verse summaries embedded in the text are mnemonic colophons in sūtra style, listing topics covered in the preceding sūtra section. The term rendered "ceremonial wood" refers to the ritual slab or wooden implement associated with certain Vinaya acts; the precise referent of "ཚུལ་ཤིང" (tshul shing) as a Vinaya technical term — possibly the boundary marker-wood or vote-stick — is not entirely transparent from the Tibetan alone, but "ceremonial wood" is the conventional rendering in this context. The term "paṇḍaka" (ma ning) refers to a person of indeterminate or non-normative sex, a Vinaya category of persons excluded from ordination. "Sending by proxy" in the final verse summary renders "མངགས་ཏེ་གཏང་བ" and refers to the rule against delegating the performance of certain Vinaya acts to a messenger. The verse summary lists five topics in paired form — requesting forbearance, the boundary, hair-shaving, overturning the latrine-stand with threats, rebuking, and condemning the lineage — which serve as mnemonic headers for the dialogue units that follow, a standard Vinaya compositional device.

The phrase rendered "condemning the lineage" translates a term referring to a monk who disparages or speaks against the royal or noble clan, a Vinaya offense that triggers formal banishment proceedings; the exact social context is a lineage of noble patronage rather than a monastic lineage. The phrase rendered "the one who performed the ordination has acted in a manner that is past and done" renders a somewhat compressed Tibetan formulation about the validity of ordination when a censure act is outstanding; the meaning is that the ordination ceremony is technically complete and valid, but the officiating monk's action (having ordained someone under censure) is a past transgression. This is a genuinely technical Vinaya point and the rendering follows the most natural reading.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source text, corresponding to a fascicle break; no text has been omitted beyond what the source provides. The phrase rendered "suspension by days" versus "suspension by intention" reflects a Vinaya distinction between a transgression that is provisionally deferred for a set number of days versus one that is held in abeyance by deliberate mental resolve. The former counts as technically unsuspended in the full doctrinal sense.

The phrase "remainder offense with the Saṅgha" renders the Vinaya category saṃghāvaśeṣa, a class of offense that requires formal Saṅgha procedure rather than simple individual confession.

The technical sequence at the end — penalty, penalty raised from the basis, restoration, appeasement, appeasement raised from the basis, and restoration with appeasement — reflects a standard set of Vinaya formal acts associated with the rehabilitation of a penalized monk; the precise Tibetan terms for these acts have been rendered as faithfully as possible in their procedural sense. The phrase rendered "drinking smoke" in the summary verse refers to the practice of fumigating or smoking items — likely alms-bowls or implements — for purification or preservation, a recognized Vinaya topic. The summary verse is an aide-mémoire listing the topics treated in the chapter, and its items do not form a continuous narrative.

The dialogue involving Upāli presents a slightly compressed exchange in the Tibetan; the second speaker in "Upāli replied" is Upāli himself, answering his own formal question in the traditional catechetical style of Vinaya dialogue. The phrase rendered "food offerings" translates གཏོར་མ, which in later tantric usage specifically denotes a ritual cake offering, but in this Vinaya context it simply refers to food offerings or oblations set out for local protective deities associated with the monastery. The rendering reflects this earlier, more general sense.

The maṇḍala throughout this passage is not a tantric meditation maṇḍala but a ritual ground or demarcated area prepared for washing alms-bowls — a specifically Vinaya usage of the term.

The verse lines "through gaining such ones, one will be honored; through making offerings, one becomes worthy of offering" are syntactically compressed in the Tibetan; the rendering follows the most natural doctrinal reading. The "group of six monks" refers to the notorious Chaddasaggiya, a recurring stock group in Vinaya narratives known for repeated transgressions that occasion the Buddha's rulings. Their name is rendered here by sense.

The term rendered "snapping sound with the fingers" translates "se gol gyi sgra phyung," literally "producing the sound of a finger-snap," which is a standard gesture of respectful greeting or announcement before a deity shrine in the Vinaya context.

The venerable Ānanda appears here under his Tibetan epithet "Nye dga' bo," meaning "dear kinsman" or "beloved," which is one of the standard Tibetan renderings of the Sanskrit name Ānanda. The phrase "skilled in all eighteen scripts" reflects a canonical literary convention appearing in Vinaya narratives, not a literal historical claim. The list of eighteen scripts is a standard formulaic enumeration in Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya literature. The term rendered "carry by the strap" translates a verb meaning to make someone carry something suspended or slung; the precise implement is a carrying strap or sling for the bowl, a standard Vinaya technical usage.

The name Cundaka is a well-known disciple of Śāriputra in Vinaya literature; the Tibetan spelling is preserved as given. The phrase rendered "sky-blue color" translates a term for a particular fired glaze or color that the bowl is to take on as a sign of proper firing; some commentators describe this as a deep blue-grey or slate hue characteristic of well-fired clay. The precise shade is a matter of traditional craft knowledge rather than textual ambiguity.

The verse-summary line "the first narrative, the bath house, the third concerning the layman" is a mnemonic condensing multiple origin stories. The syntax is elliptical in the original, as is conventional for such summary verses in the Vinaya. The phrase rendered "comes to be one who has transgressed" translates a Vinaya technical expression indicating that performing such a service constitutes a formal infraction. The precise category of downfall is not specified in this passage.

The simile of the lion performing the service of a jackal is a pointed Vinaya image: an arhat of supreme attainment should not be placed in a subordinate, servile role toward one who has broken his vows entirely, as this inverts the proper order of the community and implicates the arhat in the fallen monk's continued pretense. The passage contains the canonical teaching on repaying one's parents by establishing them in the five qualities of faith, moral discipline, generosity, wisdom, and the training, which parallels the Aṅguttara Nikāya teaching on the impossibility of repaying parents by material means alone. The list of precious substances includes "asmāgarbha" rendered as agate, though this gem-name is debated; it may refer to a specific semi-precious stone. The dialogue near the end reverses the lion-and-jackal metaphor deliberately: the son, a monk with moral discipline, is the lion; the father, though a layman, is being compared favorably by the son — which causes the father's puzzled response and sets up the next section of the teaching. The final sentence ends mid-discourse and is rendered accordingly. The four divine names invoked by the caravan-leader — rendered here as Agulāng, Varuṇa, Vaiśravaṇa, and Vāsava — are transliterations of Tibetan phonetic renderings of Sanskrit divine names. Vāsava is a standard epithet of Indra. Varuṇa and Vaiśravaṇa (the god of wealth, also called Kubera) are well-known Vedic and Indian deities. The first name (Tibetan: ལྷ་གུ་ལང) is less certain; it may correspond to a local or variant divine name not easily identified with a standard Sanskrit original. The name given to the boy is rendered as "Priyā" following the feminine Sanskrit name implied by the Tibetan "bu mo mdzaʼ mo" (dear/beloved girl). The Tibetan is functioning as a calque of a Sanskrit feminine name, likely Priyā, which fits the narrative logic of giving a boy a girl's name for auspicious longevity. The kārṣāpaṇa is a standard ancient Indian copper or silver coin; it is left in Sanskrit as a proper monetary term. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, so the translation follows accordingly. The city names — Joyful, Ever Joyous, Full of Joy — render three progressively named cities in what appears to be a standard formulaic avadāna sequence. The Tibetan names are Dga' ba, Rtag tu ra ro ba, and Dga' ba can respectively; the middle name's literal sense is closer to "ever-resounding" or "ever-melodious" but "Ever Joyous" fits the obvious triadic pattern and the positive valence of the term.

The phrase rendered "a plank of wood" is literally "a grove of the boat" or "a section of the boat," meaning a piece of the wrecked vessel used as a floatation device; this reading is consistent with parallel avadāna narratives. The phrase rendered "fetched by karma accumulated over a long time" and the subsequent lines condense a compressed Tibetan verse structure where karma is personified as the agent that summons beings to their place of retribution; the translation preserves this sense faithfully. The verse attribution pattern — alternating between the wandering young man and the maiden — reflects the standard Tibetan sūtra dialogue verse format. The city of iron is a conventional hell-realm motif (an iron city whose gates close automatically), well attested in Avadāna and Vinaya literature. The phrase rendered "noble utterance" translates a term meaning, more literally, "a word that is prized" or "a distinguished word" — the sense is that each element of the simile is praised speech or a worthy designation of the category it represents. The rendering captures the honorific and laudatory sense intended in context.

The phrase "ascetic practice" for the term referring to a monk living on alms alone and using a specific mode of conduct reflects a standard set of dhuta practices in the Vinaya; the Tibetan indicates he is using someone else's bowl or following a strict alms discipline. The term rendered "mat" throughout is gdingba, a woven or plaited mat used for sitting. The context makes clear it is a portable sitting mat on which the monk was seated during the haircut, not a fixed furnishing.

The phrase rendered "refuse cloths" refers to scraps of discarded cloth used by the Saṅgha for cleaning purposes; the hair is to be disposed of there rather than left scattered about. The compound term rendered as "compound medicine" translates a term that likely refers to a medicated preparation involving multiple ingredients combined and processed together; the exact pharmaceutical identity is uncertain but the general sense of a combined medicinal compound is clear.

The verse at the close is a mnemonic summarizing a series of medical items permitted by the Buddha. The "Great Sage" is a standard epithet of the Buddha in such enumerative verses.

The creature called "she-bear" (dred mo) is invoked as a precedent: because a bear's partially chewed and digested meat exits her body in a form that could be used, this serves as the canonical rationale for permitting meat broth outside the normal meal time rules — a characteristic Vinaya style of reasoning from natural precedent. The seven thread materials listed present some identification challenges. The terms ལྡུམ་བུ་ཤ་ན་ཀ (śaṇaka, a hemp or cannabis-like plant), གསོ་མ (nettle fibre, Girardinia), རྩྭ་དུ་གུ་ལ (a coarse grass fibre, possibly kusa-related), ལྡུམ་བུ་ཀོ་ཏམ་པ (kautamba or jute-type fibre), and སྲིན་བལ (silk, literally "worm-wool") are rendered by their most plausible botanical identifications in the Vinaya commentarial tradition; the exact botanical referents of some of these remain debated in scholarship.

The term རྐང་གནས་པ in the verse summary could mean either a "footrest" or a "foot-stand"; the context of the prose that follows suggests a support for the feet or legs of a sick person, and it has been rendered accordingly. The phrase rendered "offense with remainder" translates a technical Vinaya term for a class of transgression that is serious but not a root defeat; the Tibetan here is "das pa dang bcas par 'gyur ro," literally "it will become accompanied by an offense," corresponding to the Sanskrit saṃghāvaśeṣa class of offenses. Alternatively, some editors read this as a more general expression for incurring a transgression; the precise category may depend on broader Vinaya context.

The "group of six monks" is a well-known Vinaya stock character, a recurring band of monks associated with misbehavior in the canonical narratives. The passage contains a complex Vinaya narrative dealing with consecration of the three monastic robes from unconventional materials. The items "par thang," "la ba," and "be'u ras" refer to the three parts of the monk's triple robe set: roughly a rectangular under-sheet, a shoulder cloth, and a small piece of cloth. The exact identification of these as technical Vinaya garment terms is secure enough, but the precise names vary across Vinaya traditions; I have rendered them functionally. The phrase rendered "combined robe" for "sbyar ma" reflects the sense of a stitched or pieced-together garment.

The "Group of Six" refers to the well-known group of misbehaving monks frequently mentioned in Vinaya narratives as a narrative foil. The verse summary near the middle of the passage is a mnemonic listing the topics of the narrative sections that follow; "a noble lady" renders བཙུན་མོ and "a horse-race" renders རྟ་བབས — the latter could alternatively mean "a horse-procession" or "a cavalry display," but context in comparable Vinaya literature favors some kind of horse-related event. The precise referent will become clear in the subsequent narrative sections. The phrase rendered "set out to travel toward Rājagṛha" translates a formulaic expression indicating the Blessed One departed traveling by stages (གཞོངས་སྤྱད་པ་སྤྱད་ཅིང), a standard Vinaya idiom for traveling by graduated stages or on tour. The same formula appears twice in close succession, likely due to a scribal repetition in the Tibetan source text. The translation absorbs the second occurrence naturally into the narrative without reproducing the apparent dittography as a separate sentence. The "twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" is a standard Abhidharma-derived image: the satkāyadṛṣṭi, the view of the transitory collection as a self, is analyzed into twenty sub-views (five aggregates taken in four ways), and stream-entry shatters all of them.

The weapon hurled at Śrīmatibuddhi is described as a wheel, probably a discus-weapon (cakra), consistent with the royal arsenal of the period as depicted in Buddhist narrative literature. The passage includes a standard doctrinal moment: the "three thoughts" that arise spontaneously for a newly born deity in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, a canonical topos found in Pāli and Sanskrit sources. The Tibetan "ཞག་ལོན་ལ" is a somewhat unusual idiom; I have rendered it as "when I have only just been born" in the sense of the newborn deity period, though it could also mean something like "when I have taken on the days," i.e., settled into the new birth. The doctrinal sense is the same either way.

The verse at the end is cut off in the source; the translation preserves this as an incomplete verse accordingly. The name "Rūpasāraṃ" (Tib. གཟུགས་ཅན་སྙིང་པོ) is the king's name meaning "essence of form"; it is kept in translation as a proper name. The text ends mid-sentence with the enumeration of the seven precious things about to begin; the translation reflects this open ending faithfully. The phrase rendered "seven aeons of formation and dissolution" translates a term referring to cosmic cycles of destruction and reformation. The verse section shifts registers abruptly into first-person recollection, consistent with the preceding prose, and the pronoun "I" refers throughout to the narrator (the Blessed One recounting past lives).

The brief summary verse near the end — describing a house with foundation, stairway, bride with terrace, plastered pillars, and painted walls — appears to be an architectural summary verse or mnemonic of a building specification, likely a colophon-style verse delimiting the narrative section. Its exact structural function within the larger text is not always transparent, but it reads as a formulaic description of the structure Anāthapiṇḍada is to build. The verse summary near the beginning appears to be a mnemonic colophon listing the topics covered in the sūtra section just concluded. The individual items — "tooth of a bull, thread, garland, one adorned with precious garlands, attendant, essence, gate of the essence" — are keyword headings for the narrative episodes treated in this passage and the one preceding it. They are left in their compressed mnemonic form as the text intends them.

The term rendered "rim of the water-spout trough" translates a compound referring to the projecting drainage element on a stūpa structure, here used as an anchor point for hanging garlands. The term ཁར་བ rendered as "copper" follows standard Tibetan lexical usage where ཁར་བ can denote copper or bronze. In the context of a hierarchy of reliquary shrine materials ascending from base to precious, copper is the most natural reading.

The term ཆག་ཆག་གདབ, literally "applying seals" or "affixing stamps," refers to the decorative practice of impressing designs made from grain mixed with butter onto the shrine surface; this is a standard ritual embellishment known from Vinaya commentaries.

The final verse fragment ending with པུས་འཁྱུད (knee-embrace or clasping at the knee) is the opening of the next section's summary verse and is cut off mid-sequence; no further context is available in this passage. The phrase rendered "the master's son Legs" reflects the Tibetan "jo bo'i sras legs," which appears to be a conventional simile for a dutiful, honest person doing exactly as told — perhaps a reference to a known stock figure. The precise identification is uncertain, but the meaning in context is clearly an ironical comparison: the wife promised obedience in exactly the words an honest person would use, while intending the opposite.

The seven types of cord include several plant-fiber terms that resist certain identification. "Flax stalk fiber" (sha na ka) and "koṭambaka" are rendered from Indic loanwords; the exact botanical referents are debated in the commentarial tradition.

The phrase rendered "knee-embrace" (bu'i 'khyud) in the verse summary and question-and-answer section refers to a type of woven or corded structural element — likely a banding or lashing used in construction. The precise carpentry or architectural function is not fully transparent from context alone. The passage contains a sequence of distinct Vinaya case-rulings interspersed with their origin stories and a summarizing verse, as is standard in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya. The verse is rendered as verse; the prose rulings as prose. The term rendered "provisions" throughout translates ཡོན་བདག's dependent clause and རྙེད་པ, which in Vinaya contexts means offerings or material gains received by the community. The phrase གནས་ཁང་ཞིག་བརྩིགས་ཏེ་བཞག་ནས could also mean "built and maintained a dwelling house," but the overall context of Saṅgha property management supports "built and placed there." The name བཟང་མོ is a woman's personal name, left as Bzang mo, the standard rendering when no Sanskrit equivalent is available. The term rendered "grain-oil" for འབྲུ་མར་ is literally "grain fat" or "sesame oil" — the precise substance is uncertain, but it refers to a vegetable or seed-based oil used both as a food additive and for practical purposes such as waterproofing or treating materials. The building-maintenance context here supports both interpretations; the rendering "grain-oil" preserves the ambiguity. The phrase rendered "alms-bowl maintenance work" translates a term for work done with the alms-bowl, likely referring to the curing or seasoning of alms-bowls, a standard Vinaya task. The translation reflects this technical sense.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, consistent with the excerpt's cutoff; the translation preserves this. The term rendered "face-scraper" refers to a small implement used to scrape the face during washing, functionally similar to a strigil. The verse summary in the middle of the passage is a mnemonic gāthā listing the various locations and implements governed by the rules that follow, a standard Vinaya device for organizing rule clusters. The phrase "transgression with expiation" renders a Vinaya technical category equivalent to the Pali pācittiya, a lesser offense requiring confession and expiation rather than a root defeat. The summarizing verse appears to be a mnemonic colophon listing the items treated in the preceding cluster of rules: water pot, wash-basin, black iron bowl, drinking cup, razor-sharpening, nail-cutting, medicinal thorns, and foot-stand. The phrase rendered "medicinal thorns" translates སྨང་ཚེར་, which likely refers to a lancet or similar pointed medical instrument used in the monastic medical context; the exact implement is not entirely certain, but "medicinal thorns" reflects the literal reading and the commentarial tradition's understanding of a pointed therapeutic tool. The verse summary lists items in abbreviated form following the same pattern as the preceding passage; "the permanent thread, the second" refers to the continuing thread of cases, and "the taking away" summarizes the category of offenses covered in this section. The exact referents of the verse's condensed list are conventional mnemonic shorthand for the series of cases just described. The verse summary near the middle of the passage is a mnemonic gāthā in highly compressed, telegraphic style. The rendering "one bearing a name but not giving the self at death" and "five to be received with trust" and "a nun who is a keeper, for the sake of the allowance" follows the Tibetan literally but the precise referents depend on the surrounding Vinaya context that is not fully present here. The verse is a section-heading mnemonic and its terms are technical markers for subsections, so the rendering is necessarily approximate.

The king's name rendered as "Rūpasāra" (Tib. གཟུགས་ཅན་སྙིང་པོ) is a Tibetan rendering of a Sanskrit name meaning "one whose essence is form" or "having bodily essence"; no standard Sanskrit reconstruction is certain, so it is given in translation.

The phrase rendered "sūtra likened to falling silk" (Tib. དར་ལ་བབ་པ་ལྟ་བུའི་མདོ་སྡེ) is an idiomatic comparison; "silk falling" may indicate a text of particular refinement or suitability, but the exact reference is not established from the text alone. The phrase rendered "prostrated at his feet" translates a term literally meaning "touched his feet" — a standard gesture of obeisance before royalty in Indian narrative literature.

The passage contains a narratively compressed and somewhat elliptical sequence involving the tīrthikas, monks, and the disputed goods. The Tibetan is ambiguous in places as to exactly who is accusing whom and who has taken what from whom. The translation follows the most coherent reading of the syntax, in which a tīrthika conceals goods in his own bundle including items belonging to monks, then when the monks notice and a dispute erupts, the tīrthikas go to the king first and make the accusation against the monks. This reading is consistent with the narrative logic of the broader context. The phrase rendered as "corner tab" refers to a small loop or tab of cloth attached at the corner of a monastic robe as a distinguishing marker; the precise form is not entirely certain from the term alone, but this is the standard Vinaya identification.

The verse spoken by the dying householder closely parallels a well-known canonical formula on impermanence found across Pāli and Sanskrit sources; it is rendered here as verse in keeping with its form in the Tibetan. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source Tibetan as provided. The declaration of the Blessed One is cut off after "together with a companion, and —"; this appears to be a passage break rather than a textual lacuna, and the continuation will follow in the next segment. The term rendered throughout as "the vow of associating together with a companion" translates a Vinaya technical term for a special dispensation allowing a nun to visit a lay patron's home alone — or here, in the company of a single companion — when circumstances such as famine make normal practice impossible. The formal ecclesiastical act (kamma) structure follows standard Vinaya procedure: motion plus one proclamation.

The final prose passage introduces a new narrative section. The kārṣāpaṇa is a standard Indian coin unit frequently mentioned in Vinaya debt-and-inheritance narratives. The somewhat compressed final sentence, in which the householder appears to be proposing a transaction — the monks distribute the deceased monk's possessions and he will recover his debt from the charnel ground — follows a recognizable Vinaya plot pattern. The phrase rendered "men of good family" translates a conventional honorific expression indicating respected lay community members who might serve as trusted mediators or witnesses. The Blessed One's instruction is that if the householder remains unconvinced, the matter should be referred to such respected laypeople rather than engaging further community resources with a recalcitrant creditor. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as it leads into the next episode; the translation preserves this open ending faithfully. The name "Nandaka" renders Tibetan ཉེ་དགའ་བོ, which is the standard Tibetan for the monk Nandaka. The term ཕྲ་མོ in the opening refers to fine or lightweight cloth, contrasted with སྦོམ་པོ, coarser or heavier cloth; the merchant's claim is that he substituted a coarser piece for the finer one the monk had ordered. The phrase གནས་ངན་ལེན་ལ་མཚུངས་པར་སྤྱོད ("behaved in a manner befitting a scoundrel") is a conventional Vinaya expression of strong lay reproach. The phrase rendered as "the determined word" translates a technical Vinaya expression meaning the fixed or established statement one makes to indicate a desired price or object without actively negotiating — speaking it up to two or three times is permitted, but going beyond into direct price-bargaining is the offense.

The "group of six" refers to the notorious six monks who recur throughout the Vinaya as habitual troublemakers.

The closing verse and narrative mark a transition to a new section of the Vinaya text concerning monastic duties in gardens or groves donated to the Saṅgha. The term rendered "father-novice" translates dge tshul pha, literally a novice who acts in a parental or senior supervisory role — a specific Vinaya institutional role. The precise nuance of "father" here is as a senior novice with a supervisory function; this is a recognized Vinaya term and the rendering follows that tradition.

The phrase "noble silence" renders 'phags pa'i mi smra ba, literally "the noble one's non-speaking," which in Vinaya usage is the technical term for the meditative silence of a noble one during formal community procedures (Skt. āryatūṣṇīmbhāva).

The verse summary in the middle of the passage appears to be a mnemonic gāthā listing key legal categories discussed in the episode; its compressed telegraphic style is intentional. The phrase rendered "making-fit-for-use had not been equalized" reflects the Tibetan technical concept of the ritual act of making food allowable for monastic consumption; the distribution was uneven, leaving some monks without a proper share, hence the discontent. The Vinaya procedure of "establishing a boundary" refers to the formal demarcation of a sīmā, the canonical boundary within which communal Vinaya acts are legally valid; the dispute turns on which sīmā takes legal precedence. The phrase rendered "taking sides in a lawsuit" translates ཆེ་བཞི་བྱས, literally "making a great four" or "making a major case," which in Vinaya legal context refers to formally pressing or supporting a legal claim before royal authority. The rendering follows the contextual sense.

The summary verse at the head of the fifth-group section is an abbreviated mnemonic list of the topics that follow; several items in it are rendered according to their narrative development in the sūtra body that follows, rather than strictly term by term.

The passage ends mid-sentence with the bodhisattva image being carried through the town on foot, indicating the text continues in the next passage. The phrase rendered "garland-vessels" translates a term referring to containers or receptacles for flower garlands used as part of the processional and festival decoration; the precise form is not entirely certain but the general sense of a vessel or tray used in garland-offerings is clear. The verse summary in the middle of the passage appears to be an editorial colophon marking the close of a canonical section, followed immediately by a fresh narrative opening that recapitulates the setting at Śrāvastī — this abrupt structural shift is a feature of the Vinaya text itself, not an error in translation. The phrase "those who arrange the lodgings" refers to the monk designated as lodging-assigner (Skt. śayanāsana-paññāpaka), a recognized Vinaya office. The phrase rendered "warming of the face" translates the Tibetan "zhalbsro," literally a warming or refreshing of the face, referring to a specific ritual or festive offering connected with bathing or anointing the face, likely a spring ceremony tied to the Buddha's birth month. The exact nature of this ceremony is not entirely transparent from the text alone; it appears to be a customary offering or ablution rite performed at a residence.

The opening verse and sentence ("If one observes them, one incurs a transgression along with the corresponding offence. This concludes the third set of verses...") belong to the framing apparatus of the Vinaya text and mark the close of the preceding section before a new narrative begins. The phrase rendered "the shadow of the rose-apple tree of Jambudvīpa" is a poetic epithet describing the Blessed One as the presiding figure over Jambudvīpa. This is a standard honorific image in Buddhist literature, though its precise ceremonial significance here may relate to a festival tied to the Buddha's awakening or birth. The Tibetan "གཎྜཱི" is the wooden sounding-board or plank (Sanskrit: gaṇḍī) used in monasteries to summon the community, here consistently rendered "wooden plank." The phrase "ཤིང་རྟ་ཕྱུང་ཤིག" literally means "send out a cart or vehicle," indicating that litters or conveyances were dispatched to transport those unable to walk; this is rendered "send out a vehicle" for clarity. The closing summary verse and its colophon appear to be a standard Vinaya structural marker, cataloguing the topics covered under a heading called "the section on individual matters." The items listed, including salutation, the strainer, vessels, the drinking bowl, sugarcane, butter, roots, and tree-trunks, are case topics treated individually in the preceding sūtras. The verse is formulaic and its rendering follows the structural logic of the Vinaya rather than any single narrative thread.

The phrase rendered "the dog" in the summary verse is puzzling in context; it likely refers to a specific ruled case involving a dog that appeared earlier in the text and is here being catalogued by a single-word mnemonic, which is standard Vinaya practice. The long sequence of epithets for the buddhas — "five limbs abandoned," "six limbs," "always abiding in the six," "three aspects of those to be tamed," and so on — are formulaic enumerations whose precise referents vary by commentarial tradition and context. The translation renders them literally, as any specific doctrinal unpacking would require a commentary. The phrase rendered "thousand hundreds" for བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་བཅུ translates literally as "ten hundreds," i.e., one thousand; the idiom here indicates supreme lordship over a thousandfold world-system.

The closing list of hell realms — reviving, black-line, crushing, crying, great crying, burning, great burning, without-respite, blister — corresponds to the standard Abhidharma enumeration of the eight hot hells and their sub-divisions; the passage breaks off mid-enumeration. The list of cold hells follows the standard Abhidharma enumeration: Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala ("Blue Lotus"), Padma ("Lotus"), and Mahāpadma ("Great Lotus") are preserved in their Sanskrit forms as they are proper names of those realms, not descriptive Tibetan phrases.

The passage ends mid-verse; the translation reflects this exactly as the supplied Tibetan breaks off incomplete.

The phrase rendered "wheel-turning monarch of power" translates a distinction between two slightly different Tibetan phrases in close succession: "stobs kyi 'khor los sgyur ba'i rgyal po" (a chakravartin specifically qualified as one of power or might) and "'khor los sgyur ba'i rgyal po" (a chakravartin more generally). The left-hand and right-hand distinction in the prophecy encoding likely reflects this gradation within the category of universal monarchs. The phrase "ten roots of aversion" renders "ཞེ་སྡང་གི་ས་བཅུ་རབ་ཏུ་བྱུང་སྟེ" / "ཞེ་སྡང་གི་ས་བཅུ་པོ་ཐོབ་པས་ན" literally as "ten grounds / bases of aversion fully arisen / obtained." The precise canonical referent of these "ten" is not specified in this passage; it may refer to the ten non-virtues rooted in aversion or to a Vinaya-specific list. The translation renders it accordingly without speculating further. The list of śrāvakas includes names that are rendered from their Tibetan phonetic forms. "Vāṣpa" renders "རླངས་པ," "Mahānāman" renders "མིང་ཆེན," and "Acyuta" renders "མ་འགགས་པ" — these are standard identifications of the five first disciples (Pañcavaggiya). "Ābhāsvara" for "འོད་སྣང" is a reasonable reading, though this name more commonly denotes a class of gods; here in the context of the great śrāvakas it may refer to a lesser-known disciple. The phrase "the four fruits of the contemplative life" renders "དགེ་སྦྱོང་གི་འབྲས་བུ་བཞི," the standard four śramaṇaphala — stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship. The passage presents a notable structural complexity toward its end: the question asked by the monks to the Blessed One transitions mid-sentence into a response from the monks themselves, which is syntactically abrupt. The Tibetan breaks off mid-narration, suggesting the translation here ends at a section boundary. The rendering follows the text as closely as possible. The "twenty peaks of the mountain of the view of the transitory collection" renders the classical Abhidharma image of the twenty-fold sakkāyadiṭṭhi, the twenty modes of the view of self, shattered at stream-entry. The verse section is rendered as verse with close adherence to doctrinal imagery. The phrase "path beyond sorrow" renders the path to nirvāṇa in contextually natural terms consistent with the house glossary. The final verse is a mnemonic summary listing topics covered in the first sūtra of a single-chapter collection. The terms are highly compressed: "gathering place" refers to the valid location for the ceremony; "a village with its surrounds" to the boundary question; "the arising of mind" to intention in ordination contexts; "the three killings" to three types of killing discussed in the Vinaya. The verse functions as a topical index, not a doctrinal statement, so some opacity in English is unavoidable.

The phrase rendered "the remainder of the Saṅgha" translates a compressed Tibetan expression; it likely refers to the quorum and remaining procedural distinctions of the Saṅgha in ordination rites. The phrase rendered "impediment-creating phenomena" translates bar chad kyi chos rnams, referring to offenses or violations that obstruct the proper completion of the restoration ceremony. This is standard Vinaya technical language.

The phrase gsing ma, rendered earlier as "ground strewn with living creatures" (a marshy or insect-infested area), recurs at the opening of this passage; the translation maintains consistency with the preceding rendering. The phrase rendered "lord of the forest" translates a term that is a respectful epithet applied to the monk in each episode — literally "lord or chief of the forest grove," functioning here as an honorific for a senior monk or the monk in question. The context makes clear it refers to the particular monk protagonist in each story.

The Prātimokṣa recitation referred to as "reciting separately" or "individually" reflects a monk who, under duress and alone, performed the Prātimokṣa recitation outside the proper communal Poṣadha assembly — the Blessed One's ruling that it was "well recited" validates this extraordinary circumstance. The phrase rendered "on the one side they are dark, on the other they are white" refers to the monastic robe: the underrobe is dark (often reddish-brown or black) and the outer portion is lighter, a detail by which the knowledgeable soldier distinguishes monks from naked tīrthika ascetics. The doctrinal point being dramatized in the army episode is that the monks would not cut the grass to free themselves because the Vinaya prohibits destroying plant-life, and they explain this precept to the king, who is moved to reverence. The offense category mentioned as "an offense against the Saṅgha that exceeded the ordinary" renders the technical Vinaya term for a saṅghāvaśeṣa (an offense requiring formal suspension by the Saṅgha), which falls short of a pārājika defeat but is more serious than a simple downfall. The summary verse near the middle of this passage appears to be a mnemonic gāthā encapsulating the legal cases treated in the preceding sūtra section. The line "whose hide is unsuitable" is a standard Vinaya shorthand for a case involving a person who cannot properly receive or carry out a Vinaya procedure — the exact referent is determined by the broader case context and is rendered literally here in keeping with the formulaic nature of such summary verses. The term མ་ལྟ་བུ་འཛིན་པ literally means "holder of the mātṛkā," referring to the proto-Abhidharma numerical matrices. This is rendered as "master of the mātṛkā" with a brief gloss on first occurrence. The term དྲུག་སྡེ refers to the notorious "group of six monks," a standing cast of wayward monks in Vinaya narratives whose misdeeds typically prompt new rules; this is rendered in context without needing special gloss. The phrase rendered "the householder Anāthapiṇḍada" renders ཁྱིམ་བདག་མགོན་མེད་ཟས་སྦྱིན, the Tibetan equivalent of Sanskrit Anāthapiṇḍada, the famous lay patron of the Buddha and donor of the Jeta Grove. His name means "feeder of the destitute."

The figure called "the god" throughout this passage refers to King Prasenajit, who is being referred to by the honorific ལྷ, a standard Tibetan royal title equivalent to Sanskrit deva used for kings. The minister is, of course, using a ruse to bring the monks to the site — the "letter from the god" is a stratagem to get them to come voluntarily and thus eventually convey the noble ones toward the king's camp.

The phrase བཞིན་བཟངས ("good sir" / "good-looking one") is a term of polite address in Vinaya narratives, used between equals or when addressing someone respectfully; it corresponds to Pāli bho, Sanskrit bhoḥ. The names Buddhaguptra and Dharmadatta appear as Sanskrit-style names embedded in the Tibetan text and refer to specific monks who are the subject of the forty-day boundary dispensation. The formal act here is a standard Vinaya羯磨 procedure; the repetition of the motion and act language is a faithful rendering of the Vinaya's formulaic style and is intentional, not scribal redundancy. The verse summary near the middle of the passage is a mnemonic gāthā (a brief verse of the Vinaya), summarizing prohibited items: the phrase "forms with essence" refers to corpse-relics or the physical remains of a person of substance; the list that follows identifies the associated prohibited meats and materials. The rendering stays close to the compressed verse style of such Vinaya summaries.

The name "Ajātaśatru" is rendered from "ma skyes dgra" (literally "enemy of the unborn") and "Devadatta" from "lha sbyin" (literally "god-given"), following standard Vinaya identifications. "Bimbisāra" is the traditional identification for "gzugs can snying po" (literally "form-essence" or "essence of form"), the father of Ajātaśatru. The same epithet "gzugs can snying po" appears in the verse and in the prose narrative, referring to King Bimbisāra. The phrase rendered "like a rhinoceros horn" echoes the famous Rhinoceros Sūtra image for the pratyekabuddha's solitary mode of practice; this is a standard doctrinal allusion. The final sentence of the Tibetan is incomplete as transmitted, ending mid-clause; the translation carries it as far as the text allows and breaks naturally at that point. The phrase rendered "offense with remainder" translates a standard Vinaya technical term for an āpatti that carries a residual consequence, specifically a thullaccaya or similar category. The Tibetan reads literally "it will come along with a transgression," indicating a formal downfall rather than a root defeat.

The "Group of Six" refers to a well-known group of six monks in Vinaya literature notorious for misconduct, whose misdeeds regularly prompt the Buddha to lay down rules.

The closing verse listing prohibited meats (dog, hawk, owl, human-flesh-eating birds, horse, mule, fox, monkey) corresponds to a recognized list of prohibited flesh in the Pāli and Sanskrit Vinaya traditions. The phrase rendered "an offense with a fault with an object" reflects the Tibetan "ཉེས་པའི་དམིགས་སུ་གྱུར་ཏེ," which literally means "it becomes an object of fault." The preceding passage establishes the standard formula "འདས་པ་དང་བཅས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ" as "an offense with remainder" (a duṣkṛta or similar minor offense), which is maintained here for consistency.

The term "རྡུལ་ཁྲོད་པ" rendered as "found in a refuse heap" refers specifically to ownerless goods cast away, a recognized category in Vinaya discussions of permissible acquisition, and the monks' statement that they "consecrated" the discarded parts is a self-justification the text treats as spurious. The phrase "medicine administered from below" is a standard Vinaya euphemism for an enema or suppository. This is clear from context and the subsequent experimental methods of administration.

The verse in the summary section is terse and elliptical, as is typical of mnemonic summaries in Vinaya texts. The line "gemstones are to be passed by mouth" likely refers to a specific rule about how certain items may or may not be transferred, preserved here as literally as readability allows.

"Kyi hud" is a Tibetan exclamation of grief and shock, here rendered phonetically as it functions as a dramatic cry; it could be rendered "Alas!" but the original repetition and its dramatic function in the narrative are better served by keeping its phonetic form. The phrase rendered "the twenty-peaked mountain of the view of the transitory collection" is a traditional Tibetan metaphorical expression for the twenty varieties of the view of self among the five aggregates (five aggregates times four modes of grasping equals twenty). This is standard Abhidharma enumeration and the image of a mountain with twenty peaks is a recognized literary convention for this doctrine.

The transition at the end is mid-sentence in the Tibetan, indicating the passage continues; the translation breaks naturally at that point. The phrase rendered "householder Ambāṭhika" preserves a proper name that appears to be a personal name in the Tibetan. The causal connection drawn — that his eating of molasses led to his realizing arhatship — is an allusion to a specific narrative in this Vinaya context, where a particular meditative or physiological benefit of molasses is implied. The text does not elaborate further here, and no emendation is required.

The final verse fragment "Either butter or grain-butter" is the opening of a mnemonic verse summarizing the preceding section's legal topics; it is intentionally incomplete here as the passage breaks off. The phrase rendered "on the basis of prior acceptance" translates a Tibetan term for a formal Vinaya procedure whereby a designated monk receives an item on behalf of the community, making it permissible for use. The text describes a case where this procedure cannot be performed because no one is available to act as the receiving party, and the Blessed One's ruling relaxes the requirement in cases of medical necessity for the sick.

The expression "seven days" throughout refers to the Vinaya rule that certain allowable medicines — including butter and grain-butter — may be kept and used for a period of seven days; beyond that limit they must not be used. The monk who "consecrated it over seven days" is using the full permitted period. The term rendered "bad food" throughout translates a Tibetan phrase denoting food that is therapeutically coarse or unwholesome, here prescribed as a medical treatment; it is a technical Vinaya category, not simply spoiled food.

The phrase "not touch it even with the tip of the finger" renders a Tibetan idiom for the finest or most delicate point of contact; "the finger-tip" or "the tip of the blade of grass" are equivalent expressions in Vinaya literature.

The title "Ekaśataka" (literally "the Hundred Singles" or "One-by-One Hundred") refers to the Vinaya text under discussion; the Tibetan renders this as "Rkyang pa," meaning "single" or "alone," a section heading within the Vinaya. The phrase rendered "a wandering alms-seeker using the road as his customary practice" translates a term for a monk who travels on almsround rather than residing in a fixed dwelling. The same term applies to the group of six monks later in the passage, where it describes their habitual wandering on the road.

The "seven objects that constitute the bases for making merit from wealth" is a standard list in the Vinaya commentarial tradition referring to meritorious acts such as building temples, providing lodging, donating furnishings, and similar deeds; the text does not enumerate them here and neither does this translation.

The name "Nandaka" appears in the Tibetan as part of the exclamation about the cloth; the preceding passage's rendering of "Nandaka" as the speaker is maintained for consistency, though the Tibetan here attributes the speech to one of the group of six without naming him individually. The attribution to Nandaka follows the convention of the preceding section. The final two lines are the opening of a mnemonic verse summarizing the rules of this fascicle; the translation renders them as they stand, incomplete, since they are the beginning of a verse that continues beyond the passage supplied. The phrase rendered "charnel ground that has an owner" reflects the Tibetan's distinction between attended or guarded charnel grounds (where someone holds custodial rights) and unattended ones from which charnel-ground cloth may licitly be gathered. The "low-caste guardian" renders "rigs ngan" literally, indicating a person of base social standing charged with overseeing the charnel ground. The clause about "carrying out the king's decrees" likely refers to the legal liability the guardian and his family faced when funerary property went missing from a site under their charge. The passage shifts between two distinct cases, each with its own ruling. The first concerns taking cloth from a shrine or temple with an owner — specifically here a heterodox temple — and the second concerns the three Dharma robes of a monk being taken from him while ill. The verse couplet at the opening appears to introduce both topics as a summary rubric.

The term rendered "temple-keeper" translates lha khang pa, literally "one of the temple/house of the deity," meaning the custodian or priest responsible for the shrine. The figure of Īśvara here refers to Śiva or a local deity of that name, serving as the dedicatee of the improvised roadside shrine.
