The Blessed One's final declaration is left incomplete in the source text as given, suggesting the passage continues in the next fascicle or section. The verse summary at the end lists several cases by name or category that would be described in subsequent sūtra passages. The names Śabdāgata and Śrīvṛddha appear to be householders or donors mentioned in those subsequent stories; they are kept in their reconstructed Sanskrit forms as proper names. The Tibetan སྒྲ་ཅན་ཟིན renders a name meaning something like "one who has seized sound" and དཔལ་སྦེད one meaning "one who nurtures glory," here given as Śabdāgata and Śrīvṛddha respectively as standard equivalents in the Vinaya tradition; some uncertainty remains about these identifications, but the doctrinal content is not affected. The phrase rendered "the dregs of sesame oil" translates a term for the residue or lees remaining after oil has been pressed or clarified — a low-quality, thin product appropriately given to junior monks. The verse hinges on this contrast between nourishing fats and thin residue.

The instruction about speaking "at the time when salt, or whichever item was distributed first, is being served — not at the time of all the others" reflects a specific Vinaya procedural rule about the timing of the abbot's instruction during a meal distribution; the precise regulatory intent is clear in context but the compressed wording of the source is somewhat elliptical. The phrase rendered "the Saṅgha of those who have gone forth, headed by Gaṅgā and the others" refers to the Nirgrantha (Jain) community. "Gaṅgā" here appears to be a personal name of a Nirgrantha elder heading that community; the Tibetan reads "gang po la sogs te rab tu byung ba'i dge 'dun," literally "the Saṅgha of those who have gone forth, headed by Gaṅgā and others." This is a Jain renunciant community, contrasted with the Buddhist Saṅgha throughout this passage.

The term rendered "Nirgrantha" corresponds to the Tibetan "gcer bu pa" (literally "the naked ones"), a standard Tibetan designation for Jain ascetics. Śrī-bhadra is identified as a Nirgrantha lay practitioner, not a Buddhist. The name rendered as "Gaṅgā" throughout refers to the leader of the naked ascetic group identified in the preceding narrative. The Tibetan "གང་པོ" here functions as a proper name.

The phrase translated as "broke wind loudly" renders "རྟ་གད་དུ་བགད་པ" literally, "made a sound like a horse's belly" — a standard classical idiom for flatulence. The contrast with the Tathāgata's dignified smile is clearly the satirical point of the episode.

The allusion "like a needle-seller who returns to the home of a needle-maker to sell needles" is a classical Tibetan proverb meaning to bring something to someone who already has it in abundance — here used to mock Gaṅgā's crude imitation of the Buddha's smile.

The passage breaks mid-sentence in the source at "he thought to himself," indicating the continuation follows. The name rendered throughout as "Fireborn" translates a Tibetan equivalent of the Sanskrit name Agnija or Jātūkarṇa-type compound meaning "born of fire," here functioning as a character's name in contrast to Gaṅgā. The precise Sanskrit original is not recoverable from this passage alone, but the meaning is transparent and the rendering is consistent.

The tree name rendered as "kādira" is a phonetic approximation of the Tibetan transliteration; this is almost certainly the Acacia catechu, a tree whose charcoal is noted for its long-burning quality. The name rendered "Meṣkī" (Tibetan me skyes kyi sring mo, literally "sister of Meṣkī" or "Fire-born's sister") designates a woman called Agnijā or a similar Sanskrit equivalent; the Tibetan me skyes means "fire-born." The text gives her as Śrībhadra's sister, so the rendering follows that relationship. The name Gaṃpa (gang pa) is a proper name left in its Tibetan phonetic form as no standard Sanskrit equivalent is recoverable from context alone. The names Śrīgupta, Gaṅgopa, and Agniprabhā are standard renderings for དཔལ་སྦེད, གང་པོ, and མེ་སྐྱེས respectively. The passage makes the narrative identity of "Bhadra" (བཟང་མོ) clear as Śrīgupta's wife who is also the sister of Agniprabhā; the syntax is compressed and the exact familial relationship is slightly ambiguous, but the traditional reading identifies her as Śrīgupta's wife who had been conspiring against the Buddha. The lotus names follow standard botanical identifications: utpala (blue lotus), padma (red lotus), kumuda (white night-blooming lotus), and puṇḍarīka (white day-blooming lotus). The divine lake Mandāka is a heavenly lotus pond in the classical Indian cosmological tradition. The phrase rendered "from without and within" for ཕྱི་ཕྱིར་དད་པ་སྐྱེས་སོ is somewhat uncertain; the Tibetan ཕྱི་ཕྱིར may mean "henceforth" or "outwardly," and some editions read this simply as "he thereafter gave rise to faith." The reading adopted here follows the sense of a turning from outer to inner conviction, which fits the narrative context.

The passage ending mid-sentence — the Blessed One perceiving Śrīgupta's intention, disposition, and character — is a deliberate break at the given passage boundary; the sentence continues in the following section. The phrase rendered "the twenty mountain-peaks of the view of the transitory collection" refers to the twenty sub-views constituting the view of the transitory collection (satkāyadṛṣṭi), a standard Abhidharma enumeration: four each applied to the five aggregates, totaling twenty. This is a conventional image in stream-entry accounts, where gnosis "shatters" these views as a vajra breaks a mountain peak.

The "four abodes that gladden the noble ones" translates a phrase that could also be rendered "the four stations of joy of the noble ones," likely referring to the four fruits of the śrāvaka path or the four foundations associated with stream-entry; the exact referent is context-dependent and commentarially variable. The phrase "incurs a transgression involving the deceased" renders a Tibetan legal formula indicating that the offence is compounded by involving the merit or intention of the deceased patron. The Vinaya context implies that reducing a stūpa below its originally intended size is a serious infringement tied to the spiritual merit already dedicated to it by the one who died. The phrase rendered "woolen ox" translates a term literally meaning a yak or ox associated with wool or fleece; in context this appears to refer to a pack animal used for carrying a proclamation board through the streets, which was a common method of public announcement.

The figure "Anāthapiṇḍada" appears here both as the name of the grove's donor and as the lay householder who offers to provide music; the text treats these as the same person, which is consistent with the tradition. The phrase rendered "proximate offense" translates a term indicating a serious infraction just short of a root downfall; the Tibetan here suggests a grave offense in the category adjacent to a formal defeat. The wooden sounding board rendered as "the wooden sounding board struck" is the gaṇḍī, a resonant plank used in Indian monastic settings to summon the community, retained in transliteration in the Tibetan. The passage ends mid-sentence, consistent with the continuity format of the source. The phrase rendered "the Group of Six" refers to the well-known group of six habitually misbehaving monks (Skt. ṣaḍvargika) who figure throughout the Vinaya narratives as negative examples. This is a standard technical reference in Vinaya literature and needs no further gloss in context.

The summary verse at the midpoint and the closing verse are section-heading gāthās typical of the Two-Part Vinaya's organizational structure; the Tibetan indicates they are verse summaries encapsulating the legal matter of each sūtra section. The final verse is cryptic and may be a mnemonic condensation of narrative content that follows in the subsequent sūtra section rather than a summary of what precedes. Its meaning cannot be fully resolved from the verse alone; it likely refers to monks and nuns in proximity and the presence of children, pointing forward to disciplinary cases treated in the next section. The senior nun's name rendered here as "Gahaladā" translates the Tibetan "གནས་བརྟན་སྦོམ་མོ་དགའ་ལྡན," which appears to be a descriptive phrase meaning something like "the stout elder nun, Gāladā" or similar. The exact Sanskrit name underlying སྦོམ་མོ་དགའ་ལྡན is uncertain; some Vinaya parallels suggest "Sthūlanandā" (the stout joyful one), which fits the Tibetan descriptors perfectly. The rendering "Gahaladā" is therefore corrected: she should be identified as the elder nun Sthūlanandā, a well-known figure in the Vinaya literature.

The final two verse-summaries are extremely condensed mnemonic stanzas cataloguing the topics of the preceding sūtra sections; their elliptical phrasing makes full explication impossible without the surrounding Vinaya context, and the translation reflects their summary character faithfully. The phrase rendered "the large cloth" for རས་ཆེན is literally "large cotton cloth" and may refer to a specific requisite garment whose precise identity in the full thirteen-piece set is debated in the commentarial tradition. The list of thirteen items here does not perfectly match every known canonical enumeration; the translation follows the Tibetan as given.

The phrase མ་ལྟ་བུ — literally "like the mother" or "the Abhidharma" — is rendered throughout as "the Abhidharma," following the standard Tibetan Vinaya convention where མ་ (literally "mother") is a standard shorthand for the Abhidharma Piṭaka, the "matrix" of the teaching. The colophon-like insertions marking "the second verse" and "the third verse of the sūtra of the third section of the Ekaṃsaka" appear to be scribal section markers within what may be a Vinaya compendium organized around the Ekaṃsaka, a section of the Vinaya dealing with individual topics. These structural markers have been rendered as plain prose in keeping with TTS requirements.

The phrase rendered "formal request followed by three proclamations" translates a technical Vinaya procedure: a motion put to the Saṅgha once, followed by three formal proclamations, constituting the most solemn category of Saṅgha act.

The brief verse summaries at the section breaks appear to be mnemonic indices for the sūtras that follow, summarizing their main topics in condensed form; they have been rendered as verse accordingly. The name translated as "Twenty-Million-Grain" renders the Tibetan "Gro-zhin bye-ba nyi-shu-pa," a literal calque of a Sanskrit name such as Viṃśatikotidhānya or similar, indicating a monk associated with an extraordinary quantity of grain. The precise Sanskrit original is uncertain but the Tibetan is transparent.

The phrase rendered "the one who asked while already knowing was the blessed buddha" is a standard Vinaya narrative formula indicating that the Buddha's question to Ānanda was rhetorical, posed with full knowledge, in order to elicit a formal statement for the record.

The term "bull-elephants that happen to recognize" (Tibetan: byang-shes) refers to trained or semi-trained elephants that have learned to respond to particular handlers or stimuli — here, the scent of their own species' fat. This is a specific technical term in the elephant-keeping tradition reflected in early Vinaya literature. The verse summaries embedded in the text are mnemonic colophon-verses serving as tables of contents for Vinaya sections; their terse, list-like style is intentional and not a translation error.

The term rendered "seed-jars" translates a unit of land measurement defined by the amount of seed used to sow it; one thousand such jar-measures indicates a very substantial agricultural donation.

The list of persons disqualified from joint formal legal proceedings includes technically defined Vinaya categories. "Paṇḍaka" refers to a person with ambiguous or deficient sexual characteristics, a recognised Vinaya category. "One whose status is unsettled" and "one who dwells separately" render technical terms for monks in irregular disciplinary standing.

"Becomes associated with what is past" renders a technical Vinaya formula indicating that an irregular sitting arrangement, if no formal offence-occasion arises, is treated as though it had already concluded without consequence. The phrase rendered "face forward" translates a Tibetan expression that likely refers to monks positioning themselves to guard their property, though it may alternatively mean to proceed or turn to face a particular direction. The sense is that monks should secure the vessels rather than simply letting them be appropriated. The term "smeared" or "made entangled" here carries the technical Vinaya sense of claiming an object by marking or contaminating it with a small amount of substance, which was a stratagem used by the group of six to reserve items for themselves. The summary verse refers to shoes being set outside, which is not discussed in the body of this passage but belongs to adjacent rulings in the broader Vinaya section, carried forward as a mnemonic summary. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as this is a continuous Vinaya text and the present excerpt ends abruptly with "Then his feet and —" reflecting the original's incomplete state at the passage boundary.

The Tibetan term rendered "greasy-goods room" or "oil storage room" is "snum pa'i zong," a specialized Vinaya architectural term for a storeroom for oil or fatty substances; the exact function is rendered as closely as context permits.

The phrase rendered "bundle them and store them" in connection with the tree ornaments reflects instructions for careful preservation of devotional decorations offered by Anāthapiṇḍada, to be reused on festival occasions — a noteworthy detail of monastery administration in this Vinaya passage. The kataka tree (Sanskrit kataka, Strychnos potatorum) is a plant traditionally used in India to clarify turbid water; its seeds cause suspended particles to coagulate and settle. The translation renders the practical instruction faithfully.

The phrase rendered "ball of cooked grain" (zan gyi chang bu) refers to a small lump of cooked rice or grain used as a makeshift clarifying agent; the Blessed One's remark that "it has no grease and will break apart" may mean it lacks the binding properties of the kataka fruit and thus will dissolve without fully clarifying — the text breaks off at this point. The verse summary near the opening is a colophon-like condensation of rulings; its syntax is terse and elliptical. The phrase rendered "the triple gateway of the sole" reflects the Tibetan "rkyang pa'i sgo gsum pa," literally "the third gateway of the single foot" — this is likely a structural sūtra heading whose precise referent within the Vinaya collection is technical; the rendering is literal and no smoother reading is clearly preferable.

The passage "do not be fastidious about vessels and balls" refers to Vinaya regulations about whether water that has been stored in sealed vessels or formed into rounded containers is permissible to drink in the afternoon — "balls" here likely refers to stoppers or rounded vessel-mouths. This is a technical Vinaya usage and the translation renders it literally as the tradition intends. The phrase rendered "dough-water" translates a term literally meaning "water from washing dough" or "water in which something has been rinsed," used as a substitute purifying liquid — the exact substance is somewhat unclear from context but is consistent with Vinaya discussions of substitute cleansing agents.

The episode of the monks carrying loads for the novices' fathers involves a series of rapid rulings; the Tibetan moves quickly through several sub-cases and the sequence has been rendered as faithfully as possible to the original logic. The phrase rendered "eat from your begging bowls" translates a directive to consume food specifically using the monks' alms bowls, which in context appears to be a ruling about the propriety of eating food that has been carried in or on the bowls during travel. The series of casuistic rulings that follow all concern whether food or liquid in a bowl retains its permitted status after contact with oil, grease, or residue — standard Vinaya purity concerns.

The comparison of the mouth to a wound in the final ruling reflects a classical Indian medical and Vinaya idiom: both the mouth and an open wound are regarded as continually exuding fluid and thus inherently difficult to render fully pure, which is why the standard of three rinses and spitting out is established as legally sufficient rather than requiring perfect cleanliness. The phrase rendered "tiger-paw bread" translates a term that likely refers to a particular shape or kind of hard travel bread; the exact referent is uncertain but the term is conventional in Vinaya contexts for a compact, portable food suitable for journeys.

The summary verses are mnemonic gāthās cataloguing the topics of the sūtra sections; they are translated straightforwardly but some items in the list are allusive shorthand whose full case-narratives appear in the surrounding text.

"Dedicate it toward the north" reflects a Vinaya ritual gesture of orientation used to render certain foods allowable; the precise significance of the northward direction in this context belongs to specialist Vinaya commentary.

The passage ends mid-sentence as supplied; the translation preserves this open ending faithfully. The phrase rendered "a novice's father" translates a literal Tibetan expression meaning the head or senior figure associated with a novice; this likely refers to the novice's preceptor or a senior layman connected to the novice. The precise referent is slightly ambiguous in this context.

The phrase "a deity at whose gate" renders the Tibetan literally; it likely refers to a deity-shrine or a deity's threshold outside of which the grain had fallen, and the grain was then stolen by thieves. The sequence of events here is somewhat compressed in the original. The expression rendered "northern sound of the ill-omened drum" is a Vinaya technical phrase indicating a specific time-signal used in monastic settings; the precise cultural referent may vary across commentarial traditions but the translation reflects the literal sense of the Tibetan.

The ladder passage is an embedded ruling on carrying and setting down the Saṅgha's property, using the image of a ladder as a procedural analogy for how to handle vessels safely; the Blessed One's declaration is broken off at the passage's end, to be continued in the next section.

The name "Namgru" (Tib. nam gru) appears to be a personal name; the epithet "Doubtful Namgru" reflects his characteristic hesitancy as narrated in the text. The passage distinguishes eight levels of recipients for generosity and assigns progressively immeasurable karmic returns — this follows the standard Vinaya gradation of "fields of merit" moving from ordinary beings through the four pairs of noble ones and up to the fully awakened Buddha.

The four special occasions for obligatory delivery of offerings — the awakening (at Bodh Gayā), the first turning of the wheel of Dharma (at Sārnāth), the great miracle (at Śrāvastī), and the descent from the divine realm (at Sāṃkāśya) — are a standard Vinaya enumeration of the four great sacred sites associated with the Buddha's life and career.

The final colophon verse is a mnemonic summary (uddāna) of the sūtra's topics, a standard feature of Vinaya texts. The phrase rendered "willow branch applied accordingly" (ཚུལ་ཤིང་བྲིམས) refers to the ceremonial use of a willow or tooth-cleaning stick in ritual context; the precise referent here is formulaic and its full significance is internal to the Vinaya procedural context. The phrase rendered "distributing it according to bodily contact from the feet to the head" translates a Tibetan idiom describing how the six divided the bedding by assigning portions corresponding to each body part from foot to head, exhausting all the bedding in the process. The exact procedural meaning is somewhat obscure but the general sense of inappropriate apportionment is clear.

The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end with "or —" as the Tibetan passage itself is incomplete at this point, ending mid-construction with the pillar-plaster usage and the word "or."

"The group of six" refers throughout to the notorious group of six wayward monks frequently mentioned in Vinaya narratives as the instigators of rule-occasions. The phrase rendered "use it as plaster in the joints of a wall" continues the preceding passage's instructions about worn bedding; "སེར་ག" (joints or cracks of a wall) and "ཞལ་ཞལ" (each joint, one by one) indicate applying plaster into individual cracks, which is the natural continuation of the cow-dung-and-earth plaster instruction.

The term "ཞལ་ཏའི་གནས་ཁང་" rendered "winter residence" (literally a warm or sheltered dwelling) is uncertain; some commentators read this as a specific type of lodging rather than strictly a winter house. The narrative sense strongly supports "winter residence" here.

The summary verses at section breaks contain technical Vinaya architectural and textile terms (མཚན་མ, མངོན་མཚན, པར་ཏང, རལ་ཚེམས) whose precise meanings are debated in the scholarly literature. The renderings given ("insignia," "clear insignia," "partition screens," "ragged stitching") follow contextual inference and the general commentarial tradition but should be regarded as provisional. The verse in the summary section is terse and condensed, as is typical of mnemonic colophon-verses in Vinaya literature; the rendering follows the most natural doctrinal reading. The phrase rendered "what went out and came back without being given" refers to items that left a donor's possession (going to a funeral) and returned to him without having been formally donated — the Blessed One then rules these may be accepted by monks when offered. The final line of the passage breaks off mid-sentence, as the source text continues beyond this excerpt. The phrase rendered "steward monk" translates a monk who performs a financial or managerial function on behalf of the community; the Tibetan zhalta byedpa'i dge slong literally means "a monk who serves as steward or agent." The instruction to "consult the senior monks" before making loans reflects the standard Vinaya requirement that community property decisions involve experienced members.

The term "star" in the verse summary is obscure in this context; it may refer to a specific type of allotment marking or a technical Vinaya category whose precise referent is unclear from this passage alone.

"Novice fathers" renders dge tshul pha dag, which refers to monks who serve as preceptors or guardians of novices. The phrase rendered "bent key" translates lde mig kyog po, which likely refers to a crooked or hooked implement used to manipulate a bolt or latch from outside — a kind of picklock or curved key. This is a routine Vinaya technical detail but may sound unusual to listeners; no better single English term is available without paraphrase.

The passage about the four categories that must not be divided — stūpa funds, Saṅgha funds, sick-care fees, and food funds — is a stock Vinaya formula establishing inalienable categories of monastery income, placed here as the Blessed One's ruling in response to the monks' diversion of the householder's donation. The yakṣa's name, rendered here as "Woolly-Bull," represents a translation of the Tibetan bal glaṅ ldan, meaning "one who has a woolly bull" or "endowed with a woolly ox." This is likely a rendering of a Sanskrit name such as Vṛṣabha-related or similar; the exact Sanskrit original is uncertain.

"Uṇika" is a transliteration of the Tibetan u ni ko; the Sanskrit original is uncertain.

The phrase "fruits of the northern forests" likely refers to produce from the Uttarakuru or northern wilderness regions in the Buddhist cosmological imagination, though here it is used geographically to mean produce sent from the north down to Rohitaka.

The "making suitable by fire" refers to the Vinaya procedure of rendering fruit or seeds ritually allowable for consumption by monks through contact with fire, a knife, or a fingernail — here the fire-touching method is specified. The term rendered "fire-screen" translates a term for a portable fire-containment device or stand used for warming; the precise implement is uncertain but the context makes clear it is a raised or enclosed structure designed to hold fire off the floor-mat and to reduce smoke when used with an external blow-pipe or bellows. The rendering "hearth-screen" for the same object in the subsequent line reflects a slightly different contextual use but refers to the same item. The five-part door-securing system described at the close presents some difficulty in identifying each implement precisely; the terms rendered here as "bar-bolt," "door-bolt," "wheel-lock," "door-chain," and "bent key" are best approximations based on Vinaya parallels, and the exact ancient mechanisms are uncertain. The proportional liability scheme that follows is internally consistent and follows the Vinaya's characteristic casuistic logic, but the fractions as enumerated in the Tibetan appear asymmetrical — "three employs two, three omitted" and "two employs three, three parts" — which may reflect a scribal issue in the source text. The translation renders the Tibetan as it stands. The term rendered "formally received" refers to the Vinaya procedure of yācanā, by which food is formally accepted from the donor's hands before being consumed, a requirement whose omission can create a transgression in certain circumstances. The Tibetan term used here, byinlen, literally means "to receive a gift," and functions as the standard rendering for this formal reception rite.

The phrase rendered "excess" in the section on robe measurement translates a Tibetan idiom meaning something that goes beyond what the rule stipulates, which in Vinaya contexts constitutes a technical infraction.

The "fascicle" count at the close is a scribal colophon marking the canonical division of the Vinaya text; "bam po" is a traditional Indian and Tibetan unit of textual division. The passage repeats two pairs of questions about "observed or not observed" and "foretold or not foretold" — the second occurrences give different answers than the first. This appears to be a deliberate structural feature of the Vinaya catechism, not a scribal error, though it is striking. The translation preserves both as they stand.

The phrase rendered "abides in attachment" versus "abides in renunciation" translates ཆགས་པ་ལ་གནས་པ and འབྱུང་བ་ལ་གནས་པ respectively; འབྱུང་བ here likely means "going forth" or "renunciation" in the technical Vinaya sense, and the answer that a transgression abides in attachment rather than in renunciation is doctrinally coherent. The phrase rendered as "morally indeterminate" translates the Tibetan term for what is neither virtuous nor non-virtuous — in Vinaya contexts this often corresponds to the category of actions that are not explicitly prohibited by scripture but are not wholesome either. The pairing here of "non-virtuous" and "morally indeterminate" with the same definitions used earlier for "ripened" and "not ripened" reflects the text's systematic cross-categorization of transgressions.

The passage on "transgressions arising from mind" and the restoration ceremony is somewhat elliptical; the sense is that a monk who fails even to intend or verbalize the poṣadha ceremony incurs a mental transgression, but unlike verbal or bodily transgressions, it is not formally cleared — though it is also not as grave as a failure to cultivate virtue roots.

The final section on "spreading the sitting mat" as a condition that determines whether an act is or is not a transgression is a standard Vinaya procedural point: the presence or absence of the mat signals whether proper protocol has been observed. The passage is a technical Vinaya legal discussion involving a nun's formal expulsion from or retention within a monastic boundary (Tibetan: མཚམས, Skt. sīmā), and the conditions under which monastic acts involving that boundary do or do not incur a transgression. The terminology around shaving the head, joining palms, and prostration appears to describe a formal act of submission or appeal by the nun in question, though the exact procedural referent in the source Vinaya text is not entirely clear from this excerpt alone. The gender of the central "monk" figure in the middle section is ambiguous in the Tibetan and may in fact refer to the nun who is the subject of the formal act; this uncertainty is consequential but unresolvable without the broader context of the vinaya passage. The five classes of transgressions referred to throughout are the standard Vinaya fivefold classification of offenses. The repeated formula "not having seen the transgression" is the technical Vinaya ground for expulsion from a communal act, distinct from the root defeat offense. The phrase rendered "reinstated individually" translates the Vinaya technical term for individual reinstatement within the Saṅgha's formal procedures. The passage's parallel structure of contrasting paired conditions is characteristic of Vinaya scholastic analysis. The text ends mid-sentence, as the passage supplied was incomplete. The passage contains a highly formulaic, catechetical structure characteristic of Vinaya abhidharma-style exposition. The repeated formula "expelled on account of not having seen the transgression, not repeating the offense, and not repeating the view toward the offense" maps onto the standard threefold grounds for the suspension act (ukkhepanīyakamma). The passage ends mid-sentence, consistent with the continuity framing. The phrase rendered "in accordance with the word of a believing layman" translates "dge bsnyen dad pa'i tshig bzhin," which specifies that the expulsion was triggered by a faithful lay person's testimony — a recognized Vinaya scenario. The categories of "directly present" and "not directly present" refer to whether the relevant person or matter is physically present before the assembly at the time of the act. The term rendered "resolution" throughout translates yi dam, which in Vinaya procedural contexts denotes the agreed-upon motion or formal determination (roughly equivalent to Sanskrit karmavācanā-related consent); the passage is part of a detailed casuistic analysis of the conditions under which a Saṅgha act is valid, exploring permutations of plurality, duality, and singularity of participants under various epistemic and procedural conditions. No single rendering perfectly captures the technical force, but "resolution" follows the established usage in the preceding rendered passage and is consistent with Vinaya technical literature. The phrase "three or five factors" recurs throughout this passage as the governing conditions that determine whether a Saṅgha act is validly performed. This refers to the standard Vinaya requirements for the legality of formal acts: three factors concern the proper formulation of the motion and announcements, and five relate to the full set of procedural conditions. The precise enumeration is left implicit in the text and depends on the broader commentarial context.

The term rendered "no remainder" and "remainder" translates a distinction between a defeated nun who loses all standing in the Saṅgha entirely versus a monk who commits an analogous act and retains residual standing. The "four root defeats not shared in common" refers to pārājika offenses specific to nuns that have no parallel in the monk's code. The phrase rendered "a place of theft" translates a term that in the Vinaya context refers to a place or situation involving theft — likely signifying someone who came to ordination under false pretenses or who participated in ordination proceedings in a fraudulent or invalid context. The doctrinal referent is the category of persons whose ordination is rendered void or suspect due to circumstances of concealment or misrepresentation. This is a technically complex Vinaya category and the rendering is approximate.
